Among the Philistines, Isaac called her his sister because he feared men would kill him for her beauty. When she overheard Isaac promising Esau a blessing, she dressed Jacob in Esau's clothes to obtain it. She later warned Jacob of Esau's plan to kill him and urged Isaac to send him to Laban. Her death is not recorded, but she was buried with Isaac in the family tomb, which Gen 49:30 identifies as the cave of Machpelah.

Zerubbabel was a descendant of David's royal line who led the first group of Jewish exiles from Babylon back to Jerusalem and directed the rebuilding of the temple. He is usually called the son of Shealtiel, though 1 Chr 3:19 names Pedaiah as his father. Easton's Bible Dictionary explains that "son" here means grandson or nephew. With Jeshua the high priest, he rebuilt the altar and began the temple work. He refused help from the peoples whom Esarhaddon had settled in the land. In the second year of Darius, the prophets Haggai and Zechariah addressed him as governor of Judah and urged him to finish the house. Haggai called him God's chosen signet. Matthew lists him among the ancestors of Jesus. Easton's identifies him with Sheshbazzar, who brought back the temple vessels and laid the foundation. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia thinks they were more probably two different governors. This entry follows the identification.

Adam was the first man in the Genesis account, formed by God and placed in the garden of Eden. His name is the ordinary Hebrew word for 'man,' which Hitchcock's Bible Names glosses as 'earthy' or 'red.' He named the animals, and God made a woman from one of his ribs. Adam called her Eve. After both ate from the forbidden tree, they hid from God, who cursed the ground for Adam's sake and clothed them in skins. Adam fathered Cain, Abel and Seth, the last at age 130, as well as other sons and daughters, and he died at 930. The genealogies in 1 Chr 1:1 and Luke 3:38 begin with him. Paul contrasts Adam, in whom all die, with Christ as 'the last Adam' (1 Cor 15:22, 45). The date of about 4004 BC for his creation is an inference from the genealogies.

Ahaziah was king of Judah for one year, the son of King Jehoram and Athaliah, and the youngest son of his father. He is also called Jehoahaz and Azariah. After raiders killed his older brothers, the people of Jerusalem made him king. His age at accession is given as 22 in 2 Kgs 8:26 and as 42 in 2 Chr 22:2. While visiting his wounded uncle Joram, king of Israel, at Jezreel, he rode out with him to meet Jehu and was caught up in Jehu's revolt against the house of Ahab. Kings says he was struck near Ibleam and died at Megiddo. Chronicles says he was found hiding in Samaria and killed. His death was about 886 BC, by inference from context. Athaliah then destroyed the royal family, but his sister Jehoshabeath hid his son Joash. He is distinct from Ahaziah, Ahab's son, king of Israel.

Baasha son of Ahijah, of the tribe of Issachar, was the third king of the northern kingdom of Israel and, as Easton's Bible Dictionary notes, founder of its second dynasty. While Nadab son of Jeroboam was besieging the Philistine town of Gibbethon, Baasha conspired against him, killed him, and took the throne in the third year of Asa king of Judah. He reigned twenty-four years from Tirzah, beginning about 953 BC by inference from context. He was at war with Asa throughout and fortified Ramah to cut off movement into Judah. He abandoned the work when Asa paid the king of Syria to break his alliance with Israel. The prophet Jehu son of Hanani announced that Baasha's house would end like Jeroboam's. Baasha was buried in Tirzah and succeeded by his son Elah. Zimri later killed Elah and wiped out Baasha's whole family. Later prophecies cite Baasha's house as a precedent for the fate of Ahab's house.

Gedaliah was the son of Ahikam and grandson of Shaphan, appointed by Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon to govern the people left in Judah after Jerusalem fell. He was one of several men of this name in the Bible. Based at Mizpah, he received Jeremiah, who had been released from prison into his care. He promised the Judean army captains and their men that it would go well with them if they settled in the land and served Babylon. Jews scattered in Moab, Ammon and Edom then returned to him and gathered a large harvest. Johanan son of Kareah warned him that Ishmael son of Nethaniah had been sent by Baalis king of the Ammonites to kill him, but Gedaliah did not believe it. In the seventh month Ishmael, who was of royal descent, came with ten men, ate with him, and killed him along with the Jews and Chaldeans at Mizpah.

Jehoiada, one of several men of this name, was the priest in Jerusalem (the high priest, in Easton's Bible Dictionary) who restored David's line after Queen Athaliah seized Judah's throne. His wife Jehoshabeath, King Jehoram's daughter, hid the infant Joash from Athaliah's massacre. In the seventh year Jehoiada bound the captains and guards by oath in the temple, armed them with King David's weapons, crowned and anointed Joash, and had Athaliah killed outside the temple. He made a covenant binding king and people to the LORD and reorganized the temple services. Joash did right while Jehoiada instructed him, and together they repaired the temple, using a collection chest for funds. Jehoiada died aged 130. Joash later had his son Zechariah killed. This entry takes Jesus' "Zacharias son of Barachias" (Matt 23:35) as that Zechariah, making Barachias another name for Jehoiada. Others link it with the prophet Zechariah son of Berechiah.

Jephthah was a Gileadite warrior and judge of Israel, called a mighty man of valour and the son of Gilead by a harlot. His half-brothers drove him from the family inheritance, and he lived in the land of Tob with a band of followers. When the Ammonites attacked Israel, the elders of Gilead brought him back and made him their head and captain at Mizpeh. His messages to the Ammonite king failed. The Spirit of the LORD then came on him, and he vowed to offer whatever first came out of his house if he won. He defeated Ammon, and his only child, a daughter, came out to meet him. Smith's Bible Dictionary takes Judg 11:39 to mean she was sacrificed, while some interpreters hold she was devoted to lifelong virginity. He later fought Ephraim, judged Israel six years (from about 1152 BC, by inference), and was buried in Gilead. Heb 11:32 calls him Jephthae.

Korah (Levite) was a son of Izhar, grandson of Kohath and great-grandson of Levi. Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that Izhar was a brother of Amram, which made Korah a cousin of Moses and Aaron. With the Reubenites Dathan, Abiram and On, he led a revolt in the wilderness against Moses and Aaron. Moses told Korah and his company to bring censers with incense before the LORD so that God would show whom he had chosen. The earth opened and swallowed the rebels' households and Korah's men, and fire consumed 250 men. Their censers became a reminder that only Aaron's descendants could offer incense. Korah's sons did not die. Their descendants, the Korahites, later served as gatekeepers of the tabernacle, and several psalms carry headings naming the sons of Korah. Jude 1:11, using the form Core, points to his rebellion as a warning.

Gershon, also called Gershom in several passages of Chronicles, was a son of Levi and the brother of Kohath and Merari. He is always listed first among Levi's sons, and Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries take him to be the eldest. He went down to Egypt with Jacob's family. His sons are named as Libni and Shimei. 1 Chr 23:7 names them Laadan and Shimei, so Laadan is probably another name for Libni. Num 26:59 names Jochebed as a daughter of Levi, which makes her Gershon's sister. His descendants, the Gershonites, formed one of the three main Levite families. In the wilderness they carried the tabernacle's tent, coverings and door hangings under the oversight of Ithamar, using two wagons and four oxen. In Canaan they received thirteen cities, including Golan in Bashan. Under David, Joel led 130 of them, and they served in the temple divisions.

Nebat was the father of Jeroboam, the first king of the northern kingdom of Israel after it broke away from the house of David. He is known only through the phrase "Jeroboam the son of Nebat," which appears again and again in Kings and Chronicles. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests the phrase served to distinguish this Jeroboam from the later Jeroboam son of Joash. Nebat is identified as an Ephrathite, meaning an Ephraimite, from Zereda. His wife was Zeruah, who is described as a widow at the time Jeroboam rebelled against Solomon (1 Kgs 11:26). By inference, Nebat had died by then. Nothing else is recorded about him. The name is usually explained as meaning "sight" or "aspect" (Easton's Bible Dictionary).

Zeruiah was the sister of David and the mother of Joab, Abishai and Asahel, three leading commanders of David's army (1 Chr 2:16). Her sister was Abigail, mother of Amasa. 2 Sam 17:25 calls Abigail a daughter of Nahash, while Chronicles counts both women as sisters of Jesse's sons. This entry therefore treats Zeruiah as David's half-sister, probably through a shared mother. Her husband is never named, and her sons are almost always identified by her name: "Joab the son of Zeruiah" and "Abishai the son of Zeruiah." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests this may reflect her husband's early death or her own prominence. That work also notes that, by inference from 2 Sam 2:32, he was buried at Bethlehem. David twice complains about "ye sons of Zeruiah" when they press for harsh action (2 Sam 3:39; 16:10; 19:22).

Abishai was a son of Zeruiah and brother of Joab and Asahel. 1 Chr 2:16 places Zeruiah among David's sisters, making him David's nephew. He volunteered to go with David by night into Saul's camp and urged him to kill the sleeping king, but David refused. With Joab he pursued Abner after Asahel's death and later joined in killing him. He led troops against the Ammonites, and 1 Chr 18:12 credits him with killing eighteen thousand Edomites in the Valley of Salt. During Absalom's revolt he twice asked to kill Shimei for cursing David, and he commanded a third of David's army in the decisive battle. He pursued the rebel Sheba and rescued David by killing a Philistine giant, named Ishbi-benob in 2 Sam 21:16. He was chief among a group of three of David's warriors after killing three hundred men with his spear.

Adonijah was the fourth son of David, born to Haggith at Hebron (2 Sam 3:4; 1 Chr 3:2). When David was old, Adonijah declared, "I will be king," gathered chariots, horsemen and fifty runners, and won the support of Joab and the priest Abiathar. Zadok, Benaiah, Nathan and David's mighty men did not join him. He held a sacrificial feast by the stone of Zoheleth near En-rogel, where guests hailed him as king. Nathan and Bathsheba reminded David of his oath that Solomon would reign, and Solomon was made king. Adonijah's guests scattered, and he grasped the horns of the altar, asking Solomon to swear to spare him. Later, through Bathsheba, he asked to marry Abishag the Shunammite. Solomon treated this as a claim to the kingdom and ordered his death. Easton's Bible Dictionary calls him heir-apparent after Amnon and Absalom died. Several other men share this name.

Boaz (Greek form Booz) was a wealthy landowner of Bethlehem in the tribe of Judah and a relative of Elimelech, the late husband of Naomi. When Naomi's widowed Moabite daughter-in-law Ruth gleaned in his field, he welcomed her, praised her loyalty to Naomi, shared his reapers' meal with her and told his workers to let her glean freely through the barley and wheat harvests. After Ruth came to him at night on the threshing floor, Boaz went to the town gate, where a nearer kinsman gave up his right to redeem the family land. Before the elders, Boaz bought Elimelech's property and married Ruth, an arrangement Easton's Bible Dictionary links to the levirate law. Their son Obed was the grandfather of David. Boaz's father was Salmon, and Matthew names his mother as Rachab. He appears in both genealogies of Jesus. One of the pillars of Solomon's temple bore the same name.

Jonah, son of Amittai, was a prophet of Israel from Gath-hepher, called Jonas in the New Testament. According to 2 Kgs 14:25, he foretold that Jeroboam II would restore Israel's borders, which places him in or shortly before that king's reign. This entry dates his prophecies to about 825 BC, by inference from context. The book bearing his name tells how God sent him to Nineveh, but he fled by ship from Joppa toward Tarshish. When a storm arose, the sailors cast lots, and the lot fell on him. They threw him overboard, and a great fish swallowed him. He prayed from inside it for three days and nights until it cast him onto dry land. Sent again, he warned that Nineveh would be overthrown in forty days. Angry when the city was spared, he was taught through a gourd vine. Jesus cited "the sign of the prophet Jonas" and the Ninevites' repentance.

Manasseh (son of Hezekiah), also called Manasses, was a king of Judah who succeeded his father Hezekiah at age twelve and reigned fifty-five years in Jerusalem. His mother was Hephzibah. By inference from context, he reigned from about 697 to 642 BC. Kings describes him leading Judah into idolatry worse than that of the nations driven out before Israel, building altars in the two courts of the temple, and shedding much innocent blood. Later passages blame his sins for Judah's eventual exile. Chronicles adds that Assyrian commanders took him in fetters to Babylon, where he prayed and was restored to his kingdom, acknowledging the LORD as God. He was buried in the garden of his own house, the garden of Uzza. His son Amon succeeded him, and 2 Kgs 21:19 names Amon's mother as Meshullemeth. Matthew lists Manasseh in the genealogy of Jesus.

Timotheus, the King James form of Timothy, was a disciple from the Lystra and Derbe area who became one of Paul's closest companions. His mother, Eunice, was a believing Jewish woman and his father was a Greek (Acts 16:1). He joined Paul and Silas on the second missionary journey and stayed behind at Berea before rejoining Paul at Athens and then Corinth (Acts 17:14–15; 18:5). Paul sent him on errands to Thessalonica, Macedonia, Corinth and Philippi, and he travelled with Paul into Asia (1 Thess 3:2, 6; Acts 19:22; 20:4). He is named as co-sender of several of Paul's letters, and Paul calls him his "son in the faith" (1 Tim 1:2), a phrase usually taken to mean Paul had converted him. Two letters, 1 and 2 Timothy, are addressed to him. Heb 13:23 reports his release from custody. Easton's Bible Dictionary records a tradition that he later worked in Ephesus and died a martyr there.

Abimelech (King of Gerar) was a Philistine ruler of Gerar who dealt with both Abraham and Isaac. After Abraham called Sarah his sister, Abimelech took her, but God warned him in a dream that she was a married woman. He had not touched her. He rebuked Abraham, returned Sarah with gifts of livestock and servants, and invited him to settle in his land. God then healed his household of barrenness (Gen 20:17–18). Later, with his army commander Phichol, he made a covenant with Abraham at Beersheba after a dispute over a well. In Isaac's time Abimelech discovered that Rebekah was Isaac's wife, not his sister, and ordered that no one harm them. He later asked Isaac to leave and then came to make peace with him. Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries treat Isaac's Abimelech as a later king, probably a son, and suggest the name may have been a royal title. This entry treats both accounts under one name.

Benaiah son of Jehoiada was one of David's leading warriors and later commander of Solomon's army. Several other men in the Bible share his name. He came from Kabzeel. His recorded feats include killing two champion warriors of Moab and a lion in a pit on a snowy day, which made him famous among David's mighty men (2 Sam 23:20–22). David put him over the Cherethites and Pelethites, the royal bodyguard. He also commanded the army division that served in the third month, with his son Ammizabad in his division. 1 Chr 27:5 calls either him or his father a chief priest; Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries apply the title to Jehoiada. Benaiah did not side with Adonijah, and he helped bring Solomon to Gihon to be made king. On Solomon's orders he put to death Adonijah, Joab and Shimei, then replaced Joab as head of the army. Adonijah and Shimei are identified from the surrounding narrative.

Herod Antipas was a son of Herod the Great, by Malthace according to Easton's Bible Dictionary, and ruled Galilee as tetrarch during the ministry of Jesus (Luke 3:1). He married Herodias, the wife of his brother Philip. When John the Baptist told him the marriage was unlawful, Herod imprisoned him, although he respected John and listened to him gladly. At his birthday feast the daughter of Herodias danced before his guests, and Herod promised her whatever she asked. This led to John's beheading. By inference from context, the imprisonment was about AD 27 and the execution about AD 29. Hearing of Jesus' works, Herod wondered whether John had risen from the dead. Some Pharisees warned Jesus that Herod wanted to kill him. During Jesus' trial, Pilate sent him to Herod, who mocked him and sent him back. Herod and Pilate became friends that day. Manaen, a teacher at Antioch, had been brought up with him.

Hiram, called Huram in Chronicles, was king of Tyre in the days of David and Solomon. He sent David messengers, cedar timber, carpenters and masons to build him a house (2 Sam 5:11; 1 Chr 14:1). Described as always a friend of David, he made a league with Solomon. He supplied cedar and fir for the temple, and his builders worked alongside Solomon's, in return for yearly wheat and oil. Solomon later gave him twenty cities in Galilee. They did not please him, yet he sent Solomon 120 talents of gold, and Chronicles speaks of these cities as restored to Solomon. His experienced sailors joined Solomon's fleets to Ophir and Tarshish, bringing back gold, almug wood, precious stones and ivory. This entry names his father as Huram. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that Josephus calls him son of Abibal. The same name is also borne by a Tyrian craftsman.

Joash, also called Jehoash, was a king of the northern kingdom of Israel. He was the son of Jehoahaz and grandson of Jehu, and is distinct from several others of the same name, including his contemporary Joash king of Judah. He succeeded his father in Samaria in the thirty-seventh year of Joash of Judah and reigned sixteen years, roughly 840–825 BC by inference from context. When the prophet Elisha lay dying, Joash visited him and wept over him. He defeated Ben-hadad son of Hazael of Syria three times and recovered Israelite cities lost under his father. When Amaziah king of Judah challenged him, Joash answered with a fable of a thistle and a cedar. He then captured Amaziah at Beth-shemesh, went to Jerusalem and broke down 400 cubits of its wall. He was buried in Samaria, and his son Jeroboam, in whose days Hosea and Amos prophesied, succeeded him.

Judas Iscariot was one of the twelve apostles of Jesus and the one who betrayed him. John calls him the son of Simon (John 6:71), and Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries explain his surname as "man of Kerioth," a town in Judah. The Gospels distinguish him from another apostle named Judas, the brother of James (Luke 6:16; John 14:22). He kept the group's money bag. He went to the chief priests to arrange the betrayal, and at the last supper Jesus identified him by handing him dipped bread. He led an armed crowd to a place where Jesus often met his disciples and singled Jesus out with a kiss. When Jesus was condemned, Judas regretted it and returned the thirty pieces of silver. Matt 27:5 says he then hanged himself, and the apostles later chose someone to take his place.

Nehemiah, son of Hachaliah and brother of Hanani, was a Jew living in Persia who became governor (Tirshatha) of Judah and is the narrator of the book that bears his name. His account opens at Shushan, the Persian royal residence, in the twentieth year of the king (Neh 1:1). Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies the king as Artaxerxes Longimanus and describes Nehemiah as the royal cupbearer, who obtained leave to go to Jerusalem and rebuild its walls, probably about 446 BC. As governor he stood with Ezra the priest and scribe when the law was read, telling the weeping people that the day was holy and not for mourning (Neh 8:9). He was the first to seal the covenant (Neh 10:1). Later passages remember "the days of Nehemiah the governor" alongside Ezra and Zerubbabel (Neh 12:26, 47). Several other men in the Bible share his name.

Shaphan son of Azaliah, grandson of Meshullam, was the scribe, or royal secretary, of King Josiah of Judah. In Josiah's eighteenth year the king sent him to the temple about the money collected for its repair. There the high priest Hilkiah gave him the newly found book of the law. Shaphan read it, reported to the king and read it aloud to him (2 Kgs 22:8–10). He was then one of the group sent to consult the prophetess Huldah. His family remained prominent. His son Ahikam protected Jeremiah, his son Elasah carried Jeremiah's letter to Babylon, and Baruch read Jeremiah's scroll in the chamber of his son Gemariah. His grandson Gedaliah was made governor of Judah by Nebuchadnezzar and was later murdered by Ishmael. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "coney" (rock badger). Other men in the Bible share the name.

Amalek was a son of Eliphaz, Esau's eldest son, by his concubine Timna, making him a grandson of Esau and his wife Adah (Gen 36:12). He is listed among the chiefs ("dukes") of Edom descended from Eliphaz (Gen 36:16). The list in 1 Chr 1:36 places Timna among Eliphaz's sons alongside Amalek. His name also stands for the people descended from him, the Amalekites. As a people, Amalek attacked Israel at Rephidim after the exodus and was defeated by Joshua while Moses held up his hands (Exod 17:8–13). The LORD then declared lasting war against Amalek (Exod 17:14–16; Deut 25:17–19). Amalek later joined Moab against Israel (Judg 3:13). Saul struck Amalek and captured its king Agag (1 Sam 15:2–20), and David took spoil from it (2 Sam 8:12). Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries give the name's meaning as "dweller in a valley."

Ezra was a priest and scribe of the tribe of Levi who led a company of Jewish exiles from Babylon to Jerusalem in the reign of Artaxerxes king of Persia, about 459 BC according to Easton's Bible Dictionary. His genealogy calls him the son of Seraiah. Easton's suggests he may have been a grandson, and 1 Chr 6:14–15 makes Seraiah the father of Jehozadak (Josedech). Described as "a ready scribe in the law of Moses," Ezra received a royal letter letting him draw on the treasuries and appoint judges beyond the river. In Jerusalem he mourned the people's marriages to foreign wives and led an oath and an inquiry into the matter. Later, with Nehemiah the governor, he read the law aloud from a wooden platform and led the people in worship. Jewish tradition credits him with writing Ezra and Chronicles.

Og was the Amorite king of Bashan, the region east of the Jordan, who reigned from Ashtaroth and Edrei. He is described as the last survivor of the remnant of the giants, the Rephaim. His iron bedstead, nine cubits long and four wide (about 13 by 6 feet), was said to be kept at Rabbah of the Ammonites. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that some take it to be a basalt sarcophagus. Soon after Israel defeated Sihon, Og led his people out to fight them at Edrei and was defeated and killed. Israel took his sixty cities in the region of Argob, and Moses gave his kingdom to Reuben, Gad and the half tribe of Manasseh, mainly the Machirites. Rahab, the Gibeonites, Nehemiah and the Psalms all later recall his defeat, and his former territory became one of Solomon's administrative districts (1 Kgs 4:19).

Uriah the Hittite was a soldier in King David's army, one of David's elite warriors known as the mighty men, and the husband of Bathsheba, daughter of Eliam. While Uriah was away fighting the Ammonites, David took Bathsheba. David then called Uriah back to Jerusalem and urged him to go home, but Uriah slept at the palace door, saying he would not enjoy his house while the ark, Israel and his comrades were camped in the field. David sent him back with a letter telling Joab to put him where the fighting was fiercest and then pull back, and Uriah was killed by archers on the city wall. By inference from the surrounding chapters, the city was probably Rabbah, the Ammonite capital. The prophet Nathan condemned David for killing him and taking his wife, and 1 Kgs 15:5 names this as David's one failing. Matthew's genealogy calls him Urias.

Amnon was David's firstborn son, born in Hebron to Ahinoam of Jezreel (2 Sam 3:2; 1 Chr 3:1). He became so infatuated with Tamar, the sister of his half-brother Absalom, that he made himself ill over her. His cousin Jonadab, son of David's brother Shimeah, advised him to pretend to be sick. Amnon then asked David to send Tamar to prepare food for him. When she came, he sent everyone out, forced her, and then turned on her with intense hatred and drove her away. Absalom said nothing to Amnon but hated him for what he had done. According to 2 Sam 13:23, two years later Absalom invited the king's sons to a sheep-shearing feast. There he had his servants kill Amnon once he was merry with wine. Jonadab assured David that only Amnon had died. The same name belongs to a different man, a descendant of Judah, in 1 Chr 4:20.

Baruch son of Neriah, son of Maaseiah, was the scribe and companion of the prophet Jeremiah. During the Babylonian siege, Jeremiah handed him the deeds for the field bought from his cousin Hanameel and told him to keep them safe. In the fourth year of King Jehoiakim, Baruch wrote Jeremiah's prophecies on a scroll as the prophet dictated them. Because Jeremiah was barred from the temple, Baruch read the scroll there, then read it again to the royal officials, who told him and Jeremiah to hide. After the king burned the scroll, Baruch wrote a new, expanded copy. After Jerusalem fell, Jewish leaders accused him of turning Jeremiah against them, and he was taken with the remnant that went to Egypt (Jer 43:7). Jeremiah 45 records a personal message to him. Jer 51:59 names Seraiah son of Neriah, evidently his brother. Several other people in the Bible share his name.

Hazael was a king of Syria (Aram), ruling from Damascus, in the time of Elisha. God told Elijah to anoint him king over Syria (1 Kgs 19:15), though the anointing itself is not recorded. Hazael first appears as an officer of King Ben-hadad, sent with forty camels' load of gifts to ask Elisha whether the sick king would recover. Elisha wept and foretold both the harm Hazael would do to Israel and his rise to the throne. The next day Ben-hadad was smothered with a wet cloth, and Hazael reigned in his place. Easton's Bible Dictionary takes Hazael himself to be the killer. He fought Joram of Israel at Ramoth-gilead, struck Israel throughout its territory, and oppressed it for all of Jehoahaz's reign. He captured Gath and turned toward Jerusalem until Jehoash of Judah paid him off with temple and palace treasure. His son Ben-hadad succeeded him.

Ishmael son of Nethaniah, grandson of Elishama and of the royal line, was one of the army captains who came to Gedaliah at Mizpah after the king of Babylon made Gedaliah governor. He is not the son of Abraham who bears the same name. Johanan son of Kareah warned Gedaliah that Baalis king of the Ammonites had sent Ishmael to kill him, but Gedaliah refused to believe it. In the seventh month Ishmael and ten men ate with Gedaliah at Mizpah, then killed him along with the Jews and Chaldean soldiers there. He then killed a group of arriving men and threw their bodies into the pit King Asa had made, sparing ten who offered hidden stores of food. He carried off the remaining people, including the king's daughters, toward Ammon. Johanan overtook him by the great waters of Gibeon and freed the captives, but Ishmael escaped with eight men to the Ammonites.

Jehoiachin, also called Jeconiah, Coniah and (in Matthew) Jechonias, was a king of Judah, the son of Jehoiakim and of Nehushta, daughter of Elnathan of Jerusalem. He succeeded his father and reigned in Jerusalem for only three months. 2 Kgs 24:8 gives his age at accession as eighteen, while 2 Chr 36:9 says eight and adds ten days to the reign. He surrendered to Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon and was taken into exile with his mother, wives, officials, nobles and craftsmen, about 598 BC by inference from context. Nebuchadnezzar put Zedekiah, a son of Josiah, on the throne in his place. Jeremiah declared that Coniah and his descendants would be cast out, though another prophet foretold his return. Ezekiel and Esther date events by his captivity. In the thirty-seventh year of his exile, Evil-merodach of Babylon released him from prison. His sons included Shealtiel (Salathiel), and Matthew includes him in the genealogy of Jesus.

Jehoiada was the father of Benaiah, who commanded David's Cherethites and Pelethites and later became Solomon's army commander (2 Sam 8:18; 1 Kgs 2:35). He is known almost entirely through his son's title, "Benaiah the son of Jehoiada." 2 Sam 23:20 calls Benaiah "the son of a valiant man, of Kabzeel," which may describe Jehoiada as a brave man from Kabzeel in southern Judah. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that some read the phrase as describing Benaiah himself. 1 Chr 27:5 can be read as calling Jehoiada a chief priest. This entry also includes the Jehoiada of 1 Chr 12:27, leader of the Aaronites who joined David with 3,700 men, and treats him as probably the same man. Smith's Bible Dictionary lists them separately. The name means "the LORD knows." Several other biblical men share this name.

Joshua, also called Jeshua, was the son of Josedech (Jozadak) and the high priest of the Jews who returned from exile in Babylon with Zerubbabel. He is one of several people in the Bible with this name. With Zerubbabel, the governor of Judah, he rebuilt the altar at Jerusalem and began work on the temple. They also refused to let outsiders take part in the building, as King Cyrus had commanded. The prophet Haggai addressed him by name and urged him to be strong and finish the work. In Zechariah's visions he stands before the angel of the LORD in filthy garments, with Satan opposing him, and he is later crowned with crowns of silver and gold. He was the father of Joiakim, who in turn began a line of high priests. Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests he was probably born in Babylon during the captivity.

Mary (Mother of Jesus) was the wife of Joseph and the mother of Jesus. While she was engaged to Joseph, a descendant of David, an angel told her she would bear a son, and she accepted, calling herself "the handmaid of the Lord" (Luke 1:38). Matthew and Luke say she conceived by the Holy Spirit before she and Joseph came together. She stayed with her relative Elisabeth for about three months, then travelled with Joseph to Bethlehem, where Jesus was born. She was present when the wise men came and at his presentation in the temple. The Gospels name James, Joses, Simon and Jude as Jesus' brothers, and traditions differ on whether they were Mary's own sons. She stood at the cross and later prayed with the disciples (Acts 1:14). Following Easton's Bible Dictionary, this entry treats Luke's genealogy as hers, making Heli her father. Her name is a form of Miriam.

Abijah, also called Abijam and Abia, was king of Judah, the son and successor of Rehoboam and the father of Asa. His mother was Maachah, called the daughter of Absalom (2 Chr 11:20). 2 Chr 13:2 names her Michaiah, daughter of Uriel of Gibeah. Easton's Bible Dictionary takes Michaiah as a variant of the name and 'daughter' as meaning granddaughter. Rehoboam made him chief among his brothers, intending him to be king. He began to reign in Jeroboam's eighteenth year and ruled three years in Jerusalem, about 958–956 BC by inference from context. Chronicles describes his war with Jeroboam of Israel. He addressed the northern army from Mount Zemaraim, then defeated it and took Bethel, Jeshanah and Ephrain. He had fourteen wives, twenty-two sons and sixteen daughters. He was buried in the city of David. Matthew lists him in the genealogy of Jesus. Several other people share the name.

Achish was a Philistine king of Gath, called son of Maoch (1 Sam 27:2) or Maachah (1 Kgs 2:39). David first fled to him from Saul, but when Achish's servants recognized David as the hero of Israel's victory songs, David pretended to be mad and Achish sent him away. The title of Ps 34 calls this king Abimelech. Later David returned with six hundred men and their households, and Achish gave him the town of Ziklag. David raided neighboring peoples while telling Achish he had attacked Judah, and Achish trusted him, even making him his bodyguard. When the Philistines marched against Israel, the other Philistine lords refused to let David fight, and Achish reluctantly sent him back. Shimei's runaway servants later fled to Achish early in Solomon's reign. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia takes this as the same king, still ruling decades later.

Ahikam was a royal official of Judah, the son of Shaphan and the father of Gedaliah. When the book of the law was found in the temple, King Josiah sent him with Hilkiah the priest, Shaphan the scribe and others to consult the prophetess Huldah (2 Kgs 22:12–14; 2 Chr 34:20). His father is probably that same Shaphan the scribe. Later, when priests and prophets demanded Jeremiah's death in Jehoiakim's reign (the setting given in Jer 26:1), Ahikam's support kept the prophet from being handed over to the people (Jer 26:24). After Jerusalem fell, the Babylonians made his son Gedaliah governor of those left in Judah, based at Mizpah, and placed Jeremiah in his care. Gedaliah was later murdered by Ishmael son of Nethaniah. Elasah and Gemariah, named elsewhere as sons of Shaphan (Jer 29:3; 36:10), were his brothers. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives his name's meaning as "my brother has risen up."

Hilkiah, son of Shallum and a member of the tribe of Levi, was high priest in Jerusalem during the reign of King Josiah of Judah. Josiah sent him silver gathered from the people to fund temple repairs, and while the money was being brought out he found "the book of the law" in the temple. He gave it to Shaphan the scribe, who read it to the king. Hilkiah then led a delegation to consult the prophetess Huldah, removed the objects made for Baal from the temple at Josiah's command, and joined in providing animals for Josiah's Passover. Priestly genealogies name him as the father of Azariah and an ancestor of Ezra (1 Chr 9:11 gives his father as Meshullam). This entry also counts him as the father of Gemariah, Zedekiah's envoy to Babylon (Jer 29:3), although that identification is uncertain. The Hilkiah who was the father of Eliakim in Hezekiah's day (Isa 36:3) is a different man.

Ithamar was the fourth and youngest son of Aaron and his wife Elisheba, of the tribe of Levi (Exod 6:23). He was set apart with his father and brothers to serve as a priest. After his older brothers Nadab and Abihu died for offering unauthorized fire, he and Eleazar carried on the priestly office under Aaron, and Moses instructed them about mourning and the offerings. Ithamar oversaw the accounting of the tabernacle materials and directed the Levite clans of Gershon and Merari in their tabernacle service. Under David the priests were divided by lot, with eight chief households from Ithamar's line, represented by Ahimelech, and sixteen from Eleazar's. A descendant named Daniel returned from Babylon with Ezra. Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that the high priesthood later passed to his family in Eli, for reasons not recorded. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of his name as "island of the palm-tree."

Jezebel was the daughter of Ethbaal, king of the Sidonians, and the wife of Ahab, king of Israel. Her marriage to Ahab is tied to his worship of Baal (1 Kgs 16:31). She fed 450 prophets of Baal and 400 prophets of the groves at her table. She also had the LORD's prophets killed, though Obadiah hid a hundred of them in caves. After Elijah killed the Baal prophets, she threatened his life. When Naboth refused to sell his vineyard to Ahab, she sent letters in the king's name that led to Naboth being stoned. Elijah foretold that dogs would eat her at Jezreel. After Jehu killed her son Joram, she painted her face and looked out of a window at Jezreel. She was thrown down and dogs ate her body. Her sons Ahaziah and Joram ruled Israel, and Athaliah is commonly taken as her daughter. Rev 2:20 uses her name for a false prophetess, by context in Thyatira.

Jotham was a king of Judah, the son of King Uzziah (also called Azariah) and Jerushah, the daughter of Zadok, and the father of King Ahaz. When Uzziah was struck with leprosy and lived in a separate house, Jotham took charge of the palace and governed the people on his behalf. He became king at twenty-five, began to reign in the second year of Pekah of Israel, and ruled sixteen years in Jerusalem. By inference from context, his reign began about 758 BC and he died about 742 BC. Chronicles says he grew powerful because he ordered his ways before the LORD and mentions his wars. A genealogy of the Transjordan tribes was recorded in his day. The prophets Isaiah, Hosea and Micah were active during his reign. He was buried in the city of David. He appears as Joatham in Matthew's genealogy of Jesus. Several other people in the Bible share his name.

Naomi was the wife of Elimelech, an Ephrathite of Bethlehem in Judah, and the mother of Mahlon and Chilion. The family moved to Moab, where Elimelech died. Her sons married there and, by inference from the story, also died, since Naomi urged her two daughters-in-law to go back to their mothers' homes. Ruth refused to leave her and returned with her to Bethlehem at the start of the barley harvest. When the townspeople greeted her, Naomi asked to be called Mara, which Easton's Bible Dictionary explains as meaning "bitter", because she had gone out full and come back empty. She sent Ruth to glean in the fields of Boaz, a wealthy relative of Elimelech, and advised her in her approach to him. Boaz then bought Elimelech's land from Naomi and married Ruth. Naomi nursed their son Obed, whom the neighbouring women called a son born to Naomi. Obed became the grandfather of David.

Cyrus was the king of Persia whose decree, issued in his first year, allowed the Jewish exiles to return to Jerusalem and rebuild the temple of the LORD. The Bible presents this as fulfilling a word spoken through Jeremiah (2 Chr 36:22–23; Ezra 1:1–2). He returned the temple vessels that Nebuchadnezzar had carried to Babylon, handing them through his treasurer Mithredath to Sheshbazzar, whom he made governor. He also authorized the supply of cedar from Lebanon for the work. Opponents hindered the rebuilding throughout his reign, and a search for his decree later settled the dispute under Darius. Isaiah names Cyrus as the LORD's "shepherd" and "anointed," who would subdue nations and order Jerusalem rebuilt. Daniel continued into his reign and received a vision in his third year. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes him as the conqueror of Babylon, about 538 BC, and Smith's Bible Dictionary calls him the founder of the Persian empire.

Joash, also called Jehoash, was a king of Judah, the son of King Ahaziah and Zibiah of Beersheba. Several other men share his name. When Athaliah killed the royal family, his aunt Jehosheba, wife of the priest Jehoiada, hid the infant and his nurse (2 Kgs 11:2; 2 Chr 22:11). He became king at seven and reigned forty years in Jerusalem, beginning about 879 BC by inference from context. While Jehoiada instructed him he did what was right, and he made the priests use temple money to repair the temple. He paid off Hazael of Syria with the temple and palace treasures. After Jehoiada died, Joash had Jehoiada's son killed, and a small Syrian force later defeated Judah's army. His servants conspired against him and killed him in the house of Millo, about 839 BC. His son Amaziah followed his example. Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that Matthew's genealogy of Jesus omits him.

Joram, also called Jehoram, was a son of Ahab and Jezebel who succeeded his brother Ahaziah as king of Israel. He reigned twelve years from Samaria (2 Kgs 1:17; 3:1), beginning about 897 BC by inference from context. He is distinct from his contemporary Jehoram son of Jehoshaphat, king of Judah. Early in his reign he mustered Israel and, with Jehoshaphat and the king of Edom, campaigned against Moab (2 Kgs 3). Later, with his nephew Ahaziah of Judah, the son of his sister Athaliah, he fought Hazael of Syria at Ramoth-gilead. He was wounded there and withdrew to Jezreel to recover. While he was in Jezreel, Jehu, anointed to cut off Ahab's house, conspired against him. Joram rode out to meet Jehu on the plot once owned by Naboth, cried out that there was treachery, and fled, but Jehu shot him through the heart. Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that his death ended the dynasty of Omri.

Ben-hadad, son of Tabrimon and grandson of Hezion, was a king of Syria who ruled from Damascus. Asa king of Judah sent him silver and gold from the temple and palace treasuries, and Ben-hadad responded by attacking northern Israel, striking Ijon, Dan, Abel-beth-maachah and the land of Naphtali. The accounts that follow describe a Ben-hadad who, with thirty-two allied kings, besieged Ahab in Samaria and demanded his wealth and family. He was drinking in his tents when Israel's forces routed his army, and he escaped on horseback. A year later he was defeated at Aphek, surrendered, and made a treaty with Ahab, promising to return captured cities. The name means "son of Hadad," a Syrian god, and several kings bore it. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia takes Ahab's opponent to be a later Ben-hadad, probably this king's son. This entry treats all these passages as one man.

Hadarezer, also called Hadadezer, son of Rehob, was king of the Aramean (Syrian) state of Zobah in David's time. Both spellings appear in the text, and Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning "Hadad is help." David defeated him near the Euphrates and also killed twenty-two thousand Syrians of Damascus who came to his aid. David took gold shields from Hadarezer's servants and a great deal of bronze from his cities, Betah and Berothai, which are called Tibhath and Chun in 1 Chr 18:8. Chronicles says Solomon later used this bronze for the temple's bronze sea, pillars and vessels. Toi king of Hamath, who had been at war with Hadarezer, sent gifts to congratulate David. Later Hadarezer brought Syrians from beyond the river to Helam under his commander Shobach. After their defeat, the kings subject to him made peace with Israel. Rezon, who later opposed Solomon, had fled from him.

Ishmael (Son of Hagar) was Abraham's first son, born to Hagar, the Egyptian servant of Sarah, when Abram was eighty-six (about 1910 BC, by inference from context). An angel told Hagar to name him Ishmael, meaning "God hears," because the LORD had heard her affliction. At thirteen he was circumcised on the same day as Abraham. God promised that he would father twelve princes and become a great nation, and Genesis lists his twelve sons, beginning with Nebajoth and Kedar, as princes with their own towns. Gen 21 tells how he and Hagar were later sent away and settled in the wilderness of Paran. He and Isaac together buried Abraham in the cave of Machpelah. His daughter married Esau. She is called Mahalath in Gen 28:9 and Bashemath in Gen 36:3, probably the same woman. He died at 137. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes his descendants as the Ishmaelite tribes of northern Arabia.

James (Son of Zebedee) was one of the twelve apostles, a fisherman and the brother of John. Jesus called the two brothers while they were mending nets in a boat with their father Zebedee, and they worked as partners with Simon Peter. Jesus gave James and John the name Boanerges, “sons of thunder.” With Peter and John, James belonged to an inner group that Jesus took with him to the raising of Jairus’s daughter, the Transfiguration and Gethsemane, and he was among those who questioned Jesus privately on the Mount of Olives. He and John once asked Jesus to grant whatever they wanted, angering the other ten, and offered to call down fire on a village that rejected Jesus. Herod killed him with the sword, the first recorded death among the Twelve. This entry dates it about AD 40 by inference. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives AD 44, identifies the king as Herod Agrippa and names his mother as Salome.

Meshach was the Babylonian name given to Mishael, one of the young men from Judah taken to Babylon and trained for royal service alongside Daniel, Hananiah (Shadrach) and Azariah (Abednego) (Dan 1:6–7). After their training the king found none like them, and they entered his service (Dan 1:19). Daniel shared with them the matter of the king's dream (Dan 2:17), and at Daniel's request the three were set over the affairs of the province of Babylon (Dan 2:49). When they refused to serve Nebuchadnezzar's gods or worship his golden image, the king had them bound and thrown into a furnace heated seven times hotter than usual. The flames killed the men who carried them, but the three came out unharmed. Nebuchadnezzar then praised their God, forbade anyone to speak against him, and promoted them (Dan 3:12–30). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests Mishael perhaps means "who is equal to God?"

Micaiah son of Imlah was a prophet in the northern kingdom of Israel during the reign of Ahab, who is named as the king in the surrounding chapter. His name means "who is like the LORD?" When Ahab and Jehoshaphat of Judah planned to attack Ramoth-gilead, Ahab's prophets all promised victory. Jehoshaphat asked for another prophet, and Ahab named Micaiah, whom he hated for always prophesying evil about him. Told to agree with the others, Micaiah swore to speak only what the LORD told him. He first echoed their words, then foretold disaster. Zedekiah son of Chenaanah struck him, and the king had him held under Amon the city governor. Micaiah declared that if the king returned safely, the LORD had not spoken through him. Easton's Bible Dictionary infers he had already been imprisoned and notes a view that he was the unnamed prophet of 1 Kgs 20:35–42.

Nabal was a wealthy sheep owner of the house of Caleb whose flocks grazed near Carmel in Judah, and the husband of Abigail. The text describes him as churlish and evil in his doings, while Abigail was wise and beautiful (1 Sam 25:3). When David, then living in the wilderness, sent ten young men at shearing time to greet him and ask for provisions, Nabal insulted them, asking, "Who is David?" David set out to destroy his household, but Abigail went to meet him with gifts and turned him back, saying that Nabal's name, meaning "fool," suited him. She found Nabal drunk at a lavish feast and told him nothing until morning. When she did, "his heart died within him," and about ten days later the LORD struck him and he died. David then took Abigail as his wife. She is later still called "the wife of Nabal the Carmelite."

Naboth the Jezreelite owned a vineyard in Jezreel beside the palace of Ahab king of Samaria. Ahab wanted it for a vegetable garden and offered a better vineyard or its price in money. Naboth refused to give up the inheritance of his fathers. When Ahab sulked, his wife Jezebel wrote letters in his name to the elders and nobles of Naboth's city. She told them to proclaim a fast and seat Naboth prominently. Two worthless men then falsely accused him of cursing God and the king, and he was taken outside the city and stoned to death. As Ahab went to claim the vineyard, the prophet Elijah (named in 1 Kgs 21:17) was sent to tell him that dogs would lick his blood where they had licked Naboth's. 2 Kgs 9:26 adds that Naboth's sons were also killed. Later, Jehu had the body of Ahab's son Joram thrown onto Naboth's plot.

Shadrach was the Babylonian name given to Hananiah, one of the young men of Judah who served with Daniel at the court of Nebuchadnezzar. The chief of the eunuchs renamed him, along with Daniel (Belteshazzar), Mishael (Meshach) and Azariah (Abednego). After their training, the king found none equal to these four. Daniel shared Nebuchadnezzar's troubling dream with them, and later had Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego appointed over the affairs of the province of Babylon. When the three refused to worship the king's golden image, Nebuchadnezzar had them bound and thrown into a furnace heated seven times hotter than usual. The flames killed the men who carried them, but the three came out unharmed. The king then praised their God, issued a decree protecting his worship, and promoted them. Easton's Bible Dictionary explains the name Shadrach as "Aku's command".

Ahithophel was a man of Giloh who served as King David's counsellor and later joined Absalom's revolt. His advice was regarded as if it came from the oracle of God, under both David and Absalom (2 Sam 16:23). David prayed that his counsel would be turned to foolishness and sent Hushai back to Jerusalem to defeat it. Ahithophel advised Absalom to take David's concubines and to pursue David that night with twelve thousand men, but Absalom preferred Hushai's plan. Seeing his counsel rejected, Ahithophel went home, put his household in order, hanged himself, and was buried in his father's tomb. His son Eliam was one of David's mighty men. Smith's Bible Dictionary identifies this Eliam with Bathsheba's father (2 Sam 11:3), making Ahithophel her grandfather. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia considers two different men named Eliam more likely.

Machir was the firstborn son of Manasseh and a grandson of Joseph, born to Manasseh's Aramean concubine (Josh 17:1; 1 Chr 7:14). Joseph lived to see Machir's children, who were raised on his knees (Gen 50:23). Machir married Maachah. His children included Gilead, Peresh, Sheresh and Hammoleketh, as well as a daughter who married Hezron of Judah. His descendants, the Machirites, traced their line through Gilead, and the daughters of Zelophehad belonged to this family. Machir is called a man of war. His clan took Gilead from the Amorites, and Moses gave them that land and parts of Bashan east of the Jordan. In the Song of Deborah, Machir stands for this branch of Manasseh (Judg 5:14). Easton's Bible Dictionary suggests he may have been Manasseh's only son. The name is shared with another man, Machir son of Ammiel, who appears in David's time (2 Sam 9:4).

Micah was a man from the hill country of Ephraim during the period of the judges, distinct from the prophet and others of the same name. His mother gave two hundred shekels of silver to a metalworker, who made a carved image and a cast image that were kept in Micah's house. Micah kept a shrine with an ephod and household idols (teraphim) and installed one of his sons as priest. When a young Levite from Bethlehem in Judah passed by, Micah hired him as his priest for ten shekels a year, clothing and food, believing the Lord would now favor him. Danite scouts lodged at his house. Later the Danites carried off his images and his priest, and Micah pursued them but turned back because they were too strong. Easton's Bible Dictionary sees the story as leading into Dan's settlement in the north and illustrating the lawlessness of the age.

Ornan, called Araunah in 2 Samuel, was a Jebusite living in Jerusalem in David's reign who owned a threshing floor. During the plague sent after David's census, the angel of the LORD stopped beside this threshing floor, and the prophet Gad told David to build an altar there. Ornan was threshing wheat with his four sons when he saw the angel. When the king came, Ornan bowed to the ground and offered the site as a gift, along with oxen for sacrifice, threshing tools for wood and wheat. David refused to offer what cost him nothing and insisted on paying. The accounts give different prices: fifty shekels of silver for the threshing floor and oxen (2 Sam 24:24), and six hundred shekels of gold for "the place" (1 Chr 21:25). Solomon later built the temple on this site on Mount Moriah.

Shem was one of the three sons of Noah, born when Noah was five hundred years old and named first beside his brothers Ham and Japheth (Gen 5:32; 6:10). He and his wife entered the ark and survived the flood (Gen 7:13). When Noah later lay drunk and uncovered, Shem and Japheth walked in backward and covered him, and Noah blessed "the LORD God of Shem," making Canaan his servant (Gen 9:23–27). Gen 10:21 calls him the father of all the children of Eber. Its phrase "the elder" can refer to Shem or to Japheth, and Easton's Bible Dictionary takes Shem as the eldest. His sons were Elam, Asshur, Arphaxad, Lud and Aram. Arphaxad was born two years after the flood, when Shem was a hundred, and Shem lived five hundred years more (Gen 11:10–11). Luke lists him as "Sem" in Jesus' genealogy (Luke 3:36). The word "Semitic" comes from his name.

Silas, called Silvanus in the New Testament letters, was a leading member of the Jerusalem church and a prophet (Acts 15:22, 32). After the Jerusalem Council, about AD 46 by inference from context, he and Judas Barsabas went with Paul and Barnabas to deliver the council's letter to Antioch and confirm it in person. When Paul and Barnabas parted, Paul chose Silas as his companion for the second missionary journey. At Philippi, after Paul cast a spirit out of a fortune-telling slave girl, her owners had both men seized and jailed. At midnight they prayed and sang, and the jailer came to faith. Silas went on with Paul to Thessalonica and Berea, stayed behind there with Timothy, and later rejoined Paul at Corinth. He is named with Paul and Timothy in 1 and 2 Thessalonians. Smith's Bible Dictionary considers him probably the same Silvanus who carried Peter's first letter (1 Pet 5:12), and this entry follows that view.

Sisera (army captain) was the commander of the army of Jabin, the Canaanite king who reigned in Hazor, and he lived at Harosheth of the Gentiles (Judg 4:2). He commanded nine hundred iron chariots. When Barak gathered Israel's forces on Mount Tabor at Deborah's urging, Sisera brought his army to the river Kishon, where it was routed and destroyed (Judg 4:13–16). He got down from his chariot and fled on foot to the tent of Jael, wife of Heber the Kenite, whose household was at peace with Jabin. While he lay there, Jael drove a tent peg through his temples, so that he was dead when Barak arrived (Judg 4:22). Deborah's song celebrates his defeat and pictures his mother waiting at a window for his return (Judg 5:28). Later texts recall him as an oppressor of Israel (1 Sam 12:9; Ps 83:9). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes differences between the prose and poetic accounts of his defeat.

Cain was the firstborn son of Adam and Eve. Eve said at his birth, "I have gotten a man from the LORD" (Gen 4:1). He farmed the ground, while his brother Abel kept sheep. When both brought offerings, Cain offered produce of the ground, but God did not accept his offering, and Cain grew angry. God questioned his anger. Cain then attacked Abel in the field and killed him. When God asked where Abel was, Cain answered, "Am I my brother's keeper?" (Gen 4:9). He was punished and complained that the punishment was more than he could bear. God set a mark on him so that no one would kill him and warned that anyone who did would be avenged sevenfold. Cain settled in the land of Nod, east of Eden. There he had a son, Enoch, and built a city named after him. Later passages present him as an example of wrongdoing (1 John 3:12; Jude 1:11).

Darius was a king of Persia during whose reign the rebuilding of the temple in Jerusalem resumed and was completed. He is generally identified as Darius I (Darius the Great), who followed Cyrus and Cambyses. Work on the temple had stopped because of local opposition until his second year (Ezra 4:5, 24). In that year the prophets Haggai and Zechariah began to speak, and their messages are dated by his reign (Hag 1:1; Zech 1:1). When Tattenai, the governor west of the Euphrates, wrote to Darius about the building work, the king ordered a search of the royal archives. Cyrus's earlier decree was found, and Darius confirmed it with his own decree that the work go ahead quickly. The temple was finished in the month Adar of his sixth year (Ezra 6:15). This Darius is distinct from Darius the Mede in Daniel and from Darius the Persian in Neh 12:22.

Jehoram, also called Joram, was king of Judah, the firstborn son and successor of Jehoshaphat. Several people share the name, including a king of Israel of the same period. He began to reign at thirty-two and ruled eight years in Jerusalem, roughly 893–886 BC by inference from context. On taking power he killed all his brothers and some princes of Israel. Surrounded by the Edomites, he broke out by night with his chariots. Later the Philistines and Arabians attacked him, and raiders killed his older sons, so his youngest son Ahaziah succeeded him. Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies his wife Athaliah as a daughter of Ahab and Jezebel. Their daughter Jehoshabeath (Jehosheba), wife of the priest Jehoiada, hid her nephew Joash from Athaliah. Jehoram was buried in the city of David, and Matthew lists him among the ancestors of Jesus.

Jethro was a priest of Midian and the father-in-law of Moses. He is also called Reuel (Exod 2:18) and Raguel (Num 10:29). Smith's and Easton's Bible Dictionaries suggest Reuel was his personal name and Jethro a title. Moses tended Jethro's flocks and was doing so when he came to Horeb, the mountain of God. Later Jethro let him return to Egypt with the words "Go in peace." After the exodus, Jethro brought Moses' wife Zipporah and her two sons to him in the wilderness. He praised the LORD for delivering Israel, offered sacrifices, and ate with Aaron and the elders. His son Hobab was asked to travel with Israel. In the underlying text tags, the verses naming Deuel (or Reuel), father of Eliasaph, leader of the tribe of Gad, are also counted under this entry. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treat Deuel as a separate Gadite, and this entry does not list Eliasaph as his son.

Michal was the younger daughter of King Saul and his wife Ahinoam, and David's first wife. She loved David, and Saul gave her to him after David brought proof that he had killed two hundred Philistines, double the hundred named as the bride-price. When Saul sent men to kill David, Michal warned him, let him down through a window, and laid an image in his bed to deceive the messengers. She then told her father that David had threatened her. While David was a fugitive, Saul gave her to Phalti (Phaltiel) son of Laish of Gallim. After Saul's death, David demanded her return through Ish-bosheth. When David danced before the ark as it entered Jerusalem, she despised him and mocked him, and the account adds that she had no child to the day of her death. 2 Sam 21:8 names Michal as a mother of Saul's grandsons. Easton's Bible Dictionary reads Merab there, and this entry follows that reading.

Nethaniah was the son of Elishama and the father of Ishmael, the man who assassinated Gedaliah, the governor Babylon appointed over Judah after Jerusalem fell. He is known only through his son, who is regularly called "Ishmael the son of Nethaniah." The family is described as "of the seed royal," so Nethaniah belonged to the royal line of Judah (2 Kgs 25:25; Jer 41:1). His son Ishmael came to Gedaliah at Mizpah, killed him and others there, took the remaining people captive, and escaped to the Ammonites. The name means "the Lord has given" (Hitchcock's Bible Names). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that some Septuagint manuscripts read the name as Maththanias. Several other men in the Bible share the name Nethaniah.

Phillip the Evangelist, usually called Philip, was one of the seven men chosen by the Jerusalem church to oversee the daily distribution to the needy (Acts 6:5). He is distinct from Philip the apostle. After the persecution that followed Stephen's death scattered the believers (Acts 8:1), Philip preached Christ in the city of Samaria. Many were baptized after hearing him and seeing his miracles, among them Simon the sorcerer. Directed by an angel to the desert road from Jerusalem to Gaza, he met an Ethiopian official reading Isaiah. He explained the passage as speaking of Jesus and baptized him. The Spirit then carried Philip away. He reappeared at Azotus (Ashdod) and preached through the towns as far as Caesarea. About twenty years later, by inference from context, Paul's company stayed at his house in Caesarea, and Acts 21:9 adds that he had four unmarried daughters who prophesied.

Phinehas (Levite) was the son of Eleazar and a daughter of Putiel, and grandson of Aaron the priest (Exod 6:25). At Shittim, when Israel was drawn into sin with Moab, he took a javelin and acted against the offenders. This turned away God's wrath and stopped the plague (Num 25:7, 11; Ps 106:30). He went with the army against Midian, carrying the holy instruments and trumpets (Num 31:6). Later he led the delegation sent to Reuben, Gad and half of Manasseh over the altar they had built near the Jordan, and he accepted their explanation (Josh 22:13, 30–32). He held land in the hill country of Ephraim, where Eleazar was buried (Josh 24:33). During the war with Benjamin he stood before the ark and asked the LORD whether to fight (Judg 20:28). He was the father of Abishua and an ancestor of Ezra (1 Chr 6:4; Ezra 7:5).

Rabshakeh was an officer of the king of Assyria, named in the wider account as Sennacherib (2 Kgs 18:13). During Hezekiah's reign he was sent from Lachish with Tartan, Rabsaris and a large army to demand the surrender of Jerusalem. Standing by the conduit of the upper pool, he spoke for the "great king" and asked what Hezekiah was trusting in. Hezekiah's officials Eliakim, Shebna and Joah asked him to speak in Aramaic ("the Syrian language") rather than Hebrew. He refused and shouted in Hebrew so that the people on the wall would hear. Hezekiah's message to Isaiah described his words as a reproach against the living God. Rabshakeh then rejoined the Assyrian king, who was fighting at Libnah. The same account appears in both 2 Kings and Isaiah. Smith's and Easton's Bible Dictionaries take Rabshakeh as an official title, "chief cupbearer," rather than a personal name. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives it the broader sense of chief officer.

Amon was a king of Judah, the son and successor of Manasseh and the father of King Josiah. Several other people in the Bible share the name. His mother was Meshullemeth, daughter of Haruz of Jotbah. He became king in Jerusalem at twenty-two and reigned two years, about 642–640 BC by inference from context. Chronicles says he did evil as his father had, sacrificing to the carved images Manasseh had made. Unlike Manasseh, he did not humble himself before the LORD. His servants conspired against him and killed him in his own house. The people of the land then executed the conspirators and made Josiah king. According to 2 Kgs 22:1, Josiah's mother was Jedidah, which makes her Amon's wife, and Josiah was eight when he took the throne. Jeremiah and Zephaniah name Amon as Josiah's father, and he appears in Matthew's genealogy of Jesus.

Athaliah was the daughter of Ahab and Jezebel and the wife of Jehoram, king of Judah. She is called the daughter of Omri (2 Kgs 8:26; 2 Chr 22:2), which in context means his granddaughter. Her son Ahaziah reigned only one year. When he died, she killed the royal family of Judah and ruled the land herself. Her infant grandson Joash was rescued by Jehosheba (Jehoshabeath), Ahaziah's sister and the wife of the priest Jehoiada, and hidden in the temple for six years. When Joash was crowned there, Athaliah heard the noise, came into the temple, tore her clothes and cried "Treason, Treason." She was then killed with the sword beside the king's house. Chronicles adds that her sons had broken up the house of God and given its dedicated things to the Baals. By inference from context, her reign ran from about 886 to 879 BC.

James (Brother of Jesus) is named first among the brothers of Jesus, with Joses, Simon and Judas (Matt 13:55; Mark 6:3). This entry treats him as a son of Joseph and Mary. Paul calls him "the Lord's brother" and says the risen Jesus appeared to him (Gal 1:19; 1 Cor 15:7). He became a leader of the Jerusalem church. Peter sent word to him after escaping prison, he spoke decisively at the Jerusalem Council, and Paul reported to him and the elders (Acts 12:17; 15:13; 21:18). Paul names him with Cephas and John as "pillars" (Gal 2:9). He is taken as the author of the letter of James, and Jude calls himself his brother (Jas 1:1; Jude 1:1). Easton's Bible Dictionary instead identifies him with the apostle James son of Alphaeus, "James the Less," a cousin of Jesus. This entry links him to the "Mary the mother of James and Joses" at the cross (Mark 15:40).

Jephunneh was the father of Caleb, the man from the tribe of Judah whom Moses sent with Joshua and ten others to explore Canaan (Num 13:6). He is known only through his son, who is repeatedly called "Caleb the son of Jephunneh": one of the two spies who survived the wilderness years, and the man who received Hebron as his inheritance (Num 14:30; Josh 14:13–14). Caleb is also called "the Kenezite" (Num 32:12; Josh 14:6). Smith's Bible Dictionary takes this to mean the family descended from a Kenaz, probably an Edomite clan. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that this clan became part of Judah. This entry also counts a Kenaz among his descendants. The hard-to-read 1 Chr 4:15 places a Kenaz in Caleb's family, as the son of Elah in the King James Version. The name is shared with an unrelated man of Asher (1 Chr 7:38).

Johanan son of Kareah (spelled Careah in 2 Kgs 25:23) was a Judean army captain who, with his brother Jonathan, joined Gedaliah at Mizpah after the Babylonians made Gedaliah governor. He secretly warned Gedaliah that Ishmael son of Nethaniah planned to kill him and offered to kill Ishmael first, but Gedaliah refused and said the report was false. After Ishmael murdered Gedaliah, Johanan and the other captains pursued him and freed the captives taken from Mizpah, though Ishmael escaped to the Ammonites. Johanan then joined the people in seeking guidance from Jeremiah, but he rejected the prophet's warning not to go to Egypt. He and the captains led the remnant of Judah there instead. The connected passage in Jer 43:6–7 adds that Jeremiah went with them to Tahpanhes. Several other men in the Bible share this name.

Joseph (Mary's Husband) was the husband of Mary and the legal father of Jesus, who was 'supposed' to be his son (Luke 3:23). A descendant of David from Nazareth in Galilee, he was engaged to Mary when she was found to be pregnant. Described as a just man, he planned to end the engagement quietly. An angel in a dream then told him to take her as his wife, and he did. He traveled to Bethlehem, where Jesus was born. Later dreams sent him to Egypt to escape Herod and then brought him back. He was with Mary when Jesus was presented at the Temple and on the Passover journey when Jesus was twelve. Matthew names his father as Jacob, while Luke's genealogy lists Heli. Matt 13:55 calls him a carpenter and names James, Joses, Simon and Jude as Jesus' brothers. Easton's Bible Dictionary infers that he died before Jesus' public ministry.

Nebuzar-adan was the captain of the guard serving Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon. He arrived in Jerusalem in the fifth month of Nebuchadnezzar's nineteenth year. 2 Kgs 25:8 gives the seventh day and Jer 52:12 the tenth. After the city fell, he took into exile the people still left there and those who had gone over to the Babylonians. He left some of the poorest people in Judah and gave them vineyards and fields to work. He brought Jerusalem's leading men to the king at Riblah. On Nebuchadnezzar's orders he took charge of Jeremiah and released him at Ramah, where the prophet had been bound in chains among the captives. He placed the people who remained, including the king's daughters, in the care of Gedaliah son of Ahikam. In Nebuchadnezzar's twenty-third year he deported 745 more Jews. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia explains his name as meaning "Nebo has given seed."

Pharaoh, also called Pharaoh-hophra, was the king of Egypt in the last years of the kingdom of Judah. In Jer 44:30, Jeremiah announces that God would hand him over to those seeking his life, as Zedekiah of Judah had been handed to Nebuchadrezzar of Babylon. The Pharaoh in Ezekiel's oracles is probably the same king, judging by their date and setting. Ezekiel says his great army would not help Zedekiah in the war with Babylon (Ezek 17:17). He pictures Pharaoh as a great dragon claiming the Nile as his own creation, and says his arms would be broken while Babylon's king was strengthened against Egypt. A lament portrays him brought down among the slain. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identifies him with Apries, a grandson of Pharaoh Necho who reigned about 589–570 BC and died after a revolt. Other kings of Egypt are also called Pharaoh.

Pharez (also Perez, and Phares in the New Testament) was a son of Judah and Tamar, Judah's daughter-in-law, and the twin brother of Zerah. At their birth his brother's hand appeared first, but Pharez came out ahead, and Tamar named him for this "breach" (Gen 38:29). His sons Hezron and Hamul founded the Hezronite and Hamulite clans, and his descendants were counted as the Pharzites (Num 26:20–21). Ruth 4:12 holds up his house as a model of a flourishing family, and the genealogy that follows traces the line from Pharez through Hezron to David. His descendants stayed prominent: one commanded David's army for the first month, and 468 of them lived in Jerusalem after the exile (Neh 11:6). Matthew and Luke list him among the ancestors of Jesus. His birth is placed at about 1721 BC, by inference from context.

Phillip the Apostle, usually called Philip, was one of the twelve apostles of Jesus and came from Bethsaida in Galilee, the hometown of Andrew and Peter (John 1:44). Jesus found him and told him to follow, and Philip then brought Nathanael, telling him to "come and see" the one Moses and the prophets wrote about (John 1:43–46). He appears in every list of the Twelve (Matt 10:3; Mark 3:18; Luke 6:14). Before the feeding of the five thousand, Jesus asked him where bread could be bought, and Philip replied that two hundred pennyworth would not be enough (John 6:5–7). Some Greeks later approached him asking to see Jesus, and he passed the request on with Andrew (John 12:21–22). At the Last Supper he asked Jesus to show them the Father (John 14:8–9). He was with the apostles in the upper room after the ascension (Acts 1:13). According to tradition noted in Easton's Bible Dictionary, he later preached in Phrygia and died at Hierapolis.

Shechem was the son of Hamor the Hivite, the prince of the region around the Canaanite city that shared his name, when Jacob camped there on his return from Padan-aram (Gen 33:18–19). After Shechem took Jacob's daughter Dinah and lay with her, he asked his father to get her for him as a wife, and he offered Jacob's family whatever they asked (Gen 34:2, 34:4, 34:11). Jacob's sons answered deceitfully that the marriage could happen only if every male in the city was circumcised. Shechem and Hamor persuaded the townsmen to agree, and while the men were still recovering, Simeon and Levi killed Hamor and Shechem and took Dinah from Shechem's house (Gen 34:13, 34:24–26). Later passages recall him as the son of Hamor, from whose family Jacob bought land, and the Greek form of his name appears in Acts 7:16 as Sychem (Josh 24:32; Judg 9:28).

Shimei son of Gera was a Benjamite from Bahurim and a member of Saul's family. When David fled Jerusalem during Absalom's rebellion, Shimei followed him along a hillside, cursing him as a "bloody man" and throwing stones and dust. After Absalom's defeat he hurried down with the men of Judah and fell before David as the king crossed the Jordan. Abishai urged that he be executed, but David swore not to kill him. Near death, David reminded Solomon of Shimei's curse (1 Kgs 2:8). Solomon ordered Shimei to build a house in Jerusalem and never leave it, on pain of death, and Shimei agreed. Three years later he went to Achish at Gath to bring back two runaway servants. Solomon summoned him, charged him with breaking his oath and with his wrongs against David, and had him executed, by Benaiah according to 1 Kgs 2:46. Several other men in the Bible share this name.

Abigail was the wife of Nabal, a wealthy and harsh man of the house of Caleb living at Carmel in Judah. She is described as intelligent and beautiful. When Nabal insulted messengers sent by David, a servant warned her. She quickly loaded donkeys with bread, wine, meat, grain, raisins and figs, rode out to meet David, and bowed before him. David blessed God for sending her. About ten days later Nabal died, by inference from the wider chapter, and David sent for Abigail to marry him. She went with five maidservants and became his wife. She lived with David at Gath, was taken captive at Ziklag, and moved with him to Hebron. There she bore his second son, called Chileab in 2 Sam 3:3 and Daniel in 1 Chr 3:1. Another Abigail, David's sister, also appears in the Bible.

Asahel was a son of Zeruiah and brother of Joab and Abishai. Because 1 Chr 2:16 lists Zeruiah among the sisters of Jesse's sons, he was David's nephew. He was famous for his speed, described as "light of foot as a wild roe." After David's men defeated Abner's forces near Gibeon, Asahel chased Abner and ignored repeated warnings to turn aside. Abner then killed him with the butt end of his spear. Asahel was buried in his father's tomb at Bethlehem. Later Joab, with Abishai, killed Abner at Hebron in revenge for their brother. Asahel is named among David's thirty mighty men, and as captain for the fourth month, "and Zebadiah his son after him." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests this honor may have been held through Zebadiah after Asahel's death. Other men in the Bible share this name.

Ham was one of the three sons of Noah. He is always listed between Shem and Japheth (Gen 5:32; 6:10). Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia take him to be the youngest, pointing to Gen 9:24, while Smith's Bible Dictionary treats him as the second son. He and his wife entered the ark with Noah's family and came out after the Flood, which is dated to about 2348 BC by inference from context. Later, when Noah lay drunk, Ham saw his father's nakedness and told his two brothers. In the account that follows, Noah's curse falls on Ham's son Canaan (Gen 9:25). Ham's sons were Cush, Mizraim, Phut and Canaan, ancestors of peoples traditionally linked with Ethiopia, Egypt, Libya and Canaan. The Psalms use "the land of Ham" as a poetic name for Egypt (Ps 105:23). Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of his name as "hot."

Jehoahaz was king of Israel, the son and successor of Jehu, and the father of Joash (also spelled Jehoash). He is one of several people in the Bible with this name. He began to reign in Samaria in the twenty-third year of Joash king of Judah and ruled seventeen years, roughly 857–840 BC by inference from context. Throughout his reign Hazael king of Syria oppressed Israel and reduced his army to fifty horsemen, ten chariots and ten thousand foot soldiers. Jehoahaz pleaded with the LORD, who heard him because of Israel's suffering. He was buried in Samaria and succeeded by his son, who recovered from Ben-hadad son of Hazael the cities taken from Jehoahaz in war. Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that he continued the religious practices of the house of Jeroboam. Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests the deliverer later given to Israel was probably Jehoash or Jeroboam II.

Jeroboam, usually called Jeroboam II, was king of the northern kingdom of Israel. He was the son of Joash (also called Jehoash) and succeeded him on the throne in Samaria (2 Kgs 13:13; 14:16). He began to reign in the fifteenth year of Amaziah of Judah and ruled forty-one years, about 825–784 BC by inference from context (2 Kgs 14:23). Through him Israel was delivered, and he recovered Damascus and Hamath for Israel (2 Kgs 14:27–28). The prophets Hosea and Amos were active during his reign (Hos 1:1; Amos 1:1). Amos foretold that God would rise against his house with the sword, and Amaziah the priest of Bethel reported this to the king as a conspiracy (Amos 7:9–11). At his death his son Zachariah succeeded him but reigned only six months (2 Kgs 14:29; 15:8). He is distinct from the earlier Jeroboam son of Nebat, Israel's first king.

Kareah, also spelled Careah in 2 Kgs 25:23, was the father of Johanan and Jonathan, two army captains who joined Gedaliah, the governor Babylon appointed at Mizpah after the fall of Jerusalem. Kareah himself appears only as a name identifying his sons, and nothing is told of his own life. His son Johanan warned Gedaliah that Ishmael son of Nethaniah planned to kill him, but Gedaliah would not believe it. After the murder, Johanan led the captains against Ishmael and recovered the captives he had taken from Mizpah. Johanan later rejected Jeremiah's warning not to go to Egypt and led the remnant of Judah there. According to Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries, the name means "bald."

Manoah was a man of Zorah from the tribe of Dan and the father of Samson. His wife had been unable to have children until an angel of the LORD appeared to her and promised a son (Judg 13:2). Manoah then prayed for the messenger to come again and teach them how to raise the child. The angel returned, and Manoah asked how the boy should be brought up (Judg 13:8–13). He offered to prepare a young goat for the visitor, but was told to make a burnt offering to the LORD instead. He also asked the visitor's name. When Manoah offered the goat on a rock, the angel rose up in the altar's flame. Only then did Manoah realize who the visitor was, and he feared that he and his wife would die because they had seen God (Judg 13:15–22). Samson was later buried in Manoah's burial place between Zorah and Eshtaol (Judg 16:31). His name is usually taken to mean "rest."

Mary Magdalene was a follower of Jesus and a leading witness of his death, burial and resurrection. Her name probably reflects her hometown, Magdala on the Sea of Galilee (Easton's Bible Dictionary). Luke lists her among women healed of evil spirits who traveled with Jesus, noting that seven devils had gone out of her (Luke 8:2). She watched the crucifixion (Mark 15:40; John 19:25) and saw where the body was laid (Mark 15:47).
