After the Sabbath she brought spices and found the stone rolled away from the tomb (Mark 16:1; John 20:1). The risen Jesus appeared first to her. She recognized him when he spoke her name and then told the disciples (Mark 16:9; John 20:16–18). Later tradition linked her with the sinful woman of Luke 7. The Gospels do not make that connection, and this entry treats them as distinct.

Mephibosheth, also called Merib-baal, was the son of Jonathan and grandson of King Saul. He was five when news came of Saul and Jonathan's deaths, and his nurse dropped him as she fled, leaving him lame in both feet (2 Sam 4:4). David later brought him to Jerusalem, gave him Saul's land to be farmed by Saul's servant Ziba, and had him eat regularly at the king's table (2 Sam 9:10–13). He had a young son, Micah. During Absalom's revolt Ziba met the fleeing David with supplies and was granted all of Mephibosheth's property (2 Sam 16:1–4). When David returned, Mephibosheth came to meet him unwashed and ungroomed. By his own account Ziba had deceived him, and he told the king to let Ziba take everything (2 Sam 19:24–30). David later spared him because of his oath to Jonathan (2 Sam 21:7). Another son of Saul bore the same name.

Ner was a Benjamite of King Saul's family and the father of Abner, the commander of Saul's army (1 Sam 14:50; 2 Sam 2:8). He is almost always named only as Abner's father. 1 Sam 14:50–51 calls Ner Saul's uncle and names his father as Abiel, and 1 Chr 9:36 lists Ner alongside Kish, Saul's father, among the sons of a Benjamite family. This makes Ner and Kish brothers and Saul and Abner first cousins, the view of Easton's Bible Dictionary that this entry follows. Abiel is probably the same man as the Jeiel of 1 Chr 9:35, whose wife was Maachah. 1 Chr 8:33, by contrast, says Ner fathered Kish, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia therefore calls Ner Saul's grandfather. The name means "lamp" according to Hitchcock's Bible Names.

Sennacherib was a king of Assyria who invaded Judah in the fourteenth year of King Hezekiah and captured its fortified cities (2 Kgs 18:13; Isa 36:1). While he besieged Lachish, he sent officials to Jerusalem to mock Hezekiah's trust and demand surrender. Hezekiah prayed against him, and Isaiah answered that the prayer had been heard. Sennacherib then withdrew and lived at Nineveh. The surrounding passages (2 Kgs 19:35–37) say an angel struck down his army, and that his sons Adrammelech and Sharezer later killed him, with another son, Esar-haddon, succeeding him. Easton's Bible Dictionary dates his reign from about 705 to 681 BC. This entry also includes Sargon, the Assyrian king whose commander took Ashdod (Isa 20:1). Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries treat Sargon as Sennacherib's father and predecessor.

Ahimaaz was the son of Zadok the priest, a Levite, and one of several men in the Bible with this name. During Absalom's revolt, David sent Zadok back to Jerusalem with Ahimaaz and Jonathan son of Abiathar so the two could relay news to him (2 Sam 15:27, 36). Waiting at En-rogel, they received word through a servant girl and escaped Absalom's men who searched for them (2 Sam 17:17, 20). After the battle in which Absalom died, Ahimaaz pressed Joab to let him run, outran the Cushite messenger, and told David of the victory. When asked about Absalom, he said only that he had seen a great tumult (2 Sam 18:19–29). The genealogies place him in the priestly line as father of Azariah (1 Chr 6:8–9, 53). Easton's Bible Dictionary treats him as Zadok's successor as high priest. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia regards his later career as unknown.

Amoz was the father of the prophet Isaiah. He is known only through the phrase "Isaiah the son of Amoz," which appears in the headings of Isaiah's prophecies (Isa 1:1; 2:1; 13:1) and in the accounts of Isaiah's dealings with King Hezekiah in 2 Kings, 2 Chronicles and Isaiah. Since Isaiah prophesied in the days of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz and Hezekiah, Amoz presumably lived in Judah in the eighth century BC. The Bible records nothing else about him. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "strong" and notes a view that he was the "man of God" of 2 Chr 25:7–8. Smith's Bible Dictionary reports a rabbinical tradition that he was a brother of King Amaziah of Judah. He should not be confused with the prophet Amos, whose name is spelled differently in Hebrew.

Barak was the son of Abinoam, from Kedesh in Naphtali, who led Israel against the Canaanite commander Sisera. The prophet Deborah summoned him and told him the LORD commanded him to gather ten thousand men of Naphtali and Zebulun at Mount Tabor. Barak agreed to go only if Deborah went with him. She went, but said the honor would not be his, because Sisera would fall into the hand of a woman. At her word Barak came down from Tabor, the LORD routed Sisera's chariots and army, and Barak pursued them to Harosheth of the Gentiles. Following Sisera, he found him already dead in the tent of Jael. Deborah and Barak then sang the victory song of Judges 5. Hebrews 11:32 names him among the people of faith. This entry dates the deliverance to about 1278 BC, an estimate inferred from context. His name means "lightning" (Easton's Bible Dictionary).

Gad was a prophet in David's time, called "David's seer" or "the king's seer" (2 Sam 24:11; 2 Chr 29:25). While David was a fugitive from Saul, Gad told him to leave his stronghold for Judah, and David went to the forest of Hareth. Years later, after David counted the people, Gad brought him the LORD's choice of three punishments: famine, flight from enemies, or plague. When the plague ended, Gad told David to build an altar on the threshing floor of Araunah, called Ornan in Chronicles. Chronicles credits him with a book recording David's acts and a share in commanding the Levites' music in the temple. Jewish tradition holds that Gad and Nathan completed the books of Samuel, which is why this entry names him as a writer of them. He is distinct from Jacob's son Gad and others of that name.

Hamor was a Hivite, called "prince of the country" around the city of Shechem, and the father of Shechem in the time of Jacob. Jacob bought a field from Hamor's sons for a hundred pieces of money, and Joseph's bones were later buried there. After his son Shechem seized and violated Jacob's daughter Dinah, Hamor went to Jacob to ask for her as Shechem's wife. Jacob's sons replied deceitfully, demanding that the city's men be circumcised. Hamor and Shechem persuaded the men at the city gate to agree. Afterward Jacob's sons, named as Simeon and Levi in the surrounding narrative, killed Hamor, Shechem and the men of the city. Generations later the people of Shechem were still called "the men of Hamor" (Judg 9:28). Acts 7:16 gives his name in Greek form as Emmor. Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that the name means "donkey."

Hezron was a son of Pharez (Perez), a grandson of Judah, and the brother of Hamul (Gen 46:12; 1 Chr 2:5). He is listed among Jacob's family who went down to Egypt, and his descendants formed the Hezronite clan of the tribe of Judah (Num 26:21). His sons included Jerahmeel, his firstborn, Ram, and Chelubai, who is evidently the Caleb named a few verses later (1 Chr 2:9, 18, 25). At sixty he married the daughter of Machir, the father of Gilead, and she bore him Segub. After Hezron died at Caleb-ephrathah, his wife Abiah bore his son Ashur, the father of Tekoa (1 Chr 2:21, 24). Through Ram he was an ancestor of David (Ruth 4:18–19). He appears as Esrom, the Greek form of his name, in the genealogies of Jesus (Matt 1:3; Luke 3:33). The name Hezron is also borne by other people in the Bible.

Hushai the Archite was a loyal friend of King David, called "the king's companion" in 1 Chr 27:33. When David fled Jerusalem during Absalom's rebellion, Hushai met him at the top of the Mount of Olives with his coat torn and earth on his head, a sign of mourning. He then returned to the city as Absalom arrived and greeted Absalom as king, claiming loyalty to whoever the LORD and Israel chose. Asked to weigh in after Ahithophel had given his advice, Hushai argued that David and his men were dangerous fighters and that Ahithophel's plan was unwise. Absalom and the men of Israel preferred Hushai's counsel, and he passed both plans to the priests Zadok and Abiathar. "Archite" probably refers to the Archites, a clan or place on the border of Benjamin (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia). Baanah, one of Solomon's district officers, was probably his son.

Jeduthun (Ethan) was a Levite of the clan of Merari and son of Kishi, also spelled Kushaiah. He was one of the three chief musicians appointed in King David's time, alongside Heman and Asaph (1 Chr 6:44; 15:17, 19). The names Ethan and Jeduthun appear in matching lists of these three leaders, and Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries treat them as probably the same man, as this entry does. He played bronze cymbals, gave thanks before the LORD, and prophesied with the harp (1 Chr 16:41–42; 25:1, 3). His six sons served under his direction, and some were gatekeepers (1 Chr 16:42; 25:3, 6). Shimei, the sixth son, is probably the one named in 1 Chr 25:17. He is called "the king's seer" (2 Chr 35:15). His descendants still served in Solomon's and Hezekiah's days (2 Chr 5:12; 29:14). His name heads Psalm 77, which Smith's takes to indicate his choir.

Kish, called Cis in Acts 13:21, was a Benjamite of the family of Matri, described as "a mighty man of power," and the father of Saul, Israel's first king. 1 Sam 9:1 traces his ancestry through Abiel back to Aphiah. The only story told about him is that he sent Saul and a servant to look for his lost donkeys, a search that led Saul to Samuel. Saul's and Jonathan's bones were later buried in Kish's tomb at Zelah in Benjamin. His link to Ner is unclear. 1 Sam 14:51 suggests Kish and Ner were both sons of Abiel, while 1 Chr 8:33 and 9:39 say Ner fathered Kish. Smith's Bible Dictionary takes the Kish listed among the sons of Jehiel and Maachah (1 Chr 9:36) as a different man, an uncle of Saul's father. This entry follows the view that he is Saul's father and a brother of Ner and Abdon. Several other biblical men share the name.

Omri was a king of Israel, the northern kingdom, and father of Ahab. He was captain of the army besieging Gibbethon when Zimri killed King Elah, and the troops made him king in the camp that same day. He then besieged Tirzah. Half the people backed a rival, Tibni son of Ginath, until Omri's side prevailed and Tibni died. He reigned twelve years, beginning in the 31st year of Asa of Judah (about 929 BC, by inference from context), six of them at Tirzah. By 1 Kgs 16:24 he then built Samaria, where he was buried. The text says he did worse evil than all before him, and Micah later condemns the "statutes of Omri." Athaliah, mother of King Ahaziah of Judah, is called his daughter. Through her he is linked to the royal line of Judah. Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that the Moabite Stone records him oppressing Moab. Several other men in the Bible share his name.

Remaliah was the father of Pekah, the army captain who killed King Pekahiah in Samaria and took the throne of Israel, reigning twenty years (2 Kgs 15:25, 27). Nothing is recorded about Remaliah himself. His name survives only in the phrase "son of Remaliah," used of Pekah in Kings, Chronicles and Isaiah, including the accounts of Pekah's alliance with Rezin of Syria against Judah and King Ahaz. Isaiah repeatedly refers to Pekah only as "the son of Remaliah" or "Remaliah's son" without naming him (Isa 7:4–5, 9; 8:6). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests this may be a contemptuous reference to the family's humble origins. The name is usually explained as meaning "adorned by the Lord" (Easton's Bible Dictionary) or "protected by the Lord" (Smith's Bible Dictionary).

Ruth was a Moabite woman who married Mahlon, son of the Bethlehem family of Elimelech and Naomi, who had settled in Moab (Ruth 1:4; Ruth 4:10). After her husband died, she refused to leave her mother-in-law. Her sister-in-law Orpah turned back, but Ruth vowed that Naomi's people and God would be her own (Ruth 1:14–16). The two women reached Bethlehem at the start of the barley harvest (Ruth 1:22). There Ruth gleaned in the fields of Boaz, a relative of Elimelech, who told her to stay with his workers (Ruth 2:2, 2:8). She asked Boaz to act as a near kinsman (Ruth 3:9). He redeemed Naomi's land and married Ruth to keep the dead man's name alive on his inheritance (Ruth 4:5, 4:10). She bore Obed (Ruth 4:13), and Matthew names her in the genealogy of Jesus (Matt 1:5).

Tamar was a daughter of King David and the full sister of Absalom, named in 1 Chr 3:9 alongside David's sons. Her name means "palm tree" (Hitchcock's Bible Names). She is described as beautiful, and her half-brother Amnon became infatuated with her. On the advice of his cousin Jonadab, Amnon pretended to be ill and asked David to send Tamar to prepare food for him. When she brought the cakes into his room, he raped her. Tamar put ashes on her head, tore her richly colored robe, and went away crying. Absalom told her to keep quiet, and she lived desolate in his house. Absalom hated Amnon for what he had done and later had him killed. The same name belongs to other women in the Bible, so this Tamar is distinguished as David's daughter.

Ziba was a servant of the house of Saul who, when David asked whether anyone of Saul's family survived, told him of Jonathan's lame son Mephibosheth, living in the house of Machir at Lodebar. David gave Mephibosheth all of Saul's property and ordered Ziba, with his fifteen sons and twenty servants, to farm the land for him. During Absalom's revolt Ziba met the fleeing David with two donkeys, bread, raisins, summer fruit and wine. He claimed that Mephibosheth had stayed in Jerusalem hoping to regain his grandfather's kingdom, and David then gave Ziba everything that belonged to Mephibosheth. When David returned, Ziba and his household crossed the Jordan ahead of him. Mephibosheth then told David that Ziba had deceived him (2 Sam 19:26–27), and David ordered the two to divide the land. Easton's Bible Dictionary takes Ziba's report to have been a slander.

Abihu was the second son of Aaron and his wife Elisheba, and brother of Nadab, Eleazar and Ithamar, of the tribe of Levi. His name means "he is my father" (Hitchcock's Bible Names). With his father and older brother Nadab, he went part of the way up Mount Sinai with Moses and seventy elders of Israel to worship at a distance. He and his brothers were set apart to serve as priests alongside Aaron. Abihu and Nadab later offered "strange fire" before the LORD in their censers, fire the LORD had not commanded, and both died before the LORD in the wilderness of Sinai. They had no children, so Eleazar and Ithamar carried on the priestly office. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggest the brothers may have been drunk, since a ban on priests drinking wine follows soon after in Leviticus 10.

Agrippa was the king who came with Bernice to Caesarea to greet the new Roman governor Festus (Acts 25:13). He is usually identified as Herod Agrippa II. Easton's Bible Dictionary calls him the son of Herod Agrippa I, born at Rome about AD 27, brother of Bernice and Drusilla, and ruler of the former territories of Philip and Lysanias. Festus told him about Paul, a prisoner he could bring no clear charge against, and Agrippa asked to hear Paul himself. The next day, amid great ceremony, Festus brought Paul before him so that he would have something to write to the emperor (Acts 25:23–26). Paul addressed his defense to Agrippa and asked whether he believed the prophets. Agrippa replied, "Almost thou persuadest me to be a Christian." He later told Festus that Paul could have been freed if he had not appealed to Caesar. This entry dates the hearing to about AD 56, by inference; Easton's places it in AD 59.

Andrew was one of the twelve apostles of Jesus, the brother of Simon Peter and, like him, a son of Jonas. He came from Bethsaida and fished on the Sea of Galilee, where Jesus called the two brothers to follow him. John's Gospel says he first followed Jesus after hearing John the Baptist speak, and the next verse says he then brought his brother Simon. The brothers shared a house, probably in Capernaum by inference from the context. At the feeding of the five thousand Andrew pointed out a boy with loaves and fishes. With Philip he brought to Jesus some Greeks who wanted to see him. He joined Peter, James and John in questioning Jesus privately on the Mount of Olives, and he was with the apostles in the upper room after the ascension. Smith's Bible Dictionary records traditions that he preached widely and was crucified at Patrae in Achaia.

Eber (Heber) was a descendant of Shem in the line from Noah to Abraham. He was the son of Salah and grandson of Arphaxad (Gen 10:24; 1 Chr 1:18). He fathered Peleg at thirty-four and lived another 430 years, having other sons and daughters (Gen 11:16–17). By inference from the genealogy, he was born about 2281 BC. His two named sons were Peleg, so called because "in his days was the earth divided," and Joktan (Gen 10:25). Shem is described as "the father of all the children of Eber" (Gen 10:21), and Easton's Bible Dictionary regards Eber as the founder of the Hebrew people. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia links his name, meaning "the other side," to the word "Hebrew." In Balaam's oracle (Num 24:24), "Eber" probably stands for his descendants as a people. Luke 3:35 names him Heber in the ancestry of Jesus.

Gehazi was the servant of the prophet Elisha, mentioned in three episodes of 2 Kings. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "valley of vision." In the story of the Shunammite woman, he summoned her for Elisha and pointed out that she had no son and that her husband was old. When her child later died, he tried to push her away from the prophet at Mount Carmel. Elisha then sent him ahead with his staff to lay on the boy's face, but the child did not wake. After Elisha refused Naaman's gifts, Gehazi ran after the Syrian commander to take something from him, then told Elisha he had gone nowhere. In the verses that follow (2 Kgs 5:26–27), Elisha declares that Naaman's leprosy will cling to him. Later he described Elisha's deeds to the king, whom Easton's and Smith's dictionaries identify as Joram, just as the Shunammite arrived.

Hagar was an Egyptian slave woman who served Sarai, the wife of Abram (Abraham). Because Sarai had no children, she gave Hagar to Abram as a wife after he had lived ten years in Canaan. When Hagar conceived, she looked down on her mistress, and later she fled from Sarai. On the way, an angel met her and asked where she was going. She bore Abram a son, Ishmael, when Abram was eighty-six, about 1910 BC by inference from context. Later, Sarah saw Ishmael mocking, and Abraham sent Hagar and the boy away with bread and water. They wandered in the wilderness of Beersheba, where the angel of God called to Hagar from heaven and told her that God had heard the boy. In Gal 4:24–25 Paul, spelling her name Agar, uses her in an allegory of the covenant from Mount Sinai.

Heman was a Levite of the Kohathite clan, son of Joel and grandson of Shemuel (Samuel), and one of the chief singers in David's organization of worship (1 Chr 6:33). The Levites appointed him with Asaph and Ethan to sound bronze cymbals when the ark was brought to Jerusalem. He and Jeduthun then served with trumpets, cymbals and other instruments to give thanks to the LORD. David set apart the families of Asaph, Heman and Jeduthun to 'prophesy' with harps, lyres and cymbals. Heman is called 'the king's seer in the words of God,' and he had fourteen sons and three daughters, who sang under his direction in the house of the LORD. His family sang at the dedication of Solomon's temple, and his descendants Jehiel and Shimei served under Hezekiah. Easton's Bible Dictionary links him with the heading of Psalm 88. Other men named Heman also appear in the Bible.

Heth was a son of Canaan, named second after Sidon, the firstborn, in the table of nations (Gen 10:15; 1 Chr 1:13). He is regarded as the ancestor of the Hittites, and in Genesis his descendants appear as "the sons" or "children of Heth," a people living near Hebron in Abraham's time. Abraham bought from them, through Ephron the Hittite, the field and cave of Machpelah as a family burial place. He paid four hundred shekels of silver in a public transaction at the city gate (Gen 23:3–20). Abraham and Sarah were later buried there (Gen 25:10). Rebekah's distress over the "daughters of Heth" whom Esau had married led her to urge that Jacob not take a wife from among them (Gen 27:46). Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary give the name's meaning as "dread" or "terror."

Hur was a man of the tribe of Judah who assisted Moses during the wilderness journey. In Israel's battle with Amalek he climbed the hill with Moses and Aaron, and when Moses' hands grew heavy, Aaron and Hur held them up on either side until sunset (Exod 17:10–12). When Moses went up Mount Sinai, he left Aaron and Hur with the elders to settle any disputes (Exod 24:14). Through his son Uri, Hur was the grandfather of Bezalel, the craftsman who made the tabernacle and its bronze altar. Chronicles names him as the firstborn son of Caleb and Ephratah and calls him 'the father of Bethlehem.' His descendants included Shobal, founder of Kirjath-jearim. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats Moses' helper and Bezalel's grandfather as possibly two men. This entry follows Josephus, who identifies them as one man and makes him the husband of Miriam, Moses' sister, a view Easton's Bible Dictionary also gives.

Josedech, also called Jehozadak and Jozadak, was a priest of the tribe of Levi in the high-priestly line, the son of Seraiah (1 Chr 6:14). When Nebuchadnezzar took Judah and Jerusalem into exile, Jehozadak was carried away captive (1 Chr 6:15). Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that his father Seraiah was executed at Riblah (2 Kgs 25:18–21) and that Jehozadak never served as high priest himself. Easton's Bible Dictionary suggests he probably died in Babylon. He is mostly remembered as the father of Joshua (Jeshua), the high priest who returned with Zerubbabel, rebuilt the altar and led the rebuilding of the temple. Haggai and Zechariah address Joshua by his father's name. Ezra 7:1 calls Ezra "son of Seraiah," which is why this entry treats Ezra as his brother. Since Ezra lived much later, the phrase may instead mean a descendant.

Martha was a woman of Bethany, the sister of Lazarus and Mary, and one of those Jesus is said to have loved (John 11:5). Luke tells how she welcomed Jesus into her house in an unnamed village. She was busy with serving and asked him to tell Mary to help her, and Jesus replied that she was anxious about many things (Luke 10:38–41). John names Bethany as the sisters' town. When Lazarus died, Martha went out to meet Jesus. She said her brother would not have died had he been there, and she affirmed that he would rise at the last day. She objected when Jesus ordered the tomb opened, because Lazarus had been dead four days. Later, at the supper in Bethany where Mary anointed Jesus, Martha served while Lazarus sat at the table (John 12:2). Because the house is called hers, the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia infers that she was the elder sister.

Miriam was the daughter of Amram and Jochebed of the tribe of Levi, and the sister of Aaron and Moses, born in Egypt (Num 26:59; 1 Chr 6:3). She is probably the unnamed sister who watched over the infant Moses in the Nile (Exod 2:4). Smith's Bible Dictionary takes her to be the eldest of the three. Called "the prophetess," she led the women with timbrels and dancing in a song of triumph after the crossing of the Red Sea. Later she and Aaron spoke against Moses over his marriage to an Ethiopian woman. She became leprous and was shut out of the camp for seven days, and the people did not move on until she was brought back. Deut 24:9 recalls this as a warning, and Micah names her with Moses and Aaron as leaders God sent before Israel. She died and was buried at Kadesh, about 1452 BC by inference from context. Other women in the Bible share her name.

Nadab was the firstborn of the four sons of Aaron and his wife Elisheba, a man of the tribe of Levi, with Abihu, Eleazar and Ithamar as his brothers. He went up Mount Sinai with Moses, Aaron, Abihu and seventy elders of Israel, who were told to worship at a distance. He and his brothers were set apart with their father to serve as priests. Nadab and Abihu later offered "strange fire" with incense in their censers, which the LORD had not commanded, and both died before the LORD in the wilderness of Sinai. Lev 10:2 records that fire came out from the LORD and consumed them. What exactly made the fire "strange" is not spelled out. Smith's Bible Dictionary takes it as fire not taken from the altar, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia as fire not authorized by the Law. He had no children, so the priesthood passed through Eleazar and Ithamar.

Portius Festus (spelled Porcius in the King James text) was the Roman governor who succeeded Felix in Judea, finding Paul still a prisoner at Caesarea (Acts 24:27). Three days after arriving he went up to Jerusalem but ruled that Paul's case be heard at Caesarea (Acts 25:1–4). Wanting to please the Jewish leaders, he offered Paul a trial in Jerusalem. Paul appealed to Caesar instead, and after consulting his council Festus granted the appeal (Acts 25:9–12). When King Agrippa and Bernice visited, Festus explained the case and arranged a hearing (Acts 25:13–24). During Paul's defence he shouted that much learning had driven Paul mad (Acts 26:24). Agrippa later told him Paul could have been freed had he not appealed (Acts 26:32). This entry dates these events to about AD 56 by inference. Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries place his arrival about AD 60 and say he died in office within two years.

Thomas was one of the twelve apostles of Jesus, named in every list of the apostles. His name means "twin," and John's Gospel adds that he was called Didymus, the Greek word for twin. Most of what is known about him comes from John. When Jesus decided to return to Judea after Lazarus died, Thomas urged the other disciples to go too, "that we may die with him." Later he asked Jesus how they could know the way when they did not know where he was going. He was absent when the risen Jesus first appeared to the disciples and, according to John 20:25, refused to believe without touching the wounds. Eight days later Jesus appeared again and invited him to do so, and Thomas answered, "My Lord and my God." He was afterward among the disciples by the Sea of Galilee and among the eleven in the upper room in Jerusalem. Easton's Bible Dictionary mentions a suggestion that Thomas, Matthew and James son of Alphaeus were brothers.

Titus was a Greek Christian and a close companion and co-worker of Paul. Paul took him to Jerusalem with Barnabas, and he was not required to be circumcised (Gal 2:1–3). Paul calls him his brother, his partner and fellow helper, and his own son in the common faith (2 Cor 2:13; 8:23; Titus 1:4). Paul sent him to Corinth, where he began the church's collection and was asked to finish it. Paul looked for him anxiously, and Titus later met him in Macedonia and comforted him with news from Corinth (2 Cor 2:13; 7:6–14; 8:6, 16; 12:18). The letter to Titus is addressed to him, and its next verse (Titus 1:5) says Paul had left him in Crete. In Paul's last letter Titus has gone to Dalmatia (2 Tim 4:10). Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that he is never named in Acts.

Tobiah, called "the servant" and "the Ammonite," was one of the chief opponents of Nehemiah's rebuilding of Jerusalem's walls. With Sanballat the Horonite and Geshem the Arabian he was angered by Nehemiah's arrival, mocked the work, and jeered that a fox could break down the stone wall (Neh 4:3). He and Sanballat hired a prophet to frighten Nehemiah. Tobiah kept up a correspondence with nobles of Judah and sent letters to intimidate Nehemiah. Neh 6:18 explains these ties: he was son-in-law of Shecaniah, and his son Johanan married the daughter of Meshullam son of Berechiah. Later the priest Eliashib, who was allied to him, gave him a room in the temple courts. When Nehemiah returned to Jerusalem, he threw out Tobiah's belongings. His name means "the Lord is good" (Hitchcock's Bible Names). Several other people in the Bible share the name.

Zerah (also spelled Zarah, and Zara in Matt 1:3) was a son of Judah by his daughter-in-law Tamar and the twin brother of Pharez (Perez). At their birth his hand appeared first and the midwife tied a scarlet thread on it, but Pharez was born ahead of him, so Zerah counts as the younger twin (Gen 38:27–30). He is listed among Judah's five sons, with his half-brothers Er, Onan and Shelah, in the household that went down to Egypt with Jacob. He headed the Zarhite clan of Judah. 1 Chr 2:6 names his sons as Zimri, Ethan, Heman, Calcol and Dara. Zabdi, named as his son in Josh 7:1, is probably the same man as Zimri. Through Zabdi, Zerah was the ancestor of Achan, whose theft at Jericho brought wrath on Israel. His descendants also appear among those living in Jerusalem after the exile. Other biblical figures share the name.

Ahijah was a prophet from Shiloh, called "the Shilonite," active in the days of Solomon and Jeroboam. This is one of several men named Ahijah in the Bible. Meeting Jeroboam alone in a field outside Jerusalem, he tore his own new garment into twelve pieces as a sign that the kingdom would be divided and Jeroboam would rule part of it (1 Kgs 11:29–30). Rehoboam's refusal to listen to the people is presented as the fulfilment of this word (1 Kgs 12:15; 2 Chr 10:15). Later, when Jeroboam's son fell sick, Jeroboam sent his wife in disguise to Ahijah, who was by then blind with age. Forewarned by the LORD, Ahijah recognized her and gave her heavy news: the child's death and the destruction of Jeroboam's house, both of which came to pass (1 Kgs 14:2–6, 18; 15:29). Chronicles cites a written "prophecy of Ahijah the Shilonite" as a source for Solomon's reign (2 Chr 9:29).

Ahimelech was a priest at Nob in Saul's reign, the son of Ahitub. When David arrived alone while fleeing Saul, Ahimelech was afraid. David claimed to be on secret business for the king and asked for a weapon (1 Sam 21:1–8). The same chapter says Ahimelech gave him the consecrated bread and Goliath's sword. Doeg the Edomite reported this to Saul, who summoned Ahimelech and the priests of his family. Ahimelech defended David as Saul's most faithful servant, but Saul condemned him and his whole house to death. His son Abiathar escaped and fled to David with an ephod. Following Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries, this entry treats him as probably the same man as Ahiah son of Ahitub, a great-grandson of Eli, who wore the ephod in Saul's camp and was told to bring the ark. Some instead take Ahiah to be his brother.

Amasa was the son of Jether and Abigail, and a cousin of Joab, whose mother Zeruiah was Abigail's sister. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes Abigail as David's sister, which would make Amasa David's nephew. His father is called Ithra an Israelite in 2 Sam 17:25 but Jether the Ishmeelite in 1 Chr 2:17. During Absalom's revolt, Absalom made Amasa commander of his army in place of Joab. After the revolt failed, David promised Amasa command of his own army instead of Joab. Sent to gather the men of Judah against the rebel Sheba son of Bichri, Amasa took longer than the three days he was given. At the great stone in Gibeon, Joab greeted him as a brother and stabbed him to death. David later charged Solomon to avenge this killing, and Solomon called Amasa captain of the host of Judah. Others in the Bible share this name.

Amminadab was a man of the tribe of Judah, the son of Ram and a descendant of Judah through Perez and Hezron (Ruth 4:19; Luke 3:33). His son Nahshon was the leader of Judah during the wilderness journey. He headed the tribe's census, led its camp and march, and brought the first offering at the dedication of the altar (Num 1:7; 2:3; 7:12; 10:14). His daughter Elisheba married Aaron and bore him Nadab, Abihu, Eleazar and Ithamar (Exod 6:23). Amminadab appears in the line leading to David (Ruth 4:19–20; 1 Chr 2:10). Matthew and Luke include him, spelled Aminadab, in the genealogy of Jesus (Matt 1:4; Luke 3:33). The name, explained in Hitchcock's Bible Names as "my people is liberal," is borne by other men in the Bible as well. This entry concerns the ancestor in Judah's line.

Amram was a Levite, a son of Kohath and brother of Izhar, Hebron and Uzziel, and the father of Aaron, Moses and Miriam. He married Jochebed, his father's sister, described as a daughter of Levi born in Egypt. According to Exod 6:20 he lived 137 years, and Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that he died in Egypt. His line held a distinguished place among the Levites: Aaron and his sons were set apart to handle the most holy things and burn incense, and later lists of Levites still trace families back to him through Shubael. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests that "son of Kohath" may mean a more distant descendant, because other genealogies of the same period show more generations. This entry follows the text as it reads. The name, meaning "exalted people," is also borne by other people in the Bible.

Bathsheba, also called Bath-shua, was the daughter of Eliam and the wife of Uriah the Hittite when King David asked who she was (2 Sam 11:3). The surrounding chapter tells how David lay with her, had Uriah killed in battle and then married her. Their first child died. She later bore Solomon (2 Sam 12:24), and 1 Chr 3:5 lists four sons born to her in Jerusalem: Shimea (Shammua), Shobab, Nathan and Solomon. That verse calls her father Ammiel, which Easton's Bible Dictionary treats as another name for Eliam. When David's son Adonijah claimed the throne, the prophet Nathan urged her to go to the aged king, and she secured David's promise that Solomon would succeed him. As queen mother she sat at Solomon's right hand and brought him Adonijah's request to marry Abishag. Matt 1:6 names her, as Uriah's former wife, in the genealogy of Jesus.

Gilead was the son of Machir and grandson of Manasseh, of the tribe of Joseph. His family, the Gileadites, formed a major branch of Manasseh (Num 26:29). Numbers 26 lists his sons as Jeezer (elsewhere Abiezer), Helek, Asriel, Shechem, Shemida and Hepher, each the head of a clan (Num 26:30). Through Hepher he was the great-grandfather of Zelophehad, whose daughters asked Moses for an inheritance (Num 27:1; Josh 17:3). The heads of his clans later raised the question of their marriages (Num 36:1). His sister was Hammoleketh, Peresh and Sheresh were his brothers, and another sister married Hezron of Judah (1 Chr 2:21). The region of Gilead east of the Jordan was given to his father Machir (Josh 17:1). The Gilead named as Jephthah's father (Judg 11:2) is probably a later man of the same name, or possibly the clan itself.

Haggai was a prophet in Judah after the return from exile in Babylon. The book that bears his name is credited to him. He delivered a series of messages dated to the second year of King Darius of Persia, about 520 BC by inference from context. They were addressed to Zerubbabel the governor, Joshua the high priest, and the people, urging them to resume rebuilding the temple in Jerusalem. The leaders and people obeyed his words, and he assured them that the LORD was with them. He also questioned the priests about ritual uncleanness to make a point about the nation. Ezra pairs him with Zechariah son of Iddo and credits their prophesying with helping the elders finish the temple. Nothing is recorded of his family or tribe, as Smith's Bible Dictionary notes. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of his name as "feast."

Hannah was one of the two wives of Elkanah and the mother of the prophet Samuel. Her husband loved her and favored her, but she was childless while his other wife, Peninnah, had children (1 Sam 1:2, 1:5). On a yearly visit to the sanctuary at Shiloh she prayed silently in deep distress, and Eli the priest at first thought she was drunk until she explained that she had poured out her soul before the LORD. After the family returned home to Ramah she conceived and bore a son, naming him Samuel because she had asked him of the LORD. She kept him at home until he was weaned, then brought him to Shiloh to remain in the LORD's service. Her song of thanksgiving is recorded in 1 Sam 2:1–10. She later had three more sons and two daughters. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of her name as "favour" or "grace."

Ish-bosheth was a son of Saul who ruled Israel, apart from Judah, after his father's death. Abner, the commander of Saul's army, brought him to Mahanaim, east of the Jordan, and made him king there. He was forty years old and reigned two years, while Judah followed David (2 Sam 2:8–10). Abner and Ish-bosheth's men fought David's forces at Gibeon (2 Sam 2:12–15). When Ish-bosheth accused Abner of taking Saul's concubine Rizpah, Abner answered angrily and, as the following verses tell, went over to David (2 Sam 3:7–8). At David's demand, Ish-bosheth returned Michal, David's wife, taking her from Phaltiel (2 Sam 3:14–15). Rechab and Baanah killed him while he rested at noon and brought his head to David at Hebron. David had them executed and buried the head in Abner's tomb (2 Sam 4:5–12). In 1 Chr 8:33 he is called Eshbaal. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of Ish-bosheth as "a man of shame."

Japheth was one of the three sons of Noah, usually listed last after Shem and Ham (Gen 5:32; 6:10). He and his wife entered the ark with Noah's family and came out after the Flood (Gen 7:13; 9:18). When Noah lay drunk and uncovered, Japheth and Shem walked backward with a garment and covered him without looking. Noah then said, "God shall enlarge Japheth," adding that he would dwell in the tents of Shem (Gen 9:23, 27). The name probably plays on the Hebrew for "enlarge," though Easton's Bible Dictionary also notes a derivation meaning "beautiful" or "fair." Gen 10:21 can be read as calling either Shem or Japheth the elder, so his birth order is uncertain. His seven sons were Gomer, Magog, Madai, Javan, Tubal, Meshech and Tiras (Gen 10:2; 1 Chr 1:5). Smith's Bible Dictionary links his descendants with the Mediterranean coastlands, Europe and much of Asia.

Lazarus was a man of Bethany, the brother of Martha and of Mary, the Mary who anointed Jesus (John 11:1–2). Jesus loved all three (John 11:5). When Lazarus fell sick and died, Jesus first spoke of his death as sleep and then told his disciples plainly that he was dead (John 11:11, 14). At the tomb Jesus called out, "Lazarus, come forth," and he was raised from the dead. Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that he had lain four days in the tomb. Six days before Passover, Lazarus sat at the table at a supper for Jesus in Bethany (John 12:1–2). Crowds came to see him, and the chief priests plotted to kill him as well as Jesus (John 12:9–10). The name is a form of Eleazar, meaning "God helps" (Smith's Bible Dictionary). Another Lazarus, the beggar in Jesus' parable in Luke, is a different figure.

Mary (sister of Lazarus) was a woman of Bethany who lived with her sister Martha and brother Lazarus, and is one of several women named Mary in the New Testament. When Jesus visited the sisters, Mary sat at his feet listening to him, and he said she had chosen the good part, which would not be taken from her (Luke 10:39, 42). When Lazarus fell ill and died, many Jews came to comfort the sisters. Mary stayed in the house while Martha went to meet Jesus. When Martha called her, she went out quickly, fell at his feet and said that her brother would not have died if he had been there. After Lazarus was raised, many who had come to Mary believed in Jesus. Later, at a meal in Bethany, she anointed Jesus' feet with a pound of costly spikenard ointment and wiped them with her hair. Nothing is known of her later life.

Melchisedec, also spelled Melchizedek, was king of Salem and priest of the most high God in Abraham's time. When Abraham returned from defeating the kings who had captured Lot, Melchisedec brought out bread and wine and blessed him (Gen 14:18; Heb 7:1). The next verse, Gen 14:20, adds that Abraham gave him a tenth of the spoils. Nothing is said of his ancestry. Ps 110:4 speaks of one sworn by the LORD to be "a priest for ever after the order of Melchizedek." The Letter to the Hebrews quotes this line repeatedly and applies it to Jesus. It contrasts this priesthood with the Levitical priesthood of Aaron and notes that Levi was still in Abraham's body when Melchisedec met him (Heb 7:10–11). Salem is commonly identified with Jerusalem. Easton's and Smith's Bible dictionaries mention an old Jewish tradition that identified him with Noah's son Shem.

Naaman was the commander of the army of the king of Syria (Aram), a respected and valiant man through whom the LORD had given Syria victory, but who had leprosy. A young girl taken captive from Israel served his wife and spoke of a prophet in Samaria. Naaman came to the king of Israel with a letter from his own king, then went with his horses and chariot to Elisha's house. He was angry at first that the prophet did not come out to heal him in person. After bathing seven times in the Jordan, as told in 2 Kgs 5:14, he was healed. He asked for two mules' loads of earth and vowed to sacrifice to no god but the LORD. Elisha refused his gifts, but Elisha's servant Gehazi took silver and clothing from him and was struck with Naaman's leprosy. Easton's Bible Dictionary places him under Ben-hadad II. Jesus mentions his cleansing in Luke 4:27.

Nahshon, son of Amminadab, was the leader, or "prince," of the tribe of Judah during Israel's years in the wilderness after the Exodus. His sister Elisheba married Aaron, which made him Aaron's brother-in-law. He was named as Judah's representative at the first census of the tribes. He commanded Judah's army, which camped on the east side of the tabernacle and marched first when the camp moved. When the tabernacle was dedicated, he brought the first of the tribal offerings, on the first day. The genealogies list him in the line from Judah through Ram and Amminadab to his son Salmon (also called Salma), then Boaz, and on to David. Matthew and Luke include him, in the Greek form Naasson, in the ancestry of Jesus. Easton's Bible Dictionary concludes from Num 26:64–65 that he died in the wilderness before Israel entered Canaan.

Pekah son of Remaliah was a king of the northern kingdom of Israel. A captain under King Pekahiah, he conspired with Argob, Arieh and fifty men of Gilead, killed Pekahiah in the palace at Samaria and took the throne (2 Kgs 15:25). He is said to have reigned twenty years, from about 759 to 739 BC by inference from context. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that other chronologies make his reign later and shorter. Allied with Rezin king of Syria, he made war on Judah. According to 2 Chr 28:6 he killed 120,000 men in one day, and he besieged Ahaz in Jerusalem without taking it (2 Kgs 16:5; Isa 7:1). In his days Tiglath-pileser of Assyria seized Gilead, Galilee and Naphtali and carried their people captive. Hoshea son of Elah then conspired against him, killed him and reigned in his place. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives his name's meaning as "open-eyed."

Shealtiel, also called Salathiel, was a son of King Jehoiachin (Jeconiah) of Judah. Matthew places his birth after the deportation to Babylon (1 Chr 3:17; Matt 1:12). Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries give the meaning of his name as "asked of God." He is known almost entirely as the father of Zerubbabel, the governor of Judah who led returning exiles. Zerubbabel rebuilt the altar and began work on the temple in Jerusalem with the high priest Jeshua, and Ezra, Nehemiah and Haggai repeatedly call him "son of Shealtiel." As the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes, 1 Chr 3:19 instead names Shealtiel's brother Pedaiah as Zerubbabel's father. This may reflect adoption or a levirate marriage, or Shealtiel may have been Zerubbabel's grandfather. This entry follows the majority of passages in calling him Zerubbabel's father. Luke 3:27 also lists him among the ancestors of Jesus.

Uzziel, whose name means "God is my strength" according to Smith's Bible Dictionary, was a Levite, the fourth son of Kohath, and brother of Amram, Izhar and Hebron. Since Amram was the father of Moses and Aaron, Uzziel was their uncle, and Lev 10:4 calls him "the uncle of Aaron." His sons Mishael, Elzaphan and Zithri are named in Exod 6:22. Moses called Mishael and Elzaphan to carry their dead relatives out of the camp. By inference from the surrounding passage, these were Aaron's sons Nadab and Abihu. Elizaphan later became chief of the Kohathite families. Uzziel's line continued as a Levitical clan. Amminadab led 112 of its members in David's time. Michah and Jesiah (Isshiah), named as his sons in Chronicles, were probably later descendants heading branches of the family. Several other people in the Bible share the name.

Zebedee was a Galilean fisherman and the father of James and John, two of Jesus' twelve apostles (Matt 10:2). He appears in person only once, at the calling of his sons, about AD 27 by inference from context. Jesus found James and John in a boat with their father, mending nets, and when he called them they left Zebedee in the boat with the hired servants and followed him (Matt 4:21; Mark 1:19–20). The mention of hired servants suggests a family business of some size, and Luke 5:10 describes the sons as partners with Simon Peter. Elsewhere Zebedee is named only to identify his sons, the "sons of Zebedee." His wife, "the mother of Zebedee's children," asked Jesus for places of honor for them and was present at the crucifixion (Matt 20:20; 27:56). Comparing Matt 27:56 with Mark 15:40, Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies her as Salome.

Apollos was a Jew born at Alexandria, described as eloquent and "mighty in the scriptures," who came to Ephesus (Acts 18:24). The verses that follow say he knew only John's baptism until Priscilla and Aquila explained the way of God to him more fully (Acts 18:25–26). He then went on to Achaia and was working at Corinth when Paul arrived in Ephesus. In 1 Corinthians, Paul notes that the believers at Corinth had split into groups, some claiming to follow him and others Apollos or Cephas. Paul describes Apollos and himself as servants through whom the Corinthians believed: "I have planted, Apollos watered." Paul urged him to visit Corinth again, but Apollos chose to wait for a better time. He is last mentioned traveling with Zenas the lawyer, whom Titus was asked to help on their way. According to Smith's Bible Dictionary, later tradition made him bishop of Caesarea.

Arphaxad (Arpachshad in the Revised Version) was a son of Shem, listed among his brothers Elam, Asshur, Lud and Aram. Gen 11:10 says he was born two years after the flood, when Shem was 100 years old, which this entry places at about 2346 BC, by inference from context. At 35 he fathered Salah (Shelah), and he lived another 403 years and had other sons and daughters, a total of 438 years. Through Salah and Eber his line leads to Abraham. Luke's genealogy of Jesus also includes him, but Luke 3:36 places a Cainan between Arphaxad and Salah, while Genesis and 1 Chronicles have Arphaxad as Salah's father directly. According to Easton's Bible Dictionary, he lived in Mesopotamia, and the Jewish historian Josephus regarded him as the ancestor of the Chaldeans.

Artaxerxes was a king of Persia during whose reign Ezra and Nehemiah went to Jerusalem. In his seventh year Ezra led priests, Levites and other Israelites from Babylon to Jerusalem (Ezra 7:7; 8:1). Ezra carried a letter from the king that called him "king of kings" and ordered the treasurers west of the Euphrates to supply whatever Ezra needed (Ezra 7:12, 21). In his twentieth year Nehemiah, who served him wine, was allowed to go to Judah. He governed there until the king's thirty-second year and then returned to court (Neh 2:1; 5:14; 13:6). Ezra 6:14 also names him among the kings whose orders lay behind the temple work. Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries identify him as Artaxerxes I Longimanus, son of Xerxes, who reigned about 464–425 BC. This entry follows that view. Several Persian kings bore the name, and the Artaxerxes of Ezra 4 may be a different ruler.

Barabbas was a prisoner held in Jerusalem during the Roman trials of Jesus, about AD 30 by inference from context. Matthew calls him a notable prisoner (Matt 27:16), Mark says he was bound with rebels and had committed murder in an insurrection (Mark 15:7), and John calls him a robber (John 18:40). At the feast, Pilate offered the crowd the release of either Barabbas or Jesus. Persuaded by the chief priests and elders, the crowd demanded Barabbas, and Pilate, wanting to satisfy them, released him and handed Jesus over to be crucified (Matt 27:20–26; Mark 15:11–15; Luke 23:18). His name is Aramaic for "son of the father," according to the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia, which also notes that a few ancient manuscripts of Matthew give his name as "Jesus Barabbas." Nothing more is known of him or of the uprising he took part in.

Bilhah was the servant woman whom Laban gave to his daughter Rachel as her maid when Rachel married Jacob (Gen 29:29). Because Rachel had no children, she gave Bilhah to Jacob as a wife so that she could have children through her (Gen 30:3–4). Bilhah bore Jacob two sons, Dan and Naphtali, about 1755 and 1754 BC by inference from context (Gen 30:5–7; Gen 35:25). Elsewhere she is called Jacob's concubine, and Genesis reports that Jacob's eldest son Reuben slept with her (Gen 35:22). Later Jacob alludes to this in his final words to Reuben (Gen 49:4), and Easton's Bible Dictionary connects it with Reuben's loss of the birthright. Her sons and Naphtali's sons are counted as her descendants, seven persons in all, among those who went down to Egypt (Gen 46:25; 1 Chr 7:13). Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of her name as "timid" or "bashful."

Cornelius was a Roman centurion of the Italian band, a military unit stationed at Caesarea (Acts 10:1). His messengers described him as a just man who feared God and was well regarded by the Jewish people (Acts 10:22). While praying at the ninth hour, he saw an angel in a vision. The angel told him his prayers and alms had been remembered by God and directed him to send for Peter (Acts 10:3, 30–31). He sent two household servants and a devout soldier to Joppa, where they found Peter (Acts 10:7, 17, 21). When Peter arrived, Cornelius had gathered his relatives and close friends, and he fell at Peter's feet (Acts 10:24–25). Later verses in the chapter (Acts 10:44–48) describe his household being baptized. Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries treat him as the first Gentile convert to Christianity. The meeting is dated here to about AD 38, by inference from context.

Elkanah was the father of the prophet Samuel, a man of Ramathaim-zophim in the hill country of Ephraim whose home was at Ramah (1 Sam 1:1; 2:11). The son of Jeroham, he had two wives: Peninnah, who had sons and daughters, and Hannah, who was at first childless. Each year he went up with his household to offer sacrifice, probably at Shiloh, which 1 Sam 1:3 names as the place of worship. He gave portions to Peninnah and her children, comforted the grieving Hannah, and let her stay home until Samuel was weaned. After Samuel was left to serve under Eli the priest, Eli blessed Elkanah and his wife. 1 Sam 1:1 calls him an Ephrathite, while the genealogies in 1 Chr 6:27, 34 place him among the Levites. Easton's Bible Dictionary takes him as a Levite of the line of Heman the singer. Several other men in the Bible share his name.

Enoch (father of Methuselah), also spelled Henoch, was a descendant of Adam through Seth. He was the son of Jared and the father of Methuselah. Jared was 162 when Enoch was born, and Enoch was 65 when Methuselah was born. Genesis says that afterward Enoch "walked with God" for 300 years and had other sons and daughters. His life lasted 365 years, and then "he was not; for God took him" (Gen 5:24). Heb 11:5 explains this as his being taken so that he did not see death, because he had pleased God. Jude 1:14 calls him "the seventh from Adam" and quotes a prophecy of his about the Lord coming with ten thousands of his saints. He also appears in the genealogies of 1 Chr 1:3 and Luke 3:37. Easton's Bible Dictionary distinguishes him from Enoch the son of Cain. Working from the genealogy's figures, this entry dates his life to about 3382–3017 BC.

Ephron was a Hittite, the son of Zohar, who lived among the people of Heth and owned the field and cave of Machpelah near Mamre in Canaan. When Abraham sought a burial place for his wife Sarah, he asked the Hittites to approach Ephron for him. Ephron answered Abraham publicly at the city gate, before the assembled townspeople. Abraham insisted on paying, and he weighed out four hundred shekels of silver, after which the field, the cave and its trees were formally made over to him (Gen 23:16–17). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes the elaborate courtesy of the exchange and the large sum paid. The site continued to be identified as Ephron's field when Abraham was buried there and when Jacob asked to be buried with his fathers (Gen 25:9; Gen 49:29–30). The name is commonly explained as meaning "fawn-like" (Smith's Bible Dictionary).

Herod, usually called Herod the Great, was king of Judaea when John the Baptist and Jesus were born (Matt 2:1; Luke 1:5). When wise men from the east came to Jerusalem looking for a newborn king, Herod was troubled. He questioned them privately about when the star had appeared. Warned in a dream, they went home by another route, and Joseph fled with Mary and the child to Egypt. Furious at being outwitted, Herod had every boy aged two and under in and around Bethlehem killed. After his death, about 4 BC by inference from context, his son Archelaus ruled Judaea. Other sons, Herod Antipas and Philip, appear later in the Gospels, and two different sons bore the name Philip. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him as an Idumean whom Rome made king, who rebuilt the Jerusalem temple and died at Jericho.

Izhar was a Levite, the second of the four sons of Kohath and a grandson of Levi. His brothers were Amram, Hebron and Uzziel (Exod 6:18; 1 Chr 6:2; 1 Chr 23:12). Since Amram was the father of Moses and Aaron (Exod 6:20), Izhar was their uncle. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "oil." Numbers 3:19 spells it Izehar. His sons were Korah, Nepheg and Zichri (Exod 6:21). Korah later led a revolt against Moses (Num 16:1). Another son or descendant, Shelomith, is named as chief of the Izharite family in David's time (1 Chr 23:18). The singer Heman traced his ancestry back through Izhar (1 Chr 6:38). In 1 Chr 6:22 the son of Kohath who fathered Korah is called Amminadab. This entry treats him as Izhar, and Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests the different name arose in copying.

Kedar was the second son of Ishmael, listed after the firstborn Nebaioth in the genealogies of Gen 25:13 and 1 Chr 1:29. His name became the name of an Arab tribe descended from him, and most later mentions refer to that people, not to the man himself. The prophets describe Kedar as a people of the eastern desert who kept flocks and traded lambs, rams and goats with Tyre (Ezek 27:21; Isa 60:7). They were known for their archers (Isa 21:17), lived in villages (Isa 42:11), and their dark tents became a figure of speech (Song 1:5). Isaiah and Jeremiah announced a coming judgement on them, with Jeremiah naming Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon (Jer 49:28). Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia place the tribe in northwest Arabia near the borders of Palestine. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "blackness."

John Mark was an early Christian from Jerusalem, known by the Jewish name John and the Roman name Mark (Marcus). Believers met to pray at the house of his mother Mary, and Peter went there after his release from prison (Acts 12:12). Col 4:10 links him to Barnabas. The KJV reads "sister's son," while Easton's Bible Dictionary calls him Barnabas's cousin. Barnabas and Saul brought him from Jerusalem, and he assisted them in Cyprus on the first missionary journey, about AD 45 by inference from context. He then left them at Perga and returned to Jerusalem. Paul later refused to take him again, and after a sharp disagreement Barnabas sailed with Mark to Cyprus. Mark was afterward with Paul as a fellow worker, and Paul asked for him as useful in the ministry. Peter calls him "my son." Early church tradition names him as the author of the Gospel of Mark.

Nahor (brother of Abraham) was a son of Terah, born at Ur of the Chaldees, and brother of Abram (Abraham) and Haran. He married Milcah, the daughter of his brother Haran, so his wife was also his niece. Abraham was later told that Milcah had borne Nahor eight sons, among them Bethuel, the father of Rebekah. Gen 22:24 adds four more sons by his concubine Reumah. Nahor's family stayed in Mesopotamia when Abraham moved to Canaan. Gen 24:10 speaks of "the city of Nahor," where Abraham's servant found Rebekah as a wife for Isaac. Rebekah's brother Laban is called "the son of Nahor," meaning his descendant, since he was Bethuel's son. Laban later called on "the God of Nahor" when he made a covenant with Jacob. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary suggest that Nahor may have been older than Abraham, even though he is listed after him.

Neriah was the son of Maaseiah and the father of two men named in the book of Jeremiah. He is known only through his sons, who are repeatedly identified as "son of Neriah." One was Baruch, the scribe who wrote down Jeremiah's words on a scroll, read them in the temple, rewrote them after King Jehoiakim burned the first scroll, and later went to Egypt with Jeremiah (Jer 36:4, 36:32; 43:6). The other was Seraiah, described as a "quiet prince," who travelled to Babylon with King Zedekiah in his fourth year (Jer 51:59). Both sons are traced through Neriah to Maaseiah (Jer 32:12; 51:59), which shows they were brothers. Nothing is recorded of Neriah's own life. His name is usually taken to mean "lamp of the LORD" (Smith's Bible Dictionary).

Sanballat was the leading opponent of Nehemiah when Nehemiah came to rebuild the walls of Jerusalem. He is called "the Horonite". Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia take this to mean he came from Horonaim in Moab, while others connect the name with Beth-horon. Easton's Bible Dictionary says he held authority in Samaria. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that papyri from Elephantine in Egypt name a Sanballat as governor of Samaria. With Tobiah the Ammonite and Geshem the Arabian, he was grieved at Nehemiah's arrival, mocked the builders and accused them of rebelling against the king. As the wall neared completion, he repeatedly invited Nehemiah to meet in the plain of Ono, intending him harm. He sent an open letter, and with Tobiah he hired a prophet to frighten him. A grandson of the high priest Eliashib became Sanballat's son-in-law, and Nehemiah drove that man away.

Seth was the third son of Adam and Eve named in Genesis, born after Cain killed Abel. Eve named him, saying God had appointed her another child in place of Abel (Gen 4:25). Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "appointed" or "substitute." Adam was 130 years old when Seth was born (Gen 5:3). At 105 Seth fathered Enos, and in that generation people began to call on the name of the LORD (Gen 4:26). He also had other sons and daughters and died at the age of 912 (Gen 5:6–8). Working from these ages, his life is dated to about 3874–2962 BC. Seth appears as "Sheth" at the head of the genealogy in 1 Chr 1:1, and he is listed in Jesus' ancestry in Luke 3:38. This entry links the "children of Sheth" in Num 24:17 to him. Smith's Bible Dictionary reads that phrase as a common noun meaning "sons of tumult."

Terah, called Thara in Luke 3:34, was the son of Nahor and the father of Abram (Abraham), Nahor and Haran, whom he fathered after reaching the age of seventy. His son Haran died in Ur of the Chaldees and left a son, Lot. Terah then set out from Ur with Abram, Sarai and Lot, intending to go to Canaan. They stopped at Haran and settled there, and Terah died in Haran at the age of 205. Joshua later recalled that Terah's family lived beyond the river, meaning the Euphrates, and served other gods. Genesis 11 calls Sarai his daughter-in-law, but in Gen 20:12 Abraham says she is also his father's daughter by another mother, which is why she is counted among Terah's children. By inference from the genealogy, he lived about 2126–1921 BC. He appears in the genealogies of 1 Chr 1:26 and of Jesus in Luke.

Vashti was the queen of the Persian king Ahasuerus, whom the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identifies with Xerxes. Easton's Bible Dictionary explains her name as meaning "beautiful." While the king held a great feast, she hosted a feast for the women in the royal house. When the king sent his chamberlains to bring her before his guests wearing the royal crown so that he could show off her beauty, she refused, and he was furious. His adviser Memucan argued that her refusal wronged the whole empire and would encourage wives everywhere to despise their husbands. He proposed an unalterable decree that she never again come before the king and that her royal position go to another. The king agreed, and Esther was later crowned queen in her place. Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests Vashti was a lesser wife given the title of queen. This entry follows the narrative's consistent title of "queen," as does the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia.

Abel was the second son of Adam and Eve, the brother of Cain and of Seth, who was born after Abel's death. He kept sheep, while Cain farmed the land (Gen 4:2). When the brothers brought offerings to the LORD, Abel brought firstborn animals from his flock and their fat, and the LORD looked with favor on him and his offering (Gen 4:4). Later, while they were in the field, Cain attacked and killed him, then claimed not to know where he was (Gen 4:8–9). Eve named her next son Seth as one appointed in Abel's place (Gen 4:25). In the New Testament Jesus calls him "righteous Abel," the first in a line of innocent people killed (Matt 23:35; Luke 11:51). Hebrews says he offered a better sacrifice than Cain by faith (Heb 11:4). Easton's Bible Dictionary explains his name as meaning "breath" or "vanity."

Beor was the father of Balaam, the diviner from Pethor in Mesopotamia whom Balak king of Moab hired to curse Israel. Beor himself is known only through his son: every mention of him is the phrase "Balaam the son of Beor." It appears in Balak's summons, in Balaam's own oracles, in the account of Balaam's death among the Midianites, and in later recollections of the episode by Moses, Joshua and Micah. In 2 Pet 2:15 the name appears as Bosor. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia explains Bosor as the Greek form of Beor. The same name belongs to other people in the Bible, such as the father of Bela, an early king of Edom. They should not be confused with Balaam's father. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "burning" or "torch."

Bethuel was the son of Nahor, Abraham's brother, and his wife Milcah, which made him Abraham's nephew. He was the youngest of the eight sons Milcah bore to Nahor, and he was the father of Rebekah and Laban (Gen 22:22–23). When Abraham's servant came to find a wife for Isaac, Rebekah introduced herself as Bethuel's daughter (Gen 24:24). Bethuel speaks only once, together with Laban, agreeing that the match came from the LORD (Gen 24:50). Even there Laban takes the more prominent role, which the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia explains by the custom of a brother looking after his sister's welfare. It also notes that Josephus says Bethuel was already dead by then. He is called "Bethuel the Syrian" of Padanaram. Later Isaac sent Jacob to "the house of Bethuel" to find a wife among Laban's daughters (Gen 25:20; 28:2, 5). The name is often taken to mean "dweller in God."

Caiaphas was the Jewish high priest during the ministry, trial and death of Jesus. Luke 3:2 names him with Annas as high priest when John the Baptist began preaching, and John 18:13 says Annas was his father-in-law. The chief priests, scribes and elders met at his palace to plot against Jesus, and in council he said it was expedient for one man to die for the people (John 11:49; 18:14). After his arrest Jesus was brought to Caiaphas, where the scribes and elders had gathered, and was then taken from him to the Roman judgment hall (Matt 26:57; John 18:24, 28). Caiaphas also appears among the high priest's family gathered to examine Peter and John (Acts 4:6). Smith's Bible Dictionary gives his full name as Joseph Caiaphas. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia dates his term about AD 18–36, and Easton's Bible Dictionary gives AD 27–36.

Deborah was a prophetess, the wife of Lapidoth, who judged Israel in the period before the monarchy. She sat under a palm tree named after her, between Ramah and Bethel in the hill country of Ephraim, and the Israelites came to her to have their disputes decided. She went with Barak to Kedesh, where he gathered ten thousand men of Zebulun and Naphtali, and told him that the honour of defeating Sisera, the Canaanite commander, would go to a woman. At Mount Tabor she gave Barak the signal to attack. Afterward she and Barak sang a victory song (Judg 5), in which she calls herself "a mother in Israel." The victory is dated here to about 1278 BC, an estimate inferred from context. Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that "wife" of Lapidoth might also be read as "woman" of Lapidoth. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the name's meaning as "bee." Another Deborah, Rebekah's nurse, appears in Genesis.

Eliakim son of Hilkiah was the official "over the household", the palace administrator, under King Hezekiah of Judah. When the Assyrian army threatened Jerusalem, he led the delegation, with Shebna the scribe and Joah the recorder, that met the Assyrian officer Rabshakeh outside the city wall. He asked Rabshakeh to speak in Aramaic ("the Syrian language") rather than Hebrew, so that the people on the wall would not understand. The officials then went to Hezekiah with their clothes torn and reported his words. Hezekiah sent Eliakim, dressed in sackcloth, to the prophet Isaiah. The same events appear in both 2 Kings and Isaiah. In an oracle, Isaiah calls him "my servant Eliakim" (Isa 22:20). Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia read that oracle as Eliakim replacing Shebna as palace administrator. Several other people in the Bible share his name.

Gaal was the son of Ebed. He came to Shechem with his brothers during the rule of Abimelech, the son of Gideon (Jerubbaal), and the men of Shechem put their trust in him (Judg 9:26). He openly challenged Abimelech's right to rule, urging the Shechemites to serve the descendants of Hamor instead (Judg 9:28). Zebul, the city's governor, was angered and secretly warned Abimelech that Gaal was fortifying the city against him (Judg 9:30–31). When Abimelech's men came out of ambush, Gaal at first took them for shadows on the mountains, as Zebul suggested. He then led the Shechemites out to fight but was defeated, and Zebul drove him and his brothers out of Shechem (Judg 9:35–41). Nothing more is recorded of him. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of his name as "contempt", and Easton's Bible Dictionary gives "loathing".

Hivite is named in the table of nations as a son of Canaan, but the name stands for a people descended from him rather than for one individual (Gen 10:17; 1 Chr 1:15). The Hivites were one of the peoples living in Canaan before Israel arrived. In Jacob's time Hamor the Hivite, father of Shechem, was prince of the region around Shechem (Gen 34:2), and Esau married a descendant of Zibeon the Hivite (Gen 36:2). They appear regularly in lists of nations God promised to drive out before Israel (Exod 23:28; 34:11) and among the peoples whose kings heard of Joshua's victories. One group lived "under Hermon in the land of Mizpeh" in the north (Josh 11:3). Easton's Bible Dictionary takes the name to mean "villagers" and places them from Hermon south to Gibeon. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that some passages may confuse Hivite with the similar name Horite.

Jonadab, also called Jehonadab, was the son of Rechab and the ancestor of the Rechabites. When Jehu was moving against the house of Ahab, Jonadab came out to meet him. Jehu asked whether his heart was loyal, took his hand and brought him up into his chariot (2 Kgs 10:15). He went with Jehu into the house of Baal when the Baal worshippers were gathered there (2 Kgs 10:23). Jonadab commanded his descendants never to drink wine and to live in tents. Centuries later, in Jeremiah's time, they were still keeping this command. Jeremiah set their obedience against Judah's failure to listen to God, and announced that Jonadab would never lack a descendant to stand before the LORD (Jer 35:6–19). Easton's Bible Dictionary describes him as the founder of a tribe bound by this vow. Several other men in the Bible share the name Jonadab.

Laadan was a Levite, a son of Gershon (also spelled Gershom) and grandson of Levi. He and his brother Shimei are named as the two founders of the Gershonite families (1 Chr 23:7). STEPBible and Smith's Bible Dictionary identify him with Libni, whom Exodus, Numbers and 1 Chronicles list as Gershon's first son alongside Shimei. His sons were Jehiel the chief, Zetham and Joel (1 Chr 23:8), and 1 Chr 26:21 names the Jehielites among the heads of his line. 1 Chr 23:9 lists a Shimei whose sons were heads of Laadan's houses, and this entry treats that Shimei as Laadan's son, distinct from his brother. The name Jahath is linked to him because 1 Chr 6:43 calls Jahath a son of Gershom. However, 1 Chr 6:20 makes Jahath Libni's son, which is how Smith's reads it. An Ephraimite elsewhere also bears the name Laadan.

Pharaoh, a title of the kings of Egypt (meaning "great house" according to Smith's Bible Dictionary), here refers to the Egyptian king of the time of David and Solomon. Solomon made an alliance with him and married his daughter, bringing her to the city of David until his palace, the temple and Jerusalem's wall were finished. He later moved her to a house built for her. This Pharaoh captured and burned the Canaanite city of Gezer and gave it to his daughter as a wedding gift. He also received Hadad the Edomite, who had fled from David. He gave Hadad a house, food and land, and married him to the sister of his queen, Tahpenes. Their son Genubath grew up among Pharaoh's sons. Smith's Bible Dictionary treats Hadad's protector and Solomon's father-in-law as possibly different kings. This entry treats them as one person.

Rezin was a king of Syria (Aram) who ruled from Damascus in the time of Jotham and Ahaz, kings of Judah. He first moved against Judah late in Jotham's reign, and then joined Pekah son of Remaliah, king of Israel, in attacking Jerusalem and besieging Ahaz. They could not take the city. Isaiah told Ahaz not to fear these "two tails of smoking firebrands" (Isa 7:4) and called Rezin "the head of Damascus." During the campaign Rezin drove the Jews out of the port of Elath. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes a reading in which Elath passed to the Edomites instead. Ahaz then appealed to the king of Assyria, who captured Damascus, deported its people to Kir and killed Rezin. Easton's Bible Dictionary dates this to 732 BC, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia calls him the last king of Damascus.

Zacharias was a priest of the division of Abia (Abijah) in the days of Herod, king of Judaea, and the husband of Elisabeth, who was also of priestly descent. Both were old and childless. While he served in the temple, an angel told him his prayer had been heard and that Elisabeth would bear a son to be named John. Zacharias asked how he could know this, given their age. The people outside wondered why he stayed so long in the temple. Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that he was struck mute for his unbelief until the child was born. When relatives wanted to name the baby Zacharias after his father, he confirmed the name John, was filled with the Holy Ghost, and prophesied. His son grew up to be John the Baptist. The name is the Greek form of Zechariah and is shared by others in the Bible, as Smith's Bible Dictionary notes.

Zalmunna was one of two kings of Midian, always named together with Zebah, whom Gideon pursued and killed. While chasing them east of the Jordan, Gideon asked the men of Succoth for bread for his exhausted troops. Their leaders refused, mockingly asking whether he already had the kings in his hand, and Gideon threatened to punish them on his return. The two kings were at Karkor with about fifteen thousand men, all that remained of the eastern armies after a hundred and twenty thousand had fallen. Gideon attacked, routed the host and captured both kings, then showed them to the men of Succoth. When questioned, they admitted killing men at Tabor who resembled Gideon, whom he identified as his brothers. Gideon killed them and took the ornaments from their camels' necks. Ps 83:11 later recalls Zebah and Zalmunna as examples of defeated enemy princes.

Zebah was one of two kings of Midian, always named with Zalmunna, who led the eastern invaders defeated by Gideon in the time of the judges. As Gideon chased them east of the Jordan, the leaders of Succoth refused his exhausted men bread, doubting he would ever capture the kings (Judg 8:5–7). Zebah and Zalmunna were camped at Karkor with about fifteen thousand survivors when Gideon routed their army and took them alive (Judg 8:10–12). Easton's Bible Dictionary places Karkor probably in the Hauran. Asked about men they had killed at Tabor, the kings said each resembled a king's son. The next verse (Judg 8:19) shows these were Gideon's brothers. Gideon then killed both kings himself and took the ornaments from their camels' necks (Judg 8:21). Ps 83:11 later recalls their fate. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "victim" or "sacrifice."

Zelophehad was a man of the tribe of Manasseh. He was the son of Hepher, of the family of Gilead, and descended through Machir from Manasseh son of Joseph (Num 27:1; Josh 17:3). He had no sons, only five daughters: Mahlah, Noah, Hoglah, Milcah and Tirzah (Num 26:33). Num 27:3 says he died in the wilderness. His daughters asked Moses for their father's share of the land, and the request was granted, so his inheritance passed to them (Num 27:7). Later the leaders of Gilead's families worried that the land would pass to another tribe if the daughters married outside it. It was ruled that the daughters should marry within their father's tribe (Num 36:2, 6), and they married sons of their father's brothers (Num 36:10–11). Smith's Bible Dictionary reads 1 Chr 7:15 as making him Hepher's second son.

Abiram (son of Eliab) was a member of the tribe of Reuben and a brother of Dathan and Nemuel. With Dathan, On son of Peleth, and the Levite Korah, he led a revolt against Moses and Aaron during Israel's time in the wilderness (Num 16:1; 26:9). When Moses summoned the two brothers, they refused to come (Num 16:12). Moses then went to them, followed by the elders. The congregation was told to move away from their tents, and Dathan and Abiram stood at their doors with their wives and children (Num 16:24–27). The earth opened and swallowed them along with their households, tents and possessions (Deut 11:6; Ps 106:17). This was distinct from the rest of Korah's company, for Num 26:11 notes that Korah's sons survived. Later passages recall the event as a warning to Israel. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "high father."

Anak was the son of Arba, after whom the city of Hebron was first called "the city of Arba" (Josh 15:13; 21:11). He was the ancestor of the Anakim, a people remembered for their great height. His descendants Ahiman, Sheshai and Talmai are called his children or sons, though the phrase may mean descendants rather than immediate sons. They lived at Hebron when the twelve spies explored Canaan. The spies reported that beside these "giants" they felt like grasshoppers (Num 13:33), and a saying arose: "Who can stand before the children of Anak!" (Deut 9:2). After the conquest Hebron was given to Caleb, who drove out the three sons of Anak (Josh 15:14; Judg 1:20). Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "long-necked", while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "a collar" or "ornament".

Belshazzar was king of Babylon, called king of the Chaldeans, in the book of Daniel. He held a great feast for a thousand of his lords. While drinking, he ordered the gold and silver vessels that Nebuchadnezzar had taken from the temple in Jerusalem to be brought so that he, his nobles, wives and concubines could drink from them (Dan 5:1–2). According to the same chapter, a hand then wrote on the wall, and the king was badly shaken (Dan 5:9). Daniel interpreted the writing and rebuked him for not humbling himself. Belshazzar rewarded Daniel with scarlet clothing, a gold chain and the rank of third ruler in the kingdom, and was killed that same night. Daniel dates two visions to his first and third years. Daniel calls Nebuchadnezzar his father, which Smith's Bible Dictionary takes to mean ancestor. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Babylonian inscriptions make him the eldest son of Nabonidus, probably ruling alongside his father.

Bezaleel was the chief craftsman who built the tabernacle and its furnishings during Israel's time in the wilderness. He was the son of Uri and grandson of Hur, of the tribe of Judah (Exod 31:2; 1 Chr 2:20). God is said to have called him by name for the work, and Moses announced this to the people (Exod 35:30). Together with Aholiab and other skilled workers, he carried out all the work of the sanctuary as the LORD had commanded Moses (Exod 36:1–2; 38:22). He made the ark of acacia wood (Exod 37:1), and the bronze altar he made still stood before the tabernacle in Solomon's day (2 Chr 1:5). Easton's Bible Dictionary says he worked mainly in metal, wood and stone, while Aholiab, under him, oversaw the textiles. The name is usually explained as "in the shadow of God." Another man of the same name appears in Ezra 10:30.

Bichri was the father of Sheba, the Benjamite who led a revolt against King David soon after Absalom's rebellion. He is known only through his son, who is called "Sheba the son of Bichri" throughout 2 Samuel 20. Sheba sounded a trumpet and called Israel to abandon David.
