Joab's forces pursued him to a walled city, where its people cut off his head and threw it over the wall to Joab (2 Sam 20:1, 20:22). The name means "first-born" (Hitchcock's Bible Names). Smith's Bible Dictionary calls Bichri an ancestor of Sheba rather than strictly his father. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests the name may mean "descendant of Becher," linking the family to Becher, a son of Benjamin. This entry treats Bichri simply as Sheba's father, as the phrase "son of Bichri" most directly reads.

Chemosh was the national god of the Moabites, who are called "the people of Chemosh" in an old song quoted at Num 21:29 and again in Jeremiah's oracle against Moab (Jer 48:46). In Judg 11:24 Jephthah, answering the king of Ammon, speaks of the land "Chemosh thy god" gives. Smith's Bible Dictionary reads this as Chemosh appearing as an Ammonite god too, while the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia connects it to the Moabite cities under dispute. Solomon built a high place for Chemosh on the hill facing Jerusalem, and this worship is named among the reasons for taking part of the kingdom from his line (1 Kgs 11:7, 33). King Josiah, the king in that chapter's context, later defiled the shrine (2 Kgs 23:13). Jeremiah foretold that Chemosh would go into captivity with his priests and princes, and that Moab would be ashamed of him (Jer 48:7, 13). Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that on the Moabite Stone King Mesha credits his victories over Israel to Chemosh.

Darius, called Darius the Mede, was the son of Ahasuerus and of Median descent. In the Book of Daniel he took over the kingdom of the Chaldeans (Babylon) at about sixty-two years old (Dan 5:31; Dan 9:1). He appointed 120 princes over the kingdom (Dan 6:1). Persuaded by his officials, he signed a binding decree (Dan 6:6–9), and in that account Daniel was thrown into the lions' den. Afterward Darius wrote to all peoples throughout his realm (Dan 6:25). Daniel prospered in his reign and in that of Cyrus the Persian (Dan 6:28), and later visions are dated to his first year (Dan 9:1; Dan 11:1). He is not named outside Daniel, and his historical identity is debated. Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests he was Astyages, the last Median king. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identifies him with Gubaru, whom Cyrus appointed governor of Babylon. Several other kings in the Bible share the name Darius.

Dathan was a man of the tribe of Reuben, a son of Eliab and brother of Abiram and Nemuel (Num 26:9). With Abiram and On son of Peleth, he joined Korah the Levite in a rebellion against the leadership of Moses and Aaron in the wilderness (Num 16:1). When Moses summoned Dathan and Abiram, they refused to come (Num 16:12), so Moses went to them with the elders of Israel. The people were told to move away from the tents of Korah, Dathan and Abiram, and Dathan and Abiram stood at the doors of their tents with their wives and children (Num 16:24–27). The earth then opened and swallowed them, their households, their tents and their possessions (Deut 11:6; Ps 106:17). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that Eliab was a son of Pallu, son of Reuben. Later passages recall the event as a well-known warning.

Dinah was the daughter of Jacob and Leah, born after Leah's six sons (Gen 30:21), probably about 1750 BC by inference from context. Her name is usually explained as meaning "judged" or "vindicated" (Easton's Bible Dictionary). While Jacob's family was living near the city of Shechem, she went out to see the local women. Shechem, son of the ruler Hamor, violated her and then sought to marry her. Jacob's sons answered deceitfully, agreeing to the marriage if the men of the city were circumcised. On the third day, while the men were still in pain, her full brothers Simeon and Levi attacked the city, killed Hamor, Shechem and all the males, and took Dinah out of Shechem's house. She is later named among Jacob's family who went down to Egypt (Gen 46:15). She is Jacob's only daughter mentioned by name.

Ehud son of Gera was a left-handed Benjamite whom the LORD raised up as a deliverer when Israel was under Eglon, king of Moab (Judg 3:15). Sent to deliver Israel's tribute, he hid a two-edged dagger about a cubit long on his right thigh. He then told Eglon, who was alone in his private upper room, that he had a message from God, and stabbed him with his left hand (Judg 3:16, 3:20–21). He locked the doors behind him, escaped to Seirath, and, as the wider account tells it, led Israel to victory over Moab at the fords of the Jordan. The text places this about 1360 BC by inference from context. After his death Israel again did evil (Judg 4:1). This entry treats him as the Ehud of 1 Chr 8:6, whose sons, including Naaman, Ahiah, Gera, Uzza and Ahihud, were family heads at Geba. Because the name belongs to several people, that identification is uncertain.

Eliphaz was the firstborn son of Esau by his wife Adah (Gen 36:4, 10, 15). His sons Teman, Omar, Zepho, Gatam and Kenaz became clan chiefs ("dukes") in Edom. His concubine Timna bore him Amalek, who is also counted among the chiefs descended from him (Gen 36:11–12, 15–16). Gen 36:16 names a chief Korah in his line as well. This Korah is distinct from Esau's son Korah by Oholibamah (Gen 36:14), which is why the name appears here both as a son and as a half-brother. The list in 1 Chr 1:36 counts Timna among his sons, probably as a clan name. Easton's Bible Dictionary calls him the father of several Edomite tribes. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "God is his strength." Several people share the name. Job's friend Eliphaz the Temanite is a different man, though his title probably links him to the clan of Teman.

Elisabeth was the wife of Zacharias, a priest of the division of Abia, and the mother of John the Baptist. She was herself descended from Aaron, and the angel Gabriel calls her a relative ("cousin" in the King James Version) of Mary. She lived in the days of Herod, king of Judea. She and Zacharias were elderly and childless because she was barren, until an angel told Zacharias that she would bear a son named John. After she conceived, she kept herself in seclusion for five months. In her sixth month Mary visited her home. When Elisabeth heard Mary's greeting, the child leaped in her womb and she was filled with the Holy Spirit. In due time she gave birth to a son. By inference from context, these events fall around 6–5 BC. Her name comes from the Hebrew Elisheba, meaning "God is my oath" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia).

Enos, also spelled Enosh, was the son of Seth and grandson of Adam. Genesis 4:26 records his birth and adds that at that time people began to call on the name of the LORD. Easton's Bible Dictionary offers two readings of this remark: that people began to call themselves by the Lord's name, setting themselves apart from idolaters, or that they began to call on the Lord in a public and earnest way. Seth fathered Enos at 105. Enos fathered Cainan at 90, had other sons and daughters, and died at 905. By inference from these ages, he was born about 3769 BC and died about 2864 BC. His name, which Smith's Bible Dictionary renders "mortal man," appears in the genealogy of 1 Chr 1:1 and in Luke's genealogy of Jesus (Luke 3:38).

Felix was the Roman governor of Judea to whom Paul was sent under guard from Jerusalem, about AD 56 by inference from context. The commander Claudius Lysias addressed him in a letter as "most excellent governor" (Acts 23:24–26). Felix heard the Jewish leaders' charges and Paul's defense but, knowing more about "that way," postponed a decision until Lysias arrived. Later, with his Jewish wife Drusilla, he sent for Paul and heard him speak about faith in Christ. When Paul spoke of righteousness, self-control and coming judgment, Felix trembled and sent him away. Acts 24:26 adds that he hoped Paul would give him money. After two years Porcius Festus replaced him, and Felix left Paul in prison to please the Jews. Smith's Bible Dictionary says Claudius appointed him about AD 53 and that Drusilla was a daughter of Herod Agrippa I.

Gog is the leader addressed in Ezekiel's prophecy as "the chief prince of Meshech and Tubal," of the land of Magog (Ezek 38:2–3; 39:1). Ezekiel is told to prophesy against him. In the latter days, when Israel is living in safety, Gog comes up against the land "as a cloud to cover the land," and God's fury rises against him (Ezek 38:14–18). He and his multitude are then buried in Israel, in a valley east of the sea that is renamed the valley of Hamongog, meaning "multitude of Gog" (Ezek 39:11). Revelation takes up the names: "Gog and Magog" stand for the nations gathered from the four quarters of the earth for a final battle (Rev 20:8). Interpreters differ on whether Gog stands for a historical ruler or a symbolic figure. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the name's meaning as "roof; covering." A Reubenite in 1 Chr 5:4 has the same name but is a different person.

Hananiah son of Azur was a prophet from Gibeon who publicly opposed Jeremiah in the temple during the fourth year of Zedekiah king of Judah. Speaking before the priests and the people, he declared in the Lord's name that within two full years God would break the yoke of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon from the neck of all nations. As a sign, he took the wooden yoke Jeremiah was wearing and broke it. Jeremiah was then told to answer that the wooden yokes would be replaced by yokes of iron, and to tell Hananiah that the Lord had not sent him and that he was making the people trust in a lie. Hananiah died in the seventh month of that same year. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him as a Benjamite and a false prophet. His name is shared by several other people in the Bible.

Hanun was the son of Nahash and succeeded him as king of the Ammonites. When Nahash died, David sent servants to console Hanun, saying he wanted to show kindness to him as his father had shown kindness to David. The Ammonite princes persuaded Hanun that the envoys had really come to spy out the city and overthrow it. Hanun shaved off half of each man's beard, cut their garments off at the buttocks and sent them away. Realizing they had made themselves hateful to David, Hanun and the Ammonites spent a thousand talents of silver hiring chariots and horsemen from Mesopotamia, Syria-maachah and Zobah. The war that followed went against the Ammonites (2 Sam 10). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives the name's meaning as "favored." The name is also borne by other men in the Bible.

Hebron was a Levite, the third of the four sons of Kohath, and so a grandson of Levi. His brothers were Amram, Izhar and Uzziel, and the genealogies list the four of them in the same order (Exod 6:18; Num 3:19; 1 Chr 6:2). He became the head of a Levite family. Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that his descendants were called the Hebronites. In David's time, Eliel led eighty men of the sons of Hebron who helped bring the ark of the covenant up to Jerusalem (1 Chr 15:9). When David organized the Levites, the family was counted under four heads: Jeriah the first, Amariah the second, Jahaziel the third and Jekameam the fourth (1 Chr 23:19; 24:23). These were probably later descendants and not his immediate sons. Several other people in the Bible share the name Hebron, which is also the name of a well-known town in Judah.

Hoshea son of Elah was the last king of the northern kingdom of Israel, not to be confused with others of the same name. He conspired against King Pekah, killed him and took his throne (2 Kgs 15:30). He reigned nine years in Samaria, beginning in the twelfth year of Ahaz of Judah, about 730 BC by inference from context (2 Kgs 17:1). When Shalmaneser king of Assyria came against him, Hoshea submitted and paid tribute. Later he sent messengers to So king of Egypt and stopped the yearly payment, so the Assyrian king imprisoned him (2 Kgs 17:3–4). Shalmaneser besieged Samaria in Hoshea's seventh year, and after three years the city fell and its people were deported to Assyria (2 Kgs 17:6; 18:9–10). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the annals of Tiglath-pileser III claim he appointed Hoshea king.

Jehoahaz was a king of Judah, a son of Josiah and Hamutal, the daughter of Jeremiah of Libnah. After Josiah's body was brought back from Megiddo, "the people of the land" anointed Jehoahaz king in Jerusalem at age twenty-three. He reigned only three months, about 609 BC by inference from context. Pharaoh Necho then removed him, made his brother Eliakim king under the new name Jehoiakim, and took Jehoahaz to Egypt, where he died. Jeremiah calls him Shallum and declares that he would never return (Jer 22:11). 1 Chr 3:15 lists Shallum as Josiah's fourth son. Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that the ages given in Kings make Jehoiakim the elder, so the people chose Jehoahaz over an older brother. His brother Zedekiah, a later king, had the same mother, Hamutal. Several other people in the Bible, including a king of Israel, also bear the name Jehoahaz.

Jeshua, son of Azaniah, was a leading Levite after the return from exile in Babylon. His name is a form of Joshua, according to Smith's and Hitchcock's dictionaries. His descendants, counted with those of Kadmiel, numbered seventy-four among the returning Levites. When work on the temple began, he and his sons stood with Kadmiel to direct the workmen. Later, when Ezra read the law, Jeshua was among the Levites who helped the people understand it. He also led public prayer and praise from the stairs, and his name heads the Levites who sealed the covenant in Neh 10:9. Because the name appears over several generations and was shared by others, including the high priest Jeshua, it is uncertain whether every mention refers to the same man. It may sometimes stand for the family he headed, as Smith's Bible Dictionary takes it.

Joash was an Abiezrite of Ophrah and the father of Gideon, one of the judges of Israel. He owned the oak at Ophrah where the angel of the LORD appeared while Gideon was threshing wheat in hiding from the Midianites. Judg 6:25 shows that the altar of Baal Gideon tore down belonged to his father. When the men of the town demanded that Joash hand over his son to be killed for this, Joash refused. He replied that anyone who pleaded for Baal should be put to death, and that if Baal were a god he could defend himself. Gideon is repeatedly called "the son of Joash," and was later buried in his father's tomb at Ophrah. The Abiezrites were probably a clan of the tribe of Manasseh (Josh 17:2). Easton's Bible Dictionary treats the name as a shortened form of Jehoash. Several other people in the Bible share the name.

Kadmiel was a Levite whose family returned from exile in Babylon with Zerubbabel. In the lists of returnees his descendants are counted with those of Jeshua and Hodaviah, seventy-four in all (Ezra 2:40; Neh 7:43). When the foundation of the temple was laid, Kadmiel and his sons joined Jeshua in overseeing the workmen on the house of God (Ezra 3:9). The name appears again among the Levites who led the people in confession and praise from the stairs (Neh 9:4–5), among those who sealed the covenant (Neh 10:9), and among the Levites who came up with Zerubbabel (Neh 12:8). Neh 12:24 names a chief Levite, Jeshua the son of Kadmiel. Because the name spans many decades, these later mentions may refer to the family or to a descendant of the same name rather than to one man, as Smith's Bible Dictionary implies. The name is usually explained as "before God."

Maachah was a wife of Rehoboam king of Judah and the mother of King Abijah, and also of Attai, Ziza and Shelomith. She is called the daughter of Abishalom or Absalom, and also "Michaiah the daughter of Uriel of Gibeah" (2 Chr 13:2). Easton's Bible Dictionary reconciles these by taking Uriel as her father and Absalom's daughter Tamar as her mother, which makes her Absalom's granddaughter. This entry follows that view. Rehoboam loved her more than any of his other wives and concubines, and he made her son Abijah chief among his brothers so that he would become king. She is also called the mother of Asa, Abijah's son. Smith's Bible Dictionary takes this to mean grandmother, a woman who held the rank of king's mother. Asa removed her from that position because she had made an idol in a grove, and he burnt the idol at the brook Kidron.

Mahli (spelled Mahali in Exod 6:19) was a son of Merari and a grandson of Levi. With his brother Mushi he heads one of the two family branches of the Merarite Levites in the genealogies (Num 3:20; 1 Chr 6:19). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia calls him the founder of the Mahlite family and gives the name's meaning as "a sick or weak one." His sons are named as Eleazar and Kish (1 Chr 23:21), and Eleazar had no sons (1 Chr 24:28). Another line runs through Libni (1 Chr 6:29). 1 Chr 24:26 also names Jaaziah among Merari's sons. In Ezra's day a capable man "of the sons of Mahli" was brought to join the return from Babylon (Ezra 8:18), which shows the family still existed. The name is shared by others, including a nephew of his, a son of Mushi.

Mary (wife of Cleophas) was one of the women who stood near the cross of Jesus, named in John 19:25 with his mother and Mary Magdalene. The wording can be read as calling her the sister of Jesus' mother, or as listing those two women separately, and it is uncertain which is meant. This entry identifies her with the Mary called the mother of James the less and of Joses in the other Gospels, and with "the other Mary" in Matthew, because she appears in the same group of women. On that view she watched the crucifixion from a distance, saw where Jesus was buried, sat facing the tomb, bought spices with Mary Magdalene and Salome after the Sabbath, and helped report the empty tomb to the apostles. These events are dated to about AD 30 by inference. Hitchcock's Bible Names treats her name as the same as Miriam.

Matthew, also called Levi, was a tax collector who became one of the twelve apostles of Jesus. While he sat at his tax booth, Jesus told him, "Follow me," and he got up and followed (Matt 9:9). The parallel accounts in Mark and Luke call him Levi, and Mark names his father as Alphaeus (Mark 2:14; Luke 5:27). Easton's Bible Dictionary places his booth at Capernaum. Levi then held a large feast in his house for Jesus, attended by many tax collectors and others (Luke 5:29). Matthew appears in every list of the twelve, where Matt 10:3 calls him "the publican," and he was with the other apostles in the upper room after Jesus' ascension (Acts 1:13). Tradition names him as the author of the Gospel of Matthew. His name is usually explained as "gift of the LORD." The New Testament does not record his later life or death.

Menahem son of Gadi was a king of Israel. He came up from Tirzah to Samaria, killed Shallum son of Jabesh and took the throne (2 Kgs 15:14). He then attacked Tiphsah and its territory because the town would not open its gates to him, and he ripped open its pregnant women. He began to reign in the thirty-ninth year of Azariah king of Judah and ruled ten years in Samaria, from about 772 to 761 BC by inference from context. When Pul king of Assyria invaded, Menahem paid him a thousand talents of silver to secure his support for his rule. He raised the sum by charging each wealthy man in Israel fifty shekels, and the Assyrian king withdrew. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identifies Pul with Tiglath-pileser III, whose inscriptions name Menahem of Samaria. His son Pekahiah succeeded him.

Micah, also spelled Micha, was the son of Mephibosheth, who is called Meribbaal in Chronicles, and so was a grandson of Jonathan and a great-grandson of King Saul. He is mentioned as Mephibosheth's young son in the account of David's kindness to Mephibosheth, which also notes that Ziba's household served Mephibosheth (2 Sam 9:12). The genealogies of the tribe of Benjamin name his four sons: Pithon, Melech, Tarea (also spelled Tahrea), and Ahaz (1 Chr 8:34–35; 9:40–41). Through him Saul's family line continued. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia explains the name as a short form of Micaiah, meaning "who is like Yah?" He is a different man from the Micah of Ephraim in the Book of Judges, whose carved image was taken by the Danites.

Molech was a god worshipped by the Ammonites. His name probably means "king" (Hitchcock's Bible Names), and Easton's Bible Dictionary notes he is also called Milcom and Malcham. His worship involved making children "pass through the fire," which is generally understood as child sacrifice. The law in Leviticus forbids this practice, and anyone in Israel who gave a child to Molech was to be stoned. It also warns of judgment on a community that ignored the offence. Solomon built a high place for Molech on the hill facing Jerusalem, which Easton's identifies as the Mount of Olives. The rite was later practiced at Topheth in the valley of Hinnom. A king defiled that site to end the practice, Josiah by inference from the surrounding chapter of 2 Kgs 23. Jeremiah condemned Judah for building high places there to offer sons and daughters to Molech.

Mushi was a Levite, the second of the two sons of Merari and so a grandson of Levi. He and his brother Mahli are named as the founders of the Merarite families of the Levites (Exod 6:19; Num 3:20). His descendants were called the Mushites, as Easton's Bible Dictionary notes from Num 3:33 and 26:58. 1 Chronicles names his three sons as Mahli, Eder and Jeremoth (Jerimoth), so one son shared the name of Mushi's brother. These sons appear in the lists of Levite houses organized for service in David's time. 1 Chr 24:26 also mentions Jaaziah alongside Merari's sons, which is why he is counted as a brother here, though the verse is difficult. Mushi also appears in a Levite genealogy in 1 Chr 6:47, which by context traces the ancestry of the temple musician Ethan. Easton's gives the meaning of his name as “receding.”

Peleg was a son of Eber and brother of Joktan, in the line of Shem. His name means "division," and Genesis explains it by saying that "in his days was the earth divided" (Gen 10:25; 1 Chr 1:19). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia links this to the scattering of peoples at Babel in Gen 11:1–9. Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries instead see a split within Eber's own family, with Joktan's descendants moving into Arabia. This entry follows the second view. Peleg fathered Reu at thirty and lived another 209 years, 239 in all, having other sons and daughters. Through Reu he was an ancestor of Abraham (Gen 11:20–26). Luke's genealogy of Jesus includes him under the Greek form Phalec (Luke 3:35). By inference from the chronology in Genesis, he lived from about 2247 to 2008 BC.

Pharaoh-nechoh, also called Necho, was a king of Egypt in the late 7th century BC. STEPBible Proper Names identifies him as Neco II. He marched north to the Euphrates to fight at Carchemish, and Josiah king of Judah went out to oppose him. Necho warned Josiah off with words that 2 Chronicles describes as coming "from the mouth of God," but Josiah fought anyway and was killed at Megiddo. The date is about 609 BC, by inference from context. Necho then put Josiah's son and successor Jehoahaz in chains at Riblah in Hamath and imposed a tribute of a hundred talents of silver and a talent of gold. He made another son, Eliakim, king in his place, renamed him Jehoiakim, and took Jehoahaz to Egypt, where he died. Jehoiakim taxed the people to pay the tribute. Jer 46:2 records Necho's later defeat by Nebuchadnezzar at Carchemish.

The Queen of Sheba was a ruler who travelled to Jerusalem to visit King Solomon after hearing of his fame. She came to test him with hard questions, bringing a large company and camels loaded with spices, gold and precious stones, and she talked with him about everything on her mind (2 Chr 9:1). After seeing his wisdom and the house he had built, she gave him 120 talents of gold and a quantity of spices never matched afterward. Solomon in turn gave her whatever she asked, and she returned to her own country with her servants. The account appears in both 1 Kings 10 and 2 Chronicles 9 with only small differences. Jesus later refers to her as "the queen of the south" (Matt 12:42; Luke 11:31). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that Arab tradition calls her Bilqis, and Ethiopian legend names her Maqeda and says she bore Solomon a son.

Salah, also spelled Shelah, was a descendant of Shem and the father of Eber in the line that leads to Abraham. In Genesis and 1 Chronicles he is the son of Arphaxad, who fathered him at age thirty-five (Gen 11:12; 1 Chr 1:18, 24). Luke's genealogy of Jesus, which follows the Greek Septuagint, places Cainan between Arphaxad and Salah (Luke 3:35–36), making Salah Arphaxad's grandson. This entry follows that line in naming Cainan as his father. Salah fathered Eber at age thirty and lived another 403 years, having other sons and daughters (Gen 11:14–15). That makes a lifespan of 433 years, placed here at about 2311–1878 BC by inference from the genealogy. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the name's meaning as "mission" or "sending," and Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "sprout."

Sheba, son of Bichri, was a Benjamite who led a revolt against King David soon after Absalom's rebellion. 2 Sam 20:21 also calls him a man of the hill country of Ephraim, probably meaning where he lived. Easton's Bible Dictionary explains the setting: a dispute had broken out between Judah and the other tribes over bringing the king back. Sheba blew a trumpet and declared, "We have no part in David," and the men of Israel followed him, while Judah stayed loyal. David feared Sheba would do more harm than Absalom and sent Abishai with the royal troops after him. Joab killed Amasa along the way and took part in the pursuit. Sheba took refuge in the fortified town of Abel-beth-maacah. Joab besieged it until a wise woman persuaded the townspeople to cut off Sheba's head and throw it over the wall, which ended the revolt. Several other people in the Bible share the name Sheba.

Shebna was the scribe, or royal secretary, at the court of King Hezekiah of Judah. When the Assyrian officer called the Rabshakeh came to Jerusalem, Shebna went out to meet him with Eliakim son of Hilkiah, who was over the household, and Joah son of Asaph, the recorder. The three asked him to speak in Aramaic ("the Syrian language"), which they understood, rather than in Hebrew in the hearing of the people on the wall. They returned to Hezekiah with their clothes torn and reported his words. Hezekiah then sent Shebna, Eliakim and the senior priests, dressed in sackcloth, to the prophet Isaiah. The same account appears in both 2 Kings and Isaiah. Isa 22:15–25 speaks of a Shebna who was steward of the palace and was to be replaced by Eliakim. Smith's Bible Dictionary takes him to be the same man, later serving as scribe. Easton's Bible Dictionary mentions the view that the scribe was a different person. This entry covers the scribe.

Shelah was the third son of Judah and his Canaanite wife, the daughter of Shua. He was born at Chezib, after his brothers Er and Onan (Gen 38:5; 1 Chr 2:3). After Er and Onan died, Judah told their widow Tamar to wait until Shelah was grown, fearing that he too would die. When Shelah came of age, however, Judah did not give him to her as a husband (Gen 38:11, 14). Tamar then disguised herself and conceived Pharez and Zerah by Judah himself. Judah later admitted she had been more in the right, because he had withheld Shelah (Gen 38:26). Shelah is listed among Judah's sons in Jacob's family that went to Egypt (Gen 46:12). He became the ancestor of the Shelanites, a clan of Judah (Num 26:20). His descendants included Er, Laadah and linen-working families of the house of Ashbea (1 Chr 4:21), and, in the following verse, Jokim, Joash and Saraph.

Tubal was a son of Japheth and grandson of Noah, named fifth among Japheth's seven sons in the Table of Nations (Gen 10:2; 1 Chr 1:5). Elsewhere in the Bible the name refers to the people descended from him, who are usually paired with Meshech. Ezekiel lists Tubal with Javan and Meshech as traders who sold slaves and bronze vessels in the markets of Tyre (Ezek 27:13). He also counts Meshech and Tubal among the fallen nations in the grave (Ezek 32:26), and calls Gog "the chief prince of Meshech and Tubal" (Ezek 38:2–3; 39:1). Isaiah names Tubal among distant nations that will hear of God's glory (Isa 66:19). Josephus linked the Tubalites with the Iberians, between the Black and Caspian Seas. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia instead identifies them with the Tibarenoi of Greek writers and the Tabali of Assyrian inscriptions, in Asia Minor southeast of the Black Sea.

Uzzah (spelled Uzza in Chronicles) was a son of Abinadab, in whose house the ark of God had been kept. His brother Ahio is named with him, and another brother, Eleazar, was set apart to keep the ark according to 1 Sam 7:1. When David set out to bring the ark to Jerusalem, Uzzah and Ahio drove the new cart that carried it from Abinadab's house (2 Sam 6:3; 1 Chr 13:7). At the threshing floor called Nachon's in Samuel and Chidon's in Chronicles, the oxen stumbled, and Uzzah reached out and took hold of the ark. The LORD's anger was kindled against him, and he died there beside the ark. David was displeased and named the place Perez-uzzah, meaning 'breach upon Uzzah.' Easton's Bible Dictionary links the event to the law in Num 4:15 forbidding anyone to touch the holy things. His name means 'strength.'

Zimri was a king of the northern kingdom of Israel who held the throne for only seven days, about 929 BC by inference from context. He commanded half the royal chariots. He plotted against King Elah, son of Baasha (named in 1 Kgs 16:8), and killed him while Elah was drunk at the house of his steward Arza in Tirzah, in the twenty-seventh year of Asa king of Judah. He then wiped out Baasha's whole family, which the text presents as fulfilling the word of the prophet Jehu. The army, which was besieging the Philistine town of Gibbethon, responded by making its commander Omri king. When Omri took Tirzah, Zimri went into the palace, set it on fire over himself and died. His name later served as a byword for killing one's master, when Jezebel used it to greet Jehu (2 Kgs 9:31). Several other men in the Bible share this name.

Achan, son of Carmi, was a man of the tribe of Judah, descended through Zabdi from Zerah. He took items from the spoil of Jericho that had been devoted to God, and the Lord's anger fell on Israel (Josh 7:1). After Israel's defeat at Ai, Joshua brought the tribe forward group by group and household by household, and Achan was singled out (Josh 7:18). Urged by Joshua to confess, he admitted his sin (Josh 7:19–20). He was brought with the silver, a garment, a wedge of gold, his family and all his possessions to the valley of Achor (Josh 7:24), where, as the account goes on to say, he was stoned and burned. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the text is not explicit about what happened to his family. Later passages recall that his sin brought wrath on all Israel (Josh 22:20), and 1 Chr 2:7 calls him Achar, “the troubler of Israel.”

Ahaziah was a king of Israel, the son and successor of Ahab and Jezebel. He reigned two years from Samaria, beginning in the seventeenth year of Jehoshaphat of Judah (about 897 BC, by inference from context). He proposed that his sailors join Jehoshaphat's in a shipping venture. 1 Kgs 22:49 says Jehoshaphat refused, while 2 Chr 20:35–37 says the two kings did join forces, and the prophet Eliezer declared that the ships would be wrecked. They were broken before they could sail to Tarshish. Chronicles says Ahaziah acted very wickedly. After falling through a lattice in his upper room, he sent messengers to ask Baalzebub, the god of Ekron, whether he would recover. The following narrative tells how Elijah intercepted them and foretold the king's death. Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that Moab revolted during his reign. His brother Joram succeeded him. He is distinct from the later Ahaziah, king of Judah.

Amos was a prophet whose words make up the Book of Amos. He came from Tekoa in Judah, which Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies with modern Tekua, about 12 miles south-east of Bethlehem. He prophesied concerning the northern kingdom of Israel during the reigns of Uzziah of Judah and Jeroboam son of Joash of Israel, "two years before the earthquake" (Amos 1:1). His ministry is dated here to about 788 BC, by inference from context. He described himself as no professional prophet or prophet's son but a herdsman and a gatherer of sycamore fruit. He recorded visions such as a plumb line and a basket of summer fruit, each announcing judgment on Israel. Amaziah, the priest of Bethel, reported to Jeroboam that Amos had conspired against him by predicting the king's death and Israel's exile, and told Amos to go back to Judah. Several other men in the Bible share this name.

Barzillai was a wealthy, elderly Gileadite from Rogelim, east of the Jordan, who supported King David during Absalom's revolt. When David fled to Mahanaim, Barzillai joined Shobi and Machir in bringing supplies to him and his followers. The text describes him as "a very great man" of eighty who had provided for the king throughout his stay there. After Absalom's defeat, Barzillai escorted David across the Jordan. David invited him to live at his court in Jerusalem, but he declined because of his age. The king kissed and blessed him, and Barzillai returned home. Later verses (2 Sam 19:37–38) show that he sent his son Chimham in his place. On his deathbed David told Solomon to show kindness to Barzillai's sons and let them eat at the royal table. Several men in the Bible share this name. The ISBE notes that the name probably means "man of iron."

Bela, also spelled Belah, was the firstborn son of Benjamin and the head of the Belaite clan within the tribe of Benjamin. He appears among the family of Jacob that went down to Egypt, and in the census lists of Benjamin's clans. The lists of his sons differ. Num 26:40 gives Ard and Naaman. 1 Chr 7:7 names Ezbon, Uzzi, Uzziel, Jerimoth and Iri, heads of families with 22,034 fighting men. 1 Chr 8:3 begins another list with Addar, Gera and Abihud. Some of these names, such as Ard, Gera and Naaman, also appear as Benjamin's own sons in Gen 46:21. This probably reflects later clan groupings recorded as descendants of Bela, though the passages do not explain it. Several other people in the Bible share the name Bela.

Cainan (antediluvian patriarch), also called Kenan, was a descendant of Adam through Seth who lived before the Flood. He was the son of Enos, born when his father was ninety (Gen 5:9). At seventy he fathered Mahalaleel. He then lived another 840 years, had other sons and daughters, and died at the age of 910 (Gen 5:12–14). The genealogy in Chronicles lists him as Kenan (1 Chr 1:2), and Luke includes him among the ancestors of Jesus (Luke 3:37). Easton's Bible Dictionary counts him as the fourth patriarch before the Flood. By inference from the ages given in Genesis 5, this entry places his birth about 3679 BC and his death about 2769 BC. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of his name as "possessor" or "purchaser." He is a different person from the later Cainan, son of Arphaxad, named in Luke 3:36.

Caleb, also called Chelubai, was a man of the tribe of Judah. He was the son of Hezron and the brother of Jerahmeel and Ram (1 Chr 2:9, 18, 42), and he is known only from the genealogies of 1 Chronicles. His wife Azubah, along with Jerioth, bore Jesher, Shobab and Ardon. After Azubah died he married Ephrath, who bore Hur. His concubines Ephah and Maachah also bore him children, among them Shaaph and Sheva, and his daughter was Achsah. Several of his sons are named as the 'fathers', or founders, of towns such as Ziph, Madmannah and Gibea. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes the view that 'Carmi' among the sons of Judah in 1 Chr 4:1 stands for Chelubai, and this entry follows that view. He is a different person from Caleb son of Jephunneh, the spy. Smith's Bible Dictionary makes this Caleb the spy's grandfather through Hur.

Dagon was the national god of the Philistines. After Samson was captured, the Philistine lords gathered to offer him a great sacrifice, crediting him with their victory (Judg 16:23). Dagon's temple there is usually placed at Gaza, where Samson had been taken. When the Philistines captured the ark of the covenant, they set it beside Dagon's image in his temple at Ashdod. On two mornings the image was found fallen face down before the ark, and the second time its head and hands lay broken off on the threshold. From then on, Dagon's priests and worshippers would not step on that threshold (1 Sam 5:2–5). Saul's head was later fastened in Dagon's temple (1 Chr 10:10). The name is commonly linked to the Hebrew word for "fish," and Easton's and Smith's Bible dictionaries describe the idol as part man, part fish. Hitchcock's Bible Names also gives "corn" as a possible meaning.

Daughter of Lot - Younger is the unnamed younger of Lot's two daughters in Genesis 19. When the men of Sodom surrounded Lot's house, Lot offered his two unmarried daughters to them to protect his guests (Gen 19:8). At dawn the angels took Lot, his wife and the two daughters by the hand and led them out before the city was destroyed, about 1897 BC by inference from context. Lot's sons-in-law refused to leave (Gen 19:14). Whether they were engaged to these daughters or married to others is unclear. Lot later left Zoar and lived in a mountain cave with both daughters (Gen 19:30). There, following her older sister's plan, she conceived a child by her father (Gen 19:36). Gen 19:38 says she named her son Ben-ammi, ancestor of the Ammonites. Because Lot fathered both Ben-ammi and her sister's son Moab, both boys were also her half-brothers.

The Daughter of Pharaoh was the Egyptian princess who found and adopted the infant Moses. She came down to bathe at the river, probably the Nile, with her maidens, saw a basket among the reeds, and sent her maid to fetch it (Exod 2:5). Moses' sister offered to find a Hebrew nurse, and the princess agreed, paying the child's own mother to nurse him (Exod 2:7–9). When the boy was older he was brought to her and became her son. She named him Moses, saying she had drawn him out of the water (Exod 2:10). Stephen recalls that she raised him as her own son (Acts 7:21), and Hebrews says Moses, when grown, refused to be called her son (Heb 11:24). The text names neither her nor her father. Easton's Bible Dictionary suggests she was probably a daughter of Seti I and notes that Josephus calls her Thermuthis. Other daughters of Pharaoh, such as Solomon's wife, are different women.

Elihu, son of Barachel the Buzite and of the family of Ram, is the young man who speaks near the end of the Book of Job. He had waited in silence while Job and his three friends argued, because they were older than he (Job 32:4, 32:6). When the friends could find no answer for Job, he became angry with Job for justifying himself rather than God, and angry with the friends as well (Job 32:2, 32:5). He then gave a series of speeches, introduced again at Job 34:1, 35:1 and 36:1, which run through chapter 37. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia links the Buzites with Buz, the brother of Uz named in Gen 22:21, and counts four speeches in all. His name is usually explained as "He is my God." Several other men in the Bible share the name Elihu.

Jared was one of the patriarchs before the Flood in the line of Seth, the son of Mahalaleel and the father of Enoch, who in turn fathered Methuselah. Genesis records that his father was 65 when Jared was born, that Jared was 162 when Enoch was born, and that he lived another 800 years and had other sons and daughters. He died at 962 years, the second-longest lifespan recorded in the Bible after Methuselah's. The King James Version spells his name Jered in the genealogy of 1 Chr 1:2, and Luke includes him among the ancestors of Jesus. The name is usually taken to mean "descent" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia). That work also notes a proposed link with Irad in Cain's line (Gen 4:18). By inference from the genealogy's figures, his life is dated here to about 3544–2582 BC.

Javan was a son of Japheth and grandson of Noah. He is listed fourth among Japheth's seven sons, alongside Gomer, Magog, Madai, Tubal, Meshech and Tiras, and was the father of Elishah, Tarshish, Kittim and Dodanim (Gen 10:2–4; 1 Chr 1:5, 7). Like many names in this list, Javan also stands for a people and land descended from him. Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies it with the Greeks, especially the Ionians, and the name is later used for Greece. Isaiah names Javan among distant nations, and Ezekiel lists it among the trading partners of Tyre, dealing in slaves and bronze goods (Isa 66:19; Ezek 27:13). The Javan in Ezek 27:19 trades iron and spices. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia take that one to be a separate place, possibly in southern Arabia.

Jonadab was a nephew of King David, the son of David's brother Shimeah, also called Shammah, of the tribe of Judah. He was a friend of his cousin Amnon, David's son, and is described as a very shrewd man. He advised Amnon to pretend to be sick so that David would send Amnon's half-sister Tamar to cook for him, which led to her rape. After Absalom had Amnon killed in revenge and a report reached David that all his sons were dead, Jonadab told the king that only Amnon had died and that Absalom had planned it since the assault on Tamar. This entry also identifies him with Jonathan, son of Shimea, who killed a Philistine champion at Gath (described in 2 Sam 21:20 as a huge man with six fingers on each hand). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes he may also be the Jonathan called David's 'uncle' (possibly 'relative'), a counsellor and scribe. Smith's Bible Dictionary treats these men separately.

Lamech (father of Noah) was a descendant of Seth in the genealogy of Genesis 5, the son of Methuselah and the father of Noah. Methuselah fathered him at 187. Lamech fathered Noah at 182, then lived another 595 years and had other sons and daughters, dying at 777. The next verse, Gen 5:29, records that he named Noah, saying the child would bring comfort from the hard toil of working ground that the Lord had cursed. Comparing his age with Noah's age at the flood (Gen 7:6) suggests he died about five years before the flood. He appears in the lists of 1 Chr 1:3 and in Luke's genealogy of Jesus (Luke 3:36). He is a different man from Lamech the descendant of Cain in Gen 4. The dates sometimes given for him, about 3130–2353 BC, are estimates worked out from the genealogy.

Mahalaleel (line of Seth) was a patriarch who lived before the flood, the son of Cainan and a descendant of Seth. According to Genesis 5, his father was seventy when he was born. Mahalaleel fathered Jared at sixty-five, lived another 830 years, had other sons and daughters, and died at the age of 895. Through Jared he was an ancestor of Enoch, Methuselah and Noah. The Chronicler lists him between Kenan and Jered in the genealogy from Adam (1 Chr 1:2). Luke's genealogy of Jesus, tracing the line back to Adam, uses the Greek form of his name, Maleleel (Luke 3:37). This entry dates his life to about 3609–2714 BC, by inference from the ages given in Genesis.

Meshech was the sixth son of Japheth and a grandson of Noah, listed in the Table of Nations (Gen 10:2; 1 Chr 1:5). The name also stands for the people descended from him. Ezekiel regularly pairs Meshech with Tubal. They traded slaves and bronze vessels in the markets of Tyre (Ezek 27:13), they appear among the slain nations in the realm of the dead (Ezek 32:26), and Gog of the land of Magog is called their chief prince (Ezek 38:2–3; 39:1). The spelling Mesech appears in Ps 120:5, where the name stands for a distant, hostile people. Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries both identify the tribe with the Moschi, who lived in the mountains between the Black and Caspian Seas, on the borders of Armenia. A different Meshech, listed among the sons of Shem, appears in 1 Chr 1:17.

Methuselah was the son of Enoch, the father of Lamech, and the grandfather of Noah, listed among the descendants of Seth before the Flood. According to Genesis, Enoch became his father at sixty-five. Methuselah himself became the father of Lamech at 187 and had other sons and daughters. He lived 969 years, the longest lifespan recorded in the Bible. Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that he died in the year of the Flood. This follows from adding the ages given in Gen 5:25–28 and Gen 7:6, and it fits the dates used here, about 3317 to 2348 BC, which are estimates inferred from these genealogies. His name is usually explained as "man of the dart" or "man of the javelin." He appears in the genealogy of 1 Chr 1:3, and in Luke's genealogy of Jesus under the Greek form Mathusala.

Nahor (father of Terah), also spelled Nachor, was the son of Serug and the grandfather of Abraham. Genesis records that Serug fathered him at age thirty, and that Nahor fathered Terah at twenty-nine. He then lived another 119 years and had other sons and daughters, a total lifespan of 148 years (Gen 11:22–25). His life is placed at about 2155–2007 BC, by inference from the genealogy's figures. He appears in the line of descent from Shem to Abraham in 1 Chr 1:26, and Luke lists him as "Nachor" among the ancestors of Jesus (Luke 3:34). He shares his name with his grandson Nahor, Terah's son and Abraham's brother. The "Nachor" named in Josh 24:2 as Terah's son is that grandson, not this man. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "snorting."

Rahab was a prostitute living in Jericho whose house was where the two spies lodged when Joshua sent them from Shittim to scout the land (Josh 2:1). When the king of Jericho ordered her to hand them over, she hid them and later sent them away by another route (Josh 2:3; Jas 2:25). Because of this, she and everyone in her house were spared when Israel destroyed the city. The spies brought out her father, mother, brothers and the rest of her family, and she went on living among the Israelites (Josh 6:17, 23, 25). Hebrews 11:31 cites her as an example of faith, and James 2:25 as an example of being justified by works. Matt 1:5 names a Rahab as the wife of Salmon and mother of Boaz in Jesus' genealogy. Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries identify her with this woman. The name is spelled differently in Hebrew from the poetic name Rahab used for Egypt.

Rechab was the father of Jonadab, also spelled Jehonadab. He is known only through his son, who is regularly called "the son of Rechab." Jonadab rode with Jehu in his chariot and went with him into the house of Baal when Jehu destroyed Baal worship in Israel (2 Kgs 10:15, 23). Jonadab's descendants, known after his father as the Rechabites, kept Jonadab's command not to drink wine. Jeremiah held up their obedience as an example, and God promised that Jonadab the son of Rechab would never lack a man to stand before him (Jer 35:6–19). Easton's Bible Dictionary describes Rechab as the father of Jehonadab and so the forefather of the Rechabites. 1 Chr 2:55 links the house of Rechab with the Kenites. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the name's meaning as "square" or "chariot with team of four horses." Others in the Bible share the name, including a son of Rimmon in 2 Sam 4.

Shimei, also spelled Shimi, was a son of Gershon and grandson of Levi. The genealogies of the tribe of Levi list him with his brother Libni (Exod 6:17; Num 3:18; 1 Chr 6:17). In 1 Chr 23:7 his brother is named Laadan, apparently another name for Libni or for the same family line. His sons Jahath, Zina, Jeush and Beriah headed divisions of the Gershonite Levites in David's time. Zina appears as Zizah in the following verse. 1 Chr 23:9 also names a Shimei whose sons were heads of Laadan's houses. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia takes that Shimei to be a copying error for one of Laadan's sons. His descendants formed a Levitical clan, and Zech 12:13 names "the family of Shimei" among the households that mourn apart. Several other men in the Bible share this name.

Stephen was one of the seven men chosen by the early church in Jerusalem to serve the community, described as full of faith and of the Holy Spirit (Acts 6:5). Easton's Bible Dictionary calls him one of the seven deacons and the first Christian martyr. He performed great wonders and miracles among the people (Acts 6:8). Members of the synagogue of the Libertines, along with men from Cyrene, Alexandria, Cilicia and Asia, disputed with him (Acts 6:9). He was seized and brought before the council, where he gave a long speech, the longest in Acts. He was then stoned, praying, "Lord Jesus, receive my spirit" (Acts 7:59). Devout men buried and mourned him (Acts 8:2). Saul later recalled standing by, approving his death and guarding the clothes of those who killed him (Acts 22:20). The persecution that followed scattered believers as far as Phoenicia, Cyprus and Antioch (Acts 11:19).

Tamar was the daughter-in-law of Judah, married first to his firstborn son Er (Gen 38:6). Hitchcock's Bible Names gives her name's meaning as "palm tree." After Er died, she was given to his brother Onan, who also died (Gen 38:8–10). Judah sent her back to her father's house to live as a widow until his third son, Shelah, grew up, because he feared Shelah might also die (Gen 38:11). Shelah was never given to her. When she heard that Judah was going to Timnath to shear sheep (Gen 38:13), she conceived by him, as the chapter goes on to tell. When told she was pregnant, Judah ordered her burned (Gen 38:24), but then admitted she was more in the right than he was (Gen 38:25–26). She bore twins, Pharez (Perez) and Zerah (1 Chr 2:4), about 1721 BC by inference from context. As Thamar, she appears in Jesus' genealogy (Matt 1:3). Several other women share her name.

The giant in Gath was the Philistine ancestor of four huge warriors from Gath who fought against Israel and were killed by David and his servants (2 Sam 21:22; 1 Chr 20:8). He is never named. The Hebrew term behind "the giant" (rapha) may refer to one father or, more broadly, to a race of giants. Easton's Bible Dictionary links such giants to the Anakim, from whom Goliath came. This entry treats him as a single person. His descendants were Ishbi-benob, who nearly killed David (2 Sam 21:16); Saph, called Sippai in Chronicles, killed by Sibbechai the Hushathite (2 Sam 21:18; 1 Chr 20:4); and an unnamed man with six fingers on each hand and six toes on each foot (2 Sam 21:20; 1 Chr 20:6). Goliath and Lahmi are counted among them by inference from the related verses, 2 Sam 21:19 and 1 Chr 20:5.

Zechariah was a Levite of David's time, the firstborn son of Meshelemiah (also called Shelemiah), with brothers Jediael, Zebadiah, Jathniel, Elam, Jehohanan and Elioenai. He served as gatekeeper at the entrance of the tabernacle. When lots were cast for the temple gates, his lot fell to the north gate, and he is described as "a wise counsellor." This entry also includes a Zechariah listed among the Levites of the second rank who played harps (psalteries) when the ark was brought to Jerusalem and who served next to Asaph in the worship that followed, as well as a priest named Zechariah who blew trumpets before the ark. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia and Smith's Bible Dictionary treat the gatekeeper, the musician and the trumpeter as possibly different men. The name was common and was understood to mean "Yah remembers."

Zilpah was the maidservant whom Laban gave to his daughter Leah when Leah married Jacob. When Leah stopped having children, she gave Zilpah to Jacob as a wife, a common way for a childless or no-longer-bearing wife to gain children through her servant. Zilpah bore Jacob two sons, Gad and then Asher, both born in Paddan-aram, about 1753 and 1752 BC by inference from context. Gad and Asher became the ancestors of two of the tribes of Israel. Genesis 37:2 calls Zilpah and Bilhah Jacob's wives and places the young Joseph with their sons while tending the flocks. The list of those who went down to Egypt counts sixteen descendants through Zilpah (Gen 46:18). The meaning of her name is uncertain: Easton's Bible Dictionary gives "drooping" and Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "a trickling."

Zippor was the father of Balak, the king of Moab who, alarmed by Israel's victories over the Amorites, sent for Balaam son of Beor to curse Israel (Num 22:2–4; Josh 24:9). Zippor is known only through his son, who is repeatedly called "Balak the son of Zippor" in the account in Numbers, and again in later recollections of the episode by Joshua and by Jephthah (Judg 11:25). Balaam addresses Balak with the same formula in one of his oracles (Num 23:18). Nothing is said about Zippor's own life, and the text does not state whether he was himself a king. Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that it is not known whether he was the "former king of Moab" mentioned in Num 21:26. His name means "bird," with "sparrow" offered as a more specific sense by Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries.

Adah was one of the wives of Esau. She was a Hittite woman, the daughter of Elon (Gen 36:2), and she bore Esau's son Eliphaz (Gen 36:4, 10). Through Eliphaz she was the ancestor of several chiefs ("dukes") of Edom, including Korah, Gatam and Amalek. Amalek was born to Eliphaz by his concubine Timna but is still counted among Adah's descendants (Gen 36:12, 16). Gen 26:34 calls Esau's Hittite wife, the daughter of Elon, Bashemath. Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries therefore treat Adah and Bashemath as the same woman, and this entry follows that view. The lists of Esau's wives differ between Gen 26:34, Gen 28:9 and Genesis 36, where Bashemath is the name of a different wife, Ishmael's daughter. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that there is too little evidence to settle this. Another Adah, the wife of Lamech, appears in Gen 4:19.

Ahimelech, also called Abimelech, was a priest under King David, named as a son of Abiathar. He is listed with Zadok son of Ahitub as one of David's priests (2 Sam 8:17; 1 Chr 18:16), and he represented the priestly line of Ithamar when David organized the priests into divisions, while Zadok represented the line of Eleazar (1 Chr 24:3). He witnessed the recording and casting of lots for these divisions (1 Chr 24:6, 31). His brother is named as Jonathan, known from later passages as Abiathar's son. Elsewhere Abiathar is himself called the son of an earlier Ahimelech, the priest of Nob (1 Sam 30:7). For this reason Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that many scholars read 2 Sam 8:17 as "Abiathar the son of Ahimelech." This entry follows the text as written and treats him as Abiathar's son. Several people in the Bible share this name.

Ahinoam was a woman from Jezreel who became one of David's wives during the years he was fleeing from Saul (1 Sam 25:43). This Jezreel is probably the town in the hill country of Judah rather than the northern city of that name. She and Abigail lived with David at Gath under King Achish (1 Sam 27:3). Both were taken captive when the Amalekites raided Ziklag, and the following account in 1 Sam 30:18 says David recovered his two wives (1 Sam 30:5). She went with him to Hebron when he became king of Judah (2 Sam 2:2). There she bore Amnon, David's firstborn son (2 Sam 3:2; 1 Chr 3:1). Her name is always listed before Abigail's, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia takes 1 Sam 25:43 to mean David had married her earlier. The name is shared with Saul's wife, a different woman.

Ammihud was a man of the tribe of Ephraim, one of the two tribes descended from Joseph. He was the father of Elishama, who led Ephraim during the wilderness journey after the Exodus. Elishama helped take the census, commanded Ephraim's camp on the west side of the tabernacle, brought the tribe's offering on the seventh day of the altar's dedication, and led its host when Israel set out (Num 1:10; 2:18; 7:48, 53; 10:22). In the Ephraimite genealogy Ammihud is the son of Laadan and father of Elishama (1 Chr 7:26). The next verse continues the line to Non and his son Joshua, so Smith's Bible Dictionary counts Ammihud as an ancestor of Joshua. The name is explained as "my kinsman is glorious" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia) or "people of praise" (Hitchcock's Bible Names). Several other men in the Bible share the name.

Aquila was a Jew born in Pontus who, with his wife Priscilla, had recently come from Italy after the emperor Claudius ordered all Jews to leave Rome (Acts 18:2). Paul met them at Corinth and, according to Acts 18:3, stayed and worked with them because they shared the trade of tentmaking. When Paul left Corinth, the couple sailed with him, and Acts 18:19 says they remained at Ephesus. There they heard Apollos, named in Acts 18:24, speaking boldly in the synagogue and explained the way of God to him more accurately. Paul calls them his helpers in Christ Jesus and sends them greetings (Rom 16:3; 2 Tim 4:19). They also sent greetings along with the church that met in their house (1 Cor 16:19). The name means "eagle" (Hitchcock's Bible Names). Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that when they became Christians is uncertain.

Bashemath was a daughter of Ishmael, the son of Abraham, and the sister of Nebajoth. She became one of Esau's wives. Genesis 36 calls her Bashemath, but the earlier narrative in Gen 28:9 calls her Mahalath. That verse says Esau married her in addition to the wives he already had. Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that all three of Esau's wives have different names in the Edomite genealogy than in the narrative. Gen 26:34 also mentions a Bashemath who was the daughter of Elon the Hittite. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests that name may be a mix-up with Adah or a textual variation. This entry follows the identification of Ishmael's daughter with Mahalath. She bore Esau a son, Reuel, whose sons Nahath, Zerah, Shammah and Mizzah became chiefs ("dukes") in Edom. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of her name as "fragrant" or "pleasing."

Cush (son of Ham) was the first-named son of Ham, listed before his brothers Mizraim, Phut (Put) and Canaan in the table of nations (Gen 10:6; 1 Chr 1:8). Easton's Bible Dictionary calls him probably the eldest. His sons were Seba, Havilah, Sabtah, Raamah and Sabtecha, and through Raamah he was the grandfather of Sheba and Dedan (Gen 10:7; 1 Chr 1:9). He was also the father of Nimrod, who "began to be a mighty one in the earth" (Gen 10:8; 1 Chr 1:10). In the surrounding passage, these descendants stand for peoples and regions. Easton's notes that the land of Cush seems to take its name from him. In the Old Testament that name usually refers to the lands south of Egypt, rendered "Ethiopia" in the King James Version. Some writers have also linked it with parts of Arabia and Mesopotamia. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "blackness."

Delilah was a woman from the valley of Sorek whom Samson loved (Judg 16:4). The Philistine lords offered her silver to learn the secret of his great strength and how he could be bound (Judg 16:5). Three times she asked, and three times Samson gave false answers. She tied him with new ropes and even wove his seven locks of hair into a loom while men lay in wait, and each time he broke free. When he finally told her everything, she summoned the Philistine lords, who came with the money in hand (Judg 16:18). Later in the chapter his hair is shaved while he sleeps, and he is captured. The text does not state her nationality. Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries take her to be a Philistine, while the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that this is presumed rather than stated and that she is not called Samson's wife.

Ebed-melech was an Ethiopian eunuch who served in the royal household of Judah during the last years before Jerusalem fell. The king of the time was Zedekiah, as Jer 38:5 indicates. When officials put the prophet Jeremiah into a muddy dungeon to die, Ebed-melech left the palace and appealed to the king, who was sitting in the Benjamin Gate. The king ordered him to take thirty men and lift Jeremiah out. Ebed-melech fetched old worn-out rags from a storeroom under the treasury, lowered them on cords, and told Jeremiah to pad his armpits with them so the ropes would not hurt him as he was pulled up. Afterward Jeremiah was told to bring him a message from the LORD: disaster was coming on the city, but, as the following verses state, Ebed-melech himself would be spared. His name means "servant of the king," according to Hitchcock's Bible Names.

Eliab son of Helon was the leader of the tribe of Zebulun during Israel's wilderness journey. He is named among the tribal heads who helped Moses take the census (Num 1:9). In the camp arrangement he was captain of Zebulun, which camped alongside Judah and Issachar (Num 2:7). On the third day of the offerings for the dedication of the altar, he brought Zebulun's gifts, including peace offerings of oxen, rams, goats and lambs (Num 7:24, 29). When Israel set out from Sinai, he commanded Zebulun's company (Num 10:16). Smith's Bible Dictionary gives his name's meaning as "God is my father." Several other men in the Bible share the name. The best known is David's eldest brother (1 Sam 17:28), a different person who is not the subject of this entry.

Elimelech was a man of Bethlehem in Judah, described as an Ephrathite, and the husband of Naomi and father of Mahlon and Chilion. His name means "my God is king." During a famine in the days of the judges (Ruth 1:1, the verse just before he is named), he moved his family to the country of Moab, where he died, leaving Naomi with their two sons (Ruth 1:2–3). Both sons later died in Moab as well. Boaz, the wealthy man in whose field Ruth gleaned, belonged to Elimelech's family (Ruth 2:1, 3). After Naomi returned to Bethlehem, Elimelech's parcel of land was put up for redemption, and Boaz bought all that had belonged to Elimelech and his sons in front of the town elders (Ruth 4:3, 9). Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries place him in the Hezronite family of the tribe of Judah.

Eliphaz the Temanite was one of Job's three friends, with Bildad the Shuhite and Zophar the Naamathite. When they heard of Job's disasters, they arranged to come together to mourn with him and comfort him (Job 2:11). Eliphaz opens each of the three rounds of speeches (Job 4:1; 15:1; 22:1), and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats him as the leading spokesman of the friends. His title links him to Teman, a place in Edom associated elsewhere with wisdom (Jer 49:7). At the end of the book the LORD addresses Eliphaz directly, saying his anger burns against him and his two friends because they had not spoken rightly of him as Job had. The three then did as the LORD commanded, and the LORD accepted Job's prayer for them (Job 42:7, 9). Several other men in the Bible share the name Eliphaz, including a son of Esau.

Elishama son of Ammihud was the leader of the tribe of Ephraim during Israel's journey through the wilderness. When Moses took the census at Sinai, he was named as the man from Ephraim, one of the sons of Joseph, to help with it (Num 1:10). He was captain of Ephraim's camp, which was stationed on the west side and marched under its own standard (Num 2:18; 10:22). On the seventh day of the altar's dedication he brought Ephraim's offering, which included peace offerings of oxen, rams, goats and lambs (Num 7:48, 53). The Ephraimite genealogy in 1 Chronicles lists him as the son of Ammihud (1 Chr 7:26). The next verse names his son Nun and his grandson Joshua, so Smith's Bible Dictionary identifies him as Joshua's grandfather. His name means 'God has heard,' and several other men in the Bible share it.

Er was the firstborn son of Judah, born to him by the daughter of Shua, a Canaanite woman. His younger full brothers were Onan and Shelah. Judah arranged his marriage to Tamar. Genesis says Er was wicked in the sight of the LORD and that the LORD killed him, though the text does not describe what he did. He died in Canaan without children, before Jacob's family went down to Egypt. After his death Tamar bore twins, Pharez and Zerah, to Judah himself, so they were Er's half-brothers. Er is still named among Judah's sons in the later genealogies. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "watchful," and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "watchman." The name is shared by several people in the Bible; this entry concerns Judah's son.

Goliath was a Philistine champion from Gath whose height is given as six cubits and a span (1 Sam 17:4), about ten and a half feet by the reckoning of Easton's Bible Dictionary. He came out from the Philistine army to challenge Israel, and David heard his words (1 Sam 17:23). David killed him in the valley of Elah, about 1067 BC by inference from context. His sword was later kept wrapped in a cloth behind the ephod at Nob, and the priest gave it to David (1 Sam 21:9; 22:10). Goliath's brother, named Lahmi in 1 Chr 20:5, was killed by Elhanan (2 Sam 21:19). 2 Sam 21:22 describes such warriors as born to 'the giant in Gath.' The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia takes the Goliath of 2 Sam 21:19 as a different, younger man. This entry follows Chronicles in treating Lahmi as his brother.

Heber was a son of Beriah and a grandson of Asher, the son of Jacob. He and his brother Malchiel appear among Asher's descendants in the list of Jacob's family who went down to Egypt (Gen 46:17), and he is named again in the Asherite genealogy of Chronicles (1 Chr 7:31). In the census taken in the wilderness he is the ancestor of a clan called the Heberites within the tribe of Asher (Num 26:45). His children were Japhlet, Shomer, Hotham and their sister Shua (1 Chr 7:32). Shomer is probably the same person as the Shamer named a few verses later in that genealogy. Nothing else is recorded about him. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia takes the name to mean "associate." Several other men in the Bible are also called Heber, and they should not be confused with this Asherite.

Herod Agrippa I was the ruler called simply "Herod the king" in Acts 12. Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies him as a grandson of Herod the Great who eventually ruled his grandfather's whole kingdom. He moved against the church in Jerusalem. He had the apostle James killed (Acts 12:2) and then imprisoned Peter, who was chained between soldiers until an angel freed him. After Peter escaped, Herod questioned the guards, ordered them put to death, and went down from Judea to Caesarea. There the people of Tyre and Sidon, whose food came from his territory, sought peace with him through his chamberlain Blastus. On a set day he sat on his throne in royal robes and gave a speech. Acts 12:23 says an angel then struck him and he died. This entry dates his death to about AD 45 by inference from context, while Easton's gives AD 44.

Ittai the Gittite was a man from Gath, the Philistine city, who served King David during Absalom's rebellion. When David fled Jerusalem, he urged Ittai to go back, since he was a foreigner and an exile. Ittai refused and swore to stay with the king in life or death, so David let him cross over with all his men and their children (2 Sam 15:19–22). Later David divided his army into three parts under Joab, Abishai and Ittai, and charged all three commanders in everyone's hearing to deal gently with Absalom (2 Sam 18:2, 5, 12). Easton's Bible Dictionary suggests he commanded the six hundred men who had followed David since his wandering years, and places this muster at Mahanaim. He is not mentioned again. The name is shared by another Ittai, one of David's mighty men, who is a different person.

Jabin (king of Hazor) was a Canaanite ruler, also called "king of Canaan," who reigned from Hazor in northern Israel and oppressed the Israelites during the time of the judges. Sisera, based at Harosheth of the Gentiles, commanded his army (Judg 4:2). Judg 4:3 adds that Jabin had nine hundred iron chariots and oppressed Israel for twenty years. This entry dates the oppression to about 1298 BC, by inference from context. Through Deborah, God promised Barak victory over Sisera's forces at the river Kishon. After that defeat, Sisera fled to the tent of Jael, because Jabin was at peace with the house of Heber the Kenite. Israel then pressed on until Jabin was destroyed, and Ps 83:9 later recalls his downfall. He shares his name and city with the king of Hazor defeated by Joshua (Josh 11:1–10). Easton's Bible Dictionary treats the two as separate kings.

Jael was the wife of Heber the Kenite who killed Sisera, commander of the army of Jabin king of Hazor, after the Canaanites were defeated by Barak. Sisera fled on foot to her tent because Heber's household was at peace with Jabin (Judg 4:17). Jael went out, invited him in, told him not to be afraid and covered him with a mantle. While he lay asleep and exhausted, she drove a tent peg through his temples into the ground with a hammer. When Barak arrived in pursuit, she showed him Sisera lying dead (Judg 4:22). The Song of Deborah mentions "the days of Jael" as a time when the roads were deserted, and calls her "blessed above women" for the deed (Judg 5:24). Her name means "mountain goat" according to Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary.

Jerahmeel was a man of the tribe of Judah, the firstborn son of Hezron (1 Chr 2:9, 25). His brothers included Ram and Chelubai, who is called Caleb in 1 Chr 2:42. By his first wife, who is not named, he had Ram (his firstborn), Bunah, Oren, Ozem and Ahijah. A second wife, Atarah, bore him Onam. The genealogy follows his line through several generations and closes with the words "These were the sons of Jerahmeel" (1 Chr 2:33). His grandsons through Ram were Maaz, Jamin and Eker. Smith's Bible Dictionary treats him as the founder of the Jerahmeelites, a clan in southern Judah mentioned in 1 Sam 27:10. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "the mercy, or the beloved, of God." Other people in the Bible share this name and should not be confused with him.

Joah son of Asaph was the recorder, a royal official in charge of records, under King Hezekiah of Judah. With Eliakim son of Hilkiah, who was over the household, and Shebna the scribe, he went out to meet the Rabshakeh, the envoy of the Assyrian king, outside Jerusalem. The three officials asked the envoy to speak to them in the Syrian language (Aramaic), which they understood, rather than in Hebrew in the hearing of the people on the wall. They then returned to Hezekiah with their clothes torn and reported the Rabshakeh's words. The account appears in both 2 Kings and Isaiah. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia dates these events to about 701 BC, during the Assyrian siege. His name is usually explained as "the LORD is brother." Other men in the Bible share the name Joah.

Joktan was the second of the two sons of Eber and the brother of Peleg (Gen 10:25; 1 Chr 1:19). Through Eber he descended from Shem, according to the genealogy in Genesis 10. Peleg's line continues toward Abraham in Gen 11, while Joktan's thirteen sons are listed separately. They are Almodad, Sheleph, Hazarmaveth, Jerah, Hadoram, Uzal, Diklah, Ebal, Abimael, Sheba, Ophir, Havilah and Jobab (Gen 10:26–29; 1 Chr 1:20–23). Many of these names match peoples or regions of southern Arabia, such as Sheba and Hazarmaveth (probably modern Hadramaut). Gen 10:30 places their territory between Mesha and Sephar. Easton's Bible Dictionary notes an Arab tradition that Joktan, called Qahtan in Arabic, was the ancestor of the purest tribes of central and southern Arabia. The meaning of his name is uncertain. Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionary give "little" or "small."

Jonathan, son of the priest Abiathar, was one of several men in the Bible with this name, which means "given of God" (Hitchcock's Bible Names). During Absalom's revolt, David sent Zadok and Abiathar back to Jerusalem with their sons Ahimaaz and Jonathan, who were to carry news of events in the city to the king. The two waited at En-rogel so they would not be seen entering the city. A servant girl brought them information, and they passed it on to David. When Absalom's servants searched for them, a woman told the pursuers they had crossed the brook, and the men returned to Jerusalem without finding them. Later, at Adonijah's feast, Jonathan arrived with the news that David had made Solomon king. His brother Ahimelech appears elsewhere as a priest (2 Sam 8:17). Easton's Bible Dictionary calls Jonathan the last recorded descendant of Eli.

Joseph (of Arimathea) was a rich man from the town of Arimathea who asked for and buried the body of Jesus after the crucifixion, about AD 30 by inference from context. Mark and Luke call him an honourable counsellor, which Easton's Bible Dictionary takes to mean a member of the Sanhedrin, the Jewish ruling council. Luke describes him as a good and just man, and Mark says he waited for the kingdom of God. Matthew and John call him a disciple of Jesus, and John adds that he kept this secret for fear of the Jewish authorities. That evening he went boldly to Pilate and asked for the body. Pilate confirmed the death with the centurion and then released it to him. Joseph wrapped the body in clean linen. Connected passages describe Nicodemus helping him (John 19:39) and the body being laid in Joseph's own new rock-cut tomb. Easton's identifies Arimathea with Old Testament Ramah.

Meraioth was a priest of the tribe of Levi, descended from Aaron through Eleazar, who appears only in genealogies. He was the son of Zerahiah and the father of Amariah, in the line of high priests that leads to Zadok (1 Chr 6:6–7, 52). The genealogy of Ezra also names him as an ancestor (Ezra 7:3). That list is shortened, since there Azariah follows Meraioth directly. In 1 Chr 9:11 and Neh 11:11, a Meraioth stands between Ahitub and Zadok in the ancestry of a chief officer of the temple. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia take this as probably a different, later man of the same name. Others read it as the same ancestor in a compressed list. This entry follows the line in 1 Chronicles 6. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the name's meaning as "bitterness" or "rebellious."

Meremoth son of Urijah was a priest in Jerusalem after the exile, from the family of Koz (Smith's Bible Dictionary links this with Hakkoz). When Ezra arrived, Meremoth weighed the silver, gold and temple vessels brought from Babylon, assisted by Eleazar and the Levites Jozabad and Noadiah (Ezra 8:33). During Nehemiah's rebuilding of the wall he repaired two sections, the second running the length of Eliashib's house, probably the high priest named in Neh 3:1 (Neh 3:4, 21). This entry also connects him with the Meremoth who sealed Nehemiah's covenant (Neh 10:5) and with the priest Meremoth listed among those who returned with Zerubbabel (Neh 12:3). That priestly house, later headed by Helkai, appears as Meraioth (Neh 12:15), which the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats as a scribal variant. Because Zerubbabel's return came about a century earlier, these mentions may refer to an ancestor or to the family rather than the same man.

Milcah (wife of Nahor) was the daughter of Haran and the wife of Nahor, Abraham's brother. Since Haran was also a brother of Abraham and Nahor, she married her uncle. Her sister was Iscah, and Gen 11:27 names Lot as another child of Haran, making him her brother. After the near-sacrifice of Isaac, Abraham received news that Milcah had borne eight sons to Nahor: Huz, Buz, Kemuel, Chesed, Hazo, Pildash, Jidlaph and Bethuel (Gen 22:21–22). Through Bethuel she was the grandmother of Rebekah. Rebekah is repeatedly identified by this lineage, both when Abraham's servant first meets her at the well and when he retells the story to her family. Hitchcock's Bible Names and Smith's Bible Dictionary give the meaning of her name as "queen."

Nathanael was a disciple of Jesus from Cana in Galilee who appears only in the Gospel of John. His name means "gift of God." Philip told him they had found the one Moses and the prophets wrote about, Jesus of Nazareth. Nathanael asked whether anything good could come out of Nazareth, and Philip answered, "Come and see." Jesus greeted him as "an Israelite indeed, in whom is no guile" and said he had seen him under the fig tree before Philip called him. Nathanael then called Jesus the Son of God and the King of Israel. Later he was among the disciples together at the Sea of Tiberias when the risen Jesus appeared (John 21:2). Because John never names Bartholomew, and the other Gospels pair Bartholomew with Philip but never mention Nathanael, he is commonly identified with Bartholomew, as Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries note.

Obadiah was the official in charge of King Ahab's household in Israel, one of several men of this name in the Bible. The text says he feared the Lord greatly, and when Queen Jezebel was killing the prophets of the Lord, he hid a hundred of them in caves in two groups of fifty and supplied them with bread and water. During a severe drought, Ahab sent him to search the land's springs and brooks for grass to keep the horses and mules alive, the two men dividing the country between them. On his way Obadiah met the prophet Elijah, recognized him and bowed to the ground. He then went and told Ahab, who came out to meet Elijah. His name means "servant of the Lord" (Hitchcock's Bible Names). He is distinct from the prophet whose book bears the same name.

Obed was the son of Boaz and Ruth, the father of Jesse, and the grandfather of King David, a member of the tribe of Judah. When he was born, the women of Bethlehem named him and declared, "There is a son born to Naomi" (Ruth 4:17). The phrase reflects that the child continued the family line of Naomi, Ruth's mother-in-law, whose husband and sons had died earlier in the book. Apart from the story of his birth, Obed appears only in genealogies: those at the end of Ruth and in 1 Chronicles, and both genealogies of Jesus, in Matthew and Luke. Matthew notes that he was born of Ruth. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of his name as "servant" or "workman." Several other men in the Bible share the name.

Onan was the second son of Judah by the daughter of Shua, a Canaanite woman, and the brother of Er and Shelah. After the LORD put Er to death, Judah told Onan to marry his brother's widow and father children who would count as Er's, a custom later set out in law in Deut 25:5. The widow is named Tamar in Gen 38:6. Onan knew any child would not be counted as his own, so he spilled his seed on the ground to avoid giving his brother an heir. Gen 38:10 says the LORD was displeased and put him to death as well. He died in Canaan before Jacob's family moved to Egypt, and the tribal lists of Judah record his death. His half-brothers Pharez and Zerah were later born to Judah by Tamar. Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries give the meaning of his name as "strong."

Othniel son of Kenaz was a warrior of Judah and the first of Israel's judges.
