He captured the city that Caleb had promised to reward with his daughter Achsah, and so won her as his wife (Josh 15:17; Judg 1:13). The surrounding verses name the city as Kirjath-sepher, later called Debir. He is called "Caleb's younger brother," which may mean that Othniel himself or his father Kenaz was Caleb's brother. The STEPBible proper names index takes him as Caleb's nephew. After Israel cried to the Lord, Othniel was raised up as a deliverer, about 1410 BC by inference from context. Judg 3:8 names the oppressor as Cushan-rishathaim of Mesopotamia. The land then had rest for forty years. His sons were Hathath and probably Meonothai (1 Chr 4:13). In David's time, the captain Heldai was counted as "of Othniel," apparently a family descended from him.

Phinehas was a son of Eli who served with his brother Hophni as a priest of the LORD at Shiloh (1 Sam 1:3). Several people in the Bible share the name, and this one is distinct from the earlier Phinehas, Aaron's grandson. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia call him Eli's second or younger son. According to 1 Sam 2:12–17, Eli's sons treated the sacrifices with contempt, and a prophet warned Eli that both would die on the same day. When Israel brought the ark of the covenant from Shiloh into battle against the Philistines, the two brothers went with it. The ark was captured, both were killed, and a messenger brought the news to Eli. According to 1 Sam 4:19–22, Phinehas's wife went into labor on hearing of his death, named her son Ichabod, and died. Another son, Ahitub, became the father of Ahiah, a priest in Saul's day.

Priscilla, also called Prisca (2 Tim 4:19), was the wife of Aquila, a Jew from Pontus. She is never mentioned without him. The couple had recently come from Italy because the emperor Claudius had ordered all Jews to leave Rome. Paul met them in Corinth, about AD 49 by inference from context. The surrounding verse, Acts 18:3, adds that he stayed and worked with them as a fellow tentmaker. Later they sailed with Paul toward Syria, and Acts 18:19 says they remained at Ephesus. There they heard Apollos speak in the synagogue, took him aside, and explained the way of God to him more accurately. Paul calls them his helpers in Christ Jesus. Writing from Asia, he sends greetings from them and from the church that met in their house. As Easton's Bible Dictionary notes, her name sometimes comes before her husband's.

Ram was a son of Hezron in the tribe of Judah, and a brother of Jerahmeel and Chelubai (Caleb) (1 Chr 2:9). Ashur and Segub, also listed as his siblings, appear later in the same chapter as Hezron's sons by other wives. Ram was the father of Amminadab and the grandfather of Nahshon, who was called prince of the children of Judah (1 Chr 2:10). The genealogy in Ruth 4:19 places him in the line that leads to King David. In the King James New Testament his name appears in its Greek form, Aram, in the genealogies of Jesus (Matt 1:3–4; Luke 3:33). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that some texts of Luke read "Arni" here. The name probably means "high" or "exalted." He is a different person from Ram, the son of Jerahmeel and so Ram's nephew, who appears later in 1 Chronicles 2.

Reu was a descendant of Shem through Eber, the son of Peleg and the father of Serug, in the family line that leads to Abraham. Genesis records that Peleg was thirty when Reu was born, and that Reu was thirty-two when he fathered Serug. He lived another 207 years and had other sons and daughters, a total lifespan of 239 years. 1 Chr 1:25 repeats his place in the line from Shem to Abraham. In Luke's genealogy of Jesus he appears under the Greek form Ragau, son of Phalec (Peleg) and father of Saruch (Serug). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia and Smith's Bible Dictionary both identify Ragau as the same person. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of his name as "his friend" or "his shepherd." His dates of about 2217–1978 BC are estimates inferred from the genealogical figures.

Reuel was a son of Esau and his wife Bashemath (Gen 36:4, 36:10). Genesis 36:3 identifies this Bashemath as a daughter of Ishmael. His half-brothers were Eliphaz, the son of Adah, and Jeush, Jaalam and Korah (1 Chr 1:35). Reuel had four sons, Nahath, Zerah, Shammah and Mizzah (Gen 36:13; 1 Chr 1:37). Each became a chief (the King James Version says "duke") of a clan descended from Reuel in the land of Edom (Gen 36:17). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives the name's meaning as "God is his friend." Several other people in the Bible share the name, most notably Moses' father-in-law (Exod 2:18). This entry concerns only the Edomite son of Esau.

Salmon, also called Salma, was a man of the tribe of Judah, the son of Nahshon and the father of Boaz. He appears only in genealogies: the line from Judah to David at the end of Ruth, the Judahite lists in 1 Chronicles, and the genealogies of Jesus in Matthew and Luke, which spell his father's name Naasson and his son's Booz. Matthew 1:5 names the mother of Boaz as Rachab. She is commonly identified with Rahab of Jericho, and STEPBible's proper-names index describes Salmon as Rahab's husband. Through Boaz and Ruth he was the great-great-grandfather of King David. Smith's Bible Dictionary links him with Bethlehem, noting that a Salma is called the father of Bethlehem in the line of Caleb (1 Chr 2:51, 54). It suggests this explains why he is also counted among Caleb's descendants, though whether that Salma is the same man is not certain.

Serug was a descendant of Shem, the son of Reu and the father of Nahor, which makes him the great-grandfather of Abraham through Nahor's son Terah. Reu fathered him at age thirty-two, and Serug fathered Nahor at thirty, then lived another two hundred years and had other sons and daughters (Gen 11:20–23). That gives a lifespan of 230 years, as Smith's Bible Dictionary notes. 1 Chronicles repeats his place in the line from Shem to Abraham, and Luke's genealogy of Jesus includes him under the Greek form Saruch (Luke 3:35). His name is usually explained as meaning "branch." Taking the ages in Genesis at face value, he would have lived from about 2185 to 1955 BC, an estimate inferred from context. Nothing else is recorded about him.

Shishak was a king of Egypt in the time of Solomon and Rehoboam. When Solomon sought to kill Jeroboam, Jeroboam fled to Shishak in Egypt and stayed there until Solomon died (1 Kgs 11:40). In the fifth year of Rehoboam, Shishak came up against Jerusalem. The Chronicler presents this as the result of Judah's unfaithfulness, announced by the prophet Shemaiah. When the leaders humbled themselves, Jerusalem was spared destruction. Shishak still carried off the treasures of the temple and the palace, including the gold shields Solomon had made. He is generally identified with Sheshonk I, founder of Egypt's Twenty-second Dynasty, whose list of conquests in Palestine is carved on the temple wall at Karnak (Smith's and Easton's Bible Dictionaries). Easton's Bible Dictionary suggests that the invasion was urged by Jeroboam. That link is an inference rather than something these verses state.

Tilgath-pilneser is the spelling used in Chronicles for Tiglath-pileser, king of Assyria, who also appears in 2 Kgs 15:29 and 16:7. He carried the Reubenites, Gadites and half tribe of Manasseh into exile at Halah, Habor, Hara and the river Gozan, among them Beerah, a Reubenite prince (1 Chr 5:6, 26). When Ahaz of Judah turned to him for help, he came but distressed him rather than strengthening him (2 Chr 28:20). This entry identifies him with Pul, who received a thousand talents of silver from Menahem of Israel to secure his throne (2 Kgs 15:19). Easton's Bible Dictionary explains Pul as his throne-name in Babylon, though 1 Chr 5:26 names the two side by side, and some treat them as separate kings. This entry also links him with "king Jareb" (Hos 5:13; 10:6), which the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia takes as an epithet meaning roughly "King Contentious". Whom that title refers to is uncertain.

Zechariah was a prophet to the Jews who had returned from exile, and the author of the book that bears his name. He calls himself the son of Berechiah and grandson of Iddo the prophet (Zech 1:1), while Ezra calls him simply “the son of Iddo.” Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests that Berechiah may have died early, leaving Iddo as the head of the family. His prophecies are dated from the eighth month of the second year of King Darius of Persia (about 520 BC, by inference from context) to the fourth year of Darius. Alongside Haggai, he spoke to the people of Judah and Jerusalem, and Ezra credits the two prophets' preaching with the elders' success in rebuilding and finishing the temple. Easton's and Smith's dictionaries describe him as being of priestly descent. Several other men in the Bible share his name.

Zephaniah son of Maaseiah was a priest in Jerusalem during the reign of Zedekiah, the last king of Judah. He held the rank of "second priest," below the chief priest Seraiah. Zedekiah sent him twice to the prophet Jeremiah: once with Pashur son of Melchiah to inquire of the LORD as Babylon threatened the city (Jer 21:1), and once with Jehucal to ask Jeremiah to pray for them (Jer 37:3). Shemaiah, a prophet among the exiles in Babylon, wrote to Zephaniah urging him to restrain Jeremiah, but Zephaniah read the letter aloud to Jeremiah (Jer 29:24–29). Smith's Bible Dictionary takes him to have been an overseer of the temple. After Jerusalem fell, the Babylonian captain of the guard seized him with Seraiah and others, and 2 Kgs 25:21 says they were put to death at Riblah. He is distinct from the prophet Zephaniah and others who bore the name.
A Pharisee in whose house “a woman of the city which was a sinner” anointed our Lord’s feet with ointment (Luke 7:36-38).

Abidan, son of Gideoni, was the leader of the tribe of Benjamin during Israel's time in the wilderness after the Exodus. He was one of the tribal heads named to help Moses take the census at Sinai (Num 1:11). In the arrangement of the camp, he was captain of Benjamin, which camped on the west side with Ephraim and Manasseh (Num 2:22). When the tribal leaders brought offerings at the dedication of the tabernacle's altar, Abidan presented Benjamin's gifts on the ninth day. These included peace offerings of two oxen, five rams, five male goats and five year-old lambs (Num 7:60, 65). When Israel set out from Sinai, he commanded Benjamin's company on the march (Num 10:24). His name is usually explained as "father is judge" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia) or "father of judgment" (Hitchcock's Bible Names).

Abiel (meaning "God is my father," according to Hitchcock's Bible Names) was a Benjamite, the son of Zeror and an ancestor of King Saul. 1 Sam 9:1 calls him the father of Kish, Saul's father, and 1 Sam 14:51 calls him the father of Ner, whose son was Abner, Saul's commander. However, 1 Chr 8:33 and 9:39 say that Ner was the father of Kish, so the generations are hard to align. Easton's Bible Dictionary takes "father" in 1 Sam 9:1 to mean grandfather, making Abiel the father of Ner. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treat Kish and Ner as brothers, both sons of Abiel. This entry follows the STEPBible identification of Abiel with Jehiel, the "father of Gibeon," who lived in Gibeon with his wife Maachah (1 Chr 9:35). That passage goes on to list his ten sons, including Kish and Ner. Several other people in the Bible share the name.

Abinadab was a son of King Saul, listed among Saul's sons in the genealogies alongside Jonathan, Malchishua and Eshbaal (Ish-bosheth). He was killed by the Philistines together with his father and his brothers Jonathan and Malchishua. The surrounding narrative places this battle on Mount Gilboa (1 Sam 31:1). 1 Sam 14:49 names Saul's sons as Jonathan, Ishui and Melchishua but does not mention Abinadab. For this reason many, including the STEPBible names index, take Ishui (Ishvi) to be another name for Abinadab, and this entry follows that view. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats Ishvi under a separate heading. His mother was Ahinoam, Saul's wife (1 Sam 14:50). His sisters were Merab and Michal. Armoni and Mephibosheth were his half-brothers, Saul's sons by his concubine Rizpah (2 Sam 21:8). The name is generally explained as "my father is willing." Several other men in the Bible share it.

Abishag was a young woman from Shunem, a town that Smith's Bible Dictionary places in the tribe of Issachar. She was chosen after a search throughout Israel for a beautiful young woman to attend King David in his extreme old age. She served as his personal attendant, and she was present in the king's chamber when Bathsheba came to urge him to name Solomon as his successor. The surrounding passage (1 Kgs 1:4) adds that David did not have sexual relations with her. After David's death, his son Adonijah asked Bathsheba to request Abishag from Solomon as his wife. Solomon treated the request as a bid for the throne. He replied that his mother might as well ask the kingdom for his elder brother, and the account that follows (1 Kgs 2:25) records that he had Adonijah put to death. Nothing further is said of Abishag.

Adoniram, son of Abda, was the royal official "over the tribute", meaning the forced labor levy, in Israel. He is also called Adoram and Hadoram. Most reference works, including Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia, take these as one man who held the office under David, Solomon and Rehoboam, and this entry follows that view. Under David he appears as Adoram in the list of officials (2 Sam 20:24). Under Solomon he directed the 30,000 laborers sent to Lebanon in rotating shifts of 10,000, each working one month there and two months at home (1 Kgs 4:6; 1 Kgs 5:14). When the northern tribes rebelled against Rehoboam, the king sent him to them, and the Israelites stoned him to death. Rehoboam then fled to Jerusalem in his chariot (1 Kgs 12:18; 2 Chr 10:18).

Agag was a king of the Amalekites in the time of Saul. When Saul attacked the Amalekites, he took Agag alive and killed the people. Saul and his army spared Agag, along with the best of the sheep and cattle, instead of destroying everything as commanded (1 Sam 15:8–9). Saul then told Samuel he had obeyed the Lord and brought back Agag (1 Sam 15:20). Samuel had Agag brought to him, and Agag came saying, "Surely the bitterness of death is past." Samuel answered that as Agag's sword had made women childless, so his own mother would be childless, and he cut Agag in pieces before the Lord at Gilgal (1 Sam 15:32–33). The name is also used of another Amalekite ruler in Num 24:7, and Easton's Bible Dictionary treats Agag as a name borne by more than one Amalekite king. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives its meaning as "roof" or "upper floor."

Ahiezer the son of Ammishaddai was the leader of the tribe of Dan during Israel's time in the wilderness. He was named as Dan's representative to help Moses take the census (Num 1:12). In the arrangement of the camp he served as captain of Dan, whose standard was on the north side (Num 2:25). On the tenth day of the offerings for the dedication of the altar, he brought Dan's gifts as prince of the tribe, including peace offerings of oxen, rams, goats and lambs (Num 7:66, 71). When Israel marched, Dan's camp went last as the rear guard, with Ahiezer over its host (Num 10:25). His name means "brother of help" or "my brother is help." The name is shared by another man in the Bible, a warrior who joined David at Ziklag, who is a different person.

Ahilud is known only as the father of two officials in the royal administration of Israel. His son Jehoshaphat served as recorder, the official chronicler of the kingdom, under David and continued in that post under Solomon (2 Sam 8:16; 2 Sam 20:24; 1 Kgs 4:3; 1 Chr 18:15). A Baana son of Ahilud was one of Solomon's twelve district officers, responsible for a region including Taanach, Megiddo and Beth-shean (1 Kgs 4:12). Whether the two fathers are the same man is uncertain. Smith's Bible Dictionary leaves the question open, while the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia assumes they are one person. This entry follows that identification and treats Jehoshaphat and Baana as brothers. Nothing else is recorded about Ahilud himself. His name is usually explained as meaning something like "brother of one born" or "child's brother."

Ahira was the son of Enan and the leader of the tribe of Naphtali during Israel's time in the wilderness after the Exodus. He was named as Naphtali's representative to help Moses and Aaron take the census of the fighting men (Num 1:15). In the arrangement of the camp he was captain of Naphtali, which camped on the north side with Dan and Asher (Num 2:29). At the dedication of the altar he brought his tribe's offering on the twelfth and last day, including the peace offerings described in Num 7:83. When Israel set out from Sinai, he commanded Naphtali's troops on the march (Num 10:27). The meaning of his name is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives "brother of evil" (that is, unlucky) or "my brother is friend," and Hitchcock's Bible Names adds "brother of the shepherd."

Ahitub was a priest of Eli's family, the son of Phinehas, the grandson of Eli, and the brother of Ichabod (1 Sam 14:3). His son Ahiah wore the ephod in Saul's camp, and his son Ahimelech was the priest at Nob. Saul summoned Ahimelech and all the priests of his father's house after Doeg the Edomite reported that David had been helped there. Only Ahimelech's son Abiathar escaped (1 Sam 22:9–20). Smith's Bible Dictionary treats Ahiah and Ahimelech as the same man and traces the family through Eli to Ithamar. Easton's Bible Dictionary says Ahitub became high priest when Eli died, though the verses here do not state this. His name means "brother of goodness," according to Hitchcock's Bible Names. Several other men in the Bible share the name.

Ahitub was a Levite of the priestly line, the son of Amariah and the father of Zadok, who served as one of the priests under King David (2 Sam 8:17; 1 Chr 18:16). The genealogy of the priests in 1 Chronicles traces his descent through Meraioth and Amariah, and continues through Zadok to Ahimaaz (1 Chr 6:7–8, 52). Smith's Bible Dictionary places him in the house of Eleazar, the son of Aaron, which follows from that same line of descent. Nothing is recorded of his own life or service. The name means "brother of goodness," according to Hitchcock's Bible Names. Several other men named Ahitub appear in the Bible, including a priest of Eli's family who was the father of Ahimelech, and a later Ahitub in the same genealogy. This entry concerns Zadok's father.

Aholiab, son of Ahisamach of the tribe of Dan, was a skilled craftsman appointed to help Bezaleel make the tabernacle and its furnishings during Israel's time in the wilderness (Exod 31:6). He is described as an engraver, a designer, and an embroiderer in blue, purple and scarlet yarn and fine linen (Exod 38:23). Along with Bezaleel, he was given the ability to teach others the work (Exod 35:34). Moses called the two of them, together with every skilled worker willing to take part, to carry out the work on the sanctuary as the LORD had commanded (Exod 36:1–2). Modern translations spell his name Oholiab. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Hitchcock's Bible Names give its meaning as "tent of the father."

Aholibah is a symbolic name for Jerusalem in Ezekiel's allegory of two sisters (Ezek 23:4). She and her elder sister Aholah, who stands for Samaria, are pictured as women who belonged to the Lord and bore him sons and daughters. Later in the chapter both are condemned as unfaithful wives who took foreign lovers. Aholibah is described as watching her sister's fate and then becoming even more corrupt than she was (Ezek 23:11). The Lord announces that he will turn her former lovers against her and bring them on her from every side (Ezek 23:22). Ezekiel is told to declare the abominations of both sisters (Ezek 23:36), and they are called "the lewd women" (Ezek 23:44). Easton's Bible Dictionary and Hitchcock's Bible Names give the name's meaning as "my tent is in her," and the STEPBible names list takes her to represent the southern kingdom of Judah.

Aholibamah was one of the wives of Esau. Genesis 36 calls her the daughter of Anah, the daughter of Zibeon the Hivite. This entry reads that phrase as making Anah her mother, a daughter of Zibeon. She bore Esau three sons in Canaan, Jeush, Jaalam and Korah, who later became chiefs ("dukes") among the Edomites. This entry also identifies her with Judith, the daughter of Beeri the Hittite, whom Esau married at forty (Gen 26:34). That would make Beeri her father. Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests Judith may have been her original name. The two lists of Esau's wives differ in names and ancestry, so the match is an inference. STEPBible traces her to Seir the Horite, following the Horite genealogy later in Genesis 36. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning "my tabernacle is exalted." The name is also borne by an Edomite chief in the same chapter.

Akkub was a Levite gatekeeper ("porter") at the temple in Jerusalem after the return from exile in Babylon. He is listed with Shallum, the chief, and with Talmon and Ahiman among the porters who lived in Jerusalem (1 Chr 9:17). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia places him on duty at the east gate. The "children of Akkub" appear among the gatekeeper families who returned from Babylon (Ezra 2:42; Neh 7:45). Akkub and Talmon also lead the 172 gatekeepers in Nehemiah's day (Neh 11:19), and Akkub is named among those guarding the storehouses at the gates (Neh 12:25). Because these references span several generations, the name probably stands for a gatekeeping family as well as an individual. Other men named Akkub appear elsewhere in the Bible. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives the name's meaning as "pursuer."

Ammishaddai was a man of the tribe of Dan, known only as the father of Ahiezer, the tribe's leader during the wilderness journey after the Exodus. Every mention of him occurs in the phrase "Ahiezer the son of Ammishaddai." His son was named as Dan's representative at the census (Num 1:12) and as captain of the Danite camp, which was stationed on the north side of the tabernacle (Num 2:25). Ahiezer also brought Dan's offering on the tenth day of the altar's dedication (Num 7:66, 71), and he led the Danite host, which marched last as the rear guard of all the camps (Num 10:25). Nothing is recorded of Ammishaddai himself. His name contains Shaddai, "Almighty." Easton's Bible Dictionary renders it "people of the Almighty," while the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives "Shaddai is my kinsman."

Anah was a son of Seir the Horite, one of the early inhabitants of the land of Seir, later Edom. His brothers were Lotan, Shobal, Zibeon, Dishon, Ezer and Dishan, and Timna was his sister (Gen 36:20; 1 Chr 1:38). He is listed among the chiefs, or "dukes," of the Horites (Gen 36:29). His children were a son, Dishon, who had the same name as one of Anah's brothers, and a daughter, Aholibamah (Gen 36:25). Dishon's sons were Amram, Eshban, Ithran and Cheran (1 Chr 1:41). Several men in the Bible are named Anah. Another Anah in the same chapter is a son of Zibeon (Gen 36:24), and Esau's wife Aholibamah is called the daughter of an Anah (Gen 36:2), so it is uncertain which Anah is meant in some passages. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats Seir as the land itself personified as the ancestor of its tribes.

Ananias (Disciple at Damascus) was a follower of Jesus living in Damascus who was sent to Saul (later Paul) after Saul's encounter with Jesus on the road, about AD 32 by inference from context. In a vision the Lord told him to go to Saul, who in turn had seen a vision of a man named Ananias coming to lay hands on him so he could see again. Ananias objected that he had heard how much harm Saul had done to believers in Jerusalem. He went anyway, laid his hands on Saul, called him "Brother Saul," and said Jesus had sent him so that Saul would regain his sight and be filled with the Holy Spirit. Recounting the event later, Paul described him as devout according to the law and well regarded by the Jews of Damascus. Smith's Bible Dictionary notes a tradition that he later became bishop of Damascus and died a martyr.

Aristarchus was a Macedonian from Thessalonica and one of Paul's travelling companions. During the riot in Ephesus, the crowd seized him and Gaius and rushed them into the theatre (Acts 19:29). He was later among the group that went with Paul from Greece through Macedonia toward Asia (Acts 20:4). He also sailed with Paul on the voyage to Rome, which included the shipwreck and the stay on Malta (Acts 27:2). In Paul's letters to the Colossians and to Philemon, Aristarchus sends greetings. Paul calls him his "fellowprisoner" in Col 4:10 and his fellow worker in Phlm 1:24, so he was probably with Paul during his imprisonment, usually taken to be at Rome. His name means "best ruler." Smith's Bible Dictionary records a tradition that he became bishop of Apamea, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes a tradition that he was martyred under Nero.

Asshur was a son of Shem, listed alongside his brothers Elam, Arphaxad, Lud and Aram in the table of nations (Gen 10:22; 1 Chr 1:17). Easton's Bible Dictionary calls him Shem's second son. In the King James wording of Gen 10:11, Asshur went out of the land of Shinar and built Nineveh, Rehoboth and Calah. Many translations instead read this verse as saying that Nimrod went out into Assyria and built those cities. This entry follows the King James reading, as Easton's does. Asshur is generally taken as the ancestor who gave his name to Assyria, and the name often stands for that people or nation. In Balaam's oracles, Asshur carries the Kenites away captive and is itself afflicted by ships from Chittim (Num 24:22, 24). Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that the Assyrians' chief god also bore the name Asshur.

Azariah was one of four young men from Judah, together with Daniel, Hananiah and Mishael, who were taken to Babylon and trained for service at the court of King Nebuchadnezzar (Dan 1:6). The chief of the eunuchs gave him the Babylonian name Abednego (Dan 1:7), the name by which he is better known. He was placed under the steward Melzar with his companions (Dan 1:11). When the king examined them, none of the other young men matched these four, so they entered the king's service (Dan 1:19). When Daniel needed to learn the king's dream, he told Azariah and the other two what was happening (Dan 2:17). Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries describe him as probably of the royal family of Judah. As Abednego, he later survived the fiery furnace in Daniel 3. Several other people in the Bible share the name Azariah, a common Hebrew name meaning roughly "the Lord has helped."

Benaiah was a Levite in David's time who took part in bringing the ark of God to Jerusalem. He is listed among the Levites of the second rank, alongside the gatekeepers (1 Chr 15:18), and among those who played psalteries "on Alamoth," a musical term of uncertain meaning, possibly a high register (1 Chr 15:20; 16:5). A Benaiah is also named among the priests who blew trumpets before the ark and who were afterward assigned to sound them there continually (1 Chr 15:24; 16:6). Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treat the Levite musician and the priestly trumpeter as two different men. This entry brings these mentions together under one name. The name means "the Lord has built." Several other men in the Bible share it.

Beriah was a son of Asher and a grandson of Jacob, listed with his brothers Imnah, Ishvah and Ishvi and his sister Serah. He appears among the family members who went down with Jacob to Egypt (Gen 46:17). His sons were Heber and Malchiel, and 1 Chr 7:31 adds that Malchiel was the father of Birzavith. In the census of Numbers he is the ancestor of the Beriite clan of the tribe of Asher, and his two sons founded the Heberite and Malchielite clans (Num 26:44–45). Spellings of his brothers' names vary slightly between the lists. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "in evil" or "a gift". Several other men in the Bible share the name Beriah, including a son of Ephraim and a Benjamite, and they should not be confused with this son of Asher.

Bildad the Shuhite was one of Job's three friends, along with Eliphaz the Temanite and Zophar the Naamathite. When they heard of Job's disasters, they arranged to come together from their own homes to mourn with him and comfort him (Job 2:11). Bildad speaks in each of the three rounds of debate with Job, in Job 8, 18 and 25. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes his speeches as severe and stern. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that his third speech is the friends' last. "Shuhite" probably links him to Shuah, a region east or southeast of Israel, or to his ancestor Shuah, a son of Abraham by Keturah (Gen 25:2). The exact place is unknown. At the end of the book, Bildad and the other two friends do what the LORD commands them, and the LORD accepts Job's prayer for them (Job 42:9).

Chedorlaomer was a king of Elam in the time of Abraham, and the leading figure among four allied eastern kings: Amraphel of Shinar, Arioch of Ellasar and Tidal "king of nations". The kings of Sodom, Gomorrah and three neighbouring cities served him for twelve years and rebelled in the thirteenth. In the fourteenth year he and his allies marched west, defeating the Rephaim, Zuzim and Emim, and then met the five kings in battle, "four kings with five". The surrounding chapter says they carried off Abraham's nephew Lot. Abraham pursued and defeated them, and the king of Sodom met him on his return from "the slaughter of Chedorlaomer". Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies him with Kudur-Lagamar of Babylonian inscriptions. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia reads the name as meaning "servant of Lagamar", an Elamite deity, and notes that scholars are divided over the identification.

Cushi was the messenger Joab sent to tell King David what had happened in the battle against Absalom's rebels (2 Sam 18:21). The name probably means "the Cushite," that is, a man from Cush (roughly ancient Nubia or Ethiopia), and the Revised Version renders it that way. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him as apparently attached to Joab's household. After Cushi set out, Ahimaaz son of Zadok persuaded Joab to let him run too, took the route through the plain, and arrived first (2 Sam 18:22–23). When Cushi reached David he announced that the Lord had avenged the king on his enemies. Asked whether Absalom was safe, he answered indirectly that he wished all the king's enemies would be as that young man was, conveying Absalom's death (2 Sam 18:31–32). The name Cushi is also borne by other people in the Bible.

Daughter of Pharaoh was an Egyptian princess, the daughter of a Pharaoh king of Egypt, whom Solomon married to seal an alliance with Egypt (1 Kgs 3:1). Her father is not named, and several other women in the Bible share this title. Solomon first brought her to live in the city of David while he finished building his palace, the temple and the wall of Jerusalem. He then built her a house of her own, designed like the porch of his palace (1 Kgs 7:8), and she moved up into it, after which he built the Millo (1 Kgs 9:24). According to 2 Chr 8:11, Solomon said his wife should not live in the house of David because places the ark of the LORD had entered were holy. She is named first among the many foreign wives Solomon loved (1 Kgs 11:1). Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that this marriage is the first mention of a link between Israel and Egypt since the Exodus.

Diana was the goddess worshipped at Ephesus, called Artemis by the Greeks and Diana by the Romans (Easton's Bible Dictionary). She appears in Acts 19, where the silversmith Demetrius, who made silver shrines for her, stirred up fellow craftsmen against Paul's preaching. He warned that their trade was in danger and that her temple, revered by "all Asia and the world," would be despised. The crowd shouted "Great is Diana of the Ephesians" and kept up the cry for about two hours. The town clerk calmed them by reminding them that Ephesus was the guardian of her worship and of an image said to have fallen from Jupiter. Easton's describes her temple as one of the seven wonders of the ancient world. Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that the Ephesian goddess differed from the Roman Diana and was closer to eastern goddesses such as Astarte.

Dishan was a son of Seir the Horite and one of the Horite chiefs ("dukes" in the King James Version) in the land of Seir, later called Edom. He is named last among Seir's seven sons, after Lotan, Shobal, Zibeon, Anah, Dishon and Ezer, and Timna is also counted among the siblings here. Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries call him Seir's youngest son, apparently from this order. His sons were Uz and Aran (Gen 36:28; 1 Chr 1:42). He appears only in the parallel genealogies of Genesis 36 and 1 Chronicles 1, where the Horite clans are listed alongside the descendants of Esau. His name closely resembles that of his brother Dishon. Easton's and Smith's dictionaries give its meaning as "antelope," while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "a threshing."

Ebed was the father of Gaal, and is known only through his son, who is called "Gaal the son of Ebed" throughout Judges 9. Gaal came to Shechem with his brothers and won the confidence of its men (Judg 9:26). He then spoke openly against Abimelech, the son of Jerubbaal (Gideon), and urged the city to stop serving him (Judg 9:28). Zebul, the city's ruler, warned Abimelech in secret that Gaal and his brothers were fortifying Shechem against him (Judg 9:30–31), and Abimelech's forces came out of hiding to attack while Gaal stood at the city gate (Judg 9:35). Nothing is said about Ebed himself. His name means "servant," according to the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia and Hitchcock's Bible Names. The name is shared by other men in the Bible, who are separate people.

Ebiasaph, also spelled Abiasaph, was a Levite of the line of Korah and head of one of the Korahite families. Exodus names him with Assir and Elkanah as a son of Korah (Exod 6:24), and 1 Chr 6:37 calls him Korah's son. The list in 1 Chr 6:22–23, though, places him after Assir and Elkanah, which may make him a later descendant. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that these lists seem to skip names on purpose. His name probably means "my father has gathered." Through his son Assir he was an ancestor of Heman the singer, whose line 1 Chr 6:33–37 traces back to Korah. Through his son Kore he was an ancestor of Shallum and Meshelemiah, Korahite gatekeepers of the sanctuary (1 Chr 9:19). In 1 Chr 26:1 he appears in the short form Asaph, a different person from David's musician of that name.

Elam was the ancestor of a family group of Jews who returned to Jerusalem after the exile in Babylon. His descendants, called "the children of Elam," numbered 1,254 in the list of those who came back with Zerubbabel (Ezra 2:7; Neh 7:12). Smith's Bible Dictionary dates this return to about 536 BC or before. A later group of seventy men from the same family, led by Jeshaiah son of Athaliah, came with Ezra (Ezra 8:7). Members of the family appear again in the dispute over marriages to foreign women. Shechaniah son of Jehiel, one of Elam's descendants, admitted the wrong to Ezra and proposed a remedy (Ezra 10:2), and six men of the family are named among those who had married foreign wives (Ezra 10:26). Nothing is recorded about Elam himself. Several other people in the Bible share the name.

Eliab was a man of the tribe of Reuben, the son of Pallu and the father of Nemuel, Dathan and Abiram (Num 26:8–9). His name means "God is my father" according to Smith's Bible Dictionary. He is remembered almost entirely through his sons Dathan and Abiram, who joined Korah the Levite and On son of Peleth in a revolt against Moses and Aaron (Num 16:1). When Moses summoned them, they refused to come (Num 16:12). Deuteronomy recalls how the earth opened and swallowed Dathan and Abiram along with their households, tents and possessions (Deut 11:6). Deut 11:6 calls Eliab "the son of Reuben," meaning a descendant of Reuben, since Num 26:8 makes him Reuben's grandson through Pallu. Several other men in the Bible share the name Eliab, and this entry concerns only the Reubenite.

Eliab was the firstborn son of Jesse, of the tribe of Judah, and the eldest brother of David. His name means "God is father." When Samuel came to anoint a king from among Jesse's sons, he saw Eliab and assumed he was the LORD's anointed. In the next verse (1 Sam 16:7), God tells Samuel not to judge by appearance or height, and David is chosen instead. Eliab and his brothers Abinadab and Shammah followed Saul to war against the Philistines. When David came to the camp and asked about Goliath, Eliab angrily accused him of pride and of leaving his sheep just to watch the battle. His daughter Abihail became a wife of King Rehoboam. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia takes the Elihu named as David's brother in 1 Chr 27:18 to be Eliab under another name. Several other men in the Bible are also called Eliab.

Eliasaph was the leader of the tribe of Gad during Israel's wilderness journey after the Exodus. He was one of the tribal heads named to help Moses take the census at Sinai (Num 1:14), and he served as captain of Gad's camp (Num 2:14). On the sixth day of the dedication of the altar he brought Gad's offering (Num 7:42, 47), and he led Gad's division when the camp set out (Num 10:20). His father is usually called Deuel, but Num 2:14 reads Reuel. Reuel is also the name of Moses' father-in-law, who is elsewhere called Jethro (Exod 2:18), but that Reuel was a priest of Midian, while Eliasaph's father belonged to the tribe of Gad, so this entry does not link the two. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives the name's meaning as "God has added." Several other people in the Bible share the name.

Elizaphan, also spelled Elzaphan, was a Levite of the clan of Kohath and a son of Uzziel, Aaron's uncle, which made him a cousin of Moses and Aaron. Moses called him and his brother Mishael to carry their dead kinsmen out of the camp from before the sanctuary. From the surrounding chapter these were Aaron's sons Nadab and Abihu (Lev 10:1–4). In the wilderness census he was appointed chief of the Kohathite families (Num 3:30). His name later stood for a Levite family. In David's time Shemaiah led 200 'sons of Elizaphan' (1 Chr 15:8), and under Hezekiah, Shimri and Jeiel of that line served among the Levites (2 Chr 29:13). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives the name's meaning as 'God has protected.' He is distinct from another man of the same name in the Bible.

Elizur, son of Shedeur, was the leader of the tribe of Reuben during Israel's wilderness journey. He was one of the tribal heads chosen to help Moses and Aaron take the census of Israel (Num 1:5). In the arrangement of the camp he was captain of Reuben, whose standard stood on the south side of the tabernacle (Num 2:10), and when the people set out from Sinai he led Reuben's company on the march (Num 10:18). At the dedication of the altar, as prince of Reuben, he brought his tribe's offering on the fourth day, including peace offerings of oxen, rams, goats and lambs (Num 7:30, 35). His name means "my God is a rock," according to the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia.

Enan was a man of the tribe of Naphtali and the father of Ahira, who led that tribe during Israel's time in the wilderness. He is known only through his son's name, "Ahira the son of Enan," which appears five times in Numbers. Ahira was chosen to help Moses with the census at Sinai (Num 1:15). He served as captain of Naphtali in the camp arrangement (Num 2:29). He brought his tribe's offering on the twelfth day of the altar dedication (Num 7:78, 83) and commanded Naphtali's division on the march (Num 10:27). Nothing is recorded of Enan himself. His name is usually explained as "having eyes" or "having fountains" (Smith's Bible Dictionary; International Standard Bible Encyclopedia). Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "cloud."

Ezer was a Horite chief, one of the sons of Seir the Horite, the native people of the land of Seir, later Edom. He is listed with his brothers Lotan, Shobal, Zibeon, Anah, Dishon and Dishan, and is named among the "dukes" (clan chiefs) descended from Hori (Gen 36:21, 30; 1 Chr 1:38). His sons were Bilhan, Zaavan and Akan. 1 Chr 1:42 spells the last two Zavan and Jakan. Timna appears among his siblings because Gen 36:22 calls her Lotan's sister, which makes her a daughter of Seir by inference. Hitchcock's Bible Names and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia give the meaning of his name as "help." Several other people in the Bible share the name, and this Ezer should not be confused with them.

Gamaliel, son of Pedahzur, was the leader of the tribe of Manasseh during Israel's time in the wilderness. He was one of the tribal heads named to help Moses and Aaron take the census of Israel at Sinai (Num 1:10). In the arrangement of the camp he was captain of Manasseh, which camped beside Ephraim on the west side of the tabernacle (Num 2:20). At the dedication of the altar he brought his tribe's offering on the eighth day, the same gifts each tribal leader presented, including peace offerings of oxen, rams, goats and lambs (Num 7:54, 59). When Israel set out from Sinai, he commanded Manasseh's company on the march (Num 10:23). His name means "recompense of God" according to Smith's Bible Dictionary. He is a different person from the Pharisee and teacher of the law named Gamaliel in the New Testament.

Gershom was the elder son of Moses and his wife Zipporah, born in Midian while Moses lived there in exile. Moses named him for that exile, saying, "I have been a stranger in a strange land" (Exod 2:22). Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning as "a stranger here." Gershom and his younger brother Eliezer later came with their mother and Jethro to meet Moses in the wilderness (Exod 18:3). Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies him as the son Zipporah circumcised on the way to Egypt (Exod 4:24–26), though that passage does not name the child. As a Levite, Gershom's line was counted among the Levitical families, and his son Shebuel (also spelled Shubael) served as chief and as ruler of the treasures under David. The STEPBible names index links him to Jonathan, a priest for the Danites (Judg 18:30). Several other men in the Bible share the name.

Gideoni was a man of the tribe of Benjamin and the father of Abidan, who led the Benjamites during Israel's time in the wilderness. He is known only as part of his son's name, "Abidan the son of Gideoni." That phrase appears when Abidan is named as Benjamin's representative at the census (Num 1:11), as captain of the tribe in the camp arrangement (Num 2:22), as the prince who brought Benjamin's offering on the ninth day of the altar dedication (Num 7:60, 65), and as commander of the tribe's company when the camp set out (Num 10:24). Nothing is recorded about Gideoni himself. By inference from these passages, he belonged to the generation before the exodus. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "a cutting down," and Hitchcock's Bible Names treats it as the same as Gideon.

Gomer (son of Japheth) is the first-named son of Japheth, son of Noah, in the Table of Nations. His brothers were Magog, Madai, Javan, Tubal, Meshech and Tiras, and his sons were Ashkenaz, Riphath and Togarmah (Gen 10:2–3; 1 Chr 1:5–6). Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries call him Japheth's eldest son, which follows from his being listed first. In Ezek 38:6 Gomer, together with "the house of Togarmah of the north quarters" and their troops, appears as a people among the forces allied with Gog, so the name stands for a nation as well as an ancestor. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identifies this people with the Gimirra of Assyrian records and the Cimmerians of Greek writers, northern tribes who moved into Asia Minor in the 7th century BC. Easton's and Smith's go further and trace the Celtic peoples to Gomer. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "complete."

Hadad was an Edomite of the royal family whom God raised up as an adversary to Solomon (1 Kgs 11:14). As a small child he fled to Egypt with some of his father's Edomite servants. By inference from the surrounding verses (1 Kgs 11:15–16), this was to escape Joab's slaughter of the men of Edom in David's time. In Egypt he won Pharaoh's favor and married the sister of Queen Tahpenes. Their son Genubath was raised in Pharaoh's household (1 Kgs 11:20). When Hadad heard that David and Joab were dead, he asked Pharaoh to let him return to his own country. 1 Kgs 11:25 counts the trouble Hadad caused alongside that of Rezon, who reigned in Syria. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia describes Hadad as stirring up Edom against Israelite rule. Several other people in the Bible share the name, including a son of Ishmael and an early king of Edom.

Haggith was one of King David's wives and the mother of Adonijah, David's fourth son. She is named only as Adonijah's mother. He was born in Hebron during the years David reigned there, before he moved his capital to Jerusalem (2 Sam 3:2–5; 1 Chr 3:1–4). Her son is repeatedly called "Adonijah the son of Haggith," including in the account of his attempt to make himself king as David grew old, which the prophet Nathan reported to Bathsheba, the mother of Solomon. Adonijah's later visit to Bathsheba after Solomon became king also uses this name. Nothing else is recorded about Haggith herself. Her name is usually taken to mean "festive" or "festal" (Easton's Bible Dictionary; International Standard Bible Encyclopedia).

Hammedatha was the father of Haman, the official whom King Ahasuerus of Persia promoted above all his princes and who plotted to destroy the Jews in the book of Esther. He is known only through his son, who is repeatedly called "Haman the son of Hammedatha the Agagite" (Esth 3:1; 3:10; 8:5; 9:24). The text says nothing about Hammedatha himself. The title "Agagite" may describe the family as a whole, though it is attached to Haman's name, and its origin is not explained in these verses. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia takes the name to be Persian, meaning "given by the moon," while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "he that troubles the law." His grandsons, Haman's ten sons, were killed when the Jews defended themselves (Esth 9:10).

Hanani was a seer in Judah during the reign of King Asa. According to 2 Chr 16:7, he came to Asa and rebuked him for relying on the king of Syria rather than on the LORD, warning that the Syrian army had therefore escaped his hand. The following verses report that Asa was angered and put him in prison. Hanani is also named as the father of the prophet Jehu, who spoke the word of the LORD against Baasha king of Israel and later confronted King Jehoshaphat of Judah. Jehu's writings recorded Jehoshaphat's acts. 2 Chr 19:2 calls Jehoshaphat's challenger "Jehu the son of Hanani the seer," which supports treating the seer and the father as one man. Smith's Bible Dictionary allows that the father may have been a different Hanani, and Easton's Bible Dictionary says he was probably the same. This entry follows the single-person view. The name means "gracious."

Haran (brother of Abraham) was a son of Terah and a brother of Abram and Nahor (Gen 11:26–27). He was the father of Lot and of two daughters: Milcah, who married her uncle Nahor, and Iscah (Gen 11:27, 29). Haran died in Ur of the Chaldees, where he was born, while his father Terah was still alive (Gen 11:28). Afterward Terah took Haran's son Lot, along with Abram and Sarai, from Ur toward Canaan (Gen 11:31). Sarah is counted among his siblings because Gen 20:12 describes her as Terah's daughter by a different mother. His place in the birth order is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary calls him the eldest son, while Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treat him as the youngest. He is a different figure from the town of Haran, where the family later settled (Gen 11:31).

Harim was a priest whose name was given to the third of the twenty-four priestly divisions drawn by lot to serve in turn at the house of God (1 Chr 24:8). Smith's Bible Dictionary places this arrangement in the days of David. The priestly family called the children of Harim, 1,017 strong, appears in the lists of those who returned from Babylon with Zerubbabel (Ezra 2:39; Neh 7:42), and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats them as his descendants. In Ezra's time five priests of this family, Maaseiah, Elijah, Shemaiah, Jehiel and Uzziah, are named among those who had married foreign wives (Ezra 10:21). A second group of 'sons of Harim' appears later in the same chapter (Ezra 10:31). By inference from the context, they stand among the lay Israelites listed from Ezra 10:25 on, so they probably belonged to a separate, non-priestly family of the same name.

Helon was a man of the tribe of Zebulun, known only as the father of Eliab, the leader of that tribe during the wilderness period. He is never mentioned on his own. His name appears only in the phrase "Eliab the son of Helon", which identifies his son in several roles. Eliab is named as Zebulun's representative at the census (Num 1:9) and as captain of the tribe in the camp arrangement (Num 2:7). He brought Zebulun's offering on the third day of the dedication of the altar (Num 7:24, 29), and he led the tribe's company when Israel set out on the march (Num 10:16). Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "strong", and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia as "valorous". Hitchcock's Bible Names offers "window; grief."

Hepher was a son of Gilead, the grandson of Machir and great-grandson of Manasseh son of Joseph, and the ancestor of the Hepherites, one of the clans of the tribe of Manasseh. He appears among Gilead's sons with Abiezer, Asriel, Helek, Shechem and Shemida, and his descendants received a share of land along with the other Manassite clans. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary call him Gilead's youngest son, since he is named last in Num 26:32. He is best known through his son Zelophehad, who had no sons but five daughters, Mahlah, Noah, Hoglah, Milcah and Tirzah. These daughters came forward to claim their father's inheritance. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of his name as "a digger." Several other men in the Bible share the name Hepher, and they should not be confused with this one.

Hezron was a son of Reuben, the firstborn of Jacob. He is named third among Reuben's four sons, after Hanoch and Pallu and before Carmi. He appears in the list of Jacob's family who went down to Egypt (Gen 46:9) and in the genealogies of the heads of Reuben's fathers' houses (Exod 6:14; 1 Chr 5:3). In the census taken in the wilderness, his descendants are counted as the Hezronites, one of the clans of the tribe of Reuben (Num 26:6). Nothing else is recorded about his life. The name was shared by others. 1 Chr 2:24, which mentions a Hezron who died in Caleb-ephratah, belongs by context to a different man, the Hezron of the tribe of Judah descended from Perez, and not to Reuben's son. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "enclosed" or "surrounded by a wall."

Hilkiah was the father of Eliakim, the official in charge of King Hezekiah's palace household in Judah. He is known only through his son, who is regularly called "Eliakim the son of Hilkiah." Eliakim, with Shebna the scribe and Joah the recorder, went out to meet the Assyrian officer Rabshakeh at Jerusalem's wall and then reported his words to Hezekiah (2 Kgs 18:18, 26, 37; Isa 36:22). Isaiah also names Eliakim as God's servant who would replace Shebna (Isa 22:20). Nothing is said about Hilkiah himself. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests his name was given mainly to tell his son apart from others called Eliakim. The name means "Yah is my portion." Several men in the Bible share it, including the high priest under Josiah, who is a different person.

Hiram, also called Huram, was a skilled bronze worker from Tyre whom King Solomon brought to Jerusalem to make the bronze furnishings for the temple. He is a different person from King Hiram of Tyre, Solomon's ally, who sent him. The connected passages say his father was a man of Tyre and his mother a widow, from the tribe of Naphtali according to 1 Kgs 7:14 and of Dan according to 2 Chr 2:14. He made the lavers, pots, shovels, basins, fleshhooks and other vessels, all of polished bronze, and finished the work Solomon gave him. The nearby 1 Kgs 7:46 says the casting was done in clay ground in the Jordan valley between Succoth and Zarethan. The phrase "Huram his father" in 2 Chr 4:16 is explained in Easton's Bible Dictionary as "Huram-abi," either a personal name or a title of respect meaning something like "master."

Hophni was one of the two sons of Eli, the priest at Shiloh, and the brother of Phinehas. Both brothers served as priests of the Lord at the sanctuary there (1 Sam 1:3). The surrounding chapter of 1 Samuel describes the brothers as worthless men who abused their office by seizing sacrificial meat and behaving immorally (1 Sam 2:12–17, 22). A man of God then announced judgment on Eli's house, and as a sign of it Hophni and Phinehas would both die on the same day (1 Sam 2:34). When Israel was fighting the Philistines, the ark of the covenant was brought from Shiloh to the camp, and the two brothers went with it (1 Sam 4:4). In the battle that followed the ark was captured and both of them were killed. A messenger brought the news to Eli (1 Sam 4:11, 17). Easton's Bible Dictionary places this battle at Aphek and gives the meaning of the name as "pugilist" or "client."

Immer was a priest whose name was given to the sixteenth of the twenty-four priestly divisions organized in David's time (1 Chr 24:14). His descendants, the "children of Immer," numbered 1,052 among those who returned from exile in Babylon (Ezra 2:37; Neh 7:40). Two of them, Hanani and Zebadiah, were among the priests who had married foreign wives in Ezra's day (Ezra 10:20). Jeremiah 20:1 names Pashur, the chief officer in the temple who opposed Jeremiah, as "the son of Immer the priest." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats this Immer as a separate priest of Jeremiah's time. This entry groups all these references under one name, since "son of" may simply mark Pashur as a member of Immer's priestly family. Because the name is shared by several people, the exact identification is uncertain.

James (Son of Alphaeus) was one of the twelve apostles chosen by Jesus. He appears in every list of the Twelve, named by his father Alphaeus, which sets him apart from James son of Zebedee. After the ascension he was among the eleven in the upper room in Jerusalem, where Matthias was later chosen to replace Judas Iscariot. This entry treats him as the brother of Thaddaeus. That reading takes the King James phrase "Judas the brother of James" (Luke 6:16; Acts 1:13) to refer to him, with Luke's Judas matching Thaddaeus in the other lists. The Greek can also mean "son of James," as the STEPBible proper-names index takes it. Since Levi is also called son of Alphaeus (Mark 2:14), the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests the two may have been brothers. Many identify him with James "the Less" (Mark 15:40), and Easton's Bible Dictionary also identifies him with James the Lord's brother.

Jason was a resident of Thessalonica who hosted Paul and Silas during their stay there. Jews who rejected Paul's preaching stirred up a mob that attacked Jason's house looking for the missionaries. When they could not find them, they dragged Jason and some other believers before the city rulers. They accused him of harboring men who acted against Caesar's decrees by proclaiming another king, Jesus. The rulers took security from Jason and the others and then released them. By inference, this pledge was linked to the missionaries leaving the city, since they departed that night (Acts 17:10). A Jason is also among Paul's "kinsmen" who send greetings in Rom 16:21. Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries take him to be probably the same man. Smith's also notes a conjecture that he is the Secundus of Acts 20:4. The name was a common Greek form used by Jews named Joshua.

Jehu son of Hanani was a prophet who delivered the word of the LORD against Baasha, king of Israel, and his house. He condemned Baasha for doing evil and following the ways of Jeroboam (1 Kgs 16:1, 7). That prophecy was fulfilled when Zimri destroyed Baasha's whole family (1 Kgs 16:12). Much later Jehu went out to meet King Jehoshaphat of Judah and rebuked him for helping the ungodly. The context makes clear this meant his alliance with Ahab (2 Chr 19:2). Jehu also wrote an account of Jehoshaphat's acts, which was included in the book of the kings of Israel (2 Chr 20:34). Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests his father was probably the seer Hanani who confronted King Asa (2 Chr 16:7). It also notes that about thirty years separate his two recorded appearances, so he probably began prophesying young. He is distinct from Jehu the king of Israel who shares his name.

Joses was one of the brothers of Jesus, named with James, Simon and Judas (Jude) when the people of Nazareth questioned Jesus' background. They asked whether he was not the carpenter, or the carpenter's son, whose mother was Mary (Matt 13:55; Mark 6:3). This entry treats Joses as a son of Joseph and Mary. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the Greek of Matt 13:55 reads "Joseph," as the Revised Version renders it. The Gospels also mention a Mary "the mother of James and Joses" among the women who watched the crucifixion from a distance and later saw where Jesus was buried (Matt 27:56; Mark 15:40, 47). Mark calls this James "the less." It is uncertain whether these sons are the same as Jesus' brothers. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia considers it possible, while many readers take this Mary to be a different woman.

Kenaz was the father of Othniel, the first judge of Israel, and of Seraiah (1 Chr 4:13). He is known only through his sons. Othniel captured a Canaanite city for Caleb and received Caleb's daughter Achsah as his wife. He later delivered Israel from Cushan-rishathaim, after which the land had rest forty years. The phrase "Othniel the son of Kenaz, Caleb's younger brother" can be read two ways. Easton's Bible Dictionary takes Kenaz to be Caleb's younger brother and so a son of Jephunneh, and this entry follows that reading. Others take the brother to be Othniel himself. Easton's also notes that the family remained prominent down to David's time (1 Chr 27:15). Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the name's meaning as "this purchase" or "this lamentation." Several other men in the Bible are also named Kenaz.

Lebbaeus Thaddaeus was one of the twelve apostles chosen by Jesus. Matthew calls him “Lebbaeus, whose surname was Thaddaeus” and Mark calls him Thaddaeus. Luke and Acts list “Judas the brother of James” at the same point in their lists, and the names are generally taken as one man. He is probably the “Judas, not Iscariot” who asked Jesus how he would show himself to the disciples and not to the world (John 14:22). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia reads the Greek as “Judas of James,” meaning son of James. This entry follows the King James “brother” and takes that James to be James son of Alphaeus, which makes Alphaeus his father. After the ascension he was with the eleven in the upper room. Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies him with Jude, author of the epistle, and Smith's Bible Dictionary notes a tradition linking him with the church at Edessa.

Lotan was the first-named son of Seir the Horite, whose family lived in the land later known as Edom before Esau's descendants settled there (Gen 36:20; 1 Chr 1:38). Smith's Bible Dictionary calls him the eldest son, probably because he heads every list of Seir's sons. His brothers were Shobal, Zibeon, Anah, Dishon, Ezer and Dishan, and his sister was Timna, who is named alongside him in both genealogies (Gen 36:22; 1 Chr 1:39). He had two sons, Hori and Homam. Genesis spells the second name Hemam and Chronicles spells it Homam. Lotan also appears among the Horite chiefs, called "dukes" in the King James Version (Gen 36:29). Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "coverer."

Magog was the second of the seven sons of Japheth, Noah's son, named in the table of nations alongside Gomer, Madai, Javan, Tubal, Meshech and Tiras (Gen 10:2; 1 Chr 1:5). Elsewhere the name refers to a people or land. Ezekiel speaks of "Gog, the land of Magog," whose ruler is chief prince of Meshech and Tubal, and says God will send fire on Magog (Ezek 38:2; 39:6). In Rev 20:8, "Gog and Magog" stand for the nations of the four quarters of the earth gathered for battle. The people's identity is uncertain. Josephus links the Magogites with the Scythians, a view also taken by Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries. Others connect the name with Gyges (Gugu), king of Lydia. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that Magog may simply be a variant of Gog.

Mattithiah (meaning "gift of Yah," according to the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia) was a Levite musician in the time of King David and one of the sons of Jeduthun. Several men in the Bible share this name. He and his brothers served under their father, who prophesied with the harp to give thanks and praise to the LORD (1 Chr 25:3). When the temple musicians were divided by lot into twenty-four groups, the fourteenth lot fell to Mattithiah, whose group of sons and relatives numbered twelve (1 Chr 25:21). A Mattithiah also appears among the Levites of the second rank who played harps when the ark was brought to Jerusalem (1 Chr 15:18, 21). He was later appointed to minister before the ark under Asaph (1 Chr 16:5). Reference works differ on whether these passages describe one man. This entry treats them as the same person.

Meshelemiah was a Levite of the Korahite clan, son of Kore and descended from Asaph. He headed one of the divisions of gatekeepers (porters) at the sanctuary. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary place him in the reign of David. He had seven sons. Zechariah the firstborn, Jediael, Zebadiah and Jathniel are named here, and Elam, Jehohanan and Elioenai in the following verse (1 Chr 26:3). His sons and relatives together numbered eighteen able men. When lots were cast to assign the gates, the east gate fell to him, under the shorter name Shelemiah. His son Zechariah, described as a wise counsellor, received the north gate. Zechariah is also remembered as keeper of the door of the tabernacle. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia further identifies Meshelemiah with the Shallum of 1 Chr 9:17–31 and the Meshullam of Neh 12:25.

Michael is the angel described in Daniel as "one of the chief princes," who came to help the heavenly messenger speaking to Daniel when the prince of the kingdom of Persia opposed him for twenty-one days (Dan 10:13). He is called the prince of Daniel's people, the one who stands with that messenger (Dan 10:21), and "the great prince" who will stand up for Israel at a time of unparalleled trouble, when those written in the book will be delivered (Dan 12:1). Jude calls him "the archangel" and says that when he disputed with the devil over the body of Moses, he did not bring a railing accusation but said, "The Lord rebuke thee" (Jude 1:9). In Revelation, Michael and his angels fight against the dragon in a war in heaven (Rev 12:7). Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "who is like God?" Other men in the Bible share the name.

Nathan was a son of King David and Bathsheba, born in Jerusalem. He was one of four sons Bathsheba bore to David, along with Shammua (or Shimea), Shobab and Solomon. 1 Chr 3:5 calls his mother Bathshua the daughter of Ammiel. He should not be confused with Nathan the prophet of David's court. Luke's genealogy of Jesus runs through this Nathan rather than through Solomon, naming Mattatha as his son. Easton's Bible Dictionary takes Luke's list to be the genealogy of Mary. Zech 12:12 speaks of the mourning of "the family of the house of Nathan" beside the house of David. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats this as a family name, and it probably refers to this son's descendants, though the reference is not certain. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "given."

Nebajoth, also spelled Nebaioth, was the firstborn son of Ishmael and heads the list of Ishmael's twelve sons, followed by Kedar, Adbeel, Mibsam and the others (Gen 25:13; 1 Chr 1:29). His sister married Esau. She is called Mahalath in Gen 28:9 and Bashemath in Gen 36:3, probably two names for the same woman. The name also stands for the tribe descended from him. Isaiah pairs "the rams of Nebaioth" with "the flocks of Kedar" as offerings brought to God's altar (Isa 60:7), which points to a herding people. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia note that Josephus and Jerome identified this tribe with the Nabataeans, whose capital was Petra. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia adds that the two names are spelled with different Hebrew consonants, so the link is uncertain.

Nethaneel, son of Zuar, was the leader of the tribe of Issachar during Israel's time in the wilderness after the Exodus. He was named as Issachar's representative to help Moses and Aaron take the census of Israel's fighting men (Num 1:8). In the arrangement of the camp, Issachar pitched its tents next to Judah on the east side of the tabernacle, with Nethaneel as its captain (Num 2:5). When the tribal leaders brought gifts for the dedication of the altar, he presented his offering on the second day. It included animals for peace offerings (Num 7:18, 23). When the camp set out from Sinai, he commanded Issachar's division (Num 10:15). Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "given of God." Several other men in the Bible bear this name, and this entry concerns only the son of Zuar.

Nicodemus was a Pharisee and "a ruler of the Jews" who appears only in John's Gospel. He came to Jesus by night, and in the conversation that followed he asked how a grown man could be born a second time and how such things could be (John 3:1–9). Later, when the chief priests and Pharisees were moving against Jesus at the time of the Feast of Tabernacles, Nicodemus, "being one of them," spoke up in their council. The surrounding passage shows him objecting that the law does not judge a man without first hearing him. After the crucifixion he joined Joseph of Arimathea, as the context of John 19 indicates, bringing about a hundred pounds of myrrh and aloes for Jesus' burial. Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies him as a member of the Sanhedrin. His name means "victory of the people" (Hitchcock's Bible Names).

Nimshi was the father of Jehoshaphat and the grandfather of Jehu, the army commander who became king of northern Israel and overthrew the house of Ahab. He is known only through his descendant. The fuller form of Jehu's lineage, "Jehu the son of Jehoshaphat the son of Nimshi" (2 Kgs 9:2, 14), shows Nimshi to be the grandfather. Elsewhere Jehu is simply called "the son of Nimshi," in the sense of a descendant, when God tells Elijah to anoint him (1 Kgs 19:16), when a watchman recognizes his furious driving (2 Kgs 9:20), and in the Chronicler's account of Ahaziah's death (2 Chr 22:7). That Jehu was usually named after his grandfather suggests Nimshi was the better-known figure of the family, though nothing more is recorded about him. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "rescued from danger."

Ocran was a man of the tribe of Asher, known only as the father of Pagiel. He appears solely in the phrase "Pagiel the son of Ocran" in the book of Numbers. There his son is named as Asher's representative at the census taken in the wilderness (Num 1:13). Pagiel also led Asher's tribe in the camp around the tabernacle and on the march (Num 2:27; Num 10:26), and he brought Asher's offering on the eleventh day of the altar's dedication (Num 7:72, 77). Ocran therefore probably lived during the Exodus generation or shortly before it, though nothing else is recorded about him. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of his name as "a disturber," and Smith's Bible Dictionary renders it "troubled." Some reference works spell the name Ochran.

Pagiel was the son of Ocran and the leader of the tribe of Asher during Israel's time in the wilderness. He is named among the tribal heads who helped Moses take the census of Israel (Num 1:13). In the arrangement of the camp he was captain of Asher, which camped next to Dan, by inference from the context on the north side of the tabernacle (Num 2:27). When the altar was dedicated, each tribal prince brought gifts on his own day, and Pagiel brought Asher's offering on the eleventh day. His gifts matched those of the other princes and included peace offerings of oxen, rams, goats and lambs (Num 7:72, 77). When Israel set out from Sinai, he commanded Asher's troops (Num 10:26). His name is usually explained as "God's intervention" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia) or "God allots" (Easton's Bible Dictionary).

Pallu was the second of the four sons of Reuben, Jacob's firstborn. His brothers were Hanoch, Hezron and Carmi, and he appears second in every list of them. Genesis 46:9 spells his name Phallu and places him among the family members who went down to Egypt with Jacob. Exodus 6:14 names him as the head of a father's house within Reuben. In the wilderness census he is the founder of the Palluite clan of the tribe (Num 26:5). His son was Eliab, and the next verse, Num 26:9, names Eliab's sons as Nemuel, Dathan and Abiram, the Dathan and Abiram who later joined Korah's rebellion. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests that Peleth in Num 16:1 may be the same man. Smith's Bible Dictionary and that encyclopedia take the name to mean "distinguished".

Pashur, son of Malchijah, was a priest and the ancestor of a priestly family that returned from exile in Babylon. The genealogies of Adaiah, a priest who lived in Jerusalem after the return, trace his line back to Pashur. 1 Chr 9:12 gives a short form of the line, and Neh 11:12 gives a longer one that names Pashur's son Zechariah. The family known as the children of Pashur numbered 1,247 among those who came back from exile (Ezra 2:38; Neh 7:41). Later, several of its members were among the priests who had married foreign wives in Ezra's time (Ezra 10:22). Several men in the Bible share this name. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both suggest he may be the Pashur son of Malchiah who served as an official under King Zedekiah (Jer 38:1), but this identification is uncertain.

Pedahzur was a man of the tribe of Manasseh, known only as the father of Gamaliel, the leader of that tribe during the wilderness period after the Exodus. He appears solely in Gamaliel's identifying phrase "Gamaliel the son of Pedahzur." That phrase is used when Gamaliel is named to help Moses take the census (Num 1:10), when he is set as captain of Manasseh in the camp (Num 2:20), when he brings his tribe's offering on the eighth day of the altar's dedication (Num 7:54, 59), and when he leads Manasseh's company on the march (Num 10:23). Nothing else is recorded about Pedahzur himself. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "rock of redemption," and Hitchcock's Bible Names renders it "strong or powerful savior" or "stone of redemption."

Pharaoh here is the Egyptian king who oppressed the Israelites in the years before and around the birth of Moses. "Pharaoh" was the title of Egypt's rulers, so the name belongs to several different kings in the Bible. This one set taskmasters over the Hebrews and made them build the store cities of Pithom and Raamses for him (Exod 1:11). When the Hebrew midwives failed to kill newborn boys, he ordered his people to throw every Hebrew son into the river (Exod 1:19, 22). His daughter found the infant Moses in a basket among the reeds (Exod 2:5). Later, when he heard that Moses had killed an Egyptian, he tried to kill him, and Moses fled to Midian (Exod 2:15). His identity is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that he was long thought to be Ahmose I, but it favors Seti I, father of Rameses II.

Pharaoh in these passages is the king of Egypt in the time of King Hezekiah of Judah, probably the late eighth century BC. When the Assyrian king Sennacherib threatened Jerusalem, Judah looked to this Pharaoh for help. The Assyrian envoy mocked that hope, calling Egypt a broken reed that pierces the hand of anyone who leans on it (2 Kgs 18:21; Isa 36:6). Isaiah likewise condemned those who went down to Egypt to rely on Pharaoh's strength, warning that it would bring them shame (Isa 30:2–3). He also ridiculed the counsellors of Pharaoh at Zoan (Isa 19:11), probably the same king or one close in time. The Bible does not give this king's personal name, and the title was used for many Egyptian rulers. Smith's Bible Dictionary identifies him with Sethos, a king named by Herodotus. The nearby account in 2 Kgs 19:9 mentions Tirhakah, king of Ethiopia, marching against Sennacherib.

Rehum was one of the leaders who returned to Jerusalem with Zerubbabel after the Babylonian exile. He is listed among the heads of the returning community in Ezra 2:2, and the parallel list in Neh 7:7 gives the name as Nehum, which the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia takes as a copying variant. Neh 12:3 names a Rehum among the priests who went up with Zerubbabel. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests this should probably read Harim, the priestly house whose head in the next generation was Adna (Neh 12:15). A Harim also appears among the priests who sealed the covenant in Nehemiah's day (Neh 10:5). This entry treats these names as one figure. Smith's Bible Dictionary instead distinguishes the leader of Ezra 2:2 from the priestly Rehum of Neh 12:3. Because the name is shared by several people, the exact identifications remain uncertain.

Seraiah was a Levite priest, the son of Azariah and the father of Jehozadak (also called Josedech), in the high-priestly line recorded in 1 Chr 6:14. He served as chief priest in Jerusalem when the city fell to Babylon in the reign of Zedekiah. The captain of the guard took him prisoner, along with Zephaniah the second priest and the three doorkeepers (2 Kgs 25:18; Jer 52:24). The following verses (2 Kgs 25:21; Jer 52:27) report that he was put to death at Riblah. Ezra the scribe is called "the son of Seraiah, the son of Azariah" (Ezra 7:1). Since Ezra lived long after the exile, this probably means he was a descendant rather than a son. Nehemiah 11:11 names a Seraiah "son of Hilkiah" as ruler of the house of God. The ancestry there overlaps with this line, but it is uncertain whether it refers to the same man or a later namesake.

Shallum was a Levite in the high-priestly line descended from Aaron. He was the son of Zadok and the father of Hilkiah (1 Chr 6:12–13). Ezra the scribe traced his own ancestry through him (Ezra 7:2). In 1 Chr 9:11 and Neh 11:11 he appears as Meshullam, in genealogies of Azariah and Seraiah, who are each called "the ruler of the house of God". Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both treat Shallum and Meshullam as the same man and regard him as a high priest. Smith's places him probably in the reign of Amon, which fits his son being the Hilkiah who served as high priest under Josiah. The texts themselves give only his place in the family line. Several other men in the Bible are also named Shallum or Meshullam.

Shallum son of Kore was a Levite of the Korahite family who served as chief of the gatekeepers ("porters") of the sanctuary. 1 Chr 9:19 traces his line through Kore and Ebiasaph back to Korah and says he and his kin guarded the gates of the tabernacle, as their fathers had kept the entry. His firstborn son Mattithiah was in charge of the baked goods made in pans (1 Chr 9:31). "The children of Shallum" appear among the gatekeeper families who returned from exile (Ezra 2:42; Neh 7:45). Easton's Bible Dictionary places him in the reign of David. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identifies him with the gatekeeper called Meshelemiah or Shelemiah in 1 Chr 26. Several other men in the Bible share the name Shallum.

Shammah was the third son of Jesse of the tribe of Judah, and an older brother of David. When the prophet Samuel came to Bethlehem to anoint a king, Jesse had Shammah pass before him, but Samuel said the LORD had not chosen him (1 Sam 16:9). He was one of Jesse's three eldest sons, with Eliab and Abinadab, who followed Saul to war against the Philistines (1 Sam 17:13). He is also called Shimeah (2 Sam 13:3) and Shimma (1 Chr 2:13). As Shimeah he was the father of Jonadab, a shrewd friend of Amnon, who later told David that only Amnon, not all the king's sons, had been killed by Absalom's order (2 Sam 13:32). Reference works such as the Tyndale House proper names list also link him to a son Jonathan, named in a later passage. Several other men in the Bible share the name Shammah.

Shedeur was a man of the tribe of Reuben, known only as the father of Elizur. Elizur was the leader of Reuben during the wilderness journey after the exodus from Egypt. He was chosen to help Moses with the census (Num 1:5) and served as captain of Reuben's camp, which was stationed on the south side of the tabernacle (Num 2:10). On the fourth day of the dedication of the altar he brought his tribe's offering (Num 7:30, 35), and he led Reuben's host when the camp set out (Num 10:18). Nothing is recorded about Shedeur himself apart from his son. The meaning of the name is uncertain. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "darter of light," and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives "daybreak" while noting a proposed reading, "Shaddai is flame." Hitchcock's Bible Names offers "light of the Almighty."

Shelumiel, son of Zurishaddai, was the leader of the tribe of Simeon during Israel's time in the wilderness after the exodus. He was named as Simeon's representative when Moses took the census (Num 1:6). In the arrangement of the camp, Simeon camped beside Reuben on the south side, with Shelumiel as its captain (Num 2:12). When the tribal leaders brought gifts for the dedication of the altar, he presented Simeon's offering on the fifth day, including animals for peace offerings (Num 7:36, 41). When Israel set out from Sinai, he commanded Simeon's contingent (Num 10:19). The meaning of his name is uncertain. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "friend of God," and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests "at peace with God."
