The Greek Old Testament spells the name Salamiel, and the book of Judith traces Judith's ancestry back to him.

Shemaiah was a prophet, called "the man of God," in the reign of Rehoboam king of Judah. When Rehoboam gathered an army to win back the northern tribes that had broken away under Jeroboam, God's word came to Shemaiah. The surrounding verses (1 Kgs 12:23–24) show that he told the king not to fight, and the troops went home. Later, when Shishak king of Egypt invaded Judah, Shemaiah told Rehoboam and the princes gathered in Jerusalem that because they had forsaken the LORD, the LORD had left them in Shishak's hand. After they humbled themselves, he announced that Jerusalem would not be destroyed, though some deliverance only would be granted. Chronicles names "the book of Shemaiah the prophet" as a record of Rehoboam's acts. Several other men in the Bible share this name, which means "the LORD hears" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia).

Sherebiah was a Levite of the period after the exile who came to Jerusalem with Ezra. When Ezra asked for Levites to join his group at the river Ahava, Sherebiah was brought, along with his sons and relatives, eighteen men in all (Ezra 8:18). Ezra then set him apart with Hashabiah and others to carry the silver, gold and vessels given for the temple (Ezra 8:24). Later, in Nehemiah's time, he was among the Levites who helped the people understand the law as Ezra read it (Neh 8:7), and he stood with other Levites to lead the people in confession and praise (Neh 9:4–5). Smith's Bible Dictionary adds that he signed the covenant (Neh 10:12). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the name may also refer to a Levite family, since it recurs in later lists. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives its meaning as "singing with the Lord."

Shobal was a son of Seir the Horite, one of the original inhabitants of the land later known as Edom, and he is listed second among Seir's sons (Gen 36:20; 1 Chr 1:38). His brothers were Lotan, Zibeon, Anah, Dishon, Ezer and Dishan, and Timna was his sister. He is also named among the Horite chiefs, called "dukes" in the King James Version (Gen 36:29). His sons were Alvan, Manahath, Ebal, Shepho and Onam (Gen 36:23). In 1 Chr 1:40 two of these names appear in slightly different forms, Alian and Shephi, probably variant spellings of the same names. Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries describe him as the second son of Seir. The name Shobal is shared by several people in the Bible, and this entry concerns only the Horite chief.

Sibbechai the Hushathite was one of David's mighty men and a commander in his army. In a battle with the Philistines he killed a descendant of the giants, called Saph in 2 Sam 21:18, where the battle is placed at Gob, and Sippai in 1 Chr 20:4, where it is placed at Gezer. He appears among David's warriors as Sibbecai in 1 Chr 11:29. In the parallel list at 2 Sam 23:27 the same position is held by Mebunnai the Hushathite, which reference works such as Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia take as the same man, the difference probably arising from the similar Hebrew spelling of the two names. He was the eighth of the monthly army captains, leading a division of 24,000 in the eighth month, and belonged to the Zarhites, a clan of Judah. "Hushathite" probably refers to his hometown.

Talmon was a Levite gatekeeper ("porter") at the temple in Jerusalem, named with Shallum, Akkub and Ahiman among the gatekeepers in 1 Chr 9:17. The name also marks a family of gatekeepers: "the children of Talmon" appear among those who returned from exile in Babylon with Zerubbabel (Ezra 2:42; Neh 7:45). Talmon is listed again with Akkub among the gatekeepers living in Jerusalem in Nehemiah's time (Neh 11:19), and among the porters who guarded the storehouses at the gates (Neh 12:25). Because these mentions span several generations, it is uncertain whether they refer to one man, to several men of the same family, or to the family as a whole. Smith's Bible Dictionary takes Talmon as the head of a family of door-keepers whose descendants kept the hereditary office after the exile.

Tirzah was one of the five daughters of Zelophehad, a descendant of Manasseh son of Joseph through Machir, Gilead and Hepher (Num 27:1; Josh 17:3). Because Zelophehad had no sons, she and her sisters Mahlah, Noah, Hoglah and Milcah came forward about their father's inheritance. By inference from the surrounding passages, they were granted land among his clan in place of male heirs (Num 26:33; Num 27:1; Josh 17:3). Later, the sisters married sons of their father's brothers, which kept the land within their tribe (Num 36:11). Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary call her the youngest, since she is usually named last, although Num 36:11 lists her second. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of her name as "pleasing". The same name belongs to the city of Tirzah, a royal city of the northern kingdom (1 Kgs 15:33), which is a separate place.

Tychicus was a Christian from the province of Asia and a companion of Paul. He was one of the group who traveled with Paul on the journey from Greece and Macedonia toward Jerusalem (Acts 20:4). Paul calls him "a beloved brother and faithful minister in the Lord" and sent him to bring news of Paul's circumstances to the believers at Ephesus and Colossae (Eph 6:21; Col 4:7). By inference, he probably carried those letters. In later letters Paul mentions sending him to Ephesus (2 Tim 4:12) and considered sending him or Artemas to Titus in Crete (Titus 3:12). Easton's Bible Dictionary takes him to have been with Paul at Rome. Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests he and Trophimus may have been the two brothers who helped Titus with the collection for the believers in Judea. His name means "by chance" or "fortunate."

Uri was a man of the tribe of Judah, the son of Hur and the father of Bezaleel, the craftsman God called by name to make the tabernacle and its furnishings (Exod 31:2; 38:22). He is known only through his son, who is regularly identified as "the son of Uri, the son of Hur". The genealogy in 1 Chr 2:20 records the line Hur, Uri, Bezaleel. By inference from 1 Chr 2:19, Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him as a grandson of Caleb son of Hezron. His listed brothers, including Shobal, Salma and Hareph, are named as sons of Hur in the Judah genealogies of 1 Chr 2:50–51 and 1 Chr 4:3–4. His name is usually explained as "fiery", or "my light" according to Hitchcock's Bible Names. Several other men in the Bible share the name Uri.

Urijah, also called Uriah, was a priest in Jerusalem during the reign of King Ahaz of Judah. When Ahaz went to Damascus to meet Tiglath-pileser king of Assyria, he saw an altar there and sent its design to Urijah. Urijah built a copy before the king returned (2 Kgs 16:10–11). Ahaz then ordered that the regular morning and evening offerings, the king's sacrifices and the people's offerings all be made on this new "great altar," while the old bronze altar was kept for the king to enquire by. Urijah did everything the king commanded (2 Kgs 16:15–16). Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary describe him as high priest. The "Uriah the priest" whom Isaiah took as a reliable witness (Isa 8:2) is probably the same man, as Smith's Bible Dictionary holds, and this entry follows that view. Other people in the Bible share the name.

Zebul was the ruler of the city of Shechem and the officer of Abimelech, son of Jerubbaal (Gideon), during Abimelech's rule there (Judg 9:28, 30). When Gaal son of Ebed stirred up the Shechemites against Abimelech, mocking both him and "Zebul his officer," Zebul grew angry. By inference from the surrounding verses (Judg 9:31–33), he secretly warned Abimelech, who was living at Arumah, and urged him to come against the city. As Abimelech's troops approached, Zebul at first told Gaal that he was only seeing the shadows of the mountains. Then he challenged Gaal to back up his boasts and go out and fight (Judg 9:36, 38). After Gaal was defeated, Zebul drove him and his brothers out of Shechem (Judg 9:41). The name is usually taken to mean "habitation" (Hitchcock's Bible Names; Easton's Bible Dictionary).

Zedekiah son of Chenaanah was a prophet at the court of Ahab king of Israel. Easton's Bible Dictionary calls him a false prophet. When Ahab and Jehoshaphat of Judah consulted the prophets about going to war against the Syrians at Ramoth-gilead, Zedekiah made horns of iron and declared in the LORD's name that with them Ahab would push the Syrians until they were destroyed. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia takes him to be the leader and spokesman of the 400 court prophets. When the prophet Micaiah foretold disaster, Zedekiah struck him on the cheek and mockingly asked which way the Spirit of the LORD had gone from him to speak to Micaiah. The story is told both in 1 Kings 22 and in its parallel, 2 Chronicles 18. His name means "the LORD is my righteousness." Several people share the name. He is distinct from Zedekiah the last king of Judah, whose blinding is recorded in Jer 39:7.

Zerahiah was a priest of the tribe of Levi, descended from Aaron through Eleazar, in the high-priestly line recorded in 1 Chronicles. He was the son of Uzzi, grandson of Bukki, and the father of Meraioth (1 Chr 6:6, 51). Ezra the scribe traced his ancestry through him (Ezra 7:4). His name is usually explained as meaning "the Lord has risen." Nothing is recorded of his life beyond these genealogies. The lists in 1 Chr 9:11 and Neh 11:11 name a "Meraioth, the son of Ahitub" in the ancestry of the chief priests. Following STEPBible's Tyndale House name index, this entry treats that Ahitub as another name for Zerahiah, since Zerahiah's son was Meraioth. The fuller list in 1 Chronicles 6 also has a later Ahitub, the father of Zadok, so the identification is uncertain. Several other people in the Bible share the name Zerahiah.

Zibeon was a son of Seir the Horite, one of the original inhabitants of the land of Seir, later Edom. His brothers were Lotan, Shobal, Anah, Dishon, Ezer and Dishan, and Timna was his sister. He is listed among the Horite chiefs ("dukes" in the King James Version). His sons were Ajah, also spelled Aiah, and Anah. This Anah is remembered for finding "the mules" in the wilderness while tending his father's donkeys, a phrase some translations render as "hot springs." Genesis 36:2 also names a Zibeon the Hivite as the father of Anah, whose daughter Aholibamah married Esau. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both take him to be this same Horite Zibeon. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives the name's meaning as "hyena"; Smith's gives "robber."

Zuar was a man of the tribe of Issachar, known only as the father of Nethaneel, who led that tribe during the wilderness period after the exodus. Each of his five mentions comes in the phrase "Nethaneel the son of Zuar." They describe Nethaneel as the tribe's representative at the census (Num 1:8), as captain of Issachar's camp next to Judah (Num 2:5), as the prince who brought the tribe's offering on the second day of the altar's dedication (Num 7:18, 23), and as commander of Issachar's host when Israel set out from Sinai (Num 10:15). Nothing else is recorded about Zuar himself. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia give the meaning of his name as "littleness" or "little one."

Zurishaddai was a man of the tribe of Simeon, known only as the father of Shelumiel. Shelumiel was chosen to help Moses count Israel in the wilderness (Num 1:6) and served as captain of the Simeonites. He led them when they camped beside the tribe of Reuben (Num 2:12) and when they set out on the march (Num 10:19). On the fifth day of the offerings for the dedication of the altar, he presented Simeon's gifts (Num 7:36, 41). By inference, Zurishaddai himself belonged to Simeon and lived in the generation before the exodus. Nothing more is recorded about him. His name means "my rock is the Almighty" (Smith's Bible Dictionary), which combines the Hebrew word for rock with Shaddai, a title for God.

Abiezer was a descendant of Manasseh son of Joseph and the founder of a clan within that tribe. In Num 26:30 he appears as Jeezer, a son of Gilead, whose descendants were the Jeezerites. Josh 17:2 lists the children of Abiezer among the Manassite families that received a share of land. Easton's Bible Dictionary, drawing on 1 Chr 7:18, makes him instead a son of Hammoleketh, Gilead's sister. This entry follows the listing as a son of Gilead. His clan later produced the judge Gideon. When Gideon blew the trumpet, Abiezer gathered to him (Judg 6:34), and Gideon spoke of the "vintage of Abiezer" while calming the men of Ephraim (Judg 8:2). Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning as "father of help." Several other men in the Bible share this name.

Abinadab was a man of Kirjath-jearim whose house sheltered the ark of the LORD after the Philistines sent it back. The men of the town brought the ark to his house "in the hill" and consecrated his son Eleazar to look after it (1 Sam 7:1). According to 1 Sam 7:2 it stayed there twenty years. When David later moved it, Abinadab's sons Uzzah and Ahio drove the new cart that carried it from the house, with Ahio walking ahead (2 Sam 6:3–4; 1 Chr 13:7). The following verses record that Uzzah died after touching the ark. The "Gibeah" of 2 Samuel is probably not a separate town but the Hebrew word for "hill," pointing to the same hilltop house. Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries describe him as a Levite. Several other men in the Bible share his name, including a son of Jesse and a son of Saul.

Abinoam was the father of Barak, the Israelite commander who, with the prophetess Deborah, led the army that defeated the Canaanite forces under Sisera. He is known only through his son, who is called "Barak the son of Abinoam" each time the name appears (Judg 4:6, 12; 5:1, 12). Barak was summoned from Kedesh-naphtali, so the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia describes Abinoam as a man of that town, a reasonable inference from the passage. Twice the phrase comes in the Song of Deborah, which celebrates the victory (Judg 5:1, 12). Nothing else is recorded about him. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "father of kindness," and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives "father of pleasantness." Smith's Bible Dictionary dates the period to about 1300 BC, an estimate.

Abishua was a Levite priest, the son of Phinehas and grandson of Eleazar, Aaron's son. He appears only in genealogies of Aaron's descendants, where he is named as the father of Bukki, who in turn was the father of Uzzi (1 Chr 6:4–5, 50). Ezra 7:5 traces Ezra's own priestly ancestry back through Abishua to Aaron. Smith's Bible Dictionary places him in the line of the high priests, and because his father Phinehas and grandfather Eleazar held that office, he is probably to be counted among them, though the verses themselves do not say he served as high priest. Nothing else is recorded of his life. The name is shared by another man, a Benjamite descendant of Bela, who is a different person. The meaning of the name is uncertain; suggestions include "father of deliverance" (Smith's) and "father of wealth" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia).

Achsah was the daughter of Caleb. Her name probably means "anklet," according to Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries. Caleb promised her as a wife to the man who would attack and capture Kirjath-sepher, also called Debir. Othniel the son of Kenaz took the city and so received her in marriage. Othniel is described as Caleb's younger brother, though the wording may also be read as making him a younger kinsman, as the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia puts it. The account appears twice, in Joshua and again in Judges. The verses that follow in both books (Josh 15:18–19; Judg 1:14–15) tell how she asked her father for land and springs of water, and he gave her the upper and lower springs. Her brothers Iru, Elah and Naam are named in a genealogy of Caleb's family (1 Chr 4:15).

Ahaz was a Benjamite descendant of King Saul. He was the son of Micah and the brother of Pithon, Melech and Tarea (spelled Tahrea in 1 Chr 9:41). He appears only in the two parallel genealogies of Saul's family in 1 Chronicles. The surrounding verses trace Micah back to Merib-baal, son of Jonathan, so Ahaz was Jonathan's great-grandson. Easton's Bible Dictionary calls him Jonathan's grandson. His son is called Jehoadah in 1 Chr 8:36 and Jarah in 1 Chr 9:42. Both lists give the same descendants, Alemeth, Azmaveth and Zimri, followed by Moza, so the two names probably refer to one person spelled differently. Nothing else is recorded about him. He is a different person from the better-known Ahaz, king of Judah. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the name's meaning as "one that takes or possesses."

Ahijah was the father of Baasha, the man who seized the throne of the northern kingdom of Israel. He is known only through his son, who is repeatedly called "Baasha the son of Ahijah." The family belonged to the tribe of Issachar (1 Kgs 15:27). Baasha conspired against King Nadab, killed him at Gibbethon, and then reigned over Israel from Tirzah for twenty-four years, beginning in the third year of Asa king of Judah (1 Kgs 15:33). Ahijah's name appears again when prophets compare the coming downfall of Ahab's house to the fate of "the house of Baasha the son of Ahijah" (1 Kgs 21:22; 2 Kgs 9:9). Nothing else is recorded about him. Several other men in the Bible share the name, and this one should not be confused with Ahijah the prophet of Shiloh. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives the meaning of the name as "brother of Yahweh."

Aholah is a figurative woman in Ezekiel's allegory of two sisters, the elder of the pair, with Aholibah as her younger sister. Ezekiel 23:4 states plainly that Aholah stands for Samaria, capital of the northern kingdom of Israel, and Aholibah for Jerusalem. Both sisters are said to belong to the LORD and to bear sons and daughters. Aholah is then accused of playing the harlot by doting on the Assyrians, her neighbours, which pictures Samaria's political and religious ties with Assyria. Later the prophet is told to judge both sisters and declare their abominations, and they are called lewd women. The name appears in modern translations as Oholah. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives its meaning as "his tent" or "his tabernacle." She is a symbolic figure, not a historical person.

Aiah was the father of Rizpah, a concubine of King Saul. He appears only as part of her name, "Rizpah the daughter of Aiah". Nothing is said about his own life, family line or home. His daughter comes into the account twice. First, Ishbosheth accused Abner of sleeping with her after Saul's death (2 Sam 3:7). Later, her two sons by Saul, Armoni and Mephibosheth, were handed over by David and put to death. Rizpah then guarded their bodies on a rock from the beginning of harvest until the rains came, and David was told what she had done (2 Sam 21:8–11). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia takes the name to mean "falcon" and lists a different Aiah, an Edomite son of Zibeon, elsewhere in Genesis.

Alphaeus was the father of James, one of the twelve apostles, who is called "James the son of Alphaeus" in every list of the Twelve to tell him apart from James the son of Zebedee. Nothing is recorded about Alphaeus himself. This entry also counts Lebbaeus Thaddaeus as his son. That follows from reading "Judas the brother of James" in Acts 1:13 and Luke 6:16 as the same apostle called Thaddaeus in Matthew and Mark. His name appears in the Acts list of apostles gathered in the upper room before Matthias was chosen to replace Judas. Several people share the name. Mark 2:14 calls Levi, also known as Matthew, a son of Alphaeus, and STEPBible's proper-name index treats both apostles as his sons. Easton's and Smith's Bible dictionaries identify Alphaeus with Clopas, the husband of the Mary mentioned in John 19:25.

Amorite is named in the table of nations as a son, or more likely a descendant people, of Canaan, listed alongside the Jebusite and the Girgasite (Gen 10:16; 1 Chr 1:14). The name stands both for an ancestor and for the nation traced to him, one of the peoples living in the land before Israel. Amos recalls the Amorite as a people as tall as cedars and strong as oaks, whom God destroyed before Israel. He calls Canaan "the land of the Amorite" that Israel came to possess after the exodus and forty years in the wilderness (Amos 2:9–10). Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries explain the name as "highlanders" or "mountaineers." They place the Amorites in the hill country west of the Dead Sea and toward Hebron, and east of the Jordan in the kingdoms of Sihon and Og. Easton's adds that the name was sometimes used broadly for the inhabitants of Canaan in general.

Annas was a Jewish high priest and the father-in-law of Caiaphas, who was high priest in the year Jesus was crucified (John 18:13). Luke dates the start of John the Baptist's ministry to the time when "Annas and Caiaphas" were high priests (Luke 3:2). After Jesus' arrest he was taken first to Annas, who questioned him and then sent him bound to Caiaphas (John 18:13, 24). Only John records this hearing. Annas appears again among the high priest's family at Jerusalem when Peter and John were brought to trial, about AD 30 by inference from context (Acts 4:6). Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries place his own term as high priest at AD 7–14, before Roman officials removed him. They explain his continued title in different ways. He may have kept the title because the office was held for life under the law of Moses, or he may have led the Sanhedrin or served as Caiaphas's deputy.

Arioch was the captain of the royal guard under King Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon, appearing in Daniel 2. When the king's wise men could not tell him his dream and its meaning, Arioch was appointed to carry out the order to kill all the wise men of Babylon. Daniel, who was among those to be killed, spoke to him with tact and asked why the decree was so hasty, and Arioch explained the matter. After the dream was revealed to Daniel, he went to Arioch, asked him to spare the wise men and to bring him before the king. Arioch hurried Daniel in, introducing him as a man from the captives of Judah who could give the interpretation. He is a different person from Arioch, king of Ellasar, who fought in Abraham's time (Gen 14:1).

Azariah was a priest of the tribe of Levi, the son of Hilkiah and the father of Seraiah, in the line of high priests descended from Zadok (1 Chr 6:13–14). His father Hilkiah was probably the high priest of King Josiah's reign, and Smith's Bible Dictionary identifies his son Seraiah with the chief priest put to death by Nebuchadnezzar. Ezra the scribe traces his descent through Seraiah and Azariah to Hilkiah (Ezra 7:1). There "son" likely means descendant, since generations seem to be skipped. 1 Chr 9:11 names an Azariah son of Hilkiah as "ruler of the house of God," probably the same man. Jer 29:3 mentions a Gemariah son of Hilkiah, who is likely his brother. The name was common among priests, and this Azariah is easily confused with others who bore it.

Azel was a Benjaminite descended from King Saul, named in the family line of Saul that appears twice in 1 Chronicles (1 Chr 8:37–38; 9:43–44). Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "noble." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia traces his descent through Saul's son Jonathan, which matches the surrounding verses (1 Chr 8:33–36), where the line runs from Jonathan through Merib-baal and Micah down to Moza. The genealogy names Moza's son Binea, followed by Rapha (or Rephaiah), Eleasah and Azel, each called "his son." This wording can mean successive generations, but this entry treats Binea as Azel's father and Rephaiah and Eleasah as his brothers. Azel had six sons: Azrikam, Bocheru, Ishmael, Sheariah, Obadiah and Hanan. Nothing else is recorded about him.

Baalhanan son of Achbor was one of the early kings of Edom, listed among the rulers who reigned there before Israel had a king. He succeeded Saul (spelled Shaul in 1 Chr 1:49), and after his death Hadar, called Hadad in 1 Chr 1:50, took the throne (Gen 36:38–39). Unlike several other kings in the list, no city is named for him, and nothing more is recorded of his reign. The name means "Baal is gracious" or "the lord is gracious," according to the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia. The same name is borne by at least one other man in the Bible. This entry concerns the Edomite king.

Baal-zebub was the god of the Philistine city of Ekron. He is mentioned only in the account of Ahaziah, king of Israel. After Ahaziah fell through a lattice in his upper room in Samaria and was injured, he sent messengers to ask Baal-zebub whether he would recover (2 Kgs 1:2). The angel of the LORD sent Elijah to meet the messengers and ask whether there was no God in Israel, so that they had to consult the god of Ekron. Elijah announced that Ahaziah would not leave his bed but would die (2 Kgs 1:3, 6, 16). The name means "lord of flies." Easton's Bible Dictionary explains it as a title for a god believed to ward off plagues of flies. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats the reason for the name as uncertain and notes only that he was known as a god who gave oracles.

Baanah was a son of Rimmon, a Beerothite of the tribe of Benjamin, and the brother of Rechab. He and Rechab were captains of raiding bands under Ishbosheth, Saul's son (2 Sam 4:2). The brothers came to Ishbosheth's house in the heat of the day while he lay resting at noon, entered as though to fetch wheat, struck him down, and escaped (2 Sam 4:5–6). They brought his head to David, probably hoping for a reward, but David answered them with an oath (2 Sam 4:9). The following verses of the same chapter, as Easton's Bible Dictionary summarizes, record that David had them put to death and their mutilated bodies hung up beside the pool at Hebron. The name Baanah is shared by several other people in the Bible, and this entry concerns only Rechab's brother.

Bartholomew was one of the twelve apostles chosen by Jesus. His name appears only in the lists of the Twelve (Matt 10:3; Mark 3:18; Luke 6:14) and among the eleven gathered in the upper room in Jerusalem after the ascension (Acts 1:13). As one of the Eleven he was presumably present when Matthias was chosen to replace Judas. The name means "son of Tolmai", so it is probably a family name rather than a personal one. In the first three Gospels he is always paired with Philip, while John's Gospel never mentions him but pairs Philip with Nathanael. For this reason many, including Easton's Bible Dictionary, identify Bartholomew with Nathanael, though the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes this has not been conclusively established. Later traditions, mentioned in Smith's Bible Dictionary, say he preached in India or Armenia.

Bela son of Beor was a king of Edom, the first named in the list of kings who reigned in Edom before any king reigned over the Israelites. His city was Dinhabah, a place not otherwise identified. When Bela died, Jobab son of Zerah of Bozrah succeeded him. The same brief account appears in Gen 36:32–33 and 1 Chr 1:43–44. Smith's Bible Dictionary places his reign about eight generations before Saul. Because his father shares the name Beor with the father of Balaam, some interpreters have linked the two, but the text makes no such connection. Several other people in the Bible are also named Bela, and this king should not be confused with them.

Ben-hadad, son of Hazael, was a king of Syria (Aram), ruling from Damascus. He is often called Ben-hadad III to set him apart from earlier kings of the same name. He succeeded his father on the throne (2 Kgs 13:24). Together with Hazael he is named as an oppressor of Israel (2 Kgs 13:3). After Hazael's death, Jehoash son of Jehoahaz, king of Israel, defeated Ben-hadad three times and recovered the Israelite cities that Syria had taken from his father Jehoahaz (2 Kgs 13:25). The prophet Amos announced fire on the house of Hazael that would consume "the palaces of Benhadad" (Amos 1:4). Easton's Bible Dictionary takes this as a reference to his defeats in war. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the name's meaning as "son of Hadad," Hadad being a Syrian god.

Carmi was the fourth and last-named son of Reuben, Jacob's firstborn, and the brother of Hanoch, Pallu and Hezron. He is listed among the descendants of Jacob who went down to Egypt (Gen 46:9), and he appears again among the heads of the fathers' houses of Reuben (Exod 6:14) and in the Reubenite genealogy of 1 Chr 5:3. In the census taken in the wilderness he is named as the ancestor of the clan of the Carmites within the tribe of Reuben (Num 26:6). Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "vine dresser," and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "my vineyard." Nothing else is recorded about his life. The same name belongs to other men in the Bible, including a man of the tribe of Judah, so this Carmi should not be confused with them.

Chenaanah was the father of Zedekiah, one of the prophets at the court of Ahab king of Israel. He is known only through his son's name. When Ahab and Jehoshaphat king of Judah were deciding whether to attack Ramoth-gilead, Zedekiah son of Chenaanah made iron horns and announced that the king would push the Syrians until they were destroyed (1 Kgs 22:11; 2 Chr 18:10). When the prophet Micaiah predicted defeat instead, Zedekiah struck him on the cheek (1 Kgs 22:24; 2 Chr 18:23). Nothing else is said about Chenaanah himself. Smith's Bible Dictionary allows that he may have been an earlier ancestor rather than Zedekiah's immediate father. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia distinguishes him from another man of the same name, a Benjamite, and explains the name as related to "Canaan".

Chimham was a man whom the aged Barzillai the Gileadite offered to King David in his own place when David crossed back over the Jordan after Absalom's rebellion. Barzillai asked to return home to die in his own city and asked the king to treat Chimham as he saw fit. David agreed and promised to do for Chimham whatever Barzillai wished (2 Sam 19:37–38). Chimham then went on with the king to Gilgal (2 Sam 19:40). The text calls him Barzillai's "servant," but Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia take him to be probably Barzillai's son. Centuries later, Jer 41:17 mentions "the habitation of Chimham" near Bethlehem, where refugees stopped on their way to Egypt. From this, both dictionaries infer that David gave Chimham land at Bethlehem, which kept his name, possibly as the site of a lodging place.

Daughter of Lot - Older was the elder of Lot's two daughters, called "the firstborn" in Genesis. She escaped with her father and sister when Sodom was destroyed, about 1897 BC by inference from context, and the three of them came to live in a cave. Believing there was no man left to marry them and that their father was old, she proposed to her younger sister that they make Lot drunk and lie with him to preserve his family line (Gen 19:31–34). She went to him first, and he did not know when she lay down or rose. The next day she urged her sister to do the same. She bore a son named Moab, whom the text identifies as the ancestor of the Moabites (Gen 19:37). Because Lot was the father of both sisters' children, her son Moab and her sister's son Ben-ammi were half-brothers to her as well as her sons and nephew.

Dishon was the fifth son of Seir the Horite, listed with his brothers Lotan, Shobal, Zibeon, Anah, Ezer and Dishan, and with a sister, Timna (Gen 36:21; 1 Chr 1:38). He was one of the Horite chiefs, or 'dukes,' who ruled in the land of Seir, later known as Edom, before and alongside Esau's descendants (Gen 36:30). His sons are named as Hemdan, Eshban, Ithran and Cheran (Gen 36:26). The name was also borne by his nephew, a son of Anah (Gen 36:25), and because the list of Dishon's sons comes right after that mention, which Dishon fathered them is uncertain. This entry follows the reading that makes them sons of Seir's son Dishon. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as 'antelope,' while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives 'fatness' or 'ashes.'

Doeg was an Edomite in the service of King Saul, described as the chief of Saul's herdsmen and as set over his servants. He happened to be at Nob, "detained before the LORD," on the day the priest Ahimelech helped David, who was fleeing from Saul. Doeg later reported what he had seen to the king. When Saul ordered him to attack the priests of Nob, Doeg killed eighty-five men who wore the linen ephod. Afterward David told Abiathar, the son of Ahimelech who escaped, that he had known Doeg would inform Saul, and he took responsibility for the deaths of Abiathar's family. The heading of Ps 52 links that psalm with Doeg's report to Saul, as Easton's Bible Dictionary notes. The Septuagint describes his job as tending mules, according to the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia.

Eglon was a king of Moab during the period of the judges. After the Israelites again did evil, the LORD strengthened him against Israel, and Israel served him for eighteen years (Judg 3:12, 14). Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that he allied with Ammon and Amalek and took Jericho, the "city of palm trees," as his base, drawing on the surrounding verse (Judg 3:13). This entry places that subjugation at about 1378 BC, a date inferred from context. When Israel cried to the LORD, Ehud son of Gera, a left-handed Benjamite, was raised up as a deliverer. He brought Eglon a tribute present (Judg 3:15, 17). The text describes Eglon as a very fat man. The continuing account (Judg 3:21–22) records that Ehud killed him with a hidden dagger during a private audience, which ended the Moabite oppression. He is a different figure from the Canaanite city of the same name.

Elah was the son of Baasha and succeeded him as king of Israel after Baasha died and was buried in Tirzah (1 Kgs 16:6). He began to reign in Tirzah in the twenty-sixth year of Asa king of Judah and ruled for two years (1 Kgs 16:8). This entry dates his reign to about 930 BC, an estimate inferred from context; the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia places it in 888–887 BC. The writer of Kings groups his sins with his father's, saying both led Israel to sin and provoked the LORD with their idols (1 Kgs 16:13), and refers readers to the chronicles of the kings of Israel for the rest of his acts (1 Kgs 16:14). The surrounding verses (1 Kgs 16:9–10) say that Zimri, one of his chariot commanders, killed him while he was drunk in Tirzah. He was the last king of Baasha's line. Several other men in the Bible share the name Elah.

Elah was the father of Hoshea, the last king of the northern kingdom of Israel. He is known only through his son, who is repeatedly called "Hoshea the son of Elah" in 2 Kings. Hoshea conspired against King Pekah, killed him and took the throne (2 Kgs 15:30). He then reigned in Samaria for nine years (2 Kgs 17:1), and in his seventh year Shalmaneser king of Assyria besieged the city (2 Kgs 18:9). Nothing is said about Elah himself, including whether he held any rank. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates him to about 729 BC or earlier, an estimate drawn from his son's reign. The name means "oak" or "terebinth" according to the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia. Several other men in the Bible share the name, among them a king of Israel, and this Elah should not be confused with them.

Eliashib was a high priest of the Jews after the return from exile, in the time of Nehemiah. He was the son of Joiakim and grandson of Jeshua, and the father of Joiada (Neh 12:10). His name marks a generation in the records of Levite and priestly family heads kept until the reign of Darius the Persian (Neh 12:22). Johanan is called his son in Neh 12:23, probably meaning his grandson or descendant, since Joiada stands between them in the line. One of Joiada's sons married a daughter of Sanballat the Horonite, and Nehemiah drove him away (Neh 13:28). Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies him with the Eliashib who rebuilt part of Jerusalem's wall near the Sheep Gate (Neh 3:1) and who gave Tobiah the Ammonite a room in the temple (Neh 13:4, 7). Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "the God of conversion."

Eliezer was the second son of Moses and his wife Zipporah, and the younger brother of Gershom. He was probably born in Midian, where Moses lived after fleeing Egypt. His name means "God is help" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia). Moses explained it by saying that the God of his father had been his help and had saved him from Pharaoh's sword (Exod 18:4). According to Easton's Bible Dictionary, Eliezer stayed with his mother and brother at the home of Jethro, Zipporah's father, while Moses returned to Egypt, and they rejoined Moses after the exodus. As a descendant of Moses he belonged to the tribe of Levi. He had only one son, Rehabiah, whose descendants became very numerous (1 Chr 23:15–17). A later line of his descendants served among the Levites who looked after the temple treasuries (1 Chr 26:25). Several other people in the Bible share the name Eliezer.

Ephratah, also called Ephrath, was the wife Caleb son of Hezron married after the death of his first wife Azubah. She bore him Hur, who is called her firstborn (1 Chr 2:19, 2:50; 4:4). Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary take her to be the grandmother of Caleb the spy, through her son Hur. Her descendants are tied to Bethlehem. Hur is called "the father of Bethlehem," and 1 Chr 2:51 gives that title to Salma, one of Hur's sons. STEPBible's proper-name index therefore treats her, through Hur or Salma, as the founder of the town. This probably explains why Bethlehem was also known as Ephratah, the name used in Mic 5:2. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of her name as "abundance" or "bearing fruit."

Eve was the first woman in the Bible, the wife of Adam and the mother of Cain, Abel and Seth. Her creation is described in Gen 2:21–22, where she is formed from Adam's side. Adam named her Eve "because she was the mother of all living" (Gen 3:20), and Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "life" or "living." Genesis 3 tells how the serpent deceived her into eating the forbidden fruit, which she also gave to Adam. Paul refers to this when he warns that the serpent "beguiled Eve through his subtilty" (2 Cor 11:3), and 1 Tim 2:13 notes that Adam was formed first, then Eve. When Cain was born she said, "I have gotten a man from the LORD" (Gen 4:1). Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that the biblical account of her closes with the birth of Seth.

Gabriel is an angel named in the books of Daniel and Luke, the only angel besides Michael named in the Bible. In Daniel he appears in human form. A voice beside the Ulai river tells him to make Daniel understand a vision, which Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies as the vision of the ram and the goat. Later, while Daniel is praying at the time of the evening offering, Gabriel comes to him swiftly and touches him, and the surrounding passage records his message about the seventy weeks. In Luke he identifies himself as one who stands in God's presence. He is sent to announce good news to the priest Zacharias, which the context shows is the coming birth of John the Baptist. Six months later he is sent to Nazareth in Galilee, to Mary, to announce the birth of Jesus. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that Scripture never calls him an archangel. His name is variously explained as "man of God" or "God is my strength."

Gemariah, son of Shaphan the scribe, was a royal official (one of the "princes") in Jerusalem during King Jehoiakim's reign. Baruch read Jeremiah's prophecies to the people from Gemariah's chamber in the upper court of the temple, at the entrance of the New Gate (Jer 36:10). His son Michaiah heard the reading and reported it to the officials meeting in the scribe's chamber of the palace, and Gemariah was among them (Jer 36:11–12). When the king burned the scroll, Gemariah, with Elnathan and Delaiah, had urged him not to, but the king refused (Jer 36:25). His father is probably the Shaphan who served as scribe under King Josiah (2 Kgs 22:3), and his brothers Ahikam and Elasah also appear in Jeremiah (Jer 26:24; 29:3). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives the name's meaning as "Yahweh has accomplished." A different Gemariah, son of Hilkiah, appears in Jer 29:3.

Gera was the father, or possibly a more distant ancestor, of Shimei, the Benjamite from Bahurim who cursed King David. Gera himself never appears in the narrative. He is named only in the phrase "Shimei the son of Gera." Shimei belonged to the family of the house of Saul and cursed David at Bahurim when the king fled toward Mahanaim (2 Sam 16:5; 1 Kgs 2:8). The surrounding narrative places this flight during Absalom's rebellion. Shimei later met David at the Jordan and fell down before him (2 Sam 19:16, 18). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that Gera, meaning "grain," was a family name in the tribe of Benjamin. On that reading, "son of Gera" may mean a descendant of a Benjamite clan ancestor rather than Shimei's immediate father. Several men in the Bible bear this name, and it is uncertain how they relate to one another.

Geshem, also called Gashmu, was an Arabian who joined Sanballat the Horonite and Tobiah the Ammonite in opposing Nehemiah's rebuilding of the wall of Jerusalem after the return from exile. When the work began, the three mocked the Jews and accused them of rebelling against the Persian king (Neh 2:19). Once the wall was finished except for its gates, Geshem and Sanballat invited Nehemiah to meet them in a village on the plain of Ono, a proposal Nehemiah understood as a plot to harm him (Neh 6:1–2). Sanballat's open letter then cited Gashmu as the source of a rumor that Nehemiah meant to make himself king (Neh 6:6). Gashmu is generally taken as another form of the same name. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both suggest he was probably the chief of an Arab tribe living south of Judah.

Hadad the son of Bedad was one of the early kings of Edom, listed among the rulers who reigned there before any king ruled over Israel. He succeeded Husham, and his royal city was Avith, a place whose location is unknown. He is remembered for defeating Midian "in the field of Moab" (Gen 36:35; 1 Chr 1:46). After his death, Samlah of Masrekah became king in his place (Gen 36:36; 1 Chr 1:47). The list of Edomite kings in Genesis is repeated almost word for word in 1 Chronicles. Several other men in the Bible share the name Hadad, including a later Edomite prince who opposed Solomon, so this Hadad should be kept distinct from them. Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests the name may have served as a royal title, much like Pharaoh. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives its meaning as "joy" or "noise."

Hanameel was the son of Shallum and a cousin of the prophet Jeremiah, since Shallum was Jeremiah's uncle. His name is often explained as meaning "God has been gracious" (Easton's Bible Dictionary). The LORD told Jeremiah that Hanameel would come and ask him to buy his field at Anathoth, in the territory of Benjamin, because the right of redemption belonged to Jeremiah as next of kin. Hanameel then came to Jeremiah in the court of the prison and made the offer. Jeremiah took it as the word of the LORD and bought the field for seventeen shekels of silver. The deed of purchase was handed to Baruch son of Neriah in front of Hanameel, the witnesses who signed it, and the Jews sitting in the prison court. By context this happened while the Babylonians were besieging Jerusalem, and the purchase served as a sign that land would again be bought and sold in Judah.

Hanoch was a son of Reuben, Jacob's firstborn, and so a grandson of Jacob. He is named first in every list of Reuben's sons, alongside his brothers Pallu, Hezron and Carmi, which suggests he was the eldest, as Smith's Bible Dictionary takes him to be. He appears among Jacob's descendants who went down to Egypt (Gen 46:9), and among the heads of the fathers' houses of Reuben (Exod 6:14). In the wilderness census he is the ancestor of the Hanochites, one of the clans of the tribe of Reuben (Num 26:5). The Reubenite genealogy in 1 Chr 5:3 repeats his name. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of his name as "dedicated." The same Hebrew name is borne by a son of Midian, a different person.

Hashabiah was a Levite of the period after the Babylonian exile. This entry treats him as a single person, though reference works divide these verses among several men of the same name. A Hashabiah was among the Levites recruited to travel from Babylon to Jerusalem with Ezra, listed with Jeshaiah of the sons of Merari (Ezra 8:19). Ezra then set apart Sherebiah, Hashabiah and ten others to guard the gold, silver and temple vessels on the journey (Ezra 8:24). Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary call this second man a chief priest, but since Sherebiah and Hashabiah appear just before as Levites, the same men are probably meant. A Hashabiah also sealed the covenant under Nehemiah (Neh 10:11) and is named among the chief Levites who led praise and thanksgiving in alternating groups (Neh 12:24).

Hatach was one of the chamberlains of King Ahasuerus of Persia, assigned by the king to attend Queen Esther. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary describe him as a eunuch, and the name is also spelled Hathach. When Mordecai mourned in sackcloth at the king's gate, Esther sent Hatach to find out what had happened and why (Esth 4:5). He went out to Mordecai in the city square in front of the gate (Esth 4:6). The surrounding passage shows that Mordecai told him about Haman's plot against the Jews and asked that Esther plead with the king. Hatach brought this message back to Esther (Esth 4:9) and then carried her reply to Mordecai (Esth 4:10). He is mentioned only in this exchange. Easton's gives the meaning of his name as "verity," while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "he that strikes."

Heber the Kenite was the husband of Jael, in the time of the judge Deborah. He descended from Hobab, the father-in-law of Moses, but had separated from the other Kenites and set up his tent by the plain of Zaanaim near Kedesh (Judg 4:11). His household was at peace with Jabin king of Hazor. For that reason the Canaanite commander Sisera, fleeing on foot after his army's defeat, went to the tent of Jael. There she killed him with a tent peg while he slept (Judg 4:17, 21). The Song of Deborah praises Jael as "the wife of Heber the Kenite" (Judg 5:24). The text records nothing Heber himself did beyond his move and his peace with Jabin. Several other men in the Bible share the name Heber, and this entry concerns only the Kenite.

Herodias was the wife of Herod Antipas, the tetrarch of Galilee, and had earlier been the wife of his brother Philip (Luke 3:19). John the Baptist rebuked Herod over this marriage, and Herodias held a grudge against John and wanted him killed but could not do it (Mark 6:19). At Herod's birthday feast her daughter danced and pleased Herod, who promised to give the girl whatever she asked (Matt 14:6; Mark 6:22). The fuller accounts in Matthew 14 and Mark 6 say that, prompted by her mother, she asked for John's head, and John was beheaded in prison. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes Herodias as a granddaughter of Herod the Great through his son Aristobulus and a sister of Agrippa I. It says she left Herod Philip to marry Antipas, her step-uncle, and later went with him into exile at Lugdunum in Gaul.

Hoglah was one of the five daughters of Zelophehad, a descendant of Manasseh son of Joseph through Machir, Gilead and Hepher. Her sisters were Mahlah, Noah, Milcah and Tirzah. In most lists she is named third (Num 26:33; Josh 17:3). Because their father died without sons, the sisters came before Moses to ask for a share of his land (Num 27:1). The surrounding passage records that their request was granted, and Joshua 17 records that they later received land among the families of Manasseh. Under a further ruling, the sisters married their father's brothers' sons, so the inheritance stayed within their tribe (Num 36:11). Easton's Bible Dictionary, Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia take her name to mean "partridge." Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "his festival or dance."

Hosah was a Levite of the family of Merari who served as a gatekeeper ("porter" in the King James Version) in David's time. He was appointed with Obed-edom to guard the ark after David brought it to Jerusalem (1 Chr 16:38). In the later list of gatekeeper divisions, his sons are named as Simri, Hilkiah, Tebaliah and Zechariah. Simri was not the firstborn, but his father made him chief. Altogether Hosah's sons and relatives numbered thirteen. When duties were assigned by lot, Hosah and Shuppim received the west side, including the gate Shallecheth by the ascending causeway. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of his name as "trusting." A town in Asher's territory (Josh 19:29) has the same name in the King James Version but is unrelated to this man.

Husham was one of the early kings of Edom, listed among the rulers who reigned there before Israel had a king (the list in Gen 36 opens with that note). He came from the land of Teman, or the Temanites, a region of Edom named after Teman, a grandson of Esau. He succeeded Jobab, and when he died he was followed by Hadad son of Bedad, who defeated Midian in the country of Moab and ruled from the city of Avith (Gen 36:34–35; 1 Chr 1:45–46). The list never says Husham was his predecessor's son, so the kingship apparently did not pass from father to son. Nothing else is recorded about him. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives the meaning of his name as "alert."

Iddo was the grandfather of the prophet Zechariah, through his son Berechiah (Zech 1:1, 7). He is one of several men in the Bible with this name. Ezra twice calls Zechariah "the son of Iddo" (Ezra 5:1; 6:14). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that Ezra treats Iddo as Zechariah's father, while Zechariah names him as grandfather. Probably Ezra uses "son" in the broader sense of descendant, or names the better-known ancestor. In the King James wording of Zech 1:1 and 1:7, the title "the prophet" sits beside Iddo's name, though it may instead refer to Zechariah. Nehemiah 12:4 and 12:16 list an Iddo among the priests who returned from exile with Zerubbabel, with a Zechariah later heading his family. By inference this is the same man, which fits the STEPBible description of him as a priest in post-exilic Judah. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "timely" or "lovely."

Imla, also spelled Imlah, was the father of Micaiah, the prophet whom the king of Israel sent for when Jehoshaphat of Judah asked for one more prophet of the LORD to consult before they went to war together (1 Kgs 22:8–9; 2 Chr 18:7–8). Imla himself is known only as part of his son's name. The narrative names the king as Ahab elsewhere in the same account. Kings uses the form Imlah and Chronicles uses Imla. Smith's Bible Dictionary allows that he may have been a more distant ancestor rather than Micaiah's father, and it gives the meaning of the name as "whom God will fill up." Easton's Bible Dictionary renders it "replenisher." Nothing else is recorded about him.

Jaalam was a son of Esau (Edom) and his wife Aholibamah, the daughter of Anah. He is named second of her three sons, between his brothers Jeush and Korah, and he was born in the land of Canaan before Esau moved away (Gen 36:5, 14). His half-brothers Eliphaz and Reuel were Esau's sons by other wives. Jaalam is also listed as a "duke," or clan chief, among the Edomites, which suggests a clan descended from him (Gen 36:18). The genealogy in 1 Chr 1:35 repeats his name among Esau's sons. Nothing else is recorded about him. Modern translations spell the name Jalam, and Easton's Bible Dictionary gives its meaning as "concealer."

Jachin was a son of Simeon and so a grandson of Jacob. He is listed fourth among Simeon's sons in the family that went down to Egypt with Jacob (Gen 46:10), and again in the genealogy of Exod 6:15. In the census of Numbers 26 he appears as the founder of the Jachinites, one of the clans of the tribe of Simeon (Num 26:12). The list in 1 Chr 4:24 gives the name Jarib in the same position. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia take Jarib to be the same man, and Smith's Bible Dictionary calls this a possibility. That list also gives his brothers Jemuel and Zohar as Nemuel and Zerah. The name Jachin, meaning "he will establish," was also borne by other people in the Bible.

Jair was the son of Segub and a descendant of Judah through Hezron, who held twenty-three cities in Gilead (1 Chr 2:22). He is also called "the son of Manasseh", probably because, as 1 Chr 2:21 explains, his grandfather Hezron married a daughter of Machir son of Manasseh. When Israel was settling the land east of the Jordan, Jair captured small towns in Gilead and named them Havoth-jair, "the villages of Jair" (Num 32:41). He also took the whole region of Argob in Bashan as far as the borders of the Geshurites and Maachathites, and the name Bashan-havoth-jair lasted afterward (Deut 3:14). In Solomon's time, the towns of Jair and the region of Argob belonged to the administrative district of the son of Geber at Ramoth-gilead (1 Kgs 4:13). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes a tradition identifying him with the judge Jair of Judg 10:3–4. Several other men in the Bible share the name.

Jamin was a son of Simeon and so a grandson of Jacob. He is listed second among Simeon's sons, after Jemuel (called Nemuel in Num 26:12 and 1 Chr 4:24), in the list of Jacob's family that went down to Egypt (Gen 46:10) and again in the family list in Exodus 6:15. His brothers are given as Jemuel, Ohad, Jachin, Zohar and Shaul, though 1 Chr 4:24 gives a shorter list that includes Jarib and Zerah. Zerah is probably another form of Zohar, and Jarib probably another form of Jachin. Jamin founded a clan within the tribe of Simeon, the Jaminites, who were counted in the census in Num 26:12. His name means "right hand" according to Smith's Bible Dictionary. Several other men in the Bible share the name, and this entry concerns only Simeon's son.

Jedaiah was a priest who lived in Jerusalem after the return from the Babylonian exile. Nehemiah 11:10 lists him among the priests who settled in the city and calls him the son of Joiarib. The parallel list in 1 Chr 9:10 names Jedaiah and Jehoiarib side by side rather than as father and son. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes him simply as a priest in Jerusalem after the Exile. A Jedaiah also appears next to Joiarib among the priests who returned with Zerubbabel (Neh 12:6). In the next generation, under the high priest Joiakim, a man named Uzzi led the priestly family called by Jedaiah's name (Neh 12:19). The name was shared by several men, including a second priest in the same list, so it is uncertain whether all these passages refer to one person. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the name's meaning as "the hand of the Lord" or "confessing the Lord."

Jehiel, also called Jehieli, was a Gershonite Levite of the family of Laadan in David's time. In 1 Chr 23:8 he is named as the chief of Laadan's sons, listed alongside Zetham and Joel. In 1 Chr 26:21–22, however, Zetham and Joel are called "the sons of Jehieli" and are placed over the treasures of the house of the Lord. This entry follows the second passage in treating them as his sons. Smith's Bible Dictionary explains Jehieli as "a Jehielite," meaning a member of Jehiel's family, which may account for the difference between the two lists. When the leaders gave gifts for building the temple, those who had precious stones handed them over to the temple treasury through "Jehiel the Gershonite" (1 Chr 29:8). This was probably the same man, consistent with his family's role over the treasures. Several other men in the Bible share the name.

Jehoshaphat, son of Ahilud, was the royal recorder under King David and later under Solomon. He is named in the lists of David's chief officials, alongside Joab as army commander (2 Sam 8:16; 1 Chr 18:15) and Adoram as overseer of forced labour (2 Sam 20:24). He still held the office at the start of Solomon's reign (1 Kgs 4:3). The recorder probably kept the official records of the court. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes the post as a high-ranking state office, something like a chancellor. Baana son of Ahilud, one of Solomon's district governors in 1 Kgs 4:12, is taken here to be his brother, on the inference that the two share the same father. This Jehoshaphat is a different person from King Jehoshaphat of Judah and from others who bear the name, which means "the Lord is judge."

Jeiel, also called Jehiah, was a Levite in David's time who served when the ark of God was brought to Jerusalem. He is listed among the Levites "of the second degree" and the gatekeepers (1 Chr 15:18). He was one of the musicians who played harps on the Sheminith, probably a term for a musical setting (1 Chr 15:21). He was appointed with Obed-edom as doorkeeper for the ark (1 Chr 15:24), where the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia takes "Jehiah" as another form of the same name. When Asaph led the music before the ark, Jeiel played psalteries and harps (1 Chr 16:5). That verse names Jeiel twice, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia takes the first Jeiel there to be the Jaaziel of 1 Chr 15:18, a different man. Smith's Bible Dictionary calls this Jeiel a Merarite. Several other men in the Bible share the name.

Jemuel was a son of Simeon and grandson of Jacob. He is named first among Simeon's sons in Gen 46:10 and Exod 6:15, and Smith's Bible Dictionary takes him to be the eldest. Genesis 46 lists him among Jacob's descendants who went down to Egypt. In Num 26:12 and 1 Chr 4:24 he is called Nemuel, and Numbers names the clan descended from him, the Nemuelites, as one of the families of the tribe of Simeon. His brothers were Jamin, Ohad, Jachin, Zohar and Shaul. Some of their names also vary between lists: Zohar appears as Zerah, Jachin as Jarib, and Ohad is left out of the later lists. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests that Nemuel is probably the original form of the name. That work treats its meaning as unclear, while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "God's day." Nothing else is recorded about him.

Jeremiah was a priest of the period after the Babylonian exile, named only in Nehemiah. He is listed among the priests and Levites who went up to Jerusalem with Zerubbabel and Jeshua (Neh 12:1). He became the head of a priestly family, and in the days of the high priest Joiakim that family was led by Hananiah (Neh 12:12). A Jeremiah also appears among those who sealed the covenant under Nehemiah (Neh 10:2) and in the procession at the dedication of Jerusalem's walls (Neh 12:34). This entry treats all four mentions as one person. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia instead separates the returnee with Zerubbabel from the covenant signer, and identifies the signer with the man in the procession. The later lists may use the family's name rather than refer to the original priest himself. The name is shared by several people in the Bible, including the prophet.

Jeshua was a priest whose name is linked here with a priestly family and with the son of Jozadak. In David's arrangement of the priests, the ninth course fell by lot to Jeshua (1 Chr 24:11). Easton's Bible Dictionary treats him as head of that ninth order. After the exile, 973 priests of the house of Jeshua, counted among the descendants of Jedaiah, returned to Jerusalem (Ezra 2:36; Neh 7:39). Ezra 10:18 names Jeshua son of Jozadak, some of whose descendants had married foreign wives. Other passages, such as Ezra 3:2 and Hag 1:1, where he is called Joshua, present this son of Jozadak as the high priest who led the return alongside Zerubbabel. It is uncertain whether the Jeshua of David's time and the son of Jozadak are best treated as one figure or several. This entry combines the references under the father Jozadak.

Jether, also called Ithra (2 Sam 17:25), was the father of Amasa, whom Absalom made commander of his army in place of Joab. Jether's wife was Abigail, sister of Zeruiah, Joab's mother. The nearby verse 1 Chr 2:16 names Abigail as a sister of David, so Amasa was a nephew of the king and a cousin of Joab. The texts differ on Jether's background: 2 Sam 17:25 calls him an Israelite, while 1 Chr 2:17 calls him an Ishmaelite. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both prefer the reading 'Ishmaelite'. Jether is known only through his son. In 1 Kgs 2:5 and 1 Kgs 2:32, Amasa 'the son of Jether' is remembered as a commander whom Joab killed. The name Jether is shared by several other people in the Bible.

Jeush was a son of Esau (Edom) by his wife Aholibamah, the daughter of Anah. He was born in the land of Canaan with his full brothers Jaalam and Korah. He is named first of the three, and Easton's Bible Dictionary calls him the oldest (Gen 36:5, 14). His half-brothers Eliphaz and Reuel were Esau's sons by other wives (1 Chr 1:35). In the list of Edomite leaders Jeush appears as a "duke," meaning a chief or clan head, among the chiefs descended from Aholibamah (Gen 36:18). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia takes the name to mean probably "he protects" or "he comes to help." Nothing else is recorded about him. Several other men in the Bible share the name, so this Jeush should be kept distinct from them.

Jezaniah son of Hoshaiah, described as "the son of a Maachathite," was one of the Judean army captains still in the field after Babylon captured Jerusalem. When Gedaliah was appointed governor, Jezaniah and his men came to him at Mizpah along with Ishmael, Johanan and others (2 Kgs 25:23, where he is called Jaazaniah; Jer 40:8). After Gedaliah's murder he stood with Johanan and the people when they asked Jeremiah to seek the LORD's guidance (Jer 42:1). When the answer told them not to go to Egypt, Azariah son of Hoshaiah joined Johanan in accusing Jeremiah of lying (Jer 43:2). This entry follows Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia in treating this Azariah as the same man. The ISBE notes that the Greek Septuagint also reads "Azariah" at Jer 42:1.

Jezreel was the first child of the prophet Hosea and his wife Gomer, and the older brother of Lo-ruhamah and Lo-ammi. The LORD told Hosea to give him this name as a sign that he would soon punish the house of Jehu for "the blood of Jezreel" and end the kingdom of Israel (Hos 1:4). The phrase probably refers to the killings Jehu carried out at the city of Jezreel when he seized the throne (2 Kgs 9–10). The name also points to the valley of Jezreel, where Israel's "bow" would be broken (Hos 1:5). Later in the book the same name is used in a hopeful sense. It speaks of a great "day of Jezreel" when Judah and Israel would be reunited under one head (Hos 1:11), and of the land answering Jezreel with grain, wine and oil (Hos 2:22). This draws on the name's meaning, "God sows." Several other people and a city in the Bible share the name.

Jobab son of Zerah was one of the early kings of Edom listed in Genesis and 1 Chronicles. He came from Bozrah, an Edomite city, and succeeded Bela as king (Gen 36:33; 1 Chr 1:44). When he died, Husham of the land of the Temanites reigned in his place (Gen 36:34; 1 Chr 1:45). The list places these kings before any king reigned over Israel, so Jobab belongs to a very early period. Nothing more is recorded about his reign. Some have tried to link him with Job of the book of Job, but the text does not make this connection. The name Jobab is shared by several other men in the Bible, and this entry concerns only the Edomite king. Bozrah is usually identified with modern Buseirah in southern Jordan. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "sorrowful, hated", and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests "howling".

Joel was the firstborn son of the prophet Samuel and the brother of Abiah. He was a Levite of the Kohathite line. When Samuel grew old, he appointed Joel and Abiah as judges in Beersheba. The next verse, 1 Sam 8:3, says the brothers took bribes and perverted justice, and this led Israel's elders to ask for a king. In the King James text of 1 Chr 6:28, Samuel's firstborn is called Vashni. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia explain that Joel's name probably dropped out of that verse, and that "Vashni" is really the Hebrew word for "and the second." Read that way, the verse names Joel first and then Abiah, and this entry treats the two names as one person. Joel was the father of Heman, a singer whom the Levites appointed in David's time. Several other men in the Bible share the name Joel.

Joiada was a priest of the tribe of Levi in the Persian period, the son of Eliashib the high priest and great-grandson of Jeshua, according to the high-priestly line in Neh 12:10–11. His name means "the LORD knows" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia). STEPBible's proper-names index describes him as succeeding his father as high priest. Neh 12:11 names his son as Jonathan, the father of Jaddua, while Neh 12:22 lists Johanan after Joiada among the generations by which Levites and priests were recorded. This entry treats Johanan as his son, probably the same person as Jonathan. Neh 13:28 reports that another of Joiada's sons married a daughter of Sanballat the Horonite, an opponent of Nehemiah, and Nehemiah drove him away.

Joiarib, also called Jehoiarib, was a priest whose name stands for a priestly family in Jerusalem after the return from exile in Babylon. He is listed among the priests who lived in the city (1 Chr 9:10; Neh 11:10) and among the priests who came back with Zerubbabel (Neh 12:6). In the next generation, Mattenai is named as head of the family of Joiarib (Neh 12:19). Neh 11:10 calls Jedaiah "the son of Joiarib," which is why this entry lists Jedaiah as his son. The parallel list in 1 Chr 9:10, however, names Jedaiah and Jehoiarib side by side, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests the text should probably read "Jedaiah and Joiarib." Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries call him the founder of one of the priestly courses, linking him with the Jehoiarib of 1 Chr 24:7. Several people in the Bible share this name.

Jonas was the father of Simon Peter and, by inference, of Andrew, since John 1:40 calls Andrew Simon Peter's brother. He is known only from the way Jesus addressed his son. When Andrew brought Simon to Jesus, Jesus called him "Simon the son of Jona" and gave him the name Cephas (John 1:42). After the resurrection, at a meal by the Sea of Tiberias, Jesus addressed him three times as "Simon, son of Jonas" while asking whether Peter loved him (John 21:15–17). Matthew 16:17 likewise calls Peter "Simon Bar-jona." The name appears in different forms. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia note that the Revised Version reads "John" in these passages, following Greek manuscripts that have Ioanes. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests that Jonas may be a shortened form of that name, or that he may have had a double name. Nothing else is recorded about him.

Josiah, son of Zephaniah, was a man living in Jerusalem in the time of the prophet Zechariah, after the return from exile in Babylon. Zechariah was told to go to his house on the same day that Heldai, Tobijah and Jedaiah arrived from Babylon, and to take silver and gold from them to make crowns for Joshua the high priest (Zech 6:10). The crowns were then to be kept in the temple as a memorial, linked to these men and to "Hen the son of Zephaniah" (Zech 6:14). Smith's Bible Dictionary takes Hen to be another name for Josiah, and this entry follows that view. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that "hen" means "favor," and that the verse may instead be read as "for the kindness of the son of Zephaniah." The text there is uncertain. Nothing more is known about him.

Jotham was the youngest son of Gideon, who is also called Jerubbaal. He was the only one to escape when his half-brother Abimelech killed Gideon's other seventy sons on one stone at Ophrah, because he hid himself. When the men of Shechem made Abimelech king, Jotham stood on the top of Mount Gerizim and called out to them. In the verses that follow (Judg 9:8–15) he told the parable of the trees choosing a bramble as king, which Easton's Bible Dictionary calls the earliest parable. He ended with a curse on Abimelech and Shechem. He then fled to Beer and lived there out of fear of Abimelech. The location of Beer is uncertain. The chapter closes by saying that his curse came upon the men of Shechem. Several other people in the Bible share his name, including a later king of Judah.

Keturah was a wife of Abraham, whom he took after the events of Genesis 24. By inference from the order of the narrative, this was probably after Sarah's death, as Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary both state. Genesis calls her a wife (Gen 25:1), while 1 Chronicles calls her Abraham's concubine (1 Chr 1:32). She bore him six sons: Zimran, Jokshan, Medan, Midian, Ishbak and Shuah. Her descendants included Jokshan's sons Sheba and Dedan and Midian's sons Ephah, Epher, Hanoch, Abida and Eldaah, all counted as "the children of Keturah." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia takes her sons to represent Arab tribes south and east of Canaan. Her name is usually understood to mean "incense." Nothing is recorded of her origin or nationality.

Korah was a son of Esau by his wife Aholibamah, the daughter of Anah and granddaughter of Zibeon. He is listed with his full brothers Jeush and Jaalam, and Smith's Bible Dictionary calls him the third son of this marriage. His half-brothers included Eliphaz and Reuel. Korah was born in the land of Canaan before Esau moved to the hill country of Seir (Gen 36:5). He is also named among the "dukes," or clan chiefs, descended from Aholibamah (Gen 36:18), which suggests that an Edomite clan bore his name. The genealogy in 1 Chr 1:35 repeats his place among Esau's sons. The name, perhaps meaning "baldness," is shared by several men in the Bible. This Korah is distinct from the better-known Levite of that name who rebelled against Moses.

Lamech (descendant of Cain) was the son of Methusael and belonged to the line of Cain, five generations after Cain himself (Gen 4:18). He took two wives, Adah and Zillah. He is the first man in Genesis said to have more than one wife (Gen 4:19). The verses that follow (Gen 4:20–22) name his children: Jabal and Jubal by Adah, and Tubal-cain and a daughter, Naamah, by Zillah. Lamech is remembered for a short poem spoken to his wives. In it he says he has killed a man for wounding him, and he claims that if Cain is avenged sevenfold, he will be avenged seventy-sevenfold (Gen 4:23–24). Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that this has been called "Lamech's sword-song." Smith's Bible Dictionary links it with Tubal-cain's metalworking. He is a different person from Lamech the father of Noah, who belongs to the line of Seth (Gen 5).

Lazarus is the poor beggar in the parable Jesus tells in Luke 16 about a rich man and a beggar. He lay at the rich man's gate covered with sores (Luke 16:20). After both men died, the rich man, in torment, looked up and saw Lazarus far off at Abraham's side, "in his bosom" (Luke 16:23). The rich man asked Abraham to send Lazarus to dip his fingertip in water and cool his tongue (Luke 16:24). Abraham replied that the rich man had received good things in his lifetime and Lazarus evil things, but now Lazarus was comforted while the rich man was tormented (Luke 16:25). He is the only named character in any of Jesus' parables. He is distinct from Lazarus of Bethany, the brother of Mary and Martha, whom Jesus raised from the dead in John 11. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the name's meaning as "assistance of God."

Lydia was a woman from the city of Thyatira who sold purple goods and lived in Philippi, where she met Paul during his second missionary journey, about AD 47 by inference from context. She already worshipped God, which the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia takes to mean she was a Gentile convert to Judaism. While she listened to Paul, the Lord opened her heart to his message. The next verse, Acts 16:15, records that she and her household were baptized and that she persuaded Paul and his companions to stay at her house. After Paul and Silas were released from prison, they went to her house, met the believers there, encouraged them, and left. Easton's Bible Dictionary calls her the first person in Europe to accept Christianity. Her trade and her ability to host guests suggest she had some wealth. Thyatira lay in the region of Lydia, so her name may simply mean "the Lydian woman."

Mahlah was one of the five daughters of Zelophehad, of the tribe of Manasseh son of Joseph. Her sisters were Noah, Hoglah, Milcah and Tirzah. She is usually named first among them, and Smith's Bible Dictionary takes her to be the eldest. Her father had no sons, so the sisters came forward together to claim his inheritance (Num 27:1). The ruling in their favour allowed daughters to inherit when there was no son. A later decision required such heiresses to marry within their father's tribe, and Mahlah and her sisters married their cousins, the sons of their father's brothers (Num 36:11). Their claim was honoured when the land was divided in Joshua's time (Josh 17:3). The name may mean "sickness" or "song"; the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats its origin as doubtful. A Mahlah of the same tribe also appears in 1 Chr 7:18.

Mahlon was a son of Elimelech and Naomi, an Ephrathite from Bethlehem in Judah, and the brother of Chilion. During a famine he went with his family to Moab, where they settled. Easton's Bible Dictionary takes him to be the elder son and gives the meaning of his name as "sickly". The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia renders it "invalid". Ruth 4:10 identifies him as the husband of Ruth the Moabitess. Mahlon and his brother both died in Moab, leaving Naomi without her sons or her husband. Later, at the gate of Bethlehem, Boaz bought from Naomi everything that had belonged to Elimelech, Chilion and Mahlon. He also took Ruth as his wife "to raise up the name of the dead upon his inheritance", so that Mahlon's name would not be cut off. By inference from this, Mahlon died without children.

Malchi-shua was one of the sons of King Saul. His name is usually explained as "king of help" (Easton's Bible Dictionary) or "my king saves" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia). The genealogies of Saul's family name him among Saul's sons with Jonathan, Abinadab and Eshbaal, also called Ish-bosheth (1 Chr 8:33; 9:39), and an earlier list in 1 Sam 14:49 includes him too. His mother is taken to be Ahinoam, whom 1 Sam 14:50 names as Saul's wife. Armoni and Mephibosheth were half-brothers, sons of Saul by Rizpah (2 Sam 21:8). Malchi-shua was killed by the Philistines together with his brothers Jonathan and Abinadab when they pursued Saul and his sons. The surrounding narrative places this battle on Mount Gilboa, where Saul also died (1 Sam 31:2; 1 Chr 10:2). Nothing else is recorded about him.

Mattaniah, son of Micha (or Micah), was a Levite descended from Asaph, the temple musician. He lived in Jerusalem after the return from exile. Nehemiah calls him the leader who began the thanksgiving in prayer, which suggests he directed the temple singers (Neh 11:17; 12:8). His grandfather is named Zichri in 1 Chr 9:15 and Zabdi in Neh 11:17, probably two forms of the same name. A Mattaniah also appears with Bakbukiah among the gatekeepers who guarded the storehouses at the gates (Neh 12:25). Because he is again paired with Bakbukiah, the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia takes this to be the same man. Since several men in the Bible share the name, some of these identifications are uncertain. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "gift, or hope, of the Lord."

Merab was the elder of King Saul's two daughters, sister of Michal and Jonathan. Her mother was probably Ahinoam, who is named as Saul's wife in the next verse after her own listing. Saul offered Merab to David as his wife on condition that he fight the Philistines, hoping David would die in battle. When the time for the marriage came, she was given instead to Adriel the Meholathite. 2 Sam 21:8 says that Adriel's five sons were born to Michal, and these sons were handed over to the Gibeonites and put to death (2 Sam 21:9). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia takes Michal's name there as a scribal slip for Merab. An ancient Targum explains that Merab bore the sons and Michal raised them. This entry follows the view that the five sons were Merab's, which is why Michal appears as another name for her.

Milcah (daughter of Zelophehad) was one of the five daughters of Zelophehad, a descendant of Manasseh son of Joseph, along with Mahlah, Noah, Hoglah and Tirzah. Her father had no sons (Num 26:33; Josh 17:3). The sisters came together to ask for a share of land in their father's name (Num 27:1), and the surrounding chapter records Moses granting their request. Later, to keep the land within the tribe, Milcah and her sisters married sons of their father's brothers (Num 36:11). Joshua 17 describes the daughters receiving their inheritance among the clans of Manasseh. She is usually named fourth among the sisters, though the order varies. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of her name as "queen." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes a view that the sisters' names may also reflect places, with Milcah perhaps linked to a place called Beth-milcah.

Mizraim was the second-named son of Ham, listed after Cush and before Phut and Canaan in the Table of Nations (Gen 10:6; 1 Chr 1:8). He is named as the ancestor of the Ludim, Anamim, Lehabim, Naphtuhim, Pathrusim, Casluhim and Caphthorim (Gen 10:13; 1 Chr 1:11). These names appear to stand for peoples rather than single individuals. Elsewhere in the Hebrew Bible, Mizraim is the usual name for Egypt, so he is generally understood as the ancestor, or personification, of the Egyptians. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary explain the word as a dual form, probably referring to the two regions of Upper and Lower Egypt. Easton's adds that the modern Arabic name for Egypt, Misr, comes from the same root. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning "tribulations."

Moza was a Benjamite descendant of King Saul, named only in the two parallel genealogies of Saul's family in 1 Chronicles. He was the son of Zimri and the father of Binea (1 Chr 8:36–37; 9:42–43). Through Zimri's line he traced back to Ahaz.
