The earlier verses of the same lists (1 Chr 8:33–35; 9:39–41) show this line running from Saul through Jonathan, Merib-baal (Mephibosheth) and Micah to Ahaz. The two lists differ slightly in detail. Zimri's father is called Jehoadah in one and Jarah in the other, and Binea's son appears as Rapha or Rephaiah. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary both describe him simply as a son of Zimri of Saul's posterity. Nothing is recorded about his life beyond his place in the genealogy. The name is also borne by a different man, a son of Caleb in the line of Judah (1 Chr 2:46).

Nadab was the son of Jeroboam, the first king of the northern kingdom of Israel. He succeeded his father on the throne (1 Kgs 14:20). He began to reign in the second year of Asa king of Judah and ruled Israel for two years (1 Kgs 15:25), about 954 BC by inference from context. While Nadab and the Israelite army were besieging Gibbethon, a town then held by the Philistines, Baasha son of Ahijah, of the tribe of Issachar, conspired against him and killed him there (1 Kgs 15:27). Baasha then took the throne. Easton's Bible Dictionary places Gibbethon in the territory of Dan and notes that Baasha went on to wipe out Jeroboam's whole family (1 Kgs 15:29). The rest of Nadab's acts are said to be recorded in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Israel (1 Kgs 15:31). Several other men in the Bible share the name Nadab.

Nimrod was a son of Cush and grandson of Ham. In the list of nations he is the first to become "a mighty one in the earth" (Gen 10:8; 1 Chr 1:10). He was remembered as "a mighty hunter before the LORD," and his name became a proverb (Gen 10:9). The verses that follow, Gen 10:10–12, say his kingdom began with Babel, Erech, Accad and Calneh in the land of Shinar, in southern Mesopotamia. This entry dates that beginning to about 1822 BC, an estimate inferred from context. Those verses then describe the building of Nineveh, Calah and other cities in Assyria. The King James Version credits this to Nimrod, while another rendering credits Asshur. Micah 5:6 mentions "the land of Nimrod" alongside Assyria. Easton's Bible Dictionary takes this as Assyria or Shinar, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia takes it as Babylonia. Nimrod has not been identified with any known historical king.

Noah (daughter of Zelophehad) was one of the five daughters of Zelophehad, of the tribe of Manasseh son of Joseph. Her sisters were Mahlah, Hoglah, Milcah and Tirzah. Her father had no sons (Num 26:33; Josh 17:3). The sisters came before Moses together to ask for a share of land in their father's name (Num 27:1). The surrounding passages say this request was granted, and that they later received land among their father's kin (Num 27:7; Josh 17:4). To keep that inheritance within their tribe, Noah and her sisters married sons of their father's brothers (Num 36:11). Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that her name is spelled differently in Hebrew from that of Noah of the flood, and gives its meaning as "motion." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives it as "movement." Nothing else is recorded about her individually.

Oreb was a prince of Midian during the Midianite oppression of Israel in the time of Gideon. His name means "raven" (Easton's Bible Dictionary). After Gideon's surprise attack routed the Midianite camp, the men of Ephraim captured Oreb and his fellow prince Zeeb. They killed Oreb at a rock that was called "the rock Oreb", probably named after him, and brought the heads of both princes to Gideon across the Jordan (Judg 7:25). When the Ephraimites complained that Gideon had not called them sooner, he calmed them by saying that their capture of Oreb and Zeeb outweighed his own achievement (Judg 8:3). Later writers recalled his defeat as a byword for God's judgment on Israel's enemies. A psalm asks that hostile nobles be made like Oreb and Zeeb (Ps 83:11), and Isaiah compares a coming blow against Assyria to "the slaughter of Midian at the rock of Oreb" (Isa 10:26).

Pahath-moab was the ancestor of a large Jewish family group whose descendants returned from the Babylonian exile. The name means "governor of Moab" according to Easton's Bible Dictionary, or "sheik of Moab" according to the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia, which suggests the clan was probably named after an ancestor who held that title. His descendants came back with Zerubbabel through two family lines, Jeshua and Joab, numbering 2,812 in Ezra 2:6 and 2,818 in the parallel list in Neh 7:11. A further 200 males came with Ezra, led by Elihoenai son of Zerahiah. Eight men of this family are named among those who had married foreign wives. Because the name is shared by several people, and later passages such as Neh 3:11 and Neh 10:14 use it for the clan or its head, it is not always clear which individual is meant.

Pashur, son of Immer, was a priest and chief officer in the temple at Jerusalem in the time of Jeremiah. When he heard Jeremiah prophesying disaster, he struck the prophet and put him in the stocks at the upper Gate of Benjamin beside the temple (Jer 20:1–2). On releasing him the next day, Pashur was told by Jeremiah that the LORD had renamed him Magormissabib, meaning "terror on every side" (Jer 20:3). Jeremiah also announced that Pashur and his household would go into captivity, and that he would die and be buried in Babylon along with the friends to whom he had prophesied lies (Jer 20:6). Smith's Bible Dictionary places the episode in the reign of Jehoiakim. He is distinct from Pashur son of Malchiah, another opponent of Jeremiah, since the name is shared by several people in the Bible.

Pharaoh (during Abraham's Journey) was the unnamed king of Egypt when Abram (Abraham) went down to Egypt during a famine, about 1921 BC by inference from context. His officials praised the beauty of Abram's wife Sarai to him, and she was taken into his house (Gen 12:15). Abram had presented her as his sister, as the surrounding passage explains. The LORD then struck Pharaoh and his household with great plagues because of Sarai (Gen 12:17). Pharaoh summoned Abram and asked why he had not said she was his wife (Gen 12:18). He then had his men send Abram away with his wife and all his possessions (Gen 12:20). The text does not give his name, and "Pharaoh" is a royal title meaning "great house." Easton's Bible Dictionary suggests he was probably one of the Hyksos, or "shepherd kings," a foreign Semitic dynasty ruling from Zoan (Tanis).

Rechab was a son of Rimmon from Beeroth, a town counted as part of the tribe of Benjamin. He and his brother Baanah served Ishbosheth, Saul's son, as captains of raiding bands. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes these as leaders of predatory troops. The two brothers came to Ishbosheth's house in the heat of the day while he lay resting at noon. They entered as though to fetch wheat, stabbed him, and escaped. The surrounding narrative goes on to say that they carried his head to David at Hebron, expecting a reward. David answered them with an oath and ordered them put to death (2 Sam 4:8–12). Several other men in the Bible share the name, among them the father of Jehonadab, from whom the Rechabites took their name. This entry concerns only the son of Rimmon.

Rehum was a Persian official, called "the chancellor," who with Shimshai the scribe and their associates wrote a letter to King Artaxerxes opposing the rebuilding of Jerusalem (Ezra 4:8–9). His title probably means "master of decree" or commander. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia describes him as a high-ranking officer, and Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests he was a kind of lieutenant-governor of the province. The letter was sent on behalf of several peoples settled in Samaria and the region west of the Euphrates. The king replied to Rehum and his companions, and when his answer was read to them, they hurried to Jerusalem and forced the Jews to stop their work (Ezra 4:17, 23). His name means "merciful" according to Hitchcock's Bible Names. Several other men in the Bible share the name Rehum. This entry concerns the Persian official.

Rizpah, daughter of Aiah, was a concubine of King Saul. After Saul's death, his son Ishbosheth accused Abner, the army commander, of sleeping with her. The verses that follow describe this quarrel as what drove Abner to side with David (2 Sam 3:7). She bore Saul two sons, Armoni and Mephibosheth, who is not the son of Jonathan with the same name. During a famine in David's reign, David handed both sons over to the Gibeonites along with five of Saul's grandsons, and all seven were put to death. Rizpah spread sackcloth on a rock and guarded the bodies from birds by day and wild animals by night, from the start of the harvest until the rain fell. When David heard of it, he had their bones buried with those of Saul and Jonathan, according to 2 Sam 21:12–14. Easton's Bible Dictionary estimates her vigil at about five months and gives her name's meaning as "coal" or "hot stone."

Samlah was one of the early kings of Edom, listed among the rulers who reigned there before any king ruled over Israel. He came from Masrekah, a town whose location is unknown. He succeeded Hadad and was followed by Saul (called Shaul in 1 Chr 1:48) of Rehoboth by the river (Gen 36:36–37; 1 Chr 1:47–48). The list does not present these kings as a father-to-son dynasty, since each is identified by his own home town rather than by descent. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests this points to Edom being a confederacy at the time, with the king's city serving as its chief city. Nothing else is recorded about his reign. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "garment."

Seir was a Horite, the ancestor of the Horite clans who lived in the land later called Edom before the descendants of Esau settled there. Gen 36:20–21 and 1 Chr 1:38 name his seven sons as Lotan, Shobal, Zibeon, Anah, Dishon, Ezer and Dishan, and describe them as chiefs (“dukes”) of the Horites in the land of Edom. Timna is also counted among his children. Gen 36:22 calls her the sister of Lotan, so she was probably Seir's daughter. The region is called “the land of Seir” (Gen 36:30), and the person and the territory share the name. It is uncertain whether the land was named after him or he after it. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes him as one of the chiefs of Edom. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as “hairy” or “goat.”

Seraiah was a priest who returned from exile in Babylon with Zerubbabel and Jeshua. He heads the list of priests and Levites who went up with them (Neh 12:1). In the next generation, under the high priest Joiakim, Meraiah led the priestly family named after him (Neh 12:12). The name Seraiah also appears first among the priests who set their seal to Nehemiah's covenant (Neh 10:2). Because that list comes generations after the return, the name there probably stands for the priestly house rather than the man himself. A Seraiah is also listed among the leaders who came with Zerubbabel (Ezra 2:2). This entry treats all these mentions as one figure, following the STEPBible proper names index. Smith's Bible Dictionary instead separates the leader of Ezra 2:2 from the priest. Several other people in the Bible share the name, which Hitchcock's Bible Names renders "prince of the Lord."

Shallum son of Jabesh was a king of Israel who took the throne by killing King Zachariah. He conspired against Zachariah, struck him down in public, and reigned in his place (2 Kgs 15:10). The surrounding passage shows that the "him" of that verse is Zachariah. Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that this ended the dynasty of Jehu. Shallum began to reign in the thirty-ninth year of Uzziah king of Judah and lasted only a full month in Samaria. Then Menahem son of Gadi came up from Tirzah, killed him, and took the throne (2 Kgs 15:13–14). His other acts and his conspiracy were written in the chronicles of the kings of Israel (2 Kgs 15:15). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests his father's name may point to Gilead. This entry dates his reign to about 772 BC, inferred from context; the ISBE places it about 758 BC. Several other biblical figures share his name.

Shaphat was the father of the prophet Elisha, who succeeded Elijah. He is known only through his son, who is repeatedly called "Elisha the son of Shaphat." The family was from Abel-meholah (1 Kgs 19:16). When Elijah found Elisha, he was plowing with twelve yoke of oxen, which suggests, by inference, that Shaphat's household owned considerable farmland (1 Kgs 19:19). The same patronymic identifies Elisha when he is introduced to King Jehoshaphat (2 Kgs 3:11), and again when the king of Israel vows to have him beheaded (2 Kgs 6:31). Nothing else is recorded about Shaphat himself. The name, meaning "judge" according to Hitchcock's Bible Names, is shared by several other people in the Bible, among them the Simeonite spy listed in Num 13:5. This entry concerns only Elisha's father.

Shaul was one of the early kings of Edom. He came from Rehoboth by the river, succeeded Samlah, and was followed on the throne by Baal-hanan the son of Achbor (Gen 36:37–38; 1 Chr 1:48–49). The King James Version calls him Saul in Genesis and Shaul in Chronicles. He appears in the list of kings who ruled Edom before any king reigned over Israel (Gen 36:31). The identity of "the river" is uncertain. The STEPBible proper-names index takes it to be the Euphrates, which is how the river is usually meant in the Old Testament. Others place Rehoboth by a stream within Edom. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "asked." He is a different person from King Saul of Israel and from others who share the name.

Shaul was a son of Simeon and a grandson of Jacob, named among those who went down to Egypt with Jacob (Gen 46:10). He is described as the son of a Canaanitish woman, which sets him apart from his brothers Jemuel (also called Nemuel), Jamin, Ohad, Jachin (also called Jarib) and Zohar (also called Zerah) (Exod 6:15; 1 Chr 4:24). He became the ancestor of the Shaulites, one of the clans of the tribe of Simeon counted in the wilderness census (Num 26:13). The genealogy in Chronicles continues his line through his son Shallum, as the verse after 1 Chr 4:24 records. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of his name as "asked." The same name, usually spelled Saul in English, belongs to several other people in the Bible, including Israel's first king.

Shavsha was the royal scribe, or state secretary, under King David. He appears in the lists of David's chief officials alongside the priests Zadok and Abiathar's son, though the name is spelled differently in each list. It is Shavsha in 1 Chr 18:16, Seraiah in the parallel list at 2 Sam 8:17, and Sheva in 2 Sam 20:25. Under Solomon, Elihoreph and Ahiah, "the sons of Shisha," held the same office (1 Kgs 4:3). Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia take Shisha to be another form of the same name, so this entry treats them as one man whose sons succeeded him. The ISBE notes that his father's name is never given and that his name sounds foreign. It suggests he may have been a non-Israelite, possibly chosen because the office involved correspondence with other nations. Which spelling is original is uncertain. The ISBE describes Shavsha as the generally preferred form.

Shemaiah was a priest, or the head of a priestly family, in the period after the return from exile in Babylon. He is listed among the priests who came back with Zerubbabel (Neh 12:6). In the time of the high priest Joiakim, the head of the family of Shemaiah was Jehonathan (Neh 12:18), which suggests the name had come to stand for a priestly house. A Shemaiah also appears among the priests who sealed Nehemiah's covenant (Neh 10:8), and the name occurs in the procession at the dedication of Jerusalem's rebuilt wall (Neh 12:34). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats all of these as one of the priestly courses, and this entry follows that view. Smith's Bible Dictionary instead takes the Shemaiah of Neh 12:34 as a separate person, one of the leaders of Judah. The name means "the LORD hears," and several other people in the Bible share it.

Shethar-boznai was a Persian official in the province west of the Euphrates ("beyond the river") who, with the governor Tatnai and their associates, challenged the Jews rebuilding the temple in Jerusalem. They asked who had authorized the building and its walls (Ezra 5:3). They then sent a letter to King Darius, joined by companions called the Apharsachites (Ezra 5:6). Smith's Bible Dictionary identifies this king as Darius Hystaspes (Darius I). Darius answered by ordering them to keep away from the work and leave the builders alone (Ezra 6:6). Shethar-boznai and the others promptly carried out the king's instructions (Ezra 6:13). He appears only alongside Tatnai, and his exact office is not stated, though the order of names suggests he ranked below the governor. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his Persian name as "star of splendour."

Shimshai was a scribe, or secretary, who served alongside Rehum the chancellor in the Persian administration of the province beyond the Euphrates. Together with their companions, a group drawn from several peoples settled in Samaria and the surrounding region, they wrote a letter to King Artaxerxes opposing the rebuilding of Jerusalem by the Jews who had returned from exile. Easton's Bible Dictionary connects this opposition with the rebuilding of the temple, while the letter itself speaks of the city. The king replied to Rehum, Shimshai and their associates in Samaria. When his answer was read to them, they went to Jerusalem in haste and forced the Jews to stop the work. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "sunny," and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that it appears to come from the Hebrew word for the sun, though its origin is uncertain.

Shobach was the commander of the army of Hadarezer (Hadadezer), king of the Syrians of Zobah, in the time of David. After the Ammonites and their hired Syrian allies were beaten by Israel, Hadarezer called up Syrian forces from beyond the river, which Easton's Bible Dictionary takes to be the Euphrates. They gathered at Helam with Shobach leading them (2 Sam 10:16). David defeated them there. Shobach was struck down in the battle and died on the field (2 Sam 10:18). The parallel account in 1 Chronicles spells his name Shophach and tells the same story, though its casualty figures differ: seven thousand charioteers and forty thousand foot soldiers, against seven hundred chariots and forty thousand horsemen in Samuel (1 Chr 19:16, 18). Smith's Bible Dictionary dates these events to about 1034 BC.

Shobal was a man of the tribe of Judah, named in the genealogies of 1 Chronicles as a son of Hur and as "the father of Kirjathjearim," which probably means the founder or leading figure of that town's clan rather than a literal parent (1 Chr 2:50). The KJV wording of 1 Chr 2:50 can also be read as making him a son of Caleb, as Smith's Bible Dictionary takes it. This entry follows the reading that makes Hur his father. His descendants included Haroeh and half of the Manahethites (1 Chr 2:52). In 1 Chr 4:1–2 he appears among the "sons," meaning descendants, of Judah, as father of Reaiah, whose line produced the Zorathites. Haroeh and Reaiah are probably the same person under variant spellings, though this is inferred. The name Shobal is shared with others, including a Horite chief of Edom, and is not to be confused with him.

Simon Zelotes was one of the twelve apostles chosen by Jesus, about AD 28 by inference from context. Matthew and Mark call him "Simon the Canaanite" (Matt 10:4; Mark 3:18), while Luke calls him "Simon called Zelotes" (Luke 6:15; Acts 1:13). Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary explain that "Canaanite" here does not mean a native of Canaan. They take it as an Aramaic term whose Greek equivalent is "Zelotes," meaning "zealot." On this view he probably belonged to the Zealots, a Jewish faction known for strict devotion to the law of Moses, before his call. After Jesus' ascension he was among the eleven apostles gathered in the upper room in Jerusalem, shortly before Matthias was chosen to replace Judas (Acts 1:13). Beyond his place in the apostle lists, the Bible records nothing else about him.

Simon was the father of Judas Iscariot, the disciple who betrayed Jesus. He is known only through his son, who is repeatedly called "Judas Iscariot, Simon's son" in John's Gospel, including at the last supper when Jesus handed Judas the dipped bread (John 13:26). Nothing else is recorded about his life, home or occupation. Because the surname Iscariot is usually taken to mean "man of Kerioth," Simon probably came from the same place, though this is an inference. The name Simon, a shortened form of Simeon, was common, and several men in the New Testament bear it. Passages such as Mark 1:30 and Luke 5:3 concern Simon Peter, and Luke 7:40–44 concerns a Pharisee named Simon who hosted Jesus. These are different men from the father of Judas described in this entry.

Simon the Sorcerer was a man in a city of Samaria who practised sorcery and amazed the people there, presenting himself as someone great (Acts 8:9). When Philip preached in Samaria, about AD 31 by inference from context, Simon believed and was baptized. He then stayed close to Philip, astonished at the miracles and signs he saw (Acts 8:13). When the apostles came and he saw that the Holy Spirit was given through the laying on of their hands, he offered them money for that power (Acts 8:18). Peter rebuked him sharply, as the surrounding passage records, and Simon asked the apostles to pray to the Lord for him so that what they had spoken would not happen to him (Acts 8:24). The text does not say what became of him afterward. Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that the term "simony," meaning the buying of spiritual office, comes from his name. He is often called Simon Magus.

Simon the Tanner was a man of Joppa, a tanner by trade, in whose house the apostle Peter stayed for many days after raising Dorcas (Acts 9:43). His house stood by the sea (Acts 10:6, 32). While Peter was lodging there, he had a vision, and the men sent by the Roman centurion Cornelius arrived at the gate asking for Simon's house (Acts 10:17). The angel's directions to Cornelius identify Peter's whereabouts by naming his host, which distinguishes this Simon from Simon Peter himself. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary describe him as a Christian, an inference from his hosting the apostle. Smith's suggests the seaside location was for the water tanning needed, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia adds that tanners worked outside town for sanitation and because the trade was ritually unclean for Jews. The events are dated about AD 38, by inference from context.

Tatnai (also spelled Tattenai) was a Persian governor of the province "on this side the river," meaning the territory west of the Euphrates, in the reign of King Darius. Smith's Bible Dictionary identifies this king as Darius Hystaspes and dates the episode to about 520 BC. When the Jews who had returned from exile were rebuilding the temple in Jerusalem, Tatnai came with Shetharboznai and their companions and asked who had authorized the work (Ezra 5:3). They then sent a letter to Darius reporting the building and asking that the royal records be checked (Ezra 5:6). Darius found the earlier decree of Cyrus and ordered Tatnai and his associates to stay away from the work (Ezra 6:6), and by inference from the surrounding passage, to support it from royal revenue. Tatnai and his colleagues promptly carried out the king's instructions (Ezra 6:13).

Togarmah was a son of Gomer and grandson of Japheth, listed with his brothers Ashkenaz and Riphath in the Table of Nations (Gen 10:3; 1 Chr 1:6). The name also refers to a people descended from him, called "the house of Togarmah." Ezekiel describes them trading horses, horsemen and mules in the markets of Tyre (Ezek 27:14). Elsewhere he places them in "the north quarters" as part of the forces gathered with Gog (Ezek 38:6). Their homeland is not stated in the text. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both identify it with Armenia, the ISBE favouring southeastern Armenia or a region connected with it. The ISBE notes that the Armenians themselves traced their ancestry to a figure they called Thorgom, a form of the name. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives its meaning as "which is all bone."

Toi was king of Hamath in the time of David. He is also called Tou in 1 Chr 18:9–10. Hadadezer (Hadarezer), king of Zobah, had been at war with him. When Toi heard that David had defeated Hadadezer's whole army, he sent his son Joram to greet David, to ask after his welfare and to congratulate him on the victory. Joram brought gifts of silver, gold and bronze. The Chronicles account names the son Hadoram. Smith's Bible Dictionary places Hamath on the Orontes River in Syria and describes the gifts as an act of homage to David. Smith's also dates the embassy to about 1036 BC, an estimate rather than a date stated in the text. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "who wanders," while Smith's gives "erring."

Tola was a son of Issachar and the founder of the Tolaite clan within the tribe of Issachar. He is always listed first among Issachar's four sons, alongside Puah (also spelled Phuvah or Pua), Jashub (called Job in Gen 46:13) and Shimron, so Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries take him to be the eldest. He appears in the list of Jacob's family who went down to Egypt, and in the wilderness census his descendants are counted as the family of the Tolaites. His six sons, Uzzi, Rephaiah, Jeriel, Jahmai, Jibsam and Shemuel, were heads of households, and in David's day their descendants numbered 22,600 fighting men. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of his name as "worm" or "scarlet." The name is shared by others, including the later judge Tola, who also came from Issachar.

Uzzi was a Levite and descendant of Aaron, the son of Bukki and the father of Zerahiah. He appears only in genealogies of the priestly line that runs from Aaron through Eleazar and Phinehas to Zadok (1 Chr 6:5–6, 51). Ezra's ancestry also passes through him (Ezra 7:4). Sources differ on whether he held the high priesthood. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia calls him a high priest. Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that, although he was an ancestor of Zadok, he may never have served in that office, and it places him somewhat before Eli. The verses themselves list him only as a link in the family line and record nothing else about him. The name, perhaps meaning "my strength," is shared by several other men in the Bible.

Zabdi was a man of the tribe of Judah, the son of Zerah and the grandfather of Achan through his son Carmi (Josh 7:1, 7:18). When the lot was cast to find who had taken the forbidden plunder from Jericho, it fell first on the family of the Zarhites and then on Zabdi, before narrowing to his household and to Achan (Josh 7:17–18). He is probably the same man as Zimri, listed in 1 Chr 2:6 as one of the five sons of Zerah alongside Ethan, Heman, Calcol and Dara. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both make this identification, and the latter explains the difference in spelling as an easy confusion of similar Hebrew letters. This entry follows that view. The name is shared by several other people in the Bible, and Zabdi may be a more distant ancestor of Achan than the genealogy's simple "son of" wording suggests.

Zadok was a priest of the tribe of Levi who appears only in genealogies of the high-priestly line. He is named as the son of Ahitub and the father of Shallum (1 Chr 6:12). He is a later member of the line, distinct from the better-known Zadok of David's time. Ezra traces his own descent through him (Ezra 7:2). Two parallel lists name his son Meshullam rather than Shallum, probably another form of the same name. Through that son he is an ancestor of Hilkiah and of the priests Azariah and Seraiah, each called "the ruler of the house of God" (1 Chr 9:11; Neh 11:11). These two lists also place Meraioth between Zadok and Ahitub. Smith's Bible Dictionary takes Meraioth's name there as a copyist's insertion, and it suggests this second Zadok may himself have entered the list by copying. Nothing further is recorded about him. His name means "just" or "righteous."

Zerah, also called Zohar, was one of the sons of Simeon, the son of Jacob, and so belonged to the tribe of Simeon. Genesis and Exodus list him as Zohar among Simeon's six sons, alongside Jemuel, Jamin, Ohad, Jachin and Shaul (Gen 46:10; Exod 6:15). In the census of Numbers and in the genealogy of 1 Chronicles he appears as Zerah, and Numbers names him as the founder of the Zarhite family within Simeon (Num 26:13; 1 Chr 4:24). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia and Smith's Bible Dictionary treat Zohar and Zerah as two forms of the same name, and this entry follows that view. Nothing more is recorded about his life. Several other men in the Bible are also named Zerah.

Zophar the Naamathite was one of Job's three friends, with Eliphaz the Temanite and Bildad the Shuhite. When they heard of Job's troubles, they arranged to come together from their own homes to mourn with him and comfort him (Job 2:11). Zophar speaks twice in the debate that follows (Job 11:1; 20:1). He does not give a third speech, as Eliphaz and Bildad do. At the end of the book, God tells the three friends to offer sacrifices and have Job pray for them. They do as commanded, and the LORD accepts Job's prayer (Job 42:9). Easton's Bible Dictionary takes "Naamathite" to mean a man from an unknown place called Naamah. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia doubts it was the Naamah in Judah, since Job and his other friends came from outside Israel. The meaning of his name is uncertain; suggestions include "sparrow" and "chirping."

Abiezer was a man from Anathoth, a town of Benjamin, who is listed among David's mighty men, the elite group of warriors known as "the thirty" (2 Sam 23:27; 1 Chr 11:28). The King James Version spells his town-name in several ways (Anethothite, Antothite, Anetothite), all referring to Anathoth. He also appears as the captain of the army division that served David in the ninth month of each year, a rotating course of twenty-four thousand men, and is identified there as a Benjamite (1 Chr 27:12). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia takes the warrior and the divisional captain to be the same man, and this entry follows that view. His name means "father of help." Several other men in the Bible share the name Abiezer, so he should not be confused with them.

Abigail was a sister of Zeruiah, a half-sister of King David, and the mother of Amasa. She is a different person from Abigail the wife of Nabal, who later married David. 1 Chr 2:16 counts her among the sisters of Jesse's sons, while 2 Sam 17:25 calls her the daughter of Nahash. This entry therefore treats her as David's half-sister, probably sharing a mother with him but having a different father. Her husband is called Ithra an Israelite in 2 Sam 17:25 and Jether the Ishmaelite in 1 Chr 2:17. Smith's Bible Dictionary takes these as the same man and reads "Ishmaelite" in both places. Her son Amasa was made commander of Absalom's army in place of Joab, who was Abigail's nephew through Zeruiah. Hitchcock's Bible Names explains her name as meaning "the father's joy."

Abijah, a name meaning "the Lord is my father" (Hitchcock's Bible Names), was a priest or priestly family of the period after the return from exile in Babylon. He appears among the priests who returned with Zerubbabel (Neh 12:4, read with Neh 12:1). In the next generation, under the high priest Joiakim, a priestly household called by his name was headed by Zichri (Neh 12:17). An Abijah is also listed among the priests who set their seal to Nehemiah's covenant to keep God's law (Neh 10:7). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia tentatively treats these as one man, and this entry follows that view. Because the lists span many decades, Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests the name may stand for a priestly family, perhaps linked to the earlier priestly division of Abijah (1 Chr 24:10). Several other people in the Bible share this name.

Abinadab was the second son of Jesse of the tribe of Judah and an older brother of King David. When Samuel came to Bethlehem to anoint a new king, Jesse had his sons pass before the prophet. Abinadab followed his elder brother Eliab, and Samuel declared that the LORD had not chosen him either (1 Sam 16:8). Later, he and his brothers Eliab and Shammah, Jesse's three eldest sons, followed Saul to war against the Philistines. This was the campaign in which Goliath issued his challenge (1 Sam 17:13). The genealogy of Judah also names him as Jesse's second son (1 Chr 2:13). His name is usually taken to mean "my father is willing" or "father of willingness" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia; Hitchcock's Bible Names). Several other men in the Bible share the name, including a son of Saul.

Achbor was the father of Baalhanan, one of the kings who ruled Edom before Israel had kings. Baalhanan took the throne after the death of Saul (called Shaul in 1 Chr 1:49) and was followed by Hadar (Gen 36:38–39). The text says nothing about Achbor himself and names him only to identify his son. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia counts Baalhanan as the seventh of the eight Edomite kings in the list and gives the meaning of Achbor's name as "mouse." Easton's Bible Dictionary describes Achbor as an Edomite king. The same name belongs to a different man, an official in the court of King Josiah of Judah, who is a separate person.

Achbor son of Michaiah was an official of King Josiah of Judah. He was one of five men, along with Hilkiah the priest, Ahikam son of Shaphan, Shaphan the scribe and Asahiah, whom the king sent to ask the Lord about the book of the law found in the temple (2 Kgs 22:12). The group went to the prophetess Huldah in Jerusalem and consulted her (2 Kgs 22:14). The parallel account in 2 Chr 34:20 calls him Abdon son of Micah. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests he is probably the same Achbor named in Jer 26:22 and 36:12 as the father of Elnathan, an official under King Jehoiakim. The name Achbor is shared by other people in the Bible, including the father of an Edomite king.

Adah (wife of Lamech) was the first of the two wives of Lamech, a descendant of Cain; the other was Zillah. She bore Jabal, described as the father of those who live in tents and keep livestock. Her other son was Jubal, whom Gen 4:21 names as Jabal's brother and the father of those who play the harp and pipe. Adah and Zillah are the wives Lamech addresses in his short poem, in which he tells them he has killed a man for wounding him. Her name is usually explained as meaning "adornment" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia) or "ornament, beauty" (Smith's Bible Dictionary). She should not be confused with the later Adah who was one of Esau's wives.

Adin was the ancestor of a family whose descendants returned to Judah from exile in Babylon. The list of those who came back with Zerubbabel gives the children of Adin as 454 (Ezra 2:15), while the parallel list in Nehemiah gives 655 (Neh 7:20). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia explains the difference by suggesting that one copy of the list was made later and brought up to date. A later group of 50 men from the same family came with Ezra, led by Ebed the son of Jonathan (Ezra 8:6). Smith's Bible Dictionary adds that an Adin is named among the leaders who sealed Nehemiah's covenant (Neh 10:16), probably representing the family as a whole. Little is known of Adin himself beyond the family that bore his name. The name is usually taken to mean "adorned" or "delicate."

Adoni-bezek was a Canaanite ruler at Bezek, whose name means "lord of Bezek." After Joshua's death, the men of Judah, with Simeon according to the surrounding passage (Judg 1:3), fought him at Bezek and defeated the Canaanites and Perizzites there. He fled but was caught, and his captors cut off his thumbs and big toes. He then said that seventy kings whose thumbs and big toes he had cut off had gathered scraps under his table, and that God had paid him back for what he had done. He was brought to Jerusalem and died there. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the Septuagint confuses him with Adoni-zedek, king of Jerusalem, and treats the two as different names. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates these events to about 1425 BC.

Adonikam was the ancestor of a family group, the "children of Adonikam," who returned to Jerusalem from exile in Babylon. The list of returnees who came with Zerubbabel counts them as 666 in Ezra 2:13 and as 667 in the parallel list in Neh 7:18. A later group of his descendants came up with Ezra, led by Eliphelet, Jeiel and Shemaiah, with sixty males (Ezra 8:13). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia leaves open whether that later group is counted within the earlier total or is in addition to it. Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests the Adonijah who seals the covenant in Neh 10:16 may be the same family name. The name is usually understood to mean "my lord has risen up" or "the Lord is raised." Nothing else is recorded about Adonikam himself.

Ahiman was one of the three sons of Anak, along with Sheshai and Talmai, who lived at Hebron when the Israelite spies explored Canaan (Num 13:22). The Anakim were remembered as people of great size, and Easton's Bible Dictionary describes the three brothers as giants. Joshua 15:14 says Caleb drove them out of Hebron, and Judges 1:10 says the men of Judah killed them when they attacked the Canaanites of Hebron, formerly called Kirjath-arba. The two accounts probably describe the same conquest from different angles, with Caleb leading Judah's forces. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "brother of the right hand." The name is also borne by at least one other man in the Bible, a Levite gatekeeper in Chronicles, who is a separate person.

Ahio was a son of Abinadab, in whose house at Gibeah ("the hill") the ark of God had been kept. When David first tried to bring the ark to Jerusalem, Ahio and his brother Uzzah drove the new cart that carried it. Ahio walked in front of the ark, probably guiding the oxen, as Easton's Bible Dictionary describes. The parallel account in 1 Chr 13:7 tells the same story. By earlier passages such as 1 Sam 7:1, the house was at Kiriath-jearim, and his brother Eleazar had been set apart to keep the ark there. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that about a century may have passed since the ark arrived, so "sons" may mean descendants. Ancient Greek translations treat the name as a common noun meaning "his brother" or "his brothers." The name is shared by several other people in the Bible.

Ahisamach was a man of the tribe of Dan, known only as the father of Aholiab (Oholiab), the craftsman who worked with Bezalel on the tabernacle in the wilderness. He appears only in the phrase "Aholiab, the son of Ahisamach, of the tribe of Dan," which comes up three times in Exodus. In those passages his son is named as appointed to help make what God commanded, as gifted to teach others, and as an engraver, skilled workman and embroiderer in blue, purple, scarlet and fine linen. Nothing else is said about Ahisamach himself. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives the meaning of his name as "my brother supports." Smith's Bible Dictionary gives it as "brother of help." Smith's dates him to about 1490 BC, an estimate drawn from the setting of the Exodus.

Ahitub was a Levite in the high priestly line descended from Aaron. He was the son of Amariah and the father of Zadok, and through Zadok an ancestor of Shallum (1 Chr 6:11–12). Ezra 7:2 traces Ezra the scribe's ancestry back through this same line, so Ahitub was one of Ezra's forebears. This Ahitub comes later in the genealogy than the better-known Ahitub whose son Zadok served as priest under David (1 Chr 6:7–8). Because the names Amariah, Ahitub and Zadok repeat in the list, the two are probably separate people bearing family names that were reused, though some readers take the repetition as a copying duplication. This entry treats him as a distinct person. Nothing else is recorded about him. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "brother of goodness."

Amariah was a priest, or a priestly family named after him, in the period after the return from exile. Neh 12:2 lists Amariah among the priests who came back to Jerusalem with Zerubbabel. Neh 10:3 names Amariah among the priests who sealed the covenant in Nehemiah's day. Neh 12:13 records that a man named Jehohanan headed the house of Amariah when Joiakim was high priest. Because these mentions span several generations, many readers take the later ones to refer to a priestly house carrying the founder's name rather than to the same man. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats them as one priest and calls him Jehohanan's father. The name means "the Lord has said." Several other men in the Bible share it.

Amaziah was the priest of Bethel in the northern kingdom of Israel during the reign of Jeroboam II, and the opponent of the prophet Amos. He sent word to King Jeroboam accusing Amos of conspiring against him and saying the land could not bear his words (Amos 7:10). He then told Amos, whom he called a seer, to flee to Judah, earn his living there, and prophesy there instead (Amos 7:12). Amos answered that he was not a prophet or a prophet's son but a herdsman and a gatherer of sycamore fruit (Amos 7:14). Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries describe him as a priest of the golden calf worship at Bethel, which by inference connects him with the shrine Jeroboam I set up there. The name, meaning "the strength of the Lord" according to Hitchcock's Bible Names, is also borne by several other people in the Bible, including a king of Judah.

Ammiel was the father of Machir of Lo-debar, and he is known only through his son. Machir sheltered Mephibosheth, the lame son of Jonathan, in his house at Lo-debar until King David sent for him (2 Sam 9:4–5). Later, when David fled from Absalom to Mahanaim, Machir was one of the men who brought him supplies (2 Sam 17:27). Lo-debar lay east of the Jordan in Gilead. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia describes Ammiel as a Benjamite, though the verses themselves do not name his tribe. The name means "my kinsman is God" or, according to Smith's and Hitchcock's dictionaries, "people of God." Several other men in the Bible share the name, so this Ammiel should not be confused with them. Nothing else is recorded about him.

Anah was the mother of Aholibamah, one of Esau's wives, and the daughter of Zibeon the Hivite (Gen 36:2). Through Aholibamah she was the grandmother of Jeush, Jaalam and Korah, who became chiefs (“dukes”) in Edom (Gen 36:14, 18). The Hebrew text calls Anah “the daughter of Zibeon,” and this entry follows that reading in treating her as a woman. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the Septuagint, Samaritan Pentateuch and Syriac versions read “son.” That reading would make Anah the same person as the son of Zibeon who found hot springs in the wilderness (Gen 36:24), and Smith's Bible Dictionary takes Anah as male. This entry names her husband as Beeri. That probably rests on identifying Aholibamah with Judith, “the daughter of Beeri the Hittite,” whom Gen 26:34 names as Esau's wife. Several people in the Bible share the name Anah.

Ananias (Husband of Sapphira) was a member of the early church in Jerusalem. With his wife Sapphira he sold a piece of property (Acts 5:1). He kept back part of the price and brought the rest to the apostles, presenting it as the full amount. Peter confronted him, asking why Satan had filled his heart to lie to the Holy Spirit and to keep back part of the price of the land (Acts 5:3). On hearing these words Ananias fell down and died, and great fear came on everyone who heard about it (Acts 5:5). The surrounding passage adds that Sapphira, who knew of the deception, died the same way about three hours later. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that his offense was pretending to give everything, not keeping part, since giving was voluntary. His name is a Greek form of the Hebrew Hananiah, meaning "Yah has been gracious."

Arad was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, one of the sons of Beriah, named in a genealogy alongside Zebadiah and Ader (1 Chr 8:15). His brothers were Ahio, Shashak, Jeremoth, Zebadiah, Ader, Michael, Ispah and Joha. In the surrounding passage Beriah appears among the descendants of Elpaal, and with Shema he is said to have driven out the inhabitants of Gath (1 Chr 8:12–13). For this reason the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia places Arad among Elpaal's descendants. Nothing else is recorded about him. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "a wild ass." He is a different figure from the Canaanite "king Arad" of the south who fought Israel in the wilderness (Num 21:1; 33:40). That phrase probably refers to the king of the town of Arad in the Negev.

Aram (son of Shem) was one of the five sons of Shem named in the Table of Nations, along with Elam, Asshur, Arphaxad and Lud (Gen 10:22). His own sons were Uz, Hul, Gether and Mash (Gen 10:23). The parallel list in 1 Chr 1:17 names the same four directly after Aram among "the sons of Shem" and gives Mash as Meshech. By inference from Genesis, they are Aram's sons, listed in Chronicles as part of Shem's wider line. STEPBible's proper-names index presents Aram as the ancestor of the Aramean people. Easton's Bible Dictionary explains that the name, meaning "high" or "highlands," was also used for the upland region stretching from northeast of Palestine to the Euphrates, roughly the Syria and Mesopotamia of later Greek and Roman writers. Damascus eventually became its chief city. The Bible records nothing about Aram beyond these genealogies.

Arba was a leading figure among the Anakim, described in Josh 14:15 as "a great man among the Anakims" and twice called the father of Anak. The city of Hebron was earlier named Kirjath-arba, "city of Arba," after him. When the Israelites settled the land, this city in the hill country of Judah was given to Caleb son of Jephunneh as his share, and its surrounding pasturelands were later assigned to the priestly families of Levi (Josh 21:11). Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia regard him as the ancestor of the Anakim, the tall people the Israelites feared, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia also treats him as the reputed founder of the city. His name means "four," so Kirjath-arba can also be read as "city of four." Nothing else is recorded about his life.

Artaxerxes was a king of Persia to whom opponents of the Jews returned from exile sent letters of complaint about Jerusalem. Bishlam, Mithredath, Tabeel and their companions wrote to him in Aramaic (the "Syrian tongue"), and Rehum the chancellor and Shimshai the scribe sent a letter against the city on behalf of the men living west of the Euphrates (Ezra 4:7–11). The following verses of the chapter record his reply ordering the work to stop. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes him as the king who obstructed the rebuilding, and it and Smith's Bible Dictionary identify him with Smerdis, the usurper who briefly held the Persian throne about 522 BC. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia considers it more likely that he was Artaxerxes I. Several Persian kings bore this name, and this entry treats the king of Ezra 4 as a person in his own right.

Asahiah was a royal official of King Josiah of Judah, described as "a servant of the king's" (2 Kgs 22:12). After Hilkiah the priest found the book of the law in the temple, Josiah sent Asahiah with Hilkiah, Ahikam son of Shaphan, Achbor son of Michaiah and Shaphan the scribe to ask the LORD about the book's words. The group went to the prophetess Huldah, who lived in Jerusalem, and consulted her. The parallel account in 2 Chr 34:20 spells his name Asaiah and lists the same delegation, though it names Achbor as Abdon son of Micah. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both give the meaning of the name as "the LORD has made." Nothing else is recorded about him, and his exact office at court is not stated.

Asaph is known only as the father of Joah, one of the three officials King Hezekiah of Judah sent out to meet the Assyrian envoy Rabshakeh during the siege of Jerusalem. Joah went with Eliakim, who was over the household, and Shebna the scribe, and the three later returned to Hezekiah with their clothes torn to report the envoy's words (2 Kgs 18:18, 37; Isa 36:22). The phrase "Joah the son of Asaph the recorder" can be read two ways. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the Tyndale House proper-names index give the title "recorder" to Asaph, while Smith's Bible Dictionary gives it to Joah. This entry presents both readings without choosing between them. Smith's also suggests that "son" may mean descendant, and that this Asaph may be the well-known Levite musician of David's time. Because several men bear the name, his identity is uncertain. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives its meaning as "who gathers together."

Asenath was the Egyptian wife of Joseph, son of Jacob. She was the daughter of Potipherah, priest of On, a city usually identified with Heliopolis near modern Cairo. Pharaoh gave her to Joseph in marriage when he raised Joseph to authority over Egypt and gave him the Egyptian name Zaphnathpaaneah (Gen 41:45). She bore Joseph two sons, Manasseh and Ephraim, before the years of famine began (Gen 41:50; Gen 46:20). Her name is Egyptian, and its meaning is explained in different ways. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives "gift of the sun-god." Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia connect it with the goddess Neith, meaning something like "belonging to Neith." Hitchcock's Bible Names offers "peril" or "misfortune." Apart from her marriage and her sons, the text records nothing more about her.

Ashbel was a son of Benjamin, the youngest son of Jacob. In the list of Jacob's family who went down to Egypt, he is named third among Benjamin's sons, after Bela and Becher (Gen 46:21). The genealogy in 1 Chr 8:1 calls him Benjamin's second son, after Bela the firstborn. The census of Israel's tribes in the wilderness names him as the ancestor of a Benjaminite clan, the Ashbelites (Num 26:38). Nothing else is recorded about his life. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "reproof of God," while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "an old fire."

Ashkenaz (spelled Ashchenaz in 1 Chr 1:6) was a son of Gomer and grandson of Japheth, listed with his brothers Riphath and Togarmah in the Table of Nations (Gen 10:3; 1 Chr 1:6). His name also stands for a people or kingdom descended from him. In Jer 51:27 the prophet calls the kingdoms of Ararat, Minni and Ashchenaz to gather against Babylon. Because Ashkenaz is grouped there with Ararat and Minni, Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia place the people in or near Armenia. Easton's adds that they probably lived near the Black Sea. Smith's Bible Dictionary links the name with Lake Ascanius in northern Asia Minor and mentions a view connecting it with the Germanic peoples. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning "a fire that spreads."

Ashtoreth was a goddess of the Zidonians (Sidonians), the people of the Phoenician coast, whose worship King Solomon took up in his later years along with that of the Ammonite god Milcom (1 Kgs 11:5). Her worship is named among the reasons given for the division of Solomon's kingdom (1 Kgs 11:33). Solomon built a high place for her east of Jerusalem, on the "mount of corruption," and centuries later King Josiah defiled it together with the shrines of Chemosh and Milcom (2 Kgs 23:13). Easton's Bible Dictionary describes her as the chief female deity of the Phoenicians, often paired with Baal, and identifies her with the Assyrian Ishtar and the Greek Astarte. It links her with the "queen of heaven" mentioned in Jeremiah. Reference works differ on her character: Easton's calls her a moon goddess, while Smith's Bible Dictionary connects her with the planet Venus.

Augustus was the title of the first Roman emperor, Gaius Octavius (Octavian), and of the emperors who followed him. Luke 2:1 says a decree from Caesar Augustus ordered a registration for taxation of "all the world," which Luke places at the time of Jesus' birth. Easton's Bible Dictionary explains that the name means "majesty" or "venerable." The Roman senate gave it to Octavian in 27 BC, and he ruled until his death in AD 14, when Tiberius succeeded him. In Acts 25:21 and 25:25 the governor Festus uses the same title for the emperor of his own day. He tells Agrippa and Bernice that Paul has appealed to Augustus and will be sent to Caesar. That ruler was not Octavian but a later emperor, probably Nero, by inference from the date of about AD 56. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats this second use separately, under the general title of emperor.

Azariah was a priest of the tribe of Levi in the high-priestly line descended from Aaron through Zadok, listed as the son of Johanan and the father of Amariah (1 Chr 6:10–11). The Chronicler adds that he served as priest in the temple Solomon built in Jerusalem. Smith's Bible Dictionary places his high priesthood in the reigns of Abijah and Asa, after Solomon. Another view holds that the note about Solomon's temple belongs to the earlier Azariah, son of Ahimaaz, who served under Solomon (1 Kgs 4:2). This entry follows the reading that ties the note to Johanan's son. Ezra's genealogy names an Azariah as the father of Amariah and calls him the son of Meraioth (Ezra 7:3). That list is shortened and skips several generations, so it probably refers to this same man. The name is shared by several people in the Bible.

Azariah, whose name means "the Lord has helped" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia), is the name of a man, or possibly more than one man, in the book of Nehemiah. One Azariah is listed among the leaders who came back from exile in Babylon with Zerubbabel and Jeshua (Neh 7:7). The parallel list in Ezra 2:2 has Seraiah in that place. An Azariah is named among the priests who sealed the covenant under Nehemiah (Neh 10:2). An Azariah also took part in the procession at the dedication of Jerusalem's rebuilt wall (Neh 12:33). Smith's Bible Dictionary treats the returning leader as a separate person and identifies the covenant-sealer and the man at the dedication as probably the same priest. STEPBible's Tyndale House names list treats all three mentions as one priest, and this entry follows that grouping. The name was common, so the identification is uncertain.

Azgad was the ancestor of an Israelite family whose descendants returned from exile in Babylon. The list of those who came back with Zerubbabel numbers "the children of Azgad" at 1,222 in Ezra 2:12, while the parallel list in Neh 7:17 gives 2,322. The difference is probably due to copying variation between the two lists. A later group of 110 males from the same family, led by Johanan son of Hakkatan, returned with Ezra (Ezra 8:12). Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia also note that someone named Azgad, presumably representing this family, was among the leaders who sealed the covenant in Nehemiah's time (Neh 10:15). The name is often explained as "strong is Gad" or "strength of fortune." Because the name is shared by more than one person, the references cannot all be tied to a single individual with certainty.

Bakbukiah was a Levite in Jerusalem after the return from exile in Babylon. Nehemiah 11:17 names him "the second among his brethren," ranked after Mattaniah, who led the thanksgiving in prayer. Nehemiah 12:9 places him with Unni among Levites who stood opposite their fellow Levites "in the watches," probably singing in alternating groups. By the context of that list, this group came back with Zerubbabel. Nehemiah 12:25 lists him with Mattaniah and others as gatekeepers guarding the thresholds of the gates. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats these three mentions as possibly three different Levites. This entry follows the view that they are one man, since he appears with Mattaniah in both Neh 11:17 and Neh 12:25. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives the name's meaning as "the Lord pours out," while Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "wasting of Jehovah."

Bani was the ancestor of a family that returned to Judah from exile in Babylon, apparently with Zerubbabel. Ezra's list of returnees counts 642 "children of Bani" (Ezra 2:10). The parallel list in Nehemiah calls him Binnui and gives 648 (Neh 7:15). Smith's Bible Dictionary treats the two forms as variants of the same name, and the small difference in numbers is typical of these two parallel lists. Later, some men of this family were among those who had married foreign wives and agreed to send them away: Meshullam, Malluch, Adaiah, Jashub, Sheal and Ramoth (Ezra 10:29). Bani himself is known only as the head of this family line. Several other men in Ezra and Nehemiah share the names Bani and Binnui, including Levites, so it is not always clear which one a given passage means.

Bani was a Levite in Jerusalem in the time of Ezra and Nehemiah. He was one of the Levites who helped the people understand the law while Ezra read it publicly (Neh 8:7). He was also among the Levites who called the assembled people to stand and bless the Lord during the day of confession and prayer (Neh 9:5). A Bani appears in the list of Levites who sealed the covenant led by Nehemiah (Neh 10:13). This entry treats these mentions as one man, as Smith's Bible Dictionary does. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia separates the teacher of Neh 8:7 from the covenant signer of Neh 10:13. Because several Levites of this period were named Bani, and Neh 9:4 names a Bani as well, it is uncertain how many individuals these verses describe. The name is usually explained as meaning "built" or "posterity."

Bebai was the ancestor and head of an Israelite family whose descendants returned to Jerusalem from exile in Babylon. The list of returnees in Ezra 2:11 counts the "children of Bebai" as 623, while the parallel list in Neh 7:16 gives 628. The difference is a variation between the two copies of the same register. Later, four men of this family, Jehohanan, Hananiah, Zabbai and Athlai, are named among those who had married foreign wives and agreed to put them away during Ezra's reforms (Ezra 10:28). Ezra 8:11 also names a Zechariah son of Bebai, who led another group back with Ezra, and the name appears among those who sealed the covenant in Neh 10:15. Bebai himself is known only through his descendants. The name is shared by more than one person, and Smith's Bible Dictionary gives its meaning as "fatherly."

Becher was a son of Benjamin, the youngest son of Jacob. He appears second in the list of Benjamin's sons in Gen 46:21, among the family who went down to Egypt with Jacob, and again in 1 Chr 7:6, where Benjamin's sons are given as Bela, Becher and Jediael. Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that he is left out of the list in 1 Chr 8:1, and the clan list of Benjamin in Numbers 26 also does not name him. 1 Chr 7:8 names his nine sons: Zemira, Joash, Eliezer, Elioenai, Omri, Jerimoth, Abiah, Anathoth and Alameth. Anathoth and Alameth are also the names of Benjamite towns, which suggests that some of these names may stand for family settlements. The name, meaning "firstborn" or "young camel," is shared by others, including an Ephraimite in Num 26:35.

Ben-hadad was a king of Syria (Aram) who ruled from Damascus in the time of the prophet Elisha. Smith's Bible Dictionary calls him Ben-hadad II, son of an earlier Ben-hadad. The name means "son of Hadad" and was borne by several Syrian kings. He gathered his whole army and besieged Samaria, Israel's capital (2 Kgs 6:24). The account that follows tells of a severe famine in the city and the sudden overnight flight of the Syrian camp (2 Kgs 7). Later, when Elisha came to Damascus, Ben-hadad was ill. He sent his officer Hazael with a gift of forty camel-loads to ask whether he would recover (2 Kgs 8:7–9). The next day he was smothered with a wet cloth, and Hazael took the throne (2 Kgs 8:15). Easton's Bible Dictionary takes Hazael as the killer, while Smith's allows it may have been his servants. Both estimate a reign of about thirty years.

Benaiah the Pirathonite was one of David's thirty mighty warriors, listed among them in 2 Sam 23:30 and 1 Chr 11:31. His title connects him with Pirathon, a town in the hill country of Ephraim that was also the home of the judge Abdon (Judg 12:13–15), and 1 Chr 27:14 confirms he was an Ephraimite. He commanded the division that served the king in the eleventh month of the year, a force of 24,000 men. His name means "the Lord has built" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia). He should not be confused with the better-known Benaiah son of Jehoiada, the commander of David's bodyguard, who is listed separately among the mighty men. Several other men in the Bible also share the name.

Berechiah (also spelled Berachiah) was a Levite, the son of Shimea and the father of Asaph, the leading musician appointed in David's time (1 Chr 6:39; 1 Chr 15:17). His name means "the Lord blesses." The genealogy he appears in traces Asaph's line back to Gershom, so Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him as a Gershonite Levite. A Berechiah is also named as one of two doorkeepers for the ark, alongside Elkanah, when David brought it to Jerusalem (1 Chr 15:23). Views differ on whether this doorkeeper is the same man. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia list him as a separate person. The Tyndale House proper-names index treats them as one Levite who served during David's reign, and this entry follows that view. Because several men in the Bible bear this name, the identification remains uncertain.

Berechiah was the son of Meshezabeel and the father of Meshullam, a man who helped rebuild the walls of Jerusalem under Nehemiah. He is known only through his son. Meshullam repaired one section of the wall next to Meremoth (Neh 3:4) and another section opposite his own chamber (Neh 3:30). Meshullam's daughter married Johanan, the son of Tobiah, Nehemiah's opponent. The surrounding context identifies Tobiah as the "him" of Neh 6:18, and this marriage was one of the family ties that gave Tobiah supporters in Judah. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia explains the name as meaning "Yahweh blesses." Several other men in the Bible bear the same name, and this Berechiah should not be confused with them.

Bernice was a Jewish princess who came with King Agrippa to Caesarea to greet Festus, the newly arrived Roman governor of Judea (Acts 25:13). This was about AD 56, by inference from context. The next day she entered the hearing room with Agrippa "with great pomp," together with military commanders and the city's leading men, when Paul was brought out to make his defense (Acts 25:23). When Paul finished speaking, she rose with the king and the governor and left to discuss the case (Acts 26:30). Acts does not state how she was related to Agrippa. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary identify her as the eldest daughter of Herod Agrippa I and the sister of Agrippa II, and say she had earlier been married to her uncle Herod, king of Chalcis. Easton's adds that she later sided with the Romans in the Jewish war and lived in Rome. Her name means "bringing victory."

Bigvai was the ancestor of a large family group that returned to Judah from exile in Babylon. The list of returnees who came back with Zerubbabel counts 2,056 of his descendants (Ezra 2:14), while the parallel list in Neh 7:19 gives 2,067. A later group of his descendants, led by Uthai and Zabbud with seventy other men, traveled to Jerusalem with Ezra (Ezra 8:14). Smith's Bible Dictionary dates the first return to about 536 BC. The name was shared by several people. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia links this ancestor with the Bigvai named among the leaders who came back with Zerubbabel (Ezra 2:2; Neh 7:7). The verses here, however, name him only as the founder of a family, so whether he is the same man is uncertain.

Bilgah, also spelled Bilgai, was a priest, or the head of a priestly family, after the Babylonian exile. He appears among the priests who returned to Jerusalem with Zerubbabel and Jeshua (Neh 12:5; the list begins at Neh 12:1). Smith's Bible Dictionary dates this return to about 536 BC. A generation later, in the days of the high priest Joiakim, the family of Bilgah was headed by Shammua (Neh 12:18). Bilgai is named among the priests who sealed the covenant in Nehemiah's time (Neh 10:8). This entry follows the STEPBible Proper Names and Smith's Bible Dictionary in treating Bilgai as the same name. Because the covenant was sealed decades after the first return, that signature probably represents the family rather than the original priest. The name is also borne by the head of the fifteenth priestly division in David's time (1 Chr 24:14), a different person.

Bukki was a priest of the tribe of Levi, the son of Abishua and the father of Uzzi, in the line of Aaron's son Eleazar. The genealogy in 1 Chronicles places him four generations after Aaron (Aaron, Eleazar, Phinehas, Abishua, Bukki) (1 Chr 6:5; 1 Chr 6:51). Smith's Bible Dictionary and the STEPBible names index count him in the line of the high priests. He also appears in the ancestry of Ezra the scribe, listed between Abishua and Uzzi (Ezra 7:4). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that his name appears as Boccas in 1 Esdras 8:2 and as Borith in 2 Esdras 1:2. Nothing is recorded about his life beyond these genealogies. The name Bukki is shared by at least one other man in the Bible.

Carmi was a man of the tribe of Judah, the son of Zabdi and the father of Achan, who took forbidden plunder from Jericho and brought trouble on Israel (Josh 7:1, 18). His line ran back through Zabdi to Zerah, one of Judah's sons. Carmi himself appears only in these genealogies and plays no part in the narrative. In 1 Chr 2:7 his son is called Achar, "the troubler of Israel," a form that plays on the Hebrew word for trouble. The Chronicles genealogy names Zimri rather than Zabdi as a son of Zerah, and Easton's Bible Dictionary calls Carmi the son of Zimri. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that Zimri and Zabdi are probably the same man, as the Greek Septuagint also takes them. His name may mean "vine dresser" or "my vineyard." Other men in the Bible also bear the name Carmi, including a son of Reuben.

Chilion was one of the two sons of Elimelech and Naomi, Ephrathites from Bethlehem in Judah, and the brother of Mahlon. Easton's Bible Dictionary calls him the younger son. During a famine the family moved to Moab and settled there (Ruth 1:2). After Elimelech died, the brothers married Moabite women named Orpah and Ruth (Ruth 1:4). Ruth 4:10 names Ruth as Mahlon's widow, so Orpah was by inference Chilion's wife, as Easton's also states. Both brothers died in Moab, leaving Naomi without husband or sons (Ruth 1:5). Later, at Bethlehem, Boaz formally acquired from Naomi everything that had belonged to Elimelech, Chilion and Mahlon, with the elders and people as witnesses (Ruth 4:9). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia takes his name to mean "pining" or "wasting away." Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "finished, complete."

Demas was a companion and co-worker of the apostle Paul. He is named alongside Luke in the greetings that close Paul's letter to the Colossians (Col 4:14), and in Philemon Paul calls him one of his "fellowlabourers," together with Mark, Aristarchus and Luke (Phlm 1:24). Both letters are usually placed during Paul's first imprisonment at Rome, about AD 57 by inference from context, so Demas was probably with Paul there. In a later letter, 2 Timothy, Paul writes that Demas had left him, "having loved this present world," and had gone to Thessalonica (2 Tim 4:10). Nothing more is recorded about him. Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests his name is probably a shortened form of Demetrius, and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives its meaning as "popular."

Demetrius was a silversmith at Ephesus who made silver shrines for Diana (the Greek Artemis), a trade that brought good profit to the local craftsmen (Acts 19:24). According to Easton's Bible Dictionary, these were small models of the goddess's temple or statue sold to visitors. Seeing Paul's preaching as a threat to this business, he stirred up the craftsmen and set off the riot in Ephesus, about AD 53 by inference from context. The town clerk later calmed the crowd by telling Demetrius and his fellow craftsmen to take any complaint to the courts and the proconsuls (Acts 19:38). The name also appears in 3 John 1:12, where John commends a Demetrius whom everyone speaks well of. Most reference works, including Smith's Bible Dictionary, treat him as a different man. Smith's notes that he could possibly be the silversmith after conversion but considers this very doubtful.

Dodo was an Ahohite, the father of Eleazar, who was one of the three chief warriors among David's mighty men. Eleazar stood with David against the gathered Philistines when the men of Israel had withdrawn (2 Sam 23:9; 1 Chr 11:12). "Ahohite" probably refers to descent from Ahoah, a Benjamite family. Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies Dodo with Dodai the Ahohite, who commanded the division of David's army that served in the second month, a division of twenty-four thousand men with Mikloth as a leader (1 Chr 27:4). Smith's Bible Dictionary calls this identification probable, and this entry follows it. Some read Dodai there as a scribal shortening of "Eleazar son of Dodai." Several other people in the Bible share the name Dodo. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives its meaning as "his uncle."

Dorcas, also called Tabitha, was a disciple at Joppa, the port town on the Mediterranean coast (modern Jaffa), known for her good works and gifts to the poor (Acts 9:36). Tabitha is Aramaic and Dorcas its Greek equivalent. According to Easton's Bible Dictionary, both mean "gazelle." Among her charities she made coats and garments, which the widows showed to Peter as they wept beside her body in an upper room (Acts 9:39). The wider account in Acts 9 says she fell ill and died while Peter was at nearby Lydda, where he had healed Aeneas, and the disciples sent for him. Peter sent everyone out of the room, knelt and prayed, then said, "Tabitha, arise." She opened her eyes and sat up (Acts 9:40). This happened about AD 38, a date inferred from context. The same chapter reports that many in Joppa came to believe as a result.

Eleasah was a Benjamite in the family line of King Saul, named in the genealogy that runs from Saul through Jonathan to later generations (1 Chr 8:37; 9:43). Both lists say that Moza fathered Binea, then name Rapha (called Rephaiah in 1 Chr 9:43), Eleasah and Azel, each followed by "his son." This can be read as a chain of generations, making Eleasah the son of Rapha, as Smith's Bible Dictionary and the STEPBible names index read it. It can also be read as a list of Binea's sons, and this entry follows that reading, treating Eleasah as Binea's son and the brother of Rephaiah and Azel. This entry also identifies him with Eshek, the "brother" of Azel, whose sons were Ulam the firstborn, Jehush and Eliphelet (1 Chr 8:39). Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treat Eshek as a separate descendant of Saul. Nothing else is recorded about him, and other men in the Bible share his name.

Eleazar was a Levite of the clan of Merari, the son of Mahli and grandson of Merari, and the brother of Kish (1 Chr 23:21). A further brother, Libni, is named in 1 Chr 6:29, which lists Libni as a son of Mahli. Eleazar died without sons, leaving only daughters, and these daughters married their cousins, the sons of Kish (1 Chr 23:22). The list of Levite divisions repeats that he had no sons (1 Chr 24:28). The marriages within the family probably kept his branch's line and inheritance among Mahli's descendants, a practice that matches the rule for heiresses in Num 36. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives the meaning of his name as "God is helper." Several other men in the Bible share the name, including Aaron's son the priest, but this Eleazar is known only from these brief notes in Chronicles.

Eliab was a Levite in the time of King David, one of several men in the Bible with this name, which means "God is my father" (Smith's Bible Dictionary). He is named among the Levites "of the second degree" whom David's chief Levites appointed to serve when the ark of the covenant was brought up to Jerusalem. In that list the whole group is called porters, or gatekeepers (1 Chr 15:18). He was also one of the musicians who played psalteries, stringed instruments, "on Alamoth" (1 Chr 15:20), a musical term whose exact meaning is uncertain. Once the ark was placed in its tent, Eliab was among the Levites who served before it under Asaph, the chief musician, again playing psalteries and harps while Asaph sounded the cymbals (1 Chr 16:5). Nothing further is recorded about him.

Eliada was a son of David born in Jerusalem, one of the sons born after David established himself there. He appears only in the lists of those sons, always between Elishama and Eliphalet, near the end, so that, as Smith's Bible Dictionary notes, he is the second youngest (2 Sam 5:16; 1 Chr 3:8). In 1 Chr 3:8 he is counted among nine sons who follow those of Bathsheba. The parallel list in 1 Chr 14:7 calls him Beeliada. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives the meaning of that form as "the Lord knows," and Eliada means much the same, "God knows." Nothing else is recorded about his life. The name Eliada is also borne by other men in the Bible, who are different people.

Eliashib was the high priest in Jerusalem when the city walls were rebuilt under Nehemiah, about 445 BC by inference from context (Smith's Bible Dictionary gives 446 BC). He and his fellow priests rebuilt the Sheep Gate, set up its doors, and consecrated the wall as far as the towers of Meah and Hananel (Neh 3:1). His house stood along the wall, and other builders repaired the sections reaching to its door and to its far end (Neh 3:20–21). Connected passages add more. Neh 12:10 names him as the son of Joiakim and grandson of Jeshua. Neh 13:4–7 says a priest named Eliashib gave Tobiah a room in the temple, and Neh 13:28 says a grandson of Eliashib the high priest married a daughter of Sanballat. The name is shared by several people in the Bible.

Elihu was an ancestor of the prophet Samuel, the father of Jeroham and grandfather of Elkanah, Samuel's father. In 1 Sam 1:1 his father is called Tohu. The genealogies of the Levites in 1 Chronicles list the same man as Eliab, son of Nahath (1 Chr 6:27), and as Eliel, son of Toah (1 Chr 6:34). Nahath, Tohu and Toah are probably variant forms of one name. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both treat Elihu, Eliab and Eliel as the same person. 1 Samuel describes the family as living in Ramathaim-zophim in the hill country of Ephraim and calls Elkanah an Ephrathite. The Chronicles genealogy places the line among the Kohathite Levites, which Smith's Bible Dictionary follows, and this entry counts Elihu as belonging to the tribe of Levi. Elihu is known only from these family lists.

Eliphalet, also spelled Eliphelet, was a son of King David born in Jerusalem after David made it his capital. His name means "God is deliverance" or "God of deliverance" (Easton's Bible Dictionary; Hitchcock's Bible Names). He appears last in each list of David's Jerusalem-born sons, following Elishama and Eliada (called Beeliada in 1 Chr 14:7). In 1 Chr 3:8 he closes a group counted as nine, in addition to the four sons of Bathsheba. Smith's Bible Dictionary calls him apparently the last of David's sons. The Chronicles lists also contain an earlier son with a similar name, Eliphelet or Elpalet. This has led some to count two separate sons, while others treat the names as a duplication. This entry treats Elpalet as a separate brother. Nothing is recorded about Eliphalet beyond his name and place in these lists.

Elishama was the scribe, or royal secretary, at the court of King Jehoiakim of Judah. He is one of several men of this name in the Bible. When Baruch's scroll of Jeremiah's prophecies was read in the temple, Micaiah went down to the scribe's chamber in the king's house, where Elishama sat with the other princes (Jer 36:12). After hearing the scroll read, the officials left it in Elishama's chamber and went to report its contents to the king (Jer 36:20). Jehoiakim then sent Jehudi to fetch it from there, and Jehudi read it aloud before the king and his princes (Jer 36:21). Smith's Bible Dictionary dates these events to about 605 BC. That date is an estimate inferred from context. The name means "God has heard" or "God hears."

Elishua was a son of David born in Jerusalem after David made the city his capital. He appears only in the lists of David's sons born there, named next to Ibhar and before Nepheg or Elpalet (2 Sam 5:15; 1 Chr 14:5). His mother is not named, but these lists place him apart from the sons born earlier at Hebron, such as Amnon, Absalom and Adonijah. The parallel list in 1 Chr 3:6 gives the name Elishama at the same point. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary treat the two as the same person, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests that Elishama there is probably a copyist's misreading of Elishua. This entry follows that identification. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning "God is my salvation." Nothing more is recorded about his life.

Elnathan son of Achbor was a royal official in Judah during the reign of King Jehoiakim. The king sent him to Egypt with other men to bring back the prophet Uriah, who had prophesied against Jerusalem. According to the following verse (Jer 26:23), Uriah was brought back and executed (Jer 26:22). Later Elnathan was among the princes gathered in the scribe's chamber of the palace when Baruch's reading of Jeremiah's scroll was reported to them (Jer 36:12). When Jehoiakim burned the scroll, Elnathan, together with Delaiah and Gemariah, urged him not to, but the king would not listen (Jer 36:25). Smith's Bible Dictionary identifies him with Elnathan of Jerusalem, the father of Nehushta and maternal grandfather of King Jehoiachin (2 Kgs 24:8). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats that identification as possible. His name means "God has given." Several other men in the Bible share the name.
