Elpaal was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, named in the genealogy of 1 Chronicles 8. He was a son of Shaharaim by his wife Hushim, and the brother of Abitub (1 Chr 8:11). His half-brothers were Shaharaim's sons by another wife, Hodesh. The list credits Elpaal with many sons, including Eber, Misham and Shamed. The clause "who built Ono, and Lod" is usually read as referring to Shamed, though it may cover the family as a whole. Lod is the later Lydda, the modern city of Lod. A second group of sons, including Ishmerai, Jezliah and Jobab, appears in 1 Chr 8:17–18. Beriah and Shema are also counted among his sons here, by inference from how the list runs on. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him as the founder of a numerous family. His name is usually explained as "God has wrought" or "God's work."

Epaphras was a Christian worker from Colossae and a companion of Paul. Paul calls him "our dear fellowservant" and "a faithful minister of Christ," and says the Colossians had learned the gospel from him (Col 1:7). This suggests, as Easton's Bible Dictionary notes, that he probably founded the church there. Paul describes him as "one of you," a servant of Christ who prayed earnestly that the Colossians would stand mature and complete in God's will (Col 4:12). The next verse adds that he worked hard for the believers in Laodicea and Hierapolis as well. In the letter to Philemon, Paul calls him "my fellowprisoner" (Phlm 1:23). He was therefore with Paul during his first Roman imprisonment, dated to about AD 57 by inference from context. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that his name is a shortened form of Epaphroditus, but he is usually treated as a different person from the Philippian messenger of that name.

Ephah is named first among the children of Midian, son of Abraham by his wife Keturah. The others are Epher, Hanoch (also spelled Henoch), Abida and Eldaah (Gen 25:4; 1 Chr 1:33). The name later stands for a people or region descended from this line. Isa 60:6 pairs Ephah with Midian as sources of camels and dromedaries that will come with travellers from Sheba, bringing gold and incense. By inference, the descendants were camel-herding traders in the Arabian desert. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes a proposal that Ephah matches an Arab group named in Assyrian records of the 8th century BC. The name probably means "darkness," though Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "weary" or "tired." Several other people in the Old Testament are also called Ephah.

Erastus was a companion and helper of Paul. While Paul was based at Ephesus, he sent Erastus and Timothy ahead into Macedonia, describing them as two of those who served him, while he himself stayed on in Asia (Acts 19:22). An Erastus described as the city's treasurer (the KJV says "chamberlain") sent greetings to the Christians at Rome in Paul's letter written from Corinth (Rom 16:23). In his last letter Paul notes that Erastus stayed behind at Corinth (2 Tim 4:20). It is uncertain whether these passages refer to one man or more. Smith's Bible Dictionary treats the Corinthian treasurer as separate from Paul's travelling companion. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the same man might have left a civic office to take up mission work. The link to Corinth in two of the three passages makes a single Erastus plausible. The name means "beloved."

Esar-haddon was a king of Assyria, the son and successor of Sennacherib. According to 2 Kgs 19:37 and Isa 37:38, he came to the throne after his brothers Adrammelech and Sharezer killed their father with the sword while he worshipped in the house of his god Nisroch, then fled to Armenia. Ezra 4:2 records that the people living around Samaria in Zerubbabel's time traced their settlement there to Esar-haddon, who had brought them to the land. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia dates his reign to about 680–668 BC, from Assyrian sources, and describes his rebuilding of Babylon and his conquest of Egypt. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both suggest that Manasseh of Judah was probably brought before him as a prisoner at Babylon, as 2 Chr 33:11 describes, since he was the Assyrian king who ruled from Babylon.

Ezra was a priest listed among the priests and Levites who came back from Babylon to Jerusalem with Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel and the high priest Jeshua (Neh 12:1). He is distinct from the better-known Ezra the scribe, who arrived later. His name became the name of a priestly family: in the next generation, in the days of the high priest Joiakim, that family was headed by Meshullam (Neh 12:13). An Ezra also took part in the procession at the dedication of Jerusalem's wall (Neh 12:33). The STEPBible proper-names index treats him as the same man, and this entry follows that view, though the long gap in time leaves the identification open. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia explains the name as a shortened form of Azariah, "the LORD has helped," and links him with the Azariah of Neh 10:2.

Gallio was the Roman "deputy" (proconsul) of Achaia when Paul was working in Corinth. Some Jews of the city rose up together against Paul and brought him before Gallio's judgment seat. Before Paul could speak, Gallio told the accusers that he would hear them if the case involved a real wrong or crime. The surrounding verses show that he regarded the dispute as a question of their own law and dismissed it. Afterward the Greeks beat Sosthenes, the chief ruler of the synagogue, in front of the court, and "Gallio cared for none of those things." Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies him as the elder brother of the philosopher Seneca and notes that contemporaries described him as affable. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia dates his term of office to about AD 51–53.

Gareb was one of David's mighty warriors, named in the lists of David's elite fighting men (2 Sam 23:38; 1 Chr 11:40). Both lists call him an Ithrite and place him next to Ira, another Ithrite. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia explains "Ithrite" as a member of the Ithrite family, one of the clans of Kiriath-jearim (1 Chr 2:53). It also notes that some read the word slightly differently, which would make him a native of the town of Jattir. Nothing else is recorded about his life or deeds. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "a scab." The same name appears in Jer 31:39 for a hill near Jerusalem, but that is a place and is separate from this warrior.

Gatam was a son of Eliphaz and so a grandson of Esau, since Eliphaz was Esau's son by his wife Adah (Gen 36:10, the verse just before the list). He is named fourth among Eliphaz's sons, after Teman, Omar and Zepho and before Kenaz (Gen 36:11; 1 Chr 1:36). In Gen 36:16 he appears among the "dukes", or clan chiefs, descended from Eliphaz in the land of Edom, alongside his brothers Korah and Amalek. This suggests that Gatam was the ancestor and head of an Edomite clan that bore his name. Smith's Bible Dictionary places him somewhat after 1760 BC, an estimate drawn from context. The meaning of his name is uncertain: Smith's gives "a burnt valley", while Hitchcock's Bible Names offers "their lowing" or "their touch". Nothing more is recorded about him.

Gedor was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, one of the sons of Abiel (also called Jeiel) and his wife Maachah. He appears in the two parallel genealogies of the family that settled at Gibeon, listed among his brothers Abdon, Zur, Kish, Baal, Ner, Nadab, Ahio, Zacher (Zechariah) and Mikloth (1 Chr 8:31; 1 Chr 9:37). Nothing is recorded about him beyond his name. The surrounding lists trace King Saul's line through Gedor's brother Ner, so Gedor belonged to the family from which Saul came. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia and the STEPBible names list both describe him as an ancestor of Saul, a term used loosely here for a member of Saul's forebears' household. The mention of "Jeroham of Gedor" in 1 Chr 12:7 probably refers to a town of that name rather than to this man.

Gera was a member of the tribe of Benjamin. Gen 46:21 lists him among the sons of Benjamin who went down to Egypt with Jacob. The Benjamite genealogy in 1 Chr 8 names Gera again, alongside Shephuphan and Huram. Judg 3:15 calls Ehud, the left-handed deliverer who brought Israel's tribute to Eglon king of Moab, "the son of Gera, a Benjamite." This entry treats these mentions as one person, the father of Ehud. Because the judges' period comes long after Benjamin's sons, "son" there may mean a descendant rather than a direct child. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats Gera as a Benjamite family name and says the Gera of Judges was Ehud's "father, or ancestor." Several people in the Bible bear this name, so the identifications are uncertain.

Ginnethon was a priest named among those who set their seal to the covenant made under Nehemiah, in which the returned community pledged to keep the law (Neh 10:6). The name also appears as a priestly family. Ginnetho, probably a variant spelling, is listed among the priests who came back from exile with Zerubbabel (Neh 12:4). In the next generation, in the days of the high priest Joiakim, Meshullam was head of the priestly house of Ginnethon (Neh 12:16). The covenant signer may have been an individual of that name or someone sealing on behalf of the family, since many names in that list match priestly houses. Which reading applies is uncertain. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "gardener."

Guni was a son of Naphtali and so a grandson of Jacob through Bilhah, Rachel's servant. He is listed with his brothers Jahzeel, Jezer and Shillem among the family members who went down with Jacob to Egypt (Gen 46:24). In the census of Numbers he appears as the ancestor of the Gunites, one of the clans of the tribe of Naphtali (Num 26:48). The genealogy in 1 Chr 7:13 repeats the list, calling the brothers "the sons of Bilhah" because they descended from her through Naphtali. That verse spells two of the names differently, Jahziel for Jahzeel and Shallum for Shillem. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "a garden" or "a covering." The name Guni is also borne by at least one other man in the Bible, so this entry is limited to Naphtali's son.

Hadad was a king of Edom, the last in the list of Edomite kings who reigned before Israel had a king. He succeeded Baal-hanan son of Achbor. His city was Pau (Pai in 1 Chr 1:50), and his wife was Mehetabel, daughter of Matred and granddaughter of Mezahab. Genesis 36:39 spells his name Hadar, while 1 Chronicles has Hadad. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both take Hadar to be a copyist's variant of Hadad. After his death, 1 Chronicles goes on to list the chiefs ("dukes") of Edom. Easton's places his reign at about the time of Saul. Several other people in the Bible are named Hadad, including an earlier Edomite king, Hadad son of Bedad, in the same list. This Hadad is distinguished by his city and his wife.

Hamul was a son of Pharez (Perez) and a grandson of Judah, and the brother of Hezron. He is listed among the family of Jacob that went down to Egypt (Gen 46:12), so he belongs to the tribe of Judah. In the census taken in the wilderness, his descendants form a clan called the Hamulites (Num 26:21), making him the founder of one of Judah's family groups. The genealogy in 1 Chr 2:5 names him again alongside Hezron. Smith's Bible Dictionary calls him the younger son, probably because Hezron is always named first. Pharez was Judah's son by Tamar, as Gen 38 relates. The meaning of his name is usually given as "pitied" or "spared" (Easton's Bible Dictionary; International Standard Bible Encyclopedia). Nothing else is recorded about his life.

Hamutal was a wife of King Josiah of Judah and the mother of two later kings, Jehoahaz and Zedekiah. She was the daughter of a man named Jeremiah from Libnah, a town in Judah. He is probably not the prophet Jeremiah, who came from Anathoth. She is named only in the standard notices that open the reigns of her sons. Jehoahaz became king at twenty-three and reigned three months in Jerusalem (2 Kgs 23:31). Zedekiah became king at twenty-one and reigned eleven years (2 Kgs 24:18; Jer 52:1). That Josiah was their father comes from the surrounding passages, which call Jehoahaz the son of Josiah and make Zedekiah the uncle of King Jehoiachin. Jehoiakim, whose mother was Zebudah, was by inference their half-brother. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "kinsman of the dew." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that it also appears in the form "Hamital."

Hashum was the ancestor of a family whose descendants returned from exile in Babylon to Jerusalem and Judah with Zerubbabel. The list in Ezra gives their number as 223 (Ezra 2:19). The parallel list in Nehemiah gives 328 (Neh 7:22). The two lists differ in several figures. Ezra 10:33 names seven men of this family, among them Mattenai, Zabad, Eliphelet, Manasseh and Shimei, who had married foreign wives and agreed to put them away during Ezra's reforms. Nothing is recorded about Hashum himself. Smith's Bible Dictionary connects this family with the Hashum who sealed the covenant under Nehemiah (Neh 10:18), but that may be a different man of the same name. Several people in the Bible bear the name. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives its meaning as "silence" or "their hasting."

Hegai, also spelled Hege in Esth 2:3, was the king's chamberlain at the Persian court of King Ahasuerus. He was keeper of the women in the palace at Shushan. When the king ordered fair young virgins from every province to be gathered so a new queen could be chosen, they were placed in Hegai's custody in the house of the women, and he oversaw their preparations for purification (Esth 2:3, 8). Esther was among those brought to him. When her turn came to go in to the king, she asked for nothing beyond what Hegai advised (Esth 2:15). Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries describe him as a eunuch, which is how the Hebrew word rendered "chamberlain" is often understood. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates his service to about 474 BC. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives possible meanings of the name, including "meditation."

Heleb, son of Baanah, was a Netophathite, a man from the town of Netophah in Judah, and one of David's mighty warriors (2 Sam 23:29). The parallel list in 1 Chr 11:30 spells his name Heled. This entry also identifies him with Heldai the Netophathite, who served as captain of the twelfth of David's monthly divisions. Each division had 24,000 men and served for one month of the year (1 Chr 27:15). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia describes this identification as probable, resting on the shared hometown and the closely related names. The phrase "of Othniel" in 1 Chr 27:15 probably means he belonged to the family line of Othniel, the early judge from Judah. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name Heleb as "fatness."

Helez was one of David's mighty warriors, listed among "the thirty" of his elite fighting men. In 2 Sam 23:26 he is called "the Paltite," while 1 Chr 11:27 calls him "the Pelonite." The two titles probably refer to the same man, and the difference is most likely a variation in the copying of the name. 1 Chr 27:10 adds that Helez the Pelonite came from the tribe of Ephraim. In David's organization of the kingdom he commanded the division of 24,000 men that served in the seventh month of the year. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives the meaning of his name as "vigor," and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "armed; set free." The name Helez is shared by more than one person in the Bible, so this man should be kept distinct from others who bear it.

Hodevah was a Levite whose descendants were among the Levites who returned from exile in Babylon. In the list of returnees, his descendants are counted together with those of Jeshua and Kadmiel, seventy-four in all (Neh 7:43). The parallel list in Ezra 2:40 spells his name Hodaviah, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes a further reading, Hodeiah, treating these as minor variations of the same name. Ezra 3:9 names the "sons of Judah" alongside Jeshua and Kadmiel as overseeing the workmen rebuilding the house of God. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identifies this Judah with Hodaviah, since the two names have nearly the same meaning, "praise." Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him as a Levite who seems to have given his name to an important family. The return is usually dated to about 538 BC, an estimate drawn from context.

Hodijah was a Levite in Jerusalem in the time of Ezra and Nehemiah. He was one of the Levites who helped the people understand the law when Ezra read it publicly, while the people stood in their places (Neh 8:7). He was also among the Levites who led the people in worship, calling them to stand up and bless the LORD (Neh 9:5). A Levite named Hodijah appears among those who set their seal to the covenant (Neh 10:10), and Smith's Bible Dictionary takes this to be probably the same man. The name is shared by several people in the Bible, and another Levite and a leader of the people with this name appear in the same covenant list, so how many individuals these verses refer to is not certain. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "majesty of Jehovah."

Hori was a son of Lotan and a grandson of Seir the Horite, among the early inhabitants of the land of Seir before the Edomites. His brother is called Hemam in Gen 36:22 and Homam in 1 Chr 1:39. Both lists also name Timna as Lotan's sister. In Gen 36:30 the name appears in the phrase "the dukes that came of Hori." Since the chiefs listed there (Dishon, Ezer and Dishan) are sons of Seir, that verse probably uses the name for the Horite people as a whole rather than for this individual. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "cave-dweller," and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "a prince; freeborn." Nothing else is recorded about him. Several people in the Bible share this name.

Hosea was a prophet, the son of Beeri, and the author of the book that bears his name, the first of the minor prophets. His name means "salvation." Hos 1:1 dates his ministry to the reigns of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz and Hezekiah of Judah and Jeroboam son of Joash of Israel, roughly from about 785 BC onward, by inference from context. Smith's Bible Dictionary estimates a career of about fifty-nine years. Easton's Bible Dictionary, among others, places him in the northern kingdom of Israel, partly because of his familiarity with places in Ephraim. At the start of his prophecy the LORD told him to marry "a wife of whoredoms" as a sign of the land's unfaithfulness. His wife was Gomer, and his children Jezreel, Lo-ruhamah and Lo-ammi carried symbolic names, as the following verses of Hosea 1 relate. In Rom 9:25 Paul quotes him under the Greek form of his name, Osee.

Huram was a member of the tribe of Benjamin who appears in the tribal genealogies, and this entry treats him as the same man called Huppim and Hupham. Genesis lists Huppim among the sons of Benjamin who went down to Egypt with Jacob (Gen 46:21). Numbers names Hupham as the founder of the clan of the Huphamites, listed next to Shupham and the Shuphamites (Num 26:39). In 1 Chr 8:5 Huram appears beside Shephuphan (probably Shupham) in a list that places him among the sons of Bela, Benjamin's firstborn, which would make him Benjamin's grandson. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary describe Huram as Bela's son. The STEPBible proper names index (Tyndale House) takes Huppim, Hupham and Huram as one descendant of Benjamin, and this entry follows that view. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that his exact line of descent is hard to establish. Several other men in the Bible share the name Huram.

Ibhar was one of the sons born to David in Jerusalem, after David moved his capital there from Hebron. He appears only in the three lists of those sons (2 Sam 5:15; 1 Chr 3:6; 1 Chr 14:5), and in each list his name comes soon after Solomon's. 1 Chronicles 3 distinguishes these Jerusalem-born sons from the children of David's concubines, so Ibhar was probably the son of one of David's wives, as the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes. His mother is not named, and nothing else is recorded about his life. His name means "he chooses" or "chosen," usually understood as "God chooses" (Easton's Bible Dictionary; Hitchcock's Bible Names). As a son of David he belonged to the tribe of Judah.

Iddo was a seer and prophet in Judah whose writings the Chronicler names as sources for the reigns of Solomon, Rehoboam and Abijah. His "visions" against Jeroboam son of Nebat are listed with the works of Nathan and Ahijah as records of Solomon's acts (2 Chr 9:29). A work of Iddo the seer "concerning genealogies" is cited, along with the book of Shemaiah, for Rehoboam's reign (2 Chr 12:15). The "story" of the prophet Iddo is given as the record of Abijah's ways and sayings (2 Chr 13:22). None of these writings has survived, and nothing else is told of his life. Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that he has been identified with Oded, the father of the prophet Azariah. Several other men in the Bible share the name Iddo.

Ikkesh was a man of Tekoa, a town in Judah, and the father of Ira. He is known only through his son. Ira was one of David's mighty men, listed among "the thirty" (2 Sam 23:26; 1 Chr 11:28). He also served as captain of the army division on duty in the sixth month, a division of 24,000 men (1 Chr 27:9). The label "the Tekoite" is attached to Ira's name in each passage, and it probably identifies the family as coming from Tekoa. Nothing else is recorded about Ikkesh himself. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives the meaning of his name as "crooked," and Smith's Bible Dictionary gives it as "perverse." Smith's dates him to before 1046 BC, an estimate based on his son's service under David.

Imnah was the first-named son of Asher, one of the sons of Jacob, and so belonged to the tribe of Asher. His brothers were Ishuah (also spelled Isuah), Isui (Ishuai) and Beriah, and his sister was Serah. He appears in the list of Jacob's descendants who went down to Egypt (Gen 46:17) and in the Chronicler's genealogy of Asher (1 Chr 7:30). In the census of Numbers he is called Jimna, the ancestor of the clan of the Jimnites (Num 26:44). The King James Version spells his name Jimnah, Jimna and Imnah; these are the same Hebrew name. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both treat him as Asher's firstborn, an inference from his place at the head of each list. The meaning of the name is uncertain, with suggestions including "prosperity" or "good fortune." Another man in the Bible shares this name.

Ira the son of Ikkesh was a man from Tekoa, a town in Judah south of Bethlehem, and one of King David's mighty warriors known as "the thirty" (2 Sam 23:26; 1 Chr 11:28). In the list of David's monthly army divisions he appears as the captain for the sixth month, in charge of a division of 24,000 men (1 Chr 27:9). Several other men in the Bible share the name Ira, including another of David's warriors, Ira the Ithrite, so he is identified here by his father and hometown. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the name's meaning as "watchman."

Isui was the third son of Asher and a grandson of Jacob. He is named among Asher's sons in the list of Jacob's family who went down to Egypt (Gen 46:17), and again in the genealogy of Asher in 1 Chr 7:30, where the King James Version spells his name Ishuai. In the census taken in the plains of Moab, his descendants appear as a clan of the tribe of Asher, the family of the Jesuites, founded by Jesui (Num 26:44). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives the Hebrew form as Ishvi and the meaning as "equal," while Smith's Bible Dictionary links the name to ideas of evenness or quiet. Nothing else is recorded about him beyond his place in these family lists, where his brothers were Imnah, Isuah and Beriah, and his sister was Serah.

Jabesh was the father of Shallum, who killed King Zachariah of Israel and took his throne. Zachariah is named in the surrounding passage and by Easton's Bible Dictionary. Jabesh appears only in the phrase "Shallum the son of Jabesh," which is repeated three times in the account. Shallum began to reign in the thirty-ninth year of Uzziah king of Judah and ruled in Samaria for just one month before Menahem son of Gadi came from Tirzah and killed him. Smith's Bible Dictionary counts Shallum as the fifteenth king of Israel. Nothing else is recorded about Jabesh himself. Some interpreters read "son of Jabesh" as pointing to Shallum's origin in the town of Jabesh in Gilead. This entry treats Jabesh as the name of his father. The name is usually taken to mean "dry" or "dryness."

Jahzeel was the first-named of the four sons of Naphtali, and so a grandson of Jacob through Bilhah, Rachel's servant. His brothers were Guni, Jezer and Shillem. He is listed among the members of Jacob's household who went down to Egypt (Gen 46:24). In the census of the tribes taken in the wilderness he appears as the founder of the clan of the Jahzeelites within the tribe of Naphtali (Num 26:48). The genealogy in 1 Chronicles spells his name Jahziel and calls his brothers "the sons of Bilhah," meaning her descendants through Naphtali (1 Chr 7:13). Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary give the meaning of the name as "allotted by God" or "whom God allots," while Hitchcock's Bible Names offers "God hastens" or "divides." Nothing else is recorded about him.

Japhia was one of the sons of King David born to him in Jerusalem, after David had moved his capital there from Hebron. He appears only in the three lists of these sons (2 Sam 5:15; 1 Chr 3:7; 1 Chr 14:6), always named next to his brother Nepheg. Nothing else is recorded about his life. The lists in Chronicles, though not the one in 2 Samuel, also include a brother Nogah. According to 1 Chronicles 3, the sons born in Jerusalem included Solomon and Nathan, sons of Bathsheba, and the other sons are not assigned to particular mothers there, so Japhia's mother is unknown. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests the name may mean "tall," while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "enlightening" or "appearing." The name is also borne by other people in the Bible, including a king of Lachish, and they should not be confused with this son of David.

Jashub was the third of the four sons of Issachar, and so a grandson of Jacob, listed with his brothers Tola, Puah and Shimron (1 Chr 7:1). In the list of Jacob's family who went down to Egypt he is called Job (Gen 46:13). The Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation, reads Jashub there, as the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes. In the census of the tribes in the wilderness he is named as the ancestor of the Jashubites, one of the clans of the tribe of Issachar (Num 26:24). The name is usually taken to mean "he returns." Nothing further is recorded about his life. The same name is borne by at least one other man in the Bible, so the references need to be kept apart.

Jedaiah was a priest who headed the second of the twenty-four priestly divisions. When David's reign organized the priests by lot, the second lot fell to him (1 Chr 24:7). His descendants, described as "of the house of Jeshua," were among the priests who returned from exile in Babylon, numbering 973 (Ezra 2:36; Neh 7:39). Smith's Bible Dictionary takes these returning priests to be the descendants of the same Jedaiah, and this entry follows that view. The link rests on the shared name and priestly role, since the texts do not state it outright. The name is usually explained as meaning "knowing the LORD" (Easton's Bible Dictionary) or "praise the LORD" (Smith's Bible Dictionary). Several other men in the Bible share the name, so not every mention of a Jedaiah refers to this person.

Jediael was a son of Benjamin. He is named in 1 Chr 7:6 as one of three sons, alongside Bela and Becher. His son was Bilhan, whose seven sons included Jeush, Ehud and Ahishahar. The clan descended from Jediael was counted by its family heads at 17,200 fighting men fit for war (1 Chr 7:11). His name does not appear in the lists of Benjamin's sons in Gen 46:21 and Num 26:38. Smith's Bible Dictionary records the common view that he is the same person as Ashbel, though it says this is not certain. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes a suggestion that this list originally referred to Zebulun, with the name read as Jahleel (Gen 46:14). This entry treats him as a son of Benjamin. Several other men in the Bible share the name, which probably means "known of God."

Jehiel was a Levite musician in the time of David, one of several men in the Bible with this name. He is listed among the Levites "of the second degree," the second rank of singers and gatekeepers appointed when the ark of the covenant was brought up to Jerusalem (1 Chr 15:18). In that procession he was one of the group who played psalteries (harps or lyres) "on Alamoth," a musical term of uncertain meaning, perhaps referring to a high pitch or a particular style (1 Chr 15:20). After the ark was placed in its tent, he was named among the Levites serving under Asaph, the chief musician, in the ongoing worship before the ark (1 Chr 16:5). Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "God lives."

Jehudi son of Nethaniah was an official at the court of King Jehoiakim of Judah, named in Jer 36 when Jeremiah's prophecies were read and destroyed. His ancestry is traced back through Shelemiah to Cushi. The princes sent him to bring Baruch, Jeremiah's scribe, with the scroll Baruch had read to the people. Later the king sent Jehudi to fetch the scroll from the room of Elishama the scribe, and Jehudi read it aloud to the king and the princes standing beside him. After Jehudi had read three or four columns, the scroll was cut with a knife and thrown into the fire on the hearth, until all of it was burned. The text says only "he" cut it, and this is usually understood to mean the king. His name means "a Jew." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that his name and the name Cushi ("Ethiopian") may point to a foreign origin.

Jeremiah was a man from Libnah, a town in Judah, known only as the father of Hamutal. Hamutal was the mother of two kings of Judah: Jehoahaz, who reigned three months in Jerusalem, and Zedekiah, who reigned eleven years (2 Kgs 23:31; 2 Kgs 24:18; Jer 52:1). Both kings were sons of Josiah, so Hamutal was Josiah's wife, as Easton's Bible Dictionary notes. That made Jeremiah of Libnah the grandfather of these two kings. He is a different person from the prophet Jeremiah and from several other men who share the name. Nothing else is recorded about him. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "exaltation of the Lord."

Jeroham was the father of Elkanah and so the grandfather of the prophet Samuel. Samuel's birth to Elkanah and Hannah follows later in the same chapter. 1 Sam 1:1 names Jeroham's father as Elihu and places the family at Ramathaim-zophim in the hill country of Ephraim. The genealogies of 1 Chr 6 list him among the Levite descendants of Kohath, where his father appears as Eliab (1 Chr 6:27) and Eliel (1 Chr 6:34). These are probably variant forms of the same name. The description of Elkanah as an "Ephrathite" has been read as tribal (Ephraimite, as in the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia) or as referring to where the family lived. This entry follows the Chronicles genealogy in placing him in the tribe of Levi. The name means "may he be compassionate," and some Greek manuscripts render it Jerahmeel. Several other people in the Bible share the name.

Jezer was the third of the four sons of Naphtali, listed after Jahzeel and Guni and before Shillem. He appears among the members of Jacob's family who went down to Egypt (Gen 46:24). In the census taken in the wilderness he is named as the ancestor of the Jezerites, one of the clans of the tribe of Naphtali (Num 26:49). The genealogy in 1 Chr 7:13 repeats the same four brothers, spelling two names slightly differently (Jahziel and Shallum), and calls them "the sons of Bilhah." Bilhah was Naphtali's mother, so the phrase most likely counts them as her descendants through him. The name is usually explained as meaning "form" or "purpose" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia), though Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "power." Nothing else is recorded about him.

Johanan was a high priest of the Persian period, the son of Joiada and father of Jaddua. Nehemiah 12:11 calls him Jonathan in the line of high priests, and International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats the two names as the same man. His name means "Yahweh has been gracious." He belonged to the priestly line of the tribe of Levi. The heads of Levite and priestly families were recorded in the days of Eliashib, Joiada, Johanan and Jaddua, and the Levite chronicles ran until his time (Neh 12:22–23). Neh 12:23 calls him "the son of Eliashib." Since Neh 12:10 makes Eliashib the father of Joiada, this probably means grandson or descendant. Smith's Bible Dictionary says he succeeded his father as high priest, sometime before 332 BC. Several other people in the Bible share this name.

Joiakim was a high priest of the tribe of Levi in the period after the return from exile. He was the son of Jeshua (called Joshua elsewhere), who was the son of Jozadak, and he was the father of Eliashib, who in turn was the father of Joiada (Neh 12:10). Nehemiah uses his time in office as a point of reference, listing the priests who were heads of families "in the days of Joiakim" (Neh 12:12). It also places a list of Levites in his days alongside the days of Nehemiah the governor and Ezra the priest and scribe (Neh 12:26). Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary describe him as high priest and as his father's successor, which fits his place in the line of high priests. Smith's dates him to before 446 BC. His name means "the LORD raises up."

Jokshan was the second son of Abraham by Keturah, listed after Zimran and before Medan, Midian, Ishbak and Shuah (Gen 25:2; 1 Chr 1:32). Through Abraham he was a half-brother of Isaac and of Ishmael, the son of Hagar. He fathered Sheba and Dedan, and through Dedan he was the grandfather of the Asshurim, Letushim and Leummim (Gen 25:3). These names appear to stand for peoples or tribes as well as individuals, probably groups living in the Arabian region. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "snarer," and Smith's Bible Dictionary as "fowler." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes a suggestion that Jokshan may be another form of Joktan, whose descendants also include a Sheba (Gen 10:25–29). Nothing else is recorded about him beyond these genealogies.

Judas Barsabas was a leader in the early Jerusalem church who was chosen, along with Silas, to carry the decision of the Jerusalem Council to the believers at Antioch. Acts calls the two men "chief men among the brethren." They travelled with Paul and Barnabas, and the council's letter says they would confirm its contents in person. The council is dated to about AD 46, by inference from context. At Antioch, Judas and Silas, described as prophets, encouraged and strengthened the believers with a long address. The next verse, Acts 15:33, says they were later sent back in peace to those who had sent them. His surname, Barsabas, means "son of Sabas." Because Joseph Barsabas, a candidate to replace Judas Iscariot (Acts 1:23), had the same surname, some suggest the two were brothers, but the text does not say so. The name Judas is the same as Judah.

Jude was one of the brothers of Jesus, a son of Mary and of Joseph the carpenter. The people of Nazareth name him with James, Joses and Simon when they question where Jesus' teaching came from. Matthew calls him Judas and Mark calls him Juda (Matt 13:55; Mark 6:3). The author of the Letter of Jude calls himself "the servant of Jesus Christ, and brother of James" (Jude 1:1). This entry, like the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia and Smith's Bible Dictionary, takes him to be this brother of Jesus, with the James he mentions being James the brother of Jesus. Easton's Bible Dictionary instead connects the writer with the apostle Judas, also called Lebbaeus or Thaddaeus. Smith's notes that whether these are the same man is disputed. Through Joseph's family he belonged to the tribe of Judah.

Kenaz was a son of Eliphaz and a grandson of Esau, listed in the genealogies of Edom (Gen 36:11; 1 Chr 1:36). His brothers were Teman, Omar, Zepho (or Zephi) and Gatam. Amalek was also a son of Eliphaz, by the concubine Timna according to Gen 36:12, and Korah appears alongside them among the chiefs descended from Eliphaz. Kenaz is named as one of the 'dukes', or clan chiefs, among the descendants of Esau (Gen 36:15). STEPBible's proper-names index treats Kenaz as one of the clans of Edom. A chief named Kenaz also appears in the later list of Edomite chiefs in Gen 36:42, which may refer to the same clan. The name is shared by other people, including the father or ancestor of Othniel in Israel, who should be kept distinct. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning as 'this purchase' or 'this lamentation.'

Kish was a Levite of the clan of Merari, a son of Mahli and brother of Eleazar, named in the lists of Levite families drawn up in David's time (1 Chr 23:21). His brother Eleazar died without sons, leaving only daughters, and Kish's sons married them (1 Chr 23:22). This probably kept Eleazar's family line and inheritance within the clan, much like the rule for heiresses in Num 36. A later list names Kish's son Jerahmeel, apparently as the head of a Levite family descended from him (1 Chr 24:29). The genealogy in 1 Chr 6:29 names a Libni in Mahli's line, which is why Libni is also counted here as a brother. Several men in the Bible are called Kish, and this Levite is a different person from Kish the Benjamite, father of King Saul. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "a bow."

Kore was a Levite of the Korahite family, listed as the son of Ebiasaph and a descendant of Korah (1 Chr 9:19). His brother was Assir. His sons Shallum and Meshelemiah led families of gatekeepers, or porters, who guarded the entrances of the tabernacle and later the temple (1 Chr 9:19; 26:1). 1 Chr 26:1 calls Meshelemiah one "of the sons of Asaph," probably a shortened form of Ebiasaph. Easton's Bible Dictionary follows that verse in calling Kore "the son of Asaph." Smith's Bible Dictionary places his sons in the reign of David. It also reads "the sons of Kore" in 1 Chr 26:19 as "the sons of the Korhite," referring to the Korahite clan as a whole. Shallum and Meshelemiah may be the same man under two forms of the name, but the text does not say so. Several other people in the Bible are also called Kore.

Luke, also called Lucas, was a physician and companion of the apostle Paul. Paul calls him "the beloved physician" (Col 4:14), lists him among his fellow workers (Phlm 1:24), and in what reads as one of his last letters writes that "only Luke is with me" (2 Tim 4:11). Luke is traditionally held to be the author of the Gospel of Luke and the book of Acts. The "we" passages in Acts suggest the writer joined Paul at Troas, traveled to Philippi, rejoined him later on the journey to Jerusalem, and sailed with him through the shipwreck at Malta to Rome. Smith's Bible Dictionary infers that he was a Gentile, since Paul names him apart from those "of the circumcision" (Col 4:11), and records a tradition that he came from Antioch in Syria. His conversion, later life and death are uncertain.

Maaseiah was the father of Zephaniah, a priest in Jerusalem in the last years of the kingdom of Judah. He is known only through his son, who is always identified as "Zephaniah the son of Maaseiah." King Zedekiah twice sent Zephaniah to the prophet Jeremiah, once to ask about Nebuchadnezzar's attack (Jer 21:1) and once to ask Jeremiah to pray for the nation (Jer 37:3). Zephaniah also received letters sent from Babylon to Jerusalem (Jer 29:25). The phrase "the priest" in these verses can be read as describing either the son or the father. Easton's Bible Dictionary takes it to refer to Zephaniah, while the STEPBible names index treats Maaseiah himself as a priest. Since priesthood was hereditary, both were probably of priestly families. His name means "work of the LORD." Several other men in the Bible share it.

Machir son of Ammiel was a man of Lodebar, a town east of the Jordan, in whose house Jonathan's lame son Mephibosheth was living when King David looked for surviving members of Saul's family. After Ziba told David where Mephibosheth was, David sent and brought him from Machir's house (2 Sam 9:4–5). Later, when David fled from Absalom's rebellion and reached Mahanaim, Machir was one of three men who came to meet him, along with Shobi of Rabbah and Barzillai the Gileadite. The following verses (2 Sam 17:28–29) say they brought bedding, food and supplies for David and his people. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him as a powerful chief who served the house of Saul and then David. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the name's meaning as "selling" or "knowing." He is distinct from the better-known Machir, son of Manasseh.

Maharai the Netophathite was one of David's mighty men, the elite warriors listed in 2 Sam 23:28 and 1 Chr 11:30. His title links him to Netophah, a town near Bethlehem in Judah. He also appears in David's military organization as the tenth of twelve commanders who each served one month of the year in rotation. His division of 24,000 men was on duty in the tenth month (1 Chr 27:13). The same verse describes him as one of the Zarhites, the descendants of Zerah, son of Judah. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia takes this to mean he belonged to the family of Zerah and lived in Netophah. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "impetuous."

Mahli was a Levite of the clan of Merari, the son of Mushi and grandson of Merari, the son of Levi (1 Chr 6:47). His brothers were Eder and Jeremoth (also spelled Jerimoth), and the three are listed as the sons of Mushi among the Levite family heads in David's arrangements (1 Chr 23:23; 24:30). In the genealogy of the temple singer Ethan, Mahli's son is Shamer. The surrounding verses make this clear, though the supplied verse names only Mahli. He shares his name with his uncle Mahli, Merari's other son, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes the repetition. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "sick," and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia as "a sick or weak one." Because several men in these Levite lists bear the name, telling them apart depends on the father named in each passage.

Malchiel was a son of Beriah and a grandson of Asher, one of the sons of Jacob. He is named with his brother Heber among Asher's descendants who went down to Egypt with Jacob (Gen 46:17). In the census of the tribes taken in the wilderness he appears as the founder of a clan called the Malchielites (Num 26:45). The genealogies of Chronicles add that he was the father of Birzavith (1 Chr 7:31). Nothing else is recorded about him. The name is usually explained as meaning "God is king" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia), or "God is my king, or counselor" in Hitchcock's Bible Names.

Malluch was a priest, or the head of a priestly family, of the period after the return from Babylon. He appears among the priests who returned with Zerubbabel and Jeshua (Neh 12:2). His family is listed again in the next generation as "Melicu", whose head was Jonathan in the days of the high priest Joiakim (Neh 12:14). The name also appears among the priests who sealed the covenant in Nehemiah's time (Neh 10:4). Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia take the signer of the covenant to be probably the same priestly line, and they treat Melicu as another form of Malluch. This entry follows that view. Because several men in the Bible bear this name, the identifications are not certain. The name is usually explained as meaning "counsellor".

Mamre was an Amorite, the brother of Eshcol and Aner, who lived in the land of Canaan in Abram's time. Abram was living by the "plain of Mamre" (in Hebrew, probably the oaks or terebinths of Mamre), a place evidently named after him or associated with him, when news came that his nephew Lot had been taken captive. Mamre and his brothers were allies of Abram (Gen 14:13), and by inference from the passage they went with him to rescue Lot. Afterward Abram refused any share of the recovered goods for himself but asked that Aner, Eshcol and Mamre receive their portion (Gen 14:24). Easton's Bible Dictionary describes him as an Amorite chief in alliance with Abraham. The same place, the plains of Mamre, is where the LORD later appeared to Abraham (Gen 18:1). Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "rebellious," "bitter," or "set with trees."

Memucan was one of the seven princes of Persia and Media at the court of King Ahasuerus. These men "saw the king's face" and held the highest rank in the kingdom (Esth 1:14). When Queen Vashti refused the king's summons to appear at his feast, Ahasuerus asked these counsellors what should be done. Memucan spoke for them. He argued that Vashti had wronged not only the king but every prince and people in the provinces, because her example might lead wives everywhere to disregard their husbands (Esth 1:16). He recommended that she be removed as queen and her position given to another, with a royal decree announcing the decision. The king and the princes approved, and Ahasuerus acted on his advice (Esth 1:21). The name is probably of Persian origin, and Easton's Bible Dictionary gives its meaning as "dignified."

Meshullam son of Berechiah and grandson of Meshezabeel was one of the men who repaired the wall of Jerusalem under Nehemiah. He is listed working on a section next to Meremoth son of Urijah (Neh 3:4), and later as repairing the stretch opposite his own chamber (Neh 3:30). He is generally taken to be one man named twice, though the second mention could in principle refer to a different section he took on. His daughter married Johanan, son of Tobiah, the Ammonite official who opposed Nehemiah. Nehemiah notes this marriage as one reason many in Judah were bound by oath to Tobiah (Neh 6:18). The name Meshullam was common after the exile and is shared by several other men in the Bible, so he should be distinguished from them.

Michah was a Levite of the family of Uzziel, a branch of the Kohathite clan. In the lists of Levites arranged in King David's time, he is named as the first, or chief, of the sons of Uzziel, with Jesiah (also spelled Isshiah) second (1 Chr 23:20; 24:25). His son Shamir is named after him (1 Chr 24:24). Elizaphan, Mishael and Zithri are also counted among his brothers. Since those three appear elsewhere as sons of the Uzziel of Moses' generation, "sons of Uzziel" here probably names the clan descended from Uzziel rather than his immediate children. Smith's Bible Dictionary takes his name to mean "who is like God?" and notes that it is a form of Micah. The setting in David's reign is inferred from the surrounding chapters, which describe David organizing the Levites.

Mikloth was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, listed in the genealogy of the family of Saul as a son of the founder of Gibeon and his wife Maachah (Easton's Bible Dictionary). Chronicles names that father Jehiel, or Jeiel. This entry follows the view that he is the same man as Abiel, whom 1 Sam 9:1 calls the father of Kish, so Mikloth appears as a brother of Kish, Ner, Abdon, Zur, Baal, Nadab, Gedor, Ahio and Zacher (also called Zechariah). Mikloth became the father of Shimeah, spelled Shimeam in the parallel list, and his family lived in Jerusalem alongside their relatives. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that comparing the two lists shows his name has dropped out of the end of 1 Chr 8:31. The name is shared by others, including a commander under David mentioned in 1 Chr 27:4.

Milcom was the national god of the Ammonites, called in 1 Kgs 11:5 "the abomination of the Ammonites." Solomon, influenced by his foreign wives, worshipped Milcom along with Ashtoreth of the Sidonians and Chemosh of Moab, and this is given as a reason the kingdom would be divided after him (1 Kgs 11:33). Solomon had built a high place for Milcom east of Jerusalem, on the right side of what was later called the Mount of Corruption. Centuries afterward King Josiah, the king referred to in 2 Kgs 23:13, defiled it as part of his reforms. The name is usually understood to come from the word for "king." Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning "their king," and Smith's Bible Dictionary "great king." Both Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treat Milcom as closely connected with, or the same as, Molech. Some scholars instead regard the two as separate deities.

Miniamin was a priest, or the head of a priestly family, in the period after the return from Babylon. Under the spelling Miamin he is listed among the priests who came back with Zerubbabel (Neh 12:5), and Easton's Bible Dictionary calls him a chief priest. A Mijamin appears among the priests who sealed the covenant in Nehemiah's time (Neh 10:7). In the days of the high priest Joiakim, the house "of Miniamin" is named among the priestly families, though the name of its head at that time has dropped out of the text (Neh 12:17). This entry treats the three spellings as one priestly line, as Easton's does. Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests the covenant signer may have been a descendant of the earlier Miamin. The name, which means "from the right hand," was borne by several people, so these identifications are not certain.

Mizzah was a son of Reuel and a grandson of Esau through Esau's wife Bashemath. He is listed as the youngest of Reuel's four sons, with his brothers Nahath, Zerah and Shammah (Gen 36:13; 1 Chr 1:37). Genesis also names him among the "dukes", or clan chiefs, descended from Reuel in the land of Edom (Gen 36:17). This suggests that his name came to stand for an Edomite clan as well as for an individual. Nothing else is recorded about him. The meaning of the name is uncertain: Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "fear", the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives "strong" or "firm", and Hitchcock's Bible Names offers "defluxion from the head."

Moadiah was a priest, or a priestly family named after him, in the period after the return from exile. Nehemiah lists Maadiah among the priests who came back from Babylon with Zerubbabel (Neh 12:5). In the next generation, in the days of the high priest Joiakim, Piltai was head of the priestly house of Moadiah (Neh 12:17). Since the two lists run in parallel, Maadiah and Moadiah are generally taken as spellings of the same name. This entry also identifies him with Maaziah, one of the priests who sealed the covenant under Nehemiah (Neh 10:8), as the STEPBible proper-names index does. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treat Maaziah under a separate heading. Because the covenant came generations after the first return, the name in Neh 10:8 probably stands for the priestly family rather than the original man.

n: Mother of the Wife of Simon
bio: The Mother of the Wife of Simon was the mother-in-law of Simon Peter, the apostle. The three Gospels that tell her story all say she lay sick with a fever in Simon's house, which Luke calls "a great fever" (Luke 4:38). Mark and Luke place this immediately after Jesus left the synagogue, and Mark's wider context sets it in Capernaum. People told Jesus about her and asked him to help (Mark 1:30; Luke 4:38). The accounts go on to say that he healed her, that the fever left her, and that she got up and served them. That evening many other sick people were brought to the house to be healed. The event is dated to about AD 27, an estimate inferred from context. Her name is not given, and nothing else is recorded about her.

Naamah was a wife of King Solomon and the mother of Rehoboam, his successor as king of Judah. Each of the three verses that mention her names her as Rehoboam's mother and calls her an Ammonite, a formula repeated in the official summaries of his reign in 1 Kgs 14:21, 31 and 2 Chr 12:13. She was probably one of the foreign women Solomon married, among whom 1 Kgs 11:1 lists Ammonites. Easton's Bible Dictionary calls her the daughter of the king of Ammon. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that an addition in the Greek Septuagint makes her the daughter of Hanun son of Nahash, king of Ammon. Through her son she belongs to the royal line of David, and Rehoboam appears in the genealogy of Jesus in Matt 1:7, though she is not named there. Her name, meaning "pleasant," is also borne by the sister of Tubal-cain in Gen 4:22.

Nahash was king of the Ammonites in the time of Saul. He besieged Jabesh-gilead, east of the Jordan. When its men offered to make a treaty and serve him, he agreed only on condition that he gouge out every man's right eye, as a disgrace on all Israel (1 Sam 11:1–2). According to the rest of the chapter, the town sent word to Saul, who gathered an army and routed the Ammonites (Easton's Bible Dictionary summarizes 1 Sam 11:1–11). Samuel later recalled that this threat from Nahash was the moment the people insisted on having a king (1 Sam 12:12). Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "snake" or "serpent." Several men in the Bible share the name, including an Ammonite king who was later friendly to David. Whether he is this same man or a successor is uncertain, and this entry covers only the king of Saul's day.

Nahash was a king of the Ammonites and the father of Hanun, who succeeded him on the throne. He had shown kindness to David at some point, and when Nahash died, David sent servants to Hanun to comfort him over his father's death (2 Sam 10:2; 1 Chr 19:1–2). The text does not say what that kindness was. Whether he is the same Nahash of Ammon who besieged Jabesh-gilead and was defeated by Saul (1 Sam 11) is uncertain. Many readers take them to be one king, possibly hostile to Saul and so friendly to David, while others think they may be two rulers of the same name. A Shobi son of Nahash from Rabbah, the Ammonite capital, later brought supplies to David (2 Sam 17:27) and may have been his son. Several other men in the Bible share the name, which means "snake" or "serpent" according to Hitchcock's Bible Names.

Nahath was a son of Reuel and a grandson of Esau through Esau's wife Bashemath. His brothers were Zerah, Shammah and Mizzah. He is listed first among Reuel's sons, and Smith's Bible Dictionary takes him to be the eldest. Genesis 36 names him as one of the "dukes", or clan chiefs, who came from Reuel in the land of Edom, so his line was probably one of the Edomite clans (Gen 36:17). The genealogy in 1 Chr 1:37 repeats his name among Reuel's sons. Nothing else is recorded about him. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "rest". Several other people in the Bible share the name Nahath, and this entry concerns only the Edomite chief.

Nahath was a Levite of the clan of Kohath and an ancestor of the prophet Samuel. His name appears in different forms in the genealogies: Tohu in 1 Sam 1:1, Toah in 1 Chr 6:34, and Nahath in 1 Chr 6:26. Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries both describe him as a Kohathite Levite, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats the three forms as one person. 1 Sam 1:1 calls him the son of Zuph and the father of Elihu, the great-grandfather of Samuel's father Elkanah. 1 Chr 6:26 lists Nahath as the son of Zophai, which is probably another form of Zuph. His son's name also varies, appearing as Eliel in 1 Chr 6:34. Nothing else is recorded about him. Other men in the Bible share the name Nahath, so the context matters when the name appears.

Nepheg was one of the sons of King David born in Jerusalem, after David had moved his capital there from Hebron. He appears only in the three lists of those sons, each time between Elishua or Nogah and Japhia (2 Sam 5:15; 1 Chr 3:7; 14:6). His mother is not named, and the text records nothing about his life beyond his place among David's children. The Chronicles lists include Nogah next to him, a name missing from the list in 2 Samuel. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia give the meaning of his name as "sprout" or "shoot," while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "weak" or "slacked." The name is shared by another man, a Levite who was a son of Izhar and a brother of Korah (Exod 6:21), and he should not be confused with this son of David.

Obadiah, also called Abda, was a Levite descended from Jeduthun through Galal who lived in Jerusalem after the return from exile in Babylon. In 1 Chr 9:16 he is called Obadiah son of Shemaiah. The parallel list in Neh 11:17 names him Abda son of Shammua, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia and Smith's Bible Dictionary treat the two as the same man. The name means "servant of the Lord." Smith's also identifies him with the Obadiah listed among the gatekeepers who guarded the storerooms at the gates in Neh 12:25, and this entry follows that view. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia instead counts that gatekeeper as a separate person. Because several men in the Bible bear the name Obadiah, the identification is not certain.

Omar was a son of Eliphaz, the firstborn son of Esau, which made him a grandson of Esau. He is named second among Eliphaz's sons, after Teman, in the genealogy of Esau's descendants in Gen 36:11, and again in the parallel list in 1 Chr 1:36. His brothers included Zepho, Gatam and Kenaz, and the Chronicles list also includes Amalek. Gen 36:15 calls him a "duke," meaning a chief or clan leader, among the Edomite chiefs descended from Esau, so a clan of Edom probably bore his name. Nothing else is recorded about him. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "eloquent," and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests it may be connected with a Hebrew word meaning "speak."

On, son of Peleth, was a man of the tribe of Reuben who joined Korah, Dathan and Abiram when they gathered men to challenge the leadership of Moses and Aaron during the wilderness period (Num 16:1). His name appears only in this opening verse. As Smith's Bible Dictionary notes, he is not mentioned again in the rest of the account of the revolt, and he is absent from the description of its outcome, when the ground swallowed Dathan and Abiram. Whether he withdrew from the rebellion or simply goes unnamed afterward is not stated. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of his name as "pain," "force" or "iniquity." The other two verses listed here use "on" only as an ordinary English word and do not refer to him.

Parosh was the ancestor and head of an Israelite family that returned to Jerusalem from exile in Babylon. The lists of returnees in Ezra 2:3 and Nehemiah 7:8 count 2,172 of his descendants, the largest lay family in those lists. Seven men from this family appear in Ezra 10:25 among those who had married foreign wives in Ezra's time. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia adds that part of the family came back later with Ezra (Ezra 8:3, spelled "Pharosh" in the King James Version). It also notes that a descendant named Pedaiah helped rebuild the city walls (Neh 3:25), and that the name appears among those who sealed Nehemiah's covenant (Neh 10:14). Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the name's meaning as "a flea." Several people in the Bible share this name. Nothing is recorded about Parosh himself beyond his descendants.

Pekahiah was a king of Israel, the son and successor of Menahem. He began to reign in Samaria in the fiftieth year of Azariah (Uzziah) king of Judah and ruled for two years. His other acts were recorded in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Israel. The surrounding passage adds that he continued the worship practices begun by Jeroboam (2 Kgs 15:24). It also says that Pekah son of Remaliah, one of his captains, conspired with fifty men of Gilead and killed him in the palace at Samaria, then took the throne (2 Kgs 15:25). This entry dates his reign to about 761–759 BC, by inference from context, following Easton's Bible Dictionary. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives 759–757 BC, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that many scholars place it later, after 738 BC. His name is usually explained as "the LORD has opened (the eyes)."

Phichol was the chief captain, or army commander, of Abimelech, the Philistine king of Gerar. He went with Abimelech to Abraham, who acknowledged that God was with Abraham, and was present when the two made a covenant at Beersheba, after which they returned to the land of the Philistines (Gen 21:22, 32). A commander of the same name later went with Abimelech and Ahuzzath to Isaac to make a similar treaty (Gen 26:26). Because the two episodes are separated by many years, it is uncertain whether this is the same man or a successor bearing the same name or title. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the STEPBible proper names index treat him as one person active in the days of both Abraham and Isaac. The meaning of the name is unclear: Easton's Bible Dictionary gives "great," Smith's gives "strong," and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "the mouth of all."

Philip was a son of Herod the Great and the first husband of Herodias. He is mentioned only in connection with the imprisonment of John the Baptist. His brother Herod Antipas, the tetrarch, married Herodias, and John rebuked him for it. That rebuke led Herod to have John bound and put in prison (Matt 14:3; Mark 6:17; Luke 3:19). The Gospels call Herodias "his brother Philip's wife," which shows she was still regarded as Philip's wife when Herod took her. Easton's Bible Dictionary adds that he was the father of Salome, and it calls him Herod Philip I. He is a different person from Philip the tetrarch, his half-brother of the same name, who ruled territories to the north-east. Several other people in the New Testament are also named Philip, including the apostle and the evangelist. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "a lover of horses."

Phut, also spelled Put, was the third of the four sons of Ham listed in the Table of Nations, after Cush and Mizraim and before Canaan (Gen 10:6; 1 Chr 1:8). Through Ham he was a grandson of Noah. Unlike his brothers, he is given no listed descendants. Elsewhere the name stands for a people or land descended from him. Ezek 27:10 names men of Phut, together with Persia and Lud, serving as soldiers in the army of Tyre. Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that the prophets place Phut in Africa, probably near Egypt, and gives the views that it was Libya or Nubia. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia points out that the Greek translation of the prophets renders it "Libya", and it discusses another common identification with the Egyptian Punt, in the Somali region, perhaps reaching across the Red Sea into Yemen. The exact location remains uncertain.

Poti-pherah was an Egyptian priest of On, the city later known as Heliopolis, near modern Cairo. His daughter Asenath was given to Joseph as his wife by Pharaoh when Pharaoh raised Joseph to authority over Egypt and gave him the Egyptian name Zaphnathpaaneah (Gen 41:45). Through Asenath, Poti-pherah became the grandfather of Joseph's two sons, Manasseh and Ephraim, who were born in Egypt before the years of famine (Gen 41:50; Gen 46:20). Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that the Hebrew title may mean either priest or prince of On. His name is probably Egyptian, and it is often compared with that of Potiphar, the officer who bought Joseph, though the two are distinct men in the narrative. Nothing else is recorded about him.

Puah was the second-listed of the four sons of Issachar and a grandson of Jacob. His brothers were Tola, Jashub and Shimron. Genesis 46:13 names him Phuvah among the family members who went down to Egypt with Jacob, and Numbers 26:23 spells his name Pua and calls him the ancestor of the Punites, one of the clans of the tribe of Issachar counted in the wilderness census. 1 Chr 7:1 repeats him in the genealogy of Issachar. Jashub appears as Job in Genesis 46:13. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "mouth" or "splendid." Nothing else is recorded about his life. The name is shared by other people in the Bible, including one of the Hebrew midwives in Egypt and the father of the judge Tola, so he should not be confused with them.

Rehabiah was a Levite, the only son of Eliezer. By inference from 1 Chr 23:15, which names Eliezer as a son of Moses, he was Moses' grandson, as Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary also state. In 1 Chronicles 23:17 he is called the chief of Eliezer's line and is said to have had very many sons, so his descendants became a Levitical family in their own right. In the later list of Levite family heads, Isshiah is named as the first of Rehabiah's sons (1 Chr 24:21). A line of descent in 1 Chr 26:25 traces Rehabiah, then Jeshaiah, Joram, Zichri and Shelomith, who was a treasurer of dedicated gifts. This entry treats Jeshaiah as his son. Jeshaiah may be the same person as Isshiah, but that is uncertain. The name is usually explained as "the Lord has enlarged" (Easton's Bible Dictionary).

Rimmon was a man of Beeroth, a town counted as part of the tribe of Benjamin, and the father of Baanah and Rechab. His sons were captains of raiding bands serving Ish-bosheth, Saul's son. They went to Ish-bosheth's house in the heat of the day while he lay resting at noon and killed him. They then brought the news to David, who answered them with an oath (2 Sam 4:9). Rimmon himself appears only as part of his sons' identification, "the sons of Rimmon the Beerothite." Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that Beeroth was one of the four Gibeonite cities (Josh 9:17). The name is usually understood to mean "pomegranate." Rimmon is also the name of several places in the Bible and should not be confused with them.

Serah was the daughter of Asher and a granddaughter of Jacob. She appears in the list of those who went down to Egypt with Jacob, where she is named after her four brothers, Jimnah (Imnah), Ishuah (Isuah), Isui and Beriah, as "their sister" (Gen 46:17). The same list of Asher's children is repeated in the tribal genealogies of Chronicles (1 Chr 7:30). In the census of Israel taken in the wilderness she is again named as Asher's daughter. There the King James Version spells her name Sarah, though the Hebrew name is the same (Num 26:46). She is one of very few women named in these tribal lists, and the text gives no reason for her inclusion. Nothing else is recorded about her. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of her name as "abundance" or "princess."

Shalmaneser was a king of Assyria in the time of Hoshea, the last king of the northern kingdom of Israel. He marched against Hoshea, who submitted as his vassal and paid him tribute (2 Kgs 17:3). In Hoshea's seventh year, which was Hezekiah's fourth, he came up against Samaria and besieged it (2 Kgs 18:9). The surrounding account says the siege lasted three years before the city fell and Israel was exiled (2 Kgs 17:5–6; 18:10–11). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identifies him as Shalmaneser IV, reigning from about 727 BC. It notes that Sargon claimed the final capture, so Shalmaneser may have died or been deposed during the siege. The "Shalman" who spoiled Beth-arbel in Hos 10:14 may be a shortened form of his name, as Easton's Bible Dictionary holds. Others suggest a Moabite king named Salamanu. This entry follows the identification with Shalmaneser.

Shammah was a son of Reuel and a grandson of Esau through Esau's wife Bashemath. He is named third among Reuel's four sons, after Nahath and Zerah and before Mizzah (Gen 36:13; 1 Chr 1:37). In the list of Edom's chiefs he appears as "duke Shammah," one of the clan leaders descended from Reuel in the land of Edom (Gen 36:17). Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both describe him as a tribal chief of Edom. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of his name as "desolation" or "astonishment." Nothing more is recorded about him. Several other men in the Bible share the name Shammah, including a brother of David and one of David's mighty men. This Edomite chief is a different person.

Shammua was a son of King David, born in Jerusalem after David made the city his capital. He is listed first among the sons born there, ahead of Shobab, Nathan and Solomon (2 Sam 5:14; 1 Chr 14:4). In 1 Chr 3:5 he is called Shimea, and that verse names all four as sons of Bathshua daughter of Ammiel, a variant spelling of Bathsheba. Easton's Bible Dictionary treats Shimea and Shammua as the same person. That makes Shammua a full brother of Solomon and a member of the tribe of Judah. Nothing more is recorded about his life beyond these lists. Several other men in the Bible share the name Shammua, so he should be kept distinct from them.

Shebaniah was a Levite in the time of Ezra and Nehemiah, one of several men of that name in the Bible. When the returned exiles gathered for fasting and confession after the reading of the Law, he was among the Levites who stood on the stairs and cried aloud to the LORD (Neh 9:4). He is also named among the Levites who called the people to stand up and bless the LORD their God for ever (Neh 9:5). His name appears again among the Levites who sealed the covenant with Nehemiah to keep God's law (Neh 10:10). Whether all three mentions refer to one man is not certain, though Smith's Bible Dictionary treats them as the same person. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes the name might stand for a Levitical family rather than an individual. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "increased by Jehovah."

Shebaniah was a priest, or the priestly family named after him, in the period after the return from exile in Babylon. As Shechaniah, he appears in the list of priests who came back from captivity with Zerubbabel (Neh 12:3). The surrounding verse, Neh 12:1, identifies the group. Smith's Bible Dictionary and Easton's Bible Dictionary take Shechaniah and Shebaniah as the same name, and this entry follows that view. A Shebaniah is also among the priests who set their seal to Nehemiah's covenant (Neh 10:4). In the next generation, under the high priest Joiakim, Joseph was head of the priestly house of Shebaniah (Neh 12:14). Since these lists span several generations, the name probably refers to a family line as well as its founder. Several other men in the Bible bear the name, including Levites, and are distinct from this priest.

Shelomith was a Levite in King David's reign, descended from Moses' son Eliezer through a line of descendants: Rehabiah, Jeshaiah, Joram, Zichri and then Shelomith, whose father was Zichri (1 Chr 26:25). The parallel listing in 1 Chr 23:15–17 identifies this Eliezer as Moses' son, as Smith's Bible Dictionary also does. Shelomith and his relatives were in charge of the treasuries of dedicated things. These were gifts that David, the heads of families and the army commanders had set apart, mostly from the spoils of war, to maintain the house of the Lord. Earlier dedications were also placed under his care, including those of Samuel the seer, Saul, Abner and Joab (1 Chr 26:26–28). Some sources spell the name Shelomoth. Several other people in the Bible share this name, so this man should not be confused with them.

Shemaiah was a Levite, the firstborn of the sons of Obed-edom, listed among the gatekeepers in David's reign (1 Chr 26:4). His younger brothers included Jehozabad, Joah, Sacar, Nethaneel, Ammiel, Issachar and Peulthai. His sons were Othni, Rephael, Obed, Elzabad, Elihu and Semachiah. They are described as mighty men of valour who held leading positions in their father's family, and Elzabad's brothers are called strong men (1 Chr 26:6–7). The surrounding chapter organizes the temple gatekeepers into divisions, so Shemaiah's family probably served in that role. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia counts him among the Korahite Levites, and Smith's Bible Dictionary dates him to about 1014 BC. The name means "the Lord hears" and is shared by several other people in the Bible.

Shemaiah the Nehelamite was a prophet among the Jewish exiles in Babylon who opposed Jeremiah. He is one of several men in the Bible with this name, which Hitchcock's Bible Names takes to mean "one who hears or obeys the Lord." "Nehelamite" probably points to his family or home town, though no such place is otherwise known. Jeremiah was told to deliver a message to him (Jer 29:24). The surrounding verses (Jer 29:25–29) say that Shemaiah had sent letters from Babylon to Zephaniah the priest in Jerusalem, urging him to restrain Jeremiah. In response, Jeremiah sent word to all the exiles that the LORD had not sent Shemaiah and that he had led them to trust in a lie. Because he had taught rebellion against the LORD, he and his descendants would be punished. None of his line would remain among the people, and he would not live to see the good the LORD planned for them.

Shemida (also spelled Shemidah) was a son of Gilead in the tribe of Manasseh, son of Joseph. Through Gilead's father Machir, as Num 26:29 traces the line, he was a great-grandson of Manasseh. He was the ancestor of the Shemidaites, one of the clans of Manasseh counted in the census in the plains of Moab (Num 26:32). When the land was divided under Joshua, his descendants were among the Manassite families who received a share of territory, apparently west of the Jordan, alongside the clans of Abiezer, Helek, Asriel, Shechem and Hepher (Josh 17:2). 1 Chr 7:19 names his sons as Ahian, Shechem, Likhi and Aniam. One of these sons shares the name Shechem with one of Shemida's brothers. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of his name as "name of knowledge," and Smith's Bible Dictionary renders it "wise."

Shemiramoth was a Levite musician in David's time. He was one of the Levites of the second rank appointed to accompany the ark of the covenant when it was brought up to Jerusalem (1 Chr 15:18). Among the musicians he played the psaltery, a stringed instrument, "on Alamoth," which probably refers to a higher pitch or register (1 Chr 15:20). After the ark was placed in its tent, he was among those Asaph led in ministering before it with psalteries and harps (1 Chr 16:5). Another Levite named Shemiramoth was sent by Jehoshaphat to teach the Law in Judah (2 Chr 17:8). He is a separate person from a later reign, although the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats the name as belonging to a Levitical family. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives its meaning as "the height of the heavens."

Shephatiah was the ancestor of a family whose descendants returned from exile in Babylon to Jerusalem and Judah. The lists of returnees who came back with Zerubbabel count 372 members of this family (Ezra 2:4; Neh 7:9). A later group of 80 males from the same family, led by Zebadiah son of Michael, travelled with Ezra (Ezra 8:8). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats these as one family that returned in two stages. Nothing is recorded about Shephatiah himself beyond his name, which means "the Lord has judged." Several other people in the Bible share the name, and this family ancestor should not be confused with them.

Sherebiah was a Levite in the time of Nehemiah. He appears among the Levites who put their seal to the covenant to keep God's law (Neh 10:12, read with the surrounding list of Levites). He is also listed among the chief Levites who led praise and thanksgiving in alternating groups, following the arrangement attributed to David (Neh 12:24). Nehemiah 12:8 names a Sherebiah among the Levites connected with the thanksgiving. The context of that list ties it to those who returned from exile with Zerubbabel, so it may refer to an earlier man or to a family name carried by later Levites. Because several Bible figures share this name, how these mentions relate is uncertain. This entry follows the STEPBible Proper Names index in treating them as one Levite who sealed the covenant and led worship. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "singing with the Lord."

Sheshai was one of the three sons of Anak, named with his brothers Ahiman and Talmai, who lived at Hebron when Moses sent spies into Canaan (Num 13:22). The Anakim were remembered as people of great size, which is why some reference works call Sheshai a giant. Joshua 15:14 says Caleb drove the three sons of Anak out of Hebron. Judges 1:10 reports that the tribe of Judah attacked the Canaanites of Hebron, formerly called Kirjath-arba, and killed Sheshai, Ahiman and Talmai. The two accounts are usually read as describing the same conquest, with Caleb leading Judah's forces. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests the name may have belonged to an old Hebron clan rather than a single person. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "noble," while Hitchcock's Bible Names offers "six," "mercy" or "flax."

Sheshan was a man of the tribe of Judah, the son of Ishi and a descendant of Appaim in the Jerahmeelite clan of the genealogy in 1 Chronicles 2. The text says he had no sons, only daughters, and that he gave one of his daughters as wife to his Egyptian servant Jarha. She bore Attai, through whom Sheshan's line is traced for several generations. The same chapter also names Ahlai as Sheshan's child. Because Sheshan had no sons, Ahlai is probably a daughter, perhaps the one who married Jarha, though the text does not say so directly. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both identify him as a descendant of Jerahmeel son of Hezron. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of his name as "lily" or "joy."

Shillem was the fourth-named son of Naphtali, one of the sons of Jacob, and so a grandson of Jacob through Bilhah, Rachel's servant. He appears in the list of Jacob's family who went down to Egypt, alongside his brothers Jahzeel, Guni and Jezer (Gen 46:24). In the census taken in the wilderness he is named as the ancestor of the Shillemites, one of the clans of the tribe of Naphtali (Num 26:49). The genealogy in 1 Chr 7:13 lists the same four brothers but gives his name as Shallum, a variant form of the same name. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia describes him as the youngest son of Naphtali, probably from his place at the end of each list. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "requital" or "retribution." Nothing more is recorded about him.

Shimron was the fourth son of Issachar, son of Jacob, and the founder of the Shimronite clan in the tribe of Issachar. His brothers were Tola, Puah and Jashub. He appears among those who went down to Egypt with Jacob, where the brother called Jashub elsewhere is named Job (Gen 46:13).
