The census in the wilderness counts the Shimronites as one of Issachar's families (Num 26:24), and he is listed again in the Chronicles genealogy of the tribe (1 Chr 7:1). Nothing else is recorded about him. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia give the meaning of his name as "watch" or "watchman," and Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "watch-height." He is a different figure from the Canaanite town of Shimron in Zebulun's territory.

Shobab was a son of King David, born in Jerusalem. He appears only in the three lists of David's Jerusalem-born children (2 Sam 5:14; 1 Chr 3:5; 1 Chr 14:4), where he is named second, after Shammua (called Shimea in Chronicles) and before Nathan and Solomon. 1 Chr 3:5 says these four were the sons of Bathshua the daughter of Ammiel, a form of the name of Bathsheba. That makes him a full brother of Solomon and a half-brother of the sons born to David at Hebron, such as Amnon, Absalom and Adonijah. Nothing else is recorded about his life. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "rebellious," while Hitchcock's Bible Names offers "returned" or "turned back." The name Shobab is also borne by at least one other man in the Bible, a descendant of Judah through Caleb, who should not be confused with this son of David.

Shuah was a Canaanite man whose daughter became the wife of Judah, son of Jacob. According to Gen 38:2, Judah met her while staying near Hirah the Adullamite, married her, and had children with her. 1 Chr 2:3 names their three sons as Er, Onan and Shelah and spells the father's name Shua. His daughter's own name is never given; she is called only "the daughter of Shuah" (Gen 38:12), and her death is recorded before Judah went up to Timnath for the sheepshearing. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "wealth," while Hitchcock's Bible Names offers "ditch," "swimming" or "humiliation." Several other people in the Bible share this name, including a son of Abraham by Keturah, but this Shuah is the Canaanite father-in-law of Judah.

Shubael, also called Shebuel, was a Levite descended from Moses through Moses' son Gershom. He is named as the chief of the sons of Gershom (1 Chr 23:16) and appears among the descendants of Amram, Moses' father, with a son or descendant named Jehdeiah (1 Chr 24:20). He is described as "ruler of the treasures" (1 Chr 26:24), placed in the setting of David's organization of the Levites for temple service. The text calls him "the son of Gershom," which the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia takes as grandson of Moses. Easton's Bible Dictionary and other reference works treat him as a later descendant, since the lists belong to David's time. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests Shubael is probably the original form of the name. Several other people in the Bible bear the same name.

Shupham was a son of Benjamin and the founder of a Benjamite clan, the Shuphamites, listed in the census of Num 26:39. His name appears in several forms. Genesis 46:21 calls him Muppim and counts him among the sons of Benjamin who went down to Egypt with Jacob. In 1 Chr 8:5 he appears as Shephuphan. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia also links him with Shuppim in 1 Chr 7:12. It notes that the original form of the name is almost impossible to recover, and that the name probably means a kind of serpent. Because 1 Chr 8:3–5 lists Shephuphan among the sons of Bela, Smith's Bible Dictionary treats him there as Benjamin's grandson. This entry follows the Genesis and Numbers lists, which make him a son of Benjamin. The difference may reflect a family later counted under Bela's line. Nothing else is recorded about him.

Shuthelah was a son of Ephraim and the head of the Shuthalhite family within the tribe of Ephraim (Num 26:35). In the census list of Numbers he heads his brothers Becher and Tahan, and his own son Eran founded the Eranite family (Num 26:36). The genealogy in 1 Chronicles names his son as Bered and traces a line of descendants after him (1 Chr 7:20). Later verses in that chapter mention his brothers Ezer and Elead, killed by men of Gath, and Beriah, born afterward. Smith's Bible Dictionary takes the line beginning in 1 Chr 7:20 to lead down to Joshua son of Nun, which would make Shuthelah his ancestor. The name appears again a generation or more later in the same Chronicles list, so more than one man may have borne it. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives its meaning as "plant" or "verdure."

Simon was a man from Cyrene, a city on the north coast of Africa in present-day Libya, whom the Roman soldiers forced to carry the cross of Jesus on the way to the crucifixion, about AD 30 by inference from context. Matthew, Mark and Luke all record the incident. Mark and Luke add that he was coming in from the country and passing by when he was seized, and Luke says he carried the cross behind Jesus (Luke 23:26). Mark alone names him as the father of Alexander and Rufus (Mark 15:21), which suggests his sons were known to Mark's readers. Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests this Rufus may be the one greeted in Rom 16:13. Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that Cyrene had a large Jewish community and suggests Simon may have been among the men of Cyrene who later preached in Antioch (Acts 11:20). He is one of several men in the Bible named Simon.

Stephanas was a Christian of Corinth whose household was the first in the Roman province of Achaia to accept the gospel. Paul calls it the "firstfruits of Achaia" and says it had devoted itself to serving fellow believers. His household was one of the few Paul baptized personally at Corinth. Stephanas later came to Paul, probably at Ephesus, with Fortunatus and Achaicus, and Paul says they made up for the Corinthians' absence. Paul urged the church to respect and follow such workers. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests these three men brought the Corinthians' letter to Paul and probably carried 1 Corinthians back in reply. Easton's Bible Dictionary mentions a suggestion that he was the Philippian jailer of Acts 16. His name means "crown" (Hitchcock's Bible Names).

Talmai was one of the three sons, or descendants, of Anak, along with Ahiman and Sheshai. They lived at Hebron when the Israelite spies passed through the hill country of Canaan (Num 13:22). The Anakim were known as men of great size, a reputation reflected in the spies' report in the surrounding chapter. During the conquest, Caleb drove Talmai and his brothers out of Hebron (Josh 15:14). Judges 1:10 says the men of Judah attacked the Canaanites of Hebron, formerly called Kirjath-arba, and killed Sheshai, Ahiman and Talmai. The two accounts probably describe the same campaign, with Caleb leading Judah's forces. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats the name as possibly that of a clan rather than a single person. Talmai of Hebron is distinct from other men of the same name in the Bible, such as Talmai king of Geshur.

Talmai, son of Ammihud, was king of Geshur in the time of David. Geshur was a small kingdom, described by the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia as Aramean, which probably lay east of the Jordan near the Sea of Galilee. Talmai's daughter Maacah became one of David's wives, and she was the mother of Absalom, David's third son, born at Hebron (2 Sam 3:3; 1 Chr 3:2). After Absalom had his half-brother Amnon killed, he fled to his grandfather Talmai in Geshur, while David mourned for his son every day (2 Sam 13:37). The marriage probably reflects a political alliance between David and the Geshurite king. Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests Talmai was a minor ruler dependent on David. The name Talmai is shared by other people in the Bible, including a son of Anak at Hebron (Num 13:22), who should not be confused with this king.

Teman was a son of Eliphaz and a grandson of Esau. He heads the list of Eliphaz's sons in both genealogies, alongside Omar, Zepho (Zephi in 1 Chr 1:36), Gatam and Kenaz. Chronicles also lists Timna and Amalek with this group. Because Eliphaz was Esau's firstborn, Teman belonged to the leading line of Esau's descendants. Genesis names him first among the 'dukes', or clan chiefs, descended from Eliphaz. The name, which Smith's Bible Dictionary and Hitchcock's Bible Names explain as meaning 'the south,' was also borne by an Edomite clan and district. STEPBible's proper-names index links that clan with a reputation for wisdom. By inference, later references to Teman in Edom, and to Job's friend Eliphaz the Temanite (Job 2:11), trace back to this line. Since the name refers to more than one person or group, which mentions mean the individual and which mean the clan is not always certain.

Timna was a concubine of Eliphaz, Esau's son, and the mother of Amalek (Gen 36:12). 1 Chr 1:39 names a Timna as the sister of Lotan, one of the sons of Seir the Horite. Smith's Bible Dictionary presumes that the two are the same woman, and this entry follows that view, which makes her a daughter of Seir and a sister of Lotan, Shobal, Zibeon, Anah, Dishon, Ezer and Dishan. That would mean a Horite woman was joined to Esau's line. In the list of Eliphaz's descendants at 1 Chr 1:36, Timna's name appears next to Amalek's, apparently a shortened form of the Genesis account. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the name Timna also appears for a chief or clan of Edom, so several figures bear it.

Trophimus was a Christian from Ephesus, in the Roman province of Asia, who traveled with Paul. He was one of the companions who went with Paul from Greece through Macedonia into Asia near the end of his third missionary journey (Acts 20:4). He went on with Paul to Jerusalem. There, people who had seen the two together in the city assumed that Paul had brought him into the temple. Because Trophimus was evidently a Gentile, that belief set off the riot in which Paul was seized and arrested (Acts 21:29). Paul later wrote that he had left Trophimus sick at Miletus, a coastal city not far from Ephesus (2 Tim 4:20). Easton's Bible Dictionary takes this to refer to a later occasion not recorded in Acts. Some, including Smith's Bible Dictionary, have suggested he was the unnamed brother sent with Titus to Corinth.

Urijah, also spelled Uriah, was a priest of the period after the return from exile in Babylon. He is known only as the father of Meremoth and the son of Koz. His son Meremoth, called "the son of Uriah the priest," received and weighed the silver, gold and temple vessels that Ezra's company brought to Jerusalem (Ezra 8:33). Meremoth also repaired two sections of Jerusalem's wall under Nehemiah, including the stretch beside the high priest Eliashib's house (Neh 3:4, 21). Smith's Bible Dictionary identifies Koz with the priestly family of Hakkoz, head of the seventh course of priests, and dates Urijah to about 458 BC. Nothing more is recorded about him, and he should be kept distinct from several other men in the Bible with the same name.

Urijah, son of Shemaiah of Kirjath-jearim, was a prophet in Judah during the reign of King Jehoiakim. He prophesied in the name of the LORD against Jerusalem and the land of Judah, delivering a message that matched Jeremiah's. When Jehoiakim, his officers and the princes heard his words, the king tried to have him put to death. Urijah fled in fear to Egypt, but he was brought back. The verse between these accounts, Jer 26:22, says Jehoiakim sent Elnathan son of Achbor and other men to fetch him. The king killed him with the sword and threw his body into the common people's burial ground. His story appears in Jeremiah 26 as a contrast to Jeremiah, who was spared when he spoke the same message. Several other men in the Bible share the name Urijah, also spelled Uriah.

Wife of Simon was the wife of the apostle Simon Peter. She is never named, and she appears only indirectly: the Gospels mention her when Jesus came to Simon's house and found her mother lying sick with a fever (Matt 8:14; Mark 1:30; Luke 4:38). Luke and Mark place this visit right after Jesus left the synagogue, and the surrounding passages set it in Capernaum, where Mark describes the home as the house of Simon and Andrew. By inference, her mother was living in the household. Nothing else is recorded about her in these accounts. Paul's later remark in 1 Cor 9:5 that Cephas (Peter) took a believing wife with him on his travels probably refers to her, which would suggest she accompanied him in his later work.

Zacchaeus was a rich chief tax collector at Jericho whom Jesus met while passing through the town on his way to Jerusalem, about AD 30 by inference from context (Luke 19:2). The wider passage says he was short and climbed a sycamore tree to see Jesus over the crowd. When Jesus reached the spot, he called Zacchaeus by name, told him to come down quickly, and said he must stay at his house that day (Luke 19:5). Zacchaeus then stood and announced that he would give half his goods to the poor and repay fourfold anyone he had cheated by false accusation (Luke 19:8). Jesus followed the meeting with the parable of the pounds. Smith's Bible Dictionary infers that Zacchaeus was a Jew, from his name and from Jesus calling him a son of Abraham. Easton's Bible Dictionary links his wealth to Jericho's profitable customs trade.

Zaccur was a Levite, the first-named of the sons of Asaph, David's chief musician. He and his brothers Joseph, Nethaniah and Asarelah (called Jesharelah in 1 Chr 25:14) served under their father's direction and "prophesied" with music by the king's order (1 Chr 25:2). When David's musicians were divided by lot into twenty-four courses, the third lot fell to Zaccur, whose group of sons and kinsmen numbered twelve (1 Chr 25:10). Easton's Bible Dictionary describes him as chief of one of these courses of singers. Nehemiah 12:35 names a Zaccur son of Asaph as an ancestor of Zechariah, a trumpeter at the dedication of Jerusalem's wall, and Smith's Bible Dictionary takes him to be the same man. Several other men in the Bible share the name, which Smith's gives as meaning "mindful."

Zachariah was a king of the northern kingdom of Israel and the son of Jeroboam (Jeroboam II), whom he succeeded on the throne (2 Kgs 14:29). He began to reign in Samaria in the thirty-eighth year of Azariah king of Judah, and he ruled for only six months (2 Kgs 15:8). The surrounding verses (2 Kgs 15:9–10) say he did evil as his fathers had done and that Shallum son of Jabesh conspired against him, killed him publicly and took the throne. Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that his death ended the dynasty of Jehu, and it holds that about ten years passed between his father's death and his accession. Other records of his reign were kept in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Israel (2 Kgs 15:11). Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of his name as "memory of the Lord."

Zacharias, also called Zechariah, was the son of Jehoiada the priest and lived in the reign of King Joash of Judah. After Jehoiada's death, the Spirit of God came on him. He stood above the people and warned that because they had forsaken the LORD, the LORD had forsaken them (2 Chr 24:20). The next verses say the people stoned him in the temple court at the king's command. Jesus refers to the killing of a Zacharias 'between the temple and the altar' and pairs him with Abel (Matt 23:35; Luke 11:51). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that 2 Chronicles is the last book of the Hebrew Bible, so he was seen as its last recorded martyr, as Abel was the first. Matthew calls him 'son of Barachias.' Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests Barachias may have been his grandfather, and some early Greek writers linked this Zacharias to John the Baptist's father. This entry follows the identification with Jehoiada's son.

Zattu was the ancestor of a large Israelite lay family that returned from exile in Babylon to Judah with Zerubbabel. Ezra's list gives the descendants of Zattu as 945 (Ezra 2:8). Nehemiah's parallel list gives 845 (Neh 7:13), probably a copying difference between the two lists. In Ezra's later reform, six men of this family, Elioenai, Eliashib, Mattaniah, Jeremoth, Zabad and Aziza, are named among those who had married foreign wives (Ezra 10:27). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the family's head appears as Zatthu among the leaders who sealed Nehemiah's covenant (Neh 10:14), and that the Greek Septuagint reads the name in Ezra 8:5. Easton's Bible Dictionary likewise takes Zatthu to be probably the same name. Nothing is recorded about Zattu himself beyond his family.

Zeeb was one of two princes of Midian, always named alongside Oreb, during the Midianite invasion of Israel that Gideon defeated. His name means "wolf" according to Easton's Bible Dictionary. After the Midianites were routed, the Ephraimites captured both leaders and killed Zeeb at a winepress that took his name, the "winepress of Zeeb." They brought his head and Oreb's to Gideon across the Jordan (Judg 7:25). When the Ephraimites complained that Gideon had not called them sooner, he calmed them by pointing out that God had given these princes into their hands (Judg 8:3). Psalm 83 later recalls Oreb and Zeeb in a prayer that Israel's enemies might meet the same end (Ps 83:11). Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests he was caught at a later stage of the fighting, probably at a ford farther down the Jordan.

Zepho was a son of Eliphaz, Esau's firstborn, and so a grandson of Esau. He is listed with his brothers Teman, Omar, Gatam and Kenaz (Gen 36:11). He also appears among the "dukes", or clan chiefs, descended from Esau, which makes him one of the early tribal leaders of Edom (Gen 36:15). The parallel genealogy in 1 Chr 1:36 spells his name Zephi. Amalek, born to Eliphaz's concubine Timna, and Korah, who is named among the chiefs of Eliphaz, are counted as his brothers. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "watch-tower." Nothing else is recorded about him.

Zerah was a son of Reuel and a grandson of Esau through Esau's wife Bashemath. His brothers were Nahath, Shammah and Mizzah (Gen 36:13; 1 Chr 1:37). He is named among the "dukes," or clan chiefs, descended from Reuel in the land of Edom (Gen 36:17). Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "rising (of the sun)." Several other men in the Bible share the name, including the father of Jobab, a king of Edom (Gen 36:33). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia lists that Zerah as a separate person from this chief, and this entry treats them as distinct. Nothing more is recorded about him beyond these genealogies.

Zeresh was the wife of Haman, the chief official of the Persian king in the book of Esther. When Haman came home angry that Mordecai would not honor him, he gathered his friends and Zeresh (Esth 5:10). She and the friends advised him to build a gallows fifty cubits high and ask the king the next morning to have Mordecai hanged on it, and Haman had it built (Esth 5:14). After Haman was forced to honor Mordecai publicly, he told Zeresh and his friends what had happened. She and his wise men warned him that if Mordecai was a Jew, Haman would not prevail against him but would surely fall (Esth 6:13). The meaning of her name is uncertain. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia take it as Persian for "gold", while Easton's Bible Dictionary gives "star of Venus".

Zillah was one of the two wives of Lamech, a descendant of Cain, the other being Adah (Gen 4:19). She bore Tubal-cain, described as an instructor of every craftsman in bronze and iron. Naamah is named as Tubal-cain's sister and is generally taken to be Zillah's daughter as well (Gen 4:22). Zillah and Adah are the wives Lamech addresses in his short poem about killing a man who had wounded him (Gen 4:23). Her name is often explained as meaning "shadow" or "shade", a link to the Hebrew word for shadow that the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives as possible. Lamech's marriage to two wives is the first mention of more than one wife in the Bible.

Zipporah was the wife of Moses and a daughter of Jethro, the priest of Midian, who is also called Reuel (Exod 2:18). After Moses fled Egypt and settled with her family, her father gave her to him in marriage (Exod 2:21). She bore him two sons, Gershom and Eliezer (Exod 2:22; 18:3–4). On the journey back to Egypt, when the Lord sought to kill Moses, Zipporah circumcised her son with a sharp stone and called Moses "a bloody husband" (Exod 4:24–26). Moses later sent her back to her father, and Jethro brought her and the sons to him in the wilderness (Exod 18:2–6). Num 10:29 calls Hobab the son of Reuel, which probably makes him her brother. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives her name's meaning as "bird." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia thinks the "Cushite woman" of Num 12:1 is probably Zipporah, though others take her to be a second wife.

Zuph, also called Zophai, was a Levite of the Kohathite line and an ancestor of Elkanah, the father of the prophet Samuel. He appears in the genealogy that opens 1 Sam 1:1, where Elkanah of Ramathaim-zophim in the hill country of Ephraim is traced back through Jeroham, Elihu and Tohu to Zuph. The Levite genealogies in 1 Chronicles name him as the son of an earlier Elkanah and the father of Nahath (1 Chr 6:26, 35). Nahath there probably corresponds to Tohu in 1 Samuel, by comparing the two lists. The town name Ramathaim-zophim, and the "land of Zuph" in 1 Sam 9:5, probably come from his name or his clan. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that some scholars read the word in 1 Sam 1:1 as "Zuphite," a clan name, rather than as a personal name. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "honeycomb."

Abdon was a judge of Israel, the son of Hillel, from the town of Pirathon. He succeeded Elon as judge (Judg 12:13). The verse between the two cited here, Judg 12:14, says he had forty sons and thirty grandsons who rode on seventy donkeys, and that he judged Israel for eight years. When he died he was buried in Pirathon in the land of Ephraim, in the hill country of the Amalekites (Judg 12:15). His judgeship is dated to about 1129 BC, an estimate inferred from context. Easton's Bible Dictionary counts him as the tenth judge of Israel and suggests he is probably the Bedan named in 1 Sam 12:11. The name Abdon belongs to several people in the Bible, and this entry concerns the judge.

Abdon was a Benjamite named as the firstborn son in the family that settled at Gibeon, listed in the genealogies of 1 Chr 8:30 and 1 Chr 9:36. His father is called Jeiel, "the father of Gibeon," in the surrounding verse (1 Chr 9:35), a name also given as Abiel. His mother was Maachah. His younger brothers included Zur, Kish, Baal, Nadab, Ner, Gedor, Ahio, Zacher and Mikloth. Ner appears among them only in the second list. Since the same genealogy makes Ner the grandfather of King Saul (1 Chr 8:33), Abdon was by inference Saul's great-uncle, as the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes. Nothing is recorded about his life beyond his name and place in the family. The name, perhaps meaning "service," is shared by several other people in the Bible, including a judge of Israel, and should not be confused with them.

Abiah was the second son of the prophet Samuel. He and his older brother Joel served as judges in Beersheba, where their father had appointed them (1 Sam 8:2). The following verse, 1 Sam 8:3, says the brothers did not follow their father's ways but took bribes and perverted justice. Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that this caused the discontent that led Israel's elders to ask Samuel for a king. 1 Chr 6:28 lists him among the Levites as Samuel's son, naming the firstborn "Vashni" rather than Joel. Joel is named in 1 Chr 6:33, so Vashni is probably a textual variant or alternate name for the elder brother. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of his name as "the Lord is my father." Several other people in the Bible bear this name or its variant Abijah.

Abida was one of the five sons of Midian, listed alongside his brothers Ephah, Epher, Hanoch (also spelled Henoch) and Eldaah. Midian was a son of Abraham by Keturah, so Abida was Abraham's grandson. Both genealogies that mention him count these descendants among "the children of Keturah" (Gen 25:4; 1 Chr 1:33). Nothing else is recorded about him. Easton's Bible Dictionary takes him to have been, apparently, the head of an Arab tribe, since the names in this list are generally understood to stand for peoples descended from Midian. His name is commonly explained as meaning "father of knowledge" or "my father knows." The King James Version spells it Abidah in Genesis and Abida in Chronicles.

Abihail was the father of Esther, the Jewish woman who became queen to the Persian king Ahasuerus, and the uncle of Mordecai (Esth 2:15). Since Mordecai is described as Esther's cousin and as having taken her as his own daughter, Abihail had probably died while she was young. Esth 2:7 says that both her parents were dead. He is named only to identify Esther, both when she went in to the king and when she and Mordecai wrote to confirm the observance of Purim (Esth 9:29). Nothing else is recorded about him, though Esth 2:5 traces Mordecai's family to the tribe of Benjamin, so Abihail likely belonged to it too. The name, which Hitchcock's Bible Names explains as "father of strength," is shared by several other people in the Old Testament, and this entry concerns only Esther's father.

Abijah was the mother of King Hezekiah of Judah and the daughter of a man named Zechariah. She is named in 2 Chr 29:1, while the parallel account in 2 Kgs 18:2 gives her name in the shorter form Abi. Her name means "the Lord is my father" (Hitchcock's Bible Names). She was the wife of King Ahaz, Hezekiah's father and predecessor. Through her son she belongs to the royal line of David, which the Gospel of Matthew traces in its genealogy of Jesus. Easton's Bible Dictionary suggests her father may be the Zechariah whom Isaiah called as a reliable witness (Isa 8:2), but this identification is uncertain. Several other people in the Bible, both men and women, share the name Abijah.

Abijah was a priest whose name was given to the eighth of the twenty-four priestly divisions. These divisions were assigned by lot to take turns serving at the sanctuary (1 Chr 24:10). The surrounding chapter places the arrangement in David's reign. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes him as a descendant of Eleazar, son of Aaron. His name means "the Lord is my father" or "Yahweh is father." Centuries later, in the days of Herod king of Judea, the priest Zechariah, husband of Elizabeth, is said to belong to "the course of Abia," the Greek form of the name (Luke 1:5). Zechariah is known from the same chapter as the father of John the Baptist. Several other people in the Bible are also called Abijah, including a king of Judah and a son of Jeroboam. This entry refers only to the priest who headed the eighth division.

Abimael was a son of Joktan, named in the Table of Nations in Gen 10:28 and in the matching genealogy in 1 Chr 1:22. He is listed between Obal (called Ebal in Chronicles) and Sheba, ninth of Joktan's thirteen sons. Neighboring verses in these lists, outside the passages given here, make Joktan a son of Eber and a descendant of Shem. Nothing else is recorded about Abimael himself. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia explains his name as "my father is God" and regards it as South Arabian, like several names in the list. Hitchcock's Bible Names renders it "a father sent from God." Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries take it as "father of Mael," and Smith's suggests he was probably the ancestor of an Arabian tribe. As with his brothers, his name may stand for a people as well as an individual.

Abishur was a man of the tribe of Judah who appears only in the genealogy of Jerahmeel's descendants in 1 Chronicles. He was a son of Shammai, son of Onam, and his brother was Nadab (1 Chr 2:28). His wife was Abihail, and she bore him two sons, Ahban and Molid (1 Chr 2:29). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia counts him as a great-grandson of Jerahmeel and Atarah, tracing the line through Onam, Atarah's son in the surrounding verses. Nothing else is recorded about his life. His name is usually explained as "my father is a wall" or "father of the wall." Easton's Bible Dictionary takes this to mean "mason."

Abital was one of the wives of King David and the mother of his son Shephatiah. She appears only in the parallel lists of the sons born to David at Hebron, where Shephatiah is counted as the fifth son (2 Sam 3:4; 1 Chr 3:3). By inference from the context of those lists, she married David during his seven-year reign at Hebron, before he moved his capital to Jerusalem. Nothing else is recorded about her family or life. Easton's Bible Dictionary calls her David's fifth wife, following her son's place in the list. Her name is usually explained as "my father is dew" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia) or "father of dew" (Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary).

Achbor was the father of Elnathan, an official at the court of King Jehoiakim of Judah. He is mentioned only through his son, who was sent to Egypt to bring back the prophet Urijah (Jer 26:22) and who later sat with the princes in the scribe's chamber when Jeremiah's scroll was read (Jer 36:12). Several men in the Bible bear this name. Many readers identify him with Achbor son of Michaiah, the court official whom King Josiah sent with others to consult the prophetess Huldah (2 Kgs 22:12, 14). That would place him in the royal service a generation before his son, but the identification is an inference and is not stated in the text. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "a rat" or "bruising."

Adaiah son of Jeroham was a priest who lived in Jerusalem after the return from exile in Babylon. He is one of several men in the Bible with this name. His family line runs through Pashur to Malchijah (1 Chr 9:12). The fuller genealogy in Neh 11:12 adds Pelaliah, Amzi and Zechariah between Jeroham and Pashur, so the Chronicles list is probably abbreviated. Nehemiah counts him among the priests' kinsmen who did the work of the house of God, a group numbering 822. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "adorned by Jehovah." Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "the witness of the Lord."

Adaiah was a Levite of the Gershonite branch who appears in the genealogies of 1 Chronicles 6. In the list of Gershom's descendants he is called Iddo, son of Joah and father of Zerah (1 Chr 6:21). In the ancestry of Asaph, the singer whom David set over temple music, he appears as Adaiah, father of Zerah, with his own father named as Ethan (1 Chr 6:41–42). The two lists line up generation for generation, so Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treat Iddo and Adaiah as the same man, and this entry follows that view. On the same reasoning Joah and Ethan would be two names for his father. Nothing beyond his place in these lines is recorded. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name Adaiah as "adorned by the LORD". Several other men in the Bible share the name.

Adbeel was the third son of Ishmael, Abraham's son by Hagar, named after Nebajoth and Kedar in the list of Ishmael's twelve sons (Gen 25:13; 1 Chr 1:29). That made him a grandson of Abraham. Nothing else is said about him in the Bible. The siblings shown here include Bashemath, who appears elsewhere as Ishmael's daughter and a wife of Esau. Like his brothers, Adbeel was probably the ancestor of an Arabian tribe, as Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary suggest. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that a north Arabian tribe of this name appears in Assyrian records, living somewhere southwest of the Dead Sea. The meaning of the name is uncertain. Suggestions include "miracle of God" (Easton's), "offspring of God" (Smith's), "God's discipline" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia) and "cloud of God" (Hitchcock's Bible Names).

Adoni-zedek was the king of Jerusalem when Joshua led Israel into Canaan. His name means "lord of righteousness" or "lord of justice." He heard that Joshua had destroyed Jericho and Ai and that the people of Gibeon had made peace with Israel. He then sent to four other kings, Hoham of Hebron, Piram of Jarmuth, Japhia of Lachish and Debir of Eglon, and called on them to join him in attacking Gibeon (Josh 10:1, 3). The rest of the chapter tells what happened next. Joshua came to Gibeon's aid and routed the allied armies. The five kings hid in a cave at Makkedah, and Joshua later had them taken out, put to death and hung on trees. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that his name closely resembles that of Melchizedek, an earlier king of Salem in Abraham's time.

Adrammelech was a son of Sennacherib, king of Assyria. With his brother Sharezer he killed their father with the sword while Sennacherib was worshipping in the house of his god Nisroch. The two brothers then escaped to the land of Armenia (the region of Ararat), and another brother, Esarhaddon, became king in his father's place (2 Kgs 19:37; Isa 37:38). Both accounts place the murder after Sennacherib's failed campaign against Jerusalem and his return home. Smith's Bible Dictionary places the temple at Nineveh, the Assyrian capital, and gives the name's meaning as "splendor of the king." The same name also belongs to a god worshipped by the people of Sepharvaim, who is a different figure from this son of Sennacherib.

Adriel was the son of Barzillai, a Meholathite, probably meaning a man from Abel-meholah. Saul's daughter Merab had been promised to David, but she was given to Adriel as his wife instead (1 Sam 18:19). Later, five sons connected with Adriel were among the seven descendants of Saul whom David handed over to the Gibeonites (2 Sam 21:8). The Hebrew text of that verse says that Michal, Saul's other daughter, brought up these sons for Adriel. Easton's Bible Dictionary explains this in two ways: either Michal raised them as though they were her own, or "Michal" should read "Merab." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia takes the second view and treats the sons as children of Adriel and Merab. The name is usually explained as "flock of God" or "my help is God." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia regards it as an Aramaic form of the Hebrew name Azriel.

Aeneas was a man living at Lydda who had been bedridden for eight years with paralysis. Lydda is named in the surrounding passage (Acts 9:32) and in Smith's Bible Dictionary; it is probably the modern town of Lod in Israel. While Peter was traveling among the believers there, he found Aeneas and said to him, "Aeneas, Jesus Christ makes you whole: get up and make your bed," and Aeneas got up at once. The account that follows (Acts 9:35) says the healing led people of Lydda and Sharon to turn to the Lord. Soon afterward Peter went on to nearby Joppa, where he raised Dorcas. These events are dated to about AD 38, by inference from context. Nothing else is recorded about Aeneas, including whether he was already a believer. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of his name as "praised" or "praiseworthy."

Agabus was a Christian prophet from Judea in the early church, mentioned twice in Acts. At Antioch, where he had come with other prophets from Jerusalem, he stood up and, moved by the Spirit, foretold a great famine across the world. Acts notes that it happened in the reign of the emperor Claudius (Acts 11:28), and Smith's Bible Dictionary points out that the historian Josephus records a severe famine in Judea under Claudius. Years later, while Paul was staying at Caesarea on his way to Jerusalem, Agabus came down from Judea to meet him (Acts 21:10). The following verses describe him binding his own hands and feet with Paul's belt to show that Paul would be bound in Jerusalem. Easton's Bible Dictionary suggests he was probably one of the seventy disciples sent out by Jesus. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of his name as "a locust."

Ahab, son of Kolaiah, was a prophet among the people of Judah exiled in Babylon. He is a different person from the better-known King Ahab of Israel. In his letter to the exiles, Jeremiah condemned Ahab and Zedekiah son of Maaseiah for prophesying lies in the LORD's name. He announced that God would hand them over to Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, who would kill them in front of the exiles (Jer 29:21). Their fate would become a curse used among the captives: "The LORD make thee like Zedekiah and like Ahab, whom the king of Babylon roasted in the fire" (Jer 29:22). Smith's Bible Dictionary takes this to mean he was burned to death. The next verse, Jer 29:23, also accuses the two men of adultery. Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that nothing more is known of him. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "uncle" or "father's brother."

Ahiam was one of David's mighty men, the warriors known as "the thirty." He appears only in the two parallel lists of these heroes. In 2 Sam 23:33 he is called the son of Sharar the Hararite, while 1 Chr 11:35 gives his father's name as Sacar; this entry follows the name Sharar. "Hararite" probably refers to a place or clan, perhaps in the hill country, though its exact meaning is uncertain. In the Samuel list his name follows Shammah the Hararite, which may suggest a family or regional connection, though the text does not say so. The name is usually taken to mean "mother's brother" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia; Easton's Bible Dictionary). Nothing further is recorded about his deeds.

Ahio was a Benjamite listed among the sons of the founder or leader of Gibeon and his wife Maachah in the genealogies of 1 Chr 8:31 and 1 Chr 9:37. The parallel list in 1 Chr 9:35 calls the father Jehiel. This entry identifies him with Abiel, whom 1 Sam 9:1 names as the father of Kish. Ahio's brothers included Kish and Ner, so he belonged to the extended family of King Saul, as the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes. Nothing is recorded about his life beyond his place in these lists. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "his brother." According to the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia, Greek copies often translate the word as an ordinary noun rather than a name. Several other men in the Bible share the name, including the son of Abinadab who walked before the ark (2 Sam 6:3).

Aholibamah is a name listed among the chiefs ("dukes") of Edom, the descendants of Esau, in Gen 36:41 and the matching list in 1 Chr 1:52. It appears alongside Elah and Pinon, with no further detail. The introduction to the list (Gen 36:40) says the chiefs are named by their families and places, so many readers take Aholibamah here as the name of a clan or district rather than an individual. The same name belongs to one of Esau's wives, the daughter of Anah (Gen 36:2, 14). The chiefdom may have taken its name from her line, which would explain why this entry treats the name as female, but the link is an inference and not stated in the text. Because several people share the name, the identification is uncertain. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives its meaning as "my tabernacle is exalted."

Ajah was a son of Zibeon and a brother of Anah, part of the Horite clans of Seir listed alongside the descendants of Esau in Edom. Genesis 36:24 gives the King James spelling Ajah, while the parallel genealogy in 1 Chr 1:40 spells it Aiah. Nothing is recorded about him beyond his place in these lists. By inference from the surrounding chapter, Zibeon was a son of Seir the Horite, and Ajah's brother Anah was the father of Aholibamah, one of Esau's wives. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives the name's meaning as "falcon", and Smith's Bible Dictionary as "clamor". Smith's also suggests that Ajah probably died before his father, since the line is traced through Anah. He is a different person from Aiah, the father of Saul's concubine Rizpah.

Akan was a son of Ezer and a brother of Bilhan and Zavan (Zaavan), listed among the Horites, the people who lived in the land of Seir before Esau's descendants settled there. He appears only in genealogies. Genesis 36:27 calls him Akan, while the parallel list in 1 Chr 1:42 gives the name as Jakan. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia take the two names as the same person, and some English versions spell the Chronicles form Jaakan. His father Ezer is named in Genesis 36 as one of the sons of Seir the Horite and as a Horite chief. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "he twists," and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives "twisted." Nothing more is recorded about him.

Alemeth was a Benjamite named in the genealogy of King Saul's family. He was a son of Jarah and a brother of Azmaveth and Zimri. Zimri's line continued through his son Moza. The two copies of this genealogy differ on his father's name. 1 Chr 9:42 calls him Jarah, while 1 Chr 8:36 calls him Jehoadah. Easton's Bible Dictionary treats these as two names for the same man, and this entry follows Jarah. In both lists his grandfather was Ahaz, who descended from Saul through Jonathan. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia counts Alemeth as the fifth generation after Jonathan. Nothing else is recorded about him. The name probably means "concealment" or "covering." The same name is used for a Levitical town of Benjamin, also spelled Alameth or Almon, but that is a place, not this person.

Alexander was a man named by Paul in his letters to Timothy as an opponent. In 1 Tim 1:20 he is paired with Hymenaeus as one of those who had abandoned faith and a good conscience. Paul says he has "delivered" both men "unto Satan" so that they would learn not to blaspheme, which Easton's Bible Dictionary understands as excommunication from the church. In 2 Tim 4:14 Paul writes that "Alexander the coppersmith" did him much harm and leaves his punishment to the Lord. Whether these two passages refer to the same man is uncertain. Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests they may, and this entry treats them together. The name was common, and the New Testament mentions other men called Alexander, including a son of Simon of Cyrene and a Jew put forward during the riot at Ephesus. Their link to this Alexander is unclear.

Allon was a man of the tribe of Simeon, the son of Jedaiah and the father of Shiphi. He appears only in the genealogy of his great-grandson Ziza, which traces the line back through Jedaiah, Shimri and Shemaiah (1 Chr 4:37). Ziza was among the Simeonite leaders who, in the days of Hezekiah king of Judah, moved into the area of Gedor and took over pastureland there. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes Ziza as a prince of his tribe in Hezekiah's reign. The name means "oak." The same word appears in Josh 19:33, in the border list of Naphtali, but there it is a place name, or possibly just the word "oak" (the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia prefers this reading). It refers to a different thing, not to this man.

Almodad was the first-named of the thirteen sons of Joktan, listed in the genealogy of the nations descended from Shem (Gen 10:26; 1 Chr 1:20). His brothers included Sheleph, Hazarmaveth, Jerah, Hadoram, Uzal, Diklah, Ebal, Abimael, Sheba, Ophir, Havilah and Jobab. Nothing is recorded about him beyond his place in these lists. Like several of Joktan's sons, his name is usually taken to stand for a people as well as a person. Easton's Bible Dictionary calls him the founder of an Arabian tribe, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia describes the name as south Arabian. The meaning of the name is uncertain. Easton's gives "immeasurable," Smith's Bible Dictionary "measure," Hitchcock's Bible Names "measure of God," and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia "the beloved" or "God is beloved."

Alvah was one of the chiefs (the King James Version says "dukes") of Edom who descended from Esau. He appears in Gen 36:40 among chiefs named "according to their families, after their places." The parallel list in 1 Chr 1:51 spells his name Aliah, a minor shift in Hebrew spelling noted by the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia. Because the list is arranged by families and places, the name may stand for a clan or its district as well as for one man. Tyndale House's STEPBible proper-names list places him in the line of Esau's son Eliphaz. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia also suggests he may be the same as Alvan, a descendant of Seir (Gen 36:23). This entry treats Alvah as a separate person. Nothing else is recorded about him.

Alvan was a son of Shobal and is listed with his brothers Manahath, Ebal, Shepho and Onam in Gen 36:23. The parallel genealogy in 1 Chr 1:40 spells his name Alian. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia explains this as a small change in one Hebrew letter. The surrounding passage in Genesis 36 names Shobal as a son of Seir the Horite, one of the peoples who lived in the land of Seir, later Edom. By that context Alvan belonged to the Horite clans there, as Smith's Bible Dictionary also describes him. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "tall," though the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia marks that meaning as uncertain. Nothing is recorded about him beyond his place in these two lists.

Amariah was a Levite in the priestly line descended from Aaron through Eleazar. He was the son of Meraioth and the father of Ahitub (1 Chr 6:7). He appears only in genealogies, in the list of Levi's descendants and again in the list of Aaron's line (1 Chr 6:52). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia calls him the grandfather of Zadok, who served as priest in David's time, since both lists continue from Ahitub to Zadok. Easton's Bible Dictionary suggests he was probably the last high priest of Eleazar's line before the office passed to Eli, of the line of Ithamar. His name is usually taken to mean "the Lord has said." Several other men in the Bible share this name, including a later Amariah in the same priestly genealogy, so the references need to be kept apart.

Amariah was a Levite of the priestly line of Aaron, the son of Azariah and the father of Ahitub (1 Chr 6:11). His father Azariah is described in the preceding verse as the one who served as priest in the temple Solomon built, which places Amariah in the line of chief priests after Solomon's time. Ezra 7:3 names him among the ancestors of Ezra the scribe. That list is shortened and skips several generations found in 1 Chronicles, so it names his father as Azariah son of Meraioth. The STEPBible proper-names index (Tyndale House) identifies him as the high priest under King Jehoshaphat, by inference the chief priest Amariah mentioned in 2 Chr 19:11. This entry follows that identification, though several men in the Bible share the name and the link is not certain. The name means "the LORD has said."

Amariah was a Levite, listed as the second of the four sons of Hebron, after Jeriah and before Jahaziel and Jekameam. His name appears in two lists in 1 Chronicles that set out the Levitical families in the time of King David (1 Chr 23:19; 24:23). Hebron was one of the sons of Kohath (1 Chr 23:12), so Amariah belonged to the Kohathite branch of the tribe of Levi. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treat him as the head of a Levitical house when David organized the Levites into divisions. Because "son" in these genealogies can also mean a later descendant, he may have lived several generations after Hebron. The name, meaning "the Lord has said," was borne by several people in the Bible. Nothing else is recorded about this one.

Amasai was a Levite of the family of Kohath, named in the genealogies of 1 Chronicles 6 as a son of Elkanah and brother of Ahimoth (1 Chr 6:25). He was the father of Mahath, and through this line an ancestor of the prophet Samuel. The singers' genealogy traces Heman the singer back through Samuel, and in it Amasai appears as the father of Mahath (1 Chr 6:35). Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary both identify him as part of Samuel's ancestry, and Smith's places him among the Kohathites. Nothing is recorded about his life beyond these family links. Several other men in the Bible share the name Amasai and should not be confused with him. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning "strong," while Smith's gives "burdensome."

Amittai was the father of the prophet Jonah. He is known only through his son, who is called "Jonah the son of Amittai" both in the account of Jeroboam II's reign and at the opening of the book of Jonah (2 Kgs 14:25; Jonah 1:1). The text says nothing else about him. Since 2 Kgs 14:25 describes Jonah as being from Gath-hepher, Amittai's family probably lived there too. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia places Gath-hepher in the tribal territory of Zebulun. By inference from his son's ministry under Jeroboam II, Amittai probably lived in the northern kingdom of Israel in the early eighth century BC. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary give the meaning of his name as "true," and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives "faithful."

Amminadab was a Levite in the time of King David, chief of the descendants of Uzziel, whose group numbered 112 men (1 Chr 15:10). Uzziel was a son of Kohath, so Amminadab belonged to the Kohathite branch of the Levites, as Smith's Bible Dictionary notes. David summoned him with other Levite leaders and the priests Zadok and Abiathar when he prepared to bring the ark of the covenant up to Jerusalem (1 Chr 15:11). By inference from the following verses, these leaders were told to purify themselves and to carry the ark. Several other men in the Bible share the name Amminadab, and this one should not be confused with them. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "my people is liberal."

Amok was a priest listed among the chief priests in the days of Jeshua the high priest (Neh 12:7). The surrounding list in Nehemiah 12 names the priests who came back from exile in Babylon with Zerubbabel and Jeshua, so Amok was probably one of that first group of returnees. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates the return to about 536 BC, an estimate drawn from context. A generation later, in the time of the high priest Joiakim, the priestly family named after Amok was headed by a man called Eber (Neh 12:20). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia takes Amok to be Eber's forefather. The name is usually understood to mean "deep," and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "a valley" or "a depth." Nothing else is recorded about him.

Amon was the ancestor of a family listed among the descendants of "Solomon's servants" who returned from exile in Babylon. Nehemiah's list names him Amon (Neh 7:59). The parallel list in Ezra calls him Ami (Ezra 2:57), and the two are generally taken as the same person. Both lists place his family next to those of Shephatiah, Hattil and Pochereth of Zebaim. The surrounding passages count Solomon's servants together with the Nethinim, the temple servants, as the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes. Nothing more is recorded about him. He should not be confused with others of the same name, such as Amon the king of Judah, son of Manasseh. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "faithful" or "true," and Smith's Bible Dictionary renders it "builder."

Amon was the governor of the city, probably Samaria, in the time of Ahab king of Israel. When the prophet Micaiah predicted that Ahab would die in the battle at Ramoth-gilead, contradicting the court prophets, the king ordered that he be taken back to Amon and to Joash the king's son (1 Kgs 22:26; 2 Chr 18:25). In the following verse the king orders that Micaiah be held in prison on bread and water until the king returns safely, so Amon was apparently responsible for keeping him in custody. The passage does not name the city, but the setting at Samaria leads Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia to call him governor of Samaria. He is mentioned only in this account, and he is a different person from Amon king of Judah, the son of Manasseh.

Amraphel was king of Shinar, the lowland region of southern Mesopotamia later known as Babylonia, in the time of Abram. Genesis 14 names him first among four eastern kings, alongside Arioch king of Ellasar, Chedorlaomer king of Elam and Tidal king of nations (Gen 14:1). These four fought against five kings of the cities of the plain, including Sodom and Gomorrah, in the vale of Siddim (Gen 14:9). In that list Chedorlaomer comes first, which suggests he led the alliance. The wider chapter tells how the eastern kings won the battle and carried off goods and captives, among them Abram's nephew Lot, until Abram pursued and defeated them. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identify Amraphel with the Babylonian king Hammurabi. The latter notes that the different form of the name and the absence of this campaign from Hammurabi's known records leave the identification open. Amraphel is not mentioned elsewhere in the Bible.

Anah was a son of Zibeon and brother of Ajah (spelled Aiah in 1 Chr 1:40). He belonged to the Horites, the descendants of Seir listed in Genesis 36 alongside the family of Esau. Genesis 36:24 remembers him as the Anah who found "the mules" in the wilderness while he was feeding his father's donkeys. The Hebrew word translated "mules" appears only here and its meaning is uncertain. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that it is often rendered "hot springs," and that Jewish tradition took it to mean mules, crediting Anah with first breeding them. The name was shared by other Horites, including a brother of Zibeon (Gen 36:20), and it is debated which Anah was the father of Esau's wife Aholibamah. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "one who answers" or "afflicted."

Anamim is named as one of the sons of Mizraim, the son of Ham, in the Table of Nations (Gen 10:13) and in its repeated genealogy (1 Chr 1:11). His brothers are listed as Ludim, Lehabim, Naphtuhim, Pathrusim, Casluhim and Caphthorim. The plural ending "-im" suggests the name stands for a people rather than a single individual. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary both describe the Anamim as a tribe descended from Mizraim, the Hebrew name for Egypt. On that basis they were probably a people living in or near Egypt, although the text gives no location and their exact identity is unknown. Nothing else is recorded about them beyond their place in these two lists. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives possible meanings of the name as "a fountain," "answer" or "affliction."

Ananias (High Priest) was the Jewish high priest in Jerusalem when Paul was arrested there. When Paul stood before the Council and began his defence, Ananias ordered those standing beside him to strike Paul on the mouth (Acts 23:2). Five days after Paul had been sent to the governor Felix at Caesarea, Ananias went down there with some of the elders and a speaker named Tertullus to bring charges against him (Acts 24:1). The verses here do not describe the rest of his life. Smith's Bible Dictionary adds that he was the son of Nebedaeus, was appointed high priest by Herod king of Chalcis in about AD 48, was removed from office shortly before Felix left the province, and was later killed by the Sicarii at the start of the Jewish war against Rome. He is a different person from the other men named Ananias in Acts.

Anath was the father of Shamgar, who came after Ehud and delivered Israel by killing six hundred Philistines with an ox goad (Judg 3:31). He is known only through his son, who is twice called "Shamgar the son of Anath." The second mention, in the Song of Deborah, uses "the days of Shamgar the son of Anath" to date a time when the highways were deserted and travelers kept to side paths (Judg 5:6). Nothing else is recorded about Anath himself. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary take the name to mean "answer." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that it matches the name of Anat, a Canaanite and Phoenician goddess who was also worshipped in Egypt and is paired with the war goddess Astarte in Egyptian inscriptions of the 18th Dynasty.

Aner was an Amorite living near Hebron in the time of Abram, the brother of Eshcol and Mamre. The three brothers were allies of Abram (Gen 14:13). When a fugitive brought news that Lot had been taken captive by an invading coalition of kings, Abram set out to rescue him. By inference from Gen 14:24, Aner and his brothers went with him. After the victory Abram refused any share of the plunder for himself, but he asked that Aner, Eshcol and Mamre be given their portion. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes him as a Canaanite chief. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the names Mamre and Eshcol are also place names in the Hebron area, and suggests that Aner may likewise be linked to a local place, possibly a range of hills. Nothing more is recorded about him.

Appaim was a man of the tribe of Judah, named in the genealogy of 1 Chronicles 2 as a son of Nadab and the brother of Seled. Because Seled died without children, the family line of Nadab continued through Appaim (1 Chr 2:30). His son was Ishi, whose son Sheshan was in turn the father of Ahlai (1 Chr 2:31). Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia place him in the house of Jerahmeel, a major clan of Judah. This follows from the surrounding verses of the same genealogy, which trace Nadab back to Jerahmeel. The name is usually explained as meaning "nostrils" or "face" (Hitchcock's Bible Names). Nothing is recorded about him beyond his place in this family list.

Arah was the ancestor of a family whose descendants returned from exile in Babylon to Judah with Zerubbabel, probably about 536 BC, as Smith's Bible Dictionary dates it. The list of returning families in Ezra gives his descendants as 775 (Ezra 2:5). The parallel list in Nehemiah gives 652 (Neh 7:10). The difference is not explained in the text. He may be the same person as the Arah of Neh 6:18, whose son Shechaniah was the father-in-law of Tobiah the Ammonite, an opponent of Nehemiah's rebuilding of Jerusalem. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes this identification, but it is not certain. Several people in the Bible bear this name, including an Asherite in 1 Chr 7:39. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives its meaning as "the way" or "a traveler."

Aran was a Horite, a son of Dishan and brother of Uz, named in the genealogy of the descendants of Seir the Horite, the inhabitants of the land later occupied by Edom (Gen 36:28). The same pair of sons appears again in the parallel list in 1 Chr 1:42. Dishan was one of the sons of Seir and a chief among the Horites, so Aran belongs to one of the clans of that people. Nothing else is recorded about him. Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries take the name to mean "wild goat," and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that many Horite names in this genealogy appear to be animal names, though it also records that the meaning of this particular name is uncertain.

Archippus was a Christian known to the apostle Paul and mentioned only in two of his letters. In Philemon he is greeted alongside Philemon and Apphia and the church that met in their house, and Paul calls him "our fellowsoldier" (Phlm 1:2). At the end of Colossians, Paul asks the church to tell Archippus to take care to complete the ministry he had received in the Lord (Col 4:17). By inference from these letters he probably lived in or near Colossae and held some recognized role in the church there. Because he is named so closely with Philemon and Apphia, Easton's Bible Dictionary suggests he was a member of Philemon's household, probably his son. His name means "master of the horse." A later church tradition describes him as bishop of Laodicea.

Areli was a son of Gad and a grandson of Jacob, named last among Gad's seven sons in the list of Jacob's family who went down to Egypt (Gen 46:16). His brothers were Zephon (Ziphion), Haggi, Shuni, Ozni (called Ezbon in Genesis), Eri and Arod (Arodi). In the wilderness census of Numbers his descendants appear as a clan of the tribe of Gad, the Arelites (Num 26:17). Nothing else is recorded about him. The meaning of his name is uncertain. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "heroic", Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "the light or vision of God", and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests a form related to "God's lioness" or "God's hearth".

Arioch (king of Ellasar) was one of four eastern kings, along with Amraphel of Shinar, Chedorlaomer of Elam and Tidal "king of nations," who made war together in the days of Abraham (Gen 14:1). Genesis 14:9 describes them as "four kings with five," meaning they fought a coalition of five local kings. The surrounding verses show that coalition was led by the rulers of Sodom and Gomorrah, and that Chedorlaomer was its overlord. Nothing else is recorded about Arioch himself. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identify him with Eri-Aku, a king of Larsa known from Babylonian inscriptions, and take Ellasar to be Larsa in southern Mesopotamia, probably the site now called Senkereh. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the name's meaning as "long, great, tall." He is a different person from the Arioch who served as captain of the guard in the Book of Daniel.

Arkite is the name given in the table of nations to one of the descendants of Canaan, son of Ham. He is listed among Canaan's offspring alongside Zidon, Heth, the Jebusite, Amorite, Girgasite, Hivite, Sinite, Arvadite, Zemarite and Hamathite (Gen 10:17; 1 Chr 1:15). Like most names in this list, it reads as the name of a people group rather than a single individual. It probably refers to the inhabitants of the town of Arka in northern Phoenicia. Easton's Bible Dictionary places Arka about 12 miles north of Tripoli, near the northern end of the Lebanon range. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia adds that the town appears in Assyrian inscriptions as Irkatah and was taken by Tiglath-pileser III in 738 BC. The two verses that mention the Arkite say nothing beyond the name and its place in Canaan's line.

Arod was a son of Gad, one of the sons of Jacob, and an ancestor of the tribe of Gad. Genesis 46:16 calls him Arodi and lists him among Gad's sons in the family that went down with Jacob to Egypt. His brothers were Ziphion (Zephon), Haggi, Shuni, Ezbon (Ozni), Eri and Areli. In the census of Israel's clans in Num 26:17 he appears as Arod, founder of the family of the Arodites. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia counts him as Gad's sixth son, and Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "wild ass." Nothing else is recorded about him.

Arvadite is listed as a son of Canaan, son of Ham, in the table of nations in Gen 10:18 and its parallel in 1 Chr 1:16. He is named with the Zemarite and the Hamathite, just before the note that the families of the Canaanites later spread abroad. As with the other names in this list, the term probably refers to a people or clan rather than a single individual, presented as descending from Canaan. By inference, the Arvadites were the inhabitants of Arvad, a Phoenician island city whose men Ezek 27:8 and 27:11 describe as rowers and soldiers serving Tyre. Arvad is generally identified with the modern island of Arwad, off the coast of Syria. The Bible records nothing else about the Arvadite himself.

Asaiah was a Levite in the time of King David and the chief of the clan descended from Merari, one of Levi's three sons. He led 220 of his kinsmen when David gathered the Levites (1 Chr 15:6). David then called him, along with the priests Zadok and Abiathar and other Levite leaders, to take part in bringing the ark of the covenant to Jerusalem (1 Chr 15:11). The surrounding chapter shows this was the ark's move from the house of Obed-edom to the city of David. The genealogy in 1 Chr 6:30 lists an Asaiah among Merari's descendants, and Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia take him to be the same man. His name means "the Lord has made." Several other people in the Bible share the name.

Asaph was a Levite named as an ancestor of Mattaniah, a Levite who lived in Jerusalem after the return from exile in Babylon. In 1 Chr 9:15 the line runs Mattaniah son of Micah, son of Zichri, son of Asaph. The parallel list in Neh 11:17 gives the same line with Zabdi in place of Zichri, probably another form of the same name. There Mattaniah is described as the leader who began the thanksgiving in prayer, a role tied to the temple singers. Since several men in the Bible are called Asaph, it is uncertain who this one is. Smith's Bible Dictionary considers him most probably the same as Asaph the well-known Levite musician of David's time. If so, "son of Asaph" would mark Mattaniah as a distant descendant within that family of singers rather than a grandson. The name is usually taken to mean "gatherer" or "collector."

Ashur was a man of the tribe of Judah, the son of Hezron and his wife Abiah. He was born after his father died at Caleb-ephratah (1 Chr 2:24), which makes him a brother of Jerahmeel, Ram and Caleb, and a half-brother of Segub. He is called "the father of Tekoa," which Smith's Bible Dictionary takes to mean the founder of that town in Judah, probably near modern Khirbet Tequ'a south of Bethlehem. He had two wives, Helah and Naarah (1 Chr 4:5). The verses that follow, 1 Chr 4:6–7, name his sons: Naarah bore Ahuzam, Hepher, Temeni and Haahashtari, and Helah bore Zereth, Jezoar and Ethnan. This entry also counts Coz among his sons, by inference from his place in the list at 1 Chr 4:8. Some reference works, such as the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia, spell the name Ashhur.

Asriel was a man of the tribe of Manasseh, son of Joseph, and the founder of the clan known as the Asrielites (Num 26:31). In the census list of Numbers 26 he appears among the sons of Gilead, alongside Abiezer, Helek, Shechem, Hepher and Shemida. This entry follows that view, which makes him a great-grandson of Manasseh through Gilead and Machir, as Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him. Joshua 17:2 names the same six as "the male children of Manasseh" in the broader sense of descendants, and records that their families received a share of land in the allotment to the rest of Manasseh. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that 1 Chr 7:14 presents an Asriel as born to Manasseh by an Aramean concubine. The meaning of the name is uncertain. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "help of God."

Assir was a Levite, a son of Korah, listed with Elkanah and Abiasaph (also spelled Ebiasaph) as the founders of the Korahite families in Exod 6:24. Through Korah he descended from Kohath, the son of Levi. 1 Chr 6:22 traces the same line from Kohath through Amminadab and Korah to Assir. Exod 6:21 names Korah's father as Izhar, so Amminadab there is probably another name for Izhar, though this is an inference. In Chronicles the names that follow Assir appear to run as a line of descent rather than as a list of brothers, so the relationship of Assir to Elkanah and Ebiasaph is presented differently in the two passages. This entry follows Exodus in treating them as brothers. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia give the meaning of his name as "captive." Several other men in the Bible share the name.

Assir was a Levite descended from Korah, named in the genealogies of 1 Chronicles 6 as the son of Ebiasaph and the father of Tahath (1 Chr 6:23, 6:37). His name means "captive" or "prisoner" according to Smith's Bible Dictionary and Hitchcock's Bible Names. He appears in the line that led to Samuel the prophet, and the second list traces through him the ancestry of Heman the singer, whose genealogy begins at 1 Chr 6:33. His brother Kore is probably the Kore named as a son of Ebiasaph in 1 Chr 9:19, an ancestor of the gatekeepers. Nothing else is recorded about him. The name was shared by several people, including another Assir who was a son of Korah and so this Assir's great-grandfather (1 Chr 6:22), so this man is told apart mainly by his place in the family line.

Ater was the ancestor of a family whose descendants, counted through a line called "of Hezekiah," numbered ninety-eight among the exiles who returned from Babylon to Judah with Zerubbabel (Ezra 2:16; Neh 7:21). The phrase "Ater of Hezekiah" probably marks a branch of Ater's family descended through a man named Hezekiah, and this entry treats Hezekiah as his son. It may instead be a way of telling this Ater apart from others who share the name. Smith's Bible Dictionary adds that the family was also represented among the leaders who signed the covenant with Nehemiah (Neh 10:17). Nothing else is recorded about Ater himself. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "left hand" or "shut." Several people in the Bible bear this name, including a family of gatekeepers listed in the same return lists.

Ater was the ancestor or head of a family of temple gatekeepers ("porters" in the King James Version) whose descendants returned from exile in Babylon to Jerusalem. He appears only in the parallel lists in Ezra 2:42 and Neh 7:45. There his family is named with those of Shallum, Talmon, Akkub, Hatita and Shobai, gatekeeper families that together numbered 139 in Ezra and 138 in Nehemiah. Smith's Bible Dictionary places this return under Zerubbabel, the leader named in the surrounding lists. Nothing else is recorded about Ater himself. The same name belongs to other men in the Bible, including the ancestor of another returning family listed in the same chapters, so this gatekeeper should be kept distinct from them. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "left hand" or "shut."

Attai was a descendant of Judah in the line of Jerahmeel, named only in the genealogy of 1 Chronicles 2. His mother was a daughter of Sheshan, who had no sons and gave her in marriage to Jarha, his Egyptian servant. She is probably Ahlai, the name listed as Sheshan's child in 1 Chr 2:31, and this entry follows that reading. Through this marriage Sheshan's line continued. Attai was the father of Nathan, and Nathan was the father of Zabad, after whom the genealogy goes on for several more generations. Smith's Bible Dictionary identifies this Zabad with the Zabad listed among David's mighty men in 1 Chr 11:41. Several other men in the Bible share the name Attai, which Smith's renders as "opportune" and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia as "timely."

Azaliah was the son of Meshullam and the father of Shaphan, the scribe who served King Josiah of Judah. He is known only through his son's genealogy. In Josiah's eighteenth year, the king sent Shaphan to the temple, and the Chronicles account adds that Shaphan went with Maaseiah the governor of the city and Joah the recorder to oversee repairs to the house of the Lord (2 Kgs 22:3; 2 Chr 34:8). In the Kings account, this errand led to the discovery of the book of the law. Nothing is recorded about Azaliah's own life. By inference from his son's career, he probably lived in Jerusalem in the generation before Josiah's reforms. His name is usually explained as meaning "the Lord has set aside" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia) or "whom the Lord reserved" (Smith's Bible Dictionary).

Azareel, also called Adiel, was a priest of the family of Immer and the father of Maasiai (called Amashai in Neh 11:13). The two genealogies list Maasiai among the priests who lived in Jerusalem after the return from exile in Babylon. They trace the line differently. In 1 Chr 9:12 Adiel is the son of Jahzerah, son of Meshullam, son of Meshillemith. In Neh 11:13 Azareel is the son of Ahasai, son of Meshillemoth. Smith's Bible Dictionary treats the two passages as describing the same family, and the STEPBible proper-names index identifies Adiel and Azareel as one person. This entry follows that view. The name probably means "God has helped" (Hitchcock's Bible Names: "help of God"), and Adiel is usually explained as "ornament of God." Several other men in the Bible are also named Azareel.

Azariah was a Levite priest of the line of Zadok, the son of Ahimaaz and the father of Johanan in the priestly genealogy of 1 Chr 6:9. His name means "the Lord has helped." Since Ahimaaz was himself a son of Zadok (1 Chr 6:8), this Azariah was Zadok's grandson. 1 Kgs 4:2 lists "Azariah the son of Zadok the priest" first among King Solomon's chief officials. Views differ on whether that is the same man. Smith's Bible Dictionary takes "son" there to mean grandson and holds that Azariah succeeded Zadok as high priest under Solomon, perhaps because Ahimaaz had died first. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats the official of 1 Kgs 4:2 as a separate son of Zadok. This entry follows the single-person identification. The name Azariah was common, especially among priestly families, so care is needed in telling its bearers apart.

Azariah was a man of the tribe of Judah, named in the genealogy of Jerahmeel, the son of Hezron. He was the son of Jehu, the son of Obed, and the father of Helez, whose son was Eleasah (1 Chr 2:38–39). The surrounding passage traces this line back to the marriage of Sheshan's daughter to Jarha, his Egyptian servant (1 Chr 2:34–35), so Azariah descended from that union. Nothing else is recorded of him in these verses. Several other men in the Bible share his name, which the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia renders as "Yahweh has helped." Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests he was probably the Azariah son of Jehu who was one of the captains of hundreds who joined the priest Jehoiada against Queen Athaliah (2 Chr 23:1). That identification rests on the shared name and father, and the genealogy itself does not confirm it.

Azariah was the chief priest of Judah during the reign of King Uzziah. When Uzziah entered the temple to burn incense, Azariah followed him in with eighty priests, described as valiant men (2 Chr 26:17). The surrounding passage, 2 Chr 26:16–19, records that the priests opposed the king because burning incense was reserved for priests descended from Aaron. While Uzziah was angry with them, leprosy appeared on his forehead. Azariah and the other priests saw it and drove him out of the temple, and the king himself hurried to leave, because the LORD had struck him (2 Chr 26:20). Easton's Bible Dictionary places him as a contemporary of the prophets Isaiah, Amos and Joel. The name, shared by many people in the Bible, is explained in Hitchcock's Bible Names as "he that hears the Lord."

Azariah was the chief priest of the house of Zadok during the reign of King Hezekiah of Judah. When Hezekiah asked about the heaps of offerings the people had brought, Azariah answered that since the giving began the priests had had enough to eat with plenty left over, and that the large surplus was the result of the LORD's blessing (2 Chr 31:10). He is also called the ruler of the house of God, and under his authority, with the king's command, Levites were appointed as overseers of the stored tithes and offerings (2 Chr 31:13). Smith's Bible Dictionary says he worked with Hezekiah in purifying the temple and restoring its services, and that he succeeded Urijah, high priest under Ahaz. Several other men in the Bible share the name Azariah, which was especially common in priestly families. Smith's gives its meaning as "whom the Lord helps."

Azariah, son of Maaseiah and grandson of Ananiah, was one of the people who rebuilt the wall of Jerusalem under Nehemiah. Like several others in the list of builders, he repaired the stretch of wall beside his own house. His section lay between the part repaired by Benjamin and Hashub and the part repaired by Binnui son of Henadad. Binnui's work ran from Azariah's house to the turning of the wall at the corner (Neh 3:23–24). Smith's Bible Dictionary dates this work to about 446 BC, the period of Nehemiah. The name means "the Lord has helped" and was common in Israel, especially among priestly families. Several men in the Bible are called Azariah, so this one should be kept separate from others of the same name, including other Azariahs in Nehemiah.

Azariah, also called Uzziah, was a Levite of the clan of Kohath who appears only in the genealogies of 1 Chronicles 6. In the list of Kohath's descendants he is named Uzziah, son of Uriel and father of Shaul (1 Chr 6:24). In the parallel line tracing the ancestry of Heman the singer back to Kohath, an Azariah appears as son of Zephaniah and father of Joel (1 Chr 6:36). Smith's Bible Dictionary takes the two as the same man, which places him among the ancestors of Samuel the prophet and of Heman. This entry follows that identification and gives his father and son as named in 1 Chr 6:24. The two lists name his neighbors differently, so how the lines line up is uncertain. His name means "the Lord has helped." Several other people in the Bible share this name.

Azmaveth was one of the warriors listed among David's mighty men, the elite group known as "the thirty." He is called "the Barhumite" in 2 Sam 23:31 and "the Baharumite" in 1 Chr 11:33. Smith's Bible Dictionary takes both forms to mean he came from Bahurim, a village near Jerusalem, and so was probably a Benjamite. Nothing else is recorded about his deeds or family. The name is shared by several other men in the Bible, including a son of Jehoadah in Saul's line and an official over David's treasuries. The two lists of David's warriors are the only places where this Azmaveth clearly appears, so whether he is the same man as any of the others is uncertain. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "strong death."

Azmaveth was a descendant of King Saul, listed in the two genealogies of Saul's family in 1 Chronicles. He was a son of Jarah, a name given as Jehoadah in the parallel list (1 Chr 8:36; 1 Chr 9:42), and his brothers were Alemeth and Zimri. The surrounding verses trace this line from Saul through Jonathan, Merib-baal (Mephibosheth), Micah and Ahaz, so Azmaveth was a great-great-great-grandson of Jonathan. Nothing else is recorded about him, and the line continues through his brother Zimri rather than through him. Several other men in the Bible share the name, including one of David's mighty men, and they should not be confused with this Azmaveth. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "strong unto death."

Azor was an ancestor of Jesus who appears only in the genealogy in Matthew's Gospel. He was the son of Eliakim and the father of Sadoc (Matt 1:13–14). He belongs to the part of the list that runs from Zerubbabel (Zorobabel), after the exile to Babylon, down to Joseph, so he probably lived in the centuries after the return from exile. As a descendant of David, he belonged to the tribe of Judah. Nothing else is recorded about him, and he is not named in the Old Testament or in Luke's genealogy. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "a helper," and Hitchcock's Bible Names adds "a court."
