Azrikam was a Benjamite and the first-named of the six sons of Azel. His brothers were Bocheru, Ishmael, Sheariah, Obadiah and Hanan. He appears only in the genealogy of Saul's family, which is given twice, in nearly identical form, in 1 Chr 8:38 and 1 Chr 9:44. In both lists Azel descends from King Saul through Jonathan and Merib-baal (Mephibosheth), which makes Azrikam a distant descendant of Saul. Smith's Bible Dictionary calls him Azel's eldest son, apparently because he is named first. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives the name's meaning as "my help has arisen." Nothing else is recorded about him. Several other men in the Bible share the name Azrikam, and they should not be confused with this one.

Azrikam was a Levite of the clan of Merari, son of Hashabiah and father of Hasshub (spelled Hashub in Neh 11:15). He appears only in genealogies, as the grandfather of Shemaiah, a Levite listed among those who settled in Jerusalem after the return from exile (1 Chr 9:14; Neh 11:15). Nehemiah traces the line further back to Bunni, while Chronicles places it within the sons of Merari. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates him to before 536 BC, an estimate drawn from his place in these lists. His name is usually explained as "my help has arisen" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia). Several other men in the Bible bear the same name, and this entry concerns only the Levite.

Azubah was the daughter of Shilhi and the mother of Jehoshaphat, king of Judah. She is named only in the regnal summaries of her son, which record that he was thirty-five when he began to reign and that he reigned twenty-five years in Jerusalem (1 Kgs 22:42; 2 Chr 20:31). Since Jehoshaphat succeeded his father Asa, she was Asa's wife, probably one of his queens. Through this royal line she belongs to the ancestry traced in the genealogy of Jesus. Nothing else is told about her or about her father Shilhi. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of her name as "forsaken," and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives "desolation." The same name is borne by a different woman, a wife of Caleb son of Hezron, so the two should not be confused.

Azubah was a wife of Caleb son of Hezron, a descendant of Judah, named in the genealogy of 1 Chr 2:18. The verse is hard to read. It mentions both Azubah and Jerioth, and says "her sons" were Jesher, Shobab and Ardon. Some read Jerioth as a second wife, and others read her as a daughter. This entry follows the common reading, given in the STEPBible names index, that these three were Azubah's sons. After Azubah died, Caleb married Ephrath, who bore him Hur (1 Chr 2:19). Smith's Bible Dictionary and Hitchcock's Bible Names give the meaning of her name as "forsaken." The name belongs to more than one person. A different Azubah, daughter of Shilhi, was the mother of King Jehoshaphat (1 Kgs 22:42).

Baal was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, named in the family lists of 1 Chronicles as one of the sons of the "father of Gibeon" and his wife Maachah. He was fourth in the list, after the firstborn Abdon, then Zur and Kish. His other brothers included Ner, Nadab, Gedor, Ahio, Zacher (Zechariah) and Mikloth. The surrounding passage calls his father Jehiel (1 Chr 9:35), and Easton's Bible Dictionary names him that way. This entry identifies the father with Abiel, who appears as the father of Kish in 1 Sam 9:1. Because Ner and Kish belong to the line of King Saul in these lists, Baal was a member of Saul's extended family, though nothing is recorded about him beyond his name. The name means "master" or "lord" and is shared by several others in the Bible.

Baanah was a man from Netophah, a town near Bethlehem in Judah, and the father of Heleb, one of the elite warriors known as David's mighty men. He appears only in the two parallel lists of those warriors, where his son is called Heleb in 2 Sam 23:29 and Heled in 1 Chr 11:30. The difference is probably a copying variation of the same name. The text says nothing more about Baanah himself. In both verses the description "the Netophathite" sits close to his name. Grammatically it most naturally describes the son, though it is often applied to the father as well (Smith's Bible Dictionary calls Baanah a Netophathite). Several other men in the Bible are also named Baanah. They include one of the assassins of Ish-bosheth and one of Solomon's district officers, and this Baanah should be kept distinct from them.

Baanah was one of the leaders who returned with Zerubbabel from exile in Babylon to Jerusalem. His name closes the list of leading men in Ezra 2:2 and in the parallel list in Neh 7:7, which come just before the count of the returning people of Israel. Nothing else is recorded about him in these passages. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates the return to about 536 BC, and like the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia it suggests he may be the same Baanah who sealed the covenant in Neh 10:27. That identification is possible but not certain, because several men in the Bible share this name. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "in the answer" or "in affliction."

Bakbuk was the ancestor of a family of temple servants, known as the Nethinim, whose descendants returned from exile in Babylon to Jerusalem with Zerubbabel. The "children of Bakbuk" appear in the list of returning exiles in Ezra 2:51, and the same list is repeated in Neh 7:53. In both lists they are named among the temple servants, between the families of Hakupha and Harhur. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates the return to before 536 BC. The name probably means "bottle." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests it may imitate the gurgling sound of liquid poured from a bottle, and notes that the same family appears as Acub in 1 Esdras 5:31. Nothing is recorded about Bakbuk himself beyond his name as the head of this family line.

Baladan was the father of Merodach-baladan (called Berodach-baladan in 2 Kgs 20:12), the king of Babylon who sent letters and a gift to King Hezekiah of Judah after hearing of his illness and recovery. He appears only in this identifying phrase in two parallel passages, and the Bible says nothing else about him. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia explain the name as meaning "he (Merodach) has given a son," while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "one without judgment." Assyrian inscriptions of Sargon call Merodach-baladan the son of Yakin. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia takes Yakin to be the founder of his dynasty rather than his father. It also suggests that "Baladan" may be a shortened form of the father's full name, possibly that of an earlier king also called Merodach-baladan.

Barachel was a Buzite, of the kindred of Ram, and the father of Elihu, the young man who spoke to Job after Job's three older friends had finished (Job 32:2, 6). He is known only from these two verses, which name him to identify his son. Nothing else is said about his life. His name is usually explained as meaning "God has blessed" (Easton's Bible Dictionary, Smith's Bible Dictionary). "Buzite" probably links the family to Buz, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia points to that name and to Ram for comparison. In Gen 22:21 Buz appears as a son of Nahor, Abraham's brother, so the family was probably of Aramean descent. That connection is inferred and is not stated in Job.

Barkos was the ancestor of a family of temple servants, the Nethinim, whose descendants returned from exile in Babylon with Zerubbabel. The "children of Barkos" appear in the list of returning exiles, between the Nethinim families of Bakbuk-era names and those of Sisera and Tamah (Ezra 2:53; Neh 7:55). That the family belongs to the temple servants is inferred from where the name falls in the list. Nothing else is recorded about Barkos himself. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates the return to about 536 BC, an estimate. The name is often explained as meaning "painter" (Easton's Bible Dictionary) or "party-colored" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia), though the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia marks this meaning as uncertain. It also notes that the same family appears as Barchus in 1 Esdras 5:32.

Barzillai was the ancestor of a priestly family whose descendants returned from the Babylonian exile with Zerubbabel. He married one of the daughters of Barzillai the Gileadite and took his wife's family name (Ezra 2:61; Neh 7:63). That Gileadite is probably the wealthy elder who supplied David during Absalom's revolt (2 Sam 17:27; 19:31–39). The verses that follow in each list (Ezra 2:62; Neh 7:64) say that this family searched for its genealogical record and could not find it, so its members were excluded from the priesthood as unclean. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that 1 Esdras 5:38 gives his original name as Jaddus (Addus in the King James Version). Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "made of iron." Nothing else is known of him, and he should be kept separate from the other men named Barzillai.

Bazluth was the ancestor of a family of temple servants (the Nethinim) whose descendants returned from the Babylonian exile to Judah. His name appears only in the parallel lists of returning exiles, where "the children of Bazluth" are named between other servant families such as those of Mehida and Harsha (Ezra 2:52). Nehemiah's version of the same list spells the name Bazlith (Neh 7:54). Smith's Bible Dictionary places this return with Zerubbabel in about 536 BC, a date inferred from context. The surrounding lists suggest that these families served at the temple. Nothing is recorded about Bazluth himself beyond his name, and the text does not say when he lived.

Bedad was the father of Hadad, one of the kings who ruled Edom before Israel had a king. He is known only from the list of Edomite kings in Gen 36:35 and its parallel in 1 Chr 1:46. Both passages say that Hadad succeeded Husham, defeated Midian in the territory of Moab, and ruled from a city called Avith. Nothing is recorded about Bedad himself, and the text does not say whether he was a king. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia and Hitchcock's Bible Names give the meaning of his name as "alone" or "solitary." Smith's Bible Dictionary places him sometime before 1093 BC, an estimate drawn from the chronology of the passage.

Ben-ammi was the son of Lot and Lot's younger daughter, and the ancestor of the Ammonites (Gen 19:38). According to the surrounding account in Genesis 19, after Sodom was destroyed Lot lived in a cave with his two daughters. Believing no man was left to marry them, the daughters made their father drunk and each conceived a child by him. The older daughter's son was Moab, so Moab was both Ben-ammi's half-brother and his cousin. The name is usually explained as "son of my people" (Hitchcock's Bible Names, Smith's Bible Dictionary) or "son of my kinsman" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia). Genesis says he is "the father of the children of Ammon unto this day." The nation descended from him, Ammon, appears later in Ps 83:7 among the peoples allied against Israel, though Ben-ammi himself is named only once.

Benaiah was the father of Pelatiah, one of the leaders of the people in Jerusalem whom the prophet Ezekiel saw in a vision. In that vision Ezekiel was brought to the east gate of the temple, where twenty-five men were gathered, among them "Pelatiah the son of Benaiah" and Jaazaniah son of Azur, described as princes of the people (Ezek 11:1). As Ezekiel prophesied against these men, Pelatiah died, and the prophet cried out in distress (Ezek 11:13). Benaiah himself is known only as Pelatiah's father, and nothing else is recorded about him. Several other men in the Bible share his name, which the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia renders as "Yahweh has built." He is probably distinct from the others, though the text does not say so directly.

Beno was a Levite of the clan of Merari, named as a son of Jaaziah in the list of Levite families in 1 Chr 24:26–27. He appears with his brothers Shoham, Zaccur and Ibri, who are counted among "the sons of Merari by Jaaziah." The name means "his son," according to Smith's Bible Dictionary and Hitchcock's Bible Names. Because the Hebrew word can be read either as a personal name or simply as "his son," the wording of these verses is somewhat unclear. This entry follows the reading that treats Beno as a personal name, as the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia does. Nothing else is recorded about him.

Beor was the father of Bela, the first king named in the list of rulers who reigned in Edom before Israel had a king. Bela's city was Dinhabah (Gen 36:32; 1 Chr 1:43). Nothing else is recorded about Beor himself, and nothing in the text says whether he was a king. He should be kept distinct from another Beor, the father of the prophet Balaam (Num 22:5), since the name is shared by more than one person in the Bible. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "burning" or "torch", and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia tentatively suggests "destroyer."

Berechiah was the father of the prophet Zechariah and the son of Iddo, according to the opening of the book of Zechariah (Zech 1:1, 7). Nothing else is said about him. His son received his visions in the second year of King Darius, probably Darius I of Persia, around 520 BC by inference from context, during the rebuilding of Jerusalem after the exile. Elsewhere, Ezra 5:1 and 6:14 call Zechariah simply "the son of Iddo." This is usually explained by Hebrew "son" also meaning grandson, or by the possibility that Berechiah died young and Zechariah was linked directly to his better-known grandfather. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "blessed of Jehovah." Several other men in the Bible share the name, and this entry refers only to Zechariah's father.

Beriah was a Benjamite, a son of Elpaal, listed in the genealogy of Benjamin in 1 Chronicles 8. He and his brother Shema were heads of the families living in Aijalon, and they drove out the inhabitants of Gath (1 Chr 8:13). Easton's Bible Dictionary describes the two brothers as founders of Aijalon who expelled the Gittites. Michael, Ispah and Joha are named as his sons (1 Chr 8:16). Read as one continuous list, 1 Chr 8:14–16 also gives Ahio, Shashak, Jeremoth, Zebadiah, Arad and Ader as his sons, and this entry follows that reading. His other brothers, named in 1 Chr 8:12 and 8:17–18, include Eber, Misham, Shamed, Meshullam and Heber. Several other men in the Bible are also called Beriah, so this one should be kept separate from them.

Beriah was a Levite, the youngest of the four sons of Shimei, whose brothers were Jahath, Zizah (called Zina in 1 Chr 23:10) and Jeush. He appears only in the list of Levite families drawn up when David organized the Levites for service. From the surrounding chapter, this Shimei was probably a descendant of Gershon, so Beriah belonged to the Gershonite branch of the tribe. The STEPBible Proper Names index places him in David's reign. Because Beriah and Jeush had few sons, their descendants were not counted as separate households. They were reckoned together as a single father's house. The name is shared by several other men in the Bible, including sons of Asher and Ephraim and a Benjaminite, and this Beriah should be kept distinct from them. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "in fellowship" or "in envy."

Besai was the ancestor of a family of temple servants, the Nethinim, whose descendants returned from exile in Babylon to Judea with Zerubbabel. "The children of Besai" appear in the list of returning families in Ezra 2:49 and again in the parallel list in Neh 7:52. Nothing else is recorded about Besai himself, and the name is known only as the head of this family group. The meaning of the name is uncertain. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "sword", the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives "downtrodden", and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "a despising". The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia also notes that the same family appears as Basthai in the apocryphal book of 1 Esdras.

Bezai was the ancestor of a family group listed among the exiles who returned from Babylonian captivity to Jerusalem and Judah with Zerubbabel. Nothing is recorded about Bezai himself. Only his descendants are counted. Ezra 2:17 gives their number as 323, while the parallel list in Neh 7:23 gives 324. Small differences like this between the two lists are common. Bezai probably stands for the head of a clan or family house rather than someone who made the journey himself. The name is shared by more than one person. A Bezai is also named in Neh 10:18 among the leaders who sealed the covenant in Nehemiah's time, probably a representative of the same family. The meaning of the name is uncertain: Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "conqueror" and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia tentatively suggests "shining."

Bigthana, also spelled Bigthan, was one of King Ahasuerus's chamberlains who guarded the door of the palace in Persia. Esth 2:21 says that he and another doorkeeper, Teresh, became angry and plotted to attack the king while Mordecai was sitting at the king's gate. Mordecai learned of the plot and reported it. The following verses of the same chapter say the two men were hanged and the matter was written in the royal chronicles. Later, when the king could not sleep and had those records read to him, he found the account of how Mordecai had exposed Bigthana and Teresh (Esth 6:2). This led to Mordecai being honored. The King James Version calls him a chamberlain, and Easton's Bible Dictionary describes him as a eunuch. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "gift of God."

Bigvai was one of the leaders who returned from the Babylonian exile with Zerubbabel. He is named among the men listed at the head of the register of returning Israelites, alongside Jeshua, Nehemiah, Mordecai and others (Ezra 2:2; Neh 7:7). Nothing more is said of him personally in these verses. Smith's Bible Dictionary takes him to be one of the chiefs of Zerubbabel's expedition and connects him with the Bigvai whose family later signed the covenant (Neh 10:16). The same name also heads a large family of returnees in the lists, so it is uncertain whether all these mentions refer to one man or to a clan bearing his name. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "in my body," while Smith's gives "happy."

Bilhan was a son of Ezer, named first among his three sons alongside Zaavan (Zavan) and Akan (Jakan) in the genealogy of Gen 36:27, which is repeated in 1 Chr 1:42. From the surrounding chapter, Ezer was one of the sons of Seir the Horite, so Bilhan belonged to the Horite clans living in the land of Seir, later Edom, before and alongside Esau's descendants. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him as a Horite chief dwelling in Mount Seir, and the STEPBible proper names index counts him among the chiefs of Edom. Nothing else is recorded about him. The spellings of his brothers' names differ slightly between the two lists. The name is shared by at least one other man, a Benjamite in a later genealogy, who is a different person.

Bilshan was one of the leaders who returned from exile in Babylon with Zerubbabel. He appears in the list of men at the head of the returning Israelites, given in Ezra 2:2 and repeated in Neh 7:7. In both lists he comes right after Mordecai. Nothing else is recorded about him. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary explain the name as meaning "eloquent." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes other possible meanings and records that 1 Esdras calls him Beelsarus. It also notes that rabbinic tradition read Bilshan as a surname of the Mordecai named just before him. Smith's dates the return to about 536 BC.

Binea was a man of the tribe of Benjamin and a descendant of King Saul. He appears only in the two parallel genealogies of Saul's family, where he is named as the son of Moza (1 Chr 8:37; 1 Chr 9:43). Following the line back through these lists, Moza descended from Saul's son Jonathan through Jonathan's son Merib-baal, also known as Mephibosheth. After Binea the lists name Rapha, called Rephaiah in 1 Chr 9:43, then Eleasah, then Azel. This entry treats all three as his children. However, the repeated phrase "his son" can also be read as a chain of successive generations, with Rephaiah as Binea's son, Eleasah as Rephaiah's son, and Azel as Eleasah's son. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of his name as "son of the Lord". Nothing else is recorded about him.

Binnui was a Levite of the period after the return from exile in Babylon. Nehemiah 10 names him among the Levites who set their seal to the covenant made under Nehemiah, identifying him as one of the sons of Henadad (Neh 10:9). A Binnui also appears in the list of Levites in Neh 12:8, alongside Jeshua and Kadmiel. That list, by its context, names those who came up from exile with Zerubbabel. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats both mentions, together with Ezra 8:33, as the same man, a Levite of Ezra's time, and this entry follows that view. STEPBible's proper-name index links him with Bani, a Levite who helped teach the Law and lead prayers in Nehemiah's day. Because several men bear this name, the identification is not certain. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives its meaning as "building."

Bocheru was one of the six sons of Azel, a Benjamite, listed with his brothers Azrikam, Ishmael, Sheariah, Obadiah and Hanan. He appears only in a genealogy that is given twice in nearly identical form (1 Chr 8:38; 1 Chr 9:44). The surrounding verses trace this family back through Jonathan to King Saul, so Bocheru belonged to Saul's line many generations after him. Nothing else is recorded about him. Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that he is a son of Azel "according to the present Hebrew text." The Hebrew letters of the name can also be read as "his firstborn," and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning "the first born." On that reading the word would describe Azrikam rather than name a separate son, which would sit oddly with the stated total of six. This entry follows the text as it stands and treats Bocheru as a son of Azel.

Bohan was a man called "the son of Reuben," known only because a boundary marker, "the stone of Bohan," was named after him. The stone marked the border between the tribal lands of Judah and Benjamin. It stood near the Jordan valley, between Beth-hoglah and Beth-arabah on one side and En-shemesh and the ascent of Adummim on the other (Josh 15:6; 18:17). He does not appear in the genealogies of Reuben's sons, as the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes. So "son of Reuben" may mean a descendant of Reuben rather than a son, which is why Smith's Bible Dictionary simply calls him a Reubenite. Nothing else is recorded about him, and the site of the stone has not been identified. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives the meaning of his name as "thumb."

Bukkiah was a Levite, the first-named of the fourteen sons of Heman listed in 1 Chr 25:4. Heman was one of the leaders of music appointed under David. His sons were set apart to prophesy with harps, lyres and cymbals in the worship of the house of the Lord, according to the surrounding passage. When the temple musicians were divided into twenty-four groups by lot, the sixth lot fell to Bukkiah. His group, made up of him, his sons and his relatives, numbered twelve (1 Chr 25:13). Smith's Bible Dictionary places him among the Kohathite Levites, since Heman belonged to that clan. It gives the meaning of his name as "wasting from Jehovah," and Hitchcock's Bible Names renders it "the dissipation of the Lord." He is not mentioned anywhere else.

Canaanitish woman is the unnamed mother of Shaul, one of the six sons of Simeon, the son of Jacob. She is mentioned only in the family lists of Simeon's sons, in Gen 46:10 among those who went down to Egypt with Jacob and in Exod 6:15 among the families of Simeon. Shaul is the only son in these lists whose mother is singled out, and by inference she was probably Simeon's wife or concubine. Her people are noted because they set her apart from the other mothers in the family. Her name, her history and her exact relationship to Simeon are not recorded. Shaul's descendants later appear as one of the clans of Simeon.

Caphthorim (also spelled Caphtorim) is listed among the descendants of Mizraim (Egypt) in the table of nations, alongside Ludim, Anamim, Lehabim, Naphtuhim, Pathrusim and Casluhim (Gen 10:14; 1 Chr 1:12). The plural -im ending marks the name as a people group, not a single individual. Later passages connect this people with a land called Caphtor: Deut 2:23 says the Caphtorim came out of Caphtor and destroyed the Avvim, who lived in villages as far as Gaza, and Amos 9:7 and Jer 47:4 say the Philistines came from Caphtor. In the genealogies, however, the note about the Philistines' origin follows Casluhim, so how the two peoples relate is not fully clear. Caphtor is commonly identified with Crete, though other locations, such as the Egyptian coast or southern Asia Minor, have also been proposed.

Casluhim is a name in the Table of Nations, listed among the descendants of Mizraim (Egypt) alongside the Ludim, Anamim, Lehabim, Naphtuhim, Pathrusim and Caphtorim. The plural form suggests a people or tribe rather than a single individual, as with the other names in the list. Both Gen 10:14 and 1 Chr 1:12 add that the Philistines came from the Casluhim. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests that this note may originally have belonged after Caphtorim, since other passages link the Philistines with Caphtor. Easton's Bible Dictionary places the original home of the Casluhim probably in Lower Egypt, along the coast toward the southern border of Palestine, and gives the name's meaning as "fortified." Nothing else is recorded about them.

Chenaniah was a chief of the Levites during David's reign who led the music when the ark of the covenant was brought up to Jerusalem. He was placed in charge of the song because he was skilled at it, and he gave instruction in it (1 Chr 15:22). In the procession he is named "the master of the song with the singers," walking with the Levites who carried the ark while David wore a linen robe and ephod (1 Chr 15:27). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the Hebrew word rendered "song" can also mean "carrying," so he may have directed the carrying of the ark. Easton's Bible Dictionary takes him to be probably a Kohathite and distinct from the Chenaniah of 1 Chr 26:29, who held an outside office. The ISBE treats the two as one man. This entry covers only the Chenaniah of 1 Chr 15. His name means roughly "established by the Lord."

Cheran was a son of Dishon, named only in the genealogy of the Horites, the people descended from Seir who lived in the land later held by Edom. His brothers were Hemdan, Eshban and Ithran (Gen 36:26). The parallel list in 1 Chr 1:41 repeats the four names but gives Amram in place of Hemdan. Both lists follow a mention of Dishon as a son of Anah. The surrounding chapter also names a Dishon as a son of Seir and a Horite chief, so it is uncertain which Dishon is meant. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats Cheran as a Horite clan name as well as a personal one. Nothing else is recorded about him. The meaning of the name is uncertain. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "lyre," Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "anger," and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes Dillmann's derivation from a word for "lamb."

Chushan-rishathaim was a king of Mesopotamia who ruled over Israel for eight years in the period of the judges (Judg 3:8). The text says the LORD gave Israel into his hand because of the people's wrongdoing. The oppression ended when Othniel, on whom the Spirit of the LORD came, went to war against him and won (Judg 3:10). Othniel is named in the surrounding verses as the son of Kenaz, Caleb's younger brother. The date of about 1418 BC is an estimate inferred from context. "Mesopotamia" here translates Aram-naharaim, the region of the upper Euphrates. The name is variously explained: Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "chief of two governments," Easton's Bible Dictionary offers "Cush of double wickedness" or "governor of two presidencies," and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "blackness of iniquities." He is otherwise unknown, and his identity outside the Bible is uncertain.

Claudius (4th Roman Emperor) was the ruler of the Roman Empire during part of the apostles' ministry, reigning from AD 41 to 54 according to Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary. He succeeded Caligula. Acts names him twice. The prophet Agabus foretold a great famine "throughout all the world," which Luke says came to pass in the days of Claudius Caesar (Acts 11:28). Classical writers, cited by the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia, also describe his reign as a time of bad harvests and scarcity. Claudius also ordered all Jews to leave Rome, which is why Aquila and Priscilla had recently come from Italy when Paul met them in Corinth (Acts 18:2). The Roman historian Suetonius links the expulsion to Jewish unrest. Its date is uncertain: Easton's gives AD 49, and others suggest about AD 50 or later.

Cleophas is the name the King James Version uses in John 19:25 for the husband of Mary, one of the women who stood by the cross of Jesus. This entry treats him as the same man as Cleopas, one of the two disciples who met the risen Jesus on the road to Emmaus and asked him if he was the only visitor to Jerusalem who had not heard what had happened there (Luke 24:18). Whether the two are one person is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary allows that they may be, and also mentions a possible link with Alphaeus (Matt 10:3). Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treat them as different men, pointing out that Cleopas is a Greek name, a short form of Cleopatros, while Clopas (the Revised Version spelling in John) is Aramaic. Nothing more is recorded about him.

Cononiah was a Levite in the reign of King Hezekiah of Judah. He was put in charge of the offerings, tithes and dedicated gifts that the people brought to the temple, and his brother Shimei served as his second in command. Ten overseers, including Jehiel, Azaziah and Mahath, worked under the two brothers. They were appointed by the king and by Azariah, the ruler of the house of God (2 Chr 31:12–13). Smith's Bible Dictionary takes the name to mean "appointed by the Lord" and dates his service to about 726 BC. The name also appears in the form Conaniah, the spelling used in the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia and other reference works. That form is also given to a later Levite leader in Josiah's time, who is a different person.

Cozbi was a Midianite woman, the daughter of Zur, who was head over a people and of a chief house in Midian (Num 25:15). She was killed during the plague connected with Israel's worship of Baal of Peor, while the Israelites were camped at Shittim. The wider account in Numbers 25:6–14 tells that an Israelite named Zimri, son of Salu and a leader among the Simeonites, brought her into the camp, and that Phinehas the priest killed them both. God then told Moses to treat the Midianites as enemies, because they had led Israel astray at Peor and in the matter of Cozbi, 'the daughter of a prince of Midian' (Num 25:18). Her father Zur is probably the same Zur later named among the five Midianite kings killed in Numbers 31:8. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of her name as 'deceitful.'

Crispus was the chief ruler of the Jewish synagogue at Corinth during Paul's mission there. Acts 18:8 records that he believed in the Lord together with his whole household, and that many other Corinthians who heard also believed and were baptized. Writing later to the Corinthian church, Paul names Crispus as one of only two people there, along with Gaius, whom he baptized personally (1 Cor 1:14). His conversion took place about AD 50, by inference from context, around the time Paul wrote his letters to the Thessalonians. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that Sosthenes appears as synagogue ruler soon afterward (Acts 18:17), probably as his successor, and records a tradition that Crispus later became bishop of Aegina. His name means "curled" according to Hitchcock's Bible Names.

Daniel was the second son of David, born at Hebron during David's reign there. His mother was Abigail, formerly the wife of Nabal the Carmelite, whom David married after Nabal's death (1 Sam 25). He is named Daniel in 1 Chr 3:1, while the parallel list in 2 Sam 3:3 calls him Chileab. Some take the two as names for the same man. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the Greek reading and the shape of the Hebrew text suggest that "Chileab" may have arisen from a copying error in Samuel. The name Daniel means "God is my judge." Apart from his place in these birth lists, nothing more is recorded about him, and he plays no part in the later struggles over David's throne. He is distinct from the prophet Daniel and others who bear the same name.

Daniel was a priest descended from Ithamar, the son of Aaron, and was among the family heads who returned with Ezra from Babylon to Jerusalem (Ezra 8:2). A Daniel also appears among the priests who sealed the covenant drawn up under Nehemiah (Neh 10:6). Smith's Bible Dictionary treats these as two entries but suggests they may be the same man, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia lists both passages under one person. This entry follows that identification. The name means "God is my judge." He is not the prophet Daniel of the book of Daniel, who lived earlier, during the exile itself.

Darkon was the ancestor of a family counted among the descendants of "Solomon's servants" who returned from exile in Babylon to Judah with Zerubbabel (Ezra 2:56; Neh 7:58). Nothing is recorded about Darkon himself, only that his descendants appear in both versions of the list of returning exiles. The context shows that the family belonged to the group called Solomon's servants, which the lists place alongside the temple servants (Nethinim). Smith's Bible Dictionary dates the return to about 536 BC, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the parallel list in 1 Esdras gives the name as Lozon. The meaning of the name is uncertain. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "scatterer," the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia "carrier," and Hitchcock's Bible Names "of generation" or "of possession."

The Daughter of Herodias was the young woman who danced at the birthday feast of Herod Antipas, ruler of Galilee, and pleased him and his guests (Matt 14:6; Mark 6:22). Her mother, Herodias, had been the wife of Herod's brother Philip before marrying Herod. Herod swore to give the girl whatever she asked. According to the surrounding verses in both Gospels, she consulted her mother and, at her prompting, asked for the head of John the Baptist on a dish. Herod regretted his oath but had John beheaded in prison, and the head was brought to her, and she gave it to her mother. The Gospels do not name her. The Jewish historian Josephus names a daughter of Herodias as Salome, and Christian tradition has generally identified the dancer with her.

Daughter of Shuah was a Canaanite woman who became the wife of Judah, son of Jacob. Her own name is not given. She is identified only through her father, Shuah (or Shua), a Canaanite. Judah met her while staying near his friend Hirah the Adullamite and married her (Gen 38:2). She bore him three sons, Er, Onan and Shelah (1 Chr 2:3). According to the surrounding account in Genesis 38, Shelah was born at Chezib, and she died some years later, before the events involving Tamar. The Hebrew phrase in 1 Chr 2:3 can also be read as a name, Bath-shua, meaning "daughter of Shua." Her firstborn son Er is described as evil in the LORD's sight and was put to death (1 Chr 2:3).

Dedan (son of Raamah) was a son of Raamah and a grandson of Cush, named with his brother Sheba in the Table of Nations in Gen 10:7 and again in the genealogy of 1 Chr 1:9. He belongs to the line of Ham, since Cush was a son of Ham. Nothing is recorded about his life. He is distinct from another Dedan, a son of Jokshan and grandson of Abraham through Keturah, although the two lists share the names Sheba and Dedan. Easton's Bible Dictionary connects his descendants with the Dedanites mentioned in Isa 21:13 and Ezek 27:15, and suggests they probably settled among the Cushite peoples on the north-west coast of the Persian Gulf. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "low country."

Dedan (son of Jokshan) was a grandson of Abraham through Keturah, whom 1 Chr 1:32 calls Abraham's concubine. His father Jokshan was one of Keturah's six sons, and his brother was Sheba. Genesis names Dedan's sons as Asshurim, Letushim and Leummim. These plural forms are probably the names of tribes or peoples rather than individuals (Gen 25:3). Easton's Bible Dictionary says his descendants settled near the borders of Edom and probably lived as herders. A separate Dedan appears among the descendants of Ham in the table of nations (Gen 10:7). The prophets also mention a people or region called Dedan, and it is not always clear which line they mean. This entry concerns only the son of Jokshan.

Delaiah was the ancestor of a family that returned from exile in Babylon to Judah, probably with Zerubbabel. His descendants are listed with those of Tobiah and Nekoda. The total for the three families is 652 in Ezra 2:60 and 642 in Neh 7:62. The surrounding passage (Ezra 2:59; Neh 7:61) groups these families with people who could not show their ancestral house or prove they were of Israelite descent, so by inference their genealogy had been lost. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates the return to about 536 BC. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes Delaiah as the head of one of the returning bands, while the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats him as a family ancestor. Smith's gives the name's meaning as "freed by Jehovah." Several other men in the Bible share this name, and it is not known whether this Delaiah is connected with any of them.

Delaiah son of Shemaiah was one of the princes, or royal officials, at the court of King Jehoiakim of Judah. He was sitting with the other officials in the scribe's chamber of the palace when Micaiah reported the contents of Jeremiah's scroll, which Baruch had read aloud in the temple (Jer 36:12). The officials then had Baruch read it to them and reported it to the king. When Jehoiakim cut up the scroll and burned it, Delaiah, together with Elnathan and Gemariah, urged the king not to burn it, but he refused to listen (Jer 36:25). Smith's Bible Dictionary dates these events to about 604 BC. The name, which several people in the Bible share, is explained as "God has raised" by the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia and as "freed by Jehovah" by Smith's.

Diklah was one of the thirteen sons of Joktan, a descendant of Shem through Eber, named in the table of nations in Gen 10:27 and in the parallel genealogy at 1 Chr 1:21. His brothers included Almodad, Sheleph, Hazarmaveth, Jerah, Hadoram, Uzal, Sheba, Ophir, Havilah and Jobab. The passages give only his name. Like the other names in this list, it probably stands for a tribe or region as well as a person. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both take the name to mean "palm grove" or "place of palms." They suggest it points to a palm-growing district, probably in southern Arabia, where the settlements of Joktan's descendants are generally placed. The exact location is unknown.

Dishon was a son of Anah and brother of Aholibamah, listed among the Horite clans in the genealogies connected with Esau's family (Gen 36:25). STEPBible's proper names index identifies him as a grandson of Seir the Horite through Anah. His sister is probably the Aholibamah who became one of Esau's wives (Gen 36:2). 1 Chr 1:41 names his sons as Amram, Eshban, Ithran and Cheran. The parallel list in Gen 36:26 gives the same sons but has Hemdan in place of Amram, probably a variant spelling of the same name. The name Dishon was also borne by another Horite, a son of Seir and so probably this man's uncle (Gen 36:21), and the two are easily confused. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "fatness" or "ashes." Nothing else is recorded about him.

Dodanim is listed as the fourth son of Javan in the Table of Nations, alongside his brothers Elishah, Tarshish and Kittim (Gen 10:4; 1 Chr 1:7). Since Javan was a son of Japheth (Gen 10:2), Dodanim was Japheth's grandson. As with the other names in this list, Dodanim probably stands for a people descended from him as well as an individual. In the Hebrew text of 1 Chr 1:7, and in the Greek Septuagint and Samaritan versions of Genesis, the name appears as Rodanim (the King James Version reads Dodanim in both places). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia prefers the Rodanim reading and links the people with the inhabitants of the island of Rhodes. Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries connect them with the Dardani of Illyricum and the region of Troy. The text itself does not settle the identification, and this entry does not decide between these views.

Dodo was a man of Bethlehem and the father of Elhanan, one of David's mighty men known as "the thirty." He is mentioned only in the two parallel lists of David's warriors, where his son appears right after Asahel, the brother of Joab (2 Sam 23:24; 1 Chr 11:26). Nothing else is recorded about him. The name is shared by other men in the Bible, and Smith's Bible Dictionary treats this Bethlehemite as a different person from them. This Elhanan should probably also be kept apart from Elhanan the son of Jaare-oregim, who is credited with killing a Philistine giant (2 Sam 21:19). Smith's gives the meaning of the name as "loving," and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "his uncle."

Dumah was one of the twelve sons of Ishmael, the son of Abraham and Hagar, and so a grandson of Abraham. He appears only in the parallel genealogies of Gen 25:14 and 1 Chr 1:30, listed between his brothers Mishma and Massa. His name means "silence." Nothing is recorded of his life. Smith's Bible Dictionary takes him to be the probable founder of an Ishmaelite tribe in Arabia whose territory carried his name, and connects this with the oracle concerning Dumah in Isa 21:11. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that Arabic geographers credited him with founding the oasis town of Dumat al-Jandal, probably the modern al-Jawf in northern Saudi Arabia. It adds that the Isaiah oracle may concern that place. These links between the person, the tribe and the town are traditional inferences, not statements of the biblical text.

Ebal (son of Shobal) was one of the five sons of Shobal, listed with his brothers Alvan, Manahath, Shepho and Onam in Gen 36:23. The parallel list in 1 Chr 1:40 names the same brothers, with Alvan spelled Alian and Shepho spelled Shephi. Shobal was a son of Seir the Horite (Gen 36:20), so Ebal belonged to the Horite clans who lived in the land of Seir. Their genealogy is set alongside the family of Esau. Nothing else is recorded about him. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "stone" or "bare mountain," and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "ancient heaps." He is a different person from the Ebal son of Joktan, and the name is also shared by Mount Ebal in Canaan.

Ebal (son of Joktan) was one of the thirteen sons of Joktan, a descendant of Shem through Eber, listed in the Table of Nations. Genesis calls him Obal (Gen 10:28), and the parallel genealogy in Chronicles spells the name Ebal (1 Chr 1:22). In both lists he appears between Hadoram's brother Uzal and his brothers Abimael and Sheba. Nothing else is recorded about him. Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests that, like the rest of Joktan's family, he was apparently the founder of an Arab tribe, since many of Joktan's sons bear names linked with peoples or regions of southern Arabia. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "ancient heaps", while Smith's Bible Dictionary renders it "stripped bare". He is a different person from Ebal the son of Shobal, a descendant of Seir, and his name is separate from Mount Ebal.

Eder was a Levite, the second of the three sons of Mushi, listed between his brothers Mahli and Jeremoth (called Jerimoth in 1 Chr 24:30). Mushi was a son of Merari, so Eder belonged to the Merarite branch of the tribe of Levi. He appears only in the lists of Levitical families in 1 Chronicles 23–24, which set out the divisions of the Levites for service at the end of David's reign. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes him as appointed to the Levitical office, and Smith's Bible Dictionary places him in David's time. Nothing else is recorded about him. His name probably means "flock." He is a different person from the Benjamite Eder named elsewhere in Chronicles, and the name is also used for a tower and a town in the Old Testament.

Eglah was one of David's wives and the mother of Ithream, his sixth son. Ithream was born while David reigned at Hebron, before he moved his capital to Jerusalem (2 Sam 3:5; 1 Chr 3:3). She appears only in these two parallel lists of David's sons, and she is the only mother in them described specifically as "David's wife." Nothing else is recorded about her family or background. Her name means "heifer" (Easton's Bible Dictionary). Easton's also mentions a Jewish tradition that identifies Eglah with Michal, Saul's daughter. This entry treats her simply as the wife named in the lists.

Ehi was a son of Benjamin, named among the ten sons of Benjamin in the list of Jacob's family who went down to Egypt (Gen 46:21). He belonged to the tribe of Benjamin. This entry identifies him with Aharah, whom 1 Chr 8:1 lists as Benjamin's third son, after Bela the firstborn and Ashbel. The Benjamite genealogies differ in their names and order, and some names in Gen 46:21 appear in other lists as later descendants. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both suggest that Ehi may also be the same person as Ahiram, the third son in Num 26:38, and possibly Aher in 1 Chr 7:12. The Tyndale House proper-names index treats Ahiram, Aharah and Ehi as one man. This entry lists Ahiram separately as a brother. Nothing else is recorded about Ehi beyond his name and place in the family.

Elah was one of the chiefs, called "dukes" in the King James Version, of Edom, the people descended from Esau. He appears in the list of Edomite chiefs at the end of Genesis 36, and the same list is repeated in 1 Chr 1:52. Nothing else is recorded about him. The list may name clan leaders or the clans and districts they headed, since some names in it also appear elsewhere as places. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia describes him as the head of a clan and gives the meaning of the name as "oak" or "terebinth." Several other men in the Bible share the name Elah, including a king of Israel and a son of Caleb. They are separate people and should not be confused with this Edomite chief.

Elam (son of Shem) was the first-named son of Shem and so a grandson of Noah, listed in the table of nations alongside his brothers Asshur, Arphaxad, Lud and Aram (Gen 10:22). The genealogy in 1 Chr 1:17 repeats the list but also counts Uz, Hul, Gether and Meshech among Shem's sons, where Genesis names them as sons of Aram. The text records nothing about Elam's life. Like several names in this table, his name was also the name of a people and a land. Easton's Bible Dictionary connects him with the country of Elam east of Babylonia, whose capital was Susa and whose inhabitants were the Elamites. It explains the name as meaning "high" or "highland," while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives other meanings, including "a young man."

Eldaah was the fifth and last-named son of Midian, listed with his brothers Ephah, Epher, Hanoch (Henoch) and Abida in the two genealogies that record him (Gen 25:4; 1 Chr 1:33). Midian was a son of Abraham by Keturah, so Eldaah was Abraham's grandson, and both passages count him among "the children of Keturah." Nothing else is recorded about him. Because Midian gave his name to the Midianites, Eldaah's line was probably one of the clans of that people, though the text does not say so directly. The meaning of his name is uncertain. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests "God has called," while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "knowledge of God."

Eldad was one of the elders of Israel in the wilderness, named alongside Medad in Num 11:26–27. Both men were among those whose names had been written down when Moses gathered seventy elders to share the burden of leading the people. They stayed in the camp instead of going out to the tabernacle with the others. Even so, the spirit rested on them, and they prophesied in the camp. A young man ran to tell Moses. In the wider passage, Joshua urged Moses to stop them, but Moses refused and said he wished all the Lord's people were prophets. Easton's Bible Dictionary links the episode to the Gospel accounts in which the disciples tried to stop someone casting out demons in Jesus' name. The name is usually taken to mean "God has loved" or "favored of God."

Eleasah was a man of the tribe of Judah, named only in a genealogy of 1 Chronicles. He was the son of Helez, the son of Azariah, and the father of Sisamai, whose son was Shallum (1 Chr 2:39–40). The surrounding passage traces this line through the family of Jerahmeel, a descendant of Judah through Hezron. It begins with the marriage of Sheshan's daughter to his Egyptian servant Jarha (1 Chr 2:34–35), so Eleasah probably belonged to that branch. Nothing else is recorded about him. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "whom God made." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that in Hebrew it is the same name as Elasah, which is borne by other men in the Bible. This Eleasah should not be confused with them.

Eleazar, son of Dodo the Ahohite, was one of the three most prominent warriors among David's mighty men. 2 Sam 23:9 says he was with David when they defied the Philistines gathered for battle after the men of Israel had withdrawn. The verse that follows in that passage describes him striking down Philistines until his hand was tired and stuck to his sword. The parallel account in 1 Chronicles places a similar stand with David at Pasdammim, which the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia equates with Ephes-dammim. Easton's Bible Dictionary counts him among the three who broke through the Philistine lines to bring David water from the well of Bethlehem, and assigns him to the tribe of Benjamin. "Ahohite" probably refers to descent from Ahoah. His name means "God is helper." He is distinct from several other men named Eleazar, including Aaron's son, the priest.

Elhanan was a warrior of David's time who fought the Philistines. 1 Chr 20:5 calls him the son of Jair and says he killed Lahmi, the brother of Goliath the Gittite, whose spear shaft was like a weaver's beam. The parallel account in 2 Sam 21:19 calls him the son of Jaare-oregim, a Bethlehemite, and places the battle at Gob. Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that the words "the brother of" in 2 Sam 21:19 were added in the King James Version to match Chronicles, and that the Revised Version leaves them out. It places the exploit late in David's reign, while Smith's Bible Dictionary dates it to about 1020 BC. In both accounts the giant is linked to Goliath, whom David killed in 1 Sam 17. The name means "God has been gracious." Several men in the Bible share it, including Elhanan son of Dodo, one of David's thirty mighty men.

Elhanan, son of Dodo of Bethlehem, was one of David's mighty warriors, listed among "the thirty" (2 Sam 23:24; 1 Chr 11:26). In both lists his name comes right after Asahel, the brother of Joab, so Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him as the first named of the thirty. His name means "God has been gracious" or "whom God gave." Nothing more is recorded about his deeds. Several men in the Bible bear this name, including the Elhanan credited with killing a Philistine giant. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that some scholars think these may be the same man, while others treat them as separate people. This entry treats the son of Dodo as a distinct person.

Eliahba was one of David's mighty men, the elite group of warriors known as "the thirty." He appears in both lists of these men, in 2 Sam 23:32 and 1 Chr 11:33, and each time he is called "the Shaalbonite." That title probably means he came from Shaalbim (also spelled Shaalabbin), a town in the territory originally given to Dan. Nothing else is recorded about his life or deeds. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia give the meaning of his name as "God hides," while Hitchcock's Bible Names renders it "my God the Father."

Eliam was the father of Bathsheba, the wife of Uriah the Hittite, who later became King David's wife. He is named when David asks who the woman is and is told she is "the daughter of Eliam" (2 Sam 11:3). In 1 Chr 3:5 he is called Ammiel, and his daughter Bathshua, the mother of Shimea, Shobab, Nathan and Solomon. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia explains the two forms as the same two parts of the name in reverse order. Through Solomon, Eliam stands in the line that Matthew traces to Jesus, where Bathsheba appears as "her that had been the wife of Urias" (Matt 1:6). Several men in the Bible share the name. Some readers identify him with Eliam son of Ahithophel, one of David's mighty men (2 Sam 23:34), but neither of the verses here makes that connection.

Eliashib was a priest in Jerusalem in Nehemiah's time who had charge of the storerooms of the temple and was closely connected with Tobiah, an Ammonite official who had opposed Nehemiah's work (Neh 2:10). According to the surrounding account, while Nehemiah was away at the Persian court, Eliashib cleared a large room once used for storing grain offerings, incense and tithes and gave it to Tobiah. When Nehemiah returned to Jerusalem and learned of it, he threw Tobiah's belongings out and had the rooms purified (Neh 13:5–9). Because the name is shared by several people, his identity is uncertain. Many readers take him to be the high priest Eliashib of Neh 3:1 and 13:28, whose grandson married into Sanballat's family, while others treat him as a separate priest. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "the God of conversion."

Eliathah was a Levite, one of the fourteen sons of Heman, and a musician appointed for the temple service in the time of King David (1 Chr 25:4). When the musicians were divided by lot into twenty-four courses, the twentieth lot fell to Eliathah, and his course numbered twelve, made up of him, his sons and his relatives (1 Chr 25:27). Heman was one of the three chief musicians under David, along with Asaph and Jeduthun, according to the surrounding passage in 1 Chronicles 25. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary explain the name as meaning "to whom God will come" or "to whom God comes." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives "God has come," and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "thou art my God." Nothing else is recorded about him.

Eliel was a Levite leader in David's time, chief of the descendants of Hebron, and he led eighty of his kinsmen (1 Chr 15:9). Hebron here is a family name, not the town. Hebron was a son of Kohath, so Eliel belonged to the Kohathite branch of the Levites, as Smith's Bible Dictionary notes. He was one of the Levite heads David summoned, along with the priests Zadok and Abiathar, when the ark of the covenant was moved from the house of Obed-edom to Jerusalem (1 Chr 15:11). From the surrounding chapter, David called these leaders so they could consecrate themselves and carry the ark. His name is usually taken to mean "God is God" or "my God is God." Several other men in the Bible are also named Eliel, including some of David's mighty men, and this one should not be confused with them.

Elioenai was a man of the tribe of Judah, a descendant of David through the royal line of Jeconiah, named in the post-exile genealogy of 1 Chronicles 3. He was the first-listed of the three sons of Neariah, alongside Hezekiah and Azrikam (1 Chr 3:23). Smith's Bible Dictionary takes this order to mean he was the eldest and traces Neariah back to Shemaiah. Elioenai had seven sons: Hodaiah, Eliashib, Pelaiah, Akkub, Johanan, Dalaiah and Anani (1 Chr 3:24). Nothing else is recorded about him. Several other men in the Bible share his name, which Smith's Bible Dictionary renders as "my eyes are toward the Lord."

Elipheleh was a Levite of the "second degree" listed among the gatekeepers (KJV "porters") in 1 Chr 15:18. He was one of the men David's Levite leaders appointed for the music when the ark of the covenant was brought up to Jerusalem, the city of David. In 1 Chr 15:21 he appears with Mattithiah, Mikneiah, Obededom, Jeiel and Azaziah as one of those who played harps "on the Sheminith," a musical term of uncertain meaning, perhaps referring to an eight-stringed instrument or to a lower pitch. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "God will distinguish him." Smith's Bible Dictionary identifies him as a Merarite Levite. Nothing else is recorded about him.

Elishah was a son of Javan, listed first among his four sons in the Table of Nations, with Tarshish, Kittim and Dodanim as his brothers (Gen 10:4; 1 Chr 1:7). Javan was a son of Japheth, so Elishah was a great-grandson of Noah. The name, like those of his brothers, probably also stands for a people or region descended from him. Easton's Bible Dictionary connects Javan's line with the peoples of Greece and notes a suggestion that Elishah's descendants settled the Peloponnesus, known in part as Elis. Easton's also links him with "the isles of Elishah" in Ezek 27:7, a coastland that supplied blue and purple cloth to Tyre. Others have connected that name with Cyprus or with Carthage in North Africa. The exact identification remains uncertain.

Elishama was one of the sons of King David born to him in Jerusalem. He appears in the list of David's Jerusalem-born children, named next to last, just before Eliada (called Beeliada in 1 Chr 14:7) and Eliphalet (2 Sam 5:16; 1 Chr 14:7). The same list appears a third time in 1 Chr 3:8. His mother is not named, and nothing else is recorded about his life. The surrounding passages place these births after David moved his capital to Jerusalem and took more wives and concubines there. The name means "God has heard" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia). Several other people in the Bible share this name, including another Elishama listed earlier among David's sons in 1 Chr 3:6, who is probably the same person called Elishua in the parallel lists. This entry concerns the son named near the end of the list.

Elishama was the father of Nethaniah and the grandfather of Ishmael, the man who killed Gedaliah, the governor the Babylonians left in charge of Judah, at Mizpah in the seventh month after Jerusalem fell (2 Kgs 25:25; Jer 41:1). Both accounts describe the family as "of the seed royal," meaning it descended from the kings of Judah. Elishama is mentioned only to identify his grandson, and nothing else is recorded about him. The name, meaning "God has heard," belongs to several men in the Bible. Some have suggested he may be the same as Elishama the scribe in Jer 36:12, but the text does not make that link. This entry treats him as the grandfather of Ishmael only. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia lists him separately among the men of this name.

Eliud was a man listed in Matthew's genealogy of Jesus, in the part of the line that runs from the Babylonian exile down to Joseph. He was the son of Achim and the father of Eleazar, whose son Matthan was the father of Jacob, the father of Joseph (Matt 1:14–15). That makes Eliud the great-great-grandfather of Joseph, four generations before him, as the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes. As a descendant of David in this line, he belonged to the tribe of Judah. Nothing else is recorded about him, and he does not appear in Luke's genealogy of Jesus. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of his name as "God is my praise." Smith's Bible Dictionary renders it "God his praise."

Elkanah was a Levite of the family of Korah, the son of Izhar. Exod 6:24 names him with Assir and Abiasaph (also spelled Ebiasaph) as the sons of Korah, from whom the Korahite families descended. This entry follows that account in treating him as Korah's son. In 1 Chr 6:22–23 the same names appear in a line of descent, each called "his son," which could make Elkanah a grandson of Korah through Assir. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary both prefer that reading. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that he was one of Korah's sons who, according to Num 26:11, did not die when Korah was destroyed. His name is usually explained as "God has possessed" or "God has created." Several other men in the Bible are also called Elkanah.

Elkanah was a Levite of the clan of Kohath, named in the genealogies of 1 Chronicles 6 and counted among the ancestors of the prophet Samuel (STEPBible Proper Names). In one list of Kohath's descendants he follows Shaul and is the father of Amasai and Ahimoth (1 Chr 6:25). In the parallel line traced back from Heman the singer, he is the father of Amasai and the son of Joel (1 Chr 6:36). This entry follows the first list in naming Shaul as his father. The two lists are probably variant forms of the same line, with Shaul and Joel standing in the same position. Several other men in the Bible share the name, including Samuel's father and other Elkanahs in the same chapter, so identifying him in each verse depends on context. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the name's meaning as "the zeal of God."

Elkanah was a Levite of the clan of Kohath who appears only in the genealogies of 1 Chronicles 6. He was the son of Mahath and the father of Zuph. His name is one of several Elkanahs in the same family line, which makes the lists hard to untangle. In 1 Chr 6:26 his son is called Zophai, probably another form of the name Zuph given in 1 Chr 6:35. The second list traces the ancestry of Heman, a temple singer in David's time (1 Chr 6:33), back through the prophet Samuel to Kohath. By inference from that list and from 1 Sam 1:1, which names Zuph as an ancestor of Samuel's father, also called Elkanah, this Elkanah was a distant forefather of Samuel. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia explains the name as "God has possessed."

Elon was a Hittite whose daughter married Esau, the son of Isaac. Gen 26:34 calls her Bashemath and says Esau married her, along with Judith daughter of Beeri the Hittite, when he was forty years old. The later list of Esau's wives in Gen 36:2 names Elon's daughter as Adah. The two lists of Esau's wives differ in their names, and the passages do not explain this. Most readers take Bashemath and Adah to be two names for the same woman, and this entry follows that view, which is why Adah appears here as his daughter. Esau's wives are described as daughters of Canaan, so Elon was evidently one of the Hittite inhabitants of the land. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "oak" or "strong." Several other people in the Bible share the name Elon.

Elon was the second of the three sons of Zebulun, listed between his brothers Sered and Jahleel among the family of Jacob who went down to Egypt (Gen 46:14). In the census of the tribes taken in the wilderness, he appears as the ancestor of the Elonites, one of the clans of the tribe of Zebulun (Num 26:26). Nothing else is recorded about him. His name probably means "oak" or "terebinth," according to Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia. Several other men in the Bible share the name, including a judge of Israel from the same tribe, but this entry concerns only the son of Zebulun.

Elon was a man from the tribe of Zebulun who judged Israel for ten years (Judg 12:11). He followed Ibzan of Bethlehem and was succeeded by Abdon, as the surrounding verses of Judges 12 show. Easton's Bible Dictionary counts him as the eleventh of the Hebrew judges. The text records no deeds or battles from his time in office, only its length, his death, and his burial at Aijalon in the territory of Zebulun (Judg 12:12). This Aijalon is a different place from the better-known Aijalon in the territory of Dan. His judgeship is dated here to about 1139 BC, an estimate inferred from context. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives the meaning of his name as "terebinth," a kind of tree. Several other people in the Bible share the name Elon, so this entry concerns only the judge.

Elpalet was a son of David, one of the children born to him after he settled in Jerusalem. He is named only in the two lists of David's sons in Chronicles: as Elpalet in 1 Chr 14:5 and as Eliphelet in 1 Chr 3:6, where he follows Ibhar and Elishama (or Elishua). His mother is not named. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "God of deliverance." Both lists also name a later son called Eliphalet or Eliphelet, so David appears to have had two sons with nearly the same name. The parallel list in 2 Samuel 5 names only one, which has led some interpreters to suggest that Elpalet died young and the name was given again to a younger brother. The text does not say this, so it remains an inference.

Elymas was a Jewish sorcerer and false prophet whom Barnabas and Saul (Paul) met at Paphos, on the island of Cyprus, about AD 45 by inference from context. His Jewish name was Bar-jesus, and Acts gives Elymas as the interpretation of that name, meaning "sorcerer" (Acts 13:6, 8). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia explains Elymas as a Greek form of an Aramaic or Arabic word for a wise man or magician. He was attached to the Roman proconsul (the "deputy") Sergius Paulus, and when the proconsul sought to hear the apostles, Elymas opposed them and tried to turn him away from the faith. The account that follows in Acts 13:9–12 says Paul declared that Elymas would be blind for a time, he was struck blind, and the proconsul then believed.

Enoch (son of Cain) was the son of Cain and his wife, and the first of Cain's descendants named in Genesis. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary describe him as Cain's eldest son. Cain built a city and named it Enoch after him (Gen 4:17). Easton's notes that this is the first city mentioned in Scripture. By inference from Gen 4:16, it stood in the land of Nod, east of Eden, though its location cannot be fixed. The Hebrew sentence could also be read as saying that Enoch himself built the city. This entry follows the usual reading, with Cain as the builder. Enoch was the father of Irad, and through him the ancestor of Mehujael, Methusael and Lamech (Gen 4:18). Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of his name as "dedicated." He is a different man from Enoch the son of Jared, who appears in Seth's line in Genesis 5.

Epaphroditus was a member of the church at Philippi who served as its messenger to the apostle Paul. He carried the Philippians' gift to Paul, which Paul acknowledges as fully supplying his needs (Phil 4:18), and he stayed to look after Paul. Paul calls him "my brother, and companion in labour, and fellowsoldier" (Phil 2:25). The surrounding verses (Phil 2:26–30) say he fell seriously ill, nearly dying, while doing this work, and then recovered. Paul decided to send him home, and by inference he carried the letter to the Philippians with him. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia places these events during Paul's first imprisonment in Rome. The name, meaning "lovely" or "handsome," was common at the time. Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that Epaphras is a shortened form of it. Whether he is the same man as Epaphras of Colossae is uncertain, and this entry treats them as separate people.

Epher was a son of Midian and so a grandson of Abraham through his wife Keturah. He appears second in the list of Midian's five sons, with his brothers Ephah, Hanoch (spelled Henoch in 1 Chr 1:33), Abida and Eldaah, all counted among the descendants of Keturah (Gen 25:4; 1 Chr 1:33). Nothing else is recorded about him, and he is probably named as the ancestor of a clan within the Midianite peoples. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia give the meaning of his name as "calf" or "young deer," while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "dust" or "lead." The name is shared by other men in the Bible, including figures in the genealogies of Judah and Manasseh, who are different people from this son of Midian.

Eri was one of the sons of Gad, Jacob's son, and so a member of the tribe of Gad. He appears in the list of Jacob's descendants who went down to Egypt (Gen 46:16), and in the wilderness census he is named as the ancestor of the Erites, one of the Gadite clans (Num 26:16). His brothers were Ziphion (Zephon), Haggi, Shuni, Ezbon, Arodi (Arod) and Areli. The two lists differ slightly in spelling, and Ezbon in Genesis is probably the same person as Ozni in Numbers. Nothing else is recorded about him. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "watchful", while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "my city".

Eshban was a Horite, one of four sons of Dishon, listed in the genealogy of the people of Seir in Gen 36:26 and repeated in 1 Chr 1:41. His brothers were Ithran and Cheran, and a fourth brother is called Hemdan in Genesis but Amram in Chronicles. Chronicles places this Dishon as a son of Anah. Genesis 36 also mentions a Dishon who was a son of Seir, so which Dishon was Eshban's father is open to question. This entry follows the Chronicles reading. Nothing is recorded about Eshban beyond his name and family. The Tyndale House proper-names index describes him as a Horite chief in the land of Seir. The meaning of his name is uncertain: Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "wise man," the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests "thoughtful" or "intelligent," and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "fire of the sun."

Eshcol was an Amorite, the brother of Mamre and Aner, who lived near Abram in the area of Mamre, close to Hebron. The three brothers were allies of Abram (Gen 14:13). When Abram went after the kings who had captured his nephew Lot, Eshcol and his brothers went with him. After the victory, Abram refused to keep any of the recovered goods for himself, but he insisted that Aner, Eshcol and Mamre receive their share (Gen 14:24). The name means "cluster of grapes." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia and the STEPBible proper-names list connect him with the valley of Eshcol near Hebron, where Moses' spies later cut a large cluster of grapes (Num 13:23). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia presents this link as possible rather than certain. Smith's Bible Dictionary places these events about 1912 BC.

Eshton was a man named in the genealogies of the tribe of Judah. According to 1 Chr 4:11, he was the son of Mehir, whose father was Chelub, the brother of Shuah. Eshton fathered Beth-rapha, Paseah and Tehinnah, and Tehinnah is called the father of Ir-nahash. The passage closes by calling this family "the men of Rechah," a place or clan otherwise unknown. Some of these names, such as Beth-rapha and Ir-nahash, look like place names, so the list may record the founders of settlements as well as individual descendants, though the text does not say so directly. Nothing else is recorded about Eshton. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "effeminate," while the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia renders it "uxorious."

Ethan was a man of the tribe of Judah, one of the five sons of Zerah listed in 1 Chr 2:6, alongside Zimri (called Zabdi in Josh 7:1), Heman, Calcol and Dara. The STEPBible Proper Names index identifies him as a grandson of Judah, since Zerah was a son of Judah by Tamar (Gen 38:30). His only recorded son was Azariah. The name is shared by several men in the Bible. 1 Kgs 4:31 compares Solomon's wisdom to that of Ethan the Ezrahite, Heman, Chalcol and Darda. Because three of those names match Zerah's sons, some readers take them to be the same family, while others see them as different men, since that verse calls them sons of Mahol. This entry treats Ethan son of Zerah only as the genealogy presents him. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the name's meaning as "strong."

Ethan was a Levite of the Gershonite branch of the tribe of Levi. He was the son of Zimmah and the father of Adaiah, and he appears in the family line of Asaph, the temple singer (1 Chr 6:42). The other Gershonite genealogy in the same chapter names Zimmah's son as Joah, followed by Iddo, Zerah and Jeaterai (1 Chr 6:21). Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both take Joah and Ethan to be the same man, and this entry follows that view. By the same comparison, Iddo probably corresponds to Adaiah. Nothing is recorded about his life beyond his place in these genealogies. Several other men in the Bible are also called Ethan, so he should not be confused with Ethan the Ezrahite or Ethan the Merarite singer.

Evi was one of five kings of Midian killed by the Israelites in the war against Midian near the end of Moses' life. Numbers 31:8 names him first among the five, with Rekem, Zur, Hur and Reba, and says Balaam son of Beor was killed at the same time. Joshua 13:21 recalls the same event when describing the land given to the tribe of Reuben. There Evi and the others are called princes of Midian and "dukes of Sihon," which suggests they were local rulers allied with or subject to Sihon, the Amorite king of Heshbon. According to the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia, the battle took place while Israel was camped on the plains of Moab. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "desire," while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "unjust."

Evil-merodach was a king of Babylon who, in the first year of his reign, released Jehoiachin, the exiled king of Judah, from prison. This happened in the thirty-seventh year of Jehoiachin's captivity, in the twelfth month. 2 Kgs 25:27 gives the twenty-seventh day and Jer 52:31 the twenty-fifth. The verses that follow in both accounts say he spoke kindly to Jehoiachin, gave him a seat above the other kings with him, and provided for him at the royal table for the rest of his life. Reference works identify him as the son and successor of Nebuchadnezzar. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives his Babylonian name as Amel-Marduk, 'man of Marduk,' and says dated tablets show a reign of a little over two years. Easton's Bible Dictionary dates it about 562–560 BC. Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionary both report that he was murdered by his brother-in-law Neriglissar, who succeeded him.

Ezekiel was a priest and prophet, the son of Buzi, who received the word of the LORD while living among the Jewish exiles in the land of the Chaldeans by the river Chebar (Ezek 1:3). The book of Ezekiel is attributed to him. Easton's Bible Dictionary places him among the captives taken to Babylon with King Jehoiachin, about 597 BC, and his prophetic activity is dated here to about 593 BC, by inference from context. According to the same dictionary, he had a house in exile, was often consulted by the elders, and lost his wife suddenly. God made Ezekiel himself a sign to the people: what he did, they would do, and when it happened they would know that he was the Lord GOD (Ezek 24:24). Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "the strength of God." The time and manner of his death are not recorded.

Gadi was the father of Menahem, who seized the throne of the northern kingdom of Israel. He is known only from the phrase "Menahem the son of Gadi" in 2 Kgs 15:14 and 15:17, which tell how Menahem came up from Tirzah to Samaria, killed King Shallum son of Jabesh and reigned in his place. Menahem began to reign in the thirty-ninth year of Azariah king of Judah and ruled ten years in Samaria. Nothing else is recorded about Gadi himself. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives the meaning of his name as "fortunate," and Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him as a Gadite, that is, a member of the tribe of Gad, a view probably drawn from the form of the name.

Gahar was the ancestor of a family of temple servants (the Nethinim) whose descendants returned to Jerusalem from exile in Babylon with Zerubbabel. The "children of Gahar" appear in the list of returning families in Ezra 2:47 and again in the parallel list in Neh 7:49. In both lists they are named next to the family of Giddel. That these families were temple servants, and that they returned under Zerubbabel, comes from the surrounding context of the lists. Nothing else is recorded about Gahar himself. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "lurking-place," and Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "hiding-place." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the same family is called Geddur in 1 Esdras 5:30.

Gaius was a Christian at Corinth, one of the few people there whom Paul baptized personally, alongside Crispus (1 Cor 1:14). In Rom 16:23 a Gaius sends greetings and is called Paul's host and host of the whole church. Since Paul probably wrote Romans from Corinth, this entry follows the common view that the two references describe the same man, a believer whose home received Paul and served as a meeting place for the congregation. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both take this view. Several other men named Gaius appear in the New Testament, including a Macedonian companion of Paul seized by the crowd at Ephesus and the recipient of 3 John. Easton's Bible Dictionary connects the Corinthian host with the Macedonian traveller. How these figures relate to one another is uncertain. The name, a common Roman one, means "lord" according to Hitchcock's Bible Names.

Galal was a Levite, the son of Jeduthun and father of Shemaiah. He appears only in genealogies of the Levites who lived in Jerusalem after the return from the Babylonian exile. 1 Chr 9:16 names his grandson Obadiah, son of Shemaiah. The parallel list in Neh 11:17 names a grandson Abda, son of Shammua. Shammua and Shemaiah are probably the same person, and Obadiah and Abda the same descendant. Jeduthun is elsewhere known as a leader of temple music, so Galal's family probably served among the temple singers, as the STEPBible Proper Names describes him. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia distinguishes him from another Levite named Galal mentioned just before, in 1 Chr 9:15. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "a roll" or "a wheel."

Gamaliel was a Pharisee and teacher of the law in Jerusalem in the first century AD, respected by all the people and a member of the council (the Sanhedrin). When the apostles were brought before the council for preaching, he had them sent out briefly and then advised caution (Acts 5:34).
