The surrounding passage records his argument that if their work was of human origin it would fail, but if it was from God it could not be overthrown. The council followed his advice and released the apostles after a beating, an event dated here to about AD 30 by inference from context. Paul later said he had been brought up in Jerusalem "at the feet of Gamaliel" and trained strictly in the law (Acts 22:3). Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries identify him with the famous rabbi Gamaliel, grandson of Hillel. The name is also borne by an earlier Israelite, a leader of the tribe of Manasseh in Numbers.

Gazzam was the ancestor or head of a family of temple servants (the Nethinim) whose descendants returned from the Babylonian exile with Zerubbabel. The "children of Gazzam" appear in the list of returning exiles in Ezra 2:48 and again in the parallel list in Neh 7:51, where they are named among other temple-servant families such as those of Rezin, Nekoda and Uzza. Nothing else is recorded about Gazzam himself. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates the return to about 536 BC, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives the name's meaning as "devouring." Hitchcock's Bible Names instead renders it "the fleece of them." The same family appears as "Gazera" in the apocryphal book 1 Esdras.

Gedaliah was a Levite musician, one of the six sons of Jeduthun, who served under their father's direction in the worship organized in David's time, prophesying with the harp to give thanks and praise to the LORD (1 Chr 25:3). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives his name as meaning "Yahweh is great." His brothers were Zeri (probably the same as Izri, named later in the chapter), Jeshaiah, Hashabiah, Mattithiah and Shimei. Verse 3 says six but names only five, and Shimei, who appears later in the list, is generally taken as the sixth. When the musicians were divided by lot into twenty-four courses, the second lot fell to Gedaliah, whose group of brothers and sons numbered twelve (1 Chr 25:9). Several other people in the Bible share his name, including the governor of Judah appointed after the fall of Jerusalem. This Gedaliah is mentioned only in these two verses.

Gether was a son of Aram and a grandson of Shem, named third of Aram's four sons in the Table of Nations alongside Uz, Hul and Mash (Gen 10:23). The parallel genealogy in 1 Chr 1:17 lists him directly among the sons of Shem without naming Aram as his father. In the Chronicles list the brother called Mash in Genesis appears as Meshech. Like the other names in this table, Gether probably stands for both an individual ancestor and the people descended from him. He is mentioned nowhere else in the Bible. Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that no satisfactory trace of a people descended from him has been found, so any tribe or region linked to his name remains unknown. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "the vale of trial or searching," while Smith's gives "fear."

Gibeon, also called Gibbar, is the name under which a family group of 95 people appears among the exiles who returned from Babylon with Zerubbabel. Ezra 2:20 calls them "the children of Gibbar," while the parallel list in Neh 7:25 gives the same number under the name "the children of Gibeon." This entry treats both names as one ancestor or family head. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes Gibbar as the father of some who returned. Because many names in these lists are towns rather than people, "Gibeon" may instead refer to the people of the city of Gibeon, the Hivite town that made a treaty with Joshua. In Nehemiah the name stands near other place names, which makes that reading likely there. Nothing else is recorded about this person.

Giddalti was a Levite, one of the fourteen sons of Heman, the king's seer, listed among the musicians David organized for service in the house of the Lord (1 Chr 25:4). When these musicians were divided by lot into twenty-four courses, the twenty-second lot fell to Giddalti. His group of twelve, made up of himself, his sons and his relatives, served in that turn (1 Chr 25:29). The surrounding chapter describes these families as prophesying with harps, lyres and cymbals, so Giddalti was probably one of the temple's instrumental musicians. His name is usually understood to mean "I magnify (God)" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia) or "I have trained up" (Smith's Bible Dictionary). Several of Heman's sons have names that some scholars read together as a line of a psalm or prayer, but the text presents them simply as individuals. Nothing else is recorded about him.

Giddel was the ancestor, or head, of a family of temple servants (the Nethinim) whose descendants returned from the Babylonian exile to Jerusalem and Judah with Zerubbabel. The "children of Giddel" appear in the list of returning temple servants in Ezra 2:47 and again in the parallel list in Neh 7:49. Nothing else is recorded about him. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia give the name's meaning as "very great." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia also notes that the parallel list in 1 Esdras gives the name as Cathua. The same name belongs to another man elsewhere in the returnee lists, an ancestor of a family of Solomon's servants, who is a separate person from this one.

Giddel was the ancestor of a family listed among the descendants of "Solomon's servants" who returned from exile in Babylon to Judah with Zerubbabel. His name appears only in the parallel lists of returnees in Ezra 2:56 and Neh 7:58, where the "children of Giddel" are named alongside the families of Jaalah and Darkon. Nothing else is recorded about him. The return is usually dated to about 536 BC, the date Smith's Bible Dictionary gives, by inference from context. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the parallel list in 1 Esdras gives the name as Isdael. The name probably means "great" or "very great." Another Giddel, the head of a family of temple servants, appears in the same lists, so the name belongs to more than one person, and this entry concerns only the ancestor of Solomon's servants.

Ginath was the father of Tibni, the man whom half the people of Israel tried to make king after the death of Zimri, while the other half followed Omri (1 Kgs 16:21). Omri's supporters prevailed, Tibni died, and Omri became king (1 Kgs 16:22). Ginath is mentioned only to identify his son, and nothing else is recorded about him, including his tribe or home. The setting suggests he lived in the early ninth century BC, an estimate inferred from context. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "protection," while Hitchcock's Bible Names connects it with "a garden."

Girgasite (also spelled Girgashite) is listed in the table of nations as a son of Canaan, the son of Ham. He is named with the Jebusite and the Amorite (Gen 10:16; 1 Chr 1:14). Like his brothers, the name stands for a people descended from him rather than for an individual whose life is recorded. Easton's Bible Dictionary counts him as Canaan's fifth son. Later passages name the Girgashites among the peoples living in Canaan before the Israelites, including Gen 15:21, Deut 7:1 and Josh 3:10. Where they lived is not known. Easton's suggests central western Palestine. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes a proposed link with the Gergesenes east of the Sea of Galilee (Matt 8:28). It also notes that Josephus said nothing was known of the people.

Habaiah was the ancestor of a priestly family whose descendants returned from exile in Babylon. In the lists of returnees, "the children of Habaiah" appear among the priests, alongside the families of Koz and Barzillai (Ezra 2:61; Neh 7:63). Smith's Bible Dictionary places this return with Zerubbabel. The verses that follow in both lists (Ezra 2:62; Neh 7:64) say these priestly families searched for their genealogical records and could not find them, so they were barred from serving as priests. The STEPBible Proper Names list likewise describes Habaiah's descendants as excluded from the priesthood for lack of records. Nothing is recorded about Habaiah himself beyond his place as the family's ancestor. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of his name as "the hiding of the Lord," and Smith's Bible Dictionary renders it "whom Jehovah hides."

Habakkuk was a prophet of Judah and the writer of the Old Testament book that bears his name. The book opens by calling its message "the burden which Habakkuk the prophet did see" (Hab 1:1), and its final chapter is a prayer of his set "upon Shigionoth," probably a musical or poetic term (Hab 3:1). The book records his questions to God about injustice and God's answers, including the coming of the Chaldeans (Hab 1:6). That suggests he worked in the years before the Babylonian invasions. Nothing certain is known of his life beyond what the book itself says. Smith's Bible Dictionary places him around the twelfth or thirteenth year of King Josiah, about 630 BC. This entry dates his prophecies to about 607 BC, an estimate inferred from context. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of his name as "he that embraces" or "a wrestler."

Hachaliah was the father of Nehemiah, the Jewish official who served at the Persian court in Shushan and later became governor of Judah. He is known only through his son, who is identified as "the son of Hachaliah" at the opening of his book and again in the list of those who sealed the covenant. Hachaliah is also counted as the father of Hanani, probably because Nehemiah calls Hanani his brother (Neh 1:2; Neh 7:2), though "brother" there could mean a close relative. Nothing else is recorded about Hachaliah's life. Smith's Bible Dictionary explains the name as "whom Jehovah enlightens," while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "who waits for the Lord."

Hadar was one of the twelve sons of Ishmael, Abraham's son by Hagar. He appears only in the lists of Ishmael's sons, named alongside brothers such as Tema, Jetur, Naphish and Kedemah (Gen 25:15). The parallel list in 1 Chr 1:30 spells his name Hadad. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the two spellings come from a small difference in the Hebrew text, and that the Revised Version reads "Hadad" in both places. Like his brothers, he was probably regarded as the ancestor of an Arabian tribe, by inference from the context of these genealogies, though nothing further is recorded about him or any people descended from him. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "power" or "greatness." Ishmael also had a daughter, Bashemath, who married Esau.

Hadoram was a son of Joktan, listed fifth among his thirteen sons in the Table of Nations (Gen 10:27) and again in the parallel genealogy of 1 Chr 1:21. Through Joktan he descended from Shem by way of Arphaxad, Shelah and Eber, making him about the sixth generation after Noah. His brothers included Sheba, Ophir and Havilah, and nothing is recorded about him beyond his name. Like the other sons of Joktan, he is generally taken to stand for a people or tribe as well as an individual. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes him as the founder of an Arab tribe, while Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that, unlike the territories of several of his brothers, his settlements have not been identified. He should not be confused with Hadoram the son of Tou, king of Hamath, who appears in David's time.

Hagabah was the ancestor of a family of temple servants (the Nethinim) whose descendants returned from exile in Babylon to Judah with Zerubbabel. His name appears only in the list of returning families, where "the children of Hagabah" are counted among the temple servants (Ezra 2:45). The parallel list spells the name Hagaba (Neh 7:48). According to the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia, the name means "locust." That work also notes that he is similar to, but listed separately from, Hagab, another ancestor of temple servants named in Ezra's list. Nothing else is recorded about him beyond his place in these lists.

Haggi was the second son of Gad and a grandson of Jacob. He appears in the list of Jacob's descendants who went down to Egypt (Gen 46:16), where he is named after his brother Ziphion. His other brothers were Shuni, Ezbon, Eri, Arodi and Areli. In the census taken in the wilderness (Num 26:15), he is named as the ancestor of the Haggites, one of the clans of the tribe of Gad. Some of his brothers' names differ between the two lists: Ziphion appears as Zephon, Arodi as Arod, and Ezbon is matched in Numbers by Ozni. The name probably means "festive," according to Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia. Nothing else is recorded about Haggi or his descendants.

Hakupha was the ancestor of a family of temple servants (the Nethinim) whose descendants returned from exile in Babylon to Jerusalem with Zerubbabel. "The children of Hakupha" appear in the list of returning families in Ezra 2:51 and again in the parallel list in Neh 7:53. In both lists they are named between the families of Bakbuk and Harhur. The verses give no further details about Hakupha himself, and the name may refer to a family line rather than to a single known individual. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats it as a family name among the Nethinim and gives its meaning as "incitement." Smith's Bible Dictionary renders it "bent," and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "a commandment of the mouth."

Hamathite is the name given to one of the descendants of Canaan, son of Ham, in the Table of Nations. He is named last among Canaan's sons, after Zidon, Heth, the Jebusite, the Amorite, the Girgasite, the Hivite, the Arkite, the Sinite, the Arvadite and the Zemarite. Genesis adds that after these "the families of the Canaanites spread abroad" (Gen 10:18). The same list is repeated in 1 Chr 1:16. Smith's Bible Dictionary treats the name as a family or people descended from Canaan rather than a single individual. The form of the name suggests a link with the people of Hamath, a city on the Orontes River in Syria (modern Hama), though the verses do not state this directly. Nothing else is recorded about him.

Hammelech is named in the King James Version as the father of two men in the book of Jeremiah. His son Jerahmeel was one of three men the king, Jehoiakim by the context of the chapter, ordered to arrest Baruch the scribe and Jeremiah the prophet, though they were hidden (Jer 36:26). His son Malchiah owned the muddy cistern in the court of the prison into which Jeremiah was lowered with ropes (Jer 38:6). The Hebrew ha-melekh means "the king," and views differ on whether it is a personal name. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia read it as "the king," as the American Standard Version translates it. On that reading these men were royal sons, possibly of different kings, since Zedekiah reigned by the time of Jer 38. Easton's Bible Dictionary takes it as probably a proper name, and this entry follows that view.

Hanan was one of the six sons of Azel, a man of the tribe of Benjamin descended from King Saul through Jonathan's line. He appears only in two nearly identical genealogies, where he is listed last among his brothers Azrikam, Bocheru, Ishmael, Sheariah and Obadiah (1 Chr 8:38; 1 Chr 9:44). Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia call him the youngest son, a reading drawn from his place at the end of the list. Nothing else is recorded about him. The name, meaning "gracious," is shared by several other men in the Bible, so he should not be confused with them.

Hanan was the ancestor or head of a family of Nethinim, the temple servants, whose descendants returned from exile in Babylon to Jerusalem with Zerubbabel. The "children of Hanan" appear in the list of returning families in Ezra 2:46 and again in the parallel list in Neh 7:49. Nothing else is recorded about him beyond his name. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates the return to about 536 BC, and the name is usually explained as meaning "gracious" or "merciful." Several other men in the Bible are also called Hanan, and this entry refers only to the one named in the temple servants' lists.

Hanan was a Levite in Jerusalem after the return from exile. He was one of the men who, alongside Ezra's public reading of the law, helped the people understand what was being read while they stood in their places (Neh 8:7). A Levite named Hanan also appears among the Levites who put their seal to the covenant made in Nehemiah's time (Neh 10:10). Smith's Bible Dictionary takes this to be probably the same man, since he is listed there with several of the same companions, including Hodijah, Kelita and Pelaiah. This entry follows that identification. Smith's dates the events to about 446 BC. The name means "gracious" or "merciful." Several other men in the Bible are also called Hanan.

Hanani was a Levite musician, one of the fourteen sons of Heman listed in 1 Chr 25:4. Heman was one of the leaders of music in worship during David's reign. When the singers and musicians were divided by lot into twenty-four courses, or rotating groups, for service at the sanctuary, the eighteenth lot fell to Hanani. His group of twelve was made up of him, his sons and his relatives (1 Chr 25:25). His brothers included Hananiah, Mattaniah, Uzziel and Jerimoth, who each led a course of their own. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia give the meaning of his name as "gracious." Several other men in the Bible are also named Hanani, and this one should not be confused with them.

Hanani was a brother of Nehemiah, and so a son of Hachaliah. Neh 1:2 calls him "one of my brethren," a phrase that could mean a close relative in general, but Neh 7:2 calls him "my brother." He came with some men of Judah to Nehemiah, probably at the Persian royal city of Susa named in the surrounding verses. Nehemiah questioned them about the Jews who had survived the exile and about Jerusalem, and their report led to Nehemiah's mission to rebuild the city. After the wall was finished, Nehemiah put Hanani, together with Hananiah the ruler of the palace, in charge of Jerusalem. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes this as charge over the city gates, while Smith's Bible Dictionary calls him a governor of the city under Nehemiah. The name means "gracious" and is shared by several other people in the Bible.

Hananiah was a son of Zerubbabel, the governor who led Jews back from exile in Babylon. He belonged to the tribe of Judah and to the royal line of David, and probably lived in the late sixth century BC, after about 536 BC, which Smith's Bible Dictionary gives as an estimate. His brother Meshullam and sister Shelomith are named with him, and 1 Chr 3:20 lists five more siblings. 1 Chr 3:21 names his sons Pelatiah and Jesaiah, then lists 'the sons of' Rephaiah, Arnan, Obadiah and Shechaniah. This entry treats all six as his children, though the verse can also be read as a separate list of related families or as a chain of later generations. Smith's Bible Dictionary identifies him with Joanna in Luke's genealogy of Jesus. His name means 'the Lord has been gracious.' Several other men in the Bible share the name.

Hananiah was a Levite, one of the fourteen sons of Heman, who was one of the chief musicians organized under King David. He is listed with his brothers in 1 Chr 25:4. When lots were cast to set the order of service for the temple musicians, the sixteenth lot fell to Hananiah. He served with his sons and relatives, a group of twelve (1 Chr 25:23). The surrounding chapter places this arrangement in David's reign. The name means roughly "the Lord has been gracious" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia) and was common in Israel, so this Hananiah should be kept distinct from several others of the same name.

Harhur was the ancestor of a family of temple servants (the Nethinim) whose descendants returned from exile in Babylon to Judah with Zerubbabel. His name appears only in the two parallel lists of returning exiles, where "the children of Harhur" are named between the families of Hakupha and Bazluth (Ezra 2:51; Neh 7:53). The surrounding verses in both lists place these families among the Nethinim, the group who assisted the Levites in the temple. Nothing else is recorded about Harhur himself, and whether he was a single ancestor or the name of a clan is not stated. The name is usually explained as meaning "fever" or "inflammation" (Easton's Bible Dictionary, Smith's Bible Dictionary). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia also suggests "free-born" and notes a parallel form, Hasour, in the apocryphal 1 Esdras 5:31.

Hariph was the ancestor of a family of 112 people who returned to Jerusalem and Judah from exile in Babylon, in the group listed with Zerubbabel (Ezra 2; Neh 7). Hariph appears in Nehemiah's version of the list (Neh 7:24). The parallel list in Ezra gives the same family, with the same number, under the name Jorah (Ezra 2:18), so the two names are taken to refer to the same family. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes the group as the descendants of Hariph. Nothing else is recorded about Hariph himself. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia also links him to the Hariph who sealed Nehemiah's covenant (Neh 10:19), perhaps as a family head acting for the clan. Because several people share the name, that connection is uncertain.

Harsha was the ancestor of a family of temple servants (the Nethinim) whose descendants returned from exile in Babylon to Judah. The "children of Harsha" appear in the list of returnees in Ezra 2:52, and again in the parallel list in Neh 7:54. In both lists the name stands next to Bazluth (Bazlith) and Mehida. The context places them among the groups who came back with Zerubbabel. Nothing else is recorded about Harsha himself. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the corresponding list in 1 Esdras gives the name as "Charea." The meaning of the name is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives "worker" or "enchanter," Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "deaf," and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "workmanship" or "a wood."

Hashabiah was a Levite of the clan of Merari, named only in genealogies. He was the son of Bunni and the father of Azrikam. Through Azrikam and Hasshub he was an ancestor of Shemaiah, one of the Levites who lived in Jerusalem after the return from exile in Babylon (1 Chr 9:14; Neh 11:15). The two lists give the same line from Shemaiah back to Hashabiah. Chronicles traces it to Merari, and Nehemiah adds Hashabiah's father Bunni. Several other people in the Bible share the name, so this Hashabiah should not be confused with them. Smith's Bible Dictionary treats the two verses as separate entries, but this entry takes them as one man because the genealogies match. The name is usually explained as meaning "the Lord regards" or "the estimation of the Lord" (Hitchcock's Bible Names).

Hashabiah was a Levite musician, one of the sons of Jeduthun (also called Ethan), who served in the worship arranged in David's time. 1 Chr 25:3 names him among Jeduthun's sons, alongside Gedaliah, Zeri (Izri), Jeshaiah and Mattithiah, who worked under their father's direction as he prophesied with the harp to give thanks and praise the LORD. That verse counts six sons but names only five; the sixth is probably Shimei, who appears later in the same chapter. When the temple musicians were divided by lot into twenty-four groups, the twelfth lot fell to Hashabiah, and his group of sons and relatives numbered twelve (1 Chr 25:19). Smith's Bible Dictionary dates this to about 1014 BC and calls him the fourth son of Jeduthun. Several other men in the Bible share this name. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives its meaning as "the estimation of the Lord."

Hasrah, also called Harhas, was the father of Tikvah (or Tikvath) and the grandfather of Shallum, husband of the prophetess Huldah. He is known only from the account of King Josiah's reign. Hilkiah the priest and the king's officials went to consult Huldah about the book of the law found in the temple. Her husband's family line is given there in two parallel forms. 2 Kgs 22:14 spells the name Harhas, and 2 Chr 34:22 spells it Hasrah. The title "keeper of the wardrobe" follows Hasrah's name in both verses, but the wording does not make clear whether it belongs to him or to Shallum. Easton's Bible Dictionary takes it as Hasrah's office and explains it as care of the priestly garments. Nothing else is recorded about him.

Hasshub was a Levite of the clan of Merari, known only as a link in a family line. He was the son of Azrikam and the father of Shemaiah, a Levite listed among those who lived in Jerusalem after the return from the Babylonian exile (1 Chr 9:14; Neh 11:15). The two lists trace the same line back to Hashabiah. Chronicles places the family among the sons of Merari, while Nehemiah adds the name Bunni. The King James Version spells his name Hasshub in Chronicles and Hashub in Nehemiah. The name probably means "considerate" or "intelligent," according to the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia and Smith's Bible Dictionary. Several other men named Hashub appear in Nehemiah, and one Hebrew lexicon treats two of them as the same person. Whether this Levite is also one of them is uncertain.

Hasupha was the ancestor or head of a family of Nethinim, the temple servants, whose descendants returned to Jerusalem from exile in Babylon. The family appears in the lists of those who came back with Zerubbabel, named second among the temple servants after Ziha and before Tabbaoth (Ezra 2:43). The parallel list spells the name Hashupha (Neh 7:46), and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes the form Asipha in 1 Esdras 5:29. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates this first return to about 536 BC. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "uncovered", and Smith's gives "stripped". Nothing else is recorded about him beyond his family's place in these lists.

Hatipha was the ancestor of a family of temple servants (the Nethinim) whose descendants, "the children of Hatipha," returned from exile in Babylon. The family appears in the list of returnees recorded in Ezra 2:54 and repeated in Nehemiah 7:56, where it is named last among the temple-servant families, right after the children of Neziah. Smith's Bible Dictionary places this return with Zerubbabel, about 536 BC. Nothing else is known of Hatipha himself, and the name may stand for a clan rather than a single remembered individual. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary give the meaning of the name as "captured" or "captive." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the same family appears as "Atipha" in the parallel list in 1 Esdras 5:32.

Hatita was the ancestor of a family of temple gatekeepers ("porters") whose descendants returned from exile in Babylon to Judah. The "children of Hatita" appear in the list of returnees in Ezra 2:42 and its parallel in Neh 7:45. There they are one of six gatekeeper families, alongside those of Shallum, Ater, Talmon, Akkub and Shobai. The six families together numbered 139 in Ezra and 138 in Nehemiah. The lists place this return under Zerubbabel, which Smith's Bible Dictionary dates to about 536 BC. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia describes Hatita as the head of a family and notes that the corresponding list in the apocryphal book of 1 Esdras gives the name as "Ateta." Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary give the name's meaning as "exploration" or "exploring." Nothing else is known about him.

Hattil was the ancestor of a family group listed among the descendants of "Solomon's servants" who returned to Judah from exile in Babylon. His name appears in the parallel lists of returnees in Ezra 2:57 and Neh 7:59, alongside Shephatiah, Pochereth of Zebaim, and Ami (called Amon in Nehemiah). Nothing else is recorded about him. By inference from the surrounding lists, "Solomon's servants" were a hereditary class associated with temple service, probably descended from laborers conscripted under Solomon. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the same family is called Agia in 1 Esdras 5:34. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "howling for sin."

Hattush was a priest named in the lists of Nehemiah. Neh 12:2 includes him among the priests who came back from exile in Babylon with Zerubbabel and Jeshua, and Neh 10:4 names him among those who set their seal to the covenant made in Nehemiah's day. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the Tyndale House proper-names index describe him as a priest who returned with Zerubbabel. The two lists are separated by many decades, so the names may refer to a priestly family or to two different men. Several other men in the Bible share the name, including a descendant of David who returned with Ezra. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes some doubt about whether that descendant of David and this priest are the same person. This entry treats Hattush as the priest of Nehemiah's lists.

Havilah (son of Cush) was one of the sons of Cush, the son of Ham, named in the Table of Nations. He appears alongside his brothers Seba, Sabtah, Raamah and Sabtecha in Gen 10:7, and the list is repeated in 1 Chr 1:9. Nimrod is also called a son of Cush in the verse that follows (Gen 10:8). Nothing else is recorded about him. As with many names in this genealogy, his name probably also stands for a people or region descended from him. He should be kept distinct from Havilah the son of Joktan, a descendant of Shem (Gen 10:29), and from the land of Havilah mentioned elsewhere, although some interpreters connect the names. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "circle," while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "that suffers pain."

Havilah (son of Joktan) was one of the thirteen sons of Joktan named in the Table of Nations, listed between his brothers Ophir and Jobab (Gen 10:29; 1 Chr 1:23). Joktan was a son of Eber in the line of Shem, which makes Havilah a Semite. He should not be confused with Havilah the son of Cush (Gen 10:7), a Hamite, or with the land of Havilah mentioned elsewhere in Genesis. Nothing is recorded about his life. Like many names in this list, his name probably also stood for a people or region descended from him. By inference from his brothers' names, such as Sheba and Ophir, which are usually connected with southern Arabia, that people was probably located in Arabia. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "that suffers pain" or "that brings forth."

Hazarmaveth was a son of Joktan, a descendant of Shem through Eber, named third among Joktan's thirteen sons in the Table of Nations (Gen 10:26) and in the parallel genealogy of 1 Chr 1:20. His brothers include Almodad, Sheleph, Jerah, Sheba, Ophir and Havilah. Nothing is recorded of his life beyond his place in these lists. His name is usually taken to mean "court of death" or "dwelling of death." Like several of Joktan's sons, he appears to represent both an ancestor and a people or region. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary link the name with Hadramaut, an ancient province and people of southern Arabia on the Indian Ocean coast east of modern Yemen. Smith's notes that the region was known in antiquity for trade with India and Africa.

Hebron was a member of the tribe of Judah, listed among the descendants of Caleb the brother of Jerahmeel in the genealogy of 1 Chr 2. His four sons were Korah, Tappuah, Rekem and Shema. The wording of 1 Chr 2:42 is difficult. It names Mesha as Caleb's firstborn and the father of Ziph, then speaks of "the sons of Mareshah the father of Hebron." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia and Tyndale House's STEPBible name list call Hebron a son of Mareshah. Another reading links him directly to Mesha, and this entry follows that one, treating Mesha as his father. Several names in this list, including Ziph, Mareshah, Hebron and Tappuah, are also towns in Judah, so the genealogy may partly describe the clans that settled them. He is a different person from others in the Bible named Hebron.

Helah was one of the two wives of Ashur, the "father of Tekoa," in the genealogy of the tribe of Judah. Her fellow wife was Naarah (1 Chr 4:5). Her sons are named as Zereth, Jezoar and Ethnan (1 Chr 4:7). This entry also counts Coz as her son. He is named in the next verse (1 Chr 4:8), directly after her sons, and is probably read as continuing her line, though the text does not say so outright. Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries give the meaning of her name as "rust." Nothing more is recorded about her beyond this genealogical mention.

Helek was a son of Gilead and a descendant of Manasseh, son of Joseph. He founded the Helekite family, one of the clans of Manasseh listed in the census taken on the plains of Moab (Num 26:30). His brothers were Abiezer (called Jeezer in Numbers), Asriel, Shechem, Hepher and Shemida. When the land was divided under Joshua, the children of Helek were among the Manassite families who received a share of territory, apparently west of the Jordan, set apart from the portion already given east of the river (Josh 17:2). Smith's Bible Dictionary calls him Gilead's second son, following the order of the Numbers list. His name means "portion" (Hitchcock's Bible Names). Nothing else is recorded about him.

Helem was one of the exiles who had come back from Babylon in the time of the prophet Zechariah. Zechariah was told to take silver and gold from him and from Tobijah and Jedaiah, have crowns made, and set one on the head of Joshua the high priest (Zech 6:10–11). The crowns were then to be kept in the temple of the LORD as a memorial to Helem, Tobijah, Jedaiah and Hen the son of Zephaniah (Zech 6:14). The same man appears as Heldai in Zech 6:10. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both take Helem and Heldai to be one person, and this entry follows that view. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the Septuagint reads Helem as an ordinary word rather than a name. The setting is usually dated to about 520 BC, an estimate drawn from context.

Hemdan was a Horite, listed first among the sons of Dishon, with his brothers Eshban, Ithran and Cheran (Gen 36:26). He appears in the genealogy of the Horite clans descended from Seir, which Genesis sets alongside the descendants of Esau in the land of Edom. In the parallel list at 1 Chr 1:41 the King James Version calls him Amram. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both explain this as a difference in the Hebrew spelling: the Chronicles name is properly read Hamran, which the Revised Version uses, and it refers to the same man as Hemdan. 1 Chr 1:41 also makes his father Dishon a son of Anah. Smith's Bible Dictionary takes the name Hemdan to mean "pleasant." Nothing more is recorded about him beyond these two genealogical entries.

Henadad was a Levite whose descendants formed a family of Levites in the community that returned from exile in Babylon. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "favour of Hadad." When the foundations of the second temple were laid, the sons of Henadad, with their sons and fellow Levites, joined Jeshua and Kadmiel in overseeing the workmen on the house of God (Ezra 3:9). In Nehemiah's time a Levite named Binnui, "of the sons of Henadad," was among those who set their seal to the covenant to keep God's law (Neh 10:9). Nehemiah 3:18 and 3:24 also name Bavai and Binnui, sons of Henadad, among those who repaired Jerusalem's wall. Henadad himself is known only through his descendants. It is not certain whether every mention refers to the same ancestor, though the references are usually taken together as one Levite family.

Henoch was a son of Midian and so a grandson of Abraham through Keturah, the wife Abraham took after Sarah's death. He is listed third among Midian's five sons, with his brothers Ephah, Epher, Abida and Eldaah, in the genealogy of Keturah's descendants (Gen 25:4; 1 Chr 1:33). Genesis spells his name Hanoch, while the King James text of 1 Chronicles has Henoch. In Hebrew it is the same name as Enoch, which Smith's Bible Dictionary glosses as "dedicated." Like his brothers, he was presumably regarded as an ancestor of a Midianite clan or tribe, though the text records nothing about him beyond his place in the family line. He should not be confused with Enoch the son of Cain, Enoch the father of Methuselah, or Hanoch the son of Reuben.

Hephzi-bah was the wife of King Hezekiah of Judah and the mother of his son and successor Manasseh. She is named only once, in the notice of Manasseh's accession, which says he became king in Jerusalem at twelve and reigned fifty-five years (2 Kgs 21:1). As the mother of a Judean king she belongs to the royal line that Matthew's genealogy of Jesus traces through Hezekiah and Manasseh, though she is not named there. Her name means "my delight is in her" (Hitchcock's Bible Names; International Standard Bible Encyclopedia). The same word appears in Isa 62:4 as the new name given to restored Jerusalem, in place of "Forsaken," because the LORD delights in her. There it is a symbolic name for the city, not a reference to the queen, as both Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treat the two uses separately.

Hezekiah is a man named in the lists of Jewish exiles who returned from Babylon to Judah, where "the children of Ater of Hezekiah" number ninety-eight (Ezra 2:16; Neh 7:21). The short phrase is read in different ways. It may mean that Ater's family was traced through, or belonged to, a branch called Hezekiah, or that Hezekiah was linked to Ater's line as his son. This entry follows the second reading and lists Ater as his father. The STEPBible proper-names index describes him as an ancestor of returning exiles, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia counts him among the returned exiles. Nothing else is recorded about him. He should not be confused with King Hezekiah of Judah or with others who share the name. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the name's meaning as "strength of the Lord."

Hezrai the Carmelite was one of David's mighty men, the elite warriors listed in 2 Sam 23:35. The parallel list in 1 Chr 11:37 gives his name as Hezro, and Smith's Bible Dictionary treats the two forms as the same man. "Carmelite" probably marks him as coming from Carmel, a town in the hill country of Judah near Maon, rather than from Mount Carmel in the north. This is an inference, since the passages do not say which Carmel is meant. Nothing more is recorded about him beyond his place in the list of David's warriors. The neighbouring name also differs between the two lists: Paarai the Arbite in Samuel and Naarai the son of Ezbai in Chronicles. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of his name as "an entry or vestibule."

Hilkiah was a priest among those who returned to Jerusalem from exile in Babylon. Nehemiah 12 lists him among "the chief of the priests and of their brethren in the days of Jeshua" the high priest (Neh 12:7). By inference from the opening of the chapter, he was part of the group that came back with Zerubbabel and Jeshua. In the next generation, under the high priest Joiakim, the priestly family named after Hilkiah was headed by Hashabiah (Neh 12:21), so his name continued as the name of a priestly house. Nothing else is recorded about him. He is different from several other men named Hilkiah, including the high priest in King Josiah's time. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "God is my portion."

Hillel was the father of Abdon, one of the judges of Israel, and is known only from his son's record in Judg 12:13 and 12:15. Both verses call him (or perhaps Abdon, since the Hebrew phrasing allows either reading) a Pirathonite, a native of Pirathon in the land of Ephraim, where Abdon was later buried. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia take the title as describing Hillel himself, and this entry follows that reading. Nothing else is recorded about his life. His name means "praising" or "he greatly praised," according to Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia. He should not be confused with the famous Jewish teacher Hillel of the first century BC, who does not appear in the Bible.

Hirah was a man from Adullam, a town in the lowlands of Judah, and a friend of Judah son of Jacob. When Judah left his brothers, he turned aside to stay with Hirah (Gen 38:1). It was in this region that Judah married the daughter of Shuah. Later, after his wife died, Judah went up to his sheepshearers at Timnath together with "his friend Hirah the Adullamite" (Gen 38:12). Further on in the same chapter (Gen 38:20), Judah sends his friend the Adullamite to deliver a young goat and recover the pledge he had left with the woman he had met on the way, who was in fact his daughter-in-law Tamar. Hirah cannot find her. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the Septuagint and the Vulgate call him Judah's "shepherd" rather than his friend. Nothing else is recorded about him.

Hobab was a Midianite relative of Moses by marriage. Moses invited him to travel with Israel to the land God had promised, saying Israel would treat him well (Num 10:29). In the verses that follow, Hobab at first declines, and Moses presses him to stay because he knows the wilderness camping places. Judg 4:11 names him as the ancestor of Heber the Kenite, which links him to the Kenites who settled among Israel. Num 10:29 calls him the son of Raguel (Reuel), and Moses' father-in-law. Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that he has often been identified with Jethro himself. It also notes that the Hebrew word in Judg 4:11 can mean any male relative by marriage, so it may mean brother-in-law there. This entry follows the view that Hobab was a son of Jethro (Reuel) and a brother of Zipporah, which made him Moses' brother-in-law. The name means "beloved."

Homam was a son of Lotan and a brother of Hori, listed among the Horites, the people of Seir, in the genealogies of Edom. He appears only in these lists. 1 Chr 1:39 spells his name Homam, while the parallel list in Gen 36:22 gives it as Hemam. Both verses add that Lotan's sister was Timna, so Timna was Homam's aunt. Lotan is named in the same chapter (Gen 36:20) as a son of Seir the Horite, which makes Homam a grandson of Seir. These Horite clans lived in the land of Seir alongside Esau's descendants, which is why they appear in the Edomite records. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "destruction" or "exterminating." Hitchcock's Bible Names renders it "making an uproar."

Hoshaiah was the father of Jezaniah, one of the leaders of the Judeans left in the land after the Babylonians destroyed Jerusalem. He is known only through his son. In Jer 42:1 Jezaniah son of Hoshaiah comes with Johanan son of Kareah and the army captains to ask Jeremiah for guidance. In Jer 43:2 it is Azariah son of Hoshaiah who joins Johanan in accusing Jeremiah of lying when the prophet warns them not to go to Egypt. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia, following the Septuagint, treats Jezaniah and Azariah as probably the same man, and this entry follows that view, making Hoshaiah the father of one son known by two names. The name means "the Lord helps" or "whom the Lord saves." Several people in the Bible share this name, and nothing more is recorded about this Hoshaiah.

Hotham was a man of the tribe of Asher, a son of Heber and a brother of Japhlet, Shomer (also spelled Shamer) and their sister Shua (1 Chr 7:32). Heber was a son of Beriah, Asher's son, so Hotham was Asher's great-grandson. This entry follows the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia and Easton's Bible Dictionary in identifying him with Helem, named in 1 Chr 7:35 as the brother of Shamer. There his sons are listed as Zophah, Imna, Shelesh and Amal. The difference between the two names is probably a variation in how the name was copied, though the identification is an inference from the flow of the genealogy. Smith's Bible Dictionary lists the two names in separate entries. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of Hotham as "a seal." Nothing else is recorded about him.

Hothir was a Levite, one of the fourteen sons of Heman, whom 1 Chr 25:4 lists thirteenth among his brothers. Heman is called "the king's seer" in the same chapter, and Smith's Bible Dictionary therefore counts Hothir as a Kohathite Levite. He belonged to the families that David set apart for music in the house of God, playing cymbals, psalteries and harps under their fathers' direction. When the musicians were divided by lot into twenty-four groups of twelve, the twenty-first lot fell to Hothir, "he, his sons, and his brethren" (1 Chr 25:28). Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of his name as "excelling" or "remaining," and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives "abundance." Nothing else is recorded about him.

Hul was the second of the four sons of Aram and a grandson of Shem, named in the Table of Nations alongside his brothers Uz, Gether and Mash (Gen 10:23). The parallel genealogy in 1 Chr 1:17 lists the same names directly after Shem's sons, with Mash appearing as Meshech. By comparison with Genesis, this is probably a shortened form of the list in which Aram's sons follow straight on. Nothing is recorded of Hul as an individual. As with others in the Table of Nations, his name likely also stands for a people descended from him. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia calls that people uncertain in identity and location, while Smith's Bible Dictionary favors the district near the foot of the Lebanon mountains. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "circle," and Hitchcock's Bible Names as "pain" or "infirmity."

Huldah was a prophetess who lived in Jerusalem during the reign of King Josiah. She was the wife of Shallum, keeper of the wardrobe, whose ancestry is given as son of Tikvah, son of Harhas in 2 Kgs 22:14, and as son of Tikvath, son of Hasrah in 2 Chr 34:22. The priest Hilkiah and other officials sent by the king, including Ahikam, Achbor, Shaphan and Asahiah, went to consult her. The surrounding chapters show that this was about the book of the law recently found in the temple. She lived in the part of the city the King James Version calls "the college". Easton's Bible Dictionary explains this as the Mishneh, or "second quarter", possibly a district between the inner and outer walls, though its exact location is unknown. Easton's gives the meaning of her name as "weasel". Smith's Bible Dictionary dates the consultation to about 623 BC.

Huppim was a son of Ir, named with his brother Shuppim in 1 Chr 7:12. Their sister Maachah married Machir, the son of Manasseh (1 Chr 7:15), so the family was linked by marriage to the tribe of Manasseh. The verse naming him sits at the end of a list of Benjamin's descendants, and Ir is probably the same as Iri, a grandson of Benjamin named a few verses earlier (1 Chr 7:7). A Huppim also appears among Benjamin's sons in Gen 46:21, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests the name is probably a variant of Hupham, whose family is listed in Num 26:39. The same encyclopedia notes that his exact line of descent is hard to establish, and the STEPBible name index places him either as a descendant of Ir or as a son of Machir. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning as "a chamber covered" or "the sea-shore."

Hur was one of five kings of Midian killed by the Israelites in the time of Moses, along with Evi, Rekem, Zur and Reba. Balaam son of Beor was killed in the same campaign (Num 31:8). The surrounding chapter presents this war as Israel's revenge on Midian for the events at Peor, and Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that Phinehas led the Israelite force. Joshua 13:21 lists the same five men as princes of Midian and as "dukes of Sihon," the Amorite king who ruled from Heshbon, so they were apparently local rulers subordinate to or allied with Sihon. They lived in the land later given to the tribe of Reuben. Several other men in the Bible are named Hur, including the companion of Moses and Aaron, and this Midianite ruler should not be confused with them. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the name's meaning as "liberty," "whiteness" or "hole."

Hurai was one of David's mighty men, the elite group of warriors listed in 1 Chr 11:32. He is described as being "of the brooks of Gaash," probably meaning the ravines or valleys near Mount Gaash in the hill country of Ephraim, where Joshua was later buried. The parallel list in 2 Sam 23:30 gives his name as Hiddai, and the two forms are generally taken to refer to the same man. The difference probably comes from a copying variation, since the Hebrew letters involved look alike. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia explain the name Hurai as meaning "linen-worker" or "linen-weaver." Nothing else is recorded about him beyond his place in these two lists.

Hushim was the son of Dan and the only son listed for him among the family members of Jacob who went down to Egypt (Gen 46:23). In the census of the tribes taken in the wilderness he is called Shuham, and his descendants, the Shuhamites, make up the whole of the tribe of Dan's listed families (Num 26:42). Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that the form Hushim is plural, as though it named a clan rather than a single person, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia likewise treats it as a family name. This entry follows the view that Hushim and Shuham are the same individual, the ancestor of the Danite clan. The name Hushim is also borne by other people in the Bible, including a Benjamite and a wife of Shaharaim, who should not be confused with this son of Dan.

Hushim was one of the two wives of Shaharaim, a man listed in the genealogy of the tribe of Benjamin. The other wife was Baara. According to 1 Chr 8:8, Shaharaim had children in the country of Moab after he had "sent them away." This is usually read to mean that he divorced or dismissed Hushim and Baara, which suggests that Hushim's children were born before that separation. By Shaharaim, Hushim had two sons, Abitub and Elpaal. The verses that follow (1 Chr 8:12–18) trace Elpaal's descendants, among them the builders of Ono and Lod. The name Hushim is shared by other people in the Bible, including a son of Dan (Gen 46:23) and a Benjamite listed in 1 Chr 7:12. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia explains the name as meaning "hasters."

Hymenaeus was a man named twice in Paul's letters to Timothy as someone who had turned away from the faith. In 1 Tim 1:20 he is grouped with Alexander among those who had "made shipwreck" of their faith, and Paul says he has "delivered" both "unto Satan, that they may learn not to blaspheme." In 2 Tim 2:17 he is paired with Philetus as a teacher whose words spread "as doth a canker." The next verse says they claimed that the resurrection had already happened and were overturning the faith of some. Most readers, including the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia, take both passages to refer to the same man. Because Timothy was working in Ephesus, that work places him there by inference. The name comes from Hymen, the Greek god of marriage, as Smith's Bible Dictionary notes.

Ibzan was a judge of Israel from Bethlehem who succeeded Jephthah, as the context of Judg 12:7 indicates, and was buried in his hometown when he died. Judg 12:9 adds that he had thirty sons and thirty daughters, arranged marriages for all of them with people from outside his clan or town, and judged Israel for seven years. His judgeship is placed at about 1146 BC, by inference from context. Easton's Bible Dictionary counts him as the tenth judge and gives his name the meaning "illustrious." Which Bethlehem was his home is uncertain. Smith's Bible Dictionary takes it to be Bethlehem of Zebulun, while the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the text does not say whether it was that town or Bethlehem of Judah. Jewish tradition in the Talmud identifies Ibzan with Boaz of Bethlehem in Judah. After Ibzan, Elon judged Israel (Judg 12:11).

Iddo was a priest named among those who returned from exile to Jerusalem with Zerubbabel and Jeshua, listed in Neh 12:4. His name later stood for a priestly family: in the next generation, in the days of the high priest Joiakim, that family was headed by Zechariah (Neh 12:16). The STEPBible proper names index likewise treats him as a returning priest whose name passed to a priestly house. Because Ezra and Zechariah call the prophet Zechariah a descendant of 'Iddo', many readers identify this family head with the prophet, though the text here does not say so. Several other men in the Bible share the name Iddo, so the exact links between them are uncertain. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives the meaning of the name as 'decked' or 'adorned'.

Ilai was an Ahohite and one of David's mighty men, the elite warriors listed in 1 Chr 11:29. In the parallel list at 2 Sam 23:28 the same man appears as Zalmon the Ahohite, so Ilai and Zalmon are taken as two names for one person. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both make this identification. "Ahohite" probably marks him as a descendant of Ahoah, a Benjamite family. The same label is given to other warriors in David's lists. Beyond his place in these rosters, nothing more is recorded about him.

Immer was the ancestor of a priestly family that lived in Jerusalem after the return from the Babylonian exile. He appears in two parallel genealogies of the priests who settled there. 1 Chr 9:12 traces Maasiai back through Meshillemith to Immer, and Neh 11:13 traces Amashai back through Meshillemoth, probably a variant spelling of the same son's name. Smith's Bible Dictionary treats him as the founder of an important priestly family, and links it with the sixteenth course of temple service assigned to Immer in 1 Chr 24:14. Because several people in the Bible bear this name, it is uncertain whether these references all point to one man or to different members of the same family line. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the name's meaning as "saying" or "speaking," and Smith's gives "talkative."

Ira the Ithrite was one of David's mighty warriors, listed among the Thirty in 2 Sam 23:38 and in the parallel list in 1 Chr 11:40. In both lists he appears next to Gareb, another Ithrite. The Ithrites were probably a family or clan from Kiriath-jearim (1 Chr 2:53). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the Hebrew could instead be read "Jattirite," meaning a man from the town of Jattir in Judah. It also suggests he may be the same person as Ira the Jairite, David's chief minister, though this is uncertain. Several men in the Bible share the name Ira, and this entry treats the warrior as a separate person. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "watchman."

Iram was one of the chiefs (the King James Version says "dukes") of Edom, the people descended from Esau. He is the last name in the list of Edomite chiefs in Gen 36:43, which says these chiefs are named "according to their habitations in the land of their possession." This suggests that Iram may be the name of a clan or district as well as a person. The parallel list in 1 Chr 1:54 repeats the name. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes him as chief of an Edomite tribe in Mount Seir, and Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "belonging to a city." Nothing more is recorded about him, and Smith's notes that no further identification has been found.

Irijah was a captain of the guard at the Benjamin Gate of Jerusalem in the last years of the kingdom of Judah. He was the son of Shelemiah and grandson of Hananiah. When the prophet Jeremiah tried to leave the city through that gate, Irijah arrested him and accused him of deserting to the Chaldeans (the Babylonians). Jeremiah denied it, but Irijah would not listen and took him to the princes (Jer 37:13–14). The surrounding verses add that Jeremiah was leaving for the land of Benjamin while the Babylonian siege was briefly lifted, and that the princes then beat him and imprisoned him. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates the incident to about 589 BC. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives the name's meaning as "Yah sees," while Hitchcock's Bible Names renders it "the fear of the Lord."

Ishbak was a son of Abraham and Keturah, and the fifth of their six sons. His brothers were Zimran, Jokshan, Medan, Midian and Shuah, and Isaac and Ishmael were his half-brothers. His name appears only in the two lists of Keturah's sons (Gen 25:2; 1 Chr 1:32), and nothing else is recorded about him. 1 Chr 1:32 calls Keturah Abraham's concubine. By inference from the surrounding chapter, Ishbak was among the sons Abraham sent away eastward with gifts, away from Isaac (Gen 25:6). Smith's Bible Dictionary regards him as the ancestor of a tribe in northern Arabia. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that these names probably stand for tribes, though the tribe of Ishbak has not been identified with certainty. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "leaving."

Ishmael was one of the six sons of Azel, a Benjamite in the family line of King Saul. He appears only in two matching genealogies, 1 Chr 8:38 and 1 Chr 9:44, where his brothers are named as Azrikam, Bocheru, Sheariah, Obadiah and Hanan. The surrounding lists trace this line from Saul through his son Jonathan and then Merib-baal (Mephibosheth), so Ishmael was a distant descendant of Saul, as Smith's Bible Dictionary notes. Nothing else is recorded about him. His name, usually understood to mean "God hears," was shared by several other people in the Bible, including Abraham's son by Hagar, and he should not be confused with them.

Isshiah was a Levite named as a son of Uzziel in the lists of Levite families from King David's time. In 1 Chr 23:20 the King James Version spells his name Jesiah and calls him the second son, after his brother Michah. 1 Chr 24:25 calls him Isshiah, again Michah's brother, and names his son Zechariah as head of a family among the Levites. Smith's Bible Dictionary identifies this Uzziel as the son of Kohath, making Isshiah a Kohathite. Exod 6:22 names Mishael, Elzaphan and Zithri as sons of Kohath's son Uzziel, which is why they are counted as his brothers here. Because these lists come many generations after Kohath, "son of Uzziel" in Chronicles probably means a descendant of Uzziel's family line rather than a literal son. Nothing more is recorded about him.

Isuah, also spelled Ishuah (and Ishvah in some references), was the second son of Asher and a grandson of Jacob. He appears in two genealogical lists of Asher's children, alongside his brothers Imnah (Jimnah), Isui (Ishuai) and Beriah and their sister Serah (Gen 46:17; 1 Chr 7:30). Genesis places him among the family members who went down to Egypt with Jacob. Nothing else is recorded about him. The clan list of Asher in Num 26:44 names Jimnah, Jesui and Beriah but not Isuah, which may mean that no clan descended from him, though the text does not say so. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "quiet."

Ithran was a Horite, one of the sons of Dishon, listed among the descendants of Seir the Horite, the early inhabitants of the land of Edom. His brothers were Hemdan, Eshban and Cheran (Gen 36:26). The parallel list in 1 Chr 1:41 gives the same names, except that Hemdan appears as Amram, and it makes Dishon the son of Anah. Genesis also has an earlier Dishon who was a son of Seir, so it is not entirely certain which Dishon was Ithran's father. Nothing further is recorded about him. Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests he was probably the head of a Horite clan, by inference from the list of Horite chiefs in the same chapter. The name is usually taken to mean "excellent" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia). A different Ithran, from the tribe of Asher, appears elsewhere in Chronicles.

Ithream was the sixth son of David, born to him by his wife Eglah while David reigned at Hebron (2 Sam 3:5; 1 Chr 3:3). Both lists of David's Hebron-born sons place him last, after Amnon, the son called Daniel or Chileab, Absalom, Adonijah and Shephatiah, each of whom had a different mother. Solomon and David's other sons born later in Jerusalem were his half-brothers. As a son of David, he belonged to the tribe of Judah. Nothing else is recorded about his life, and Eglah appears only as his mother. Reference works explain his name differently: the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives "residue of the people," Smith's Bible Dictionary "abundance of people," and Hitchcock's Bible Names "excellence of the people."

Ittai, also called Ithai, was the son of Ribai, from Gibeah in the territory of Benjamin, and one of David's mighty warriors. He appears in the list of David's thirty heroes in 2 Sam 23:29, and again in the parallel list in 1 Chr 11:31, where his name is spelled Ithai. Nothing else is recorded about him beyond his name, his father, his home town and his place among David's elite fighters. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary both identify him as a Benjamite among David's thirty. Several people in the Bible share the name. This Ittai should be distinguished from Ittai the Gittite, the Philistine from Gath who stayed loyal to David during Absalom's revolt.

Izri was a Levite musician, one of the six sons of Jeduthun, who served in the worship organized under King David. In 1 Chr 25:3 he is called Zeri and is listed among the sons who prophesied with the harp under their father's direction, giving thanks and praise to the LORD. When the musicians were divided by lot into twenty-four groups of twelve, the fourth lot fell to Izri, together with his sons and relatives (1 Chr 25:11). Reference works such as the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treat Izri and Zeri as two spellings of the same man's name, and this entry follows that view. His role suggests he served in the reign of David, by inference from the surrounding chapter.

Jaala, also spelled Jaalah, was the ancestor of a family that returned from exile in Babylon to Judah with Zerubbabel, probably around 538–536 BC by inference from context. He is known only as a name in the parallel lists of returnees in Ezra 2:56 and Neh 7:58, where his descendants appear beside those of Darkon and Giddel. The surrounding passage places these families among the descendants of "Solomon's servants," a group counted together with the temple servants (the Nethinim). Smith's Bible Dictionary accordingly calls them descendants of Solomon's slaves, while Easton's Bible Dictionary groups Jaala with the Nethinim. Nothing more is recorded about him or his family. Easton's and Smith's dictionaries give the meaning of the name as "wild she-goat."

Jaaziah was a Levite of the clan of Merari, named only in the list of Levite families in 1 Chr 24:26–27. That list is part of the arrangement of Levites in King David's time. It names Mahli and Mushi as Merari's sons and then gives a line "of Jaaziah," whose sons were Beno, Shoham, Zaccur and Ibri. This entry treats Jaaziah as a third son of Merari alongside Mahli and Mushi. Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that he may instead have been a later descendant. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia describes the Hebrew text here as difficult and mentions a reading in the Greek Septuagint that some connect with the name Uzziah. The meaning of the name is given variously as "comforted by the Lord" (Easton's Bible Dictionary) or "the Lord strengthens" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia).

Jaaziel was a Levite of the second rank whom the Levite leaders appointed, at David's command, as one of the musicians when the ark was brought up to Jerusalem (1 Chr 15:18). He is listed among a group of brethren who also served as gatekeepers. In the same passage he appears as Aziel, which Smith's Bible Dictionary takes as a shortened form of the same name. Aziel is named among the Levites who played psalteries (harps) "on Alamoth," a musical term of uncertain meaning (1 Chr 15:20). Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "comforted by God." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia renders it "God strengthens." That encyclopedia also notes that some scholars, following the Septuagint, read the name as Uzziel. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates these events to about 1014 BC.

Jabez was a man named in the genealogies of Judah, described as more honorable than his brothers. His mother gave him his name because she bore him in sorrow. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia explains this as wordplay: the Hebrew name sounds like a word meaning "he causes pain," and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives its meaning as "sorrow" or "trouble." Jabez prayed to the God of Israel, asking to be blessed, to have his territory enlarged, to have God's hand with him, and to be kept from harm so that it would not grieve him. The same play on sorrow appears in the prayer itself. The text records that God granted his request. His exact place in Judah's family line is not stated, but Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that the passage sits within a genealogy connected with Bethlehem.

Jachin was a priest, or a priestly family, listed among those living in Jerusalem after the return from the Babylonian exile. He appears beside Jedaiah and Jehoiarib (Joiarib) in the parallel lists of 1 Chr 9:10 and Neh 11:10. In Nehemiah the list names those who settled in Jerusalem when part of the returning population was chosen by lot to live in the city. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia connect the name with Jachin, head of the twenty-first course of priests in David's time (1 Chr 24:17). On that view, the name here probably refers to the priestly family descended from that head rather than to a single man. The name probably means "he will establish." Several other men in the Bible share the name.

Jacob was the son of Matthan and the father of Joseph, the husband of Mary, in Matthew's genealogy of Jesus (Matt 1:15–16). He appears only in that list, which traces the royal line from David through Solomon, so he belonged to the tribe of Judah. Nothing else is recorded about his life. He is a different man from the patriarch Jacob, son of Isaac, whose name Hitchcock's Bible Names explains as meaning "that supplants" or "the heel." Luke's genealogy names Joseph's father as Heli (Luke 3:23), and the two lists differ for several generations. Some explain this by taking Luke's line as Mary's ancestry, others by a levirate marriage or an adoption that gave Joseph both a natural and a legal father. This entry follows Matthew's account, in which Jacob is Joseph's father.

Jada was a man of the tribe of Judah named only in the genealogy of 1 Chronicles 2. He was a son of Onam and a brother of Shammai (1 Chr 2:28). He had two sons, Jether and Jonathan, and the text notes that Jether died without children (1 Chr 2:32). Onam is described in the surrounding verses as a son of Jerahmeel by his wife Atarah, so Jada belonged to the Jerahmeelite line of Judah. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes this and calls him a grandson of Jerahmeel. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of his name as "knowing." Nothing else is recorded about him.

Jaddua was a priest of the tribe of Levi in the line of high priests that descended from Eliashib, Nehemiah's contemporary. In Neh 12:11 he is called the son of Jonathan. Neh 12:22 lists the succession as Eliashib, Joiada, Johanan and Jaddua, so Jonathan and Johanan are probably the same man. That verse also says the heads of priestly and Levitical families were recorded up to the reign of "Darius the Persian." Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary call Jaddua the last high priest named in the Old Testament. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identifies this Darius as Darius III, the last Persian king, who was defeated by Alexander the Great. It also links Jaddua with Josephus's account of Alexander entering Jerusalem. His name means "known." Other people in the Bible share the name.

Jahath was a Levite of the Gershonite line, named as the first of four sons of Shimei in the list of Levite families drawn up in David's last years (1 Chr 23:10). His brothers were Zina (called Zizah in the next verse, probably the same person), Jeush and Beriah. Jahath is called the chief, or head, of these families, with Zizah second. Because Jeush and Beriah had few sons, their descendants were counted together as a single father's house (1 Chr 23:11). Easton's Bible Dictionary calls him a grandson of Gershom (Gershon), and Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him as head of a later house within the family of Gershom. Nothing further is recorded about him. The name Jahath belongs to several other men in the Bible, mostly Levites, and he should not be confused with them.

Jahaziel was a Levite, the third of the four sons of Hebron, with Jeriah, Amariah and Jekameam as his brothers. Hebron belonged to the Kohathite branch of the tribe of Levi, so Smith's Bible Dictionary describes Jahaziel as a Kohathite. He is named only in two lists from the time of David: one dividing the Levites into their family groups for service at the house of the Lord (1 Chr 23:19), and a repeated list of Levitical families (1 Chr 24:23). By inference from that setting, he headed one of the Hebronite family lines in David's reign. Nothing else is recorded about him. The name, often explained as "God sees," belongs to several different men in the Bible, and this Jahaziel should not be confused with them.

Jahleel was the third of the three sons of Zebulun, and so a grandson of Jacob and Leah. His brothers were Sered and Elon. He is named among Jacob's descendants who went down to Egypt (Gen 46:14). In the census taken in the plains of Moab he appears as the ancestor of the Jahleelites, one of the three family groups of the tribe of Zebulun (Num 26:26). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that "son" in these lists may refer to a clan as much as to an individual. Nothing else is recorded about him. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "hoping in Jehovah," and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "waiting for, or beseeching, or hope in, God."

Jair was the father of Elhanan, a warrior in David's time who killed a brother of Goliath the Gittite during a later war with the Philistines. The incident is recorded twice. 2 Sam 21:19 places the battle at Gob, calls Elhanan a Bethlehemite, and names his father Jaare-oregim. The parallel account in 1 Chr 20:5 names the father Jair and gives the slain giant's name as Lahmi. Both passages describe the giant's spear shaft as being like a weaver's beam. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia explains the longer form as a copying slip: "oregim" means "weavers" and also appears at the end of the same verse in Hebrew, so it was probably repeated by mistake. This entry treats Jaare-oregim and Jair as one man. Nothing else is recorded about him. He is distinct from the other men named Jair in the Bible.

Jair was a man from Gilead, east of the Jordan, who judged Israel for twenty-two years after Tola (Judg 10:3). His judgeship is dated here to about 1192 BC, an estimate inferred from context. The next verse, Judg 10:4, adds that he had thirty sons who rode thirty donkeys and held thirty towns in Gilead known as Havoth-jair. He died and was buried in Camon (Judg 10:5), a place whose location is uncertain but was probably in Gilead. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the name's meaning as "my light" or "who diffuses light." Several other men in the Bible share the name, including a descendant of Manasseh who captured towns in Gilead and the father of Mordecai. This entry concerns the judge.

Jairus was a ruler of a synagogue in Galilee who came to Jesus, fell at his feet and begged him to come to his house (Mark 5:22; Luke 8:41). The surrounding accounts in Mark 5 and Luke 8 tell why. His only daughter, about twelve years old, was dying. On the way to the house Jesus healed a woman who had suffered from bleeding, and meanwhile word came that the girl had died. Jesus went in with Peter, James, John and the girl's parents, raised her to life, and told them to give her something to eat. Matthew 9 tells the same story without naming the father. The town is not named in these verses. Easton's Bible Dictionary places the synagogue at Capernaum, while Smith's Bible Dictionary says only that it was probably in a town near the western shore of the Sea of Galilee.

Japhlet was a man of the tribe of Asher, named in the Asherite genealogy in 1 Chronicles. He was a son of Heber, and his brothers were Shomer (also spelled Shamer) and Hotham, with a sister named Shua (1 Chr 7:32). His own sons were Pasach, Bimhal and Ashvath (1 Chr 7:33). The surrounding verses (1 Chr 7:30–31) make Heber a son of Beriah and grandson of Asher, so Japhlet was a great-grandson of Asher. Smith's Bible Dictionary explains his name as meaning "whom God delivers," while the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia tentatively gives "he escapes." Nothing else is recorded about him.

Jarah was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, a descendant of King Saul, named in the genealogy of Saul's family as the son of Ahaz and the father of Alemeth, Azmaveth and Zimri. Through Zimri his line continued to Moza and later generations. The surrounding verses (1 Chr 9:39–41; 8:33–35) trace his ancestry back through Ahaz, Micah and Merib-baal (Mephibosheth) to Jonathan, Saul's son. The same genealogy appears twice. In 1 Chr 8:36 he is called Jehoadah, and in 1 Chr 9:42 Jarah. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the Greek Septuagint and some Hebrew manuscripts read Jadah in the second passage. It suggests this is probably the original form, a shortened equivalent of Jehoadah. His name may mean "honeycomb." Nothing else is recorded about him.

Jarha was an Egyptian servant of Sheshan, a member of the Jerahmeelite clan of the tribe of Judah. Sheshan had daughters but no sons, so he gave one of his daughters to Jarha as his wife, and she bore him a son, Attai (1 Chr 2:34–35). The daughter is not named in these verses. This entry identifies her as Ahlai, by inference from 1 Chr 2:31, where Ahlai is listed as Sheshan's child even though Sheshan had no sons. The genealogy that follows in 1 Chronicles 2 traces a long line of descendants through Attai. For this reason the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia describes Jarha as the founder of a house within the Jerahmeelites. Smith's Bible Dictionary places him around the time of Eli, but the text itself gives no date. The meaning of his name is unknown.

Jasher is the name in the title of "the book of Jasher," a lost writing quoted twice in the Old Testament. The name means "upright," and early translations render the title "the Book of the Upright One" or "the Book of Just Ones," so it may describe the book's subject rather than name an author. Nothing else is known of any person called Jasher, and whether one existed is uncertain. The book is cited as the source of the account of the sun standing still during Joshua's battle against the Amorites (Josh 10:13). It is also cited as the source of David's lament over Saul and Jonathan, known as the Song of the Bow (2 Sam 1:18). Easton's Bible Dictionary suggests it was probably a national collection of songs praising Israel's heroes. Smith's Bible Dictionary adds that it was probably written in verse and is wholly lost.

Jashobeam was one of David's leading warriors. He is named first among David's mighty men and called a Hachmonite and "the chief of the captains" (some translations read "chief of the three"). He is said to have used his spear against three hundred men, killing them at one time (1 Chr 11:11). The parallel list in 2 Sam 23:8 names this hero Josheb-basshebeth the Tachmonite and gives the number as eight hundred. A Jashobeam son of Zabdiel commanded the first of David's twelve monthly army divisions, with 24,000 men (1 Chr 27:2). This entry treats him as the same man as the chief warrior, as Easton's Bible Dictionary does. Because the name was shared by several people, the identification is not certain. A Korhite Jashobeam who joined David at Ziklag (1 Chr 12:6) may also be the same person, though the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that opinions differ.

Jeaterai was a Levite of the Gershonite branch, the son of Zerah, named at the end of a line of descent from Gershom in 1 Chr 6:21. He is generally identified with Ethni, son of Zerah, who appears in the ancestry of Asaph the singer in 1 Chr 6:41. There Ethni's son is Malchiah (1 Chr 6:40). The two lists differ in places: Zerah's father is Iddo in one and Adaiah in the other. Smith's Bible Dictionary treats the two names in separate entries. The Tyndale House proper-names index identifies them as one man, and this entry follows that view. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of Jeaterai as "searching out." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives Ethni as "gift." Nothing else is recorded about him.

Jebusite is listed in the Table of Nations as a son, or descendant, of Canaan, the son of Ham. He appears alongside the Amorite, the Girgasite and other Canaanite groups (Gen 10:16; 1 Chr 1:14). The name works both as an individual ancestor and as the people who claimed descent from him. Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies them as the original inhabitants of Jebus, the city later known as Jerusalem, and notes that they appear often among the nations of Canaan the Israelites were to dispossess. According to the same dictionary, their king Adonizedek was defeated by Joshua (Josh 10:1, 23). The Jebusites held Jebus until David captured it and made it his capital. David later bought from Araunah the Jebusite the site where the temple was afterwards built (2 Sam 24:16–25; 1 Chr 21:24–25).

Jecoliah, also spelled Jecholiah, was a woman of Jerusalem who was the mother of King Uzziah of Judah. Both accounts of Uzziah's reign name her when they record that he became king at sixteen and reigned fifty-two years in Jerusalem (2 Kgs 15:2; 2 Chr 26:3). In 2 Kings her son is mostly called Azariah. She was the wife of King Amaziah, Uzziah's father and predecessor. Her name probably means "the Lord is able" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia) or "strong through the Lord" (Smith's Bible Dictionary). Nothing else is recorded about her. She belongs to the royal line traced in Matthew's genealogy of Jesus, where her son appears as Ozias or Uzziah (Matt 1:8–9).

Jedaiah was one of the chief priests who returned from exile to Jerusalem with Zerubbabel and Jeshua. In Neh 12:7 he is the last name in a list of priestly leaders described as "the chief of the priests and of their brethren in the days of Jeshua." The same list already has a Jedaiah in the previous verse, so the text appears to name two different priests with this name, and this entry covers the second. A later list of priestly family heads in the time of the high priest Joiakim (Neh 12:12) names two Jedaiah families. In this one, Nethaneel led the family descended from this Jedaiah (Neh 12:21), while Uzzi led the other. Little else is known about him.
