Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the name's meaning as "the hand of the Lord" or "confessing the Lord."

Jedaiah was one of the exiles who had come back from Babylon in the time of the prophet Zechariah. He is named with Heldai and Tobijah as the people from whom Zechariah was told to take silver and gold on the same day. He was also to go to the house of Josiah son of Zephaniah (Zech 6:10). From this metal crowns were made and set on the head of Joshua the high priest. The crowns were then kept in the temple of the LORD as a memorial to Helem (probably the same man as Heldai), Tobijah, Jedaiah and Hen son of Zephaniah (Zech 6:14). Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him as a priest in the days of Jeshua the high priest, though the passage itself does not give his office. The name is shared by several other men in the Bible, including priests listed in Chronicles, Ezra and Nehemiah.

Jeduthun was a Levite, the father of Galal, known only as an ancestor in the lists of Levites who settled in Jerusalem after the return from the Babylonian exile. Through Galal his descendants included Obadiah son of Shemaiah (1 Chr 9:16), who is called Abda son of Shammua in the parallel list (Neh 11:17). That list places this family among the Levites connected with the temple's thanksgiving and prayer. Several men in the Bible share the name, so it is uncertain whether this Jeduthun is the same as the musician David appointed to lead worship. Because his descendants appear among the temple singers, that identification is quite possible, but this entry treats him separately. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "his law" or "giving praise."

Jehoaddan was the mother of Amaziah, king of Judah, and the wife of King Joash (also called Jehoash). She came from Jerusalem. She is known only from the notices that open Amaziah's reign, which say he became king at twenty-five and reigned twenty-nine years in Jerusalem (2 Kgs 14:2; 2 Chr 25:1). Naming the king's mother is a regular feature of these accounts of Judah's kings. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the written Hebrew text of 2 Kgs 14:2 spells her name Jehoaddin, the form used in the Revised Version. The meaning of the name is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives "Jehovah his ornament," and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "pleasure, or time, of the Lord." As mother of a king in David's royal line, she belongs to the line that Matthew's genealogy of Jesus follows, although Matthew's list does not name Amaziah.

Jehoshabeath, also called Jehosheba (2 Kgs 11:2), was a daughter of King Jehoram of Judah and sister of King Ahaziah. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives the meaning of her name as "Yahweh is an oath." She was married to Jehoiada the priest, and Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that she is the only recorded case of a royal princess marrying a high priest. When Athaliah had the king's sons killed after Ahaziah's death, Jehoshabeath took Ahaziah's young son Joash and hid him and his nurse in a bedchamber, saving his life. The following verse, 2 Kgs 11:3, says he stayed hidden in the temple for six years. Smith's and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggest she may have been Jehoram's daughter by a wife other than Athaliah. This entry follows the view that Athaliah was her mother.

Jehoshaphat was the son of Nimshi and the father of Jehu, who became king of Israel. He is named only in the account of Jehu's anointing and revolt, where Jehu is twice identified as "the son of Jehoshaphat the son of Nimshi": once when Elisha sends a young prophet to find and anoint him at Ramoth-gilead (2 Kgs 9:2), and again when Jehu conspires against King Joram (2 Kgs 9:14). Nothing else is recorded about his life. Elsewhere, in 1 Kgs 19:16 and 2 Kgs 9:20, Jehu is called simply "son of Nimshi". As the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes, Jehoshaphat's name is left out there, so Nimshi, Jehu's grandfather, stands as the better-known family name. His name means "the Lord judges." He should not be confused with Jehoshaphat king of Judah or others who share the name.

Jehozabad was one of two royal servants who conspired against King Joash (Jehoash) of Judah and killed him. Joash was buried in the city of David, and his son Amaziah became king (2 Kgs 12:21). His fellow conspirator was Jozachar, also called Zabad, the son of Shimeath. Kings calls Jehozabad the son of Shomer, while Chronicles calls him the son of Shimrith, a Moabite woman (2 Chr 24:26). Smith's Bible Dictionary treats Shomer and Shimrith as the same name. The surrounding passage in 2 Chronicles says the conspiracy came in revenge for Joash's killing of the son of Jehoiada the priest, and 2 Kgs 14:5 records that Amaziah later executed the servants who had killed his father. The name means "Yahweh has bestowed" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia). Several other people in the Bible share this name.

Jekameam was a Levite, the fourth son of Hebron, listed after his brothers Jeriah, Amariah and Jahaziel. He appears only in the Levite genealogies of 1 Chronicles, which set out the families of Levi in the setting of David's organization of the Levites for temple service (1 Chr 23:19; 1 Chr 24:23). The same chapter names Hebron as a son of Kohath, so Jekameam probably belonged to the Kohathite branch of the tribe. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia describes him as the head of a Levitical house and explains his name as probably meaning "may the kinsman establish." Nothing else is recorded about him.

Jerah was a son of Joktan, a descendant of Shem through Eber, named in the Table of Nations (Gen 10:26) and in the parallel genealogy in 1 Chr 1:20. He is listed fourth among Joktan's thirteen sons, after Almodad, Sheleph and Hazarmaveth. His brothers included Sheba, Ophir and Havilah. Nothing is recorded of his life. The name means "moon" or "month" in Hebrew. Like his brothers, he is probably meant as the ancestor of a people or tribe, and Smith's Bible Dictionary places that tribe in southern Arabia. No district called Jerah has been identified. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes places named Yurakh in Yemen and Yarach in the Hijaz, along with several Arabian place-names built on the word for "moon." It adds that moon worship in southern Arabia made such names common, so no single location can be fixed.

Jeremoth, also spelled Jerimoth, was a Levite listed as one of the three sons of Mushi, alongside his brothers Mahli and Eder (1 Chr 23:23). Mushi was a son of Merari, so Jeremoth belonged to the Merarite branch of the tribe of Levi, as Smith's Bible Dictionary and Easton's Bible Dictionary note. He appears only in the genealogies of 1 Chronicles, in the lists of Levite families arranged for service in the time of David. The second list gives his name as Jerimoth and counts the brothers among "the sons of the Levites after the house of their fathers" (1 Chr 24:30). Nothing further is recorded about him. Several other people in the Bible share the name Jeremoth or Jerimoth, and this Levite should not be confused with them. The name is commonly explained as meaning "heights" or "eminences."

Jeriah was a Levite, the firstborn of the four sons of Hebron, followed by Amariah, Jahaziel and Jekameam. He appears in the lists of Levitical families drawn up when David organized the Levites for service (1 Chr 23:19; 1 Chr 24:23). Through Hebron, a son of Kohath, he belonged to the Kohathite branch of the tribe of Levi, and as firstborn he probably headed the Hebronite house. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both identify him with Jerijah, named in 1 Chr 26:31 as chief of the Hebronites, a man whose kin were found in Jazer of Gilead in David's fortieth year. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives the meaning of his name as "founded of Yahweh," while Hitchcock's Bible Names renders it "fear, or throwing down, of the Lord."

Jerimoth, also spelled Jeremoth, was a Levite and one of the fourteen sons of Heman listed among the musicians David organized for service at the sanctuary (1 Chr 25:4). The surrounding chapter describes Heman's sons as leading worship with cymbals, harps and lyres under their father's direction. When the musicians were divided by lot into twenty-four groups of twelve, the fifteenth lot fell to Jeremoth, who served together with his sons and relatives (1 Chr 25:22). The two spellings almost certainly refer to the same man, since both appear in the same list of Heman's sons. Smith's Bible Dictionary places his service in David's reign, about 1014 BC, a date inferred from context. Several other men in the Bible share this name, and this entry concerns only Heman's son.

Jeroham was a priest, known only as an ancestor of Adaiah, one of the priests who lived in Jerusalem after the return from exile. Nehemiah 11:12 names him as the son of Pelaliah and traces his line back through Amzi, Zechariah and Pashur to Malchiah. Adaiah appears there among the 822 priests who did the work of the temple. 1 Chronicles 9:12 gives a shorter version of the same line, calling Jeroham the son of Pashur. This is probably the same person, with the intervening generations left out, and Easton's Bible Dictionary also suggests the two passages refer to one man. This entry treats them as the same. Several other men in the Bible share the name, which the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia takes to mean "may he be compassionate."

Jerushah was the wife of King Uzziah of Judah and the mother of his son and successor, King Jotham. She is named only in the brief notices that open Jotham's reign, which record that he became king at twenty-five and reigned sixteen years in Jerusalem (2 Kgs 15:33; 2 Chr 27:1). 2 Kings spells her name Jerusha. Both passages call her the daughter of Zadok. Nothing more is said about this Zadok, and it is uncertain whether he is connected to any other man of that name. Easton's Bible Dictionary explains her name as meaning "possessed," that is, by a husband. Because Jotham appears as Joatham in the line of descent given in Matt 1:9, Jerushah is, by inference, an ancestor in the genealogy of Jesus, though she is not named there.

Jeshaiah was a Levite of the line of Moses, the son of Rehabiah and the father of Joram. In 1 Chr 24:21 he appears as Isshiah, the first of Rehabiah's sons. In 1 Chr 26:25 he is part of a line running from Eliezer through Rehabiah, Jeshaiah, Joram and Zichri to Shelomith. The surrounding passage (1 Chr 26:26) names Shelomith as the man over the treasuries of dedicated things. The wider chapter (1 Chr 23:15–17) shows that this Eliezer was a son of Moses, so Easton's Bible Dictionary calls Jeshaiah a Kohathite Levite. Smith's Bible Dictionary places the lists in the reign of David, though Jeshaiah himself may have lived earlier as an ancestor in the line. Several other men in the Bible share this name.

Jeshaiah was a Levite, one of the sons of Jeduthun, the musician who led his sons in prophesying with the harp to give thanks and praise to the LORD (1 Chr 25:3). His name means "salvation of the LORD" or "deliverance of Yah," according to Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia. When the temple singers were divided by lot into twenty-four courses in David's time, the eighth lot fell to Jeshaiah, whose group of sons and relatives numbered twelve (1 Chr 25:15). The list in 1 Chr 25:3 counts six sons of Jeduthun but names only five. Shimei, who is counted among the brothers here, probably supplies the missing name, since he appears in the later list of lots (1 Chr 25:17). Izri is likely the same person as Zeri (1 Chr 25:11). Several other men in the Bible bear the name Jeshaiah.

Jesharelah was a Levite musician, one of the sons of Asaph, who led the seventh of the twenty-four divisions of temple musicians organized under King David. In 1 Chr 25:2 he is called Asarelah and is listed with his brothers Zaccur, Joseph and Nethaniah. All of them served under their father's direction and "prophesied according to the order of the king," which the surrounding chapter connects with music on harps, lyres and cymbals. When the duties were assigned by lot, the seventh lot fell to Jesharelah, and his group, made up of his sons and relatives, numbered twelve (1 Chr 25:14). Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary give the meaning of the name as "upright toward God." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests the name may stand for a family of musicians as well as an individual.

Jeshua was the ancestor of one branch of the family of Pahath-moab, alongside a second branch descended from Joab. He is mentioned only in the lists of exiles who returned from Babylon to Judah. Ezra 2:6 counts 2,812 descendants of Pahath-moab through Jeshua and Joab, while the parallel list in Neh 7:11 gives 2,818. Here Jeshua and Joab are treated as sons of Pahath-moab, although the lists could also mean more distant descendants. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes the Pahath-moab clan as probably one of the chief families of Judah. Jeshua is another form of the name Joshua. Several other people in the Bible share the name, including the high priest of the return, and they should be kept distinct from this ancestral figure.

Jether was a man of the tribe of Asher, listed in the genealogy of 1 Chronicles 7 as the father of Jephunneh, Pispah and Ara. He is probably the same person as Ithran, named in the preceding verse among the sons of Zophah alongside Bezer, Hod, Shamma, Shilshah and Beera. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both make this identification, and this entry follows it. The two names are closely related in Hebrew: Jether is usually explained as meaning "abundance" or "excellence" and Ithran as "excellent." The Asher genealogy describes these families as heads of their fathers' houses and as valiant warriors (1 Chr 7:40), so Smith's Bible Dictionary calls Jether the chief of a family of warriors. Nothing else is recorded about him. Several other men in the Bible share the name Jether.

Jetheth was one of the chiefs (the King James Version says "dukes") of Edom who descended from Esau. He appears in the list of Edomite chiefs named "according to their families, after their places" (Gen 36:40), which is repeated in 1 Chr 1:51 after the death of King Hadad. Because the list ties each chief to a family and a place, the name may stand for a clan or district as well as an individual. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests the name may be a variant of Jether or Ithran, a Horite name in Gen 36:26. The meaning of the name is uncertain. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "a nail", Easton's Bible Dictionary "a peg, or a prince", and Hitchcock's Bible Names "giving". Nothing else is recorded about him.

Jetur was one of the twelve sons of Ishmael, Abraham's son by Hagar. He appears only in the lists of Ishmael's sons, between Tema and Naphish (Gen 25:15; 1 Chr 1:31). Nothing is told of his life. His brothers included Nebajoth, Kedar, Adbeel, Dumah and Tema, and his sister Bashemath became a wife of Esau. Like several of Ishmael's sons, Jetur's name also stands for a tribe descended from him. In 1 Chr 5:19 the tribes of Reuben and Gad and the half-tribe of Manasseh fight against the Hagrites and Jetur. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia and Smith's Bible Dictionary link this people with the Itureans of New Testament times, whose region, Ituraea, is named in Luke 3:1. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "an enclosure." Hitchcock's Bible Names offers "order" or "mountainous."

Jeush was a Levite, one of the four sons of Shimei listed in David's organization of the Levites (1 Chr 23:10). Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia place this Shimei among the Gershonites, which fits the surrounding passage. Jeush's brothers were Jahath, the chief, and Zizah (called Zina in 1 Chr 23:10), along with Beriah. Because Jeush and Beriah did not have many sons, the two were counted together as a single father's house in the Levitical reckoning (1 Chr 23:11). The context sets this in David's reign, and Smith's Bible Dictionary dates it to about 1014 BC. The name is probably understood as "he protects" or "he comes to help" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia). Several other men in the Bible share the name Jeush, so this one should be kept distinct from them.

Joab was a descendant of Pahath-moab whose family returned from exile in Babylon to Judah. In the lists of returning exiles, the line of Pahath-moab is counted through two branches, Jeshua and Joab. Together these branches numbered 2,812 according to Ezra 2:6 and 2,818 according to the parallel list in Neh 7:11. Joab's name therefore probably stands for a clan or ancestral house rather than an individual who made the journey himself. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats this Joab as a family of returned exiles. Ezra 8:9 later mentions a group called the sons of Joab, which may be the same family or a related one. This Joab is not the same person as Joab the commander of David's army. Several people in the Bible share the name, which means "the Lord is father."

Joanna was the wife of Chuza, the steward of Herod, probably Herod Antipas, tetrarch of Galilee, as Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary take it. Luke names her among a group of women, including Mary Magdalene and Susanna, who traveled with Jesus during his second tour of Galilee (about AD 28, by inference from context) and supported him and his disciples from their own means (Luke 8:3). The preceding verse says these women had been healed of evil spirits and illnesses. Joanna appears again after the crucifixion. She was with Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James, and other women who reported to the apostles what they had found at the empty tomb (Luke 24:10). Smith's Bible Dictionary takes both passages to refer to the same woman. The name Joanna is borne by more than one person in the Bible, but only these two verses refer to this Joanna.

Joash was a man called "the king's son" in the account of King Ahab's final campaign against Ramoth-gilead. When the prophet Micaiah foretold disaster, the king of Israel ordered him taken back to Amon, the governor of the city, and to Joash, to be held in custody (1 Kgs 22:26; 2 Chr 18:25). This entry follows the common view, found in Easton's Bible Dictionary, that he was a son of Ahab, which would make him a brother of Ahaziah and Joram, both later kings of Israel, and of Athaliah. Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests he was a younger son who held some subordinate authority while his father was alive. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that "the king's son" may also be a title for a royal officer, as it seems to be in Jeremiah. Several other people in the Bible share the name Joash.

Jobab (son of Joktan) is the last of the thirteen sons of Joktan named in the Table of Nations, listed after his brothers Ophir and Havilah (Gen 10:29; 1 Chr 1:23). Through Joktan, son of Eber, he belonged to the line of Shem. Nothing is recorded of him beyond his name and place in the genealogy. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes him as the founder of an Arabian tribe, which fits the setting of Joktan's descendants, who settled in the east (Gen 10:30). The name's meaning is uncertain. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "a desert," the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests "howling," and Hitchcock's Bible Names offers "sorrowful, hated." He should not be confused with the other men named Jobab in the Bible, such as the early king of Edom.

Jochebed was a daughter of Levi, born to him in Egypt, and the wife of Amram. She was the mother of Aaron, Moses and their sister Miriam (Num 26:59). Exod 6:20 calls her Amram's father's sister. Since Exod 6:18 names Amram as a son of Kohath, she was Kohath's sister and Amram's aunt, as Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary note. Her brothers were Gershon, Kohath and Merari, the heads of the main Levite clans. Her name is usually explained as "the LORD is glory" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia). She is probably the unnamed Levite woman of Exod 2:1–10 who hid her infant son for three months and then placed him in a basket among the reeds of the Nile. Moses' birth is dated here to about 1571 BC, by inference from context.

Joel was a Levite in the time of David who led the clan descended from Gershom, one of Levi's sons. He is called its chief, at the head of 130 of his kinsmen (1 Chr 15:7). When David prepared to bring the ark of the covenant to Jerusalem, he summoned the priests Zadok and Abiathar together with Joel and the other Levite leaders, Uriel, Asaiah, Shemaiah, Eliel and Amminadab (1 Chr 15:11). From the surrounding chapter, these men were charged with consecrating themselves and carrying the ark. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests he is probably the same Joel named among the Gershonite leaders in 1 Chr 23:8 and 26:22, though this is not certain. Several other men in the Bible share the name Joel.

Joel was a Levite of the Gershonite clan, descended from Laadan, who served in the time of King David. He appears in the lists of Levites drawn up when David organized their duties, in the setting of 1 Chr 23:1–6. With his brother Zetham he was in charge of the treasures of the house of the LORD (1 Chr 26:22). The two passages present the family differently. In 1 Chr 23:8, Jehiel, Zetham and Joel are listed together as three sons of Laadan. In 1 Chr 26:22, Zetham and Joel are called sons of Jehieli, meaning Jehiel. This entry follows the second passage and treats Joel as Jehiel's son and Zetham's brother. Smith's Bible Dictionary takes both verses to describe the same man and places him about 1014 BC. Several other men in the Bible are also named Joel.

Joel, the son of Pethuel, was a prophet to whom "the word of the LORD" came, and the book of Joel bears his name (Joel 1:1). Easton's Bible Dictionary counts him as the second of the twelve minor prophets and notes that nothing is known of his life beyond his book. The Tyndale House proper-names list describes him as a prophet of Judah whose message combined judgment and hope. His date is uncertain. This entry places his prophecies about 820 BC, an estimate inferred from context, though the book itself gives no date. In the New Testament, Peter quoted him on the day of Pentecost, saying the events in Jerusalem were "that which was spoken by the prophet Joel" (Acts 2:16). The name, popularly taken to mean "the LORD is God," is shared by several other men in the Bible.

Johanan was a member of the tribe of Levi in the high-priestly line descended from Aaron. He appears only in the genealogy of 1 Chr 6, as the son of Azariah and the father of another Azariah (1 Chr 6:9–10). Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that his grandfather Ahimaaz was the son of Zadok, the priest of David's time. The genealogy adds that Johanan's son Azariah was the one who served as priest in the temple Solomon built in Jerusalem. Nothing else is recorded about Johanan himself. His name means "Yahweh has been gracious" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia). It was shared by several other people in the Bible, so he should be kept distinct from other men called Johanan. In the Hebrew Bible these verses are numbered 1 Chr 5:35–36.

Jonathan was one of David's mighty men, the elite group of warriors listed in 2 Sam 23 and 1 Chr 11. 1 Chr 11:34 calls him "Jonathan the son of Shage the Hararite," and this entry follows that naming of his father. In the parallel list at 2 Sam 23:32–33 his name is followed directly by "Shammah the Hararite." Some readers, including the STEPBible proper-names index, take this to mean he was the son of Shammah, possibly the same Shammah son of Agee the Hararite praised earlier in that chapter. "Hararite" probably refers to a place or clan whose location is uncertain. Nothing is recorded about his deeds beyond his place on the list. His name means "Yahweh has given" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia). He is distinct from Jonathan the son of Saul and from several other men of the same name.

Jonathan was a man of the tribe of Judah, listed in the genealogy of Jerahmeel's descendants in 1 Chronicles. He was a son of Jada, the brother of Shammai, and his brother Jether died without children (1 Chr 2:32). Jonathan's sons were Peleth and Zaza, and the passage closes by counting these among "the sons of Jerahmeel" (1 Chr 2:33). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia therefore calls him a Jerahmeelite. Because Jether left no heirs, this branch of Jada's family probably continued only through Jonathan, by inference from the passage. His name means "the LORD has given" (Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "given of God"). Nothing else is recorded about him, and he should not be confused with the several other men named Jonathan in the Bible, such as Saul's son.

Jonathan was a scribe in Jerusalem during the final years of the kingdom of Judah, in the reign of Zedekiah. His house had been turned into a prison, and the princes who were angry with Jeremiah beat the prophet and confined him there (Jer 37:15). Jeremiah later begged King Zedekiah not to send him back to Jonathan's house, fearing he would die there (Jer 37:20). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia also connects him with Jer 38:26, where Jeremiah repeats this plea. The name means "Yahweh has given." Nothing more is recorded about him, and he is distinct from the several other men named Jonathan in the Bible, including Saul's son.

Joram was the son of Toi (spelled Tou in Chronicles), king of Hamath. When David defeated Hadadezer king of Zobah, who had been at war with Toi, Toi sent Joram to David to greet him and congratulate him on the victory. Joram brought gifts of silver, gold and bronze vessels (2 Sam 8:10). The parallel account in 1 Chr 18:10 calls him Hadoram. The name Joram means "the LORD is exalted". Hadoram contains the name of the god Hadad instead, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that many commentators prefer the form Hadoram in 2 Samuel as well. Several other people in the Bible are also named Joram, including kings of Israel and Judah. This Joram is a different person, a prince of Hamath.

Joseph (son of Asaph) was a Levite, one of the four sons of the musician Asaph. With his brothers Zaccur, Nethaniah and Asarelah (called Jesharelah in 1 Chr 25:14), he served under his father's direction among those who "prophesied" in the temple worship, by inference with music, as the surrounding chapter describes, according to the king's arrangement (1 Chr 25:2). That king is David, which places Joseph in David's reign. When the temple musicians were divided by lot into twenty-four courses, the first lot fell to Joseph, making him head of the first division (1 Chr 25:9). Easton's Bible Dictionary describes him in these terms. Unlike the leaders of the following courses, the verse does not state the number of his group. Nothing else is recorded about him. His name is commonly explained as meaning "increase" or "addition."

Joshbekashah was a Levite, one of the fourteen sons of Heman listed among the musicians organized for temple service in David's time (1 Chr 25:4). When the musicians' duties were assigned by lot, the seventeenth lot fell to him, and he served with his sons and relatives in a group of twelve (1 Chr 25:24). Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "a seat in a hard place" and calls him head of the seventeenth course of musicians. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that some commentators read the last eight or nine names in the list of Heman's sons, including this one, as the words of a prayer or poetic lines rather than personal names. This entry treats Joshbekashah as a person, as the lot assignment in 1 Chr 25:24 does.

Joshua was a man of Beth-shemesh, called "the Bethshemite," who owned the field where the cart carrying the ark of the LORD stopped after the Philistines sent it back to Israel. The cart halted beside a great stone in his field. The people there split up the wood of the cart and offered the cows that had drawn it as a burnt offering to the LORD (1 Sam 6:14). The ark was set on that stone, called the great stone of Abel, which the writer says was still standing in Joshua's field "unto this day" (1 Sam 6:18). Nothing else is recorded about him, and he is distinct from the better-known Joshua son of Nun and others who share the name. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "saviour" or "whose help is Jehovah."

Jucal, also called Jehucal, was the son of Shelemiah and an official at the court of Zedekiah, the last king of Judah. King Zedekiah sent him with Zephaniah the son of Maaseiah the priest to ask the prophet Jeremiah to pray to the Lord for them (Jer 37:3). Easton's Bible Dictionary places this during the final Babylonian siege of Jerusalem under Nebuchadnezzar. Later Jucal was one of four officials, with Shephatiah, Gedaliah son of Pashur, and Pashur son of Malchiah, who heard Jeremiah tell the people what was coming (Jer 38:1). The verses that follow say these officials urged the king to put Jeremiah to death, and the prophet was then lowered into a cistern. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia takes both forms of the name to mean probably "Yahweh is able."

Judah was a man named in the lists of Nehemiah 12. One of several people in the Bible with this name, which means "praised," he appears in Neh 12:8 among the Levites who returned from exile with Zerubbabel, alongside Jeshua, Binnui, Kadmiel, Sherebiah and Mattaniah, who led the thanksgiving songs. A Judah is also named in Neh 12:34 among those who walked in the first procession at the dedication of Jerusalem's rebuilt wall. This entry treats both mentions as one person. Tyndale House's STEPBible Proper Names describes him as a Levite who helped lead the thanksgiving choir at the dedication. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia lists the two as separate men, treating the Judah of Neh 12:34 as one of the leaders of Judah. The verses give no further details about him.

Julius was a Roman centurion of "Augustus' band," usually understood as the Augustan cohort. Paul and some other prisoners were placed in his charge when it was decided they should sail to Italy. By inference from the preceding chapters, the voyage began at Caesarea, where Paul had been held. The next day, at Sidon, Julius treated Paul kindly and let him go ashore to visit friends and be cared for. Later in the same chapter, the centurion (presumably still Julius) at first trusted the ship's master over Paul's warning (Acts 27:11). During the shipwreck he stopped the soldiers from killing the prisoners because he wanted to save Paul (Acts 27:43). Easton's Bible Dictionary describes him as showing Paul friendly regard in many ways. This entry dates the journey to about AD 56–57, by inference from context. Smith's Bible Dictionary places it around AD 60.

Kedemah was the last-named of the twelve sons of Ishmael, the son of Abraham and Hagar. He appears only in the two genealogies of Ishmael's descendants (Gen 25:15; 1 Chr 1:31), alongside brothers such as Nebajoth, Kedar, Dumah, Tema and Jetur. Smith's Bible Dictionary takes him to be the youngest. Nothing else is recorded about his life. The surrounding passage in Genesis presents Ishmael's twelve sons as princes of tribes living in the regions east of Egypt toward Assyria, so Kedemah was probably regarded as the founder of a tribal group of the northern Arabian desert. His name is usually understood to mean "eastward" or "toward the east" (Easton's Bible Dictionary). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia links it with the Hebrew word for "the East." A sister, Bashemath, who later married Esau, is also counted among Ishmael's children.

Kelita was a Levite in Jerusalem in the time of Ezra and Nehemiah. When Ezra read the law to the assembled people, Kelita was one of the Levites who helped them understand what was read while they stood in their places (Neh 8:7). His name appears again among the Levites who set their seal to the covenant made under Nehemiah (Neh 10:10). The surrounding context shows that this list belongs to the Levites. Ezra 10:23 mentions "Kelaiah (the same is Kelita)" among the Levites who had married foreign wives. Smith's Bible Dictionary treats him as the same man and says he returned with Ezra. The meaning of the name is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives "dwarf" and Smith's gives "assembly."

Kenaz was one of the chiefs ("dukes" in the King James Version) of Edom, the people descended from Esau. He is named in the closing list of Edomite chiefs in Gen 36:42, repeated in 1 Chr 1:53. The surrounding passage presents these chiefs by their families and places, so the name may stand for a clan or district as well as a person. Smith's Bible Dictionary identifies him with Kenaz the son of Eliphaz, Esau's son, who appears earlier in the same chapter among the chiefs descended from Eliphaz. This entry follows that identification, though it is not certain that the two lists name the same man. The name is shared by several people in the Bible, including the father of Othniel and a grandson of Caleb. Smith's gives its meaning as "hunting," while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "this purchase" or "this lamentation."

Keros was the ancestor of a family of temple servants, the Nethinim, whose descendants returned from exile in Babylon to Judah with Zerubbabel. The family appears in the list of returning exiles in Ezra 2:44 and in its parallel in Neh 7:47, placed between the families of Ziha and Siaha (spelled Sia in Nehemiah) and Padon. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both class him among the Nethinim, a group assigned to serve at the temple. The context of the lists supports this, since the surrounding names belong to that section. Nothing is recorded about Keros himself beyond his name and his descendants. The meaning of the name is uncertain. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "curved", Hitchcock's Bible Names "crooked", and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia tentatively suggests "fortress."

Kishi was a Levite of the clan of Merari, the son of Abdi and the father of Ethan, one of the chief singers whom David's Levites appointed to lead music at the house of the Lord. He appears only in genealogies of Ethan. In 1 Chr 6:44 his line is traced back through Abdi and Malluch to Merari, and Ethan stands on the left hand of the singers. In 1 Chr 15:17 the same man is called Kushaiah, a name the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia renders "bow of Yah." Ethan is widely identified with Jeduthun, another leading musician of David's time, and this entry follows that identification. Nothing more is recorded about Kishi himself.

Kittim was a son of Javan and grandson of Japheth, listed with his brothers Elishah, Tarshish and Dodanim in the Table of Nations (Gen 10:4; 1 Chr 1:7). No personal details are given. As with the other names in this list, Kittim stands both for an individual ancestor and for the people descended from him. Elsewhere the Bible uses the name for a coastal or island people of the Mediterranean, such as the "isles of Chittim" in Jer 2:10 and Ezek 27:6. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that Josephus linked the name to Kition, an ancient city on Cyprus. On that basis the name is often associated with Cyprus in a narrower sense, and more broadly with the islands and coastlands of the western Mediterranean. Smith's Bible Dictionary points out that the King James Version spells the name Kittim in these two verses and Chittim elsewhere.

Koz was the ancestor of a priestly family whose descendants returned from the Babylonian exile with Zerubbabel. He is named alongside Habaiah and Barzillai in the parallel lists of Ezra 2:61 and Neh 7:63. The verses that follow in both lists (Ezra 2:62; Neh 7:64) say these families searched for their genealogical records but could not find them, so they were barred from serving as priests until their status could be settled. STEPBible Proper Names (Tyndale House) gives the name as Hakkoz, reflecting the Hebrew form with the article. Some connect this family with Hakkoz, head of the seventh priestly division in 1 Chr 24:10, and with Meremoth son of Uriah son of Koz, who later served in the temple (Ezra 8:33; Neh 3:4), but these links are uncertain. Several people in the Bible share this name.

Koz was the father of Urijah and the grandfather of Meremoth, who repaired two sections of Jerusalem's wall under Nehemiah. One section lay beside the stretch repaired by Meshullam, and the other ran from the door of the high priest Eliashib's house to its far end. Koz is known only through this family line. Smith's Bible Dictionary treats Koz as the same name as Hakkoz, and the STEPBible name index describes Hakkoz as a priestly name. On that view Koz may be the ancestor of a priestly family rather than Meremoth's literal grandfather. The Hakkoz family appears in Ezra 2:61 among priests who could not prove their descent, and Ezra 8:33 calls Meremoth son of Uriah a priest. Because similar names belong to several people, it is uncertain how closely these passages connect.

Laish was the father of Phalti, also called Phaltiel. He appears only as the father of the man to whom Saul gave his daughter Michal, David's wife, after David fled from Saul's court (1 Sam 25:44). Later, Saul's son Ishbosheth took Michal back from Phaltiel and returned her to David (2 Sam 3:15). The family is described as being "of Gallim," a town that 1 Sam 25:44 connects with Phalti. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identifies Laish as a Benjamite, which fits Gallim's probable location in the territory of Benjamin, north of Jerusalem. According to Smith's Bible Dictionary and Hitchcock's Bible Names, the name means "lion." He should not be confused with the city of Laish in the far north, which the tribe of Dan captured and renamed Dan. Nothing else is recorded about him.

Lebanah was the ancestor of a family of temple servants (the Nethinim) who returned from exile in Babylon to Judah with Zerubbabel. He is known only from the lists of returning exiles. In Ezra 2:45 his descendants appear between other temple-servant families, alongside those of Hagabah and Akkub. The parallel list in Neh 7:48 spells the name Lebana and places it with Hagaba and Shalmai. Nothing else is recorded about him, and the name probably refers to the founder or head of the family group rather than to someone who made the journey himself. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "white."

Lehabim is named in the Table of Nations as a son, or descendant people, of Mizraim, the son of Ham whose name is the Hebrew word for Egypt (Gen 10:13; 1 Chr 1:11). The plural ending suggests a people group rather than a single individual, and the same list gives his siblings as Ludim, Anamim, Naphtuhim, Pathrusim, Casluhim and Caphthorim. Neither passage says anything more about him. Smith's Bible Dictionary identifies the Lehabim with the Lebu (or Rebu) of Egyptian inscriptions, an early people living west of Egypt in North Africa, from whom Libya took its name. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia similarly connects them with the Lubim mentioned elsewhere in the Bible, and suggests that one name may be a variant of the other. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "flames".

Lemuel was a king whose words open the last chapter of Proverbs. Prov 31:1 calls them a prophecy, or oracle, that his mother taught him. In her advice she addresses him by name and warns that kings and princes should not drink wine or strong drink (Prov 31:4). The ISBE notes that the following acrostic poem on the capable wife (31:10–31) may come from the same source. Nothing else is known of him for certain. Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries record that rabbinic commentators identified him with Solomon. Smith's adds that others take him for the chief of an Arab tribe, possibly a brother of Agur (Prov 30:1). The ISBE mentions a proposal to read the word translated "prophecy" as a place name, making him "king of Massa" after Ishmael's son Massa (Gen 25:14). The name is usually explained as "dedicated to God."

Lo-ruhamah was the daughter of the prophet Hosea and his wife Gomer, born after her brother Jezreel and before her brother Lo-ammi. Her name means "not pitied" or "no mercy." God told Hosea to give her this name as a sign that he would no longer show mercy to the house of Israel but would take them away (Hos 1:6). After Gomer weaned her, she gave birth to Lo-ammi (Hos 1:8). Smith's Bible Dictionary describes the name as pointing to the ruin of the northern kingdom of Israel. Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that later in the book the name is reversed, when God says he will have mercy on her who had not obtained mercy (Hos 2:23). Nothing else is recorded about her life.

Lucius was a Christian named twice in the New Testament. Lucius of Cyrene was one of the prophets and teachers in the church at Antioch, alongside Barnabas, Simeon called Niger, Manaen and Saul, when that church sent Barnabas and Saul out on their first missionary journey, about AD 45 by inference from context (Acts 13:1). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests he was probably one of the men of Cyprus and Cyrene who first preached to Greeks at Antioch (Acts 11:20). Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that his name is Latin, while his home town suggests he was a Jew from Cyrene in North Africa. A Lucius also sends greetings in Paul's letter to the Romans, where Paul calls him one of his kinsmen (Rom 16:21). Whether this is the same man is uncertain. Easton's treats them as one person, and Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that some hold this view.

Lud was a son of Shem, and so a grandson of Noah. He is named fourth among Shem's sons in the genealogies of Gen 10:22 and 1 Chr 1:17. His brothers were Elam, Asshur, Arphaxad and Aram. Nothing is recorded about his life. He appears only in these lists, which trace peoples back to Noah's descendants. Easton's Bible Dictionary, Smith's Bible Dictionary and the Tyndale House proper-names index all connect him with the Lydians, a people of western Asia Minor in what is now western Turkey, and present him as their probable ancestor. He is a different figure from the Ludim, whom Gen 10:13 lists among the descendants of Mizraim (Egypt). Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "strife."

Ludim is named as the first of the sons of Mizraim, the son of Ham whose name is the Hebrew word for Egypt, in the table of nations (Gen 10:13; 1 Chr 1:11). His brothers were Anamim, Lehabim, Naphtuhim, Pathrusim, Casluhim and Caphthorim. The name has a plural ending, as do the other names in this list, so it probably refers to a people descended from Mizraim rather than to a single individual. Easton's Bible Dictionary takes the Ludim to be probably the same as the people called Lud, who appear alongside African nations as fighters in the Egyptian army in Jer 46:9. Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests they lived west of Egypt, perhaps farther than any other people descended from Mizraim. Nothing else is recorded about him.

Maacah (also spelled Maachah) was one of King David's wives and the mother of Absalom, David's third son. She was the daughter of Talmai, king of Geshur, a small kingdom probably lying east of the Sea of Galilee. Both lists of David's sons name her, placing Absalom among the sons born to David at Hebron (2 Sam 3:3; 1 Chr 3:2). Easton's Bible Dictionary describes Geshur as belonging to the old native population of the region, and the marriage probably formed a political alliance between David and Talmai. Later passages connect this family tie to Absalom's story: after killing his half-brother Amnon, Absalom fled to his grandfather Talmai in Geshur (2 Sam 13:37–38). His sister Tamar (2 Sam 13:1) was probably also Maacah's daughter, though the text does not name her mother. Nothing more is recorded about Maacah herself.

Maachah (wife of Machir) was the wife of Machir, a son of Manasseh, and the mother of Peresh and Sheresh (1 Chr 7:15–16). She is named only in this genealogy of the tribe of Manasseh. She is described as the sister of Huppim and Shuppim. An earlier verse, 1 Chr 7:12, calls Huppim and Shuppim "the children of Ir" in a Benjamite list, so this entry gives Ir as her father, by inference from that passage. The Hebrew of 1 Chr 7:15 is difficult, and its wording about who is whose sister is unclear. This entry follows the plain statement of 1 Chr 7:16, which calls Maachah the wife of Machir. She named her son Peresh. His brother Sheresh had sons named Ulam and Rakem. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of her name as "pressed down" or "worn."

Maachah was the wife of Jehiel, the "father of Gibeon," meaning probably its founder or leading settler, in the genealogy of Saul's family in 1 Chronicles (1 Chr 8:29; 9:35). The name is shared by several people in the Bible. The surrounding verses name her sons as Abdon, Zur, Kish, Baal, Ner, Nadab, Gedor, Ahio, Zacher and Mikloth. Her husband appears here as Abiel. By inference, Jehiel is the same man as Abiel, since 1 Sam 9:1 and 14:51 call Kish and Ner sons of Abiel. The STEPBible proper names index identifies her as the mother of Kish, the father of King Saul. However, 1 Chr 9:39 makes Ner the father of Kish and grandfather of Saul, so her son Kish may instead have been Saul's great-uncle. The genealogies leave this uncertain. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of her name as "pressed down."

Maachah, also called Maoch, was the father of Achish, king of the Philistine city of Gath. He is known only through his son. As Maoch, he is named when David and his six hundred men went over to Achish to escape Saul (1 Sam 27:2). As Maachah, he is named when two of Shimei's servants ran away to Achish early in Solomon's reign (1 Kgs 2:39). The two accounts are several decades apart, so some readers take the two kings named Achish to be different men, perhaps grandfather and grandson. This entry follows Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia, which treat Maoch and Maachah as one person, the father of a single Achish. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "oppression." Several other people in the Bible share the name Maachah.

Maaseiah was a Levite of the second rank whom David appointed when the ark was brought up to Jerusalem from the house of Obed-edom. He is listed with his fellow Levites among the gatekeepers ("porters") in 1 Chr 15:18. In 1 Chr 15:20 he is named again among the musicians assigned to play psalteries (harps or lyres) "on Alamoth," probably a musical term for a high register. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes him as a porter for the ark, while Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia emphasise his role as a musician. The two verses together suggest he served in both capacities. His name means "the work of the Lord." Several other men in the Bible bear the same name, and nothing further is recorded about this one.

Maaseiah was the father of Neriah and so the grandfather of two brothers who appear in the book of Jeremiah. One was Baruch, to whom Jeremiah handed the deed of the field he bought at Anathoth (Jer 32:12). The other was Seraiah, who went with King Zedekiah to Babylon in the fourth year of his reign and carried Jeremiah's message against Babylon (Jer 51:59). Nothing else is recorded about Maaseiah himself. The name, meaning "work of the Lord" according to Hitchcock's Bible Names, belongs to several men in the Bible. The Hebrew spelling in these verses is Mahseiah, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia and STEPBible use that form for him. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him as a priest, which the two verses here do not state.

Maasiai was a priest of the family of Immer who lived in Jerusalem after the return from exile in Babylon. He appears in the list of priests in 1 Chr 9:12, where he is called the son of Adiel, and descends through Jahzerah, Meshullam and Meshillemith from Immer. Nehemiah 11:13 names a priest Amashai, son of Azareel, son of Ahasai, son of Meshillemoth, son of Immer, in its list of Jerusalem's residents in Nehemiah's time. Smith's Bible Dictionary takes the two as apparently the same man, and this entry follows that view. The two lists name different fathers and intermediate ancestors, though both reach back to Immer. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives his name the meaning "work of the Lord."

Madai was one of the seven sons of Japheth, the son of Noah, and a brother of Gomer, Magog, Javan, Tubal, Meshech and Tiras. He appears only in the genealogies of the nations in Gen 10:2 and its repetition in 1 Chr 1:5, and no personal details are recorded. His name is the same Hebrew word used elsewhere in the Bible for the Medes, and he is generally regarded as their ancestor. Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that Mada is the name by which the Medes appear on Assyrian monuments. Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests the list may be naming peoples rather than individual sons, so that the entry means the Medes were counted among Japheth's descendants. The Medes lived in the region south and southwest of the Caspian Sea, in what is now northwestern Iran.

Magdiel was one of the chiefs, called "dukes" in the King James Version, of Edom, the people descended from Esau. His name appears near the end of the list of Edomite chiefs given "according to their habitations" in Gen 36:43, and again in the parallel list in 1 Chr 1:54, both times paired with Iram. Because the chiefs are listed by where they lived, the name may stand for a clan or district as well as a person. Nothing more is recorded about him. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "prince of God," while Hitchcock's Bible Names renders it "declaring God" or "chosen fruit of God."

Mahath, also called Ahimoth, was a Levite of the clan of Kohath who appears only in the genealogies of 1 Chronicles 6. In 1 Chr 6:35 he is the son of Amasai and the father of Elkanah, in the line that runs back from Heman the singer, appointed in David's time, through Samuel's ancestors to Kohath. The parallel list in 1 Chr 6:25 gives the name as Ahimoth and names him with Amasai as sons of an earlier Elkanah. That makes the two brothers there rather than father and son. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats the two names as probably the same person, and this entry follows that view. The name Mahath is shared by others, including a Levite in Hezekiah's reign mentioned in 2 Chronicles. Whether that man is connected to this one is uncertain. The ancestor is otherwise known only by name.

Mahazioth was a Levite, one of the fourteen sons of Heman listed in 1 Chr 25:4. Heman was one of the chief musicians appointed in David's time, and his sons served in the music of the house of the Lord. When the musicians were divided by lot into twenty-four courses, the twenty-third fell to Mahazioth, who served with his sons and relatives, twelve in all (1 Chr 25:30). Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary identify Heman's family as Kohathite. Easton's gives the meaning of the name as "visions." Nothing more is recorded about him.

Maher-shalal-hash-baz was a son of the prophet Isaiah and his wife, called "the prophetess" (Isa 8:3). His name means roughly "swift is the spoil, speedy is the prey." Before his birth, the LORD told Isaiah to write the name in large letters on a scroll or tablet (Isa 8:1). When the child was born, Isaiah was told to give him that name. The verses that follow (Isa 8:4) explain it as a sign. Before the boy could say "my father" or "my mother," the king of Assyria would carry off the wealth of Damascus and Samaria. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both read the name as a symbol of the coming Assyrian attack on Syria and Israel, the kingdoms of Rezin and Pekah. He was the brother of Shear-jashub, Isaiah's other son, whose name was also symbolic (Isa 7:3).

Malcham was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, a son of Shaharaim by his wife Hodesh. He appears only in the Benjamite genealogy of 1 Chr 8:9, where he is listed with his brothers Jobab, Zibia and Mesha. The next verse adds Jeuz, Shachia and Mirma as further sons of Shaharaim. The surrounding passage says Shaharaim had these sons in the country of Moab after sending away his wives Hushim and Baara, whose sons, including Abitub and Elpaal, were Malcham's half-brothers. Nothing else is recorded about him. The same Hebrew form occurs in Zeph 1:5, but there it is not this man. Easton's Bible Dictionary takes it as the national idol of the Ammonites, by whom some in Judah swore. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "their king."

Malchijah, also spelled Malchiah, was a priest named only as an ancestor in the genealogy of Adaiah, one of the priests who lived in Jerusalem after the return from exile. He was the father of Pashur, and through him an ancestor of Adaiah son of Jeroham (1 Chr 9:12). The parallel list in Nehemiah traces the same line in more detail, naming Pashur's descendants Zechariah, Amzi and Pelaliah before Jeroham, and places Adaiah among the priests who did the work of the temple (Neh 11:12). Several men in the Bible bear this name, so his identity with any other Malchijah is uncertain. He may be connected with the Malchijah whose family headed the fifth priestly division (1 Chr 24:9), and his son may be the Pashur son of Melchiah mentioned in Jer 21:1, but the text does not say so directly.

Mallothi was a Levite, one of the fourteen sons of Heman, the singer whom David appointed with Asaph and Jeduthun to lead music in the house of the Lord (1 Chr 25:4). Heman belonged to the Kohathite clan of Levi, so Mallothi was a Kohathite. When the musicians were organized into twenty-four rotating divisions by lot, the nineteenth lot fell to Mallothi, and he headed a group of twelve made up of himself, his sons and his relatives (1 Chr 25:26). He is mentioned nowhere else. His name is usually taken to mean "my fullness" (Easton's Bible Dictionary), though the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia renders it "my discourse." The fact list here gives his brother as Shubael, while 1 Chr 25:4 has Shebuel; these are generally understood as variant spellings of the same name.

The man of great stature was an unnamed Philistine warrior who fought against Israel in a battle at Gath during David's reign. He stood out for his size and for having six fingers on each hand and six toes on each foot, twenty-four in all (2 Sam 21:20; 1 Chr 20:6). Both accounts say he was born to "the giant" in Gath. The phrase may mean a direct son or more broadly a descendant of a race of giants. This entry treats him as a son, and therefore as a brother of the other giants named in these passages: Goliath, Ishbi-benob, Lahmi and Sippai. The verses that follow in both accounts (2 Sam 21:21; 1 Chr 20:7) say he taunted Israel and was killed by Jonathan, son of David's brother Shimea. His own name is never given.

Manahath was a son of Shobal and a descendant of Seir the Horite, listed among the early inhabitants of Mount Seir (Gen 36:23; 1 Chr 1:40). His brothers were Alvan, Ebal, Shepho and Onam. In 1 Chronicles some of the brothers' names are spelled differently (Alian for Alvan, Shephi for Shepho). Shobal himself appears in Genesis 36 as one of the sons of Seir and a Horite chief. Nothing more is recorded about Manahath beyond his place in these genealogies. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia regards him as the ancestor who gave his name to one of the ancient clans of Mount Seir that was later conquered and absorbed into Edom. He should be kept distinct from the place called Manahath mentioned elsewhere in 1 Chronicles.

Mash was the fourth son of Aram and a grandson of Shem, listed among the descendants of Noah in the Table of Nations (Gen 10:23). The parallel genealogy in 1 Chr 1:17 gives the name as Meshech and places Aram's sons directly after the sons of Shem, without repeating Aram's name before them. His brothers were Uz, Hul and Gether. Nothing more is recorded about him. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the Greek Septuagint reads Mosoch in both passages, but it treats Mash as the original form, since Meshech is otherwise the name of a son of Japheth. The name probably also stands for a tribe descended from him. Smith's Bible Dictionary and Easton's Bible Dictionary connect it with Mons Masius, the mountain range that classical writers placed on the northern edge of Mesopotamia, between the Tigris and Euphrates.

Massa was a son of Ishmael and so a grandson of Abraham. He appears only in the two genealogies of Ishmael's twelve sons, where he is listed seventh, between Dumah and Hadar (called Hadad in 1 Chr 1:30). His brothers included Nebajoth, Kedar and Tema, and his sister was Bashemath. Nothing is recorded about his life. His name is usually taken to mean "burden" (Hitchcock's Bible Names). Easton's Bible Dictionary describes him as the founder of a nomadic Arabian tribe living in the desert toward Babylonia, and Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests his descendants may be the Masani, whom the ancient geographer Ptolemy placed in eastern Arabia. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes an alternative rendering of Prov 31:1 that calls Lemuel "king of Massa," which would point to a tribe or place named after him.

Matred was the daughter of Mezahab and the mother of Mehetabel, who married Hadar (called Hadad in 1 Chr 1:50). Hadar was one of the kings who ruled Edom before Israel had kings, and his city was Pau, or Pai in Chronicles. Matred appears only in this genealogical note, which Genesis and 1 Chronicles repeat almost word for word, and nothing else is recorded about her. The Hebrew phrasing is ambiguous. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the Septuagint and Peshitta treat Matred as a man, the son of Mezahab, which would make Matred Mehetabel's father. This entry follows the reading of Matred as a woman and Mehetabel's mother. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives the name's meaning as "expulsion," Smith's Bible Dictionary as "pushing forward," and Hitchcock's Bible Names as "wand of government."

Mattan was a priest of Baal in Jerusalem, killed in front of Baal's altars when the people of the land tore down the house of Baal (2 Kgs 11:18; 2 Chr 23:17). The surrounding accounts place this in the uprising led by the priest Jehoiada, which removed Queen Athalia and put the young Joash on the throne. The Baal temple and its altars and images were smashed during the same action. Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests that Mattan probably came to Jerusalem with Athalia from Samaria, where her family, the house of Ahab, had promoted Baal worship. The name means "a gift." Several other people in the Bible share the name, among them the father of Shephatiah in the time of Jeremiah. This entry concerns only the priest of Baal.

Mattaniah was a Levite, one of the fourteen sons of Heman, who led one of the families of musicians organized for temple worship in the time of David (1 Chr 25:4). When lots were cast to set the order of service, the ninth lot fell to Mattaniah, and his group of sons and relatives numbered twelve (1 Chr 25:16). The surrounding chapter describes these musicians as serving with cymbals, harps and lyres. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia also connect Heman's sons with sounding the horn, drawn from the reference to lifting up the horn in 1 Chr 25:5. His name is usually explained as "gift of the LORD." Several other men in the Bible share the name, including the original name of King Zedekiah, and this entry concerns only the son of Heman.

Mattaniah was a Levite of the family of Asaph, the temple singers. He is named only in genealogies in Nehemiah, as the son of Michaiah (also spelled Micha). Through his son Hashabiah he was an ancestor of Uzzi, overseer of the Levites in Jerusalem after the return from exile (Neh 11:22). Through his son Shemaiah he was an ancestor of Zechariah, who played a trumpet at the dedication of the rebuilt city wall (Neh 12:35). Because he appears several generations above men active in Nehemiah's day, he probably lived somewhat earlier, though the line itself belongs to Nehemiah's period. A Levite called Mattaniah son of Micah, of Asaph's line, also appears in 1 Chr 9:15 and may be the same man. The name is shared by several people in the Bible. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives its meaning as "gift, or hope, of the Lord."

Matthias was the disciple chosen to take the place of Judas Iscariot among the twelve apostles. After Jesus' ascension, the believers in Jerusalem put forward two candidates, Joseph called Barsabas (also known as Justus) and Matthias (Acts 1:23). They cast lots, the lot fell on Matthias, and he was counted with the eleven apostles (Acts 1:26). By inference from the surrounding passage, he met Peter's stated requirement of having been with the disciples from John's baptism until the ascension, so that he could serve as a witness of the resurrection. The event is dated to about AD 30, by inference from context. His name probably means "gift of God" (Easton's Bible Dictionary). Nothing more is said of him in the Bible. Later traditions, noted in Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia, place his preaching and death variously in Ethiopia, Judea or Jerusalem.

Medad was one of the elders of Israel chosen during the wilderness journey, in the account of the seventy elders whom Moses gathered to share the burden of leading the people. He and another man, Eldad, were among those registered, but they stayed in the camp instead of going out to the tabernacle. The spirit rested on them there as well, and they prophesied in the camp (Num 11:26). A young man ran to report this to Moses (Num 11:27). The following verses, Num 11:28–29, tell how Joshua urged Moses to stop them, and Moses replied that he wished all the Lord's people were prophets. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives the meaning of his name as "affectionate", and notes that later Jewish tradition, including a lost apocalyptic Book of Eldad and Modad, supplied the content of their prophecy.

Medan was a son of Abraham and Keturah, the woman Abraham took after Sarah's death. He is listed third among six brothers: Zimran, Jokshan, Medan, Midian, Ishbak and Shuah (Gen 25:2). 1 Chr 1:32 repeats the list and calls Keturah Abraham's concubine. Through Abraham he was a half-brother of Isaac and Ishmael. Nothing is recorded about his life. The surrounding passage (Gen 25:6) says Abraham gave gifts to the sons of his concubines and sent them away eastward, away from Isaac, so Medan probably settled somewhere east of Canaan. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the tribe named after him and its territory remain unidentified. It treats a link with the Midianites as unlikely because Midian appears beside him as a separate brother. The name is usually taken to mean "strife" or "judgment."

Mehetabel was the wife of Hadad, one of the kings who ruled Edom before Israel had a king. She is mentioned only in the list of Edomite kings, where her husband succeeds Baal-hanan son of Achbor and reigns from a city called Pau (Gen 36:39), spelled Pai in the parallel list (1 Chr 1:50). Genesis gives her husband's name as Hadar, while Chronicles has Hadad. The two forms differ by a single letter in Hebrew and are generally taken as the same king. Both passages describe her as the daughter of Matred and the daughter, or granddaughter, of Mezahab. It is unclear whether Mezahab was Matred's father or mother. Her name is usually explained as "God does good" or "favored of God" (Smith's Bible Dictionary). A man in Nehemiah's time bore a related name.

Mehida was the ancestor of a family of temple servants (Nethinim) whose descendants returned from exile in Babylon. "The children of Mehida" appear in the list of returning exiles in Ezra 2:52 and again in the parallel list in Neh 7:54. In both lists they come between the families of Bazluth (Bazlith) and Harsha. The lists connect the returning groups with Zerubbabel, and Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both place this family among those who came back with him. Nothing is recorded about Mehida himself beyond his name, which functions here as a family name. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that 1 Esdras 5:32 gives the name as "Meeda" and takes it to mean "renowned," while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning as "a riddle" or "sharpness of wit."

Mehunim, also spelled Meunim, is the ancestral name of a family of temple servants (Nethinim) listed among those who returned from the Babylonian exile with Zerubbabel (Ezra 2:50; Neh 7:52). The name appears only as a family heading, so nothing is known of an individual by this name. It is a plural form, and Easton's Bible Dictionary connects it with the Meunim, or Maonites, a people of the region south and southeast of Judah whom Uzziah defeated (2 Chr 26:7) and who were displaced in Hezekiah's day (1 Chr 4:41). On that view, this family probably descended from Meunite captives or foreigners who had been assigned to serve at the temple. This entry treats Mehunim as the name of a family line among the temple servants.

Melchiah, also spelled Malchiah, was the father of Pashur, an official in Jerusalem during the reign of King Zedekiah. His name means roughly "the LORD is king." He appears only in his son's name. Zedekiah sent Pashur son of Melchiah, with the priest Zephaniah, to consult Jeremiah (Jer 21:1). Pashur son of Malchiah was also among the officials who heard Jeremiah's warnings to the people and, as the following verses tell, had him imprisoned (Jer 38:1). Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia describe Melchiah as a priest. This probably connects him with the priestly Pashur son of Malchijah listed in 1 Chr 9:12. Jer 38:6 names a cistern belonging to "Malchiah the son of Hammelech," into which Jeremiah was lowered. Whether that Malchiah is the same man is uncertain.

Melech was a Benjamite, a descendant of King Saul, named as the second of the four sons of Micah. His brothers were Pithon, Tarea (also spelled Tahrea) and Ahaz. He appears only in the two parallel genealogies of Saul's family (1 Chr 8:35; 1 Chr 9:41). The surrounding verses trace this line from Saul through Jonathan to Merib-baal, the son of Jonathan better known as Mephibosheth, and then to Micah. That makes Melech Mephibosheth's grandson and Jonathan's great-grandson, as Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia note. His name means "king." Nothing more is recorded about his life. The line continues through his brother Ahaz rather than through him.

Melzar was an official at the Babylonian court. The chief of the eunuchs put him in charge of Daniel, Hananiah, Mishael and Azariah, young men from Judah who were being trained for royal service (Dan 1:11). Daniel spoke with him about their food. The verses in between describe a ten-day trial of vegetables and water, so Melzar probably agreed to that test. Afterward he took away the king's food and wine they had been given and fed them pulse, meaning vegetables (Dan 1:16). The King James Version treats Melzar as a personal name. Other readings take the Hebrew word, which has the article ("the melzar"), as a job title. Smith's Bible Dictionary renders it "the steward," and Easton's Bible Dictionary suggests it means a chief butler. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia links it to a Babylonian word for a guardian. This entry follows the King James reading of a named individual.

Mered was a man of the tribe of Judah, named in a fragmentary genealogy as one of the sons of Ezra (spelled Ezrah in some translations), alongside Jether, Epher and Jalon (1 Chr 4:17). He married Bithiah, described as the daughter of Pharaoh (1 Chr 4:18). The passage is hard to follow, but it probably means that Miriam, Shammai and Ishbah, the father of Eshtemoa, were Bithiah's children. Mered also had a wife called Jehudijah. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia reads this name as a description, "the Jewess," which sets her apart from the Egyptian wife. It also suggests that the Hodiah of 1 Chr 4:19 is the same woman, whose descendants include Keilah the Garmite. His name means "rebellion." Smith's Bible Dictionary mentions a tradition that identifies him with Caleb and Moses.

Meshillemith was a priest, the son of Immer, who appears only as an ancestor in two lists of priests living in Jerusalem after the return from the Babylonian exile. In 1 Chr 9:12 he is the father of Meshullam and an ancestor of the priest Maasiai. Nehemiah 11:13 spells his name Meshillemoth and names him as an ancestor of Amashai, one of the priestly heads of families in Jerusalem. The two genealogies give different names between him and his descendants, and they are usually taken as parallel versions of the same family line. His father Immer probably stands for the priestly family of that name rather than a single generation. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "recompense." Nothing else is recorded about him.

Meshullam was a priest of the family of Immer, named only in genealogies. In 1 Chr 9:12 he is the son of Meshillemith and the father of Jahzerah, and an ancestor of Maasiai, one of the priests listed among those living in Jerusalem, by context after the return from the Babylonian exile. The parallel list in Neh 11:13 traces Amashai back through Azareel and Ahasai to Meshillemoth, son of Immer. This entry treats the Ahasai of that verse as the same man as Meshullam, since both stand as son of Meshillemith or Meshillemoth. Smith's Bible Dictionary instead matches Ahasai with Jahzerah, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia describes the Nehemiah list as omitting Meshullam's name. Because the two lists differ in names and order, the exact match is uncertain. Several other men in the Bible share the name Meshullam, which was common after the exile.

Meshullam was a priest in Jerusalem in the time of Nehemiah. He appears among the priests who set their seal to the covenant the returned exiles made to keep God's law (Neh 10:7). This entry also identifies him with the Meshullam who took part in the procession at the dedication of the rebuilt city wall, named alongside Azariah and Ezra (Neh 12:33). That identification follows the STEPBible Proper Names index. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia instead treat the two mentions as separate people, and Smith's calls the second one of the princes of Judah. Meshullam was a very common name after the exile, so the link between the two verses is uncertain. The name is usually taken to mean "friend" or "devoted."

Mezahab was the father of Matred and the grandfather of Mehetabel, the wife of Hadar (called Hadad in 1 Chr 1:50), the last king listed in the list of Edom's kings. He appears only in this genealogical note, given in both Gen 36:39 and 1 Chr 1:50. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary explain the name as meaning "waters of gold." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that Jewish commentators such as Abarbanel took the name to mean he was very wealthy, with gold in his house as plentiful as water. It also mentions that the name may instead refer to a place, possibly the same as Dizahab. The wording "daughter of Matred, the daughter of Mezahab" can be read either way. This entry treats Mezahab as a man, Matred's father, following the dictionaries. Nothing more is recorded about him.

Mibsam was one of the twelve sons of Ishmael, Abraham's son by Hagar. He is listed fourth, after Nebajoth, Kedar and Adbeel, in the genealogy of Ishmael's descendants in Gen 25:13, which is repeated in 1 Chr 1:29. Nothing else is recorded about him. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes him as the head of an Arab tribe, in line with the way Ishmael's sons are presented as founders of tribal groups. His sister Bashemath (also called Mahalath) later married Esau. The name is usually taken to mean "sweet odor" or "perfume" (Smith's Bible Dictionary, Hitchcock's Bible Names). Another Mibsam, a descendant of Simeon, appears in a separate genealogy, and the two should not be confused.

Mibzar was one of the chiefs ("dukes" in the King James Version) of Edom, the nation descended from Esau. He appears only in the closing list of Edomite chiefs, between Teman and Magdiel, in Gen 36:42 and its parallel in 1 Chr 1:53. Nothing else is recorded about him. The surrounding passage says these chiefs are named "according to their families, after their places," so Mibzar may stand for a clan or district as much as for an individual. His name means "fortress." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that Eusebius linked the name with Mibsara, a sizeable village under Petra that still existed in his day.

Micah the Morasthite was a prophet of Judah, credited with the book that bears the name. According to Mic 1:1, the word of the Lord came to Micah during the reigns of Jotham, Ahaz and Hezekiah, kings of Judah, and concerned both Samaria and Jerusalem. This entry dates the prophecies to about 754 BC, an estimate inferred from context. Easton's Bible Dictionary takes "Morasthite" to mean a native of Moresheth-gath (compare Mic 1:14) and treats Micah as a contemporary of Isaiah. The title also sets this prophet apart from others with the same name, such as Micaiah son of Imlah. Much later, during Jeremiah's trial, Micah's warning from Hezekiah's day was quoted: Zion would be plowed like a field and Jerusalem would become heaps (Jer 26:18). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia explains the name as a shortened form meaning "who is like Yah?"

Micha (also spelled Micah) was a Levite descended from Asaph, the temple musician, and the father of Mattaniah. Mattaniah led the thanksgiving in prayer among the Levites who settled in Jerusalem after the Babylonian exile. The two genealogies name Micha's father differently: 1 Chr 9:15 calls him Zichri, while Neh 11:17 calls him Zabdi. This entry follows Zichri. The two names are probably variant forms for the same ancestor. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes the family as Gershonite Levites and gives the name's meaning as "who is like God?" Hitchcock's Bible Names treats it as the same name as Micaiah. Several other people in the Bible share this name, and this Micha should not be confused with them.

Michaiah was a Levite of the family of Asaph, the temple singers, named only in genealogies in Nehemiah. He was the son of Zaccur and the father of Mattaniah. Through Mattaniah he was an ancestor of Zechariah son of Jonathan, who played a trumpet at the dedication of Jerusalem's rebuilt wall (Neh 12:35). The same line appears in Neh 11:22, where the name is spelled Micha. There his descendant Uzzi son of Bani is named as overseer of the Levites in Jerusalem after the return from exile. Smith's Bible Dictionary identifies him with the Micha of 1 Chr 9:15, the son of Zichri, an identification that rests on the matching descendant Mattaniah. The name is shared by several people in the Bible. Hitchcock's Bible Names treats it as the same name as Micah.

Michaiah was the father of Achbor, one of the officials whom King Josiah sent to ask the Lord about the Book of the Law found in the temple (2 Kgs 22:12). In the parallel account he is called Micah, and his son is named Abdon rather than Achbor (2 Chr 34:20). The two passages describe the same delegation, so they are taken to refer to the same father and son, recorded under variant names. According to the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia, Micah is a shortened form of the name, which means "who is like Yah?" Nothing else is recorded about Michaiah himself. His son's place among Josiah's leading officials suggests a family of some standing at court. Several other people in the Bible have the same name, and he should not be confused with them.

Michaiah was the son of Gemariah and grandson of Shaphan, and he lived in Jerusalem in the time of King Jehoiakim. He heard Baruch read Jeremiah's scroll of the LORD's words to the people (Jer 36:11). The surrounding passage places that reading in his father Gemariah's chamber in the temple court. Michaiah then went to the royal palace and told the assembled officials everything he had heard (Jer 36:13). According to the following verse, the officials then sent for Baruch to read the scroll to them. His grandfather Shaphan was probably the royal scribe of King Josiah's day, which suggests the family held office at court. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "who is like God?" Several people in the Bible share this name, and this Michaiah appears only in this one episode.

Mikneiah was a Levite of the second rank in David's time. He appears among the brothers appointed to serve alongside the leading musicians Heman, Asaph and Ethan when the ark was brought up to Jerusalem. In 1 Chr 15:18 he is listed with men described as "porters," or gatekeepers. In 1 Chr 15:21 he is named among those who played harps "on the Sheminith," a term of uncertain meaning, probably a musical setting or pitch. Smith's Bible Dictionary takes his name to mean "possession of Jehovah" and describes him as both a gatekeeper of the ark and a member of the musical band. Nothing further is recorded about him.

Mishael was a Levite of the Kohathite clan, a son of Uzziel and so a cousin of Moses and Aaron, since Uzziel was Aaron's uncle (Lev 10:4). Exodus lists him first among Uzziel's sons, with Elzaphan and Zithri (Exod 6:22). Elzaphan is also spelled Elizaphan, and 1 Chronicles names Michah and Isshiah as further sons of Uzziel. Mishael's one recorded act came after Aaron's sons Nadab and Abihu died for offering unauthorized fire. Moses called Mishael and Elzaphan to carry the bodies away from the sanctuary and out of the camp (Lev 10:4). The following verse says they carried them out in their tunics. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia takes the name to mean "who is equal to God?" The same name belongs to other people, including Daniel's companion, who were not this man.

Mishma was one of the twelve sons of Ishmael, Abraham's son by Hagar. He appears only in the genealogical lists of Ishmael's descendants, named after his brother Mibsam and before Dumah and Massa (Gen 25:14; 1 Chr 1:30). Nothing else is recorded about his life. The context of Genesis 25, which presents Ishmael's sons as princes of their tribes, suggests he headed one of the Ishmaelite clans. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes him as the founder of an Arab tribe. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "a hearing," and Hitchcock's Bible Names adds "obeying." The name is shared by several people in the Bible, including a later descendant of Simeon, who should not be confused with this son of Ishmael.

Mishma was a member of the tribe of Simeon named in the genealogy of 1 Chronicles 4. The list traces a line through Shallum to Mibsam, and then to Mishma.
