The sons of Mishma are given as Hamuel, Zacchur and Shimei. Read as a chain of father to son, this makes Hamuel his son and Zacchur and Shimei later descendants. Smith's Bible Dictionary reads Mishma as a brother of Mibsam, while this entry follows the reading of him as Mibsam's son. Nothing else is recorded about him. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "hearing" or "obeying." The same name belongs to another man, a son of Ishmael (Gen 25:14), who is a different person.

Mispereth was one of the leaders named among those who came back from exile in Babylon with Zerubbabel, the first group of returning exiles. The name appears only in two parallel lists of returnees. Neh 7:7 gives the form Mispereth, while Ezra 2:2 spells it Mispar (Mizpar in some King James printings, according to the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia). Both forms are generally taken to refer to the same person, since the two lists match closely, and Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "number." Nothing more is recorded: no family, tribe or later role is mentioned. The name stands alongside figures such as Jeshua, Nehemiah and Mordecai at the head of the list, which suggests, by inference, a position of some prominence among the returning community.

Mordecai was one of the leaders who came back from exile in Babylon to Jerusalem with Zerubbabel. He appears among them in Ezra 2:2 and again in the parallel list at Neh 7:7, where he is named alongside Jeshua, Nehemiah, Bilshan and others at the head of the register of returning Israelites. Nothing else is recorded about him. Several people in the Bible share this name, and this Mordecai is usually kept distinct from Esther's cousin in the Persian court, who lived in Susa decades later. Both lists date the return to the early years after the exile, probably the late 500s BC by inference from context. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "contrition; bitter; bruising."

The Mother of Zebedee's children was the wife of Zebedee and the mother of the apostles James and John. Matthew records that she came to Jesus with her two sons, knelt before him, and made a request. The following verses (Matt 20:21) say she asked that her sons sit at his right and left hand in his kingdom. In Mark's parallel account (Mark 10:35) James and John make the request themselves. She appears again among the women who had followed Jesus from Galilee and watched his crucifixion from a distance, about AD 30 by inference from context. Where Matthew names her at the cross, Mark 15:40 names Salome, so she is often identified as Salome. Some also infer from John 19:25 that she was the sister of Jesus' mother. Both identifications are inferences, and Matthew never gives her name.

Naaman was a member of the tribe of Benjamin, a son of Bela and so a grandson of Benjamin. Numbers 26:40 names him with his brother Ard as the sons of Bela and as the founder of the clan called the Naamites. 1 Chr 8:4 lists him among Bela's sons, alongside brothers such as Addar, Gera, Abihud, Abishua and Ahoah. A Naaman also appears among the sons of Benjamin himself in Gen 46:21, in the list of those who went down to Egypt with Jacob. Smith's Bible Dictionary takes this to be the same man, which would mean the genealogies sometimes count a grandson among a patriarch's sons. Smith's gives the name's meaning as "pleasantness." He is a different person from Naaman the Syrian army commander healed of leprosy in 2 Kgs 5.

Naarah was one of the two wives of Ashur, the father of Tekoa, named in the genealogy of the tribe of Judah. Her fellow wife was Helah. Naarah bore Ashur four sons: Ahuzam, Hepher, Temeni and Haahashtari (1 Chr 4:5–6). Her name means "a girl" or "maiden," according to the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia and Smith's Bible Dictionary. Easton's Bible Dictionary calls her the second of Ashur's wives, following the order in which the two are named. "Father of Tekoa" probably means that Ashur founded or led the town of Tekoa rather than that he had a son of that name. Nothing else is recorded about Naarah. She should not be confused with Naarah (or Naarath), a town on the border of Ephraim (Josh 16:7).

Nadab was a man of the tribe of Judah, named in the genealogy of 1 Chronicles 2 as a son of Shammai and brother of Abishur (1 Chr 2:28). His grandfather was Onam, who, according to the surrounding verses (1 Chr 2:25–26), was a son of Jerahmeel. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia accordingly places him among Jerahmeel's descendants. Nadab had two sons, Seled and Appaim. Seled died without children (1 Chr 2:30), so the line continued through Appaim, whose descendants are listed in the verses that follow. Nothing else is recorded about him. The name is shared by other men, including Aaron's son and a king of Israel, who are different people. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives the meaning of the name as "noble," and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "free and voluntary gift" or "prince."

Nadab was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, named only in the genealogies of 1 Chronicles as a son of the family settled at Gibeon. His mother was Maachah, and this entry gives his father as Abiel. The fuller list in 1 Chr 9:35 names the 'father of Gibeon' as Jehiel. Nadab appears in two near-identical lists of the sons, which name Abdon as the firstborn, followed by Zur, Kish, Baal, Ner and Nadab, and then others such as Gedor, Ahio, Zacher and Mikloth. Smith's Bible Dictionary calls him 'a son of Gibeon.' Nothing else is recorded about him. His name probably means 'noble' or 'generous.' He is distinct from the other men called Nadab in the Bible, such as Aaron's son and the king of Israel who succeeded Jeroboam.

Naharai was one of David's mighty men, the warriors named in the lists of 2 Sam 23 and 1 Chr 11. He is called a Beerothite (spelled Berothite in Chronicles), meaning he came from Beeroth, probably the Benjaminite town of that name. Both lists say he was armourbearer to Joab the son of Zeruiah, the commander of David's army. Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that some printings of the Authorized Version spell his name Nahari in 2 Samuel. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "snorer", while Hitchcock's Bible Names renders it "my nostrils" or "hot, anger". Nothing else is recorded about him beyond these two parallel lists.

Naphish was a son of Ishmael, Abraham's son by Hagar. He is named eleventh of Ishmael's twelve sons, next to last, between Jetur and Kedemah, in Gen 25:15 and again in 1 Chr 1:31. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "refreshment." Like his brothers, he was probably regarded as the founder of a tribe named after him. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identifies this tribe with "Nephish" in 1 Chr 5:19. That passage lists Nephish among the Hagrite peoples defeated by the Reubenites, Gadites and half-tribe of Manasseh east of the Jordan. The same work links Naphish with the "Nephusim" listed among the temple servants in Ezra 2:50. These connections rest on the similar names rather than on any direct statement in the text.

Naphtuhim is named as a son of Mizraim in the Table of Nations (Gen 10:13), and again in the matching list in 1 Chr 1:11. He is listed alongside Ludim, Anamim, Lehabim, Pathrusim, Casluhim and Caphthorim. The plural ending, like those of his brothers, suggests the name stands for a people descended from Mizraim, the ancestor of Egypt, rather than a single individual. Nothing more is recorded about him. Where this people lived is uncertain. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes several proposals, mostly placing them in Lower Egypt, such as the people around Memphis or the inhabitants of the Nile Delta. Easton's Bible Dictionary mentions a link with Napata, far to the south on the Nile. The STEPBible Proper Names index places them in northern Egypt, which is the view most commonly followed.

Nathan was a man from Zobah connected with one of David's mighty men, the elite warriors listed in 2 Samuel 23 and 1 Chronicles 11. He is not the prophet Nathan or David's son of that name. In 2 Sam 23:36 he is the father of Igal, one of the warriors. The parallel list at 1 Chr 11:38 instead has "Joel the brother of Nathan." The two lists differ, and it is not clear whether Igal or Joel is the original name, or whether Nathan was the warrior's father or his brother. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that one early Greek manuscript reads "son" in the Chronicles verse, which would bring the two lists closer together. This entry records both relationships, Igal as his son and Joel as his brother. Zobah was probably the Aramean kingdom north of Israel. The name Nathan means "given" or "giver."

Neariah was a descendant of King David in the royal line of Judah that continued after the Babylonian exile. He was one of the sons of Shemaiah, son of Shechaniah. His brothers were Hattush, Igeal, Bariah and Shaphat. The verse gives the total as six, though it names only five, so Shemaiah himself may be included in the count (1 Chr 3:22). Neariah had three sons, Elioenai, Hezekiah and Azrikam (1 Chr 3:23). Smith's Bible Dictionary places him at about 350 BC, an estimate worked out from the genealogy. Smith's gives the meaning of his name as "servant of Jehovah," while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "child of the Lord." Several people in the Bible share the name. One is a Simeonite captain named in 1 Chr 4:42, who is a different man.

Nehemiah was one of the leaders who came back from exile in Babylon to Jerusalem with Zerubbabel. He appears only in the lists of returning exiles, where he is named third, after Zerubbabel and Jeshua, among the men who headed the first return (Ezra 2:2; Neh 7:7). He is a different man from the better-known Nehemiah, the governor who rebuilt Jerusalem's walls. That Nehemiah arrived about a century later, and Smith's Bible Dictionary likewise treats this one as a separate leader of the earlier expedition. Nothing else is recorded about him. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "consolation" or "repentance of the Lord."

Nekoda was the ancestor of a family of temple servants (the Nethinim) whose descendants returned to Jerusalem from exile in Babylon. The family appears in the list of returnees in Ezra 2:48 and again in the parallel list in Neh 7:50, between the descendants of Rezin and those of Gazzam. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia describes Nekoda as the head of this family of Nethinim. Nothing else is recorded about Nekoda as an individual. The verses do not say whether Nekoda was a man or a woman, and this entry treats Nekoda as female. The same name belongs to a different family in the same lists (Ezra 2:60; Neh 7:62), whose members could not prove their Israelite descent. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "painted" or "inconstant."

Nekoda was the ancestor of a family that returned to Judah from the Babylonian exile but could not prove its Israelite descent. The surrounding passage (Ezra 2:59; Neh 7:61) says these returnees came from places such as Tel-melah and Tel-harsa and could not show their father's house or lineage. The descendants of Nekoda are listed with those of Delaiah and Tobiah, and the three families together numbered 652 in Ezra and 642 in Nehemiah. The text gives no further details about Nekoda personally. The name is shared by another Nekoda, whose descendants were among the temple servants (Ezra 2:48), and the two should be kept apart. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "painted" or "inconstant."

Nephusim was the ancestor or founder of a family whose descendants returned from exile in Babylon to Jerusalem. The family appears in the list of returnees in Ezra 2:50, and the parallel list in Neh 7:52 gives the name as Nephishesim. Both lists place these families in the section naming the Nethinim, or temple servants, so the family was probably one of the groups that served at the temple. Smith's Bible Dictionary treats the two spellings as the same name and, following the Hebrew scholar Gesenius, takes Nephishesim as the proper form. STEPBible's proper-name index likewise describes the Nephushesim as a family of temple servants who came back from captivity. Nothing more is recorded about the man himself, and the name may refer to a clan rather than to a single individual.

Nergal-sharezer was a Babylonian official, one of the princes of Nebuchadnezzar who entered Jerusalem when it fell and sat in the middle gate (Jer 39:3). The name appears twice in that verse, so Smith's Bible Dictionary takes it to refer to two different officials. One of them carries the title Rabmag, probably meaning a chief of the magi or a senior court officer. Nergal-sharezer the Rabmag was among the officials sent by Nebuzaradan, the captain of the guard, to have Jeremiah released from the court of the prison (Jer 39:13). The name means "O Nergal, protect the king" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia). Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries identify him with Neriglissar, who later took the Babylonian throne after Evil-merodach, son of Nebuchadnezzar, and reigned about 559–556 BC. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia also reports this view. Jerusalem's fall is usually dated about 587 BC.

Nethaniah was a Levite musician of David's time, one of the sons of Asaph who prophesied under their father's direction "according to the order of the king" (1 Chr 25:2). His brothers are named as Zaccur, Joseph and Asarelah. Asarelah is apparently the same person as the Jesharelah of 1 Chr 25:14. When the temple musicians were divided into twenty-four groups by lot, the fifth lot fell to Nethaniah, and his group of sons and relatives numbered twelve (1 Chr 25:12). The name means "gift of the Lord" or "Yah has given" (Hitchcock's Bible Names; International Standard Bible Encyclopedia). Several other men in the Bible share this name, and this Nethaniah is distinct from them. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates him to about 1015 BC, an estimate drawn from the setting in David's reign.

Neziah was the ancestor of a family of temple servants (the Nethinim) whose descendants returned from the Babylonian exile to Judah. The "children of Neziah" appear in the list of returning exiles in Ezra 2:54 and again in the parallel list in Neh 7:56, placed between the families of Bazluth and Hatipha. The verses themselves only name the family. The identification with the Nethinim comes from where the name falls in the list, among the temple servants, as Smith's Bible Dictionary notes. Smith's links this return with Zerubbabel and dates it to about 536 BC, an estimate inferred from context. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the same family is called "Nasi" or "Nasith" in 1 Esdras 5:32. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "victory" or "pure," while Hitchcock's Bible Names renders it "conqueror" or "strong." Nothing more is known about Neziah himself.

Nogah was one of the sons of King David born to him in Jerusalem, listed between Eliphelet and Nepheg in the two lists of David's Jerusalem-born children (1 Chr 3:7; 1 Chr 14:6). His name means "splendor" or "brightness." Nothing more is recorded about his life. The parallel list in 2 Sam 5:14–16 does not include him, as the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes. That encyclopedia also points out that the same name in its Greek form, Naggai, appears in Luke's genealogy of Jesus (Luke 3:25), though that is a different person. Smith's Bible Dictionary places the births of David's Jerusalem sons roughly between 1050 and 1015 BC, an estimate drawn from context. As a son of David, Nogah belonged to the tribe of Judah.

Nohah was a son of Benjamin, listed as the fourth son in the Benjamite genealogy of 1 Chr 8:2. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "rest." This entry identifies him with Naaman, who is named among the sons of Benjamin who went down to Egypt with Jacob in Gen 46:21. The lists of Benjamin's sons differ considerably between Genesis, Numbers and Chronicles, so this match is an inference. Elsewhere a Naaman appears as a grandson of Benjamin through Bela (Num 26:40; 1 Chr 8:4), which suggests that the genealogies arrange the family in different ways. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia proposes that the phrase "a resting-place" in Judg 20:43 should be read as the place name Nohah, possibly where his family settled. Nothing else is recorded about him.

Obadiah was one of the six sons of Azel, listed in the genealogy of King Saul's family in the tribe of Benjamin. His brothers were Azrikam, Bocheru, Ishmael, Sheariah and Hanan. The same list of Azel's sons appears twice, in 1 Chr 8:38 and again in 1 Chr 9:44. The surrounding verses trace Azel's line back through Jonathan's son Merib-baal to Saul, so Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia describe Obadiah as a descendant of Saul. Nothing else is recorded about him. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of his name as "servant of the Lord." Several other men in the Bible share this name, including the prophet, and this Obadiah should not be confused with them.

Obed was a man of the tribe of Judah who appears only in a genealogy in 1 Chronicles. He was the son of Ephlal and the father of Jehu, and his line continued through Jehu's son Azariah (1 Chr 2:37–38). The surrounding passage (1 Chr 2:34–35) traces this family through the clan of Jerahmeel. It descends from Sheshan, who had no sons and gave his daughter in marriage to Jarha, his Egyptian servant. Obed was a later descendant of that marriage, as the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia and Smith's Bible Dictionary both note. His name is usually taken to mean "servant" or "worker" (Hitchcock's Bible Names). Nothing else is recorded about him. He should not be confused with other men of the same name, such as Obed the grandfather of David.

Oded was the father of Azariah, the prophet whom the Spirit of God came upon during the reign of King Asa of Judah (2 Chr 15:1). Asa's reign is dated roughly to the late 10th and early 9th centuries BC. In 2 Chr 15:8 the prophecy that moved Asa to take courage, remove the idols from Judah, Benjamin and the captured towns of Ephraim, and restore the Lord's altar is called "the prophecy of Oded the prophet." Since the message in the passage is spoken by Azariah, the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests the verse means "the prophecy of Azariah the son of Oded." Others take it to mean that Oded was himself a prophet, which is how STEPBible's names index describes him. His name is usually explained as meaning "restorer" or "sustainer." A different Oded, a prophet in Samaria in the time of Ahaz, appears in 2 Chr 28:9.

Ohad was a son of Simeon and a grandson of Jacob, listed third among Simeon's six sons in Gen 46:10 and Exod 6:15. His brothers were Jemuel, Jamin, Jachin, Zohar and Shaul, the last of whom was the son of a Canaanite woman. Zohar appears as Zerah in later lists. In Genesis he is named among Jacob's family who went down to Egypt. Exodus counts these sons as the founding families of the tribe of Simeon. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that Ohad does not appear in the list of Simeon's clans in Num 26:12–14, so he probably left no separate clan. Nothing else is recorded about him. The meaning of his name is uncertain: Easton's Bible Dictionary gives "united" or "power," and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "praising" or "confessing."

Onam was a son of Shobal and a grandson of Seir the Horite. He is named in the list of Seir's descendants given alongside the genealogy of Esau's family in Edom. His brothers were Alvan, Manahath, Ebal and Shepho (Gen 36:23). The parallel list in 1 Chr 1:40 gives the same five names with slight spelling differences, Alian for Alvan and Shephi for Shepho. Shobal's descent from Seir comes from the surrounding verses of the genealogy. Nothing more is recorded about Onam beyond his place in these lists. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives the meaning of his name as "vigorous." The same name belongs to another man in the Bible, a descendant of Judah through Jerahmeel, who should not be confused with this Horite.

Onam was a member of the tribe of Judah, listed in the genealogy of Jerahmeel's family. He was the son of Jerahmeel by a second wife, Atarah (1 Chr 2:26). His brothers Ram, Bunah, Oren, Ozem and Ahijah are named in the preceding verse as Jerahmeel's sons, and were probably his half-brothers by Jerahmeel's first wife. Onam had two sons, Shammai and Jada, and through Shammai the line continued to Nadab and Abishur (1 Chr 2:28). Nothing else is recorded about him. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "strong" and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia as "vigorous"; the latter suggests the name may be connected with Onan, son of Judah. The name is shared by at least one other person, a Horite descendant of Seir in Edom (Gen 36:23), who should not be confused with this Onam.

Onesimus was a man from Colossae whom the apostle Paul calls "my son," saying he had become his spiritual father while Paul was in prison (Phlm 1:10). Paul's short letter to Philemon is an appeal on his behalf. In that letter Paul asks Philemon to receive him "not now as a servant, but above a servant, a brother beloved" (Phlm 1:16) and offers to repay anything he owes (Phlm 1:18). This indicates that Onesimus was Philemon's slave and had left his master, perhaps after some wrong. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes him as a runaway who reached Rome, where Paul was held. Paul sent him back with Tychicus and introduced him to the Colossian church as "a faithful and beloved brother, who is one of you" (Col 4:9), so he was probably a native or resident of Colossae. His name means "useful," and Paul plays on this meaning in Phlm 1:11.

Onesiphorus was a Christian whom Paul remembers warmly in his second letter to Timothy. Paul prays for mercy on his household because Onesiphorus often refreshed him and was not ashamed of his chains. The following verses (2 Tim 1:17–18) add that when he came to Rome he searched hard for the imprisoned Paul until he found him, and that he had served in many ways at Ephesus. Paul's closing greetings ask Timothy to greet his household, alongside Prisca and Aquila. Since Timothy was probably at Ephesus, Smith's Bible Dictionary and Easton's Bible Dictionary take Onesiphorus to have been an Ephesian whose home and family stayed there. His name means "bringing profit." Because Paul twice greets his household rather than the man himself, some interpreters, as the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes, think he may have died by the time of writing, though this cannot be known.

Ophir was a son of Joktan, listed among his thirteen sons in the Table of Nations (Gen 10:29) and again in the genealogy of 1 Chr 1:23. Joktan descended from Shem through Eber, so Ophir belongs to the Semitic line. His brothers included Sheba, Havilah, Jobab, Hazarmaveth and Almodad. Smith's Bible Dictionary counts him as the eleventh son. The text records nothing else about him personally. Like several of his brothers, his name probably also stands for a people or region. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia connects him with the land of Ophir, the source of the gold that Solomon's ships brought back from Ezion-geber. It places that land most likely in southeastern Arabia, though India and Africa have also been proposed. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "fruitful region."

Orpah was a Moabite woman who married into the family of Elimelech and Naomi, an Israelite family from Bethlehem living in Moab. Ruth 1:4 says Naomi's two sons married Moabite women, Orpah and Ruth, and stayed there about ten years. Her husband was Chilion, an inference from Ruth 4:10, which names Ruth as the wife of Mahlon. After both sons died, Orpah set out with Naomi toward Judah. When Naomi urged her daughters-in-law to go back to their own families, Orpah wept, kissed her goodbye and returned to her people, while Ruth stayed with Naomi (Ruth 1:14). The meaning of her name is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives "forelock or fawn," Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "gazelle," and Hitchcock's Bible Names links it to the Hebrew word for "neck."

Ozni was a son of Gad and the founder of the Oznite family, one of the clans of the tribe of Gad listed in the census taken in the wilderness (Num 26:16). In the list of Jacob's descendants who went down to Egypt he appears to be called Ezbon (Gen 46:16). The two lists name Gad's sons in matching order, and Ezbon stands where Ozni does, so Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treat the names as referring to the same man. This entry follows that identification. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of Ozni as "an ear" or "my hearkening." His brothers were Zephon, Haggi, Shuni, Eri, Arod and Areli. Nothing further is recorded about him.

Padon was the ancestor of a family of temple servants (the Nethinim) whose descendants returned from the Babylonian exile with Zerubbabel. His name appears only in the two parallel lists of returning exiles, between the families of Keros and Siaha (Sia in Nehemiah), within the section on the temple servants (Ezra 2:44; Neh 7:47). Nothing else is recorded about him personally, and he probably lived well before the return, since the lists name family groups by their forebears. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives the meaning of the name as "redemption" and identifies him with the "Phaleas" of 1 Esdras 5:29. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates the return of his descendants to before 529 BC.

Pathrusim is named in the Table of Nations as one of the descendants of Mizraim, son of Ham, listed alongside Ludim, Anamim, Lehabim, Naphtuhim, Casluhim and Caphthorim (Gen 10:14; 1 Chr 1:12). The plural ending marks the name as a people rather than a single individual. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia explain it as "the people of Pathros," a branch of the Egyptians, since Mizraim is the Hebrew name for Egypt. Pathros appears elsewhere in the prophets, for example Jer 44:1 and Ezek 29:14, as a region of Egypt where Judeans later lived. It is usually identified with Upper (southern) Egypt, the Nile valley south of the Delta. Nothing else is recorded about the Pathrusim beyond the two parallel genealogical lists.

Pedaiah was a son of Jehoiachin (also called Jeconiah), the king of Judah taken captive to Babylon, and so belonged to the royal line of the tribe of Judah. He is named among Jehoiachin's seven sons, alongside Shealtiel, Malchiram, Shenazar, Jecamiah, Hoshama and Nedabiah (1 Chr 3:18). By inference he was born during the Babylonian exile, as the STEPBible proper-names index notes. His sons were Zerubbabel and Shimei (1 Chr 3:19). Elsewhere, as in Ezra 3:2, Zerubbabel is called the son of Shealtiel, Pedaiah's brother. Smith's Bible Dictionary mentions a suggestion that Zerubbabel became Shealtiel's heir because Shealtiel had no children of his own. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes other possible explanations. The name means "the Lord redeems," and several other men in the Bible share it.

Pelaiah was a Levite in Jerusalem in the time of Ezra and Nehemiah. He was one of a group of Levites who helped the people understand the law while Ezra read it aloud to the gathered assembly, and the people stood in their places as they listened (Neh 8:7). A Levite named Pelaiah also appears among the Levites who set their seal to the covenant of commitment led by Nehemiah (Neh 10:10). Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treat these as the same man, and this entry follows that view, though the name is shared by more than one person in the Bible. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that he is called Phalias in 1 Esdras 9:48. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates these events to about 445 BC. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of his name as "the Lord's secret or miracle."

Pelatiah son of Benaiah was one of the "princes of the people" in Jerusalem whom the prophet Ezekiel saw in a vision. The spirit brought Ezekiel to the east gate of the temple, where he saw twenty-five men, among them Jaazaniah son of Azur and Pelatiah (Ezek 11:1). Ezekiel was told to prophesy against these men, whom the surrounding passage describes as devising mischief and giving wicked counsel in the city. While Ezekiel was prophesying, Pelatiah died, and Ezekiel fell on his face and cried out, asking whether God would make a full end of the remnant of Israel (Ezek 11:13). His name means "the LORD delivers" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia). Several other men in the Bible share the name Pelatiah; this one is known only from Ezekiel's vision.

Peninnah was one of the two wives of Elkanah, a man from the hill country of Ephraim. The other was Hannah, the mother of Samuel. Unlike Hannah, who was childless, Peninnah had children (1 Sam 1:2). When Elkanah offered sacrifices at the yearly festival, he gave portions to Peninnah and to all her sons and daughters (1 Sam 1:4). The verses that follow describe her as Hannah's rival, who provoked Hannah year after year because Hannah had no children (1 Sam 1:6–7). This is also how the STEPBible proper names list from Tyndale House describes her. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia calls her Elkanah's second wife. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of her name as "coral" or "pearl" and dates her to about 1125 BC, an estimate drawn from context.

Perida was the ancestor of a family listed among the descendants of "Solomon's servants" who returned from exile in Babylon. The family appears in the parallel lists of returnees in Ezra and Nehemiah, where it is named between the families of Sotai and Sophereth. Nehemiah 7:57 spells the name Perida, while Ezra 2:55 has Peruda, a small difference in the Hebrew spelling for the same person. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that he also appears as Pharida in 1 Esdras 5:33. Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries place this return under Zerubbabel, which Smith dates to before 536 BC. Nothing else is recorded about Perida himself. The meaning of the name is uncertain: Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "grain, kernel," the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia "recluse," and Hitchcock's Bible Names "separation; division."

Phaltiel was the son of Laish from Gallim and the second husband of Michal, Saul's daughter. After David fled from Saul, Saul gave Michal, who was already David's wife, to him. 1 Sam 25:44 calls him Phalti. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "deliverance of the Lord." Later, after Saul's death, Ishbosheth took Michal away from Phaltiel and returned her to David. The surrounding passage explains that David demanded this as a condition for his agreement with Abner (2 Sam 3:14). The next verse says Phaltiel followed her, weeping, as far as Bahurim, until Abner ordered him to go home (2 Sam 3:16). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia also notes a different Phaltiel, a "captain of the people" in the apocryphal book of 2 Esdras, who is not the same man.

Phaseah, also spelled Paseah, was the ancestor of a family of Nethinim, or temple servants, whose descendants returned from exile in Babylon. "The children of Paseah" appear in the list of those who came back with Zerubbabel (Ezra 2:49), and the same family is named as "the children of Phaseah" in the parallel list in Neh 7:51. In both lists the family is grouped with the descendants of Uzza and other temple-servant families. Nothing is recorded about Phaseah himself beyond his name. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives its meaning as "lame," and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia renders it "limping." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia also equates this family with "Phinoe" in the corresponding list of 1 Esdras 5:31. This Phaseah is distinct from another Paseah named in the genealogies of Judah.

Phurah was Gideon's servant, who went with him by night to the edge of the Midianite camp before Gideon's attack. God told Gideon that if he was afraid to go down to the camp alone, he should take Phurah with him and listen to what the enemy was saying, so that he would be encouraged to attack (Judg 7:10–11). The two reached the outposts of the armed men in the camp, where, as the following verses tell, Gideon overheard a soldier describing a dream that foretold Midian's defeat. Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests Phurah was probably Gideon's armor-bearer, comparing Jonathan's armor-bearer in 1 Sam 14:1. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the word for "servant" literally means "young man" and spells the name Purah. The name is usually taken to mean "branch" or "bough." He is not mentioned anywhere else.

Pinon was one of the chiefs, called "dukes" in the King James Version, of Edom, the nation descended from Esau. He appears only in the list of Edomite chiefs in Gen 36:41 and its parallel in 1 Chr 1:52, where he is named between Elah and Kenaz. Smith's Bible Dictionary takes such a chief to be the head or founder of a tribe within Edom. The surrounding list in Genesis says these chiefs are named by their families and their places, so Pinon may also be the name of a clan or a district. Some interpreters connect it with Punon, a stopping place of Israel in the wilderness (Num 33:42), though that link is an inference. The meaning of the name is given as "darkness" in Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia, and as "pearl" or "gem" in Hitchcock's Bible Names. Nothing else is recorded about him.

Pithon was a Benjamite, the first-named of the four sons of Micah, listed with his brothers Melech, Tarea (also spelled Tahrea) and Ahaz (1 Chr 8:35; 1 Chr 9:41). He appears only in the two parallel genealogies of King Saul's family in 1 Chronicles. The surrounding verses show that his father Micah was the son of Merib-baal, the name Chronicles uses for Mephibosheth, Jonathan's son. That makes Pithon a great-grandson of Jonathan and a descendant of Saul, as Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia also note. Nothing else is recorded about him. The meaning of his name is uncertain. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "harmless," while Hitchcock's Bible Names suggests "mouthful" or "persuasion."

Pochereth was the ancestor of a family listed among the descendants of Solomon's servants who returned from exile in Babylon. He appears only in the parallel return lists in Ezra 2:57 and Neh 7:59, where he is called "Pochereth of Zebaim." The surrounding passage (Ezra 2:55–58) places this group with the temple servants, and Smith's Bible Dictionary connects the family with the return led by Zerubbabel. Nothing else is recorded about him. The phrase "of Zebaim" could point to a place or clan, but it is often read as part of a single compound name, Pochereth-hazzebaim, which many modern translations render as Pokereth-Hazzebaim. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "cutting of the mouth of warfare." It is unclear whether Pochereth was an individual or a name preserved for a family line.

Potiphar was the Egyptian official who bought Joseph as a slave. He is described as an officer of Pharaoh and "captain of the guard," a title the King James margin renders "chief of the executioners." Easton's Bible Dictionary suggests he probably headed a force that combined military and civil police duties. Joseph's brothers sold him to traders, called both Midianites and Ishmeelites, who brought him down to Egypt and sold him to Potiphar (Gen 37:36; Gen 39:1). The rest of Genesis 39 says Joseph won his trust and ran his household. Potiphar's wife then falsely accused Joseph, and Potiphar had him put in prison. Nothing more is said of Potiphar after this. His name is usually taken to mean "belonging to the sun" or "dedicated to Ra," and it closely resembles Potipherah, the name of Joseph's later father-in-law.

Publius was "the chief man" of the island of Malta when Paul and his companions were shipwrecked there, about AD 57 by inference from context. He owned estates near the place where they came ashore, and he welcomed them and lodged them hospitably for three days (Acts 28:7). His father was sick with fever and dysentery. Paul went in to him, prayed, laid his hands on him and healed him (Acts 28:8). The Greek title translated "chief man" (protos, "first") was probably an official title. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that it appears on an inscription from the nearby island of Gozo, and Smith's Bible Dictionary takes Publius to have been the governor. A later tradition says that Publius became the first bishop of Malta and afterward bishop of Athens.

Raamah was a son of Cush and grandson of Ham, listed in the Table of Nations among Noah's descendants. His brothers were Seba, Havilah, Sabtah, Sabtecha and Nimrod, and his sons were Sheba and Dedan (Gen 10:7; 1 Chr 1:9). Like many names in this genealogy, Raamah probably stands both for an ancestor and for the people or region descended from him. Ezek 27:22 later mentions merchants of Sheba and Raamah trading spices, precious stones and gold with Tyre, which suggests a trading people, usually placed in Arabia. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "greatness" or "thunder." Nothing else is recorded about him.

Rab-mag appears in the King James text as one of the princes of the king of Babylon who came in and sat in the middle gate of Jerusalem when the city fell to Nebuchadnezzar's army in the reign of Zedekiah (Jer 39:3). He is named again among the officials whom Nebuzaradan, the captain of the guard, sent at the time Jeremiah was released from the prison court (Jer 39:13). The King James text lists Rab-mag as if it were a name, and this entry treats it as a person. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia and Smith's Bible Dictionary, however, take it as a title, probably meaning "chief of the magi" or chief prince, held by the Nergal-sharezer named just before it. Smith's Bible Dictionary further suggests this Nergal-sharezer is probably the later Babylonian king the Greeks called Neriglissar.

Rab-saris was one of the high officials of Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, who entered Jerusalem when the city fell and sat in the middle gate with the other Babylonian princes (Jer 39:3). He was also among the officials who, with Nebuzaradan the captain of the guard, sent to have Jeremiah released from the court of the prison (Jer 39:13). The name means "chief of the eunuchs" (Hitchcock's Bible Names), and Smith's Bible Dictionary says it is probably the title of an office rather than a personal name. Read that way, it may describe the man named just before it in each verse, Sarsechim in Jer 39:3 and Nebushasban in Jer 39:13. Whether both verses refer to the same person is uncertain. The same title is used for an Assyrian officer sent to Hezekiah in 2 Kgs 18:17, a different man from an earlier period.

Ram was the firstborn son of Jerahmeel, a member of the tribe of Judah known only from the genealogy in 1 Chronicles 2. His father Jerahmeel was the firstborn of Hezron, and his brothers were Bunah, Oren, Ozem and Ahijah. Onam is also counted among Jerahmeel's sons, and according to 1 Chr 2:26 he was born to a second wife named Atarah, so he was probably Ram's half-brother. Ram's own sons were Maaz, Jamin and Eker. Nothing else is recorded about him. Several people in the Bible bear the name Ram. This one should be kept distinct from his uncle Ram, Jerahmeel's brother and a son of Hezron, who appears in the line leading to David (1 Chr 2:9–10; Ruth 4:19). Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "elevated" or "sublime."

Rapha was a son of Benjamin, the youngest son of Jacob, and so belonged to the founding generation of the tribe of Benjamin. In the Benjamite genealogy of 1 Chr 8:1–2 he is named as Benjamin's fifth son, after Bela, Ashbel, Aharah and Nohah. This entry identifies him with Rosh, who appears among the sons of Benjamin in the list of Jacob's family that went down to Egypt (Gen 46:21). The identification follows the STEPBible proper-name index from Tyndale House. It is an inference, because the Benjamite lists in Genesis, Numbers and Chronicles differ considerably in their names and order. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of Rapha as "tall" and of Rosh as "head." A different Rapha, a descendant of Saul, appears later in the same chapter (1 Chr 8:37). Nothing else is recorded about this son of Benjamin.

Reaiah was a man of the tribe of Judah, a son of Shobal, who is called the father of Kirjathjearim. He appears only in the genealogies of 1 Chronicles. 1 Chr 4:2 names him as the father of Jahath, whose sons Ahumai and Lahad headed the families of the Zorathites. He is probably the same person as Haroeh, listed in 1 Chr 2:52 as a son of Shobal alongside half of the Manahethites. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests that "Reaiah" should probably be read in place of "Haroeh" there, though both spellings may be copying variants, and this entry treats the two names as one man. The ISBE also calls him the founding ancestor of a Calebite family. His name means "the Lord has seen" (Hitchcock's Bible Names: "vision of the Lord"). The name Reaiah is also borne by other men in the Bible.

Reaiah was the ancestor of a family of temple servants (the Nethinim) whose descendants returned from exile in Babylon to Jerusalem. The family is named in both lists of returning exiles (Ezra 2:47; Neh 7:50), and Smith's Bible Dictionary places the return with Zerubbabel, before about 536 BC by inference from context. Nothing else is recorded about Reaiah himself, and the name may stand for a family or clan rather than a single known individual. The name means "the Lord has seen" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia). Several other people in the Bible share the name, and this Reaiah should not be confused with them.

Reba was one of five Midianite rulers killed by the Israelites under Moses, along with Evi, Rekem, Zur and Hur. Balaam son of Beor died in the same campaign (Num 31:8). Numbers calls the five "kings of Midian," while Joshua calls them "princes of Midian" and "dukes of Sihon," the Amorite king who ruled from Heshbon (Josh 13:21). This suggests they were local chiefs living in that region and allied with or subject to Sihon. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Hitchcock's Bible Names take the name to mean "fourth." Nothing else is recorded about him.

Reelaiah was one of the leading men who returned from exile in Babylon with Zerubbabel. His name appears in the list of those who came back with Zerubbabel and Jeshua in Ezra 2:2. In the parallel list in Neh 7:7 he is called Raamiah. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia counts him among twelve chiefs named at the head of the list, notes that 1 Esdras 5:8 gives the name as Resaias, and says it is almost impossible to decide which form is original, though it leans toward Reelaiah. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of Raamiah as "thunder of the Lord." Nothing more is recorded about him beyond his place among these leaders of the return.

Rehob was the father of Hadadezer, king of Zobah, an Aramean (Syrian) kingdom north of Israel. He is known only through his son. Hadadezer is called "the son of Rehob" when David defeated him as Hadadezer went to recover his border at the Euphrates River (2 Sam 8:3). He is named again in the list of spoil David dedicated, which included spoil taken from Hadadezer (2 Sam 8:12). Nothing else is recorded about Rehob himself, and it is not stated whether he was also a king. The name, which Hitchcock's Bible Names explains as meaning "breadth" or "space," is shared by other people in the Bible and is also used as a place name. This Rehob should not be confused with them.

Rekem was one of five kings of Midian killed by the Israelites in the time of Moses, along with Evi, Zur, Hur and Reba. Numbers 31:8 records their deaths in Israel's war against Midian, the same campaign in which Balaam son of Beor was killed with the sword. Joshua 13:21 recalls the event when describing the land east of the Jordan. It calls these five "princes of Midian" and "dukes of Sihon", meaning chieftains linked to Sihon, the Amorite king who ruled from Heshbon. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "variegation." The same name belongs to other people in the Bible, including a man of Judah and a town of Benjamin, but this entry concerns only the Midianite king.

Rekem was a man of the tribe of Judah, named in the genealogy of 1 Chr 2 as one of the four sons of Hebron, alongside Korah, Tappuah and Shema. He was the father of Shammai. Nothing else is recorded about him. This Hebron belongs to the line of Caleb within Judah's genealogy, and some of the names in this list, such as Tappuah, also appear as towns in Judah. For that reason the names may stand partly for clans or settlements as well as for individuals, though the text presents them as father and sons. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "variegation." Several other people in the Bible share the name Rekem, including a Midianite king killed in Moses' time. This entry concerns only the son of Hebron.

Rephaiah was a son of Binea in the family line of King Saul, from the tribe of Benjamin. He appears only in the two parallel genealogies of Saul's descendants. He is called Rephaiah in 1 Chr 9:43 and Rapha (Raphah) in 1 Chr 8:37. By inference from the surrounding verses (1 Chr 8:33–36; 9:39–42), his grandfather Moza descended from Saul through Jonathan and Merib-baal, so Rephaiah belonged to a late generation of Saul's line. The text says nothing about his life. This entry treats Eleasah and Azel as his brothers, though the repeated phrase "his son" can also be read as a line of descent, with Eleasah as Rephaiah's son and Azel as his grandson. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives the meaning of the name as probably "Yah is healing." Several other men in the Bible share the name.

Rezin was the ancestor of a family of temple servants, the Nethinim, whose descendants returned from exile in Babylon to Judah with Zerubbabel. The family appears in the list of returnees in Ezra 2:48 and again in the parallel list in Neh 7:50, both times beside the families of Nekoda and Gazzam or Reaiah. The context of the return places this before about 536 BC, a date Smith's Bible Dictionary also gives. Nothing else is recorded about Rezin himself. He is different from Rezin the king of Syria (Aram), who allied with Israel against Judah in the time of Ahaz. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "firm," while Hitchcock's Bible Names offers "good-will" or "messenger."

Ribai was a Benjamite from Gibeah, known only as the father of Ittai, one of David's mighty men. He is named in the two parallel lists of David's warriors, where his son is called Ittai in 2 Sam 23:29 and Ithai in 1 Chr 11:31. Both passages place the family in Gibeah of the tribe of Benjamin, the hometown of King Saul. Nothing else is recorded about Ribai himself. Smith's Bible Dictionary takes the name to mean "pleader with Jehovah", while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "strife". His lifetime would fall before or during David's reign, by inference from his son's service.

Riphath was the second of the three sons of Gomer, Japheth's son, listed with his brothers Ashkenaz and Togarmah in the Table of Nations (Gen 10:3) and again in the genealogy of 1 Chr 1:6. Nothing else is recorded about him. Like the other names in these lists, his name was probably understood as the ancestor of a people. The Hebrew text of 1 Chr 1:6 reads Diphath, a spelling the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes, while the King James Version keeps Riphath in both places. Identifications of his descendants vary. Josephus, as cited by the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia and Easton's Bible Dictionary, linked them with the Paphlagonians on the southern coast of the Black Sea. Smith's Bible Dictionary connects the name with the Rhipaean mountains, which it takes to be the Carpathian range. This entry does not settle between these views.

Romamti-ezer was one of the fourteen sons of Heman, a Levite who led music at the sanctuary in King David's time (1 Chr 25:4). Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of his name as "exaltation of help," and Easton's Bible Dictionary gives "elevation of help." David's musicians were divided by lot into twenty-four courses for service. Romamti-ezer received the twenty-fourth and last lot, and his group of his sons and his brothers numbered twelve (1 Chr 25:31). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes a view held by some commentators: the last eight or nine names in the list of Heman's sons, including this one, may originally have been the words of a poetic prayer rather than personal names. This entry follows 1 Chr 25:31, which treats Romamti-ezer as the head of a course of singers.

Sabtah was the third of the five sons of Cush, son of Ham, named in the Table of Nations (Gen 10:7). 1 Chr 1:9 repeats the list and spells his name Sabta. His brothers were Seba, Havilah, Raamah and Sabtecha. Nimrod is also counted among his brothers because Gen 10:8 says Cush fathered Nimrod, though he is named apart from the list. Nothing else is recorded about Sabtah himself. Many names in this genealogy also stand for the peoples or regions descended from them, so Sabtah probably also represents a people. Its location is uncertain and the verses do not identify it. The meaning of the name is given differently by different reference works: Easton's Bible Dictionary gives "rest," Smith's Bible Dictionary "striking," and Hitchcock's Bible Names "a going about" or "old age."

Sabtecha was a son of Cush and a grandson of Ham, named in the Table of Nations in Gen 10:7 and again in the parallel genealogy in 1 Chr 1:9. He is listed fifth among the sons of Cush, after Seba, Havilah, Sabtah and Raamah, and Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary both describe him as the fifth son. Nimrod, also called a son of Cush, is named separately in the following verses. Nothing further is recorded about Sabtecha's life. Like other names in the Table of Nations, his name probably stood for a people or region descended from him, but neither passage says where they lived, and any identification remains uncertain.

Sallu was a priest listed among the chief priests who returned from the Babylonian exile in the days of Jeshua the high priest (Neh 12:7), which places him in the first return led by Zerubbabel. A later list of priestly family heads from the next generation names Kallai as head of the house "of Sallai" (Neh 12:20). Sallai is probably the same name as Sallu, used here for the family descended from him, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats the two as one priestly family. By inference from the surrounding passage, this later list belongs to the time of the high priest Joiakim, Jeshua's son. Nothing else is recorded about him. The name Sallu is also borne by a Benjamite living in Jerusalem, a different person.

Salma was a man of the tribe of Judah, named in the genealogy of 1 Chronicles as a son of Hur. The surrounding passage makes Hur the firstborn of Ephrathah and a descendant of Caleb (1 Chr 2:50). Salma is called "the father of Bethlehem." This probably means he founded the town or was the ancestor of its people, as the STEPBible Proper Names index takes it. His "sons" are listed largely as places and clans: Bethlehem, the Netophathites, Ataroth (the house of Joab), half of the Manahethites, and the Zorites. These were probably settlements and groups in the Bethlehem area. The same name appears in 1 Chr 2:11 for Salma (Salmon), the father of Boaz of Bethlehem. Whether the two are the same man is uncertain, and this entry treats Salma as the son of Hur. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning "peace; perfection."

Salome was one of the women who followed Jesus and were present at his death and resurrection. Mark names her among the women watching the crucifixion from a distance, along with Mary Magdalene and Mary the mother of James the less and Joses (Mark 15:40). After the Sabbath she and the same two women bought spices to anoint Jesus' body and went to the tomb early on the first day of the week (Mark 16:1). These are the only places she is named. Comparing the parallel list in Matt 27:56, which names "the mother of Zebedee's children" in her place, Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries identify her as the wife of Zebedee and mother of James and John, the woman who asked for places of honor for her sons (Matt 20:20). They also suggest she was probably the sister of Jesus' mother mentioned in John 19:25. These identifications are inferences, and this entry treats them as probable.

Seba was the first-named son of Cush, the son of Ham, in the table of nations (Gen 10:7; 1 Chr 1:9). His brothers were Havilah, Sabtah, Raamah and Sabtecha. Nimrod is also called a son of Cush in the following verse (Gen 10:8). Seba should not be confused with Sheba, his nephew through Raamah, who is named in the same verse. Like many names in this list, Seba probably stands for a people as well as a person. Later passages mention Seba as a distant land alongside Sheba, Egypt and Ethiopia (Ps 72:10; Isa 43:3), and Isa 45:14 speaks of the Sabeans as tall men. These links point, by inference, to a people in the region of Cush, usually placed in northeast Africa. Its exact location is uncertain. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "a drunkard" or "that turns."

Segub was a man of the tribe of Judah, the son of Hezron by the daughter of Machir, the father of Gilead. Hezron married her when he was sixty years old (1 Chr 2:21). Segub's brothers were Caleb, Jerahmeel and Ram, and Ashur was his half-brother. Segub was the father of Jair, who held twenty-three cities in the land of Gilead (1 Chr 2:22). Because his mother came from Machir's family of the tribe of Manasseh, his line probably explains why his son Jair held towns in Gilead, Machir's territory. Elsewhere Jair is called a son of Manasseh, which reflects this descent. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "fortified" or "raised." Smith's Bible Dictionary dates him to about 1682 BC, an estimate based on context. The name is shared with at least one other man in the Bible, so references to Segub need to be told apart.

Seraiah son of Tanhumeth was one of the army captains who came with their men to Gedaliah at Mizpah after the king of Babylon made Gedaliah governor of Judah following the fall of Jerusalem. He is named alongside Ishmael son of Nethaniah, Johanan son of Kareah and Jaazaniah (Jezaniah). In 2 Kgs 25:23 he is called a Netophathite, meaning a man from Netophah, a town near Bethlehem. In the parallel list in Jer 40:8 that label is attached instead to the sons of Ephai, who are named right after him. Nothing more is recorded about him. Several other men in the Bible share the name Seraiah, which Hitchcock's Bible Names explains as "prince of the Lord" and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia as "Yah hath prevailed."

Seraiah was a man of the tribe of Judah, named in its genealogy as a son of Kenaz and brother of Othniel (1 Chr 4:13). He was the father of Joab, described as "the father of the valley of Charashim," a name meaning the Valley of Craftsmen. The text explains the name with the note "for they were craftsmen," so Joab was probably the founder or leading figure of a settlement of skilled workers (1 Chr 4:14). Othniel, his brother, is by inference the same Othniel who appears elsewhere as the first judge of Israel. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia calls Seraiah the younger brother, presumably because he is listed second. The name, which the same work explains as "Yah hath prevailed," is shared by several other men in the Bible. This Joab is distinct from David's commander of the same name.

Seraiah was the son of Neriah and grandson of Maaseiah. He was the brother of Baruch, Jeremiah's scribe, whom Jer 32:12 and 36:4 also call a son of Neriah. He travelled with King Zedekiah of Judah to Babylon in the fourth year of Zedekiah's reign. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates this to about 594 BC, an estimate drawn from context. The King James Version calls him "a quiet prince." Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that the Revised Version renders this "chief chamberlain," and Smith's suggests he was the officer in charge of the royal caravan. Jeremiah gave him a written message announcing Babylon's coming ruin and told him to read it aloud when he arrived. The surrounding passage (Jer 51:60–64) adds that he was then to tie a stone to the scroll and throw it into the Euphrates, as a sign that Babylon would sink and not rise again. Several other men in the Bible share his name.

Sered was a son of Zebulun and so a grandson of Jacob and Leah. His brothers were Elon and Jahleel. He appears in the list of Jacob's family who went down to Egypt (Gen 46:14). Because he is named first in both lists, Smith's Bible Dictionary calls him Zebulun's firstborn. In the census taken in the wilderness of Moab, he is named as the ancestor of the Sardites, one of the family groups of the tribe of Zebulun (Num 26:26). Nothing else is recorded about him. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "fear," while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "dyer's vat."

Shage the Hararite was the father of Jonathan, one of the warriors listed among David's mighty men in 1 Chr 11:34. The parallel list in 2 Sam 23:32–33 reads "Jonathan, Shammah the Hararite" at the same point. Smith's Bible Dictionary takes this to mean that Shage and Shammah are the same man, and this entry follows that view by treating Shammah as another name for him. On that reading, the original text probably said "Jonathan son of Shammah" in Samuel. The STEPBible name index further links him with Shammah the son of Agee the Hararite, whom 2 Sam 23:11 praises for holding his ground against the Philistines. That would make Shage himself a renowned warrior of David's time, around 1000 BC by inference from context. "Hararite" probably means he came from the hill country, though the exact place is uncertain.

Shallum was the husband of Huldah the prophetess, who lived in Jerusalem in the reign of King Josiah. He is called the son of Tikvah (Tikvath in Chronicles) and the grandson of Harhas (Hasrah in Chronicles). The title "keeper of the wardrobe" follows these names. It is usually taken to describe Shallum himself, though the wording could also refer to his grandfather. Easton's Bible Dictionary understands the wardrobe as the temple vestments. Shallum is mentioned only to identify Huldah, when Hilkiah the priest and the king's officials went to consult her, by context about the book of the law found in the temple (2 Kgs 22:14; 2 Chr 34:22). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests he was probably the uncle of Jeremiah named in Jer 32:7. Several other men in the Bible share the name Shallum.

Shallum was a man of the tribe of Judah named in the genealogy of 1 Chronicles 2. He was the son of Sisamai and the father of Jekamiah, whose son was Elishama (1 Chr 2:40–41). By the surrounding context, his line belongs to the descendants of Jerahmeel through Sheshan, whose daughter married his Egyptian servant Jarha. The STEPBible proper-names index likewise places him in Judah's line through Jerahmeel. Nothing else is recorded about him beyond his place in this family list. The name Shallum is shared by several other people in the Bible, including a king of Israel and the husband of the prophetess Huldah, so this Shallum should not be confused with them.

Shalmai was the ancestor of a family of Nethinim, the temple servants, whose descendants returned to Jerusalem from exile in Babylon with Zerubbabel. He is known only from the two parallel lists of returning exiles (Ezra 2:46; Neh 7:48), where "the children of Shalmai" appear next to the families of Hagab or Hagaba and Hanan. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates the return to about 536 BC, an estimate drawn from context. The spelling of the name differs between versions and manuscripts. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives the Ezra form as Shamlai and the Nehemiah form as Salmai, while the King James Version reads Shalmai in both places. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning as "my garment," and Smith's gives "my thanks." Nothing more is recorded about him.

Shamer, also called Shomer, was a man of the tribe of Asher who appears only in the Asherite genealogy of 1 Chronicles. He was a son of Heber, and his brothers were Japhlet and Hotham, with a sister named Shua (1 Chr 7:32). His sons were Ahi, Rohgah, Jehubbah and Aram (1 Chr 7:34). The two spellings occur in neighbouring verses of the same list and are taken to refer to the same person, as Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary both note. The name is usually understood to mean "keeper". Nothing else is recorded about him beyond his place in the family line. Several other men in the Bible bear similar names, so he should be distinguished from them.

Shamgar, son of Anath, was a deliverer of Israel in the period of the judges, mentioned right after the account of Ehud. Judg 3:31 says he killed six hundred Philistines with an ox goad and so also delivered Israel. Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that an ox goad was a long, sharp-pointed stick used for driving cattle. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia observes that this verse is the first mention of the Philistines troubling Israel. The Song of Deborah recalls "the days of Shamgar" alongside the days of Jael as a time when the roads were deserted and travellers kept to back paths (Judg 5:6). This suggests he lived shortly before or overlapping with Deborah and Barak, and Easton's treats them as probably contemporaries for a time. Nothing else is recorded about him or his father Anath.

Shammah the Harodite was one of David's mighty warriors, listed among the elite group known as "the thirty" in 2 Sam 23:25. The parallel list in 1 Chr 11:27 calls him Shammoth the Harorite. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia takes "Harorite" as a copying variant of "Harodite" and suggests he probably came from Harod, the spring where Gideon camped (Judg 7:1). Smith's and Easton's Bible Dictionaries also identify him with Shamhuth the Izrahite, the commander of the fifth monthly division of David's army in 1 Chr 27:8. His name is spelled differently in each passage, and beyond his place in these lists nothing more is recorded about him. Several other men in the Bible share the name Shammah, including one of David's brothers and another of David's mighty men. This entry concerns only the Harodite.

Shammai was a man of the tribe of Judah, named in the genealogy of Jerahmeel, son of Hezron. He was a son of Onam and the brother of Jada, and his sons were Nadab and Abishur (1 Chr 2:28). His brother Jada's line is traced next, through Jada's sons Jether and Jonathan (1 Chr 2:32). Nothing further is recorded about his life. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "desolate." Several other men in the Bible bear the name Shammai, and this one should not be confused with them. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia lists him first among them and identifies him as a Jerahmeelite.

Shammai was a man of the tribe of Judah, named only in the genealogy of 1 Chronicles 2. He was the son of Rekem and the father of Maon, and Maon in turn was the "father of Bethzur" (1 Chr 2:44–45). From the surrounding verses (1 Chr 2:42–43), this line descends from Caleb through Hebron, whose son was Rekem, so Shammai probably belonged to the Calebite clans of southern Judah. Maon and Beth-zur are also the names of towns in the hill country of Judah, so "father of" here may mean the founder or leading figure of a settlement rather than only a parent. Nothing else is recorded about him. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "desolate." The name is shared by other men in the Judahite genealogies, so this Shammai should not be confused with them.

Sharar was a Hararite, the father of Ahiam, one of the warriors listed among David's mighty men (2 Sam 23:33). In the parallel list in 1 Chr 11:35 he is called Sacar. The difference between the two names probably comes from copying of the text, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia regards Sharar as the more likely original reading. The description "Hararite" probably refers to his family or place of origin, perhaps the hill country, though its exact meaning is uncertain. Nothing more is recorded about him beyond his son's place in David's roll of heroes. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes him as one of David's heroes, but in both lists it is his son Ahiam who is named among the mighty men.

Sharezer was a son of Sennacherib, king of Assyria, and a brother of Adrammelech and Esarhaddon. While Sennacherib was worshipping in the temple of his god Nisroch, Sharezer and Adrammelech killed him with the sword and fled to the land of Armenia. The Hebrew calls this land Ararat, a mountainous region north of Assyria. Their brother Esarhaddon then became king (2 Kgs 19:37; Isa 37:38). Both accounts place the killing after Sennacherib's failed campaign against Jerusalem in Hezekiah's reign. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia explains the name as Assyrian for "protect the king." It notes that the Babylonian Chronicle speaks of a single, unnamed son as the murderer. Some scholars, following an ancient writer quoted by Eusebius, read his full name as Nergal-sharezer. A different man named Sharezer appears in Zech 7:2.

Shashak was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, named in the Benjamite genealogy of 1 Chronicles 8. He is listed with Ahio and Jeremoth (1 Chr 8:14). This entry follows Smith's Bible Dictionary in treating him as a son of Beriah. By inference from the surrounding verses, that makes him a descendant of Elpaal, since Beriah appears among Elpaal's descendants and as a family head connected with Aijalon. The list itself does not spell out the relationship, so his exact place in it is somewhat uncertain. Eleven sons are credited to him, including Ishpan, Heber, Eliel, Abdon, Zichri, Hanan, Hananiah, Elam, Antothijah, Iphedeiah and Penuel (1 Chr 8:25). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia describes him as the founder of a Benjamite family. Smith's gives the meaning of his name as "longing"; Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "a bag of linen."

Shaul was a Levite of the clan of Kohath who appears in the genealogies of 1 Chronicles 6. In 1 Chr 6:24 he closes a line of descent from Kohath that runs through Tahath, Uriel and Uzziah. The parallel ancestry of the singer Heman, which traces back through the prophet Samuel, has a Joel son of Azariah and father of Elkanah at the same point (1 Chr 6:36). For this reason the two names are usually taken as the same man, and this entry follows that view. Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests that Joel may be a copying variant of Shaul, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia calls him a Levite ancestor of Samuel. The two lists give his father as Uzziah and as Azariah, which are probably alternate forms of one name. Several other people in the Bible are also called Shaul.

Sheariah was one of the six sons of Azel, a Benjamite descended from King Saul through Jonathan. He appears only in the genealogy of Saul's family, which is given twice in nearly identical words (1 Chr 8:38; 1 Chr 9:44). His brothers were Azrikam, Bocheru, Ishmael, Obadiah and Hanan. The surrounding lists trace Azel's line back through Jonathan's son Merib-baal (Mephibosheth) to Saul, so Sheariah belonged to a late generation of Saul's descendants. Nothing is recorded about his life beyond his name and place in the family. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "valued by Jehovah," while Hitchcock's Bible Names offers "gate of the Lord" or "tempest of the Lord."

Sheba (son of Raamah) was a son of Raamah and a grandson of Cush, listed with his brother Dedan in the Table of Nations (Gen 10:7) and again in the genealogy of 1 Chr 1:9. Beyond these two genealogical entries, nothing is recorded about him personally. He is usually understood as the ancestor of a people. Easton's Bible Dictionary says his descendants settled with those of Dedan along the Persian Gulf. He should be kept distinct from Seba, his father's brother, named in the same verse, and from other men called Sheba, including the son of Joktan in the line of Shem (Gen 10:28). Which Sheba gave rise to the kingdom whose queen visited Solomon is uncertain. The name has been interpreted in Hitchcock's Bible Names as meaning "oath" or "repose," among other suggestions.

Sheba (son of Joktan) was one of the thirteen sons of Joktan, a descendant of Shem through Eber, named in the table of nations in Gen 10:28 and again in 1 Chr 1:22. He appears only in these lists, with brothers including Ophir, Havilah, Jobab and Abimael, and nothing is told of his life. Many of Joktan's sons are taken as names of peoples or regions in Arabia. Easton's Bible Dictionary calls Sheba probably the founder of the Sabeans, and the STEPBible proper-names index links him with the ancient kingdom of Sheba in southern Arabia, known for its wealth and trade. The name is shared by others, such as a son of Raamah in the line of Ham (Gen 10:7) and a grandson of Abraham through Jokshan (Gen 25:3). Which of these lines the later kingdom of Sheba descends from is uncertain.

Sheba was a son of Jokshan and a grandson of Abraham through Keturah, whom 1 Chr 1:32 calls Abraham's concubine. His brother was Dedan, whose sons Asshurim, Letushim and Leummim are also named (Gen 25:3). The genealogies list him without any further detail. The name Sheba is shared by several people in the Bible, including a descendant of Shem through Joktan (Gen 10:28) and a descendant of Ham through Cush (Gen 10:7). Those two also have a brother or relative named Dedan, which suggests the names stand for related Arabian peoples or tribes. STEPBible Proper Names connects this Sheba with the peoples of southern Arabia, and the name may be linked to the land of Sheba known from the story of its queen. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "oath" or "captivity."

Shechaniah was a member of the royal line of David, in the tribe of Judah. He appears in the list of David's descendants after the Babylonian exile in 1 Chr 3. This entry treats him as a son of Hananiah, whom 1 Chr 3:19 names as a son of Zerubbabel, and as a brother of Pelatiah, Jesaiah, Rephaiah, Arnan and Obadiah. The wording of 1 Chr 3:21 is compressed, though. It can also be read as naming separate family branches without saying how each one connects to Hananiah. Shechaniah's son was Shemaiah, whose sons were Hattush, Igeal, Bariah, Neariah and Shaphat. The verse counts them as six, although only five names appear. The STEPBible proper names index traces his line back to David through Jeconiah. Several other men in the Bible share this name.

Shechaniah, son of Jehiel and one of the descendants of Elam, spoke for the people when Ezra learned that many returned exiles had married foreign wives. He admitted that they had sinned against God by taking wives from the peoples of the land, but he said there was still hope for Israel (Ezra 10:2). The following verses show him proposing a covenant to send those wives away and urging Ezra to act. A Jehiel of the sons of Elam also appears in Ezra 10:26 among the men who had married foreign wives, which may be his father. This entry also treats him as the Shechaniah whose son Shemaiah repaired part of Jerusalem's wall in Nehemiah's time (Neh 3:29). Easton's Bible Dictionary describes that Shechaniah only as Shemaiah's father. Because several men share this name, it is uncertain whether these two passages refer to the same person.

Shechem was a son of Gilead in the tribe of Manasseh and the ancestor of the Shechemite clan. Numbers lists him among Gilead's sons, with Abiezer, Asriel, Helek, Hepher and Shemida, each the founder of a family within Manasseh (Num 26:31). When Joshua divided the land, these six clans received their own allotment, west of the Jordan by inference from the passage, apart from the Makirites who held Gilead and Bashan (Josh 17:2). Through Manasseh he belonged to the wider tribe of Joseph. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "back" or "shoulder." He should not be confused with Shechem the son of Hamor in Genesis, who shares the name, or with the city of Shechem, although the clan may have been linked to that region.

Shelemiah was the father of Jehucal, also called Jucal, an official in the reign of King Zedekiah of Judah. He is known only through his son. King Zedekiah sent Jehucal with the priest Zephaniah to ask Jeremiah to pray for the people (Jer 37:3). Later Jucal was one of the officials who heard Jeremiah's message to the people (Jer 38:1). By inference from the next verses, those officials pressed the king to have Jeremiah put to death, which is why Easton's Bible Dictionary describes Shelemiah as the father of one of Jeremiah's accusers. The two verses spell his son's name differently, and according to the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia the Hebrew form of Shelemiah's name also differs slightly between them. Nothing more is recorded about him. Several other men in the Bible share his name.

Sheleph was the second of the thirteen sons of Joktan named in the Table of Nations, listed after Almodad and before Hazarmaveth and Jerah (Gen 10:26; 1 Chr 1:20). Through Joktan he belonged to the line of Shem, by way of Eber. His brothers included Sheba, Ophir and Havilah, names that are elsewhere linked with regions of Arabia. The two verses that mention him give only his name and place in the list. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "a drawing forth." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that Sheleph is also the name of a Yemenite tribe or district in southern Arabia, known from Sabean inscriptions and Arabian geographers. On that basis he is probably to be understood as the ancestor or namesake of a people living there, as with several of Joktan's other sons.

Shelomoth was a Levite of the family of Izhar, a branch of the Kohathite clan. In 1 Chr 23:18 he is called Shelomith and described as the chief of the sons of Izhar, in the list of Levite families organized under David. In 1 Chr 24:22 he appears as Shelomoth, head of the Izharites, with Jahath named among his sons. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both treat the two spellings as the same man. This entry follows that view. Exod 6:21 names Korah, Nepheg and Zichri as sons of Izhar but does not mention Shelomith. Because the Chronicles lists are set in David's time, "son of Izhar" there probably means a descendant and family head rather than an immediate son. The same may be true of Jahath. Nothing else is recorded about him.

Shema was a man of the tribe of Judah, listed in the genealogy of 1 Chronicles 2 as one of the four sons of Hebron, along with Korah, Tappuah and Rekem (1 Chr 2:43). He was the father of Raham, who in turn is called the father of Jorkoam (1 Chr 2:44). Hebron here appears within the line of Caleb, and some of the names in this list, including Hebron, Tappuah and possibly Jorkoam, are also place names in Judah. They may therefore stand partly for clans or settlements as well as individuals, though the text presents them as a family line. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "hearing" or "obeying." Several other men in the Bible share the name Shema, and this one is known only from these two verses.

Shemaiah son of Hasshub was a Levite of the clan of Merari who lived in Jerusalem after the return from the Babylonian exile. Both lists of Jerusalem's resettled inhabitants trace his line through Hasshub (spelled Hashub in Nehemiah), Azrikam and Hashabiah. 1 Chr 9:14 places him among the sons of Merari, while Neh 11:15 adds the name Bunni to the line. The two passages are generally taken to describe the same man, and this entry treats them that way. He is one of several people in the Bible named Shemaiah, a name meaning "the Lord hears" and borne most often by priests, Levites and prophets, according to the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia. Nothing more is recorded about him beyond his ancestry and his place among the Levites settled in Jerusalem.

Shemaiah was a Levite of the family of Jeduthun, the son of Galal and the father of Obadiah. He appears only in genealogies of Levites who lived in Jerusalem after the return from exile. 1 Chr 9:16 names him as Obadiah's father. The parallel list in Neh 11:17 gives the same line under slightly different names, "Abda the son of Shammua, the son of Galal, the son of Jeduthun." For this reason Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treat Shammua as another form of Shemaiah and Abda as another form of Obadiah. The context in Nehemiah, which places him among the singers led by Mattaniah, suggests that his family served in the temple music. Several other men in the Bible share the name Shemaiah, which the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes was common among priests, Levites and prophets.

Shemaiah was a Levite in the time of David, the chief of the family descended from Elizaphan. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identifies this as a clan of the Kohathite branch of the Levites, which matches Num 3:30, where Elizaphan leads the Kohathites. Shemaiah led two hundred of his relatives when David organized the Levites to carry the ark of the covenant from the house of Obed-edom up to Jerusalem. David called for him, along with other Levite leaders and the priests Zadok and Abiathar, and told them to prepare themselves for this task. His name means "the LORD hears." Several other men in the Bible share the name, and this Shemaiah should not be confused with them.

Shephatiah was the fifth son of David, born to him by his wife Abital. He is named only in the two parallel lists of the sons born to David at Hebron, during the years David ruled from that city before moving to Jerusalem. In both lists he comes after Adonijah, the son of Haggith, and before Ithream, the son of Eglah. The surrounding passage states that these sons were born in Hebron (2 Sam 3:5). Smith's Bible Dictionary dates his birth to about 1050 BC, an estimate. Nothing further is recorded about his life. Abital appears only as his mother, and no other children of hers are named. His name means "the Lord has judged" or "judged by the Lord." Several other men in the Bible are also called Shephatiah and should not be confused with this son of David.

Shephatiah was an ancestor whose descendants were listed among the families of "Solomon's servants" who returned from exile in Babylon to Jerusalem and Judah. His name appears in two parallel lists of returnees (Ezra 2:57; Neh 7:59), next to Hattil, Pochereth of Zebaim, and Ami, who is called Amon in Nehemiah.
