The surrounding passage groups Solomon's servants with the temple servants and gives a combined total of 392 for both groups (Ezra 2:58), so the size of Shephatiah's own family is not stated. The phrase "Solomon's servants" probably refers to descendants of workers who served King Solomon. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that 1 Esdras gives his name as Saphat. The name means "the Lord has judged." Several other men in the Bible share this name, and this one is otherwise unknown.

Shepho was a son of Shobal and a descendant of Seir the Horite, listed with his brothers Alvan, Manahath, Ebal and Onam among the inhabitants of the land of Seir (Gen 36:23). The parallel genealogy in 1 Chr 1:40 spells his name Shephi and gives Alvan as Alian. The surrounding passage in Genesis 36 traces the Horite clans who lived in Seir, later Edom, before and alongside Esau's descendants. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia describes him as a Horite chief. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "bareness," while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "desert." Nothing more is recorded about him beyond his place in these lists.

Shilhi was the father of Azubah, the mother of King Jehoshaphat of Judah. He is mentioned only in the two parallel notices of Jehoshaphat's accession, which give the king's age as thirty-five and his reign as twenty-five years in Jerusalem (1 Kgs 22:42; 2 Chr 20:31). Since Jehoshaphat was the son of King Asa, Azubah was presumably Asa's wife, which made Shilhi the maternal grandfather of Jehoshaphat. Jehoshaphat appears in Matthew's genealogy of Jesus, which links Shilhi to that line through his daughter. Nothing else is recorded about him. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "armed." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes a suggestion that "Shilhi" may be a form of Shilhim, a town in Judah (Josh 15:32), and so could name Azubah's birthplace instead of her father. This entry follows the usual reading of Shilhi as a personal name.

Shimeath was the parent of Jozachar, also called Zabad, one of the two royal servants who conspired against King Joash of Judah and killed him. 2 Kgs 12:21 names the killer simply as "Jozachar the son of Shimeath." The parallel account in 2 Chr 24:26 calls him "Zabad the son of Shimeath an Ammonitess," describing Shimeath as a woman from Ammon. Smith's Bible Dictionary and Tyndale House's proper-names list follow Chronicles and identify Shimeath as his mother. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the name in Kings reads as masculine, which makes Shimeath the father there, and suggests that the writer of Chronicles took the name's final letter as a feminine ending. This entry lists Shimeath as male. Nothing else is recorded about Shimeath.

Shimei, son of Elah, was an official of David and Solomon. He is one of several men in the Bible with this name. When Adonijah tried to claim David's throne, Shimei was among those who did not side with him, along with Zadok the priest, Benaiah, Nathan the prophet, Rei and David's mighty men (1 Kgs 1:8). A Shimei son of Elah later appears among Solomon's twelve district officers, who supplied food for the king and his household. His district was the territory of Benjamin (1 Kgs 4:18). This entry treats the two mentions as the same man, following Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia. The latter suggests that Solomon appointed him because of his loyalty. Smith's Bible Dictionary lists the two separately. The Jewish historian Josephus calls him "the friend of David."

Shimei was a man of the tribe of Simeon, the son of Zacchur and a descendant of Simeon through Mishma (1 Chr 4:26). Mishma himself appears in the preceding verse as a descendant of Simeon's son Shaul. Shimei is noted for having an unusually large family of sixteen sons and six daughters. The text contrasts this with his relatives, who had few children, so that the clan as a whole did not grow as large as the tribe of Judah (1 Chr 4:27). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia places him in the time of David. It links his many descendants to the Simeonite expansion described later in the same chapter, into Gerar and Mount Seir in Hezekiah's day. Several other men in the Bible share the name Shimei, which possibly means "hear me."

Shimei was a Levite in the reign of King Hezekiah of Judah and the brother of Cononiah. When Hezekiah restored temple worship, the people brought in offerings, tithes and dedicated things, which were stored in chambers at the temple. Cononiah was put in charge of these contributions, and Shimei ranked next under him (2 Chr 31:12). Ten other Levites, including Jehiel, Azaziah and Benaiah, served as overseers under the two brothers. They were appointed at the command of Hezekiah and of Azariah, the ruler of the house of God (2 Chr 31:13). Shimei is a common name in the Bible, and Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests he may be the same as the Levite Shimei of Heman's family listed just before this passage, though this is uncertain. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "that hears" or "my fame."

Shimrith, also called Shomer, was the parent of Jehozabad, one of the royal servants who conspired against and killed King Joash of Judah. The other conspirator was Jozachar, also called Zabad, son of Shimeath. Joash was buried in the city of David, and his son Amaziah became king (2 Kgs 12:21). In 2 Kgs 12:21 the name appears as Shomer, while the parallel account in 2 Chr 24:26 gives the feminine form Shimrith and describes her as a Moabitess. Easton's Bible Dictionary, Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia take Shimrith to be Jehozabad's mother. Smith also notes that Shomer in Kings could be read as a father's name. This entry treats Shimrith as male, following the Kings reading of Shomer as a father. Nothing else is recorded about this person.

Shobai was the ancestor of one of the families of temple gatekeepers (the "porters" of the King James Version) whose descendants returned to Jerusalem from exile in Babylon. His family is listed with those of Shallum, Ater, Talmon, Akkub and Hatita, and the gatekeepers of these six families together numbered 139 in Ezra 2:42 and 138 in the parallel list at Neh 7:45. Smith's Bible Dictionary places this return with Zerubbabel, before about 536 BC. Nothing further is recorded about Shobai himself. The meaning of his name is uncertain: Easton's Bible Dictionary gives "captors," Smith's Bible Dictionary "glorious," and Hitchcock's Bible Names "turning captivity."

Shuah was a son of Abraham by Keturah, the wife Abraham took after Sarah's death and whom 1 Chr 1:32 calls his concubine. He is named last of her six sons, after Zimran, Jokshan, Medan, Midian and Ishbak, which made him a half-brother of Isaac and Ishmael. Nothing is recorded of his life beyond these two genealogies. Genesis 25:6 says Abraham gave gifts to the sons of his concubines and sent them away eastward, so Shuah was probably among them. The STEPBible proper-names index says his descendants formed a tribe, and many link this people with Bildad 'the Shuhite' in Job 2:11, though that connection is inferred. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as 'wealth', while Hitchcock's Bible Names offers 'ditch' or 'humiliation'. Several other people in the Bible bear the same or a similar name.

Shubael, also called Shebuel, was a Levite musician and one of the fourteen sons of Heman. He is named fourth among them in 1 Chr 25:4 under the form Shebuel. In the casting of lots that divided the temple musicians into twenty-four rotating groups, the thirteenth lot fell to Shubael, whose group of his sons and relatives numbered twelve (1 Chr 25:20). Heman's sons served under their father in the music of worship, and the surrounding passage describes these musicians as appointed in David's time to prophesy with lyres, harps and cymbals. Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that Heman's sons had the duty to "lift up the horn" in the temple service. Several other men in the Bible share this name, including a descendant of Moses, and they should be kept distinct from this son of Heman.

Shuni was a son of Gad, the son of Jacob, and the ancestor of the Shunite family within the tribe of Gad. He appears in the list of Jacob's descendants who went down with him into Egypt (Gen 46:16). He appears again in the census of Israel taken in the plains of Moab, where his line is counted as the clan of the Shunites (Num 26:15). His brothers were Zephon (Ziphion), Haggi, Ozni (called Ezbon in Genesis), Eri, Arod (Arodi) and Areli. Nothing else is recorded about him. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "fortunate," while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "changed" or "sleeping."

Shuppim was a descendant of Benjamin, named with his brother Huppim as one of "the children of Ir" in the genealogy of 1 Chr 7:12. Smith's Bible Dictionary takes Ir to be the same man as Iri, son of Bela and grandson of Benjamin, which would make Shuppim a great-grandson of Benjamin. In 1 Chr 7:15 he and Huppim are named as brothers of Maachah, who became the wife of Machir of the tribe of Manasseh. Apart from these genealogical notes, the text records nothing more about him. The name Shuppim belongs to more than one person in the Bible, and this entry covers only the Benjamite son of Ir.

Sia was the ancestor of a family of temple servants (the Nethinim) whose descendants returned from the Babylonian exile to Jerusalem. The "children of Sia" appear in the list of returning families in Neh 7:47, between the families of Keros and Padon. The parallel list in Ezra 2:44 spells the name Siaha. Smith's Bible Dictionary connects the family with the return led by Zerubbabel and notes that the apocryphal book 1 Esdras gives the name as Sud. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives its meaning as "moving" or "help." Nothing else is recorded about Sia himself. He is known only as the founder of this family line.

Simeon was a man living in Jerusalem at the time of Jesus' birth. Luke describes him as just and devout, waiting for "the consolation of Israel," and says the Holy Spirit was upon him (Luke 2:25). When Mary and Joseph brought the infant Jesus to the temple, Simeon took the child in his arms and praised God. His words of praise are traditionally known as the Nunc Dimittis, from their opening words in Latin. He then blessed the parents and told Mary that her child was set for the fall and rising again of many in Israel and would be a sign spoken against (Luke 2:34). According to Hitchcock's Bible Names, his name means "that hears" or "that is heard." Several other people in the Bible share the name Simeon, including a son of Jacob, and they are distinct from this man.

Simon was one of the brothers of Jesus, named alongside James, Joses and Judas (Jude) when people in Jesus' hometown questioned where his teaching came from. They asked, "Is not this the carpenter's son?" and were offended at him (Matt 13:55; Mark 6:3). Matthew lists Simon third among the brothers and Mark lists him last. Nothing more is recorded about him in these passages. Interpreters have long differed on how Jesus' "brethren" were related to him, with some taking them as cousins or as Joseph's sons from an earlier marriage. This entry follows the view that Simon was a son of Joseph and Mary, and so of the tribe of Judah. Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that some writers identify him with Symeon, who later led the church in Jerusalem, and others with Simon the Canaanite. The name Simon is shared by several people in the Bible.

Simon, known as "the leper," was a man of Bethany in whose house Jesus was staying or dining shortly before his death. During the meal a woman broke open an alabaster jar of very costly ointment of spikenard and poured it on Jesus' head (Matt 26:6; Mark 14:3). Matthew and Mark do not name the woman. Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies her as Mary, drawing on the related account in John 12:1–3, which places an anointing at Bethany in a home connected with Lazarus, Martha and Mary. Simon's title probably describes a past condition, since lepers were kept apart from others under the law. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both suggest he may have been healed by Jesus, though the text does not say so. He should not be confused with the several other men named Simon in the Bible.

Sinite is listed as a son of Canaan in the Table of Nations, named between the Arkite and the Arvadite (Gen 10:17; 1 Chr 1:15). As with most of Canaan's descendants in these lists, the name is in a gentilic form ("the Sinite"). It refers to the ancestor of a people, or to the people themselves, rather than to an individual whose life is described. His brothers include Zidon, Heth, the Jebusite, the Amorite, the Girgasite, the Hivite, the Arkite, the Arvadite, the Zemarite and the Hamathite. Nothing else is recorded about him. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes the Sinite as an inhabitant of a place called Sin near Arka. Smith's Bible Dictionary places the tribe in the northern part of the Lebanon region. This fits the neighbouring names, which point to towns along the Phoenician coast and in Syria.

Sippai, also called Saph, was a Philistine warrior described as one of "the sons of the giant," that is, a descendant of the Rapha or Rephaim. He was killed by Sibbechai the Hushathite, one of David's warriors, in a battle with the Philistines during David's reign (about 1050 BC by Smith's Bible Dictionary's estimate). 2 Sam 21:18 places the battle at Gob and calls him Saph. The parallel account in 1 Chr 20:4 places it at Gezer and calls him Sippai. The surrounding passage (2 Sam 21:22) groups him with Ishbi-benob, Goliath (or Lahmi, Goliath's brother, in Chronicles) and an unnamed man of great stature as giants born to "the giant in Gath." This may mean a common father or simply a common ancestry. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes a suggestion that he was Goliath's son, which the text does not settle. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the name's meaning as "threshold."

Sisera was the ancestor of a family of temple servants (Nethinim) whose descendants returned to Jerusalem from the Babylonian exile with Zerubbabel. He is known only from the parallel lists of returnees in Ezra 2:53 and Neh 7:55, where "the children of Sisera" appear alongside the families of Barkos and Tamah. Nothing else is recorded about him. He is a different person from Sisera, the Canaanite army commander in the book of Judges. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes there is no evidence that this family descended from the earlier Sisera. Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests the name points to Canaanite captives assigned to humble duties in the temple. The return is usually dated to about 538–536 BC.

Sister of Tahpenes was an unnamed Egyptian woman, the sister of Queen Tahpenes, wife of the Pharaoh who ruled Egypt during the reign of Solomon. Pharaoh gave her in marriage to Hadad the Edomite, a member of Edom's royal family who had fled to Egypt as a boy and won Pharaoh's favour (1 Kgs 11:19). She bore Hadad a son, Genubath. Her sister Tahpenes weaned the child in Pharaoh's house, and Genubath grew up in Pharaoh's household among Pharaoh's own sons (1 Kgs 11:20). Through this marriage Hadad became tied to the Egyptian royal family. Her name is not given, and nothing more is recorded about her.

The sons of Jashen were men listed among David's mighty warriors in 2 Sam 23:32. Their father appears as Jashen there and as Hashem the Gizonite in the parallel list at 1 Chr 11:34, so "Gizonite" probably names the family's home town. Neither passage gives the sons' names or their number. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats the two names as the same person, and Smith's Bible Dictionary counts the sons of Hashem as members of David's guard. In both lists the phrase is followed by the name Jonathan. Some readers take Jonathan to be one of these sons, but the wording leaves this uncertain, since 1 Chr 11:34 calls him "the son of Shage the Hararite."

Sopater was a believer from Berea in Macedonia who travelled with Paul. Acts 20:4 lists him first among the companions who went with Paul into Asia as he left Greece for Jerusalem, along with Aristarchus, Secundus, Gaius, Timothy, Tychicus and Trophimus. This entry links him to Paul's mission in Macedonia and Greece, dated about AD 54 by inference from context. The Revised Version adds that he was the son of Pyrrhus, a detail the King James Version omits. Easton's, Smith's and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia all take him to be probably the same man as Sosipater, a longer form of the same name. In Rom 16:21 Sosipater, with Timothy, Lucius and Jason, sends greetings to the Christians in Rome, and Paul calls him a kinsman, which the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia understands as a fellow Jew. This entry follows that identification. His name means roughly "saviour of his father."

Sophereth was the ancestor of a family counted among "the children of Solomon's servants" in the lists of exiles who returned from Babylon to Jerusalem and Judah (Ezra 2:55; Neh 7:57). Smith's Bible Dictionary places this return with Zerubbabel, before about 536 BC. The name appears only in these two parallel lists, which name nothing about Sophereth beyond the family line. In Ezra the Hebrew carries the definite article, so the Revised Version reads "Hassophereth" there, as the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning as "scribe" or "numbering," and Smith's gives "writing." This entry treats Sophereth as female, a reading suggested by the feminine ending of the name. The name may also have been the title of an office, such as a scribe, rather than a personal name, so whether it refers to a single individual is uncertain.

Sosthenes was the chief ruler of the synagogue at Corinth during Paul's mission there. Acts 18:17 records that after Gallio, the Roman governor, refused to hear the Jewish leaders' case against Paul, a crowd of Greeks seized Sosthenes and beat him in front of the judgment seat, and Gallio paid no attention. The text does not explain why he was attacked. Paul later names "Sosthenes our brother" as co-sender of 1 Corinthians (1 Cor 1:1). Whether this is the same man is uncertain. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia calls it possible, and the Tyndale House proper names index treats them as one person who later joined Paul's work. Other interpreters see two different men. This entry follows the single-person view. The events at Corinth date to about AD 49–51, an estimate from context. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "savior" or "strong."

Sotai was the ancestor, or founder, of a family counted among "the children of Solomon's servants" in the lists of exiles who returned from Babylon to Jerusalem and Judah (Ezra 2:55; Neh 7:57). The two lists are near-identical, and in both his family is named first in this group, ahead of Sophereth and Peruda (Perida). Solomon's servants were probably descendants of laborers or attendants assigned to royal or temple service in Solomon's time. Smith's Bible Dictionary places this return with Zerubbabel, before about 536 BC, which is an inferred date. Nothing is recorded about Sotai himself beyond his name. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives its meaning as "binding," and Smith's gives "changeful."

Tabbaoth was the ancestor of a family of Nethinim, or temple servants, whose descendants were among the exiles who returned from Babylon to Judah. The family appears third in the list of temple servants, after the families of Ziha and Hasupha, in both versions of the list of returnees (Ezra 2:43; Neh 7:46). Smith's Bible Dictionary places their return with Zerubbabel, before about 536 BC. Nothing is recorded of Tabbaoth himself. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary give the meaning of the name as "rings". The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests the family may have been named after a place rather than a person, and notes the same family in 1 Esdras 5:29.

Tahath was a Levite of the Kohathite clan, the son of Assir, named in two genealogies of Levi's descendants in 1 Chronicles 6. In the first list, which traces the line of Kohath, he comes after Assir and is followed by his son Uriel, then Uzziah and Shaul (1 Chr 6:24). In the second, which traces the ancestry of Heman the temple singer, he again appears as the son of Assir, son of Ebiasaph, son of Korah (1 Chr 6:37). There the next name, from the preceding verse, is Zephaniah rather than Uriel. The two lists probably refer to the same man and follow different lines of his descendants, though the reason for the difference is not explained. Several other people in the Bible share the name Tahath. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives its meaning as "fear" or "going down."

Tahpenes was a queen of Egypt, the wife of the Pharaoh who took in Hadad the Edomite. The surrounding passage in 1 Kings 11 shows that Hadad had fled to Egypt as a boy when David's forces struck Edom. Pharaoh favored him so much that he gave him Tahpenes' sister, who is not named, as his wife (1 Kgs 11:19). Their son Genubath was weaned by Tahpenes in Pharaoh's house and grew up among Pharaoh's own sons (1 Kgs 11:20). The text does not name the Pharaoh she was married to. Smith's Bible Dictionary places her around 1000 BC, in the time of David and Solomon, which fits the setting of the passage. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meanings "standard," "flight" or "temptation" for her name, though its origin is probably Egyptian.

Tahrea was a son of Micah in the genealogy of the tribe of Benjamin that traces the descendants of King Saul. He is listed with his brothers Pithon, Melech and Ahaz (1 Chr 9:41). The earlier copy of the same list spells his name Tarea (1 Chr 8:35), and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats that form as a copyist's slip for Tahrea. The verses just before each list name Micah as the son of Merib-baal (Mephibosheth), son of Jonathan, son of Saul, which makes Tahrea a great-great-grandson of Saul. Smith's Bible Dictionary accordingly calls him a grandson of Mephibosheth. Nothing else is recorded about him beyond his name and family. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "cunning", while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "anger" or "wicked contention."

Tamah, also spelled Thamah (and Temah in some modern translations), was the ancestor of a family of temple servants who returned from exile in Babylon. His name appears only in the two parallel lists of returning exiles, in Ezra 2:53 and Neh 7:55. There his descendants are named alongside the families of Barkos and Sisera. The surrounding lists place these families among the Nethinim, the servants assigned to assist at the temple. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes them as returning with Zerubbabel. Nothing else is recorded about Tamah himself, and it is not clear whether he was a real individual or a name used for a family group.

Tanhumeth was the father of Seraiah, one of the army captains who came with their men to Gedaliah at Mizpah after the king of Babylon made Gedaliah governor of Judah following the fall of Jerusalem. Tanhumeth himself does nothing in the text and appears only as Seraiah's father. In 2 Kgs 25:23 the description "the Netophathite" follows his name, which suggests the family came from Netophah, a town near Bethlehem. In the parallel list in Jer 40:8 the same term is attached instead to the sons of Ephai. Smith's Bible Dictionary places him before about 582 BC, a date inferred from the context of Gedaliah's governorship. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of his name as "consolation."

Tarshish (son of Javan) is named in the Table of Nations as one of the four sons of Javan, alongside Elishah, Kittim and Dodanim (Gen 10:4; 1 Chr 1:7). Since Javan was a son of Japheth, Tarshish was a great-grandson of Noah. Nothing is recorded of him beyond his name. As with his brothers, the name probably stands for a people or region as much as for an individual, and the STEPBible proper-names index links him with the ancient city of Tarshish, the distant seaport mentioned often elsewhere in the Old Testament. That place's location is uncertain, and it is commonly placed somewhere in the western Mediterranean. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "contemplation" or "examination." He is distinct from the other men named Tarshish in the Bible.

Tartan was the title of a senior Assyrian military commander. In the King James Version it reads like a personal name, but the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia and Smith's Bible Dictionary explain it as an official rank, Assyrian tartanu or turtanu, probably the commander-in-chief and the highest official after the king. It appears in two passages. In Isa 20:1, Sargon king of Assyria sends the Tartan against the Philistine city of Ashdod, and he captures it. In 2 Kgs 18:17, the king of Assyria, named as Sennacherib in the surrounding narrative, sends the Tartan with the Rabsaris and the Rabshakeh from Lachish to Jerusalem with a large army. They stop by the conduit of the upper pool to confront King Hezekiah. Because these events happened under two different kings, the two passages probably refer to two different men who held the same office. Neither man's personal name is known.

Tema was a son of Ishmael, Abraham's son by Hagar. He appears ninth among Ishmael's twelve sons in the genealogy of Gen 25:13–15, and in the parallel list in 1 Chr 1:29–30. Bashemath was his sister. The surrounding passage describes these twelve sons as princes of their own tribes (Gen 25:16), so Tema was probably regarded as the founder of a people. STEPBible's proper-names index links him with the ancient Arabian city of Tema. That place is mentioned elsewhere for its caravans and its people (Job 6:19; Isa 21:14; Jer 25:23) and is generally identified with the oasis of Tayma in northwestern Saudi Arabia. Nothing else is recorded about Tema himself. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "admiration" or "perfection."

Teman was one of the chiefs ("dukes" in the King James Version) of Edom, named in the list of chiefs descended from Esau in Gen 36:42 and repeated in 1 Chr 1:53. He appears between the chiefs Kenaz and Mibzar. The surrounding passage (Gen 36:40–43) says these chiefs are named after their families and their places, so the name may refer to a clan or district as much as to an individual. Several people in the Bible share the name. Earlier in the same chapter a Teman is named as a grandson of Esau through Eliphaz and as a chief, and some readers take the two as the same figure or clan. This entry treats the chief in the closing list separately. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the name's meaning as "the south."

Teresh was one of two chamberlains of the Persian king Ahasuerus who guarded the palace door. Esth 2:21 says he and his fellow doorkeeper Bigthan (also spelled Bigthana) became angry and plotted to harm the king. The following verses, Esth 2:22–23, say that Mordecai, who sat in the king's gate, learned of the plot and told Queen Esther, who reported it to the king. After an inquiry both men were hanged, and the matter was written in the royal chronicles. Later, when the king could not sleep and had the chronicles read to him, he heard the account of Mordecai's report against Teresh and Bigthana (Esth 6:2). This led to Mordecai being honored. Smith's Bible Dictionary takes the name to mean "strictness," and Easton's Bible Dictionary gives "severe."

Tertullus was an orator, probably a professional advocate, who came with Ananias the high priest and the elders to present their case against Paul before Felix, the Roman governor (Acts 24:1). The setting was Caesarea, where Paul had been sent, and this entry dates the hearing to about AD 56, an estimate inferred from context. Tertullus opened his speech by praising Felix for the peace and reforms the nation enjoyed under him (Acts 24:2). The following verses (Acts 24:5–6) describe how he went on to accuse Paul of stirring up unrest among Jews throughout the world, of leading the sect of the Nazarenes, and of trying to profane the temple. His name is a diminutive of the Latin Tertius, "third." Smith's Bible Dictionary infers he was of Roman or Italian origin, while the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that Roman names were common among Greeks and Jews, so his background is uncertain.

Theophilus was the man to whom the Gospel of Luke and the Acts of the Apostles are addressed. The author says he wrote his orderly account so that Theophilus would have it (Luke 1:3). Acts opens by addressing him again and referring back to that "former treatise" about what Jesus did and taught (Acts 1:1). His name means "friend of God" or "loved by God." Luke calls him "most excellent," the same title Paul uses for the Roman governors Felix and Festus (Acts 23:26; 26:25). From this, Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary conclude that he was probably a person of rank, perhaps a Roman official. Some have suggested the name stands for any Christian reader, but the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia takes the title to point to a real individual. Nothing more is known of him, and later traditions about his life are uncertain.

Tibni was the son of Ginath and a rival of Omri for the throne of Israel. After Zimri's brief reign ended in his death, the people of Israel split into two factions: half followed Tibni to make him king, and half followed Omri (1 Kgs 16:21). Omri's supporters eventually prevailed, Tibni died, and Omri became sole king (1 Kgs 16:22). The text does not say how Tibni died. Comparing the date of Zimri's reign in 1 Kgs 16:15 with the start of Omri's reign in 1 Kgs 16:23 suggests the contest lasted about four years. This entry places it at roughly 929–925 BC, by inference from context. Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that Omri was the army's choice, while Tibni was probably backed by the people of Tirzah. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes him as a man of some standing. These two verses are the only biblical mentions of him.

Tidal was the "king of nations" (Hebrew goyim, sometimes rendered Goiim) named in Gen 14:1 as one of four eastern kings in the days of Abraham, allied with Chedorlaomer king of Elam, Amraphel king of Shinar and Arioch king of Ellasar. Together these four fought against five kings of the cities of the plain, in the battle in the vale of Siddim (Gen 14:9). Genesis says nothing else about him, and what "nations" he ruled is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary takes goyim as Gutium, a land east of the Tigris and north of Elam. Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests he led various nomadic tribes. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia links his name with Tudhula in a late Babylonian text and with the Hittite royal name Tudhaliya, suggesting he may have been a Hittite ruler, though it treats the identification as uncertain. The Greek Septuagint renders his name Thargal.

Tikvah, also spelled Tikvath, was the son of Hasrah and the father of Shallum, the husband of the prophetess Huldah. He is mentioned only in her genealogy, in the account of how King Josiah's officials consulted Huldah in Jerusalem after the book of the law was found in the temple (2 Kgs 22:14; 2 Chr 34:22). His father's name appears as Harhas in Kings and Hasrah in Chronicles. Either Shallum or Tikvah's line is described as "keeper of the wardrobe"; the wording does not make clear which. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "hope" and notes that the Chronicles form is properly read Tokhath. It places him before about 632 BC, a date inferred from the time of Josiah. The name Tikvah is also borne by at least one other man in the Bible.

Timnah was one of the chiefs, called "dukes" in the King James Version, descended from Esau and listed among the leaders of Edom. He heads the list of chiefs named "according to their families, after their places" in Gen 36:40, and the same list is repeated in 1 Chr 1:51, where it follows the death of King Hadad. Because these chiefs are named by their places, Timnah may be the name of a clan or district as well as a person. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests there was probably a place called Timna in Edom, noting that the early writers Eusebius and Jerome knew of a Thamna there. The name also recalls Timna, Esau's son's concubine and Lotan's sister, mentioned earlier in Genesis 36, though any link is uncertain. Nothing further is recorded about him. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "forbidding."

Tiras was a son of Japheth and a grandson of Noah. He appears only in the genealogy of the nations descended from Noah after the flood, which names him last among Japheth's seven sons, after Gomer, Magog, Madai, Javan, Tubal and Meshech (Gen 10:2; 1 Chr 1:5). Easton's Bible Dictionary takes this to mean he was the youngest. Nothing else is recorded about him. As with the other names in this list, Tiras was probably understood as the ancestor of a people. Ancient commentators, including Josephus, linked him with the Thracians. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia prefers a connection with the Tursenioi, seafaring peoples of the Aegean coasts sometimes identified with the Etruscans, and mentions a further suggestion that Tiras is the same as Tarshish. Which people the name stands for remains uncertain.

Tirhakah was a king of Ethiopia (Cush) whose army marched out to fight Sennacherib of Assyria during the Assyrian invasion of Judah in the reign of King Hezekiah. When Sennacherib heard that Tirhakah was coming against him, he sent messengers back to Hezekiah with a further demand that Jerusalem surrender (2 Kgs 19:9; Isa 37:9). These two parallel verses are his only mentions in the Bible. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identifies him with Taharqa, a ruler of Egypt and Cush, called Tarqu in Assyrian inscriptions. It dates his reign from about 693 to 667 BC and says he was later defeated by the Assyrian kings Esarhaddon and Ashurbanipal and died in Cush. Because Sennacherib's campaign is usually dated to 701 BC, before that accession, some suggest Tirhakah was acting for an earlier pharaoh, while others think two campaigns have been combined.

Tobiah was the ancestor of a family that returned from exile in Babylon with Zerubbabel, probably before about 536 BC by inference from context. His descendants were listed with those of Delaiah and Nekoda, totaling 652 in Ezra 2:60 and 642 in the parallel list at Neh 7:62. The surrounding passage (Ezra 2:59; Neh 7:61) places these families among returnees who could not show their father's house or prove they were of Israelite descent. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both treat Tobiah as the head or namesake of this family. Nothing else is known of him. The name, meaning "the Lord is good" according to Hitchcock's Bible Names, is shared by several people, and this Tobiah is distinct from Tobiah the Ammonite who opposed Nehemiah.

Tobijah was one of the returned exiles who came from Babylon to Jerusalem in the time of the prophet Zechariah. He is named with Heldai and Jedaiah. Zechariah was told to take silver and gold from these men and make crowns, which were set on the head of Joshua the high priest (Zech 6:10–11). Afterward the crowns were to be kept in the temple of the LORD as a memorial to Tobijah and his companions (Zech 6:14). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the Greek Septuagint translates his name as a descriptive word rather than as a personal name. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates the episode to about 519 BC. The name Tobijah means "the LORD is good" and belongs to several people in the Bible. This Tobijah should not be confused with the others who bear it.

Ulam was a member of the tribe of Manasseh, one of the two tribes descended from Joseph, named in the genealogy of 1 Chr 7. His grandparents were Machir, Manasseh's son, and Machir's wife Maachah. His father was Sheresh, brother of Peresh, and his brother was Rakem. He is recorded as the father of Bedan. The family is summed up as descendants of Gilead, son of Machir. The Hebrew of 1 Chr 7:16 says only that "his sons" were Ulam and Rakem, so the father could be either Sheresh or Peresh. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia takes him as a son of Peresh and treats the name as a Manassite clan, while this entry follows the reading that makes him Sheresh's son. Nothing else is recorded about him. The name is shared by at least one other man in the Bible, so this Ulam should not be confused with others of the same name.

Ulam was a Benjaminite, the firstborn of Eshek, with younger brothers Jehush and Eliphelet (1 Chr 8:39). Eshek was the brother of Azel, whose line the genealogy traces back through Jonathan to King Saul. Smith's Bible Dictionary accordingly calls Ulam a descendant of the house of Saul. Since Azel was the son of Eleasah (1 Chr 8:37), this entry links Ulam to Eleasah, though the verse itself names Eshek as his father. Ulam's sons were remembered as mighty warriors and archers, and his descendants grew to 150 sons and grandsons (1 Chr 8:40). They close the Benjamite genealogy of this chapter. Smith's Bible Dictionary and Hitchcock's Bible Names explain the name as meaning "porch," while the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives "preceding." The name is shared with at least one other man, a descendant of Manasseh.

Ulla was a member of the tribe of Asher, named in the Asherite genealogy of 1 Chronicles 7 as the father of three sons, Arah, Haniel and Rezia (1 Chr 7:39). The list does not say who Ulla's father was. This entry follows the view, given in Tyndale House's STEPBible proper names, that Ulla is the same man as Shual, one of the sons of Zophah, alongside Suah, Harnepher, Beri, Imrah and others (1 Chr 7:36). On that view his brothers include Beera, Bezer, Hod, Shamma, Shilshah and Jether, the remaining sons of Zophah named in the same passage. Other reference works, such as the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia, treat Shual and Ulla as two separate Asherites. The meaning of the name Ulla is uncertain. Nothing further is recorded about him beyond his place in the genealogy.

Unni was a Levite of the second rank whom the chief Levites appointed, at David's command, as one of the musicians when the ark was brought up to Jerusalem from the house of Obed-edom. He is listed among the brethren of the second degree in 1 Chr 15:18, a group that also included gatekeepers. In 1 Chr 15:20 he appears among those who played psalteries, or harps, set to "Alamoth," a musical term of uncertain meaning that may refer to a higher pitch. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him as one of the doorkeepers, while Easton's Bible Dictionary describes him as a psaltery player. Both roles fit the two verses. The name is shared by another Levite who returned from exile with Zerubbabel (Neh 12:9), a different man from a much later period. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the name's meaning as "afflicted" or "that answers."

Uriel was a Levite of the clan of Kohath, son of Tahath, named in the Kohathite genealogy of 1 Chr 6:24, where his son is Uzziah. The parallel line of descent for the singer Heman (1 Chr 6:33–38) names Zephaniah son of Tahath, father of Azariah, at the same point. This entry follows the common view, given in the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia and in STEPBible, that Zephaniah and Uriel are the same man. On that view his son appears as both Uzziah and Azariah, two names also used interchangeably for a later king of Judah. Because Heman's line runs through Elkanah and Samuel, Easton's Bible Dictionary calls him an ancestor of the prophet Samuel. Nothing else is recorded of him. Several other men in the Bible are also called Uriel, including a Kohathite leader in David's time (1 Chr 15:5).

Uriel was a Levite and the chief of the clan of Kohath in the time of King David. He led a group of 120 of his kinsmen (1 Chr 15:5). When David prepared to bring the ark of the covenant up to Jerusalem, he called for the priests Zadok and Abiathar and for six Levite leaders, with Uriel named first (1 Chr 15:11). From the surrounding passage, these leaders were told to consecrate themselves and to carry the ark properly, after an earlier failed attempt. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes him as the chief of the Kohathites at the time the ark was brought to Jerusalem. Hitchcock's Bible Names treats the name as having the same meaning as Uriah. Several other men in the Bible share the name, including a Kohathite ancestor and a man from Gibeah, and they should be kept distinct from this Uriel.

Uz (son of Aram) was a son of Aram and a grandson of Shem, listed in the Table of Nations with his brothers Hul, Gether and Mash (Gen 10:23). The parallel genealogy in 1 Chr 1:17 names the same four directly after Shem's sons, without the phrase "the children of Aram," and gives Mash as Meshech. By inference from Gen 10:23, the Chronicles list is a shortened form, and Uz is Aram's son rather than Shem's. Nothing else is recorded about him. Like many names in these lists, his may also stand for a people descended from him. Other men named Uz appear elsewhere in Genesis, a son of Nahor and a descendant of Seir, and Job is said to have lived in a "land of Uz." Any link between these and Aram's son is uncertain. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "counsel" or "words."

Uz (son of Dishan) was a Horite, a descendant of Seir, the people who lived in the land of Seir before the Edomites. He appears only in the genealogies of Gen 36:28 and 1 Chr 1:42, which name him and his brother Aran as the sons of Dishan. Dishan was one of the sons of Seir the Horite and a chief in that land, as the surrounding verses of Genesis 36 show. Easton's Bible Dictionary counts Uz among the Horite chiefs in the land of Edom. The verses themselves record nothing about him beyond his name and family. He is distinct from the other men named Uz in the Bible, such as the son of Aram and the son of Nahor. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "counsel" or "words."

Uzal was one of the sons of Joktan, a descendant of Shem, named in the list of nations in Gen 10:27 and again in 1 Chr 1:21. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia count him as Joktan's sixth son. Nothing is recorded about his life beyond his place in these genealogies, where he stands between his brothers Hadoram and Diklah. Like his brothers, he is generally taken as the ancestor of a people of southern Arabia. Easton's Bible Dictionary sees him as the founder of an Arab tribe whose name probably passed to their territory and chief city. Smith's and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia link the name with Awzal, the old name of San'a, the capital of Yemen. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia also suggests that Ezek 27:19 may mention Uzal as a place, depending on how one obscure Hebrew word is read.

Uzza is the man after whom the "garden of Uzza" in Jerusalem was named. It was the burial place of two kings of Judah. King Manasseh was buried there, in the garden of his own house (2 Kgs 21:18), and his son Amon was later buried in his tomb in the same garden (2 Kgs 21:26). The text says nothing else about Uzza himself. Because the garden belonged to Manasseh's house, it was probably near the royal palace. It may have been named after an earlier owner, or possibly after the Uzzah who died beside the ark in David's time, but neither connection is stated in the text. The name is shared by several other people in the Bible, and this entry refers only to the Uzza of the garden.

Uzza was the ancestor of a family of temple servants, known as the Nethinim, whose descendants returned from exile in Babylon to Judah. The "children of Uzza" appear in the list of returning families in Ezra 2:49 and again in the parallel list in Neh 7:51. In both lists they stand among the temple-servant families, next to the descendants of Paseah (spelled Phaseah in Nehemiah). Smith's Bible Dictionary places this return with Zerubbabel, before about 536 BC. Nothing else is recorded about Uzza himself, and the lists probably name him only as the head of a family line. The name means "strength" and is shared by several other men in the Bible, including the man who touched the ark in David's time. This Uzza appears to be a separate person.

Uzzi was a son of Tola and a grandson of Issachar, listed first among Tola's six sons in the genealogy of the tribe of Issachar (1 Chr 7:2). His brothers were Rephaiah, Jeriel, Jahmai, Jibsam and Shemuel. Together they are called heads of their father's house and valiant men, and the family is said to have numbered 22,600 fighting men in the days of David. Uzzi's son was Izrahiah, whose five descendants, Michael, Obadiah, Joel, Ishiah and Izrahiah himself, are described as chief men (1 Chr 7:3). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats him as the founder of a family within Issachar, and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of his name as "my strength." Several other men in the Bible share the name, and this Uzzi is known only from these two verses.

Uzziel was a Levite and one of the fourteen sons of Heman, one of the leading musicians in David's time. He is named third among Heman's sons in 1 Chr 25:4. The same man is called Azareel in the list of the twenty-four groups of temple musicians chosen by lot, where the eleventh lot fell to him, with his sons and relatives making a group of twelve (1 Chr 25:18). Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary both treat the two names as one person, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that one major Greek manuscript of the Septuagint reads Azarael in verse 4 as well. The name Uzziel means "God is my strength." Several other people in the Bible share this name, so he should not be confused with them. Nothing more is recorded about him.

Zabad, also called Jozachar, was one of the two royal servants who conspired against King Joash of Judah and killed him. 2 Chronicles names him Zabad, son of Shimeath, an Ammonite woman. His fellow conspirator was Jehozabad, son of Shimrith, a Moabite woman (2 Chr 24:26). The parallel account in 2 Kgs 12:21 calls him Jozachar son of Shimeath and says the two men struck the king down. Joash was buried in the city of David, and his son Amaziah succeeded him. The surrounding verse in Chronicles (2 Chr 24:25) explains that the conspiracy followed the death of Zechariah son of Jehoiada. Smith's Bible Dictionary takes Jozachar to be probably the more accurate form of the name. Several other men in the Bible are also named Zabad, and this entry concerns only Joash's assassin.

Zabad was a man of the tribe of Judah, listed in the genealogy of the Jerahmeelite clan in 1 Chronicles. He was the son of Nathan and the father of Ephlal, whose son was Obed (1 Chr 2:36–37). By inference from the surrounding verses, his line traces back to Sheshan, a Jerahmeelite who had no sons and gave his daughter in marriage to Jarha, his Egyptian servant. Their son Attai was Nathan's father, which makes Zabad Sheshan's great-great-grandson. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests the name may be a shortened form of Zebadiah, meaning "the Lord has given." Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning "dowry" or "endowed." Several other men in the Bible share this name, and nothing beyond his place in this family list is recorded about this Zabad.

Zaccai was the ancestor of a family whose descendants, 760 in number, returned from exile in Babylon to Jerusalem and Judah. The figure is the same in both lists of returning families (Ezra 2:9; Neh 7:14). Both lists place this return under Zerubbabel's leadership, and Smith's Bible Dictionary dates it to before 536 BC. Nothing else is recorded about Zaccai himself, and it is unclear whether the name refers to one individual or serves as a family or clan name. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "pure." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia links the name to Zabbai, though the connection between the two is uncertain.

Zacher was a Benjamite listed among the sons of the founder of Gibeon and his wife Maachah in the genealogies of 1 Chronicles. He appears in 1 Chr 8:31, and the parallel list in 1 Chr 9:37 calls him Zechariah. The father is named Jehiel or Jeiel in the surrounding verses. This entry identifies him with Abiel, who in 1 Sam 9:1 is the father of Kish. His brothers included Abdon, Zur, Kish, Baal, Ner, Nadab, Gedor, Ahio and Mikloth. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia says he lived in Gibeon and, as a brother of Kish, was an uncle of King Saul. Nothing is recorded about him beyond his place in these family lists. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "memorial."

Zadok was the father of Jerushah (also spelled Jerusha), the mother of King Jotham of Judah. Both accounts of Jotham's reign name her as "the daughter of Zadok" when they introduce the king, who began to reign at twenty-five and ruled sixteen years in Jerusalem (2 Kgs 15:33; 2 Chr 27:1). Since Jotham was the son of King Uzziah (also called Azariah), Jerushah was Uzziah's wife, which made Zadok the king's father-in-law and Jotham's maternal grandfather. Through Jotham, who appears in Matthew's genealogy of Jesus, Zadok is connected to that line. Nothing else is recorded about him, and he should not be confused with the better-known priest Zadok of David's time or the other men of the same name. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "just" or "justified."

Zavan, also spelled Zaavan, was a son of Ezer and brother of Bilhan and Akan (called Jakan in 1 Chr 1:42). He appears only in the genealogy of the Horites, the people who lived in the land of Seir before the Edomites. In Genesis 36 Ezer is listed among the sons of Seir the Horite and as one of the Horite chiefs, so Zavan was a grandson of Seir. Genesis gives the name as Zaavan (Gen 36:27), while 1 Chronicles has Zavan (1 Chr 1:42). Smith's Bible Dictionary and the STEPBible names index describe him as a Horite chief. Easton's Bible Dictionary counts him among the "dukes of Edom" and gives the meaning of his name as "terror." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia considers the meaning uncertain but notes a possible root meaning "to tremble." Nothing else is recorded about him.

Zechariah, spelled Zachariah in 2 Kgs 18:2, was the father of Abi, also called Abijah, who was the mother of King Hezekiah of Judah. That made him Hezekiah's maternal grandfather. He is mentioned only in the parallel notices that open the accounts of Hezekiah's reign. Both state that Hezekiah became king at twenty-five and reigned twenty-nine years in Jerusalem. Nothing else is recorded about him, including his tribe, his position, or when he lived beyond being a generation before Hezekiah. The name means roughly "the Lord remembers" and was very common in the Old Testament, so he should not be confused with the many other men called Zechariah. Because Hezekiah appears in the line of kings in Matthew's genealogy of Jesus (Matt 1:9–10), this Zechariah is counted among Jesus' ancestors through Hezekiah's mother.

Zedekiah son of Maaseiah was a prophet among the Jewish exiles in Babylon, one of several men in the Bible with this name, which means "the Lord is my justice" (Hitchcock's Bible Names). In Jeremiah's letter to the exiles, the Lord condemns him and Ahab son of Kolaiah for prophesying lies in his name, and declares that Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon will kill them in front of the people. Their fate was to become a curse used by the exiles: "The LORD make thee like Zedekiah and like Ahab, whom the king of Babylon roasted in the fire." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia understands their message as a promise of an early return from captivity, and draws on the next verse, Jer 29:23, which also charges them with adultery. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates these events to about 595 BC.

Zelek was an Ammonite listed among David's mighty men, the elite warriors named in 2 Sam 23 and 1 Chr 11. He appears only in these two parallel lists, identified simply as "Zelek the Ammonite," which shows that David's renowned fighters included men of foreign origin. Nothing else is recorded of his deeds or family. In both lists his name comes just before Naharai the Beerothite, who is described as armourbearer to Joab son of Zeruiah. The Hebrew wording could be read as applying that title to Naharai alone, and this entry follows that reading, so Zelek is not himself called Joab's armourbearer. The meaning of his name is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives it as "cleft," while the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats it as unknown.

Zemarite is the name of a Canaanite people listed among the descendants of Canaan, son of Ham, in the table of nations (Gen 10:18; 1 Chr 1:16). Like the other names in the list, such as the Amorite, Hivite and Jebusite, it stands for a tribe or clan rather than a single individual, and here it is treated as a son of Canaan. It appears between the Arvadite and the Hamathite, which suggests a home in the north, along the Phoenician coast. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia link the name to Zemar, or Sumur, an important Phoenician city mentioned in the Amarna letters. They place it probably at the village of Sumra on the coast between Tripoli and Arvad. Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that older interpreters placed the tribe at Emesa, modern Homs. Beyond the genealogies, the Bible says nothing more about them.

Zephaniah was the father of Josiah, a man living in Jerusalem after the return from Babylon. In Zech 6:10 the prophet Zechariah is told to go to Josiah's house with Heldai, Tobijah and Jedaiah, who had come from the captivity, and to make crowns from their silver and gold. Zech 6:14 gives the crowns as a memorial in the temple to Helem, Tobijah, Jedaiah and "Hen the son of Zephaniah." Hen is usually taken as another name for Josiah, though the word may instead mean "kindness." Smith's Bible Dictionary treats Zephaniah as Hen's father too, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia allows that one or more fathers may be meant. Easton's Bible Dictionary calls Josiah a priest. The name, meaning "the LORD has treasured" or "hidden," was shared by several people. This Zephaniah is not the prophet of that name.

Zephon was a son of Gad, one of the sons of Jacob, and the ancestor of the Zephonites, a clan of the tribe of Gad. Genesis names him Ziphion in its list of Gad's sons who went down to Egypt with Jacob (Gen 46:16). Numbers, in the census of Israel taken in the wilderness, gives the name as Zephon (Num 26:15). Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both treat the two forms as the same person. His brothers were Haggi, Shuni, Ozni, Eri, Arod and Areli. Ozni appears to correspond to the Ezbon of Genesis, and Arod to Arodi. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "watch," and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia tentatively suggests "gaze." Nothing else is recorded about him.

Zerah was the father of Jobab, who followed Bela as king of Edom in the period before Israel had kings (Gen 36:33; 1 Chr 1:44). The verses describe him as "of Bozrah," a major Edomite city probably at modern Buseirah in southern Jordan. The wording could also be read as calling Jobab himself a man of Bozrah. The STEPBible Proper Names index takes Zerah to be from Bozrah and counts him among the Edomite royal line. Nothing else is recorded about him. Several other men in the Bible share the name, including a son of Judah and an Edomite chief descended from Esau, and it is uncertain whether this Zerah is the same person as any of them. Hitchcock's Bible Names treats the name as the same as Zarah, which it explains as meaning "east" or "brightness."

Zerah was a Levite of the Gershonite clan named in the genealogies of 1 Chronicles 6. In one list he is the son of Iddo and the father of Jeaterai, in a line descending from Gershom (1 Chr 6:21). In another he is the son of Adaiah and the father of Ethni, in the ancestry of Asaph, the singer appointed by David (1 Chr 6:41). Smith's Bible Dictionary and the Tyndale House STEPBible names index treat these as the same man, which suggests that Iddo and Adaiah are two forms of one name and that Jeaterai and Ethni may also correspond. This entry follows that identification, though the two lists do not match exactly. Nothing else is recorded about him. Several other people in the Bible share the name, which Smith's Bible Dictionary explains as meaning "rising" of the sun.

Zetham was a Levite of the Gershonite clan in the time of David, mentioned only in 1 Chronicles. In 1 Chr 23:8 he is listed with Jehiel and Joel as one of the three sons of Laadan. In 1 Chr 26:22 he and his brother Joel appear as "sons of Jehieli" and are placed over the treasures of the house of the LORD. The two passages can be read differently. Zetham may be Jehiel's brother and a son of Laadan, or Jehiel's son and Laadan's grandson. This entry follows the second reading and treats Jehiel as his father. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes a proposal by the scholar Curtis that 1 Chr 26:22 should read "Jehiel and his brethren, Zetham and Joel." Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "olive planter."

Zibeon was a Hivite whose descendant Aholibamah (Oholibamah) became one of Esau's wives. Genesis calls her "the daughter of Anah the daughter of Zibeon," which makes Zibeon her grandfather through Anah (Gen 36:2). Through Aholibamah, Zibeon was the ancestor of Esau's sons Jeush, Jaalam and Korah (Gen 36:14). The Hebrew wording leaves it open whether "daughter of Zibeon" refers to Aholibamah or to Anah. This entry treats Anah as Zibeon's child, and the STEPBible proper-names index likewise calls him Oholibamah's grandfather. The name is shared by more than one person. Later in the same chapter a Zibeon son of Seir the Horite has a son named Anah (Gen 36:20, 24), and many readers take him to be the same man, described there as a Horite rather than a Hivite. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "iniquity that dwells."

Zibiah was a woman from Beersheba, in the far south of Judah, and the mother of King Joash (also called Jehoash) of Judah. She is named only in the formal introductions to her son's reign, which say he became king at seven years old, in the seventh year of Jehu of Israel, and reigned forty years in Jerusalem. Her husband was King Ahaziah of Judah. Connected passages such as 2 Kgs 11:1–3 explain that after Ahaziah's death the young Joash was hidden from Queen Athaliah until he could be crowned. Through her son she belongs to the royal line of David that is traced in the genealogies of Jesus. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia takes her name to mean probably "gazelle" and notes that some Greek manuscripts give it as Abia. Nothing else about her is recorded.

Zichri was a Levite of the family of Asaph, the temple musician, and the father of Micah (spelled Micha in Nehemiah). He appears only in the genealogy of his grandson Mattaniah, who lived in Jerusalem after the return from exile. Mattaniah was the one who led the thanksgiving in prayer (1 Chr 9:15; Neh 11:17). The parallel list in Neh 11:17 gives Zichri's name as Zabdi. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary also link him with the Zaccur named in Mattaniah's line at Neh 12:35. "Son of Asaph" may mean a later descendant rather than a direct son, since genealogies often skip generations. Zichri himself is known only through these lists, so he probably lived some generations before Nehemiah's time. Several other men in the Bible share the name Zichri, including Levites mentioned in Exod 6:21 and 1 Chr 26:25.

Zidon, also spelled Sidon, was the firstborn son of Canaan, a grandson of Noah through Ham, according to the table of nations (Gen 10:15; 1 Chr 1:13). His brothers included Heth and the ancestors of the Jebusites, Amorites, Girgasites, Hivites, Arkites, Sinites, Arvadites, Zemarites and Hamathites. Nothing is told of his life beyond his place in these genealogies. Easton's Bible Dictionary connects him with the Phoenician coastal city of Sidon, about 25 miles north of Tyre, saying the city took its name from him. The STEPBible proper-names list likewise treats him as the ancestor of the Sidonian people. In this reading the person stands at the head of a people and a city that appear often in later biblical history. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "hunting" or "fishing."

Ziha was the ancestor of a family of Nethinim, the temple servants, whose descendants returned from exile in Babylon to Jerusalem. They head the list of Nethinim in the record of returning exiles in Ezra 2:43, and the same list appears again in Neh 7:46. Smith's Bible Dictionary places this return under Zerubbabel, about 536 BC. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia also links the name to a Ziha who oversaw the Nethinim in Neh 11:21. Because several people bear this name, it is uncertain whether that overseer is the family's ancestor, a later member of the family, or a different man. The meaning of the name is unclear. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "brightness" or "drought," and Smith's gives "parched."

Zimmah was a Levite of the clan of Gershom, named in the genealogies of 1 Chronicles. In the line of the singer Asaph he appears as the son of Shimei and the father of Ethan (1 Chr 6:42). The following verse makes Shimei a son of Jahath, son of Gershom. In the list of Gershom's descendants, a Zimmah is called the son of Jahath, son of Libni (1 Chr 6:20). Smith's Bible Dictionary treats these as possibly the same man, which would mean one list omits a generation. This entry follows the identification as Shimei's son and Ethan's father. The name is shared by more than one person in the Bible, so other mentions may refer to different individuals. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives its meaning as "thought" or "wickedness," and Smith's gives "purpose."

Zimran was a son of Abraham and Keturah, the woman Abraham took after Sarah's death. He is listed first among her six sons, followed by Jokshan, Medan, Midian, Ishbak and Shuah (Gen 25:2; 1 Chr 1:32). This made him a half-brother of Isaac and Ishmael. Genesis calls Keturah Abraham's wife, while 1 Chronicles calls her his concubine. Gen 25:6 says that Abraham gave gifts to the sons of his concubines and sent them away eastward, away from Isaac. That probably included Zimran. As Smith's Bible Dictionary notes, no descendants of his are recorded. The meaning of his name is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives "celebrated," Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "song" or "vine," and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia derives it from a word for wild sheep or goat. That encyclopedia also mentions a proposed link with the "Zimri" of Jer 25:25 and with places in Arabia.

Zimri was a Benjamite and a descendant of King Saul, named in the two genealogies of Saul's family in 1 Chronicles. He was a son of Ahaz's son, the brother of Alemeth and Azmaveth, and the father of Moza. The father's name differs between the lists: 1 Chr 8:36 calls him Jehoadah and 1 Chr 9:42 calls him Jarah. These are probably two forms of the same name, and this entry follows the Jarah form. Both lists trace the line from Saul through Jonathan and Merib-baal (Mephibosheth) to Micah and Ahaz. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both identify him as Saul's descendant. Nothing else is recorded about him. He should not be confused with other men called Zimri, such as the short-reigning king of Israel.

Ziph was a son of Jehaleleel, named in the genealogy of Judah's descendants together with his brothers Ziphah, Tiria and Asareel (1 Chr 4:16). Nothing else is recorded about him. The name Ziph is also used for a town and wilderness in Judah, where Saul searched for David (1 Sam 26:2). Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that two towns in Judah bore the name. Whether this man is connected with any of those places is not stated. Because the Chronicles genealogies sometimes list clan founders whose names match towns, a link is possible, but it remains uncertain. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that Greek manuscripts differ on the name. Codex Alexandrinus reads Ziphai, while Codex Vaticanus has the quite different form Ameachei.

Zizah was a Levite of the Gershonite branch, the second son of Shimei. His brothers were Jahath, the chief, and Jeush and Beriah (1 Chr 23:10–11). He appears in the list of Levite family heads that David organized for service. The same man is called Zina in 1 Chr 23:10 and Zizah in the next verse. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the Septuagint and Vulgate read "Ziza" in both verses, as does one Hebrew manuscript in verse 10. It suggests that Zina is a variant spelling of the same name. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "abundance." Nothing more is recorded about him.

Zohar was the father of Ephron the Hittite, the man from whom Abraham bought the field and cave of Machpelah near Mamre as a family burial place. He is known only through his son: Abraham asks the people of the land to plead with "Ephron the son of Zohar" on his behalf when seeking a grave for Sarah (Gen 23:8), and the same description is used when Isaac and Ishmael later bury Abraham in that cave (Gen 25:9). Nothing else is recorded about him. Since Ephron is called a Hittite, Zohar was presumably a Hittite too, one of the people living around Hebron in Abraham's day. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of his name as "white" or "bright", and Smith's Bible Dictionary renders it "light". The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia regards the meaning as uncertain. The same name is borne by other men elsewhere in the Old Testament.

Zophah was a man of the tribe of Asher, named in the tribe's genealogy in 1 Chronicles. He is listed as a son of Helem, alongside his brothers Imna, Shelesh and Amal (1 Chr 7:35). This Helem is usually taken to be Hotham, son of Heber, mentioned a few verses earlier. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the Tyndale House proper-name index both make this identification, and this entry follows it. Zophah had a large family. Suah, Harnepher, Beri and Imrah are among the sons named in 1 Chr 7:36, and the list of his descendants continues in the following verses. Easton's Bible Dictionary calls him a chief of Asher, which fits the genealogy's description of these men as heads of their fathers' houses. Nothing else is recorded about him. The meaning of his name is uncertain.

Zur was one of five kings of Midian killed by the Israelites in their war against Midian in the time of Moses. The others were Evi, Rekem, Hur and Reba, and Balaam son of Beor was killed in the same campaign (Num 31:8). Josh 13:21 recalls the same five as princes of Midian and describes them as dukes, or subordinate chiefs, of Sihon king of the Amorites, living in his country. Num 25:15 names a Zur, head of a leading family in Midian, as the father of Cozbi, the Midianite woman killed alongside Zimri by Phinehas. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identifies that Zur with this king. His name means "rock." Several other men in the Bible share the name, so this entry covers only the Midianite leader.

Zur was a Benjamite who lived at Gibeon, the second son listed after the firstborn Abdon in the family of the founder of Gibeon and his wife Maachah (1 Chr 8:30; 9:36). His father is named here as Abiel. The Chronicles genealogy calls the father of Gibeon Jehiel (1 Chr 9:35), and Abiel is the name given to Saul's ancestor in 1 Sam 9:1, so this entry treats the two as the same man. Zur's brothers included Kish, Baal, Ner, Nadab, Gedor, Ahio, Zacher and Mikloth, and so he belonged to the same clan from which King Saul came. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes a suggestion that he may be connected with Zeror in 1 Sam 9:1. Nothing more is recorded of him. His name means "rock," and several other people in the Bible share it.

Abagtha was one of the seven chamberlains, or eunuchs, who served in the presence of King Ahasuerus of Persia. He is named only in Esth 1:10, alongside Mehuman, Biztha, Harbona, Bigtha, Zethar and Carcas. On the seventh day of the king's feast, when Ahasuerus was merry with wine, he gave these seven men a command. The following verse shows the command was to bring Queen Vashti before him. Easton's Bible Dictionary also links him to Esth 2:21. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identifies Ahasuerus as Xerxes and notes that the name is Persian, one of many Persian features in the Book of Esther. The meaning of the name is uncertain. The same encyclopedia suggests "fortunate one," Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "God-given," and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "father of the wine-press." Nothing more is recorded about him.

Abda was the father of Adoniram, one of King Solomon's chief officials. He is known only as a name in the list of Solomon's officers, where his son Adoniram is said to have been "over the tribute" (1 Kgs 4:6). Easton's Bible Dictionary explains this as the forced labour, which the Revised Version calls the "levy". Nothing else is recorded about Abda himself. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests the name may be a shortened form meaning "servant of Yahweh", and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "servant" or "servitude". Another man named Abda appears among the Levites in Nehemiah's time, but he is a different person from Adoniram's father.

Abdeel was the father of Shelemiah, one of three men King Jehoiakim ordered to seize Baruch the scribe and Jeremiah the prophet, though the LORD hid them (Jer 36:26). He is known only as Shelemiah's father and appears in this single verse. The king is not named in the verse itself, but the surrounding chapter identifies him as Jehoiakim, who had just burned the scroll of Jeremiah's prophecies. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia give the meaning of his name as "servant of God," while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "a vapor; a cloud of God."

Abdi was a Levite of the clan of Merari, the son of Malluch and the father of Kishi. He appears only in the genealogy of Ethan, the Merarite singer who stood on the left hand in the temple music that David organized (1 Chr 6:44). That makes Abdi Ethan's grandfather. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that this would place him around the time of King Saul. His name probably means "servant" and is perhaps short for "servant of the LORD." Several other men in the Bible share the name, so this Abdi should not be confused with them.

Abdi was a Levite of the clan of Merari and the father of Kish, one of the Levites who rose up at King Hezekiah's call to cleanse and rededicate the temple at the start of his reign (2 Chr 29:12). Abdi himself is known only as Kish's father. He probably lived a generation before Hezekiah. His name means "my servant" (Hitchcock's Bible Names), probably a shortened form of "servant of the LORD" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia). The name is shared by several people. Another Merarite Levite called Abdi appears in the singer Ethan's ancestry (1 Chr 6:44). Some identify him with this man, but the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats them as two people, and this entry follows that view.

Abdi was a man of the family or clan of Elam who lived in the time of Ezra, after the return from exile in Babylon. He appears only in the list of men who had married foreign wives (Ezra 10:26). The surrounding chapter shows that these men agreed to send those wives away. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that he was not a Levite but a layman, "of the sons of Elam," and takes the name as probably a shortened form of "servant of the Lord." Hitchcock's Bible Names gives its meaning as "my servant." The name Abdi is also borne by other people in the Bible, including a Levite of Merari's line, so this Abdi should not be confused with them. Nothing else is recorded about him.

Abdiel was a man of the tribe of Gad, the son of Guni and the father of Ahi, named in the Gadite genealogy of 1 Chronicles. The verse calls Ahi, or possibly the family line as a whole, "chief of the house of their fathers." The surrounding passage places the Gadites in Gilead and Bashan east of the Jordan. It says their genealogies were recorded in the days of Jotham king of Judah and Jeroboam king of Israel (1 Chr 5:16–17), so Abdiel probably lived in or before that period. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates him to about 758 BC, an estimate drawn from that context. His name means "servant of God." Nothing else is recorded about him.

Abdon was a son of Shashak and a member of the tribe of Benjamin. He appears only once, in the Benjamite genealogy of 1 Chr 8:23, where he is listed with his brothers Zichri and Hanan. The full list of Shashak's sons in that passage also includes Antothijah, Elam, Eliel, Hananiah, Heber, Iphedeiah, Ishpan and Penuel. Nothing else is recorded about him. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia places him among the Benjamites said to have lived in Jerusalem, possibly in Nehemiah's time, though it notes that the date is unclear. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "servile," and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests "service." Several other people in the Bible share the name, including a judge of Israel, and there was also a Levitical town called Abdon in Asher. This Abdon should not be confused with them.

Abiah was the wife of Hezron, a grandson of Judah, in the genealogy of Judah's descendants. According to 1 Chr 2:24, after Hezron died at Caleb-ephratah, Abiah bore him a son, Ashur, described as the father of Tekoa. This suggests the child was born after his father's death. "Father of Tekoa" probably means Ashur was the founder or leading figure of the town of Tekoa rather than the father of a person named Tekoa. This is the only verse that mentions her, and the Hebrew of the verse is difficult, so some details of the passage are uncertain. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of her name as "the Lord is my father." The same name is borne by several other people in the Bible, and she should not be confused with them.

Abiah was a member of the tribe of Benjamin, one of the nine sons of Becher listed in the Benjamite genealogy at 1 Chr 7:8. Becher was himself a son of Benjamin, so Abiah was Benjamin's grandson. His brothers were Zemira, Joash, Eliezer, Elioenai, Omri, Jerimoth, Anathoth and Alameth. Nothing else is recorded about him beyond his place in this list. The Hebrew name is often written Abijah, and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives its meaning as "the Lord is my father." Several other people in the Bible share the name, and this Abiah should not be confused with them.

Abiel the Arbathite was one of David's mighty men, the elite warriors listed in 1 Chr 11:32. The parallel list in 2 Sam 23:31 calls him Abi-albon, and Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary treat the two names as referring to the same man. "Arbathite" probably means he came from Beth-arabah, a town on the border between Judah and Benjamin near the Jordan valley. This is an inference from the form of the name. His name is usually explained as "God is father" or "my father is God" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia). Nothing else is recorded about him beyond his place in the list of David's warriors.

Abiezer was a member of the tribe of Manasseh, named in its genealogy as a son of Hammoleketh and a brother of Ishod and Mahalah (1 Chr 7:18). By inference from the surrounding verses, Hammoleketh was the sister of Gilead, Machir's son, which would make Abiezer a great-grandson of Manasseh through his mother's line. STEPBible Proper Names also places him among Manasseh's descendants. He is probably the ancestor of the Abiezrite clan of Manasseh, which Josh 17:2 lists among the tribe's family groups and to which Gideon later belonged (Judg 6:11), though this link is drawn from those connected passages rather than stated in 1 Chr 7:18. The name, which Hitchcock's Bible Names renders "father of help," is shared by several people in the Bible, including one of David's warriors from Anathoth.

Abihail was a Levite, the father of Zuriel. In Moses' time Zuriel was chief of the families descended from Merari, one of Levi's sons. During the census of the Levites in the wilderness, Zuriel's clan was assigned to camp on the north side of the tabernacle (Num 3:35). Abihail is known only through his son, and nothing more is recorded about him. By inference from the setting, he lived around the time of the Exodus, and Smith's Bible Dictionary places him as a contemporary of Moses. The name means "father of strength" (Hitchcock's Bible Names). Several other people in the Old Testament share it, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia counts five, so this Merarite should not be confused with the others.

Abihail was the wife of Abishur and the mother of his sons Ahban and Molid, named in the genealogy of the tribe of Judah (1 Chr 2:29). The surrounding genealogy places Abishur in the line of Hezron and Jerahmeel, so she belongs to the Jerahmeelite branch of Judah, as the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia also notes. Nothing more is recorded about her. The name, which Smith's Bible Dictionary and Hitchcock's Bible Names explain as "father of strength," is borne by several people in the Old Testament, both men and women. This Abihail should not be confused with the others, such as the father of Queen Esther.

Abihail was a member of the tribe of Gad, named in the Gadite genealogy of 1 Chronicles as the son of Huri. His ancestry is traced back through Jaroah, Gilead, Michael, Jeshishai and Jahdo to Buz. His seven sons were Michael, Meshullam, Sheba, Jorai, Jachan, Zia and Heber. The surrounding passage places these Gadite families in Gilead and Bashan, east of the Jordan. It says their genealogies were recorded in the days of King Jotham of Judah and King Jeroboam of Israel (1 Chr 5:17). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia counts him among the heads of the tribe of Gad. Nothing else is recorded about him. Several other people in the Bible share the name, which Hitchcock's Bible Names explains as "father of strength."

Abihail was a woman of the tribe of Judah named in 2 Chr 11:18 in connection with King Rehoboam's marriages. She is called the daughter of Eliab son of Jesse, David's eldest brother; Smith's Bible Dictionary takes 'daughter' here to mean descendant. Readings of the verse differ. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary treat her as a second wife of Rehoboam, and this entry follows that view. On this reading, the sons listed in the next verse, Jeush, Shamariah and Zaham (2 Chr 11:19), are hers. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia and the Tyndale House proper-names index instead take her as the mother of Mahalath, so that she was the wife of Jerimoth, David's son.
