Either way, the verse shows marriage within David's extended family. The name is shared by several other people in the Bible.

Abihud was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, named as one of the sons of Bela in the genealogy of 1 Chr 8:3. Bela was Benjamin's firstborn, which made Abihud a grandson of Benjamin. In that list he appears alongside Addar and Gera, and the wider genealogy counts several brothers, among them Abishua, Naaman and Ahoah. The name is usually taken to mean "father of majesty" or "my father is majesty." Easton's Bible Dictionary suggests he is the same man as the Ahihud named a few verses later, in 1 Chr 8:7. Nothing else is recorded about him, and he should not be confused with the Abiud of Matthew's genealogy of Jesus, a different person.

Abijah was a son of Jeroboam, the first king of the northern kingdom of Israel, and a brother of Nadab, who later succeeded their father on the throne. He is one of several people in the Bible with this name, which means "the Lord is my father" (Hitchcock's Bible Names). 1 Kgs 14:1 records that he fell sick. The surrounding narrative in 1 Kgs 14 says Jeroboam sent his wife in disguise to the aged, blind prophet Ahijah to ask whether the boy would recover. Ahijah recognized her and foretold the boy's death. He said Abijah alone of Jeroboam's family would be buried and mourned, because in him "some good thing toward the Lord" was found. The child died as his mother returned home, and all Israel mourned him. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him as dying in childhood.

Abimelech, son of Jerubbesheth, is the man Joab mentions in 2 Sam 11:21. There Joab anticipates David's anger at soldiers who went too close to the wall of Rabbah, and recalls that Abimelech died at Thebez when a woman threw a piece of a millstone down on him from the wall. Jerubbesheth is another form of Jerubbaal, the name given to Gideon, so this is Gideon's son Abimelech. Judges 8–9 tells his story, and Smith's Bible Dictionary summarizes it. He was born to Gideon's concubine from Shechem. After his father's death he killed his brothers, leaving only Jotham alive, and the people of Shechem made him king. After a three-year reign he put down a revolt in Shechem and then attacked Thebez, where the woman struck him. The name means "father of the king," and several other men in the Bible bear it.

Abinadab was the father of one of King Solomon's twelve district officers, who in turn supplied food for the king's household, as the surrounding list in 1 Kings 4 explains. That son is called simply "the son of Abinadab" in the King James Version, or Ben-Abinadab in the Revised Version. He governed the whole region of Dor on the Mediterranean coast and married Solomon's daughter Taphath (1 Kgs 4:11). Nothing else is recorded about Abinadab himself. This entry follows Smith's Bible Dictionary in treating him as the officer's father. Easton's Bible Dictionary applies the name to the officer himself. The name is usually taken to mean "father of willingness" or "my father is willing." Several men in the Bible bear this name, so it is uncertain whether he is the same as any other Abinadab.

Abiram was the firstborn son of Hiel the Bethelite and the brother of Segub, Hiel's youngest son. He is mentioned only in 1 Kgs 16:34, which reports that during Ahab's reign Hiel rebuilt Jericho, laying its foundation "in Abiram his firstborn" and setting up its gates "in his youngest son Segub." The verse presents this as fulfilling the word spoken through Joshua, whose curse in Josh 6:26 warned that whoever rebuilt Jericho would lose his eldest and youngest sons. Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries take Abiram's death as the outcome of that curse. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia mentions a possible alternative, that Hiel offered his sons as foundation sacrifices. This entry follows the more common reading, that Abiram died when the foundation was laid. He is a different man from Abiram son of Eliab, who joined Korah's rebellion in the wilderness.

Abishua was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, listed in 1 Chr 8:4 among the sons of Bela, Benjamin's firstborn, which makes him Benjamin's grandson. Nothing is recorded about him beyond his place in this genealogy, where he is named alongside Addar, Gera, Abihud, Naaman and Ahoah. The brothers listed with him here combine this list with a different list of Bela's sons in 1 Chr 7:7, which names Ezbon, Uzzi, Uzziel, Jerimoth and Iri. The meaning of the name is uncertain. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "father of deliverance", Hitchcock's Bible Names "father of salvation", and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests "father of wealth". The same name belongs to another man, a priest descended from Aaron through Phinehas, who should not be confused with this Benjamite.

Abitub was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, named once in the Benjamite genealogy of 1 Chronicles. He was a son of Shaharaim by his wife Hushim, and his full brother was Elpaal (1 Chr 8:11). From the surrounding verses (1 Chr 8:8–10), Shaharaim also had sons by another wife, Hodesh, while living in the country of Moab: Jobab, Zibia, Mesha, Malcham, Jeuz, Shachia and Mirma, who were Abitub's half-brothers. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia takes Abitub to have been born in Moab, though the passage does not say clearly where Hushim's sons were born. Nothing else is recorded about him. Through his brother Elpaal, the genealogy goes on to name descendants who built the towns of Ono and Lod (1 Chr 8:12). Easton's Bible Dictionary and Hitchcock's Bible Names give the meaning of his name as "father of goodness."

Abiud was a man of the tribe of Judah named in Matthew's genealogy of Jesus as the son of Zerubbabel and the father of Eliakim (Matt 1:13). Nothing else is recorded about him, and Matthew is the only book that uses this name. The children of Zerubbabel listed in 1 Chr 3:19–20 include Meshullam, Hananiah, their sister Shelomith, Hashubah, Ohel, Berechiah, Hasadiah and Jushab-hesed. This entry counts Abiud among those children, although his name does not appear in that list. Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies him with Juda in Luke's genealogy (Luke 3:26) and with Obadiah in 1 Chr 3:21. Smith's Bible Dictionary and Hitchcock's Bible Names give the name's meaning as "father of praise," and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests "my father is majesty."

Achaicus was a Christian from Corinth who, with Stephanas and Fortunatus, came to the apostle Paul. Paul wrote that he was glad of their coming, because they had supplied what was lacking on the Corinthians' part (1 Cor 16:17). This probably means that their presence made up for Paul's absence from the church. By inference from the context, Paul was writing from Ephesus (1 Cor 16:8). Easton's Bible Dictionary suggests the three men came to consult him about the church's affairs and probably carried the Corinthians' letter that Paul mentions in 1 Cor 7:1. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia infers from 1 Cor 16:15–18 that Achaicus was among the church's leaders, whom Paul urged the believers to recognize. His name means "belonging to Achaia," the Roman province that included Corinth. Nothing else is recorded about him.

Achim was an ancestor of Jesus named in Matthew's genealogy, the son of Sadoc and the father of Eliud (Matt 1:14). He is mentioned nowhere else in the Bible. He belongs to the part of the line that follows the return from exile in Babylon, so the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia describes him as a descendant of Zerubbabel. That places him in the royal line of the tribe of Judah. Nothing is recorded about his life beyond his place in the list. Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests that the Hebrew form of his name would be Jachin, a short form of Jehoiachin, meaning "the Lord will establish." Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meanings "preparing," "revenging," or "confirming."

Achsa is the form of the name Achsah used in the King James Version at 1 Chr 2:49, where she is named as the daughter of Caleb in the genealogy of the tribe of Judah. The verse closes a list of Caleb's descendants by his concubine Maachah, and the brothers grouped with her here are sons of Caleb by several mothers. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both treat her as the same woman as Achsah, the daughter of Caleb whom Josh 15:16–17 and Judg 1:12–13 describe as given in marriage to Othniel after he captured Kirjath-sepher. Because the Caleb of 1 Chronicles 2 is traced through Hezron, while the Caleb of Joshua is called the son of Jephunneh, how the two Calebs relate is not certain. This entry follows the reference works in identifying her with Achsah.

Adaiah was a man of Boscath and the father of Jedidah, the mother of King Josiah of Judah. That made him Josiah's maternal grandfather (2 Kgs 22:1). He is mentioned only in this one verse, which gives Josiah's age at his accession and the length of his reign. Boscath is usually taken to be the same as Bozkath, a town in the lowlands of Judah listed in Josh 15:39. Smith's Bible Dictionary places that town there. Because Josiah appears in Matthew's genealogy of Jesus (Matt 1:10–11), Adaiah belongs to that family line through his daughter. Smith's Bible Dictionary explains the name as "adorned by the LORD," while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "the witness of the Lord." Several other men in the Bible share the name Adaiah. Nothing else is recorded about this one.

Adaiah was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, named in its genealogy as one of the sons of Shimhi, listed alongside Beraiah and Shimrath (1 Chr 8:21). His other brothers named in the same list are Jakim, Zichri, Zabdi, Elienai, Zilthai and Eliel. Smith's Bible Dictionary takes his father Shimhi to be the same man as Shema in 1 Chr 8:13. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia goes further and traces this Shema through Elpaal to Shaharaim, whose family is listed among the Benjamites. Nothing else is recorded about Adaiah beyond his name and family. The name means "Yahweh has adorned" according to Smith's and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia. Several other people in the Bible share the name, so this Adaiah should not be confused with them.

Adaiah was the father of Maaseiah, one of the captains of hundreds whom the priest Jehoiada brought into a covenant in the seventh year, as he prepared to act (2 Chr 23:1). The surrounding chapter shows this was the plot to remove Queen Athaliah and crown the young Joash as king of Judah. Adaiah himself is known only through his son and does nothing in the narrative. Smith's Bible Dictionary calls him Maaseiah's "ancestor" rather than his father, since "son of" in Hebrew can mean a more distant descendant. The name, which the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia renders "Yahweh has adorned," belongs to several men in the Bible. This Adaiah should not be confused with the others of the same name.

Adaiah was one of the descendants of Bani listed in Ezra 10:29 among the men of Israel who had married foreign wives after the return from exile in Babylon. The surrounding chapter describes how these men agreed, at Ezra's urging, to send away their foreign wives. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that he was a layman rather than a priest or Levite, since he appears among the 'sons of Bani' and not in the priestly or Levitical lists. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates the episode to about 459 BC. The name means 'Yahweh has adorned' according to Smith's and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia, while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives 'the witness of the Lord.' Several other men in the Bible share the name Adaiah. Nothing more is recorded about this one.

Adaiah was one of the Israelite men in Ezra's time who had married foreign wives, named in the list of those who agreed to send them away (Ezra 10:39). He appears only once, in a run of names with nothing else said about him. The setting is inferred from the surrounding chapter, where Ezra led the returned exiles to give up such marriages. Which family group he belonged to is uncertain. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia place him among the descendants of Bani, possibly a second Bani in the list. The STEPBible names list from Tyndale House describes him as a priest descended from Harim. Several other men in the Bible share the name Adaiah, and it is not clear whether he is the same as any of them. The name is usually explained as "the Lord has adorned."

Adaiah was a man of the tribe of Judah who appears only in the family line of Maaseiah, one of the Judahites who lived in Jerusalem in Nehemiah's time (Neh 11:5). He was the son of Joiarib and the father of Hazaiah. By that genealogy he was Maaseiah's great-great-grandfather, so he probably lived several generations before the return from exile. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia place him in the line of Perez, son of Judah. Nothing else is recorded about him. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "adorned by the LORD," and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "the witness of the Lord." Several other people in the Bible share the name Adaiah and should not be confused with him.

Adalia was one of the ten sons of Haman, the Persian official who plotted to destroy the Jews in the reign of Ahasuerus. He appears only in the list of Haman's sons at Esth 9:8. By inference from the surrounding passage (Esth 9:6–10), he was killed with his brothers in Shushan when the Jews defended themselves on the day set for their destruction. Smith's Bible Dictionary counts him as the fifth son and gives the meaning "a fire-god." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia regards the name as probably Persian, with its meaning unknown. Nothing else is recorded about him.

Addar was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, named first among the sons of Bela, Benjamin's firstborn, in the genealogy at 1 Chr 8:3. That makes him a grandson of Benjamin. His name probably means "glorious" or "mighty." Nothing else is recorded about him. Easton's Bible Dictionary, Smith's Bible Dictionary and the STEPBible proper-names list identify him with Ard, who appears as a son of Bela in Num 26:40 and as a son of Benjamin in Gen 46:21. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that he is sometimes counted as one of Benjamin's own sons. This entry lists Ard among Addar's brothers, along with Gera, Abihud, Abishua, Naaman, Ahoah and others drawn from the different lists of Bela's sons. On that view the two names refer to separate people, though the equation of Addar with Ard is widely held.

Addi is a man named only once in the Bible, in Luke's genealogy of Jesus, which traces the line back from Joseph to Adam. He appears as the son of Cosam and the father of Melchi (Luke 3:28). In Luke's list he stands three generations above Salathiel, the father of Zerubbabel. By inference from his position in the list, which runs through David's son Nathan rather than through the kings, he would have lived some generations before the Babylonian exile and belonged to the tribe of Judah. Nothing else is recorded about him. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "ornament."

Ader was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, named once in the Benjamite genealogy of 1 Chr 8:15. He is listed among the sons of Beriah, alongside Zebadiah, Arad, Michael, Ispah, Joha and others. Nothing further is recorded about his life. The surrounding passage describes Beriah as one of the heads of the families living in Aijalon, so Ader probably belonged to that community, by inference from context. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "flock" and notes that the Hebrew form is more accurately Eder. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia likewise treats "Ader" as the King James spelling of Eder, the form used in most modern translations. He is distinct from other men named Eder in the Bible.

Adiel was a leader in the tribe of Simeon, named in a list of Simeonite family heads in 1 Chr 4:36. The surrounding passage, which continues past this verse, describes these men as princes in their families whose households grew large. In the days of King Hezekiah they went to the valley of Gedor, attacked the people living there, including Hamites and Meunites, and settled in their pasture lands. Easton's Bible Dictionary calls him a family head of Simeon. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both take part in the Gedor raid as his, and Smith's dates it to about 711 BC, an estimate drawn from context. The name is usually explained as "ornament of God." Several other men in the Bible share the name Adiel, and this one should not be confused with them.

Adiel was the father of Azmaveth, the official in charge of King David's treasures (1 Chr 27:25). He is known only through his son's name in the list of David's administrators. Nothing else about his life or tribe is recorded. Smith's Bible Dictionary calls him an ancestor of Azmaveth, since "son of" can refer to a more distant forebear. It dates the period to about 1050 BC, an estimate inferred from the timing of David's reign. Smith's and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia give the name's meaning as "ornament of God," and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "the witness of the Lord." Several other men in Chronicles bear the same name, including a Simeonite leader and a priest's ancestor. This Adiel is distinguished from them only by his connection to Azmaveth.

Adin was one of the leaders of the people who sealed the written covenant in the time of Nehemiah, when the community in Jerusalem pledged to keep the law of God after returning from exile. His name appears in Neh 10:16 within the list that begins with "the chief of the people" in Neh 10:14, alongside Adonijah and Bigvai. The text gives no further details about him. The name also appears elsewhere as the head of a family whose descendants returned from Babylon (Ezra 2:15; Neh 7:20). Bigvai is a family name in those same lists, so this Adin may stand for that family rather than for a single individual. Whether he is the same person is uncertain, and the name is shared by several people in the Bible. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives its meaning as "adorned" or "dainty."

Adina was a Reubenite, the son of Shiza, named among David's mighty men in 1 Chr 11:42. He is described as a captain, or chief, of the Reubenites, with thirty men under him. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that he appears in the part of the Chronicler's list that adds names not found in the parallel list of David's warriors in 2 Samuel 23. Smith's Bible Dictionary places him among David's captains east of the Jordan, which fits the territory of the tribe of Reuben. His name is usually explained as meaning "slender" (Easton's Bible Dictionary) or "adorned" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia). Nothing else is recorded about him.

Adino the Eznite is named in 2 Sam 23:8 as the first and chief of David's mighty men, called the Tachmonite who "sat in the seat," chief among the captains. He is credited with killing eight hundred men with his spear at one time. The Hebrew of this verse is difficult, and its reading is debated. The parallel list in 1 Chr 11:11 names the chief warrior Jashobeam, a Hachmonite, says he lifted up his spear, and gives the number slain as three hundred. Many scholars therefore take "Adino the Eznite" as a garbled form of that phrase rather than a personal name. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the Septuagint keeps the names Adino and Eznite, and it suggests judgment be suspended. This entry follows the King James reading, which treats Adino as another name for the same chief warrior. Neither name appears anywhere else in the Bible.

Adlai was the father of Shaphat, one of the officials over King David's property. He is mentioned only once, in a list of David's stewards, where Shaphat son of Adlai is named as the man in charge of the royal herds that grazed in the valleys. A different official, Shitrai the Sharonite, oversaw the herds in the plain of Sharon (1 Chr 27:29). Nothing else is recorded about Adlai himself. By inference from the list, he lived in or before the time of David. The meaning of his name is uncertain. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "justice of Jehovah," the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives "lax, weary," and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "my witness; my ornament."

Admatha was one of the seven princes of Persia and Media at the court of King Ahasuerus, listed third in Esth 1:14 among Carshena, Shethar, Tarshish, Meres, Marsena and Memucan. These men "saw the king's face" and "sat the first in the kingdom." In other words, they had direct access to the king and held the highest rank under him. From the surrounding passage, they were the advisers the king consulted when Queen Vashti refused his summons. Nothing else is recorded about Admatha himself. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the Septuagint gives only three names in this list. The meaning of the name is uncertain. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "given by the highest," while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "a cloud of death."

Adna was a man of the family of Pahath-moab who appears in the list of Israelites found to have married foreign wives in Ezra's time (Ezra 10:30). The surrounding chapter describes how, after the return from exile in Babylon, these men agreed to send away their foreign wives as part of Ezra's reforms. He is one of eight men named from Pahath-moab. The events fall in the mid-fifth century BC; Smith's Bible Dictionary dates them to about 459 BC, an estimate drawn from context. The name is usually explained as meaning "pleasure" or "delight" (Hitchcock's Bible Names). Several people in the Bible share this name, including a priest in Nehemiah's day, and this Adna should not be confused with them. Nothing else is recorded about him.

Adna was a priest in Jerusalem after the return from exile. He is listed as head of the priestly family of Harim in Neh 12:15. The surrounding list in Nehemiah 12 places him in the days of Joiakim, son of Jeshua the high priest, a generation after the first exiles returned from Babylon. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates this to about 500 BC; that date is an estimate drawn from context. Nothing more is recorded about him. The name, which Hitchcock's Bible Names explains as meaning "pleasure" or "delight," is shared by several people in the Bible, including a man of the family of Pahath-moab who had married a foreign wife (Ezra 10:30). This entry concerns only the priest of Harim's family.

Adnah was a man of the tribe of Manasseh, one of the "captains of the thousands" of Manasseh who came over to David as he went to Ziklag (1 Chr 12:20). The surrounding passage places this when David was leaving the Philistine camp, and Smith's Bible Dictionary describes Adnah as deserting Saul to join David and fighting with him against the Amalekite raiders; the next verse speaks of these men helping David against the band, which is read as that pursuit. Smith's and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia give the meaning of the name as "pleasure." The name Adnah is shared by more than one person in the Bible, and this entry concerns only the Manassite captain. Nothing more is recorded about him.

Adnah was a commander from the tribe of Judah in the army of King Jehoshaphat. He is named first among the captains of thousands from Judah and is called "the chief." Under him were 300,000 "mighty men of valour" (2 Chr 17:14). The context places him in Jehoshaphat's reign over Judah, as part of the king's organized military force. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests he may have been the commander-in-chief of the army. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "pleasure," while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "eternal rest." The name is shared by another man in the Bible, a warrior of Manasseh who joined David. This entry concerns only the commander under Jehoshaphat, who is known from this single verse.

Adonijah was a Levite in the reign of King Jehoshaphat of Judah. He is named in a list of Levites whom Jehoshaphat sent out, together with several officials and the priests Elishama and Jehoram, to teach the people (2 Chr 17:8). The surrounding passage says they carried the Book of the Law and went through the cities of Judah giving instruction. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia dates this mission to Jehoshaphat's third year. His name means "my lord is the LORD" (Smith's Bible Dictionary). Nothing else is recorded about him. He should not be confused with other men of the same name, such as David's son Adonijah, who tried to claim the throne.

Adonijah was one of the men who set their seal to the covenant made under Nehemiah after the return from exile, pledging to keep the Law of God. He appears in Neh 10:16 between Bigvai and Adin. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia place him among the "chiefs of the people" listed in that part of the chapter, while the STEPBible proper-names index describes him as a Levite. Smith's Bible Dictionary identifies him with Adonikam, whose family appears among the returned exiles, which would make the name stand for that clan. His name means "my lord is the LORD." Nothing else is recorded about him, and he should not be confused with other men of the same name, such as David's son.

Adrammelech was a god worshipped by the people of Sepharvaim, named together with Anammelech as one of the two gods of that city. According to 2 Kgs 17:31, after Assyria resettled foreigners in Samaria, the Sepharvite settlers kept up his worship there and burned their children in fire to him. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes him as a form of the sun-god. Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that his rites resembled those of Molech, and suggests he represented the male power of the sun, with Anammelech as the female counterpart. The name is usually explained as meaning something like "splendor" or "glory of the king." The same name belongs to a different person, a son of the Assyrian king Sennacherib who helped kill his father (2 Kgs 19:37; Isa 37:38). That man is a separate figure from this god.

Agag is a king named in Balaam's oracle over Israel, which says that Israel's king "shall be higher than Agag" (Num 24:7). The verse does not say who he was, but Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies him as a king of the Amalekites living at the time of the Exodus. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggest that Agag may have been a title used by Amalekite kings, much as Pharaoh was used in Egypt. This entry covers only the Agag of Balaam's oracle. A different Agag, also an Amalekite king, was later spared by Saul and then put to death by Samuel (1 Sam 15). Some readers take the name in Balaam's oracle as pointing ahead to that later king. The meaning of the name is uncertain, and older works offer readings such as "flame" or "violent."

Agee was a Hararite, the father of Shammah, one of David's three most prominent mighty men (2 Sam 23:11). He is named only in that verse, which introduces Shammah's stand against the Philistines in a field of lentils after the rest of the people had fled. The epithet "the Hararite" may describe Agee or his son, and probably points to a home in the hill country or to a family or clan name. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary give the name the meaning "fugitive." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes a textual puzzle. 1 Chr 11:34 names "Jonathan the son of Shagee the Hararite," while the parallel list in 2 Sam 23:32–33 has "Jonathan, Shammah the Hararite." On one reading Agee was Jonathan's grandfather. On another, "Agee" and "Shagee" are the same name, which would make Jonathan and Shammah brothers.

Agur was the son of Jakeh, named in Prov 30:1 as the author of the sayings collected in Proverbs 30. The verse calls his words "the prophecy" (or "oracle") and says he addressed them to Ithiel and Ucal, who are otherwise unknown. Nothing else is recorded about him, and his time and place are not stated. The meaning of his name is uncertain: Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries give "gatherer" or "collector," while the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia also allows "hireling." Smith's describes him as an unknown Hebrew sage who spoke or collected the sayings. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that his chapter includes a well-known prayer asking for neither poverty nor riches (Prov 30:7–9) and several numerical proverbs.

Aharhel was a man of the tribe of Judah, named once in the genealogies of Judah as the son of Harum (1 Chr 4:8). The verse says that Coz fathered Anub and Zobebah, and then mentions "the families of Aharhel the son of Harum." That wording suggests Aharhel founded a clan known by his name. How he and Harum relate to Coz is unclear. Smith's Bible Dictionary calls the passage an obscure fragment of Judah's genealogies. Nothing else is recorded about him. The meaning of his name is uncertain. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "behind the breastwork," while Hitchcock's Bible Names offers several possibilities, including "another host" and "a brother's sheep."

Ahasbai was the father of Eliphelet, one of the warriors listed among David's mighty men in 2 Sam 23:34. The verse calls him "the son of the Maachathite," which probably means Ahasbai himself was a Maachathite, someone from Maacah. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests this could be either Abel-beth-maacah in northern Israel or, more probably, the Aramean kingdom of Maacah east of the upper Jordan. Nothing else is recorded about him. The parallel list in 1 Chr 11:35 gives different names at this point, "Eliphal the son of Ur." Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both explain the difference as damage to the text in copying. The name is usually taken to mean "blooming." By inference from David's reign, he lived about 1050 BC.

Ahban was a man of the tribe of Judah, named only in the genealogies of 1 Chronicles. He was the son of Abishur and his wife Abihail, and Molid was his brother (1 Chr 2:29). The surrounding genealogy traces Abishur's line back through Shammai and Onam to Jerahmeel, a descendant of Judah through Perez and Hezron. Nothing else is recorded about Ahban's life. Smith's Bible Dictionary takes his name to mean "brother of the wise" or "discreet," and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives "brother of an intelligent one," marking that meaning as uncertain.

Aher is named once in the Bible, in 1 Chr 7:12, as the father of Hushim. The verse comes at the end of a list of Benjamin's descendants, and Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both treat him as a Benjamite. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the name means "another" and may be a shortened form. Both works suggest he may be the same man as Ahiram, a son of Benjamin in Num 26:38, or Aharah in 1 Chr 8:1. The STEPBible proper-names index, by contrast, links him to the tribe of Asher as a son of Shemer. The brief and compressed wording of the verse leaves his exact place in the genealogy uncertain. This entry follows the Benjamite reading suggested by the verse's context and records only what the verse states: that Hushim was his son.

Ahi was a member of the tribe of Gad, named in the Gadite genealogy of 1 Chronicles as the son of Abdiel and grandson of Guni. He is described as "chief of the house of their fathers", meaning the head of a family clan (1 Chr 5:15). The surrounding passage places the Gadites in Gilead and Bashan, east of the Jordan, and says their genealogies were recorded in the days of Jotham king of Judah and Jeroboam king of Israel. Smith's Bible Dictionary accordingly dates him to about 758 BC, an estimate drawn from that context. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "my brother". The name Ahi is borne by more than one person in the Bible. This Ahi should not be confused with the Asherite of the same name in 1 Chronicles 7. Nothing further is recorded about him.

Ahi was a man of the tribe of Asher, listed in the Asherite genealogy as the first of the sons of Shamer, with his brothers Rohgah, Jehubbah and Aram (1 Chr 7:34). Shamer is probably the same man called Shomer, son of Heber, two verses earlier in 1 Chr 7:32. The STEPBible proper names index identifies him the same way. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "my brother." Because the Hebrew word can also be read as an ordinary noun, some translations render the verse as "the sons of Shamer his brother" rather than treating Ahi as a personal name. This entry follows the King James reading, which takes Ahi as a son. Nothing else is recorded about him. He is distinct from another Ahi, a man of the tribe of Gad named in 1 Chr 5:15.

Ahiah was one of the officials of King Solomon. He and his brother Elihoreph served together as scribes, or royal secretaries, and both are called sons of Shisha (1 Kgs 4:3). Shisha is probably the same man as Shavsha, David's scribe (1 Chr 18:16), who is also called Seraiah (2 Sam 8:17) and Sheva (2 Sam 20:25). If so, the office passed from father to sons. Smith's Bible Dictionary counts him among Solomon's princes, since he is named in the list of high officials. His name is often spelled Ahijah. Smith's gives its meaning as "friend of Jehovah," and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "brother of the Lord." Several other people in the Bible share this name. Nothing more is recorded about this Ahiah.

Ahiah was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, named in the Benjamite genealogy of 1 Chr 8:7 alongside Naaman and Gera. The surrounding passage, which lists "the sons of Ehud" (1 Chr 8:6), indicates that he was a son of Ehud, and this entry follows that reading. Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries instead describe him as a son of Bela, Benjamin's firstborn, since Bela's line opens the chapter. The verse also notes that "he removed them" and then names Uzza and Ahihud, who are listed here as his brothers. The wording is compressed, and who carried out the removal is not clear. The Revised Version spells his name Ahijah, which Smith's Bible Dictionary renders "friend of Jehovah" and Hitchcock's Bible Names renders "brother of the Lord." Several other people in the Bible bear the same name. Nothing else is recorded about him.

Ahian was a son of Shemida in the genealogy of the tribe of Manasseh, one of the two tribes descended from Joseph. He is named first among Shemida's four sons, with Shechem, Likhi and Aniam, in 1 Chr 7:19, and nothing more is recorded about him. The chapter places Shemida among the descendants of Manasseh. Num 26:32 and Josh 17:2 also list Shemida as the founder of a Manassite clan, which suggests that Ahian belonged to that family line. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives the meaning of his name as "brotherly." Hitchcock's Bible Names renders it "brother of wine."

Ahiezer was the son of Shemaah the Gibeathite and the brother of Joash. He is named as the chief of a group of warriors who came to David at Ziklag (1 Chr 12:3). The surrounding passage describes these men as kinsmen of Saul from the tribe of Benjamin, skilled with bow and sling, who joined David while he was still kept away from Saul. Easton's Bible Dictionary calls him the chief of the Benjamite slingers, while Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him as leading a body of archers. "Gibeathite" probably means he came from Gibeah, Saul's hometown in Benjamin. His name is usually taken to mean "brother is help." He should not be confused with the other Ahiezer, the leader of the tribe of Dan during the wilderness period.

Ahihud, son of Shelomi, was the prince, or leader, of the tribe of Asher. He appears in the list of tribal leaders whom the LORD named to Moses to divide the land of Canaan west of the Jordan among the tribes (Num 34:27). The surrounding passage shows that these men were to work with Eleazar the priest and Joshua in assigning each tribe its inheritance. Nothing else is recorded about him. The meaning of his name is uncertain. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives "brother is majesty" and Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "brother of renown." Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that the Hebrew spelling differs from another Ahihud in the Bible, a Benjamite named in the genealogies of 1 Chronicles, so the two should not be confused.

Ahihud was a member of the tribe of Benjamin, named in the Benjamite genealogy at 1 Chr 8:7. This entry treats him as a son of Ehud, whose sons are listed as Naaman, Ahiah and Gera, followed by Uzza and Ahihud. The verse is hard to follow, however. It says of the first three that "he removed them," probably referring to a forced move of these families, and then that "he begat Uzza, and Ahihud." Some readers therefore take Gera as Ahihud's father. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia calls the passage obscure and probably damaged in transmission. Easton's Bible Dictionary links him with the line of Bela, Benjamin's son. The name is usually explained as "brother is majesty." Nothing else is recorded about him, and he should not be confused with others of the same name, such as the Asherite leader in Num 34:27.

Ahijah was one of the sons of Jerahmeel, of the tribe of Judah. He is mentioned only in the genealogy of 1 Chr 2:25, which names Jerahmeel as the firstborn of Hezron and lists his sons as Ram the firstborn, Bunah, Oren, Ozem and Ahijah. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia describe Jerahmeel as a great-grandson of Judah. The next verse, 1 Chr 2:26, says Jerahmeel had another wife, Atarah, who was the mother of Onam, so Onam was probably Ahijah's half-brother. Because that verse speaks of "another wife," some interpreters have suggested that "Ahijah" here may be the name of Jerahmeel's first wife. This entry follows the usual reading, which treats Ahijah as a son. The name, often explained as "brother of the LORD," belongs to several different people in the Bible. Nothing more is recorded about this one.

Ahijah the Pelonite was one of David's mighty men. He is named in the list of David's warriors at 1 Chr 11:36, next to Hepher the Mecherathite. Nothing else is recorded about him. The parallel list in 2 Sam 23:34 has "Eliam the son of Ahithophel the Gilonite" at roughly the same place, and Easton's Bible Dictionary treats Ahijah and Eliam as the same man. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes the correspondence between the two lists, which probably arose from differences in how the names were copied. The name Ahijah means "brother of the Lord" or "my brother is the Lord." Several other men in the Bible share this name, so this Ahijah should not be confused with Ahijah the prophet of Shiloh or with others called Ahijah.

Ahijah was a Levite who was in charge of the treasuries of the house of God and of the treasuries of the dedicated things (1 Chr 26:20). The surrounding chapter describes how the Levites' duties were organized, and Smith's Bible Dictionary places him in the reign of David. Nothing else is recorded about him, and he is one of several men in the Bible named Ahijah. The name is usually explained as "brother of the Lord" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia). That encyclopedia also notes that the Greek translation of this verse reads "and their brethren" instead of a personal name, a reading many scholars accept. This entry follows the Hebrew text as translated in the King James Version, which names Ahijah.

Ahijah was one of the men who set their seal to the covenant made under Nehemiah, in which the community returned from exile pledged to keep the law of God. He is named only in Neh 10:26, alongside Hanan and Anan. The verse falls within the list that begins at Neh 10:14 with "the chief of the people," so he was probably a lay leader, and Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him as one of the "heads of the people." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia counts him as a Levite, and the Tyndale House proper-names list calls him a priest. This entry follows the reading as a head of the people. Nothing else is recorded about him, and several other men in the Bible share his name. The name is usually explained as "brother of the LORD" or "my brother is the LORD."

Ahimaaz was the father of Ahinoam, the wife of King Saul. He is mentioned only once, in 1 Sam 14:50, which names Saul's wife and her father alongside Abner, the commander of Saul's army. Nothing else is recorded about him, and he should not be confused with others of the same name, such as the son of Zadok the priest. The meaning of the name is uncertain. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests "my brother is rage" or "brother of rage", Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "brother of anger", and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "a brother of the council." Smith's Bible Dictionary places him before 1093 BC, an estimate drawn from his connection to Saul's reign.

Ahimaaz was one of the twelve district officers King Solomon appointed to supply food for the royal household, each for one month of the year. His district was Naphtali (1 Kgs 4:15). The surrounding passage lists these officers, which is why he is understood as a governor or commissary officer there. He married Basmath, a daughter of Solomon, and so was the king's son-in-law. Several people in the Bible are called Ahimaaz. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that this man may possibly be Ahimaaz the son of Zadok the priest, though nothing in the text confirms it. This entry treats him as a separate person. The name is usually taken to mean "brother of anger" or "my brother is rage" (Smith's Bible Dictionary; International Standard Bible Encyclopedia), while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "a brother of the council."

Ahiman was one of the gatekeepers ("porters") named in 1 Chr 9:17, listed with Shallum, Akkub, Talmon and their relatives, with Shallum as their chief. Smith's Bible Dictionary calls him a Levite porter. The setting is open to two readings. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia place him among the temple guardians after the Exile, since the surrounding chapter lists those who lived in Jerusalem. The STEPBible proper-names index places his service in David's reign, reading the list alongside the chapter's later reference to gatekeepers appointed by David and Samuel. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia compares the parallel list in Neh 11:19, which names Akkub and Talmon but not Ahiman. He is a different person from Ahiman the son of Anak at Hebron. His name is often explained as "brother of the right hand" or "my brother is fortune."

Ahimelech was a Hittite who was among David's companions while David was hiding from Saul in the wilderness. He is mentioned only once. When David found Saul's camp in the wilderness of Ziph, he asked Ahimelech and Abishai son of Zeruiah which of them would go down with him into the camp at night. Abishai volunteered, and nothing more is said of Ahimelech (1 Sam 26:6). His presence shows that David's band included foreigners, as did his later forces, which counted Uriah the Hittite among them. The name is usually explained as "my brother is king" or "brother of a king" (Hitchcock's Bible Names; International Standard Bible Encyclopedia). Several people in the Bible share this name. This Ahimelech should not be confused with Ahimelech the priest of Nob, who helped David earlier in his flight from Saul.

Ahinadab, son of Iddo, was one of the twelve district officers King Solomon appointed over Israel. According to 1 Kgs 4:7, which introduces the list, each officer provided food for the king and his household for one month of the year. Ahinadab's district was Mahanaim, a town east of the Jordan in Gilead, and by inference the surrounding territory as well (1 Kgs 4:14). Nothing else is recorded about him or his father. The meaning of his name is understood in different ways: Easton's Bible Dictionary gives "brother of liberality," Smith's Bible Dictionary "noble brother," and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia "brother of willingness" or "my brother is willing."

Ahinoam was the wife of King Saul and the daughter of Ahimaaz. She is named once, in 1 Sam 14:50, in a brief summary of Saul's family and court that also names Abner as commander of his army. The preceding verse lists Saul's children, and by inference from that context she is taken as the mother of Jonathan, Malchi-shua, Merab and Michal. Abinadab, a son of Saul who died with his father in battle according to 1 Sam 31:2, is also counted among her children here. Nothing else is recorded about her life. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia explains her name as "my brother is pleasantness." She is a different person from Ahinoam of Jezreel, one of David's wives. Her father Ahimaaz is also distinct from the later priest of that name.

Ahio was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, listed in the genealogy of 1 Chr 8 among the sons of Beriah, alongside brothers such as Shashak and Jeremoth. By inference from the surrounding verses, Beriah and Shema were family heads of the inhabitants of Aijalon who drove out the people of Gath (1 Chr 8:13), and 1 Chr 8:16 closes the list as 'the sons of Beriah.' The Tyndale House proper-names index (STEPBible) instead counts Ahio as a son of Elpaal, Beriah's father. This entry follows the reading that makes him Beriah's son. Nothing else is recorded about him. The name probably means 'brotherly' or 'his brother.' The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the Greek Old Testament renders it as an ordinary word, 'his brother.' Other men bear the same name, including the son of Abinadab who walked before the ark (2 Sam 6:3).

Ahiram was a son of Benjamin and the ancestor of the Ahiramites, one of the Benjamite clans counted in the census taken in the plains of Moab (Num 26:38). He is third in that list, after Bela and Ashbel. His name is usually taken to mean "exalted brother" or "my brother is exalted." The lists of Benjamin's sons in other books do not match exactly, and Ahiram may appear there under other forms. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both connect him with Ehi in Gen 46:21, possibly a shortened form of the name. They also note that Aharah in 1 Chr 8:1 and Aher in 1 Chr 7:12 may be the same man, though this is uncertain. This entry lists Ehi separately among his brothers.

Ahishahar was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, the last-named of the seven sons of Bilhan in the Benjamite genealogy of 1 Chr 7:10. His brothers were Jeush, Benjamin, Ehud, Chenaanah, Zethan and Tharshish. Bilhan was a son of Jediael, and the surrounding passage traces Jediael back to Benjamin, son of Jacob. That makes Ahishahar a great-grandson of the tribe's founder, though Smith's Bible Dictionary calls Bilhan Benjamin's grandson. The brother named Benjamin shares his name with the patriarch but is a different man. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives the meaning of the name Ahishahar as "brother of dawn." He appears only in this one verse, and nothing else is recorded about him. By inference from the context, which counts men of valor by their fathers' houses, he was the head of one of the family groups within this branch of Benjamin.

Ahishar was one of King Solomon's chief officials. He was "over the household," meaning he managed the royal palace and its affairs. He appears only once, in the list of Solomon's high officers in 1 Kgs 4:6, where he is named alongside Adoniram, who was in charge of forced labor. Nothing else is recorded about his family or career. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia take his name to mean "brother of song" or "my brother has sung," while Hitchcock's Bible Names also offers "brother of a prince." Later passages show that the office of the one "over the household" carried considerable authority in the kingdoms of Israel and Judah, so Ahishar probably ranked among the most important figures at Solomon's court.

Ahlai was a member of the tribe of Judah, descended through Jerahmeel, Onam, Appaim and Ishi, and named in 1 Chr 2:31 as the child of Sheshan. That verse says only "children," but 1 Chr 2:34 adds that Sheshan had no sons, only daughters, so Ahlai is understood as his daughter. STEPBible's proper-names index takes her this way, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes both readings. The same passage says Sheshan gave a daughter in marriage to his Egyptian servant Jarha, and she bore Attai, through whom the family line continued (1 Chr 2:34–35). That daughter is probably Ahlai, by inference from the passage. The name is shared with another Ahlai, the father of Zabad, one of David's mighty men (1 Chr 11:41). Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the name's meaning as "beseeching; sorrowing; expecting."

Ahlai was the father of Zabad. He is known only from 1 Chr 11:41, where Zabad son of Ahlai appears in the list of David's mighty men, the elite warriors of his army, named immediately after Uriah the Hittite. Nothing else is recorded about Ahlai himself. The same name belongs to another person in the Bible, a daughter of Sheshan in the genealogy of Judah (1 Chr 2:31, 34). The two are distinct, and this entry concerns the father of Zabad. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia explains the Hebrew name as meaning "O would that!", while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "beseeching; sorrowing; expecting."

Ahoah was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, one of the sons of Bela, Benjamin's firstborn. He appears only once, in the list of Bela's sons at 1 Chr 8:4, with Abishua and Naaman. His name may mean "brotherly." Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries take Ahiah in 1 Chr 8:7 to be the same man. Easton's also identifies him with Iri, who is named among Bela's sons in 1 Chr 7:7. Both dictionaries connect him with the Ahohites, a clan named after an Ahoah (2 Sam 23:9, 28; 1 Chr 11:12, 29; 27:4). Members of that clan included Dodo, father of Eleazar, and Zalmon (also called Ilai), two of David's mighty men. By inference, these men descended from this Benjaminite. Beyond his place in the genealogy, nothing more is recorded about him.

Aholibamah was a daughter of Anah and the sister of Dishon. She appears in the genealogy of the Horites, the earlier inhabitants of Seir (Edom). Gen 36:25 names her as Anah's only daughter. By inference from the verse before it (Gen 36:24), her father is Anah the son of Zibeon. Esau's wife Aholibamah is described in Gen 36:2 and 36:14 as the daughter of Anah, the daughter of Zibeon, so she is probably the same woman. Through that marriage the Horite line would have joined Esau's family. Because several people in the Bible carry this name, including an Edomite chief in Gen 36:41, the identification is likely but not certain. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "my tabernacle is exalted."

Ahumai was a man of the tribe of Judah, named only in the genealogy of 1 Chr 4:2. He was a son of Jahath and a brother of Lahad. His grandfather was Reaiah, son of Shobal. The verse says these were "the families of the Zorathites," so Ahumai and Lahad were apparently founders or heads of clans linked with Zorah, a town in the lowland of Judah. Smith's Bible Dictionary takes him to be the head of one of these families. Nothing else is recorded about him. The meaning of his name is uncertain. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia tentatively gives "brother of water," and Hitchcock's Bible Names offers both "a meadow of waters" and "a brother of waters."

Ahuzam was a man of the tribe of Judah, named in the genealogy of 1 Chr 4:6 as the first of four sons born to Ashur by his wife Naarah. His full brothers were Hepher, Temeni and Haahashtari. Ashur also had another wife, Helah, whose sons Zereth, Jezoar, Ethnan and Coz were Ahuzam's half-brothers, according to the verse that follows in the same genealogy. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the spelling Ahuzzam and identifies Ashur as the father or founder of Tekoa, drawing on the opening of this family list (1 Chr 4:5). Smith's renders the name as "possession," and Hitchcock's Bible Names as "their taking or possessing vision." Nothing more is recorded about him beyond his place in this family line.

Ahuzzath was one of the friends of Abimelech, king of Gerar, mentioned only once. He went with Abimelech and Phichol, the commander of Abimelech's army, to meet Isaac after Isaac had moved away from Gerar (Gen 26:26). By inference from the surrounding passage, the meeting took place at Beersheba, where the two sides swore an oath and made a covenant of peace. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests that the title "friend" may mean a royal adviser or minister, and that his name, meaning "possession," ends in a way that recalls Philistine names such as Gath and Goliath. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates the event to about 1877 BC, an estimate drawn from context.

Akkub was one of the seven sons of Elioenai, listed in the genealogy of David's royal line in the tribe of Judah (1 Chr 3:24). His brothers were Hodaiah, Eliashib, Pelaiah, Johanan, Dalaiah and Anani. The surrounding genealogy traces this family through King Jehoiachin and Zerubbabel, so Akkub belongs to the generations after the Babylonian exile. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia call him a descendant of Zerubbabel. Easton's Bible Dictionary simply describes him as a descendant of David. Nothing else is recorded about him beyond his name and place in the list. Several other men in the Bible share the name Akkub, including Levite gatekeepers and the head of a family of temple servants, but this entry refers only to the son of Elioenai. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives the name's meaning as "pursuer."

Akkub was the ancestor or head of a family of Nethinim, the temple servants, whose descendants are listed among the exiles who returned from Babylon to Jerusalem and Judah (Ezra 2:45). The list in Ezra 2 records the groups who came back with Zerubbabel. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates this return to about 536 BC. Nothing else is said about this Akkub himself. He appears only as a family name. Notably, the parallel list in Nehemiah 7 does not include his family. The name Akkub is shared by several other men in the Old Testament, including a gatekeeper and a descendant of David, and this entry is distinct from them. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives meanings for the name such as "footprint" or "supplanting."

Akkub was one of the men named in Neh 8:7 who helped the people understand the law when Ezra read it publicly in Jerusalem after the return from exile. He is listed with Jeshua, Bani, Sherebiah and others, and the verse groups them with "the Levites" who explained the reading while the people stood in their places. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him as a Levite who assisted Ezra in expounding the law. Nothing more is recorded about him. The name Akkub is shared by several people in the Bible, including a gatekeeper family and a descendant of David. Whether this Akkub is connected to any of them is uncertain, so this entry treats him as a distinct individual known only from this passage.

Alameth was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, one of the nine sons of Becher listed in the genealogy at 1 Chr 7:8. His brothers were Zemira, Joash, Eliezer, Elioenai, Omri, Jerimoth, Abiah and Anathoth. Becher was himself a son of Benjamin, which makes Alameth a grandson of Benjamin, as Easton's Bible Dictionary notes. Nothing is recorded of his life beyond his name. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the name more properly as Alemeth, meaning "covering," while the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia renders it "concealment." The ISBE also suggests that his name survived as that of a town near Anathoth, the Levitical city called Alemeth (Allemeth) in 1 Chr 6:60. His brother Anathoth likewise shares his name with that nearby town.

Alexander was a son of Simon of Cyrene, the man who was passing by on his way in from the country when the soldiers made him carry Jesus' cross (Mark 15:21). His brother was Rufus. Mark names the two sons without explaining who they were. By inference, they were probably known to Mark's first readers, since he identifies Simon through them. Some have linked Rufus with the Rufus greeted in Rom 16:13, but nothing in the text confirms a connection, and nothing further is recorded about Alexander himself. Several other men named Alexander appear in the New Testament, and there is no clear reason to identify this Alexander with any of them. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "one who assists men."

Alexander (Son of Simon) was a man in Jerusalem who was present when Peter and John were questioned by the Jewish leaders, about AD 30 by inference from context. Acts 4:6 lists him with Annas the high priest, Caiaphas, John and "as many as were of the kindred of the high priest." Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries take him to be a relative of Annas, a member of the high-priestly family who sat in on the hearing before the Sanhedrin. Nothing more is recorded of him. The title of this entry calls him a son of Simon, but Acts 4:6 does not name his father. Mark 15:21 mentions an Alexander whose father was Simon of Cyrene, and whether that is the same man is uncertain. Several other men named Alexander also appear in the New Testament. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "one who assists men."

Alexander (Jew of Ephesus) was a Jewish man who took part in the riot at Ephesus. The riot was stirred up by Demetrius the silversmith against Paul's preaching, about AD 53 by inference from context. During the uproar, the Jews of the city pushed Alexander forward from the crowd, and he motioned with his hand, intending to make a defence before the people (Acts 19:33). Easton's Bible Dictionary suggests that he was probably meant to show that the Jews had no connection with Paul. According to the next verse, the crowd recognized him as a Jew and drowned him out by shouting for about two hours in praise of the goddess Artemis (Diana), so his speech was never given. Easton's also notes that he may be the same person as Alexander the coppersmith mentioned in 2 Tim 4:14, though the name was common and the link is uncertain.

Alphaeus was the father of Levi, the tax collector whom Jesus called to follow him as he sat at his tax booth (Mark 2:14). The parallel account in Matthew 9:9 names the tax collector Matthew, so Alphaeus is identified as the father of the apostle Matthew, as Easton's Bible Dictionary also states. Nothing further is recorded about him. The same name belongs to the father of another apostle, James "the son of Alphaeus," in the lists of the Twelve. Whether these are the same man is uncertain. The Gospels never call Matthew and James brothers, and many readers treat them as two different men named Alphaeus. This entry concerns Matthew's father.

Amal was a man of the tribe of Asher, named once, in the Asherite genealogy, as one of the four sons of Helem, along with Zophah, Imna and Shelesh (1 Chr 7:35). The verse calls Helem the brother of the man named just before. The earlier list in 1 Chr 7:32 names Shomer and Hotham as brothers, sons of Heber. So Helem is probably another form of the name Hotham, and this entry follows that identification in treating Hotham as Amal's father. Nothing else is recorded about Amal. His name means "labor" or "toiler" according to Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia. Hitchcock's Bible Names also gives the meaning "iniquity."

Amariah was the chief priest in Judah during the reign of King Jehoshaphat. When Jehoshaphat appointed judges in Jerusalem, he named Amariah as the one over them "in all matters of the LORD". Zebadiah son of Ishmael, ruler of the house of Judah, handled "all the king's matters", and the Levites served as officers (2 Chr 19:11). Amariah therefore had charge of religious cases within the king's judicial reforms. Easton's Bible Dictionary suggests he is probably the Amariah named in the priestly genealogy at 1 Chr 6:9, and Smith's Bible Dictionary calls him the son of Azariah. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats that identification as possible. Several other men in the Bible share the name, which is usually taken to mean "the LORD has said".

Amariah was a man who served during the reign of King Hezekiah of Judah, one of six assistants named under Kore, the Levite in charge of the freewill offerings (2 Chr 31:14–15). Working in the cities of the priests, these men handed out the offerings brought to the temple to their fellow priests and Levites by their divisions, giving fairly to young and old alike. The surrounding passage sets this in Hezekiah's reorganization of temple worship and support. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia and the Tyndale House proper-names index treat him as a Levite, while Easton's Bible Dictionary lists him among the high priests of Hezekiah's time. This entry follows the Levite reading, which fits his place under Kore. His name means "the Lord has said." Several other men in the Bible bear the same name, and nothing else is recorded about this one.

Amariah was one of the Israelite men listed in Ezra's time as having married foreign wives, who agreed to send them away during Ezra's reforms after the return from exile. He is named only once, alongside Shallum and Joseph, in Ezra 10:42. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia place him among the descendants of Bani, the family group whose list begins earlier in the same chapter. Nothing else is recorded about him. The name, meaning "the Lord has said" or "the Lord promises," is shared by several other men in the Old Testament, and he should not be confused with them.

Amariah was a man of the tribe of Judah, from the clan of Perez, named only in a genealogy in Neh 11:4. He was the son of Shephatiah and the father of Zechariah, and an ancestor of Athaiah, one of the Judahites who lived in Jerusalem when the city was resettled in Nehemiah's time. Amariah himself therefore probably lived some generations before the return from exile. His name means "the Lord has said" or "the Lord promises." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia compares this line with the similar list of Judahite settlers in 1 Chr 9:4, which names an Imri, and suggests Amariah may belong to the same family. Several other men in the Bible share the name Amariah, and this one is known only from this single verse.

Amariah was an ancestor of the prophet Zephaniah, named only in the genealogy that opens Zephaniah's book (Zeph 1:1). He was the son of Hizkiah and the father of Gedaliah, making him Zephaniah's great-grandfather. Zephaniah prophesied in the days of Josiah king of Judah, so Amariah probably lived two or three generations earlier. Hizkiah is the same Hebrew name as Hezekiah, and many interpreters take him to be King Hezekiah of Judah. If so, Amariah was a son of that king and Zephaniah was of royal descent, though the verse does not call Hizkiah a king. Nothing else is recorded about him. Several other men in the Bible share the name, which Hitchcock's Bible Names explains as "the Lord says."

Amasa son of Hadlai was one of the leaders of the tribe of Ephraim in the northern kingdom of Israel during the reign of Ahaz, king of Judah. After Pekah's Israelite army defeated Judah and brought a large number of captives to Samaria, the prophet Oded warned the returning soldiers against enslaving their kinsmen. Amasa and three other heads of Ephraim, Azariah, Berechiah and Jehizkiah, then stood up against the returning troops (2 Chr 28:12). The surrounding passage records that they refused to let the captives be brought in, and that the captives were clothed, fed and returned to Jericho. Smith's Bible Dictionary calls him a prince of Ephraim. He is a different man from the better-known Amasa who commanded Absalom's army, since the name is shared by several people in the Bible.

Amasai was the leader of a group of men from Benjamin and Judah who came to David while he was an outlaw fleeing from Saul. When David questioned their loyalty, the spirit came upon Amasai, described as chief of the captains, and he declared that they belonged to David and were on his side. He wished peace to David and to his helpers, because David's God was helping him. David then accepted the men and made them captains of his band (1 Chr 12:18). Sources differ on where this happened. Smith's Bible Dictionary places it at Ziklag, while Easton's Bible Dictionary suggests the stronghold, probably of Adullam. This entry treats the place as uncertain. The name is shared by several men in the Bible. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives its meaning as "burdensome," while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "strong."

Amasai was a priest, one of seven named in 1 Chr 15:24 who blew trumpets before the ark of God when David had it brought up to Jerusalem. The other trumpeters were Shebaniah, Jehoshaphat, Nethaneel, Zechariah, Benaiah and Eliezer. Obed-edom and Jehiah served as doorkeepers for the ark on the same occasion. Easton's Bible Dictionary places this during the ark's move from the house of Obed-edom, where it had been kept for a time. Nothing else is recorded about him. Several other men in the Bible share the name Amasai, and this priest should be kept distinct from them. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "burdensome," while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "strong."

Amasai was a Levite of the Kohathite clan, known only as the father of Mahath. His son was one of the Levites who came forward when King Hezekiah called for the temple to be cleansed and its worship restored, as described in 2 Chr 29:12. Amasai himself does not take part in the account, and the verse records nothing else about him. Mahath is listed as a Kohathite, so Amasai probably belonged to that clan as well. The same pairing of names, Mahath son of Amasai, also appears in the much earlier Kohathite genealogy of 1 Chr 6:35. That suggests these names ran in the family, though the two men are probably different people. Several other men in the Bible are also called Amasai. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "strong," and Smith's Bible Dictionary gives it as "burdensome."

Amasiah, son of Zichri, was one of the military commanders of Judah during the reign of King Jehoshaphat. He appears only in 2 Chr 17:16, in a list of the king's army chiefs stationed in Jerusalem, where he is named next after Jehohanan. He commanded two hundred thousand "mighty men of valour." The verse singles him out as one who "willingly offered himself unto the LORD," a phrase Easton's Bible Dictionary compares with the volunteers praised in Judg 5:9. The text does not say what form this self-offering took. His name is usually explained as meaning "Yah bears" or "sustained by the LORD" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia; Easton's Bible Dictionary). Nothing else is recorded about him, and his father Zichri, a common name in the Old Testament, cannot be identified with any other person of that name.

Amaziah was a man of the tribe of Simeon, known only as the father of Joshah, who appears in a list of Simeonite clan leaders in 1 Chr 4:34. The surrounding passage (1 Chr 4:38–41) describes these leaders as princes of their families who, in the days of King Hezekiah of Judah, moved toward Gedor in search of pasture and settled there. By inference, Amaziah lived a generation before that time, but nothing else is said about him. Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies Joshah as one of the Simeonite chiefs in Hezekiah's time. Hitchcock's Bible Names and Smith's Bible Dictionary give the meaning of the name as "the strength of the Lord." Several other people in the Bible share the name Amaziah, including a king of Judah. This Amaziah should not be confused with them.

Amaziah was a Levite named only in the genealogy of 1 Chr 6:45, where he is listed as the son of Hilkiah and the father of Hashabiah. The surrounding passage traces the ancestry of Ethan, one of the Levite singers David appointed for the music of worship, back through Merari, son of Levi. Easton's Bible Dictionary accordingly places Amaziah among the descendants of Merari in Ethan's family line. He would therefore have lived several generations before Ethan. STEPBible's proper-names index links him with the time of David. Nothing else is recorded about him. The name, which Hitchcock's Bible Names explains as "the strength of the Lord," was borne by several other men in the Bible, including a king of Judah. This Levite should not be confused with them.

Ammiel, son of Gemalli, was the man from the tribe of Dan among the twelve spies Moses sent to explore the land of Canaan (Num 13:12). By inference from the wider account, he was not Joshua or Caleb, so he was one of the ten spies who brought back a discouraging report. Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that these ten died by a plague (Num 14:37). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia explains the name as meaning "my kinsman is God," while Smith's and Hitchcock's dictionaries give "people of God." The name Ammiel belongs to several different men in the Old Testament, and this entry refers only to the spy from Dan.

Ammiel was a Levite named as the sixth of eight brothers in the list of temple gatekeepers in 1 Chr 26:5. The surrounding passage (1 Chr 26:4) presents these brothers as the sons of Obed-edom, and Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries identify Ammiel that way. This entry records his father as Shimei. His brothers were Shemaiah, Jehozabad, Joah, Sacar, Nethaneel, Issachar and Peulthai. The chapter belongs to the account of the duties assigned to the Levites in David's time, so he probably served as a doorkeeper during David's reign, as the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia states. The verse closes the list with the remark that God had blessed the family. Nothing else is recorded about him. Several other men in the Bible share his name, which Hitchcock's Bible Names takes to mean "the people of God."

Ammihud was a man of the tribe of Simeon and the father of Shemuel. He is named only once, in Num 34:20, where his son Shemuel appears in the list of tribal leaders chosen to divide the land of Canaan among the tribes after Israel entered it. Nothing else is recorded about Ammihud himself. The name was shared by several other people in the Old Testament, such as the Ephraimite father of Elishama and the Naphtalite father of Pedahel, and this Simeonite should be kept distinct from them. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia explains the name as "my kinsman is glorious," while Smith's Bible Dictionary and Hitchcock's Bible Names give its meaning as "people of praise."

Ammihud was the father of Pedahel, the leader of the tribe of Naphtali named in Num 34:28. Pedahel was one of the tribal leaders chosen to help divide the land of Canaan among the Israelites, and the surrounding passage describes that appointment. Ammihud himself is known only as Pedahel's father, and nothing more is said about him. Several other men in the Bible share the name Ammihud, including fathers of leaders from the tribes of Ephraim and Simeon, so this one should not be confused with them. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia explains the name as "my kinsman is glorious," while Smith's Bible Dictionary and Hitchcock's Bible Names give "people of praise."

Ammihud was the father of Talmai, king of Geshur, a small Aramean kingdom northeast of Israel. He appears only once, at 2 Sam 13:37, which says that Absalom fled to Talmai son of Ammihud after killing his brother Amnon. A connected passage, 2 Sam 3:3, says David's wife Maacah was the daughter of Talmai king of Geshur, so Ammihud was probably the great-grandfather of Absalom through his mother. Some Hebrew manuscripts spell the name Ammihur, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia prefers that reading. It gives the meaning "my kinsman is glorious," while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "people of praise." Several other people in the Bible are also called Ammihud. Nothing more is recorded about this one.

Ammihud was a man of the tribe of Judah, descended through Pharez (Perez), son of Judah. He was the son of Omri and the father of Uthai. He appears only in a genealogy in 1 Chr 9:4, which traces Uthai's line back through Ammihud, Omri, Imri and Bani to Pharez. The surrounding chapter lists people who lived in Jerusalem after the return from exile, so Uthai was probably one of those settlers. Ammihud himself may have lived somewhat earlier, but the text does not say. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "people of praise." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia renders it "my kinsman is glorious." Several other men in the Old Testament share the name, and this Ammihud should not be confused with them. Nothing else is recorded about him.

Ammizabad was the son of Benaiah, the warrior who was mighty among David's thirty champions and ranked above them. He is named only in 1 Chr 27:6, in the list of the twelve army divisions that served King David in monthly rotation. Benaiah commanded the division for the third month, and the verse says that in his course was Ammizabad his son. This is usually taken to mean that Ammizabad served under his father in that division, perhaps as his second-in-command or as his successor in the post, as the STEPBible Proper Names suggest. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary explain the name as "people of the giver," meaning God. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia renders it "my kinsman has made a present." Nothing more is recorded about him.

Amnon was a son of Shimon, named with his brothers Rinnah, Ben-hanan and Tilon in the genealogy of the tribe of Judah (1 Chr 4:20). Nothing else is recorded about him, and Shimon's own place in the family line is not stated. Because the surrounding list in 1 Chronicles 4 traces the descendants of Judah, he is generally taken to be a Judahite, as the STEPBible proper names index describes him. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "faithful." He is a different person from the better-known Amnon, the eldest son of King David.

Amos is an ancestor of Jesus listed in Luke's genealogy, the son of Naum and the father of Mattathias (Luke 3:25). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia places him eighth before Joseph, the husband of Mary. Since Luke's line runs through David and Judah, he belongs to the tribe of Judah by inference from the genealogy. He lived in the period after the Babylonian exile, judging by his position in the list. Nothing else is recorded about him. He is a different person from the prophet Amos, whose book appears among the Old Testament prophets, and the name is shared by others in the Bible. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "loading" or "weighty."

Amplias was a Christian in Rome whom Paul greets near the end of his letter to the Romans, calling him "my beloved in the Lord" (Rom 16:8). He is mentioned nowhere else in the Bible, and nothing more is known of him. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia explains that Amplias, the form used in the King James Version, is a shortened form of the Latin name Ampliatus, which is how the Revised Version renders it. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives its meaning as "large" or "extensive." Smith's Bible Dictionary dates the letter, and so this greeting, to about AD 55. The warm description suggests a close personal tie to Paul, though the text does not say how they knew each other.

Amram was one of the descendants of Bani listed in Ezra 10:34, in the time of Ezra. He appears in the roll of Israelite men who had married foreign wives after the return from exile in Babylon. By inference from the surrounding chapter, those named agreed to send these wives away as part of the reform Ezra led. Smith's Bible Dictionary places the event around 459 BC. Nothing else is recorded about him. He should not be confused with Amram the father of Moses, Aaron and Miriam, who has the same name. The name is usually explained as meaning "exalted people."

Amzi was a Levite of the family of Merari, named only in the genealogy of 1 Chr 6:46. He was the son of Bani and the father of Hilkiah. The surrounding passage (1 Chr 6:31–47) traces the ancestry of Ethan, one of the Merarite singers David appointed to lead music at the tabernacle. By inference from that context, Amzi was an ancestor of Ethan, several generations back, and descended from Merari through Mahli and Shamer. The STEPBible proper names index describes him as a temple musician, a role tied to his family line. Nothing else is recorded about his life. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of his name as "strong, mighty." The name Amzi belongs to more than one person in the Bible. Another Amzi appears in the priestly genealogy of Neh 11:12 and is a different man.

Amzi was a priest named in the family line of Adaiah, one of the priests living in Jerusalem in Nehemiah's time after the return from exile. Neh 11:12 lists him as the son of Zechariah and the father of Pelaliah, and traces the line back through Pashur to Malchiah. Adaiah's family belonged to the 822 priests who 'did the work of the house', meaning the temple. Nothing else is recorded about Amzi himself. Because he appears several generations before Adaiah, he may have lived well before the exile ended, though the text gives no dates. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives the name's meaning as 'my strength'. The name is shared by at least one other man, a Levite in the genealogy of 1 Chr 6, and this entry treats the two as different people.

Anaiah was one of thirteen men who stood on a wooden platform with Ezra the scribe when Ezra read the Book of the Law to the people gathered in Jerusalem. He stood on Ezra's right, between Shema and Urijah (Neh 8:4). The verse does not give his role. Smith's Bible Dictionary takes him to be probably a priest, while the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia calls him a Levite who helped Ezra with the reading. The same encyclopedia suggests he may be the Ananias named in the parallel account in 1 Esdras 9:43. His name means "Yah has answered." The name is shared by more than one person. An Anaiah also appears among the leaders who sealed the covenant in Neh 10:22. That man may or may not be the same person, and the text does not say.

Anaiah was one of the men who set their seal to the written covenant made in Nehemiah's time, when the community returned from exile pledged to keep the law of God. His name, meaning "Yah has answered," appears only in a list of names (Neh 10:22). From its place in the chapter, the list seems to belong to the section headed "the chief of the people" (Neh 10:14). Smith's Bible Dictionary accordingly calls him one of the heads of the people, while the Tyndale House STEPBible proper-names list describes him as a priest. This entry follows the reading of him as a lay leader.
