The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests he may be the same Anaiah who stood beside Ezra during the public reading of the law (Neh 8:4). Nothing else is recorded about him, and because several people share the name, his identity is uncertain.

Anammelech was one of the gods of Sepharvaim, worshipped by the Sepharvites after the king of Assyria settled them in Samaria in place of the deported Israelites (see 2 Kgs 17:24). 2 Kgs 17:31 names him alongside Adrammelech and says the Sepharvites burned their children in fire to both gods. The name is usually explained as "Anu is king" (Easton's Bible Dictionary) or "Anu is the prince" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia), linking it to the Mesopotamian sky god Anu. Smith's Bible Dictionary calls him Adrammelech's companion god, worshipped with rites like those of Molech. Easton's describes Anammelech as a female moon deity paired with Adrammelech as the sun, while this entry treats the god as male. Where the god came from is uncertain, because some identify Sepharvaim with Sippar in Babylonia and others with a Syrian city, possibly Sibraim near Damascus.

Anan was one of the Israelites who put their seal to the written covenant made under Nehemiah after the return from exile in Babylon. He appears only once, in the list of signers at Neh 10:26, between Hanan and Malluch. The surrounding list groups the signers into priests, Levites and "chiefs of the people," and Anan falls in this last group of lay leaders, as Smith's Bible Dictionary notes. Nothing else is recorded about his family or his role. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary both give the meaning of his name as "cloud." Smith's dates the sealing of the covenant to about 410 BC, an estimate rather than a date stated in the text.

Anani was the seventh and last-named son of Elioenai, listed in the genealogy of the royal line of David in the tribe of Judah (1 Chr 3:24). His brothers were Hodaiah, Eliashib, Pelaiah, Akkub, Johanan and Dalaiah. The genealogy places him among the descendants of Zerubbabel, so he probably lived several generations after the return from the Babylonian exile, as the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes. Nothing else is recorded about him, and he is often taken to be the last generation the Chronicler records in this line. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests the name may be a shortened form of Ananiah, meaning "Yah has covered". Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "protected by Jehovah", and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "a cloud".

Ananiah is named only as the grandfather of Azariah, who repaired a section of Jerusalem's wall beside his own house when the city was rebuilt under Nehemiah (Neh 3:23). Ananiah's son Maaseiah was Azariah's father. Nothing else is recorded about Ananiah himself. Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests he was probably a priest, perhaps because priests are mentioned among the nearby workers in the same chapter. By inference from the setting, he lived some generations before the rebuilding, which took place around the mid-400s BC. His name, meaning roughly "the Lord has covered" or "protected by the Lord," should not be confused with the town of Ananiah, which is mentioned elsewhere in Nehemiah.

Anathoth was a son of Becher and a grandson of Benjamin, named in the genealogy of the tribe of Benjamin in 1 Chr 7:8. He is listed as one of nine sons of Becher, alongside Zemira, Joash, Eliezer, Elioenai, Omri, Jerimoth, Abiah and Alameth. Nothing else is recorded about him. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "answers to prayer," while Hitchcock's Bible Names offers "answer," "song" or "poverty." The same name belongs to a Levitical town in Benjamin, the hometown of Jeremiah, and to a man who signed the covenant in Nehemiah's time. Because he and his brother Alameth are listed together, and Alameth's name resembles the nearby town of Alemeth, some suggest these names may be linked to Benjamite settlements, but the text does not say so.

Anathoth was one of the leaders of the people who set their seal to the covenant made in the time of Nehemiah, after the return from exile in Babylon (Neh 10:19). His name appears in a list of signers alongside Hariph and Nebai. Nothing else is recorded about him. The name is shared by others in the Bible, including a Benjamite listed in the genealogies of Chronicles, and it is also the name of a priestly town in Benjamin, the home of Jeremiah. Whether this signer had any connection with the town or its family is not stated. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates the covenant to about 410 BC. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "answer," "song" or "poverty," while Smith's renders it "answers to prayer."

Andronicus was a Christian greeted by Paul at the close of his letter to the Romans, named together with Junia (Rom 16:7). Paul calls the two his "kinsmen," which may mean relatives or, more broadly, fellow Jews; Easton's Bible Dictionary describes Andronicus as a Jewish Christian. Paul also calls them his fellow prisoners, so they had evidently been imprisoned at some point, though the verse does not say when or where. They were "of note among the apostles," a phrase read either as well known to the apostles or as outstanding apostles themselves. Paul adds that they were in Christ before him, meaning they became believers earlier than he did. Since the greeting is sent to Rome, he was probably living there when the letter was written. Junia may have been his wife or another relative, but the text does not say. His name is Greek and is usually given as meaning "man-conquering."

Aniam was a son of Shemida and a member of the tribe of Manasseh, one of the two tribes descended from Joseph. He appears only once, in the genealogy of Manasseh in 1 Chr 7:19, which lists him with his brothers Ahian, Shechem and Likhi. Nothing else is recorded about him. Shemida himself appears elsewhere as a son of Gilead, whose family formed one of the clans of Manasseh (Num 26:32; Josh 17:2). Aniam therefore belonged to that clan, though the text gives no details of his life or descendants. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia explain the name as "sighing" or "lament of the people."

Anna was a prophetess in Jerusalem, the daughter of Phanuel, from the tribe of Asher. Luke describes her as very old. She had been married for seven years before she was widowed (Luke 2:36). The following verses, Luke 2:37–38, add that she was a widow of about eighty-four, that she never left the temple, and that she worshipped there with fasting and prayer night and day. They also say that when the infant Jesus was presented in the temple, she came in at that moment, gave thanks to God, and spoke about him to everyone in Jerusalem who was looking for redemption. Easton's Bible Dictionary places her alongside other women called prophetesses in the Bible, such as Miriam, Deborah and Huldah. Her name is the Greek form of the Hebrew Hannah and means "grace."

Antipas was a Christian at Pergamum (Pergamos) who was put to death for his faith. He is named only once, in the message to the church at Pergamum in Rev 2:13. There the risen Christ calls him "my faithful martyr," a phrase that can also be translated "my faithful witness." The verse says he was killed among the believers there, in the city described as the place "where Satan's seat is." The church is praised for holding fast and not denying the faith even in the days when Antipas died, so his death evidently happened some time before Revelation was written. Nothing more is known of him for certain (Easton's Bible Dictionary). Smith's Bible Dictionary records a tradition that he was bishop of Pergamum. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the name is a shortened form of Antipater.

Antothijah was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, named once in the Benjamite genealogy of 1 Chronicles 8. He is listed with Hananiah and Elam in 1 Chr 8:24, and the next verse groups these names among the sons of Shashak. His brothers include Ishpan, Heber, Eliel, Abdon, Zichri, Hanan, Iphedeiah and Penuel. Nothing else is recorded about him beyond his place in this family list, which belongs to the line of Elpaal's descendants living in or near Jerusalem. His name is also spelled Anthothijah in some reference works, such as the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives its meaning as "answers" or "songs of the Lord." The name probably resembles that of Anathoth, a town in Benjamin's territory, though no link between the two is stated.

Anub was a man of the tribe of Judah, named once in the genealogy of Judah as a son of Coz (1 Chr 4:8). The same verse names Zobebah and "the families of Aharhel the son of Harum" in the same line of descent, and this entry treats Harum as Anub's brother. Smith's Bible Dictionary connects Coz with the family of Ashur, the father of Tekoa, from the surrounding verses, though the passage does not state the link directly. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives the father's name as Hakkoz and suggests the name Anub means "ripe," while Smith's Bible Dictionary renders it "confederate." Nothing else is recorded about him.

Apelles was a Christian at Rome whom Paul greets in his letter to the Romans, calling him "approved in Christ" (Rom 16:10). The phrase suggests he had been tested in some way and proved faithful, though the text does not say how. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that Apelles was a common name in the period. Nothing else about him is recorded in the Bible. Smith's Bible Dictionary reports a later tradition that he became bishop of Smyrna or of Heraclea. In the same verse Paul goes on to greet the household of Aristobulus, but the text does not say whether Apelles was connected with that household.

Aphiah was a man of the tribe of Benjamin and an ancestor of King Saul, Israel's first king. He appears only in the genealogy that introduces Saul's father Kish, where the line runs from Kish back through Abiel, Zeror and Bechorath to Aphiah (1 Sam 9:1). Bechorath is named as his son. The verse ends by calling the man "a Benjamite, a mighty man of power." Grammatically this description could refer either to Aphiah, the last name in the list, or to Kish, who opens the verse. Most readers take it to describe Kish. Nothing else is recorded about Aphiah. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "refreshed," while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "speaking, blowing."

Aphses was a priest whose family received the eighteenth of the twenty-four divisions of priests, assigned by lot to serve in turn at the sanctuary (1 Chr 24:15). The surrounding chapter places this arrangement in the time of King David, who organized the descendants of Aaron into these rotating courses with the help of Zadok and Ahimelech. Aphses is probably the head of a priestly family rather than someone known for any personal deeds, since he is mentioned only in this list. Aphses is the King James spelling, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the Revised Version renders the name Happizzez. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives its meaning as "the dispersion."

Apollyon is the Greek name, meaning "destroyer," given in Rev 9:11 to the angel of the bottomless pit, whose Hebrew name is Abaddon. In John's vision he is king over the locust-like creatures that come up out of the pit when the fifth trumpet sounds. The Hebrew word abaddon means ruin or destruction. Elsewhere in the Old Testament, as Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia note, it names a place: the realm of the dead, set alongside Sheol, death and the grave in passages such as Job 26:6, Job 28:22 and Prov 15:11. Revelation is the only place where the word becomes a personal name for the angel who rules that realm. Smith's Bible Dictionary observes that the Greek text makes clear Abaddon here is the angel, not the abyss. John Bunyan later used the name Apollyon for the adversary in The Pilgrim's Progress.

Apphia was a Christian woman named in the opening greeting of Paul's letter to Philemon, where she is called "our beloved Apphia" (some manuscripts and the Revised Version margin read "the sister"). She is greeted with Philemon, with Archippus, and with the church that met in Philemon's house (Phlm 1:2). Because the letter deals with one household, many interpreters, including Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia, consider her probably Philemon's wife and possibly the mother of Archippus, though the text does not say so. By inference from Col 4:9, 17, which mention Onesimus and Archippus, the household was at Colossae. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes a Greek church tradition that commemorates her on November 22 and says she was martyred with Philemon under Nero. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the name's meaning as "fruitful."

Ara was a man of the tribe of Asher, named as one of the three sons of Jether in the genealogy of Asher's descendants (1 Chr 7:38). His brothers were Jephunneh and Pispah. Nothing else is recorded about him; he appears only in this list. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes Jether as the head of a family of Asherites. The meaning of the name is uncertain. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "lion," Hitchcock's Bible Names offers "cursing" or "seeing," and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats the meaning as unknown.

Arah was a man of the tribe of Asher, named first among the three sons of Ulla in the Asherite genealogy of 1 Chronicles, with his brothers Haniel and Rezia (1 Chr 7:39). Nothing else is recorded about him. Ulla does not appear elsewhere in the list, so his place in the family line is unclear. The STEPBible Proper Names index treats Ulla as another form of Shual, a son of Zophah named a few verses earlier in the same genealogy. The name Arah is usually explained as meaning "traveler" or "wayfarer" (Hitchcock's Bible Names; Smith's Bible Dictionary). Several other people in the Bible share the name, including the ancestor of a family that returned from exile with Zerubbabel, but they should not be confused with this Asherite.

Arah was the father of Shechaniah, a man of Judah in Nehemiah's day. He is mentioned only to identify his son, whose son-in-law was Tobiah, one of the opponents of Nehemiah's rebuilding of Jerusalem's walls. Because of this marriage tie, and because Tobiah's son Johanan had married into the family of Meshullam son of Berechiah, many in Judah were bound by oath to Tobiah (Neh 6:18). Several people in the Bible bear the name Arah, including the head of a family whose descendants returned from exile with Zerubbabel (Ezra 2:5; Neh 7:10). This Arah may have belonged to that family or been its ancestor, but the text does not say. Nothing else is recorded about him. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "the way" or "a traveler."

Aram (son of Kemuel) was a grandson of Nahor, Abraham's brother. He is named only once, in the list of Nahor's sons by his wife Milcah that was reported to Abraham after the near-sacrifice of Isaac (Gen 22:21). There his father Kemuel is called "the father of Aram." Nothing else is recorded about him. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both treat him as distinct from Aram the son of Shem (Gen 10:22), the ancestor of the Arameans. Some readers note a possible link between this Aram's name and the Aramean peoples who lived around Nahor's family in Mesopotamia, but the text does not make that connection. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "high."

Aram (tribe of Aher) was a man of the tribe of Asher, listed as one of the four sons of Shamer, together with his brothers Ahi, Rohgah and Jehubbah (1 Chr 7:34). He appears only in this genealogy of Asher's descendants, and nothing else is recorded about him. His father Shamer is probably the same man called Shomer two verses earlier, a son of Heber, which by inference makes Aram a great-great-grandson of Asher through Beriah (1 Chr 7:30–32). He should not be confused with Aram the son of Shem or with the land of Aram (Syria), which share the name. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "highness" or "magnificence."

Archelaus was a son of Herod the Great who ruled Judea after his father's death. Matthew mentions him once: when Joseph returned from Egypt with Mary and the young Jesus, he heard that Archelaus was reigning in Judea in place of his father. Joseph was afraid to go there, and after a warning in a dream he went instead to Galilee (Matt 2:22). His brothers included Herod Antipas and Philip. According to Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries, his mother was Malthace, a Samaritan, and he was brought up in Rome with Antipas. When Herod died, about 4 BC, the kingdom was divided among the brothers, and Archelaus received Judea, Samaria and Idumea. Smith's notes that his official title was ethnarch rather than king. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia records that the Romans removed him for misgovernment in AD 6, and Smith's adds that he was banished to Vienne in Gaul.

Ard is named as one of the sons of Benjamin, Jacob's youngest son, in the list of Jacob's family who went down to Egypt during the famine (Gen 46:21). He appears last among the ten sons given there and was part of the Tribe of Benjamin. Nothing else is recorded about him. The lists of Benjamin's sons in Num 26 and 1 Chr 7–8 differ from Genesis, which explains brothers named here such as Ahiram, Shupham, Jediael and Rapha. In Num 26:40 an Ard appears as a son of Bela, Benjamin's firstborn, and as the ancestor of the Ardites. That may be the same man counted as a grandson, or a separate person with the same name. The name is shared by more than one person, so the identification is uncertain. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives its meaning as "one that commands" or "he that descends."

Ard was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, a son of Bela and so a grandson of Benjamin. He appears in the census of Israel taken in the plains of Moab, where he and his brother Naaman are named as the sons of Bela and the ancestors of two Benjamite clans. His descendants were the Ardites (Num 26:40). Other sons of Bela, including Gera, Abihud, Abishua and Ahoah, are named in the Benjamite genealogies of 1 Chronicles 7 and 8. Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies Ard with Addar, listed among Bela's sons in 1 Chr 8:3. This entry treats Addar as a separate brother. Genesis 46:21 lists an Ard among Benjamin's own sons, so the name is shared, and how that Ard relates to this one is uncertain. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "one that commands" or "he that descends."

Ardon was a man of the tribe of Judah, named in the genealogy of 1 Chr 2:18 as one of the sons of Caleb, the son of Hezron. He is listed third after Jesher and Shobab. The verse names two women, Azubah, Caleb's wife, and Jerioth, and its wording leaves unclear which of them was the mother of these sons. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary take Azubah as his mother. This Caleb, a descendant of Judah through Perez and Hezron, is generally distinguished from the better-known Caleb son of Jephunneh. Nothing else is recorded about Ardon. The meaning of his name is uncertain: Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "fugitive," Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "ruling," and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia calls it unknown.

Aretas was the king whose governor (ethnarch) held Damascus with a garrison in order to arrest the apostle Paul, who escaped by being let down through a window in the wall in a basket (2 Cor 11:32–33). The parallel account in Acts 9:24–25 describes the same escape but credits the plot to the Jews of the city. Aretas was a common name among Arabian rulers, and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives its meaning as "agreeable" or "virtuous." This one is generally identified as Aretas IV, king of the Nabataeans, whose capital was Petra. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia, drawing on Josephus, describe him as the father-in-law of Herod Antipas. Antipas left his daughter to marry Herodias, and war between the two followed. How Aretas came to control Damascus is unclear. Easton's holds that he seized it about AD 37. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia thinks it more probable that the emperor Caligula granted it to him.

Argob is a man named in 2 Kgs 15:25, in the account of how Pekah son of Remaliah, a captain of King Pekahiah of Israel, conspired against the king and killed him in the palace at Samaria with the help of fifty men of Gilead. Argob and Arieh are named alongside the king in that verse, but the wording is obscure. One reading, followed by STEPBible's proper names index and by this entry, takes them as men who were with Pekahiah, probably his officers, and who were struck down with him. Others read them as fellow conspirators with Pekah. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the Latin Vulgate treats both names as places, and that the Jewish commentator Rashi took Argob to be part of the royal palace. Nothing else is recorded about him.

Aridai was one of the ten sons of Haman, the Persian official who plotted to destroy the Jews in the days of Queen Esther. He is named only once, in the list of Haman's sons at Esth 9:9. The surrounding passage, Esther 9, reports that the Jews killed these ten sons in Shushan on the day set for the Jews' destruction, and that their bodies were afterward hanged at Esther's request. Smith's Bible Dictionary counts him as the ninth son and gives the meaning of his name as "the strong." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests a link to a Persian name meaning "delight of Hari," but notes that the text of the name is very uncertain. Nothing else is recorded about him.

Aridatha was one of the ten sons of Haman, the official who plotted to destroy the Jews of the Persian Empire in the reign of King Ahasuerus. He is named only once, in the list at Esth 9:8, where Smith's Bible Dictionary counts him as the sixth son. The surrounding passage reports that the Jews killed Haman's ten sons in Shushan on the day the decree against them was overturned, and that their bodies were later hanged at Esther's request. His brothers were Parshandatha, Dalphon, Aspatha, Poratha, Adalia, Parmashta, Arisai, Aridai and Vajezatha. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests the name may come from the Persian Hari-data, meaning "given by Hari," and notes that the Greek Septuagint spells it Pharadatha. Nothing else is recorded about him.

Arieh is a man named in 2 Kgs 15:25 in the account of how Pekah son of Remaliah, a captain of King Pekahiah of Israel, conspired against the king and killed him in the palace at Samaria. Arieh and Argob are named alongside the assassination, but the Hebrew wording leaves their role unclear. Easton's Bible Dictionary takes Arieh to have been one of the royal bodyguard killed with Pekahiah. Smith's Bible Dictionary allows either that view or that he was one of Pekah's accomplices, along with the fifty men of Gilead. This entry treats him, as the STEPBible notes do, as a man who was with the king at the time of the attack, probably one of his officials. Smith's dates the event to about 757 BC, an estimate drawn from context. The name means "lion." Nothing else is recorded about him.

Ariel was one of the "chief men" whom Ezra summoned at the river Ahava while he was gathering the exiles returning from Babylon to Jerusalem (Ezra 8:16). Ezra had found no Levites among the returning company, and the surrounding passage shows that he sent this group to Iddo at a place called Casiphia to bring back ministers for the house of God. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both describe Ariel as one of this delegation. Nothing else is recorded about his family or later life. The name is usually explained as "lion of God" (Hitchcock's Bible Names), and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives "lioness of God." The same word appears elsewhere in the Bible with other meanings, including a poetic name for Jerusalem and an "altar hearth," but those uses are unrelated to this man.

Arisai was one of the ten sons of Haman, the official of the Persian king Ahasuerus who plotted to destroy the Jews. He is named only once, in the list of Haman's sons at Esth 9:9. By inference from the surrounding passage, he was killed by the Jews in Shushan when they defended themselves on the day Haman had set for their destruction. Smith's Bible Dictionary counts him as the eighth son and gives the meaning of the name as "lion-like." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia instead treats the name as probably Persian, of unknown meaning. The wider chapter records that the bodies of Haman's sons were afterward hanged at Queen Esther's request. Nothing else is known about him.

Aristobulus was a man living in Rome whose household Paul greets in Rom 16:10. Paul greets the members of his household rather than Aristobulus himself, so he may have died, been away, or not been a believer, though the verse does not say which. His name means "best counselor." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests he was probably a grandson of Herod the Great and a brother of Herod Agrippa, a wealthy man close to the emperor Claudius. It notes J. B. Lightfoot's suggestion that his "household" were slaves who stayed together after his death and passed to the emperor while keeping their former master's name. Some of them were Christians. Smith's Bible Dictionary records a tradition that Aristobulus was one of the seventy disciples and preached the gospel in Britain. The Tyndale House proper-names index takes him to have been a prominent believer in Rome.

Armoni was a son of King Saul by Rizpah, the daughter of Aiah, and the brother of Mephibosheth (not Jonathan's son of the same name). His name means "belonging to the palace" according to the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia, or "inhabitant of a fortress" in Easton's Bible Dictionary. He appears only in 2 Sam 21:8. There, during a famine in David's reign, the Gibeonites demanded seven of Saul's descendants because Saul had tried to wipe them out. David handed over Armoni and his brother Mephibosheth, together with five of Saul's grandsons. The surrounding verses say the Gibeonites put them to death and hung up their bodies at Gibeah. Rizpah then kept watch over the bodies until rain came. Ish-bosheth, who briefly ruled Israel after Saul's death, was also his brother, and Jonathan, Michal and Merab were among his half-siblings.

Arnan was a man of the tribe of Judah and a descendant of David through Solomon, named only once, in the royal genealogy of 1 Chr 3:21. He belonged to the line of Zerubbabel, who led Jews back from exile in Babylon. This entry treats him as a son of Hananiah, whom the preceding verse names as Zerubbabel's son, and as brother of Pelatiah, Jesaiah, Rephaiah, Obadiah and Shechaniah. The Hebrew wording is uncertain, though. It lists "the sons of Arnan" as one of several families without clearly linking them to Hananiah, so Arnan's exact place in the line is open. The Greek Septuagint reads the verse as a chain of fathers and sons and spells his name Orna. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives the meaning "joyous" and describes him as the founder of a family. Nothing else is recorded about him.

Artemas was a companion of the apostle Paul, named only in Titus 3:12. Paul tells Titus that he plans to send either Artemas or Tychicus to him in Crete, and that once one of them arrives, Titus should hurry to join Paul at Nicopolis, where Paul had decided to spend the winter. By inference from the passage, Artemas was trusted enough to take over Titus's work among the churches of Crete. Nothing more is recorded about him in the Bible. The name is Greek, probably a masculine form of Artemis or a shortened form of Artemidorus, a common name in Asia Minor (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia). A later tradition, noted in Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia, counts him among the seventy disciples and makes him bishop of Lystra.

Arza was the steward in charge of the royal household at Tirzah, then the capital of the northern kingdom of Israel. He is mentioned only once. While King Elah was drinking himself drunk in Arza's house, Zimri, who commanded half of the king's chariots, plotted against him (1 Kgs 16:9). The surrounding passage shows that Zimri then killed Elah and seized the throne. The king is not named in the verse itself, but the context identifies him as Elah son of Baasha. Smith's Bible Dictionary calls Arza prefect of the palace. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the wording is not entirely clear, and that Arza could have been Zimri's servant rather than Elah's. This entry follows the more common reading that he served Elah. Nothing else is known of him, including whether he took any part in the plot.

Asa was a Levite, the son of Elkanah and the father of Berechiah, named once in the genealogy of 1 Chr 9:16. His son Berechiah appears in the list of Levites living in Jerusalem after the return from exile in Babylon. The verse says the family lived in the villages of the Netophathites, probably settlements around Netophah, near Bethlehem. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both describe Asa this way. Nothing else is recorded about his life. The name means "physician" or "healer" (Hitchcock's Bible Names). Several people in the Bible share this name, and this Asa should not be confused with the better-known King Asa of Judah.

Asahel was one of the Levites whom King Jehoshaphat of Judah sent out, together with princes and the priests Elishama and Jehoram, to teach the people in the cities of Judah. The surrounding verses describe the group taking the book of the law of the Lord with them as they went through the towns (2 Chr 17:7–9). Asahel is named only in this list, and nothing else is recorded about him. He is one of several men in the Bible who share the name, and he should not be confused with Asahel the brother of Joab, who belongs to the time of David. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates this teaching mission to about 910 BC, and that date is an estimate. The name is usually explained as meaning "made by God" or "creature of God."

Asahel was a Levite in the reign of King Hezekiah of Judah, one of ten overseers who served under Cononiah and his brother Shimei. They were appointed by the king's command and by Azariah, the ruler of the house of God (2 Chr 31:13). Going by the surrounding passage, their work was to look after the tithes, offerings and dedicated things that the people brought to the temple storerooms. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the STEPBible proper-names index both describe him as having charge of these gifts. His name is usually explained as "made by God." Several other men in the Bible are also called Asahel, among them the brother of Joab and Abishai, but this Levite is mentioned only here and is a separate person.

Asahel was the father of Jonathan, a man of Ezra's time, after the return from exile. He is named only in Ezra 10:15. His son Jonathan and Jahaziah son of Tikvah had a part in the inquiry into the returned exiles who had married foreign wives. The Hebrew can be read two ways. The King James Version says the two men were "employed about this matter," meaning they oversaw it. Other readings, including the Revised Version text and STEPBible's proper names, have them opposing the plan. This entry follows the King James wording given in the verse. Nothing else is recorded about Asahel himself. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him as a priest and notes that 1 Esdras calls him Azael. The name means "God has made." Several other men in the Bible share this name, including a nephew of David.

Asaiah was a leader of a family of the tribe of Simeon, named in a list of Simeonite chiefs in 1 Chr 4:36. The surrounding passage says these men were princes in their families whose households increased greatly, and that in the days of King Hezekiah of Judah they went to the region of Gedor looking for pasture for their flocks. There they attacked the people living in the area, including the Meunim, and settled in their place. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia counts Asaiah among those who took part in this incursion. Nothing else is recorded about him. His name means "the Lord has made" or "the Lord has wrought" (Hitchcock's Bible Names). Several other men in the Bible share the name, and this Simeonite should not be confused with them.

Asaiah was a Levite of the clan of Merari, named in 1 Chr 6:30 as the son of Haggiah. He appears only in a genealogy that traces the descendants of Merari, son of Levi, through Mahli, Libni, Shimei, Uzza, Shimea and Haggiah. Nothing is recorded about his life or activities. STEPBible's Tyndale House proper-names index describes him as an ancestor of Ethan the singer, one of the Levitical musicians of David's time. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "the Lord hath wrought." Several other men in the Bible share the name, including a Merarite leader in David's day, a Simeonite chief and an official of King Josiah. This entry treats this Asaiah as a separate person known only from this genealogy.

Asaiah was a man of Judah, named in 1 Chr 9:5 as the firstborn among the Shilonites, who lived in Jerusalem with his sons. The chapter lists people who resettled in Jerusalem, generally understood as the return from exile in Babylon. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates this to about 536 BC. "Shilonite" probably refers to descent from Shelah, son of Judah, rather than to the town of Shiloh. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both identify him with Maaseiah, son of the Shilonite, in the parallel list of Jerusalem's residents in Neh 11:5. His name means "the Lord has made." Several other men in the Bible share the name, so he should not be confused with them.

Asaph was the keeper of the king's forest under the Persian king Artaxerxes in Nehemiah's time. When Nehemiah got permission to go and rebuild Jerusalem, he also asked the king for a letter to Asaph ordering him to supply timber. The timber was for beams for the gates of the fortress beside the temple, for the city wall, and for the house Nehemiah would live in, and the king granted the request (Neh 2:8). The Hebrew word for forest here can mean a royal park or 'paradise', as Smith's Bible Dictionary notes. Where this forest was is not stated. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes Asaph as a Jew holding high office at the Persian court, probably because his name is Hebrew. Nothing else is recorded about him. He should not be confused with the better-known Asaph, the musician of David's time, or with others who bore the name.

Asareel was a son of Jehaleleel, named in the genealogies of the tribe of Judah in 1 Chr 4:16. He is listed with his brothers Ziph, Ziphah and Tiria, and nothing else is recorded about him. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "whom God has bound (by an oath)," while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "the beatitude of God." Modern versions often spell the name Asarel. Jehaleleel's own link to the main lines of Judah's descendants is not stated in the passage, so Asareel's exact place in the tribe's family tree is uncertain.

Ashpenaz was the master of the eunuchs, a chief court official, under the Babylonian king Nebuchadnezzar, who is named in Dan 1:1. The king ordered him to bring certain young Israelites of royal and noble families from among the captives so they could be trained for service in the palace (Dan 1:3). He is named only in this verse. The 'prince of the eunuchs' later in the same chapter, who gave Daniel and his companions Babylonian names and heard Daniel's request not to eat the king's food, is probably the same man, by inference from the passage. Easton's Bible Dictionary equates his office with the 'Rabsaris' title of the court. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as 'horse-nose,' while the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests the name is more likely Babylonian than Persian in origin.

Ashriel was a man of the tribe of Manasseh, named at the head of the list of Manasseh's sons in 1 Chr 7:14. The verse says he was born to a woman it calls only "she," and it sets him apart from Machir, the father of Gilead, whose mother was Manasseh's Aramean concubine. This entry follows that reading and treats Ashriel as a son of Manasseh and a half-brother of Machir. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the name more properly as Asriel and takes it to mean "vow of God." Num 26:31 and Josh 17:2 name an Asriel among the descendants of Gilead, and STEPBible Proper Names (Tyndale House) identifies Ashriel with him, which would make him Manasseh's great-grandson rather than his son. The unclear wording of 1 Chr 7:14 leaves the exact relationship uncertain.

Ashvath was a man of the tribe of Asher, named in the genealogy of 1 Chr 7:33 as one of the sons of Japhlet, with his brothers Pasach and Bimhal. Japhlet appears earlier in the same list as a son of Heber, a grandson of Asher through Beriah (1 Chr 7:30–32), which places Ashvath several generations down from Asher himself. Nothing else is recorded about him. His name appears only in this one verse, and he is known solely as part of Asher's family line.

Asiel was a man of the tribe of Simeon, named only in the Simeonite genealogy of 1 Chr 4:35. He was the father of Seraiah and, through Seraiah and Josibiah, the great-grandfather of Jehu. Jehu appears in a list of Simeonite clan leaders. By inference from the surrounding passage, these leaders lived in the reign of Hezekiah, when they expanded their families' grazing lands, so Asiel himself probably lived some generations earlier. Nothing else is recorded about him. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "created by God," and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "the work of God."

Asnah was the ancestor or head of a family of temple servants (the Nethinim) whose descendants, "the children of Asnah," appear in the list of exiles who returned from Babylon to Judah with Zerubbabel (Ezra 2:50). Nothing else is recorded about him. His family is named alongside other temple-servant families, such as those of Mehunim and Nephusim. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia give the meaning of the name as "thornbush." His family does not appear in the parallel list of returnees in Nehemiah 7, which suggests it was either left out there or listed under another name.

Asnappar was the ruler called "the great and noble Asnappar" in a letter sent by officials in Samaria to the Persian king Artaxerxes. The letter says he had brought various nations over and settled them in the cities of Samaria and the region west of the Euphrates (Ezra 4:10). He is named only here. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the STEPBible proper names index both identify him, probably, with the Assyrian king Ashurbanipal, son and successor of Esarhaddon. Easton's dates the start of his reign to about 668 BC and notes his great library of clay tablets at Nineveh. On that view, the passage refers to a later stage of the Assyrian resettlement of Samaria after the fall of the northern kingdom. The name appears as Osnappar in some modern translations.

Aspatha was one of the ten sons of Haman, the official of the Persian king Ahasuerus who plotted to destroy the Jews. He is named only once, third in the list of Haman's sons in Esth 9:7, after Parshandatha and Dalphon. His brothers were Poratha, Adalia, Aridatha, Parmashta, Arisai, Aridai and Vajezatha. From the surrounding passage, the ten sons were killed in Shushan when the Jews defended themselves on the day Haman had set for their destruction. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him as Haman's third son, following the order of the list. The name is probably Persian, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes a suggested meaning of "given by a sacred horse." Nothing else is recorded about him.

Asshurim is named in Gen 25:3 as one of the sons of Dedan, alongside Letushim and Leummim. Dedan was a son of Jokshan, and the surrounding passage makes Jokshan a son of Abraham by his wife Keturah, so Asshurim belongs to the line of Abraham through Keturah, as the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes. The name has a plural ending in Hebrew, as do the names of his two brothers. This suggests that the verse may be naming a tribe or people descended from Dedan rather than a single individual. The Bible gives no further details about him or his descendants. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "liers in want" or "beholders."

Asyncritus was a Christian living in Rome whom Paul greeted near the end of his letter to the Romans (Rom 16:14). He is named first in a group of five men, together with Phlegon, Hermas, Patrobas and Hermes, followed by "the brethren which are with them." That wording suggests these men belonged to the same circle of believers, possibly a house church meeting in Rome, though the text does not say so directly. Nothing else is recorded about him. His name is Greek and, according to Smith's Bible Dictionary and Hitchcock's Bible Names, means "incomparable."

Atarah was a wife of Jerahmeel and the mother of Onam. She appears only once, in the genealogy of the tribe of Judah in 1 Chr 2:26. That verse calls her Jerahmeel's "other wife," which sets her apart from the first wife, whose sons are listed in the verse before. She is therefore probably a second wife, though the text does not say which marriage came first. Through Onam, her descendants make up a separate branch of the Jerahmeelite line, traced in the verses that follow. Jerahmeel himself was a son of Hezron and a great-grandson of Judah. Her name means "crown," according to Smith's Bible Dictionary and Hitchcock's Bible Names. Nothing else is recorded about her.

Ater was one of the men who set their seal to the covenant made in Nehemiah's time, when the community in Jerusalem pledged to keep the law of Moses (Neh 10:17). He appears in the part of the list given to the leaders of the people, so he was probably a family or clan head rather than a priest or Levite. Because the name is placed next to Hizkijah, he may represent the family called 'the children of Ater of Hezekiah' among the exiles who returned from Babylon (Ezra 2:16; Neh 7:21). This is an inference from the names, not something the verse states. Several people in the Bible share the name, so other references may concern different individuals. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives its meaning as 'left hand' or 'shut'.

Athaiah was a man of the tribe of Judah who lived in Jerusalem after the return from exile in Babylon. Nehemiah 11:4 names him first among the people of Judah who settled in the city. It traces his line through his father Uzziah and then Zechariah, Amariah, Shephatiah and Mahalaleel, back to Perez, the son of Judah. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both take him to be the same man called Uthai in the parallel list at 1 Chr 9:4, although the ancestors named there differ. The meaning of his name is uncertain. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives "Yahweh is helper", Smith's gives "whom Jehovah made", and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "the Lord's time".

Athaliah is a name in the genealogy of the tribe of Benjamin, listed in 1 Chr 8:26 among the children of Jeroham. Athaliah's siblings were Shamsherai, Shehariah, Eliah, Jaresiah and Zichri. The surrounding passage (1 Chr 8:27–28) describes Jeroham's family as heads of Benjamite households who lived in Jerusalem, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia accordingly describes this Athaliah as a Benjamite who lived there. Nothing else is recorded about this person. The name is shared by others in the Bible, most notably the queen who seized the throne of Judah (2 Kgs 11), and this entry should not be confused with her. The name's meaning is uncertain: Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "the time of the Lord," while the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests "whom Yahweh has afflicted."

Athaliah was a man of the family of Elam and the father of Jeshaiah. He is known only from the list in Ezra 8:7 of family heads who travelled from Babylon to Jerusalem with Ezra, where his son Jeshaiah is named as leading seventy men of the sons of Elam. The verse gives Athaliah only as Jeshaiah's father, so nothing more is known of his life. His name is the same as that of the better-known Queen Athaliah of Judah, and he should not be confused with her. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "the time of the Lord."

Athlai was one of the "sons of Bebai" named in Ezra 10:28. By context, this means he belonged to the family or clan descended from Bebai, not necessarily that he was Bebai's own son. He appears in the list of men who had married foreign wives and, after Ezra's reforms in Jerusalem following the return from exile, agreed to send them away. Three other men of the same family are listed with him: Jehohanan, Hananiah and Zabbai. Nothing else is recorded about him. The meaning of his name is uncertain. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "whom Jehovah afflicts", and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "my hour or time".

Attai was a warrior from the tribe of Gad who joined David before David became king. He is named sixth in a list of Gadite leaders (1 Chr 12:11). The surrounding passage, read in context, describes these men as experienced fighters with faces like lions and as swift as gazelles. It says they crossed the Jordan when it was in flood to come over to David at his stronghold in the wilderness, and that each became a captain in his army. Smith's Bible Dictionary places their joining in the wilderness. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia connects it with David's time at Ziklag. The name may mean "timely." This name is shared by several people in the Bible, including a descendant of Judah and a son of King Rehoboam, but this Gadite is known only from this one verse.

Attai was a son of King Rehoboam of Judah and his wife Maachah, the daughter of Absalom. He is named second among her four children, after Abijah and before Ziza and Shelomith (2 Chr 11:20). Smith's Bible Dictionary therefore calls him Rehoboam's second son by Maachah. As Rehoboam's son he was a grandson of Solomon and a member of the tribe of Judah, and he was probably born in Jerusalem, the royal city. Through his father he also had half-brothers, Jeush, Shamariah and Zaham. His full brother Abijah was chosen to succeed Rehoboam as king, but nothing more is recorded about Attai himself. Several other men in the Bible share the name, and he should not be confused with them. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "opportune".

Azaniah was the father, or possibly a more distant ancestor, of Jeshua, a Levite. He is known only from Neh 10:9, where "Jeshua the son of Azaniah" heads the list of Levites who put their seal to the covenant made in Nehemiah's time, after the return from exile. Nothing else is recorded about Azaniah himself, and it is not clear whether he was still alive at that time. Smith's Bible Dictionary explains his name as "whom the Lord hears," and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives a similar meaning, "Yahweh has given ear."

Azarael was a musician who took part in the dedication of the rebuilt wall of Jerusalem in Nehemiah's time. He is named among the "brethren" of Zechariah, a descendant of Asaph, in one of the two great thanksgiving choirs that processed on the wall. These men played "the musical instruments of David the man of God", with Ezra the scribe leading them (Neh 12:36). The preceding verse names Zechariah as the son of Jonathan, and this entry treats Azarael as Jonathan's son too. However, "brethren" may mean kinsmen or fellow musicians rather than full brothers. Smith's Bible Dictionary calls him a Levite musician. STEPBible Proper Names describes him as a priest, since the group is connected with the priests' sons mentioned just before. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats the name as a form of Azarel. Nothing more is recorded about him.

Azareel was one of the warriors listed among the Korhites who joined David, named alongside Elkanah, Jesiah, Joezer and Jashobeam in 1 Chr 12:6. The opening verses of the chapter place this list among the men who came to David at Ziklag while he was still in hiding from Saul. They were skilled with bow and sling, and many were Benjamites. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him as a Korhite who joined David in his retreat at Ziklag, and dates this to about 1060 BC. "Korhites" may refer to descendants of a Korah, but which family is meant is not clear from this verse alone. His name means "help of God" (Hitchcock's Bible Names). Several other men in the Bible share this name, and nothing more is recorded about this Azareel.

Azareel son of Jeroham was the leader, or prince, of the tribe of Dan during the reign of David. He appears only in 1 Chr 27:22, at the end of a list of officers placed over the tribes of Israel. Smith's Bible Dictionary connects the list with the time when David numbered the people, which the surrounding passage goes on to describe. Nothing else is recorded about him or his father Jeroham. His name means "God helps" or "help of God" (Hitchcock's Bible Names). Several other men in the Bible share the name Azareel, and none of them can be identified with this tribal leader.

Azareel was one of the Israelites listed in Ezra 10:41 among the men who had married foreign wives in the time of Ezra, after the return from exile in Babylon. In the surrounding passage these men agreed to send away their foreign wives. Smith's Bible Dictionary places him among the descendants of Bani, inferred from the list's structure (compare Ezra 10:34), and dates the event to about 459 BC, an estimate drawn from context. Nothing else is recorded about him. The name, meaning "God helps" or "help of God" according to Hitchcock's Bible Names, is shared by several other men in the Bible, including a warrior who joined David and a temple musician. This Azareel should not be confused with them.

Azariah, son of Nathan, was one of King Solomon's chief officials. He was placed "over the officers" (1 Kgs 4:5). These were probably the twelve district governors listed just after him, who each supplied the royal household with provisions for one month of the year. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia accordingly calls him captain of Solomon's tax collectors. His brother Zabud, also a son of Nathan, served as principal officer and "the king's friend." Which Nathan was their father is uncertain. Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests he may have been David's son Nathan, which would make Azariah David's grandson. Others connect him with Nathan the prophet, who was closely tied to Solomon's accession. The name Azariah means "the Lord has helped" and was borne by several people in the Bible, so this man should be kept distinct from others of the same name.

Azariah was a man of the tribe of Judah, named as the son of Ethan in the genealogy of 1 Chr 2:8. He is the only son of Ethan listed there, and nothing else is recorded about him. The surrounding genealogy places Ethan among the sons of Zerah, son of Judah, so Azariah belonged to the Zerahite clan by inference from context. Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests that Zerahiah may be the better reading of his name in this verse. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia links his father with Ethan the Wise. The name Azariah means "the Lord has helped" and was common in Israel, especially among priestly families, so this man should be kept distinct from the many others who bore it.

Azariah son of Oded was a prophet in Judah during the reign of King Asa. 2 Chr 15:1 records that the Spirit of God came upon him. From the passage that follows, he went out to meet Asa after a military victory and urged the king and the people to seek the Lord, promising that God would be with them if they did. Easton's Bible Dictionary credits his message with prompting a great national reformation, in which Asa removed idols and renewed the altar of the Lord. In 2 Chr 15:8 the prophecy is attributed simply to "Oded the prophet," which Smith's Bible Dictionary takes as a shortened reference to Azariah himself. His name, which Smith's renders "whom the Lord helps," was common in Israel, and he should not be confused with the several other men called Azariah in the Bible.

Azariah was one of the sons of Jehoshaphat king of Judah and a brother of King Jehoram. He belonged to the tribe of Judah and was probably born in Jerusalem. The list in 2 Chr 21:2 is unusual because it names two different sons of Jehoshaphat called Azariah. This entry is one of them, but the text gives nothing that tells the two apart. The verse calls Jehoshaphat "king of Israel," which here means the king of Judah. The next verses (2 Chr 21:3–4) say that after Jehoram became king, he killed all his brothers with the sword. By inference, that is how Azariah died, in Jerusalem in about 889 BC, a date estimated from context. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "he that hears the Lord." Several other people in the Bible share the name.

Azariah was one of the sons of Jehoshaphat king of Judah, of the tribe of Judah, and a brother of King Jehoram. 2 Chr 21:2 lists two sons of Jehoshaphat named Azariah, so this entry refers to one of the two, and the text gives nothing to tell them apart. His other brothers were Jehiel, Zechariah, Michael and Shephatiah. The verse calls Jehoshaphat "king of Israel," though he ruled the southern kingdom of Judah. The surrounding passage says Jehoshaphat gave these sons gifts of silver, gold and fortified cities in Judah, but left the kingdom to Jehoram, the firstborn (2 Chr 21:3). When Jehoram had secured his rule, he killed all his brothers with the sword, so Azariah probably died then (2 Chr 21:4). Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "he that hears the Lord."

Azariah son of Jeroham was one of the captains of hundreds whom the priest Jehoiada brought into a covenant with him in the seventh year (2 Chr 23:1). By inference from the surrounding passage, this was the plot to overthrow Queen Athaliah and crown the young Joash, the surviving heir of David's line, as king of Judah. He is named alongside four other commanders, one of whom, Azariah son of Obed, bore the same name. The seventh year refers, by context, to the seventh year of Athaliah's reign, during which Joash had been kept hidden in the temple. Nothing else is recorded about him, and several other people in the Bible share his name. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of Azariah as "he that hears the Lord."

Azariah son of Obed was one of the military commanders, called captains of hundreds, who entered into a covenant with the priest Jehoiada in 2 Chr 23:1. The same verse names a second commander called Azariah, the son of Jeroham, so the two are told apart by their fathers. The pact took place in the seventh year, which by inference from the preceding passage (2 Chr 22:12) means the seventh year of Queen Athaliah's rule, while the young prince Joash was hidden in the temple. The following verses describe these commanders helping Jehoiada crown Joash and remove Athaliah. Nothing else is recorded about this Azariah, and because many men in the Bible share the name, he should not be confused with the others. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "he that hears the Lord."

Azariah, son of Johanan, was one of the leading men of Ephraim in the northern kingdom of Israel during the reign of Ahaz, king of Judah. Smith's Bible Dictionary calls him one of the captains of Ephraim. In 2 Chr 28:12 he stands up with Berechiah, Jehizkiah and Amasa against the soldiers coming back from war. From the surrounding chapter, those soldiers were Pekah's army returning with captives taken from Judah, and these leaders objected to making their own kinsmen slaves. By inference from the same passage, they helped see that the captives were clothed, fed and sent back to Jericho. His name is usually explained as "the Lord has helped." Several other men in the Bible are also called Azariah, and this one is known only from this single verse.

Azariah was a Levite of the Kohathite clan whose son Joel was among the Levites who came forward when King Hezekiah called for the temple to be cleansed (2 Chr 29:12). He is known only as Joel's father. Azariah himself does not appear to take part, and nothing else is recorded about him. He should not be confused with another Azariah in the same verse, the son of Jehalelel, who belonged to the Merarite clan and served alongside Joel. The names Joel and Azariah also appear together in the earlier Kohathite genealogy of Heman the singer (1 Chr 6:36). Families often repeated names, so the two lists may refer to different men. The name is shared by many people in the Bible. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives its meaning as "he that hears the Lord."

Azariah, son of Jehalelel, was a Levite of the clan of Merari who lived in the reign of King Hezekiah of Judah. He appears only in 2 Chr 29:12, in the list of Levites who stepped forward when Hezekiah called on the priests and Levites to consecrate themselves and cleanse the temple in Jerusalem. He is named there alongside Kish son of Abdi as representing the Merarites, while other men stood for the Kohathites and Gershonites. Nothing more is recorded about him. He should not be confused with Azariah the Kohathite, father of Joel, named in the same verse, or with the many other men of this name in the Bible. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "he that hears the Lord."

Azariah was one of the men who helped the people understand the law when Ezra read it publicly in Jerusalem after the return from exile (Neh 8:7). He is named in a list with Jeshua, Bani, Sherebiah and others who explained the reading while the people stood in their places. The verse's wording leaves it slightly unclear whether every name in the list belongs to the Levites mentioned at its end. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both treat him as a Levite who assisted Ezra. Nothing else is recorded about him. The name, usually explained as "the Lord has helped," was common in Israel, especially in priestly families, and he should not be confused with the many other men called Azariah.

Azaz was a man of the tribe of Reuben, named only in the Reubenite genealogy of 1 Chr 5:8. He was the son of Shema, the grandson of Joel, and the father of Bela. The verse says this family lived in Aroer and its territory reached as far as Nebo and Baal-meon, towns east of the Dead Sea in the land later held by Reuben. Nothing else is recorded about Azaz himself. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "strong," and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "strong one." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia renders it "powerful."

Azaziah was a Levite musician in the time of King David. He was one of six men assigned to play harps "on the Sheminith" when David brought the ark of the covenant up to Jerusalem from the house of Obed-edom (1 Chr 15:21). "Sheminith" is probably a musical term, possibly referring to a lower pitch or an eight-stringed instrument, though its exact meaning is uncertain. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that his name does not appear in the earlier list of Levites in 1 Chr 15:18. The name means "the Lord is strong" or "the Lord strengthens." Several people in the Bible bear this name. This entry refers only to the harpist named in this passage.

Azaziah was an Ephraimite, known only as the father of Hoshea, who led the tribe of Ephraim (1 Chr 27:20). The verse belongs to a list of the chief officers over the tribes of Israel during the reign of David. The surrounding passage links this list to the time David counted the people, so Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia place Hoshea's leadership then. Nothing else is recorded about Azaziah himself. His name is usually explained as meaning "the Lord strengthens" or "strength of the Lord." Several other men in the Bible share the name, including a Levite musician in David's time and a Levite overseer under Hezekiah. This Azaziah is a different person from them.

Azaziah was a Levite in the reign of King Hezekiah of Judah. He was one of ten overseers who worked under Conaniah (spelled Cononiah in the KJV) and his brother Shimei. Hezekiah and Azariah, the ruler of the house of God, appointed them to look after the offerings, tithes and dedicated things the people brought to the temple (2 Chr 31:13). The surrounding passage describes how these gifts were stored in chambers prepared in the temple, so the overseers' work was probably to manage those stores. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both describe him as having charge of the temple offerings. His name is usually taken to mean "the Lord is strong" or "the Lord strengthens." Nothing else is recorded about him. Other men named Azaziah appear elsewhere in the Bible and should not be confused with him.

Azbuk was the father of a Nehemiah who ruled half the district of Beth-zur and repaired a section of Jerusalem's wall in the days of the governor Nehemiah. His son's stretch of the work ran to a point opposite the tombs of David, to the man-made pool, and to the "house of the mighty" (Neh 3:16). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that this son is a different man from the governor Nehemiah, though they lived at the same time. Smith's Bible Dictionary allows that Azbuk may have been a more distant ancestor rather than the immediate father, since "son of" can carry that wider sense. Azbuk is mentioned only in this verse, and nothing more is known about him.

Azgad was one of the leaders of the people who set their seal to the written covenant made in the time of Nehemiah, when the returned exiles pledged to keep God's law (Neh 10:15). He appears in a list of names with no further detail. In the surrounding passage this group is called the "chief of the people," and many of the names in it match families of returned exiles listed earlier. So Azgad here probably stands for the head or representative of the family of Azgad, whose descendants are counted among those who came back from Babylon in Ezra 2:12 and Neh 7:17. Because the name is used for more than one person or family, he cannot be identified with certainty. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "a strong army" or "a gang of robbers."

Aziza was a man of the family of Zattu who lived in Judah after the return from exile in Babylon. He appears only once, in the list of men who had married foreign wives in Ezra's time (Ezra 10:27). The surrounding chapter shows that these men agreed to send their foreign wives away as part of the reforms Ezra led. He is named together with five others from the same family: Elioenai, Eliashib, Mattaniah, Jeremoth and Zabad. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him as a layman, as opposed to a priest or Levite, and gives the meaning of his name as "strong." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia renders it "the powerful" and notes that the parallel list in 1 Esdras 9:28 has the name Zardeus in his place. Nothing else is recorded about him.

Azmaveth was the father of Jeziel and Pelet, two of the warriors who came over to David (1 Chr 12:3). The surrounding passage (1 Chr 12:1–2) places these men among the Benjamites, Saul's own tribe, who joined David at Ziklag while he was still in hiding from Saul. It describes them as archers and slingers who could use either hand. By inference, Azmaveth was also a Benjamite, and the STEPBible Proper Names index describes him that way. Nothing else is recorded about him. Several men in the Bible share the name, and some readers connect this Azmaveth with Azmaveth the Barhumite, one of David's mighty men (1 Chr 11:33). The text does not settle the question, so this entry treats him as a separate person. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "strong death."

Azmaveth son of Adiel was the official in charge of King David's treasures, according to the list of royal administrators in 1 Chr 27:25. In the same verse, Jehonathan son of Uzziah oversaw the storehouses in the fields, cities, villages and fortresses. That suggests Azmaveth's charge was the king's central treasury, probably kept in Jerusalem, though the verse does not say where it was. Easton's Bible Dictionary places his service in the time of both David and Solomon. Several other men in the Bible bear the name Azmaveth, including one of David's mighty men. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that some identify the treasurer with one or more of them. This entry treats him as the son of Adiel named in this verse. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "strong death."

Azriel was one of the heads of a father's house in the half-tribe of Manasseh that lived east of the Jordan. In 1 Chr 5:24 he is listed with Epher, Ishi, Eliel, Jeremiah, Hodaviah and Jahdiel, all described as mighty men of valour, famous men, and family heads. The surrounding passage places this half-tribe in the land from Bashan to Mount Hermon. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia links him with the people of his tribe whom the king of Assyria later carried into exile, as the following verses report. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates him to about 741 BC, an estimate drawn from that context. His name means "God's help." Several other men in the Bible share the name, and this Azriel is known only from this single verse.

Azriel was a man of the tribe of Naphtali and the father of Jerimoth. He is mentioned only once, in the list of tribal leaders during King David's reign, where Jerimoth son of Azriel is named as the officer over Naphtali (1 Chr 27:19). Nothing else is recorded about Azriel himself. Smith's Bible Dictionary calls him Jerimoth's ancestor rather than his father, since "son of" in such lists can mean a more distant descendant. His name means "God's help" or "whom God helps". The same name belongs to other men in the Bible, and this entry covers only the Naphtalite.

Azriel was the father of Seraiah, one of three men whom the king ordered to arrest Baruch the scribe and Jeremiah the prophet. The order followed the king's burning of the scroll of Jeremiah's prophecies, but the LORD hid the two men (Jer 36:26). From the surrounding chapter, the king was Jehoiakim of Judah. Smith's Bible Dictionary places these events about 605 BC. Azriel himself appears only as part of his son's name, and nothing else is recorded about him. Several other men in the Bible share the name, which the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia and Smith's Bible Dictionary translate as "God's help." Nothing links this Azriel to any of them.

Azrikam was a man of the tribe of Judah, one of the three sons of Neariah, along with his brothers Elioenai and Hezekiah (1 Chr 3:23). He appears only in the genealogy of David's royal line in 1 Chronicles 3, which traces the family through King Jehoiachin and Zerubbabel into the generations after the exile. This places Azrikam among the later descendants of Zerubbabel, as Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia note. Nothing is recorded about his life beyond his place in this list. The name, which the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia renders "my help has arisen," is shared by several other men in the Bible, including a Levite and an official of King Ahaz. This Azrikam should be kept distinct from them.

Azrikam was an official of King Ahaz of Judah, described as "the governor of the house," probably meaning the officer in charge of the royal palace. He was killed by Zichri, a warrior from Ephraim, who also killed the king's son Maaseiah and Elkanah, who was "next to the king" (2 Chr 28:7). By context, this happened during the invasion of Judah by Pekah, king of Israel, in the reign of Ahaz. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates it to about 738 BC. The name is usually explained as "my help has arisen" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia). Several other men in the Bible share the name Azrikam, and this one is mentioned only in this single verse.

Azur was the father of Hananiah, the prophet from Gibeon who confronted Jeremiah in the temple in the fourth year of Zedekiah king of Judah (Jer 28:1). He is known only from this one verse, which identifies his son by name and hometown. Smith's Bible Dictionary calls him a Benjamite of Gibeon, an inference from the town, which lay in Benjamin's territory. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes Hananiah as a false prophet. Smith's gives the more exact form of the name as Azzur, and Hitchcock's Bible Names explains it as meaning "he that assists" or "is assisted." Several other people in the Bible bear the same name, and nothing links this Azur to any of them.

Azur was the father of Jaazaniah, one of the twenty-five men Ezekiel saw in a vision at the door of the east gate of the temple in Jerusalem. Jaazaniah and Pelatiah son of Benaiah are singled out there as "princes of the people" (Ezek 11:1), and the passage goes on to describe them as leaders whom Ezekiel was told to prophesy against. Nothing is recorded about Azur himself beyond his son's name. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the name more properly as Azzur and explains it as "he that assists." The same name belongs to other people in the Bible, such as the father of the prophet Hananiah in Jeremiah 28 and a leader who sealed the covenant in Nehemiah 10. Nothing in the text links this Azur to either of them.

Azzan was a man of the tribe of Issachar, known only as the father of Paltiel. Paltiel was the prince, or leader, of Issachar named among the tribal representatives chosen to divide the land of Canaan among the tribes (Num 34:26). The context of the surrounding chapter, where God names these leaders to Moses, places this near the end of Israel's wilderness journey, before the crossing of the Jordan. Nothing else is recorded about Azzan himself. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "very strong," while the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests "strong" or "thorn."

Azzur was one of the leaders of the people who set their seal to the covenant made under Nehemiah after the return from exile in Babylon. He appears only in the list of those who signed it, between Ater and Hizkijah in Neh 10:17. By inference from the surrounding chapter, he signed among the heads of the people rather than the priests or Levites. Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests the name probably stands for a family rather than a single individual. It notes that the Hebrew name is the same one elsewhere spelled Azur, and gives its meaning as "one who helps." Nothing else is recorded about him, and whether he is connected to the others who bear the name Azur is uncertain.

Baal was a man of the tribe of Reuben, named in the Reubenite genealogy of 1 Chr 5:5 as the son of Reaia and the father of Beerah. The following verse, 1 Chr 5:6, describes Beerah as a prince of the Reubenites whom Tiglath-pileser king of Assyria carried into exile. That would place Baal's life, by inference, in the generation or two before the Assyrian deportations of the eighth century BC. Nothing else is recorded about him. His name means "lord" or "master" (Hitchcock's Bible Names). It is the same word used for the Canaanite god Baal, and several people and places in the Bible share it. This Baal should not be confused with the Benjamite of the same name in Saul's family line.

Baalhanan the Gederite was the official who managed King David's olive trees and sycomore-fig trees in the "low plains" (1 Chr 27:28). Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies these lowlands as the Shephelah, the foothills between the Judean hills and the coastal plain. He appears in a list of stewards in charge of the king's property, and in the same verse a man named Joash oversees the stores of oil. "Gederite" probably means he came from Geder or Gederah, though which town is meant is uncertain. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives the name's meaning as "the Lord is gracious" and describes him as a gardener in David's service. The same name belongs to another person in the Bible, an early king of Edom, who is a different individual.

Baalis was king of the Ammonites at the time Jerusalem fell to Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon. After the fall, the Babylonians appointed Gedaliah son of Ahikam as governor over those left in Judah. Johanan son of Kareah and other army captains warned Gedaliah that Baalis had sent Ishmael son of Nethaniah to kill him, but Gedaliah did not believe them (Jer 40:14). The following chapter of Jeremiah records that Ishmael did murder Gedaliah at Mizpah and then tried to escape to the Ammonites. This supports the view, found in Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia, that Baalis instigated the assassination. His motive is not stated. The meaning of the name is uncertain. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "a rejoicing" or "a proud lord," and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests it may be a form of Baalim.

Baana son of Ahilud was one of the twelve officers Solomon appointed over Israel. According to the surrounding passage (1 Kgs 4:7), each officer supplied food for the royal household for one month of the year. Baana's district included Taanach, Megiddo and all of Beth-shean near Zarethan below Jezreel, stretching from Beth-shean to Abel-meholah and beyond Jokneam. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes this as Jezreel and the north of the Jordan valley. Easton's Bible Dictionary calls him one of Solomon's purveyors. He was the brother of Jehoshaphat son of Ahilud, whom 1 Kgs 4:3 names as Solomon's recorder. Several men in the Bible bear the name Baana. This one is distinct from Baana son of Hushai, another of Solomon's district officers (1 Kgs 4:16).

Baana was the father of Zadok, one of the men who repaired a section of Jerusalem's wall under Nehemiah's leadership (Neh 3:4). He is known only from this single mention, which identifies his son. Nothing is recorded of Baana's own life or role, and he may not have been alive at the time of the rebuilding. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates the work on the wall to about 446 BC. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives the name's meaning as "son of oppression" and notes that a similar name belongs to two of Solomon's district officers (spelled "Baanah" in the King James Version). Because several people in the Bible bear this or a closely similar name, this Baana should not be confused with them.

Baanah son of Hushai was one of the twelve district officers King Solomon appointed over Israel, responsible for Asher and Aloth (1 Kgs 4:16). By inference from the surrounding passage (1 Kgs 4:7), each of these officers supplied food for the king and his household for one month of the year. Easton's Bible Dictionary accordingly calls him one of Solomon's purveyors, and Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him as a commissariat officer. Asher was the tribal territory in the northwest of the country, and Aloth was probably a place or district near it, though its location is uncertain. Some have suggested his father was Hushai the Archite, David's friend and counselor, but the text does not say so. The name Baanah is shared by several other men in the Bible, including a captain under Saul's son Ish-bosheth and another of Solomon's officers, Baanah son of Ahilud.

Baanah was one of the chiefs of the people who set their seal to the covenant made in Nehemiah's time, when the returned exiles pledged to keep God's law. His name appears in the list of signatories, beside Malluch and Harim (Neh 10:27). By inference from the surrounding passage, the covenant was sealed after the public reading of the law and the confession recorded in Nehemiah 8–9. Nothing else is recorded about him. Several other men in the Bible share the name Baanah, among them one of Ish-bosheth's murderers and one of Solomon's district officers. Some suggest this Baanah may be the man of the same name who returned from exile with Zerubbabel (Ezra 2:2; Neh 7:7), or a family head of that name, but the text does not settle this. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "in the answer" or "in affliction."

Baara was one of the wives of Shaharaim, a member of the tribe of Benjamin, named once in the genealogies of 1 Chronicles. 1 Chr 8:8 says Shaharaim had children in the land of Moab after he had sent away Hushim and Baara, his two wives. The phrase "sent them away" is usually read as divorce. The next verse names Hodesh as the wife by whom he had children in Moab, and a later verse in the same chapter credits sons to Hushim. No children are named for Baara, and nothing else is recorded about her. The meaning of her name is uncertain. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "brutish," the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives "the burning one," and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "a flame; purging."

Baaseiah was a Levite named only once, in the genealogy of Asaph the singer in 1 Chr 6:40. That verse makes him the son of Malchiah and the father of Michael. The surrounding passage traces Asaph's line back through Gershom, son of Levi, so Baaseiah belonged to the Gershonite branch of the tribe of Levi. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the STEPBible proper-names index both describe him this way. Nothing else is recorded about his life. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives the name's meaning as "the Lord is bold." It also suggests the name may be a variant of Maaseiah, "the work of the Lord," a form that some Greek manuscripts support. Smith's dictionary dates him to about 1310 BC. That date is an estimate worked out from his place in the genealogy, not something the text states.

Bakbakkar was a Levite named in the list of those who lived in Jerusalem, recorded in 1 Chr 9:15. He appears alongside Heresh, Galal and Mattaniah. In the surrounding passage, this list describes the Levites who settled in Jerusalem, probably after the return from exile in Babylon, by inference from the context of the chapter. The verse traces Mattaniah's ancestry back to Asaph, the temple musician. Smith's Bible Dictionary takes Bakbakkar to be apparently a descendant of Asaph as well. Nothing else is recorded about him. The meaning of his name is uncertain: Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "admirable," and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives "investigator." Some readers have linked him with Bakbukiah, a Levite in the similar list in Nehemiah 11, but the text does not make this identification.

Bani was a man of the tribe of Gad who appears in the list of David's mighty warriors, the elite fighters known as "the thirty" (2 Sam 23:36). He is called simply "Bani the Gadite" and is named next to Igal son of Nathan of Zobah. Nothing else is recorded about him, his family or his deeds.
