The parallel list of David's warriors in 1 Chr 11:38 has "Mibhar the son of Haggeri" at this point, so some take the two names as variant forms of the same entry, though this is uncertain. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives the meaning of the name as "posterity", while Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "built". Several other men in the Bible are named Bani, mostly Levites and returned exiles in the books of Ezra and Nehemiah. This Bani is distinct from them.

Bani was a Levite named in the family line of Ethan, one of the temple musicians in 1 Chr 6:46. He was the son of Shamer and the father of Amzi. The surrounding passage traces Ethan's ancestry back through the Levite clan of Merari. In context, Ethan was one of the men David put in charge of singing at the place of worship (1 Chr 6:31–47). Smith's Bible Dictionary accordingly describes Bani as a Levite of the line of Merari and a forefather of Ethan. Nothing else is recorded about him. Several other men in the Bible share the name Bani, and this entry refers only to the Merarite Levite of this genealogy.

Bani was a man of the tribe of Judah, descended from Pharez (Perez) son of Judah. He appears only in the genealogy of Uthai, one of the people of Judah who lived in Jerusalem after the return from exile (1 Chr 9:4). There he is named as the father of Imri and an ancestor of Uthai through Imri, Omri and Ammihud. Bani himself probably lived several generations before the return. Nothing else is recorded about him. Several other men in the Bible share the name Bani, and this entry concerns only the Judahite of the line of Pharez, as Smith's Bible Dictionary also identifies him. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives the meaning of the name as "posterity", while Smith's gives "built".

Bani is named in Ezra 10:34 as the head of a family whose members appear in the list of Israelites who had married foreign women after the return from exile in Babylon. Maadai, Amram and Uel are the first of the men listed under his name. By inference from the surrounding chapter, those named agreed under Ezra's leadership to send away their foreign wives. The STEPBible proper names index (Tyndale House) counts Bani himself among the men who had married foreign women and agreed to put them away. The verse does not make clear whether Bani was a living man or a more distant ancestor whose name marked the family. The name is shared by several people in the Bible, and another Bani family appears earlier in the same list (Ezra 10:29), so this entry treats him as a separate person, though the relationship between the two is uncertain.

Bani was an Israelite named in Ezra 10:38 among the men who had married foreign women in the time of Ezra, after the return from exile in Babylon. His name appears in a list that the surrounding chapter presents as men who agreed to send away their foreign wives. By inference from the list's structure, he seems to belong to a group introduced earlier as "the sons of Bani" (Ezra 10:34), and Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him that way. In that case he would be a member of that family who shared its founder's name. Nothing else is recorded about him. Several other men in Ezra and Nehemiah are also called Bani, and it is unclear whether any of them is the same person.

Bani was a Levite, known only as the father of Rehum, who led a group of Levites in repairing a section of Jerusalem's wall under Nehemiah (Neh 3:17). The verse names him only to identify his son, so nothing else is recorded about his life. He is taken to be a Levite because his son is listed among the Levites; Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him as a Levite. The work on the wall dates to the return from exile in the Persian period. Several other men in Ezra and Nehemiah share the name Bani, including Levites in the same period, and it is uncertain whether any of them is this same person. This entry treats him as a separate individual.

Bani was a Levite who stood on the stairs with other Levites and cried out loudly to the LORD during the assembly of fasting and confession held in Jerusalem in the time of Nehemiah (Neh 9:4). The surrounding chapter places this after the return from exile, when the Israelites gathered in sackcloth to confess their sins and hear the law read (Neh 9:1–3). The verse names two Levites called Bani, one after Jeshua and another after Sherebiah, so it is not certain which of them this entry refers to. The two may also be easy to confuse with other men of the same name in Ezra and Nehemiah. Bani is one of the most common names of the period, and the text gives no family line or further details that would tell these men apart.

Bani was one of the chiefs of the people who set their seal to the covenant made in Nehemiah's time, when the community that had returned from exile pledged to keep the law of God. In the list at Neh 10:14 he appears among the lay leaders, after Parosh, Pahath-moab, Elam and Zatthu. Several of these names also appear as family names in the lists of returned exiles, so Bani here probably stands as the head or representative of a family group rather than as a private individual. This is an inference from the pattern of the list. The name, which the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia explains as meaning "posterity," is shared by several men in Ezra and Nehemiah, including Levites. Which of the other mentions, if any, refer to this same leader is uncertain, and nothing more is recorded about him.

Bani was a Levite descended from Asaph, named only in a genealogy in Neh 11:22. He was the son of Hashabiah and the father of Uzzi, who served as overseer of the Levites at Jerusalem in Nehemiah's time. The same line traces his ancestry back through Mattaniah and Micha. Since the passage places this family among "the sons of Asaph," the singers who were in charge of the work of the house of God, Bani's household probably belonged to the Temple musicians. Nothing else is recorded about him. Several other men in the Bible bear the name Bani, and this one should not be confused with them. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives the name's meaning as "posterity," while Smith's Bible Dictionary renders it "built."

Bariah was a man of the tribe of Judah, one of the sons of Shemaiah, son of Shechaniah, in the genealogy of David's royal line in 1 Chr 3:22. His brothers were Hattush, Igeal, Neariah and Shaphat. The verse lists five names but gives the total as six, and Easton's Bible Dictionary explains this by counting the father Shemaiah along with his sons. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia places him among David's descendants through Solomon. Because the surrounding genealogy follows the royal line after the exile, he probably lived in the post-exilic period, and Smith's Bible Dictionary dates him before about 410 BC. His name is usually taken to mean "fugitive." Nothing else is recorded about him.

Barsabas Justus, whose given name was Joseph, was one of two men put forward by the early believers in Jerusalem to replace Judas Iscariot among the twelve apostles (Acts 1:23). He bore two further names: Barsabas, often explained as "son of Sabas" (Smith's Bible Dictionary), and the Latin surname Justus. By inference from the surrounding passage (Acts 1:21–22), he had been among the followers who were with the apostles throughout Jesus' ministry, from John's baptism to the ascension, which made him eligible to serve as a witness of the resurrection. The other candidate was Matthias. After prayer the group cast lots, and the lot fell to Matthias, who was added to the eleven. This episode is set about AD 30, by inference from context. Nothing further is recorded of Joseph Barsabas. He is distinct from Judas Barsabas of Acts 15, though some have suggested the two were related.

Bartimaeus, son of Timaeus, was a blind beggar who sat beside the road outside Jericho as Jesus left the city with his disciples and a large crowd (Mark 10:46). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia explains the name as Aramaic "bar" (son) joined to a Greek or Greek-like "Timaeus", so it may simply mean "son of Timaeus". The verses that follow in Mark (Mark 10:47–52) tell how he called out to Jesus and received his sight. The healing is dated to about AD 30, by inference from context, during Jesus' last journey to Jerusalem. Parallel accounts tell a similar story: Luke 18:35–43 places it as Jesus approached Jericho and does not name the man, and Matt 20:29–34 describes two blind men. Easton's Bible Dictionary takes Bartimaeus to be one of those two, while some scholars read the accounts as separate incidents.

Baruch, son of Zabbai, was one of the men who repaired the walls of Jerusalem under Nehemiah after the return from exile. Neh 3:20 says he "earnestly" repaired a second section of the wall, running from the angle or turning of the wall to the door of the house of Eliashib the high priest. The text gives no further details about him, and he should be kept distinct from other men of the same name, such as Jeremiah's scribe. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates the rebuilding to about 446 BC. The name means "blessed." He is probably the same Zabbai's son as no one else named elsewhere, though a Zabbai also appears among those who put away foreign wives in Ezra's time, and whether that man was his father is uncertain.

Baruch was one of the priests who set their seal to the covenant made in Nehemiah's time, when the community that had returned from exile in Babylon pledged to keep the law. His name appears in the list of priests at Neh 10:6, between Ginnethon and the next signatory. The heading of the list at Neh 10:8 identifies these men as priests, and Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests the name may stand for a priestly family rather than a single individual. The name means "blessed." Nothing else is recorded about him. He should be kept distinct from other men called Baruch, most notably Jeremiah's scribe and Baruch the son of Zabbai, who repaired part of the wall of Jerusalem.

Baruch was a man of the tribe of Judah, known only from a genealogy in Neh 11:5. He was the son of Col-hozeh and the father of Maaseiah, and his ancestry is traced back through Hazaiah, Adaiah, Joiarib and Zechariah to Shiloni. His son Maaseiah is listed among the people of Judah who lived in Jerusalem after the return from exile in Babylon. The surrounding passage suggests that the family belonged to Judah's clan of Perez, and Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both describe Baruch as a descendant of Perez. Nothing else is recorded about him. Several other men in the Bible share the name, including Jeremiah's scribe, and this Baruch should not be confused with them. According to Hitchcock's Bible Names, the name means "blessed."

Barzillai the Meholathite was the father of Adriel and is mentioned only once, in 2 Sam 21:8. His five grandsons, the sons of Adriel, were among the seven descendants of Saul whom King David handed over to the Gibeonites. The KJV text says Saul's daughter Michal "brought up" these sons for Adriel. Because 1 Sam 18:19 says Saul's daughter Merab was given to Adriel the Meholathite, the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that Adriel's wife may have been either Michal or Merab. The STEPBible names index describes the boys as sons Michal adopted. The title "Meholathite" probably means he came from Abel-meholah. He is a different man from the better-known Barzillai the Gileadite, who supported David. The name is usually taken to mean "man of iron."

Basmath was a daughter of King Solomon and the wife of Ahimaaz, the officer responsible for the district of Naphtali (1 Kgs 4:15). Ahimaaz was one of the twelve district governors who each provided food for the king's household for one month of the year. Her sister Taphath was likewise married to one of these governors, which suggests that Solomon tied some of his officials to the royal family by marriage. Her brother Rehoboam later succeeded Solomon as king. Her name means "fragrant" or "pleasing," according to Smith's Bible Dictionary. She is mentioned only in this one verse. The English spelling Basemath is shared with a wife of Esau, but they are different women. It is uncertain whether her husband is the same Ahimaaz who was the son of the priest Zadok.

Bavai, son of Henadad, was ruler of half the district of Keilah in Nehemiah's day and helped rebuild the walls of Jerusalem. He is named only in Neh 3:18, which says he repaired a section of the wall after "their brethren," probably the Levites named in the verse before. Keilah was a town in the lowlands of Judah, so Bavai seems to have led workers from his own district. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates this work to about 446 BC. Later in the same chapter, Neh 3:24 names another son of Henadad, Binnui, who repaired a different section. Some readers take Bavai and Binnui as two forms of one name. The usual reading treats them as brothers, and this entry follows that view.

Bealiah was one of the warriors who came to David at Ziklag while David was still in hiding from Saul. He is named only once, in a list of these men (1 Chr 12:5). The surrounding passage describes them as relatives of Saul from the tribe of Benjamin, men armed with bows who could sling stones and shoot arrows with either the right or the left hand. Easton's Bible Dictionary counts him among David's warriors of the sling and bow. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia explain his name as meaning "the LORD (Yahweh) is Lord." Nothing else is recorded about him.

Bebai was the father, or more likely the ancestor, of Zechariah, who led twenty-eight men of the family of Bebai back to Jerusalem with Ezra (Ezra 8:11). The verse speaks of "the sons of Bebai," so the name probably refers to the founder of a family clan rather than Zechariah's immediate father. STEPBible Proper Names describes Zechariah as a descendant of Bebai. A family group called the children of Bebai also appears among those who returned from exile earlier, as recorded in Ezra 2 and Nehemiah 7. Nothing else is known about Bebai himself. The name is shared by several people in the Bible, and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives its meaning as "void, empty."

Bebai was one of the leaders of the people who put their seal to the written covenant made in Nehemiah's time, in which the community in Jerusalem pledged to keep the law of Moses (Neh 10:15). He appears in a list of the chiefs of the people, between Azgad and Hodijah. Many names in this list, Bebai among them, match the family groups that returned from exile in Babylon (Ezra 2:11 counts a large group as the descendants of Bebai). So he probably signed as the head or representative of that family rather than only as an individual. Nothing else is recorded about him, and the name is shared by several people in the Bible. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives the meaning of the name as "fatherly," while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "void, empty."

Becher was a son of Ephraim and the ancestor of an Ephraimite clan called the Bachrites (or Becherites). He appears in the census of Israel taken in the plains of Moab, where Num 26:35 lists him between his brothers Shuthelah and Tahan as the head of one of Ephraim's families. His other brothers, Ezer, Elead and Beriah, are named in the Ephraimite genealogy of 1 Chr 7:20–23. That genealogy does not name Becher, and Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both take him to be the Bered it lists there. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of his name as "first begotten" or "first fruits." The name is shared with others, notably a son of Benjamin (Gen 46:21), and this entry refers only to the Ephraimite.

Bechorath was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, named only in the genealogy of Kish in 1 Sam 9:1. He was the son of Aphiah and the father of Zeror, which makes him the great-great-grandfather of Kish. Since the next verse introduces Kish's son Saul, Bechorath was an ancestor of King Saul. Nothing else is recorded about him. Smith's Bible Dictionary takes the name to mean "first-born," and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "first fruits." Smith's also links him with Becher, a son of Benjamin listed in 1 Chr 7:8, and treats Bechorath as Becher's grandson. That connection is not stated in the passage itself. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia spells the name Becorath.

Bedan is a deliverer of Israel named by Samuel in his farewell speech, listed with Jerubbaal (Gideon), Jephthah and Samuel himself as leaders the LORD sent to rescue the people from their enemies (1 Sam 12:11). His name may mean "son of judgment." No judge called Bedan appears in the Book of Judges, so who he was is uncertain. The Septuagint, Syriac and Arabic versions read "Barak" here, and the Aramaic paraphrase reads "Samson" (Smith's Bible Dictionary). Easton's Bible Dictionary considers it most likely a shortened form of Abdon, the judge in Judg 12:13. This entry does not settle on any one of these identifications. The name is also borne by a different man, a descendant of Manasseh.

Bedan was a man of the tribe of Manasseh, named as the son of Ulam in the genealogy of 1 Chr 7:17. That verse ends by counting this family among the descendants of Gilead, the son of Machir, the son of Manasseh, so Bedan belonged to the Gileadite clans of the half-tribe descended from Joseph's son Manasseh. The preceding verse (1 Chr 7:16) makes Ulam a son of Peresh, whose mother was Maachah, Machir's wife. Nothing else is recorded about him. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "son of judgment." The name is also used of a different figure in 1 Sam 12:11, one of the deliverers of Israel named by Samuel, who is not the same man.

Bedeiah was an Israelite named in the list of men in Ezra's time who had married foreign wives (Ezra 10:35). The list groups names by family. By inference from the context of Ezra 10:34, he belonged to the descendants of Bani, as Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both note. The surrounding chapter records that these men agreed to send away their foreign wives during the reforms led by Ezra after the return from exile. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates this to about 458 BC, an estimate inferred from context. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia explains his name as meaning "servant of Yah." Nothing else is known about him.

Beera was a man of the tribe of Asher, named as a son of Zophah in the tribal genealogy of 1 Chr 7:37. He is the last of the sons listed there. His brothers in the same list include Bezer, Hod, Shamma, Shilshah and Ithran, along with Suah, Harnepher, Beri, Imrah and Ulla. Jether, also counted here among his brothers, is probably the same person as the Ithran named in this verse, since the two forms of the name are closely related. Nothing else is recorded about Beera beyond his place in the genealogy. According to Smith's Bible Dictionary and Hitchcock's Bible Names, his name means "a well." He should not be confused with Beerah, a Reubenite leader taken captive by the Assyrians, whose name is spelled differently in English.

Beerah was a prince, or leader, of the tribe of Reuben. He was the son of Baal and appears in the Reubenite genealogy of 1 Chr 5. Tilgath-pilneser (Tiglath-pileser III), king of Assyria, carried him away captive (1 Chr 5:6). That places him in the eighth century BC, when Assyria conquered the Israelite territories east of the Jordan and deported their people. 2 Kgs 15:29 describes Tiglath-pileser taking Gilead and carrying its inhabitants to Assyria, and 1 Chr 5:26 names the Reubenites among those deported. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates his captivity to about 738 BC. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives the meaning of his name as "expounder." Nothing else is recorded about him.

Beeri was a Hittite, the father of Judith, whom Esau married at the age of forty along with Basemath the daughter of Elon (Gen 26:34). The name is shared by several people in the Bible, and this Beeri is mentioned only in this one verse. The later list of Esau's wives in Gen 36:2–3 gives different names, and harmonizers have tried to match the two lists in different ways. One common reconciliation, which Smith's Bible Dictionary points to and this entry follows, takes Judith to be the same woman as Aholibamah and links Beeri with Anah, whom that list names as Aholibamah's parent. This is why Aholibamah is shown here as his daughter and Anah is connected with him. Easton's Bible Dictionary instead identifies Judith with Adah. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "my well."

Beeri was the father of the prophet Hosea and is known only from the opening verse of the book of Hosea (Hos 1:1). That verse dates Hosea's prophetic work to the reigns of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz and Hezekiah, kings of Judah, and of Jeroboam son of Joash, king of Israel. By inference, Beeri lived in the eighth century BC; Smith's Bible Dictionary places him before 725 BC. Nothing else is recorded about him. Another man named Beeri, a Hittite and the father of Esau's wife Judith, appears in Genesis, and this one should not be confused with him. The name is usually connected with the Hebrew word for "well." Hitchcock's Bible Names gives its meaning as "my well," while the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia renders it "expounder."

Bela was a man of the tribe of Reuben, the son of Azaz, son of Shema, son of Joel. He appears only once, in the Reubenite genealogy of 1 Chr 5:8. That verse says he lived in Aroer and that his people's territory reached as far as Nebo and Baal-meon, towns east of the Jordan in the region north of the Arnon River. The following verses, read in context, describe his family spreading eastward toward the Euphrates because their livestock had multiplied in Gilead. His tie to Reuben comes from the surrounding genealogy, though the exact link between Joel and Reuben's sons is not spelled out. Smith's Bible Dictionary calls his father Ahaz rather than Azaz. Several other men in the Bible share the name Bela, including a king of Edom and a son of Benjamin. This Bela should be kept distinct from them.

Ben was a Levite named in 1 Chr 15:18 among the musicians and gatekeepers of the "second degree" whom the Levite leaders appointed at David's command when the ark of the covenant was brought up to Jerusalem. His name means "son." He appears in a list alongside Zechariah, Jaaziel, Obed-edom and others, and nothing else is recorded about him. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the text here may be uncertain, because the name is missing when the same group is listed again in 1 Chr 15:20 and does not appear in the Septuagint. On that reading, "Ben" may be part of a neighboring name rather than a separate person. This entry treats him as the individual Levite named in the verse.

Ben-hanan was a son of Shimon, named in the genealogy of the tribe of Judah in 1 Chr 4:20. His brothers were Amnon, Rinnah and Tilon. The verse belongs to a list of Judah's descendants, but Shimon's own link to the main family line is not stated, so his exact place in the tribe is unclear. Nothing else is recorded about Ben-hanan, and this is the only verse that mentions him. His name means "son of grace" or "son of the gracious one," according to Hitchcock's Bible Names and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia.

Ben-zoheth was a man of the tribe of Judah, named once in the genealogies of 1 Chronicles as a son of Ishi and brother of Zoheth (1 Chr 4:20). His name means "son of Zoheth." Smith's Bible Dictionary reads it that way, which could suggest he was Zoheth's son and so Ishi's grandsonsuggested. The verse itself lists both Zoheth and Ben-zoheth among the sons of Ishi, and this entry follows that reading, as does the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning "son of separation." Nothing else is recorded about him.

Benaiah was a man of the tribe of Simeon, named in a list of Simeonite clan leaders in 1 Chr 4:36. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him as one of the "princes" of the families of Simeon. By inference from the surrounding passage (1 Chr 4:38–41), these leaders' families grew large, and in the days of Hezekiah, king of Judah, they moved toward Gedor in search of pasture and attacked the people living there, including the Meunim. STEPBible's proper names index follows this reading and places Benaiah among the men who took part. Nothing else is recorded about him. His name is usually explained as "the Lord has built" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia). Several other men in the Bible share this name, including David's commander Benaiah son of Jehoiada, and this Simeonite should be kept distinct from them.

Benaiah was the father of Jehoiada, who is named in 1 Chr 27:34 as one of King David's counselors, following Ahithophel in that role. Nothing else is said about Benaiah himself. This Benaiah is one of several men with the name, which the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia explains as "Yahweh has built." That dictionary links this entry to the better-known Benaiah son of Jehoiada, the commander of David's bodyguard. This suggests that the father and son may be the same family, with the names possibly appearing in reverse order here. Following the verse as written, this entry treats Benaiah as Jehoiada's father.

Benaiah was a Levite of the family of Asaph, known only from a genealogy in 2 Chr 20:14. He was the son of Jeiel and the father of Zechariah, which made him the grandfather of Jahaziel, the Levite on whom the Spirit of the LORD came in the assembly during the reign of King Jehoshaphat. The line continues back through Jeiel to Mattaniah. Nothing else is recorded about him, and since he is listed two generations before Jahaziel, he probably lived somewhat earlier than Jehoshaphat's time. Several other men in the Bible share the name Benaiah. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives its meaning as "Yahweh has built."

Benaiah was a Levite in the time of King Hezekiah of Judah, called a Levite in Smith's Bible Dictionary. He was one of ten overseers who served under Cononiah and his brother Shimei, by order of Hezekiah and Azariah, the ruler of the house of God (2 Chr 31:13). The surrounding passage shows that Cononiah and Shimei were in charge of the offerings, tithes and dedicated gifts brought into storerooms prepared in the temple. Benaiah and the other overseers probably helped manage these stores for the priests and Levites. Nothing else is recorded about him, and he should not be confused with several other men of the same name in the Bible. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "made by the Lord," while Hitchcock's Bible Names renders it "son of the Lord."

Benaiah was a man of Israel, a descendant of Parosh, named in the list of those who had married foreign wives in the time of Ezra (Ezra 10:25). By inference from the surrounding chapter, he lived among the Jews who had returned from exile in Babylon, and he was among those who agreed to send away their foreign wives when Ezra led the community in a reform. He appears in the part of the list covering ordinary Israelites rather than priests, Levites, singers or gatekeepers. Nothing else is recorded about him. Several other men in the Bible share the name Benaiah, including others in the same list, and this one should not be confused with them. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "son of the Lord."

Benaiah was a man descended from Pahath-moab who is listed in Ezra 10:30 among the Israelites of the returned community who had married foreign wives. By inference from the surrounding chapter, he was one of those who agreed to send away these wives during the reforms led by Ezra after the return from exile. He is known only from this list, and nothing else is recorded about him. The name Benaiah is shared by several other men in the Bible, including more than one in this same chapter of Ezra, so he should not be confused with them. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "son of the Lord."

Benaiah was one of the men listed in Ezra 10 who had married foreign wives during Ezra's reforms after the return from exile. He appears only in Ezra 10:35. By inference from the surrounding verses, he belonged to the descendants of Bani (Ezra 10:34), and he was among those who agreed to send away their foreign wives and children (Ezra 10:44). Nothing else is known about him. Several other men in the Bible share the name, and he should not be confused with them, including other Benaiahs in the same list. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "son of the Lord."

Benaiah was one of the descendants of Nebo named in Ezra's list of Israelite men who had married foreign wives (Ezra 10:43). By inference from the surrounding chapter, this was in the time after the return from exile in Babylon, when Ezra led the community to separate from such marriages, and those named agreed to send their wives away. The list says nothing more about him. Several other men in the Bible share the name, including a well-known commander under David and Solomon, but nothing in the text links this Benaiah to any of them. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "son of the Lord."

Benhail was one of the princes, or officials, of Judah whom King Jehoshaphat sent out in the third year of his reign to teach in the cities of Judah (2 Chr 17:7). He is named alongside Obadiah, Zechariah, Nethaneel and Michaiah. By inference from the following verses, these princes travelled with a group of Levites and priests, taking the book of the law of the Lord with them. STEPBible's proper-names index describes Benhail as a Levite, while the verse itself counts him among the king's princes. His name is usually explained as meaning "son of strength" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia; Hitchcock's Bible Names), and Smith's Bible Dictionary also gives "son of the host." He is mentioned nowhere else in the Bible.

Beninu was a Levite named among those who set their seal to the written covenant made in the time of Nehemiah, after the return from exile in Babylon. He appears only once, in the list of Levite signatories, between Hodijah and Bani (Neh 10:13). That he was a Levite comes from the context of the list, which in Neh 10:9 begins naming the Levites who sealed the agreement. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both explain the name as meaning "our son." Nothing else is recorded about his family or his life.

Benjamin was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, named in the genealogy of 1 Chr 7:10 as one of the seven sons of Bilhan. His brothers were Jeush, Ehud, Chenaanah, Zethan, Tharshish and Ahishahar. Bilhan was a son of Jediael, and the surrounding passage traces Jediael back to the patriarch Benjamin (1 Chr 7:6), so this man carried the name of his tribe's ancestor. The following verse (1 Chr 7:11) describes these descendants of Jediael as heads of their fathers' houses and men of valor, and Smith's Bible Dictionary accordingly calls him the head of a family of warriors. Nothing else is recorded about him. He should not be confused with the patriarch Benjamin, Jacob's youngest son, or with other men of the same name. The name means "son of the right hand," according to Hitchcock's Bible Names.

Benjamin was an Israelite in the time of Ezra, listed among the men who had married foreign wives (Ezra 10:32). He appears alongside Malluch and Shemariah in a group that, by the surrounding passage, belonged to the "sons of Harim" (Ezra 10:31), as Smith's Bible Dictionary also notes. The context of Ezra 10 shows that these men agreed to send away their foreign wives during Ezra's reforms after the return from exile. Nothing more is recorded about him. He is distinct from the more famous Benjamin, the youngest son of Jacob, and from other men of the same name. The name is usually explained as meaning "son of the right hand" (Hitchcock's Bible Names).

Benjamin was a man of Jerusalem who, together with Hashub, repaired a section of the city wall opposite their house during the rebuilding led by Nehemiah after the return from exile (Neh 3:23). The next section was repaired by Azariah son of Maaseiah. Nothing more is said about his family or background. The name, which Hitchcock's Bible Names explains as meaning "son of the right hand," is shared by several people in the Bible, most famously Jacob's youngest son. A Benjamin is also named among those who took part in the dedication of the rebuilt wall (Neh 12:34), and he may be the same man, though the text does not say so.

Benjamin was one of the men named among those who took part in the procession at the dedication of the rebuilt wall of Jerusalem in Nehemiah's time (Neh 12:34). He appears in a list with Judah, Shemaiah and Jeremiah, in the company that walked along the wall behind Hoshaiah and half the leaders of Judah. The surrounding passage places the list just before the priests' sons with trumpets, and STEPBible Proper Names (Tyndale House) identifies him as a priest, the view this entry follows. Some readers take "Judah and Benjamin" here as standing for the tribes rather than for individuals. Whether he is the same as the Benjamin who repaired part of the wall in Neh 3:23, or the Benjamin of Ezra 10:32, cannot be determined. The name, shared by several people in the Bible, means "son of the right hand" (Hitchcock's Bible Names).

Bera was king of Sodom in the time of Abram, one of five kings of the cities of the plain who went to war against an alliance of four eastern kings led by Chedorlaomer of Elam (Gen 14:2). The same chapter says these cities had served Chedorlaomer for twelve years before rebelling. Their armies met in the Vale of Siddim, where the five kings were defeated and the king of Sodom fled. After Abram rescued his nephew Lot and recovered the captives and goods, the king of Sodom went out to meet him. He offered Abram the goods in exchange for the people, but Abram refused to keep anything (Gen 14:17, 21–24). Bera is named only once, in Gen 14:2, but he is probably the unnamed king of Sodom in these later verses. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "gift" or "son of evil."

Berachah was one of the warriors who came to David at Ziklag, named in a list in 1 Chr 12:3. The surrounding chapter describes these men as kinsmen of Saul from the tribe of Benjamin. They joined David while he was still hiding from Saul, and they were skilled with the bow and the sling. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary both identify Berachah as a Benjamite on this basis. His name means "blessing." Nothing else is recorded about him. He should not be confused with the Valley of Berachah, a place named in a later period of Israel's history. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates his joining David to about 1054 BC, an estimate drawn from context.

Beraiah was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, named once in the Bible, in the Benjamite genealogy of 1 Chronicles 8. He is listed as one of the sons of Shimhi, alongside his brothers Adaiah, Shimrath, Jakim, Zichri, Zabdi, Elienai, Zilthai and Eliel (1 Chr 8:21). Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him as a chief man of Benjamin, in line with the chapter's presentation of these names as heads of families. His name is usually explained as meaning "the LORD has created" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia), while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "the choosing of the Lord." Nothing more is recorded about his life.

Berechiah was a son of Zerubbabel and a member of the royal line of David in the tribe of Judah. He appears only in the genealogy of David's descendants in 1 Chr 3:20, where he is named within a group of five brothers: Hashubah, Ohel, Berechiah, Hasadiah and Jushab-hesed. The previous verse lists Zerubbabel's other children, Meshullam, Hananiah and their sister Shelomith. Abiud is also counted as a sibling here because Matt 1:13 names an Abiud as a son of Zerubbabel. Since Zerubbabel led the return from exile in Babylon, Berechiah probably lived in Judah after the return, though nothing is recorded about his life. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives the meaning of his name as "Yahweh blesses." Several other people in the Bible share the name, including the father of the prophet Zechariah, and they should not be confused with this Berechiah.

Berechiah, son of Asa and grandson of Elkanah, was a Levite named in the list of those who lived in Jerusalem after the return from exile in Babylon. He appears alongside Obadiah, a descendant of Jeduthun, among the Levites in that list. The verse says the family lived in the villages of the Netophathites. Netophah was a town near Bethlehem, so these settlements were probably in that area. It is not clear whether the phrase about the villages applies to Berechiah himself or to his ancestor Elkanah. STEPBible's Tyndale House name index calls him a Levite gatekeeper, while Smith's Bible Dictionary simply calls him a Levite. Nothing else is recorded about him. Several people in the Bible share the name Berechiah, which means "the Lord blesses," and this one should not be confused with the others.

Berechiah, son of Meshillemoth, was one of the leaders of the tribe of Ephraim during the reign of Ahaz, king of Judah. When the army of the northern kingdom of Israel came home from war against Judah with a large number of Judean captives, Berechiah and three other Ephraimite leaders stood up against the returning soldiers (2 Chr 28:12). The surrounding passage shows that they opposed keeping their fellow Israelites as slaves, and the captives were then clothed, fed and sent back to Jericho. Easton's Bible Dictionary counts him among seven Ephraimite chieftains. His name means "the LORD blesses." Several other men in the Bible share this name, and this Berechiah is known only from this one episode.

Bered was a descendant of Ephraim, son of Joseph, named only in the genealogy of Ephraim's line in 1 Chr 7:20. The verse lists him as the son of Shuthelah and the father of Tahath, which makes him a grandson of Ephraim, as Easton's Bible Dictionary also reads it. Eran, who is listed as a son of Shuthelah in Num 26:36, is shown here as his brother. Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests Bered may be the same person as Becher in Num 26:35, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia points to Becher for comparison. The name probably means "hail" (Hitchcock's Bible Names). Nothing else is recorded about his life.

Beri was a man of the tribe of Asher, named as one of the sons of Zophah in the genealogy of Asher's descendants in 1 Chr 7:36. His brothers listed with him include Suah, Harnepher, Shual and Imrah, and the list continues in the next verse with Bezer, Hod, Shamma, Shilshah, Ithran (or Jether) and Beera. Nothing else is recorded about him beyond his place in this family line. The meaning of his name is uncertain. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "a well," the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives "wisdom," and Hitchcock's Bible Names offers "my son" or "my corn."

Beriah was a son of Ephraim, born after Ephraim's sons Ezer and Elead were killed by the men of Gath while raiding their cattle (1 Chr 7:21–22). Ephraim mourned them for many days. When his wife later bore him another son, he named him Beriah "because it went evil with his house," which links the name to the family's misfortune (1 Chr 7:23). Easton's Bible Dictionary and the Tyndale House proper-names index both explain the name this way. The following verses list his descendants. His daughter Sherah is said to have built the Beth-horons (1 Chr 7:24). Rephah and Resheph follow, though the text does not make clear whether they were Beriah's own sons. The line then runs down to Joshua son of Nun (1 Chr 7:25–27). Several other men in the Bible share the name Beriah.

Besodeiah was the father of Meshullam, who is known only from Neh 3:6. In Nehemiah's account of rebuilding Jerusalem's walls, Meshullam son of Besodeiah worked with Jehoiada son of Paseah to repair the Old Gate. They laid its beams and set up its doors, locks and bars. Nothing else is recorded about Besodeiah himself. He presumably lived in the generation before the rebuilding, which this account places in the Persian period after the return from exile. Smith's Bible Dictionary takes his name to mean "in the secret of the Lord," and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia reads it as "in the confidence or counsel of Yah." Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "counsel of the Lord."

Beth-rapha was a son of Eshton, named in the genealogy of Judah in 1 Chr 4:12 alongside his brothers Paseah and Tehinnah. The passage groups these men as "the men of Rechah." Nothing else is recorded about him. Because the name begins with "Beth" (house), it may stand for a family, clan or settlement rather than a single individual, as other names in these Chronicles genealogies do. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes, however, that it cannot now be linked with any particular place or clan. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning "house of health."

Bezai was one of the leaders of the people who set their seal to the covenant made in Nehemiah's time, when the community that had returned from exile in Babylon committed itself in writing to keep the law of God. He is named in a list of the chiefs of the people (Neh 10:18) and nothing else is recorded about him. The name also belongs to a family whose members returned from Babylon with Zerubbabel (Ezra 2:17; Neh 7:23). The Bezai who sealed the covenant was probably the head of that family, signing on its behalf, though the text does not say so directly. The meaning of the name is uncertain. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia tentatively suggests "shining," and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "eggs."

Bezaleel was one of the sons, or descendants, of Pahath-moab named in Ezra's list of men who had married foreign wives after the return from exile (Ezra 10:30). By inference from the surrounding chapter, he was among those who agreed to send away these wives and their children under the reform led by Ezra. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates these events to about 458 BC, and the name is usually explained as meaning "in the shadow of God." Nothing else is recorded about him. He should not be confused with the better-known Bezaleel, the craftsman of the tabernacle in Exodus, or with others who share the name.

Bezer was a man of the tribe of Asher, named in the Asherite genealogy of 1 Chronicles as a son of Zophah. He appears in a list of eleven sons that includes Suah, Harnepher, Beri, Imrah, Hod, Shamma, Shilshah, Beera and Ulla. The verse that names him also names Ithran, and the next verse in the chapter mentions Jether. This entry treats the two as the same brother. By inference from the surrounding genealogy, Zophah was a son of Helem, which places Bezer in a line descending from Asher through Heber. Smith's Bible Dictionary counts him among the heads of the houses of Asher. Nothing else is recorded about him. Reference works explain his name differently: "strong" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia), "gold ore" (Smith's) or "vine branches" (Hitchcock's). He is distinct from Bezer, the city of refuge east of the Jordan.

Bigtha was one of the seven chamberlains who served in the presence of King Ahasuerus of Persia, according to Esth 1:10. On the seventh day of the king's feast, when he was merry with wine, Ahasuerus ordered these seven men, Mehuman, Biztha, Harbona, Bigtha, Abagtha, Zethar and Carcas, to bring Queen Vashti before him. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary describe the chamberlains as eunuchs who had charge of the king's harem. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identifies Ahasuerus with Xerxes, and Smith's places the event about 483 BC. Bigtha is mentioned only in this verse. Some take him to be the same man as Bigthan, a palace official who later plotted against the king (Esth 2:21). The names are similar, but this entry treats Bigtha as the chamberlain of Esth 1:10 alone.

Bigvai was one of the leaders of the people who set their seal to the written covenant made in the time of Nehemiah, in which the returned community of Judah pledged to keep the law of God (Neh 10:16). His name appears in the list of the "chief of the people" that begins at Neh 10:14, between Adonijah and Adin. Nothing more is told about him personally. The name Bigvai is shared by several people. It belongs to a leader who returned from Babylon with Zerubbabel and to a large family of returned exiles (Ezra 2:2, 14; Neh 7:7, 19). Since many names in this list match family names from those earlier lists, this Bigvai probably signed as head or representative of that family, though this is an inference. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "in my body."

Bilgah was a priest in the time of David and the head of the fifteenth of the twenty-four divisions, or courses, into which the priests were organized for service at the sanctuary. The lots were cast to set the order in which these priestly families would serve, and the fifteenth lot fell to Bilgah, just before Immer (1 Chr 24:14). Nothing else is recorded about him personally. The name appears again for other men, including a priest who returned from exile with Zerubbabel and one who sealed Nehemiah's covenant, the latter spelled Bilgai in the KJV. These later bearers may represent the same priestly family or division, but they are distinct individuals. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "ancient countenance," while Smith's Bible Dictionary renders it "first-born."

Bilhan was a member of the tribe of Benjamin, named in the genealogy of 1 Chr 7:10 as the son of Jediael. That verse lists his seven sons: Jeush, Benjamin, Ehud, Chenaanah, Zethan, Tharshish and Ahishahar. His son Benjamin bears the same name as the tribe's ancestor, and his son Ehud should not be confused with the judge Ehud son of Gera. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia describes his sons as heads of houses within their tribe, by inference from the surrounding passage, which counts Jediael's descendants as fighting men. Nothing more is recorded about him. The name Bilhan is also borne by a Horite chief descended from Seir, a different person.

Bimhal was a man of the tribe of Asher, named in 1 Chr 7:33 as one of the three sons of Japhlet, along with his brothers Pasach and Ashvath. He appears only in this genealogy of Asher's descendants, and nothing else is recorded about his life. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "circumcised."

Binnui was a Levite of the time of Ezra, known only as the father of Noadiah. According to Ezra 8:33, on the fourth day after Ezra's company arrived in Jerusalem from Babylon, the silver, gold and vessels they had brought for the temple were weighed in the house of God. This was done under the priest Meremoth son of Uriah, with Eleazar son of Phinehas, and with the Levites Jozabad son of Jeshua and Noadiah son of Binnui. The verse gives no further details about Binnui himself. Several other men named Binnui appear in Ezra and Nehemiah, and whether any of them is the same person is uncertain. Smith's Bible Dictionary treats this Binnui as a separate Levite, and this entry follows that view. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "building."

Binnui was one of the descendants of Pahath-moab named in Ezra 10:30. He appears in the list of men who had married foreign wives in the time of Ezra, after the return from exile in Babylon. By inference from the surrounding passage, the men on this list agreed to send away their foreign wives as part of Ezra's reforms, and the STEPBible Proper Names index describes him this way. Nothing else is recorded about him. Several other men in the books of Ezra and Nehemiah bear the same name, so he should not be confused with them. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "building," while Smith's Bible Dictionary renders it "familyship."

Binnui was an Israelite named in Ezra 10:38 among the men who had married foreign wives in the period after the return from exile in Babylon. By inference from the surrounding list, which is introduced as "the sons of Bani" a few verses earlier, he belonged to that family group. TIPNR describes him the same way and says he divorced his foreign wife during Ezra's reforms, which is what the men in this list pledged to do. Nothing else is recorded about him. Some translations read the words "Bani, and Binnui" in this verse as "of the sons of Binnui," which would make Binnui the head of a family rather than an individual. This entry follows the King James reading, which treats him as one person. Several other men in Ezra and Nehemiah share the name, and it is uncertain whether any of them is the same man. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "building."

Binnui was the son of Henadad and one of the workers who rebuilt Jerusalem's wall under Nehemiah after the return from exile. Nehemiah 3:24 says he repaired a section of the wall running from the house of Azariah to the turning of the wall at the corner. Several men in the Bible bear this name, so his identity beyond this verse is uncertain. Neh 10:9 lists a Levite named Binnui "of the sons of Henadad" among those who sealed the covenant, and Neh 3:18 names a Bavai son of Henadad among the builders. Either or both may be the same man, which would suggest he belonged to a Levite family descended from Henadad, though this is only an inference. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "building."

Birsha was the king of Gomorrah in the time of Abraham. He is named only once, in Gen 14:2, among five kings of the cities of the plain: Bera of Sodom, Birsha of Gomorrah, Shinab of Admah, Shemeber of Zeboiim, and the king of Bela, also called Zoar. The kings Chedorlaomer, Amraphel, Arioch and Tidal made war against these five. The rest of the chapter describes the battle in the vale of Siddim, the defeat of Sodom and Gomorrah, and Abram's rescue of his nephew Lot. By inference, Birsha was among the kings who fled that battle, though he is not named again. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "son of wickedness." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests the name may have been altered in transmission, or chosen by the writer to mean "with wickedness."

Birzavith is named in the genealogy of the tribe of Asher as the child of Malchiel, who was a son of Beriah and grandson of Asher (1 Chr 7:31). She is mentioned only in this one verse, and nothing else is recorded about her. This entry treats Birzavith as a woman, Malchiel's daughter. Some readers take the name instead as a place. In the Chronicles genealogies, "father of" can mean the founder or leading figure of a town, and STEPBible Proper Names (Tyndale House) notes that Birzaith may have been a town connected with Malchiel. Smith's Bible Dictionary simply describes it as a name in the genealogies of Asher. The spelling also varies, with Birzaith given as an alternative form.

Bishlam was one of the men who, in the days of Artaxerxes king of Persia, wrote a letter to the king with Mithredath, Tabeel and their companions (Ezra 4:7). The letter was written in Aramaic, which the King James Version calls "the Syrian tongue." From the surrounding chapter, which describes opposition to the Jews returning from exile, the letter was probably a complaint against them. The STEPBible Proper Names index describes him as a Samaritan official who opposed the rebuilding of Jerusalem. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats him as one of three foreign colonists and notes that 1 Esdras gives the name as Belemus. The name may mean "in peace," and the Greek Septuagint renders the word as that phrase rather than as a name. This entry follows the reading of Bishlam as a personal name. Nothing else is known about him.

Bithiah was a daughter of Pharaoh who married Mered, a descendant of Judah, and appears only in the genealogy of 1 Chr 4:18. Her children are named as Miriam, Shammai and Ishbah the father of Eshtemoa. They are listed in the preceding verse, and by inference from the passage's phrase "these are the sons of Bithiah" that list belongs to her. Mered also had a wife called Jehudijah. The Revised Version renders this name "the Jewess," which sets her apart from the Egyptian Bithiah. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that "Pharaoh" could mean an Egyptian king or could be a Hebrew personal name. This entry follows the more common reading of an Egyptian princess. Her name means "daughter of the Lord" (Hitchcock's Bible Names; Smith's Bible Dictionary), which the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia takes to suggest she had adopted the worship of Israel's God.

Biztha was one of the seven chamberlains who served in the presence of King Ahasuerus of Persia, and the second named in the list in Esth 1:10. On the seventh day of the king's feast, when Ahasuerus was merry with wine, he sent these seven men to bring Queen Vashti before him. The word translated "chamberlains" usually means eunuchs, and Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both describe Biztha as a eunuch of the royal household. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identifies Ahasuerus with Xerxes and suggests the name may come from a Persian word meaning "bound," and so "eunuch." Smith's dates the event to about 483 BC. Nothing more is recorded about him.

Blastus was the chamberlain, or personal attendant, of King Herod in Acts 12:20. This Herod is identified as Herod Agrippa I by Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries. When Herod was angry with the people of Tyre and Sidon, they came to him together and asked for peace, because their land depended on the king's territory for its food supply. To do this they first won Blastus over as their friend, so that he could act as their go-between with the king. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests they probably gained his help with a bribe, though the text does not say how. Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that such officials usually had great influence with their masters. Blastus is mentioned nowhere else in the Bible. His name is Greek and is usually explained as meaning "sprout" or "shoot."

Bukki son of Jogli was the leader of the tribe of Dan named in Num 34:22 among the men chosen to divide the land of Canaan among the tribes. In the surrounding passage, the LORD tells Moses to appoint one leader from each tribe to assist Eleazar the priest and Joshua in giving out the land west of the Jordan. Smith's Bible Dictionary counts him as one of the ten men chosen for this task, because Reuben, Gad and half of Manasseh had already received land east of the Jordan. Nothing else is recorded about him. He should not be confused with another Bukki, a priestly descendant of Aaron named in later genealogies such as 1 Chr 6:5.

Bunah was a man of the tribe of Judah, named second among the sons of Jerahmeel, the firstborn of Hezron, in the genealogy of 1 Chr 2:25. His brothers listed there are Ram the firstborn, Oren, Ozem and Ahijah. The next verse, 1 Chr 2:26, says Jerahmeel had another wife, Atarah, who was the mother of Onam, so Onam was probably Bunah's half-brother. Through Hezron, Bunah belonged to the line of Perez, son of Judah, as Smith's Bible Dictionary notes. Nothing else is recorded about him, and no descendants are listed for him. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of his name as "building" or "understanding."

Bunni was a Levite in the time of Nehemiah. He was one of eight Levites, listed with Jeshua, Bani, Kadmiel, Shebaniah, Sherebiah, a second Bani and Chenani, who stood on the stairs and cried out loudly to the LORD during the public gathering of fasting and confession after the return from exile (Neh 9:4). By inference from the surrounding chapter, these Levites led the people in prayer and confession of sin, and STEPBible Proper Names describes him in this way. Smith's Bible Dictionary identifies him simply as one of the Levites of Nehemiah's day. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "building me." The name Bunni belongs to more than one person in the Bible, and this entry covers only the Levite of Neh 9:4. Nothing more is recorded about his family or later life.

Bunni was one of the leaders of the people who set their seal to the written covenant made in Nehemiah's time, when the community in Jerusalem pledged to keep the law. He appears only in the list of signatories, between Bani and Azgad (Neh 10:15), and nothing else is told about him. Several of the names around his, such as Azgad and Bebai, also appear as family names among those who returned from exile (Ezra 2). So "Bunni" here may stand for a family or clan head rather than a single individual, though this is an inference. The name is also borne by Levites mentioned elsewhere in Nehemiah, and it is uncertain whether any of them is the same man. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "building me."

Bunni was a Levite named as an ancestor of Shemaiah, one of the Levites living in Jerusalem after the return from exile. The genealogy in Neh 11:15 traces Shemaiah back through Hashub, Azrikam and Hashabiah to Bunni, making Bunni Hashabiah's father and Shemaiah's great-great-grandfather. Because he stands several generations back in that line, he probably lived well before Nehemiah's day, as Smith's Bible Dictionary notes. Nothing else is recorded about him. The parallel list in 1 Chr 9:14 has "of the sons of Merari" where Nehemiah has "the son of Bunni," and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia takes the two readings as variants of the same text. This entry follows the wording of Nehemiah. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "building me." Several other men in the Bible share the name, so he should not be confused with them.

Buz was the second son of Nahor, Abraham's brother, and his wife Milcah. He is named in the list of Nahor's children reported to Abraham after the binding of Isaac, where he follows his elder brother Huz, the firstborn, and comes before Kemuel. Among his brothers was Bethuel, the father of Rebekah. Nahor also had sons by his concubine Reumah. Buz is probably the ancestor of the Buzites. Elihu, who speaks in the book of Job, is called "the Buzite" (Job 32:2), and both Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary take him to be a descendant of Buz. The name, which Hitchcock's Bible Names renders as "despised" or "plundered," is also borne by another man in the genealogies of Gad. A people or region called Buz appears in Jer 25:23 as well.

Buz was a man of the tribe of Gad, named only once, at the very end of a family line in 1 Chr 5:14. He was the father of Jahdo and the most distant ancestor listed for Abihail, whose descendants are traced back through Huri, Jaroah, Gilead, Michael, Jeshishai and Jahdo to Buz. The surrounding chapter places these Gadites in the region of Bashan and Gilead east of the Jordan, so his family probably belonged there. Easton's Bible Dictionary calls him one of the chiefs of the tribe of Gad. Nothing else is recorded about his life. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "despised" or "plundered." The same name belongs to other figures in the Bible, notably a son of Abraham's brother Nahor, and this Gadite should not be confused with them.

Buzi was the father of the prophet Ezekiel and is known only from Ezek 1:3. There Ezekiel is introduced as "the priest, the son of Buzi" when the word of the Lord came to him in the land of the Chaldeans by the river Chebar. Because Israel's priesthood passed from father to son, Buzi was probably himself of a priestly family, and STEPBible's proper-names index describes him as a priest. The verse says nothing else about him, including whether he lived to see the exile in Babylonia that his son shared. Smith's Bible Dictionary and Hitchcock's Bible Names give the meaning of his name as "contempt" or "my contempt."

Cainan (son of Arphaxad) appears in Luke's genealogy of Jesus as the son of Arphaxad and the father of Salah, placing him three generations after Noah through Shem (Luke 3:36). Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that he is not named anywhere in the Old Testament and that he is usually called the "second Cainan," which distinguishes him from the earlier Cainan son of Enos listed in the next verse of Luke's line. In the Hebrew text of Genesis 11:12, Arphaxad is the father of Salah directly, with no Cainan between them. Cainan does appear at that point in the Greek Septuagint translation of Genesis, which is probably where Luke's list draws the name from. Nothing else is recorded about his life. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "possessor" or "purchaser."

Calcol was a man of the tribe of Judah, listed in 1 Chr 2:6 as one of the five sons of Zerah, alongside Zimri, Ethan, Heman and Dara. Since Zerah was a son of Judah by Tamar (1 Chr 2:4), Calcol was a grandson of Judah. Zimri is probably the same man called Zabdi in Josh 7:1, which is why Zabdi appears among his brothers. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary both take Calcol to be probably the same person as Chalcol in 1 Kgs 4:31, one of the famous wise men, together with Ethan, Heman and Darda, whom Solomon surpassed in wisdom. That passage calls them sons of Mahol, so the identification is likely but not certain. The name is explained as meaning "sustenance" (Easton's, Smith's) or "nourishing" (Hitchcock's Bible Names). Nothing else is recorded about him.

Candace was the queen of the Ethiopians mentioned in Acts 8:27. Her treasurer, a eunuch of great authority who had charge of all her treasure, had gone to Jerusalem to worship. On his way home he met Philip, who baptized him, in an event dated here to about AD 32 by inference from context. Candace herself does not appear in the story and is named only as his ruler. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia explain that Candace was not a personal name but a title held by a line of Ethiopian queens, much like "Pharaoh" or "Caesar." The Roman writer Pliny is cited for this. Easton's Bible Dictionary places her kingdom at Meroe in Upper Nubia, in present-day Sudan, a wealthy center of trade. Easton's also records a tradition that her treasurer converted her on his return, though Acts says nothing of this.

Carcas was the seventh of seven chamberlains who served in the presence of the Persian king Ahasuerus. On the seventh day of a royal feast, when the king was merry with wine, he ordered these chamberlains to bring Queen Vashti before him wearing her crown so that he could display her beauty (Esth 1:10). The Hebrew word for chamberlain usually means a eunuch, and Smith's Bible Dictionary describes the seven as eunuchs. Nothing else is recorded about Carcas. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "severe," while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "the covering of a lamb." The name is probably Persian in origin, so its meaning is uncertain.

Carchemish is named in 2 Chr 35:20 as the target of a campaign by Necho king of Egypt, who "came up to fight against Carchemish by Euphrates." King Josiah of Judah went out to oppose Necho on his march, after he had finished restoring the temple. The KJV wording "fight against Carchemish" can be read as naming an opponent, and this entry treats the name as a person. Elsewhere in the Bible, however, Carchemish is a city on the Euphrates (Isa 10:9; Jer 46:2), and most readers take the name here as that city. Jeremiah links it with Necho's army and its defeat by Nebuchadnezzar. The city is generally identified with the ruins near modern Jerablus on the Turkey–Syria border. Nothing else is said about Carchemish as an individual.

Carshena was the first named of the seven princes of Persia and Media at the court of King Ahasuerus (Esth 1:14). These men "saw the king's face", meaning they had direct access to him, and they held the highest rank in the kingdom. From the surrounding passage, they were the advisers the king consulted when Queen Vashti refused to appear at his feast. Their spokesman in that episode was Memucan, and nothing further is recorded about Carshena himself. The name is probably Persian. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives its meaning as "illustrious", while Hitchcock's Bible Names offers "a lamb" or "sleeping".

Chalcol was one of four men famous for wisdom in the days of Solomon. 1 Kgs 4:31 says Solomon was wiser than all of them: Ethan the Ezrahite, Heman, Chalcol and Darda, called "the sons of Mahol." Nothing else is said about him there, and his comparison with Solomon is his only role in the passage. The name is also spelled Calcol. The same group of names (Zimri, Ethan, Heman, Calcol and Dara) appears in 1 Chr 2:6 as sons of Zerah of the tribe of Judah, so Chalcol is probably the same man. If so, "sons of Mahol" may name a family line or guild rather than a literal father. This entry follows the verse in Kings and treats Mahol as his father, with Darda, Ethan and Heman as his brothers. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "who nourishes, consumes, and sustains the whole."

Chelal was one of the descendants of Pahath-moab listed among the Israelites who had married foreign wives in the time of Ezra. He is named only once, in Ezra 10:30, in the list of men who agreed to put away these wives after Ezra's call for the community to separate from the surrounding peoples. Pahath-moab was a family group that had returned from exile in Babylon, and Chelal appears alongside seven other members of that clan. Nothing else is recorded about him. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia give the meaning of his name as "perfection," while Hitchcock's Bible Names renders it "as night."

Chelluh was one of the Israelite men listed in Ezra 10:35 as having married a foreign wife. By inference from the surrounding passage, he belonged to the group called the sons of Bani (Ezra 10:34). The list records those who agreed, under Ezra's reforms after the return from exile in Babylon, to send away the foreign wives they had married. Nothing else is known about him. Some versions and reference works give his name as Cheluhi, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia lists him under that form. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "completed," while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "all."

Chelub was a man of the tribe of Judah, named only in the genealogy at 1 Chr 4:11, which calls him the brother of Shuah and the father of Mehir, whose son was Eshton. He is linked here with Rechah as his ancestor, probably because the next verse ends this short family list with "these are the men of Rechah" (1 Chr 4:12). The name may be a variant form of Caleb. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that some scholars have read the verse as referring to Caleb son of Hezron, and the STEPBible proper-names index treats Chelub as a brother of Caleb and a son of Hezron. This entry follows the link to Rechah. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning "a basket." He should not be confused with another Chelub, the father of Ezri, who appears later in Chronicles. Nothing further is recorded about him.

Chelub was the father of Ezri, the officer whom King David put in charge of the farm laborers who worked the royal fields (1 Chr 27:26). He is named only to identify his son in a list of the officials who managed David's property, and nothing else is recorded about him. The name is shared by other people in the Bible, including a man of Judah in the genealogy of 1 Chr 4:11, who is probably a different person. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "a basket."

Chenaanah was a member of the tribe of Benjamin, listed fourth among the seven children of Bilhan, son of Jediael, in the Benjamite genealogy of 1 Chr 7:10. The verse names them as Jeush, Benjamin, Ehud, Chenaanah, Zethan, Tharshish and Ahishahar. The next verse (1 Chr 7:11) describes this family as heads of their fathers' houses and mighty warriors, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia places them in the time of David. Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests the family probably belonged to the clan of Bela. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia explains the name as a feminine form of "Canaan," noting that others read it as "toward Canaan." Nothing else is recorded about this person. The name is shared with others in the Bible, including the father of the prophet Zedekiah in the reign of Ahab (1 Kgs 22:11).

Chenani was a Levite named only in Neh 9:4. He was one of eight Levites who stood on the stairs, probably a raised platform, and cried out loudly to the Lord at the assembly where the returned exiles gathered to fast, confess their sins and renew their commitment to God in Nehemiah's time. The others were Jeshua, Bani, Kadmiel, Shebaniah, Bunni, Sherebiah and a second Bani. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives the name's meaning as "planted", while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "my pillar". The same encyclopedia notes that these names may stand either for individual men or for Levitical families. If they were families, they probably sang a well-known psalm. If they were individuals, they probably led the people in a special prayer. Nothing else is recorded about him.

Chenaniah was a Levite of the Izharite clan, descended from Izhar son of Kohath. In David's organization of the Levites, he and his sons were assigned to "the outward business over Israel," serving as officers and judges (1 Chr 26:29). By inference from the context, this meant duties away from the temple service itself, probably administrative and judicial work among the people. The name is shared with another Levite, Chenaniah, who led the singing when the ark was brought to Jerusalem (1 Chr 15:22, 27). Some readers identify the two as the same man, but the text does not say so, and this entry treats the Izharite on his own. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the name's meaning as "preparation," "disposition," or "strength of the Lord."

Chesed was a son of Nahor, Abraham's brother, and his wife Milcah. He appears only once, in the list of Nahor's eight sons by Milcah that was reported to Abraham after the near-sacrifice of Isaac (Gen 22:22). His brothers were Huz, Buz, Kemuel, Hazo, Pildash, Jidlaph and Bethuel, the father of Rebekah. Nahor also had sons and a daughter by his concubine Reumah. Smith's Bible Dictionary counts Chesed as the fourth son and gives the name's meaning as "increase," while Easton's Bible Dictionary renders it "gain." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia links the name with the Hebrew Kasdim, the people known in English Bibles as the Chaldeans, and suggests Chesed was probably their ancestor. The Bible says nothing further about his life.

Chislon was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, known only as the father of Elidad. In Num 34:21, Elidad is named as Benjamin's representative among the tribal leaders chosen to help divide the land of Canaan among the tribes once Israel entered it. Nothing else is recorded about Chislon himself. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia describes him as a prince of Benjamin, though the verse gives that role to his son. The name is usually understood to mean "strength" or "confidence". Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "hope, trust". Smith's Bible Dictionary dates the setting to about 1450 BC. Any such date is an estimate inferred from context rather than stated in the text.

Chloe was a woman mentioned only in 1 Cor 1:11, where Paul says that people "of the house of Chloe" had told him about quarrels and divisions among the believers at Corinth. The phrase probably refers to members of her household, such as family members, servants or slaves, who had traveled between Corinth and Paul, who was likely writing from Ephesus. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests she lived in either Corinth or Ephesus and that the messengers were probably Christian slaves. Whether Chloe herself was a believer is not stated, though it is commonly presumed. Her name means "green herb" or "tender shoot." Nothing else is known about her.

Chuza was the steward of Herod, the official who managed the ruler's household and property, and the husband of Joanna. He is mentioned only once, in Luke 8:3, where Joanna appears among the women who traveled with Jesus and supported him from their own means. The Herod meant is probably Herod Antipas, tetrarch of Galilee, who ruled there during Jesus' ministry; Smith's Bible Dictionary identifies Chuza as his house-steward. The text says nothing more about Chuza himself. It does not say whether he shared his wife's support for Jesus. Joanna is named again in Luke 24:10 among the women at the empty tomb, which suggests her continued involvement, but Chuza does not appear there. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of his name as "the seer" or "prophet."

Claudia was a Christian woman who, together with Eubulus, Pudens, Linus and "all the brethren," sent greetings to Timothy at the close of Paul's second letter to him (2 Tim 4:21). Because Paul appears to be writing from Rome, she was probably a member of the church there. Nothing more is known about her for certain. Later tradition adds details. The Apostolical Constitutions name her as the mother of Linus, whom Irenaeus and Eusebius list as a bishop of Rome. Easton's Bible Dictionary mentions a conjecture that she was the wife of Pudens and a British princess, the daughter of King Cogidubnus. That theory rests on an epigram by the poet Martial about a couple named Claudia and Pudens. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that these identifications rest on very little evidence. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "lame."

Claudius Lysias was the Roman commander of the garrison in Jerusalem who sent Paul under guard to the governor Felix at Caesarea, with a letter that opens with his own name and greeting (Acts 23:26). The surrounding chapters, where he appears as the "chief captain", say he rescued Paul from a mob at the temple, bound him and questioned him. He let Paul speak to the crowd and stopped short of having him scourged once he learned Paul was a Roman citizen (Acts 21:31–40; 22:24–29). After a stormy session of the Sanhedrin and news of a plot against Paul's life, he sent him to Felix, by inference about AD 56. In Acts 22:28 the commander says he bought his citizenship. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both take him to be a Greek who adopted the Roman name Claudius when he became a citizen.

Clement was a Christian whom Paul names in Phil 4:3 as one of his fellow workers in spreading the gospel, whose names, Paul says, are in the book of life. He is mentioned alongside women who had worked with Paul, and Paul asks his "true yokefellow" to help them. Since the letter was written to the church at Philippi, he was probably a member of that congregation, as Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries take him to be. The name means "mild" or "merciful." Ancient church writers such as Origen and Eusebius identified him with Clement, later bishop of Rome and author of a letter to the Corinthians. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the name was common and that this identification can be neither proved nor disproved. This entry treats him simply as Paul's coworker at Philippi.

Col-hozeh was the father of Shallun, who repaired the Fountain Gate of Jerusalem in Nehemiah's time. Shallun rebuilt and roofed the gate, set up its doors, locks and bars, and repaired the wall of the pool of Siloah by the king's garden as far as the stairs down from the City of David (Neh 3:15). The title "ruler of part of Mizpah" most naturally belongs to Shallun, though the wording could also be read as describing Col-hozeh. Nothing else is recorded about this man. The same name appears in Neh 11:5 for an ancestor of Maaseiah of the tribe of Judah, and it is unclear whether these are the same person. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "every prophet."

Col-hozeh was the son of Hazaiah and the father of Baruch. He appears only in the family line of Maaseiah, his grandson, who was one of the people living in Jerusalem in Nehemiah's time after the return from exile (Neh 11:5). By inference from the surrounding passage, this family belonged to the tribe of Judah and traced its descent back through Joiarib and Zechariah to Shiloni. Nothing else is recorded about him. The same name belongs to the father of Shallun, who repaired the Fountain Gate (Neh 3:15). Whether the two are the same man is uncertain, and this entry treats Col-hozeh of Neh 11:5 on his own. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "every prophet."

Conaniah was one of the chief Levites during the reign of King Josiah of Judah. According to 2 Chr 35:9, he and his brothers Shemaiah and Nethaneel, along with Hashabiah, Jeiel and Jozabad, gave the Levites 5,000 sheep and goats and 500 oxen for the Passover offerings. This was the large Passover that Josiah held in Jerusalem, which the surrounding chapter places in Josiah's eighteenth year. His name is usually explained as meaning "the Lord has established." A Levite with a very similar name, spelled Cononiah in the King James Version, was put in charge of the tithes and offerings in Hezekiah's time (2 Chr 31:12). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats the two as separate men. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes Conaniah as a Levite placed over the tithes brought into the temple. Nothing else is recorded about him.

Concubine the Aramitess is an unnamed woman mentioned once, in the genealogy of Manasseh in 1 Chr 7:14. She was a concubine, probably of Manasseh, the son of Joseph, since the verse lists the sons of Manasseh and then refers to "his concubine." She is called an Aramitess, meaning a woman from Aram, the region of the Arameans (Syria). She was the mother of Machir, who is described as the father of Gilead. Other passages, such as Num 26:29 and Gen 50:23, name Machir as Manasseh's son, which supports the inference that Manasseh was her partner. The wording of the verse is difficult. It says Ashriel was born to an unnamed "she" and then sets the Aramitess apart as Machir's mother, so the relationship between the two women, and between the two sons, is uncertain. Nothing else is recorded about her.

Cosam was a man named only in Luke's genealogy of Jesus, where he appears as the son of Elmodam and the father of Addi (Luke 3:28). Luke traces this line backward from Jesus through Joseph, and Smith's Bible Dictionary places Cosam in the line of Joseph the husband of Mary. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that he stands five generations before Zerubbabel. By inference from the order of the list, he probably lived in the period of the kings of Judah, before the Babylonian exile, as a descendant of David through Nathan rather than through the royal line of Solomon. Nothing else is recorded about him. Hitchcock's Bible Names and Smith's Bible Dictionary give the meaning of his name as "divining" or "a diviner."
