Coz was a man of the tribe of Judah who is named only in 1 Chr 4:8, where he is the father of Anub and Zobebah and is linked to the families of Aharhel son of Harum. The verse does not state who his parents were. Because it directly follows the list of Helah's sons by Ashhur (1 Chr 4:5–7), he is probably a son of Ashhur and Helah. That would make Zereth, Jezoar and Ethnan his brothers, and Ashhur's sons by his other wife, Naarah, his half-brothers. This entry treats Harum as his son, by inference from the same verse. The name means "thorn" (Hitchcock's Bible Names). The Revised Version renders it "Hakkoz" (Easton's Bible Dictionary). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia distinguishes him from the priestly family of Hakkoz mentioned in 1 Chr 24:10 and Ezra 2:61.

Crescens was a companion and coworker of Paul, mentioned only once in the Bible. In 2 Tim 4:10, Paul, writing during his imprisonment, says that Crescens had gone to Galatia, a region in central Asia Minor, at the same time that Titus had gone to Dalmatia and Demas had left for Thessalonica. Unlike Demas, Crescens is not said to have deserted Paul, so he probably went to Galatia on church work, by inference from the context. His Latin name means "growing" or "increasing." Easton's Bible Dictionary suggests he was probably a Christian from Rome. Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionary both note a tradition that he was one of the seventy disciples sent out by Jesus. A later church tradition also links him with founding a church at Vienne in Gaul. Nothing more about him is recorded in the Bible.

Cushi was the father of Shelemiah and the great-grandfather of Jehudi, the man the princes of Judah sent to bring Baruch and the scroll of Jeremiah's prophecies he had read to the people (Jer 36:14). He is known only from this genealogy. His lifetime would have been about three generations before Jeremiah's, by inference from the line of descent. The name means "a Cushite." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that with the article it marks a person of Cushite origin, as with the messenger in 2 Sam 18, and that it later came to be used as a personal name. The same name belongs to other people in the Bible, including the father of the prophet Zephaniah, and they should not be confused with this man.

Cushi was the father of the prophet Zephaniah and the son of Gedaliah. He is named only in the opening line of the book of Zephaniah, which traces the prophet's ancestry back four generations through Cushi, Gedaliah and Amariah to Hizkiah (Zeph 1:1). Since Zephaniah prophesied in the days of Josiah king of Judah, Cushi probably lived in Judah in the generation before, around the reigns of Manasseh and Amon, by inference from the passage. Nothing else is recorded about him. The name Cushi is shared by several people in the Bible. Among them are the messenger who brought news of Absalom's death to David and an ancestor of Jehudi in the time of Jeremiah. This entry concerns only Zephaniah's father.

Cyrenius was the Roman governor of Syria when the census or registration took place that brought Joseph and Mary to Bethlehem around the time of Jesus' birth (Luke 2:2). Cyrenius is the King James spelling of the Greek form of the Latin name Quirinius, and Smith's Bible Dictionary and Easton's Bible Dictionary give his full name as Publius Sulpicius Quirinius. According to Smith's, he was a Roman consul and became governor of Syria in AD 6, after Archelaus was removed. How his governorship fits the date of Jesus' birth has long been discussed. Smith's suggests he served twice as governor, first around 4–1 BC. Easton's proposes that he governed Cilicia, then joined to Syria, before later serving as governor of Syria itself. Smith's connects a later census to the one mentioned in Acts 5:37.

Dalaiah was a man of the tribe of Judah, one of the seven sons of Elioenai, and so a member of the royal line of David. He appears only in the genealogy of David's descendants in 1 Chr 3:24. He is the sixth son listed, after Hodaiah, Eliashib, Pelaiah, Akkub and Johanan, and before Anani. The surrounding genealogy traces this family through Jeconiah (Jehoiachin) and Zerubbabel, which places Dalaiah several generations after the Babylonian exile. Nothing else is recorded about him. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him as a descendant of the royal family of Judah and gives the meaning of his name as "freed by Jehovah." Hitchcock's Bible Names renders it "the poor of the Lord." The name is often spelled Delaiah, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats it under that form.

Dalphon was the second of the ten sons of Haman, the Persian official who plotted to destroy the Jews in the reign of King Ahasuerus. He is named only in Esth 9:7, in the list of Haman's sons killed by the Jews in the fortress city of Shushan when the day set for their destruction was turned against their enemies. The surrounding verses go on to describe the bodies of the ten sons being hanged at Esther's request (Esth 9:13–14). His name's meaning is uncertain. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "swift", the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives "crafty", and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "the house of caves". Nothing else is recorded about him.

Damaris was a woman of Athens who believed Paul's message after he spoke at the Areopagus, about AD 48 by inference from context. Acts 17:34 names her alongside Dionysius the Areopagite as among those who joined Paul and believed, while others mocked or put off hearing more. Nothing else is recorded about her. That she is one of only two converts named may suggest she was a woman of some standing, as the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes, comparing the prominent Greek women who believed at Berea. Chrysostom and others, as Smith's Bible Dictionary reports, held that she was the wife of Dionysius, though the verse itself does not say so. Her name is often explained as meaning "heifer" (Easton's Bible Dictionary), perhaps from a related Greek word, while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "a little woman."

Dara was one of the five sons of Zerah in the tribe of Judah, named with his brothers Zimri, Ethan, Heman and Calcol (1 Chr 2:6). Zerah was a son of Judah and Tamar (1 Chr 2:4), so Dara was Judah's grandson. The brother called Zimri here is probably the same man as the Zabdi named as Zerah's son in Josh 7:1. Dara appears only in this genealogy, and nothing else is recorded about him. Because the names Ethan, Heman and Calcol also appear in 1 Kgs 4:31 alongside a Darda, among the wise men whom Solomon surpassed, many readers take Dara and Darda to be the same person. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that Darda is called a son of Mahol there, which leaves the link uncertain. It gives the meaning of Darda as "pearl of wisdom."

Darda was a wise man named, with his brothers Heman and Chalcol and with Ethan the Ezrahite, as a standard against which Solomon's wisdom is measured. 1 Kgs 4:31 calls them "the sons of Mahol" and says Solomon was wiser than all of them. The verse records nothing else about him. The similar list in 1 Chr 2:6, where the name appears as Dara, places him among the sons of Zerah, son of Judah. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes both lines of descent. "Sons of Mahol" may name his father, which is the reading this entry follows. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "pearl of wisdom," and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "home of knowledge." Rabbinic tradition read the name as "the generation of knowledge," taken to mean the wilderness generation.

Darius, called "Darius the Persian," was a king of Persia named in Neh 12:22 as the limit of a record. The Levite heads of families, and also the priests, were registered in the days of the high priests Eliashib, Joiada, Johanan and Jaddua, up to his reign. Nothing else is said about him in this passage. Because several Persian kings bore the name Darius, which one is meant is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary both identify him most likely as Darius II (Ochus or Nothus), son of Artaxerxes Longimanus, who reigned about 424–405 BC. Both also mention the view that he was Darius III (Codomannus), the last Persian king, who was defeated by Alexander the Great about 336–330 BC. This entry follows the Darius II identification as the more probable one. He should not be confused with Darius the Mede or with the other kings of this name.

Daughter of Machir is an unnamed woman mentioned once in the genealogy of Judah. Her father Machir was the son of Manasseh, so she belonged to the Joseph tribes. She was the sister of Gilead, and other passages in 1 Chronicles name Peresh, Sheresh and Hammoleketh among Machir's children. According to 1 Chr 2:21, Hezron, a grandson of Judah, married her when he was sixty years old, and she bore him a son, Segub. The next verse says Segub was the father of Jair, who held towns in Gilead. Her marriage linked a line of Judah with Manasseh's territory east of the Jordan. Her own name is not recorded.

Daughter of Meshullam is an unnamed woman mentioned only in Neh 6:18. She was the daughter of Meshullam son of Berechiah and married Johanan, the son of Tobiah. From the surrounding passage (Neh 6:17), this Tobiah is Tobiah the Ammonite, one of Nehemiah's main opponents during the rebuilding of Jerusalem's walls. The verse explains that many in Judah were bound by oath to Tobiah because of family ties. He was the son-in-law of Shechaniah son of Arah, and his son had married this woman. Her father is probably the same Meshullam son of Berechiah who repaired sections of the wall in Neh 3:4 and 3:30, so her marriage linked a family active in the rebuilding with Nehemiah's adversary. Nothing else is recorded about her.

Daughter of Putiel is the unnamed woman described in Exod 6:25 as "one of the daughters of Putiel." She married Eleazar, the son of Aaron, and bore him a son, Phinehas. The verse appears in a genealogy of the Levites that lists the heads of their ancestral families. Nothing else is recorded about her, and the Bible gives neither her own name nor any further details about her father Putiel. Her son Phinehas went on to become a prominent priest in later passages such as Num 25:7–13, where he is promised a lasting priesthood.

Debir was the king of Eglon, one of five Amorite kings in southern Canaan. Adonizedek king of Jerusalem summoned him, along with the kings of Hebron, Jarmuth and Lachish, to join an alliance against Gibeon after Gibeon made peace with Joshua and Israel (Josh 10:3). Later in the same chapter the alliance is defeated at Gibeon. The five kings flee and hide in a cave at Makkedah, where they are shut in until Joshua returns from pursuing their armies. He then puts them to death and hangs them on five trees (Josh 10:16–26), as Easton's Bible Dictionary summarizes. Debir is named only in Josh 10:3. The other kings are named again later in the chapter, but he is referred to there only as the king of Eglon. His name is the same as that of the Canaanite town of Debir, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives its meaning as "oracle."

Deborah was the nurse of Rebekah, the wife of Isaac. She is named only at her death, recorded while Jacob and his household were at Bethel. She was buried below Bethel under an oak, and the tree was then called Allonbachuth, meaning "oak of weeping" (Gen 35:8). Smith's Bible Dictionary identifies her with the unnamed nurse who left the house of Bethuel with Rebekah when she went to marry Isaac (Gen 24:59). If so, she had served the family for many years and, by inference, was living with Jacob's household in her old age. Her name is usually understood to mean "bee." She is distinct from Deborah the prophet and judge of Israel in the book of Judges, who shares the name.

Dekar was the father of one of King Solomon's twelve district officers, who is known only as "the son of Dekar" (Hebrew Ben-deker). Nothing is said about Dekar himself, and his son's own name is not given. According to 1 Kgs 4:9, the son of Dekar was responsible for the district that included Makaz, Shaalbim, Beth-shemesh and Elon-beth-hanan. Smith's Bible Dictionary places this district in the western part of the hill country of Judah and Benjamin. From the surrounding passage, each of these officers supplied food for the king and his household for one month of the year. The name is usually linked to a Hebrew root meaning "to pierce". On that basis Smith's Bible Dictionary renders it "a lancer", while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "force".

Delaiah was a priest in the time of David who headed the twenty-third of the twenty-four divisions into which the priests were organized. The divisions were assigned by lot to take turns serving at the sanctuary, and the twenty-third turn fell to Delaiah (1 Chr 24:18). Nothing else is recorded about him. The name is usually explained as meaning "the Lord has drawn up" or "raised," though Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "freed by Jehovah" and Hitchcock's Bible Names "the poor of the Lord." Several other men in the Bible share the name, and this priest should not be confused with them.

Delaiah was the son of Mehetabeel and the father of Shemaiah. He is mentioned only once, in Neh 6:10, as part of his son's lineage. There Nehemiah describes visiting Shemaiah, who was "shut up" in his house and urged Nehemiah to hide inside the temple because enemies were coming to kill him at night. The following verses of the same chapter say that Tobiah and Sanballat had hired Shemaiah to frighten Nehemiah. Nothing is recorded about Delaiah himself, so he probably lived in Jerusalem in the generation before Nehemiah's time. Several other people in the Bible share his name. Reference works explain the name differently: Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "freed by Jehovah," the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives "God has raised," and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "the poor of the Lord."

Diblaim was the father of Gomer, the woman the prophet Hosea married (Hos 1:3). He is named only in that verse, where Gomer is called "the daughter of Diblaim," and nothing else is recorded about him. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia describes him as a native of northern Israel, where Hosea worked, and the STEPBible proper names index also treats him as Gomer's father. Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries instead take Diblaim to be Gomer's mother. This entry follows the view that Diblaim was her father. The name is generally understood to mean "two cakes," probably pressed cakes of figs. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning "cluster of figs."

Dibri was a man of the tribe of Dan, named only as the father of Shelomith. He appears in Lev 24:11, where his daughter is identified as the mother of a man who blasphemed the name of the LORD during the wilderness period and was brought to Moses. The surrounding passage says this grandson's father was an Egyptian, and that the man was stoned outside the camp as punishment. Dibri himself plays no part in the account. He is mentioned only to identify the family and tribe of the offender's mother. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia tentatively gives the meaning of his name as "eloquent," and Hitchcock's Bible Names renders it "an orator."

Dionysius was an Athenian who believed Paul's message when Paul preached in Athens, probably around AD 48 by inference from context. Acts 17:34 names him first among the few who joined Paul, together with a woman named Damaris and others. He is called "the Areopagite," which most likely means he belonged to the Areopagus, the city's council that met on Mars Hill, where Paul had just given his speech earlier in the same chapter. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him as an eminent Athenian and explains the name as meaning "devoted to Dionysus," the Greek god of wine. Scripture says nothing more about him. Church tradition, noted in Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia, holds that he became the first bishop of Athens. Other traditions say he was martyred, and one links him with Saint Denis of Paris. A set of mystical writings was later circulated under his name, and Smith's dates these to the sixth century.

Diotrephes was a member of a church addressed in the letter of 3 John. The writer says that Diotrephes "loves to have the preeminence" among the believers there and refuses to receive the writer and his companions (3 John 1:9). The following verse, 3 John 1:10, adds that he spoke against the writer with malicious words, refused to welcome traveling fellow believers, stopped others who wanted to welcome them, and put them out of the church. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests that his love of preeminence may mean he held some office in the church and was misusing it. Nothing else is known of him. His Greek name means "nourished by Zeus" (Smith's Bible Dictionary), or "nourished by Jupiter" in Hitchcock's Bible Names.

Dodavah was a man of Mareshah, a town in Judah, known only as the father of the prophet Eliezer. Eliezer prophesied against King Jehoshaphat of Judah for allying himself with Ahaziah king of Israel, announcing that the LORD had broken his works. As a result, the ships the two kings had built were wrecked and never sailed to Tarshish (2 Chr 20:37). The verse does not make clear whether "of Mareshah" refers to Dodavah or to his son, but it is usually taken as the family's hometown. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes Dodavah as a man of Maresha in Judah and gives the meaning of his name as "love of the Lord." Hitchcock's Bible Names gives simply "love." Nothing else is recorded about him.

Dodo was a man of the tribe of Issachar, the father of Puah and the grandfather of Tola. Tola arose after Abimelech to defend Israel as one of its judges and lived at Shamir in the hill country of Ephraim (Judg 10:1). Dodo appears only in this genealogical note, and nothing else is recorded about him. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes him simply as a descendant of Issachar. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "his uncle." Several other men in the Bible share this name, including fathers of warriors in David's army. This Dodo should be kept distinct from them.

Drusilla was the Jewish wife of Felix, the Roman governor of Judea. Acts 24:24 records that some days after Paul's hearing before Felix at Caesarea, Felix came with Drusilla, sent for Paul, and heard him speak about faith in Christ. By inference from context, this happened during Paul's custody there, about AD 56. The Bible says nothing more about her. Drawing on the Jewish historian Josephus, Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identify her as the youngest daughter of Herod Agrippa I, the king of Acts 12, and a sister of Bernice. They say she was first married to Azizus, king of Emesa, and that Felix persuaded her to leave him. Smith's Bible Dictionary adds that he did this through a Cypriot sorcerer named Simon. Easton's states that she and her son died in the eruption of Mount Vesuvius in AD 79. Her name is traditionally explained as meaning "watered by the dew."

Ebed, son of Jonathan, was one of the family heads who came back from Babylon to Jerusalem with Ezra. He belonged to the descendants of Adin and brought fifty males of his family with him (Ezra 8:6). The name means "servant," according to Smith's Bible Dictionary and Hitchcock's Bible Names. Smith's notes that many manuscripts read the name as Eber. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identifies him with Obeth in the parallel list of 1 Esdras 8:32, in the Apocrypha. Another Ebed, the father of Gaal in the book of Judges, is a different man who shares the name. Nothing more is recorded about this Ebed beyond his place in Ezra's list of returning exiles.

Eber (a Benjamite) was a son of Elpaal, from the tribe of Benjamin. He appears only once, in the Benjamite genealogy at 1 Chr 8:12, where he is named first among Elpaal's sons, followed by Misham and Shamed. Easton's Bible Dictionary calls him the oldest of the three. The same verse says the towns of Ono and Lod were built. The wording leaves it open whether Shamed alone built them or the brothers together did. Later in the chapter (1 Chr 8:17–18), more men are listed as sons of Elpaal, including Zebadiah, Meshullam, Hezeki, Heber, Ishmerai, Jezliah and Jobab. Earlier verses in the chapter trace Elpaal back to Shaharaim and his wife Hushim. This Eber is separate from the Benjamite Eber listed among the sons of Shashak (1 Chr 8:22), and from the ancestor Eber in Genesis. Nothing else is recorded about him.

Eber (Amok Family Head) was a priest who led the priestly family of Amok after the return from exile in Babylon. He is named once, in a list of priestly family heads (Neh 12:20). The surrounding passage places this list in the days of the high priest Joiakim, son of Jeshua (Neh 12:12), which would make Eber's generation the one after the first returnees. Amok himself appears earlier in the same chapter among the priests who came back with Zerubbabel (Neh 12:7). Easton's Bible Dictionary connects Eber with the time of Zerubbabel. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates him to about 445 BC. Nothing more is recorded about him. He is different from the better-known Eber of Genesis, the ancestor of Abraham, and from several other men of the same name.

Eden was a Levite of the Gershonite clan, the son of Joah son of Zimmah. He is named among the Levites who rose up at King Hezekiah's call to cleanse the temple in Jerusalem and restore its worship after it had been neglected (2 Chr 29:12). The verse lists two Levites from each of the three Levite clans, Kohath, Merari and Gershon, and Eden and his father represent the Gershonites. An Eden also appears in 2 Chr 31:15 among the Levites who helped distribute the temple offerings to the priestly cities under Hezekiah. That may well be the same man, but the text does not say so. The name is shared by several people and is distinct from the garden of Eden. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives its meaning as "pleasure" or "delight."

Eden was a Levite in the reign of King Hezekiah of Judah. He was one of six men who served 'next' to Kore, the Levite placed over the freewill offerings (by inference from the preceding verse, 2 Chr 31:14). Working in the cities of the priests, these men handed out the tithes, contributions and dedicated gifts to their fellow priests and Levites according to their divisions, giving fairly to old and young alike. STEPBible Proper Names describes him as one of the Levites Hezekiah appointed to this task. A Gershonite Levite named Eden, son of Joah, also appears among those who cleansed the temple at the start of Hezekiah's reign (2 Chr 29:12). He may be the same man, but the text does not say so. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as 'pleasure' or 'delight.'

Ehud was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, one of the seven sons of Bilhan, listed in the Benjamite genealogy of 1 Chr 7:10. His brothers were Jeush, Benjamin, Chenaanah, Zethan, Tharshish and Ahishahar. Bilhan was a son of Jediael, who in the surrounding verses is a son of Benjamin, so Easton's Bible Dictionary describes this Ehud as Benjamin's great-grandson. Nothing else is recorded about him. He is a different person from the better-known Ehud son of Gera, the left-handed Benjamite judge who killed Eglon king of Moab. Whether the Ehud named in a later Benjamite list in 1 Chronicles 8 is the same man is uncertain. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "he that praises."

Eker was a man of the tribe of Judah, named once in the genealogies of 1 Chronicles. He was one of three sons of Ram, listed after his brothers Maaz and Jamin (1 Chr 2:27). His father Ram was the firstborn of Jerahmeel, which places Eker among the Jerahmeelites, as the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes. Jerahmeel was a son of Hezron and a grandson of Perez, son of Judah (1 Chr 2:9). Nothing else is recorded about Eker. Smith's Bible Dictionary takes his name to mean "a rooting up," and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives "root." Hitchcock's Bible Names offers "barren, feeble."

Eladah was a descendant of Ephraim, son of Joseph, named once in the Ephraimite genealogy of 1 Chr 7:20. The line runs Ephraim, Shuthelah, Bered, Tahath, Eladah, Tahath, which makes Eladah the son of one Tahath and the father of another. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia spells the name Eleadah. The STEPBible proper-names index describes him as a son of Ephraim, meaning a descendant rather than an immediate son, and as an ancestor of Joshua. That link follows from the same genealogy, which later reaches Nun and his son Joshua (1 Chr 7:27). Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the name's meaning as "the eternity of God." Nothing else is recorded about him.

Elah was the father of Shimei, one of the twelve officers King Solomon appointed to supply food for the royal household. Shimei was responsible for the territory of Benjamin (1 Kgs 4:18). Elah himself is known only as Shimei's father. The verse gives no details about his life, and it does not say whether he held any office. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia explains the name as meaning "oak" or "terebinth." Several other men in the Bible are also named Elah, including a king of Israel and the father of King Hoshea. Nothing in the text links this Elah to any of them.

Elah was a son of Caleb son of Jephunneh, the man who served as one of the spies Moses sent into Canaan. He appears only in the genealogy of Judah at 1 Chr 4:15, which names him second of Caleb's three sons, between his brothers Iru and Naam, and records that his son was Kenaz. His sister Achsah is known from other passages, such as Josh 15:16–17, where Caleb gives her in marriage to Othniel. This Kenaz, Elah's son, is probably a different man from the Kenaz who was Othniel's father, since the name recurs within Caleb's family. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia explains the name Elah as meaning "oak" or "terebinth." Several other men in the Bible share the name, including a king of Israel, so this Elah should be kept distinct from them. Nothing further is recorded about his life.

Elah, son of Uzzi and grandson of Michri, was a Benjamite named in 1 Chr 9:8. He appears in the list of people who lived in Jerusalem after the return from exile in Babylon. Several other Benjamites are named alongside him, among them Ibneiah son of Jeroham and Meshullam son of Shephathiah. By inference from the surrounding passage (1 Chr 9:7–9), he was one of the leading men of the families of Benjamin who settled in the city. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia describes him as one of the chiefs of the tribes when the country was resettled. Nothing else is recorded about him. He should not be confused with the several other men named Elah in the Bible, including a king of Israel. The name is usually taken to mean "oak" or "terebinth."

Elam was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, named as a son of Shashak in the Benjamite genealogy of 1 Chronicles 8. He appears in a list of Shashak's sons that includes Ishpan, Heber, Eliel, Abdon, Zichri, Hanan, Hananiah, Antothijah, Iphedeiah and Penuel. Nothing is recorded about his life beyond his place in this family line. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him as a chief man of Benjamin, probably drawing on the summary in the same chapter that calls these men heads of fathers' houses who lived in Jerusalem. Several other people in the Bible share the name Elam, including a son of Shem and the ancestor of a family that returned from exile. This entry concerns only the Benjamite son of Shashak.

Elam was a Levite of the family of Korah, the fifth of seven sons of Meshelemiah, named in the list of temple gatekeepers organized in the time of King David (1 Chr 26:3). His brothers were Zechariah, Jediael, Zebadiah, Jathniel, Jehohanan and Elioenai. The surrounding chapter assigns these Korahite families to guard the gates of the house of the Lord, so Elam probably served as a gatekeeper, as STEPBible's proper-names index describes him. Smith's Bible Dictionary places him in David's reign, about 1014 BC. Nothing else is recorded about him. Several other men in the Bible share the name Elam, and this one should not be confused with them.

Elam was one of the "chief of the people" named in Neh 10:14 among the leaders who set their seal to the covenant made in Nehemiah's time, after the return from exile in Babylon. By inference from the surrounding chapter, this covenant was a written pledge to keep the law of Moses. Nothing else is recorded about him personally. His name appears alongside Parosh, Pahath-moab, Zattu and Bani, which are also the names of large family groups listed among the returning exiles (Ezra 2:3–10; Neh 7:8–15, where "the children of Elam" are counted). So this Elam probably signed as head or representative of the family of Elam rather than as a single individual, though the text does not say so directly. Several people in the Bible share the name, and this entry treats the covenant signer as a separate figure. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the name's meaning as "a young man" or "a secret."

Elam was a priest or Levite in Nehemiah's time. He appears only in a list of eight men who took part in the dedication of the rebuilt wall of Jerusalem, where they stood while the singers sang loudly under their overseer Jezrahiah (Neh 12:42). Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him as one of the priests who accompanied Nehemiah at that dedication. The context suggests the group formed part of one of the two thanksgiving processions on the wall, as described in the surrounding passage. Nothing further is recorded about him. Several other people in the Bible share the name Elam, and this man should not be confused with them. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the name's meaning as "a young man" or "a secret," while Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "eternity."

Elasah was one of the sons, or descendants, of Pashur listed in Ezra 10:22 among the men who had married foreign wives in the time of Ezra. The surrounding passage places the descendants of Pashur among the priests, so Elasah was probably a priest, as Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him. By inference from the context of Ezra 10, he was among those who agreed to send away their foreign wives during Ezra's reforms after the return from exile in Babylon. Nothing more is recorded about him. His name means "God has made" according to the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia. Several people in the Bible bear this name, and this Elasah should not be confused with the others, such as the son of Shaphan who carried Jeremiah's letter to the exiles.

Elasah son of Shaphan was one of two men King Zedekiah of Judah sent to Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon. The other was Gemariah son of Hilkiah. Jeremiah 29:3 says they also carried the letter Jeremiah wrote to the Jewish exiles in Babylon. The mission is undated in the text, and Smith's Bible Dictionary places it about 594 BC. His name means "God has made" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia). Elasah is probably the son of Shaphan, the royal scribe under King Josiah (2 Kgs 22:3). That would make him a brother of Ahikam, who protected Jeremiah (Jer 26:24), and of Gemariah son of Shaphan, in whose chamber Baruch read Jeremiah's scroll (Jer 36:10). That Gemariah is a different man from the Gemariah son of Hilkiah who travelled with Elasah. The name Elasah is also borne by another person in the Bible.

Elead was a member of the tribe of Ephraim who, along with Ezer, was killed by the men of Gath, described as people born in that land, when they came down to take away their cattle (1 Chr 7:21). The verse is commonly read, as in the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia, as describing a cattle raid by the Ephraimites, though its wording could also mean the men of Gath came to take Ephraim's cattle. The genealogy is ambiguous about his exact place in the family. This entry treats him as a son of Ephraim, matching the next verse, in which Ephraim mourns for his sons. Smith's Bible Dictionary calls him more generally a descendant of Ephraim. His name is explained as "God has testified" or "witness of God." Nothing else is recorded about him.

Eleazar was a son of Abinadab of Kiriath-jearim. After the Philistines returned the ark of the LORD and it had been at Beth-shemesh, the men of Kiriath-jearim brought it to Abinadab's house on the hill and consecrated Eleazar to keep it (1 Sam 7:1). The following verse says the ark stayed there twenty years. Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that he was set apart to take charge of the ark but would not have been allowed to touch it, comparing the rules for Levitical care of holy objects in Num 3:31 and 4:15. Ahio and Uzzah, who later drove the cart when David moved the ark (2 Sam 6:3), are also called sons of Abinadab. By inference they were Eleazar's brothers. His name means "God is helper." Several other people in the Bible share the name Eleazar.

Eleazar son of Phinehas was one of the men who received and weighed the silver, gold and temple vessels that Ezra's company brought from Babylon to Jerusalem. On the fourth day after their arrival, the treasure was weighed in the house of God by Meremoth son of Uriah the priest, with Eleazar beside him and the Levites Jozabad and Noadiah (Ezra 8:33). The verse does not make his own status clear. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia calls him a priest who accompanied Ezra from Babylon, Easton's Bible Dictionary describes him as working alongside the priests, and Smith's Bible Dictionary calls him a Levite. His name means "God is helper." He is distinct from the much earlier Eleazar son of Aaron, whose own son was also named Phinehas. Several other people in the Bible share the name Eleazar.

Eleazar was one of the descendants of Parosh who appear in the list of Israelite laymen who had married foreign wives in the time of Ezra (Ezra 10:25). The surrounding chapter records that these men agreed to send away their foreign wives as part of Ezra's reforms after the return from exile in Babylon. Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that he was a layman rather than a priest or Levite, which fits the heading "of Israel" under which he is listed. Nothing else is recorded about him. Eleazar was a common name, shared by several people in the Bible, most notably Aaron's son the priest, and this man should not be confused with them. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "help of God."

Eleazar was one of the men who took part in the dedication of the rebuilt wall of Jerusalem under Nehemiah, about 446 BC by inference from context. He is named in a list of eight who stood with the singers in one of the processions, while the singers sang loudly under their overseer Jezrahiah (Neh 12:42). Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia describe him as a priest, and the STEPBible proper names index calls him a priest or Levite. The verse itself gives no family or title, so his exact role is inferred from the setting of the dedication ceremony. His name means "God is helper." Several other men in the Bible share this name, and nothing further is known of this one.

Eleazar was an ancestor of Jesus named in Matthew's genealogy, the son of Eliud and the father of Matthan (Matt 1:15). Through Matthan he was the grandfather of Jacob and the great-grandfather of Joseph, the husband of Mary. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia places him three generations before Joseph. He belongs to the part of the genealogy after the return from exile in Babylon, and as a descendant of David he was of the tribe of Judah. Nothing else is recorded about him beyond his place in this list. His name means "God is helper" or "help of God," and several other men in the Bible share it, among them Aaron's son, the priest who succeeded him. This Eleazar should not be confused with them.

Eliab was a warrior of the tribe of Gad, listed third among the Gadite leaders who joined David before he became king (1 Chr 12:9). The surrounding passage (1 Chr 12:8–15) describes these Gadites as mighty men trained for war, with faces like lions and as swift as gazelles, who left their tribe and came to David's stronghold in the wilderness while he was hiding from Saul. Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries place his joining at that wilderness stronghold, while the Tyndale House proper-names index links it with David's time at Ziklag, where the chapter opens (1 Chr 12:1). Nothing more is recorded about him. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "God is my father." He is one of several men named Eliab in the Bible and should not be confused with David's eldest brother or with the Zebulunite tribal leader of Moses' time.

Eliada was a Benjamite commander in the army of King Jehoshaphat of Judah. 2 Chr 17:17 calls him "a mighty man of valour" and says he led 200,000 men from the tribe of Benjamin, armed with bow and shield. He appears in a list of Jehoshaphat's military leaders and the troops under each, all of whom served the king in Jerusalem alongside the garrisons stationed in Judah's fortified cities. Nothing else is recorded about him. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates him to about 945 BC. The name, usually taken to mean "God knows" or "known by God" (Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "knowledge of God"), is also borne by other men in the Bible, including a son of David, so this Eliada should not be confused with them.

Eliadah was the father of Rezon, a man God raised up as an adversary to King Solomon (1 Kgs 11:23). He is known only through his son. Rezon had fled from his master Hadadezer, king of Zobah, so Eliadah was probably an Aramean of that region, though this is an inference from the passage. Easton's Bible Dictionary places the family among the Arameans of Zobah and describes Rezon as captain of a raiding band that troubled Solomon. Nothing else is recorded about Eliadah himself. His name is sometimes spelled Eliada, and he should not be confused with other men of that name in the Old Testament, such as a son of David.

Eliah was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, named as one of the sons of Jeroham in the genealogy of 1 Chr 8:27. His brothers were Shamsherai, Shehariah, Athaliah, Jaresiah and Zichri. Smith's Bible Dictionary counts him among the chief men of the tribe, in line with the passage's description of these families as heads of their fathers' houses who lived in Jerusalem (1 Chr 8:28). Nothing else is recorded about him. His name means "my God is the Lord" (Smith's Bible Dictionary). It is the same Hebrew name as Elijah, and several other men in the Bible bear it, so he should not be confused with Elijah the prophet or with others of that name.

Eliah was one of the sons of Elam, a family of Israelite laymen, named in the list of men who had married foreign wives in the time of Ezra (Ezra 10:26). The surrounding chapter describes how these men agreed to put away their foreign wives after the return from Babylon. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "my God is Jehovah," and it is a form of the name Elijah. Several other people in the Bible bear the same name, and nothing further is recorded about this man beyond his place in the list.

Eliakim was a priest in Nehemiah's time who took part in the dedication of the rebuilt wall of Jerusalem. He is named first in a group of seven priests who played trumpets in one of the two thanksgiving processions that went around the wall (Neh 12:41). From the surrounding passage, this group probably walked in the company that went with Nehemiah. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates the event to about 446 BC. The name means "God raises up" or "God sets up." Several other men in the Bible share the name, including the palace official under King Hezekiah and the son of Josiah who became King Jehoiakim. Nothing more is recorded about this priest.

Eliakim was a descendant of Zerubbabel who appears in Matthew's genealogy of Jesus, in the line of the tribe of Judah. He was the son of Abiud and the father of Azor (Matt 1:13), which makes him a grandson of Zerubbabel, the leader of the return from exile in Babylon. He lived after the exile, but nothing else is recorded about him. Because he and his immediate descendants do not appear in the Old Testament, Matthew's list is the only source for him. Smith's Bible Dictionary identifies his father Abiud with a son of Zerubbabel named in other genealogies and calls Eliakim the eldest son, but this rests on harmonizing different lists. The name, meaning "God raises up" or "God sets up," was shared by several people in the Bible, including a palace official under King Hezekiah and a king of Judah later renamed Jehoiakim. This Eliakim is a different person from both.

Eliakim is an ancestor of Jesus named in the genealogy in Luke's Gospel. Luke 3:30 lists him as the father of Jonan, and the list continues in Luke 3:31 by naming his father as Melea. He belongs to the stretch of the genealogy between David and the exile, which runs through David's son Nathan rather than through Solomon. For that reason he is counted among the tribe of Judah. Nothing else is recorded about him, and he appears nowhere else in the Bible. Several other men in the Bible share his name, including a palace official under King Hezekiah and the king of Judah later renamed Jehoiakim. This Eliakim should not be confused with them. The name means "God sets up" according to the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia, or "raised up by God" according to Smith's Bible Dictionary.

Eliam was the son of Ahithophel the Gilonite and one of David's elite warriors known as "the thirty," listed in 2 Sam 23:34. His father, Ahithophel, is probably the same Gilonite who served as David's counselor and later joined Absalom's revolt (2 Sam 15:12). "Gilonite" points to the town of Giloh in the hill country of Judah (Josh 15:51). Apart from his place in this roll of mighty men, nothing else is recorded about him. The name is shared by more than one person. Easton's Bible Dictionary suggests he may be the same Eliam named as the father of Bathsheba in 2 Sam 11:3, which would make Ahithophel Bathsheba's grandfather. This entry treats the warrior separately. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "the people of God."

Eliasaph son of Lael was a Levite named as chief of the Gershonites, the clan descended from Levi's son Gershon, during Israel's time in the wilderness (Num 3:24). The passage comes from the census and organization of the Levites at Sinai. There the Gershonites were assigned to camp behind the tabernacle on its west side and to care for its curtains, coverings and hangings. As head of the clan, Eliasaph probably oversaw that work. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia explains the name as "God has added." Several men in the Bible bear the name Eliasaph. He should be kept distinct from Eliasaph son of Deuel (or Reuel), the leader of the tribe of Gad in the same book. Nothing further is recorded about him.

Eliashib was a man of the tribe of Judah, one of the seven sons of Elioenai, named in the genealogy of David's royal line in 1 Chr 3:24. His brothers were Hodaiah, Pelaiah, Akkub, Johanan, Dalaiah and Anani. The genealogy traces this family through King Jeconiah, and Smith's Bible Dictionary describes Eliashib as one of the latest descendants of the royal family of Judah. That would place him well after the return from exile in Babylon, by inference from his position near the end of the list. Nothing else is recorded about him. The name, usually explained as "God restores," belongs to several other men in the Bible, including a high priest in Nehemiah's time. This Eliashib should be kept distinct from them.

Eliashib was a priest in the time of King David. He gave his name to the eleventh of the twenty-four divisions, or courses, into which the priests were organized to take turns serving at the sanctuary (1 Chr 24:12). By inference from the surrounding chapter, he was the head of a priestly family descended from Aaron, through either Eleazar or Ithamar, and his division's turn of service was set by lot. Nothing else is recorded about him. The name, which Smith's Bible Dictionary explains as meaning "God restores," belongs to several men in the Bible. Among them are a high priest in Nehemiah's day and men of the return from exile, and this priest should not be confused with them.

Eliashib was the father of Johanan (also spelled Jehohanan), whose chamber at the temple in Jerusalem Ezra entered after rising from before the house of God. There Ezra fasted from bread and water, mourning the unfaithfulness of the returned exiles who had married foreign wives (Ezra 10:6). The name means "God restores," according to the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia. Several men in the Bible share this name. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests this Eliashib is probably the same person as the high priest Eliashib of Nehemiah's time, and Neh 12:23 does mention a Johanan son of Eliashib among the Levite heads of families. STEPBible's proper names index likewise describes him as a priest in Ezra's day. The verse itself gives no further detail about him, so the identification remains an inference. In the apocryphal book 1 Esdras he is called Eliasib.

Eliashib was one of the singers among the Levites in the time of Ezra. He is named in Ezra 10:24 in the list of men who had married foreign wives. From the surrounding chapter, this list records those who agreed to send away their foreign wives during Ezra's reforms after the return from exile. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him as a singer who had married a foreign wife, and gives the meaning of his name as "whom God restores." Nothing else is recorded about him. Several other men in the Bible share the name, including the high priest Eliashib of Nehemiah's day and other men named in the same list in Ezra 10. This entry concerns only the singer.

Eliashib was one of the sons, or descendants, of Zattu listed in Ezra 10:27. He appears among the Israelite men who had married foreign wives and who agreed, during Ezra's reforms after the return from exile, to send those wives away. The surrounding chapter describes this pledge, and the list he belongs to names those who took part. Nothing more is recorded about him. The name, which Smith's Bible Dictionary explains as "whom God restores," was borne by several men of this period, including a high priest in Nehemiah's time and others in the same list in Ezra 10. This Eliashib should not be confused with them.

Eliashib was one of several men of this name in the Bible. He appears only in the list of Israelites who had married foreign women during Ezra's reforms after the return from exile. By inference from the surrounding passage, he is named among the 'sons of Bani' (Ezra 10:34), meaning he belonged to the family or clan of Bani. Ezra 10:44 says the men on this list had taken foreign wives, and the wider chapter describes their agreement to send them away. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates these events to about 458 BC, a date inferred from context. Nothing else is recorded about him. The name is usually taken to mean 'God restores' (Smith's Bible Dictionary). Because the name was common, he should not be confused with Eliashib the high priest or the other Eliashibs in the lists of Ezra and Nehemiah.

Elidad, son of Chislon, was the leader from the tribe of Benjamin named in Num 34:21 among the men chosen to divide the land of Canaan among the tribes. The surrounding passage (Num 34:16–29) presents these leaders as appointed, one from each tribe, to work with Eleazar the priest and Joshua in assigning the territory west of the Jordan. His name is usually taken to mean "God has loved" or "beloved of God." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests he may be the same person as Eldad, though the text does not say so. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates his appointment to about 1452 BC, an estimate based on context. Nothing else is recorded about him.

Eliel was one of the heads of families in the half-tribe of Manasseh that settled east of the Jordan. In 1 Chr 5:24 he is listed with Epher, Ishi, Azriel, Jeremiah, Hodaviah and Jahdiel, and they are described as mighty men of valour, famous men and heads of their fathers' houses. The surrounding passage places this group in the land from Bashan to Mount Hermon and goes on to tell of their later deportation by the Assyrians. Easton's and Smith's Bible dictionaries identify him only as a chief of eastern Manasseh. The STEPBible name index places him in the time of King David, though the verse gives no date. Smith's dictionary takes the name to mean "to whom God is strength." Several other men in the Bible are also named Eliel, and nothing more is known about this one.

Eliel was a Benjamite listed among the sons of Shimhi in the genealogy of the tribe of Benjamin in 1 Chr 8:20. His brothers were Jakim, Zichri, Zabdi, Elienai, Zilthai, Adaiah, Beraiah and Shimrath. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him as a chief man in the tribe of Benjamin, and the surrounding list names the sons of Shimhi as heads of families who lived in Jerusalem. Shimhi is probably the same man called Shema elsewhere in the chapter, by inference from context, though this is uncertain. Nothing else is recorded about him. Smith's gives the name's meaning as "to whom God is strength." Several other men in the Bible are also called Eliel, and this one should not be confused with them.

Eliel was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, named in the genealogy of 1 Chronicles 8 as one of the sons of Shashak. He appears in a list with his brothers Ishpan and Heber (1 Chr 8:22), alongside Abdon, Zichri, Hanan, Hananiah, Elam, Antothijah, Iphedeiah and Penuel. The passage groups these men among the heads of Benjamite families who lived in Jerusalem, so Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him as a Benjamite chief. Nothing else is recorded about him. The name, usually explained as "God is my God" or "God is strength," was borne by several other men in the Bible, and this Eliel should not be confused with them.

Eliel the Mahavite was one of David's mighty men, the warriors listed in 1 Chr 11 as the heroes of David's guard. He is named only once, in 1 Chr 11:46, where he appears alongside Jeribai and Joshaviah, the sons of Elnaam, and Ithmah the Moabite. His title "the Mahavite" probably refers to his hometown or clan, but no place called Mahavah or Mahav is mentioned elsewhere, so its meaning is uncertain. Nothing more is recorded about his deeds or family. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "to whom God is strength," and Hitchcock's Bible Names renders it "God, my God." Several other men in the Bible share the name Eliel, including another of David's warriors named in 1 Chr 11:47, and this entry concerns only the Mahavite.

Eliel was one of the warriors named in the list of David's mighty men near the end of 1 Chr 11. He appears in 1 Chr 11:47 alongside Obed and Jasiel the Mesobaite, but nothing else is said about him: no father, home town or deeds are given. The name is shared by several people in the Bible. Another Eliel, called the Mahavite, appears in the verse just before, so this list seems to contain two different men of the same name. STEPBible's proper-names index describes this Eliel as coming from Meholah. Smith's Bible Dictionary takes the name to mean 'to whom God is strength,' while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives 'God, my God.'

Eliel was one of the warriors from the tribe of Gad who joined David before he became king. He is listed seventh among eleven Gadite leaders in 1 Chr 12:11. By inference from the surrounding passage, these men left their tribe east of the Jordan and came to David's stronghold in the wilderness. They are described as skilled with shield and spear and as swift as gazelles, and they crossed the Jordan when it was in flood. Reference works place the episode differently. Smith's Bible Dictionary sets it while David was hiding from Saul in the wilderness of Judah, while Easton's Bible Dictionary connects it with David's stay at Ziklag. Nothing else is recorded about him. Several other men in the Bible share the name Eliel, which Smith's Bible Dictionary explains as "to whom God is strength."

Eliel was one of ten overseers appointed in the reign of King Hezekiah to help manage the offerings, tithes and dedicated gifts brought to the house of God. He served under Cononiah and his brother Shimei, who had chief charge of these stores, by the command of Hezekiah and of Azariah, the ruler of the temple (2 Chr 31:13). The surrounding passage places this work in the storerooms of the temple. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the STEPBible proper-names index describe him as a Levite, which fits the context, and Smith dates his service to about 726 BC. He is known only from this verse. The name, meaning roughly "my God is God" or "God is strength," is shared by several other men in the Old Testament, including warriors of David, and this Eliel should be kept distinct from them.

Elienai was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, named in the Benjamite genealogy of 1 Chronicles 8. He is listed as one of the nine sons of Shimhi, along with Jakim, Zichri, Zabdi, Zilthai, Eliel, Adaiah, Beraiah and Shimrath (1 Chr 8:19–21). Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him as a chief man in the tribe, probably by inference from the later statement in the same chapter that the men listed were heads of families who lived in Jerusalem. Nothing else is recorded about him. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "my eyes are toward God," and Hitchcock's Bible Names renders it "the God of my eyes." His father Shimhi is probably the same person as the Shema of 1 Chr 8:13, though the identification is uncertain.

Eliezer (Abraham's Steward) was the man in charge of Abram's household, described as "Eliezer of Damascus" (Gen 15:2). Abram named him when he complained to God that he had no children. The following verse shows that, without a son, this servant would inherit Abram's estate, and the TIPNR proper-names index describes him as Abraham's potential heir before Ishmael and Isaac were born. The Revised Version renders "steward" as "possessor" of the house. Easton's Bible Dictionary suggests he was probably the unnamed senior servant whom Abraham later sent to his family's homeland in Mesopotamia to find a wife for Isaac (Gen 24), though that chapter does not give the servant's name. Hitchcock's Bible Names takes the name to mean "help of my God." No other passage clearly mentions him by name.

Eliezer was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, one of the nine sons of Becher named in a genealogy in 1 Chr 7:8. His brothers were Zemira, Joash, Elioenai, Omri, Jerimoth, Abiah, Anathoth and Alameth. Becher was a son of Benjamin (1 Chr 7:6), which, as Easton's Bible Dictionary notes, makes Eliezer a grandson of Benjamin. Nothing else is recorded about him. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives the meaning of his name as "God is help." Several other people in the Bible share the name, including Abraham's servant and a son of Moses, and they should not be confused with this Eliezer.

Eliezer was one of seven priests who blew trumpets before the ark of God in the time of King David (1 Chr 15:24). The surrounding chapter describes the ark being brought up from the house of Obed-edom to Jerusalem, and he took part in that procession with Shebaniah, Jehoshaphat, Nethaneel, Amasai, Zechariah and Benaiah. Nothing else is recorded about him. His name means "God is help" according to the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia. Several other men in the Bible share the name Eliezer, including Abraham's servant and a son of Moses, and this priest should not be confused with them.

Eliezer, son of Zichri, was the ruler of the tribe of Reuben during King David's reign. He appears in a list of the chief officers over the tribes of Israel (1 Chr 27:16), a list in which Shephatiah son of Maachah led the neighbouring Simeonites. The context of 1 Chronicles 27, which records David's administrative organization, places him in David's time, as Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia also note. Nothing further is recorded about him. The name, meaning "God is help" according to the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia, is shared by several other men in the Bible, and this Eliezer should not be confused with them.

Eliezer, son of Dodavah and from Mareshah, was a prophet in the reign of King Jehoshaphat of Judah. He is known only from 2 Chr 20:37. There he condemns Jehoshaphat for joining with Ahaziah, king of Israel, to build ships meant to sail to Tarshish. He announces that the LORD has broken Jehoshaphat's works, and the ships are then wrecked before they can make the voyage. Mareshah was a town in the lowlands of Judah. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "help, or court, of my God." Several other men in the Bible share the name Eliezer, and Easton's Bible Dictionary notes others in Ezra and in Luke's genealogy. This prophet should not be confused with them.

Eliezer was one of the leading men Ezra sent for while the returning exiles were camped by the river Ahava on their way from Babylon to Jerusalem (Ezra 8:16). He is named first in a list of men described as "chief men." The surrounding passage explains why Ezra sent for them: on reviewing the group he found no Levites among it, and he sent these leaders to Iddo at Casiphia to bring ministers for the temple. Nothing else is recorded about this Eliezer. The name, which Hitchcock's Bible Names explains as meaning "help of my God," belongs to several people in the Bible. This one should probably be kept distinct from the Eliezers in Ezra 10 who had married foreign wives, though that cannot be settled from the text.

Eliezer was a priest in the time of Ezra, one of several men of this name in the Bible. He belonged to the family of Jeshua son of Jozadak, the high priest who led the priests home from exile, and he is listed among Jeshua's descendants or relatives who had married foreign wives (Ezra 10:18). The next verse, Ezra 10:19, says that these men pledged to send their wives away and offered a ram as a guilt offering. Nothing else is recorded about him, and he should not be confused with the other men named Eliezer, such as the Levite and the layman listed later in the same chapter. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "help, or court, of my God."

Eliezer was a Levite in the time of Ezra, named in a list of Levites who had married foreign women (Ezra 10:23). Judging from the surrounding chapter, this list belongs to Ezra's reform among the Jews who had returned from exile in Babylon. In that reform, men who had taken wives from the surrounding peoples agreed to send them away. Nothing else is recorded about this Eliezer, and he should not be confused with the several other men of the same name in the Bible. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "help, or court, of my God."

Eliezer (Son of Harim) was an Israelite of the family of Harim, named in Ezra 10:31 alongside Ishijah, Malchiah, Shemaiah, Shimeon and others. The verse belongs to the list of men who had married foreign wives, drawn up during Ezra's reforms after the return from exile in Babylon. By inference from the surrounding chapter (Ezra 10:3, 19, 44), he was among those who agreed to send these wives away. "Son of Harim" probably means that he belonged to the Harim clan rather than that Harim was his own father. Nothing else is recorded about him, and he should not be confused with the several other men named Eliezer in the Bible. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "help, or court, of my God."

Eliezer was an ancestor of Jesus named only in the genealogy in Luke's Gospel, which traces Jesus' line back through David to Adam. Luke 3:29 lists him as the son of Jorim and the father of Jose. His place in the list falls between David and the Babylonian exile, so he belonged to the tribe of Judah and lived during the period of the kings, by inference from his position in the genealogy. Nothing else is recorded about him, and he is distinct from the several other men in the Bible who share his name. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives the name's meaning as "God is help."

Elihoenai was a son of Zerahiah and a member of the family of Pahath-moab. He led 200 men of that family who returned from exile in Babylon to Jerusalem with Ezra (Ezra 8:4). Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "my eyes are toward Jehovah" and dates the return to about 459 BC. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia lists him under the spelling Eliehoenai. He is mentioned only in this one verse, so nothing more is known of him.

Elihoreph was one of King Solomon's scribes, or royal secretaries. He is named with his brother Ahiah among Solomon's chief officials, and both are called the sons of Shisha (1 Kgs 4:3). Shisha is probably the same man as Shavsha, who served as scribe under David (1 Chr 18:16) and is called Seraiah in 2 Sam 8:17 and Sheva in 2 Sam 20:25. This entry follows that identification. If it is correct, the brothers took over their father's office in the royal court. Nothing else is recorded about Elihoreph. The meaning of his name is uncertain. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "God is his reward," the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia tentatively suggests "God of autumn," and Hitchcock's Bible Names offers "god of winter, or of youth."

Elihu was one of the captains of thousands from the tribe of Manasseh who went over to David as he traveled to Ziklag (1 Chr 12:20). He is named in a list of seven Manassite commanders who joined David's growing force. The surrounding chapter places this after David left the Philistine army, and Smith's Bible Dictionary sets it on the eve of the battle of Gilboa, where Saul died. The name is usually explained as "He is my God" or "my God is He". Several other men in the Bible are also called Elihu, including the young speaker in the book of Job. This Manassite is mentioned only in this one verse, and nothing more is known about him.

Elihu was a Levite in the time of David, one of the sons of Shemaiah listed in 1 Chr 26:7 alongside Othni, Rephael, Obed, Elzabad and Semachiah. The verse calls Elihu and Semachiah among the "strong men" of the family. The surrounding chapter places Shemaiah's family within the household of Obed-edom, which was assigned to guard the gates of the sanctuary. Easton's Bible Dictionary accordingly describes Elihu as one of the temple porters appointed under David, and Smith's Bible Dictionary identifies him as a Korahite Levite. Nothing further is recorded about him. His name probably means "He is my God." Several other men in the Bible share the name, including Job's young companion, and they should not be confused with this gatekeeper.

Elihu was a man of the tribe of Judah, described as "one of the brethren of David" and named as the leader of Judah in the list of tribal chiefs under King David (1 Chr 27:18). This entry treats him as a son of Jesse and a brother of David, Eliab, Abinadab, Shammah, Nethaneel, Raddai and Ozem. His exact identity is uncertain. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia takes the name as another form of Eliab, David's eldest brother (1 Sam 16:6). Others note that 1 Sam 16:10 implies Jesse had eight sons while 1 Chr 2:13–15 names only seven, so Elihu may be the unnamed one. Because "brethren" can also mean a wider kinsman, he may simply have been a relative of David. His name means "he is my God." Several other people in the Bible share the name.

Elijah was a man of the family of Harim, one of the men named in the list of those who had married foreign wives in the time of Ezra (Ezra 10:21). The surrounding passage places the sons of Harim among the priests, so this Elijah was probably of priestly descent, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia describes him as a man of priestly rank. By inference from the wider chapter, he was among those who agreed to put away their foreign wives during Ezra's reforms after the return from Babylon. Nothing else is recorded about him. He should not be confused with the prophet Elijah or with others who share the name, which means "Yah is God" according to the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia.

Elika was a Harodite listed among David's mighty men, the group of elite warriors known as "the thirty" (2 Sam 23:25). He is named right after Shammah the Harodite, who came from the same place, probably Harod, the spring or town near which Gideon camped. Nothing else is recorded about him. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that his name does not appear in the parallel list of David's warriors in 1 Chronicles 11. The meaning of his name is uncertain: Easton's Bible Dictionary gives "God is his rejector," and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "pelican of God."

Elioenai was a man of the tribe of Simeon, named in a list of Simeonite clan leaders in 1 Chr 4:36. Smith's Bible Dictionary calls him the head of a Simeonite family. The surrounding passage explains that the men in this list were princes in their families whose households grew greatly (1 Chr 4:38). It also says that in the days of King Hezekiah they moved toward Gedor to find pasture for their flocks and drove out the people living there (1 Chr 4:39–41). On that basis the STEPBible Proper Names index places him in Hezekiah's reign. Nothing else is recorded about him. Several other men in the Bible share the name, and this Elioenai should not be confused with them. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "my eyes are toward the Lord."

Elioenai was a member of the tribe of Benjamin, one of the nine sons of Becher listed in the genealogy at 1 Chr 7:8. His brothers were Zemira, Joash, Eliezer, Omri, Jerimoth, Abiah, Anathoth and Alameth. Becher was himself a son of Benjamin, which makes Elioenai a grandson of Benjamin. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him as the head of one of the families descended from Becher, and it gives the meaning of his name as "my eyes are toward the Lord." Nothing else is recorded about him. Several other men in the Bible bear the same name, and this Benjamite should not be confused with them.

Elioenai was a Levite, the seventh son of Meshelemiah, named in the list of temple gatekeepers in 1 Chr 26:3. His brothers were Zechariah, Jediael, Zebadiah, Jathniel, Elam and Jehohanan. From the surrounding chapter, Meshelemiah's family belonged to the Korahite branch of the Levites. They were among the divisions of doorkeepers organized for the house of the Lord, which by context dates to the later years of King David's reign. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him as a Korahite Levite and one of these doorkeepers. Smith's gives the meaning of his name as "my eyes are toward the Lord." Nothing more is recorded about him. Several other men in the Bible share the name Elioenai, and this entry concerns only the son of Meshelemiah.

Elioenai was a priest of the family of Pashur, listed in Ezra 10:22 among the men who had married foreign wives in the time of Ezra, after the return from exile. The verse itself names him only as one of the sons of Pashur, alongside Maaseiah, Ishmael, Nethaneel, Jozabad and Elasah. His being a priest is inferred from the surrounding passage, which groups these names under the priests who had taken foreign wives and who agreed to send them away in response to Ezra's reforms. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "my eyes are toward the Lord" and suggests he may be the same Elioenai who appears among the priests at the dedication of Jerusalem's rebuilt wall (Neh 12:41). Several other men in the Bible share this name, so the identification is uncertain.

Elioenai was an Israelite of the family of Zattu, named in Ezra 10:27 in the list of men who had married foreign wives after the return from exile in Babylon. The surrounding chapter records that these men agreed to send their foreign wives away at Ezra's call. This would have been around 458 BC, the date Smith's Bible Dictionary gives, inferred from the context of Ezra's reforms. Nothing else is recorded about him. The name, which Smith's Bible Dictionary explains as "my eyes are toward the Lord," is borne by several other men in the Old Testament, including a priest of the family of Pashhur in the same list and descendants in the genealogies of Chronicles. The man named here should not be confused with them.

Elioenai was a priest who blew a trumpet at the dedication of the rebuilt wall of Jerusalem in Nehemiah's time. In Neh 12:41 he is named among seven priests with trumpets, alongside Eliakim, Maaseiah, Miniamin, Michaiah, Zechariah and Hananiah. By inference from the surrounding passage, this group marched in one of the two companies that processed along the wall before gathering at the temple. Nothing else is recorded about him. Several other men in the Bible bear the same name, and it is uncertain whether this priest is the same as any of them, such as the priest of the family of Pashhur who had married a foreign wife (Ezra 10:22). This entry treats him as a separate person. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "toward him are mine eyes."

Eliphal, son of Ur, was one of David's mighty men, the elite warriors listed in 1 Chr 11:35. Nothing else is recorded about him. His name is usually taken to mean "God has judged" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia), though Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "a miracle of God." The parallel list of David's warriors in 2 Samuel 23 has Eliphelet the son of Ahasbai, the son of the Maachathite, at the corresponding place. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia, following a footnote in the Revised Version, treat the two as the same man, with the names differing between the two lists. This entry presents him under the Chronicles form of the name.

Eliphelet son of Ahasbai was one of David's mighty men, the elite group of warriors listed in 2 Sam 23. He appears only once, in that roster (2 Sam 23:34). The King James wording, "the son of Ahasbai, the son of the Maachathite," is usually read as meaning that Ahasbai was a Maachathite, probably from Maacah or the town of Abel-beth-maacah in the far north. Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies him with "Eliphal the son of Ur" in the parallel list at 1 Chr 11:35, where the names differ. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "God of deliverance" and counts him among the thirty warriors of David's guard. Several other people in the Bible share the name Eliphelet, including sons of David, and they should not be confused with this warrior.

Eliphelet was a Benjamite, the third son of Eshek, and is named after his older brothers Ulam and Jehush in the genealogy of King Saul's family (1 Chr 8:39). Eshek is called the brother of Azel, so by inference from the surrounding list (1 Chr 8:37–38) he and Azel were sons of Eleasah, making Eliphelet a descendant of Eleasah and, further back, of Saul through Jonathan. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary both describe him this way. Smith's gives the meaning of his name as "the God of deliverance" and places him before 536 BC. That date is an estimate, not stated in the text. Nothing is recorded about his life beyond his place in this family line. The name Eliphelet is shared by several other men in the Bible, including a son of David and one of David's warriors, and these should not be confused with him.

Eliphelet was one of the descendants of Adonikam who returned from exile in Babylon to Jerusalem with Ezra. In Ezra's list of family heads who traveled with him, he is named first among "the last sons of Adonikam," alongside Jeiel and Shemaiah, and the three led a group of sixty men (Ezra 8:13). Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him as one of the leaders of this family group and gives the name's meaning as "the God of deliverance." It dates the return to about 459 BC. Nothing more is recorded about him. The name Eliphelet is shared by several other men in the Bible, including a son of David and one of David's mighty men, and this entry refers only to the returning exile.

Eliphelet was one of the descendants of Hashum listed in Ezra 10:33 among the men who had married foreign wives in the time of Ezra. The list he appears in, in Ezra 10, records those who agreed to put away these wives after Ezra's reforms among the returned exiles in Jerusalem. Smith's Bible Dictionary takes the name to mean "God of deliverance" and dates the episode to about 458 BC. Nothing else is recorded about him. The name Eliphelet is shared by several other men in the Bible, including a son of David, and this Eliphelet should be kept distinct from them.

Elishama, son of Jekamiah, was a descendant of Judah who is named only once, in the genealogy at 1 Chr 2:41. This genealogy traces the line of Jerahmeel, a great-grandson of Judah, through Sheshan's daughter and her Egyptian husband Jarha, down to Shallum, Jekamiah and finally Elishama, the last name in the list. Nothing is recorded about his life beyond his place in this family line. The name means "God has heard," according to the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia. Several other men in the Bible share the name, including a prince of Ephraim, a son of David and a royal scribe, but this Elishama appears to be a different person from all of them.

Elishama was a priest in the reign of King Jehoshaphat of Judah. He and another priest, Jehoram, were sent with a group of Levites to accompany the king's officials. By inference from the surrounding passage (2 Chr 17:7–9), the group went through the cities of Judah teaching the people from the book of the law of the Lord. He appears only in 2 Chr 17:8, and nothing more is recorded about him. Several other men in the Bible share the name, which means "God has heard" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia). This Elishama should not be confused with them. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates his time to about 912 BC.

Elishaphat, son of Zichri, was one of the five "captains of hundreds" whom Jehoiada the priest brought into a covenant in the seventh year, at the start of the plot to overthrow Queen Athaliah and crown the young Joash king of Judah (2 Chr 23:1). He appears only in this verse. The surrounding chapter describes the plan these commanders carried out, so he probably took part in guarding Joash and in the events that ended Athaliah's reign, though he is not named again. His name means "God is judge" or "whom God has judged" (Easton's Bible Dictionary; International Standard Bible Encyclopedia). Smith's Bible Dictionary dates these events to about 877 BC.

Elisheba was the wife of Aaron, Moses' brother, and the mother of his four sons, Nadab, Abihu, Eleazar and Ithamar (Exod 6:23). She was the daughter of Amminadab and the sister of Nahshon, so she came from the tribe of Judah. Smith's Bible Dictionary identifies her brother Nahshon as the leader of Judah's camp named in Num 2:3. Because Aaron's sons became the priestly line, the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia calls her the foundress of the entire Levitical priesthood. Her marriage linked the priestly family of Levi with a leading family of Judah. Her name is usually explained as "God is an oath" or "God swears" (Easton's Bible Dictionary), and Hitchcock's Bible Names treats it as the same name as Elisabeth. She is mentioned by name only once in the Bible.

Elizaphan, son of Parnach, was the prince, or chief, of the tribe of Zebulun named in Num 34:25. The surrounding chapter lists the tribal leaders whom the LORD appointed to divide the land of Canaan among the Israelites, with Eleazar the priest and Joshua. Elizaphan was to represent Zebulun in that division, which places him late in the wilderness period, as Israel prepared to enter the land. Nothing else is recorded about him. The name means "God has protected" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia). Several people in the Bible bear this name, including a Levite leader of the Kohathites, and this Zebulunite should not be confused with them.

Elkanah was a Levite named only in a genealogy in 1 Chr 9:16. He was the father of Asa and the grandfather of Berechiah. The surrounding chapter lists the Levites who lived in Jerusalem, and Berechiah's family is described as living in the villages of the Netophathites, probably near Netophah, south of Jerusalem. Nothing else is recorded about Elkanah himself. His name is shared by several other people in the Bible, including the father of Samuel, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats this Elkanah as a separate Levite. The name is usually explained as "God has possessed" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia) or "God-provided" (Smith's Bible Dictionary).

Elkanah was one of the Korahites who joined David at Ziklag, listed with Jesiah, Azareel, Joezer and Jashobeam in 1 Chr 12:6. By inference from the opening of the chapter, these men came to David while he was still kept away from Saul, and they were counted among the warriors who helped him. The surrounding list marks them as skilled fighters, able to use the bow and sling with either hand. Nothing else is recorded about him. Several other men in the Bible share the name, including the father of Samuel, and this Elkanah should be kept distinct from them. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "God-provided," and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives "God has possessed."

Elkanah was a Levite who, with Berechiah, served as a doorkeeper for the ark of the covenant (1 Chr 15:23). The surrounding chapter shows that he held this post when David brought the ark up to Jerusalem, as one of the Levites the leaders of the tribe appointed to the music and service for that occasion. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests he may be the same man as another Levite Elkanah named in Chronicles, but this is uncertain. Several men in the Bible bear this name, which means "God has possessed" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia) or "the zeal of God" (Hitchcock's Bible Names). Nothing further is recorded about him.

Elkanah was a high official of Ahaz king of Judah, described as "next to the king" (2 Chr 28:7). The phrase probably means he held the second-highest position at court, a chief minister or deputy to the king. He was killed by Zichri, a warrior of Ephraim, along with the king's son Maaseiah and Azrikam, the governor of the palace. By inference from the surrounding chapter, this happened during the invasion of Judah by Pekah king of Israel, when Judah suffered heavy losses. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates these events to about 739 BC. The name, which several other men in the Bible also bear, is usually explained as "God has possessed" or "God has created" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia). Nothing more is recorded about this Elkanah.

Elmodam was an ancestor of Jesus named only once, in the genealogy given in Luke's Gospel, which traces the line back through Joseph (Luke 3:28). He is listed as the son of Er and the father of Cosam.
