In Luke's list he belongs to the stretch of names between David and the Babylonian exile, coming through David's son Nathan rather than through the royal line of kings, so he was presumably of the tribe of Judah. Nothing else is recorded about him, and the period he lived in can only be inferred from his position in the list. Some modern editions spell the name Elmadam, the form used by STEPBible's Tyndale House proper names list. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives its meaning as "the God of measure, or of the garment," while Smith's Bible Dictionary gives simply "measure."

Elnaam was the father of Jeribai and Joshaviah, two men named among David's mighty warriors in the list at 1 Chr 11:46. He is mentioned only in this verse, and nothing else is recorded about him. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation, reads the verse differently and counts Elnaam himself as one of the warriors. This entry follows the Hebrew text, which makes him their father. His name is usually explained as meaning "God is delight" or "God his delight" (Smith's Bible Dictionary). Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "God's fairness."

Elnathan was a man of Jerusalem whose daughter Nehushta was the mother of King Jehoiachin of Judah, which made him the king's maternal grandfather (2 Kgs 24:8). His name means "God has given" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia; Hitchcock's Bible Names). He belongs to the genealogy of Jesus through this grandson, since Jehoiachin (Jechonias) appears in the royal line in Matt 1:11–12. Elnathan himself is not named there. Several men in the Bible share this name. Some interpreters identify him with Elnathan son of Achbor, an official under King Jehoiakim mentioned in Jer 26:22 and 36:12, 25. That would fit, because Jehoiakim was Jehoiachin's father, but the text does not confirm it. This entry treats him only as Nehushta's father.

Elnathan was one of the men Ezra sent for while his returning group camped by the river Ahava. Ezra 8:16 names three men called Elnathan: two among the "chief men" and one among the "men of understanding." The verse does not say which of the three this entry refers to. They may be three different people, or the repetition may reflect copying in the text. By inference from the surrounding passage (Ezra 8:15–17), Ezra had found no Levites in his company, so he sent these leaders to Iddo at Casiphia to bring ministers for the temple. Nothing more is recorded about this Elnathan. He is distinct from other men of the same name in the Bible. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "God hath given" or "the gift of God."

Elnathan was one of the men Ezra summoned at the river Ahava while gathering exiles to return from Babylon to Jerusalem (Ezra 8:16). The name appears three times in this one verse: two Elnathans are listed among the "chief men," and a third is named with Joiarib as one of the "men of understanding," probably teachers. This entry refers to one of these men, but the text gives no way to tell which, and nothing else is recorded about him. By inference from the surrounding passage, Ezra had found no Levites in his company and sent this group to Iddo at Casiphia to bring back ministers for the temple. The name is shared by other people in the Bible. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives its meaning as "God hath given" or "the gift of God."

Elnathan was one of the men Ezra sent for while his company of returning exiles camped by the river Ahava. The name appears three times in Ezra 8:16: twice among the "chief men" and once, alongside Joiarib, among the "men of understanding." It is unclear which of these three this entry refers to, and some readers treat the repetition as a possible copying error. From the surrounding passage, Ezra had found no Levites among the travelers, so he sent this group to Iddo at Casiphia to bring back ministers for the temple. Nothing else is recorded about him. The name, which Hitchcock's Bible Names explains as "God hath given," also belongs to other men, such as Jehoiachin's grandfather and the son of Achbor in Jeremiah's time. They are separate people.

Eluzai was one of the warriors who came over to David at Ziklag, while David was still keeping away from Saul. He appears only once, in a list of fighting men in 1 Chr 12:5, alongside Jerimoth, Bealiah, Shemariah and Shephatiah the Haruphite. The surrounding passage (1 Chr 12:1–7) describes these men as skilled archers and slingers who could use either hand, and as kinsmen of Saul from the tribe of Benjamin. So Eluzai was a Benjamite, by inference from that context. Nothing else is recorded about him. His name is usually explained as "God is my strength" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia; Hitchcock's Bible Names), though Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "God is my praise."

Elzabad was a warrior from the tribe of Gad, listed ninth among the Gadite fighters who joined David (1 Chr 12:12). The surrounding passage, which is not quoted here, describes these men as skilled with shield and spear and fierce as lions. They left their tribe to join David at his stronghold in the wilderness while he was being hunted by Saul, and they crossed the Jordan when it was in flood. The STEPBible proper names index links his joining David with Ziklag, where the chapter's list of supporters begins. The name means "God has given" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia). Another man named Elzabad, a Levite gatekeeper of the family of Obed-edom, appears in 1 Chr 26:7 and is a different person.

Elzabad was a Levite named among the sons of Shemaiah in the list of temple gatekeepers in 1 Chronicles 26. He is listed with his brothers Othni, Rephael, Obed, Elihu and Semachiah, and the text notes that his brothers were "strong men" (1 Chr 26:7). By inference from the surrounding chapter, Shemaiah was a son of Obed-edom, so Elzabad belonged to Obed-edom's family of gatekeepers. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia describe him as a Korahite doorkeeper. The STEPBible name index places this service in the time of David. His name is usually taken to mean "God has given." The name is also borne by a different man, a warrior from the tribe of Gad who joined David (1 Chr 12:12), who should not be confused with this Levite.

Epaenetus was a Christian living in Rome whom Paul greets in his letter to the Romans, calling him "my wellbeloved" (Rom 16:5). Paul describes him as the "firstfruits" of his region for Christ, meaning one of the first people there to become a believer. The King James Version reads "of Achaia," the Roman province of southern Greece. Many manuscripts instead read "of Asia," meaning the Roman province in western Asia Minor, and the Revised Version follows that reading. Easton's Bible Dictionary considers "Asia" probably correct, and the STEPBible proper names index also calls him the first convert in Asia. His greeting comes right after the greeting to the church that met in the house of Priscilla and Aquila. This suggests he may have been connected with that household, though that is an inference. Nothing more is known of him. His name means "commendable."

Ephah was a concubine of Caleb, named in the genealogy of the tribe of Judah in 1 Chr 2:46. She bore him three sons, Haran, Moza and Gazez. The same verse adds that Haran fathered a son named Gazez, so the name may belong to both a son and a grandson, or the line may be recorded in two ways. The surrounding chapter traces the descendants of Hezron, so this Caleb is probably Caleb son of Hezron (compare 1 Chr 2:18, 42) rather than Caleb son of Jephunneh, the spy sent by Moses. Several people in the Bible share the name Ephah, including a son of Midian (Gen 25:4) and a man listed just after her in 1 Chr 2:47. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives the name's meaning as "darkness", and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "weary" or "tired". Nothing else is recorded about her.

Ephah was a child of Jahdai and a member of the tribe of Judah, named only in 1 Chr 2:47. Ephah's siblings were Regem, Jotham, Geshan (also spelled Gesham), Pelet and Shaaph. The verse appears in the genealogy of Caleb's descendants, though it does not say how Jahdai himself was connected to Caleb. The verse groups Ephah among Jahdai's "sons", and Smith's Bible Dictionary describes Ephah as a son, while this entry treats Ephah as female. Nothing else is recorded about this person. The name is shared by others, including Caleb's concubine Ephah, mentioned in the previous verse (1 Chr 2:46), who is a different person. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "weary" or "tired", and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives "darkness".

Ephai was a man from Netophah whose sons were among the Judean army officers who came to Gedaliah at Mizpah after the Babylonians appointed him governor of those left in Judah (Jer 40:8). Netophah was a town near Bethlehem, as its pairing with Bethlehem in Neh 7:26 suggests. Ephai himself is known only through his sons, who are not named. The written Hebrew text spells the name Ophai, while the traditional reading is Ephai. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives its meaning as "gloomy." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia holds that these sons were later killed along with Gedaliah when Ishmael son of Nethaniah murdered the governor and the Judeans with him. That is an inference from Jer 41:3, which does not name them.

Epher was a man of the tribe of Judah, listed as the third of four sons of Ezra in the genealogy of Judah (1 Chr 4:17). His brothers were Jether, Mered and Jalon. This Ezra is a different person from the scribe of the same name, and nothing else is recorded about Epher beyond his place in the family list. The name is shared by several people in the Bible, including a grandson of Abraham through Midian and a head of a family in the half-tribe of Manasseh, so this Epher should be kept distinct from them. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives the meaning of the name as "calf" or "young deer," while Hitchcock's Bible Names offers "dust" or "lead."

Epher was one of the heads of the families of the half-tribe of Manasseh that lived east of the Jordan. In 1 Chr 5:24 he is the first named in a list of seven clan leaders described as mighty men of valour and famous men. The surrounding passage says these eastern tribes later turned from God and were carried into exile by the Assyrian king Tiglath-pileser. Easton's Bible Dictionary therefore counts Epher's family among those taken captive. Nothing else is recorded about him. The same name belongs to other people in the Bible, including a son of Midian and a man of Judah, and they should not be confused with him. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "dust" or "lead."

Ephlal was a man of the tribe of Judah, named only in the genealogy of 1 Chr 2:37, where he is the son of Zabad and the father of Obed. The surrounding list traces the line of Jerahmeel, son of Hezron, so Ephlal belonged to the Jerahmeelite clan within Judah, as Smith's Bible Dictionary also notes. By inference from the wider passage, this line came down from Sheshan, whose daughter married an Egyptian servant named Jarha. Nothing else is recorded about Ephlal beyond his place in this family line. His name is usually explained as meaning "judgment" (Smith's Bible Dictionary; International Standard Bible Encyclopedia), and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "judging" or "praying."

Ephod was a man of the tribe of Manasseh, known only as the father of Hanniel. In Num 34:23 Hanniel son of Ephod is named as the prince, or leader, of the tribe of Manasseh, one of the sons of Joseph. The surrounding chapter shows that these tribal leaders were appointed to help divide the land of Canaan among the Israelite tribes. Nothing else is recorded about Ephod himself. His name is spelled the same as the ephod, the priestly garment often mentioned in the Old Testament, but the text does not link the two.

Er was a son of Shelah, the son of Judah, and so a grandson of Judah within the tribe of Judah. He is named only once, in a genealogy at 1 Chr 4:21, where he is called "the father of Lecah." Lecah was probably a town or clan rather than a single son, since Chronicles often uses "father of" for the founder of a settlement. His brothers were Laadah, the father of Mareshah, along with Jokim, Joash and Saraph. The same verse links Shelah's descendants with families of fine linen workers of the house of Ashbea. He should not be confused with his uncle Er, Judah's firstborn, after whom he was probably named. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "watchman."

Er is a man named only in Luke's genealogy of Jesus. He was the son of Jose and the father of Elmodam (Luke 3:28). Jose appears in the next verse of the list, and some translations render his name as Joshua. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia places Er in the seventh generation before Zerubbabel. He belongs to the stretch of Luke's line that runs from David's son Nathan down to Shealtiel and Zerubbabel, so he counts as a member of the tribe of Judah. Nothing else is recorded about him. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "watchman." He should not be confused with other men called Er, such as Judah's eldest son or Judah's grandson, the son of Shelah.

Eran was a son of Shuthelah and a grandson of Ephraim, belonging to the tribe of Ephraim within the descendants of Joseph. He appears only once, in the census taken in the wilderness (Num 26:36), where he is named as the ancestor of the Eranites, a family or clan within the tribe. In that census, Shuthelah heads the main Ephraimite clan and Eran's family is listed as a branch of it. Bered, his brother, is probably the Bered named in the Ephraimite genealogy at 1 Chr 7:20, which lists him as a son of Shuthelah. Nothing else is recorded about Eran's life. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives the meaning of his name as "watcher" or "watchful."

Eshtemoa the Maachathite is named once, in the genealogy of Judah at 1 Chr 4:19, as a son of Hodiah, the sister of Naham. This entry treats Mered as his father. That is an inference from the surrounding verses (1 Chr 4:17–18), which describe Mered's two wives. On that reading, Ishbah, Miriam and Shammai, the children of Mered's other wife, would be Eshtemoa's half-siblings. The same verse also names the father of Keilah the Garmite among Hodiah's sons. Eshtemoa shares his name with a town in the hill country of Judah, and the town Keilah is mentioned beside him. For that reason he is often understood as the ancestor or founder of the people who settled there, though the passage does not say so directly. The meaning of the label "Maachathite" here is uncertain. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "the bosom of a woman."

Esli was an ancestor of Jesus named only in Luke's genealogy, where he appears as the son of Nagge and the father of Naum (Luke 3:25). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia counts him as the tenth generation before Joseph, the husband of Mary, and suggests his name probably stands for the Hebrew name Azaliah. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives its meaning as "near me" or "he who separates." Because Luke's list places him between Zerubbabel (Luke 3:27) and Joseph, he probably lived in the centuries after the return from the Babylonian exile. As part of the line Luke traces back through David, he belonged to the tribe of Judah. Nothing else is recorded about him.

Ethan the Ezrahite was a man famous for his wisdom. 1 Kgs 4:31 names him first in a list of renowned sages, along with Heman, Chalcol and Darda, the sons of Mahol, to show that Solomon was wiser than all of them. The heading of Psalm 89 names Ethan the Ezrahite as its author. "Ezrahite" probably points to descent from Zerah of Judah, since 1 Chr 2:6 lists Ethan, Heman, Calcol and Dara as sons of Zerah. Easton's Bible Dictionary instead places him in the tribe of Levi, linking him with the Levite singer Ethan of David's time. The name is shared by several people in the Bible, so how these figures relate is uncertain. This entry treats him as the wise man of 1 Kings and the author of Psalm 89.

Ethbaal was king of the Sidonians and the father of Jezebel, who married King Ahab of Israel (1 Kgs 16:31). This marriage is mentioned as the setting for Ahab's turn to serving and worshipping Baal. His name is usually taken to mean "with Baal." Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that Josephus calls him king of the Tyrians as well, and identifies him with Eithobalus, who seized the throne of Tyre and ruled for thirty-two years, about 940–908 BC. Easton's Bible Dictionary adds that he was said to have been a priest of Astarte. His link to the royal line of Judah is probably through Athaliah, Ahab's daughter, who married Jehoram of Judah (2 Kgs 8:18, 26). If she was Jezebel's daughter, Ethbaal was an ancestor of the later Davidic kings, though the text does not say directly who her mother was.

Ethnan was a man of the tribe of Judah, named in the genealogy of 1 Chr 4:7 as one of the sons of Helah, alongside Zereth and Jezoar. The surrounding passage (1 Chr 4:5–6) explains that Helah was one of the two wives of Ashur, called the father, probably meaning the founder, of Tekoa. Ashur's other wife, Naarah, bore Ahuzam, Hepher, Temeni and Haahashtari, who were Ethnan's half-brothers. Coz, named next in 1 Chr 4:8, is also treated here as a brother, though the text does not state his parentage directly. His name is usually taken to mean "gift" or "hire," as in Smith's Bible Dictionary and Hitchcock's Bible Names. Nothing else is recorded about him.

Eubulus was a Christian who sent greetings to Timothy at the close of Paul's second letter to him (2 Tim 4:21). He is named alongside Pudens, Linus, Claudia and "all the brethren." Because the letter is usually understood to have been written while Paul was imprisoned in Rome, Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia take Eubulus to be a member of the church there. The ISBE adds that his Greek name suggests he was probably a Gentile by birth. The name means "prudent" or "good counselor," according to Hitchcock's Bible Names. Nothing more is recorded about him, and this is his only mention in the Bible.

Eunice was the mother of Timothy (called Timotheus in the King James Version) and the daughter of Lois. Paul names her in 2 Tim 1:5, recalling the sincere faith that lived first in Lois, then in Eunice, and then in Timothy. Her name is Greek, meaning "good victory" according to Hitchcock's Bible Names. Acts 16:1, which tells how Paul found Timothy at Lystra, describes his mother as a Jewish believer and his father as a Greek, so she probably lived in Lystra. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia infers that she came to faith during Paul's first visit to the city. It also connects her with 2 Tim 3:15, which says Timothy had known the scriptures from childhood, and suggests she taught him there. Nothing more is recorded about her.

Euodias was a Christian woman in the church at Philippi. In Phil 4:2 Paul urges her and another woman, Syntyche, to "be of the same mind in the Lord." The appeal suggests the two had disagreed, though the letter does not say what the dispute was about. The next verse, Phil 4:3, speaks of women who "laboured with me in the gospel," and Easton's Bible Dictionary takes this to include Euodias, describing her as one who worked hard alongside Paul. Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that the name is more accurately spelled Euodia, the form used in the Revised Version and most modern translations. The name is usually explained as meaning "fragrant" or "sweet scent" (Smith's and Hitchcock's Bible Names), while Easton's gives "a good journey." She is mentioned nowhere else in the Bible.

Eutychus was a young man at Troas whose name means "fortunate" (Hitchcock's Bible Names). While Paul was preaching late into the night to the believers gathered in an upper room, Eutychus sat in a window, sank into a deep sleep, and fell from the third story. He "was taken up dead" (Acts 20:9). The surrounding passage (Acts 20:7–12) relates that Paul went down, embraced him and said his life was in him. The gathering then resumed and continued until daybreak, and the young man was brought away alive. Easton's Bible Dictionary compares the scene to the restorations performed by Elijah and Elisha. The episode is told in the "we" section of Acts, which the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia takes as an eyewitness account. It is dated here to about AD 54, an estimate inferred from context.

Ezbai was the father of Naarai, one of the warriors listed among David's mighty men in 1 Chr 11:37. Nothing else is said about him, and he appears only in this verse. The parallel list in 2 Sam 23:35 has "Paarai the Arbite" at this point, so many readers take Naarai and Paarai to be the same man. By that comparison, "son of Ezbai" in Chronicles may correspond to "the Arbite" in Samuel, though how the two readings relate is uncertain. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia give the meaning of the name as "shining," and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia adds "blooming."

Ezbon was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, the first named of five sons of Bela, Benjamin's firstborn. In 1 Chr 7:7 he and his brothers Uzzi, Uzziel, Jerimoth and Iri are called heads of their fathers' houses and mighty men of valour, and their family line is counted at 22,034 fighting men. A separate list of Bela's sons in 1 Chr 8:3–5 gives different names, among them Addar, Gera, Abihud, Abishua, Naaman and Ahoah, and those are counted here as his brothers as well. Ezbon does not appear in that second list. Nothing else is recorded about him. He should not be confused with Ezbon the son of Gad (Gen 46:16). Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "hastening to understand," and Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "working."

Ezer was a man of the tribe of Judah, named in the genealogy of 1 Chr 4:4 as one of the sons of Hur, the firstborn of Ephratah and "father of Bethlehem." He is called "the father of Hushah," which may mean he was the ancestor or founder of the town or clan of Hushah rather than the father of a person, a common usage in these lists. The STEPBible proper-names index describes him as the "father or founder" of Hushah. The name probably means "help," as the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia and Hitchcock's Bible Names give it. Several other men in the Bible share the name Ezer, and nothing beyond this single genealogical mention is recorded about him. His relationship to the other sons of Hur listed with him, such as Penuel, rests on the grouping in this genealogy.

Ezer was a son of Ephraim and so a member of the tribe of Joseph. He is mentioned only in 1 Chr 7:21, which says that he and Elead were killed by the men of Gath who were born in that land, because they had come down to take the people of Gath's cattle. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes these men of Gath as the original inhabitants of the land. The wording of the genealogy leaves it slightly unclear whether Ezer was Ephraim's son or a later descendant, but this entry follows the reading that he was Ephraim's own son. The following verses (1 Chr 7:22–23) say that Ephraim mourned many days and later had another son, Beriah, named because of this trouble. His other brothers include Shuthelah, Becher and Tahan. His name means "help" according to Hitchcock's Bible Names. Several other people in the Bible share the name Ezer.

Ezer was a warrior from the tribe of Gad who joined David while David was an outlaw avoiding King Saul. He is listed first among eleven Gadite leaders in 1 Chr 12:9. The surrounding passage (1 Chr 12:8) describes these Gadites as men of war who crossed over to David at his stronghold in the wilderness. It calls them skilled with shield and spear, with faces like lions and as swift as gazelles on the mountains. Because Ezer is named first, he was probably the chief or most senior of the group. Nothing else is recorded about him. The name, meaning "help" according to the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia, belongs to several different men in the Bible, and this Ezer should not be confused with the others.

Ezer son of Jeshua was one of the men who rebuilt the walls of Jerusalem under Nehemiah after the return from exile. Nehemiah 3:19 calls him "the ruler of Mizpah" and says he repaired a second section of the wall, facing the ascent to the armoury where the wall turned. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary identify him as a Levite. This probably follows from the surrounding passage, which lists Levites among the builders working on this stretch of the wall. His father Jeshua may be the Levite of that name mentioned elsewhere in Nehemiah, but this is not certain. The name Ezer, meaning "help" according to the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia and Hitchcock's Bible Names, is borne by several different men in the Bible, and this Ezer is known only from this one verse.

Ezer was one of the men named at the dedication of the rebuilt wall of Jerusalem in Nehemiah's time. He is the last in a list of eight names given in Neh 12:42, alongside Maaseiah, Shemaiah, Eleazar, Uzzi, Jehohanan, Malchijah and Elam. By inference from the context, this group belonged to one of the two great thanksgiving companies that processed on the wall, and it was linked with the singers led by Jezrahiah. Smith's Bible Dictionary calls him a priest, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia describes him as a musician in one of those companies. Nothing else is recorded about him. Several other men in the Bible share the name, which Hitchcock's Bible Names takes to mean "a help." The event is usually dated to about 446 BC, an estimate inferred from context.

Ezra was a man of the tribe of Judah, named only in the genealogy of 1 Chr 4:17, where he is the father of Jether, Mered, Epher and Jalon. The same verse goes on to say that "she bare" Miriam, Shammai and Ishbah, the father of Eshtemoa. The verse does not name this woman, and the following verse suggests the children belong to one of Mered's wives, so their exact place in the family is unclear. This Ezra is a different man from the well-known priest and scribe who led returning exiles to Jerusalem. Nothing else is recorded about him. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia explains the name as meaning "help," a shortened form of Azariah, "the LORD has helped," and notes that the Hebrew spelling here differs slightly from that used for the scribe.

Ezri, son of Chelub, was the official in charge of the farm laborers who worked King David's fields and tilled the ground (1 Chr 27:26). He is named in a list of David's stewards, the men who managed the king's property, including his vineyards, olive groves, herds and storehouses. Nothing more is recorded about him. His name probably means "my help" or, in a fuller form, "help of the LORD," as Hitchcock's Bible Names and Easton's Bible Dictionary give it. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates his service to about 1014 BC, an estimate drawn from the setting in David's reign. His father Chelub is otherwise unknown and should probably not be confused with the Chelub of the tribe of Judah in 1 Chr 4:11.

Fortunatus was a member of the church at Corinth who, with Stephanas and Achaicus, came to Paul while he was writing 1 Corinthians. Paul says he was glad they had come, because they had supplied what was lacking on the Corinthians' part (1 Cor 16:17). The following verse speaks of their refreshing his spirit. Paul was probably at Ephesus at the time, since he says in 1 Cor 16:8 that he will stay there until Pentecost. Easton's Bible Dictionary adds that the three men probably carried the letter back to Corinth. His name is Latin and means "fortunate" or "blessed." Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that a Fortunatus is named at the end of Clement's first letter to the Corinthians, an early Christian writing outside the Bible, and suggests he may be the same man. He appears only once in the Bible.

Gabbai was a man of the tribe of Benjamin named in the list of those who settled in Jerusalem after the return from the Babylonian exile. In Neh 11:8 he appears with Sallai, following Sallu son of Meshullam, and together they are counted with 928 people. By inference from the context of the chapter, Gabbai and Sallai were leaders or heads of Benjamite families who lived in the city. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him as apparently the head of an important Benjaminite family resident at Jerusalem, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia calls him one of the chiefs of the Benjamites there. The name is usually explained as meaning "collector" or "tax gatherer." Nothing else is recorded about him.

Gaddi, son of Susi, was the man chosen from the tribe of Manasseh, which is counted here as part of the tribe of Joseph, to be one of the twelve men Moses sent to explore the land of Canaan (Num 13:11). The surrounding chapter shows that each tribe supplied one leader for this mission. Nothing more is recorded about him. By inference from the chapter, he would have been among the ten scouts whose discouraging report led the people to refuse to enter the land, since only Joshua and Caleb are singled out as giving a favorable account. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "fortunate," and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia renders it "my fortune."

Gaddiel son of Sodi was the man from the tribe of Zebulun among the twelve men Moses sent to explore the land of Canaan (Num 13:10). The surrounding chapter describes the twelve as tribal leaders sent from the wilderness of Paran. Only Joshua and Caleb are named later for urging Israel to go in, so Gaddiel was probably among the ten whose discouraging report turned the people against entering the land, as Numbers 13–14 recounts. He is not mentioned anywhere else. His name is usually explained as "fortune of God" (Easton's Bible Dictionary, Smith's Bible Dictionary) or "blessed of God" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia).

Gaham was a son of Nahor, the brother of Abraham, by Nahor's concubine Reumah. He is named only once, in Gen 22:24, in the list of Nahor's children reported to Abraham after the testing of Isaac. His full brothers and sister were Tebah, Thahash and Maachah. Through Nahor's wife Milcah he had eight half-brothers, among them Huz, Buz, Kemuel and Bethuel, the father of Rebekah. Nothing else is recorded about him, and no descendants are named. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "sunburnt" and dates him to about 1900 BC. Like other dates for this period, that figure is an estimate inferred from context.

Gaius (of Macedonia) was a man from Macedonia who traveled with the apostle Paul. During the riot in Ephesus, stirred up by the silversmith Demetrius according to the wider account in Acts 19, the crowd seized Gaius and his fellow Macedonian Aristarchus and rushed them into the city's theater (Acts 19:29). Smith's Bible Dictionary and others suggest the mob took them because Paul himself could not be found. The riot took place during Paul's third missionary journey, about AD 53 by inference from context. Nothing more is said of what happened to Gaius. The name Gaius was common, and several men called Gaius appear in the New Testament. Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies this Gaius with Paul's host at Corinth (Rom 16:23; 1 Cor 1:14). Others treat them as different people, and this entry follows that view.

Gaius (of Derbe) was one of the companions who travelled with Paul on his last journey toward Jerusalem, at the end of his mission through Macedonia and Greece. Acts 20:4 lists him with Sopater of Berea, Aristarchus and Secundus of Thessalonica, Timothy, and Tychicus and Trophimus of Asia, all of whom went with Paul into Asia. The group probably carried the collection from the churches for the believers in Jerusalem, by inference from the context of Paul's travels. Derbe was a town in Lycaonia in southern Asia Minor that Paul had visited earlier (Acts 14:20). The New Testament names several men called Gaius, including a Macedonian companion of Paul at Ephesus (Acts 19:29), a Corinthian whom Paul baptised (1 Cor 1:14), and the recipient of 3 John. Whether any of them is the same person is uncertain. This entry treats Gaius of Derbe separately. The journey is dated about AD 54, by inference from context.

Gaius was the Christian to whom the letter known as 3 John is addressed. The writer calls himself "the elder" and greets Gaius as "wellbeloved," one whom he loves "in the truth" (3 John 1:1). Christian tradition identifies the elder as the apostle John. Easton's Bible Dictionary places Gaius in Asia Minor. The rest of the letter praises him for staying faithful to the truth and for welcoming travelling Christian workers, as the STEPBible proper-names index also notes. The name was common in the Roman world, and several men called Gaius appear in the New Testament, including companions of Paul in Macedonia, Derbe and Corinth. Whether this Gaius is any of them is uncertain, so this entry treats him as a separate person. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "lord" or "an earthly man."

Galal was a Levite named in 1 Chr 9:15 among the Levites who lived in Jerusalem, in a list that by context describes the community resettled there after the Babylonian exile. He appears alongside Bakbakkar, Heresh and Mattaniah, the son of Micah, whose descent is traced back to Asaph. Smith's Bible Dictionary counts Galal himself among the sons of Asaph, and the STEPBible Proper Names index describes him as a Levite musician descended from Asaph. The verse does not state his own ancestry, so that link rests on how the list is read. Smith's dates him to about 536 BC, an estimate drawn from the setting rather than stated in the text. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "a roll, a wheel." Several men in the Bible bear the name Galal, and this entry covers only the one in 1 Chr 9:15.

Gamul was a priest whose family received the twenty-second of the twenty-four priestly divisions when the courses of service at the sanctuary were assigned by lot (1 Chr 24:17). The surrounding chapter places this arrangement in the time of King David, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia describes Gamul as head of that course. Each division took its turn serving at the house of the Lord. Nothing else is recorded about him. His name is usually understood to mean "weaned" (Easton's Bible Dictionary, Smith's Bible Dictionary), while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "a recompense."

Garmite is a name in the tribe of Judah's genealogy at 1 Chr 4:19, which lists the sons of Hodiah, sister of Naham, as "the father of Keilah the Garmite, and Eshtemoa the Maachathite." The wording is obscure, and readings differ. Smith's Bible Dictionary takes "Garmite" to mean a descendant of Gerem, a label attached to Keilah. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia also treats it as a clan name applied to Keilah, and says the reason is unknown. This entry treats Garmite as a son of Hodiah and Mered and a brother of Eshtemoa. Hodiah's husband is inferred to be Mered from the surrounding verses. Through Mered's other wife, Bithiah, Pharaoh's daughter, he would be a half-brother of Miriam, Shammai and Ishbah (1 Chr 4:17–18). Nothing else is recorded about him.

Gazez was a man of the tribe of Judah, named only in the genealogy of 1 Chr 2:46. He was a son of Caleb by Ephah, Caleb's concubine, and his full brothers were Haran and Moza. Through Caleb he was related to a large group of other children in the same genealogy, including Mesha, Jesher, Shobab, Ardon, Jahdai and Achsa, and half-brothers such as Hur, Sheber and Tirhanah. The same verse also names a second Gazez, a son of Haran, which would make him this Gazez's nephew. It is not clear whether the verse means two separate men or repeats one name, and this entry treats the son of Caleb as a distinct person. Nothing else is recorded about him. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "a passing over."

Gazez, son of Haran, was a member of the tribe of Judah named in the genealogy of Caleb's descendants (1 Chr 2:46). His father Haran was a son of Caleb by Caleb's concubine Ephah, which makes this Gazez Caleb's grandson. The same verse also lists a Gazez among Ephah's own sons, alongside Haran and Moza, so the name appears twice in one line: once for a son of Caleb and once for a son of Haran. Whether these are two different men, an uncle and nephew sharing a name, or a single person mentioned twice is not clear from the text, and this entry treats the son of Haran as a separate individual. Nothing further is recorded about him. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "a passing over."

Geber was the father of one of the twelve district officers who supplied food for King Solomon and his household. He is known only through his son, whose name is not given in the King James Version. The son was based at Ramoth-gilead and oversaw the towns of Jair in Gilead and the region of Argob in Bashan, which had sixty large walled cities with bronze bars, a district east of the Jordan (1 Kgs 4:13). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the Revised Version treats "Ben-geber" ("son of Geber") as the officer's own name. On that reading Geber himself is not really a separate figure. Nothing else is recorded about him. The name, which means "man" or "strong one," is shared by another person in the same list of officers, so the two should not be confused.

Geber son of Uri was one of the twelve district officers King Solomon appointed to supply food for the royal household, and he is the last named in the list. His district was east of the Jordan in Gilead. It covered the former territory of Sihon king of the Amorites and of Og king of Bashan (1 Kgs 4:19). The verse calls him "the only officer which was in the land." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests this probably means one official was assigned to this large region because it could supply less than the others. That source and Smith's Bible Dictionary place his district probably south of the one held by Ben-geber, who is named earlier in the list (1 Kgs 4:13). The name Geber means "man" or "strong one." Because several people in the Bible share the name, he should be kept distinct from the others.

Gedaliah was a priest in the time of Ezra, one of the descendants of Jeshua son of Jozadak, the high priest who returned from exile in Babylon. He appears only in Ezra 10:18, in the list of priests found to have married foreign wives. The following verse (Ezra 10:19) says that these men of Jeshua's family pledged to send their wives away and offered a ram as a guilt offering, so Gedaliah was probably among those who made that pledge. Nothing else is recorded about him. The name, meaning "the LORD is great" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia), was borne by several people in the Bible. This Gedaliah is distinct from the better-known governor of Judah appointed by the Babylonians after the fall of Jerusalem.

Gedaliah son of Pashur was one of the officials in Jerusalem during the reign of King Zedekiah, shortly before the city fell to Babylon. He is named with Shephatiah son of Mattan, Jucal son of Shelemiah and Pashur son of Malchiah as having heard Jeremiah tell the people that those who stayed in the city would die, while those who surrendered to the Chaldeans would live (Jer 38:1). The following verses of the chapter show these officials asking the king to put Jeremiah to death, and Jeremiah being lowered into a muddy cistern. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes Gedaliah as one of the nobles who conspired against the prophet. His father Pashur may be the priest Pashur son of Immer who had earlier put Jeremiah in the stocks (Jer 20:1–2), but the text does not say so. Several other men in the Bible share the name Gedaliah.

Gedaliah was an ancestor of the prophet Zephaniah, named in the genealogy that opens the book of Zephaniah. He was the son of Amariah and the father of Cushi, so he was Zephaniah's grandfather (Zeph 1:1). The same verse traces the line back one more generation to Hizkiah. Many readers take Hizkiah to be King Hezekiah of Judah, though the text does not say so. Zephaniah prophesied in the days of King Josiah, so Gedaliah probably lived a couple of generations earlier, in the late eighth or early seventh century BC, by inference from the genealogy. Nothing else is recorded about him. Several other men in the Bible share his name, including the governor of Judah appointed after the Babylonian conquest, and this Gedaliah should not be confused with them. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the name's meaning as "God is my greatness."

Gemalli was a man of the tribe of Dan and the father of Ammiel, who represented Dan among the twelve men Moses sent to explore the land of Canaan (Num 13:12). He is mentioned only in this one verse, and nothing else is recorded about him. Gemalli therefore belonged to the generation that left Egypt in the exodus, but the text gives no further details of his life. His name is usually linked to the Hebrew word for "camel". The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia renders it "camel owner", and Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "camel-driver".

Gemariah son of Hilkiah was one of two envoys whom King Zedekiah of Judah sent to Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon. He traveled with Elasah son of Shaphan, and the two carried Jeremiah's letter to the Jewish exiles in Babylon (Jer 29:3). Easton's Bible Dictionary adds that the mission carried tribute from Zedekiah, and Smith's Bible Dictionary dates it to about 594 BC. His father Hilkiah is often taken to be the high priest of Josiah's reign who found the book of the law (2 Kgs 22). That would explain why this entry places Gemariah in the tribe of Levi and names Azariah as his brother, since 1 Chr 6:13 lists Azariah as a son of Hilkiah. This identification is an inference. He is a different man from Gemariah son of Shaphan in Jer 36. The name means "the LORD has accomplished."

Genubath was the son of Hadad, a member of Edom's royal family, and of the sister of Tahpenes, the wife of the Egyptian Pharaoh. His only mention, 1 Kgs 11:20, says that Tahpenes herself weaned him in Pharaoh's house and that he grew up in the royal household among Pharaoh's own sons. The surrounding passage explains how this came about: Hadad had fled to Egypt as a child when David's forces conquered Edom, and there he won Pharaoh's favor and married into the royal family. Genubath was therefore born and raised at the Egyptian court, probably during the later part of David's reign, by inference from context. According to Easton's and Hitchcock's dictionaries, his name means "theft." Nothing more is recorded about his life.

Gera was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, a son of Bela and so a grandson of Benjamin. He is named second among Bela's sons in 1 Chr 8:3, after Addar and before Abihud. The list goes on in 1 Chr 8:4–5 and names a second Gera among the same brothers, which may be a copying repetition or a second person of that name. Other brothers of his appear in a separate list of Bela's sons in 1 Chr 7:7. Gen 46:21 names a Gera as a son of Benjamin himself, and later Benjamites such as Ehud and Shimei are called sons of Gera, so the name seems to have been common in the tribe, perhaps as a family name. Several people therefore bear it, and it is uncertain how they relate. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives its meaning as "pilgrimage, combat; dispute."

Gera was a Benjamite named as one of the sons of Ehud in the genealogy of the tribe of Benjamin (1 Chr 8:7). He is listed with Naaman and Ahiah. The surrounding passage says Ehud's family were heads of households in Geba and were moved to Manahath (1 Chr 8:6), and 1 Chr 8:7 adds "he removed them". The STEPBible proper names index reads this phrase as an alternative name, Gera or Heglam, and describes him as among those carried into exile. The verse goes on to say that someone "begat Uzza, and Ahihud". The wording is unclear, but this entry counts them among Ehud's sons and so as Gera's brothers. Nothing else is recorded about him. The name was shared by several Benjamites, including a son of Benjamin, the father of the judge Ehud, and the father of Shimei. This Gera should be kept distinct from them.

Gershom was the father of Jonathan, the man who served as priest to the tribe of Dan at the carved image the Danites set up in their new territory. In Judg 18:30 the King James Version calls Gershom the son of Manasseh, and says Jonathan and his sons kept this priesthood until the land went into captivity. Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that the Revised Version reads "son of Moses" here instead. On that reading this Gershom would be Moses' son of the same name (Exod 2:22), and Jonathan his descendant. This entry follows the King James wording, which lists Manasseh as his father. Several men in the Bible bear the name Gershom, and nothing more is told about this one. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "a stranger here."

Gershom was a priest descended from Phinehas, Aaron's grandson, who returned from Babylon to Jerusalem with Ezra. In Ezra 8:2 he heads the list of family leaders who travelled with Ezra, standing for the priestly line of Phinehas, alongside Daniel for the line of Ithamar and Hattush for the line of David. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia calls him the head of a father's house and places the journey in the reign of Artaxerxes, as the surrounding chapter indicates. Nothing else is recorded about him. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "a stranger here." The same name belongs to other people in the Bible, most notably Moses' son, so this Gershom should not be confused with them.

Gesham was a son of Jahdai, named in the genealogy of the tribe of Judah in 1 Chr 2:47. The King James Version spells his name Geshan. He is listed with five brothers, Regem, Jotham, Pelet, Ephah and Shaaph. Smith's Bible Dictionary places this family within the line of Caleb. That fits the surrounding verses, which list Caleb's descendants, though Jahdai's own connection to Caleb is not stated and has to be inferred from where he appears. Nothing else is recorded about Gesham beyond his name and his place in this list.

Geuel, son of Machi, was the man from the tribe of Gad among the twelve spies Moses sent to explore the land of Canaan (Num 13:15). The surrounding chapter shows that each spy represented one tribe and that most of them returned with a discouraging report. Only Caleb and Joshua are singled out as dissenting, so Geuel was presumably among the others. He is not mentioned anywhere else. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia and Smith's Bible Dictionary give his name's meaning as "majesty of God," while Hitchcock's Bible Names renders it "God's redemption."

Gilalai was a musician who took part in the dedication of the rebuilt wall of Jerusalem in Nehemiah's time. He appears only in Neh 12:36, among the "brethren" of Zechariah who played "the musical instruments of David the man of God" in a procession led by Ezra the scribe. The preceding verse, Neh 12:35, identifies Zechariah as the son of Jonathan and one of the priests' sons with trumpets. That is why Gilalai is counted here as a son of Jonathan and a brother of Zechariah, Shemaiah, Azarael, Milalai, Maai, Nethaneel, Judah and Hanani, though "brethren" could also mean fellow members of a group. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him as one of the priests' sons and dates the event to about 446 BC. The meaning of his name is uncertain: Smith's gives "weighty" and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "a wheel."

Gilead was the father of Jephthah, the judge of Israel described as a mighty warrior. Judg 11:1 says Jephthah's mother was a prostitute and that Gilead fathered him. The next verse, Judg 11:2, adds that Gilead's wife also bore him sons, and that these half-brothers later drove Jephthah away from the family inheritance because of his birth. Nothing else is recorded about Gilead himself. His name is the same as that of the region east of the Jordan and of an earlier descendant of Manasseh, so it is not certain how far the name here refers to a specific individual rather than to the clan or territory Jephthah came from. This entry follows the plain reading, as the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia does, and treats him as Jephthah's actual father. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "the heap or mass of testimony."

Gilead was a man of the tribe of Gad, named only once, in the Gadite genealogy of 1 Chr 5:14. He was the son of Michael and the father of Jaroah, and his line is traced back through Jeshishai and Jahdo to Buz. Through Jaroah he was an ancestor of Huri, Abihail and Abihail's sons, a family the surrounding passage places among the Gadites living east of the Jordan in Bashan and the region of Gilead. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia lists him as a Gadite, and he shares his name with the land of Gilead and with other men called Gilead, including the better-known descendant of Manasseh. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "the heap or mass of testimony." Nothing else is recorded about him.

Gispa was one of two men placed over the Nethinim, the temple servants, in Jerusalem after the return from exile in Babylon. Nehemiah 11:21 says the Nethinim lived in Ophel, the hill area south of the temple, and that Ziha and Gispa were in charge of them. Nothing else is recorded about him. Some reference works spell the name Gishpa. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives its meaning as "caress," while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "coming hither." A Ziha also appears among the families of Nethinim who returned with Zerubbabel (Ezra 2:43), so Gispa's fellow overseer may have belonged to or led that family. This is an inference.

Gog was a descendant of Reuben, named once in a family line in 1 Chr 5:4. The verse traces a line of descent from Joel: Shemaiah his son, Gog his son, Shimei his son. This makes Gog the son of Shemaiah, the grandson of Joel, and the father of Shimei. The surrounding chapter lists the descendants of Reuben, Jacob's firstborn, and Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary both identify Gog as a Reubenite. Nothing else is recorded about his life. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "roof" or "covering." Several people in the Bible share this name. This Reubenite is a different figure from the Gog of the land of Magog in Ezek 38–39, a leader of nations who is mentioned again in Rev 20:8.

Gomer (wife of Hosea) was the daughter of Diblaim and the wife of the prophet Hosea, whom he married at the beginning of his prophetic work (Hos 1:3). The surrounding passage says Hosea was told to take "a wife of whoredoms" (Hos 1:2), and their marriage serves in the book as a picture of Israel's relationship with God. Gomer bore a son, Jezreel, then a daughter, Lo-ruhamah, and another son, Lo-ammi. Their names were given as signs to Israel (Hos 1:4–9). In Hos 3:1–3 Hosea is told to love an adulterous woman again and buys her back. Many readers, including the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia, take this woman to be Gomer, though she is not named there. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of her name as "to finish; complete." She is a different person from Gomer the son of Japheth.

Guni was a man of the tribe of Gad, named in the Gadite genealogy of 1 Chronicles 5. He was the father of Abdiel and the grandfather of Ahi, who is described as chief of his father's house (1 Chr 5:15). The surrounding passage places these Gadites in the land of Bashan and Gilead, east of the Jordan. Nothing else is recorded about him. The name Guni is also borne by another man in the Bible, a son of Naphtali, so the Gadite here should not be confused with him. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "a garden" or "a covering," while Smith's Bible Dictionary renders it "painted."

Haahashtari was a man of the tribe of Judah, named in the Chronicles genealogy as one of the four sons of Ashur by his wife Naarah. His brothers were Ahuzam, Hepher and Temeni (1 Chr 4:6). According to the preceding verse, Ashur, called the father of Tekoa, had two wives, Helah and Naarah. Through Helah he had further sons, Zereth, Jezoar and Ethnan, who were Haahashtari's half-brothers. Coz is listed alongside them in the same family. Nothing else is recorded about him. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of his name as "a runner," and Smith's Bible Dictionary as "the courier." Smith's allows that the name may refer to a family rather than a single man. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests the Hebrew may be a scribal variant of "the Ashurites," a label describing the names before it. This entry treats Haahashtari as an individual son of Ashur.

Habaziniah was the father of a man named Jeremiah and the grandfather of Jaazaniah, who led the Rechabites in the time of the prophet Jeremiah. He is mentioned only once, in a genealogy identifying Jaazaniah when the prophet brought the Rechabite household into a room of the temple and offered them wine, which they refused out of loyalty to their ancestor Jonadab's command (Jer 35:3). His son Jeremiah is a different person from the prophet. Smith's Bible Dictionary takes Habaziniah to have been the head of one of the Rechabite families and dates him before 589 BC. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the Revised Version spells the name Habazziniah. Nothing else is recorded about him.

Hachmoni was the father of Jehiel, a man who served at King David's court and "was with the king's sons" (1 Chr 27:32). The phrase probably means that Jehiel looked after or tutored the royal princes. He is named alongside Jonathan, David's uncle, who was a counsellor and scribe. Nothing else is recorded about Hachmoni himself. Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests that Hachmoni may have been the founder of a family rather than an immediate father, since the related name "Hachmonite" is also applied to Jashobeam, one of David's mighty men (1 Chr 11:11), whose actual father was Zabdiel. On that view "son of Hachmoni" would mean a member of the Hachmonite family. This entry treats him as Jehiel's father, as the verse reads. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "a wise man."

Hadlai was an Ephraimite, known only as the father of Amasa. His son was one of the leaders of the tribe of Ephraim who stood up against the soldiers of the northern kingdom returning from war against Judah. Those soldiers had brought back captives from Judah, and the leaders objected to keeping them (2 Chr 28:12). By context these events fell in the time of Pekah, king of Israel, and Ahaz, king of Judah, as the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes. Nothing else is recorded about Hadlai himself. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "resting," and Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "rest of God."

Hagab was the ancestor of a family of temple servants (the Nethinim) whose descendants returned from exile in Babylon to Jerusalem with Zerubbabel, as recorded in the list of returning families in Ezra 2:46. Nothing else is known of him as an individual. His name probably means "locust," according to Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that his family is listed just after the similar name Hagabah but is missing from the parallel list of returning temple servants in Neh 7:48. The return under Zerubbabel is usually dated to about 536 BC or shortly before, an estimate drawn from context rather than stated in the text.

Haggeri is named in 1 Chr 11:38 as the father of Mibhar, one of the mighty men of David listed in that chapter. Nothing else is recorded about him. In the parallel list of David's warriors at 2 Sam 23:36, the corresponding place reads "Bani the Gadite." Smith's Bible Dictionary takes that as the probable original reading, which suggests that "Mibhar the son of Haggeri" may reflect a difference in how the text was handed down. Following the same connection, the STEPBible proper-names index places Haggeri's family in the tribe of Gad. Some reference works, such as the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia, spell the name Hagri. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives its meaning as "a stranger," and Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "wanderer."

Haggiah was a Levite from the line of Merari, named once in the genealogy of the Levites at 1 Chr 6:30. There he is listed as the son of Shimea and the father of Asaiah. The surrounding verses trace Merari's descendants generation by generation, and the Merarite placement follows from that context, as Smith's Bible Dictionary also notes. Nothing else is recorded about his life. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of his name as "the Lord's feast," and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia renders it "feast of Yah." His son Asaiah may be the Merarite Asaiah who later helped bring the ark to Jerusalem under David, but the text does not make that link directly.

Hakkatan was the father of Johanan, who led the family group descended from Azgad when it returned from Babylon to Jerusalem with Ezra. Johanan brought 110 men with him (Ezra 8:12). Hakkatan is known only through this mention of his son, and nothing else is recorded about him. Whether he went back to Jerusalem himself is not stated. His name means "the little one" or "the young one" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia; Smith's Bible Dictionary). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the parallel list in 1 Esdras 8:38 gives the name as Akatan.

Hakkoz was a priest whose name was given to the seventh of the twenty-four divisions of priests. These divisions were drawn by lot in David's time to take turns serving at the sanctuary (1 Chr 24:10). Easton's Bible Dictionary describes him as the head of one of these priestly courses, and gives the name's meaning as "the thorn." Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that the same name appears as Koz in the King James Version of Ezra 2:61 and Nehemiah 3:4, 21. Those passages concern a later priestly family of that name, so the connection between the two is probably one of family descent. Beyond his place in the order of the priestly courses, nothing more is recorded about him.

Hallohesh was one of the leaders of the people who set their seal to the covenant made in the time of Nehemiah, after the return from exile. Nehemiah 10 lists him among the chiefs who pledged to keep the law. Neh 10:24 names him beside Pileha and Shobek. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia takes him to be the same man as Halohesh of Neh 3:12, whose son Shallum, ruler of half the district of Jerusalem, helped repair the city walls with his daughters. Because the two passages may refer to the same family or to different people, that link is uncertain. Smith's Bible Dictionary explains the name as "enchanter", while the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives "the whisperer". Smith's dates the covenant to about 410 BC, an estimate.

Halohesh was the father of Shallum, who helped rebuild the walls of Jerusalem under Nehemiah. He is named only to identify his son. Shallum, described as ruler of half the district of Jerusalem, repaired a section of the wall with his daughters (Neh 3:12). Smith's Bible Dictionary dates the wall repair to about 446 BC, an estimate drawn from context. Nothing else is said about Halohesh himself. A man spelled Hallohesh appears among the leaders who sealed the covenant in Neh 10:24. He may be the same person or a member of the same family, but the text does not say so.

Hammoleketh was a woman of the tribe of Manasseh, part of the wider Joseph tribes, named only in the genealogy of 1 Chr 7. She is called the sister of Gilead, so she was a daughter of Machir, Manasseh's son. Peresh and Sheresh, Machir's sons by his wife Maachah in the preceding verses, were her brothers. 1 Chr 7:18 says she bore Ishod, Abiezer and Mahalah. Her name means "the queen," according to Easton's Bible Dictionary. Her son Abiezer probably gave his name to the Abiezrite clan of Manasseh. That clan appears among Manasseh's family groups in Josh 17:2, and Gideon belonged to it, as Judg 6:11 shows. Nothing else is recorded about her.

Hamuel was a man of the tribe of Simeon, named only in the Simeonite genealogy of 1 Chr 4:26. He was the son of Mishma and the father of Zacchur, whose son was Shimei. Smith's Bible Dictionary places him in the family of Shaul, a son of Simeon, which fits the surrounding verses. It gives the meaning of his name as "heat," that is, "wrath, of God." Some reference works, including the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia, spell the name Hammuel. Nothing else is recorded about him.

Hanan was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, one of the sons of Shashak listed in the Benjamite genealogy of 1 Chronicles 8. His brothers named in the same list include Abdon, Zichri, Hananiah, Elam, Antothijah, Iphedeiah, Ishpan, Heber, Eliel and Penuel. 1 Chr 8:28 describes the men of this list as heads of their fathers' houses living in Jerusalem, and on that basis Smith's Bible Dictionary calls him one of the chief people of the tribe. Nothing else is recorded about him. The name, which means "gracious" or "merciful," is shared by several other men in the Old Testament, and this Hanan should not be confused with them.

Hanan son of Maachah was one of David's mighty warriors. He appears only once, in the extended list of heroes in 1 Chr 11:43, where he is named alongside Joshaphat the Mithnite. This part of the list goes beyond the parallel roster in 2 Samuel 23, and nothing further is recorded about his deeds or background. Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests that "son of Maachah" might mean he came from the Syrian district of Aram-maachah, though Maachah may simply be his father's name, as this entry takes it. The name Hanan means "gracious" or "merciful." Several other men in the Bible share the name, and this Hanan should not be confused with them.

Hanan was one of the men who put their seal to the covenant made under Nehemiah, in which the returned exiles in Jerusalem pledged to keep the Law of Moses. He appears only in Neh 10:22, in a list of names with no further details. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary count him among the chiefs or heads of the people, since the verse falls within the list of lay leaders (Neh 10:14–27). STEPBible's Tyndale names list describes him as a Levite. Smith dates the sealing to about 410 BC, an estimate. Several other men in the Bible share the name Hanan, including two more in the same chapter, so he should not be confused with them. The name is usually taken to mean "merciful" or "gracious."

Hanan was one of the men who set their seal to the written covenant made in Jerusalem under Nehemiah, by which the returned exiles bound themselves to keep the Law of Moses. He is named only once, in Neh 10:26, between Ahijah and Anan. That verse falls within the list of the "chief of the people" (Neh 10:14–27), and Smith's Bible Dictionary counts him among the leading laymen who signed. The STEPBible names index describes him as a Levite. This entry follows the lay identification, which places him among the heads of the people. Nothing else is recorded about him. Several other men in the Bible share the name, including a Levite named Hanan earlier in the same list (Neh 10:10), so he should not be confused with them. The name is usually explained as meaning "merciful" or "full of grace."

Hanan, son of Zaccur and grandson of Mattaniah, was one of the men Nehemiah appointed as treasurers over the temple storehouses in Jerusalem after the return from exile. He served alongside Shelemiah the priest, Zadok the scribe and Pedaiah the Levite. They were chosen because they were considered trustworthy, and their job was to distribute supplies to their fellow workers. By inference from the context, these supplies were the tithes of grain, wine and oil brought in for the Levites and singers, and Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him as a storekeeper of the provisions collected as tithes. The name means "merciful" or "full of grace," according to Smith's and Hitchcock's dictionaries. Several other men in the Bible are also named Hanan, and this one is known only from Neh 13:13.

Hanan was the son of Igdaliah, mentioned once in the Bible. His name means "gracious" or "merciful." Jeremiah brought the Rechabites into the temple in Jerusalem, to a room belonging to "the sons of Hanan." This room was next to the chamber of the princes and above the chamber of Maaseiah son of Shallum, the doorkeeper (Jer 35:4). The verse calls someone "a man of God," but it is unclear whether this means Hanan or his father Igdaliah. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia applies it to Igdaliah. The title may mean a prophet, and Hanan's "sons" may have been his disciples or followers rather than his children, though the text does not say so. The setting of the chapter places him in the time of King Jehoiakim, near the end of the kingdom of Judah. Several other people in the Bible share the name Hanan.

Hanani was a priest from the family of Immer who returned from exile in Babylon and is listed among the men who had married foreign wives in the time of Ezra. He appears with Zebadiah under the heading "of the sons of Immer" (Ezra 10:20). By inference from the surrounding chapter, he was among those who agreed to send away their foreign wives, and the priests listed alongside him pledged to do so and offered a ram as a guilt offering. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both identify him as a priest. The name, meaning "gracious," belongs to several men in the Bible, and this Hanani should not be confused with others of the same name, such as the seer of King Asa's time or Nehemiah's brother.

Hanani was one of the musicians who took part in the dedication of the rebuilt wall of Jerusalem in Nehemiah's time. He is named last in a group of eight "brethren" who played "the musical instruments of David the man of God," with Ezra the scribe leading them in the procession (Neh 12:36). The preceding verse introduces Zechariah son of Jonathan, and the group in Neh 12:36 is called his brethren. This entry treats Hanani as Jonathan's son and Zechariah's brother, though "brethren" may mean kinsmen or fellow musicians rather than full brothers. Smith's Bible Dictionary calls him a priest, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia describes him as a priest and chief musician. Nothing else is recorded about him. Several other men in the Bible share the name, which means "gracious."

Hananiah was a member of the tribe of Benjamin, named in the Benjamite genealogy of 1 Chr 8:24 as one of the sons of Shashak. His brothers listed with him include Ishpan, Heber, Eliel, Abdon, Zichri, Hanan, Elam, Antothijah, Iphedeiah and Penuel. The passage gives no details about his life beyond his place in the family line. Easton's Bible Dictionary calls him a chief of Benjamin, and Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him as the head of a Benjamite house, following the genealogy's summary of these men as heads of fathers' houses. His name means roughly "the Lord has been gracious." It was common in Israel, so he should be kept distinct from the several other men called Hananiah in the Bible.

Hananiah was one of the captains of King Uzziah of Judah. 2 Chr 26:11 describes Uzziah's army, which went out to war in organized bands. Jeiel the scribe and Maaseiah the official counted and recorded it, and the whole work was under Hananiah's direction. Easton's Bible Dictionary calls him one of Uzziah's military officers, and Smith's Bible Dictionary calls him a general. The name, meaning roughly "the Lord has been gracious," was common in Israel, and several different men in the Bible bear it. This Hananiah is known only from this one verse, and nothing more is told about his family or career.

Hananiah was a descendant of Bebai, one of the family groups of Israel, in the time of Ezra. He appears with Jehohanan, Zabbai and Athlai in Ezra 10:28. That verse belongs to the list in Ezra 10 of men who had married foreign wives and who, in response to Ezra's reforms after the return from exile in Babylon, agreed to send those wives away. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him as one of the sons of Bebai who returned with Ezra from Babylon. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia calls him a Levite and notes that he also appears in the parallel list in 1 Esdras 9:29. Nothing more is recorded about him. His name, meaning roughly "the Lord has been gracious," was common in Israel, and he should not be confused with the several other men called Hananiah.

Hananiah was one of the men who repaired the wall of Jerusalem under Nehemiah after the return from exile. Nehemiah 3:8 describes him as "the son of one of the apothecaries," a phrase usually understood to mean that he belonged to the guild of perfume or ointment makers. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia renders it this way, calling him one of the perfumers. He worked on the section next to Uzziel, a goldsmith, and the workers in this stretch fortified the city as far as the Broad Wall. Nothing else is recorded about him. The name, meaning roughly "the Lord has been gracious," was common in Israel, and several other men called Hananiah appear in the Bible. This one is not clearly identified with any of them.

Hananiah, son of Shelemiah, was one of the men who rebuilt the walls of Jerusalem under Nehemiah after the return from exile. Nehemiah 3 lists the builders section by section, and Neh 3:30 says that Hananiah and Hanun, the sixth son of Zalaph, together repaired "another piece." The phrase suggests they took on a second stretch of wall. By inference from the nearby verses, this section lay on the eastern side of the city, near the Horse Gate, as the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia places it. That work further suggests the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes he may be the same man as another Hananiah named among the wall builders. His name, common in Israel, means "the LORD has been gracious." Nothing else is recorded about him.

Hananiah was the ruler of the palace in Jerusalem in the time of Nehemiah. After the city wall was rebuilt, Nehemiah put him in charge of Jerusalem together with Nehemiah's brother Hanani. Nehemiah explains the choice by saying Hananiah was a faithful man who feared God more than many others (Neh 7:2). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia takes "the palace" to mean the fortress or citadel (the birah) guarding the temple area. Smith's Bible Dictionary connects him with the arrangements for guarding the city gates described in the following verse, and dates his appointment to about 446 BC. The name means "the LORD has been gracious" and was common in Israel, so this man is distinct from the several others called Hananiah in the Bible. Whether he is the same as any other Hananiah named in Nehemiah is uncertain.

Hananiah was one of the men who sealed the written covenant in Nehemiah's time, when the community that had returned from exile in Babylon pledged to keep God's law. He is known only from his name in the list of those who set their seal to it (Neh 10:23), where he appears between Hoshea and Hashub. The surrounding section of the list (Neh 10:14–27) names the leaders of the people. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia describes him as a Levite. Nothing else is recorded about him. The name, meaning "the Lord has been gracious," was common in Israel, and several other men named Hananiah appear in Nehemiah's time. Whether this man is the same as any of them is uncertain.

Hananiah was a priest in the generation after the return from exile in Babylon. Neh 12:12 names him as head of the priestly family of Jeremiah in the days of Joiakim. Joiakim was the high priest who succeeded his father Jeshua, according to Neh 12:10 and 12:26. The family of Jeremiah was probably named after the priest Jeremiah who came back with Zerubbabel and Jeshua (Neh 12:1). It is a different person from the prophet Jeremiah. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes Hananiah simply as a priest, son of Jeremiah. Smith's Bible Dictionary calls him the head of that priestly course. Nothing else is recorded about him. Several other men in the Bible share the name, which means roughly "the Lord has been gracious."

Hananiah was a priest who blew a trumpet at the dedication of Jerusalem's rebuilt wall in Nehemiah's time. Neh 12:41 lists him last among seven priests with trumpets, after Eliakim, Maaseiah, Miniamin, Michaiah, Elioenai and Zechariah. By inference from the surrounding chapter, this group went with the second of the two thanksgiving choirs that marched along the wall. Nothing else is recorded about him. Several other men in the Bible bear the same name, and it is uncertain whether this priest is the same as any of them, so this entry treats him as a separate person. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "grace," "mercy," or "gift of the Lord."

Hananiah was the father of Zedekiah, one of the princes of Judah during the reign of King Jehoiakim. He is known only through his son, who was among the officials sitting in the scribe's chamber of the royal palace when Micaiah son of Gemariah came to report the reading of Jeremiah's scroll by Baruch (Jer 36:12). Nothing further is recorded about Hananiah himself. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia lists him as the father of one of the princes under Jehoiakim. His name means "the LORD has been gracious" and was common in Israel, so he should be distinguished from others called Hananiah. These include the prophet who opposed Jeremiah and Daniel's companion, who was renamed Shadrach. Whether he is connected to any of them is not stated.

Hananiah was the father of Shelemiah and the grandfather of Irijah, the captain of the guard at the gate of Benjamin in Jerusalem. During the Babylonian siege, Irijah arrested the prophet Jeremiah as he was leaving the city and accused him of deserting to the Chaldeans (Jer 37:13). Hananiah is named only in this genealogical note identifying his grandson, and nothing else is recorded about him. The name, meaning "the LORD has been gracious," was common in Israel, and several other men in the Bible bear it. These include the false prophet who opposed Jeremiah, but nothing in the text links this Hananiah with any of them. Smith's Bible Dictionary places him before 589 BC, which fits a grandfather of an officer serving in Zedekiah's reign.

Haniel was a man of the tribe of Asher, named as one of the sons of Ulla alongside his brothers Arah and Rezia in the genealogy of Asher (1 Chr 7:39). Nothing else is recorded about him. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes him as a chief of the tribe of Asher, probably by inference from the next verse, which calls the descendants of Asher heads of their fathers' houses and leading men. The name is also spelled Hanniel, the form the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia uses. It is usually explained as meaning "grace of God" (Smith's Bible Dictionary) or "the gift of God" (Hitchcock's Bible Names). He should be distinguished from Hanniel son of Ephod, a leader of Manasseh in the time of Moses.

Hanniel was the son of Ephod and the leader, or prince, of the tribe of Manasseh named in Num 34:23. He was one of the tribal leaders chosen to help divide the land of Canaan among the tribes. The surrounding passage shows that these leaders were to work with Eleazar the priest and Joshua in allotting the land west of the Jordan. Manasseh is listed there as one of the two tribes descended from Joseph. The half of Manasseh that had already settled east of the Jordan did not need such a leader, so Hanniel probably represented the western half of the tribe, by inference from the passage. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives the meaning of his name as "grace of God." A different man named Hanniel, from the tribe of Asher, appears in 1 Chr 7:39.

Hanun was a man who, together with the inhabitants of Zanoah, repaired the Valley Gate of Jerusalem during the rebuilding of the city walls under Nehemiah. His group built the gate, set up its doors, locks and bars, and also repaired a thousand cubits (roughly 450 metres) of wall as far as the Dung Gate (Neh 3:13). Smith's Bible Dictionary dates this work to about 446 BC. Whether Hanun was a leader of the Zanoah group or simply one of its members is not clear; the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia counts him among the inhabitants of Zanoah. The name, meaning "favored" or "gracious," is shared by several people in the Bible, including an Ammonite king in David's time and another wall-builder in the same chapter, and this Hanun should be kept distinct from them.

Hanun, the sixth son of Zalaph, was one of the men who repaired the wall of Jerusalem under Nehemiah after the return from exile. Neh 3:30 says he worked on "another piece", a second section next to the one repaired by Hananiah son of Shelemiah. Smith's Bible Dictionary places this stretch apparently on the east side of the city and dates the work to about 446 BC, a date inferred from context. The phrase "another piece" suggests he had already worked on an earlier section, though the text does not say which. The name, meaning "favored" or "gracious," is shared by several people in the Bible. He is probably distinct from the Hanun who repaired the Valley Gate earlier in the same chapter, and from the Ammonite king of that name in David's time. Nothing else is recorded about him.

Haran (son of Caleb) was a man of the tribe of Judah, named once in the genealogy of 1 Chr 2:46. He was a son of Caleb by Caleb's concubine Ephah, and his full brothers were Moza and Gazez. The same verse says that Haran in turn fathered a son named Gazez. A brother and a son therefore share the name, and the text gives no further detail to explain this. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary both describe him only as Caleb's son by Ephah. The Caleb of this genealogy belongs to the line of Hezron in Judah. He is not to be confused with Haran the brother of Abraham, who shares the name. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "mountainous country," and Smith's renders it "a mountaineer." Nothing else is recorded about his life.

Haran (son of Shimei) was a Gershonite Levite listed in David's organization of the Levites. 1 Chr 23:9 names him with Shelomith and Haziel as the three sons of Shimei and counts them among the heads of the families descended from Laadan. From the surrounding chapter, this list belongs to the time when David, in his old age, arranged the Levites for service at the temple, so Haran probably lived during David's reign. It is unclear how this Shimei relates to the Shimei whose four sons appear in the next verse. Many readers take the Shimei of verse 9 to be a descendant of Laadan, distinct from Laadan's brother Shimei. Nothing else is recorded about Haran.
