He should not be confused with Haran the brother of Abraham. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "a mountaineer," and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "mountainous country."

Harbona was one of the seven chamberlains, or court eunuchs, who served in the presence of the Persian king Ahasuerus. He is named third in the list of officials the king ordered, on the seventh day of his feast while he was merry with wine, to bring Queen Vashti before him (Esth 1:10). Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries give the name's meaning as "ass-driver," taking it to be a Persian word. Easton's also identifies him with Harbonah in Esth 7:9, who later told the king about the gallows Haman had built for Mordecai, which led to Haman being hanged on it. The spelling differs slightly, but the same office and court make it probable that he is the same man.

Harbonah was one of the chamberlains (court officials) serving King Ahasuerus of Persia. At the banquet where Queen Esther exposed Haman's plot against the Jews, Harbonah told the king that Haman had built a gallows fifty cubits high for Mordecai, the man whose report had once saved the king's life, and that it stood at Haman's house. The king then ordered Haman hanged on it (Esth 7:9). Smith's Bible Dictionary identifies him with Harbona, one of the seven chamberlains whom the king sent to bring Queen Vashti before his guests (Esth 1:10); the spelling differs slightly in the KJV. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "his destruction" or "his sword."

Hareph was a man of the tribe of Judah, named only once, in the genealogy of 1 Chr 2:51, as "the father of Bethgader." There he appears alongside Shobal and Salma among the descendants of Caleb. The preceding verse can be read either as "the sons of Caleb the son of Hur" or as listing sons of Hur himself. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia call Hareph a son of Caleb, while this entry treats him as a son of Hur, which links him with the other sons of Hur named in this genealogy and in 1 Chr 4. In these lists "father of" a town probably means its founder or leading clan head, so Hareph was likely the ancestor of the people of Beth-gader. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of his name as "winter" or "reproach." Nothing else is recorded about him.

Harhaiah was the father of Uzziel, who repaired a section of Jerusalem's wall in the time of Nehemiah (Neh 3:8). He is named only in this one verse. The phrase "of the goldsmiths" is usually read as describing Uzziel, and perhaps the family, as belonging to the goldsmiths' guild. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both connect the goldsmith label with Harhaiah. The meaning of his name is uncertain. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "heat, or anger, of the Lord" and Smith's Bible Dictionary "the Lord is angry," while the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests "Yah protects." Smith's Bible Dictionary places him before 446 BC, an estimate drawn from the date of the wall rebuilding.

Harim was the father of Malchijah, one of the men who rebuilt Jerusalem's wall under Nehemiah after the return from exile. According to Neh 3:11, Malchijah son of Harim, together with Hashub son of Pahath-moab, repaired a second section of the wall and the Tower of the Furnaces. Nothing else is said about Harim himself. Harim is also the name of a priestly family and of a lay family among the returned exiles, and "son of Harim" may mean a member of one of these families rather than a literal son. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats Harim here as a family name and notes that it is uncertain which family is meant. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "destroyed" or "dedicated to God."

Harim was one of the men who set their seal to the written covenant made in Nehemiah's time, when the people pledged to keep the law of Moses after returning from exile. He appears in Neh 10:27 alongside Malluch and Baanah, in the part of the list that, by context (Neh 10:14), names the leaders of the people rather than the priests or Levites. He may have signed as head of a family that bore the name Harim. The name is shared by several others, including a priest who also sealed the covenant (Neh 10:5) and families named among the returned exiles (Ezra 2:32, 39), so his exact identity is uncertain. Nothing else is recorded about him. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "destroyed" or "dedicated to God."

Hariph was one of the leaders who set their seal to the written covenant made in the time of Nehemiah, when the returned exiles pledged to keep the law of God (Neh 10:19). His name appears in the list of the "chief of the people" who signed after the priests and Levites, beside names such as Anathoth and Nebai. The text gives no personal details about him. Since several names in this list match family names elsewhere, he may have signed on behalf of a clan. Neh 7:24 counts 112 "children of Hariph" among those who returned from exile, and the parallel list in Ezra 2:18 gives the name Jorah at that point. Because the name is shared by more than one person, it is uncertain exactly how this signer relates to that family.

Harnepher was a man of the tribe of Asher, named as the second of the sons of Zophah in the Asherite genealogy of 1 Chr 7:36. His brothers listed in the genealogy include Suah, Shual, Beri, Imrah, Bezer, Hod, Shamma, Shilshah, Ithran (Jether) and Beera. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes him as a chief of the tribe of Asher, reflecting the genealogy's description of these men as heads of their fathers' houses and leading men. Nothing further is recorded about him beyond his place in this list. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "panting", while Hitchcock's Bible Names renders it "the anger of a bull" or "increasing heat."

Harum was a man of the tribe of Judah, named only once, in the genealogy of Judah in 1 Chr 4:8. That verse says Coz fathered Anub and Zobebah, and then mentions "the families of Aharhel the son of Harum." This entry follows the reading that makes Harum a son of Coz and a brother of Anub and Zobebah, as the STEPBible proper names index does. The verse itself does not say so directly, and Harum's exact place in the line is unclear. Smith's Bible Dictionary calls this one of the most obscure genealogies of Judah. Harum is remembered as the father of Aharhel, whose descendants formed clans within Judah. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "elevated," and Smith's as "lofty." Nothing else is recorded about him.

Harumaph is named only once in the Bible, as the father of Jedaiah. Jedaiah was one of the men who repaired a section of Jerusalem's wall under Nehemiah after the return from exile, and he worked on the part opposite his own house (Neh 3:10). Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that Harumaph may have been Jedaiah's father or a more distant ancestor, since "son of" can carry either sense. Nothing else is recorded about Harumaph himself. Smith's gives the meaning of the name as "slit-nosed," while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "destruction."

Haruz was a man of Jotbah and the father of Meshullemeth, the mother of King Amon of Judah (2 Kgs 21:19). Since Amon was the son of King Manasseh, Meshullemeth was Manasseh's wife, which made Haruz the king's father-in-law and Amon's maternal grandfather. Amon appears in Matthew's genealogy of Jesus, which links Haruz to that line through his daughter. Haruz is named only in this verse, and nothing else is told about him. Jotbah's location is uncertain. Some place it in Galilee, while others connect it with Jotbathah, a camp from the wilderness journey. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates Haruz before 644 BC, an estimate drawn from the timing of Amon's reign. The meaning of his name is given as "eager" in Easton's Bible Dictionary, "zealous" in Smith's, and "careful" in Hitchcock's Bible Names.

Hasadiah was a man of the tribe of Judah, a descendant of the royal line of David through King Jehoiachin (Jeconiah). He appears only in the genealogy at 1 Chr 3:20, as one of a group of five: Hashubah, Ohel, Berechiah, Hasadiah and Jushab-hesed. This entry follows the reading that these five were sons of Zerubbabel, the leader of the return from Babylon, as Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia take it. That would make him a brother of Meshullam, Hananiah and Shelomith, who are listed just before. Easton's Bible Dictionary instead counts him among the sons of Pedaiah, Zerubbabel's father in this genealogy. If he was Zerubbabel's son, he probably lived in the late sixth century BC, an estimate inferred from context. His name means roughly "the Lord is kind" or "favoured by the Lord."

Hasenuah was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, named only in the genealogy of Sallu in 1 Chr 9:7. He was the father of Hodaviah, the grandfather of Meshullam, and the great-grandfather of Sallu. From the surrounding chapter, Sallu appears among the Benjamites living in Jerusalem, probably after the return from exile. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes Hasenuah as belonging to one of the chief families of the tribe. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "bristling" or "hated." Other English versions spell the name Hassenuah, as the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes. A similar name, Senuah, appears in the Benjamite list of Neh 11:9, though it is uncertain whether the same family is meant. Nothing else is recorded about him.

Hashabiah was a Levite of the clan of Merari, named only in a genealogy in 1 Chronicles. He was the son of Amaziah and the father of Malluch (1 Chr 6:45). The surrounding passage (1 Chr 6:44–47) traces the ancestry of Ethan, one of the Merarite musicians whom David put in charge of the singing at the house of the Lord, so Hashabiah appears as one of Ethan's forebears. Nothing else is recorded about him. Several other men in the Old Testament share the name, and this entry is distinct from them. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him as a Merarite Levite, and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "the estimation of the Lord."

Hashabiah was a Levite of the Hebronite clan who, with 1,700 of his relatives described as capable men, served as an officer over Israel west of the Jordan. According to 1 Chr 26:30, they handled both "the business of the LORD" and "the service of the king," which probably means they oversaw religious and royal affairs in that region. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes the Hebronites as descendants of Hebron, son of Kohath, and the surrounding chapter places this appointment among King David's arrangements for the Levites, so he probably served during David's reign. Nothing else is recorded about him. Several other men in the Bible share the name, and this one should not be confused with them. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "the estimation of the Lord."

Hashabiah son of Kemuel was the leader of the tribe of Levi during King David's reign. He appears in 1 Chr 27:16–22, a list of the chief officers over the tribes of Israel, where he is named for the Levites while Zadok is named separately for the Aaronites, the priestly line descended from Aaron. Smith's Bible Dictionary calls him prince of the tribe of Levi and dates him to about 1014 BC, an estimate inferred from context. Nothing more is recorded about him. Several other men in the Bible share the name Hashabiah, many of them Levites, so this one should not be confused with them. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "the estimation of the Lord."

Hashabiah was one of the chief Levites in the reign of King Josiah of Judah. He is named in 2 Chr 35:9 with Conaniah, Shemaiah, Nethaneel, Jeiel and Jozabad, who together gave the Levites 5,000 sheep and goats and 500 oxen as Passover offerings for the great Passover Josiah held in Jerusalem. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates this feast to about 623 BC. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the parallel account in 1 Esdras calls him Sabias. Nothing else is recorded about him. Several other men in the Bible share the name Hashabiah, which Hitchcock's Bible Names explains as "the estimation of the Lord." The text gives no reason to identify this Levite with any of them.

Hashabiah was the ruler of half the district of Keilah, a town in the lowlands of Judah, who repaired a section of the wall of Jerusalem when it was rebuilt under Nehemiah (Neh 3:17). He worked next to Rehum son of Bani, in a stretch of the wall assigned to Levites. STEPBible's proper-name index counts Hashabiah himself among these Levites, although the verse could also be read as simply placing him next to them. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates the rebuilding to about 446 BC, an estimate inferred from context. The name, which Hitchcock's Bible Names renders as "the estimation of the Lord," belongs to several other men in the Bible, mostly Levites. This entry treats the Hashabiah of Neh 3:17 as a separate person, since nothing else is known about him.

Hashabiah was a Levite named in the genealogy of Uzzi, the overseer of the Levites in Jerusalem after the return from exile (Neh 11:22). He was the son of Mattaniah and grandson of Micha, and the father of Bani, whose son Uzzi held that office. The family belonged to the sons of Asaph, the singers who were in charge of the work of the house of God. A brother named Shemaiah is also linked to him, though the verse does not mention him. Nothing else is recorded about Hashabiah himself. His name, which Hitchcock's Bible Names renders "the estimation of the Lord," is shared by several other men in the Bible, mostly Levites, so he should not be confused with them.

Hashabiah was a priest who headed the priestly family of Hilkiah in the generation after the return from exile in Babylon. He appears only in a list of the heads of priestly families (Neh 12:21). By inference from the surrounding passage, that list belongs to the days of Joiakim, the son of the high priest Jeshua, which is how Smith's Bible Dictionary dates him. Nothing else is recorded about him. Several other men in the Bible share the name Hashabiah, many of them Levites, and this priest should not be confused with them. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "the estimation of the Lord," and Smith's renders it "whom God regards."

Hashabnah was one of the leaders of the people who set their seal to the covenant made in Nehemiah's time, a written pledge by the returned exiles in Jerusalem to keep the law of Moses. He appears only once, in the list of signatories at Neh 10:25, where he is named between Rehum and Maaseiah among the "chief of the people," as distinct from the priests and Levites listed earlier in the chapter. Nothing else is recorded about his family or role. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates the sealing to about 410 BC and takes the name to mean "whom Jehovah regards," while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "the silence of the Lord."

Hashabniah was the father of Hattush, a man who helped rebuild the walls of Jerusalem under Nehemiah after the return from exile. He is known only from Neh 3:10, which places his son's repair work next to that of Jedaiah son of Harumaph. Nothing else is recorded about Hashabniah himself, and he probably lived in the generation before the rebuilding. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "whom Jehovah regards." A similar name belongs to a Levite who led the people in prayer in Neh 9:5. Because this name is shared by more than one person, it is uncertain whether the two are connected, and this entry treats the father of Hattush separately.

Hashabniah was a Levite in Jerusalem after the return from exile, in the time of Ezra and Nehemiah. He is named only once, in Neh 9:5, among the Levites who led a gathering of the people during a public fast and confession of sin. With Jeshua, Kadmiel, Bani, Sherebiah, Hodijah, Shebaniah and Pethahiah, he called on the assembly to stand up and bless the LORD, opening the long prayer recorded in that chapter. The context shows this gathering led to the written covenant the people's leaders sealed (Neh 9:38). Smith's Bible Dictionary explains the name as meaning "whom Jehovah regards" and dates the event to about 410 BC, an estimate drawn from context. The same name belongs to another man elsewhere in Nehemiah, the father of Hattush (Neh 3:10). Whether the two are related is not stated.

Hashbadana was one of the men who stood on Ezra's left hand on the wooden platform when Ezra the scribe read the Law aloud to the people gathered in Jerusalem after the return from exile (Neh 8:4). He is named alongside Pedaiah, Mishael, Malchiah, Hashum, Zechariah and Meshullam, while six others stood on Ezra's right. The text gives no further details about his family or role. Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests these men were probably Levites, though the verse does not say so, and many see them as leading men or elders. Smith's and Easton's Bible Dictionary give the meaning of his name as "considerate judge" or "consideration in judging." This is his only appearance in the Bible.

Hashub, son of Pahath-moab, was one of the men who helped rebuild the walls of Jerusalem under Nehemiah's leadership. Working alongside Malchijah son of Harim, he repaired a second section of the wall and the Tower of the Furnaces (Neh 3:11). Pahath-moab, meaning "governor of Moab," was the name of a large family that returned from exile, so "son of" here probably means he belonged to that clan rather than being a literal son. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates the wall-building to about 446 BC, a date inferred from context. The name Hashub belongs to several people in Nehemiah's time, including another wall-builder who worked opposite his own house and a Levite. It is uncertain whether any of these are the same man as this Hashub.

Hashub was a man who, together with Benjamin, repaired a section of Jerusalem's wall opposite their house during the rebuilding led by Nehemiah (Neh 3:23). The pair worked on the stretch just before Azariah son of Maaseiah, who repaired beside his own house. Nothing else is recorded about him. Several men in the Bible share this name, and another Hashub appears among the wall builders in the same chapter (Neh 3:11). Smith's Bible Dictionary treats this Hashub as a separate person from that one, and this entry does the same. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "esteemed" or "numbered."

Hashub was one of the leaders of the people who set their seal to the written covenant made in Nehemiah's time, after the return from exile in Babylon. In that covenant the community pledged to keep the law of Moses. He appears only in a list of names between Hananiah and Hoshea (Neh 10:23). By inference from the surrounding passage, he belongs to the group described as "the chief of the people," and Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him this way. The text says nothing more about him. Several other men named Hashub appear in Nehemiah and 1 Chronicles, including two who helped repair Jerusalem's wall (Neh 3:11, 23). He may be the same man as one of them, but that cannot be confirmed. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "esteemed" or "numbered."

Hashubah was a son of Zerubbabel, the governor who led exiles back from Babylon, and so a descendant of King David through Jehoiachin, in the tribe of Judah. He is named only in the genealogy of David's line at 1 Chr 3:20, where he heads a group of five: Hashubah, Ohel, Berechiah, Hasadiah and Jushab-hesed. The previous verse lists Meshullam, Hananiah and their sister Shelomith as Zerubbabel's children, so the separate count of five suggests a second group within the family. Smith's Bible Dictionary takes these five as the latter half of Zerubbabel's family, possibly born after the return to Judah. Nothing else is recorded about his life. His name is usually explained as meaning "consideration" or "esteem".

Hashum was one of the men who stood on Ezra's left hand when Ezra the scribe read the Law of Moses from a wooden platform to the assembled people in Jerusalem (Neh 8:4). He is named among thirteen men who flanked Ezra, six on his right and seven on his left, but nothing more is said about him. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him as one of the priests or Levites, which is an inference from the setting, since the verse gives no title. Several men in the Bible bear this name. A family of Hashum is listed among returning exiles and among those who sealed the covenant in Nehemiah's day, and this Hashum may have been its head or a member of it, though the text does not say so. The reading took place after the return from exile, in the time of Nehemiah.

Hashum was one of the leaders who set their seal to the covenant made in the time of Nehemiah, in which the returned exiles pledged to keep the law of God (Neh 10:18). He appears in the list of the chiefs of the people, between Hodijah and Bezai. The name is also used elsewhere for a family whose members returned from Babylon and for a man who stood with Ezra at the reading of the law. This Hashum was probably the head of that family, signing on its behalf, but this is an inference, and the name is shared by several people, so the link is uncertain. Nothing else is recorded about him. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "silence" or "their hasting."

Hassenaah is named in Neh 3:3 as the ancestor or head of a group called "the sons of Hassenaah." They rebuilt the Fish Gate when Nehemiah restored the walls of Jerusalem, probably around 446 BC, a date inferred from context. The verse says they laid the gate's beams and set up its doors, locks and bars. Nothing else is recorded about Hassenaah as an individual. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests the name is probably the same as Senaah (Ezra 2:35; Neh 7:38) with the Hebrew definite article added. Senaah appears among the groups of returning exiles, and its context there suggests a place-name. On that view, "sons of Hassenaah" may mean the people of a town rather than the descendants of one man. This entry treats Hassenaah as a male person, while noting that the name may be a place.

Hathath was a man of the tribe of Judah, named in the genealogy of 1 Chr 4:13 as a son of Othniel and grandson of Kenaz. This Othniel is probably the same Othniel son of Kenaz who captured Debir and later served as Israel's first judge (Josh 15:17; Judg 3:9–11). The King James text names only Hathath as Othniel's son. Meonothai is treated here as his brother because he appears in the next verse, and some ancient translations add his name to verse 13. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia give the meaning of his name as "terror", and Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "fearful". Nothing else is recorded about him.

Hattush was a man of the tribe of Judah, listed as a son of Shemaiah in the royal line of David that ran through King Jehoiachin (Jeconiah) after the exile (1 Chr 3:17–22). His brothers were Igeal, Bariah, Neariah and Shaphat. The verse gives the total as "six" but names only five, a difficulty that has never been settled. Some take the count to include Shemaiah himself. Many readers identify him with the Hattush "of the sons of David" who returned from Babylon with Ezra (Ezra 8:2), which would fit the generations in this genealogy, but that link is an inference. The name is also borne by other men of the same period, including a priest and a wall-builder in Nehemiah, so the identification is uncertain. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "forsaking sin."

Hattush was a descendant of David named in Ezra 8:2 among the family heads who traveled from Babylon to Jerusalem with Ezra. The surrounding passage places this return in the reign of the Persian king Artaxerxes. He stands in the list beside Gershom, of the priestly line of Phinehas, and Daniel, of the line of Ithamar, as the representative of the royal house of David. He is probably the same Hattush whom 1 Chr 3:22 lists among the descendants of Zerubbabel, in the line of David's heirs after the exile, though that link is an inference. The name is shared by other men of the post-exilic period, including a wall-builder in Nehemiah's day and a priest who signed the covenant, and it is not always clear which mentions refer to the same person. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "forsaking sin."

Hattush, son of Hashabniah, was one of the men who helped rebuild the walls of Jerusalem under Nehemiah after the return from exile. He repaired the section next to Jedaiah son of Harumaph, who worked on the stretch opposite his own house (Neh 3:10). Nothing else is recorded about him. The name Hattush belongs to several men in the Bible, including a descendant of David and a priest who returned with Zerubbabel. This Hattush is identified only by his father's name, and whether he is the same as any of the others is uncertain. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "forsaking sin."

Hazaiah was a man of the tribe of Judah, named only in the genealogy of Maaseiah son of Baruch, one of the Judahites who settled in Jerusalem after the return from exile (Neh 11:5). He was the son of Adaiah and the father of Col-hozeh, and so the great-grandfather of Maaseiah. The line traces back through Joiarib and Zechariah to Shiloni. Smith's Bible Dictionary takes Shiloni to mean the Shilonites, the descendants of Judah's son Shelah. Hazaiah himself probably lived some generations before Nehemiah's time, by inference from his place in the list. Nothing else is recorded about him. His name means "the LORD sees" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia) or "seeing the Lord" (Hitchcock's Bible Names).

Hazelelponi was a woman of the tribe of Judah, named in the genealogy of 1 Chr 4:3 as the sister of Jezreel, Ishma and Idbash, who are called sons of "the father of Etam." She is one of the few women named in this list, and nothing more is said about her. The Hebrew of the verse is difficult, and this entry follows the reading that places these siblings in the family of Hur. By inference from nearby genealogies, where Hur's descendants include Shobal, Salma, Hareph, Penuel and Ezer (1 Chr 2:50–51; 4:4), she is grouped here with them as Hur's daughter. Whether "father of Etam" refers to a person or to the founder of the town of Etam near Bethlehem is uncertain. Her name is also spelled Hazzelelponi. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives its meaning as "shade coming upon me," and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "sorrow of countenance."

Haziel was a Levite in the time of David, named once in the list of Gershonite families that David organized for service. 1 Chr 23:9 calls him one of three sons of Shimei, with his brothers Shelomith and Haran, and says they were heads of the fathers' houses of Laadan. This Shimei is probably a descendant within Laadan's line. He is distinct from the Shimei who was a son of Gershon and is named in the following verse, which is why these men count as Laadan's chiefs. Nothing else is recorded about Haziel. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives the meaning of his name as "God sees," and Smith's Bible Dictionary renders it "union of God."

Hazo was a son of Nahor, Abraham's brother, and his wife Milcah. He appears only once, in the list of Nahor's children reported to Abraham after the near-sacrifice of Isaac (Gen 22:22). His full brothers were Huz, Buz, Kemuel, Chesed, Pildash, Jidlaph and Bethuel, and Bethuel was the father of Rebekah. Nahor also had children by his concubine Reumah: Tebah, Gaham, Thahash and Maachah. Hazo is the fifth son named in the list. Nothing else is recorded about him. Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries give the meaning of his name as "vision." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests he may have been the ancestor who gave his name to a family or clan descended from Nahor.

Heber was a man of the tribe of Judah, named in the genealogy of 1 Chr 4:18 as a son of Jehudijah and as "the father of Socho." His brothers were Jered, father of Gedor, and Jekuthiel, father of Zanoah. "Father" here probably means founder or leading figure of the town of Socho (Socoh) in Judah rather than a literal parent. The verse is hard to read, and views on his father differ. This entry names Ishbah, linking him to the family listed in the preceding verse. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia and the Tyndale House proper-names index name Mered, the husband of Bithiah, Pharaoh's daughter, and treat Jehudijah as Mered's Judahite wife. Nothing else is recorded about him. The name Heber, which the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia takes to mean "associate," is shared by several other people in the Bible.

Heber was a man of the tribe of Gad, one of seven kinsmen listed together in the Gadite genealogy of 1 Chr 5:13. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes these seven as heads of Gadite families. The next verse, 1 Chr 5:14, calls the group the sons of Abihail, which is how Heber is identified as Abihail's son and as the brother of Michael, Meshullam, Sheba, Jorai, Jachan and Zia. According to 1 Chr 5:17, this genealogy was recorded in the days of Jotham king of Judah and Jeroboam king of Israel, and the STEPBible proper-names index places him in that period. The Gadites are described as living in Bashan and Gilead, east of the Jordan. Nothing more is recorded about him. Several other people in the Bible share the name Heber, and he should not be confused with them.

Heber was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, named as a son of Elpaal in the Benjamite genealogy of 1 Chr 8:17. He appears in a list with his brothers Zebadiah, Meshullam and Hezeki, and the family also included Beriah, Shema, Eber, Misham, Shamed, Ishmerai, Jezliah and Jobab. Nothing is recorded about his life beyond his place in this list. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the name may stand for a clan or family descended from Elpaal rather than a single individual. The name is usually taken to mean "associate" or "alliance". Several other people in the Bible are also called Heber, including Heber the Kenite, the husband of Jael, and a grandson of Asher. This Benjamite should not be confused with them.

Heber was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, listed as one of the sons of Shashak in the Benjamite genealogy of 1 Chronicles 8. He is named alongside his brothers Ishpan, Eliel, Abdon, Zichri, Hanan, Hananiah, Elam, Antothijah, Iphedeiah and Penuel. Nothing further is recorded about him beyond his place in this family list. By inference from the surrounding passage, Shashak's family was among the Benjamite households living in Jerusalem. Smith's Bible Dictionary identifies him simply as a Benjamite. Some modern renderings and name lists, such as the STEPBible proper names index, give his name as Eber. He should not be confused with several other men called Heber in the Bible, including Heber the Kenite, the husband of Jael.

Helez was a man of the tribe of Judah, named only in a genealogy as the son of Azariah and the father of Eleasah (1 Chr 2:39). The genealogy belongs to the line of Jerahmeel, son of Hezron, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia places him among the Jerahmeelites. In this line Azariah descends from the Egyptian servant Jarha, who married the daughter of Sheshan (1 Chr 2:34–38). Nothing else is recorded about him. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "strength." The name is borne by several people in the Bible, among them one of David's mighty men, and this Helez should not be confused with them.

Heli appears in Luke's genealogy of Jesus, where Joseph is called "the son of Heli" (Luke 3:23). The next verse names Heli's father as Matthat, placing him in a line that runs back through David to the tribe of Judah. Matthew's genealogy names Joseph's father as Jacob (Matt 1:16), and this has led to two main readings. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia take Heli as Joseph's father in Luke's account. Another long-standing view, followed by the STEPBible proper names index and by this entry, is that Luke traces Mary's line. In that case Heli was Mary's father and Jesus' maternal grandfather, and Joseph was his son-in-law. Smith's Bible Dictionary mentions a further possibility, that he was Mary's grandfather. Nothing else is recorded about him. According to Hitchcock's Bible Names, his name means "ascending."

Helkai was a priest who headed the priestly family of Meraioth in the days of Joiakim the high priest, in the generation after the return from exile in Babylon. He appears only once, in a list of the heads of priestly families serving under Joiakim (Neh 12:15). By inference from the surrounding passage, Meraioth was one of the priestly houses that had returned with Zerubbabel, and it probably corresponds to the Meremoth named earlier in the same chapter. Nothing more is recorded about him. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests his name may be a shortened form of Hilkiah, meaning "Yah is my portion," while Easton's Bible Dictionary gives its meaning as "smooth-tongued."

Heman was a man famous for his wisdom in the time of Solomon. In 1 Kgs 4:31 he is named with Ethan the Ezrahite, Chalcol and Darda, the sons of Mahol, as one of the wise men whom Solomon surpassed. Easton's Bible Dictionary connects him with the Heman listed in 1 Chr 2:6 as a son of Zerah of the tribe of Judah, together with Ethan, Calcol and Dara. On that reading, "Mahol" may name a family or a group rather than a literal father. He is linked to the Psalms because the heading of Ps 88 attributes it to "Heman the Ezrahite," a term probably meaning a descendant of Zerah. Several men in the Bible bear this name, including Heman the Levite singer of David's time (1 Chr 6:33), and some identify the psalm's author with that singer instead. This entry follows the identification with the wise man of 1 Kgs 4:31.

Heman was a son of Zerah and a grandson of Judah, listed in the genealogy of the tribe of Judah with his brothers Zimri, Ethan, Calcol and Dara (1 Chr 2:6). Zimri appears to be the same person called Zabdi in Josh 7:1. Zerah was one of the twin sons of Judah and Tamar. Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies this Heman with the Heman of 1 Kgs 4:31, one of the wise men whom Solomon is said to have surpassed. That verse also names Ethan, Calcol and Darda, which closely matches this list of brothers, although it calls them sons of Mahol. The Heman called "the Ezrahite" in the title of Psalm 88 may also belong to this family, but that is uncertain. Several men in the Bible share this name. This Heman should be kept distinct from Heman the Levite, who was a singer in David's time (1 Chr 6:33).

Hemath was the ancestor from whom a group of Kenites descended, according to the genealogy of Judah in 1 Chr 2:55. That verse names him as "the father of the house of Rechab" and links him to the families of scribes living at Jabez: the Tirathites, Shimeathites and Suchathites. In these lists "father" often means founder, so Hemath may stand for the head of a clan rather than an immediate parent. The surrounding verses place these families among the descendants of Salma, the founder of Bethlehem. Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that the name, meaning "heat", could refer to either a person or a place. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia spells it Hammath. The house of Rechab is probably the same family as Jonadab son of Rechab and the Rechabites, who appear in 2 Kings 10 and Jeremiah 35. This entry treats Hemath as a man. Nothing else is recorded about him.

Henadad is named in Neh 3:18 as the father of Bavai, who helped repair the wall of Jerusalem in Nehemiah's time and is described as ruler of half the district of Keilah. Henadad himself appears only as his son's father here. The phrase "their brethren" links Bavai with the Levites listed just before (Neh 3:17), so Henadad was probably a Levite. The name also appears elsewhere in Nehemiah's era: the sons of Henadad are among the Levites in Ezra 3:9, and a Binnui son of Henadad repairs another section of the wall in Neh 3:24. These may belong to the same Levitical family, but whether they refer to the same Henadad is uncertain. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "grace of the beloved."

Henadad was the father of Binnui, who repaired a section of Jerusalem's wall in Nehemiah's time, from the house of Azariah to the turning of the wall at the corner (Neh 3:24). Nothing else is said of him personally in this verse. Elsewhere the "sons of Henadad" appear as a Levite family that helped oversee work on the rebuilt temple (Ezra 3:9), and a Binnui "of the sons of Henadad" is named among Levites who sealed the covenant (Neh 10:9). So Henadad was probably the head of a Levite clan, and "son of Henadad" may mean a descendant rather than a direct son. A Bavai son of Henadad also worked on the wall (Neh 3:18). Because the name is shared by several people, how these references relate is uncertain. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the name's meaning as "grace of the beloved."

Hepher was a man of the tribe of Judah, the son of Ashur and his wife Naarah. He is listed second among Naarah's four sons, after Ahuzam and before Temeni and Haahashtari (1 Chr 4:6). The surrounding genealogy (1 Chr 4:5–7) calls Ashur the father of Tekoa and says he had a second wife, Helah, whose sons, including Zereth, Jezoar and Ethnan, were Hepher's half-brothers. Nothing else is recorded about him. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of his name as "a digger," and Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "a well." The same name belongs to other men in the Bible, including a son of Gilead in the tribe of Manasseh and one of David's mighty men, so he should not be confused with them.

Hepher was one of David's mighty warriors, the elite fighters listed in 1 Chr 11, where he is called "the Mecherathite" (1 Chr 11:36). Nothing else is recorded about him. The term Mecherathite appears nowhere else and probably refers to his hometown or clan, though no place called Mecherah is known. The parallel list in 2 Sam 23:34 has no Hepher at this point, and the names there differ, so some readers take "Mecherathite" as a variant of "Maachathite." The name Hepher is shared by other men in the Bible, including a descendant of Manasseh, the father of Zelophehad, and a son of Ashur of Judah. These are separate people. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "a digger," and Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "a well."

Heresh was a Levite named in the list of those who lived in Jerusalem after the return from the Babylonian exile. He appears alongside Bakbakkar, Galal and Mattaniah, a descendant of Asaph (1 Chr 9:15). By inference from the surrounding passage, which lists the priests, Levites and gatekeepers who resettled the city, he belonged to the Levites who served at the house of God. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him as a Levite attached to the tabernacle and dates him to about 536 BC. His name is usually explained as meaning "artificer" or "carpenter" (Smith's Bible Dictionary; Hitchcock's Bible Names). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that ancient Greek manuscripts render the name differently, as Rharaiel or Hares. Nothing else is recorded about him, and his family line is not given.

Hermas was a Christian living in Rome to whom Paul sent greetings near the end of his letter to the Romans. He is named in a group with Asyncritus, Phlegon, Patrobas and Hermes, along with "the brethren which are with them" (Rom 16:14), which suggests these men belonged to the same household or house church. Nothing more is said about him in the Bible. The name is a short form of several Greek names, and Hitchcock's Bible Names links it to Hermes. Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that Origen and other early writers identified him with the author of The Shepherd, a widely respected early Christian book. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia points out that the Muratorian Canon dates that author to about AD 140–155 and that the name was common. This entry treats Hermas simply as the Roman believer Paul greeted.

Hermes was a Christian in Rome to whom Paul sent greetings at the close of his letter to the Romans. He is named in a group with Asyncritus, Phlegon, Hermas and Patrobas, along with "the brethren which are with them" (Rom 16:14). That wording suggests these men belonged to the same household or house church. Nothing more is known of him from the Bible. His name is the Greek form of the god the Romans called Mercury. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that it was one of the most common slave names of the period, so he may have been a slave or a freedman, though the text does not say. Smith's Bible Dictionary records a tradition that he was one of the seventy disciples and later bishop of Dalmatia. He should not be confused with Hermas, who is named beside him in the same verse.

Hermogenes was a Christian named in 2 Tim 1:15, where Paul reminds Timothy that "all they which are in Asia" had turned away from him, Phygellus and Hermogenes among them. His name is Greek and means "born of Hermes" (the god the Romans called Mercury). Nothing else is recorded about him. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes him as once Paul's fellow worker in Asia Minor who later abandoned him, probably because of the dangers involved. It is unclear when and where the desertion happened. Some take it as an earlier rejection of Paul's authority in Ephesus. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia favors a different setting: Christians from the province of Asia who were in Rome during Paul's final imprisonment and avoided him, probably out of fear. It notes that the very next verses contrast them with Onesiphorus, who searched for Paul in Rome.

Herodion was a Christian at Rome whom Paul greets in his letter to the Romans, calling him "my kinsman" (Rom 16:11). The word can mean a blood relative, as Smith's Bible Dictionary takes it, or more broadly a fellow Jew, the reading the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia prefers. This entry leaves both possibilities open. His name suggests a link with the family of Herod. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia proposes that he may have been a freed slave of the Herods or a member of the household of Aristobulus, whom Paul greets in the verse just before (Rom 16:10). Aristobulus is often thought to be a grandson of Herod the Great. Nothing more is known about him. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates the letter to about AD 55, an estimate inferred from context.

Hesed was the father of one of Solomon's twelve district officers, who appears in 1 Kgs 4:10 only as "the son of Hesed" (Hebrew Ben-hesed). Nothing is recorded about Hesed himself beyond his son's role. The son was based in Aruboth, and his district included Sochoh and all the land of Hepher. By inference from the surrounding passage, the twelve officers each supplied food for the king's household for one month of the year. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes the son as Solomon's commissary and gives the meaning of the name as "kindness." It dates him to about 995 BC, an estimate drawn from context rather than stated in the text. The locations of Aruboth and Sochoh in this district are uncertain. They probably lay in the hill country or coastal plain west of Samaria, but no firm identification can be made from this single verse.

Hezeki was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, listed among the sons of Elpaal in the Benjamite genealogy of 1 Chr 8:17. He appears only in this list, alongside brothers such as Zebadiah, Meshullam and Heber. Elpaal is named earlier in the same chapter as a son of Shaharaim and Hushim, which places Hezeki within a Benjamite family line, and Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him as a descendant of Shaharaim. The context suggests the family was linked with towns such as Ono and Lod. Some modern translations spell the name Hizki, following the Hebrew more closely. His name probably means "strong," as Smith's Bible Dictionary notes, and it is related to the name Hezekiah. Nothing else is recorded about his life or deeds.

Hezekiah was a son of Neariah and a member of the tribe of Judah, named with his brothers Elioenai and Azrikam in 1 Chr 3:23. He appears only in this genealogy. It traces the royal line of David after the exile, through King Jeconiah (Jehoiachin), so Hezekiah was a descendant of David living after the Babylonian captivity. Nothing more is recorded about him. He is a different person from King Hezekiah of Judah and from others who share the name. The Revised Version spells his name "Hizkiah," as the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "strength of the Lord."

Hezion was the father of Tabrimon and the grandfather of Ben-hadad, the king of Syria who ruled from Damascus. He is named only in the genealogy of Ben-hadad, when King Asa of Judah sent silver and gold from the temple and palace treasuries to buy Ben-hadad's help (1 Kgs 15:18). The verse does not say whether Hezion himself was a king, though the context suggests he founded or belonged to the ruling line in Damascus. Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests he is probably the same person as Rezon, the ruler of Damascus who opposed Solomon (1 Kgs 11:23). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that Greek manuscripts render the name as Azein or Azael. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "vision."

Hezir was a priest in the time of King David whose family was given the seventeenth of the twenty-four divisions of priestly service (1 Chr 24:15). The surrounding chapter describes how these divisions were assigned by lot, each taking its turn at the sanctuary. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes the divisions as monthly courses. Easton's Bible Dictionary calls Hezir the head of the seventeenth course, and Smith's gives the name's meaning as "swine." Nothing else is recorded about him. The same name belongs to more than one person in the Bible. A later Hezir appears among the leaders who sealed the covenant in Nehemiah's time, and he is a different man.

Hezir was one of the leaders who set their seal to the covenant made in Nehemiah's time, in which the returned community in Jerusalem pledged to keep the Law of God. His name is the only thing Neh 10:20 records about him, where it appears between Magpiash, Meshullam and others. By inference from its place in the list, he belongs among the "chiefs of the people" who sealed after the priests and Levites. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both describe him as a lay head of the people. Smith's dates the sealing to about 410 BC and gives the meaning of the name as "swine." The name was shared by several people. It also belongs to the head of a priestly division in David's day (1 Chr 24:15), who is a different man.

Hiel was a man from Bethel who rebuilt the city of Jericho during the reign of King Ahab of Israel. The verse dates it only as "in his days", which by context refers to Ahab (1 Kgs 16:34). His name is usually taken to mean "God lives." The verse says he laid Jericho's foundation "in" his firstborn son Abiram and set up its gates "in" his youngest son Segub, as the LORD had said through Joshua. That word is the curse in Josh 6:26, spoken after Jericho's fall, that whoever rebuilt the city would do so at the cost of his eldest and youngest sons. Interpreters understand Hiel's loss in different ways. Easton's Bible Dictionary takes it to mean his sons died while the work went on. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia reads it as the sacrifice of the sons as foundation offerings. The text itself does not say how they died.

Hilkiah was a Levite of the family of Merari, named only in the genealogy of the Levites in 1 Chr 6:45. He was the son of Amzi and the father of Amaziah. The list traces the ancestry of Ethan, one of the Levites David appointed to lead singing at the house of the Lord, and Hilkiah's place in it comes from the surrounding context of the chapter. His name means "the Lord is my portion" (Hitchcock's Bible Names; the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia). Several other men in the Old Testament share the name, most of them connected with the priesthood, such as the high priest of Josiah's reign. This Hilkiah is a different person, known only as a link in this family line. Nothing else is recorded about him.

Hilkiah was a Levite, the second son of Hosah, named in the list of temple gatekeepers organized in David's time (1 Chr 26:11). His brothers were Simri, Tebaliah and Zechariah, and Hosah's sons and relatives numbered thirteen in all. The surrounding chapter places Hosah's family among the descendants of Merari, and Smith's Bible Dictionary accordingly calls Hilkiah a Merarite Levite. The name means "the LORD is my portion," and it is shared by several other men in the Bible, most notably the high priest in the days of King Josiah, who is a different person. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia raises the possibility that the doorkeeper Hosah's family mentioned in 1 Chr 16:38 is connected, but nothing further is recorded about this Hilkiah himself.

Hilkiah was one of six men who stood at Ezra's right hand on the wooden platform when Ezra the scribe read the law to the people gathered in Jerusalem after the return from exile (Neh 8:4). Nothing else is said about him there. Smith's Bible Dictionary takes him to have been a Levite and probably a priest, and the STEPBible proper-names index calls him a priest. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that he may be the same Hilkiah listed among the priests who returned with Zerubbabel and whose family appears in a later priestly list (Neh 12:7, 21). That identification is uncertain, because the name was common, especially among priestly families. The name means "Yahweh is my portion."

Hilkiah was a priest from Anathoth in the territory of Benjamin and the father of the prophet Jeremiah (Jer 1:1). His name means "God is my portion" according to Hitchcock's Bible Names and Smith's Bible Dictionary, or "Yah is my portion" in the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia. His brother was Shallum. This is inferred from Jer 32:7, which calls Shallum Jeremiah's uncle and names Shallum's son Hanameel as Jeremiah's cousin. Smith's Bible Dictionary places Hilkiah before 628 BC. Nothing else is recorded of him. Several men in the Old Testament share the name, most of them linked with the priesthood. The best known is the high priest who found the book of the law in Josiah's reign. Some interpreters have identified the two, but most treat Jeremiah's father as a separate priest of Anathoth, and this entry follows that view.

Hizkiah was an ancestor of the prophet Zephaniah, named at the head of the prophet's genealogy in Zeph 1:1. That verse traces Zephaniah back through Cushi, Gedaliah and Amariah to Hizkiah, which makes Hizkiah the father of Amariah and Zephaniah's great-great-grandfather. The prophecy is dated to the days of Josiah king of Judah, so Hizkiah lived several generations earlier. Smith's Bible Dictionary places him before 635 BC and gives the meaning of his name as "might of Jehovah." His name is a form of Hezekiah, and many interpreters identify him with King Hezekiah of Judah. This would explain why the genealogy is traced so far back, and the generations fit roughly between Hezekiah and Josiah. The verse itself does not call him king, so the identification remains uncertain. Nothing else is recorded about him.

Hizkijah was one of the leaders who set their seal to the covenant made in Nehemiah's day, a solemn pledge to keep the law of Moses after the return from exile in Babylon. He appears in a list of names in Neh 10:17, between Ater and Azzur. By inference from the surrounding passage, he belongs to the group headed 'the chief of the people', so he was probably a clan or family head rather than a priest or Levite. STEPBible's proper names index describes him as a clan leader among the returned exiles. His name is the same as Hezekiah's, and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives its meaning as 'the strength of the Lord.' Because Ater and Hezekiah are also linked as one family among the returnees in Ezra 2:16, Hizkijah may stand here for that family. Nothing else is recorded about him.

Hod was a man of the tribe of Asher, named once in the tribe's genealogy as one of the sons of Zophah (1 Chr 7:37). His brothers in the list include Suah, Harnepher, Beri, Imrah, Bezer, Shamma, Shilshah, Beera and others. Ithran, who appears in the same verse, is generally taken to be the Jether of the next verse. Zophah's sons are traced back to Asher through Helem, so Hod belonged to a family line within one of Asher's clans. Nothing else is recorded about him. His name is usually understood to mean "splendor" or "majesty" (Smith's Bible Dictionary; International Standard Bible Encyclopedia), while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "praise" or "confession."

Hodaiah was a man of the tribe of Judah, listed first among the seven sons of Elioenai in the genealogy of David's royal line (1 Chr 3:24). His brothers were Eliashib, Pelaiah, Akkub, Johanan, Dalaiah and Anani. The surrounding chapter traces David's descendants through the kings to Jeconiah and on past the exile, so Hodaiah belongs to a late generation of that line, after the return from Babylon. Smith's Bible Dictionary places him at about 406 BC, an estimate inferred from the genealogy. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of his name as "the praise of the Lord." Some manuscripts and translations spell the name Hodaviah. Nothing further is recorded about him.

Hodaviah was a leader of the half-tribe of Manasseh that settled east of the Jordan. He appears once, in 1 Chr 5:24, in a list of seven heads of their fathers' houses, described together as mighty men of valour and famous men. The surrounding passage places these clans in the land from Bashan to Baal-hermon and Mount Hermon, and goes on to tell how the eastern tribes were later carried into exile by the Assyrian king Tiglath-pileser. The text does not say exactly when Hodaviah lived. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates him to about 720 BC, near the time of that exile, while the STEPBible names index places him in the time of King David. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "praise ye the LORD." Several other men in the Bible share this name and should not be confused with him.

Hodaviah was a Benjamite named in the genealogy of Sallu, one of the Benjamites listed as living in Jerusalem. He was the son of Hasenuah and the father of Meshullam, which made him Sallu's grandfather (1 Chr 9:7). The surrounding list in 1 Chronicles 9 records those who resettled in Jerusalem after the Babylonian exile, so Hodaviah probably lived some generations before that return. The STEPBible proper-names index places him among the Benjamite families of post-exilic Jerusalem. Nothing else is recorded about him. The name, which Smith's Bible Dictionary renders "praise ye Jehovah," is shared by several other men in the Bible, and this Hodaviah should not be confused with them. A similar Benjamite genealogy in Neh 11:7 traces Sallu through different ancestors, and it is uncertain how the two lists relate.

Hodesh was a wife of Shaharaim, a man named in the genealogy of the tribe of Benjamin. She appears only once, in 1 Chr 8:9, which lists her sons Jobab, Zibia, Mesha and Malcham. The next verse, 1 Chr 8:10, continues the list with Jeuz, Shachia and Mirma, so she is counted as the mother of seven sons. The surrounding passage (1 Chr 8:8) says Shaharaim had children in the country of Moab after sending away his wives Hushim and Baara. By inference from that context, Hodesh was probably a later wife and her sons were born in Moab. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of her name as "new moon," while Hitchcock's Bible Names renders it "a table; news." Nothing else is recorded about her.

Hodiah was a woman of the tribe of Judah, named in the genealogy of 1 Chr 4:19 as the sister of Naham. Her sons were the ancestors of two clans: the father of Keilah the Garmite, and Eshtemoa the Maachathite. The Hebrew of this passage is difficult, and the verse says only "his wife" without naming the husband. This entry takes him to be Mered, who in the previous verse is married to Bithiah, the daughter of Pharaoh. On that reading Hodiah would be his other, Judahite wife. Smith's Bible Dictionary identifies her husband as Ezra (Ezrah) of Judah and takes her to be the same woman as Jehudijah in verse 18. The STEPBible names list gives her husband as Ishbah. Her name is usually understood to mean "majesty of the Lord."

Hodijah was a man who set his seal to the covenant made under Nehemiah, in which the returned exiles pledged to keep the Law of God (Neh 10:13). His name falls in the section of the list that names the Levites, which begins at Neh 10:9, before the list of the chiefs of the people at Neh 10:14. By that placement Smith's Bible Dictionary counts him as a Levite. STEPBible's proper-names index describes him as one of the leaders who signed the covenant. The name appears more than once in this period, including another Hodijah earlier in the same Levite list (Neh 10:10), so it is uncertain whether he is the same person as any other Hodijah. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "majesty of Jehovah." Nothing else is recorded about him.

Hodijah was one of the leaders who set their seal to the covenant made in Nehemiah's day to keep the law of God (Neh 10:18). His name appears in the section of the list that begins at Neh 10:14 with the "chief of the people." By inference from the passage, he was a lay leader, which is how Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him. Easton's Bible Dictionary calls him a Levite, and the STEPBible names index places him among the priests. This entry follows the reading of him as one of the heads of the people. The same covenant list names a Levite or Levites called Hodijah earlier (Neh 10:10, 13), and the name is shared by several people in the Bible, so it is uncertain how he relates to them. Nothing else is recorded about him.

Hoham was the king of Hebron at the time of Israel's conquest of Canaan under Joshua. Adonizedek, king of Jerusalem, sent to him and to the kings of Jarmuth, Lachish and Eglon, calling them to join an attack on Gibeon, which had made peace with Joshua (Josh 10:3). The surrounding chapter describes these five as Amorite kings. Their alliance was defeated, and the kings hid in a cave at Makkedah, where they were afterwards captured and put to death. Hoham is not named again, but he is presumably among those five kings. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary give the meaning of his name as "Jehovah impels." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives the same meaning with a question mark, and Hitchcock's Bible Names renders it "woe to them."

Horam was the king of Gezer at the time of Israel's conquest of Canaan under Joshua. When Joshua attacked the city of Lachish, Horam came up with his forces to help defend it. Joshua defeated him and his people, leaving none of them remaining (Josh 10:33). He is mentioned only in this verse, within the account of Joshua's campaign against the cities of southern Canaan. Gezer itself is not said to have been taken at this point, and by inference from the passage Horam fought away from his own city. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives the meaning of his name as "height," and Smith's Bible Dictionary as "mountainous."

Hori was a man of the tribe of Simeon, known only as the father of Shaphat. Shaphat was the Simeonite chosen as one of the twelve men Moses sent from the wilderness to explore the land of Canaan (Num 13:5). Nothing else is recorded about Hori himself. He is mentioned only to identify his son, in the way the other spies are named with their fathers. He lived during the wilderness period of Israel's history. Several people in the Bible share this name, and this entry concerns the Simeonite. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia give the name's meaning as "cave-dweller," while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "a prince" or "freeborn."

Hoshaiah was a man who took part in the dedication of the rebuilt wall of Jerusalem in Nehemiah's time. Nehemiah organized two large thanksgiving choirs that walked in opposite directions along the top of the wall. Hoshaiah walked behind the singers of one of them, leading half of the princes of Judah in the procession (Neh 12:32). Smith's Bible Dictionary dates the event to about 446 BC, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests he was probably from the tribe of Judah. Nothing else is recorded about him. His name means "whom the Lord helps" or "the salvation of the Lord." The name is shared by another man in the Bible, the father of Jezaniah or Azariah in the book of Jeremiah, but nothing links the two.

Hoshama was one of the sons of Jehoiachin (also called Jeconiah), the king of Judah who was taken captive to Babylon. He appears only in the royal genealogy of 1 Chr 3:17–18, where he is listed among seven sons along with Shealtiel, Malchiram, Pedaiah, Shenazar, Jecamiah and Nedabiah. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the list may refer to sons or more broadly to descendants of Jeconiah. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "whom Jehovah hears." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia explains it as a shortened form of Jehoshama. Nothing more is recorded about his life. By inference from his father's captivity, he was probably born or raised during the exile in Babylon.

Hoshea, son of Azaziah, was the officer over the tribe of Ephraim during King David's reign. He appears only once, in the list of tribal rulers in 1 Chr 27:16–22, where each tribe of Israel is assigned a leader. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary both describe him as the ruler of Ephraim in David's time. Nothing else is recorded about him. The name Hoshea, which Smith's Bible Dictionary glosses as "salvation," was borne by several people in the Bible. These include Joshua son of Nun, another Ephraimite, whose original name was Hoshea, and the last king of the northern kingdom of Israel. This Hoshea should be kept distinct from them.

Hoshea was one of the leaders of the people who set their seal to the covenant made in Nehemiah's time, a written pledge by the returned exiles to keep the Law of God. His name appears in the list of signatories at Neh 10:23, alongside Hananiah and Hashub, and nothing else is recorded about him. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "salvation" and dates the covenant to about 410 BC. The same name belongs to several other people in the Bible, including the last king of the northern kingdom of Israel, the son of Nun (the earlier name of Joshua), and a tribal officer under David. This Hoshea is a separate person, known only from this list.

Hothan was a man from Aroer, known only as the father of Shama and Jehiel, two brothers listed among David's mighty warriors in 1 Chr 11:44. The text calls him "the Aroerite" but does not say which Aroer is meant. Towns of that name stood beside the Arnon River east of the Jordan and in the Negev of Judah, so his home cannot be fixed with certainty. Nothing else is recorded about him. His name is spelled Hotham in many modern translations. Smith's Bible Dictionary explains it as meaning "signet ring." He should not be confused with Hotham the Asherite of 1 Chr 7:32, a different man. By inference from the list in which his sons appear, he lived in the time of David, about the late eleventh or early tenth century BC.

Huppah was a priest in the time of King David. He is named only once, in the list of the twenty-four divisions of priests who took turns serving at the sanctuary. When David organized the priesthood, the lot assigned the thirteenth turn to Huppah (1 Chr 24:13). From the surrounding passage, the divisions were drawn from the descendants of Eleazar and Ithamar, the sons of Aaron. Huppah was probably the head of a priestly family, and his name stood for the course that served in that position. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both give the meaning of his name as "protection." Nothing else is recorded about him.

Hur was the father of one of the twelve district officers King Solomon appointed over Israel to supply food for the royal household. He is known only through his son, who is listed in 1 Kgs 4:8 simply as "the son of Hur" (in Hebrew, Ben-hur) and who served in the hill country of Ephraim. Nothing else is recorded about Hur himself. The name is shared by several other people in the Bible, including the Hur who helped Aaron hold up Moses' hands during the battle with Amalek. There is no indication that this Hur is the same man as any of them. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "liberty," "whiteness" or "hole."

Hur was the father of Rephaiah, who repaired a section of Jerusalem's wall when the city was rebuilt under Nehemiah, probably in the mid-400s BC by inference from context. He is known only from Neh 3:9, which names him solely to identify his son. The verse calls someone "the ruler of the half part of Jerusalem," meaning half of the district around the city. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia takes this title to belong to Rephaiah, which fits the pattern of other district rulers named as builders in the same chapter. STEPBible's Tyndale House name list applies it to Hur himself. This entry follows the reading that Rephaiah was the ruler. Nothing else is recorded about Hur, and he should not be confused with the other men of the same name in the Bible. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the name's meaning as "liberty," "whiteness" or "hole."

Huram appears only in the phrase "Huram my father's" in 2 Chr 2:13, part of the letter King Huram (Hiram) of Tyre sent to Solomon. There the king says he is sending a skilled craftsman to help build the temple. Read this way, the phrase names the king's own father, also called Huram, as the craftsman's former master, and this entry follows that reading, treating him as the father of Hiram. Nothing else is said about him. The wording is ambiguous, though, and many translations take "Huram my father" (Huram-abi) as the name or title of the craftsman himself. In that case it would not refer to a separate person at all, and the same expression is used of the craftsman in 2 Chr 4:16. Several people in the Bible share the name. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives its meaning as "their liberty" or "their whiteness."

Huri was a man of the tribe of Gad, named only once in the Bible, in the Gadite genealogy of 1 Chr 5:14. He was the son of Jaroah and the father of Abihail, whose descendants are listed among the Gadite families living in Gilead and Bashan east of the Jordan. His line is traced back through Jaroah, Gilead, Michael, Jeshishai and Jahdo to Buz. The verse records nothing else about him. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both give the meaning of his name as "linen weaver." Hitchcock's Bible Names instead suggests "being angry," or links it with the name Huram.

Hushim was a son of Aher, named only in 1 Chr 7:12 in a short list that also mentions Shuppim and Huppim. The verse calls him "the sons of Aher," so Smith's Bible Dictionary notes the name may be plural and may refer to a family group rather than one person. Views differ on his tribe. The verse sits within Benjamin's genealogy, and Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treat him as a Benjamite. Tyndale House's STEPBible names place him in the line of Dan. That view connects him with Gen 46:23, where Hushim is Dan's son, and it would account for Dan otherwise being missing from this chapter. This entry follows the Danite reading. Nothing else is recorded about him. The name is also borne by others, including a wife of Shaharaim (1 Chr 8:8).

Huz was the firstborn son of Nahor, Abraham's brother, and his wife Milcah. He is named first in the list of Nahor's sons that was reported to Abraham after the binding of Isaac (Gen 22:21). His full brothers were Buz, Kemuel, Chesed, Hazo, Pildash, Jidlaph and Bethuel, the father of Rebekah. Nahor also had sons by his concubine Reumah. Nothing more is recorded about Huz himself. In Hebrew his name is the same as Uz, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats him under that name. STEPBible's proper-name index describes him as an Aramean, which fits his family's links to Aram. Some readers connect his name with the land of Uz, the homeland of Job, but the text does not draw that link. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates him to about 1900 BC, an estimate based on context.

Ibneiah, son of Jeroham, was a man of the tribe of Benjamin. He is named in 1 Chr 9:8 in a list of Benjamites living in Jerusalem. By inference from the context of 1 Chronicles 9, which describes those who settled in the city after the return from the Babylonian exile, he was among the resettled inhabitants of Jerusalem. The STEPBible proper-names index reads the passage this way. He appears in the same verse as Elah son of Uzzi and Meshullam son of Shephathiah. His name means roughly "the LORD builds up" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia). Smith's Bible Dictionary gives his father's name as Jehoram, a variant of Jeroham. He should not be confused with Ibnijah, a similar name in the same verse belonging to an ancestor of Meshullam. Nothing further is recorded about him.

Ibnijah was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, named only in the genealogy at 1 Chr 9:8. He was the father of Reuel, and through him the great-grandfather of Meshullam son of Shephathiah. Meshullam appears among the Benjamites listed as living in Jerusalem, a list that the surrounding chapter connects with the return after the Babylonian exile. Ibnijah himself is named only as an ancestor, so he probably lived some generations before that resettlement, although the STEPBible Proper Names index counts him among the returning Israelites. The same verse names a different man, Ibneiah son of Jeroham, whose name is spelled very similarly in Hebrew. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives the meaning of Ibnijah's name as "Yah builds up." Nothing else is recorded about him.

Ibri was a Levite of the clan of Merari, named as a son of Jaaziah in the list of Levite families in 1 Chr 24:27. His brothers there are Beno, Shoham and Zaccur. The list belongs to the arrangement of the Levites for temple service in the last years of David's reign, so by inference Ibri's family belonged to that period. The verse itself is difficult. Its phrase "by Jaaziah" may mean that these men were descendants of Merari through Jaaziah rather than his own sons. Nothing more is recorded about him. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives the meaning of his name as "a Hebrew." Hitchcock's Bible Names suggests "passing over" or "being angry."

Ichabod was a son of Phinehas and a grandson of Eli, the priest at Shiloh. He was a brother of Ahitub. His only mention in the verses supplied here is in 1 Sam 14:3, where he identifies Ahiah, who wore the ephod in Saul's camp. Ahiah was the son of Ahitub and so Ichabod's nephew. The fuller account of his birth is in 1 Sam 4:19–22. His mother went into labour when she heard that the ark of God had been captured by the Philistines and that her husband and father-in-law were dead. She named the child as she was dying, saying the glory had departed from Israel. The name is usually explained as meaning "no glory" or "inglorious" (Smith's Bible Dictionary; International Standard Bible Encyclopedia). Hitchcock's Bible Names also gives "where is the glory?" Nothing else is recorded of his life.

Idbash was a man of the tribe of Judah, named only in the genealogy at 1 Chr 4:3. He is listed with Jezreel and Ishma, and with their sister Hazelelponi, as children of "the father of Etam." Etam was probably a town near Bethlehem, so "father" likely means founder or leader of its settlement. This entry identifies that father as Hur. That is an inference from the surrounding genealogy, where Hur is called "the father of Bethlehem" (1 Chr 4:4) and his other sons, such as Shobal, Salma and Hareph, appear in 1 Chr 2:50–51. On that reading his brothers also include Penuel, Ezer and Uri. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the Greek Septuagint reads "sons of Etam." The meaning of his name is uncertain. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "stout," and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "flowing with honey." Nothing else is recorded about him.

Iddo was the father of Ahinadab, one of the twelve officers King Solomon appointed to supply food for the royal household, each for one month of the year. Ahinadab was responsible for the district of Mahanaim, a town east of the Jordan in Gilead (1 Kgs 4:14). Nothing else is recorded about Iddo himself, and he is mentioned only as Ahinadab's father. Several other men in the Bible share the name Iddo, and there is no clear basis for linking this one with any of them. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "timely." Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia spell the son's name "Abinadab" rather than the "Ahinadab" found in the King James text.

Iddo was the son of Zechariah and the leader of the half tribe of Manasseh in Gilead, the part of the tribe settled east of the Jordan River. He is named once, in a list of the officers over the tribes of Israel during King David's reign (1 Chr 27:21). The surrounding chapter shows these men served as tribal heads in David's administration, and Smith's Bible Dictionary dates his time to about 1014 BC, an estimate drawn from the setting. Nothing else is recorded about him. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "lovely," while the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests "beloved." Several other men in the Bible share the name Iddo, and this one should not be confused with them.

Iddo was the chief, or leader, of a community at a place called Casiphia in Babylonia during Ezra's return to Jerusalem. When Ezra found no Levites among the people gathered to travel with him, he sent messengers to Iddo and his brethren with instructions to ask them to send ministers to serve in the temple (Ezra 8:17). The following verses report that Levites and temple servants (Nethinim) came in response (Ezra 8:18–20). The wording of the verse is read in two ways. Smith's Bible Dictionary takes Iddo himself to be one of the Nethinim. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests that an "and" may have dropped out, so that the message went to "his brethren and the Nethinim," and it notes that 1 Esdras calls him Loddeus. Several other people in the Bible share the name Iddo, and this one is mentioned only here. The exact location of Casiphia is unknown.

Igal son of Joseph was the man chosen from the tribe of Issachar to be one of the twelve spies Moses sent from the wilderness of Paran to explore Canaan (Num 13:7). Nothing else is said about him individually. The surrounding chapters show that ten of the spies brought back a discouraging report, while only Joshua and Caleb urged the people to go in. Since he is not named among those two, Igal was presumably one of the ten. His father Joseph is not the patriarch Joseph but an otherwise unknown man of Issachar. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia takes the name to mean "he (God) redeems." Several other men in the Bible share the name Igal, so this entry is limited to the spy from Issachar.

Igal, son of Nathan of Zobah, was one of David's mighty warriors. His name appears in the list of David's champions in 2 Sam 23:36. Zobah was an Aramean kingdom north of Israel, so he was probably of Aramean origin or from a family linked to that region. The parallel list in 1 Chr 11:38 seems to name the same man as "Joel the brother of Nathan," a difference noted by the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia. This entry follows the 2 Samuel reading. His name is usually taken to mean "he (God) redeems." Nothing else is recorded about him, and he should not be confused with others of the same name, such as Igal the spy sent from the tribe of Issachar to explore Canaan.

Igdaliah was the father of Hanan, mentioned once in the Bible, in Jer 35:4. When Jeremiah brought the Rechabites into the temple, he took them to the chamber belonging to "the sons of Hanan, the son of Igdaliah, a man of God." The room was next to the chamber of the princes and above that of Maaseiah son of Shallum, the doorkeeper. The title "a man of God" could apply grammatically either to Hanan or to Igdaliah. Smith's Bible Dictionary takes it as describing Igdaliah, as a prophet or holy man, and this entry notes that reading while recognizing the ambiguity. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia describes him as the ancestor of a group that had a chamber in the temple in Jeremiah's time, so he probably lived in or before the late seventh century BC. His name means "Yah is great."

Igeal was a man of the tribe of Judah and a son of Shemaiah, named in the genealogy of King David's royal line in 1 Chr 3:22. His brothers were Hattush, Bariah, Neariah and Shaphat. The verse says the sons of Shemaiah were "six" but names only five, a difference the text leaves unexplained. By inference from the surrounding genealogy (1 Chr 3:17–21), he belonged to the generations after Jeconiah and Zerubbabel, so he probably lived in the period after the Babylonian exile. Nothing else is recorded about him. The Revised Version spells his name Igal, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives its meaning as "God redeems." He should be kept distinct from others of a similar name, such as the spy from Issachar (Num 13:7) and one of David's mighty men (2 Sam 23:36).

Immer was the father of Zadok, who repaired a section of Jerusalem's wall opposite his own house during Nehemiah's rebuilding (Neh 3:29). Nothing else is recorded about Immer himself, and he is known only through his son. Several people in the Bible share the name. Immer was also the name of a priestly family that returned from exile in Babylon, and since the priests worked on the neighbouring stretch of wall (Neh 3:28), "son of Immer" here may refer to a member of that family rather than to Immer's immediate son. This is an inference from the context and is not certain. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "saying", "speaking" or "a lamb."

Imna was a man of the tribe of Asher, named once in the tribe's genealogy as one of the sons of Helem, alongside his brothers Zophah, Shelesh and Amal (1 Chr 7:35). The verse calls Helem the brother of the man named just before, which by inference from the surrounding genealogy is Shomer (spelled Shamer in 1 Chr 7:34), son of Heber. This entry treats Helem as another name for Hotham, a third son of Heber listed in 1 Chr 7:32, and so gives Imna's father as Hotham. The identification rests on the two names appearing in matching places in the list. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "holding back." Nothing else is recorded about him.
