Imnah was a Levite known only as the father of Kore, according to 2 Chr 31:14. Kore was the gatekeeper of the east gate of the temple. During King Hezekiah's religious reforms he was put in charge of the freewill offerings given to God and handed out the Lord's offerings and the most holy gifts. The phrase "the Levite" in that verse could describe either father or son, but both would have belonged to the tribe of Levi. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates Kore's service to about 726 BC and gives the name's meaning as "holding back." Nothing else is recorded about Imnah himself. The same name belongs to other people in the Bible, including a son of Asher (Gen 46:17; 1 Chr 7:30), whose name the KJV also spells Jimnah. This Levite should not be confused with them.

Imrah was a man of the tribe of Asher, one of the sons of Zophah named in the Asherite genealogy of 1 Chr 7:36. His brothers listed there and in the next verse include Suah, Harnepher, Shual, Beri, Bezer, Hod, Shamma, Shilshah, Ithran (or Jether) and Beera. Nothing else is recorded about him beyond his place in this family list. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "stubborn", and Hitchcock's Bible Names renders it "a rebel; waxing bitter; changing". Smith's places him sometime after 1445 BC, a date inferred from the genealogy rather than stated in the text.

Imri was a man of the tribe of Judah, descended through Perez (Pharez), the son of Judah. He appears only in a genealogy in 1 Chr 9:4, which names him as the son of Bani and the father of Omri. His great-grandson Uthai is listed among the people who lived in Jerusalem, and the surrounding chapter places that list after the return from exile in Babylon. Imri himself therefore probably belonged to an earlier generation, though STEPBible's proper-names index counts him among those who settled in Jerusalem after the exile. Nothing else is recorded about him. The name is shared by at least one other person in the Bible, so this Imri should not be confused with others who bear it. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives its meaning as "speaking," "exalting," "bitter," or "a lamb."

Imri was the father of Zaccur, one of the men who rebuilt a section of Jerusalem's wall under Nehemiah after the return from exile. Zaccur worked on the stretch next to the men of Jericho, near the Sheep Gate where the rebuilding began (Neh 3:2). Nothing else is recorded about Imri himself. His name appears only as part of his son's identification, and the verse does not say whether he was still living at the time. Another man named Imri appears in a Judahite genealogy (1 Chr 9:4), and there is no clear evidence that the two are the same person. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the name's meaning as "speaking" or "exalting".

Iphedeiah was a son of Shashak and a member of the tribe of Benjamin. He appears only in the Benjamite genealogy of 1 Chronicles 8, which lists him with Penuel among the sons of Shashak (1 Chr 8:25). The surrounding list also names his brothers Ishpan, Heber, Eliel, Abdon, Zichri, Hanan, Hananiah, Elam and Antothijah. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes him as a chief of the tribe, probably reflecting the note at the end of the list that these men were heads of their fathers' houses living in Jerusalem. His name is usually explained as meaning "the Lord frees" or "the Lord redeems" (Smith's and Hitchcock's). Nothing else is recorded about him.

Ir was a descendant of Benjamin, named in 1 Chr 7:12 as the father of Shuppim and Huppim. The verse sits within a genealogy of Benjamin's family. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identifies him with Iri, a son of Bela, Benjamin's firstborn, who appears a few verses earlier in 1 Chr 7:7. This entry follows that identification. Ir is also counted here as the father of Maachah, the wife of Machir. That rests on 1 Chr 7:15, which says Machir married the sister of Huppim and Shuppim and gives her name as Maachah, so she was probably Ir's daughter. Nothing else is recorded about him. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "watchman," "city" or "vision."

Ira the Jairite was one of King David's senior officials, named at the end of the list of David's officers in 2 Sam 20:26. The King James Version calls him "a chief ruler about David." The underlying Hebrew word usually means "priest," and Easton's Bible Dictionary describes him as a priest, either a royal chaplain or a confidential adviser to the king, comparing the similar title given to David's sons in 2 Sam 8:18. The STEPBible name index also lists him as a priest under David. "Jairite" probably marks him as a descendant of, or someone from the towns of, Jair, a clan of Manasseh in Gilead, though the text does not explain the term. Nothing more is recorded about him. The name Ira is shared by several men in the Bible, including two of David's warriors, and they should not be confused with this one.

Irad was a son of Enoch and a grandson of Cain, listed in the genealogy of Cain's descendants in Gen 4:18. He was the father of Mehujael, and through him the line continued to Methusael and then to Lamech. Nothing else is recorded about his life. He belongs to the generations before the flood. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "runner" or "wild ass," and Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "fleet." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the Greek Septuagint spells his name Gaidad. His name is similar to Jared in the line of Seth (Gen 5:15–20), and some readers compare the two genealogies. This entry treats Irad as a distinct person in Cain's line, as Genesis presents him.

Iri was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, a son of Bela and so a grandson of Benjamin. He is named in 1 Chr 7:7 as the last of Bela's five sons: Ezbon, Uzzi, Uzziel, Jerimoth and Iri. They are described as heads of their fathers' houses and mighty men of valour, whose descendants were counted at 22,034. The other brothers grouped with him here, such as Addar, Gera and Naaman, come from a different list of Bela's sons in 1 Chr 8:3–5. Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests that the Ir of 1 Chr 7:12 is the same man under a shorter form of the name. Smith's gives the meaning as "belonging to a city," while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "fire" or "light." Nothing else is recorded about him.

Iru was a son of Caleb the son of Jephunneh, named in the genealogy of Judah at 1 Chr 4:15 together with his brothers Elah and Naam. Because he is listed first, Smith's Bible Dictionary calls him Caleb's eldest son. Achsah is counted as his sister. By inference from Josh 15:16–17 and Judg 1:12–13, she is the daughter whom Caleb gave in marriage to Othniel. Nothing more is recorded about Iru himself. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the Hebrew name may originally have been Ir. On that reading, the final "-u" is the word "and" belonging to the next name in the list. This entry keeps the familiar form Iru.

Iscah was a child of Haran, the brother of Abram, mentioned only once, in the note on the marriages of Abram and Nahor (Gen 11:29). That verse names Haran as "the father of Milcah, and the father of Iscah," which makes Iscah a sibling of Milcah, Nahor's wife. Lot was also a child of Haran (Gen 11:27), so Iscah was Lot's sibling too, and a niece or nephew of Abram and Nahor. The verse does not state Iscah's sex. Easton's Bible Dictionary, Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia all describe Iscah as Haran's daughter. Smith's notes that Jewish tradition identifies Iscah with Sarai, Abram's wife. Nothing else is recorded about Iscah's life. The name's meaning is given as "spy" (Easton's), "one who looks forth" (Smith's), or "he that anoints" (Hitchcock's Bible Names).

Ishbah was a man of the tribe of Judah, named once in the genealogy of 1 Chr 4:17, where he is called "the father of Eshtemoa." Eshtemoa was a town in the hill country of Judah, so "father" here probably means founder or chief of that settlement rather than a literal parent. His name is usually explained as meaning "praising" (Smith's Bible Dictionary). The verse lists him with Miriam and Shammai as children of an unnamed "she." By inference from 1 Chr 4:18, which is generally read as continuing this list, this entry takes her to be Bithiah, Pharaoh's daughter, and his father to be Mered, a son of Ezra. The same passage names Jehudijah as the mother of Jered, Heber and Jekuthiel. The wording of these verses is compressed, and how these people relate to one another is uncertain.

Ishbi-benob was a Philistine warrior described as one of "the sons of the giant" (the Rephaim, in Easton's Bible Dictionary), who tried to kill David during a battle between Israel and the Philistines late in David's reign. 2 Sam 21:16 says his bronze spearhead weighed three hundred shekels, roughly 7.5 pounds (about 3.5 kg), and that he was armed with a new sword when he attacked David, who had grown tired in the fighting. The next verse, 2 Sam 21:17, records that Abishai son of Zeruiah came to David's aid and killed him. After this, David's men swore that David would no longer go out to battle with them. The surrounding passage (2 Sam 21:15–22) names him as one of four men born to the giant in Gath, alongside figures such as Saph (Sippai) and the brother of Goliath. Easton's and Smith's dictionaries take his name to mean "dweller at Nob" or "my seat at Nob."

Ishi was a man of the tribe of Judah, named only in the genealogy of 1 Chr 2:31 as the son of Appaim and the father of Sheshan, whose child was Ahlai. The surrounding genealogy places Appaim in the family of Jerahmeel, a son of Hezron and grandson of Judah. Ishi therefore belonged to the Jerahmeelite branch of Judah, or as Smith's Bible Dictionary puts it, "one of the great house of Hezron." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that such genealogies may show membership in Judah either by blood or by adoption. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "salvation," and Smith's gives "salutary." Nothing else is recorded about him. Several other men in the Bible share the name Ishi, and this one should not be confused with them.

Ishi was a man of the tribe of Judah, named in the genealogy of 1 Chr 4:20 as the father of Zoheth and Ben-zoheth. That verse is the only mention of him. It follows a list of the sons of Shimon, and the STEPBible Proper Names index takes Ishi to be one of Shimon's sons, though the verse does not say so directly. Nothing more is recorded about his life. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia give the name's meaning as "salutary," and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "salvation." Several other men in Chronicles bear the same name, including a descendant of Judah through Jerahmeel (1 Chr 2:31), a Simeonite (1 Chr 4:42) and a leader of the half-tribe of Manasseh (1 Chr 5:24). This entry treats the Ishi of 1 Chr 4:20 as a separate person.

Ishi was a man of the tribe of Simeon, described in Smith's Bible Dictionary as the head of a Simeonite family. His four sons, Pelatiah, Neariah, Rephaiah and Uzziel, served as captains of a band of five hundred Simeonites who went to Mount Seir (1 Chr 4:42). The next verse, 1 Chr 4:43, says they struck down the surviving Amalekites there and settled in their place. The surrounding passage places these Simeonite movements in the days of Hezekiah, king of Judah (1 Chr 4:41). Nothing else is recorded about Ishi himself. The name means "salutary" according to Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia, or "salvation" according to Hitchcock's Bible Names. Several other men in the Bible share the name Ishi, including figures in the genealogies of Judah and Manasseh, and should not be confused with this Simeonite.

Ishi was one of the heads of ancestral houses in the half-tribe of Manasseh that settled east of the Jordan. In 1 Chr 5:24 he is listed with Epher, Eliel, Azriel, Jeremiah, Hodaviah and Jahdiel, who are described as mighty men of valour, famous men and heads of their fathers' houses. The surrounding passage places this half-tribe in the land from Bashan to Baal-hermon and Mount Hermon, and Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both identify him as a chief of eastern Manasseh. Nothing more is recorded about him. The name, which Smith's Bible Dictionary renders "salutary" and Hitchcock's Bible Names "salvation," is also borne by other men in the Bible, so this Ishi should not be confused with others of the same name.

Ishiah was a man of the tribe of Issachar, named in the tribe's genealogy as a son of Izrahiah and grandson of Uzzi. His brothers were Michael, Obadiah and Joel (1 Chr 7:3). The verse counts the group as "five" though it names only four sons. The fifth is probably Izrahiah himself, though Smith's Bible Dictionary takes Ishiah as the fifth of five sons. All of them are called "chief men," meaning heads of their clan. From the surrounding verses, Uzzi descended from Tola, Issachar's son. Smith's Bible Dictionary places this family in the time of David. The name is also spelled Isshiah, and Smith's Bible Dictionary gives its meaning as "whom the Lord lends." Nothing more is recorded about him. Several other men in Chronicles bear the same or a similar name, and they appear to be different people.

Ishijah was one of the "sons of Harim," a lay family group among the Israelites who had returned from exile. He is named only once, in the list in Ezra 10:31. That list records the men who had married foreign wives and, during Ezra's reforms, agreed to send them away. Nothing else is known about him. Smith's Bible Dictionary explains the name as meaning "whom Jehovah lends." It dates the event to about 459 BC, a date estimated from the context of Ezra's work in Jerusalem. Some reference works, such as the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia, spell the name Isshijah.

Ishma was a man of the tribe of Judah, named once in the genealogy of Judah's descendants. 1 Chr 4:3 lists him with Jezreel and Idbash as belonging to "the father of Etam," and names their sister Hazelelponi. "Father of Etam" may refer to the founder or leading figure of the town of Etam rather than a personal name, so the exact relationship is uncertain. This entry follows the reading that places Ishma among the descendants of Hur. By inference from the next verse, 1 Chr 4:4, which closes the list with "these are the sons of Hur," he is grouped with the other men of Hur's line, such as Shobal, Salma and Hareph. Nothing else is recorded about him. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia takes his name to mean "desolate."

Ishmael was a man of Judah known only as the father of Zebadiah, who served as "the ruler of the house of Judah" in charge of the king's matters. The context shows this was during the reign of King Jehoshaphat, who appointed judges and officials in Jerusalem (2 Chr 19:11). Ishmael himself is not described, and nothing else is recorded of his life or role. Several other men in the Bible share the name, and the verse does not link him to any of them. The name means "God hears," according to Smith's Bible Dictionary and Hitchcock's Bible Names.

Ishmael son of Jehohanan was one of the captains of hundreds in Judah whom the priest Jehoiada brought into a covenant with him in the seventh year (2 Chr 23:1). By context, the seventh year is that of Queen Athaliah's rule, and the covenant aimed to overthrow her and make the young Joash king, as the rest of 2 Chronicles 23 describes. Ishmael is named alongside Azariah son of Jeroham, Azariah son of Obed, Maaseiah son of Adaiah and Elishaphat son of Zichri. Nothing more is recorded about him. The name, meaning "God hears" according to Hitchcock's Bible Names, belongs to several people in the Bible, and this man should not be confused with Abraham's son or with the Ishmael who killed Gedaliah.

Ishmael was a priest, one of the sons (descendants) of Pashur, listed in Ezra 10:22 among the men who had married foreign wives in the time of Ezra. The surrounding passage shows that those named agreed to send away these wives as part of Ezra's reforms after the return from exile in Babylon. The name means "God hears," according to Hitchcock's Bible Names. Several other men in the Bible share the name, most famously Abraham's son by Hagar, but this Ishmael is known only from this list. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the same man appears as Ismael in the parallel list in 1 Esdras 9:22. Nothing else is recorded about him.

Ishmaiah, son of Obadiah, was the leader of the tribe of Zebulun during King David's reign. He appears only once, in a list of the chief officers over the tribes of Israel (1 Chr 27:16–22), where he is named as the ruler of Zebulun alongside Jerimoth son of Azriel, ruler of Naphtali. The text gives no further details about his life or duties. Easton's Bible Dictionary calls him a viceroy of Zebulun under David and Solomon. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia describes him as the chief of Zebulun's contingent in David's monthly rotation of tribal service, though the surrounding list is usually read as one of tribal leaders rather than military commanders. His name is usually taken to mean "the LORD hears." He should not be confused with Ishmaiah of Gibeon, a mighty man of David mentioned elsewhere in Chronicles.

Ishmerai was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, named as one of the sons of Elpaal in the Benjamite genealogy of 1 Chronicles 8. He is listed alongside Jezliah and Jobab, with other sons of Elpaal such as Eber, Misham, Shamed, Beriah, Shema, Zebadiah, Meshullam, Hezeki and Heber named in the surrounding verses. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia counts him among the heads of fathers' houses who lived in Jerusalem, following the summary later in the same chapter. Nothing else is recorded about him. His name probably means "the Lord keeps" or "guard, protector," according to Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia.

Ishod (spelled Ishhod in some translations, as in the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia) was a man of the tribe of Manasseh, named only in the Manasseh genealogy of 1 Chr 7:18. His mother was Hammoleketh, and his brothers were Abiezer and Mahalah. The verse calls Hammoleketh "his sister," and the person meant is not certain. From the preceding verse she was probably the sister of Gilead, the son of Machir. STEPBible's proper-names list takes her as the sister of Manasseh. Smith's Bible Dictionary places this family among the Manassites east of the Jordan. His name has been explained as "man of glory" (Smith's Bible Dictionary) or "a comely man" (Hitchcock's Bible Names). Nothing else is recorded about him.

Ishpan was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, named in the Benjamite genealogy of 1 Chronicles 8 as a son of Shashak. His brothers were Heber, Eliel, Abdon, Zichri, Hanan, Hananiah, Elam, Antothijah, Iphedeiah and Penuel. The surrounding passage presents these sons of Shashak among the heads of fathers' houses and chief men who lived in Jerusalem. That is noted in a verse just after his own, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia reads it the same way. Nothing else is recorded about him. The meaning of his name is uncertain. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives "he will hide," Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "hid" or "broken in two," and Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "bald."

Ismachiah was one of ten overseers who served under Cononiah and his brother Shimei during the reign of King Hezekiah of Judah. They were appointed by command of the king and of Azariah, the ruler of the house of God (2 Chr 31:13). The surrounding passage shows that their task was to manage the tithes, offerings and dedicated gifts that the people brought to the temple storerooms. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him as a Levite, which fits the context of temple service, though the verse does not say so directly. His name is generally taken to mean "the LORD sustains" or "whom the LORD upholds." He is mentioned only here, and nothing more is known about him.

Ismaiah was a man from Gibeon, called "the Gibeonite," who is named among the warriors who came over to David. 1 Chr 12:4 describes him as "a mighty man among the thirty, and over the thirty," which suggests he was both a member of David's elite group of warriors known as the Thirty and a leader within it. The surrounding chapter lists men who joined David at Ziklag while he was still in hiding from Saul, as Easton's Bible Dictionary also notes. Many of these men were Benjamites, Saul's own kinsmen. His name is also spelled Ishmaiah in some reference works. He is not mentioned in the lists of the Thirty in 2 Samuel 23 or 1 Chronicles 11, and nothing more is known of him.

Ispah, also spelled Ishpah in some versions, was a man of the tribe of Benjamin named among the sons of Beriah in the genealogy of 1 Chr 8:16. His brothers were Michael, Joha, Ahio, Shashak, Jeremoth, Zebadiah, Arad and Ader. Judging from the surrounding passage, his father Beriah was one of the Benjamite family heads linked with Aijalon (1 Chr 8:13), and the men in this list are later described as heads of families living in Jerusalem (1 Chr 8:28). Smith's Bible Dictionary likewise calls Ispah one of the heads of his tribe. Nothing else is recorded about him. The meaning of his name is uncertain. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "bald" and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "a jasper stone."

Issachar was a Levite of the Korahite line who served as a gatekeeper of the house of the Lord in the time of King David. He is named only once, in the list of gatekeeper families, as the seventh son in a family of eight brothers: Shemaiah, Jehozabad, Joah, Sacar, Nethaneel, Ammiel, Issachar and Peulthai (1 Chr 26:5). The surrounding passage (1 Chr 26:4) presents these brothers as the sons of Obed-edom, and Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both identify him that way. The list closes by noting that God blessed the family with many sons. His name, probably meaning "reward," is shared with the better-known ninth son of Jacob and the tribe descended from him, who is a different person. Nothing else is recorded about this Issachar.

Ithiel was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, named only in the genealogy of Sallu in Neh 11:7. He was the son of Jesaiah and the father of Maaseiah, and he was an ancestor of Sallu several generations back. Sallu was among the Benjamites who lived in Jerusalem after the return from exile in Babylon. Ithiel himself probably lived well before that time, by inference from the length of the line. Nothing else is recorded about him. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "God is with me." The same name belongs to a different man, one of those addressed in Prov 30:1, who is not the person described here.

Ithiel was one of two men, together with Ucal, to whom Agur son of Jakeh addressed his sayings in Prov 30:1. The verse names Ithiel twice and gives no details about who he was, though he may have been a pupil or companion of Agur. Smith's Bible Dictionary takes the name to mean "God is with me" and places the discourse at about 900 BC, an estimate rather than a date given in the text. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia says the name is only "perhaps" present here, because the Hebrew words can also be divided and read as a phrase rather than as personal names. This entry follows the reading of the King James Version, which treats Ithiel as a person. The name is shared by others in the Bible, including a Benjamite listed in Neh 11:7, who is a different man.

Ithmah was a Moabite listed among David's mighty warriors in 1 Chr 11:46. He appears in the extended roster of heroes in 1 Chronicles 11, which goes beyond the shorter list in 2 Samuel 23, and nothing else is recorded about him. His Moabite origin is notable because Moab was often at war with Israel. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia points out that a man from that nation still ranked among the king's heroes. The meaning of his name is uncertain. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "bereavedness," Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "an orphan," and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives "purity."

Izrahiah was a man of the tribe of Issachar, named in its genealogy as the son of Uzzi. His four sons were Michael, Obadiah, Joel and Ishiah. The verse counts the group as "five," probably including Izrahiah himself with his sons, and calls them all "chief men," meaning heads of families or clans. The verse before (1 Chr 7:2) names Uzzi as a son of Tola, Issachar's son, so Izrahiah was Tola's grandson, as the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia also notes. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him as a chieftain of Issachar. His name is usually explained as meaning "the LORD shines" or "the LORD appears." Nothing else is recorded about him.

Jaakobah was a man of the tribe of Simeon, named once in a list of Simeonite clan leaders in 1 Chr 4:36. By inference from the surrounding passage (1 Chr 4:38–41), these men were princes of their families whose households grew large. In the days of King Hezekiah of Judah they moved toward Gedor to find pasture for their flocks and took the land from its earlier inhabitants. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates him to about 710 BC, an estimate drawn from that context. His name is a form of Jacob. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives its meaning as "heel-catcher," and Smith's gives "supplanter." Nothing else is recorded about him.

Jaanai was a leader of the tribe of Gad, named in the genealogy at 1 Chr 5:12 alongside Joel the chief, Shapham second in rank, and Shaphat. The surrounding passage places these Gadite families in the land of Bashan, east of the Jordan, which is probably where Jaanai lived as well. Nothing else is recorded about him. Most modern translations spell his name Janai, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia lists him under that form. The meaning of the name is uncertain. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "whom Jehovah answers," Hitchcock's Bible Names offers "answering" or "afflicting," and Easton's Bible Dictionary gives "mourner."

Jaasau was an Israelite man named in the list of those who had married foreign wives in the time of Ezra, after the return from exile in Babylon (Ezra 10:37). The surrounding list in Ezra 10 groups these men by family. By inference from that context, Smith's Bible Dictionary places him among the descendants of Bani, and he was among those who agreed to send away their foreign wives during Ezra's reforms. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates this to about 459 BC. Nothing else is recorded about him. Smith's Bible Dictionary takes the name to mean "whom the Lord made," while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "doing" or "my doing." Some versions spell the name Jaasu.

Jaasiel was the son of Abner and the leader of the tribe of Benjamin during the reign of King David. He appears in the list of officers who ruled over the tribes of Israel (1 Chr 27:16–22), where he is named alongside Iddo, leader of the half-tribe of Manasseh in Gilead. His father is probably Abner the Benjamite, Saul's cousin and army commander, as Smith's Bible Dictionary takes him. That would fit a son of Abner being placed over Benjamin, though the verse does not say so. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both identify him with Jasiel the Mezobaite, one of David's mighty men in 1 Chr 11:47. The ISBE marks that identification as probable. His name is usually explained as meaning "God makes" or "made by God."

Jaazaniah was the son of Jeremiah and grandson of Habaziniah, and a leading member of the Rechabites, a family clan in the days of the prophet Jeremiah (Jer 35:3). His father Jeremiah is a different man from the prophet. When the prophet was told to bring the Rechabites into a chamber of the temple and offer them wine, he took Jaazaniah together with his brothers, his sons and the whole Rechabite household. Since he heads the list, he was probably the clan's chief at the time, as Easton's Bible Dictionary describes him. By inference from the rest of the chapter, he and his family refused the wine out of loyalty to their ancestor's commands, and the prophet held up their faithfulness as an example to Judah. His name means "the Lord hears." Several other men in the Bible share the name, and this Jaazaniah should not be confused with them.

Jaazaniah, son of Shaphan, was one of the seventy elders of Israel whom the prophet Ezekiel saw in a vision of the Jerusalem temple. He is singled out as standing among them while each man held a censer and a thick cloud of incense rose (Ezek 8:11). The surrounding passage places this scene in a chamber whose walls were covered with images of creeping things, beasts and idols, so the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia describes him as offering incense to idols. His father Shaphan is sometimes taken to be Josiah's scribe of that name, but this is not stated and remains uncertain. Several other men in the Bible share the name Jaazaniah, so he should not be confused with the others. The name means "Yah hears" according to the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia, or "whom the Lord will hear" in Hitchcock's Bible Names.

Jaazaniah son of Azur was one of the twenty-five men whom the prophet Ezekiel saw in a vision at the east gate of the temple in Jerusalem. He is named there alongside Pelatiah son of Benaiah, and both are called "princes of the people" (Ezek 11:1). In the verses that follow, Ezekiel is told that these men were devising mischief and giving wicked counsel in the city, and he is commanded to prophesy against them. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates the vision to about 593 BC. His name means "the LORD hears." Several other men in the Bible share the name, and this Jaazaniah should not be confused with Jaazaniah son of Shaphan, whom Ezekiel sees in an earlier vision (Ezek 8:11).

Jabal was a son of Lamech, a descendant of Cain, and his wife Adah. Jubal was his full brother, and Tubal-cain and Naamah, children of Lamech's other wife Zillah, were his half-siblings. Genesis names him as the father of those who live in tents and keep livestock (Gen 4:20). In other words, he is presented as the founder or first practitioner of a nomadic herding way of life, much as Jubal is linked with music and Tubal-cain with metalworking. Easton's Bible Dictionary takes the description to mean that he led a wandering life. The meaning of his name is uncertain. Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries give it as "stream," and Hitchcock's Bible Names as "which glides away." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes a suggested link with a word for "ram," which would suit a herdsman. He is mentioned only in this one verse.

Jabin was a king of Hazor, a major Canaanite city in northern Canaan, when the Israelites entered the land under Joshua. When he heard of Israel's victories, he sent messages to Jobab king of Madon and to the kings of Shimron and Achshaph to form an alliance against Joshua (Josh 11:1). The rest of Joshua 11 tells how this northern coalition gathered at the waters of Merom and was defeated. Joshua then took Hazor, killed its king and burned the city. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes this battle as the last of Joshua's recorded battles and the crowning act of the conquest, and notes that here Israel first faced Canaanite horses and chariots. The name was also borne by a later king of Hazor who oppressed Israel in the time of Deborah and Barak (Judg 4). Whether the name was a dynastic title or the two were simply namesakes is uncertain. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning "he that understands."

Jachan was a man of the tribe of Gad, named in 1 Chr 5:13 as one of seven kinsmen listed among the Gadites living in Bashan. His brothers were Michael, Meshullam, Sheba, Jorai, Zia and Heber, and the next verse names their father as Abihail. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary describe these seven as chief men or leading 'brothers' of Gad. Nothing else is recorded about him. By inference from the surrounding passage, which says the Gadite genealogies were recorded in the days of Jotham king of Judah and Jeroboam king of Israel (1 Chr 5:17), the STEPBible names index places him in Jotham's reign. The meaning of his name is uncertain: Easton's gives 'mourner', Smith's 'affliction', and Hitchcock's Bible Names 'wearing out; oppressing'.

Jachin was the priest whose family was assigned the twenty-first of the twenty-four divisions of priests that took turns serving at the sanctuary, according to the arrangement credited to David in 1 Chronicles 24. The lots for these divisions were drawn among the descendants of Eleazar and Ithamar, the sons of Aaron. Jachin's name appears only in the list itself (1 Chr 24:17), between Jakim and Gamul, and nothing more is recorded about him. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes him as the head of this twenty-first course. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "he that strengthens and makes steadfast." Several other men in the Bible share the name, including a son of Simeon and a priest of Nehemiah's time. Jachin is also the name of one of the bronze pillars at Solomon's temple. This entry refers only to the head of the priestly division.

Jadau was one of the descendants of Nebo listed in Ezra 10:43 among the Israelite men who had married foreign wives after the return from exile. The context of Ezra 10 shows that these men agreed, during Ezra's reforms, to send away their foreign wives. Nothing else is recorded about him. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates the event to about 459 BC. The spelling of his name varies in the Hebrew text. The King James Version reads Jadau, while the Revised Version reads Iddo and gives "Jaddai" in the margin. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that 1 Esdras 9:35 calls him "Edos." Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning as "his hand" or "his confession," and Smith's gives "loving."

Jaddua was one of the chiefs of the people who set their seal to the written covenant in Nehemiah's time, when the community returned from exile pledged to keep the law of Moses. His name appears in the list of signers between Zadok and Meshezabeel's group (Neh 10:21). Nothing else is recorded about him. The name, meaning "known" according to Hitchcock's Bible Names, is shared by several people in the Bible. These include a later high priest named Jaddua, who is listed among the descendants of Jeshua in Neh 12. This entry concerns only the lay leader who signed the covenant. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates the sealing to about 410 BC, an estimate inferred from context.

Jadon the Meronothite was one of the men who helped repair the wall of Jerusalem under Nehemiah. He worked alongside Melatiah the Gibeonite and the men of Gibeon and Mizpah, next to the section rebuilt by the men of Tekoa, on a stretch reaching toward the seat of the Persian governor of the province west of the Euphrates (Neh 3:7). The name probably means "he will judge" or "he will plead." The title "Meronothite" points to a place called Meronoth, but no such place is named elsewhere. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that another Meronothite, Jehdeiah, appears in 1 Chr 27:30, and that the Jewish historian Josephus gives the name Jadon to the unnamed man of God who confronted Jeroboam at Bethel. That figure is a different person from the wall builder. The work is dated to about 446 BC, by inference from context.

Jahath was a man of the tribe of Judah, named once in the genealogy of 1 Chr 4:2. He was the son of Reaiah and the grandson of Shobal, and he was the father of Ahumai and Lahad. The verse identifies these descendants as the families of the Zorathites, a name that probably links them with the town of Zorah in the lowland of Judah. Nothing else is recorded about his life. The name Jahath is also borne by several other men in the Bible, mostly Levites, and they should not be confused with this descendant of Judah. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests the name may mean "he (God) will snatch up," while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "broken in pieces" or "descending."

Jahath was a Levite, the son of Shelomoth, from the clan of the Izharites. He appears only once, in the list of Levite family heads in 1 Chr 24:22. That list belongs to the account of how the Levites were organized for temple service in David's time. Izhar was a son of Kohath, so Easton's Bible Dictionary places Jahath in the family of Kohath. Nothing else is recorded about him. Several other men in the Bible bear the name Jahath, including other Levites in the Chronicles genealogies, and he should not be confused with them. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "broken in pieces" or "descending," while Smith's Bible Dictionary renders it "union."

Jahath was a Levite descended from Merari who lived in the reign of King Josiah of Judah. Together with Obadiah, another Merarite, he was one of the overseers of the workmen repairing the temple in Jerusalem. Zechariah and Meshullam, of the Kohathite line, also supervised the work, and the passage notes that the workmen did their job faithfully (2 Chr 34:12). By inference from the surrounding chapter, this was the temple restoration carried out in Josiah's eighteenth year. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates it to about 623 BC. Nothing more is known about him. Several other men named Jahath appear in Levite and Judahite genealogies, and this one should be kept distinct from them.

Jahaziah son of Tikvah was one of the Israelites gathered in Jerusalem when Ezra called on those who had married foreign wives to separate from them after the return from exile. He is named only in Ezra 10:15, along with Jonathan son of Asahel, Meshullam and Shabbethai the Levite. The verse can be read two ways. The King James Version says he and Jonathan "were employed about this matter," which suggests they helped carry out the plan. Many modern translations read the Hebrew as saying they "stood against" it. STEPBible's Tyndale House name index takes that view, describing him as one of four men who opposed Ezra's order, and this entry follows that reading. Modern versions spell his name Jahzeiah, as the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives its meaning as "the vision of the Lord." Nothing else is known about him.

Jahaziel was one of the warriors who joined David at Ziklag, named in a list alongside Ismaiah the Gibeonite, Jeremiah, Johanan and Josabad the Gederathite (1 Chr 12:4). The surrounding chapter describes these men as coming to David while he was still kept away from Saul, and as kinsmen of Saul from the tribe of Benjamin. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the STEPBible proper-names index treat him as a Benjamite. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that he may instead have been from Judah, since the place-name attached to Josabad points toward Judean territory. This entry follows the Benjamite reading of the list. Nothing more is recorded about him. His name is usually explained as "God sees" or "God watches over." Several other men in the Bible bear the same name and should not be confused with this warrior.

Jahaziel was a priest in the time of King David, named with Benaiah as one of the two priests who blew trumpets regularly before the ark of the covenant (1 Chr 16:6). The surrounding chapter places this appointment when David brought the ark to Jerusalem and set it in the tent he had prepared, arranging ongoing worship around it. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia associate him with the ark's removal to Jerusalem. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia also notes that major Greek manuscripts of the Septuagint read the name as "Uzziel" here. The name is usually explained as meaning "God sees." Several men in the Bible bear this name, and nothing beyond this single verse connects this priest to any of them.

Jahaziel son of Zechariah was a Levite descended from Asaph, one of the families of temple musicians, who lived during the reign of King Jehoshaphat of Judah. His ancestry is traced through Zechariah, Benaiah, Jeiel and Mattaniah. When Judah faced invasion by the Moabites and Ammonites, the people gathered to seek the LORD, and the Spirit of the LORD came upon Jahaziel in the middle of the assembly. According to the verses that follow (2 Chr 20:15–17), he told Jehoshaphat and the people not to be afraid, because the battle was God's and they would not need to fight it. Easton's Bible Dictionary and other reference works describe him as encouraging the king against the invaders. His name is usually explained as "God sees." Several other men in the Bible share the name Jahaziel.

Jahaziel was the father of a family leader who returned from Babylon to Jerusalem with Ezra. Ezra 8:5 lists "the son of Jahaziel" among the sons of Shechaniah, along with three hundred men who traveled with him. The son's own name is not given in the Hebrew text as it stands. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests the verse probably originally read "of the sons of Zattu, Shecaniah the son of Jahaziel," following the parallel list in 1 Esdras 8:32. On that reading Shecaniah is Jahaziel's son, not a more distant ancestor. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates the return to before 459 BC. The name is usually explained as "God sees" or "God watches over." Several other men in the Bible share this name, and this Jahaziel is known only from this single verse.

Jahdai was a man of the tribe of Judah, named only in the genealogy of Caleb as the father of six sons: Regem, Jotham, Geshan (also spelled Gesham), Pelet, Ephah and Shaaph (1 Chr 2:47). This entry treats him as a son of Caleb, placing him among Caleb's many children in the same chapter. The verse names no parent for him and comes abruptly among the lists of sons born to Caleb's concubines, so his exact link to Caleb is unclear. Easton's Bible Dictionary calls him a descendant of Caleb of the family of Hezron. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes two views: that Jahdai was another wife or concubine of Caleb, or, which it considers more likely, a descendant whose connecting name has dropped out of the text. His name has been explained as meaning "grasper" or "Yah leads." Nothing else is recorded about him.

Jahdiel was one of the heads of family in the half-tribe of Manasseh that lived east of the Jordan. He appears only in 1 Chr 5:24, where he is the last of seven named leaders, alongside Epher, Ishi, Eliel, Azriel, Jeremiah and Hodaviah. All seven are described as mighty men of valor, famous men and heads of their fathers' houses. The surrounding verses place this group in the land stretching from Bashan toward Mount Hermon, and they go on to tell of the tribe's later unfaithfulness and its deportation by the Assyrians. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia takes his name to mean "God gives joy," and Smith's Bible Dictionary gives a similar sense, "whom Jehovah makes joyful." Nothing else is recorded about him.

Jahdo was a man of the tribe of Gad, named only once, in the genealogy of 1 Chr 5:14. He was the son of Buz and the father of Jeshishai. The line runs from him through Jeshishai, Michael, Gilead, Jaroah and Huri to Abihail, whose sons were Gadite clan leaders living in Gilead and Bashan. Smith's Bible Dictionary calls him a Gadite, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia calls him a Gileadite, after the region where this branch of Gad lived. Nothing else is recorded about him. The meaning of his name is uncertain. Smith's gives "united", and Hitchcock's Bible Names offers several possibilities, including "his joy".

Jahmai was a man of the tribe of Issachar, one of the six sons of Tola named in the tribal genealogy of 1 Chr 7:2, alongside Uzzi, Rephaiah, Jeriel, Jibsam and Shemuel. The verse calls these sons heads of their father's house and valiant men of might. It adds that in the days of David their descendants numbered 22,600, so Jahmai is probably remembered as the founder or head of a clan within the family of Tola. Tola himself is listed as a son of Issachar in 1 Chr 7:1. Nothing else is recorded about him. The meaning of his name is uncertain. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests it may be a shortened form meaning "may Yahweh protect," and Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "whom Jehovah guards." Hitchcock's Bible Names instead gives "warm" or "making warm."

Jahzerah was a priest of the family of Immer, named only in a genealogy in 1 Chr 9:12. He was the son of Meshullam and an ancestor of Maasiai, one of the priests listed among those living in Jerusalem after the return from exile. In that verse his son is Adiel. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identifies him with Ahasai (Ahzai) in the parallel list of Neh 11:13. There the line runs Amashai son of Azareel, son of Ahasai, son of Meshillemoth, son of Immer. On that identification his son would be Azareel, and Meshillemoth would match the Meshullam and Meshillemith of the Chronicles list. This entry follows that identification. Because the two lists differ in their names, the exact family links are uncertain.

Jair was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, known only as the father of Mordecai, the Jew who lived in Shushan, the Persian royal city, in the book of Esther. Esth 2:5 traces Mordecai's line as "the son of Jair, the son of Shimei, the son of Kish," so Jair was the son of Shimei. Some readers take Shimei and Kish to be more distant, well-known ancestors rather than Jair's immediate father and grandfather, since biblical genealogies sometimes skip generations. Nothing else is recorded about Jair's life. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "enlightener." Several other people in the Bible share the name Jair, and this entry concerns only Mordecai's father.

Jakeh was the father of Agur, whose sayings make up Proverbs 30. He is named only once, in the heading of that chapter (Prov 30:1), and nothing else is recorded about him. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "pious." The Hebrew of the verse is difficult. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests that the word translated "the prophecy" may instead mean "of Massa" or "the Massaite." Massa was the name of an Ishmaelite tribe and its country (compare Gen 25:14; Prov 31:1). On that reading, Jakeh and his son would have belonged to that people rather than to Israel. Whether that is so cannot be settled from the single verse.

Jakim was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, named in the genealogy of Benjamin's descendants in 1 Chr 8:19. He is listed as one of the sons of Shimhi, alongside his brothers Adaiah, Beraiah, Eliel, Elienai, Shimrath, Zabdi, Zichri and Zilthai. Shimhi appears to be the same man called Shimei elsewhere, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia describes Jakim as a son of Shimei. The passage says nothing more about him beyond his place in the family list. The name probably means "he (God) lifts up" or "God establishes," and it is related to the name Eliakim. Several people in the Bible bear the name Jakim, so this Benjamite should not be confused with others of the same name, such as the priest of that name in David's time.

Jakim was a priest whose name was given to the twelfth of the twenty-four divisions, or courses, into which the priests were organized to take turns serving at the sanctuary (1 Chr 24:12). The assignment was made by lot under David, as the surrounding chapter describes, and he is presumably the head of that family or division. Nothing else is recorded about him. The name probably means "he (God) raises up" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia), and it is shared by another man in the Bible, a Benjamite listed in the genealogies of 1 Chronicles 8. This entry concerns only the priest.

Jalon was the last-named of the four sons of Ezra listed in the genealogy of the tribe of Judah in 1 Chr 4:17. His brothers were Jether, Mered and Epher. Nothing else is recorded about him, and he appears nowhere else in the Bible. This Ezra is a different man from the later scribe of the same name, and some reference works, including the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia, spell his name Ezrah. Placing Jalon in the tribe of Judah follows from the surrounding genealogy, as Easton's Bible Dictionary notes. The meaning of his name is uncertain. Easton's gives "lodger", Smith's Bible Dictionary "abiding" and Hitchcock's Bible Names "tarrying" or "murmuring". The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats the meaning as unknown.

Jambres is named once in the Bible, in 2 Tim 3:8, where Paul pairs him with Jannes as men who "withstood Moses." Paul uses the two as an example of people who resist the truth, comparing them to false teachers of his own day. The verse gives no further detail, but by inference from the Exodus account, Jannes and Jambres are usually taken to be among Pharaoh's magicians who copied Moses' early signs in Egypt (Exod 7:11, 22). Exodus does not name those magicians. The names seem to come from Jewish tradition, which Paul draws on here. The STEPBible proper-names index describes Jambres as an Egyptian magician who opposed Moses alongside Jannes. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of his name as "poverty," "bitter," or "a rebel."

Jamin was a man of the tribe of Judah, named in the genealogy of 1 Chr 2:27 as one of the three sons of Ram, the firstborn of Jerahmeel. His brothers were Maaz and Eker, and he is listed second, between them. This made him a grandson of Jerahmeel, whose line forms one branch of Judah's descendants in the Chronicles genealogies. Nothing else is recorded about him. The name means "right hand" according to Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia. Hitchcock's Bible Names also gives "south wind." Several other people in the Bible share the name, including a son of Simeon and a Levite who helped explain the law in Ezra's time. This entry concerns only the Judahite descendant of Jerahmeel.

Jamin was one of the men named in Neh 8:7 who helped the people understand the law when Ezra read it publicly in Jerusalem after the return from exile. He is listed with Jeshua, Bani, Sherebiah, Akkub and others, alongside the Levites, while the people stood in their places. The wording leaves open whether these named men were themselves Levites. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the STEPBible proper names list treat him as a Levite, while the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia adds a question mark and notes that 1 Esdras 9:48 gives the name as Iadinus. His name means "right hand." This is his only mention, and he should be kept distinct from others of the same name, such as the son of Simeon.

Jamlech was a man of the tribe of Simeon, named in a list of Simeonite clan leaders in 1 Chr 4:34. Nothing else is recorded about him personally. The surrounding passage describes these men as princes in their families whose households grew large. According to the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia, if the account in 1 Chr 4:41 refers back to this list, he lived in the time of King Hezekiah. That verse tells how the Simeonites moved out in search of pasture and took land near Gedor. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "whom God makes king," and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia as "may he (God) cause to reign."

Janna was an ancestor of Jesus named only in the genealogy in Luke's Gospel (Luke 3:24). He is listed as the son of Joseph and the father of Melchi. This Joseph is several generations before Mary's husband Joseph and is a different man. Janna falls in the stretch of Luke's list between the return from exile and the time of Jesus, and nothing else is recorded about him. Because Luke traces this line back through David, he is counted with the tribe of Judah. Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that the Revised Version spells the name Jannai and gives its meaning as "flourishing." Hitchcock's Bible Names connects it with Jannes and offers meanings such as "who speaks or answers" or "afflicted."

Jannes is named in the Bible only once, in 2 Tim 3:8, where Paul pairs him with Jambres as men who "withstood Moses." Paul uses the two as an example of people who oppose the truth, comparing them with corrupt men of his own day. The verse does not say who they were. Smith's Bible Dictionary and Easton's Bible Dictionary identify Jannes and Jambres as Egyptian magicians at Pharaoh's court, linking them by inference with the unnamed magicians of Exod 7, who copied Moses' and Aaron's signs, such as turning rods into serpents. The Old Testament never gives the magicians' names. Paul probably drew the names from Jewish tradition current in his time, which remembered Jannes and Jambres as Moses' chief opponents in Egypt.

Japhia was king of Lachish when the Israelites entered Canaan under Joshua. After Gibeon made peace with Israel, Adonizedek king of Jerusalem appealed to him and to the kings of Hebron, Jarmuth and Eglon to join forces against Gibeon (Josh 10:3). The rest of the chapter tells how these five Amorite kings attacked Gibeon, were routed by Joshua, hid in a cave at Makkedah, and were then put to death. Japhia is not named again, but he is probably one of those five kings. The name is shared by other people in the Bible, including a son of David, so this Japhia should not be confused with them. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "enlightening" or "appearing."

Jaresiah was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, named in the Benjamite genealogy as one of the sons of Jeroham (1 Chr 8:27). His brothers are listed in the same passage as Shamsherai, Shehariah, Athaliah, Eliah and Zichri. The list belongs to a register of Benjamite family heads who lived in Jerusalem, according to the surrounding verses of the chapter. Nothing else is recorded about him. Modern translations spell the name Jaareshiah, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats Jaresiah as the King James form of that name. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives its meaning as "whom Jehovah nourishes."

Jarib was one of the "chief men" Ezra summoned while his company of returning exiles was camped by the river Ahava on the way from Babylon to Jerusalem (Ezra 8:16). The surrounding passage explains why. Ezra had found no Levites among the travelers, so he sent these leaders, along with two "men of understanding," to Iddo at Casiphia to bring back ministers to serve in the Temple (Ezra 8:15–17). The STEPBible names index and Easton's Bible Dictionary both describe him this way. Nothing else is told about him. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates the journey to 469 BC. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives meanings for the name such as "fighting" or "chiding." The same name belongs to other people, including a son of Simeon (1 Chr 4:24) and a priest of the family of Jeshua (Ezra 10:18). Whether that priest is the same man as this Jarib is uncertain.

Jarib was a priest in Ezra's time, one of several men of that name in the Bible. He belonged to the priestly family of Jeshua son of Jozadak, the high priest who had led the return from exile. Ezra 10:18 lists him with Maaseiah, Eliezer and Gedaliah among the priests found to have married foreign wives. The following verse records that these men pledged to send their wives away and offered a ram as a guilt offering. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates these events to about 459 BC. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identifies him with Joribus in the parallel account in 1 Esdras 9:19, and explains the name as meaning "he contends" or "he takes our part."

Jaroah was a man of the tribe of Gad, named only once, in a genealogy in 1 Chr 5:14. He was the son of Gilead and the father of Huri. The line runs on to Huri's son Abihail, whose descendants were Gadite family heads living in the land of Bashan and Gilead east of the Jordan. This Gilead appears to be a Gadite descendant of Buz, not the better-known Gilead son of Machir of the tribe of Manasseh. Smith's Bible Dictionary calls Jaroah a chief man of Gad and gives the meaning of his name as "moon". The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia says the meaning is unknown and notes that the text of this genealogy may not have been preserved accurately. Nothing else is recorded about him.

Jashen is a man named in the list of David's elite warriors known as "the thirty" (2 Sam 23:32). The King James text reads "of the sons of Jashen," which suggests that several of his sons served among David's mighty men, as Easton's Bible Dictionary takes it. The parallel list in 1 Chr 11:34 gives the name as Hashem and calls him "the Gizonite." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia offers another reading. It suggests that "sons of" arose from a copying error that repeated the last letters of the word before it. On that reading Jashen, possibly "the Gunite," was himself one of the thirty. This entry treats him as the father named in the King James wording, while noting that the text is uncertain. Nothing else is recorded about him. The name is usually taken to mean "sleeping."

Jashobeam was one of five Korahites, listed with Elkanah, Jesiah, Azareel and Joezer, who joined David (1 Chr 12:6). The surrounding chapter describes the men who came to David at Ziklag while he was keeping away from Saul, and STEPBible's proper-names index places this Jashobeam among them. The name belongs to several men in the Bible. This one is usually kept separate from Jashobeam the chief of David's mighty men and commander of a monthly division, though the two are sometimes identified. Here "Korhites" probably means descendants of Korah, the Levite family. Some suggest it could instead refer to a Benjamite place or clan, since the chapter lists Benjamites just before. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "the people sitting" or "captivity of the people." Nothing else is recorded about him.

Jashub was a man of the family of Bani, listed among the Israelites in Ezra's time who had married foreign wives (Ezra 10:29). By inference from the surrounding chapter, he was one of those who agreed to send away these wives after Ezra led the returned exiles in confessing intermarriage with neighboring peoples. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates this to about 459 BC, an estimate inferred from context. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the same man appears as "Jasubus" in the apocryphal book 1 Esdras 9:30. His name is usually explained as meaning "he returns." Nothing else is recorded about him. The name Jashub is also borne by other people in the Bible, among them a son of Issachar, and this entry concerns only the man named in Ezra.

Jasiel the Mesobaite is the last name in the list of David's mighty warriors in 1 Chr 11:47, where he appears alongside Eliel and Obed. The verse gives no further details about him. "Mesobaite" probably refers to his hometown or clan, but the place is otherwise unknown. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "whom God made." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests he is probably the same man as Jaasiel son of Abner, whom 1 Chr 27:21 names as leader of the tribe of Benjamin under David. If so, he would be the son of Saul's army commander Abner. That identification rests on the similar names and is not certain, and this entry treats it as a possibility only.

Jathniel was a Levite, the fourth son of Meshelemiah, named in the list of temple gatekeepers in 1 Chr 26:2. His brothers were Zechariah the firstborn, Jediael, Zebadiah, Elam, Jehohanan and Elioenai. The surrounding verse (1 Chr 26:1) places Meshelemiah's family among the Korahites, the Levite clan descended from Korah. By inference from the context of the chapter, the family served as gatekeepers in the arrangements for temple service made late in David's reign, as the STEPBible Proper Names index also describes him. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates him to about 1014 BC, an estimate drawn from context. The meaning of his name is uncertain: Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "whom God gives" and Hitchcock's Bible Names "gift of God", while the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives "God lives." Nothing else is recorded about him.

Jaziz was a Hagerite (Hagrite) who oversaw King David's flocks, probably sheep and goats. He is named in a list of the officials who managed the king's property, each responsible for a different part of the royal estate, such as the treasuries, fields, vineyards, olive groves, herds, camels and donkeys (1 Chr 27:31). His title, "Hagerite," links him to the Hagrites, a people group, so he was probably not an Israelite by descent, though the passage itself does not say so. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "whom God moves," while the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia calls the meaning uncertain. Nothing else is recorded about him.

Jeberechiah was the father of Zechariah, one of the two reliable witnesses Isaiah chose to attest a written record. The other was Uriah the priest (Isa 8:2). From the surrounding passage, the record was the large tablet inscribed with the words "Maher-shalal-hash-baz." This was a sign that Damascus and Samaria would soon be plundered, and it was later given as the name of Isaiah's son. The events fall in the reign of King Ahaz of Judah. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia places them around 734 BC, an estimate drawn from context. Nothing else is recorded about Jeberechiah himself, and his name appears only in this verse. It means "the LORD blesses." Some have linked his son with the Zechariah whose daughter Abi was Hezekiah's mother (2 Kgs 18:2), but the text does not make this connection, and it remains uncertain.

Jecamiah was a son of Jehoiachin (also called Jeconiah), the king of Judah who was taken captive to Babylon. He is named only once, in the royal genealogy of David's line at 1 Chr 3:18, alongside his brothers Malchiram, Pedaiah, Shenazar, Hoshama and Nedabiah. Shealtiel and Zedekiah also appear among Jehoiachin's sons in the surrounding verses. Since Jehoiachin spent most of his life in exile, Jecamiah was probably born or raised in Babylon, by inference from context. Smith's Bible Dictionary takes these men as adopted into the royal line after Jehoiachin's line failed; this entry follows the plain reading of the genealogy and lists him as Jehoiachin's son. Modern translations spell the name Jekamiah. It is usually explained as meaning "the Lord gathers" or "the Lord establishes." Another man named Jekamiah appears in an earlier genealogy of Judah (1 Chr 2:41) and is a different person.

Jedaiah was a man of the tribe of Simeon, named only in a genealogy in 1 Chr 4:37. He was the son of Shimri and the father of Allon, and an ancestor of Ziza. The surrounding passage lists Ziza among the Simeonite leaders whose families grew numerous and who moved in search of pasture for their flocks. Jedaiah is therefore known only as a link in that family line, and nothing else is recorded about him. Easton's Bible Dictionary calls his father Shimri a chief Simeonite and gives the name's meaning as "invoker of Jehovah." Hitchcock's Bible Names offers "the hand of the Lord" or "confessing the Lord." Several other men in the Bible bear the name Jedaiah, including priests. This entry concerns only the Simeonite.

Jedaiah, son of Harumaph, was one of the men who rebuilt the walls of Jerusalem under Nehemiah after the return from exile in Babylon. He is mentioned only once. Neh 3:10 says he repaired the section of wall opposite his own house, working beside Hattush the son of Hashabniah. Several workers in this chapter repaired the stretch nearest their homes, so Jedaiah probably lived close to the wall. Nothing else is recorded about him. Several other people in the Bible share the name Jedaiah, including priests of the same period, and he should not be confused with them. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "the hand of the Lord" or "confessing the Lord."

Jediael son of Shimri was one of the warriors listed among David's mighty men in 1 Chr 11:45, where he is named alongside his brother Joha. The verse adds the description "the Tizite," and it is unclear whether this refers to Joha alone or to both brothers. Nothing else is known about the place or family it points to. This part of the Chronicler's list goes beyond the parallel roll of heroes in 2 Samuel 23, so Jediael appears only here in that list. Easton's Bible Dictionary suggests he is probably the same Jediael of Manasseh who deserted to David at Ziklag (1 Chr 12:20), and STEPBible's proper-names index also places him in the tribe of Manasseh. Several other men in the Bible share this name, so the identification is uncertain. The name is commonly explained as meaning "known of God."

Jediael was a man of the tribe of Manasseh, one of seven "captains of the thousands" of Manasseh who joined David as he went to Ziklag (1 Chr 12:20). By inference from the surrounding passage, this happened when the Philistine leaders sent David away rather than let him fight with them against Saul, and he returned to his base at Ziklag. Smith's Bible Dictionary links this to David's pursuit of the Amalekites in 1 Sam 30:9–10. Nothing else is recorded about him. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "known of God," and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "the knowledge of God." Several other men in the Bible share the name Jediael, including a descendant of Benjamin, one of David's mighty men, and a Levite gatekeeper. Whether any of them is the same person as this captain is not stated.

Jediael was a Levite, the second son of Meshelemiah, listed among the gatekeepers of the temple in David's time (1 Chr 26:2). His brothers were Zechariah the firstborn, Zebadiah, Jathniel, Elam, Jehohanan and Elioenai. The surrounding passage, 1 Chr 26:1, places Meshelemiah's family among the Korahites, descendants of Asaph, and Easton's Bible Dictionary describes Jediael as a Korahite of the family of Ebiasaph. Nothing more is recorded about him beyond his place in this list of gatekeeping families. His name is usually explained as "known of God" or "God makes known." Several other men in the Bible share the name, so this Jediael should not be confused with them.

Jedidah was the mother of King Josiah of Judah and the daughter of Adaiah of Boscath (2 Kgs 22:1). Her name means "beloved" (Smith's Bible Dictionary; Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "well beloved; amiable"). She is named only once, in the formal note that opens the account of her son's reign. That note records that Josiah became king at eight years old and reigned thirty-one years in Jerusalem. By inference from the account of Josiah's father in the preceding chapter, she was a wife of King Amon. Boscath, also spelled Bozkath, is listed in Josh 15:39 among the towns of the lowland of Judah. Josiah appears in Matthew's genealogy of Jesus (Matt 1:10–11), which places Jedidah among the ancestors in that line, although Matthew does not name her. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates her son's birth to about 648 BC.

Jehaleleel was a man of the tribe of Judah, named only in the genealogies of 1 Chr 4:16, which lists his four sons: Ziph, Ziphah, Tiria and Asareel. Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that he and his sons appear abruptly in the list, with no stated link to the names around them, so his exact place in Judah's family tree is uncertain. The Tyndale House proper-names index (STEPBible) treats him as a son of Elah, connecting him with the preceding verse, where Elah appears among the sons of Caleb son of Jephunneh. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of his name as "praising God." The son named Ziph may be connected with the Judean town of that name, though the verse does not say so. He should not be confused with the Levite Jehalelel of a later period (2 Chr 29:12).

Jehalelel was a Levite of the Merari clan, known only as the father of Azariah. His son was one of the Levites who arose in the time of King Hezekiah to sanctify themselves and cleanse the temple, listed alongside representatives of the other Levite families, the Kohathites and the Gershonites (2 Chr 29:12). Nothing else is recorded about Jehalelel himself, and it is not clear whether he was still living at the time. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "who praises God." A man of Judah with a similar name, spelled Jehaleleel in the King James Version, appears in 1 Chr 4:16. He is a different person.

Jehdeiah was a Levite, a descendant of Amram through Shubael. He appears only in 1 Chr 24:20, in a list of the remaining Levite family heads set out in connection with David's organization of temple service, so he probably lived in or near David's time. Smith's Bible Dictionary calls him the representative of Shubael's descendants. Since 1 Chr 23:16 names Shebuel as a son of Gershom, son of Moses, Shubael is probably the same man, which would make Jehdeiah a descendant of Moses. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives the name's meaning as "may Yahweh give joy." He should not be confused with another Jehdeiah, the Meronothite who managed David's donkeys (1 Chr 27:30).

Jehdeiah the Meronothite was the official in charge of King David's donkeys, one of the overseers of the royal property listed in 1 Chr 27:30. He served alongside Obil the Ishmaelite, who looked after the camels. The title "Meronothite" probably refers to his home town, Meronoth, whose location is unknown. Smith's Bible Dictionary specifies that he had charge of the she-asses, and Easton's Bible Dictionary places his service under both David and Solomon. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives the meaning of the name as "may Yahweh give joy." The same name belongs to another man in the Bible, a Levite of David's time (1 Chr 24:20), so this officer should not be confused with him.

Jehezekel was a priest in the time of King David who received the twentieth of the twenty-four divisions into which the priests were organized for service at the house of the Lord (1 Chr 24:16). These divisions were assigned by lot, each priestly family taking its turn in the temple duties. He is mentioned only in this list. Smith's Bible Dictionary explains his name as "whom God makes strong," and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "strength of God." The Hebrew name is the same as that of the prophet Ezekiel, but nothing connects this priest with the prophet, who lived centuries later.

Jehiel was one of the warriors in the list of David's mighty men in 1 Chronicles. He is named with his brother Shama as the sons of Hothan the Aroerite (1 Chr 11:44), and Easton's Bible Dictionary describes him as one of David's guard. "Aroerite" means a man from Aroer. More than one town had that name, including one east of the Jordan near the Arnon and one in southern Judah, so it is uncertain which was his family's home. This part of the Chronicles list has no counterpart in the parallel list of David's warriors in 2 Sam 23, and nothing more is recorded about him. Several other men in the Bible are also called Jehiel.

Jehiel was the son of Hachmoni and one of the officials of King David's court. He is named once, in the list of David's officers in 1 Chr 27:32, where he is said to have been "with the king's sons." Easton's Bible Dictionary takes this to mean he was a tutor in the royal household toward the end of David's reign. Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that the exact meaning of the phrase is unclear. "Hachmoni" may be a family or clan name rather than a personal one. The related form "Hachmonite" is used of Jashobeam, one of David's mighty men, in 1 Chr 11:11. The same verse also names Jonathan, David's uncle, as a counsellor and scribe. Several other men in the Bible share the name Jehiel, which Smith's Bible Dictionary renders as "God lives."

Jehiel was one of the sons of Jehoshaphat, king of Judah, and a younger brother of Jehoram, who succeeded their father on the throne. He is named second in the list of Jehoshaphat's sons, after Azariah and before Zechariah, a second Azariah, Michael and Shephatiah. The verse calls Jehoshaphat "king of Israel," though he ruled the southern kingdom of Judah. Jehiel is one of several people in the Bible with this name. The next verses (2 Chr 21:3–4) say Jehoshaphat gave his younger sons wealth and fortified cities in Judah. Once Jehoram had secured the kingdom, he killed all his brothers. Smith's Bible Dictionary takes Jehiel to be among them, and this entry follows that reading. His death in Jerusalem is placed about 889 BC, by inference from context.

Jehiel was a Levite descended from Heman, one of the temple musicians' families. He appears in the list of Levites who answered King Hezekiah's call to purify the temple at the start of his reign (2 Chr 29:14). He is named alongside Shimei as the representatives of the sons of Heman. From the surrounding chapter, these Levites consecrated themselves and then cleansed the house of the Lord, which had been neglected. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates this to about 726 BC. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes him as one who helped Hezekiah in his work of reform. Some reference works, including the STEPBible names list, give his name as Jehuel. Several other men in the Bible are called Jehiel, and nothing more is known of this one beyond this single mention.

Jehiel was one of ten overseers who served under Cononiah and his brother Shimei during the reign of King Hezekiah of Judah (2 Chr 31:13). He was appointed at the king's command and under Azariah, the ruler of the house of God. By inference from the surrounding passage, these men looked after the offerings, tithes and dedicated gifts that the people brought to the temple storerooms. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the STEPBible proper names index both identify him as a Levite, and the context of temple service supports this. His name is usually explained as meaning "God lives." Several other men in the Bible are also called Jehiel, and nothing more is recorded about this one.

Jehiel was one of the "rulers of the house of God" in the reign of King Josiah of Judah. Together with Hilkiah and Zechariah, he gave the priests 2,600 small animals and 300 oxen for the Passover offerings at Josiah's great Passover celebration (2 Chr 35:8). The verse counts these three among Josiah's princes who gave willingly to the people, the priests and the Levites. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes him as a prince who gave generously toward restoring the temple sacrifices under Josiah. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates these reforms to about 623 BC, an estimate inferred from context. The Hilkiah named beside him is probably the high priest of that name active under Josiah, though the verse does not say so. Nothing else is recorded about this Jehiel, and he should not be confused with the several other men of the same name in the Bible.

Jehiel was the father of Obadiah, a member of the family group descended from Joab. He is named only to identify his son, who led 218 men of that family when they returned from Babylon to Jerusalem with Ezra (Ezra 8:9). Nothing else is said about Jehiel himself, and the verse does not say whether he made the journey. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "God lives" and places him before about 459 BC, a date inferred from the timing of Ezra's return. Several other men in the Bible share the name Jehiel, including another Jehiel mentioned in the book of Ezra, so this one should be kept separate from them.

Jehiel was the father of Shechaniah and belonged to the family of Elam, one of the clans who returned from exile with or before Ezra. He is named only as Shechaniah's father, in the account of Ezra's response to marriages between Israelites and foreign women. Shechaniah admitted to Ezra that the people had taken foreign wives and proposed a way forward (Ezra 10:2). Ezra 10:26 lists a Jehiel among the sons of Elam who had married foreign wives. The STEPBible Proper Names index (Tyndale House) treats him as this same man, so Shechaniah may have been confessing a fault within his own family. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "God lives." Several other men in the Bible share the name, and the text says nothing more about this one.

Jehiel was a priest of the family of Harim in the time of Ezra. He is named in Ezra 10:21 alongside Maaseiah, Elijah, Shemaiah and Uzziah. By inference from the surrounding passage, which begins its list with the priests and ends by stating that all these men had taken foreign wives, Jehiel was among those who had married women from outside Israel and agreed to send them away during Ezra's reforms after the return from exile. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates these events to about 459 BC, an estimate drawn from context. The name means "God lives." Several other men in the Bible are also called Jehiel, and this one is known only from this single mention.

Jehiel was a man of the family of Elam. He is named in Ezra 10:26 in the list of Israelites who had married foreign wives after the return from exile. By inference from the surrounding chapter, he was among those who agreed to send away their wives and children in the reform led by Ezra. Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that the name means "God lives" and describes him as a member of the same family who himself had to part with his wife. Several other men in the Bible share the name Jehiel. They include another Jehiel of the sons of Elam, named a few verses earlier in the same chapter, whose son Shechaniah first proposed the reform. This entry concerns only the man listed in Ezra 10:26. Nothing else is recorded about him.

Jehizkiah son of Shallum was one of the leaders of Ephraim in the northern kingdom of Israel during the reign of Ahaz of Judah. His name means "the LORD strengthens," as Easton's Bible Dictionary notes. Along with Azariah, Berechiah and Amasa, he stood up against the soldiers returning from war with captives from Judah (2 Chr 28:12). The surrounding passage shows that Israel's army under Pekah had taken large numbers of Judeans prisoner, and that the prophet Oded warned against keeping them as slaves. These chiefs backed that warning, and the captives were then clothed, fed and taken back to Jericho. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia dates these events to about 734 BC, while Smith's Bible Dictionary gives 738 BC. Nothing else is recorded about him.

Jehohanan was a Levite of the family of Korah, the sixth son of Meshelemiah, listed among the gatekeepers of the sanctuary in the arrangements credited to King David (1 Chr 26:3). His brothers were Zechariah, Jediael, Zebadiah, Jathniel, Elam and Elioenai. The surrounding chapter, read in context, places these gatekeepers in David's later reign, about 1000 BC by inference. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes him as head of one of the divisions of temple porters. His name means "the Lord is gracious" and is the longer form of the name John. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that one Greek textual tradition reads his name as Jehonathan. Several other men in the Bible share the name Jehohanan, and this entry concerns only Meshelemiah's son.

Jehohanan was a military commander in Judah during the reign of King Jehoshaphat. 2 Chr 17:15 lists him among the king's captains and places 280,000 men under him.
