He is named "next to" Adnah, the chief commander, which suggests he ranked second among the leaders of Judah's troops. The surrounding passage describes these men as soldiers stationed in Jerusalem who served the king, apart from the garrisons in Judah's fortified cities (2 Chr 17:13, 19). Smith's Bible Dictionary explains the name as meaning "whom Jehovah gave" and notes that John is its shortened form. Several other men in the Bible share this name, and nothing in the text links this commander to any of them.

Jehohanan was the father of Ishmael, one of the "captains of hundreds" whom the priest Jehoiada brought into a covenant with him in the seventh year (2 Chr 23:1). The surrounding account shows that this covenant was the plan to overthrow Queen Athaliah and put the young king Joash on the throne of Judah. Jehohanan himself is known only as Ishmael's father, and nothing else is recorded about him. Smith's Bible Dictionary explains the name as meaning "whom Jehovah gave" and notes that John is a shortened form of it. Several other men in the Bible share the name, and this entry refers only to the father of Ishmael.

Jehohanan was one of the descendants of Bebai listed in Ezra 10:28 among the Israelites who had married foreign wives after the return from exile. In the context of Ezra 10, these men agreed to send away their foreign wives during the reforms led by Ezra. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates this to about 459 BC. The name means "the Lord has been gracious," and John is a shortened form of it. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the parallel list in 1 Esdras 9:29 gives his name as Joannes. Several other men in the Bible share the name Jehohanan. Nothing more is known of this one beyond his place in this list.

Jehohanan was a priest in Jerusalem after the return from exile, listed as head of the priestly family of Amariah (Neh 12:13). The list he appears in names the heads of priestly families in the days of Joiakim, who was high priest after his father Jeshua. That setting comes from the surrounding verses rather than from Neh 12:13 itself. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates him to about 406 BC. The name means "the Lord has been gracious" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia), and Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that John is a shortened form of it. Several other men in the Bible share the name, and nothing beyond this single listing is recorded about this one.

Jehohanan was one of the participants in the dedication of the rebuilt wall of Jerusalem in Nehemiah's time. He is named in a list of eight men who stood with the singers during the ceremony, while the singers sang loudly under the direction of Jezrahiah (Neh 12:42). Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia describe him as a priest, by inference from the surrounding list of priests and musicians taking part in the celebration. Smith's dates the event to about 446 BC. The name means "the Lord is gracious" or "gift of the Lord," and John is its shortened form. Several other men in the Bible share this name, and nothing more is known about this particular Jehohanan beyond this one mention.

Jehoiada son of Benaiah was one of King David's counselors. He is named only in 1 Chr 27:34, in a list of David's officials, where he comes "after Ahithophel" alongside Abiathar, while Joab commanded the army. The preceding verse calls Ahithophel the king's counselor, so Jehoiada probably took over or shared that advisory role, perhaps after Ahithophel joined Absalom's revolt and died. STEPBible Proper Names describes him as Ahithophel's successor as counselor. Elsewhere David's well-known officer is Benaiah son of Jehoiada. This Jehoiada may therefore have been that Benaiah's son, named after his grandfather, though some readers suspect the two names were reversed in copying. Several other men in the Bible share the name, which Hitchcock's Bible Names renders as "knowledge of the Lord."

Jehoiada son of Paseah was one of the men who helped rebuild the walls of Jerusalem under Nehemiah. Together with Meshullam son of Besodeiah, he repaired the Old Gate. They laid its beams and set up its doors, locks and bars (Neh 3:6). Nothing else is recorded about him. Several people in the Bible share the name Jehoiada, and this one should not be confused with the better-known priest of that name. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia and other modern references give his name as Joiada, which reflects the Hebrew spelling in this verse. The name means "the Lord knows," and Hitchcock's Bible Names renders it "knowledge of the Lord." By inference from the setting of Nehemiah's work, his repairs date to the mid-400s BC.

Jehoiada was a priest mentioned once, in Jer 29:26, in a letter that Shemaiah, a man among the exiles in Babylon, sent to Jerusalem. Shemaiah tells the priest Zephaniah that the LORD has made him priest in place of Jehoiada. The letter says this priest had charge of the officers in the house of the LORD, with authority to put anyone who acted as a self-made prophet into prison and the stocks. By inference from the surrounding chapter, Shemaiah was urging Zephaniah to use that authority against Jeremiah. Who this Jehoiada was is uncertain. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that some identify him with the well-known priest of Queen Athaliah's time, while others hold that nothing more is known of him. It also observes that Zephaniah could not have directly succeeded that earlier priest. This entry treats him as a separate priest of Jeremiah's time. The name means "Yahweh knows."

Jehoiarib was a priest whose family became the first of the twenty-four divisions, or courses, of priests that took turns serving at the sanctuary. The surrounding chapter describes how, under King David, the priestly descendants of Eleazar and Ithamar were assigned their order of service by drawing lots, and the first lot fell to Jehoiarib, with Jedaiah second (1 Chr 24:7). Easton's Bible Dictionary connects him with the Jehoiarib named among the priests living in Jerusalem in 1 Chr 9:10. A similar name, Joiarib, appears among priestly families after the return from exile in Nehemiah, probably the same priestly house. Because the name may refer to the founding head of the division and also to the division that carried his name, it is uncertain how many separate individuals these mentions involve. Easton's gives the name's meaning as "the LORD defends." Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "fighting, or multiplying, of the Lord."

Jehonathan, son of Uzziah, was one of King David's royal officials. He was in charge of the storehouses in the fields, cities, villages and fortified towers (the King James Version says "castles"). Azmaveth son of Adiel oversaw the king's own treasures (1 Chr 27:25). He appears in a list of the stewards who managed David's property. The name means "the Lord has given" and is a longer form of Jonathan. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the Hebrew uses both forms of the name. Several other men in the Bible share the name, and nothing else is known about this one. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates his service to about 1014 BC, an estimate based on the period of David's reign.

Jehonathan was a Levite in the reign of King Jehoshaphat of Judah. He was one of nine Levites sent out, together with the priests Elishama and Jehoram and a group of the king's officials, to the towns of Judah (2 Chr 17:8). The surrounding passage, 2 Chr 17:7–9, says they carried the book of the law of the LORD and taught it to the people. Nothing more is recorded about him. His name is a fuller form of Jonathan, meaning "the LORD has given" according to the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia. Several other men in the Bible bear the same name, and this Levite should not be confused with them. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates the teaching mission to about 910 BC.

Jehonathan was a priest who headed the priestly family of Shemaiah in Jerusalem after the return from exile in Babylon. He is named in a list of the heads of priestly families serving in the days of Joiakim the high priest, the son of Jeshua (Neh 12:18). By inference from the surrounding list, Shemaiah here is the name of a priestly house, and an earlier Shemaiah appears among the priests who came back with Zerubbabel. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates this generation to some time after 536 BC. The name means "the Lord has given" and is a fuller form of Jonathan. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that Hebrew sometimes uses both forms for the same person. Several other men in the Bible bear this name. Nothing more is recorded about this one.

Jehoram was a priest whom King Jehoshaphat of Judah sent out, along with the priest Elishama and a group of Levites, in the third year of his reign. According to the surrounding passage (2 Chr 17:7–9), the princes, Levites and priests went through the cities of Judah teaching the people from the book of the law of the Lord. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes him as a priest sent to instruct the people. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of his name as "exaltation of the Lord." Nothing else is recorded about him. He should not be confused with others who share the name, including Jehoshaphat's own son and successor, King Jehoram of Judah, and King Jehoram of Israel.

Jehoshaphat son of Paruah was one of the twelve officers King Solomon appointed over Israel, and he was responsible for the territory of Issachar (1 Kgs 4:17). The surrounding list in 1 Kings 4 explains that each of these district officers supplied food for the king and his household for one month of the year. Easton's Bible Dictionary calls him Solomon's purveyor, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives the same account of his duty. Nothing else is recorded about him beyond his father's name. His name means "the Lord is judge" or "Yahweh has judged." He should not be confused with other men of the same name, such as Jehoshaphat king of Judah or Jehoshaphat son of Ahilud, who served David and Solomon as recorder.

Jehoshaphat was one of the seven priests who blew trumpets before the ark of God when David had it brought up to Jerusalem (1 Chr 15:24). The others named with him are Shebaniah, Nethaneel, Amasai, Zechariah, Benaiah and Eliezer, while Obed-edom and Jehiah served as doorkeepers for the ark. Nothing more is recorded about him. The name means "the Lord judges." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the Hebrew spelling here is Joshaphat, and the Revised Version renders it that way, so the King James spelling links him in name with other men called Jehoshaphat, including the king of Judah. He should not be confused with them; this entry treats him as a separate priest of David's time.

Jehozabad was a Levite, the second of the eight sons of Obed-edom named in 1 Chr 26:4–5, whose other sons were Shemaiah, Joah, Sacar, Nethaneel, Ammiel, Issachar and Peulthai. The passage lists the divisions of gatekeepers (porters) organized in David's time. By inference from its opening verse, which introduces the Korahite gatekeepers, Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia call him a Korahite. Smith's also connects his family with the south gate of the temple and the storehouse beside it, since that lot later in the chapter falls to Obed-edom and his sons (1 Chr 26:15). His name means "Yahweh has bestowed." Several other men in the Bible share the name, and this Jehozabad should not be confused with them.

Jehozabad was a military commander under King Jehoshaphat of Judah, named in a list of the king's army leaders. He led 180,000 men equipped for war (2 Chr 17:18). By inference from the surrounding passage, he belonged to the tribe of Benjamin: he is listed "next" to Eliada, a Benjamite commander, and Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both identify him as a Benjamite. His name means "the LORD has given" or "the LORD has bestowed." Several other men in the Bible share this name, and this entry concerns only the commander in Jehoshaphat's reign.

Jehu was a man of the tribe of Judah, named only in the genealogy at 1 Chr 2:38 as the son of Obed and the father of Azariah. The surrounding verses place him in the line of Jerahmeel, a son of Hezron. By inference from 1 Chr 2:34–37, he descended from the marriage of Sheshan's daughter to Jarha, an Egyptian servant, through Attai, Nathan, Zabad, Ephlal and Obed. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him as of the house of Hezron. Nothing else is recorded about him. He should not be confused with other men of the same name, such as the king of Israel or the prophet son of Hanani. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "himself who exists," while Smith's renders it "the living."

Jehu was a man of the tribe of Simeon, named in the genealogy of Simeon's descendants in 1 Chr 4:35. He was the son of Josibiah, the son of Seraiah, the son of Asiel. Several other men in the Bible share his name, and this Jehu should not be confused with the better-known king of Israel. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the Tyndale House proper-names index both identify him as a Simeonite. The surrounding passage lists him among the leaders of Simeonite families whose clans grew large and, in the days of King Hezekiah of Judah, moved toward Gedor in search of pasture for their flocks. By inference, Jehu was one of these clan heads, though nothing is recorded about him beyond his name and ancestry.

Jehu the Antothite was one of the warriors who joined David at Ziklag, named among them in 1 Chr 12:3. The surrounding passage describes these men as Benjamites, Saul's own kinsmen, who were skilled archers and slingers able to use either hand. They came to David while he was still kept away from Saul. "Antothite" probably means he came from Anathoth, a Levitical town in Benjamin north of Jerusalem. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the STEPBible proper names list both describe him as one of the Benjamite slingers or archers, and Smith's Bible Dictionary counts him among the chief heroes of Benjamin. Nothing else is recorded about him. He is a different man from the better-known Jehu who later became king of Israel, and from the prophet Jehu son of Hanani. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "himself who exists."

Jehubbah was a man of the tribe of Asher, named only once, in the Asherite genealogy of 1 Chr 7:34, as one of the four sons of Shamer, with his brothers Ahi, Rohgah and Aram. Shamer is probably the Shomer of 1 Chr 7:32, a son of Heber and grandson of Beriah, which would place Jehubbah in the house of Beriah, as Smith's Bible Dictionary notes. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia points out that the Hebrew text reads his name in more than one way: the spoken tradition gives "and Hubbah," while the written consonants suggest a form like "Yachbah." It treats the meaning of the name as unknown. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "protected" and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "hiding, binding." Nothing else is recorded about him.

Jehudijah was a woman named in the genealogy of Judah in 1 Chr 4:18 as the mother of three sons: Jered the father of Gedor, Heber the father of Socho, and Jekuthiel the father of Zanoah. These sons are described as founders of towns in Judah. The verse calls her "his wife," and the husband is unclear. This entry follows the reading that makes her the wife of Ishbah, who is the nearest man named in the preceding verse. Tyndale House's STEPBible Proper Names makes her the wife of Mered, who is said in the same verse to have married Bithiah, Pharaoh's daughter. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggest the Hebrew may be a description, "the Jewess," rather than a personal name. If so, it may set her apart from the Egyptian wife. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the name's meaning as "the praise of the Lord."

Jehush was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, the second of three sons listed for Eshek, after his older brother Ulam and before his younger brother Eliphelet (1 Chr 8:39). Eshek was the brother of Azel, and the surrounding genealogy traces this family back through Jonathan to King Saul, so Smith's Bible Dictionary calls Jehush a remote descendant of Saul. The verse names Eshek as his father. This entry connects him to Eleasah, the father of Azel in 1 Chr 8:37, and by inference also Eshek's father, so Eleasah appears to stand one generation above Jehush. Some reference works, including the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia, treat the name as a form of Jeush. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives its meaning as "to whom God hastens." Nothing else is recorded about him.

Jeiel was a chief of the tribe of Reuben, named first among the leaders of his kindred when their family genealogy was recorded (1 Chr 5:7). The surrounding passage traces Reuben's descendants through the line of Joel down to Beerah, whom the Assyrian king Tilgath-pilneser carried into exile. Jeiel and Zechariah are listed as "his brethren", that is, relatives of Beerah, so Smith's Bible Dictionary places Jeiel in the house of Joel. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes him simply as a Reubenite chief. Nothing more is recorded about him. Several other men in the Bible share the name Jeiel, and this Reubenite should not be confused with them.

Jeiel was a Levite of the family of Asaph, named only in the genealogy of Jahaziel in 2 Chr 20:14. He was the son of Mattaniah and the father of Benaiah. Through Benaiah and then Zechariah he was an ancestor of Jahaziel, on whom the Spirit of the LORD came in the assembly during the reign of King Jehoshaphat of Judah. By the line given in the verse he was Jahaziel's great-great-grandfather. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him as a Gershonite Levite, since the Asaphite singers were traced to Gershon, and calls him a forefather of Jahaziel. Nothing else is recorded about him. Several other men in the Bible share the name Jeiel, and this entry concerns only the Asaphite ancestor of Jahaziel.

Jeiel was a scribe in the service of Uzziah, king of Judah. He is mentioned only in 2 Chr 26:11, where he and Maaseiah the ruler took the count of Uzziah's army. That army was organized into bands that went out to war, under the direction of Hananiah, one of the king's captains. Jeiel's task was evidently administrative: recording the numbers of the fighting men. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes these troops as irregular raiding forces and dates the passage to about 803 BC. Nothing else is known about him, including his family. Several other men in the Bible share the name Jeiel, and this one should not be confused with them.

Jeiel was a Levite descended from Elizaphan who served in the time of King Hezekiah. He appears with Shimri in 2 Chr 29:13, in a list of Levites grouped by family. From the surrounding passage, these Levites answered Hezekiah's call to purify themselves and cleanse the temple in Jerusalem after it had been neglected. Elizaphan is known from Num 3:30 as a leader among the Levites in the wilderness period, so the 'sons of Elizaphan' here were probably a Levite family that kept his name. Some references, including the STEPBible proper names index, give the name as Jeuel, an alternative Hebrew reading of the same name. Several other men in the Bible are also called Jeiel, and this one is known only from this single mention.

Jeiel was one of the chiefs of the Levites in the reign of King Josiah of Judah. He is named with Conaniah, Shemaiah, Nethaneel, Hashabiah and Jozabad, and together they gave the Levites 5,000 small animals (sheep and goats) and 500 oxen as offerings for the great Passover that Josiah held (2 Chr 35:9). Smith's Bible Dictionary dates this Passover to about 623 BC, and explains the name as meaning "treasured of God," though the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats its meaning as unknown. Several other men in the Bible share the name Jeiel, and nothing more is recorded about this one.

Jeiel was one of the descendants of Adonikam who returned from Babylon to Jerusalem with Ezra. He appears in Ezra's list of family heads who joined the journey. Along with Eliphelet and Shemaiah, he is named among "the last sons of Adonikam," and sixty men of the family went with them (Ezra 8:13). Smith's Bible Dictionary dates this return to about 459 BC. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia and the Tyndale House proper-names index give the name as Jeuel, following a different reading of the Hebrew text; the King James Version reads Jeiel. Nothing else is recorded about him. Several other people in the Bible share the name Jeiel, and this man should not be confused with them.

Jeiel was a man of the family or clan of Nebo, listed among the Israelites in Ezra's time who had married foreign wives (Ezra 10:43). The surrounding chapter describes how, after returning from exile in Babylon, these men agreed to send away their foreign wives. His name is the first of seven given for the descendants of Nebo, a group probably named after an ancestor or a home town. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him as a layman and dates these events to about 459 BC. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the parallel list in 1 Esdras 9:35 gives his name as Juel. Nothing more is known about him. Several other men in the Bible share the name Jeiel, and this one should not be confused with them.

Jekamiah was a man of the tribe of Judah named in the genealogy of 1 Chr 2:41, where he is the son of Shallum and the father of Elishama. This list belongs to the descendants of Jerahmeel. It traces the line that, according to the earlier verses of the chapter (1 Chr 2:34–35), began when Sheshan gave his daughter in marriage to his Egyptian servant Jarha. Smith's Bible Dictionary accordingly places him in the line of Ahlai. Nothing else is recorded about him. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia takes his name to mean "may the LORD establish." He is probably a different person from the son of King Jeconiah listed in 1 Chr 3:18, whose name the KJV spells Jecamiah.

Jekuthiel was a man of the tribe of Judah, named once in the genealogies of 1 Chr 4:18 as "the father of Zanoah." His mother was Jehudijah, and his brothers were Jered, father of Gedor, and Heber, father of Socho. In these lists "father" often means the founder or leading figure of a settlement, so Jekuthiel was probably linked with the town of Zanoah in Judah's territory. The passage is hard to follow, because it does not make clear whose wife Jehudijah was. This entry follows the reading that makes Ishbah, named just before in the same genealogy, his father. The STEPBible proper names index instead treats him as a son of Mered, who is named in the same verse. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the meaning of his name is uncertain, possibly "preservation of God." Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "hope, or congregation, of the Lord." Nothing else is recorded about him.

Jemima was the first of the three daughters born to Job after his fortunes were restored, at the close of the book of Job. Her sisters were Kezia and Keren-happuch (Job 42:14). The following verses, by connection with this passage, describe Job's daughters as the most beautiful women in the land and say he gave them an inheritance alongside their brothers. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary give the meaning of her name as "dove," while Hitchcock's Bible Names renders it "handsome as the day." Nothing else is recorded about her.

Jephunneh was a man of the tribe of Asher, named in the tribe's genealogy as a son of Jether and the brother of Pispah and Ara (1 Chr 7:38). He is listed first of the three, and Smith's Bible Dictionary takes him to be the eldest. Nothing else is recorded about him. He is a different person from the better-known Jephunneh, father of Caleb, who belonged to the tribe of Judah. The meaning of the name is uncertain: Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "for whom a way is prepared," and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "he that beholds."

Jerahmeel was a Levite, the son of Kish, named in the list of Levite family heads in 1 Chr 24:29. That list belongs to the account of David organizing the Levites for service at the sanctuary. Smith's Bible Dictionary identifies him as a Merarite who stood as the representative of the family of Kish. By comparison with 1 Chr 23:21, this Kish was a son of Mahli, the son of Merari. Nothing more is recorded about him. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "the mercy, or the beloved, of God." Several other men in the Bible share the name, among them a descendant of Judah and an officer of King Jehoiakim, and they should not be confused with this Levite.

Jerahmeel the son of Hammelech was one of three men King Jehoiakim of Judah ordered to arrest Baruch the scribe and Jeremiah the prophet. The other two were Seraiah son of Azriel and Shelemiah son of Abdeel (Jer 36:26). The surrounding chapter places the order after the king had burned the scroll of Jeremiah's prophecies. The arrest failed because, the verse says, the LORD hid them. Hammelech means "the king" in Hebrew, so some translations read "the king's son," which would probably make Jerahmeel a royal prince or official. Jer 38:6 names a Malchiah son of Hammelech, into whose cistern Jeremiah was later lowered, and this entry takes him to be Jerahmeel's brother. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the name's meaning as "the mercy, or the beloved, of God." Several other people in the Bible share the name.

Jered was a man of the tribe of Judah, named once in the genealogy of 1 Chr 4:18. His mother was Jehudijah, and he is called the "father" of Gedor, which probably means he founded the town or was the ancestor of its people, as Smith's Bible Dictionary explains. His brothers Heber and Jekuthiel are likewise named as fathers of Socho and Zanoah, so the three are linked with towns in Judah. The family lines in this passage are hard to untangle, and his father is identified in different ways. This entry follows the reading that connects him with Ishbah, who is mentioned in the preceding verse (1 Chr 4:17). The STEPBible names index makes him a son of Mered, and Easton's Bible Dictionary connects him with Ezra, also named in that verse. His name is usually taken to mean "descent." He is a different person from Jared, the ancestor of Noah.

Jeremai was a man of the family of Hashum who returned to Judah after the exile and is named in Ezra's list of those who had married foreign wives (Ezra 10:33). By inference from the surrounding chapter, he was among those who agreed to send away their foreign wives as part of the reforms led by Ezra in Jerusalem. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him as a layman and dates the event to about 459 BC. Nothing else is recorded about him, and he appears only in this verse. The meaning of his name is uncertain. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "dwelling in heights," Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "my height" or "throwing forth waters," and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia calls it unknown. That encyclopedia also links him with Jeremias in the parallel list in 1 Esdras 9:34.

Jeremiah was one of the heads of families in the half-tribe of Manasseh that lived east of the Jordan. He appears in a single list in 1 Chr 5:24, alongside Epher, Ishi, Eliel, Azriel, Hodaviah and Jahdiel. All of them are described as mighty men of valour, famous men, and heads of their fathers' houses. The surrounding passage places this branch of Manasseh in the land from Bashan to Baal-hermon and Mount Hermon. It also says these Manassites were later carried into exile by the Assyrians, so he probably lived some generations before that deportation. Nothing else is recorded about him. He is a different person from Jeremiah the prophet and from the several other men of the same name in the Bible. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "exaltation of the Lord."

Jeremiah was one of the warriors who joined David at Ziklag, named in 1 Chr 12:4 alongside Ismaiah the Gibeonite, Jahaziel, Johanan and Josabad the Gederathite. The surrounding passage (1 Chr 12:1–2) describes this group as men who came to David while he was still kept away from Saul, skilled archers and slingers who could use either hand. Easton's Bible Dictionary treats him as a Benjamite slinger, since the list opens with Saul's own tribe. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes he may instead have been from Judah, because nearby names such as "the Gederathite" probably point to towns in Judah. This entry follows the Benjamite view. Nothing more is recorded about him. He is distinct from Jeremiah the prophet and from other men of the same name, including two Gadite warriors listed later in the same chapter.

Jeremiah was a warrior from the tribe of Gad who joined David while he was hiding from King Saul. He appears fifth in a list of Gadite leaders (1 Chr 12:10). The surrounding passage describes these Gadites as skilled fighters who crossed over to David at his stronghold in the wilderness, and it says the least of them was equal to a hundred men (1 Chr 12:8, 14). Easton's Bible Dictionary places his joining in the wilderness, while Tyndale House's proper-names index connects it with David's time at Ziklag. The same list names another Jeremiah as the tenth Gadite (1 Chr 12:13), so the two should be kept apart. Nothing else is recorded about this man. His name is shared with several others in the Bible, most famously the prophet. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives its meaning as "exaltation of the Lord."

Jeremiah was a warrior from the tribe of Gad, listed tenth among the Gadite fighters who joined David (1 Chr 12:13). The surrounding passage describes these Gadites as mighty men skilled with shield and spear who left their tribe to join David at his stronghold in the wilderness, while he was still kept away because of Saul (1 Chr 12:1, 8). It also calls them captains of the army (1 Chr 12:14). Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies him simply as a Gadite warrior. STEPBible places him among those who joined David while he was fleeing from King Saul. Nothing else is recorded about him. He is one of several men in the Bible named Jeremiah and is distinct from the prophet. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "exaltation of the Lord."

Jeremiah was a Rechabite, the son of Habaziniah and the father of Jaazaniah. He is mentioned only once, in Jer 35:3, where his son Jaazaniah is named first among the Rechabite household that the prophet Jeremiah brought to the temple in Jerusalem. In the surrounding chapter the prophet set wine before the Rechabites, and they refused it, keeping the command of their ancestor Jonadab son of Rechab. This Jeremiah appears only as a link in his son's lineage, and nothing is said about his own life. He is distinct from the prophet Jeremiah and from several other men of the same name. The name is usually explained as meaning something like "the Lord establishes" or "the Lord appoints." Hitchcock's Bible Names gives it as "exaltation of the Lord."

Jeremoth was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, named in the Benjamite genealogy of 1 Chronicles. He appears in a list of names that ends by calling them the sons of Beriah (1 Chr 8:14). By inference from the surrounding passage, this Beriah is the one who, with Shema, headed the families of Aijalon and drove out the people of Gath. The family probably belonged to the Benjamite leaders said later in the chapter to have lived in Jerusalem, which is how the STEPBible Proper Names describes him. Nothing else is recorded about him. The name is shared by several other men in the Bible, so this Jeremoth should not be confused with them. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "heights," and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia compares it with the similar name Jeroham in the same genealogy.

Jeremoth was one of the descendants of Elam listed in Ezra 10:26 among the men who had married foreign wives after the return from exile. The surrounding chapter describes how, under Ezra's leadership, these men agreed to send their foreign wives away, and STEPBible's proper-names index places Jeremoth in this group. He is named alongside Mattaniah, Zechariah, Jehiel, Abdi and Eliah, but nothing else is recorded about him. Several other men in the Bible bear the same name, and this Jeremoth should not be confused with them. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "eminences" or "one that fears death."

Jeremoth was one of the descendants of Zattu listed in Ezra 10:27, alongside Elioenai, Eliashib, Mattaniah, Zabad and Aziza. The surrounding chapter shows that the men in this list had married foreign women after the return from exile in Babylon, in the time of Ezra, and STEPBible Proper Names (Tyndale House) notes that he was among those who agreed to send these wives away. Nothing else is recorded about him. Several other men in the Old Testament bear the same name, and this Jeremoth should not be confused with them. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "eminences" or "one that fears death."

Jeribai was one of David's mighty men, the elite warriors listed in 1 Chronicles 11. He is named as a son of Elnaam, along with his brother Joshaviah, and the two appear next to Eliel the Mahavite and Ithmah the Moabite in the later part of the roster (1 Chr 11:46). Nothing else is recorded about him. As the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes, his name belongs to the part of the Chronicles list that has no counterpart in the shorter roster of David's warriors in 2 Sam 23. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "whom Jehovah defends," while the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia considers the meaning uncertain.

Jeriel was a man of the tribe of Issachar, one of the six sons of Tola named in the genealogy of 1 Chr 7:2. His brothers were Uzzi, Rephaiah, Jahmai, Jibsam and Shemuel. The passage calls these sons heads of their father's house and valiant men of might. It also gives the number of their descendants in the days of David as 22,600. Tola himself was a son of Issachar (1 Chr 7:1), so Jeriel belongs to an early generation of the tribe. Nothing else is recorded about him. The meaning of his name is uncertain. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives "founded of God," Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "people of God," and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "fear, or vision of God."

Jerijah was a Levite, the chief of the Hebronites, a family descended from Hebron son of Kohath, during the reign of David. In David's fortieth year a search was made through the family records, and capable, valiant men of this clan were found at Jazer in Gilead, east of the Jordan (1 Chr 26:31). Their recorded duties lay among the tribes east of the river, serving both the king and the worship of God. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia and Smith's Bible Dictionary treat him as the same person as Jeriah, named as head of the Hebronites in 1 Chr 23:19 and 24:23. The two spellings are variant forms of one Hebrew name, meaning something like "founded of the LORD." This entry follows that identification.

Jerimoth was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, named as one of the five sons of Bela in 1 Chr 7:7, alongside Ezbon, Uzzi, Uzziel and Iri. Bela was Benjamin's firstborn son (1 Chr 7:6). The verse calls these five heads of their fathers' houses and mighty men of valour, and says their descendants were counted at 22,034 in the genealogies. Other passages list Bela's sons differently: 1 Chr 8:3–5 names Addar, Gera, Abihud, Abishua, Naaman and Ahoah, and Num 26:40 names Ard. Those men also count as Jerimoth's brothers here. Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that "son" may mean a descendant rather than a direct son. Several other men in the Bible share the name Jerimoth, and this one appears only in this genealogy. Nothing more is recorded about him.

Jerimoth was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, one of the nine sons of Becher listed in the genealogy at 1 Chr 7:8. His brothers were Zemira, Joash, Eliezer, Elioenai, Omri, Abiah, Anathoth and Alameth. Becher himself appears in the same chapter as a son of Benjamin, so Jerimoth was Benjamin's grandson. Nothing else is recorded about him. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him as the head of a Benjamite house, and STEPBible's proper-names index spells the name Jeremoth. Smith's gives the meaning of the name as "heights", while Hitchcock's Bible Names renders it "he that fears or rejects death." Several other men in the Bible are named Jerimoth, and this one should not be confused with them.

Jerimoth was one of the warriors who joined David at Ziklag, named in a list alongside Eluzai, Bealiah, Shemariah and Shephatiah the Haruphite (1 Chr 12:5). The surrounding passage describes these men as kinsmen of Saul from the tribe of Benjamin who came to David while he was still kept away from Saul. They were skilled with both right and left hands in slinging stones and shooting arrows, so Easton's Bible Dictionary calls Jerimoth a Benjamite slinger. Nothing else is recorded about him. Several other men in the Bible share the name Jerimoth, and this one should not be confused with them.

Jerimoth son of Azriel was the leader of the tribe of Naphtali in the time of King David. He appears only once, in a list of the chief officers over the tribes of Israel (1 Chr 27:19). The surrounding chapter places this list in David's reign, and by inference he served as the tribe's head or prince within David's administration. Nothing else is recorded about him. Several other men in the Bible share the name Jerimoth, and this one is distinguished from them by his father's name and his tribe. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "heights," while Hitchcock's Bible Names renders it "he that fears or rejects death."

Jerimoth was a son of King David, known only as the father of Mahalath, who married David's grandson King Rehoboam of Judah (2 Chr 11:18). This made Mahalath and Rehoboam cousins. The same verse names Abihail, daughter of David's brother Eliab, alongside Mahalath. Smith's Bible Dictionary takes her as Rehoboam's second wife, while the STEPBible names index connects her to Jerimoth's family; this entry does not decide between these readings. Jerimoth does not appear in the lists of David's sons born in Hebron and Jerusalem (1 Chr 3:1–9; 2 Sam 5:14–16). He was probably the son of one of David's concubines, whose children 1 Chr 3:9 mentions without naming them. His birth in Jerusalem is likewise an inference. Several other men in the Bible share his name. Smith's gives the meaning "heights."

Jerimoth was one of ten overseers who served in the reign of King Hezekiah of Judah, working under Cononiah and his brother Shimei. They were appointed by command of the king and of Azariah, the ruler of the house of God (2 Chr 31:13). The surrounding passage describes how the people brought offerings, tithes and dedicated things to the temple, and the overseers helped manage these stores. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary identify him as a Levite, which fits the setting, since Levites handled the temple chambers. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "heights," while Hitchcock's Bible Names renders it "he that fears or rejects death." Nothing else is recorded about him. The name Jerimoth belongs to several different men in the Bible, and this one should not be confused with the others.

Jerioth is a woman named once, in the genealogy of Judah at 1 Chr 2:18. In the King James wording she appears as a wife of Caleb son of Hezron, alongside Azubah. Smith's Bible Dictionary calls her one of the elder Caleb's wives, distinguishing him from the better-known Caleb son of Jephunneh. Her name is usually taken to mean "curtains" (of a tent). The verse goes on to list the sons Jesher, Shobab and Ardon, but it is unclear whether "her sons" refers to Jerioth or to Azubah. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the Hebrew of this verse is difficult and has been read in other ways: Jerioth as a daughter of Caleb and Azubah, Azubah as the daughter of Jerioth, or Jerioth as another name for Azubah. This entry follows the reading that makes her Caleb's partner. Nothing else is known about her.

Jeroham was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, named in the Benjamite genealogy of 1 Chronicles 8 as the father of six sons: Shamsherai, Shehariah, Athaliah (here a man's name), Jaresiah, Eliah and Zichri. The list of his sons runs across 1 Chr 8:26–27 and ends with the words "the sons of Jeroham." The verse that follows describes the men in this part of the list as heads of families who lived in Jerusalem, so Jeroham's descendants were probably counted among the Benjamite households there. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him as the founder of a Benjamite family known by his name. Several men in the Bible are called Jeroham, and it is uncertain whether this one is the same as any of the others. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "high," "merciful" or "beloved."

Jeroham was the father, or possibly a more distant ancestor, of Ibneiah. Ibneiah appears in 1 Chr 9:8 among the Benjamites who settled in Jerusalem, in a list of residents usually understood as those living there after the return from exile. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the STEPBible proper names index both identify this Jeroham as a Benjamite, which fits the context of the surrounding list. Smith's Bible Dictionary takes "son" in the broader sense of descendant and dates him to some time before 588 BC. Nothing else is recorded about him. The name, which Hitchcock's Bible Names explains as "merciful" or "beloved," belongs to several men in the Bible, including the father of Elkanah and grandfather of Samuel. This Jeroham is generally treated as a separate person.

Jeroham of Gedor was the father of Joelah and Zebadiah, two of the men who came to David at Ziklag (1 Chr 12:7). By inference from the surrounding passage (1 Chr 12:1–2), these were warriors who joined David while he was still kept away from King Saul. Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies Jeroham as a Benjamite, and Smith's Bible Dictionary dates him to some time before about 1055 BC. The text itself tells us nothing about Jeroham beyond his sons and his connection with Gedor. Which Gedor is meant is uncertain. A town of that name lay in the hill country of Judah, but the context may point to a place in or near Benjamin. Several other men in the Bible are also called Jeroham, and this one should not be confused with them. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the name's meaning as "high," "merciful," or "beloved."

Jeroham was a man of the tribe of Dan, known only as the father of Azareel. In the list of tribal leaders under King David, Azareel son of Jeroham is named as the prince, or chief officer, over Dan (1 Chr 27:22). Nothing else is recorded about Jeroham himself. Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that Azareel may have been his son or a later descendant. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia explains the name as meaning "may he be compassionate." Several other men in the Bible share the name Jeroham, including the father of Elkanah and grandfather of Samuel, and this Danite should not be confused with them.

Jeroham was the father of Azariah, one of the captains of hundreds whom the priest Jehoiada brought into a covenant with him in the seventh year of Queen Athaliah's rule (2 Chr 23:1). These commanders helped Jehoiada overthrow Athaliah and place the young Joash on the throne of Judah. Nothing else is recorded about Jeroham himself; he is known only through his son. The name, which the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia renders "may he be compassionate," is shared by several men in the Bible, and this Jeroham is distinct from the others. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates him to some time before 876 BC, and that date is an estimate rather than something the text states.

Jerubbesheth is a name for Gideon, the judge of Israel, used only once, in 2 Sam 11:21. There Joab, sending news of Uriah's death to David, expects the king to recall how Abimelech the son of Jerubbesheth was killed at Thebez when a woman dropped a piece of millstone on him from the wall. The account in Judges 9 calls Abimelech's father Jerubbaal, the name Gideon received after tearing down Baal's altar (Judges 6:32). Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary both treat Jerubbesheth as another name for Gideon. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia explains that later scribes, reluctant to pronounce the name Baal, sometimes replaced "baal" with "bosheth," meaning "shameful thing." It compares Ish-bosheth, called Eshbaal in 1 Chronicles. Jerubbesheth is therefore probably an altered form of Jerubbaal.

Jesaiah was a man of the tribe of Judah, a son of Hananiah, named in the genealogy of David's royal line in 1 Chr 3:21. The verse that follows the line from David through the kings and the exile (1 Chr 3:19) shows Hananiah as a son of Zerubbabel, so Jesaiah was probably Zerubbabel's grandson. Smith's Bible Dictionary places him after 536 BC. The wording of 1 Chr 3:21 is compressed, and the 'sons of' Rephaiah, Arnan, Obadiah and Shechaniah can be read in more than one way. Some read the verse as tracing Jesaiah's family line through these men, which is why STEPBible's name list calls him a descendant of Shecaniah. This entry treats them as Jesaiah's brothers, alongside Pelatiah. His name means 'salvation of the Lord' and is a form of the name also spelled Jeshaiah. Several other men in the Bible bear it.

Jesaiah was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, named only once, as the earliest ancestor in the genealogy of Sallu son of Meshullam (Neh 11:7). Sallu was one of the Benjamites living in Jerusalem in Nehemiah's time, after the return from the Babylonian exile. The genealogy traces Sallu back through Meshullam, Joed, Pedaiah, Kolaiah, Maaseiah and Ithiel to Jesaiah, who was Ithiel's father. Since he stands seven generations before Sallu, Jesaiah probably lived well before the exile. Nothing else is recorded about him. The same Hebrew name, often spelled Jeshaiah in English, belongs to several other men in the Bible, but this Jesaiah is identified only by his place in this family line. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the name's meaning as "health, or salvation, of the Lord."

Jeshaiah, son of Athaliah, was a member of the family of Elam who returned from Babylon to Jerusalem with Ezra. Ezra 8:7 lists him as the head of the Elam family group in that company, with seventy males accompanying him. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates the return to about 459 BC. The name means "deliverance of the Lord" or "salvation of the Lord," and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that he appears as Jesias (Josias in the King James Version) in the parallel list in 1 Esdras 8:33. His father Athaliah is a man, not to be confused with the queen of the same name. Several other men in the Bible are also called Jeshaiah, and this one is known only from this single verse.

Jeshaiah was a Levite of the family of Merari who travelled with Ezra from Babylon to Jerusalem. Ezra 8:19 names him alongside Hashabiah. The two led a group of their relatives and sons, twenty men in all. The surrounding passage shows that Ezra had sent for Levites to serve at the temple because none had joined his company at first. Jeshaiah and his kinsmen were among those who answered that call. His name means "salvation of the Lord" (Smith's Bible Dictionary) or "deliverance of Yah" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the same man appears as "Osaias" in 1 Esdras 8:48. Several other people in the Bible share the name, and this entry refers only to the Merarite of Ezra's time. Nothing more is recorded about him.

Jeshebeab was a man whose family was assigned the fourteenth of the twenty-four divisions, or courses, of priests. 1 Chronicles 24 describes these divisions being drawn by lot in David's time so that the descendants of Aaron could take turns serving in the sanctuary. He is mentioned only once, in 1 Chr 6:13 of this list (1 Chr 24:13), and nothing else is recorded about him. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary take the name to mean "father's seat". The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that one manuscript of the Greek Septuagint reads the name as "Ishbaal", and another leaves it out. It suggests the Hebrew form may have been altered because the original contained the word "baal".

Jesher was a man of the tribe of Judah, listed as the first of three sons of Caleb the son of Hezron, alongside Shobab and Ardon (1 Chr 2:18). The verse names two women, Caleb's wife Azubah and Jerioth, and its wording leaves it unclear which is the mother of these sons. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary both take Azubah to be his mother. Caleb had other sons by other women, including Hur, Mesha and Gazez, so Jesher's wider family appears across the genealogy of Judah in 1 Chronicles 2. Jesher appears only in this one verse, and nothing more is recorded about his life. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "uprightness."

Jeshishai was a man of the tribe of Gad, named only once, in the genealogy of 1 Chr 5:14. He is listed as the son of Jahdo and the father of Michael, in a line of ancestors that runs back to Buz and forward to Abihail son of Huri, whose sons were among the Gadite family heads. The surrounding passage places these Gadites east of the Jordan in Gilead and Bashan. Nothing else is recorded about him. Smith's Bible Dictionary takes the name to mean "descended from an old man," and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives "aged." That encyclopedia also raises the possibility that the name stands for a family or clan as well as an individual.

Jeshohaiah was a man of the tribe of Simeon, named only once, in a list of Simeonite leaders (1 Chr 4:36). The surrounding passage calls the men in this list princes, or heads, of their families. It says their clans grew large and that in the days of King Hezekiah of Judah they moved toward Gedor in search of pasture, drove out the people living there and settled in their place. So Jeshohaiah probably lived in Hezekiah's reign, around the late 8th century BC by inference from context. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates him to about 711 BC and, drawing on the genealogy earlier in the chapter, counts him among the descendants of Shimei. It gives the name's meaning as "whom Jehovah casts down," while the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats the meaning as unknown. Nothing else is recorded about him.

Jeshua was a Levite in the reign of King Hezekiah of Judah. He is one of six men named in 2 Chr 31:15 who served "next" to Kore, the Levite placed in charge of the freewill offerings brought to the temple. Based in the cities of the priests, these men had the set duty of handing out portions to their fellow priests and Levites according to their divisions (courses), to the great and the small alike. Context places this in Hezekiah's reform of temple worship, roughly the late 8th century BC; Smith's Bible Dictionary dates it to about 726 BC. Nothing else is recorded about him. The name is another form of Joshua, and several other men in the Bible share it, so he should not be confused with the high priest Jeshua who returned from exile.

Jeshua was the father of Jozabad, one of the Levites who helped weigh the silver, gold and temple vessels brought from Babylon by Ezra's company. The weighing took place in the house of God in Jerusalem on the fourth day after the group arrived, under the priest Meremoth son of Uriah (Ezra 8:33). He is known only through his son's name, and nothing else is said about him. Because his son is counted among the Levites, Jeshua was probably a Levite himself, and Easton's Bible Dictionary describes him that way. Several men in Ezra and Nehemiah share the name Jeshua, including Levites of the returning exiles, so this Jeshua may be one of them, but the text does not say which. The name is a form of Joshua (Hitchcock's Bible Names).

Jeshua was the father of Ezer, one of the men who repaired a section of Jerusalem's wall under Nehemiah after the return from exile. He is mentioned only once, in the list of builders, where Ezer worked on a stretch facing the ascent to the armoury at the angle of the wall (Neh 3:19). The verse calls someone "the ruler of Mizpah," but the wording leaves unclear whether the title belongs to Ezer or to his father Jeshua. Nothing else is recorded about him. Several people in the Bible share the name Jeshua, and it is uncertain whether this man is the same as any of the others. Hitchcock's Bible Names treats the name as a form of Joshua.

Jeshua, son of Kadmiel, was one of the chief Levites named in Neh 12:24, alongside Hashabiah and Sherebiah. With their fellow Levites, these leaders were set in opposing groups to lead praise and thanksgiving in turns, "ward over against ward," following the arrangement attributed to David. The surrounding chapter places this list in the period after the return from exile, and the STEPBible Proper Names index places him in Nehemiah's time and links him with the dedication of Jerusalem's wall. Elsewhere Jeshua and Kadmiel appear side by side as Levite family names, so some readers take "son of" here as a way of linking the two households rather than a literal father and son. This entry follows the wording of the verse. His name is a form of Joshua, according to Hitchcock's Bible Names. Several other men in the Bible bear the same name.

Jesiah was a Korahite named among the warriors who joined David, listed with Elkanah, Azareel, Joezer and Jashobeam in 1 Chr 12:6. The surrounding chapter describes the men who came to David at Ziklag while he was still in hiding from Saul, so Jesiah was by inference one of these early supporters. Smith's Bible Dictionary places this about 1055 BC, a date estimated from context. Modern translations spell his name Isshiah, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives its meaning as "Yah exists." Smith's Bible Dictionary renders it "whom Jehovah lends." The term "Korhites" probably means he descended from Korah the Levite, though some take it to refer to a different Korah of the tribe of Judah or Benjamin. Several other men in the Old Testament bear the name Isshiah, and nothing else is known of this one.

Jesimiel was a man of the tribe of Simeon, named in a list of Simeonite clan leaders in 1 Chr 4:36. The surrounding passage describes these men as princes in their families whose households grew large. In the days of King Hezekiah they moved toward Gedor in search of pasture for their flocks and took over land held by earlier inhabitants (1 Chr 4:38–41). That places him, by inference from context, in the late 8th century BC. Smith's Bible Dictionary counts him among the family of Shimei, a Simeonite named a few verses earlier. Nothing else is recorded about him. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives the name's meaning as "God establishes," while Hitchcock's Bible Names renders it "naming, or astonishment, of God."

Jesus, also called Justus, was a Jewish Christian named by Paul at the close of his letter to the Colossians. Paul sends greetings from him together with Aristarchus and Mark, and says that these men, the only ones "of the circumcision" (that is, Jewish believers) among his fellow workers for the kingdom of God, had been a comfort to him (Col 4:11). Since Paul wrote this letter as a prisoner, Jesus Justus was probably with him during that imprisonment, as the STEPBible Proper Names index also understands it. Nothing more is known of him. His name is the Greek form of the Hebrew Joshua, which Hitchcock's Bible Names renders "savior" or "deliverer," and his Latin surname Justus means "just." The name Jesus was common among Jews of the period and is shared by several people in the Bible, including Jesus of Nazareth.

Jether was the firstborn son of Gideon, the judge who delivered Israel from the Midianites. After Gideon captured the Midianite kings Zebah and Zalmunna, he told Jether to rise and kill them. Jether would not draw his sword, because he was afraid and was still a youth (Judg 8:20). Easton's Bible Dictionary describes him as the oldest of Gideon's seventy sons. His brothers included Abimelech and Jotham. By inference from Judg 9:5, where Abimelech killed his brothers and only Jotham escaped, Jether probably died in that slaughter, though he is not named there. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of his name as "he that excels." Several other men in the Bible share the name Jether, and they should not be confused with this son of Gideon.

Jether was a man of the tribe of Judah, the son of Jada and the brother of Jonathan. He appears only in the genealogy of 1 Chr 2:32, which describes Jada as the brother of Shammai and notes that Jether died without children. His line therefore continued through his brother Jonathan. Jada belonged to the family of Jerahmeel, a descendant of Hezron, so the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia calls Jether a Jerahmeelite. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "he that excels," and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives "abundance." Several other men in the Bible share the name Jether, and this entry refers only to the son of Jada. Nothing else is recorded about him.

Jether was a man of the tribe of Judah, listed in 1 Chr 4:17 as the first of the sons of Ezra, with his brothers Mered, Epher and Jalon. This Ezra appears only in Judah's genealogy and is a different person from the later scribe of the same name. Nothing else is recorded about Jether's life or descendants. The name probably means "abundance" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia) or "he that excels" (Hitchcock's Bible Names). Several other men in the Bible are also called Jether, among them Gideon's eldest son, so this entry concerns only the Judahite named in this genealogy. The verse goes on to say "she bare Miriam, and Shammai, and Ishbah," but it does not name the mother. By inference from the following verse, the children listed there probably belong to Mered rather than to Jether.

Jeuel was a man of the tribe of Judah, a descendant of Zerah, son of Judah. He is mentioned only once, in the list of people who lived in Jerusalem (1 Chr 9:6). He is named at the head of the sons of Zerah, who with their relatives numbered six hundred and ninety. By inference from the surrounding passage, which describes the first inhabitants to resettle their towns, this places him among those who lived in Jerusalem after the return from exile in Babylon. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him as a chief man of Judah. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "snatched away by God," and Hitchcock's Bible Names offers "God hath taken away" or "God heaping up." Nothing else is recorded about him.

Jeush was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, listed as the first of the seven sons of Bilhan in 1 Chr 7:10. Bilhan was a son of Jediael, whom the nearby 1 Chr 7:6 names as a son of Benjamin, so Jeush belongs to Benjamin's line a few generations down. One of his brothers was also named Benjamin, after the tribe's ancestor. His other brothers were Ehud, Chenaanah, Zethan, Tharshish and Ahishahar. The following verse describes this family as heads of fathers' houses and mighty men of valour. Nothing else is recorded about him. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests the list may originally have belonged to Zebulun, but this entry follows the text's placement among the Benjamites. The name is shared by several other people in the Bible. The same encyclopedia gives its probable meaning as "he protects" or "he comes to help."

Jeush was a son of Rehoboam, king of Judah, named alongside his brothers Shamariah and Zaham in the list of Rehoboam's family (2 Chr 11:19). The verse says only that "she" bore these sons, after the preceding verse mentions two wives: Mahalath, a granddaughter of David, and Abihail, daughter of Eliab. Some readers, including Tyndale House's STEPBible names list, take Mahalath as the mother. Others read Abihail as a second mother, and this entry follows that view. His half-brothers Abijah, Attai and Ziza and half-sister Shelomith were children of another wife, Maachah (2 Chr 11:20), and Abijah succeeded Rehoboam as king. Jeush was probably born in Jerusalem, Rehoboam's capital. Nothing more is recorded of him. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests the name means "he protects" or "he comes to help." Several other men in the Bible share the name.

Jeuz was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, named in the genealogy of 1 Chronicles 8. He was one of the sons born to Shaharaim by his wife Hodesh. His full brothers were Jobab, Zibia, Mesha, Malcham, Shachia and Mirma, and Abitub and Elpaal were his half-brothers through Shaharaim's wife Hushim. By inference from the surrounding verses (1 Chr 8:8–9), these sons were born in the country of Moab after Shaharaim had sent away his earlier wives. The STEPBible proper-names index also places his birth in Moab. Jeuz and his brothers are described as "heads of the fathers," meaning leaders of family groups (1 Chr 8:10). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia accordingly treats him as the founder of a Benjamite family. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "counsellor." Nothing else is recorded about him.

Jeziah was an Israelite of the family of Parosh who lived after the return from exile in Babylon. He appears only once, in Ezra 10:25, in the list of men who had married foreign wives. By inference from the surrounding chapter, he was among those who agreed to send away these wives during the reforms led by Ezra. Some English versions spell his name Izziah, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia lists him under that form. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "whom Jehovah expiates." Nothing else is recorded about him.

Jeziel was a son of Azmaveth and the brother of Pelet, listed in 1 Chr 12:3 among the warriors who joined David at Ziklag. The surrounding passage, 1 Chr 12:1–2, describes these men as kinsmen of Saul from the tribe of Benjamin, skilled archers and slingers who could use either hand. They came to David while he was still unable to move freely because of Saul. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary both explain the name as meaning "assembled by God." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the Hebrew spelling varies in the text and suggests a meaning of "God gathers." His father Azmaveth may be the same man as Azmaveth the Barhumite, one of David's mighty men, but the text does not say so, and the identification is uncertain. Jeziel is mentioned nowhere else.

Jezliah was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, named as one of the sons of Elpaal in the Benjamite genealogy of 1 Chr 8:18. His brothers listed there include Ishmerai and Jobab, along with Beriah, Shema, Eber, Misham, Shamed, Meshullam, Hezeki, Heber and Zebadiah, all counted among Elpaal's descendants in the surrounding verses. Nothing else is recorded about him beyond his place in this family list. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "whom God will preserve." Some versions and reference works, such as the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia, spell the name Izliah.

Jezoar was a man of the tribe of Judah, named only in the genealogy of 1 Chr 4:7 as one of the sons of Helah, along with Zereth and Ethnan. The surrounding verses (1 Chr 4:5–6) identify Helah as one of the two wives of Ashur, called the father of Tekoa. Through Ashur's other wife, Naarah, Jezoar had the half-brothers Ahuzam, Hepher, Temeni and Haahashtari. Coz, named in the next verse (1 Chr 4:8), is counted here as a full brother, by inference from his place in the list. Nothing else is recorded about Jezoar. The Hebrew spelling of his name varies, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia lists him under the form Izhar. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives its meaning as "clear" or "white," and Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "whiteness."

Jezrahiah was the overseer, or leader, of the singers at the dedication of the rebuilt wall of Jerusalem under Nehemiah. He is mentioned only once, in Neh 12:42. That verse comes in the account of two large thanksgiving choirs that processed along the wall and then stood in the temple, where "the singers sang loud, with Jezrahiah their overseer." Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him as a Levite and dates the dedication to about 446 BC. Both points are inferred from the context of the passage rather than stated in it. His name is usually taken to mean "the Lord arises" or "the Lord shines." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia lists the name under the alternative spelling Izrahiah. Nothing else is recorded about him, including his family.

Jezreel was a man of the tribe of Judah, named in the genealogy of 1 Chr 4:3 as one of those belonging to "the father of Etam," together with Ishma and Idbash and their sister Hazelelponi. "Father of Etam" probably means the founder or leading ancestor of the town of Etam rather than a literal parent. The verses that follow (1 Chr 4:4) close the list as descendants of Hur, the firstborn of Ephratah, so this entry links Jezreel to Hur's family, alongside relatives such as Penuel, Ezer, Shobal and Salma. Smith's Bible Dictionary explains the name as "seed of God." Nothing else is recorded about him. He should not be confused with the city and valley of Jezreel or with Hosea's son of the same name.

Jibsam was a man of the tribe of Issachar, one of six sons of Tola listed in the genealogy at 1 Chr 7:2. His brothers were Uzzi, Rephaiah, Jeriel, Jahmai and Shemuel. The verse calls the sons of Tola heads of their father's house and valiant men of might. It adds that in the days of David their descendants numbered 22,600. Tola was a son of Issachar (1 Chr 7:1), so Jibsam was Issachar's grandson. He is mentioned nowhere else. Some reference works, such as the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia, spell his name Ibsam. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "pleasant," while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "their drought, their confusion."

Jidlaph was a son of Nahor, Abraham's brother, and his wife Milcah, which made him Abraham's nephew. He appears only once, in the list of Nahor's eight sons by Milcah that was reported to Abraham after the near-sacrifice of Isaac (Gen 22:20–23). In that list he is named just before Bethuel, the father of Rebekah. His full brothers were Huz, Buz, Kemuel, Chesed, Hazo, Pildash and Bethuel. Nahor also had sons by his concubine Reumah: Tebah, Gaham, Thahash and Maachah. Nothing else is recorded about Jidlaph's life or descendants. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia take his name to mean "weeping" or "he weeps." Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "he that distills water."

Joab was a man of the tribe of Judah, the son of Seraiah, named in the genealogies of 1 Chr 4:14. He is called "the father of the valley of Charashim," which most likely means he founded or led the settlement there rather than being literally a parent. The name means "valley of craftsmen," and the verse explains that its people were craftsmen. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia renders the place Ge-harashim. Smith's Bible Dictionary counts him among the descendants of Kenaz, which fits the surrounding verses, where Seraiah appears as a son of Kenaz. Nothing else is recorded about him. He should not be confused with the better-known Joab, David's nephew and army commander, or with others of the same name.

Joab was the ancestor of a family group whose descendants returned from Babylon to Jerusalem with Ezra. Ezra 8:9 records that Obadiah son of Jehiel led the "sons of Joab," with 218 men. Joab himself apparently lived well before this return, and his name stands for a clan rather than an individual traveler. Ezra 2:6 and Neh 7:11 list descendants of "Jeshua and Joab" under the family of Pahath-moab among the earlier returnees, and the STEPBible proper names index accordingly treats this Joab as a descendant of Pahath-moab. Nothing else is recorded about him. He should not be confused with Joab the commander of David's army or with other men of the same name. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "paternity" or "voluntary."

Joah was a Levite, the third son of Obed-edom, listed among the temple gatekeepers organized in David's time (1 Chr 26:4). His brothers named in the same list are Shemaiah the firstborn, Jehozabad, Sacar and Nethaneel, and the next verse, 1 Chr 26:5, adds Ammiel, Issachar and Peulthai. This entry also links him to a father named Shimei, which the verse itself does not explain. The surrounding chapter places Obed-edom's family among the divisions of porters (doorkeepers), and Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary describe Joah as a Korhite (Korahite) doorkeeper. Smith's dates him to about 1014 BC, an estimate. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives the name's meaning as "Yahweh is brother." Several other men in the Bible share the name Joah, and they should not be confused with this son of Obed-edom.

Joah son of Zimmah was a Levite of the Gershonite clan. He is named among the Levites who rose to act when King Hezekiah called on them to purify the temple, as the surrounding chapter of 2 Chronicles describes. He is listed alongside representatives of the other Levitical clans, Kohath and Merari. The Eden son of Joah named next to him in the same verse was probably his son. A Gershonite genealogy in 1 Chr 6:20–21 also lists a Joah son of Zimmah, which may point to an earlier ancestor with the same name or to names repeated within the family. Several other men in the Bible share the name Joah. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives its meaning as "fraternity" or "brother of the Lord."

Joah was a Levite of the Gershonite clan, the son of Zimmah and the father of Eden. He is named in 2 Chr 29:12 among the Levites who arose to act when King Hezekiah called on them to purify the temple at the start of his reign. Father and son are listed together as the Gershonite representatives, alongside leaders from the Kohathite and Merarite clans. A Joah son of Zimmah also appears in an earlier Gershonite genealogy (1 Chr 6:21). That may be an ancestor with the same names, since Levite families often reused names, but how the two relate is uncertain. Several other men in the Bible are also called Joah. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "fraternity" or "brother of the Lord."

Joah was the son of Joahaz and one of three officials King Josiah of Judah sent to repair the temple in the eighteenth year of his reign. This came after Josiah had purged the land and the temple. His companions were Shaphan son of Azaliah and Maaseiah, the governor of the city (2 Chr 34:8). Joah is called "the recorder," and Easton's Bible Dictionary takes this to mean the keeper of the state archives. The verse's wording could be read as giving that title to his father, but reference works generally apply it to Joah. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates the event to about 623 BC, an estimate drawn from context. His name is usually explained as "the Lord is brother." Several other men in the Bible are also called Joah, and this one should not be confused with them.

Joahaz was the father of Joah, the recorder who served King Josiah of Judah. He is named only once, in 2 Chr 34:8. That verse says that in the eighteenth year of his reign Josiah sent Joah, together with Shaphan the son of Azaliah and Maaseiah the governor of the city, to repair the house of the LORD. Nothing more is recorded about Joahaz himself. Easton's Bible Dictionary treats the name as a shortened form of Jehoahaz, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives its meaning as "Yahweh has grasped." Smith's Bible Dictionary places him before 623 BC, an estimate inferred from the date of Josiah's temple repairs. He should not be confused with the kings named Jehoahaz, who are different people.

Joanna was a man named in Luke's genealogy of Jesus, in the line of the tribe of Judah. Luke 3:27 lists him as the son of Rhesa and the father of Juda, and places him two generations after Zorobabel (Zerubbabel), the son of Salathiel (Shealtiel). He is a different person from Joanna the woman who followed Jesus, though the name is the same in English. The Revised Version spells his name Joanan, and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives its meaning as "grace or gift of the Lord." Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies him with Hananiah, the son of Zerubbabel listed in 1 Chr 3:19. Smith's Bible Dictionary mentions the same identification as one possible way of reading the line, which would make him Zerubbabel's son rather than his grandson. This entry follows Luke's text and treats him as Rhesa's son. Nothing else is recorded about him.

Joash was a man of the tribe of Judah, listed in the genealogy of Shelah, the son of Judah. He is one of several people in the Bible with this name. He appears only in 1 Chr 4:22, which names him alongside Jokim, the men of Chozeba, and Saraph. The verse says that Joash and Saraph "had the dominion in Moab," which suggests they held some authority or settled there, though no details are given. The passage ends by calling these "ancient things," an indication that the record was old even when the Chronicler wrote it. The preceding verse names Er and Laadah as sons of Shelah. Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that it is unclear whether Joash was Shelah's son or Jokim's. This entry treats him as a son of Shelah. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia explains the name as "Yahweh is strong" or "Yahweh has bestowed."

Joash was a son of Becher and a member of the tribe of Benjamin, named second among Becher's nine sons in the genealogy at 1 Chr 7:8. His brothers were Zemira, Eliezer, Elioenai, Omri, Jerimoth, Abiah, Anathoth and Alameth. Becher appears in the same chapter as a son of Benjamin (1 Chr 7:6), so Joash was a grandson of Benjamin. Smith's Bible Dictionary calls him the head of a Benjamite family and explains the name, a shortened form of Jehoash, as meaning roughly "the LORD hastens to help." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests this genealogy may originally have belonged to the tribe of Zebulun. This entry follows the Benjamite reading of the passage. Nothing else is recorded about him, and he should not be confused with the several other men named Joash in the Bible.

Joash was a son of Shemaah the Gibeathite, from Gibeah, and the brother of Ahiezer. In 1 Chr 12:3 he is listed second, after Ahiezer the chief, among the warriors who came to David at Ziklag while David was still in hiding from Saul. The surrounding passage describes these men as Benjamites, kinsmen of Saul, who were skilled archers and slingers able to use either hand. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary both identify him as one of these Benjamite recruits. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that some commentators read his father's name as Shemaiah. Nothing more is recorded about him. Several other men in the Bible share the name Joash, and this one should not be confused with them.

Joash was one of the officials who managed King David's royal property. In the list of David's stewards he is named as the man in charge of the "cellars of oil," the storehouses of olive oil (1 Chr 27:28). His post sat next to that of Baalhanan the Gederite, who oversaw the olive and sycamore trees in the lowlands, so the two roles probably formed a chain from orchard to storage. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes him as keeping the royal oil stores under both David and Solomon. Nothing else is recorded about him, including his family or origin. The name Joash, a shortened form of Jehoash, is usually explained as "Yahweh has helped" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia). Several other people in the Bible share the name, and this Joash should not be confused with them.

Jobab was a Canaanite king of Madon, a city in northern Canaan, in the time of Joshua. When Jabin king of Hazor heard of Israel's victories in the south, he sent to Jobab and to the kings of Shimron and Achshaph to form an alliance against Israel (Josh 11:1). The following verses of the same chapter say that these allied kings gathered their forces at the waters of Merom and were defeated by Joshua. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him as one of the northern chieftains routed there. By inference, Jobab is the unnamed "king of Madon" in the list of defeated kings at Josh 12:19. He is named only in Josh 11:1. The same name belongs to several other men in the Bible, including a son of Joktan, an early king of Edom, and some Benjamites. Those are different people.

Jobab was a son of Shaharaim and his wife Hodesh, listed in the genealogy of the tribe of Benjamin in 1 Chr 8:9. He is named first among Hodesh's sons, followed by Zibia, Mesha and Malcham. The next verse adds Jeuz, Shachia and Mirma. Shaharaim also had sons by another wife, Hushim, including Abitub and Elpaal, who were Jobab's half-brothers. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him as the head of a Benjamite house, based on the summary of these sons as heads of fathers' houses. Nothing else is recorded about him. Several other men in the Bible share the name, among them a descendant of Joktan, an early king of Edom and a king of Madon defeated by Joshua. This Jobab should not be confused with them. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "sorrowful, hated."

Jobab was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, named as one of the sons of Elpaal in the Benjamite genealogy of 1 Chr 8:18. He is listed with Ishmerai and Jezliah. Elpaal's other sons, named in the surrounding verses, include Eber, Misham, Shamed, Beriah, Shema, Zebadiah, Meshullam, Hezeki and Heber. Nothing more is recorded about him beyond his place in this family list. The name Jobab belongs to several different men in the Bible, including a son of Joktan, a king of Edom, a king of Madon, and another Benjamite named in the same chapter as a son of Shaharaim. This entry refers only to the son of Elpaal. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "sorrowful" or "hated."

Joed was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, named only in the genealogy of Sallu in Neh 11:7. He was the son of Pedaiah and the father of Meshullam, and Sallu was his grandson. Sallu appears in the list of Benjamites who settled in Jerusalem after the return from the Babylonian exile. Joed himself probably lived some generations earlier, since the list traces Sallu's ancestry back through several names. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the parallel list in 1 Chr 9:7 gives Sallu's line without Joed's name. Smith's Bible Dictionary explains the name as meaning "for whom the LORD is witness." Nothing else is recorded about him.

Joel was a leader of the tribe of Simeon, named in a list of Simeonite clan heads in 1 Chr 4:35. Nothing is recorded about his ancestry or family, unlike Jehu, who is named next to him with several generations of forebears. The surrounding passage calls the men on this list princes in their families.
