It says their households grew large and moved toward Gedor in search of pasture during the reign of Hezekiah king of Judah (1 Chr 4:38–41). By inference, Joel belonged to that generation and took part in the move, though he is not mentioned individually. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him as a Simeonite chief and explains the name as meaning "Jehovah is God". Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "he that wills or commands". Several other men in the Bible are also called Joel, including the prophet. This one is known only from this verse.

Joel was a member of the tribe of Reuben, named in its genealogy at 1 Chr 5:4 as the father of Shemaiah. The verse traces a line of descent from him: Shemaiah, then Gog, then Shimei. The following verses continue the line down to Beerah, a Reubenite prince whom the Assyrian king Tilgath-pilneser carried into exile (1 Chr 5:5–6). The text does not say how Joel was connected to Reuben's sons listed just before (1 Chr 5:3). Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that some interpreters make him a son of Hanoch, while others trace his descent through Carmi. His name is usually explained as meaning "the LORD is God." Several other men in the Bible share the name, and this Joel is known only from this genealogy.

Joel was a man of the tribe of Reuben, named in 1 Chr 5:8 as the father of Shema and the great-grandfather of Bela son of Azaz. Bela's family lived in Aroer and spread as far as Nebo and Baal-meon, east of the Dead Sea. The Reubenite context comes from the surrounding genealogy in 1 Chronicles 5. That chapter also mentions a Joel at 1 Chr 5:4, whose descendants begin with Shemaiah. Some readers take Shema and Shemaiah to be the same person, which would make the two Joels one man, but the text does not settle this. Several other men in the Bible share the name. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives its meaning as "he that wills or commands." Beyond his place in this family line, nothing else is recorded about him.

Joel was a man of the tribe of Gad, named first among the Gadite leaders as "the chief" in 1 Chr 5:12. The surrounding passage places these Gadites in the land of Bashan, east of the Jordan. By inference from 1 Chr 5:17, their family records were compiled in the days of Jotham king of Judah and Jeroboam king of Israel. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates him to about 782 BC, an estimate drawn from that context. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that he may be the same person as the Joel listed among the Reubenites earlier in the chapter, perhaps as head of a clan counted with either tribe. Nothing more is recorded about him. His name is usually understood to mean "the LORD is God." Several other men in the Bible share the name Joel.

Joel was a man of the tribe of Issachar, a son of Izrahiah and grandson of Uzzi, named in the genealogy at 1 Chr 7:3. His brothers were Michael, Obadiah and Ishiah. The verse gives a total of "five" but names only four sons, so the count probably includes Izrahiah himself. All of them are called "chief men," and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia describes Joel as a chief of Issachar. The surrounding verses (1 Chr 7:1–2) trace this family back through Uzzi to Tola, a son of Issachar, and go on to note the large number of fighting men the family produced. His name is usually understood to mean "the LORD is God." Nothing else is recorded about him. He should not be confused with other men of the same name, such as the prophet Joel.

Joel, the brother of Nathan, was one of David's mighty men, the elite warriors listed in 1 Chr 11:38. Nothing else is recorded about him. Smith's Bible Dictionary takes his brother to be Nathan of Zobah. The parallel list in 2 Samuel 23:36 has "Igal the son of Nathan" in about the same place. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that Codex Vaticanus of the Greek Septuagint reads "son" rather than "brother" in Chronicles, so the two names may refer to the same man. This entry follows the Chronicles wording, which calls him Nathan's brother. The name Joel is commonly taken to mean "the LORD is God." Several other men in the Bible share the name, including the prophet Joel.

Joel, son of Pedaiah, was the leader of the half-tribe of Manasseh during David's reign. He appears once, in a list of chief officers over the tribes of Israel (1 Chr 27:20). The verse does not say which half of Manasseh he led. The next verse names a separate leader for the half-tribe of Manasseh in Gilead, east of the Jordan, so Joel probably led the western half. Smith's Bible Dictionary takes this view. The STEPBible proper-names index instead places his rule in Gilead. This entry follows the western reading, based on the surrounding list. Nothing else is recorded about him. He should be kept distinct from the several other men named Joel in the Bible, including the prophet. The name is usually understood to mean "the LORD is God."

Joel, son of Azariah, was a Levite of the Kohathite clan in the reign of King Hezekiah of Judah. He is named among the Levites who responded when Hezekiah called on them to consecrate themselves and cleanse the temple in Jerusalem. He is listed with Mahath son of Amasai as the representatives of the Kohathites, alongside leaders from the Merarite and Gershonite clans (2 Chr 29:12). The surrounding chapter shows these men gathering their fellow Levites to remove what had defiled the temple, so Joel probably helped lead that work. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates this to about 726 BC. The name Joel is commonly explained as "the LORD is God" and was borne by several men in the Bible. This Joel is known only from this one verse.

Joel was one of the descendants ("sons") of Nebo listed in Ezra 10:43 among the Israelites who had married foreign wives after the return from exile in Babylon. By inference from the surrounding chapter, he was among those who agreed during Ezra's reforms to send these wives away. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates the episode to about 459 BC, an estimate drawn from context. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the same man appears as "Juel" in the parallel list in 1 Esdras 9:35. His name is usually understood to mean "the Lord is God." Several other men in the Bible share the name, including the prophet Joel, and nothing more is known of this one beyond his place in the list.

Joel, son of Zichri, was a leader of the tribe of Benjamin in Jerusalem after the return from the Babylonian exile. In the list of those who settled in the city in Nehemiah's time, he is named as overseer of the Benjamites living there, with Judah son of Senuah second over the city (Neh 11:9). That he belonged to Benjamin is inferred from context, since the verse closes the list of Benjamite families that begins at Neh 11:7. Nothing else is recorded about him. The name, usually explained as "the LORD is God" (Smith's Bible Dictionary), was borne by several people in the Bible, including the prophet Joel, and this man should not be confused with them.

Joelah was one of the warriors who joined David at Ziklag. In 1 Chr 12:7, Joelah and Zebadiah are called "the sons of Jeroham of Gedor." The surrounding passage lists the men who came to David while he was keeping away from Saul, and by inference from that context Joelah fought alongside him. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the Tyndale House proper-names index describe Joelah as a Benjamite, because the list in this part of the chapter is introduced as Saul's kinsmen. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that Joelah may instead have been a Judean, since Gedor was also the name of a town in Judah. Nothing more is recorded. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "Jehovah helps," while the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests "may he avail."

Joezer was one of the Korahites named in the list of warriors who joined David at Ziklag while he was still in hiding from Saul (1 Chr 12:6). He appears alongside Elkanah, Jesiah, Azareel and Jashobeam. The surrounding passage presents these men as part of a group of Benjaminite recruits, kinsmen of Saul, who were skilled with the bow and the sling. The label "Korhites" is not explained here. It may refer to descendants of the Levite Korah, or to a family of Benjamin or Judah with a similar name. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that he was perhaps a Judean. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes him as part of David's bodyguard, and Smith's Bible Dictionary calls him one of David's captains. His name means "the LORD is help." Nothing else is recorded about him.

Jogli was a man of the tribe of Dan, known only as the father of Bukki. In Num 34:22 Bukki son of Jogli is named as the leader of Dan among the tribal representatives chosen to help divide the land of Canaan among the tribes of Israel. Nothing else is recorded about Jogli himself, though he was presumably a Danite of some standing, since his son held this role. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggest his name means "led into exile," while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "passing over," "turning back" or "rejoicing."

Joha was a Benjamite, one of the sons of Beriah, named in the genealogy of the tribe of Benjamin in 1 Chr 8:16. He appears alongside Michael and Ispah. The surrounding verses also list Zebadiah, Arad, Ader, Ahio, Shashak and Jeremoth among Beriah's family. The nearby 1 Chr 8:13 presents Beriah as a family head among the inhabitants of Aijalon who drove out the people of Gath, so Joha probably belonged to that Aijalon clan, by inference from the passage. Nothing more is recorded about him. The name is shared by at least one other man, a son of Shimri listed among David's warriors in 1 Chr 11:45, who is a different person. Smith's Bible Dictionary takes the name to mean "the Lord gives life." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia regards its meaning as uncertain and possibly a form of Joah.

Joha was one of David's mighty warriors, named in the list of his elite fighting men in 1 Chr 11:45. He was the son of Shimri and the brother of Jediael, who appears beside him in the same list. He is called "the Tizite," probably a reference to his hometown or clan, though no place called Tiz or Tizi is otherwise known. The verse's wording leaves it unclear whether the title belongs to Joha alone or to both brothers. This section of the list has no parallel in 2 Samuel 23, and nothing more is recorded about him. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "the LORD gives life," while the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests it may be a form of Joah. The name Joha is also borne by at least one other man in the Bible, a Benjamite.

Johanan was the firstborn son of King Josiah of Judah, named first among Josiah's four sons in 1 Chr 3:15, ahead of Jehoiakim, Zedekiah and Shallum. He is not mentioned anywhere else, and he never became king. When Josiah died, the throne passed to Shallum, called Jehoahaz in 2 Kgs 23:30–31, and later to Jehoiakim and Zedekiah. Why Johanan was passed over is not explained. He may have died young, but that is only a possibility. This entry treats him as a member of the tribe of Judah, born in Jerusalem, and as a full brother of Jehoiakim. That makes Zebudah his mother, since 2 Kgs 23:36 names her as Jehoiakim's mother. Jehoahaz and Zedekiah, whose mother was Hamutal, were his half-brothers. Smith's Bible Dictionary explains his name as "gift or grace of God." Several other men in the Bible share the name.

Johanan was one of the seven sons of Elioenai, listed in the royal genealogy of the tribe of Judah in 1 Chr 3:24. His brothers were Hodaiah, Eliashib, Pelaiah, Akkub, Dalaiah and Anani. The surrounding chapter traces the line of King David through Jehoiachin and Zerubbabel, so Johanan belongs to the family of David's heirs after the return from exile in Babylon. Smith's Bible Dictionary places him in the line of Zerubbabel's descendants, through Neariah and Shemaiah, and dates him to after 406 BC. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia describes him as a post-exilic Davidic prince. Nothing else is recorded about him beyond his name. The name means "the Lord has been gracious," and several other people in the Bible share it.

Johanan was one of the warriors who came over to David at Ziklag, named in a list of mighty men in 1 Chr 12:4 alongside Ismaiah the Gibeonite, Jeremiah, Jahaziel and Josabad the Gederathite. The surrounding passage, 1 Chr 12:1–7, describes these men as kinsmen of Saul from the tribe of Benjamin who joined David while he was still hiding from Saul. Smith's Bible Dictionary accordingly calls him a valiant Benjamite. Nothing else is recorded about him. The name Johanan, meaning "gift or grace of God" according to Smith's Bible Dictionary, belongs to several different people in the Bible. This Johanan should not be confused with the Gadite warrior of the same name listed later in the same chapter.

Johanan was a warrior of the tribe of Gad, listed eighth among the Gadite fighters who came over to David (1 Chr 12:12). The surrounding passage describes these Gadites as skilled, battle-ready men who separated themselves to join David at his stronghold in the wilderness while he was still a fugitive from Saul. Easton's Bible Dictionary places this in the desert of Judah. STEPBible's proper-names index connects the list with the men who joined David at Ziklag and helped him fight raiding bands. Nothing else is recorded about him. Several other men in the Bible share the name, and this Johanan should not be confused with them. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "gift or grace of God."

Johanan was the father of Azariah, one of the leading men of the tribe of Ephraim during the reign of Ahaz king of Judah. He is known only through his son, who is named in 2 Chr 28:12 among the Ephraimite heads who stood up against the army returning from war. In the surrounding chapter, that army had brought captives from Judah to Samaria, and these leaders opposed keeping them. Nothing else is recorded about Johanan himself. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the Hebrew text spells his name in the longer form Jehohanan, meaning "the Lord has been gracious." Several other men in the Bible share the name Johanan, and this one should not be confused with them.

Johanan, son of Hakkatan, was the head of the family of Azgad among those who returned from exile in Babylon to Jerusalem with Ezra. He led 110 men of his family on the journey (Ezra 8:12). He is one of several men in the Bible named Johanan, and nothing more is recorded about him. Ezra's return took place in the reign of the Persian king Artaxerxes, as the surrounding chapter states. The name means "the Lord has been gracious" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia). The same list in the apocryphal book of 1 Esdras gives his name as Joannes.

Johanan was the son of Eliashib. He owned a chamber at the temple in Jerusalem, to which Ezra withdrew after leaving the house of God. There Ezra fasted, eating no bread and drinking no water, as he mourned the unfaithfulness of the returned exiles who had married foreign wives (Ezra 10:6). Nothing else is said of him here. The STEPBible Proper Names index describes him as a priest in Ezra's time. Many interpreters link his father with Eliashib the high priest of Nehemiah's day. Neh 12:23 also speaks of a Johanan son of Eliashib in the high priestly line, possibly a grandson called "son" in a broader sense. Whether these are the same man is uncertain, since the name was common and is shared by several people in the Bible. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives its meaning as "who is liberal or merciful."

Johanan was the son of Tobiah the Ammonite, one of the chief opponents of Nehemiah during the rebuilding of Jerusalem's walls. Nehemiah mentions him only in passing, to explain why many people in Judah were bound by oath to Tobiah. Tobiah was the son-in-law of Shechaniah son of Arah, and Johanan had married the daughter of Meshullam son of Berechiah (Neh 6:18). Earlier in the book, a Meshullam son of Berechiah is named among those who repaired sections of the wall, so these marriages probably tied Tobiah's family to people inside Jerusalem's own leadership. Nothing else is recorded about Johanan himself. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "gift or grace of God." The name was shared by several people in the Bible, and this Johanan should not be confused with the others.

John (Relative of the High Priest) was a member of the high priestly family in Jerusalem. He is named only once, alongside Annas the high priest, Caiaphas and Alexander, among those of the high priest's kindred who gathered in Jerusalem when the apostles Peter and John were brought before the council after healing a lame man (Acts 4:6). This was probably about AD 30, by inference from context. He was one of those who questioned and judged the two apostles. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes him as otherwise unknown. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia records a suggestion by the scholar Lightfoot that he was the Talmudic teacher Johanan ben Zakkai. This entry treats him simply as an otherwise unidentified relative of the high priest. His name means "the grace or mercy of the Lord," according to Hitchcock's Bible Names.

Joiarib was one of the men Ezra summoned at the river Ahava while gathering the returning exiles for the journey from Babylon to Jerusalem. In Ezra 8:16 he is named with Elnathan as "men of understanding," set apart from the "chief men" listed before them. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia renders the description as "teacher." Read with the following verse, Ezra sent this group to Iddo at Casiphia to bring Levites to serve in the house of God, as Easton's Bible Dictionary notes. Smith's Bible Dictionary calls him a layman who returned with Ezra. Nothing more is recorded about him. The name, often explained as "the LORD contends" or "the LORD defends," is shared by several other men in the Bible, and it is uncertain whether he is connected with any of them.

Joiarib was a man of the tribe of Judah, named only in the family line of Maaseiah, one of the Judahites who lived in Jerusalem after the return from the Babylonian exile (Neh 11:5). He was the son of Zechariah and the father of Adaiah, and he stood several generations before Maaseiah, whose ancestry runs back through Joiarib to Shiloni. Smith's Bible Dictionary takes "Shiloni" to mean a Shilonite, probably a descendant of Shelah son of Judah. The STEPBible name index instead places this line under Judah's son Perez. Either way, he lived some time before the return, probably in the 6th century BC or earlier, by inference from the length of the line. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia simply call him a Judahite. His name is usually taken to mean "the LORD pleads" or "contends." Several other men in the Bible bear the same name.

Jokim was a man of the tribe of Judah, named only once, in the genealogy of Judah at 1 Chr 4:22. He is listed among the descendants of Shelah, the son of Judah, alongside Er, Laadah, Joash and Saraph. Smith's Bible Dictionary calls him a son of Shelah, while Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia describe him more loosely as a descendant. The verse that names him also mentions the men of Chozeba and says that Joash and Saraph "had the dominion in Moab." It closes by noting that "these are ancient things," which suggests the compiler was drawing on old records. Nothing else is told about Jokim. His name is usually explained as meaning "the LORD raises up" and is related to the name Jehoiakim.

Jonan is a man named in Luke's genealogy of Jesus, which traces the line back from Joseph through David's son Nathan (Luke 3:30). He is listed as the son of Eliakim and the father of Joseph, and as a descendant of David he belonged to the tribe of Judah. Nothing else is recorded about him. Some reference works, including the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia, give the name as Jonam, a spelling found in some Greek manuscripts. Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests it may be a shortened form of Johanan, meaning "gift or grace of God." It places him before 876 BC, which is a rough estimate drawn from his position in the genealogy.

Jonathan was a Levite, the son of Gershom, who became priest to the tribe of Dan after the Danites set up a carved image in their new city of Dan. According to Judg 18:30, he and his sons held this priesthood until the land was taken into captivity. The KJV calls Gershom "the son of Manasseh." Easton's Bible Dictionary explains that the rabbis changed the name from Moses to Manasseh to spare the lawgiver's memory. On that reading, Jonathan was a grandson of Moses through his son Gershom (Exod 2:22). Easton's also identifies him with the young Levite from Bethlehem in Judah whose story is told in Judges 17–18. That Levite first served as household priest to Micah of Ephraim, and Danite raiders later persuaded him to go with them and carry off Micah's idols. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "given of God." Several other men in the Bible share the name.

Jonathan was the father of Ebed, one of the family of Adin, who is named in the list of those who came up from Babylon to Jerusalem with Ezra (Ezra 8:6). His son Ebed led fifty men of that family on the journey. Jonathan himself is known only as Ebed's father. Nothing is said of his own life, or of whether he lived to see the return. He is one of several men in the Bible named Jonathan, a name meaning "the LORD has given." He is a different person from Saul's son, David's friend. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the same list appears in 1 Esdras 8:32.

Jonathan son of Asahel was one of the men named when Ezra dealt with the Israelites who had married foreign wives after the return from exile (Ezra 10:15). He is one of several people in the Bible with this name, which means "the LORD has given." Ezra 10:15 names him with Jahaziah son of Tikvah, and says Meshullam and Shabbethai the Levite helped them. The Hebrew can be read two ways. The King James Version says they were "employed about this matter," meaning they managed the inquiry. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes the other reading, that they stood against the plan, and STEPBible's proper names index takes him as an opponent of the demand to put away foreign wives. This entry follows the King James wording quoted here but notes that both readings are held. Smith's Bible Dictionary calls him a priest. Nothing else is recorded about him.

Jonathan was a priest in the generation after the return from exile in Babylon. He is named once, in a list of the heads of priestly families. Nehemiah 12:14 links him to Melicu, which the surrounding list (Neh 12:12) shows to be a priestly house he represented. By inference from that context, he served while Joiakim was high priest, a generation after Zerubbabel's return. Melicu is probably the same as Malluch, one of the priests who came back with Zerubbabel (Neh 12:2). Nothing else is recorded about him. His name means "the LORD has given." Several men in the Bible share it, and he is a different person from Jonathan the son of King Saul.

Jonathan was the father of Zechariah, one of the men with trumpets at the dedication of Jerusalem's rebuilt wall in Nehemiah's time. Neh 12:35 places him in a family line running back through Shemaiah, Mattaniah, Michaiah and Zaccur to Asaph, the well-known temple musician. That makes Jonathan the son of Shemaiah and a descendant of Asaph. The following verse, Neh 12:36, names Zechariah's 'brethren': Shemaiah, Azarael, Milalai, Gilalai, Maai, Nethaneel, Judah and Hanani. This entry counts them as Jonathan's sons, although the Hebrew word can also mean kinsmen more broadly. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia describe this Jonathan as a priest. He appears only in this genealogy, and nothing else is told about him. His name means 'the LORD has given.' He is one of several men in the Bible called Jonathan.

Jonathan was a son of Kareah and brother of Johanan, mentioned once in the Bible. After the Babylonians captured Jerusalem, Jonathan and his brother were among the army officers who came with their men to Gedaliah, the governor at Mizpah (Jer 40:8). This was about 587 BC, a date Smith's Bible Dictionary gives. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia describes him as a Judahite captain. His brother Johanan becomes prominent in the chapters that follow, but Jonathan is not mentioned again. The parallel list of officers in 2 Kgs 25:23 names only Johanan son of Kareah, so it is uncertain whether Jonathan belongs in the original list. Several other men in the Bible share the name, including Saul's son, the friend of David. The name means "the LORD has given."

Jorai was a man of the tribe of Gad, one of seven brothers of the house of their fathers listed in 1 Chr 5:13: Michael, Meshullam, Sheba, Jorai, Jachan, Zia and Heber. The next verse names their father as Abihail. The surrounding passage places these Gadites in Gilead and Bashan, east of the Jordan. It says their genealogies were recorded in the days of Jotham king of Judah and Jeroboam king of Israel, so Jorai probably belongs to about that period. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "whom Jehovah teaches." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia describes him as a Gadite chief and notes that the name may stand for a clan rather than a single person. Nothing else is recorded about him.

Joram was a Levite named in a genealogy in 1 Chr 26:25. He was the son of Jeshaiah and the father of Zichri. The line traces back through Rehabiah to Eliezer, and by inference from the surrounding chapter Eliezer is the son of Moses. The line ends with Shelomith, who appears in the passage as the one in charge of the treasuries of dedicated gifts in the time of David. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes Joram as an ancestor of Shelomith. His name is usually explained as meaning "the LORD is exalted." It is a shorter form of Jehoram and is shared by several other people in the Bible, including kings of Israel and Judah. Nothing else is recorded about this Joram.

Jorim is a man named only once in the Bible, in Luke's genealogy of Jesus. Luke 3:29 lists him as the son of Matthat and the father of Eliezer. That places him in the line running from David through Nathan, so he belongs to the tribe of Judah. He lived in the generations between David and the Babylonian exile. Nothing else is recorded about him. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia takes the Greek form of his name to come from the Hebrew Joram or Jehoram. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives its meaning as "whom Jehovah has exalted." Hitchcock's Bible Names renders it "he that exalts the Lord."

Josabad the Gederathite was one of the warriors who came to David at Ziklag, while David was still hiding from Saul. He is named among a group of fighters in 1 Chr 12:4. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary describe him as one of the Benjamite archers. This follows from the surrounding passage, which presents these men as Saul's kinsmen from Benjamin who could use both bow and sling. The epithet "Gederathite" probably refers to his home town, Gederah. Its location is uncertain, but it was likely a place in Benjamin rather than the Gederah of the Judean lowlands. Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that the name is more properly spelled Jozabad, meaning "whom the Lord bestows." He is not the same person as the other men called Jozabad in Chronicles, Ezra and Nehemiah. Nothing more is recorded about him.

Jose is a man named in Luke's genealogy of Jesus, which traces the line back through David's son Nathan and so belongs to the tribe of Judah. He is called the son of Eliezer, and by inference from the order of the list he was the father of Er (Luke 3:29). Nothing else is recorded about him. Smith's Bible Dictionary treats Jose as another form of Joses. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the Greek text here reads Iesous, the equivalent of Joshua or Jesus, and that the Revised Version renders it that way. Jose is the King James spelling. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "raised" or "who pardons."

Joseph was a man of the tribe of Issachar, known only as the father of Igal. Igal was the man chosen from Issachar to be one of the twelve spies Moses sent to explore the land of Canaan, and he is listed in Num 13:7 as "the son of Joseph." Nothing else is recorded about Joseph himself. He lived probably a generation before the wilderness journey, and he should not be confused with the several other men of the same name in the Bible, such as Jacob's son Joseph. Smith's Bible Dictionary and Hitchcock's Bible Names give the meaning of the name as "increase" or "addition."

Joseph was one of the Israelite laymen listed in Ezra 10 among those who had married foreign wives after the return from exile. He is named only once, alongside Shallum and Amariah (Ezra 10:42). The surrounding chapter shows that these men agreed to send away their foreign wives during Ezra's reforms. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia places him among the sons of Bani, the family group that heads this part of the list. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates the episode to about 459 BC, an estimate inferred from context. Nothing else is recorded about him, and he should not be confused with the several other men in the Bible who share his name. According to Hitchcock's Bible Names, the name means "increase" or "addition."

Joseph was a priest who headed the priestly family of Shebaniah in the days of the high priest Joiakim, after the return from exile in Babylon. He appears only in a list of priestly family heads (Neh 12:14). By inference from the surrounding passage, which dates the list to Joiakim's time, he lived in the generation after the first returnees under Zerubbabel, Smith's Bible Dictionary places him some time after 536 BC. The family name Shebaniah probably matches the Shechaniah of Neh 12:3, a variation in spelling between the two lists. Several other people in the Bible share the name Joseph, and this one should not be confused with them. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the name's meaning as "increase" or "addition." Nothing more is recorded about him.

Joseph was an ancestor of Jesus named only in Luke's genealogy, which traces Jesus' line back through David to Adam. He was the father of Janna and, according to the next verse (Luke 3:25), the son of Mattathias. Because the line runs through David, he belonged to the tribe of Judah. Nothing else is recorded about him. Smith's Bible Dictionary places him some time after 400 BC, a date inferred from his position in the list. He should not be confused with the other men named Joseph in the same genealogy, including Mary's husband at its start (Luke 3:23) and another ancestor further back (Luke 3:30). Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "increase" or "addition."

Joseph (son of Judah) is a name in Luke's genealogy of Jesus, listed as the son of Juda and the father of Semei (Luke 3:26). Nothing else is recorded about him. Many Greek manuscripts and modern translations spell the name Josech, as the STEPBible proper-names index notes. Two other men named Joseph appear in the same genealogy (Luke 3:24, 30), as Easton's Bible Dictionary points out. The next verse continues the line back through Joanna and Rhesa to Zerubbabel, which suggests he lived a few generations after the return from the Babylonian exile. Smith's Bible Dictionary places him somewhere between 536 and 410 BC, an estimate drawn from his position in the list. His name is usually taken to mean "increase" or "addition."

Joseph was an ancestor of Jesus named in Luke's genealogy, which traces the line back from Joseph the husband of Mary through David's son Nathan. He is listed as the son of Jonan and the father of Juda (Luke 3:30). Because this line runs through David, he belongs to the tribe of Judah. Nothing else is recorded about him, and since several people in the Bible share the name, he should not be confused with the better-known men called Joseph. By inference from his place in the list, between David and the Babylonian exile, he probably lived several generations after David, though the text gives no date. The name is commonly understood to mean "increase" or "addition" (Hitchcock's Bible Names).

Joshah son of Amaziah was a man of the tribe of Simeon. He appears only once, in a list of Simeonite names in 1 Chr 4:34. The surrounding passage (1 Chr 4:38–41) describes the men on this list as leaders of their families. It says that in the days of King Hezekiah, their clans grew and moved toward Gedor in search of pasture for their flocks, driving out the earlier inhabitants and settling there. By inference from that context, Joshah was one of these Simeonite clan leaders in Hezekiah's time, probably the late 8th century BC. Nothing else is recorded about him or his father Amaziah, who is not otherwise identified. The meaning of the name is uncertain. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives "Yahweh's gift", and Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "whom Jehovah lets dwell".

Joshaphat the Mithnite was one of the warriors named in the list of David's mighty men in 1 Chr 11:43, where he appears next to Hanan the son of Maachah. His name means "the Lord judges" according to Smith's Bible Dictionary, which describes him as one of David's guard. The title "Mithnite" probably refers to his hometown or clan, but no place called Mithna is known from the Bible, so its meaning is uncertain. He is mentioned only in this verse, which belongs to the later part of the list that has no parallel in 2 Samuel 23, and nothing else is recorded about his deeds or family. He should not be confused with Jehoshaphat or the other men called Joshaphat elsewhere in Scripture.

Joshaviah was a son of Elnaam and a brother of Jeribai. Both brothers are named among David's mighty warriors in the list of 1 Chr 11:46. The verse is ambiguous about the title "the Mahavite," which follows the name Eliel and comes before the two brothers. It may belong to Eliel alone, or Eliel may also have been a son of Elnaam. Nothing else is recorded about Joshaviah. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that his name does not appear in the parallel list of David's warriors in 2 Samuel 23, which is shorter and differs in detail. Smith's Bible Dictionary explains the name as meaning "whom Jehovah makes dwell," and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "the seat, alteration, or captivity of the Lord."

Joshua was a governor of a city in Judah during the reign of King Josiah, mentioned only in 2 Kgs 23:8. A city gate was named after him, and high places stood at its entrance, on the left as one entered. Josiah broke these down as part of his reforms, when he brought the priests out of the cities of Judah and defiled the high places from Geba to Beersheba. The verse does not name the city. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia take it to be Jerusalem and call Joshua its governor, and this entry follows that reading. Smith's dates him to about 628 BC. Nothing else is known of him, and he is distinct from the better-known Joshua son of Nun and others who share the name, which means "the LORD is salvation."

Josibiah was a man of the tribe of Simeon, named only once, in a genealogy in 1 Chr 4:35. He was the son of Seraiah, the grandson of Asiel, and the father of Jehu. That verse is part of a list of Simeonite clan leaders. The surrounding passage (1 Chr 4:41) places these leaders in the days of King Hezekiah, when they moved to Gedor in search of pasture for their flocks. STEPBible Proper Names follows this reading and counts Josibiah among the Simeonite leaders of Hezekiah's reign, though it is perhaps more exact to say that his son Jehu belonged to that generation. Some English versions spell the name Joshibiah. Smith's Bible Dictionary takes it to mean "to whom God gives a dwelling," while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "the seat, or captivity of the Lord." Nothing else is recorded about him.

Josiphiah was the father, or possibly a more distant ancestor, of Shelomith, who led a group of 160 men back from Babylon to Jerusalem with Ezra (Ezra 8:10). The name is usually explained as meaning "the Lord adds" or "the Lord will increase." In the Hebrew text the verse is awkward, reading "of the sons of Shelomith; the son of Josiphiah." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests that a family name, Bani, fell out of the verse, based on the Greek Septuagint and 1 Esdras 8:36. On that reading, Shelomith son of Josiphiah was head of the Bani family group. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates the return to about 459 BC. Nothing else is recorded about Josiphiah himself.

Jotham was a man of the tribe of Judah, named once as one of the six sons of Jahdai, alongside Regem, Geshan, Pelet, Ephah and Shaaph (1 Chr 2:47). He appears in the genealogy of the descendants of Caleb, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia calls him a Calebite. The verse does not say how Jahdai is connected to Caleb's family. STEPBible's proper-name index takes Jahdai as a wife of Caleb, while Smith's Bible Dictionary simply calls Jotham a son of Jahdai. This entry treats Jahdai as his father. Nothing else is recorded about him. His name means "the LORD is perfect" or "the LORD is upright." Several other men in the Bible share the name, including the son of Gideon and the king of Judah, and he should not be confused with them.

Jozabad was one of the men of the tribe of Manasseh who left Saul's side and joined David while David was on his way to Ziklag. 1 Chr 12:20 names him among the captains of thousands from Manasseh who came over to David. By inference from the surrounding passage, this happened when David had gone with the Philistines toward battle against Saul and was then sent back to Ziklag. The same verse names two men called Jozabad in this group, and it is not clear which one this entry refers to. Several other men in the Bible also bear the name. Hitchcock's Bible Names treats Jozabad as the same name as Josabad. Nothing more is recorded about him.

Jozabad was a man of the tribe of Manasseh and one of the "captains of the thousands" of Manasseh who joined David as he went to Ziklag (1 Chr 12:20). By inference from the surrounding chapter and the account in 1 Samuel 29–30, this happened when David left the Philistine army before its battle with Saul and returned to Ziklag, and these men changed sides to support him. The same verse lists two men named Jozabad among the seven Manasseh commanders, so it is unclear which of the two this entry refers to. Nothing else is recorded about him. Hitchcock's Bible Names treats Jozabad as the same name as Josabad. Several other men in the Bible also bear this name.

Jozabad was one of ten overseers who served under Cononiah and his brother Shimei during the reign of King Hezekiah of Judah. He was appointed by command of Hezekiah and of Azariah, the chief officer of the temple. By inference from the surrounding passage, these overseers helped manage the offerings, tithes and dedicated gifts that the people brought to the temple and that were kept in its storerooms. Smith's Bible Dictionary identifies him as a Levite and dates his service to about 726 BC, an estimate drawn from context. STEPBible's Tyndale House name list describes his role as helping distribute the contributions to the priests and Levites. Smith's gives the name's meaning as "Jehovah justifies." He is mentioned only in 2 Chr 31:13. Several other men in the Bible share the name Jozabad, and this one should not be confused with them.

Jozabad was one of the chief Levites in the reign of King Josiah of Judah. At Josiah's great Passover, he joined Conaniah, Shemaiah, Nethaneel, Hashabiah and Jeiel in supplying the Levites with animals for the Passover offerings: five thousand sheep and goats and five hundred oxen (2 Chr 35:9). Nothing else is recorded about him. The name, which Smith's Bible Dictionary takes to mean "the LORD justifies," is shared by several other men in the Bible, including other Levites, so this Jozabad should not be confused with them.

Jozabad, son of Jeshua, was a Levite in the time of Ezra. After Ezra's group arrived in Jerusalem from Babylon, the silver, gold and temple vessels they had carried were weighed in the house of God on the fourth day. The priest Meremoth son of Uriah did the weighing, together with Eleazar son of Phinehas. Two Levites, Jozabad and Noadiah son of Binnui, assisted them (Ezra 8:33). Smith's Bible Dictionary dates this to about 459 BC, an estimate from context. It suggests he is probably the same man as a Levite named Jozabad mentioned elsewhere in Ezra and Nehemiah, but the identification is uncertain because several people share the name. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "Jehovah justifies."

Jozabad was a priest of the family of Pashur who lived in the time of Ezra, after the return from exile in Babylon. He appears only in the list of men who had married foreign wives (Ezra 10:22). The verse itself simply names him among the sons of Pashur. The surrounding chapter places this family among the priests, and it records that those listed agreed to send away their foreign wives. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the parallel list in 1 Esdras 9:22 gives his name as Ocidelus. His name is usually explained as meaning "the Lord has bestowed," though Smith's Bible Dictionary renders it "Jehovah justifies." Several other men in the Bible share the name Jozabad, so this one should not be confused with the Levites of the same name in Ezra and Nehemiah.

Jozabad was a Levite in the time of Ezra, listed among those who had married foreign women (Ezra 10:23). By inference from the surrounding chapter, he was one of the men who agreed to send away their foreign wives during Ezra's reform after the return from exile in Babylon. The STEPBible Proper Names index describes him the same way. Several other men in the Bible share the name Jozabad, including Levites mentioned elsewhere in Ezra and Nehemiah. Whether this Jozabad is the same as any of them is uncertain, and this entry treats him as a separate person known only from this list. Hitchcock's Bible Names treats the name as the same as Josabad.

Jozabad was one of the Levites who helped the people understand the law when Ezra read it publicly in Jerusalem after the return from exile. He is named in Neh 8:7 among thirteen men, alongside Jeshua, Bani, Sherebiah and others, who explained the reading while the people stood in their places. Nothing more is said about him in this passage. The name Jozabad is shared by several men of the same period, including Levites mentioned in Ezra and elsewhere in Nehemiah, such as a Levite who oversaw the outward business of the temple (Neh 11:16). He may be the same man as one of these, but the text does not make the identification, so it remains uncertain.

Jozabad was one of the leading Levites living in Jerusalem after the return from exile, in the time of Nehemiah. Together with Shabbethai, he oversaw the "outward business of the house of God" (Neh 11:16), meaning the outside work of the temple rather than its sacred service inside. Because several men in the Bible share this name, it is uncertain whether he is the same as the Levite Jozabad mentioned elsewhere in Ezra and Nehemiah, such as the one who helped explain the law to the people (Neh 8:7) or the son of Jeshua who received the temple treasures (Ezra 8:33). An identification with one of them is possible but not stated in the text.

Jozadak was the father of Jeshua, a priest whose family is named in Ezra 10:18. That verse lists priests of the sons of Jeshua son of Jozadak, namely Maaseiah, Eliezer, Jarib and Gedaliah, among those found in Ezra's time to have married foreign wives. Other passages call Jeshua son of Jozadak the high priest who returned from exile with Zerubbabel and helped rebuild the altar and temple (Ezra 3:2, 3:8, 5:2; Neh 12:26). By inference, Jozadak is the same man as Jehozadak, the son of the high priest Seraiah, who according to 1 Chr 6:14–15 was carried into exile when Nebuchadnezzar took Judah and Jerusalem. Haggai and Zechariah spell the name Josedech. The verse shown here records nothing about Jozadak himself beyond his being Jeshua's father.

Jubal was a son of Lamech and his wife Adah, in the line of Cain, and the brother of Jabal. His half-siblings were Tubal-cain and Naamah, Lamech's children by his other wife, Zillah. Genesis 4:21 calls him "the father of all such as handle the harp and organ," meaning he was the founder or originator of those who play musical instruments. Easton's Bible Dictionary explains that the Hebrew words translated "harp" and "organ" more properly mean a lyre and a mouth-organ or Pan's pipe, so modern translations often render them "lyre and pipe." Along with his brothers, who are linked with herding and metalworking, Jubal appears in a short list that traces early skills and crafts to Lamech's family. His name has been connected with music; Hitchcock's Bible Names gives it as "a trumpet." He is mentioned only in this one verse.

Juda is an ancestor of Jesus named in Luke's genealogy, which traces the line back from Joseph through David to Adam. He was the father of Joseph and, according to the next verse (Luke 3:27), the son of Joanna. He belongs to the generations after the Babylonian exile, between Zerubbabel and Joseph the husband of Mary. Nothing else is recorded about him. Many later Greek texts spell the name Joda, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia lists him under that form. He is not the same as several other people in the Bible with similar names, including Judah son of Jacob, who appears as Juda later in the same genealogy. Smith's Bible Dictionary identifies him with Abiud in Matthew's genealogy (Matt 1:13). The two lists differ in this section, so that identification is uncertain.

Juda was a man named in Luke's genealogy of Jesus, listed as the son of Joseph and the father of Simeon (Luke 3:30). He appears only in this list, which traces the line from David through his son Nathan. That line places Juda in the tribe of Judah. He lived several generations after David and long before the exile, though no dates are given. Nothing else is recorded about him. Juda is the Greek form of the Hebrew name Judah, which Smith's Bible Dictionary explains as meaning "praised." Several other people in the Bible share the name, and this Juda should not be confused with them. Easton's Bible Dictionary places him in Christ's maternal ancestry, reflecting the view that Luke's genealogy follows Mary's line, as distinct from Matthew's.

Judah was a Levite listed among those who had married foreign women in the time of Ezra (Ezra 10:23). He appears in the roll of priests, Levites and other Israelites who had taken wives from the surrounding peoples. From the surrounding chapter, these men agreed to send away their foreign wives. Nothing else is recorded about him, and because several people in the Bible share the name Judah, it is uncertain whether he can be linked with any other Levite of that name in the books of Ezra and Nehemiah. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "the praise of the Lord" or "confession."

Judah son of Senuah was a leader in Jerusalem in the time of Nehemiah, after the return from exile. He appears in the list of people who settled in the city, and Neh 11:9 says he was "second over the city," serving under or alongside Joel son of Zichri, the overseer. The surrounding verses, which list descendants of Benjamin, suggest he belonged to that tribe, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia calls him a Benjamite. The Hebrew phrase can mean either that he was second in command over Jerusalem or that he was in charge of the city's second district. His father's name is given in the KJV as Senuah, which the same encyclopedia renders Hassenuah. Several people in the Bible share the name Judah, which Hitchcock's Bible Names takes to mean "the praise of the Lord." Nothing more is recorded about him.

Judah was one of the musicians who played at the dedication of the rebuilt wall of Jerusalem in Nehemiah's time. He is named among the "brethren" of Zechariah son of Jonathan. Neh 12:35 makes Zechariah one of the priests' sons with trumpets, and this entry makes Judah and the others with him sons of Jonathan, though "brethren" may simply mean kinsmen or fellow musicians. They played the musical instruments of David, and Ezra the scribe led their part of the procession (Neh 12:36). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia calls him a priest and musician and suggests he may be the same as other men named Judah in Ezra and Nehemiah. Because several people share this name, that identification is uncertain. His name is usually taken to mean "praised."

Judas (of Galilee) was a rebel leader mentioned by Gamaliel in his speech to the Jewish council in Acts 5:37. Gamaliel was advising the council on how to deal with the apostles. He said that Judas rose up "in the days of the taxing," drew many people after him, and then perished, and his followers were scattered. Gamaliel names him after Theudas as a second example of a movement that came to nothing once its leader died. The "taxing" refers to a Roman registration or census. STEPBible Proper Names (Tyndale House) describes Judas as leading a revolt against the Roman census held while Quirinius was governor of Syria. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia likewise calls him a Galilean who stirred up rebellion during the enrollment. His name is the Greek form of Judah (Easton's Bible Dictionary).

Judas (Jew of Damascus) was the man in whose house Saul of Tarsus stayed in Damascus after his encounter with the risen Jesus on the road to the city. The Lord told Ananias in a vision to go to the street called Straight and ask at the house of Judas for Saul, who was praying there (Acts 9:11). Saul had been led into Damascus blind, so he was probably lodging with Judas as a guest, by inference from the surrounding passage. Nothing more is known of him. Easton's Bible Dictionary calls him a Jew of Damascus, while the STEPBible proper names index describes him as a Christian; the text itself does not say. His name is the Greek form of Judah. Easton's and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia note that a house traditionally called the "house of Judas" is still pointed out on or near Straight Street.

Julia was a Christian woman living in Rome. Paul greets her near the end of his letter to the Romans (Rom 16:15). She is named together with Philologus, Nereus and Nereus's sister, Olympas, and "all the saints which are with them." That grouping suggests they belonged to the same household or house church. Because her name is paired with Philologus, Smith's and Easton's Bible Dictionaries take her to be probably his wife. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia allows that she may have been his sister, and notes that the name Julia may point to someone connected with the imperial household. The text itself does not say how she was related to the others. Her name is the feminine form of Julius. Nothing else is recorded about her.

Junia was a Christian at Rome whom Paul greets together with Andronicus in Rom 16:7. Paul calls the two his kinsmen, which may mean blood relatives or simply fellow Jews. He also calls them his fellow prisoners, meaning they had been imprisoned at some point, perhaps with him. He says they became believers in Christ before he did, so they were among the earliest followers. Paul describes them as "of note among the apostles." This is read either as saying they were prominent apostles themselves, the reading the STEPBible names data follows, or that they were well regarded by the apostles. Some translations give the name as the masculine "Junias," but this entry treats Junia as a woman. Because the two are named as a pair, Andronicus is often taken to be her husband or brother, though the verse does not say. Smith's Bible Dictionary explains the name as "belonging to Juno."

Jushab-hesed was a son of Zerubbabel, a member of the tribe of Judah descended from King Jehoiachin's royal line. He appears only once, as the last of a group of five sons listed together, "Hashubah, and Ohel, and Berechiah, and Hasadiah, Jushabhesed, five" (1 Chr 3:20). The verse before names Zerubbabel's other children, Meshullam, Hananiah and their sister Shelomith. Because the five are counted separately, they may have been a distinct group, perhaps born later or to another mother, though the text does not say. His brother Abiud is named only in Matthew's genealogy of Jesus. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia renders his name "loving-kindness is returned" and suggests it was probably symbolic, like Shear-jashub. That would fit a family living through the return from exile, though this is an inference. Nothing else is recorded about him.

Justus was a man at Corinth described as "one that worshipped God," which probably means a Gentile who attended the synagogue without fully converting, and whose house stood next door to the synagogue (Acts 18:7). When the Jews of Corinth opposed Paul's teaching, Paul left the synagogue and went into Justus's house, apparently using it as his base for preaching during his mission to Corinth, about AD 49 by inference from context. Ancient manuscripts differ on his name. Some read "Justus" alone, while others read "Titius Justus" or "Titus Justus." Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests he may be Paul's companion Titus, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes a proposal linking him with Tertius (Rom 16:22). This entry treats him simply as the Corinthian host named in Acts 18:7. He is distinct from the other men called Justus in Acts 1:23 and Col 4:11. The name means "just" or "upright."

Kallai was a priest who headed the priestly family of Sallai in the generation after the return from exile in Babylon. He appears only once, in a list of family heads among the priests (Neh 12:20). By inference from the surrounding passage, this list belongs to the days of Joiakim son of Jeshua the high priest, as Smith's Bible Dictionary and STEPBible's proper-names index also place him. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia connects him more loosely with the priests who returned with Zerubbabel. The family of Sallai is probably the same as the "Sallu" named among the earlier returning priests earlier in the same chapter. Nothing else is recorded about him. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives the meaning of his name as "swift."

Kelaiah, also called Kelita, was a Levite listed in Ezra 10:23 among the men who had married foreign wives in the period after the return from exile. The surrounding chapter describes Ezra's reform, in which these men agreed to send away their foreign wives, so Kelaiah is understood by inference from context to have been one of those who did so. The verse itself notes that Kelaiah and Kelita are the same man. A Levite named Kelita also appears in Nehemiah, helping explain the law when Ezra read it to the people and later sealing the covenant. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that this may be the same person but says the identification is not certain. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "swift messenger of Jehovah."

Kemuel was the third son of Nahor, Abraham's brother, and his wife Milcah. He is named in the list of Nahor's children that reached Abraham after the near-sacrifice of Isaac (Gen 22:21), where he is called "the father of Aram." His full brothers were Huz, Buz, Chesed, Hazo, Pildash, Jidlaph and Bethuel, the father of Rebekah. Nahor's concubine Reumah bore his half-siblings Tebah, Gaham, Thahash and Maachah. This Aram is probably not the Aram son of Shem in the Table of Nations. Nothing else is recorded about Kemuel's life. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the name's meaning as "God hath raised up, or established him." The name is shared by other men in the Old Testament, such as a leader of the tribe of Ephraim and a Levite, who are different people.

Kemuel, son of Shiphtan, was the leader ("prince") of the tribe of Ephraim named in Num 34:24. He is listed among the tribal representatives whom the LORD designated, through Moses, to divide the land of Canaan among the Israelites. From the surrounding passage, these leaders were to work alongside Eleazar the priest and Joshua in assigning the inheritance west of the Jordan. This is his only mention in the Bible. The name is shared by other people, including a son of Nahor and a Levite father of Hashabiah, and should not be confused with them. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "congregation of God," the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives "God's mound," and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "God hath raised up."

Kemuel was a Levite whose son Hashabiah served as the ruler over the tribe of Levi in the list of tribal leaders from King David's reign (1 Chr 27:17). In that list the Aaronites, the priestly branch of the tribe, are counted separately under Zadok. Nothing else is recorded about Kemuel himself, and he is known only as Hashabiah's father. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes Hashabiah as a prince of the tribe in David's time. The Hashabiah named here may be the same as the Hashabiah of the Hebronite clan mentioned in the preceding chapter, but this is uncertain. The name Kemuel is shared by other men in the Bible, including a son of Nahor and a prince of the tribe of Ephraim, and they should not be confused with this Levite. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the name's meaning as "God hath raised up, or established him."

Kenaz was a descendant of Caleb the son of Jephunneh, named in the genealogy of the tribe of Judah. According to 1 Chr 4:15 he was a son of Elah, which makes him Caleb's grandson, as Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary both describe him. The Hebrew of the verse is a little unusual, and Smith's notes an alternative reading in the margin, so the exact wording of the relationship is not entirely certain. Nothing further is recorded about him. The name Kenaz is shared by several people in the Bible, including an Edomite chief descended from Esau and the father or ancestor of Othniel, Caleb's younger kinsman. This Kenaz should be kept distinct from them, though the name's recurrence in Caleb's family is notable, since Caleb himself is elsewhere called a Kenizzite.

Keren-happuch was the third and youngest daughter of Job, named in Job 42:14 alongside her sisters Jemima and Kezia. Her birth came in the closing part of the book, after Job's suffering ended and his fortunes were restored, as the surrounding verses describe. The next verse says no women in the land were as beautiful as Job's daughters and that he gave them an inheritance among their brothers. Her name means "horn of antimony" or "horn of eye-paint," according to the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia and Easton's Bible Dictionary. It refers to a small horn used to hold the black cosmetic that women applied to the edges of their eyelids. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning as "the horn or child of beauty." Nothing else is recorded about her.

Kezia was the second of the three daughters born to Job after his trials ended and his fortunes were restored. Her sisters were Jemima, the eldest, and Keren-happuch, the youngest (Job 42:14). The surrounding verses make her a daughter: Job 42:13 says Job had seven sons and three daughters, and Job 42:15 says no women in the land were as beautiful as Job's daughters, and that their father gave them an inheritance alongside their brothers. Smith's Bible Dictionary also calls her the second daughter. Her name is usually taken to mean "cassia," a fragrant spice related to cinnamon, and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives that meaning. Nothing else is recorded about her.

Kish son of Abdi was a Levite of the clan of Merari in the reign of King Hezekiah of Judah. He is named in 2 Chr 29:12 among the Levites who answered Hezekiah's call. Each of the three Levitical clans, Kohath, Merari and Gershon, is represented in that list by two men, and Kish appears with Azariah son of Jehalelel for the Merarites. The surrounding chapter shows these Levites consecrating themselves and cleansing the temple, so he probably took part in that work. Nothing else is recorded about him. He is not the Benjamite Kish who was the father of King Saul, and the name is shared by several other people in the Bible. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives the meaning of the name as "bow" or "power."

Kish was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, named in Esth 2:5 as the father of Shimei and the great-grandfather of Mordecai, the Jew living in Shushan who raised Queen Esther. He appears only in this genealogy, which runs Mordecai, son of Jair, son of Shimei, son of Kish. Several other men in the Bible share the name, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia lists five. Readers differ on how to take the line. Most reference works, including Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary, treat Kish as Mordecai's actual great-grandfather, and this entry follows that reading. Others suggest the names may point to well-known earlier Benjamites, such as Kish the father of King Saul, rather than to immediate ancestors. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "a bow."

Kolaiah was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, named only in the family line of Sallu, one of the Benjamites who settled in Jerusalem after the return from exile (Neh 11:7). He was the son of Maaseiah and the father of Pedaiah, and through Pedaiah, Joed and Meshullam he was an ancestor of Sallu. Nothing else is recorded about his life. Smith's Bible Dictionary places him before about 536 BC, the period of the first return from Babylon. By inference from the length of the genealogy, he probably lived some generations before Nehemiah's time. The name, which the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia renders "voice of Yah," is also borne by another man in the Bible, the father of the false prophet Ahab mentioned in Jeremiah. That man should not be confused with this Benjamite.

Kolaiah was the father of Ahab, one of two men whom Jeremiah condemned for prophesying lies in the Lord's name to the Jewish exiles in Babylon (Jer 29:21). The Lord declared that Ahab and his companion Zedekiah son of Maaseiah would be handed over to Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon and killed before the exiles' eyes. The next verse says the king roasted them in the fire, and Smith's Bible Dictionary accordingly describes Ahab as burnt by the king of Babylon. Nothing else is recorded about Kolaiah himself. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "voice of Jehovah" and places him before about 594 BC, a date inferred from context. The same name belongs to a different man, a Benjamite ancestor listed in Neh 11:7, who is distinct from this Kolaiah.

Korah was an Edomite chief (a "duke" in the King James Version) descended from Eliphaz, the son of Esau and his wife Adah. He appears only in Gen 36:16, in a list of the chiefs who came from Eliphaz in the land of Edom, alongside Gatam and Amalek. His name is often taken to mean "baldness" (Smith's Bible Dictionary; Hitchcock's Bible Names). He is not named among the sons of Eliphaz in the genealogy just before (Gen 36:11–12) or in the parallel list in 1 Chr 1:36. Because of this, some interpreters, as the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes, connect him with another Korah, Esau's son by Aholibamah (Gen 36:14, 18). This entry treats him as a separate chief listed under Eliphaz's line. Several other people in the Bible share the name Korah, including the Levite who rebelled against Moses.

Korah was a man of the tribe of Judah, listed in 1 Chr 2:43 as one of the sons of Hebron, with his brothers Tappuah, Rekem and Shema. He appears only in this genealogy, among the descendants of Caleb. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that this Hebron was the son of Mareshah. Some scholars read names in these Calebite lists as clans or towns as well as individuals, and Hebron and Tappuah are also place names in Judah, so Korah may represent a family group. The text records nothing else about him. He is distinct from other men named Korah, such as the Levite who rebelled against Moses and the son of Esau. The name probably means "baldness," according to Smith's Bible Dictionary.

Kore, son of Imnah, was a Levite who served as gatekeeper at the east gate of the temple during the reign of Hezekiah, king of Judah. As part of Hezekiah's reorganization of temple service, Kore was put in charge of the freewill offerings given to God. He was responsible for distributing the offerings presented to the LORD and the most holy things, apparently to the priests and Levites who depended on them (2 Chr 31:14). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests he probably belonged to the same family line as an earlier Kore, a gatekeeper of the Korahite clan. Several men in the Bible bear this name, and this entry concerns only the son of Imnah. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates his service to about 726 BC.

Laadah was a man of the tribe of Judah, a son of Shelah and so a grandson of Judah. He appears only once, in the genealogy of Judah's descendants at 1 Chr 4:21, where he is called "the father of Mareshah." His brothers named in the passage and its context are Er, Joash, Jokim and Saraph. Mareshah was also the name of a town in the lowlands of Judah, so "father" here may mean the founder or leading figure of that settlement rather than a literal parent, a common pattern in these Chronicles genealogies. This is an inference, and the text does not settle it. The same verse links Shelah's descendants to families of linen workers of the house of Ashbea. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of his name as "to assemble together" or "to testify."

Laadan was a member of the tribe of Ephraim, one of the tribes descended from Joseph, named only in the genealogy of 1 Chr 7:26. His father was Tahan and his son was Ammihud, whose son was Elishama. The list goes on to Joshua the son of Nun (1 Chr 7:27), so Smith's Bible Dictionary describes Laadan as an ancestor of Joshua. Elishama son of Ammihud is probably the same man who led the tribe of Ephraim in the wilderness (Num 1:10). Nothing else is recorded about Laadan's life. The name is shared by others, including a Levite of the family of Gershon (1 Chr 23:7), who is a different person. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the name's meaning as "for pleasure," "devouring" or "judgment."

Lael was a Levite of the Gershonite branch, known only as the father of Eliasaph. In Num 3:24 his son Eliasaph is named chief of the father's house of the Gershonites, the family responsible under Moses for parts of the tabernacle's coverings and hangings. Since his son held this leading role, Lael was presumably a descendant of Gershon son of Levi, though the text gives no further details of his life or ancestry. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia explains the name as meaning "belonging to God," while Hitchcock's Bible Names renders it "to God" or "to the mighty." He is mentioned in this single verse and nowhere else in the Bible.

Lahad was a man of the tribe of Judah, named once in the genealogies of 1 Chronicles. He was a son of Jahath and the brother of Ahumai. Through Jahath he descended from Reaiah son of Shobal. The verse ends by calling this line "the families of the Zorathites," so Lahad's descendants were probably counted among the clans linked with Zorah, a town in the lowlands of Judah. Nothing else is recorded about his life. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "oppression," while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "praising" or "to confess."

Lahmi was a Philistine warrior, the brother of Goliath the Gittite, killed by Elhanan the son of Jair in one of David's later wars with the Philistines (1 Chr 20:5). Like Goliath, he is described as having a spear whose shaft was as thick as a weaver's beam. The same chapter, together with 2 Sam 21:15–22, groups him with other huge warriors from Gath, including Ishbi-benob, Sippai and an unnamed man of great stature, all called descendants of 'the giant' in Gath. The parallel passage, 2 Sam 21:19, says instead that Elhanan, a Bethlehemite, killed Goliath himself. Many interpreters explain the difference as two ways of reading a similar Hebrew text, since 'Lahmi' closely resembles the word for 'Bethlehemite.' This entry follows the Chronicles account, which presents Lahmi as a separate person. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of his name as 'my bread' or 'my war.'

Lapidoth was the husband of Deborah, the prophetess who judged Israel in the period of the judges (Judg 4:4). He is named only in this one verse, and nothing else is told about him: no family, tribe, home or role in the events of Deborah's time. His name means "torches" or "lamps." Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that some have read the Hebrew phrase not as "wife of Lapidoth" but as "a woman of a fiery spirit," on the view that Lapidoth is not a personal name at all. This entry follows the common reading of the verse, which treats Lapidoth as a man's name and Deborah's husband.

Letushim was a son of Dedan, who was a son of Jokshan, listed with his brothers Asshurim and Leummim in Gen 25:3. Because Jokshan was one of the sons Abraham had with Keturah, Letushim belongs to Abraham's line through Keturah. He is mentioned only in this one genealogy, and nothing is said about his life. His name has a plural form, as do the names of his brothers, so the entry may name a people or tribe rather than a single man. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats Letushim as a Dedanite tribe of North Arabia. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him as the second son of Dedan. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the name's meaning as "hammermen" or "filemen."

Leummim was the third of the three sons of Dedan named in Gen 25:3, alongside Asshurim and Letushim. Dedan was a son of Jokshan, and Jokshan was one of the sons Abraham had by Keturah (Gen 25:1–2), which makes Leummim a descendant of Abraham through Keturah. Like the names of his brothers, Leummim has a plural form in Hebrew and means "peoples" or "nations." For this reason Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary take it as the name of a tribe or people rather than of a single individual. Easton's describes Leummim as the head of an Arabian tribe, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia places this Dedanite tribe in northern Arabia. The Bible gives no further details about him or his descendants.

Levi was an ancestor of Jesus who appears only in Luke's genealogy, which traces Jesus' line back through Joseph (Luke 3:24). He is named as the son of Melchi and the father of Matthat. As part of the line running through David, he belonged to the tribe of Judah. Nothing else is recorded about his life. The name, which Hitchcock's Bible Names takes to mean "associated with him," is shared by several people in the Bible. These include Jacob's son, who founded the tribe of Levi, and another Levi listed further back in the same genealogy. He should not be confused with either of them. Matthew's genealogy follows a different line between David and Joseph and does not mention him.

Levi is one of the ancestors of Jesus listed in Luke's genealogy, which traces the line backward from Joseph. Luke 3:29 names him as the father of Matthat, and the next verse (Luke 3:30) names his own father as Simeon. He belongs to the stretch of the genealogy between David's son Nathan and the exile, so he would have been of the tribe of Judah by descent. Nothing else is recorded about him. The name Levi belongs to several people in the Bible. He should not be confused with Levi the son of Jacob, with Matthew the tax collector (also called Levi), or with a second Levi who appears earlier in the same genealogy (Luke 3:24) as the father of a different Matthat. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "associated with him."

Libni was a Levite of the clan of Merari, named in the genealogy at 1 Chr 6:29 as the son of Mahli and the father of Shimei. The line continues through Shimei to Uzza. His brothers Eleazar and Kish are not named in this verse. A later genealogy, 1 Chr 23:21–22, names Eleazar and Kish as sons of Mahli. Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests that this Libni may be the same person as Libni the son of Gershon, named earlier in the chapter, and that something may have dropped out of the text here. That would explain why the names in this list do not match the Merarite lines elsewhere. This entry treats him as the Merarite descendant shown in the verse as it stands. Hitchcock's Bible Names takes the name to mean the same as Libnah, and Smith's gives its meaning as "white."

Likhi was a son of Shemida and a member of the tribe of Manasseh, one of the tribes descended from Joseph. He appears only once, in the genealogy of 1 Chr 7:19, which lists Shemida's sons as Ahian, Shechem, Likhi and Aniam. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes Shemida as a son of Manasseh and gives the meaning of Likhi's name as "learned." Shemida also appears among the clans of Gilead in the census lists of Numbers and Joshua, which suggests that Likhi belonged to that Manassite family line. Nothing else is recorded about him.

Linus was a Christian at Rome who sent greetings to Timothy through Paul's second letter to him. He is named with Eubulus, Pudens and Claudia among those who joined Paul in greeting Timothy, whom Paul urged to come before winter (2 Tim 4:21). The letter was written during what is usually taken as Paul's last imprisonment in Rome, so Linus was probably one of the believers still in contact with him then. The New Testament says nothing more about him. Early church tradition, beginning with Irenaeus in the second century, identifies this Linus as the first bishop of Rome after the apostles, and Smith's Bible Dictionary follows that view. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia, citing Lightfoot, notes that it is safest to say he held some prominent position in the Roman church. His name is Greek, and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives its meaning as "net."

Lo-ammi was the third child of the prophet Hosea and his wife Gomer, and their second son, after Jezreel and the daughter Lo-ruhamah. His name means "not my people." God commanded Hosea to give him this name as a sign: "for ye are not my people, and I will not be your God" (Hos 1:9). As Smith's Bible Dictionary and Easton's Bible Dictionary explain, the name stood for God's rejection of the kingdom of Israel. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia compares it with the symbolic names Isaiah gave his children. Later verses in Hosea (Hos 1:10; 2:23) take up the meaning of the name and promise that those called "not my people" will again be called God's people. Paul quotes this promise in Rom 9:25. Nothing else is known about Lo-ammi himself.

Lois was the grandmother of Timothy, Paul's younger companion, and the mother of Eunice, Timothy's mother. She is named only once in the Bible, in 2 Tim 1:5, where Paul recalls Timothy's sincere faith and says it lived first in his grandmother Lois and his mother Eunice. By inference from Acts 16:1, the family lived at Lystra, where Paul met Timothy. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests she probably became a Christian during Paul's first missionary journey (Acts 14), when Eunice and Timothy did. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both connect this verse with 2 Tim 3:15, where Timothy is said to have known the holy scriptures from childhood, and infer that Lois shared with Eunice in teaching him the Jewish Scriptures.

Lucifer is the name the King James Version uses in Isa 14:12, where the prophet addresses a figure as "Lucifer, son of the morning" who has fallen from heaven and been cut down to the ground after weakening the nations. The name comes from Latin and means "light-bearer" or "bringing light." Both the name and the epithet "son of the morning" point to a bright star, probably the morning star, the planet Venus. The surrounding passage is a taunt song against the king of Babylon (Isa 14:4), and Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary both take the title as describing that king's splendor and his downfall. Smith's Bible Dictionary also notes a long Christian tradition, going back at least to Jerome, that applies the verse to Satan's fall from heaven. This entry follows the reading of the passage as addressed to the king of Babylon and also notes the later tradition.

Lysanias was the tetrarch, or regional ruler, of Abilene, named by Luke among the rulers in power when John the Baptist began preaching. Luke dates that moment to the fifteenth year of the Roman emperor Tiberius, when Pontius Pilate governed Judea, Herod Antipas ruled Galilee and his brother Philip ruled Ituraea and Trachonitis. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia places this at about AD 26–28. Easton's Bible Dictionary locates Abilene, the district around the town of Abila, on the eastern slope of the Anti-Lebanon range near Damascus. The historian Josephus mentions an earlier Lysanias who ruled Chalcis and Abilene and was put to death about 36 BC. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that inscriptions point to a later ruler of the same name, probably a descendant, and this entry follows that view. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the name's meaning as "that drives away sorrow." Nothing else is recorded about him in the Bible.

Maachah (Daughter of Nahor) is the last-named child of Nahor, Abraham's brother, by his concubine Reumah. She is mentioned only once, in Gen 22:24, at the close of a list of Nahor's descendants. By inference from the surrounding passage (Gen 22:20), this list was reported to Abraham after the episode on Mount Moriah. Her full brothers were Tebah, Gaham and Thahash. Her half-brothers were the eight sons of Nahor's wife Milcah, among them Bethuel, whom the preceding verse names as the father of Rebekah. The verse itself does not state Maachah's sex, and the name is borne elsewhere in the Bible by both men and women. This entry follows Smith's Bible Dictionary in treating her as Nahor's daughter. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "pressed down" or "worn." Nothing further is recorded about her.

Maachah was a concubine of Caleb, a member of the tribe of Judah, listed in the genealogies of Judah in 1 Chronicles. According to 1 Chr 2:48, she bore Caleb two sons, Sheber and Tirhanah. The next verse, 1 Chr 2:49, adds that she also bore Shaaph, the father of Madmannah, and Sheva, the father of Machbenah and Gibea. Smith's Bible Dictionary identifies this Caleb as the son of Hezron, which matches the surrounding genealogy. Nothing else is recorded about her. Several other people in the Bible share the name Maachah, and she should not be confused with them. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "pressed down" or "worn."
