Maachah was the father of Hanan, who appears in the list of David's mighty warriors in 1 Chr 11:43. Nothing more is recorded about him, and the verse gives no clan or hometown, unlike many other names in the list. The name Maachah (also spelled Maacah) is shared by several people in the Bible, both men and women, as well as by a small Aramean kingdom near the upper Jordan. Some take "son of Maachah" to point to a family or regional link with that kingdom, but the text does not say so, and this entry treats Maachah as Hanan's father. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes Hanan as one of David's bodyguard. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "pressed down; worn; fastened."

Maachah was a man of the tribe of Simeon, known only as the father of Shephatiah. His son was the ruler of the Simeonites in the list of tribal leaders of Israel in 1 Chr 27:16. That list belongs to the account of David's administration, so Shephatiah served in David's reign, as Smith's Bible Dictionary also notes. Nothing else is recorded about Maachah himself. Several other people in the Bible bear the name Maachah, both men and women, and this one should not be confused with them. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the name's meaning as "pressed down" or "worn."

Maadai was one of the descendants of Bani listed in Ezra 10:34 among the men of Israel who had married foreign wives after the return from exile in Babylon. By inference from the surrounding chapter, he was among those who agreed under Ezra's leadership to send away their foreign wives. "Sons of Bani" here probably means members of the family or clan of Bani rather than his literal sons. Nothing else is recorded about him. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "ornament of Jehovah," while Hitchcock's Bible Names renders it "pleasant" or "testifying."

Maai was a Levite musician who took part in the dedication of the rebuilt wall of Jerusalem in Nehemiah's time. He is named only in Neh 12:36, among the "brethren" of Zechariah son of Jonathan, a descendant of Asaph who played the trumpet in the preceding verse (Neh 12:35). This entry treats these men as Jonathan's sons and so as Zechariah's brothers, though the word may simply mean kinsmen or fellow Levites of the Asaph line. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both describe him as an Asaphite. With the others in his group he played "the musical instruments of David the man of God" in the procession led by Ezra the scribe. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "compassionate," while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "belly; heaping up." Nothing else is known of him.

Maaseiah, son of Adaiah, was one of the "captains of hundreds" whom the priest Jehoiada brought into a covenant with him in the seventh year, according to 2 Chr 23:1. From the surrounding chapter and the parallel account in 2 Kings 11, this was the pact that ended Queen Athaliah's rule and placed the young Joash (Jehoash) on the throne of Judah. Maaseiah is named alongside four other commanders and is not mentioned elsewhere. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia calls him a Levite captain, and the Tyndale House proper-names index describes him as a priest. The name means "work of the Lord" (Hitchcock's Bible Names) and is borne by several other men in the Old Testament, so he should not be confused with the others called Maaseiah.

Maaseiah was an officer in the reign of King Uzziah of Judah. He is called "the ruler", meaning an official, in 2 Chr 26:11. Together with Jeiel the scribe, he kept the count of Uzziah's army, which went out to war in organized bands. Both men worked under Hananiah, one of the king's captains. Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests he was probably a Levite serving in a semi-military role, comparing the Levite officers of 1 Chr 23:4. His name means "work of the Lord". Several other men in the Bible share this name, and nothing links this officer to any of them. He is mentioned only in this one verse.

Maaseiah was a son of King Ahaz of Judah, called "the king's son" in his only appearance (2 Chr 28:7). This made him a brother of Hezekiah, who succeeded Ahaz as king (2 Kgs 18:1). He was killed by Zichri, "a mighty man of Ephraim," along with Azrikam, the governor of the palace, and Elkanah, who was second to the king. The surrounding passage places this during the war in which Pekah, king of Israel, invaded Judah and inflicted heavy losses. The phrase "king's son" is sometimes read as a title for a royal official rather than a literal son. This entry follows the reading that he was Ahaz's son, as Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia do. The name, meaning "work of the Lord" (Hitchcock's Bible Names), is shared by several other people in the Bible.

Maaseiah was the governor of Jerusalem under King Josiah of Judah. In the eighteenth year of Josiah's reign, after the king had purged the land and the temple of idolatry, he sent Maaseiah with Shaphan son of Azaliah and Joah son of Joahaz, the recorder, to repair the house of the Lord (2 Chr 34:8). Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that the Hebrew word behind "governor" (sar) is rendered elsewhere in the King James Version as "prince," "chief captain" or "chief ruler," so it denotes a high official of the city. The name means "work of the Lord" and was common in the late monarchy and the exile, so several men in the Bible bear it. This Maaseiah appears only in this verse. The parallel account in 2 Kings 22 names Shaphan but not Maaseiah.

Maaseiah was a priest in Ezra's time, about the mid-5th century BC by inference from context. He was one of the descendants of Jeshua son of Jozadak, the high priest who led worship among the exiles who returned from Babylon. Ezra 10:18 lists him first among the priests of Jeshua's family who had married foreign wives. The following verse says these men pledged to send their wives away and offered a ram as a guilt offering. Nothing else is recorded about him. Several other men in the Bible share the name, which Hitchcock's Bible Names interprets as "the work of the Lord." Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that four men called Maaseiah appear in Ezra's list of those with foreign wives, so this one should be kept distinct from the others.

Maaseiah was a priest, one of the descendants of Harim, who is listed among the men who had married foreign wives in the time of Ezra (Ezra 10:21). He appears in a list of five sons of Harim. The surrounding chapter records that these men agreed to send away their foreign wives. The context places him in the mid-5th century BC, after the return from exile in Babylon. Smith's Bible Dictionary counts him among four men of this name who had married foreign wives in Ezra's day. The name, which Hitchcock's Bible Names gives as meaning "the work of the Lord," was common, and several other people in the Bible bear it. Nothing more is known about him.

Maaseiah was a priest of the family of Pashur. He is listed among the men who had married foreign wives in the time of Ezra (Ezra 10:22). The surrounding passage in Ezra 10 describes how these men agreed to send away their foreign wives after the return from exile in Babylon. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the Tyndale House STEPBible names list both identify him as a priest, and that fits the context, because the sons of Pashur appear in Ezra's list of priestly families. Nothing else is recorded about him. The name, which Hitchcock's Bible Names explains as meaning "the work of the Lord," was borne by several men in the Bible. Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that four men named Maaseiah appear in Ezra's list of those who had married foreign wives, so this one should not be confused with the others.

Maaseiah was one of the descendants of Pahath-moab listed in Ezra 10:30 among the Israelite men who had married foreign women in Ezra's time. The context of Ezra 10 shows that these men agreed to put away their foreign wives after the return from exile. He was a layman, not a priest or Levite, as Smith's Bible Dictionary notes, and he appears in a group of eight sons of Pahath-moab. Nothing else is recorded about him. The name, which Hitchcock's Bible Names gives as meaning "the work of the Lord," was borne by several people in the Bible. Smith's Bible Dictionary lists four men named Maaseiah among those who had married foreign wives in this one chapter, so he should not be confused with the others of the same name.

Maaseiah, son of Ananiah, was the father of Azariah. He is known only from the genealogy given for his son in the list of those who rebuilt the walls of Jerusalem under Nehemiah. According to Neh 3:23, Azariah repaired a section of the wall beside his own house, next to the section worked on by Benjamin and Hashub. Since Azariah was active then, Maaseiah probably lived during or shortly before the return from exile in the 5th century BC. Nothing else is recorded about him. The name, meaning "the work of the Lord" (Hitchcock's Bible Names), was common in this period, and several other men called Maaseiah appear in Ezra, Nehemiah and elsewhere. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats this Maaseiah as a separate individual, and this entry does the same.

Maaseiah was one of the men who stood at Ezra's right hand on the wooden platform when Ezra the scribe read the law to the people in Jerusalem after the return from exile. He is named alongside Mattithiah, Shema, Anaiah, Urijah and Hilkiah, while another group stood on Ezra's left (Neh 8:4). The verse gives no further detail about his family or role. The STEPBible Proper Names index (Tyndale House) describes him as a Levite who assisted Ezra in reading the law. The name means "work of the Lord" and was common in this period, so several different men called Maaseiah appear in Ezra, Nehemiah and elsewhere. It is uncertain whether this man is the same as any of them.

Maaseiah was one of the men who helped the people understand the law when Ezra read it publicly in Jerusalem after the return from exile, in the time of Nehemiah (Neh 8:7). He is named in a list with Jeshua, Bani, Sherebiah and others alongside the Levites, while the people stood in their places. The wording leaves open whether these named men were themselves Levites, but Smith's Bible Dictionary and the STEPBible proper names index both describe him as a Levite, and this entry follows that view. His name means "work of the Lord" (Hitchcock's Bible Names). Several other men in the Bible are called Maaseiah, including some from Ezra's time, so it is uncertain whether this Maaseiah appears anywhere else. Nothing more is recorded about him.

Maaseiah is one of several men of this name in the Bible. This one appears only in Neh 10:25, in the list of the leaders of the people who set their seal to the written covenant made in Nehemiah's time. In that covenant the returned community of Jerusalem pledged to keep the law of Moses. He is named between Rehum and Hashabnah, and nothing else is recorded about him. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him as one of the heads of the people whose descendants signed the covenant, while the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats him as one of those who took part in sealing it. The name means "work of the Lord." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that it was common in late monarchic and exilic times, so linking him with any other Maaseiah is uncertain.

Maaseiah, son of Baruch, was a man of the tribe of Judah who lived in Jerusalem after the return from exile. He appears in Nehemiah's list of the people who settled in the city, where his ancestry is traced back through Colhozeh, Hazaiah, Adaiah, Joiarib and Zechariah to Shiloni (Neh 11:5). By inference from the surrounding passage, he is named as one of the heads of the Judahite families living in Jerusalem. "Shiloni" is often taken to mean a descendant of Shelah, son of Judah, though Smith's Bible Dictionary links him to the line of Perez. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identifies him with Asaiah, listed among the Shilonites in the parallel list at 1 Chr 9:5. The name means "work of the Lord" and was shared by several other men in the Bible.

Maaseiah was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, named only in the genealogy of Sallu in Neh 11:7. He was the son of Ithiel and the father of Kolaiah, and so an ancestor several generations back of Sallu son of Meshullam, one of the Benjamites who settled in Jerusalem after the return from exile. The verse gives no further details about his life. His name, often explained as "the work of the Lord" (Hitchcock's Bible Names), was common in the later monarchy and exile, according to the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia, and several different men in the Bible bear it. This Maaseiah should not be confused with the others of the same name, such as those listed in Ezra's time as having married foreign wives.

Maaseiah was a priest in Jerusalem in the time of Nehemiah, about the mid-5th century BC by inference from context. He appears only in Neh 12:41, in a list of seven priests who played trumpets at the dedication of the rebuilt city wall. The others were Eliakim, Miniamin, Michaiah, Elioenai, Zechariah and Hananiah. From the surrounding passage, this group probably marched with the thanksgiving company that Nehemiah himself followed around the wall to the temple. His name means "work of the Lord" (Hitchcock's Bible Names). Many men in the Bible share the name. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia counts this Maaseiah as separate from another of the same name listed in the very next verse, among the priests and singers of the same ceremony. Nothing more is recorded about him.

Maaseiah was a priest who took part in the dedication of the rebuilt wall of Jerusalem in Nehemiah's time. He is named first in a list of eight men, alongside Shemaiah, Eleazar, Uzzi, Jehohanan, Malchijah, Elam and Ezer, who stood at the ceremony while the singers sang loudly under the direction of Jezrahiah (Neh 12:42). The verse itself does not state his role, but the STEPBible Proper Names index identifies him as a priest who sang during the dedication, and the context of the processions in this chapter supports that reading. Nothing more is recorded about him. The name Maaseiah was common, especially among priests and Levites of the period, so he cannot be firmly linked to any other man of that name. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives its meaning as "the work of the Lord."

Maaseiah was the father of Zedekiah, a prophet among the Jewish exiles in Babylon whom Jeremiah condemned. In his letter to the exiles, Jeremiah names Zedekiah son of Maaseiah, together with Ahab son of Kolaiah, as men who prophesied lies in the Lord's name, and he announces that Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon would hand them over and kill them before the exiles' eyes (Jer 29:21). Nothing is recorded about Maaseiah himself beyond his being Zedekiah's father. The name, meaning "work of the Lord" according to Hitchcock's Bible Names, was common in the late monarchy and the exile, as the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes. Several other men in the Bible share it, and there is no clear way to link this Maaseiah with any of them.

Maaseiah, son of Shallum, was an official at the temple in Jerusalem during the reign of Jehoiakim, king of Judah. Jeremiah mentions him while describing where he brought the Rechabites. They were taken into the chamber of the sons of Hanan, which was next to the princes' chamber and above the chamber of Maaseiah (Jer 35:4). He is called "the keeper of the door," one of the officers who guarded the temple threshold. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia takes the title as his. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him as a Levite of high rank and compares 1 Chr 9:19, where a Shallum and his family are keepers of the gates. That connection is suggestive but not certain. His name means "work of the Lord." Several other men in the Bible share the name, and nothing else is recorded about this one.

Maath is a man named only once, in Luke's genealogy of Jesus (Luke 3:26). He is listed as the son of Mattathias and the father of Nagge. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia counts him as the twelfth generation before Joseph, the husband of Mary. Since the same list names Zerubbabel a few generations earlier and traces the line back through David, Maath probably lived after the Babylonian exile and belonged to the tribe of Judah. Nothing else is recorded about him. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "small," and Hitchcock's Bible Names offers "wiping away" or "breaking."

Maaz was a man of the tribe of Judah, named only in the genealogy of 1 Chr 2:27. He was the first-listed son of Ram, who was the firstborn of Jerahmeel, and his brothers were Jamin and Eker. Jerahmeel was a son of Hezron and a grandson of Perez, son of Judah, so Maaz belonged to the Jerahmeelite branch of Judah's descendants. This Ram, Jerahmeel's son, is different from Ram the brother of Jerahmeel, who was an ancestor of David. Nothing else is recorded about Maaz. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of his name as "wood" or "wooden."

Maaziah was a priest in the time of King David, the head of the twenty-fourth and last of the priestly divisions. According to the surrounding chapter, David organized the descendants of Aaron's sons Eleazar and Ithamar into twenty-four groups, or courses, by casting lots. Each course took its turn serving at the sanctuary, and the final lot fell to Maaziah (1 Chr 24:18). Apart from this assignment, nothing more is recorded about him. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "consolation of Jehovah." A priest with the same name appears in Nehemiah's time as one of those who sealed the covenant (Neh 10:8). He lived centuries later and is generally treated as a different man, though the shared name may reflect the continuing priestly line.

Machbanai was a warrior from the tribe of Gad who joined David while David was a fugitive from Saul. He is named only in 1 Chr 12:13, as the eleventh of eleven Gadite leaders. The surrounding passage (1 Chr 12:8–14) describes these Gadites as skilled fighters with faces like lions and as swift as gazelles, and calls them captains of the army. That context suggests Machbanai held a command, though the verse does not say how large. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the STEPBible proper names index both connect his coming to David with the period David spent at Ziklag, the setting introduced at the start of the chapter. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "bond of the Lord." Nothing else is recorded about him.

Machi was a man of the tribe of Gad, known only as the father of Geuel. Geuel was the Gadite chosen as one of the twelve men Moses sent to explore the land of Canaan, a group that included Caleb and Joshua (Num 13:15). Nothing else is recorded about Machi himself. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the Syriac Peshitta and some manuscripts of the Greek Septuagint read his name as "Machir." Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "decrease," while Hitchcock's Bible Names offers "poor" or "a smiter."

Machnadebai was one of the Israelite men listed in Ezra 10:40 among those who had married foreign wives after the return from exile in Babylon. The list in Ezra 10 records men who agreed, at Ezra's urging, to send away their foreign wives. By inference from the surrounding verses, he belonged to the group descended from Bani (Ezra 10:34), as Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both understand him. Nothing more is known about him beyond his name in this list. The meaning of the name is uncertain. Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests "what is like the liberal?", and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "smiter."

Magpiash was one of the leaders of the people who set their seal to the written covenant made in the time of Nehemiah, when the community that had returned to Jerusalem pledged to keep the law of Moses. He appears only in the list of signers, between Ahiah and Meshullam's neighbours in the list (Neh 10:20), and nothing else is recorded about him. Because the leaders in this part of the list often represent family or clan names, Smith's Bible Dictionary identifies him with Magbish, a family whose descendants returned from exile with Zerubbabel (Ezra 2:30). The name may then stand for that family rather than a single individual. Smith's gives the meaning of the name as "moth-killer," while Hitchcock's Bible Names renders it "a body thrust hard together."

Mahalah was a descendant of Manasseh, named once in the genealogies of 1 Chronicles as one of three children of Hammoleketh, along with Ishod and Abiezer (1 Chr 7:18). The verse calls Hammoleketh "his sister." From the surrounding verses, Smith's Bible Dictionary takes this to mean the sister of Gilead, so Mahalah belonged to the Manassite clan of Gilead. The text does not say whether Mahalah was male or female. This entry treats Mahalah as female. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the Revised Version spells the name Mahlah. That is the same name as one of Zelophehad's daughters, who seems to be a different person. Smith's gives the meaning of the name as "disease." Nothing else is recorded about Mahalah.

Mahalaleel was a man of the tribe of Judah, descended from Perez, who appears only in the genealogy of Athaiah in Neh 11:4. He was the father of Shephatiah, and through him an ancestor of Athaiah, one of the people of Judah who lived in Jerusalem in Nehemiah's time after the return from exile. Nothing else is recorded about him, and when he lived is not stated. His name, which Smith's Bible Dictionary renders as "praise of God," is also borne by other people in the Bible, most notably the son of Cainan in the early genealogy of Genesis. This Mahalaleel is a separate, much later individual.

Mahalath was one of the wives of Rehoboam, king of Judah and son of Solomon. She was the daughter of Jerimoth, a son of David, which made her a granddaughter of David and a cousin of her husband. Jerimoth does not appear in the main lists of David's sons, so he may have been the son of a concubine, as 1 Chr 3:9 mentions such sons without naming them. Her birthplace in Jerusalem is inferred from her family's place in the royal household. The verse naming her also names Abihail, a descendant of David's brother Eliab. The next verse (2 Chr 11:19) credits sons to "her," but it is unclear whether this means Mahalath or Abihail. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia counts her among Rehoboam's eighteen wives. She is a different person from Mahalath the daughter of Ishmael, whom Esau married (Gen 28:9).

Mahath son of Amasai was a Kohathite Levite in the reign of King Hezekiah of Judah. He is named first among the Levites who rose to answer Hezekiah's call to sanctify themselves and cleanse the temple in Jerusalem (2 Chr 29:12). Alongside Joel son of Azariah he represented the Kohathite branch of the tribe of Levi, while others came from the Merarite and Gershonite families. The surrounding chapter describes this cleansing, and in it the Levites removed the defilement that had built up in the temple. The name Mahath is borne by more than one person in the Bible. Whether this Mahath is the same as the Mahath later listed among Hezekiah's temple overseers (2 Chr 31:13) is uncertain, though the shared name and period make it possible. The genealogy of Heman in 1 Chr 6:35 also names a Mahath son of Amasai, an earlier ancestor of the same family line.

Mahath was a Levite in the reign of King Hezekiah of Judah. He was one of ten overseers who worked under Cononiah and his brother Shimei, by order of Hezekiah and Azariah, the ruler of the house of God. By inference from the surrounding passage, their task was to manage the offerings, tithes and dedicated gifts that the people brought and that were stored in the temple chambers. STEPBible Proper Names describes him as a Levite who helped distribute the tithes. Several men in the Bible bear this name. A Mahath son of Amasai, a Kohathite Levite, appears in 2 Chr 29:12 among those who cleansed the temple early in Hezekiah's reign. He may be the same man, though the text does not say so. Hitchcock's Bible Names treats the name as the same as Maath.

Mahol is named in 1 Kgs 4:31 as the father of Ethan, Heman, Chalcol and Darda, four men so famous for wisdom that the writer measures Solomon's wisdom against theirs and says Solomon surpassed them. Nothing else is told about Mahol himself. His name means "dance" (Easton's Bible Dictionary; International Standard Bible Encyclopedia). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia compares the phrase "sons of Mahol" with "sons of dance," which has led some to read it as a title for a guild of musicians or singers rather than a family. There is also a puzzle of descent. 1 Chr 2:6 lists men with nearly the same names (Ethan, Heman, Calcol and Dara) as sons of Zerah of Judah, and Ethan is called "the Ezrahite," probably meaning a descendant of Zerah. This entry follows the plain reading of 1 Kings and treats Mahol as their father.

Malachi was the prophet through whom "the burden of the word of the LORD to Israel" came, as the opening verse of the book bearing his name states (Mal 1:1). His book is the last of the minor prophets and closes the Old Testament in the traditional English order. Nothing is known of his life beyond his book. His name means "my messenger," and some have taken it as a title rather than a personal name, though Easton's Bible Dictionary treats it as his ordinary name. By inference from the issues he addresses, such as corrupt priests and marriages to foreign wives, Easton's places him in the time of Nehemiah, after Haggai and Zechariah, when the rebuilt temple was in use. This entry dates his prophecies to about 442 BC, an estimate from context. Easton's suggests about 420 BC.

Malchiah was a Levite of the Gershonite line, named in the family tree of Asaph, one of the singers David put in charge of music at the sanctuary. In 1 Chr 6:40 he appears as the father of Baaseiah and an ancestor of Asaph through Michael. The next verse names his father as Ethni, son of Zerah. This entry gives his father as Jeaterai, who appears as a son of Zerah in the parallel Gershonite list (1 Chr 6:21). The two names are probably different forms for the same man. Nothing more is recorded about Malchiah beyond his place in this genealogy. The name, also spelled Malchijah, means "the Lord is my king" according to Hitchcock's Bible Names. Several other men in the Bible share it and should not be confused with this Levite.

Malchiah was a man of Israel, one of the descendants of Parosh, listed in Ezra 10:25 among those who had married foreign wives in the time of Ezra. The surrounding chapter describes how, after returning from exile, these men agreed to send away their foreign wives. Nothing else is recorded about him. The same list of Parosh's sons also includes a Malchijah, a closely related form of the name, so the two appear to be different men of the same family line. Several other people in the Bible bear this name or its variants, and this Malchiah should not be confused with them. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "the Lord my king" or "my counselor."

Malchiah was one of the "sons of Harim", meaning a member of the family or clan descended from Harim, listed in Ezra 10:31. He appears in the list of Israelites who had married foreign wives and who, during Ezra's reforms after the return from exile, agreed to send those wives away. The passage records nothing else about him. The name, also spelled Malchijah, is usually explained as "the Lord is my king" (Hitchcock's Bible Names). Several other men in the Bible share this name, including other members of the same list in Ezra 10, so this Malchiah should not be confused with them.

Malchiah, son of Rechab, was ruler of part of the district of Beth-haccerem in Judah in the time of Nehemiah. During the rebuilding of Jerusalem's walls after the return from exile, he repaired the Dung Gate. He rebuilt it and installed its doors, locks and bars (Neh 3:14). This Rechab is probably not the ancestor of the Rechabites, though the text does not say either way. Several other men in the Bible share the name Malchiah (also spelled Malchijah), which Hitchcock's Bible Names explains as meaning "the Lord my king." This one is known only from this single verse.

Malchiah was one of the men who repaired the wall of Jerusalem under Nehemiah's leadership after the return from exile. Neh 3:31 calls him "the goldsmith's son." The phrase can also be read as marking him as a member of the goldsmiths' guild, and the STEPBible proper-names index describes him as a goldsmith himself. His section ran up to the quarters of the Nethinim (temple servants) and the merchants, opposite the Miphkad Gate, and as far as the upper room at the corner. This was probably on the eastern side of the city near the temple area, judging from the other landmarks in the chapter. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "the Lord my king." Several other men in the Bible share the name, and nothing further is known about this one.

Malchiah was one of the men who stood beside Ezra the scribe on a wooden platform when Ezra read the book of the Law aloud to the people of Jerusalem. He stood on Ezra's left, with Pedaiah, Mishael, Hashum, Hashbadana, Zechariah and Meshullam (Neh 8:4). The verse does not say what his role was. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the STEPBible proper names index describe him as a priest. His name, also spelled Malchijah, is explained in Hitchcock's Bible Names as "the Lord my king." Several other men in the Bible share this name, including others in the books of Ezra and Nehemiah. It is uncertain whether this Malchiah is the same as any of them, so this entry treats him only as the man named in Neh 8:4.

Malchiah, son of Hammelech, was the owner of the dungeon or cistern in the court of the prison in Jerusalem into which Jeremiah was lowered with ropes. It held no water, only mud, and Jeremiah sank into it (Jer 38:6). The name Hammelech means "the king", and many translations render the phrase "Malchiah the king's son", so he was probably a member of the royal family in the last years of Judah. This entry treats Jerahmeel, also called the son of Hammelech, as his brother. Jer 36:26 says Jerahmeel was sent by King Jehoiakim to arrest Baruch and Jeremiah. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the name's meaning as "the Lord my king". Several other men in the Bible share the name, and how they relate to this Malchiah is uncertain.

Malchijah was a priest whose family received the fifth of the twenty-four priestly divisions when lots were cast to organize temple service in David's reign (1 Chr 24:9). The surrounding passage describes David, with Zadok and Ahimelech, assigning the descendants of Aaron to courses that took turns serving. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes him as the head of the fifth division. His name means "Yah is king," according to the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia. Nothing else is recorded about him. Several other men in the Bible share the name, including priests and laymen of later periods, and this entry refers only to the head of the fifth priestly course.

Malchijah was a descendant of Parosh, one of the Israelite laymen listed in Ezra 10:25. The list in Ezra 10 names men who had married foreign wives after the return from exile. By inference from the surrounding chapter, he was among those who agreed to send their wives away during Ezra's reforms. The name means "Yah is king." The same verse names two men of this name among the sons of Parosh. The King James Version spells the first "Malchiah" and the second "Malchijah," and this entry refers to the second. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the parallel list in 1 Esdras 9:26 renders the two names as "Melchias" and "Asibias." Nothing more is recorded about him, and several other people in the Bible share the name.

Malchijah, son of Harim, was one of the men who rebuilt Jerusalem's wall under Nehemiah after the return from exile. Neh 3:11 says that he and Hashub son of Pahath-moab repaired "the other piece", a second section of the wall, along with the Tower of the Furnaces. His name means "Yah is king," according to the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia. Several people in the Bible share this name, and nothing more is told about this one. He may be the Malchiah listed among the sons of Harim in Ezra 10:31, who had married foreign wives, but this is not certain. Harim was also the name of a priestly family and of a lay family among the returned exiles, so it is unclear which Harim was his father or ancestor.

Malchijah was one of the men who set their seal to the covenant made in Nehemiah's time, when the community that had returned from exile pledged to keep the law of God (Neh 10:3). He appears in a list alongside Pashur and Amariah. By inference from the context, this part of the list names priests, and STEPBible Proper Names (Tyndale House) identifies him as a priest. The name means "Yah is king," according to the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia. Several men in the Bible bear this name, including others in the books of Ezra and Nehemiah, so it is uncertain whether this signatory is the same person as any of them. Nothing more is recorded about him.

Malchijah was one of the people who took part in the dedication of the rebuilt wall of Jerusalem in Nehemiah's time. He is named in a list of eight men, alongside Maaseiah, Shemaiah, Eleazar and others, who stood in the procession at the temple while the singers sang loudly under their overseer Jezrahiah (Neh 12:42). Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia describe him as a priest who served among the musicians at this celebration. The verse itself gives only his name, so his precise role is inferred from the context of the dedication ceremony. His name means "Yahweh is king," and it is shared by several other men in the Bible, including other priests and Levites of the same period. Whether he is the same as any of them is uncertain, and this entry treats him as a separate person.

Malchiram was a son of Jehoiachin (also called Jeconiah), the king of Judah who was taken captive to Babylon. He appears only in the genealogy of David's royal line in 1 Chr 3:18, listed after Shealtiel among Jehoiachin's sons, with Pedaiah, Shenazar, Jecamiah, Hoshama and Nedabiah. This makes him a member of the tribe of Judah and a descendant of David. Since Jehoiachin was taken into exile as a young man, these sons were probably born in Babylon, though the passage does not say so. Nothing else is recorded about his life. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives the meaning of his name as "uplifted king."

Malchus was the servant of the high priest whose right ear Simon Peter cut off with a sword when Jesus was arrested (John 18:10). Only John's Gospel gives his name. The setting is the garden across the Kidron valley, identified with Gethsemane in the parallel accounts of Matthew and Mark. The high priest that night was Caiaphas, so Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia call Malchus his servant. Matthew, Mark and Luke also tell of the injury but leave the servant unnamed, and Luke alone adds that Jesus touched his ear and healed him (Luke 22:51). Later in the same chapter, a relative of Malchus, also a servant of the high priest, asks Peter whether he had seen him in the garden with Jesus (John 18:26). The name is usually linked to the Semitic word for "king."

Malluch was a Levite of the clan of Merari, named in the genealogy of Ethan, one of the singers David appointed to lead music at the house of the Lord. The list traces Ethan's line back through Kishi and Abdi to Malluch, so Malluch was Abdi's father and Ethan's great-grandfather. The same verse names Malluch's father as Hashabiah (1 Chr 6:44–45). The Merarite singers stood on the left hand of Heman, the chief singer. Malluch himself is mentioned only in this genealogy, and nothing more is recorded about him. The name, which Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia take to mean "counsellor," is shared by several other men in the Old Testament, including priests and laymen of Ezra's and Nehemiah's time, who are different people.

Malluch was one of the "sons of Bani" named in Ezra 10:29, in the list of Israelite men who had married foreign wives in the time of Ezra. By inference from the surrounding chapter, he was among those who agreed to send away these wives during Ezra's reforms after the return from exile in Babylon. Nothing else is recorded about him. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia links this Bani to the line of Judah (citing 1 Chr 9:4) and identifies Malluch with the Mamuchus of 1 Esdras 9:30. Several other men in the Bible share the name, including a man of the sons of Harim in the same list. The name is usually explained as meaning "counsellor" or "reigning."

Malluch was one of the sons of Harim listed in Ezra 10:32 among the Israelites who had married foreign wives after the return from exile in Babylon. The list belongs to Ezra's reforms, when those who had taken such wives agreed to send them away. By inference from the surrounding verses (Ezra 10:31), he was counted with the descendants of Harim, as Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both note. Nothing else is recorded about him. The name, which Smith's Bible Dictionary takes to mean "counsellor," is shared by several other men in the Old Testament, including a priest and a Levite, so this Malluch should not be confused with them.

Malluch was one of the leaders of the people who set their seal to the covenant made in Nehemiah's time. In that covenant the returned community of Jerusalem pledged to keep God's law. His name appears in the list of signers in Neh 10:27, next to Harim and Baanah, among the heads of the people rather than the priests or Levites. Nothing else is recorded about him. Several other men in the Bible share the name, including a priest and a Levite, and a Malluch who signed earlier in the same list among the priests. This entry treats the signer in Neh 10:27 as a separate person, but it is uncertain whether he can be linked to any of the others. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "counsellor." Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "reigning" or "counseling."

The man of understanding was a Levite descended from Mahli, son of Merari and grandson of Levi. He was brought to Ezra when Ezra was preparing to lead a group of exiles from Babylon to Jerusalem. By inference from the surrounding chapter, Ezra had found no Levites among the travelers camped by the river Ahava and sent messengers to recruit some, and this man was among those who came. Ezra credits his arrival to the good hand of God (Ezra 8:18). The text gives no personal name. Readers take the phrase in different ways: as describing an unnamed skilled or wise Levite, as a description of Sherebiah, who is named immediately afterward, or as a proper name. This entry treats him as a separate, unnamed person.

Manaen was one of the prophets and teachers in the church at Antioch, named alongside Barnabas, Simeon called Niger, Lucius of Cyrene and Saul (Acts 13:1). The verse describes him as having been "brought up with Herod the tetrarch," meaning Herod Antipas, ruler of Galilee. The Greek word behind the phrase is often rendered "foster brother," so he was probably raised and educated alongside Antipas, perhaps as a childhood companion at court. He was present at Antioch when Barnabas and Saul were set apart for the work that began the first missionary journey, about AD 45 by inference from context. His name is the Greek form of the Hebrew Menahem, meaning "consoler." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests he may have been related to an earlier Manaen, an Essene whom Josephus says befriended Herod the Great. Nothing more is known of him.

Manasseh is named in Judg 18:30 as the father of Gershom and grandfather of Jonathan. Jonathan and his sons served as priests to the tribe of Dan at its carved image until the land went into captivity. Nothing else is said about him. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that in the Hebrew text a small letter n is written above the name, turning Moses (Mosheh) into Manasseh (Menashsheh). It holds that the name was originally Moses, changed so that Moses' name would not be tied to an idolatrous priesthood. This matches the fact that Moses had a son named Gershom (Exod 2:22), and many modern translations read "Moses" here. This entry follows the King James reading, Manasseh, while noting that identification. He is distinct from Joseph's son Manasseh and from King Manasseh of Judah. The name is usually taken to mean "causing to forget."

Manasseh was a man of the family of Pahath-moab, listed in Ezra 10:30 among the Israelites who had married foreign wives after the return from exile in Babylon. Context shows that those named in this list agreed, during Ezra's reforms, to send away their foreign wives (the STEPBible Proper Names index describes him as having divorced his). Nothing more is recorded about him. The name, meaning "causing to forget" according to the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia, was borne by several people in the Bible, including Joseph's elder son and a king of Judah. This Manasseh is a different and otherwise unknown individual. In the parallel list in 1 Esdras 9:31 he appears as Manaseas.

Manasseh was a man of the family or clan of Hashum, one of several people in the Bible with this name. He is named once, in the list in Ezra 10 of men who had married foreign wives after the return from exile in Babylon (Ezra 10:33). In context, these men agreed during Ezra's reforms to send away their wives, and STEPBible Proper Names describes him as having divorced his foreign wife. The passage records nothing else about him. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "forgetfulness" or "he that is forgotten." He should not be confused with Joseph's son Manasseh or King Manasseh of Judah.

Maon was a man of the tribe of Judah, named in the genealogy of Caleb's descendants in 1 Chr 2:45. He was the son of Shammai and the father of Bethzur. STEPBible's Tyndale House name list places him among the descendants of Caleb, which fits the surrounding list in 1 Chronicles 2. Maon and Bethzur are also the names of towns in the hill country of Judah. Because of this, the names in this passage may represent the founders or forebears of the clans that settled those towns, though the verse itself presents them simply as father and son. Nothing else is recorded about him. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "house" or "place of sin."

Marsena was one of the seven princes of Persia and Media under King Ahasuerus. Esth 1:14 names him among the nobles who "saw the king's face" and "sat the first in the kingdom," meaning they had direct access to the king and held the highest rank at court. From the surrounding passage, these seven were among the wise men "which knew the times" whom Ahasuerus consulted when Queen Vashti refused to appear at his feast. Only Memucan is recorded as speaking. Marsena is mentioned nowhere else, and nothing more is known of him. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia says the origin of his name is unknown but probably Persian. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives its meaning as "worthy," and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "bitterness of a bramble."

Mary (Mother of John Mark) was a woman of Jerusalem whose house served as a gathering place for the early believers. After an angel freed Peter from prison, about AD 40 by inference from context, he went straight to her house, where many were gathered praying (Acts 12:12). Smith's Bible Dictionary takes this as a sign of a close connection between them. Her son was John, also called Mark, who according to later chapters of Acts travelled with Paul and Barnabas. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary identify her as Barnabas's sister, drawing on Col 4:10, where the King James Version calls Mark Barnabas's "sister's son". Many modern translations read "cousin" there. Smith's also records a tradition that her house stood on the upper slope of Mount Zion and was where the disciples met at Pentecost. Her name is a form of Miriam.

Mary (of Rome) was a Christian woman whom Paul greets in his letter to the church at Rome, saying that she "bestowed much labour on us" (Rom 16:6). Nothing else is known about her, and she should not be confused with the several other women named Mary in the New Testament. Readings of the verse differ on whom her work served. The King James wording points to Paul and his companions, and Easton's Bible Dictionary describes her as someone who treated Paul with special kindness. Some ancient manuscripts read "on you" instead, and the STEPBible names index (Tyndale House) describes her as a woman who worked hard for the church in Rome. Either way, Paul singles her out for her hard work among the believers he greets by name. Hitchcock's Bible Names treats her name as the same as Miriam.

Matri was a Benjamite whose name was carried by a family, or clan, within the tribe of Benjamin, and King Saul belonged to that family. The only mention comes in the account of Saul being chosen king at Mizpah. Samuel had the tribes of Israel come forward, and the choice fell first on Benjamin. Then Benjamin's families came forward and the family of Matri was taken. Finally Saul the son of Kish was taken, but when the people looked for him he could not be found (1 Sam 10:21). Nothing else is recorded about Matri himself. He is probably the ancestor the clan was named after, by inference from the phrase "the family of Matri." Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both treat the name mainly as the name of the clan. Smith's gives its meaning as "rain of Jehovah," and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives "rainy."

Mattan was the father of Shephatiah, one of the Judean officials in Jerusalem who heard Jeremiah's message to the people during the last years of the kingdom of Judah (Jer 38:1). Nothing more is recorded about Mattan himself. His son Shephatiah was among those who then asked the king to put Jeremiah to death and lowered him into a cistern (Jer 38:4–6), as the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes. The name means "gift," according to Smith's Bible Dictionary. Several people in the Bible bear the name Mattan, including a priest of Baal killed in Jerusalem in the time of Queen Athaliah (2 Kgs 11:18). Nothing in the text links this Mattan to any of the others, so he is best treated as a separate person.

Mattaniah was a Levite descended from Asaph. He is named only once, in the family line of Jahaziel, who was moved by the Spirit of the LORD to speak before the assembly of Judah during the reign of King Jehoshaphat (2 Chr 20:14). That verse traces Jahaziel's ancestry back through Zechariah, Benaiah and Jeiel to Mattaniah, which makes Mattaniah the father of Jeiel and an earlier ancestor of Jahaziel. Nothing else is recorded about his life. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him simply as a descendant of Asaph and an ancestor of Jahaziel. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "gift, or hope, of the Lord." Several other men in the Bible are also called Mattaniah, and this one should not be confused with them.

Mattaniah was a Levite descended from Asaph, one of the "sons of Asaph" listed among the Levites who gathered when King Hezekiah ordered the temple in Jerusalem to be cleansed and restored to use (2 Chr 29:13). He is named alongside Zechariah as the representatives of the Asaph family, the line of temple singers. The surrounding chapter shows these Levites sanctifying themselves and then removing the impurities from the house of the Lord at the start of Hezekiah's reforms. His name means "gift of the Lord" (Hitchcock's Bible Names). Several other men in the Bible share the name Mattaniah, including the king better known as Zedekiah and other Levites of the Asaph line. This entry concerns only the Levite of Hezekiah's time.

Mattaniah was one of the "sons of Elam", meaning a member of the family or clan descended from Elam, named in Ezra 10:26. He appears in the list of returned exiles who had married foreign wives during Ezra's reforms. By inference from the surrounding chapter, he was among those who agreed to send these wives away (Ezra 10:19, 44). Nothing else is recorded about him. His name means "gift of the Lord" (Smith's Bible Dictionary; Hitchcock's Bible Names). Several people in the Bible share this name, including another Mattaniah listed among the descendants of Zattu in the next verse of the same list, so it is not always clear which mention refers to which man. This entry covers the man counted among the family of Elam.

Mattaniah was a man of the family of Zattu who lived in the time of Ezra, after the return from exile in Babylon. Ezra 10:27 names him among the sons of Zattu, together with Elioenai, Eliashib, Jeremoth, Zabad and Aziza. The surrounding chapter shows that this list records men who had married foreign wives and agreed to send them away during Ezra's reforms, so Mattaniah was probably one of them. His name means "gift of the Lord." Several other men in the Bible share the name, including another Mattaniah in the same list from the family of Elam (Ezra 10:26), so he should be kept distinct from them. Nothing else is recorded about him.

Mattaniah was one of the descendants of Pahath-moab listed in Ezra 10:30 among the Israelite men who had married foreign wives after the return from exile. By inference from the surrounding chapter, he was among those who agreed under Ezra's reforms to send away these wives. The STEPBible Proper Names index describes him in these terms. Nothing more is recorded about him. His name, which Hitchcock's Bible Names gives as meaning "gift, or hope, of the Lord," was borne by several other men in the Old Testament. This includes another Mattaniah, a son of a different family, named in the same list of Ezra 10. He should not be confused with King Zedekiah, whose original name was also Mattaniah.

Mattaniah was one of several men of this name in the Bible. This one appears only once, in the list of Israelites who had married foreign wives in the time of Ezra (Ezra 10:37). The surrounding list places him among the descendants, or "sons," of Bani. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the Tyndale House STEPBible names index both say that these men sent away their foreign wives at Ezra's command during his reforms after the return from exile. Nothing else is recorded about him. The name means "gift of the Lord," according to Smith's Bible Dictionary, and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "gift, or hope, of the Lord." He should not be confused with other men named Mattaniah, such as the king of Judah whose name was changed to Zedekiah.

Mattaniah was the father of Zaccur and the grandfather of Hanan, one of the men Nehemiah appointed to oversee the storehouses of the restored Jerusalem community (Neh 13:13). Hanan served alongside Shelemiah the priest, Zadok the scribe and Pedaiah the Levite. These men were chosen because they were considered trustworthy, and their job was to distribute supplies to their fellow workers. Mattaniah himself is known only through this family line. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him as a Levite, probably by inference from his grandson's role in handling the Levites' share of the offerings. His name means "gift of the LORD." Several other men in the Bible share the name, and it is uncertain whether this Mattaniah is the same as any of them.

Mattatha is a man named once in the Bible, in Luke's genealogy of Jesus, which traces Jesus' ancestry back through David to Adam. He is listed as the son of Nathan, who was a son of King David, and as the father of Menan (Luke 3:31). Because his line runs through David, he belongs to the tribe of Judah. The verse gives no details about his life beyond his place in this line of descent. He appears only in Luke's genealogy, which follows Nathan's branch of David's family rather than Solomon's royal line traced in Matthew. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of his name as "his gift."

Mattathah was one of the sons, or descendants, of Hashum named in the list of men who had married foreign wives in the time of Ezra (Ezra 10:33). By inference from the surrounding chapter, he was among those who agreed to send away these wives during Ezra's reforms after the return from exile, as the STEPBible Proper Names index also notes. He appears in that list alongside Mattenai, Zabad, Eliphelet, Jeremai, Manasseh and Shimei, and nothing more is said about him. The Revised Version spells his name Mattattah. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identifies him with the Mattathias of the parallel list in 1 Esdras 9:33, a name the King James Version gives as Matthias.

Mattathias was an ancestor of Jesus named in the genealogy in Luke's Gospel, which traces Jesus' line back through Joseph to Adam. Luke 3:25 lists him as the son of Amos, and the preceding words show he was the father of Joseph. This Joseph is a different person from Joseph, the husband of Mary. Mattathias belongs to the stretch of the genealogy between the return from exile and the time of Jesus, and as part of David's line he was of the tribe of Judah. Smith's Bible Dictionary places him after 406 BC. Nothing else is recorded about him. His name is the Greek form of Mattathiah and is usually explained as meaning "gift of the Lord." Several people in the Bible share this name, including another Mattathias who appears a few generations further on in the same list.

Mattathias was an ancestor of Jesus named in Luke's genealogy, which traces Jesus' line back through Joseph. He was the son of Semei and the father of Maath (Luke 3:26). He belongs to the part of the list between the return from exile under Zerubbabel and the time of Jesus, a stretch whose names appear nowhere else in the Bible, so nothing more is known about him. His place in the tribe of Judah follows from the genealogy, which runs through David and Judah. Smith's Bible Dictionary treats the name as the Greek form of Mattathiah, and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives its meaning as "the gift of the Lord." Several other men in Luke's genealogy and elsewhere share the name, and this entry covers only the son of Semei.

Mattenai was a man of the clan or family of Hashum who appears in the list of men who had married foreign wives in the time of Ezra (Ezra 10:33). He is named first among seven men from the sons of Hashum. From the surrounding chapter, these men agreed to send away their foreign wives as part of the reforms Ezra led after the return from exile in Babylon. Nothing more is recorded about him. The name Mattenai is shared by several people in the Bible, including another man in the same list and a priest of Joiarib's family in the days of Joiakim. This entry refers only to the descendant of Hashum.

Mattenai was one of the men of Israel listed in Ezra 10 as having married foreign wives in the period after the return from exile in Babylon. His name appears in a run of names in Ezra 10:37 that, by the arrangement of the list, belongs to the descendants of Bani (Ezra 10:34). STEPBible Proper Names (Tyndale House) describes him as a descendant of Bani who divorced his foreign wife during Ezra's reforms, when the men involved agreed to send away their foreign wives. Nothing else is recorded about him. Several other men in the Bible share the name, including another Mattenai in the same chapter among the sons of Hashum (Ezra 10:33) and a priest of that name in Nehemiah. This entry is about the man listed in Ezra 10:37.

Mattenai was a priest who headed the priestly family of Joiarib in the days of Joiakim, the high priest who succeeded Jeshua after the return from exile in Babylon. He appears only once, in the list of priestly family heads in Neh 12:19. By inference from the surrounding passage, which places this list in Joiakim's time, he lived some decades after the first return, probably in the late sixth or early fifth century BC. Smith's Bible Dictionary explains the name as a shortened form of Mattaniah, meaning "gift of the Lord." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives the meaning as "liberal." Nothing else is known about him. The same name belongs to other men in the Bible, including laymen in the time of Ezra who had married foreign wives, and this Mattenai should not be confused with them.

Matthan was an ancestor of Jesus named in Matthew's genealogy, the son of Eleazar and the father of Jacob (Matt 1:15). The next verse makes Jacob the father of Joseph, the husband of Mary, so Matthan was Joseph's grandfather, as Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary both note. He belongs to the tribe of Judah through the royal line traced from David. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "gift." Luke's genealogy names a different grandfather of Joseph, Matthat, father of Heli (Luke 3:24). Some interpreters treat Matthan and Matthat as the same man, and others see two separate lines of descent. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia discusses Matthat under this name. Nothing else is recorded about Matthan beyond his place in the list.

Matthat was an ancestor of Jesus named in Luke's genealogy. He was the son of Levi and the father of Heli (Luke 3:24). Since the preceding verse calls Jesus the supposed son of Joseph, who was the son of Heli, Matthat appears as Joseph's grandfather in this line. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes him simply as the son of Levi and father of Heli. Matthew's genealogy names a different set of ancestors for Joseph, with Matthan as his grandfather (Matt 1:15), and some readers connect the two names. Nothing more is recorded about him. Luke's list includes another, earlier Matthat, also called a son of Levi (Luke 3:29), so the name belongs to more than one person in the same genealogy. He is counted here with the tribe of Judah because Luke traces this line through David.

Matthat was an ancestor of Jesus named in the genealogy in Luke's Gospel. He is listed as the son of Levi and the father of Jorim (Luke 3:29). This places him in the stretch of the line between David and Jesus that runs through David's son Nathan rather than through Solomon. Because he appears in a lineage traced from David, this entry groups him with the tribe of Judah. Nothing else is recorded about him. The name is shared with at least one other man in the same genealogy, a later Matthat listed as the grandfather of Joseph (Luke 3:24). Easton's Bible Dictionary distinguishes this Matthat as the son of "another Levi," separate from the Levi who appears later in the list.

Mattithiah was a Levite, the firstborn son of Shallum the Korahite. He appears in the list of those who resettled in Jerusalem after the exile. There he held a permanent duty over "the things that were made in the pans" (1 Chr 9:31). By inference from the passage, this meant preparing the flat-baked items used in worship, probably the grain offerings cooked on a griddle. The STEPBible proper names index describes him as in charge of baking bread in the temple. Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies him as the eldest son of Shallum, of the family of Korah. Several other men in the Bible share the name Mattithiah, and this one is known only from this single verse.

Mattithiah was one of the descendants of Nebo listed in Ezra 10:43 among the Israelite men who had married foreign wives in the period after the return from exile. By inference from the surrounding chapter, he was one of those who agreed to put away these wives during Ezra's reforms. His name means "gift of Yah" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia), and the parallel list in 1 Esdras 9:35 gives it as "Mazitias." Nothing else is recorded about him. Several other men in the Bible bear the same name, and this Mattithiah should not be confused with them.

Mattithiah was one of thirteen men who stood on a wooden platform beside Ezra the scribe when Ezra read the book of the law publicly to the people gathered in Jerusalem after the return from exile. He is named first among the six who stood on Ezra's right hand, with Shema, Anaiah, Urijah, Hilkiah and Maaseiah (Neh 8:4). The verse does not give his family, his office or anything else about him. The STEPBible proper names index (Tyndale House) describes him as a Levite who assisted Ezra in the reading. Several other men in the Bible share the name, and it is uncertain whether this Mattithiah is the same as any of them.

Mehetabeel was the father of Delaiah and the grandfather of Shemaiah, the man who invited Nehemiah to meet him inside the temple and shut the doors because enemies were coming to kill him (Neh 6:10). He is known only from this genealogical note, which identifies Shemaiah by his father and grandfather. His name is usually understood to mean "God does good" or, in Easton's Bible Dictionary, "whose benefactor is God." The following verses show that Shemaiah had been hired by Tobiah and Sanballat to frighten Nehemiah into sinning, but nothing is said about Mehetabeel himself. The name is spelled Mehetabel in some English versions and should not be confused with Mehetabel, the wife of the Edomite king Hadar (Gen 36:39).

Mehir was a man in the genealogies of the tribe of Judah, named only in 1 Chr 4:11. He was the son of Chelub, who is described as the brother of Shuah, and he was the father of Eshton. Nothing else is recorded about his life. His place among Judah's descendants comes from the setting of the list in 1 Chronicles 4, which traces the families of Judah. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives the meaning of his name as "price" or "hire," and Hitchcock's Bible Names renders it "a reward." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia also notes that the Targum of Rabbi Joseph calls him Perug, an Aramaic name with the same meaning.

Mehujael was a descendant of Cain, named in the genealogy of Cain's line in Gen 4:18. He was the son of Irad, the grandson of Enoch son of Cain, and the father of Methusael, whose son was Lamech. That makes him the fourth generation after Cain. Nothing else is recorded about him. Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries give the meaning of his name as "smitten by God," while Hitchcock's Bible Names renders it "who proclaims God." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes the view that the genealogy of Seth's line in Genesis 5 reworks the same material, so that Mahalaleel there would correspond to Mehujael. This entry treats Mehujael as a distinct person in Cain's line, as Gen 4:18 presents him.

Mehuman was one of the seven chamberlains who served in the presence of King Ahasuerus of Persia, and he is named first in the list in Esth 1:10. On the seventh day of the king's feast, when Ahasuerus was merry with wine, he commanded these seven men to bring Queen Vashti before him, as the following verse goes on to say. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary describe the chamberlains as eunuchs and give the meaning of the name as "faithful", while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "making an uproar" or "a multitude." Easton's identifies Ahasuerus with Xerxes. Mehuman is not mentioned anywhere else in the Bible, and nothing more is known about him.

Melatiah was a man from Gibeon who helped rebuild the wall of Jerusalem under Nehemiah, after the return from exile in Babylon. Nehemiah 3 lists the groups that repaired each section. Melatiah appears in Neh 3:7 alongside Jadon the Meronothite, among the men of Gibeon and Mizpah. They worked next to the men of Tekoa, near the "throne of the governor on this side the river." This probably refers to the official seat of the Persian governor of the province west of the Euphrates. Nothing else is recorded about him. His name is generally taken to mean "the Lord delivers" or "deliverance of the Lord," as given in Smith's Bible Dictionary and Hitchcock's Bible Names.

Melchi was an ancestor of Jesus named in Luke's genealogy, which traces the line back from Joseph. He is listed as the son of Janna and the father of Levi, and he stands a few generations before Joseph, the husband of Mary (Luke 3:24). Nothing else is recorded about him. Another Melchi appears further back in the same genealogy (Luke 3:28), so the name belongs to more than one person, and this entry refers to the one in Luke 3:24. Because Luke's line runs through David, he is counted with the tribe of Judah. Smith's Bible Dictionary and Hitchcock's Bible Names give the meaning of the name as "my king" or "my counsel."

Melchi was an ancestor of Jesus named only in Luke's genealogy, which traces Jesus' descent back through David's son Nathan rather than through the kings of Judah. He is listed as the son of Addi (Luke 3:28). The neighboring verse makes him the father of Neri, whose son Salathiel (Shealtiel) appears in the generations around the Babylonian exile. By inference, Melchi lived during the later monarchy, a member of the tribe of Judah through David's family. Nothing else is recorded about him. Another Melchi, son of Janna, appears a few generations later in the same list (Luke 3:24), so the two should not be confused. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "my king" or "my counsel."

Melea was a man named only in Luke's genealogy of Jesus. Luke 3:31 lists him as the son of Menan. His son was Eliakim, named in the preceding verse. He belongs to the line that runs from David through David's son Nathan rather than through Solomon, so he was of the tribe of Judah. Melea is a few generations after Nathan: Nathan, Mattatha, Menan, then Melea. Nothing else is recorded about his life. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "fulness," while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "supplying" or "supplied."

Menan is a name in Luke's genealogy of Jesus, which traces Jesus' ancestry back through Joseph. He appears as the son of Mattatha and the father of Melea (Luke 3:31). Since Mattatha was the son of Nathan, a son of King David, Menan was a great-grandson of David through the line of Nathan rather than through Solomon, and so belonged to the tribe of Judah. Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that the Revised Version spells his name Menna. Nothing else is recorded about him, and he is mentioned nowhere else in the Bible. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "numbered," "rewarded" or "prepared."

Meonothai was a man of the tribe of Judah, named in the genealogy of 1 Chr 4:14 as the father of Ophrah. This entry treats him as a son of Othniel and a brother of Hathath. The Hebrew text of 1 Chr 4:13 names only Hathath as Othniel's son. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the King James margin, the Latin Vulgate and one Greek manuscript tradition read "the sons of Othniel, Hathath and Meonothai," which links Meonothai to Othniel. Othniel, the first judge, was the nephew of Caleb. Smith's Bible Dictionary says Othniel was the son of Caleb's younger brother. Meonothai's name probably means "my dwellings." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests his son Ophrah may have been the founder of a town of that name. Nothing else is recorded about him.

Mephibosheth was a son of King Saul by his concubine Rizpah, the daughter of Aiah, and the brother of Armoni. He should not be confused with Jonathan's son of the same name, who was Saul's grandson and whom David spared (2 Sam 21:7). During a famine in David's reign, which the surrounding passage ties to Saul's earlier killing of Gibeonites, David handed seven of Saul's descendants over to the Gibeonites: Mephibosheth, Armoni and five grandsons of Saul. The following verses say the Gibeonites hanged them on a hill at the beginning of the barley harvest, and that Rizpah guarded the bodies until the rains came (2 Sam 21:9–10). Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary both identify him as one of these seven victims. Through his father Saul he was a half-brother of Jonathan, Abinadab, Malchi-shua, Merab and Michal.

Meraiah was a priest in the days of Joiakim, the high priest who succeeded his father Jeshua after the return from exile in Babylon. He appears in Neh 12:12 in a list of the heads of the priestly families, where he is named as head of the house of Seraiah. That family is probably named after the Seraiah listed among the priests who came back with Zerubbabel earlier in the same chapter. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia connects this house with Ezra, whose ancestry Ezra 7:1 traces through a Seraiah. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "resistance", and Smith's Bible Dictionary as "rebellion". Nothing more is recorded about him.

Meremoth was a man of the family of Bani who is named in Ezra 10:36 among the Israelites who had married foreign wives after the return from exile. The surrounding list in Ezra 10 records those who agreed to send away these wives in response to Ezra's reforms. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him as a layman, not a priest or Levite. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the parallel list in 1 Esdras 9:34 appears to give his name as Carabasion. Several other men in the Bible bear the name Meremoth, and this one is distinct from them. Nothing more is recorded about him. The name is usually taken to mean "heights" or "elevations."

Meres was one of the seven princes of Persia and Media at the court of King Ahasuerus. Esth 1:14 describes these men as officials who "saw the king's face" and "sat the first in the kingdom," meaning they had direct access to the king and held the highest rank under him. By inference from the surrounding passage, Meres was among the advisers the king consulted when Queen Vashti refused to appear at his banquet, though only Memucan's advice is recorded. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him as one of Ahasuerus's seven counsellors and gives the meaning of his name as "lofty." Hitchcock's Bible Names offers a different meaning. He is mentioned only in this one verse, and nothing else is known about him.

Merodach-baladan, son of Baladan, was a king of Babylon in the time of Hezekiah, king of Judah. Isa 39:1 records that he sent letters and a gift to Hezekiah after hearing that Hezekiah had been ill and had recovered. The parallel account in 2 Kgs 20:12 gives his name as Berodach-baladan. Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that his name appears in Assyrian inscriptions. That dictionary describes two reigns: the first from about 721 to 709 BC, and a short second reign of about half a year after he regained the throne around 702 BC. It dates the embassy to Hezekiah to about 713 BC. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia describes him as a Chaldean king who fought the Assyrian kings Sargon and Sennacherib for control of Babylon. It suggests the embassy may also have sought an alliance with Judah against Assyria.

Mesha was a king of Moab in the time of the kings of Israel. According to 2 Kgs 3:4, he was a sheep breeder who paid the king of Israel a yearly tribute of a hundred thousand lambs and the wool of a hundred thousand rams. The following verses of the same chapter say that after Ahab's death Mesha rebelled against Israel. Jehoram of Israel, joined by Jehoshaphat of Judah and the king of Edom, then invaded Moab and laid it waste. Shut up in Kir-hareseth, Mesha offered his firstborn son as a burnt offering on the city wall, and the invaders withdrew. Easton's Bible Dictionary calls him the son of Chemosh-Gad and links him with the Moabite Stone, an inscription found at Dibon that records his exploits. The name is also borne by other people in the Bible.

Mesha was the firstborn son of Caleb, the brother of Jerahmeel, and belonged to the tribe of Judah. He appears only in the genealogy of 1 Chr 2:42, which calls him "the father of Ziph." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia takes this to mean he was probably the ancestor of the Ziphites, the people of the town of Ziph in Judah. The verse goes on to mention "the sons of Mareshah the father of Hebron." The STEPBible proper-names index reads Mareshah as Mesha's son and the re-founder of Hebron, and this entry follows that reading in connecting Mesha with Hebron. Some Greek manuscripts give his name as Marisa, which suggests a link with Mareshah. Smith's Bible Dictionary mentions the medieval commentator Kimchi's suggestion that his mother was Caleb's wife Azubah. The name probably means "deliverance." Several other people in the Bible share the name, including the king of Moab.

Mesha was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, one of the sons Shaharaim had by his wife Hodesh. He is named in the Benjamite genealogy of 1 Chronicles alongside his full brothers Jobab, Zibia, Malcham, Jeuz, Shachia and Mirma. Shaharaim also had sons Abitub and Elpaal by another wife, Hushim, who were Mesha's half-brothers. The surrounding verses place these births in the country of Moab, after Shaharaim had sent away his earlier wives, so Mesha was probably born there. Nothing further is recorded about him. He should not be confused with others of the same name, including Mesha the king of Moab, who rebelled against Israel in the days of Ahab's sons. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "burden" or "salvation". Smith's Bible Dictionary gives it as "freedom".

Meshezabeel was the father of Berechiah and the grandfather of Meshullam, one of the men who repaired a section of Jerusalem's wall in Nehemiah's time. He is known only from this genealogical note in Neh 3:4, which identifies Meshullam by naming his father and grandfather. Nothing else is said about Meshezabeel himself. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "delivered by God." The same name belongs to other men in Nehemiah, including a leader who sealed the covenant (Neh 10:21) and the father of Pethahiah (Neh 11:24). Whether any of these is the same person as Meshullam's grandfather cannot be determined from the text.

Meshezabeel was one of the leaders who put their seal to the covenant made in Nehemiah's time, when the returned exiles pledged to keep the law of God (Neh 10:21). His name appears among the "chief of the people," the lay heads listed after the priests and Levites. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "delivered by God" and suggests that it may stand for a family rather than a single individual. Nothing else is recorded about him. The same name is borne by other men in Nehemiah, including the grandfather of Meshullam, who helped rebuild the wall (Neh 3:4), and the father of Pethahiah (Neh 11:24). Whether any of these is the same person or belongs to the same family is uncertain.

Meshezabeel was the father of Pethahiah, a man of Judah descended from Zerah, son of Judah (Neh 11:24). He is known only through his son, who served "at the king's hand in all matters concerning the people." This is generally understood to mean that Pethahiah represented the Jews of Jerusalem at the Persian court in the time of Nehemiah. Nothing else is recorded about Meshezabeel himself. The name, which Smith's Bible Dictionary renders as "delivered by God," is shared by other men in Nehemiah: one is an ancestor of Meshullam, who helped repair the wall, and another sealed the covenant. Whether any of these is the same person as Pethahiah's father is uncertain. This entry treats him as the father of Pethahiah named in this verse.

Meshillemoth was an Ephraimite, known only as the father of Berechiah. His son was one of the leaders of the tribe of Ephraim who stood up against the soldiers of the northern kingdom when they returned from war with captives from Judah (2 Chr 28:12). From the surrounding chapter, this was during Pekah's war against Ahaz of Judah. Berechiah and the other leaders refused to let the captives be brought into Samaria as slaves. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes Meshillemoth himself as one of the tribe's chiefs, while the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives the leading role to his son. Both dictionaries say the name means "recompense." A priest in Nehemiah's time had the same name, but he is a different person.

Meshobab was a man of the tribe of Simeon, named first in a list of clan leaders in 1 Chr 4:34. The surrounding passage (1 Chr 4:38–41) describes these leaders as princes in their families whose households grew large. Looking for pasture for their flocks, they went toward Gedor and drove out the earlier inhabitants. The passage places this in the days of Hezekiah king of Judah, so Meshobab probably lived in the late 8th century BC, by inference from context. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia connects the list with the settlement near Gedor, which some read as Gerar, and with the attack on the Meunites. Nothing else is recorded about him, and his father's name is not given.

Meshullam was the father of Azaliah and the grandfather of Shaphan the scribe, who served King Josiah of Judah. He is named only once, in the genealogy given for Shaphan when Josiah sent him to the house of the LORD in the eighteenth year of his reign (2 Kgs 22:3). Nothing else is recorded about him. Many other men in the Bible bear the same name, especially in the period after the exile, as the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes, and this one should not be confused with them. The name is usually explained as meaning "devoted" or "resigned" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia), "friend" (Smith's Bible Dictionary) or "peaceable" (Hitchcock's Bible Names). Since his grandson was active in Josiah's reign, Meshullam probably lived two generations earlier, in the seventh century BC, though this is only an inference.

Meshullam was a son of Zerubbabel and a member of the tribe of Judah. He appears only in the genealogy of David's royal line after the exile in Babylon, where he is listed first among Zerubbabel's children, followed by his brother Hananiah and his sister Shelomith (1 Chr 3:19). The next verse lists five more sons, Hashubah, Ohel, Berechiah, Hasadiah and Jushab-hesed (1 Chr 3:20). Matthew's genealogy of Jesus names another son of Zerubbabel, Abiud (Matt 1:13), who does not appear in the Chronicles list. Nothing is recorded about Meshullam's life. International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the name, meaning "devoted" or "resigned," was very common after the exile, and several other men called Meshullam appear in the Bible. Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries both identify this man simply as Zerubbabel's son.

Meshullam was a member of the tribe of Gad, one of seven kinsmen listed together in the Gadite genealogy of 1 Chr 5:13 alongside Michael, Sheba, Jorai, Jachan, Zia and Heber. The following verse in that passage identifies these men as sons of Abihail. The surrounding chapter places the Gadites in Bashan, east of the Jordan, and says their genealogy was recorded in the days of Jotham king of Judah and Jeroboam king of Israel. On that basis Easton's Bible Dictionary describes him as one of the chief Gadites in Bashan in Jotham's time. Nothing else is recorded about him.
