The name Meshullam is shared by many people in the Bible, especially after the exile, and this Gadite should not be confused with them. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia takes the name to mean "devoted" or "resigned," while Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "friend."

Meshullam was a Benjamite, one of the sons of Elpaal, named in the genealogy of the tribe of Benjamin in 1 Chr 8:17. He is listed there alongside Zebadiah, Hezeki and Heber. Other brothers named in the wider list include Eber, Misham, Shamed, Beriah, Shema, Ishmerai, Jezliah and Jobab. The passage also connects Elpaal's family with the towns of Ono, Lod and Aijalon. Nothing further is recorded about him beyond his place in this family list. Several other men in the Bible share the name Meshullam, which Smith's Bible Dictionary takes to mean "friend," and this one should not be confused with them.

Meshullam was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, the son of Hodaviah and the father of Sallu. He appears only in a genealogy in 1 Chr 9:7, which traces Sallu's line back through Meshullam and Hodaviah to Hasenuah. That chapter lists the families who settled in Jerusalem after the return from the Babylonian exile, so Meshullam's line was probably among them, and the STEPBible Proper Names index places him with those Jerusalem residents. A similar list in Neh 11:7 also names a Benjamite Sallu son of Meshullam but gives a different line of ancestors, so the two lists may record the same family in different forms. Several other men in the Bible share the name Meshullam, and this one should not be confused with them. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "peaceable" or "perfect."

Meshullam son of Shephathiah was a man of the tribe of Benjamin. He appears in the list of people who lived in Jerusalem after the return from exile in Babylon. His line of descent is traced back through his father Shephathiah to Reuel and then to Ibnijah (1 Chr 9:8). The surrounding passage names him among the Benjamite heads of families who settled in the city, and Smith's Bible Dictionary likewise places him in Jerusalem after the captivity. Nothing else is recorded about him. Several other men in the Bible are also called Meshullam, including another Benjamite in the same chapter, so he should not be confused with them. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "peaceable" or "perfect," and Smith's gives "friend."

Meshullam was a Levite descended from Kohath who helped oversee the repair of the temple in Jerusalem during the reign of King Josiah of Judah. According to 2 Chr 34:12, he and Zechariah, both Kohathites, directed the workmen alongside Jahath and Obadiah, Levites of the line of Merari, and the text says the men did the work faithfully. The same verse mentions Levites skilled with musical instruments, though it does not say whether Meshullam was one of them. Smith's Bible Dictionary allows that the name here may stand for a Kohathite family rather than a single man. This verse is the only mention of him. The name was common, especially after the exile, and belongs to several other men in the Bible who should not be confused with this Levite. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives its meaning as "devoted" or "resigned."

Meshullam was one of the "chief men" Ezra summoned while preparing to lead a group of exiles from Babylon to Jerusalem (Ezra 8:16). According to the surrounding passage, Ezra had camped by the river Ahava and found no Levites among his company. He called for Meshullam and several other leaders and then sent them to Iddo at Casiphia to bring Levites and temple servants for the journey. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both describe him this way. The STEPBible name index sees him as a leader who also helped Ezra teach the Law, which links him with a Meshullam in a later passage, though that identification is not certain. The name was very common after the exile, so he is hard to tell apart from others who bore it. It is usually taken to mean "devoted" or "friend."

Meshullam was a man of Ezra's time named in Ezra 10:15, during the assembly that dealt with Israelites who had married foreign wives after the return from exile. He is mentioned together with Jonathan son of Asahel, Jahaziah son of Tikvah and Shabbethai the Levite. The verse is read in two ways. The King James wording says these men were 'employed about this matter' and that Meshullam and Shabbethai 'helped them,' and Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him as a chief man who helped Ezra end the marriages. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia and Tyndale House's STEPBible name list take the verse to mean that he opposed Ezra's plan, and the ISBE also counts him as a Levite. This entry follows the opposition reading. The name was common after the exile, so he is probably not the same as other men called Meshullam.

Meshullam was one of the descendants of Bani listed in Ezra 10:29 among the Israelites who had married foreign wives after the return from exile in Babylon. The surrounding passage in Ezra 10 records that these men agreed to send away their foreign wives, and Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him as one who put his wife away. He appears in the list alongside Malluch, Adaiah, Jashub, Sheal and Ramoth. Nothing else is recorded about him. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that Meshullam was a very common name after the exile, so he should not be confused with the other men of the same name in Ezra, Nehemiah and Chronicles. The name is usually explained as meaning "devoted" or "resigned"; Smith's gives "friend."

Meshullam, son of Besodeiah, was one of the people who helped rebuild the walls of Jerusalem under Nehemiah after the return from exile. Together with Jehoiada son of Paseah, he repaired the Old Gate. They laid its beams and set up its doors, locks and bars (Neh 3:6). Nothing else is recorded about him. The name Meshullam was very common after the exile, and several men called by it appear in Ezra and Nehemiah. This one is set apart from the others by his father's name. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia takes the name to mean "devoted" or "resigned," while Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "friend."

Meshullam was one of the men who stood beside Ezra the scribe on a wooden platform when Ezra read the book of the law aloud to the people of Jerusalem after the return from exile. He is the last named of the seven who stood at Ezra's left hand, alongside Pedaiah, Mishael, Malchiah, Hashum, Hashbadana and Zechariah (Neh 8:4). Easton's Bible Dictionary describes him as one of the principal Israelites who supported Ezra, and STEPBible's proper-names index identifies him as a priest, though the verse itself does not state his office. The name was very common after the exile, and several other men called Meshullam appear in Ezra and Nehemiah. Whether this Meshullam is the same as any of them is uncertain, so this entry treats him as a separate person known only from this occasion.

Meshullam was one of the leaders of the people who set their seal to the covenant made in Nehemiah's time, when the community returned from exile pledged to keep the law of God. He appears only in the list of signers, between Magpiash and Hezir (Neh 10:20), and nothing more is recorded about him. The name was very common after the exile, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia counts many men who bore it. Several of them appear in Nehemiah, including a priest who also sealed this covenant and a man who repaired part of Jerusalem's wall. Whether this signer is the same as any of those others is uncertain, and this entry treats him as a separate person. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives the name's meaning as "devoted" or "resigned," while Smith's Bible Dictionary renders it "friend."

Meshullam was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, the son of Joed and the father of Sallu. He appears only in a genealogy in Neh 11:7, which traces Sallu's descent through Meshullam back to Jesaiah. Sallu is listed among the Benjamites who settled in Jerusalem after the return from the Babylonian exile, so Meshullam was probably part of that same family line. STEPBible Proper Names describes him as a Benjamite living in Jerusalem after the exile. A similar list in 1 Chr 9:7 also names a Sallu son of Meshullam, but it traces the line through Hodaviah and Hassenuah, so it is uncertain whether both lists refer to the same man. Several other people in the Bible share the name Meshullam, which Hitchcock's Bible Names takes to mean "peaceable" or "perfect."

Meshullam was a priest in the time after the return from exile in Babylon. He is named only in Neh 12:13, in a list of the heads of priestly families serving in the days of Joiakim, son of Jeshua the high priest (Neh 12:12, by context). There he appears as head of the priestly family of Ezra. This Ezra is probably the priestly clan named among those who returned with Zerubbabel (Neh 12:1), not necessarily Ezra the scribe. Nothing more is recorded about him. The name Meshullam was common in this period and is shared by several other men in Ezra, Nehemiah and Chronicles, so he should not be confused with them. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "friend," while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "peaceable" or "perfect."

Meshullam was a priest in the days after the return from exile in Babylon. He was head of the priestly family of Ginnethon (Neh 12:16). The list he appears in (Neh 12:12–21) names the heads of the priestly families during the high priesthood of Joiakim, son of Jeshua, so he probably served in the generation after the first returnees. That setting is inferred from the surrounding passage; Smith's Bible Dictionary and Tyndale House's STEPBible name list place him the same way. The Ginnethon family is probably the same as the Ginnethon who signed the covenant in Neh 10:6. Nothing more is recorded about him. Several other men in the Bible bear the name Meshullam, including other priests and Levites of the same period, so care is needed to tell them apart. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "peaceable" or "perfect."

Meshullam was a gatekeeper in Jerusalem after the return from exile. Nehemiah 12:25 lists him with Mattaniah, Bakbukiah, Obadiah, Talmon and Akkub as porters who kept watch at the storehouses by the thresholds of the gates. The following verse dates this group to the days of the high priest Joiakim, and of Nehemiah and Ezra. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia accordingly places him in Joiakim's time, and the Tyndale House proper-names index describes him as a Levite gatekeeper of Nehemiah's era. The name, which may mean "devoted" or "rewarded," was very common after the exile, so he is hard to distinguish from the other men called Meshullam. Some readers link him with Shallum, head of the gatekeeping families in other lists, but this cannot be confirmed. Nothing else is recorded about him.

Meshullemeth was the wife of King Manasseh of Judah and the mother of his son and successor, Amon. She is named only once, in the notice of Amon's accession, which says he began to reign at twenty-two and ruled two years in Jerusalem (2 Kgs 21:19). She is called the daughter of Haruz of Jotbah. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that this is the earliest case in Kings where the queen mother's home town is added to her name, and that her name is the feminine form of Meshullam. Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries give its meaning as "friend." The location of Jotbah is uncertain. Through her son Amon, father of Josiah, she belongs to the royal line traced in Matthew's genealogy of Jesus, which names Manasseh and Amon but not her.

Methusael was a man in the line of Cain, named only in the genealogy of Gen 4:18. He was the son of Mehujael and the father of Lamech, which makes him the fourth generation after Cain (Cain, Enoch, Irad, Mehujael, Methusael). The following verses (Gen 4:19–24) go on to describe his son Lamech, his two wives and his children. Nothing else is recorded about Methusael himself. His name is usually understood to mean "man of God" (Smith's Bible Dictionary; Easton's Bible Dictionary gives "champion of El; man of God"), while Hitchcock's Bible Names renders it "who demands his death." He is a different person from Methuselah of Seth's line in Gen 5, although the two names look alike and both genealogies end in a man named Lamech.

Miamin was an Israelite layman of the family of Parosh who lived in Ezra's time, after the return from exile in Babylon. He is named in the list of men who had married foreign wives and who agreed, at Ezra's urging, to send them away (Ezra 10:25). The verse groups him with six others from the same family: Ramiah, Jeziah, Malchiah, Eleazar, Malchijah and Benaiah. Nothing else is recorded about him. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him as a layman who put away his foreign wife. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "the right hand." The same name, often spelled Mijamin, belongs to other men in the Old Testament, such as a priest in David's time, and these are probably different people.

Mibhar, son of Haggeri, appears in 1 Chronicles' list of David's mighty warriors, the elite fighters who served the king (1 Chr 11:38). He is named right after Joel the brother of Nathan, and nothing more is said about him. The name is often explained as meaning "choice" or "chosen." The parallel list in 2 Sam 23:36 has no Mibhar. At that point it reads "Igal the son of Nathan of Zobah, Bani the Gadite." Easton's Bible Dictionary therefore identifies Mibhar with Bani the Gadite. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests that the Chronicles wording arose from a copying change, with "Mibhar" coming from "of Zobah" and "son of Haggeri" from "Bani the Gadite." This entry treats Mibhar as the warrior named in Chronicles while noting that the two lists differ at this point.

Mibsam was a descendant of Simeon, named in the genealogy of that tribe in 1 Chr 4:25. He was the son of Shallum and the father of Mishma. The surrounding passage (1 Chr 4:24) traces this line from Simeon through his son Shaul, so Shallum was probably Shaul's son, which would make Mibsam Simeon's great-grandson. Nothing else is recorded about his life. His name is often explained as meaning "sweet smell" or "perfume" (Smith's Bible Dictionary; Hitchcock's Bible Names), though the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia marks this meaning as uncertain. The same name belongs to another man, a son of Ishmael (Gen 25:13; 1 Chr 1:29), who is a different person.

Micah was a member of the tribe of Reuben. He appears only once, in the Reubenite genealogy of 1 Chr 5:5, as the son of Shimei and the father of Reaia. The surrounding verses (1 Chr 5:4–6) place him in a line descending from Joel. The line runs through Shemaiah, Gog and Shimei to Micah, then through Reaia and Baal to Beerah, a Reubenite prince whom the Assyrian king Tiglath-pileser carried into exile. Nothing else is recorded about Micah. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia explains the name as a shortened form of Micaiah, meaning "who is like Yah?" Several other men in the Bible share the name, including the prophet Micah, and this Reubenite should not be confused with them.

Micha was one of the men who set their seal to the written covenant made in the time of Nehemiah, when the returned exiles pledged to keep the law of God. His name appears in a list alongside Rehob and Hashabiah (Neh 10:11). That list falls within the section introduced as the Levites (Neh 10:9), so he was probably a Levite, as Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him. Nothing else is recorded about him. Smith's gives the meaning of the name as "who is like God?", and Hitchcock's Bible Names treats it as the same name as Micaiah. Several other people in the Bible bear this or a similar name, including a son of Mephibosheth and a Levite of the line of Asaph. Whether this Micha is connected to any of them is uncertain.

Michael was a man of the tribe of Asher and the father of Sethur. He is known only from Num 13:13, which names Sethur as Asher's representative among the twelve men Moses sent to explore the land of Canaan. Nothing else is recorded about Michael himself. His name means "who is like God?" (Smith's Bible Dictionary). It is shared by several other people in the Bible, including the archangel Michael, and this Asherite should not be confused with them.

Michael was a member of the tribe of Gad who lived in the region of Bashan, east of the Jordan. He is listed first among seven kinsmen named in 1 Chr 5:13, alongside Meshullam, Sheba, Jorai, Jachan, Zia and Heber. The next verse, 1 Chr 5:14, identifies these men as the sons of Abihail. According to 1 Chr 5:17, the Gadite families were recorded in genealogies during the reigns of Jotham king of Judah and Jeroboam king of Israel. Easton's Bible Dictionary calls him a chief Gadite in Bashan. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "who is like God?" Nothing else is recorded about him. Several other people in the Bible share the name Michael, and this one should not be confused with them.

Michael was a man of the tribe of Gad, named only in a genealogy in 1 Chr 5:14. He was the son of Jeshishai and the father of Gilead. Through Gilead he was an ancestor of Abihail, whose sons were among the Gadite family heads in this list. The genealogy traces his own line back through Jahdo to Buz. The surrounding passage places the Gadites in Bashan, east of the Jordan, and nothing more is recorded about him. Smith's Bible Dictionary explains the name as meaning "who is like God?" and counts this Michael as one of several Gadites who bear it. The name is shared by a number of people in the Bible, including other men in Chronicles and the archangel, so this Michael should not be confused with them.

Michael was a Levite named in the ancestry of Asaph, one of the leading singers David appointed for the music of the house of the Lord. In the genealogy in 1 Chr 6:40 he is the son of Baaseiah and the grandson of Malchiah. His son Shimea appears in the line that leads down to Asaph, so Michael was one of Asaph's forefathers. Because Asaph's line is traced back through Gershom, Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary identify Michael as a Gershonite Levite. Smith's gives the meaning of the name as "who is like God?" Nothing else is recorded about him. Several other people in the Bible share the name Michael, and this one should not be confused with them.

Michael was a man of the tribe of Issachar, named first among the sons of Izrahiah, whose brothers were Obadiah, Joel and Ishiah. He belonged to the line of Uzzi, a descendant of Tola, Issachar's son (1 Chr 7:1–3). The verse calls the group "five", although it names only four sons. Izrahiah himself is probably counted as the fifth, by inference from the passage. All of them are described as "chief men", which points to leaders of family clans within the tribe. Nothing else is recorded about him. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "who is like God?" Several other men in the Bible share this name, and this Michael should not be confused with them.

Michael was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, named among the sons of Beriah in the Benjamite genealogy of 1 Chronicles. 1 Chr 8:16 lists him first in a group with Ispah and Joha. Read with the preceding verses (1 Chr 8:14–15), the same list probably also includes Ahio, Shashak, Jeremoth, Zebadiah, Arad and Ader as sons of Beriah. Nearby verses describe Beriah as a head of a family who lived in Aijalon and drove out the inhabitants of Gath (1 Chr 8:13). Nothing else is recorded about Michael himself. Smith's Bible Dictionary explains the name as meaning "who is like God?" Several other men in the Bible share the name, as does the archangel Michael, and this Benjamite should not be confused with them.

Michael was a man of the tribe of Manasseh and one of the "captains of the thousands" of Manasseh who went over to David as he went to Ziklag (1 Chr 12:20). He is named with six other Manassite commanders, including Adnah, Jozabad and Elihu. The surrounding chapter suggests this happened when David left the Philistine army before the battle in which Saul died, though that timing is inferred from context. Nothing else is recorded about him. His name means "who is like God?" (Smith's Bible Dictionary). Several other men in the Bible share the name, and this Michael should not be confused with them.

Michael was a man of the tribe of Issachar, known only as the father of Omri. Omri served as the leader of Issachar in the list of tribal chiefs during King David's reign (1 Chr 27:18). Nothing else is recorded about Michael himself. Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that he may have been Omri's father or a more distant ancestor, since 'son of' can sometimes point to a forebear. The name means 'who is like God?' and is shared by several people in the Bible, including the archangel Michael. This Michael should not be confused with them.

Michael was one of the sons of King Jehoshaphat of Judah, listed among the brothers of Jehoram, who succeeded their father as king (2 Chr 21:2). The verse calls Jehoshaphat "king of Israel," although he ruled the southern kingdom of Judah. His brothers were Azariah, Jehiel, Zechariah, a second Azariah, and Shephatiah. According to 2 Chr 21:4, when Jehoram had established himself on the throne he killed all his brothers with the sword. Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries both understand Michael to have died in this way. His death is placed here at about 889 BC in Jerusalem, an estimate inferred from the context of Jehoram's reign. The name means "who is like God?" and is shared by several other people in the Bible, including the archangel Michael, so he should not be confused with them.

Michael was the father, or possibly an earlier ancestor, of Zebadiah, a man of the family of Shephatiah. He is known only from the list of family heads who traveled from Babylon to Jerusalem with Ezra, where his son Zebadiah is named as leading eighty men of that family (Ezra 8:8). Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "who is like God?" and allows that "son of" here may mean a more distant descendant. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes a parallel to this list in 1 Esdras 8:34. The verse does not say whether Michael himself made the journey. Several other people in the Bible share the name Michael, and nothing further is recorded about this one.

Michaiah was one of five princes whom King Jehoshaphat of Judah sent out in the third year of his reign to teach in the cities of Judah (2 Chr 17:7). The verse itself only says "his reign," but the surrounding chapter makes clear the king is Jehoshaphat. The following verses add that Levites and priests went with these princes, and that they taught the people from the book of the law of the Lord as they travelled through the towns of Judah (2 Chr 17:8–9). Nothing else is recorded about this Michaiah. Several other people in the Bible share the name, and he is not known to be any of them. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "who is like God?"

Michaiah was a priest who took part in the dedication of the rebuilt wall of Jerusalem in Nehemiah's time. He is named in Neh 12:41 among seven priests who played trumpets with one of the two great thanksgiving choirs that processed along the wall. This is his only mention, and nothing else is recorded about him. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "who is like God?". Several other people in the Bible bear the same name or a close form of it (Micaiah, Micah), and this priest should not be confused with them. By inference from the setting, the dedication took place in the mid-fifth century BC, after the wall was completed under Nehemiah.

Michri was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, named only once in the Bible, as the father of Uzzi and grandfather of Elah. He appears in the genealogy of Elah in 1 Chr 9:8. That verse belongs to a list of Benjamite families who lived in Jerusalem, and it names Elah among the heads of fathers' houses there. The surrounding passage concerns those who settled in the city, usually understood as the community after the return from exile. So Michri was probably an ancestor of returned Benjamite settlers rather than a settler himself, an inference from context. Nothing else is recorded about him. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "prize of Jehovah." Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "worthy of price," and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "selling."

Mijamin was a priest whose name was given to the sixth of the twenty-four divisions of priests that David organized for service at the sanctuary (1 Chr 24:9). The divisions were assigned by casting lots, and each one was named for the head of a priestly family. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him as the chief of that sixth course. Nothing else is recorded about him. The name, which Hitchcock's Bible Names explains as meaning "right hand," also belongs to other men in Ezra and Nehemiah, including a priest who returned from exile and a man who had married a foreign wife. Because those passages fall in a much later period, they probably refer to different people, though a priestly family name could have carried on. This entry covers only the head of David's sixth division.

Mikloth was an officer in King David's army, named only in 1 Chr 27:4. David's forces were organized into twelve divisions of 24,000 men, each serving for one month of the year. Mikloth belonged to the division for the second month, which was commanded by Dodai the Ahohite. The verse calls him "the ruler" of that course, and readers have understood his role in two ways. Easton's Bible Dictionary takes him as an officer serving under Dodai, while Smith's Bible Dictionary and the STEPBible names index describe him as the leader of the second division. The wording supports his being at least a senior officer of that monthly force. The name Mikloth is also borne by a different man, a Benjamite of Gibeon listed in the family of Saul in 1 Chr 8:32 and 9:37–38, who should not be confused with this officer.

Milalai was one of the musicians who played at the dedication of the rebuilt wall of Jerusalem in Nehemiah's time. He is named only in Neh 12:36, among the "brethren" of Zechariah son of Jonathan, a descendant of Asaph (Neh 12:35). This group played "the musical instruments of David" in the procession led by Ezra the scribe. This entry treats Milalai as a son of Jonathan and a brother of Zechariah and the others named with him. The Hebrew word for "brethren" can also mean kinsmen or fellow Levites, so the exact relationship is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia call him a Levite musician. Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests he was probably a Gershonite Levite of the sons of Asaph. The name is explained as "eloquent" in Easton's and as "my talk" in Hitchcock's Bible Names.

Miniamin was a Levite in the reign of King Hezekiah of Judah. He is named in 2 Chr 31:15 as one of six men who worked under Kore, the official in charge of the freewill offerings (2 Chr 31:14, a verse not quoted here). Stationed in the cities of the priests, these men shared out the gifts and tithes to their fellow priests and Levites by their divisions, giving to old and young alike. The name is thought to mean "from the right hand" or "right hand" (Smith's Bible Dictionary; Hitchcock's Bible Names). Several other people in the Bible bear this name, including priests in the time of Nehemiah. This entry covers only the Levite of Hezekiah's day, and nothing more is recorded about him.

Miniamin was a priest who played a trumpet at the dedication of the rebuilt wall of Jerusalem in Nehemiah's time. Nehemiah 12:41 names him among seven priests, Eliakim, Maaseiah, Miniamin, Michaiah, Elioenai, Zechariah and Hananiah, who sounded trumpets in one of the two thanksgiving processions that marched around the wall. Nothing else is recorded about him. The name, which Smith's Bible Dictionary and Hitchcock's Bible Names take to mean "from the right hand," belongs to several men in the Bible, including priests of the same period. It is uncertain whether this Miniamin is the same as any of them, so this entry treats him only as the trumpeter at the wall's dedication.

Miriam was a descendant of Judah, named once in the genealogy of Ezrah's family in 1 Chr 4:17. That verse says "she bare Miriam, and Shammai, and Ishbah the father of Eshtemoa," without saying who "she" was. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests the latter half of the verse probably belongs after verse 18, which names Bithiah, the daughter of Pharaoh, as the wife of Mered. This entry follows that reading, treating Miriam as the child of Mered and Bithiah, with Shammai and Ishbah as siblings. This entry treats Miriam as female, though the Hebrew name could also be read as a man's name here, and the same encyclopedia allows for either. Nothing else is recorded about this Miriam. She is distinct from Miriam the sister of Moses and from others who bear the name.

Mirma was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, named once in the Benjamite genealogy of 1 Chronicles. He was one of the seven sons of Shaharaim by his wife Hodesh, and his full brothers were Jobab, Zibia, Mesha, Malcham, Jeuz and Shachia. Through Shaharaim's other wife, Hushim, he had two half-brothers, Abitub and Elpaal. The surrounding verses say Shaharaim had these children in the country of Moab after sending away his earlier wives, so Mirma was probably born there, as Smith's Bible Dictionary also states. Together with his brothers he is called one of the "heads of the fathers," meaning a leader of a family clan (1 Chr 8:10). Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "fraud." Nothing else is recorded about him.

Mishael was one of the men who stood on Ezra's left hand when Ezra read the Book of the Law to the people of Jerusalem from a wooden platform (Neh 8:4). He is named alongside Pedaiah, Malchiah, Hashum, Hashbadana, Zechariah and Meshullam, while six others stood on Ezra's right. Nothing else is recorded about him. The STEPBible proper-names index describes him as a Levite, though the verse itself does not give his tribe or his role. The name is usually taken to mean "who is what God is?" (Smith's Bible Dictionary) or "who is equal to God?" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia). Several people in the Bible share this name, including Daniel's companion, who was renamed Meshach in Babylon. This Mishael belongs to the period after the return from exile and appears to be a different person.

Misham was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, named in the Benjamite genealogy as one of the sons of Elpaal, alongside Eber and Shamed (1 Chr 8:12). Nothing else is recorded about him. The same verse says that Ono and Lod, with their surrounding towns, were built, but the wording most naturally credits this to Shamed rather than to Misham. Elpaal's other sons, such as Beriah, Shema, Zebadiah, Meshullam and Jobab, appear in the verses that follow. Smith's Bible Dictionary traces this family to Shaharaim, whom an earlier passage in the same chapter names as Elpaal's father (1 Chr 8:8–11). The meaning of the name is uncertain. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "purification," Easton's Bible Dictionary gives "their cleansing" or "their beholding," and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "their savior" or "taking away."

Mishmannah was a warrior of the tribe of Gad who joined David's forces. He is named only once, as the fourth in a list of Gadite fighters (1 Chr 12:10). The surrounding passage in 1 Chronicles 12 describes these Gadites as skilled with shield and spear, with faces like lions and as swift as gazelles on the mountains. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary place their joining at Ziklag, where David stayed while fleeing from Saul. The wider chapter also speaks of men coming to David at a stronghold in the wilderness, so the exact setting is drawn from the context of the chapter as a whole. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "fatness." Nothing else is recorded about him.

Mithredath was the treasurer of Cyrus king of Persia. Through him Cyrus brought out the vessels that Nebuchadnezzar had taken from the temple in Jerusalem. Mithredath counted them and handed them over to Sheshbazzar, the prince of Judah, so the returning exiles could carry them back (Ezra 1:8). The name is Persian. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia explain it as "given by Mithra" or "consecrated to Mithra." Another man named Mithredath appears later in the book of Ezra, a Persian official who wrote against the rebuilding of Jerusalem in the time of Artaxerxes. He is a different person from the treasurer described here.

Mithredath was a man who, along with Bishlam, Tabeel and their companions, wrote a letter to Artaxerxes king of Persia. The letter was written in Aramaic (the "Syrian tongue" of the King James text) and translated (Ezra 4:7). The verse does not give the letter's contents. Its setting among the efforts of local opponents to stop the Jews' rebuilding suggests it opposed the work on Jerusalem, and STEPBible Proper Names says it accused the Jews of rebuilding the city's walls. His name is Persian, meaning "gift of Mithra" according to the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia, which calls him perhaps an official. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him as a Persian officer stationed at Samaria. He is probably a different man from Mithredath the treasurer of Cyrus in Ezra 1:8, since the name was borne by more than one person.

Mnason was a Christian from Cyprus, described as "an old disciple" (an early disciple), who gave lodging to Paul and his companions near the end of Paul's journey from Miletus to Jerusalem, about AD 54 by inference from context. Disciples from Caesarea traveled with Paul's group and brought Mnason along so that the travelers could stay with him (Acts 21:16). The verse does not say exactly where his house was. Smith's Bible Dictionary and Easton's Bible Dictionary take it to have been in Jerusalem, while others place it at a stop along the road from Caesarea. Easton's understands "old disciple" to mean that he became a believer in the earliest days of the church. Smith's suggests that, as a Cypriot, he may have been a friend of Barnabas, who was also from Cyprus. He is mentioned nowhere else in the Bible.

Molid was a man of the tribe of Judah, named only in the genealogy of 1 Chr 2:29 as the son of Abishur and his wife Abihail and the brother of Ahban. Nothing else is recorded about him. The surrounding genealogy (1 Chr 2:25–28) traces Abishur back through Shammai and Onam to Jerahmeel, so Molid belonged to the Jerahmeelite clan of Judah. Smith's Bible Dictionary also places him among Jerahmeel's descendants. Smith's gives the meaning of his name as "begetter," and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "nativity" or "generation."

The Mother of Aholah and Aholibah is an unnamed figure in the allegory the prophet Ezekiel was given in Ezek 23. The passage opens by describing two women who were daughters of one mother (Ezek 23:2). She is never named and takes no action in the story. She serves only to show that the two sisters share the same origin. Later in the same chapter, Ezek 23:4 identifies Aholah as Samaria and Aholibah as Jerusalem, the capitals of the northern and southern kingdoms. By inference from the allegory, the common mother probably stands for the single people of Israel from which both kingdoms came, though the text does not say this directly. Ezek 23:3 places the sisters' early history in Egypt, which suggests that their shared origin is meant to recall the nation's beginnings there.

The Mother of Lemuel is the unnamed woman credited with the teaching recorded in Proverbs 31. Prov 31:1 introduces the chapter as "the words of king Lemuel, the prophecy that his mother taught him." The verses that follow (Prov 31:2–9) appear to give her advice: she warns her son against wasting his strength on women and against kings drinking wine, and urges him to speak up for the poor and judge fairly. Whether the closing poem about the capable wife (Prov 31:10–31) also comes from her is uncertain. Neither she nor Lemuel is identified elsewhere in the Bible. Jewish tradition takes Lemuel to be another name for Solomon, which would make her Bathsheba, but the text does not say so. Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that a king's mother held a place of special honor in Israel, as Bathsheba did.

Moza was a son of Caleb by his concubine Ephah, listed in the genealogy of the tribe of Judah. His full brothers were Haran and Gazez (1 Chr 2:46). Caleb had other sons by other wives and concubines. Moza is named only once, and nothing more is recorded about him. Opinions differ over which Caleb is meant. Smith's Bible Dictionary identifies him as Caleb the son of Hezron, which fits the surrounding genealogy. The STEPBible proper-names index takes him to be the well-known spy. This entry follows the genealogy's own setting and leaves the question open. The name Moza is shared by at least one other person, a descendant of Saul in the line of Benjamin (1 Chr 8:36–37), who is a different man.

Naam was one of the sons of Caleb the son of Jephunneh, named with his brothers Iru and Elah in the genealogy of the tribe of Judah (1 Chr 4:15). This Caleb is the man known from Numbers and Joshua as one of the spies sent into Canaan, so Naam probably belonged to the generation that settled in the land under Joshua. His sister Achsah is the daughter whom Caleb gave in marriage to Othniel, according to Josh 15:16–17. Nothing else is recorded about Naam. The same verse names Kenaz as a son of Elah but lists no descendants for Naam. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "pleasantness," and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "fair; pleasant."

Naamah (line of Cain) was the daughter of Lamech, a descendant of Cain, and his wife Zillah. She is named only once, in Gen 4:22, where she appears as the sister of Tubal-cain, the forger of bronze and iron tools. Jabal and Jubal, Lamech's sons by his other wife Adah, were her half-brothers. The genealogy gives no details about her life, and why she alone among Lamech's daughters is named is not explained. Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that she is one of only four women named in the record before the flood, and that all of them except Eve belong to Cain's line. Her name is usually taken to mean "pleasant" or "lovely." Another Naamah, an Ammonite woman who was the mother of King Rehoboam, is a different person.

Naaman was a member of the tribe of Benjamin, named in the genealogy of 1 Chronicles as one of the sons of Ehud. He appears with Ahiah and Gera in a list of family members who were "removed" (1 Chr 8:7). The preceding verse, 1 Chr 8:6, explains that Ehud's sons were heads of families in Geba and were carried away to Manahath, so this probably describes a forced relocation of the family group. The wording of 1 Chr 8:7 is difficult. It is unclear who did the removing, and Uzza and Ahihud, grouped here with Naaman's siblings, may instead be the sons of the one who removed them. Nothing else is recorded about him. He is distinct from Naaman the Syrian army commander healed under Elisha. A Benjamite Naaman also appears as a son of Bela in Num 26:40, and the two may be related within the same clan.

Naarai son of Ezbai was one of David's mighty men, listed among his warriors in 1 Chr 11:37 directly after Hezro the Carmelite. Nothing else is recorded about him. The parallel list in 2 Sam 23:35 seems to name the same man "Paarai the Arbite." Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary both treat Naarai and Paarai as one person. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the original form of his name and description is uncertain. Smith's records the view that the Chronicles form is the correct one. This entry follows the Chronicles form. The name is usually explained as meaning "youthful," though Smith's gives "handmaid."

Nagge is a man named only in the genealogy of Jesus in Luke's Gospel, which traces Jesus' ancestry back through Joseph. Luke 3:25 names him as the father of Esli. The next verse, Luke 3:26, makes him the son of Maath. He belongs to the stretch of the list between Zerubbabel and Joseph, so he probably lived in the centuries after the return from exile in Babylon. As a descendant of David, he was of the tribe of Judah. Nothing else is recorded about him, and he appears nowhere else in the Bible. Modern translations often spell his name Naggai, and Smith's Bible Dictionary cross-references him under that form. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "clearness, brightness, light."

Naham was a man of the tribe of Judah, named only in the genealogy of 1 Chr 4:19 as the brother of Hodiah. Hodiah is described there as the wife of a man whose name the verse does not repeat. By inference from the surrounding verses, this is probably Mered or Ezra, and Smith's Bible Dictionary takes the husband to be Ezra. The verse goes on to mention "the father of Keilah the Garmite, and Eshtemoa the Maachathite." The wording is hard to follow, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia calls the passage obscure. Some read it as making Naham himself a Judahite clan leader and father of Keilah. Others take Hodiah's sons to be the founders of Keilah and Eshtemoa, which were towns in Judah. His name means "comfort" or "consolation." Nothing else is recorded about him.

Nahamani was one of the leaders named alongside Zerubbabel and Jeshua at the head of the list of exiles who returned from Babylon to Jerusalem and Judah (Neh 7:7). Counting Zerubbabel, the list has twelve leaders, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia describes him as one of these twelve heads of the return. His name is missing from the parallel list in Ezra 2:2, which has only eleven names. The same encyclopedia notes that 1 Esdras 5:8 calls him Eneneus, and gives the meaning of his name as "compassionate." Nothing else is recorded about him beyond this single mention.

Nahash was the father of Abigail and Zeruiah, named only once, in 2 Sam 17:25. That verse explains that Amasa, whom Absalom made commander of his army in place of Joab, was the son of Ithra and Abigail, "the daughter of Nahash, sister to Zeruiah Joab's mother." The name means "serpent." Because 1 Chr 2:16 calls Zeruiah and Abigail sisters of David, the son of Jesse, his relationship to David's family is understood in different ways. Easton's Bible Dictionary suggests that Jesse's wife was first married to Nahash, which would make the two women David's half-sisters through their mother. A rabbinic tradition treats Nahash as another name for Jesse, and some interpreters take Nahash as the name of Jesse's wife. This entry treats Nahash as a man and the father of the two sisters. He is a different person from Nahash, the king of the Ammonites.

Nahash, whose name means "serpent", was a man of Rabbah, the Ammonite capital, and the father of Shobi. He is named only in 2 Sam 17:27, which tells how Shobi, together with Machir of Lodebar and Barzillai the Gileadite, met David at Mahanaim when David was fleeing from his son Absalom. The following verses describe the supplies they brought. The name is shared by several people in the Bible, and whether this Nahash is the same as Nahash king of the Ammonites, whose son Hanun succeeded him (2 Sam 10:1), is uncertain. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests he may be that king, and some take Shobi to be a brother of Hanun. Tyndale House's STEPBible names also treat him as the Ammonite king. If so, Shobi was a royal son who supported David after Hanun's war with Israel.

Nahath was a Levite in the reign of King Hezekiah of Judah. He was one of ten overseers who served under Conaniah (spelled Cononiah in the King James Version) and his brother Shimei. Hezekiah and Azariah, the ruler of the house of God, appointed them to take charge of the offerings, tithes and dedicated things that the people brought to the temple (2 Chr 31:13). The verse itself does not call him a Levite, but the surrounding passage concerns Levites appointed to this work, and Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both describe him that way. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates his service to about 725 BC. Nothing else is recorded about him. The name Nahath, which Hitchcock's Bible Names takes to mean "rest," also belongs to other people in the Bible, including a descendant of Esau and a Levite of Kohath's line.

Nahbi was the son of Vophsi and the representative of the tribe of Naphtali among the twelve men Moses sent from the wilderness to explore the land of Canaan (Num 13:14). He is named only in the list of these spies and does not appear again by name. By inference from the wider chapter, he was among the ten spies who brought back a discouraging report, as opposed to Joshua and Caleb. Numbers 14 records that those ten died by a plague. His name is usually taken to mean "hidden" (Easton's Bible Dictionary; Smith's Bible Dictionary), or "very secret" according to Hitchcock's Bible Names.

Nahum was the prophet whose vision is recorded in the book that bears his name, the seventh of the minor prophets. Its opening verse calls the book "the burden of Nineveh" and names him "Nahum the Elkoshite," probably meaning he came from a place called Elkosh (Nah 1:1). Nothing else is known of his life. The site of Elkosh is disputed. Smith's Bible Dictionary notes proposals for Galilee and for Alkush near Mosul in Assyria, and suggests that his imagery and language fit someone living in the land of Israel. His message foretells the fall of Nineveh, the Assyrian capital, so it was written while Assyrian power still stood. This entry dates his prophecies to about 663 BC, an estimate inferred from context; Smith's places him in the reign of Hezekiah. His name is often explained as "comfort" or "consolation."

Narcissus was a man living in Rome whose household Paul greets in Rom 16:11, addressing specifically those members of it "which are in the Lord." The wording suggests that only some of his household were Christians. It also leaves open whether Narcissus himself was a believer, or even still alive, since he himself is not greeted. Narcissus was a common name, especially among slaves and freedmen. Some have identified him with the powerful freedman of that name who served the emperor Claudius and was put to death in AD 54. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes Bishop Lightfoot's view that his slaves would then have passed into the emperor's household while keeping his name. Conybeare and Howson preferred a later favorite of Nero. Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries both describe any such identification as quite uncertain, and this entry leaves the question open.

Nathan was a man of the tribe of Judah, named once in the genealogy of 1 Chronicles as the son of Attai and the father of Zabad. By inference from the surrounding verses (1 Chr 2:34–35), he belonged to the line of Jerahmeel. His grandfather was Jarha, an Egyptian servant of Sheshan who married Sheshan's daughter because Sheshan had no sons. Nothing else is recorded about him. Several men in the Bible share the name, which Hitchcock's Bible Names explains as meaning "given" or "rewarded." Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies this Nathan with the prophet of David's and Solomon's reigns and counts Zabad among the prophet's sons at the royal court. This entry follows the reading of Nathan simply as Attai's son in Judah's family line, as the genealogy itself presents him.

Nathan was one of the "chief men" whom Ezra summoned while the returning exiles were camped by the river Ahava, on their journey from Babylon to Jerusalem (Ezra 8:16). He is listed with Eliezer, Ariel, Shemaiah, several men named Elnathan, Jarib, Zechariah and Meshullam. The following verse shows that Ezra sent this group to Iddo at Casiphia to bring Levites to serve in the temple, because none had joined the company. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia describes him as a companion of Ezra from Babylon and notes that the same list appears in 1 Esdras 8:44. Nothing more is recorded about him. Several other people in the Bible share the name Nathan, which Hitchcock's Bible Names takes to mean "given." It is uncertain whether this Nathan is the same man as anyone else of that name, such as the Nathan later listed among those who had married foreign wives.

Nathan was an Israelite named in Ezra 10:39 in the list of men who had married foreign wives in the time of Ezra, after the return from exile in Babylon. Going by the surrounding chapter, he was one of those who agreed to send these wives away. He appears among the descendants of Bani, whose family group heads this part of the list, and nothing more is recorded about him. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the parallel list in 1 Esdras 9:34 gives his name as Nathanias. Several other men in the Bible are also called Nathan, including the prophet in David's court and a son of David. This Nathan is a different person, known only from this single mention. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "given" or "giving."

Nathan-melech was a court official of Judah in the time of King Josiah, mentioned only in 2 Kgs 23:11. He is called a "chamberlain," a word Smith's Bible Dictionary takes to mean a eunuch, and the Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation, calls him "Nathan, the king's eunuch." His chamber stood in the precincts near the entrance to the house of the LORD. It serves as a landmark in the account of Josiah's reforms: the horses that earlier kings of Judah had dedicated to the sun were kept near this chamber, and Josiah removed them and burned the chariots of the sun. The text does not say whether Nathan-melech himself took part in this sun worship. His name is usually explained as meaning "gift of the king." Smith's Bible Dictionary dates him to about 628 BC, an estimate drawn from the reign of Josiah.

Naum was an ancestor of Jesus who appears only in Luke's genealogy, which traces Jesus' line back through Joseph (Luke 3:25). There he is named as the son of Esli and the father of Amos, which places him in the line of Judah in the generations after the return from exile. Nothing else is recorded about him. Naum is the King James spelling of the name rendered Nahum in some other translations, and according to Smith's Bible Dictionary it means "consolation." He is a different person from the prophet Nahum. Smith's Bible Dictionary estimates that he lived around the time of Antiochus Epiphanes, about 175 BC. That date is worked out by counting generations and is not stated in the text.

Neariah was a son of Ishi and one of four brothers, with Pelatiah, Rephaiah and Uzziel, who led five hundred men of the tribe of Simeon to Mount Seir (1 Chr 4:42). The surrounding passage places this expedition in the days of King Hezekiah of Judah. The following verse says the Simeonites struck down the remaining Amalekites there and settled in their place. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates these events to about 715 BC. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the Septuagint gives the name as "Noadiah." Smith's renders the name as "servant of Jehovah" and Hitchcock's Bible Names as "child of the Lord." He should not be confused with another Neariah, a descendant of David in the royal line listed earlier in 1 Chronicles 3.

Nebai was one of the leaders of the people whose names were set to the sealed covenant in Nehemiah's time, when the returned exiles pledged to keep the law of God (Neh 10:19). He appears in a list of "chiefs of the people" alongside Hariph and Anathoth, and nothing else is recorded about him. Smith's Bible Dictionary treats the name as standing for a family among the heads of the people rather than for a single individual. Since some names in this list match places or clans mentioned elsewhere (Anathoth, for example, is also a town), that reading is possible, but the verse itself does not settle it. The name's meaning is uncertain. Smith's gives "fruitful" and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "budding" or "speaking."

Nebo was the ancestor or head of a family whose descendants are listed in Ezra 10:43. Seven of them, Jeiel, Mattithiah, Zabad, Zebina, Jadau, Joel and Benaiah, were among the men who had married foreign wives after the return from exile in Babylon. By inference from the surrounding chapter, they agreed to send those wives away under Ezra's reform. Nothing else is recorded about Nebo himself. Because Ezra 2:29 and Neh 7:33 also mention people of a place called Nebo, the phrase "sons of Nebo" may refer to people from that town rather than to descendants of one man. This entry treats Nebo as a person. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "that speaks or prophesies."

Nebushasban was a Babylonian official who held the title Rabsaris at the time Jerusalem fell to Nebuchadnezzar. Easton's Bible Dictionary explains his name as "adorer of Nebo" or "Nebo saves me". It takes Rabsaris to mean chief chamberlain, while Smith's Bible Dictionary takes it to mean chief of the eunuchs. Smith's also suggests he probably succeeded Ashpenaz, who held the same office in Dan 1:3. He appears only in Jer 39:13. There he is named with Nebuzaradan the captain of the guard, Nergalsharezer the Rabmag, and the other princes of the king of Babylon. By the context of the passage, these officials were sent to take Jeremiah out of the court of the prison and hand him over to Gedaliah. The Bible records nothing more about him.

Nedabiah was one of the sons of Jehoiachin (also called Jeconiah), the king of Judah who was taken captive to Babylon. He is named only once, in the list of David's royal descendants after the exile, as the last of seven sons in 1 Chr 3:18. His brothers were Shealtiel, Malchiram, Pedaiah, Shenazar, Jecamiah and Hoshama. A Zedekiah is also counted among his brothers, though 1 Chr 3:16 may name him as Jehoiachin's son or as his brother, so the relationship is uncertain. Smith's Bible Dictionary calls him "apparently" a son of Jehoiachin, since the genealogy's wording leaves some room for doubt. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "moved of Jehovah." Nothing else is recorded about his life.

Nehemiah, son of Azbuk, was the ruler of half the district of Beth-zur who helped repair Jerusalem's wall in the days of Nehemiah the governor. He is mentioned only once. According to Neh 3:16, he worked on the section running to a point opposite the tombs of David, as far as the artificial pool and the "house of the mighty," probably a barracks or guardhouse for warriors. Beth-zur was a town in the hill country of Judah, south of Jerusalem, and his district appears to have been divided between two officials. He is a different man from Nehemiah son of Hachaliah, the governor who organized the rebuilding, and from others of the same name. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "consolation" or "repentance of the Lord."

Nehushta was the mother of Jehoiachin, king of Judah, and the daughter of Elnathan of Jerusalem (2 Kgs 24:8). She was the wife of King Jehoiakim, Jehoiachin's father. Her name is usually taken to mean "bronze" or "copper" (Easton's Bible Dictionary). Her son became king at eighteen and reigned in Jerusalem only three months. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that when Jerusalem fell to Babylon she was taken into exile with her son and his court. Later passages, 2 Kgs 24:12 and Jer 29:2, mention the king's mother among the captives, and she is probably the queen mother addressed in Jer 13:18. Through Jehoiachin, who appears as Jechonias in Matthew's genealogy, she belongs to the royal line traced to Jesus. Her father Elnathan is probably the official of that name in Jehoiakim's court mentioned in Jer 26:22 and 36:12, though this identification is an inference.

Nemuel was a man of the tribe of Reuben, a son of Eliab and the brother of Dathan and Abiram. He is named only once, in the census list of Reuben's descendants taken in the plains of Moab (Num 26:9). He is listed first among Eliab's sons, and Smith's Bible Dictionary takes him to be the eldest. His brothers Dathan and Abiram are remembered for joining Korah's rebellion against Moses and Aaron, but the text says nothing about Nemuel taking part. Nothing more is recorded of him. The same name belongs to a different man, a son of Simeon, in the same census chapter, so the two should be kept apart.

Nepheg was a Levite, a son of Izhar and a brother of Korah and Zichri. He is named only once, in the genealogy of Levi's descendants in Exod 6:21. Izhar was a son of Kohath (Exod 6:18), so Nepheg belonged to the Kohathite clan of the tribe of Levi, as STEPBible Proper Names notes. His brother Korah later led the rebellion against Moses together with Dathan and Abiram (Num 16). Shelomoth, also listed as his brother, is named in 1 Chr 23:18 as the chief of Izhar's descendants, though he may be a later descendant rather than a direct son. Nothing else is recorded about Nepheg. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives the meaning of his name as "sprout" or "shoot." A different Nepheg was one of David's sons born in Jerusalem (2 Sam 5:15).

Nereus was a Christian in Rome to whom Paul sent greetings near the end of his letter to the Romans (Rom 16:15). Paul greets him together with his sister, whose name is not given, and with Philologus, Julia, Olympas and "all the saints which are with them." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia takes this group to have formed a small community or house church. That encyclopedia also notes that the name Nereis appears on an inscription of the period listing servants of the emperor's household. Later church tradition, recorded in Smith's Bible Dictionary, holds that Nereus was beheaded at Terracina, probably in the reign of Nerva. A later account, the Acts of Nereus and Achilleus, calls him a chamberlain of Domitilla, a niece of the emperor Vespasian. Whether that Nereus is the man Paul greets is uncertain. Nothing more about him is recorded in the Bible.

Neri was an ancestor of Jesus named in Luke's genealogy, where he appears as the father of Salathiel and grandfather of Zorobabel (Zerubbabel) (Luke 3:27). The facts here also name his father as Melchi, as the following verse in Luke states. His line belongs to the tribe of Judah. Luke traces it back to David through David's son Nathan, so Neri probably lived around the time of the Babylonian exile. Matthew 1:12 and 1 Chr 3:17 name Jeconiah, not Neri, as Salathiel's father. Explanations offered for this include adoption, a levirate marriage, or Luke following a different line of descent, and the text does not settle the question. Smith's Bible Dictionary treats Neri as a short form of Neriah, meaning "the LORD is my lamp". Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "my light." Nothing else is recorded about him.

Nethaneel was the fourth son of Jesse of the tribe of Judah, and so a brother of King David. He appears only in the genealogy of 1 Chr 2:14, which lists Jesse's sons in birth order: Eliab, Abinadab, Shimma (Shammah), Nethaneel, Raddai, Ozem and David. Nothing else is recorded about him. His name, according to Smith's Bible Dictionary, means "given of God" and is the same name as Nathanael. Several other men in the Bible share it. The Chronicles list names seven sons, while 1 Sam 16:10–11 and 1 Sam 17:12 speak of eight. Elihu, described in 1 Chr 27:18 as one of David's brothers, is also counted among the siblings here.

Nethaneel was a priest in the time of David, one of seven priests who blew trumpets before the ark of God when it was brought up to Jerusalem (1 Chr 15:24). He is named alongside Shebaniah, Jehoshaphat, Amasai, Zechariah, Benaiah and Eliezer, while Obed-edom and Jehiah served as doorkeepers for the ark. By inference from the surrounding chapter, this was the procession that carried the ark from the house of Obed-edom to the tent David had prepared for it, as Smith's Bible Dictionary also notes. The name means "given of God" and is the same as Nathanael. Several other men in the Bible share this name, and nothing beyond this single mention identifies this priest further.

Nethaneel was a Levite in the time of King David, known only as the father of Shemaiah. In 1 Chr 24:6, Shemaiah recorded the drawing of lots that divided the priestly families of Eleazar and Ithamar into their courses. This was done before the king, the princes, Zadok the priest and Ahimelech son of Abiathar. The verse calls Shemaiah "the son of Nethaneel the scribe," and it can be read two ways. Smith's Bible Dictionary takes "the scribe" to mean Shemaiah. The STEPBible proper-names index applies it to Nethaneel. This entry follows the more common reading, in which Shemaiah was the scribe. Nethaneel is probably a Levite himself, since his son is called one. His name means "given of God." Several other men in the Bible share the name, and nothing links this Nethaneel with any of them.

Nethaneel was a Levite named in 1 Chr 26:4 as the fifth son of Obed-edom, listed after Shemaiah, Jehozabad, Joah and Sacar. The next verse (1 Chr 26:5) adds Ammiel, Issachar and Peulthai as further brothers. The passage falls within the arrangement of the temple gatekeepers' divisions in David's time, so Nethaneel was probably one of the gatekeepers. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes him as a temple porter of the Korahite family. Nothing else is recorded about him. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "given of God," and Hitchcock's Bible Names treats it as the same as Nathanael. Several other men in the Bible bear this name, and this entry concerns only the son of Obed-edom.

Nethaneel was one of the princes of Judah whom King Jehoshaphat sent out in the third year of his reign to teach in the cities of Judah. He is named alongside Benhail, Obadiah, Zechariah and Michaiah (2 Chr 17:7). The king is not named in this verse, but the surrounding chapter makes clear it is Jehoshaphat. The following verses add that Levites and priests went with these princes and that they taught from the book of the law of the Lord, as Easton's Bible Dictionary also notes. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates the mission to about 912 BC and gives the name's meaning as "given of God," the same name as Nathanael. Nothing more is recorded about him, and he should not be confused with the several other men of the same name in the Bible.

Nethaneel was a chief Levite in the reign of King Josiah of Judah. He is named only in 2 Chr 35:9, as a brother of Conaniah and Shemaiah. Together with Hashabiah, Jeiel and Jozabad, these leaders of the Levites gave the other Levites five thousand sheep and goats and five hundred oxen as offerings for the great Passover that Josiah held. "Brethren" here may mean fellow Levites rather than brothers by birth. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates this Passover to about 628 BC. The name means "given of God" and is the same as Nathanael. Several other men in the Bible share the name, so this Nethaneel should not be confused with them.

Nethaneel was one of the sons, or descendants, of Pashur listed in Ezra 10:22 among the priests who had married foreign wives in the period after the return from exile. The surrounding passage records that these men agreed to put away their foreign wives in response to Ezra's reforms. Pashur's family is grouped with the priestly houses in this list, so Nethaneel was probably a priest, and the STEPBible Proper Names index identifies him that way. Nothing more is recorded about him. Several other men in the Bible share this name, which Hitchcock's Bible Names treats as the same as Nathanael, and this Nethaneel should not be confused with them.

Nethaneel was a priest who headed the priestly family of Jedaiah after the return from exile in Babylon. Neh 12:21 lists him in a roll of priestly family heads. By inference from the surrounding passage, this roll belongs to the days of Joiakim the high priest, son of Jeshua, which Smith's Bible Dictionary places about 446 BC. The verse records only his name and the family he represented, so nothing more is known of him. His name means "given of God" and is a form of Nathanael. Several other men in the Bible share the name, and this Nethaneel should not be confused with them.

Nethaneel was one of the Levite musicians who played "the musical instruments of David" at the dedication of the rebuilt wall of Jerusalem, in the procession led by Ezra the scribe (Neh 12:36). He is named among the "brethren" of Zechariah son of Jonathan, whom the previous verse (Neh 12:35) traces back to Asaph, the musician of David's time. This entry treats Nethaneel as another son of Jonathan, so Zechariah, Shemaiah, Azarael, Milalai, Gilalai, Maai, Judah and Hanani appear as his brothers. The word "brethren" could also mean kinsmen or fellow Levites more broadly. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him as a Levite of the sons of Asaph, and Easton's Bible Dictionary calls him a priest's son. The dedication probably took place around 445 BC, by inference from context. Several other men in the Bible share this name, which means "given of God."

Nethaniah was a Levite in the reign of King Jehoshaphat of Judah. He is named in 2 Chr 17:8 among nine Levites who went out with two priests, Elishama and Jehoram. The surrounding passage explains why. In the third year of his reign Jehoshaphat sent officials to teach in the cities of Judah, and these Levites and priests went with them, carrying the book of the law of the Lord as they taught the people. Nethaniah is mentioned nowhere else, and nothing more is known about him. Several other men in the Bible share his name, so he should not be confused with them. The name means "given of the Lord" or "Yah has given" (Hitchcock's Bible Names; International Standard Bible Encyclopedia). Smith's Bible Dictionary dates his service to about 912 BC, an estimate.

Nethaniah was the father of Jehudi and the son of Shelemiah, and through Shelemiah a descendant of Cushi. He appears only once, in Jer 36:14, as part of his son's lineage. The passage tells how the princes of Judah sent Jehudi to bring Baruch and the scroll he had been reading to the people. The scroll held the words Jeremiah had dictated to him. The surrounding chapter places these events in the reign of King Jehoiakim, so Nethaniah probably lived in the late seventh century BC. Nothing more is recorded about him. His name means "Yah has given" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia) or "the gift of the Lord" (Hitchcock's Bible Names). Several other men in the Bible bear the same name, including the father of Ishmael who killed Gedaliah. This entry treats Jehudi's father as a separate person from them.

Nicanor was one of the seven men chosen by the whole body of believers in the early Jerusalem church, alongside Stephen, Philip, Prochorus, Timon, Parmenas and Nicolas (Acts 6:5). The surrounding passage explains that the seven were appointed to oversee the daily distribution of food so the apostles could devote themselves to prayer and teaching. Tradition calls them the first deacons, and Easton's Bible Dictionary describes Nicanor as one of the seven deacons. The event is dated to about AD 30, by inference from context. His name is Greek and means "conqueror" or "victorious" (Hitchcock's Bible Names). Like the other names on the list, it may suggest he came from the Greek-speaking Jewish community whose complaint led to the appointment, though that is an inference. Nothing more is recorded of him. He is a different person from the Syrian general Nicanor in the books of Maccabees.

Nicolas was one of the seven men chosen by the early Jerusalem church to serve its members, about AD 30 by inference from context. Acts 6:5 lists him last among the seven, after Stephen, Philip, Prochorus, Nicanor, Timon and Parmenas, and describes him as a proselyte of Antioch. That makes him a Gentile by birth who had converted to Judaism before becoming a follower of Jesus, and the only one of the seven whose non-Jewish origin is noted. The surrounding passage explains that the seven were appointed to oversee the daily distribution of food to widows, so the apostles could focus on prayer and preaching, and that the apostles laid hands on them (Acts 6:1–6). Later tradition calls these men the first deacons. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "victory of the people." Some early church traditions connected him with the Nicolaitans mentioned in Rev 2:6, 15, a link the biblical text itself does not make.

Noadiah son of Binnui was a Levite in the time of Ezra. According to Ezra 8:33, on the fourth day after Ezra's group reached Jerusalem from Babylon, the silver, gold and sacred vessels they had brought for the temple were weighed in the house of God. The priest Meremoth son of Uriah did the weighing, with Eleazar son of Phinehas and two Levites, Jozabad son of Jeshua and Noadiah, assisting. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the parallel account in 1 Esdras calls him Moeth son of Sabannus. His name is usually explained as meaning "Yahweh has met" or "meeting with Yahweh." The name Noadiah is shared by others in the Bible, including a prophetess who opposed Nehemiah, but this entry concerns only the Levite. Nothing more is known of him.

Noadiah was a prophetess in Jerusalem in the time of Nehemiah, about the mid-400s BC by inference from context. She is mentioned only once, in Nehemiah's prayer asking God to remember Tobiah, Sanballat, Noadiah and "the rest of the prophets" who tried to make him afraid (Neh 6:14). By inference from the surrounding chapter, this happened while Nehemiah was rebuilding Jerusalem's walls, when his opponents were trying to frighten him into stopping the work. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes her as a false prophetess who was bribed by Tobiah and Sanballat to stir up discontent in the city. The text itself says nothing more about what she said or did. Her name, often explained as "meeting with the Lord," is also borne by a Levite man in the time of Ezra (Ezra 8:33), a different person.

Nobah was an Israelite who captured the town of Kenath and its surrounding villages and renamed it Nobah after himself (Num 32:42). The verse closes an account of the tribe of Manasseh's conquests east of the Jordan, alongside those of Machir and Jair, so by inference from the passage he was probably a leader or clan head of Manasseh. Nothing else is recorded about his family or his life. A place called Nobah, mentioned near Jogbehah in Judg 8:11, may be the same renamed town, although this is uncertain. Kenath is often identified with modern Qanawat in southern Syria. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of his name as "that barks or yelps."

Obadiah was a man of the tribe of Judah and a descendant of King David, named once in the genealogy of David's royal line in 1 Chr 3:21. This entry treats him as a son of Hananiah, alongside Pelatiah, Jesaiah, Rephaiah, Arnan and Shechaniah. The verse's wording ("the sons of Rephaiah, the sons of Arnan, the sons of Obadiah") is ambiguous, and it may instead list separate Davidic families whose link to Hananiah is not stated. From the surrounding genealogy, Hananiah was a son of Zerubbabel (1 Chr 3:19), which places Obadiah in the generations after the return from exile. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates him to about 470 BC. His name means "servant of the Lord." Nothing else is recorded about him, and he is one of several men in the Bible named Obadiah.

Obadiah was a man of the tribe of Issachar, a son of Izrahiah and a grandson of Uzzi, named in the genealogy of 1 Chr 7:3. His brothers were Michael, Joel and Ishiah. The verse calls the group "five" while naming only four sons, so Izrahiah himself is probably counted among them, and all five are described as chief men. The verses just before trace Uzzi back to Tola, the firstborn son of Issachar. Nothing else is recorded about him. Smith's Bible Dictionary places him about 1014 BC, an estimate drawn from context. His name means "servant of the Lord" (Hitchcock's Bible Names). Several other men in the Bible share the name, and this Obadiah should not be confused with them, including the prophet.

Obadiah was a Gadite warrior, listed second among the Gadite leaders who came over to David (1 Chr 12:9). The surrounding passage, 1 Chr 12:8–15, describes these men as skilled fighters with faces like lions and as swift as gazelles. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary place their joining at Ziklag, while David was a fugitive from Saul. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia calls him a chief of the Gadites. His name means "servant of the Lord." Several other men in the Bible share the name, including the prophet of the book of Obadiah and the steward of King Ahab's household. Nothing else is recorded about this Obadiah.

Obadiah was a man of the tribe of Zebulun and the father of Ishmaiah, named only in 1 Chr 27:19. The verse belongs to a list of the leaders of the tribes of Israel under King David, where Ishmaiah son of Obadiah is given as the leader for Zebulun. Nothing else is recorded about Obadiah himself. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia read the verse as making Ishmaiah the tribal chief. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the Tyndale STEPBible names list describe Obadiah himself as a prince or ruler of Zebulun in David's time. This entry follows the reading that Ishmaiah held the office, which matches the wording of the list. The name means "servant of the Lord." Several other men in the Bible share it, including the prophet and a steward of King Ahab, and this Obadiah should not be confused with them.

Obadiah was one of the princes, or officials, of Judah whom King Jehoshaphat sent out in the third year of his reign to teach in the cities of Judah. He is named alongside Benhail, Zechariah, Nethaneel and Michaiah (2 Chr 17:7). The following verses, 2 Chr 17:8–9, say that Levites and priests went with these princes and that they taught the people from the book of the law of the Lord. Nothing else is recorded about this Obadiah. Several other men in the Bible share the name, which means "servant of the Lord" (Hitchcock's Bible Names), and there is no clear link between this official and any of them.

Obadiah was a Levite from the clan of Merari who served as one of the overseers of the workmen repairing the temple in Jerusalem during the reign of King Josiah. 2 Chr 34:12 names him with Jahath, another Merarite, and with Zechariah and Meshullam of the Kohathites as the men who directed the work, which the text says was done faithfully. Other Levites skilled with musical instruments were also involved. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates these repairs to about 623 BC. His name means "servant of the Lord." Several other men in the Bible share the name, and nothing further is recorded about this Obadiah.

Obadiah son of Jehiel was a family head of the clan descended from Joab. He returned from Babylon to Jerusalem with Ezra during the reign of the Persian king Artaxerxes, bringing 218 men of his family with him (Ezra 8:9). Smith's Bible Dictionary places him in the second caravan of returning exiles, the one Ezra led. His name means "servant of the Lord," according to Hitchcock's Bible Names. Nothing else is recorded about him, and he should be kept distinct from the several other men in the Bible called Obadiah, including the prophet and Ahab's household steward.

Obadiah was one of the men who set their seal to the written covenant made under Nehemiah, in which the returned community in Jerusalem pledged to keep the law of God. His name appears in a list in Neh 10:5. The names in that part of the list (Neh 10:1–8) are followed by the statement "these were the priests," so he was probably a priest. Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests the name may stand for a priestly family rather than a single individual. The name means "servant of the Lord" and is borne by several different men in the Bible. Nothing further is recorded about this Obadiah, and it is uncertain whether he is the same as any other person of that name.

Obadiah was the prophet whose message makes up the Book of Obadiah, the shortest book in the Old Testament. The book opens by calling itself "the vision of Obadiah" and presents a message from the Lord concerning Edom, the nation descended from Esau, announcing that the nations are being summoned to rise against it in battle (Obad 1:1). Nothing is recorded about his family, home or life. His name means "servant of the Lord" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia), and several other men in the Bible share it, including the steward of King Ahab's household. There is no clear basis for identifying the prophet with any of them. The date of his prophecy is uncertain. This entry places it about 585 BC, by inference from context, shortly after the Babylonian destruction of Jerusalem, when Edom is often thought to have taken advantage of Judah's fall.

Obed was one of David's mighty warriors, named near the end of the list of David's heroes in 1 Chronicles 11. He appears alongside Eliel and Jasiel the Mesobaite (1 Chr 11:47). This list continues beyond the parallel roster in 2 Samuel 23, and nothing more is recorded about him, neither his family, his hometown nor any deeds. He is a different man from the better-known Obed, son of Boaz and Ruth and grandfather of David, and from the other men of this name in the Bible. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "a servant" or "workman." Smith's Bible Dictionary places him in David's time, about 1046 BC, a date inferred from his place in the account rather than stated in the text.

Obed was a Levite, one of the sons of Shemaiah, listed among the gatekeepers of the temple in the divisions organized in David's time (1 Chr 26:7). His brothers were Othni, Rephael, Elzabad, Elihu and Semachiah. The verse notes that Elzabad's brothers were strong men. The surrounding passage (1 Chr 26:4–6) makes Shemaiah the firstborn son of Obed-edom, so Obed was probably Obed-edom's grandson. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him this way, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia counts him among the Korahite doorkeepers. Smith's dates him to about 1017 BC, an estimate drawn from context. His name is usually taken to mean "servant" or "worker" (Hitchcock's Bible Names). Several other people in the Bible are also called Obed, including the grandfather of David. This man is a different person, known only from this one list.

Obed was the father of Azariah, one of the captains of hundreds whom the priest Jehoiada brought into a covenant with him in the seventh year (2 Chr 23:1). That covenant began the uprising that removed Queen Athaliah from the throne of Judah and crowned the young Joash, as the rest of the chapter and the parallel account in 2 Kgs 11 describe. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates these events to sometime before 876 BC. Obed is known only as Azariah's father, and nothing else is recorded about him. The name, which Hitchcock's Bible Names takes to mean "servant" or "workman," belongs to several men in the Bible.
