This Obed is distinct from the better-known Obed who was the son of Ruth and Boaz and the grandfather of David.

Obil was an Ishmaelite who was in charge of King David's camels. He appears once, in the list of officials who managed the king's property (1 Chr 27:30). Next to him in that list, Jehdeiah the Meronothite oversaw the donkeys. As a descendant of Ishmael, Obil probably came from a people known for desert travel and camel herding, which may explain why he held this post. The meaning of his name is uncertain. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives "camel driver", which fits his role, and Smith's Bible Dictionary similarly renders it "chief of the camels". Hitchcock's Bible Names instead gives "that weeps". Smith's dates his service to about 1050 BC. Nothing else is recorded about him.

Oded was a prophet of the Lord in Samaria during the reign of Ahaz of Judah, when Pekah king of Israel defeated Judah and brought a large number of captives back to Samaria. Oded went out to meet the returning army and told them that God had handed Judah over to them because he was angry with Judah, but that they had killed in a rage that reached up to heaven. The following verses (2 Chr 28:10–15) record him warning them not to enslave their fellow Judeans. Some leaders of Ephraim backed him, and the captives were clothed, fed and taken back to Jericho. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates these events to about 739 BC. This Oded is distinct from another Oded named as the father of the prophet Azariah in the days of Asa (2 Chr 15:1). Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "to sustain, hold or lift up."

Ohel was a son of Zerubbabel and a member of the tribe of Judah, descended through the royal line of David. He is mentioned only once, in the genealogy of 1 Chr 3:20, where he is the second name in a group of five sons: Hashubah, Ohel, Berechiah, Hasadiah and Jushab-hesed. The preceding verse names Zerubbabel's other children, Meshullam, Hananiah and their sister Shelomith. Counting those two brothers first, Easton's Bible Dictionary calls Ohel the fourth son. Abiud is also counted among his brothers here, because Matthew's genealogy of Jesus names Abiud as a son of Zerubbabel. Why the five sons are listed separately is not explained. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both give the meaning of his name as "tent." Nothing else is recorded about his life.

Olympas was a Christian at Rome to whom Paul sent greetings near the end of his letter to the Romans (Rom 16:15). He is named in a single greeting with Philologus, Julia, Nereus and Nereus's sister, followed by "all the saints which are with them." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia takes this grouping to suggest that these believers formed a small community of their own, perhaps meeting together, within the early Roman church. The same work treats Olympas as a shortened form of the name Olympiodorus, and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives its meaning as "heavenly." Nothing else is recorded about him, and this is his only mention in the Bible.

Omri was a member of the tribe of Benjamin, one of the nine sons of Becher listed in the Benjamite genealogy at 1 Chr 7:8. His brothers were Zemira, Joash, Eliezer, Elioenai, Jerimoth, Abiah, Anathoth and Alameth. Smith's Bible Dictionary identifies Becher as a son of Benjamin, which would make Omri a grandson of Benjamin. Nothing else is recorded about him beyond his place in this family list. He is not the same person as Omri the king of Israel, father of Ahab, and the name is shared by several other people in the Bible. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "pupil of Jehovah," while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "sheaf of corn."

Omri was a man of the tribe of Judah, descended through Pharez (Perez), who appears only in a genealogy in 1 Chr 9:4. He was the son of Imri, the grandson of Bani, and the father of Ammihud. His grandson Uthai is listed among the people of Judah who lived in Jerusalem. The surrounding passage concerns those who resettled there after the exile, so Omri himself probably lived some generations earlier. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia and STEPBible's proper names index connect him with Jerusalem, but the verse places only his descendant Uthai there. Nothing else is recorded about him. He is a different man from Omri the king of Israel and from the other men of this name. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "sheaf of corn," and Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "pupil of Jehovah."

Omri, son of Michael, was the leader of the tribe of Issachar during the reign of King David. He appears in a list of the chief officers over the tribes of Israel (1 Chr 27:16–22), where he is named as the officer for Issachar. The single verse that mentions him gives no further details about his life or duties. He should not be confused with other men of the same name, most notably Omri the later king of Israel and father of Ahab. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates him to about 1030 BC, and the name is explained as "pupil of Jehovah" there and as "sheaf of corn" in Hitchcock's Bible Names.

Ophrah was a man of the tribe of Judah, named once in the genealogies of Judah as the son of Meonothai (1 Chr 4:14). Nothing else is recorded about him. The surrounding verses suggest Meonothai belonged to the family of Othniel, the son of Kenaz: the preceding verse lists Othniel's sons, and some ancient Greek manuscripts read Meonothai there as well, though the Hebrew text does not. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary give the meaning of his name as "fawn." The same name belongs to two towns in the Old Testament, one in Benjamin and one in Manasseh (the home of Gideon), but this Ophrah is a person and is not connected to either place in the text.

Oren was a man of the tribe of Judah, the third of five sons of Jerahmeel listed in 1 Chr 2:25. His father Jerahmeel was the firstborn of Hezron, and his brothers were Ram, Bunah, Ozem and Ahijah. The facts also name Onam as a sibling. The next verse (1 Chr 2:26) says Jerahmeel had a second wife, Atarah, who was Onam's mother, so Onam was probably Oren's half-brother. Oren appears only in this genealogy, and nothing more is recorded about him or his descendants. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "ash" or "pine," and Smith's Bible Dictionary as "pine tree." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that some Greek manuscripts spell the name Aran.

Othni was a Levite, the first named of the sons of Shemaiah in the list of temple gatekeepers organized in David's time (1 Chr 26:7). His brothers were Rephael, Obed, Elzabad, Elihu and Semachiah, and the verse calls members of the family "strong men." Easton's Bible Dictionary describes him as a "mighty man of valour." The surrounding chapter (1 Chr 26:4) names Shemaiah as the firstborn son of Obed-edom, so Othni was Obed-edom's grandson. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia counts the family among the Korahite Levites, and the context places him among the gatekeepers assigned to guard the sanctuary. He is mentioned nowhere else. The meaning of his name is uncertain. Easton's and Smith's dictionaries give "lion of Jehovah," and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "my time" or "my hour."

Ozem was a son of Jesse of the tribe of Judah and a brother of King David. The genealogy in 1 Chronicles names him as the sixth son, listed just before David, the seventh (1 Chr 2:15). His other brothers named there are Eliab, Abinadab, Shammah, Nethaneel and Raddai. A later passage mentions an Elihu as one of David's brothers (1 Chr 27:18). Nothing is recorded about Ozem beyond his name and his place in the family. The accounts in 1 Samuel say Jesse had eight sons (1 Sam 16:10–11; 17:12), while Chronicles lists only seven. The meaning of the name is uncertain. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "power," and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "that fasts." The name is shared by another man, a son of Jerahmeel in the same tribe (1 Chr 2:25), who is a different person.

Ozem was a man of the tribe of Judah, one of the sons of Jerahmeel, the firstborn of Hezron. He appears only in the genealogy of 1 Chr 2:25, listed fourth among Jerahmeel's sons after Ram, Bunah and Oren, and before Ahijah. The next verse (1 Chr 2:26) adds that Jerahmeel had another wife, Atarah, who was the mother of Onam, so Onam was probably Ozem's half-brother. Through Hezron, Ozem belonged to the line of Judah's son Perez, and the STEPBible names data call him a nephew of Caleb, Jerahmeel's brother. Nothing else is recorded about him. Another Ozem, a brother of David, appears in the same chapter (1 Chr 2:15), and the two should be kept distinct. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "power," while the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats its meaning as unknown.

Paarai the Arbite was one of David's mighty men, the elite warriors listed in 2 Sam 23. He appears only once, named between Hezrai the Carmelite and Bani the Gadite, and nothing more is recorded about him. The title "Arbite" probably refers to Arab, a town in the hill country of Judah, though this is inferred. The parallel list in 1 Chr 11:37 names "Naarai the son of Ezbai" at this point, and Easton's Bible Dictionary, Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia all take Naarai to be the same man, the difference in spelling probably arising in copying. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of his name as "opening," while the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests "devotee of Peor."

Pahath-moab is named in Neh 3:11 as the father of Hashub, who repaired a section of the wall of Jerusalem and the Tower of the Furnaces in Nehemiah's day. Nothing else is said about him personally. Elsewhere Pahath-moab is the name of a large family group whose members returned from exile in Babylon (Ezra 2:6; Neh 7:11), and a leader of that name joined in sealing the covenant under Nehemiah (Neh 10:14). So "son of Pahath-moab" here may mean a member of that family line rather than a literal son. The name, which probably means "governor of Moab," is shared by several people, and it is uncertain how this figure relates to the others.

Pahath-moab was one of the "chief of the people" who set their seal to the covenant made in Nehemiah's time, when the community in Jerusalem bound itself to keep the law (Neh 10:14). He appears in that list next to Parosh, Elam, Zatthu and Bani. The name means "governor of Moab." Several of the names in this list also appear elsewhere as family names. Ezra 2:6 and Neh 7:11 record a large clan called "the children of Pahath-moab" among the exiles who returned from Babylon. So this signer probably stood for that clan or was its head, rather than being a person known in any other way. Because the name is used for both a family and its leaders, it is not certain which individual is meant here.

Palal was the son of Uzai and one of the men who repaired the walls of Jerusalem under Nehemiah after the return from exile. His only mention is in the list of builders in Neh 3:25. His section lay opposite the turning, or angle, of the wall and the tower that projected from the king's upper house, near the court of the prison. Pedaiah the son of Parosh worked on the next section after him. Nothing more is known of his family or later life. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives the meaning of his name as "judge."

Palti son of Raphu was the man from the tribe of Benjamin chosen as one of the twelve leaders Moses sent from the wilderness of Paran to explore the land of Canaan (Num 13:9). Each tribe supplied one representative for this mission. By inference from the rest of Numbers 13–14, Palti was among the ten spies who brought back a discouraging report, since only Joshua and Caleb are singled out for urging Israel to enter the land. Nothing else is recorded about him. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "deliverance from the Lord," and Smith's Bible Dictionary renders it "whom Jehovah delivers." He is distinct from Phalti (also spelled Palti in some translations), the man to whom Saul gave his daughter Michal.

Paltiel son of Azzan was the leader ("prince") of the tribe of Issachar named in Num 34:26. He appears in a list of tribal leaders whom the Lord appointed, according to the surrounding passage, to work with Eleazar the priest and Joshua in dividing the land of Canaan west of the Jordan among the tribes. Nothing else is recorded about him. His name is usually explained as meaning "God delivers" or "deliverance of God" (Easton's Bible Dictionary; Smith's Bible Dictionary). Smith's Bible Dictionary dates his appointment to about 1450 BC. The same name is also borne by a different man, Michal's husband, called Paltiel in 2 Sam 3:15 and Phalti in 1 Sam 25:44, who should not be confused with this tribal leader.

Parmashta was one of the ten sons of Haman, the official who plotted to destroy the Jews of the Persian Empire. He is named only in the list of Haman's sons in Esth 9:7–10. By context these verses record the men killed by the Jews in Shushan (Susa), the Persian royal city, on the day Haman's decree was reversed, the events remembered at the festival of Purim. His brothers were Parshandatha, Dalphon, Aspatha, Poratha, Adalia, Aridatha, Arisai, Aridai and Vajezatha. The meaning of his name is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives "strong-fisted," Smith's Bible Dictionary "superior," and Hitchcock's Bible Names "a yearling bull." The name is probably Persian. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the Septuagint renders it Marmasima. Smith's dates his death to about 473 BC.

Parmenas was one of the seven men chosen by the Jerusalem church to take charge of the daily distribution of food to its widows, so that the apostles could devote themselves to prayer and teaching (Acts 6:5). By inference from context, this took place about AD 30. He is named sixth in the list, alongside Stephen, Philip, Prochorus, Nicanor, Timon and Nicolas. His name is Greek, a shortened form of Parmenides according to the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia. Like the other six, he probably came from the Greek-speaking Jewish believers whose widows had been overlooked. The seven are often called deacons, though the passage does not use that title for them. Scripture does not mention him again. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia record a tradition that he was martyred at Philippi during the reign of the emperor Trajan.

Parnach was a man of the tribe of Zebulun, known only as the father of Elizaphan. In Num 34:25 Elizaphan is named as the prince, or leader, of Zebulun among the tribal representatives chosen to help divide the land of Canaan among the Israelite tribes. Since his son was a leader in the generation that was to enter the land, Parnach probably belonged to the generation that left Egypt, though this is an inference. Nothing else is recorded about him. The meaning of his name is uncertain: the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives "gifted," while Hitchcock's Bible Names suggests "a bull striking, or struck."

Parosh was the father of Pedaiah, who repaired a section of the Jerusalem wall in Nehemiah's day. Pedaiah worked next to Palal, near the tower that projected from the king's upper palace by the court of the prison (Neh 3:25). Nothing else is said about Parosh himself. Parosh is also the name of a large family that returned from exile (Ezra 2:3; Neh 7:8), so "son of Parosh" may mean Pedaiah was a member of that clan rather than the son of a man by that name. The text does not settle this. Because several people bear this name, it is uncertain how this Parosh relates to the others. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "a flea."

Parosh was one of the chiefs of the people who set their seal to the written covenant made in the time of Nehemiah, in which the returned exiles pledged to keep the law of God (Neh 10:14). He heads the list of lay leaders who signed. Parosh is also the name of a large family that returned from Babylon with Zerubbabel (Ezra 2:3; Neh 7:8). Because the names that follow in Neh 10:14, such as Pahathmoab, Elam and Zatthu, are also family names from those return lists, this Parosh was probably the head or representative of that clan rather than a separately known individual. STEPBible's proper-names index likewise describes him as a clan leader. Several people in the Bible bear this name, and the text says nothing more about this one. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives its meaning as "a flea."

Parshandatha was one of the ten sons of Haman, the official of the Persian king Ahasuerus who plotted to destroy the Jews. He is named first in the list of Haman's sons in Esth 9:7–10. Smith's Bible Dictionary and Easton's Bible Dictionary take this placement to mean he was the eldest. The surrounding passage records that the Jews killed the ten sons in Shushan, the Persian royal city, on the day Haman's decree was meant to be carried out. His brothers were Dalphon, Aspatha, Poratha, Adalia, Aridatha, Parmashta, Arisai, Aridai and Vajezatha. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests the name may come from a Persian phrase meaning "given by prayer," and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the same meaning. Smith's dates his death to about 473 BC, which is an estimate drawn from context.

Paruah was the father of Jehoshaphat, one of the twelve officers King Solomon appointed over districts of Israel. Jehoshaphat's district was the territory of Issachar (1 Kgs 4:17). The surrounding passage explains that each of these officers supplied food for the king and his household for one month of the year. Nothing else is recorded about Paruah himself; he is known only through his son's name. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary give the meaning of his name as "flourishing," and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives "blooming." Smith's Bible Dictionary dates his son's service to about 1017 BC, an estimate drawn from the timing of Solomon's reign.

Pasach was a son of Japhlet and a member of the tribe of Asher. He is named only once, in the genealogy of Asher's descendants, where he is listed first among Japhlet's three sons, followed by his brothers Bimhal and Ashvath (1 Chr 7:33). Japhlet appears in the preceding verse as a son of Heber, which places Pasach in the line of Heber, the grandson of Asher. Nothing else is recorded about his life. The meaning of his name is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives "clearing," Smith's Bible Dictionary "cut off," and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia "divider."

Paseah was a son of Eshton, named in the genealogy of the tribe of Judah in 1 Chr 4:12. His brothers were Beth-rapha and Tehinnah, and Tehinnah is called the father of Ir-nahash. The verse closes by calling this family "the men of Rechah," a group or place that is otherwise unknown. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes the passage as an obscure fragment of Judah's genealogies, and nothing more is recorded about Paseah himself. His name is usually explained as meaning "lame" or "limping" (Smith's Bible Dictionary; International Standard Bible Encyclopedia). Other men named Paseah appear elsewhere in the Bible, and this one should not be confused with them.

Paseah was the father of Jehoiada (called Joiada in many modern translations), who worked with Meshullam son of Besodeiah to repair the Old Gate of Jerusalem in Nehemiah's time. They laid its beams and set up its doors, locks and bars (Neh 3:6). Nothing else is said about Paseah himself. He appears only as the father who identifies his son. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives the name's meaning as "limping," and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "passing over; halting." Several people in the Bible share this name, including a man in the genealogy of Judah and the ancestor of a family of temple servants who returned from exile. This entry concerns only the father of the Old Gate repairer. Whether he is connected to either of the others is not stated.

Pashur was a priest who set his seal to the covenant made in the time of Nehemiah, the written pledge by the returned exiles to keep God's law. He appears in Neh 10:3 among the priests listed after Nehemiah the governor. The verse itself gives only his name, and the priestly role follows from the context of the list. Several men in the Bible bear this name, and they are hard to tell apart. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests he may be the same as another Pashur of the same period, probably the head of the priestly family of Pashur whose descendants returned from exile. The name has been explained as meaning "splitter" or "cleaver."

Pashur the son of Melchiah was an official of King Zedekiah of Judah, one of several men in the Bible named Pashur. In Jer 21:1 Zedekiah sent him, together with Zephaniah the son of Maaseiah the priest, to ask Jeremiah to inquire of the LORD. Judging from the following verses, this was during the Babylonian attack on Jerusalem. He is probably the same Pashur son of Malchiah who appears in Jer 38:1, where he is among the officials who heard Jeremiah's warnings and urged the king to have him put to death. He is distinct from Pashur the son of Immer, the priest who had Jeremiah beaten and put in the stocks (Jer 20:1–2). Some link him to the priestly family of Pashur son of Malchijah named in 1 Chr 9:12, though this is uncertain. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "whiteness."

Pashur is known only as the father of Gedaliah, one of the royal officials in Jerusalem who heard Jeremiah's prophecies during the Babylonian siege in the reign of Zedekiah (Jer 38:1). In the passage that follows, Gedaliah and the other officials urge the king to put Jeremiah to death, and the prophet is lowered into a cistern. Nothing else is recorded about Pashur himself. Several men share this name, and he is distinct from Pashur the son of Malchiah, who is named in the same verse. Some suggest he may be the priest Pashur son of Immer, who had Jeremiah beaten and put in stocks (Jer 20:1–2), but the text does not make the link, and the identification is uncertain. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "that extends or multiplies the hole" or "whiteness."

Patrobas was a Christian in Rome whom Paul greeted by name at the close of his letter to the Romans. He appears in a group of five men, Asyncritus, Phlegon, Hermas, Patrobas and Hermes, together with "the brethren which are with them" (Rom 16:14). This suggests, by inference, that they belonged to the same household or house church. Nothing more is said about him. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the name is a shortened form of Patrobius. A wealthy freedman of the emperor Nero with that name was later put to death by Galba, and this Patrobas may have been one of his dependents. Smith's Bible Dictionary likewise observes that the name was borne by members of the imperial household. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives its meaning as "paternal."

Pedahel, son of Ammihud, was the leader of the tribe of Naphtali in the list of Numbers 34. The surrounding chapter shows that these tribal leaders were appointed, one from each tribe, to help Eleazar the priest and Joshua divide the land of Canaan among the Israelites. This is his only mention in the Bible. Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries give the meaning of his name as "whom God redeems" or "redeemed of God." His father Ammihud should not be confused with other men of that name in the Old Testament.

Pedaiah was a man from Rumah whose daughter Zebudah became the wife of King Josiah of Judah and the mother of King Jehoiakim, who began to reign at twenty-five and ruled eleven years in Jerusalem (2 Kgs 23:36). Nothing else is recorded about him. Since Jehoiakim was the father of Jeconiah, who appears in Matthew's genealogy of Jesus, Pedaiah stands in that line through his daughter. The location of Rumah is uncertain. Some connect it with Arumah near Shechem, mentioned in Judg 9:41. The name means "Yah redeems" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia). Several other men in the Bible share the name, including a son of King Jeconiah in 1 Chr 3:18–19, and they should not be confused with this Pedaiah.

Pedaiah was the father of Joel, who led the half-tribe of Manasseh among the tribal rulers listed in King David's administration (1 Chr 27:20). Nothing else is recorded about him. Because the next verse (1 Chr 27:21) names a separate leader for the half of Manasseh in Gilead, Joel's half-tribe was probably the western one, west of the Jordan, as the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia also understands it. The name means "the LORD redeems." Several other men in the Bible are also called Pedaiah, and this one is not clearly identified with any of them.

Pedaiah, son of Parosh, was one of the men who repaired the walls of Jerusalem under Nehemiah. In the list of builders, his section comes right after that of Palal son of Uzai. Palal worked near the turn of the wall and the tower projecting from the king's upper house by the court of the guard (Neh 3:25). Pedaiah's stretch therefore probably lay in the same area, on the eastern side of the city. Smith's Bible Dictionary takes "son of Parosh" to mean a member of the family of that name. Parosh was a large family that returned from exile in Babylon. Smith's dates the work to about 446 BC, an estimate from context. The name means "the Lord redeems." Several other men in the Bible share it, and this one is known only from this verse.

Pedaiah was one of the men who stood on Ezra's left on the wooden platform when Ezra the scribe read the book of the law aloud to the people of Jerusalem (Neh 8:4). He appears in a group of seven on the left, with six more on the right, but the verse gives nothing else about him: no father, no role and no further actions. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him as apparently a priest, while the STEPBible proper names index calls him a Levite. Both views rest on inference from his place beside Ezra at the public reading. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates the event to about 445 BC. Hitchcock's Bible Names explains the name as meaning "redemption of the Lord." Several other men in the Bible share this name, and this Pedaiah should not be assumed to be any of them.

Pedaiah was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, named only in the genealogy of Sallu in Neh 11:7. He was the son of Kolaiah and the father of Joed, and he was an ancestor of Sallu, one of the Benjamites who settled in Jerusalem after the return from exile in Babylon. The verse traces Sallu's line back several generations, through Meshullam, Joed, Pedaiah, Kolaiah, Maaseiah and Ithiel to Jesaiah. Pedaiah himself therefore probably lived well before the return, although the text gives no dates for him and nothing else is recorded about him. His name means "the Lord redeems" or "redemption of the Lord" (Smith's Bible Dictionary; Hitchcock's Bible Names). Several other men in the Bible share the name Pedaiah, and they should not be confused with this one.

Pedaiah was a Levite whom Nehemiah appointed as one of the treasurers over the storehouses during his reforms in Jerusalem. He served with Shelemiah the priest and Zadok the scribe, with Hanan son of Zaccur as their assistant. Nehemiah chose these men because they were considered trustworthy, and their job was to distribute the stored supplies to their fellow Levites and temple workers (Neh 13:13). The context suggests these were the tithes of grain, wine and oil brought to the temple storerooms. His name means "the LORD redeems." Several men in the Bible share this name. Smith's Bible Dictionary considers this Levite to be apparently the same Pedaiah who stood beside Ezra at the public reading of the law, probably the one in Neh 8:4, though the text does not say so directly.

Pelaiah was a son of Elioenai and one of seven brothers, along with Hodaiah, Eliashib, Akkub, Johanan, Dalaiah and Anani, listed in 1 Chr 3:24. That verse comes at the end of the genealogy of David's descendants in 1 Chronicles 3, which traces the royal line of Judah through the kings and on past the exile through Zerubbabel. This places Pelaiah several generations after the return from exile. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates him to some time after 400 BC. Nothing else is recorded about him beyond his place in this family list. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of his name as "the Lord's secret or miracle." The same name belongs to other men in the Bible, including Levites of Ezra and Nehemiah's time, and they should not be confused with this descendant of David.

Pelaliah was a member of a priestly family, named only in the genealogy of Adaiah, one of the priests who lived in Jerusalem in Nehemiah's time (Neh 11:12). He was the son of Amzi and the father of Jeroham, which made him Adaiah's grandfather. The line goes back through Zechariah and Pashur to Malchiah. Nothing else is recorded about him. The parallel list in 1 Chr 9:12 gives Adaiah's ancestry more briefly and leaves out Pelaliah, Amzi and Zechariah, a common way of shortening genealogies. The name is usually explained as "the LORD judges" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia) or "judged by Jehovah" (Smith's Bible Dictionary). Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "entreating the Lord."

Pelatiah was a man of the tribe of Judah, named in the royal genealogy of 1 Chr 3 as a son of Hananiah. The preceding verse, 1 Chr 3:19, names Hananiah as a son of Zerubbabel, so Pelatiah was Zerubbabel's grandson and a descendant of King David and Solomon, as Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia note. He is listed with Jesaiah. The verse then names the sons of Rephaiah, Arnan, Obadiah and Shechaniah. This entry treats these men as Pelatiah's brothers, though the wording can also be read as listing separate family lines. Smith's Bible Dictionary places him after 536 BC, after the return from exile, a date inferred from his descent from Zerubbabel. His name means "the Lord delivers." Several other men in the Bible share the name, and nothing more is recorded about this one.

Pelatiah was a man of the tribe of Simeon, one of the four sons of Ishi, along with Neariah, Rephaiah and Uzziel. The four brothers led a force of five hundred Simeonites to Mount Seir, the hill country of Edom south of the Dead Sea (1 Chr 4:42). The following verse, 1 Chr 4:43, says this band struck down the surviving Amalekites there and settled in their place. Smith's Bible Dictionary places the expedition in the reign of Hezekiah, about 700 BC, by inference from the surrounding context in 1 Chr 4:41. His name means "the Lord delivers." Several other men in the Bible share the name, including a descendant of David, a leader who sealed the covenant in Nehemiah's day, and a prince of Jerusalem in Ezekiel's vision. This Pelatiah is known only from this one passage.

Pelatiah was one of the men who set their seal to the covenant made in Nehemiah's time, binding the returned exiles to keep the law of God. He appears among the leaders of the people in that list, beside Hanan and Anaiah (Neh 10:22). Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him as one of the heads of the people and suggests the name may stand for a family rather than a single person. It dates the event to about 440 BC, a date inferred from context. His name means "the Lord delivers" (Hitchcock's Bible Names). Nothing else is recorded about him. Several other men in the Bible share this name, and he should not be confused with them.

Pelet was a man of the tribe of Judah, named once as one of the six sons of Jahdai in the genealogy of Judah (1 Chr 2:47). His brothers were Regem, Jotham, Gesham (spelled Geshan in the King James Version), Ephah and Shaaph. The passage does not say how Jahdai fits into the surrounding family line. He appears among the descendants of Caleb, but his exact link to them is left open. Nothing else is recorded about Pelet. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "liberation," and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives "deliverance." Other men named Pelet appear elsewhere in the Bible, among them a man of Benjamin who joined David at Ziklag and a descendant of Jerahmeel. This entry concerns only the son of Jahdai.

Pelet, son of Azmaveth and brother of Jeziel, was one of the warriors who came to David at Ziklag (1 Chr 12:3). The surrounding passage describes these men as kinsmen of Saul from the tribe of Benjamin who joined David while he was still keeping away from Saul. Easton's Bible Dictionary accordingly calls Pelet a Benjamite. Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that "son of Azmaveth" could mean either a native of the town of Azmaveth or a son of the Azmaveth who was one of David's mighty men. The name means "deliverance" or "liberation." Nothing more is recorded about him. Another man named Pelet appears in the genealogy of Judah, so the name refers to more than one person.

Peleth was a man of the tribe of Reuben and the father of On. His son joined Korah, Dathan and Abiram in their rebellion against Moses and Aaron during Israel's time in the wilderness (Num 16:1). Nothing else is recorded about Peleth himself. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "swiftness." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests he is probably the same person as Pallu, a son of Reuben, which would explain why the verse counts On among the "sons of Reuben." The name Peleth is also borne by at least one other man in the Bible, a descendant of Judah, who is a different person.

Peleth was a son of Jonathan and a brother of Zaza, named in the genealogy of the tribe of Judah at 1 Chr 2:33. He belonged to the family line of Jerahmeel, a descendant of Judah through Hezron. In context, his father Jonathan was a son of Jada, who was a son of Onam, but the passage records nothing about Peleth beyond his name and family. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia give the meaning of the name as "swiftness." The same name is borne by another man in the Bible, Peleth the father of On, a Reubenite who joined Korah's rebellion, and the two should not be confused.

Penuel was a man of the tribe of Judah, named in the genealogy of 1 Chr 4:4 as a son of Hur, the firstborn of Ephratah and "father of Bethlehem." Penuel himself is called "the father of Gedor." In these Judahite lists, "father" of a place usually means its founder or the head of the clan that settled there, so Penuel was probably regarded as the founder of the town of Gedor. That town is probably the Gedor listed among the hill-country towns of Judah in Josh 15:58. His brother Ezer is named alongside him as the father of Hushah. Nothing else is recorded about him. The name is shared with a Benjamite in 1 Chr 8:25 and with the place where Jacob wrestled. Hitchcock's Bible Names treats it as the same name as Peniel, usually understood as "face of God."

Penuel was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, named as one of the sons of Shashak in the Benjamite genealogy of 1 Chronicles 8. He appears in a list of eleven brothers that includes Ishpan, Heber, Eliel, Abdon, Zichri, Hanan, Hananiah, Elam, Antothijah and Iphedeiah (1 Chr 8:25). The chapter places Shashak's family among the Benjamite heads of households who lived in Jerusalem. Nothing else is recorded about him. The name is shared by other people in the Bible, including a man of Judah in the genealogy of 1 Chronicles 4, and it is also the name of the place where Jacob wrestled. Hitchcock's Bible Names treats the name as the same as Peniel, usually understood to mean "face of God."

Peresh was a son of Machir and his wife Maachah, listed in the genealogy of the tribe of Manasseh, one of the two tribes descended from Joseph. According to 1 Chr 7:16, his mother named him, and his brother was Sheresh. The same verse says “his sons were Ulam and Rakem,” but it does not make clear whether these were the sons of Peresh or of Sheresh. Since Machir was Manasseh’s son (1 Chr 7:14), Peresh was Manasseh’s grandson, and Gilead was his brother. Peresh appears only in this verse, and nothing else is recorded about him. The meaning of his name is explained in different ways. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia give “dung,” while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives “horseman.”

Persis was a Christian woman in the church at Rome whom Paul greeted near the end of his letter to the Romans (Rom 16:12). He calls her "the beloved Persis" and says she "laboured much in the Lord," a phrase that sets her apart from Tryphena and Tryphosa, named in the same verse, who "labour in the Lord." The past tense may suggest that her work had been done earlier. Nothing more is said about her family, origin or role. Smith's Bible Dictionary explains the name as meaning "a Persian woman," and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the name is attested in Rome for a freedwoman, so she may have come from that background, though the text does not say. Smith's dates the letter to about AD 55.

Pethahiah was a priest who headed the nineteenth of the twenty-four priestly divisions. These divisions were assigned by lot in the time of David, and each one took its turn serving at the sanctuary (1 Chr 24:16). The surrounding chapter presents the arrangement as part of David's organization of the priests descended from Eleazar and Ithamar. Pethahiah is mentioned only in this list, so nothing else is known about him. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates him to about 1020 BC, an estimate drawn from the context of David's reign. His name is usually explained as meaning "Yahweh opens" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia). Several other men in the Bible bear the same name, including a Levite in the time of Ezra and Nehemiah and an official serving the Persian king. This entry refers only to the head of the nineteenth priestly course.

Pethahiah was a Levite in the time of Ezra, named in Ezra 10:23 among the Levites who had married foreign women. In the wider passage, those listed agreed to send away these wives as part of the reform Ezra led after the return from exile in Babylon. Nothing else is recorded about him in this verse. The name, which Hitchcock's Bible Names explains as "the Lord opening" or "gate of the Lord," belongs to several men in the Bible. They include the head of a priestly division in David's time (1 Chr 24:16) and a Levite who helped lead the people's prayer of confession in Nehemiah's day (Neh 9:5). Because that Levite lived in the same period, he may be the same man as the one in Ezra 10:23, but the text does not say so, and this entry treats the connection as uncertain.

Pethahiah was a Levite in the time of Nehemiah. He was one of eight Levites, along with Jeshua, Kadmiel, Bani, Hashabniah, Sherebiah, Hodijah and Shebaniah, who called the gathered people of Jerusalem to stand and bless the LORD. This took place during the day of fasting and confession that followed the reading of the Law (Neh 9:5). The prayer that follows in the chapter recounts Israel's history. The name is often explained as meaning "the Lord opens" (Hitchcock's Bible Names). Several men in the Bible bear this name. A Levite named Pethahiah appears among those who had married foreign wives in Ezra 10:23, and some identify him with this man. That link is possible but not certain, and this entry treats only the Levite of Neh 9:5.

Pethahiah, son of Meshezabeel, was a man of the tribe of Judah, from the family of Zerah, Judah's son. He lived in the time of Nehemiah, after the return from exile. Neh 11:24 says he "was at the king's hand in all matters concerning the people." Easton's Bible Dictionary takes this to mean he held some office at the Persian court, and the STEPBible name index describes him as appointed to represent the people before the Persian king. The king in question was probably Artaxerxes, whom Nehemiah served. Nothing more is recorded about him. His name is usually explained as "Yahweh opens" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia). Several other men in the Bible share the name, so he should not be confused with them.

Pethuel was the father of the prophet Joel. He is named only once in the Bible, in the opening line of the book of Joel, where the prophet is introduced as "Joel the son of Pethuel" (Joel 1:1). Nothing else is recorded about him: his tribe, home, and lifetime are not given. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates him to before 800 BC, but this depends on how the book of Joel itself is dated, which is uncertain. The meaning of his name is also explained in different ways. Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries give "vision of God," the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives "God's opening," and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "mouth of God" or "persuasion of God."

Peulthai was a Levite listed as the eighth of the brothers Shemaiah, Jehozabad, Joah, Sacar, Nethaneel, Ammiel and Issachar, in the roster of temple gatekeepers organized in David's time. The surrounding passage (1 Chr 26:4) presents these brothers as sons of Obed-edom, and Easton's, Smith's and the Tyndale House proper-names list all identify him that way. This entry names his father as Shimei, which the passage itself does not do. The verse ends with the note that God blessed Obed-edom with these many sons. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the fuller form of his name as Peullethai and explains it as "my wages". Easton's Bible Dictionary renders it "wages of the Lord", and Hitchcock's gives "my works". Nothing else is recorded about him. Smith dates him to about 1020 BC, an estimate inferred from the setting in David's reign.

Phanuel was the father of Anna, the elderly prophetess of the tribe of Asher, according to Luke 2:36. He is mentioned only here, to identify his daughter, and nothing else is said about him. Since Anna belonged to the tribe of Asher, he did too. Luke tells how Anna, who had been widowed after seven years of marriage, met the infant Jesus when he was brought to the temple in Jerusalem. Phanuel's name is the Greek form of the Hebrew Penuel and means "face of God" (Easton's Bible Dictionary; Hitchcock's Bible Names). It is the same name Jacob gave the place where he wrestled by the Jabbok. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates Phanuel to about 80 BC, an estimate based on his daughter's great age at the time of Jesus' birth.

Pharaoh, in this entry, is the Egyptian king named only once, in the genealogy of the tribe of Judah at 1 Chr 4:18. There his daughter Bithiah is said to have been taken as wife by Mered, a descendant of Judah, and to have borne him sons. The verse gives this king no personal name and no other detail, and it does not say when he reigned. "Pharaoh" was the common title of Egypt's native kings rather than a personal name, and Smith's Bible Dictionary explains it as meaning "the great house." Because the Bible uses the same title for several different rulers, this Pharaoh cannot be securely identified with any other Pharaoh mentioned in Scripture or with a known Egyptian king. Some have suggested that "daughter of Pharaoh" may simply mean an Egyptian woman of high or royal standing, but the text itself says no more.

Pharaoh here is the king of Egypt named in Jeremiah's prophecy of the cup of the Lord's wrath. Jeremiah lists him, together with his servants, princes and all his people, among the nations made to drink it (Jer 25:19). "Pharaoh" was the standard title of Egypt's rulers rather than a personal name, so several different kings in the Bible are called by it. The passage does not name this one. Jeremiah 25:1 dates the prophecy to the fourth year of Jehoiakim king of Judah, and Jer 46:2 names the Egyptian king of that year as Pharaoh-necho, defeated at Carchemish. By inference, the ruler meant here is probably Necho, though the verse itself speaks of Egypt's king only by title. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "that disperses" or "that spoils."

Pharosh is the King James spelling, used only in Ezra 8:3, of the name elsewhere written Parosh. The name belongs to an ancestor whose descendants formed a family group among those who returned from exile in Babylon. In Ezra's list of those who went up with him to Jerusalem, Zechariah led the descendants of Pharosh, and 150 males were registered with him. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the same family appears as Parosh in other lists. Part of it had already returned with Zerubbabel (Ezra 2:3; Neh 7:8). Some of its members had married foreign wives (Ezra 10:25). One descendant, Pedaiah, helped rebuild the city walls (Neh 3:25), and a representative sealed Nehemiah's covenant (Neh 10:14). The same encyclopedia gives the name's meaning as "flea." Whether Pharosh was a single historical person or simply the family's name is not stated.

Phebe (also spelled Phoebe) was a Christian woman whom Paul commended to the believers in Rome at the close of his letter to them. He calls her "our sister" and a servant of the church at Cenchrea, the eastern port of Corinth (Rom 16:1). The Greek word translated "servant" is diakonos, and Easton's Bible Dictionary describes her as a deaconess of that church. The next verse, Rom 16:2, asks the Romans to receive her and help her in whatever she needs, because she had been a helper of many people, including Paul himself. Easton's Bible Dictionary adds that she was probably the one who carried Paul's letter to Rome. This is inferred from the commendation, which reads like an introduction for someone about to arrive. Her name means "shining" or "pure" according to Hitchcock's Bible Names.

Philemon was a Christian to whom Paul, writing as a prisoner and joined by Timothy, addressed the short New Testament letter that bears his name. Paul calls him "dearly beloved" and a "fellowlabourer" (Phlm 1:1), which suggests he took an active part in the work of the church. The rest of the letter indicates that a church met in his house, that he owed his faith to Paul, and that Paul wrote to appeal on behalf of Onesimus, a slave of his who had run away and become a Christian. He probably lived at Colossae, by inference from Col 4:9 and 4:17, which link Onesimus and Archippus to that city. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests Apphia was his wife and Archippus his son. Later tradition, noted in Smith's Bible Dictionary, makes him bishop of Colossae and a martyr under Nero.

Philetus was a man named by Paul in 2 Tim 2:17, alongside Hymenaeus, as an example of those whose teaching spreads like gangrene ("canker" in the King James Version). The next verse, 2 Tim 2:18, explains that the two had strayed from the truth by claiming that the resurrection had already happened, and that this had upset the faith of some. Several reference works, including Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia, take this to mean that they treated the resurrection as purely spiritual or figurative. Since Timothy was then probably at Ephesus, Easton's Bible Dictionary places Philetus there. Hymenaeus also appears without him in 1 Tim 1:20, and Smith's suggests Philetus may have been his follower. Nothing else is known of him. His name is Greek and is usually explained as meaning "beloved" or "amiable."

Philip was a son of Herod the Great who ruled as tetrarch of Ituraea and the region of Trachonitis. Luke 3:1 names him alongside his brother Herod Antipas, tetrarch of Galilee, to date the start of John the Baptist's ministry to the fifteenth year of Tiberius Caesar, probably around AD 28–29 by inference from context. His territories lay northeast of the Sea of Galilee, roughly in the modern Golan Heights and southern Syria. His other brothers included Archelaus. Another son of Herod also bore the name Philip: the Gospels identify a Philip as the first husband of Herodias (Mark 6:17). Whether that man is the same as the tetrarch has been debated, and this entry treats them as two different people. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "warlike" or "a lover of horses."

Philologus was a Christian in Rome to whom Paul sent greetings near the end of his letter to the Romans (Rom 16:15). He is named first in a group that includes Julia, Nereus and his sister, Olympas, and "all the saints which are with them." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests that Julia was probably his wife or sister, and that this group may have formed one of the house churches within the Roman Christian community. These are inferences from the way the names are grouped, not statements in the text. The Greek name means "fond of learning" or "lover of words." The same encyclopedia notes that the name appears in inscriptions connected with the imperial household, which may hint that he was a freedman or servant there. Nothing more is recorded about him.

Phinehas was the father of Eleazar, one of the men who helped weigh the silver, gold and temple vessels in the house of God in Jerusalem on the fourth day after Ezra's company arrived from Babylon (Ezra 8:33). He is known only through his son's name. The verse names Eleazar alongside the priest Meremoth and the Levites Jozabad and Noadiah, so Eleazar was probably of priestly or Levitical family. Smith's Bible Dictionary treats this Phinehas as a Levite of Ezra's time, but notes that the phrase may instead mean that Eleazar belonged to the family of the earlier, well-known Phinehas, grandson of Aaron. This entry treats him as Eleazar's father. Several other men in the Bible share the name.

Phlegon was a Christian living in Rome whom Paul greeted near the end of his letter to the Romans (Rom 16:14). He is named in a group with Asyncritus, Hermas, Patrobas and Hermes, along with "the brethren which are with them." That wording suggests these men belonged to the same household or house church within the Roman congregation. Nothing else about him is recorded in the Bible. His name is Greek and means "burning," according to Easton's Bible Dictionary and Hitchcock's Bible Names. Smith's Bible Dictionary notes a later tradition, recorded under the name of Hippolytus, that counts him among the seventy disciples and makes him bishop of Marathon. The New Testament itself does not mention this.

Phygellus was a believer from the Roman province of Asia, in western Asia Minor, named in 2 Tim 1:15. There Paul tells Timothy that everyone in Asia has turned away from him, and he singles out Phygellus and Hermogenes by name. The verse does not say what the turning away involved: whether they rejected Paul personally, refused to help him, or abandoned his teaching. Easton's Bible Dictionary places the incident during Paul's second imprisonment at Rome, the setting the letter itself suggests. The STEPBible proper names index connects the desertion with Paul's ministry in Asia. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "fugitive." Nothing more is known of him, and the King James Version spells the name Phygellus, while many other translations write it Phygelus.

Pildash was one of the eight sons of Nahor, Abraham's brother, by his wife Milcah. That makes him Abraham's nephew. He appears only once, in the list of Nahor's children that was reported to Abraham after the near-sacrifice of Isaac (Gen 22:22). His full brothers were Huz, Buz, Kemuel, Chesed, Hazo, Jidlaph and Bethuel. Bethuel later became the father of Rebekah. Nahor also had four children by his concubine Reumah: Tebah, Gaham, Thahash and Maachah. Nothing else is recorded about Pildash. The meaning of his name is uncertain. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "flame of fire," while the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives "steely."

Pileha was one of the leaders of the people whose names appear on the sealed covenant made in Nehemiah's time, when the returned exiles in Jerusalem pledged to keep the law of Moses. He is named only once, in a list between Hallohesh and Shobek (Neh 10:24). From context, the list belongs to the leaders who set their seal to the agreement described in the surrounding chapter. Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests the name may stand for a family rather than a single person, and gives a date of about 410 BC. The name is also spelled Pilha in some reference works, such as the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia. Nothing else is recorded about him.

Piltai was a priest in the days of Joiakim, the high priest who succeeded his father Jeshua after the return from exile in Babylon. In Neh 12:17 he is named as head of the priestly family of Moadiah, which is probably the same family as Maadiah, listed among the priests who came back with Zerubbabel (Neh 12:5). Smith's Bible Dictionary gives this identification. The surrounding passage lists the heads of priestly houses in Joiakim's generation. A gap in the same verse after Miniamin shows that the name of that family's head has dropped out of the text. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia explains his name as probably meaning "Yahweh delivers." Smith's dates him to about 445 BC. That date is an estimate drawn from the setting rather than stated in the text. Nothing else is recorded about him.

Piram was the Amorite king of Jarmuth, a city in the lowlands of Judah, at the time of Joshua's conquest of Canaan. He is named only in Josh 10:3, where Adonizedek king of Jerusalem sends to him and to the kings of Hebron, Lachish and Eglon. The following verses explain why: the five kings joined forces to attack Gibeon because it had made peace with Israel. Joshua came to Gibeon's defense and routed them, and the kings fled and hid in a cave at Makkedah. According to Josh 10:16–26, Joshua later brought them out and put them to death, so Piram was presumably among those killed. The king of Jarmuth also appears in the list of defeated kings in Josh 12:11. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "like a wild ass" or "fleet", while the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia renders it "indomitable."

Pispah was a man of the tribe of Asher, named only once, in the Asherite genealogy of 1 Chr 7:38. He is listed there as one of the three sons of Jether, alongside his brothers Jephunneh and Ara. Nothing else is recorded about his life. Jether is probably the same man called Ithran in the preceding verse (1 Chr 7:37), since the two names are closely related forms. This is an inference from the context of the passage. Pispah's brother Jephunneh shares his name with the father of Caleb, but that Jephunneh belonged to the tribe of Judah and is a different person.

Poratha was one of the ten sons of Haman, the official of the Persian king Ahasuerus who plotted to destroy the Jews. He is named only once, in the list of Haman's sons in Esth 9:8. The surrounding passage (Esth 9:6–10) records that the Jews killed these ten sons in Shushan the palace on the day set for the Jews' destruction, which became the day the Jews defended themselves. At Esther's request their bodies were afterward hanged (Esth 9:13–14). The meaning of his name is uncertain. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests it may come from a Persian word meaning "given by fate," while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "fruitful." Nothing else is recorded about him beyond his name and his place among his brothers.

Prochorus was one of the seven men chosen by the early church in Jerusalem to oversee the daily distribution of food to widows, so that the apostles could give their attention to prayer and teaching. He is named third in the list, after Stephen and Philip (Acts 6:5). The choice is dated here to about AD 30, by inference from context. Nothing more is recorded of him in the Bible. His name is Greek, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests he may have been a Hellenist, a Greek-speaking Jew, which fits the context of a complaint from the Greek-speaking widows. Smith's Bible Dictionary counts him among the "seven deacons," a traditional title for the group. According to later church tradition, also noted in the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia, he became bishop of Nicomedia and died a martyr at Antioch.

Puah was one of the two Hebrew midwives, together with Shiphrah, whom the king of Egypt addressed when he ordered that Hebrew baby boys be killed at birth (Exod 1:15). The verses that follow (Exod 1:16–21) say the midwives feared God and did not carry out the order, telling Pharaoh that Hebrew women gave birth before a midwife could arrive. God then dealt well with them and gave them households of their own. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes her in these terms, and Smith's Bible Dictionary dates the episode to about 1571 BC, an estimate drawn from context. With only two midwives named, they may have been leaders over others rather than the only midwives, though the text does not say. The name is explained as "splendid" by Smith's and as "mouth" by Hitchcock's Bible Names. Several other people in the Bible bear the same or a similar name, including a son of Issachar and the father of the judge Tola.

Puah was a man of the tribe of Issachar, the son of Dodo and the father of Tola. He is known only from Judg 10:1, which records that his son Tola rose to defend Israel after the time of Abimelech and lived at Shamir in the hill country of Ephraim. Nothing else is said about Puah himself. The name is shared by several people in the Bible. These include one of Issachar's own sons, listed elsewhere among the tribe's founding families, and one of the Hebrew midwives in Egypt. This Puah belongs to a much later generation. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "mouth", "corner" or "bush of hair".

Pudens was a Christian at Rome who sent greetings to Timothy at the close of Paul's second letter to him (2 Tim 4:21). He is named alongside Eubulus, Linus and Claudia, and "all the brethren" who were with Paul when Paul urged Timothy to come before winter. By inference from the letter, he was among those who stayed in contact with Paul during his final imprisonment in Rome. The name is Latin and is usually taken to mean "modest" or "bashful". He is not mentioned anywhere else in the New Testament. Smith's Bible Dictionary records a legend that he hosted Peter, was a friend of Paul, and was martyred under Nero. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes a conjecture that Pudens and Claudia were husband and wife, with Claudia possibly a British king's daughter, though it calls this only a supposition.

Putiel was the father of the woman whom Eleazar, son of Aaron, married. She bore Eleazar a son, Phinehas, so Putiel was Phinehas's maternal grandfather (Exod 6:25). He appears only in this verse, which closes the genealogy of the Levite family heads. The text gives neither his tribe nor his family. His daughter is not named either; she is described only as "one of the daughters of Putiel," which implies he had more than one daughter. The meaning of his name is uncertain. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "God is my fatness," while the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests "contemned by El."

Quartus was a Christian who sent greetings to the believers in Rome at the close of Paul's letter to them (Rom 16:23). Paul names him alongside Gaius, his host, and Erastus, the city treasurer, and calls him simply "a brother." Some translations render the phrase "our brother" or "the brother." Paul was probably writing from Corinth, since Gaius and Erastus are connected with that city elsewhere, so Quartus is generally taken to have been a member of the church there, as Easton's Bible Dictionary describes him. His name is Latin and means "fourth." Nothing else about him is recorded in the Bible. Smith's Bible Dictionary notes a later tradition that he was one of the seventy disciples and afterward became bishop of Berytus, modern Beirut.

Rabsaris was one of three high officials whom the king of Assyria sent from Lachish to Jerusalem, together with Tartan and Rabshakeh, at the head of a large army against King Hezekiah of Judah. The three came up to Jerusalem and stood by the conduit of the upper pool on the highway to the fuller's field (2 Kgs 18:17). The surrounding narrative names the Assyrian king as Sennacherib. The word is probably a title rather than a personal name. Smith's Bible Dictionary and Hitchcock's Bible Names give its meaning as "chief of the eunuchs," and Easton's Bible Dictionary renders it "Chief of the Heads," meaning a senior court officer. The same title appears for a Babylonian official at the fall of Jerusalem in Jer 39:3 and 39:13. That is evidently a different man holding a similar office.

Rachab is a woman named in the genealogy of Jesus in Matt 1:5, where she is the wife of Salmon and the mother of Boaz, who later married Ruth and became the great-grandfather of King David through Obed and Jesse. Rachab is the Greek form of the name Rahab, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia and Easton's Bible Dictionary both treat the names as the same. Smith's Bible Dictionary identifies her with Rahab the harlot of Jericho, who hid the Israelite spies and was spared when the city fell (Josh 2; 6). The Old Testament does not say whom that Rahab married, so her identification with Salmon's wife rests on Matthew's genealogy. This entry follows that identification. She is one of the few women named in Matthew's list, along with Tamar, Ruth and the wife of Uriah.

Raddai was one of the brothers of David, named in 1 Chr 2:14 as the fifth son of Jesse, of the tribe of Judah. He appears only in this genealogy, between Nethaneel the fourth son and Ozem the sixth, and nothing else is recorded about him. The Chronicles list gives Jesse seven sons, while 1 Sam 16:10–11 implies eight, with David the youngest. Raddai's name does not appear in the Samuel accounts of Jesse's sons, which name only Eliab, Abinadab and Shammah. The meaning of the name is uncertain. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "trampling," the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia tentatively suggests "beating down," and Hitchcock's Bible Names offers "ruling; coming down." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia also notes that some Greek manuscripts spell the name differently, for example "Rhaddai" or "Zaddai."

Raham was a man of the tribe of Judah, named only once, in the genealogy of the descendants of Caleb son of Hezron in 1 Chr 2:44. He was the son of Shema and is called "the father of Jorkoam." In these Chronicles genealogies "father" can mean the founder or leading figure of a town or clan, so Jorkoam may have been a settlement rather than a son. The TIPNR proper-names index of Tyndale House allows both readings. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "merciful," and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives "pity" or "love." Nothing else is recorded about him.

Rakem was a descendant of Manasseh, son of Joseph, named only in the genealogy at 1 Chr 7:16. That verse says that Maachah, wife of Machir, bore a son named Peresh, and that his brother was Sheresh. It then says "his sons were Ulam and Rakem." Grammatically, "his" could point to either brother. This entry follows the reading that Rakem and his brother Ulam were sons of Sheresh, which would make Rakem a grandson of Machir and a great-grandson of Manasseh, within the tribe of Joseph. The Bible records nothing else about him. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "flower garden" and places him before 1451 BC, a date inferred from his place in the family line.

Ram was the ancestor or founder of the clan to which Elihu belonged. Elihu, the son of Barachel the Buzite, was the young man who angrily answered both Job and his three friends (Job 32:2). Nothing else is recorded about this Ram, and he should not be confused with others of the same name, such as Ram in the line of Judah. The name means "high" or "exalted." Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies him with Aram, a nephew of Buz in Gen 22:21. That link fits Elihu's description as a Buzite. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia instead treats the name as possibly that of an obscure Arab tribe, and it notes the medieval rabbinic commentator Rashi's suggestion that Ram stands for Abraham. This entry treats Ram simply as Elihu's clan ancestor, which is all the verse itself states.

Ramiah was an Israelite layman of the family of Parosh who lived in the time of Ezra, after the return from exile in Babylon. He is named first among the sons of Parosh in the list of men who had married foreign wives (Ezra 10:25). The surrounding chapter describes how these men agreed to send away their foreign wives, so Ramiah was probably among those who made that pledge. Nothing else is recorded about him. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia explains his name as meaning "Yah has loosened" or "Yah is high," and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "exaltation of the Lord." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia also notes that the parallel list in 1 Esdras 9:26 gives his name as "Hiermas," which points to a Hebrew form close to Jeremiah.

Ramoth was one of the "sons of Bani" listed in Ezra 10:29 among the Israelite men who had married foreign wives after the return from exile. The context of Ezra 10 shows that those named agreed to send these wives away as part of the reform led by Ezra. Nothing else is recorded about him. The spelling of his name differs between textual traditions. The King James Version follows the form the Hebrew scribes marked to be read aloud, Ramoth. The written Hebrew form gives Jeremoth, which the Revised Versions adopt, according to the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia. That form resembles names found in nearby verses of the same list. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of Ramoth as "eminences" or "high places."

Raphu was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, known only as the father of Palti. Palti was the Benjamite chosen as one of the twelve men Moses sent to explore the land of Canaan (Num 13:9). Raphu is named only in this list of the spies, which identifies each one by tribe and by father, so nothing else is recorded about his life. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia give the meaning of his name as "healed" or "one healed." Smith's Bible Dictionary dates him to before 1490 BC, an estimate drawn from the timing of the wilderness journey.

Reaia was a man of the tribe of Reuben, named only in the genealogy of 1 Chr 5:5. He was the son of Micah and the father of Baal. Placing him among the Reubenites is an inference from the passage, which traces this line from Joel, a descendant of Reuben (1 Chr 5:1–4). It ends with Beerah, a Reubenite prince whom the Assyrian king Tilgath-pilneser carried into exile (1 Chr 5:6). Smith's Bible Dictionary describes Reaia as apparently a prince of his tribe. The verse itself records only his place in the family line. Smith's also notes that the name is the same as Reaiah, which other men in the Old Testament bear. Nothing else is told about him.

Rechab was the father of Malchiah, who is named in Neh 3:14 as "the ruler of part of Bethhaccerem." Malchiah repaired the Dung Gate when Jerusalem's walls were rebuilt under Nehemiah. He rebuilt the gate and fitted its doors, locks and bars. Rechab himself is known only as part of his son's name. Nothing else is recorded about him, so he probably lived in the generation before the wall-building, which Smith's Bible Dictionary dates to before 446 BC. Several men in the Bible share the name Rechab. Some interpreters link this man with the Rechab whose descendants, the Rechabites, appear in Jeremiah, but the text does not make that connection, and this entry treats him simply as Malchiah's father. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "rider." Hitchcock's Bible Names suggests "square" or "chariot with team of four horses."

Rechah is a name in the genealogy of Judah, mentioned only in 1 Chr 4:12, which closes a short list of descendants with the words "These are the men of Rechah." The men named include Eshton, his sons Bethrapha, Paseah and Tehinnah, and Tehinnah's son Irnahash. This entry treats Rechah as a man and the ancestor of this group. Chelub and Shuah are shown as his children by inference from the preceding verse, 1 Chr 4:11, where Chelub, the brother of Shuah, begins the line that ends with "the men of Rechah." The phrase may instead name a place, since such lists often link families to towns. Smith's Bible Dictionary takes it as probably a village in Judah, perhaps Rashiah, about three miles south of Jerusalem. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that nothing further is known about it.

Regem was a man of the tribe of Judah, named first among the six sons of Jahdai in the genealogy of 1 Chr 2:47. His brothers were Jotham, Geshan (also spelled Gesham), Pelet, Ephah and Shaaph. The verse sits within the list of Caleb's descendants, so the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia describes him as a Calebite and the probable founder of a family or clan of that name. Jahdai's own link to Caleb is not stated; by inference from the surrounding verses he belonged to the same line. Nothing else is recorded about Regem. The meaning of his name is uncertain: Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "friend," while Hitchcock's Bible Names offers "that stones" or "purple."

Regem-melech was one of the men sent, together with Sherezer and their companions, to pray before the Lord and to put a question to the priests and prophets at the house of God (Zech 7:2). The following verse shows that the question was whether to keep up the fast of the fifth month, which mourned the destruction of the temple. The passage is dated to the fourth year of Darius, while the temple was being rebuilt after the exile. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes the senders as exiled Jews. The Hebrew of the verse is difficult and can also be read to mean that the people of Bethel sent the delegation. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the name may mean "friend of the king," so some read it as a title for Sherezer rather than as a second person. This entry treats Regem-melech as a separate individual. Nothing else is known of him.

Rehob was a Levite named among those who set their seal to the written covenant of Nehemiah's day, in which the returned community of Jerusalem pledged to keep God's law. He appears only in the list of sealers at Neh 10:11, between Micha and Hashabiah. By inference from the surrounding list (Neh 10:9–13), this part of the roll names Levites. Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests the name may stand for a Levitical family rather than a single man. Nothing else is recorded about him. He should not be confused with others called Rehob in the Bible, such as the father of Hadadezer king of Zobah. The name is usually taken to mean "breadth" or "open space."

Rehum son of Bani was a Levite who helped rebuild the walls of Jerusalem under Nehemiah. Neh 3:17 names him at the head of a group of Levites who repaired a section of the wall. Hashabiah, ruler of half the district of Keilah, worked on the section next to theirs. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates this work to about 445 BC. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of his name as "merciful" or "compassionate." Several other men in the Bible are also called Rehum, including a Persian official who opposed the rebuilding of Jerusalem. This Rehum is known only from this one verse.

Rehum was one of the leaders of the people who set their seal to the covenant made in Nehemiah's time, a written pledge by the returned exiles to keep the law of God (Neh 10:25). His name appears among the "chief of the people" in the list of signers, alongside Hashabnah and Maaseiah. Nothing else is recorded about him. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates the covenant to about 410 BC, and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "merciful" or "compassionate." Several other men in the Bible are also named Rehum, including a Persian official in Ezra and a Levite who helped repair the wall of Jerusalem. Whether this signer is the same person as any of them cannot be determined from the text, so this entry treats him as a separate individual.

Rei was a man named once in the Bible, among those who did not side with Adonijah when Adonijah tried to make himself king near the end of David's reign (1 Kgs 1:8). He is listed with Zadok the priest, Benaiah son of Jehoiada, Nathan the prophet, Shimei, and David's mighty men, the group that stayed loyal to David and so backed Solomon's succession. The text gives no further details about him, and his identity is uncertain. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes several proposals: that he and Shimei were officers of David's bodyguard, or that he was Ira the Jairite, called David's priest in 2 Sam 20:26. It also notes that Josephus omits him and reads the phrase as "David's friend." That encyclopedia suggests he was probably an officer of the royal guard. The name is usually explained as meaning "friendly."

Rephael was a Levite, a son of Shemaiah, named with his brothers Othni, Obed, Elzabad, Elihu and Semachiah in the list of temple gatekeepers in 1 Chr 26:7. The surrounding passage traces Shemaiah to Obed-edom, and Smith's Bible Dictionary describes Shemaiah as Obed-edom's firstborn. The verse calls some of the brothers "strong men", and Easton's Bible Dictionary notes that this family's strength for service made them one of the divisions of porters, or gatekeepers. The Chronicler places these arrangements in the reign of David. The name means "God has healed". The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats Rephael as the founder of a family of gatekeepers and notes that the same name appears as Raphael in later Jewish writings such as Tobit. Nothing else is recorded about him.

Rephah was a member of the tribe of Joseph, listed in the genealogy of Ephraim's descendants (1 Chr 7:25). The verse says only that "Rephah was his son," and the "his" can be read in more than one way. This entry follows the reading that makes him a son of Beriah, the son Ephraim named after the loss of his other sons in the preceding verses, with Resheph and Sherah as his siblings. Smith's Bible Dictionary instead calls him a son of Ephraim. The list that follows him runs through Telah and Tahan and on to Nun and his son Joshua (1 Chr 7:26–27), so Rephah appears as an ancestor of Joshua. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats him as the founder of an Ephraimite family and notes that the Hebrew form of his name may be corrupt. Nothing else is recorded about him.

Rephaiah was a man of the tribe of Judah and a descendant of King David, named in the royal genealogy that follows the line after the exile. This entry treats him as a son of Hananiah, alongside Pelatiah, Jesaiah, Arnan, Obadiah and Shechaniah. Hananiah was a son of Zerubbabel, according to 1 Chr 3:19, so Rephaiah belongs to the generations after the return from Babylon. The wording of 1 Chr 3:21 is unclear. It lists "the sons of Rephaiah" as a separate family group, so Rephaiah may have headed a clan connected to Hananiah's line rather than being his direct son. The Greek Septuagint reads the verse as a chain of successive generations. His name probably means "Yah is healing," according to the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia. Several other men in the Bible share the name.

Rephaiah was one of four sons of Ishi, a man of the tribe of Simeon. With his brothers Pelatiah, Neariah and Uzziel, he was a captain of five hundred Simeonites who went to Mount Seir (1 Chr 4:42). The surrounding verses place this expedition in the days of Hezekiah, king of Judah, and say that the group struck down the remaining Amalekites who had escaped there and settled in their land (1 Chr 4:41, 43). The name probably means "the LORD heals" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia). Several other men in the Bible bear the same name, and this Rephaiah appears only in this one passage.

Rephaiah was a son of Tola and a grandson of Issachar, listed in the genealogy of the tribe of Issachar in 1 Chr 7:2. His brothers were Uzzi, Jeriel, Jahmai, Jibsam and Shemuel. Together they are called heads of their father's house and valiant men of might, and their descendants are said to have numbered 22,600 in the days of David. Nothing else is recorded about him. The name probably means "the LORD heals" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia). Several other men in the Bible share the name, and this Rephaiah should not be confused with them.

Rephaiah son of Hur was the ruler of half the district of Jerusalem in the time of Nehemiah. He repaired a section of the city wall when it was rebuilt after the return from exile (Neh 3:9). His section lay next to that of the men of Jericho and others listed just before him. Another official, Shallum son of Hallohesh, is also called ruler of half the district of Jerusalem (Neh 3:12), so the city was probably divided into two administrative halves. The name probably means "the LORD heals" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia). Smith's Bible Dictionary dates the work to about 441 BC. Several other men in the Bible share the name Rephaiah, but this one is known only from this verse. Nothing more is recorded about him or his father Hur.

Resheph was a descendant of Ephraim, one of the tribes descended from Joseph, named once in the Ephraimite genealogy at 1 Chr 7:25. The verse lists him after Rephah. This entry reads him as a son of Beriah, the son Ephraim named after the killing of his sons by the men of Gath (1 Chr 7:21–23), which would make Rephah and Sherah his siblings. The wording leaves open whether 'his son' refers back to Ephraim or to Beriah, and Smith's Bible Dictionary calls Resheph simply a son of Ephraim. The list continues through Telah, taken here as Resheph's son, and on down the line that leads to Joshua (1 Chr 7:27). The name means 'flame' or 'fire-bolt,' and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that it is also found in Phoenician as the name of a god. Nothing else is recorded about him.

Reuel was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, named only once, in a genealogy in 1 Chr 9:8. He was the son of Ibnijah and the father of Shephathiah, and through Shephathiah he was the grandfather of Meshullam. Meshullam appears in a list of Benjamite family heads living in Jerusalem, a list that the surrounding chapter, by inference from its context, places among the people who settled there after the return from exile. Reuel himself would therefore have lived some generations earlier, though nothing else is recorded about him. Several other people in the Bible share the name, including a son of Esau. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia give the meaning of the name as "friend of God."

Reumah was the concubine of Nahor, the brother of Abraham. She is named only once, at the end of the list of Nahor's descendants that was reported to Abraham after the near-sacrifice of Isaac. The surrounding verses list Nahor's eight sons by his wife Milcah first, and then Reumah's four children: Tebah, Gaham, Thahash and Maachah (Gen 22:24). The verse does not give the children's genders. This entry treats Maachah as a daughter, while some reference works, such as the STEPBible proper names list, describe all four as sons.
