Nothing else is recorded about her. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of her name as "lofty" or "sublime," and Smith's Bible Dictionary renders it "elevated." Smith's dates her to about 1870 BC, an estimate drawn from the patriarchal timeline.

Rezia was a man of the tribe of Asher, named as one of the three sons of Ulla, alongside his brothers Arah and Haniel, in the Asherite genealogy of 1 Chr 7:39. Nothing else is recorded about him, and Ulla himself is not clearly linked to the earlier names in the list. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "delight." Some reference works, such as the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia, list him under the spelling Rizia.

Rezon son of Eliadah was a man who fled from his master Hadadezer, king of Zobah, and whom God raised up as an adversary to Solomon (1 Kgs 11:23). The surrounding passage (1 Kgs 11:24–25) says he gathered a band of men after David defeated Zobah, took Damascus, reigned over Syria, and opposed Israel throughout Solomon's reign. Easton's Bible Dictionary connects his break with Hadadezer to David's victory over Zobah recorded in 2 Sam 8:3–8. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that many scholars identify him with Hezion, named in 1 Kgs 15:18 as the grandfather of Ben-hadad I. If so, Rezon founded the line of Syrian kings at Damascus that later fought against Israel. That identification is uncertain.

Rhesa was a man named in Luke's genealogy of Jesus as the son of Zorobabel (the Greek form of Zerubbabel) and the father of Joanna (Luke 3:27). Through this line he belongs to the tribe of Judah. He appears in only this one verse, and nothing else is told about his life. Rhesa is not among the sons of Zerubbabel listed in 1 Chr 3:19–20, and Matthew's genealogy traces the line from Zerubbabel through Abiud instead, so his place in the family cannot be checked against other passages. Smith's Bible Dictionary notes a suggestion that "Rhesa" may be a title meaning "head" or "prince" rather than a personal name. This entry treats him as a person, as Luke's wording presents him. Older name dictionaries give different meanings for the name, including "affection" (Easton's Bible Dictionary) and "will" or "course" (Hitchcock's Bible Names).

Rhoda was a servant girl in the house of Mary, the mother of John Mark, in Jerusalem. Her name means "rose." When Peter knocked at the gate after an angel freed him from Herod's prison, she came to answer (Acts 12:13). The surrounding passage (Acts 12:12–15) tells how she recognized his voice and was so overjoyed that she ran inside to tell the gathered believers without opening the door. They told her she was out of her mind, and when she insisted, they said it must be his angel. Peter kept knocking until they let him in. The event is dated here to about AD 40, by inference from context; Smith's Bible Dictionary places it about AD 44. Nothing more is recorded about her.

Rinnah was a man of the tribe of Judah, named once in the genealogy of 1 Chr 4:20 as one of the four sons of Shimon, alongside Amnon, Ben-hanan and Tilon. Nothing else is recorded about him, and Shimon himself is not otherwise identified. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the Greek Septuagint reads the verse differently, taking the "Ben" of Ben-hanan as "son of" and so making Rinnah a son of Hanan. This entry follows the Hebrew text, which lists him as Shimon's son. His name is usually understood to mean "a shout," "song" or "rejoicing" (Smith's Bible Dictionary; Hitchcock's Bible Names). Smith's dates him to about 1300 BC, an estimate from his place in the genealogy rather than anything the text states.

Rohgah was a man of the tribe of Asher, named only once in the Bible, in the Asherite genealogy at 1 Chr 7:34. He is listed as one of the sons of Shamer, along with his brothers Ahi, Jehubbah and Aram. Shamer is probably the same man called Shomer in 1 Chr 7:32, a descendant of Asher through Heber, so by inference Rohgah belonged to the line of Beriah. Nothing else is recorded about his life or deeds. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the Hebrew text has a variant written form of the name (rohaghah) alongside the form read aloud (rohgah). Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning "clamor," while Hitchcock's Bible Names renders it "filled or drunk with talk."

Rufus was a son of Simon of Cyrene, the man who was made to carry Jesus' cross on the way to the crucifixion, and the brother of Alexander. Mark identifies Simon as "the father of Alexander and Rufus" (Mark 15:21). The parallel accounts in Matthew and Luke do not name the sons, so Mark's readers probably knew these two men, by inference from the passage. A Christian named Rufus is greeted by Paul in Rom 16:13, and some interpreters identify him with this Rufus. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats the two mentions together. The name was common, however, and the link is uncertain. This entry covers the son of Simon named in Mark. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "red."

Rufus was a Christian in Rome to whom Paul sent greetings at the close of his letter to the Romans, calling him "chosen in the Lord" (Rom 16:13). Paul also greeted Rufus's mother, describing her as "his mother and mine," which suggests she had once cared for Paul like a mother, though the occasion is not recorded. The name means "red" according to Hitchcock's Bible Names, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that it was a very common name. Another Rufus appears in Mark 15:21 as a son of Simon of Cyrene, the man who carried Jesus' cross. Because Mark's Gospel is traditionally linked with the church at Rome, the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests the two may be the same man, but this cannot be confirmed, and this entry treats the Rufus of Romans on his own.

Sacar was a Levite, the fourth of the eight sons of Obed-edom listed in 1 Chr 26:4. His brothers named there are Shemaiah, Jehozabad, Joah, Nethaneel, Ammiel, Issachar and Peulthai. The passage appears in the list of the divisions of gatekeepers, or porters, for the house of the Lord, so Sacar is understood to have served as a gatekeeper. Easton's Bible Dictionary calls him a temple porter, and STEPBible places his service in the reign of King David. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats him as the founder of a family of gatekeepers. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "wages." Nothing else is recorded about him. He is a different man from Sacar the Hararite, the father of one of David's warriors (1 Chr 11:35).

Sadoc was an ancestor of Jesus named in Matthew's genealogy, the son of Azor and the father of Achim (Matt 1:14). His name is the Greek form of the Hebrew Zadok, which Hitchcock's Bible Names and Easton's Bible Dictionary explain as meaning "just" or "righteous." He belongs to the part of the line that runs from Zerubbabel, after the exile in Babylon, down to Joseph. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia describe him as a descendant of Zerubbabel, and Smith's places him at about 280 BC, an estimate reached by counting generations rather than a date the text states. Because he comes in the royal line of David, he is counted with the tribe of Judah. Nothing else is recorded about him, and he should not be confused with the better-known priest Zadok of David's time.

Salathiel is the Greek form of the name Shealtiel. In Luke's genealogy of Jesus he is named as the son of Neri and the father of Zorobabel (Zerubbabel), placing him in the line of David and the tribe of Judah (Luke 3:27). His name probably means "asked of God." Matthew's genealogy (Matt 1:12) and 1 Chr 3:17 instead call him a son of Jeconiah, the king of Judah taken into exile in Babylon. Easton's Bible Dictionary explains the difference by suggesting that Salathiel was the natural son of Neri, a descendant of David's son Nathan, and became heir to the royal line when Jeconiah's line ended. Other explanations have also been offered, such as adoption or a levirate marriage. His son Zerubbabel later led a group of exiles back to Jerusalem, and this entry places Salathiel in the generation of the Babylonian exile.

Sallai was a man of the tribe of Benjamin who lived in Jerusalem after the return from the Babylonian exile. He is named only in Neh 11:8, in the list of those who settled in the city when its population was strengthened in Nehemiah's time. The surrounding passage identifies the group as Benjamites, which Easton's Bible Dictionary also notes. Sallai appears alongside Gabbai, following a man named Sallu, and the verse gives a combined total of 928 men. It is not clear whether that figure counts the followers of Gabbai and Sallai alone or the Benjamite group as a whole, and it is possible that Sallai names a clan rather than a single person. Nothing else is recorded about him. The priestly family head called Sallai in Neh 12:20 is usually taken to be a different man.

Sallu was a man of the tribe of Benjamin named among the inhabitants of Jerusalem in 1 Chr 9:7. He was the son of Meshullam, and his ancestry is traced back through Hodaviah and Hasenuah. The surrounding chapter lists the families who settled in Jerusalem, which the context suggests was after the return from exile in Babylon. The STEPBible Proper Names index describes him as a Benjamite who lived in Jerusalem. A similar list in Neh 11:7 also names a Benjamite Sallu son of Meshullam, but with a different line of ancestors. He is probably the same man, though the two genealogies do not match exactly. The name Sallu is also borne by others in the Bible, including a priest who returned with Zerubbabel, so care is needed to keep them apart. Nothing else is recorded about him.

Sallu was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, the son of Meshullam, named among those who lived in Jerusalem after the return from the Babylonian exile. Neh 11:7 gives his ancestry through seven generations: Meshullam, Joed, Pedaiah, Kolaiah, Maaseiah, Ithiel and Jesaiah. By inference from the surrounding chapter, he was one of the Benjamite family heads listed among the leaders who settled in the city when its population was being restored. The STEPBible Proper Names index describes him as a Benjamite leader. A parallel list in 1 Chr 9:7 names a Sallu son of Meshullam among the Benjamites in Jerusalem, though it traces a different line of ancestors, so it probably refers to the same man. The name Sallu is also borne by a priest who returned with Zerubbabel (Neh 12:7), a different person.

Salu was a man of the tribe of Simeon, known only as the father of Zimri. According to Num 25:14, Zimri was killed together with a Midianite woman during the episode at Shittim, when Israelites joined in the worship of Baal of Peor. The surrounding chapter shows that Phinehas the priest was the one who killed them. The verse calls Zimri "a prince of a chief house among the Simeonites." Grammatically this title could belong to either father or son. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia applies it to Salu, as head of a Simeonite family. Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that Salu is called Salom in 1 Maccabees 2:26, and the name may mean "weighed." Nothing else is recorded about him.

Samgar-nebo was one of the princes of the king of Babylon (Nebuchadnezzar, by the surrounding context) who came in and sat in the middle gate of Jerusalem after the Babylonian army took the city (Jer 39:3). He appears only in this list of officials, alongside Nergal-sharezer, Sarsechim, the Rabsaris and the Rabmag. The name is Babylonian. Smith's Bible Dictionary renders it "sword of Nebo," while Easton's Bible Dictionary gives "be gracious, O Nebo" or "cup-bearer of Nebo" and suggests it may be a title of Nergal-sharezer rather than a separate person. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the Greek Septuagint reads the verse differently, and that some scholars regroup the names, joining "Nebo" to the following Sarsechim to match the Nebushazban of Jer 39:13. This entry treats Samgar-nebo as a distinct Babylonian official, following the order of names in the traditional Hebrew text.

Sapphira was a member of the early Jerusalem church and the wife of Ananias. According to Acts 5:1, she and her husband sold a piece of property. The surrounding passage (Acts 5:1–11) says they kept back part of the money while presenting the rest to the apostles as the full price. Ananias died after Peter confronted him with lying to God. About three hours later Sapphira, not knowing what had happened, repeated the same claim about the price and also died. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes her as a partner in both his guilt and his punishment. The event is dated to about AD 30, by inference from context. Her name is Aramaic and is usually taken to mean "beautiful" or "sapphire," as the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes, while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "that relates or tells."

Saraph was a man of the tribe of Judah, listed in the genealogy of 1 Chr 4:22 among the descendants of Shelah, Judah's son. This entry treats him as Shelah's son, alongside Er, Laadah, Jokim and Joash. The verse says that Joash and Saraph "had the dominion in Moab." It does not explain what that rule involved. Most readers take it to mean that they held power in Moab or married into it, but the Hebrew is unclear. The chronicler adds that "these are ancient things," which suggests the details came from very old records. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "burning," while the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests "noble one" and links the name to a word for burning or shining. Nothing more is known about him.

Sarsechim was one of the princes of the king of Babylon who came in and sat in the middle gate of Jerusalem when the city fell to Nebuchadnezzar's army (Jer 39:3). He appears only in this list of Babylonian officials, and nothing else is recorded about him. The text of the verse is difficult, and readings differ. The KJV, followed in this entry, treats Sarsechim as a separate name. STEPBible's Tyndale House names list joins it with the preceding "nebo" to read "Nebu-sar-sekim," a high official in Nebuchadnezzar's army. On that reading, the following word "Rabsaris," meaning chief official or chief eunuch, may be his title. Smith's Bible Dictionary calls him "prince of the eunuchs." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests a link with Nebushazban the Rabsaris of Jer 39:13. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the name's meaning as "master of the wardrobe."

Sceva was a Jew described as a "chief of the priests" at Ephesus, known only as the father of seven sons who worked as travelling exorcists during Paul's mission there, about AD 53 by inference from context (Acts 19:14). The surrounding passage tells how his sons tried to drive out an evil spirit by invoking "Jesus whom Paul preacheth". The spirit answered that it knew Jesus and Paul but not them, and the possessed man overpowered them, so that they fled wounded. The account led many in Ephesus to give up magic. What his title means is uncertain, since he could not have officiated at the Jerusalem temple while living in Asia Minor. Easton's Bible Dictionary takes him to have headed one of the priestly courses. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests he belonged to a high-priestly family or had once led a course.

Secundus was a Christian from Thessalonica who traveled with Paul when the apostle left Greece and headed for the province of Asia, near the end of the journey this entry dates to about AD 54, by inference from context. He is named only once, alongside Aristarchus, another Thessalonian, in a group that also included Sopater of Berea, Gaius of Derbe, Timothy, Tychicus and Trophimus (Acts 20:4). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that this group went ahead and waited for Paul at Troas. It also suggests he may have been one of the delegates carrying the Macedonian churches' gifts to Jerusalem, in which case he probably went with Paul that far. The name is Latin for "second", and the same encyclopedia notes that it appears in a list of Thessalonian city officials on an inscription. Nothing more is known of him.

Segub was the youngest son of Hiel of Bethel, who rebuilt Jericho during the reign of Ahab king of Israel. 1 Kgs 16:34 says Hiel laid the city's foundation at the cost of his firstborn Abiram and set up its gates at the cost of Segub. By inference, both sons died, and the verse presents this as fulfilling what the LORD had spoken through Joshua. The connected passage, Josh 6:26, records Joshua's curse on anyone who rebuilt Jericho: the builder would lose his firstborn at the foundation and his youngest son at the gates. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes two explanations for the deaths. One links them to an ancient practice of foundation sacrifice, and the other suggests an accident during the building work. The text itself does not say how Segub died. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the name's meaning as "fortified" or "raised." Another man named Segub appears in Judah's genealogy.

Seled was a man of the tribe of Judah, named in the genealogy of 1 Chr 2:30 as a son of Nadab and the brother of Appaim. The verse notes that he died without children, so his line did not continue, while the genealogy goes on through his brother Appaim. Nadab belonged to the family of Jerahmeel, and Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia accordingly describe Seled as a Jerahmeelite. Nothing else is recorded about his life. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "exultation," while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "affliction; warning."

Semachiah was a Levite, one of the sons of Shemaiah named in the list of temple gatekeepers in 1 Chr 26:7. His brothers were Othni, Rephael, Obed, Elzabad and Elihu, and the verse describes Elzabad's brothers, who include Elihu and Semachiah, as "strong men." The surrounding chapter places this family among the Korahite gatekeepers organized in the time of David. Shemaiah was a son of Obed-edom (1 Chr 26:4–6), so Semachiah was probably Obed-edom's grandson. His name is usually explained as meaning "the LORD has sustained." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests that the same name may lie behind "Ismachiah" in 2 Chr 31:13. Nothing further is recorded about him.

Semei is a man named once, in Luke's genealogy of Jesus, which runs back from Jesus through his ancestors (Luke 3:26). There he is the son of Joseph and the father of Mattathias. This Joseph, son of Juda, is a different person from Jacob's son Joseph and from Mary's husband, and he belongs to the stretch of the list between the return from exile and Jesus' birth. Because the line runs through David, Semei counts as a member of the tribe of Judah. Smith's Bible Dictionary treats the name as the Greek form of the Hebrew Shimei, and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives its meaning as "hearing" or "obeying." The Revised Version spells it Semein. Nothing else is known about him.

Senuah was a man of the tribe of Benjamin. He is known only as the father of Judah, who was "second over the city" of Jerusalem after the return from exile, serving under the overseer Joel son of Zichri (Neh 11:9). By inference from the surrounding list, Senuah belonged to the Benjamite families who settled in Jerusalem in Nehemiah's time. Smith's Bible Dictionary explains the name as meaning "bristling" and notes that the Hebrew form carries the definite article, Hassenuah, which is how some modern translations render it. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia compares 1 Chr 9:7, which names a Benjamite Hasenuah among Jerusalem's inhabitants, possibly the same family. Nothing else is recorded about him.

Seorim was a priest whose name was given to the fourth of the twenty-four divisions of priests. In 1 Chronicles 24, during the reign of David, these divisions were set by lot so that each family would take its turn at service in the sanctuary, and the fourth lot fell to Seorim (1 Chr 24:8). Nothing else is recorded about him. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary describe him as the chief of this fourth course and give the meaning of his name as "barley." Hitchcock's Bible Names offers other meanings, such as "gates," "hairs" or "tempests." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats Seorim as the name of a priestly course of the period after the exile, while the STEPBible names index takes him to be a priest of David's time who headed the division. This entry follows the passage's setting in David's reign.

Seraiah was a man of the tribe of Simeon, named only once, in a genealogy at 1 Chr 4:35. He was the son of Asiel and the father of Josibiah, which made him the grandfather of Jehu. This Jehu appears in a list of Simeonite clan leaders. The surrounding passage places these leaders in the reign of Hezekiah, when they moved to find pasture for their flocks, so Seraiah himself probably lived some generations earlier. Nothing else is recorded about him. The name means something like "the Lord has prevailed" according to the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia, or "prince of the Lord" according to Hitchcock's Bible Names. Several other men in the Bible are also called Seraiah, and this one should not be confused with them.

Seraiah, the son of Azriel, was one of three men whom the king ordered to arrest Baruch the scribe and Jeremiah the prophet, together with Jerahmeel the son of Hammelech and Shelemiah the son of Abdeel (Jer 36:26). The king was Jehoiakim of Judah. The order came after he had burned the scroll of Jeremiah's prophecies that Baruch had written down. The verse says the arrest did not happen because the LORD hid the two men. Nothing else is recorded about this Seraiah. The name is shared by several people in the Bible, and this one is distinct from the others. It is usually explained as meaning "the LORD has prevailed" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia), though Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "prince of the Lord."

Sergius Paulus was the Roman governor of Cyprus when Barnabas and Saul visited the island, about AD 45 by inference from context. The King James Version calls him the "deputy of the country". The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia explains the title as proconsul, the correct term for the governor of a senatorial province such as Cyprus was then. Acts describes him as "a prudent man" who sent for Barnabas and Saul because he wanted to hear the word of God (Acts 13:7). The surrounding passage, set at Paphos, tells how the sorcerer Elymas, who was with the proconsul, tried to turn him away from the faith and was struck blind. Sergius Paulus then believed, astonished at the teaching of the Lord (Acts 13:8–12). Easton's Bible Dictionary notes an inscription found at Rome bearing his name, which it takes to record a later post he held there.

Sethur, son of Michael, was the man from the tribe of Asher among the twelve spies Moses sent to explore the land of Canaan (Num 13:13). The surrounding chapter describes the mission: the spies were leaders chosen one from each tribe, and they went from the wilderness of Paran to scout the land and report on it. By inference from Num 13–14, Sethur was one of the ten spies who gave a discouraging report, since only Joshua and Caleb are singled out for urging Israel to go in, and the other ten are said to have died by plague. He is not mentioned anywhere else. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "hidden."

Shaaph was a man of the tribe of Judah, named as the last of six sons of Jahdai in the genealogy of 1 Chr 2:47. His brothers were Regem, Jotham, Geshan (spelled Gesham in some lists), Pelet and Ephah. Nothing else is recorded about him. Jahdai's own parentage is not stated, but because his family appears among the descendants of Caleb in 1 Chr 2, he is generally taken to belong to Caleb's line, and STEPBible's proper-names index describes Shaaph as a descendant of Caleb. The name Shaaph is also given to a different man, a son of Caleb by his concubine Maachah, mentioned a few verses later in the same chapter. The two are usually treated as separate people, and this entry covers only the son of Jahdai.

Shaaph was a man of the tribe of Judah, a son of Caleb by Maachah. The surrounding passage identifies Maachah as Caleb's concubine, and Smith's Bible Dictionary identifies this Caleb as the brother of Jerahmeel. 1 Chr 2:49 calls Shaaph "the father of Madmannah." Madmannah was also the name of a town in southern Judah, so "father" here probably means the founder or leading figure of that settlement rather than only a parent. The same verse names his brother Sheva as the father of Machbenah and of Gibea, and his sister as Achsah. Nothing else is recorded about him. The name Shaaph is shared by several people in the Bible. Another Shaaph appears just before this one, in the list of Jahdai's sons (1 Chr 2:47), and the two are usually treated as different men.

Shaashgaz was a chamberlain, or court official, of King Ahasuerus of Persia, mentioned only in Esth 2:14. He was in charge of the concubines in "the second house of the women." When the king was searching for a new queen, each young woman spent one night with him and then moved the next morning into this second house under Shaashgaz's custody. She did not go to the king again unless he took pleasure in her and called for her by name. By context, he worked alongside Hegai, who kept the women before they were brought to the king (Esth 2:8). Easton's Bible Dictionary calls him a chief eunuch and gives the name's meaning as "servant of the beautiful." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the Septuagint calls him Gai, the same name it gives Hegai, and that the origin of the name is uncertain.

Shabbethai was a Levite in the time of Ezra, after the Jews returned from exile in Babylon. He is named in Ezra 10:15, in the account of how the community dealt with men who had married foreign wives. The King James Version says Jonathan and Jahaziah were "employed about this matter" and that Meshullam and Shabbethai helped them. Many modern translations read the Hebrew as saying that these men opposed the plan. STEPBible Proper Names (Tyndale House) follows that reading and describes Shabbethai as opposing Ezra's efforts. A Levite named Shabbethai also helps explain the law to the people in Neh 8:7 and oversees outside work for the temple in Neh 11:16. He may be the same man, but this is uncertain, since several people share the name. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the name's meaning as "my rest."

Shabbethai was one of the men, apparently Levites, who helped the people understand the law when Ezra read it publicly in Jerusalem after the return from exile. Nehemiah 8:7 lists him among thirteen named helpers who explained the reading while the people stood in their places. The STEPBible proper names index treats him as a Levite who assisted in explaining the Law. The name also appears in Ezra 10:15, where a Shabbethai the Levite is linked with the inquiry into foreign marriages, and in Neh 11:16, where a Shabbethai is among the chief Levites in charge of the outside work of the temple. These may be the same man, but the text does not say so, and this entry treats only the Shabbethai of Neh 8:7. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "my rest."

Shabbethai was a Levite who lived in Jerusalem in the time of Nehemiah. Nehemiah 11:16 names him with Jozabad among the chief Levites and says the two were in charge of the "outward business of the house of God". This probably means the practical and outside affairs that supported the temple, as distinct from the worship carried on inside it. STEPBible Proper Names describes this as overseeing external affairs. A Levite named Shabbethai also appears in Ezra 10:15, during the dispute over foreign marriages, and in Neh 8:7, among those who helped the people understand the law. He may be the same man, but since the name is shared by several people, that cannot be confirmed. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "my rest".

Shachia was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, named once in the Benjamite genealogy of 1 Chronicles. He was a son of Shaharaim by his wife Hodesh. His full brothers were Jobab, Zibia, Mesha, Malcham, Jeuz and Mirma, and his half-brothers Abitub and Elpaal were sons of Shaharaim by another wife, Hushim (1 Chr 8:8–11). The text calls Shaharaim's sons "heads of the fathers," meaning leaders of family groups within the tribe (1 Chr 8:10). Nothing else is recorded about him. The spelling of his name differs among Hebrew manuscripts and ancient translations, and the Greek and Syriac versions read it as Shabiah, as the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes. Its meaning is uncertain. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives it as "protection of the Lord."

Shaharaim was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, named in the Benjamite genealogy of 1 Chronicles 8. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "double dawn." The text does not name his father, so his exact place in the family line is uncertain. According to 1 Chr 8:8, he had children in the land of Moab after he had sent away his wives Hushim and Baara. The following verses (1 Chr 8:9–11) name a third wife, Hodesh, who bore him Jobab, Zibia, Mesha, Malcham, Jeuz, Shachia and Mirma, apparently in Moab. They also say that by Hushim he had earlier fathered Abitub and Elpaal. The passage gives no reason for sending away his first wives and no explanation for his time in Moab.

Shallum was a man of the tribe of Simeon, named only in the Simeonite genealogy of 1 Chr 4:25. He was the son of Shaul and the father of Mibsam, and the line continues through Mibsam's son Mishma. The preceding verse lists Shaul among the sons of Simeon, so Shallum was probably Simeon's grandson, as Smith's Bible Dictionary takes him to be. Nothing else is recorded about him. Several other people in the Bible share the name Shallum, and this one should not be confused with them. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia counts at least twelve. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "retribution", while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "perfect" or "agreeable."

Shallum was an Ephraimite, known only as the father of Jehizkiah, one of the leaders of Ephraim named in 2 Chr 28:12. Several people in the Bible share this name, and this one is otherwise unknown. His son appears in the account of the war in which Pekah of Israel defeated Ahaz of Judah and brought many captives from Judah to Samaria. Jehizkiah and other heads of Ephraim stood up against the returning soldiers and opposed holding fellow Judeans as captives. From that context, Shallum probably lived around the reign of Ahaz, king of Judah. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes him as an Ephraimite chief. The text itself gives the leadership role to his son and says nothing further about Shallum.

Shallum was a temple gatekeeper (a "porter" in the King James Version) in Ezra's time. He is listed with Telem and Uri in Ezra 10:24, in the roll of men who had married foreign wives. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both describe him this way. The surrounding chapter records that the men on this list agreed to send away their foreign wives during Ezra's reforms after the return from exile, so Shallum was probably among them. The verse places him among the gatekeepers, right after the singer Eliashib. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that he appears as "Sallumus" in 1 Esdras 9:25. Nothing else is known of him. The name Shallum belongs to several other men in the Bible, including a king of Israel, and this gatekeeper should not be confused with them.

Shallum was one of the Israelites listed in Ezra 10:42 among the men who had married foreign wives in the period after the return from exile in Babylon. By inference from the surrounding chapter, he was one of those who agreed to send these wives away during the reforms led by Ezra the scribe. Smith's Bible Dictionary places him among the descendants of Bani, following the family heading earlier in the same list. Nothing else is recorded about him. The name Shallum is shared by several other men in the Bible, including a king of Israel, and this Shallum should not be confused with them.

Shallum the son of Halohesh was ruler of half the district of Jerusalem in the time of Nehemiah. He took part in rebuilding the city wall after the return from exile, repairing a section next to the stretch worked on by Rephaiah's neighbour in the list (Neh 3:12). The verse notes that his daughters worked alongside him, an unusual detail in a list that otherwise names men. The other half of Jerusalem's district appears to have had its own ruler, by inference from the phrase "the half part." The name Shallum is shared by about a dozen men in the Bible, according to the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia, and this one is mentioned only here. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "retribution," while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "perfect" or "agreeable."

Shallum was the uncle of the prophet Jeremiah and the father of Hanameel. He is named only once, in Jer 32:7, where the Lord tells Jeremiah that Hanameel, "the son of Shallum thine uncle," will come and ask him to buy a family field at Anathoth, because Jeremiah held the right of redemption. Shallum is described here as a brother of Hilkiah. Jer 1:1 names Hilkiah, a priest of Anathoth, as Jeremiah's father, so by inference Shallum was his father's brother and belonged to the same priestly family of Anathoth. The following verses in Jer 32 describe Jeremiah buying the field from Hanameel. Several other men in the Bible are called Shallum, and Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests this one may perhaps be the same as one of them. Nothing more is recorded about him.

Shallum was the father, or possibly an earlier ancestor, of Maaseiah. He is mentioned once, in Jer 35:4, when Jeremiah brought the Rechabites into the temple. One of the rooms there is identified as the chamber of Maaseiah the son of Shallum, located below the chamber of the princes. The verse calls one of them "the keeper of the door." The STEPBible proper names index takes this title to belong to Maaseiah, as one of the temple's threshold keepers in Jeremiah's time, and this entry follows that reading. Nothing else is said about Shallum himself. Because several men in the Bible bear this name, his identity is uncertain. Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests he may be the same as another Shallum of the period and dates him to about 630 BC. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "perfect" or "agreeable."

Shallun son of Col-hozeh was the ruler of the district of Mizpah who took part in Nehemiah's rebuilding of Jerusalem's walls after the return from exile. According to Neh 3:15, he repaired the Fountain Gate. He rebuilt and roofed it and installed its doors, locks and bars. He also rebuilt the wall of the Pool of Siloah (Shelah) beside the king's garden, as far as the stairs leading down from the City of David. His name means "retribution" according to Smith's Bible Dictionary. Some ancient manuscripts and translations spell it Shallum, but he is mentioned only in this one verse.

Shama was one of David's mighty warriors, named in the list of his heroes in 1 Chr 11:44. He and his brother Jehiel were sons of Hothan the Aroerite, so the family probably came from Aroer. There were two towns of that name, one east of the Jordan on the Arnon River and one in southern Judah, and the verse does not say which is meant. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "obedient" and counts him among David's guard. His name appears in the later part of the Chronicles list, which goes beyond the parallel roster in 2 Samuel 23, and nothing else is recorded about him.

Shamariah was a son of King Rehoboam of Judah, listed with his brothers Jeush and Zaham in 2 Chr 11:19. The preceding verse names two of Rehoboam's wives, Mahalath and Abihail, and the Hebrew does not make fully clear which of them bore these three sons. This entry follows the reading that their mother was Abihail, daughter of Eliab, David's eldest brother. His half-siblings Abijah, Attai, Ziza and Shelomith were Rehoboam's children by Maachah (2 Chr 11:20), and Abijah later succeeded his father as king. Nothing more is recorded about Shamariah. His birth in Jerusalem is inferred from his father's reign there. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "kept by Jehovah", and some versions spell it Shemariah.

Shamed was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, named in the genealogy of 1 Chr 8 as a son of Elpaal, alongside Eber and Misham. The verse credits him with building Ono and Lod with their surrounding towns. It is most naturally read as referring to Shamed alone, though it could include his brothers. Lod is probably the later Lydda of the New Testament, the modern city of Lod in Israel, and Ono lay nearby. Smith's Bible Dictionary holds that his name is properly Shamer or Shemer, and some reference works list him as Shemed. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives its meaning as "destroying", while Smith's gives "keeper". Nothing else is recorded about him.

Shamer was a Levite of the family of Merari, named once in the genealogy of the temple singers at 1 Chr 6:46. In that list he is the son of Mahli and the father of Bani, and his line runs on through Amzi and later generations. By inference from the surrounding passage (1 Chr 6:44–47), he was an ancestor of Ethan, one of the singers David appointed to lead music at the sanctuary, and Mahli was himself a descendant of Merari son of Levi. Nothing else is recorded about him. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "keeper," and Hitchcock's Bible Names adds "thorn" or "dregs." Some resources spell the name Shemer. Several people in the Bible share this name, including an Asherite also called Shamer and the Shemer from whom Omri bought the hill of Samaria. This Levite is distinct from them.

Shamhuth was the commander of the fifth of the twelve army divisions that David organized, each serving in turn for one month of the year. His division served in the fifth month and numbered 24,000 men (1 Chr 27:8). He is called "the Izrahite," probably meaning a descendant of Zerah, a clan of Judah, though the exact sense of the term is uncertain. His name appears only in this verse. Many interpreters identify him with Shammah the Harodite, one of David's mighty men (2 Sam 23:25), also called Shammoth the Harorite (1 Chr 11:27), since several other division commanders in this list also appear among those warriors. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia points readers to its entry on Shammuah for this connection. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "desolation" or "destruction."

Shamir was a Levite, the son of Michah, listed among the descendants of Uzziel in 1 Chr 24:24. The passage is part of a register of Levites who were not priests, set out in connection with the organization of temple service in David's time. Uzziel was a son of Kohath, so Shamir belonged to the Kohathite branch of the tribe of Levi, as Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both note. Smith's describes Michah as Uzziel's firstborn. The name may mean "point" or "thorn." Beyond his place in this genealogy, nothing more is recorded about him. The name Shamir is also used for towns elsewhere in the Old Testament, but those are unrelated to this man.

Shamma was a man of the tribe of Asher, named once in the genealogy of Asher's descendants in 1 Chr 7:37. He was one of the sons of Zophah, listed with his brothers Suah, Harnepher, Beri, Imrah, Bezer, Hod, Shilshah, Ithran and Beera. The Ithran of this verse is probably the same person as the Jether named in the next verse, which would account for Jether among his brothers. Nothing else is recorded about Shamma beyond his place in this family list. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "astonishment."

Shammah son of Agee the Hararite was one of the three leading warriors among David's mighty men, listed after Eleazar in 2 Sam 23:11. When the Philistines gathered as a raiding troop at a field full of lentils and the Israelites fled, Shammah stood his ground. The next verse (2 Sam 23:12) says he took his stand in the middle of the field, defended it and killed the Philistines, and that the LORD brought about a great victory. Easton's Bible Dictionary counts him among David's three mighty men. "Hararite" probably refers to his home town or clan, though its location is unknown. Several men in the Bible are named Shammah, and it is unclear whether the "Shammah the Harodite" and "Shammah the Hararite" listed later in the same chapter are the same man or relatives. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the name's meaning as "loss; desolation; astonishment."

Shammai was a descendant of Judah, named only in the genealogy at 1 Chr 4:17. Several men in the Bible share this name. He was a son of Mered, who was a son of Ezra (often spelled Ezrah). The verse lists him with his sister Miriam and his brother Ishbah, the father of Eshtemoa. The wording here is compressed, and the verse does not say who 'she' is. The next verse, 1 Chr 4:18, identifies these children as the offspring of Bithiah, the daughter of Pharaoh, whom Mered married. Mered also had children by a wife from Judah, and 1 Chr 4:18–19 links Eshtemoa and 'the Garmite' to that line, which explains the half-siblings shown in this entry. Nothing else is recorded about Shammai. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of his name as 'my name' or 'my desolations.'

Shammua son of Zaccur was the man from the tribe of Reuben chosen as one of the twelve spies Moses sent to explore the land of Canaan (Num 13:4). Each spy represented one tribe, and the surrounding chapter shows the group setting out from the wilderness of Paran. He is not named again. Because only Joshua and Caleb are singled out for urging Israel to enter the land, Shammua was probably among the ten spies who brought back a discouraging report and who, according to Num 14:36–37, died by a plague. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "renowned" and dates the mission to about 1490 BC. Several other people in the Bible share the name Shammua, and this Reubenite should not be confused with them.

Shammua was a priest in the period after the return from exile, named in Neh 12:18 as head of the priestly family of Bilgah. The surrounding passage lists the heads of the priestly houses in the days of Joiakim the high priest, who succeeded Jeshua. By inference from that context, Shammua served in the generation after the first returnees from Babylon. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates him to about 500 BC, an estimate rather than a date given in the text. His name is often explained as meaning "renowned." Nothing else is recorded about him. Several other men in the Bible share the name, including a spy sent into Canaan and a son of David, and they should not be confused with this priest.

Shamsherai was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, named in the genealogy of Benjamin's descendants in 1 Chronicles. He is listed first among the sons of Jeroham, alongside his brothers Shehariah, Athaliah, Jaresiah, Eliah and Zichri (1 Chr 8:26–27). The following verse describes the men in this part of the list as heads of their fathers' houses who lived in Jerusalem (1 Chr 8:28), so Shamsherai was probably a family leader there. Nothing else is recorded about him. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "sunlike," while Hitchcock's Bible Names renders it "there a singer or conqueror."

Shapham was a leader of the tribe of Gad who lived in Bashan, east of the Jordan. He is named only once, in the Gadite genealogy at 1 Chr 5:12, where he is listed as "the next" after Joel the chief. This probably means he ranked second in authority among the Gadite families. The surrounding passage says these Gadite records were compiled in the days of Jotham king of Judah and Jeroboam king of Israel (1 Chr 5:17). On that basis Smith's Bible Dictionary dates him to about 750 BC. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes another possibility: the lists were written down around that time, but Shapham and Joel may have lived earlier, in Saul's day, and taken part in the war against the Hagrites described in the same chapter. Nothing else is recorded about him.

Shaphan was the father of Jaazaniah, a man Ezekiel saw in a vision of the Jerusalem temple. Jaazaniah stood among seventy elders of Israel, each holding a censer, as a thick cloud of incense rose from their worship of the images carved on the temple walls (Ezek 8:11). Nothing more is said about Shaphan himself. The name, meaning "rock badger" according to the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia, belongs to several people in the Bible. The best known is Shaphan the scribe under King Josiah, whose sons served at court in Jeremiah's time. Some have suggested this Shaphan is the same man, but the verse does not say so. That encyclopedia lists him separately and describes him only as "perhaps" the father of Jaazaniah. This entry treats him as a distinct person.

Shaphat, son of Hori, was the man chosen from the tribe of Simeon as one of the twelve spies Moses sent to explore the land of Canaan (Num 13:5). Each tribe supplied one leader for the mission. By inference from the rest of Numbers 13–14, he was among the ten spies who brought back a discouraging report, since only Joshua and Caleb are singled out for their favorable account. Nothing else is recorded about him. The name, which Hitchcock's Bible Names gives as meaning "judge," is shared by several other men in the Bible, including the father of the prophet Elisha. This Shaphat should be kept distinct from them.

Shaphat was a son of Shemaiah and a member of the royal line of Judah, listed among the descendants of David in the genealogy of 1 Chr 3:22. His brothers were Hattush, Igeal, Bariah and Neariah, and his grandfather was Shechaniah. From the surrounding genealogy, which traces David's line through Zerubbabel, he probably lived in the period after the return from exile, as STEPBible's Tyndale House name list also places him. The verse totals the sons as "six" but names only five. Including Shemaiah in the count is one way to reach that number, though the verse does not say so. Nothing else is recorded about him. The name, meaning "judge" according to Hitchcock's Bible Names, is shared by several other men in the Bible, including the Simeonite spy of Num 13:5.

Shaphat was a leader of the tribe of Gad who lived in Bashan, the region east of the Jordan. He is named in a genealogy of the Gadites, listed fourth among their chief men after Joel the chief, Shapham the next, and Jaanai (1 Chr 5:12). The surrounding passage places these records in the days of Jotham king of Judah and Jeroboam king of Israel, so Smith's Bible Dictionary dates him to about 750 BC. His name means "judge" according to Hitchcock's Bible Names. Several other men in the Bible share the name, among them the Simeonite spy sent out by Moses and the father of the prophet Elisha. Nothing more is recorded about this Gadite.

Shaphat son of Adlai was one of the officials who managed King David's royal property. According to 1 Chr 27:29, he was in charge of the herds of cattle that grazed in the valleys. Another official, Shitrai the Sharonite, looked after the herds that pastured in the plain of Sharon. The verse comes from a list of the stewards who oversaw the king's possessions, which also included vineyards, olive groves, camels and flocks. Nothing else is recorded about him. The name Shaphat, which means "judge" according to Hitchcock's Bible Names, belongs to several men in the Bible. These include the Simeonite spy sent out by Moses and the father of the prophet Elisha, and this Shaphat should not be confused with them.

Sharai was an Israelite man named in the list of those who had married foreign wives during Ezra's reforms after the return from exile in Babylon. He appears only in Ezra 10:40, within a group that Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both place among the sons of Bani. By inference from the surrounding passage, he was one of the men who agreed to send away his foreign wife. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates these events to about 457 BC, an estimate drawn from context. The meaning of his name is uncertain. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "releaser," while Hitchcock's Bible Names offers "my lord," "my prince" or "my song." Nothing else is recorded about him.

Shashai was one of the Israelites listed in Ezra 10:40 among the men who had married foreign wives in the time of Ezra. Ezra's reforms called for these marriages to be dissolved, and Shashai's name appears in the closing list of those involved. The verse itself gives only his name, between Machnadebai and Sharai. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both place him among the sons of Bani, following the arrangement of the list in that chapter. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia adds that he is called Sesis in 1 Esdras 9:34. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates the episode to about 457 BC, an estimate from context. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the name's meaning as "rejoicing," "mercy" or "linen," while Smith's renders it "noble." Nothing else is recorded about him.

Sheal was one of the descendants of Bani named in the list of Israelite men who had married foreign wives in the time of Ezra (Ezra 10:29). The context of Ezra 10 shows that these men agreed to send away their foreign wives as part of Ezra's reforms after the return from exile in Babylon. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "asking," and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives "request." It also notes that Greek versions spell the name differently, and that the parallel list in 1 Esdras calls him Jasaelus. Nothing else is known about him.

Shear-jashub was a son of the prophet Isaiah. His name means "a remnant shall return." He appears only once, when the LORD told Isaiah to take him along to meet King Ahaz of Judah "at the end of the conduit of the upper pool in the highway of the fuller's field" (Isa 7:3). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that his name, like those of other prophets' children such as his brother Maher-shalal-hash-baz, was symbolic and carried a message. Isaiah later uses the same Hebrew words in Isa 10:21 to announce that a remnant of Israel will return. By inference, the boy's presence at the meeting with Ahaz was itself part of the prophet's message. Nothing more is recorded about his life.

Sheba was a member of the tribe of Gad, one of seven brothers listed among the leading families of his father's house in 1 Chr 5:13. His brothers were Michael, Meshullam, Jorai, Jachan, Zia and Heber, and his father was Abihail. The surrounding passage places these Gadites in the land of Bashan, east of the Jordan, and says their genealogies were recorded in the days of Jotham king of Judah and Jeroboam king of Israel. STEPBible's Tyndale House name index likewise describes him as a Gadite leader in Bashan in Jotham's time. Nothing else is recorded about him. Several other people in the Bible bear the name Sheba, and he should not be confused with them. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives possible meanings of the name as "captivity," "old man," "repose" or "oath."

Shebaniah was one of the priests who blew trumpets before the ark of God when David brought it up to Jerusalem (1 Chr 15:24). He is listed with Jehoshaphat, Nethaneel, Amasai, Zechariah, Benaiah and Eliezer, while Obed-edom and Jehiah served as doorkeepers for the ark. The verse calls him a priest, as do Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia, while Easton's Bible Dictionary describes him as a Levite. The surrounding chapter places the event in David's reign, and Smith's Bible Dictionary dates it to about 1043 BC. Nothing more is known of him. The name Shebaniah is shared by several other men in the Old Testament, mainly Levites of Nehemiah's time, and this Shebaniah should be kept distinct from them.

Shebaniah was one of the men who set their seal to the written covenant in Nehemiah's time, when the community that had returned from exile pledged to keep the law. He appears in Neh 10:12 in a list of names beside Zaccur and Sherebiah. The surrounding passage places this list among the Levites (Neh 10:9–13), and Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia describe him as a Levite. Easton's Bible Dictionary and STEPBible call him a priest. This entry follows the Levite reading suggested by the context. The name Shebaniah belongs to several people in the Bible, and another Shebaniah appears among the sealers of the same covenant. Beyond his sealing of the covenant, nothing more is known about him.

Sheber was a son of Caleb by his concubine Maachah, named in the genealogy of the tribe of Judah together with his brother Tirhanah (1 Chr 2:48). This Caleb is the son of Hezron listed in the same chapter. Smith's Bible Dictionary identifies him as Caleb ben-Hezron, as distinct from Caleb son of Jephunneh. The following verse names further children of Maachah, including Shaaph, Sheva and a daughter, Achsa. Sheber's half-brothers through Caleb's other wives and concubines include Hur, Haran, Moza and Gazez. Nothing else is recorded about him. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "breaking," and Hitchcock's Bible Names offers "breaking" or "hope."

Shebna was a royal official in Jerusalem, described in Isa 22:15 as the treasurer "which is over the house," meaning he was steward of the king's palace. God sends the prophet Isaiah to deliver a message to him. The verses that follow (Isa 22:16–25) rebuke him for cutting out a grand tomb for himself and announce that he will be removed from office and replaced by Eliakim son of Hilkiah. By context this was during the reign of Hezekiah. A Shebna who served as scribe, or secretary, under Hezekiah appears in 2 Kgs 18:18 and Isa 36:3, while Eliakim is there over the household. Some readers take him to be the same man in a lower post, and others take him to be a different person. Several people in the Bible share this name. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives its meaning as "who rests himself" or "who is now captive."

Shecaniah was a priest in the time of King David. He headed the family that received the tenth of the twenty-four divisions into which David divided the priests for their turns of service in the sanctuary (1 Chr 24:11). The surrounding chapter describes how these divisions were assigned by lot among the descendants of Eleazar and Ithamar, sons of Aaron. Nothing else is recorded about him personally, and his division is known by his name. The name Shecaniah is borne by several other men in the Old Testament, including priests and Levites of later periods, and this entry concerns only the head of the tenth priestly course. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "habitation of the Lord."

Shecaniah was one of the men who worked under Kore during the reign of Hezekiah, king of Judah, in distributing the offerings brought to the temple. The verse places him with Eden, Miniamin, Jeshua, Shemaiah and Amariah in the cities of the priests. There they handed out portions to their fellow priests and Levites by their divisions, to old and young alike (2 Chr 31:15). The context shows that the overseers named just before belonged to the Levites. Easton's Bible Dictionary calls Shecaniah one of the priests, while the STEPBible names index calls him a Levite. This entry follows the context of tithe distribution under Hezekiah and leaves his exact rank open. Several other men in the Bible share the name, which Hitchcock's Bible Names explains as "habitation of the Lord." Nothing more is recorded about this Shecaniah.

Shechaniah was an ancestor named in the list of family heads who returned from Babylon to Jerusalem with Ezra. Ezra 8:3 lists "the sons of Shechaniah, of the sons of Pharosh," naming Zechariah as the leader of the group, with 150 males registered by genealogy with him. The verse is read here as making Shechaniah a descendant of Pharosh (Parosh), so his line formed a branch within that larger clan. The STEPBible Proper Names index (Tyndale House) follows this reading. Some interpreters instead attach "of the sons of Shechaniah" to the end of the previous verse, which would make this Shechaniah a separate family head. Nothing else is recorded about him, and the name was borne by several other men in the Bible. He should not be confused with the Shechaniah mentioned shortly afterward in Ezra 8:5.

Shechaniah is named in the list of family heads who returned from exile in Babylon to Jerusalem with Ezra (Ezra 8:5). The verse reads "of the sons of Shechaniah; the son of Jahaziel," and three hundred males travelled with him. The wording is ambiguous. It can be read as a clan called after an ancestor named Shechaniah, led by a son of Jahaziel, or as Shechaniah himself being the son of Jahaziel and leader of the group. Some ancient versions place a clan name, Zattu, before Shechaniah, which supports the second reading. This entry follows the STEPBible Proper Names index, which treats Shechaniah as a descendant of Jahaziel who returned from exile. Nothing more is recorded about him. Several other men in the Bible bear the same name, and it is uncertain whether he is connected with any of them.

Shechaniah, the son of Arah, was the father-in-law of Tobiah, the Ammonite official who opposed Nehemiah's rebuilding of Jerusalem's walls. Nehemiah notes that many people in Judah were bound by oath to Tobiah because of this marriage tie. Tobiah's son Johanan had also married the daughter of Meshullam son of Berechiah (Neh 6:18). As Easton's Bible Dictionary notes, Shechaniah is known only as Tobiah's father-in-law. The verse does not say outright that Tobiah's wife was Shechaniah's daughter, but "son in law" implies it, and the STEPBible proper names index reads it that way. Shechaniah was probably a man of some standing in Judah, since the link to his family helped Tobiah win support there. His father Arah may belong to the family of Arah listed among the exiles who returned from Babylon, though this is not certain. Several other men in the Bible share the name Shechaniah.

Shechem was a man of the tribe of Manasseh, one of the two tribes descended from Joseph, named only in the genealogy of 1 Chr 7:19. He was a son of Shemida, and his brothers were Ahian, Likhi and Aniam. Other passages such as Num 26:32 and Josh 17:2 present Shemida as a clan head descended from Gilead, so Shechem probably belonged to the Gileadite branch of Manasseh. Smith's Bible Dictionary calls him a Gileadite. The same passage lists another Shechem, a son of Gilead, which suggests this Shechem was a namesake within the same family line. Several other people in the Bible share the name, and nothing further is recorded about this one. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "back" or "shoulder," and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "portion."

Shehariah was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, named only once, in the genealogy of Benjamin's descendants that leads up to the family of Saul. He is listed among the sons of Jeroham, together with his brothers Shamsherai, Athaliah, Jaresiah, Eliah and Zichri (1 Chr 8:26–27, by inference from the surrounding list). The genealogy groups these men among the heads of Benjamite families who lived in Jerusalem. Nothing else is recorded about him. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "dawning of the Lord," while Hitchcock's Bible Names renders it "mourning or blackness of the Lord." Smith's also dates him to about 588 BC, but that date is an estimate and the verse itself gives no indication of when he lived.

Shelemiah was an Israelite named in the list of men who had married foreign wives in Ezra's time and agreed to put them away (Ezra 10:39). The list groups the men by family, and by inference from its arrangement he belonged to the descendants of Bani, whose names run from Ezra 10:34. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia also places him among the sons of Bani and notes that 1 Esdras 9:34 calls him Selemias. Nothing else is recorded about him. A second Shelemiah appears a few verses later in the same list (Ezra 10:41), and the name is borne by several other people in the Bible, so he should not be confused with them. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "God is my perfection" or "my peace."

Shelemiah was an Israelite in Ezra's time, named in the list of men who had married foreign wives and agreed to put them away (Ezra 10:41). He appears in a group introduced as descendants of Bani. Smith's Bible Dictionary counts him as another of the sons of Bani, which reflects the fact that an earlier Shelemiah is named a verse before. Nothing else is recorded about him. The name, which Smith's Bible Dictionary explains as "repaid by Jehovah," is shared by several men in the Old Testament, and this Shelemiah should not be confused with the others of that name.

Shelemiah was the father of Hananiah, one of the men who repaired a section of Jerusalem's wall under Nehemiah's leadership after the return from exile (Neh 3:30). He is known only as his son's father, and nothing else is recorded about him. Several other men in the Bible share the name Shelemiah, and there is no clear way to link this one with any of them. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "repaid by the Lord."

Shelemiah was a priest in the time of Nehemiah, one of several people in the Bible with this name. When Nehemiah reorganized the temple storehouses, he appointed Shelemiah as a treasurer over them, together with Zadok the scribe, Pedaiah of the Levites, and Hanan son of Zaccur, son of Mattaniah, as their assistant. Nehemiah chose them because they were considered faithful, and their job was to distribute the stored supplies to their fellow priests and Levites (Neh 13:13). By inference from the surrounding chapter, this was part of Nehemiah's restoration of the tithes that had been neglected during his absence from Jerusalem. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "repaid by Jehovah," while Hitchcock's Bible Names renders it "God is my perfection" or "my peace."

Shelemiah was the son of Cushi and the father of Nethaniah. He is known only from the genealogy of his grandson Jehudi in Jer 36:14. In the reign of Jehoiakim, the princes sent Jehudi to fetch Baruch and the scroll of Jeremiah's prophecies that Baruch had read aloud to the people. Later in the same chapter, Jehudi reads that scroll to the king. Shelemiah himself plays no part in the story. His name serves to identify Jehudi by listing his ancestry back three generations. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "repaid by Jehovah." Several other men in the Bible are also called Shelemiah, and this one should not be confused with them.

Shelemiah son of Abdeel was one of three men whom the king ordered to arrest Baruch the scribe and Jeremiah the prophet, together with Jerahmeel the son of Hammelech and Seraiah the son of Azriel (Jer 36:26). The surrounding chapter shows that the king was Jehoiakim and that the order came after the scroll of Jeremiah's prophecies had been read before him and he had burned it. The arrest did not take place, because, as the verse says, "the LORD hid them." Nothing more is recorded about this Shelemiah. The name was borne by several other men in the Bible, and this one is identified only by his father's name. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the Septuagint leaves his name out of this verse. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates the episode to about 604 BC.

Shelemiah was the son of Hananiah and the father of Irijah, a captain of the guard in Jerusalem in the last years of the kingdom of Judah. He is known only through his son. At the gate of Benjamin, Irijah stopped the prophet Jeremiah, accused him of deserting to the Chaldeans (the Babylonians), and arrested him (Jer 37:13). The verse names Shelemiah only to identify Irijah, and nothing else is said about him. Smith's Bible Dictionary places him before about 589 BC, a date inferred from the setting during the Babylonian siege. Several other men in the Bible share the name Shelemiah, and there is no clear way to link this one with any of them. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "repaid by Jehovah."

Shelesh was a man of the tribe of Asher, named once in the Asherite genealogy of 1 Chr 7:35. He is listed with his brothers Zophah, Imna and Amal as a son of Helem, described there as the brother of Shomer. His father is called Hotham in this entry. The two names are probably the same man: 1 Chr 7:32 lists Hotham as a brother of Shomer (spelled Shamer in 1 Chr 7:34), so Helem in verse 35 appears to be another form of Hotham. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia call him a son of Helem, while the STEPBible proper names index joins the two names. The Greek manuscripts spell his name variously, including Seme and Selles. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives its meaning as "captain" or "prince," and Smith's gives "might." Nothing else is recorded about him.

Shelomi was a man of the tribe of Asher, known only as the father of Ahihud. In Num 34:27, Ahihud is named as the prince, or leader, of Asher among the tribal representatives chosen to help divide the land of Canaan among the Israelite tribes. Nothing else is recorded about Shelomi himself. Since his son served in the generation that was about to enter Canaan, Shelomi probably lived during the wilderness period. Smith's Bible Dictionary places him before about 1450 BC, which is an estimate inferred from context. Smith's also gives the meaning of his name as "peaceful."

Shelomith was an Israelite woman of the tribe of Dan, the daughter of Dibri. She is named only as the mother of the man who blasphemed the name of the LORD and cursed during Israel's time in the wilderness, and who was brought to Moses for judgment (Lev 24:11). The surrounding passage says her son's father was an Egyptian (Lev 24:10) and that the son was later stoned outside the camp at the LORD's command (Lev 24:14, 23). Nothing else is recorded about her. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of her name as "peaceful." Several other people in the Bible share the name Shelomith, and this entry refers only to the mother of the blasphemer.

Shelomith was a daughter of Zerubbabel and a member of the tribe of Judah, listed in the royal genealogy descending from David. 1 Chr 3:19 names her as the sister of Meshullam and Hananiah, and she is the only daughter mentioned among Zerubbabel's children. The next verse, 1 Chr 3:20, names further sons: Hashubah, Ohel, Berechiah, Hasadiah and Jushab-hesed. Matthew's genealogy of Jesus names another son, Abiud (Matt 1:13). Her father is probably the Zerubbabel who led exiles back from Babylon and served as governor of Judah, so Smith's Bible Dictionary dates her to some time after 536 BC. The same dictionary gives the meaning of her name as "peaceful." Nothing more is recorded about her. Several other people in the Bible share the name Shelomith and should not be confused with her.

Shelomith was a Levite of the clan of Gershon, named in 1 Chr 23:9 alongside Haziel and Haran as the three sons of Shimei. The three are described as heads of the fathers' houses of Laadan, one of the Gershonite family lines. The list appears in David's organization of the Levites for service, which suggests that Shelomith's household had a recognized place in that arrangement. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "peaceful" and identifies this Shelomith as a Gershonite. The STEPBible proper-names index notes the variant spelling Shelomoth. Apart from this single genealogical mention, nothing more is recorded. The name is shared by several other people in the Bible, both men and women. They include a daughter of Zerubbabel and a Levite treasurer in David's time, and they should not be confused with this person.

Shelomith was a daughter of King Rehoboam of Judah and his wife Maachah, the daughter of Absalom. She is named only once, at the end of the list of Maachah's children, after her brothers Abijah, Attai and Ziza (2 Chr 11:20). Her brother Abijah later succeeded Rehoboam as king. The surrounding passage (2 Chr 11:18–19) names Rehoboam's sons by another wife, Mahalath: Jeush, Shamariah and Zaham, who were Shelomith's half-brothers. As a member of the royal household of Judah, she was probably born in Jerusalem, Rehoboam's capital, though the text does not say so. Nothing else is recorded about her. Several other people in the Bible bear the name Shelomith, and they should not be confused with this daughter of Rehoboam.

Shelomith is named in Ezra 8:10 as the ancestor or head of a family whose descendants returned from Babylon to Jerusalem with Ezra. The verse says that from the sons of Shelomith came the son of Josiphiah, together with 160 males. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes Shelomith simply as one whose sons came back with Ezra, and gives the meaning of the name as "peaceful." A different reading is noted in the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia, which follows the Greek of 1 Esdras 8:36 in taking the verse as "of the sons of Bani, Shelomith son of Josiphiah." On that reading Shelomith was the leader of the returning group rather than its ancestor. This entry follows the wording of the verse as it stands. Several other people in the Bible share the name, and this Shelomith should not be confused with them.

Shema was a man of the tribe of Reuben, named only in a genealogy in 1 Chr 5:8. He was the son of Joel and the father of Azaz, whose son Bela lived in Aroer and held land as far as Nebo and Baal-meon, east of the Jordan. The verse gives his name only as a link in Bela's ancestry and records nothing else about him. Because the genealogy skips generations, he may be the same person as Shemaiah, listed as a descendant of Joel a few verses earlier in 1 Chr 5:4. This is an inference, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia connects the name with Shimei, the form found in some Greek manuscripts. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "hearing" or "obeying." Several other people in the Bible share the name, so he should be kept distinct from them.

Shema was a Benjamite, a son of Elpaal, named in the genealogy of Benjamin's descendants. With Beriah he is listed among the heads of the ancestral families living in Aijalon, and the two of them drove out the inhabitants of Gath (1 Chr 8:13). The verse does not say when or how this happened. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both suggest he is probably the same man called Shimhi or Shimei a few verses later in the list (1 Chr 8:21), whose sons are named there. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "hearing" or "obeying." Several other men in the Bible share the name Shema, and this one should not be confused with them.

Shema was one of the men who stood at Ezra the scribe's right hand on the wooden platform when Ezra read the Law aloud to the people gathered in Jerusalem after the return from exile (Neh 8:4). He is named second among the six who stood on Ezra's right, alongside Mattithiah, Anaiah, Urijah, Hilkiah and Maaseiah, while seven others stood on his left. Nothing more is recorded about him, and the text does not say whether he was a priest, a Levite or a lay leader. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the parallel account in 1 Esdras 9:43 calls him Sammus. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates the reading to about 458 BC. Several other men in the Bible share the name Shema, which Hitchcock's Bible Names takes to mean "hearing" or "obeying."

Shemaah was a man of Gibeah, called "the Gibeathite," and the father of Ahiezer and Joash. His sons appear at the head of a list of warriors who came over to David (1 Chr 12:3). The surrounding verses show that this list names Benjamites, Saul's own kinsmen, who joined David at Ziklag while he was still in hiding from Saul. Shemaah was therefore probably a Benjamite, which fits Gibeah, Saul's home town in Benjamin. Ahiezer is called the chief of the group. Nothing else is recorded about Shemaah himself. Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries give the meaning of his name as "rumour." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the Greek Septuagint reads "son" rather than "sons," making him the father of Joash alone. This entry follows the Hebrew text, which names both men as his sons.

Shemaiah was a man of the tribe of Judah, the son of Shechaniah, named in the genealogy of David's royal line in 1 Chr 3:22. The surrounding passage traces this line from Solomon through the kings and on to Zerubbabel and his descendants, so Shemaiah probably lived after the Babylonian exile, by inference from his place in the list. He is credited with five named sons: Hattush, Igeal, Bariah, Neariah and Shaphat. The verse totals "six", which may count Shemaiah himself among the sons of Shechaniah, or may reflect a name lost from the list. The verse also names him twice, once as Shechaniah's son and once as father of the five. His name, according to Hitchcock's Bible Names, means "one who hears or obeys the Lord." Several other men in the Bible share this name, and nothing further is recorded about this one.

Shemaiah was a man of the tribe of Simeon, named only in the genealogy of Ziza in 1 Chr 4:37. He was the father of Shimri and an ancestor of Ziza, five generations later, through Shimri, Jedaiah, Allon and Shiphi. Easton's Bible Dictionary identifies him as a Simeonite. That follows from the context: the list appears among the Simeonite clan leaders in 1 Chr 4:24–43, who are said to have spread to new pasture lands in the days of Hezekiah king of Judah (1 Chr 4:41). Nothing else is recorded about him. The name, which Hitchcock's Bible Names explains as "one who hears or obeys the Lord," belongs to several other men in the Bible, and this Shemaiah should not be confused with them.

Shemaiah was a member of the tribe of Reuben, named in the Reubenite genealogy as the son of Joel and the father of Gog (1 Chr 5:4). The list goes on through Gog to Shimei and later descendants. The passage does not give Joel's own parentage, so how this family line connects to Reuben himself is left unstated. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests he is the same man called Shema later in the same genealogy (1 Chr 5:8). Nothing else is recorded about him. The name, which means "the LORD hears" (Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "that hears or obeys the Lord"), was common in Israel and was borne by many others, especially priests, Levites and prophets. This Shemaiah should not be confused with them.

Shemaiah, son of Nethaneel, was a Levite and scribe in the time of King David. According to 1 Chr 24:6, he wrote down the divisions of the priests as they were assigned by lot. This was done in the presence of the king, the princes, Zadok the priest, Ahimelech son of Abiathar, and the heads of the priestly and Levitical families. Households were drawn alternately for the descendants of Eleazar and of Ithamar, Aaron's two surviving sons. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia describes him as the scribe who registered the names of the priestly courses. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates the event to about 1014 BC, an estimate inferred from context. His name means "the LORD hears." Several other men in the Bible are also called Shemaiah, and this entry refers only to the scribe of 1 Chr 24:6.

Shemaiah was a Levite in the reign of King Jehoshaphat of Judah. He is named first in a list of nine Levites who, together with the priests Elishama and Jehoram, went out with a group of royal officials (2 Chr 17:8). The surrounding passage, as Easton's Bible Dictionary and the STEPBible proper-names index describe it, shows that this group was sent through the cities of Judah to teach the people from the Book of the Law. Nothing else is recorded about him. Several other men in the Bible share the name, which means "the Lord hears." It was common among priests, Levites and prophets, so this Shemaiah should not be confused with the others. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates his service to about 909 BC.

Shemaiah was a Levite of the family of Jeduthun, one of the temple musicians' families, who lived in the reign of King Hezekiah of Judah. He appears in a list of Levites where he is named with Uzziel as representing the sons of Jeduthun, alongside Jehiel and Shimei of the sons of Heman (2 Chr 29:14). By inference from the surrounding passage, these Levites answered Hezekiah's call to consecrate themselves and cleanse the temple in Jerusalem after a period of neglect. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia describes him as one of those who helped purify the temple. His name is usually understood to mean "the Lord hears." Several other men in the Bible share the name, many of them priests, Levites or prophets, and this Shemaiah is known only from this one verse.

Shemaiah was a Levite in the reign of King Hezekiah of Judah. He was one of six men named in 2 Chr 31:15 who served in the cities of the priests and assisted Kore, the keeper of the east gate, who was in charge of the freewill offerings (the preceding verse names Kore). Their task was to share out the offerings and holy things to their fellow priests and Levites by their divisions, giving fairly to great and small alike. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes him as a Levite appointed to distribute the offerings of the Lord, and Smith's Bible Dictionary dates his service to about 726 BC. Nothing more is recorded about him. The name, meaning "the LORD hears," was common, especially among priests, Levites and prophets, so he should not be confused with the many other men called Shemaiah.

Shemaiah was a Levite in the reign of King Josiah of Judah. He appears only in 2 Chr 35:9, in the account of Josiah's great Passover. There he is named with his brothers Conaniah and Nethaneel, and with Hashabiah, Jeiel and Jozabad, as one of the chiefs of the Levites. Together these leaders gave the Levites five thousand lambs and young goats and five hundred cattle for the Passover offerings. The surrounding chapter places this Passover in Josiah's reign. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates it to about 628 BC, an estimate drawn from context. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the Greek Septuagint and 1 Esdras call him Samaias. The name means "the Lord hears." Several other men in the Bible share it, many of them priests, Levites or prophets, and nothing beyond this verse is known of this Shemaiah.

Shemaiah was a member of the family of Adonikam who returned from Babylon to Jerusalem with Ezra. Ezra 8:13 names him with Eliphelet and Jeiel as "the last sons of Adonikam." These three led sixty men of the family. The phrase "the last sons" probably means they came later than the earlier group of Adonikam's descendants who returned under Zerubbabel.
