Nothing more is recorded about him. The name means "the Lord hears," and it is shared by many people in the Bible, especially priests, Levites and prophets, so this Shemaiah should not be confused with the others. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the parallel list in 1 Esdras gives his name as Samaias.

Shemaiah was one of the "chief men" Ezra sent for while his returning company was camped by the river Ahava on the way from Babylon to Jerusalem (Ezra 8:16). He is named in a group with Eliezer, Ariel, Elnathan, Jarib, Nathan, Zechariah and Meshullam. From the surrounding passage, Ezra had found no Levites among the returning people and sent these leaders to Iddo at Casiphia to bring ministers for the temple. Smith's Bible Dictionary therefore describes Shemaiah as one of Ezra's messengers, and Tyndale House's proper-names index counts him as a Levite summoned to join the return. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the parallel account in 1 Esdras gives his name as "Maasmas" or "Samaias." Nothing else is recorded about him. Several other people in the Bible share the name, which means "the Lord hears."

Shemaiah was a priest of the family of Harim who lived in Ezra's time. He is one of several people with this name. Ezra 10:21 lists him among the sons of Harim. In the wider passage, these men are counted among the priests who had married foreign women, and they agreed to send those wives away at Ezra's urging. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both describe him this way. The ISBE adds that the parallel list in 1 Esdras 9:21 calls him "Sameus." Harim was one of the priestly families that returned from exile in Babylon. Nothing else is recorded about him. The name means "the Lord hears" (ISBE).

Shemaiah was an Israelite layman of the family of Harim, listed in Ezra 10:31 among the men who had married foreign wives in the time of Ezra. The surrounding chapter describes how, after returning from exile, these men agreed to send away their foreign wives, and their names were recorded family by family. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates this to about 458 BC. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the parallel list in 1 Esdras 9:32 calls him Sabbeus. The name, meaning roughly "the Lord hears," is shared by many people in the Bible, most often priests, Levites and prophets. This Shemaiah is known only from this single mention and should not be confused with the others.

Shemaiah, son of Shechaniah, was one of the people who rebuilt Jerusalem's wall under Nehemiah after the return from exile. He repaired a section next to the one done by Zadok son of Immer (Neh 3:29). He is called the keeper of the east gate, which most readers take to mean that Shemaiah himself held this post. The STEPBible Proper Names index describes him as a Levite who repaired the wall near his house. 1 Chr 3:22 also names a Shemaiah son of Shechaniah among the descendants of David. Some connect the two, but whether they are the same man is uncertain. The name was shared by several people in the Bible, and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives its meaning as "that hears or obeys the Lord."

Shemaiah, son of Delaiah and grandson of Mehetabeel, was a man in Jerusalem in Nehemiah's time, during the rebuilding of the city wall. He is described as "shut up", which probably means confined to his house, though the reason is not given. When Nehemiah visited him, Shemaiah urged him to meet inside the temple and shut its doors, warning that enemies were coming at night to kill him. The verses that follow (Neh 6:12–13) say Nehemiah saw that God had not sent him, and that Tobiah and Sanballat had hired him to frighten Nehemiah into acting wrongly and so discredit him. For this reason Easton's Bible Dictionary and the Tyndale House proper-names list call him a false prophet. His name means "heard by the Lord" according to Smith's Bible Dictionary. Several other men in the Bible share the name.

Shemaiah was a descendant of Asaph, the temple musician, and appears only in a family line in Neh 12:35. There he is named as the son of Mattaniah, the father of Jonathan, and the grandfather of Zechariah. Zechariah was one of the priests' sons who played trumpets in the procession at the dedication of Jerusalem's rebuilt wall under Nehemiah. Shemaiah himself is not described as taking part, so he probably lived a generation or two before that event. Neh 11:22 names a Hashabiah who was also a son of Mattaniah son of Micha, which is probably how this entry identifies him as Shemaiah's brother. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia gives the name's meaning as "the LORD hears." Several other people in the Bible share this name.

Shemaiah was one of the musicians who took part in the dedication of the rebuilt wall of Jerusalem in Nehemiah's time. He is named first among the 'brethren' of Zechariah son of Jonathan, a group that played the musical instruments of David while Ezra the scribe led their procession (Neh 12:36). The preceding verse, Neh 12:35, identifies Zechariah as a priest's son who played a trumpet. This entry treats Shemaiah as a son of Jonathan and a brother of Zechariah, Azarael, Milalai, Gilalai, Maai, Nethaneel, Judah and Hanani, though 'brethren' can also mean kinsmen or fellow members of a Levitical guild. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes he may stand for a singer or a clan. His name means 'the Lord hears'. Several other men in the Bible share the name.

Shemaiah was one of the men who took part in the dedication of the rebuilt wall of Jerusalem in Nehemiah's time, about 445 BC by inference from context. He is listed in Neh 12:42 among a group of eight who stood with one of the two thanksgiving processions, just before the singers sang loudly under their overseer Jezrahiah. Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries identify him as a priest. The STEPBible proper-names index treats him as a Levite connected with the singing. The verse itself names him only in the list, without giving his family or exact role. The name, which Hitchcock's Bible Names explains as "that hears or obeys the Lord," belongs to several people in the Bible, including others in Nehemiah, so this Shemaiah should not be assumed to be any of them.

Shemaiah was the father of Urijah, a prophet who spoke in the name of the LORD against Jerusalem and Judah in the same terms as Jeremiah (Jer 26:20). He is mentioned only to identify his son. The phrase "of Kirjathjearim" most naturally describes the family's home town, Kiriath-jearim, west of Jerusalem. The surrounding chapter places Urijah's preaching in the reign of King Jehoiakim, who had him pursued into Egypt and killed, so Shemaiah probably lived in the late 7th century BC. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates him to before 608 BC. Nothing else is recorded about him. Several other people in the Bible share the name, which the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia renders as "the LORD hears." It notes that the name was borne most often by priests, Levites and prophets.

Shemaiah was the father of Delaiah, one of the royal officials ("princes") gathered in the scribe's chamber of the king's house when Baruch's scroll of Jeremiah's prophecies was reported to them (Jer 36:12). The chapter sets this scene in the reign of King Jehoiakim of Judah, so Shemaiah probably lived in the late seventh century BC. Nothing else is recorded about him, and he is known only through his son. Later in the same chapter, Delaiah is one of the officials who urged the king not to burn the scroll (Jer 36:25). The name, which Hitchcock's Bible Names explains as "one who hears or obeys the Lord," was common, and several other men in the Bible are called Shemaiah. This entry refers only to Delaiah's father.

Shemariah was one of the warriors who joined David at Ziklag, named in a list of fighting men in 1 Chr 12:5. The surrounding passage describes these men as kinsmen of Saul from the tribe of Benjamin. They came to David while he was still kept away from Saul's court, and they were skilled with bow and sling. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both identify him as a Benjamite warrior. His name means "whom the LORD guards" or "kept by the LORD." Nothing more is recorded about him. Several other men in the Bible share the name Shemariah, so he should not be confused with them.

Shemariah was a man of Israel, a member of the family of Harim, who appears in the list of those who had married foreign wives in the time of Ezra. Ezra 10:32 names him alongside Benjamin and Malluch. The preceding verse places this group among "the sons of Harim," and the surrounding chapter describes how these men agreed to send away their foreign wives as part of Ezra's reforms after the return from exile. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him as a layman rather than a priest or Levite. His name means "kept by the LORD" or "whom the LORD guards." Nothing more is recorded about him. Several other men in the Bible share the name Shemariah, including one of David's warriors and a son of King Rehoboam, and this entry refers only to the man in Ezra's list.

Shemariah was an Israelite in Ezra's time whose name appears in the list of men who had married foreign wives (Ezra 10:41). By inference from the surrounding chapter, he was among those who agreed to send these wives away during the reforms led by Ezra after the return from exile in Babylon. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia places him among the descendants of Bani, the family group whose list begins earlier in the chapter. Nothing else is recorded about him. Several other men in the Bible share the name, and he should not be confused with them. The name means "the Lord guards" or "kept by the Lord."

Shemeber was the king of Zeboiim, one of the cities of the plain near Sodom. He appears only in Gen 14:2, which lists him among five local kings who went to war against Chedorlaomer of Elam and his allies. The surrounding chapter says these kings had served Chedorlaomer for twelve years and rebelled in the thirteenth. The two sides fought in the Vale of Siddim, where the five kings were defeated. Abram later pursued the victors and brought back the captives and goods that had been taken. Shemeber's name is not repeated when the kings are listed again in Gen 14:8, where he is called only the king of Zeboiim. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "soaring on high," and Hitchcock's Bible Names as "name of the strong." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes A. H. Sayce's comparison of the name with the Assyrian name Sumu-abi.

Shemer was the owner of the hill of Samaria in the northern kingdom of Israel. According to 1 Kgs 16:24 he sold the hill for two talents of silver to a king who built a city on it. From the surrounding passage, that king was Omri. The verse says the city was named Samaria after Shemer, the hill's former owner, and it later became the capital of the northern kingdom. Nothing else is recorded about him. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of his name as "guardian" or "thorn." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests that Shemer may have been an ancient clan name. It also connects the name Samaria with the idea of a "watch mountain," a reading that sits alongside the verse's statement that the city was named after Shemer.

Shemiramoth was a Levite in the reign of Jehoshaphat, king of Judah. He is named in 2 Chr 17:8 among nine Levites who, together with the priests Elishama and Jehoram, were sent out with the king's officials. The surrounding passage (2 Chr 17:7–9) explains the mission. In the third year of his reign Jehoshaphat sent these men through the cities of Judah to teach the people, taking the book of the law of the Lord with them. Nothing else is recorded about him. The same name belongs to a Levite musician in David's time (1 Chr 15:18; 16:5), who is generally treated as a different person, given the gap of more than a century between them. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "the height of the heavens."

Shemuel son of Ammihud was the leader from the tribe of Simeon chosen to help divide the land of Canaan among the tribes. He appears in a list of tribal leaders whom the LORD named to Moses, one from each tribe. These leaders were to work with Eleazar the priest and Joshua in assigning the territory west of the Jordan (Num 34:20). Nothing else is recorded about him. The name, which Smith's Bible Dictionary takes to mean "heard by God," is the same Hebrew name as Samuel. It is shared by several people in the Bible, so this Shemuel should not be confused with the others who bear it. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates the appointment to about 1450 BC, an estimate inferred from context.

Shemuel was a son of Tola and a grandson of Issachar, belonging to the tribe of Issachar. He is listed in 1 Chr 7:2 with his brothers Uzzi, Rephaiah, Jeriel, Jahmai and Jibsam as heads of their father's house. The passage calls them valiant men of might, and says their descendants numbered 22,600 in the days of David. The STEPBible Proper Names index describes him as a leader of Issachar during David's reign, though the verse may simply mean the family's numbers were counted then. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "heard by God." The same name belongs to other people in the Bible, and this Shemuel is known only from this one genealogical list.

Shenazar (spelled Shenazzar in the Revised Version) was a man of the tribe of Judah, named once in the royal genealogy of 1 Chronicles. He appears in a list of sons that continues from the previous verse, which names the sons of Jeconiah, also called Jehoiachin, the king of Judah taken captive to Babylon. His brothers included Shealtiel, Malchiram, Pedaiah, Jecamiah, Hoshama and Nedabiah. Smith's Bible Dictionary takes him as a son of Shealtiel instead, but this entry follows the reading that makes him a son of Jehoiachin. Because his father was deported, he was probably born during the Babylonian exile, as the Tyndale House proper-names list notes. Nothing else is recorded about him.

Shephathiah was a Benjamite named only in a genealogy, as the son of Reuel and the father of Meshullam (1 Chr 9:8). The verse traces the line back one step further, to Reuel's father Ibnijah. He appears in the list of Benjamites who lived in Jerusalem, which the surrounding passage presents as the city's residents after the return from exile in Babylon. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him simply as the father of Meshullam. His son Meshullam is one of the Benjamite heads of families named there. Nothing else is recorded about Shephathiah. His name is spelled a little differently from the more common Shephatiah, borne by several other men in the Old Testament, and he should not be confused with them.

Shephatiah the Haruphite was one of the warriors who came to David at Ziklag, listed in 1 Chr 12:5. The surrounding passage describes these men as relatives of Saul from the tribe of Benjamin who joined David while he was still kept away from Saul. They were skilled with both bow and sling, able to use either hand. The title "Haruphite" probably refers to his family or hometown, though its exact meaning is uncertain. His name means "the Lord has judged" (Hitchcock's Bible Names; International Standard Bible Encyclopedia). Several other men in the Bible share the name, and nothing further is recorded about this one. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates the event to about 1054 BC, and that date is an estimate.

Shephatiah son of Maachah was the leader of the tribe of Simeon during the reign of David. He appears only once, in a list of the chief officers over the tribes of Israel (1 Chr 27:16), alongside leaders such as Eliezer son of Zichri over Reuben. The list belongs to the Chronicler's account of how David organized his kingdom near the end of his life. Nothing else is recorded about Shephatiah's life or duties. His name means "the LORD has judged" or "the LORD judges," according to the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia and Hitchcock's Bible Names. Several other men in the Bible share this name, including a son of David and an official in Jeremiah's time. This Shephatiah is distinguished from them by his father, Maachah, and by his role over the Simeonites.

Shephatiah was one of the sons of King Jehoshaphat of Judah, listed with his brothers Azariah, Jehiel, Zechariah, a second Azariah and Michael in 2 Chr 21:2. Their eldest brother Jehoram succeeded Jehoshaphat as king. The verse calls Jehoshaphat "king of Israel," though he ruled the southern kingdom of Judah. The following verses say that Jehoshaphat gave these sons gifts of silver, gold and fortified cities in Judah, and that after Jehoram secured the throne he killed all his brothers with the sword (2 Chr 21:3–4). Shephatiah probably died in that purge in Jerusalem, about 889 BC by inference from context. His name means "the LORD has judged" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia). Several other men in the Bible share this name.

Shephatiah was a man of the tribe of Judah, descended through Perez, named only in the genealogy of Athaiah in Neh 11:4. He was the son of Mahalaleel and the father of Amariah. Through Amariah he was an ancestor of Athaiah, one of the men of Judah who lived in Jerusalem in the time of Nehemiah, after the return from the Babylonian exile. Nothing else is recorded about his life, and when he lived can only be placed some generations before Nehemiah's day, by inference from the length of the family line. His name means "the Lord has judged" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia). Several other men in the Bible share this name, and this Shephatiah is not clearly linked to any of them.

Shephatiah son of Mattan was an official in Jerusalem during the reign of King Zedekiah, shortly before the city fell to Babylon. He appears in Jer 38:1 with Gedaliah son of Pashur, Jucal son of Shelemiah and Pashur son of Malchiah, a group who heard Jeremiah telling the people to surrender to the Chaldeans. In the verses that follow, these men urged the king to put the prophet to death, and Jeremiah was let down into a cistern. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary both describe Shephatiah as one of the princes who opposed Jeremiah this way. His name means "the Lord has judged." Several other men in the Old Testament share the name, and nothing further is known about this one.

Sherah (also spelled Sheerah) was a woman of the tribe of Ephraim, one of the Joseph tribes. She is remembered in 1 Chr 7:24 for building Lower and Upper Beth-horon and a town named after her, Uzzen-sherah. This is unusual, because the Bible rarely credits a woman with founding towns. The verse calls her "his daughter," and the surrounding passage leaves unclear whether "his" means Ephraim or his son Beriah. Smith's Bible Dictionary takes her as Ephraim's daughter. The STEPBible name index treats her as his granddaughter through Beriah, and this entry follows that view. On that reading, Rephah and Resheph, named in the following verse, were her brothers. The two Beth-horons are generally identified with the modern villages of Beit Ur et-Tahta and Beit Ur al-Fauqa, northwest of Jerusalem. The location of Uzzen-sherah is unknown.

Sheresh was a man of the tribe of Manasseh, one of the tribes descended from Joseph. He is named only once, in the genealogy of Manasseh at 1 Chr 7:16. He was a son of Machir, Manasseh's son, and Machir's wife Maachah, and a brother of Peresh. The verse goes on to say "his sons were Ulam and Rakem." The wording could refer either to Sheresh or to Peresh, but this entry follows the reading that makes Ulam and Rakem the sons of Sheresh. Gilead and Hammoleketh, named elsewhere in the same chapter, are listed here among Machir's children and so as Sheresh's siblings. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "root." Nothing else is recorded about him.

Sherezer (also spelled Sharezer) was a man sent, together with Regemmelech and their men, to the house of God to pray before the Lord (Zech 7:2). The following verse shows that the delegation also asked the priests and prophets whether they should keep mourning and fasting in the fifth month, as they had done for many years (Zech 7:3). By inference from Zech 7:1, this took place in the fourth year of Darius, after the return from exile. Who sent him is unclear. The King James wording leaves the senders unnamed, and Easton's Bible Dictionary describes them as the exiles. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia reads the Hebrew as saying that the people of Bethel sent him, and notes that the text is difficult. It also links the name to an Assyrian phrase meaning "protect the king," while Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "prince of fire." He is a different person from Sennacherib's son of the same name.

Shethar was one of the seven princes of Persia and Media at the court of King Ahasuerus, named in Esth 1:14 alongside Carshena, Admatha, Tarshish, Meres, Marsena and Memucan. These men "saw the king's face," meaning they had direct access to him, and they held the highest rank in the kingdom. In the surrounding passage the king consults this group of advisers about Queen Vashti's refusal to appear before him, though Shethar himself is not singled out. His name is probably Persian. Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries give its meaning as "a star," while the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that it has never been satisfactorily explained. Smith's dates him to about 483 BC. That date is an estimate based on the setting of the story in the third year of Ahasuerus's reign, usually identified with Xerxes I. Nothing else is recorded about him.

Sheva was a man of the tribe of Judah, named in the genealogy of 1 Chr 2. He was a son of Caleb and Caleb's concubine Maachah, whose other sons, Sheber and Tirhanah, appear in 1 Chr 2:48. Shaaph was another of her sons. Sheva is called "the father of Machbenah" and probably also "the father of Gibea" (1 Chr 2:49). In these genealogies "father" often means the founder or leading figure of a settlement, so Machbenah and Gibea were probably towns in Judah. Their sites are unknown. The same verse names Achsah as Caleb's daughter, which links this Caleb with the Caleb whose daughter Achsah appears in the conquest accounts. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "Jehovah contends." This Sheva is a different man from Sheva, David's scribe, in 2 Sam 20:25. Nothing else is recorded about him.

Shiloni is named in the King James Version as the father of Zechariah and the earliest ancestor in the family line of Maaseiah son of Baruch. Maaseiah was one of the men of Judah who settled in Jerusalem after the return from exile in Babylon, in Nehemiah's time (Neh 11:5). Smith's Bible Dictionary takes the word as a clan name, "the Shilonite," rather than a personal name, meaning a descendant of Shelah, son of Judah. The STEPBible proper-names index likewise describes the Shilonites as descendants of Judah living in Jerusalem after the exile. The parallel list of Jerusalem's settlers in 1 Chr 9:5 speaks of "the Shilonites," which fits this reading. This entry treats Shiloni as a male ancestor while noting that the name may be a family designation. Nothing else is recorded about him.

Shilshah was a man of the tribe of Asher, named once in the Bible as one of the sons of Zophah in the genealogy of Asher's descendants (1 Chr 7:37). He appears in a list of brothers that includes Suah, Harnepher, Beri, Imrah, Bezer, Hod, Shamma and Beera. The surrounding verses trace Zophah's line back through Helem and Heber to Asher. Nothing else is recorded about Shilshah's life or deeds. The Greek manuscripts spell his name differently, for example Saleisa in Codex Vaticanus and Codex Alexandrinus, according to the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "strong," and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "three," "chief" or "captain."

Shimea was a Levite of the family of Merari, named only in the genealogy of 1 Chr 6:30. He was the son of Uzza and the father of Haggiah, and his grandson was Asaiah. The surrounding list (1 Chr 6:29) traces this line from Merari through Mahli, Libni, Shimei and Uzza, so Shimea sits in the middle of a chain of descendants, which Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary both describe as Merarite. Nothing else is recorded about his life. STEPBible's proper-names index places him in the time of King David, probably by inference from the later Asaiah who led the Merarites when the ark was brought to Jerusalem (1 Chr 15:6), if that is the same man. The name is shared by several other people in the Bible, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia links it with the related forms Shammua and Shammah.

Shimea was a Levite named in the family line of Asaph, the singer who stood at the right hand of Heman in the temple music arranged under David. In 1 Chr 6:39 he is the father of Berachiah and so Asaph's grandfather. The genealogy goes on to name his father as Michael, and it traces the line back to Gershom son of Levi, so Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary describe Shimea as a Gershonite Levite. Nothing else is recorded about him. Several people in the Bible share this name, and this entry covers only the ancestor of Asaph.

Shimeah was a Benjamite, the son of Mikloth, named in the genealogy of the family of Gibeon in 1 Chronicles 8. The verse records that Mikloth fathered Shimeah and that these relatives lived in Jerusalem alongside their kinsmen (1 Chr 8:32). Easton's Bible Dictionary describes him as a descendant of Gibeon, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia as a descendant of Jehiel, the "father" or founder of Gibeon. The parallel genealogy in 1 Chr 9:38 gives his name as Shimeam. According to the STEPBible proper names index he was a nephew of Ner, who appears in the same family list. Nothing else is recorded about him, and his dates are unknown, though Smith's Bible Dictionary tentatively places him around 536 BC. Hitchcock's Bible Names suggests the name means "that hears" or "obeys."

Shimei was a Levite of the family of Gershon, named once in the ancestry of Asaph, one of the singers David put in charge of music at the house of the Lord (1 Chr 6:39–43). He was the father of Zimmah, and through him an ancestor of Ethan and, several generations later, of Asaph. This entry names his father as Laadan, a Gershonite whose family appears in 1 Chr 23:7–9. The verse that follows in the genealogy (1 Chr 6:43) calls him the son of Jahath, son of Gershom, and Smith's Bible Dictionary follows that reading. Because the names Shimei and Jahath recur among the Gershonite families, the exact relationship is uncertain. Several other men in the Bible share this name. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives its meaning as "that hears or obeys" or "my fame."

Shimei was a Levite musician, a son of Jeduthun (also identified with Ethan), one of David's chief temple singers. When the singers were divided by lot into twenty-four courses of service, the tenth lot fell to Shimei, who led a group of twelve made up of himself, his sons and his relatives (1 Chr 25:17). Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him as chief of the tenth division of the singers. His brothers were Gedaliah, Izri (Zeri), Jeshaiah, Hashabiah and Mattithiah. The Hebrew list of Jeduthun's sons in 1 Chr 25:3 gives the total as six but names only five, so Shimei is probably the missing sixth. The sons linked with him here match the sons of Obed-edom in 1 Chr 26:4–5, and Obed-edom is called a son of Jeduthun in 1 Chr 16:38, so this entry connects Shimei with that family. The connection is uncertain. Several other men in the Bible share his name.

Shimei was a son of Pedaiah and a brother of Zerubbabel, listed in the genealogy of David's royal descendants in 1 Chr 3:19. He belonged to the tribe of Judah. Pedaiah is named in the same genealogy as a son of King Jeconiah (Jehoiachin), so Shimei was a grandson of that king. Several other men in the Bible share his name. Nothing further is recorded of him, and no descendants are listed for him, while the verse goes straight on to name Zerubbabel's children. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates him to about 536 BC, the period of the return from exile, which fits his being Zerubbabel's brother. The name is usually taken to mean "renowned" or "one who hears."

Shimei was a Reubenite named in the genealogy of the tribe of Reuben in 1 Chr 5:4. He was the son of Gog and belonged to the line descended from Joel. The next verse, 1 Chr 5:5, names his son Micah. The list continues down to Beerah, a Reubenite leader whom the Assyrian king Tilgath-pilneser carried into exile. Joel's exact connection to Reuben is not spelled out, but the surrounding passage concerns Reuben's descendants, and Easton's and Smith's Bible dictionaries both identify Shimei as a Reubenite. Nothing more is recorded about him. Several other men in the Bible share the name Shimei and should not be confused with him. Hitchcock's Bible Names explains the name as meaning "that hears" or "my fame."

Shimei was a Levite of the clan of Merari, named only in the genealogy of the Levites in 1 Chr 6:29. In that list he is the son of Libni and the father of Uzza. Here Libni appears as the son of Mahli, Merari's son, so Shimei belongs to the line descending from Merari through Mahli. This Libni is apparently distinct from the better-known Libni who was a son of Gershon, another of Levi's sons. The verse records nothing about Shimei beyond his place in this line of descent. The name Shimei is shared by several men in the Bible, including other Levites, so he should not be confused with them. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "that hears or obeys" or "my reputation."

Shimei the Ramathite was the official in charge of King David's vineyards, according to the list of royal stewards in 1 Chr 27:27. The same verse names Zabdi the Shiphmite as the man responsible for the produce of the vineyards stored in the wine cellars, so Shimei probably oversaw the vines themselves while Zabdi handled the wine. "Ramathite" probably means he came from a place called Ramah, as the Tyndale House STEPBible names list takes it. Several towns bore that name, so his hometown is uncertain. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia counts him as a man of Judah. Nothing else is recorded about him, and he should not be confused with the other men named Shimei in the Bible, a common name probably meaning "hear me" or "heard."

Shimei was a Levite descended from Heman, one of the temple singers' families. He is named with Jehiel as representing the sons of Heman among the Levites who gathered to purify the temple (2 Chr 29:14). From the surrounding chapter, this took place at the start of King Hezekiah's reign, when the king ordered the Levites to sanctify themselves and clear the temple of what had defiled it. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates the event to about 726 BC, an estimate based on context. The same passage lists Shemaiah and Uzziel for the sons of Jeduthun, another musical family. Nothing else is recorded about this Shimei. The name was common, and several other men in the Bible are called Shimei. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives its meaning as "that hears or obeys" or "my fame."

Shimei was a Levite in the time of Ezra, named among those who had married foreign wives (Ezra 10:23). He appears in the list of men found to have taken wives from the surrounding peoples after the return from exile in Babylon. By inference from the surrounding chapter, he was one of those who agreed to send these wives away, as the STEPBible Proper Names index also states. He is listed with other Levites, including Jozabad, Kelaiah (also called Kelita), Pethahiah, Judah and Eliezer. Nothing else is recorded about him. The name Shimei is shared by several other men in the Bible, and this one should not be confused with them. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives its meaning as "that hears or obeys" or "my fame."

Shimei was one of the descendants of Hashum listed in Ezra 10:33 among the Israelite men who had married foreign wives. Context shows that these men agreed, at Ezra's call after the return from Babylonian exile, to send those wives away. He appears in the list alongside Mattenai, Mattathah, Zabad, Eliphelet, Jeremai and Manasseh, all of the same family. Smith's Bible Dictionary describes him the same way, as one of the family of Hashum who put away his foreign wife at Ezra's command. Nothing else is recorded about him. The name Shimei was common and is borne by several other people in the Bible, including others in the same list in Ezra 10. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives its meaning as "that hears or obeys" or "my fame."

Shimei was one of the Israelites named in Ezra 10:38 in the list of men who had married foreign wives after the return from exile in Babylon. By inference from the surrounding passage, he was among those who agreed, under Ezra's reforms, to send these wives away. The list groups the men by family, and his name falls in the section headed "of the sons of Bani" (Ezra 10:34). For that reason Smith's Bible Dictionary calls him a son of Bani, meaning a member of that family line. It dates the event to about 459 BC, an estimate drawn from context. Nothing else is recorded about him. Several other men in the Bible share the name, and this Shimei should not be confused with them. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "that hears or obeys" or "my fame."

Shimei was a Benjamite named in the family line of Mordecai, the Jew living at the Persian palace in Shushan (Susa). Esth 2:5 traces Mordecai as "the son of Jair, the son of Shimei, the son of Kish," so Shimei was Mordecai's grandfather, or possibly a more distant ancestor. Nothing else is recorded about him. Readers differ on how to take the list. Some treat it as a straight run of generations. Others think it names famous forebears of the tribe, linking Kish with Saul's father and Shimei with the Benjamite Shimei son of Gera, who cursed David. This entry treats him simply as the Shimei of Esther 2:5. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests the name may mean "hear me (God)," and notes that it is shared by many people in the Old Testament.

Shimeon was an Israelite of the family of Harim. He is named in the list of men who had married foreign wives in the time of Ezra (Ezra 10:31). In the surrounding passage these men agreed to send away their foreign wives after Ezra's reforms in Jerusalem. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates this to about 458 BC, a date inferred from context. Shimeon is a laymen's name, not a priest's, since the sons of Harim listed here come after the priests and Levites in the chapter. The name is a form of Simeon and is usually taken to mean "hearing" or "hearkening" (Easton's Bible Dictionary). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the parallel list in 1 Esdras 9:32 gives him as "Simon Chosameus." Nothing else is recorded about him.

Shimhi was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, named only in the Benjamite genealogy of 1 Chronicles 8. The verses there list nine sons: Jakim, Zichri, Zabdi, Eliel, Zilthai, Elienai, Adaiah, Beraiah and Shimrath. These families appear to have been counted among the Benjamites living in Jerusalem. In Hebrew his name is the same as Shimei, a common name meaning "famous" or "renowned" according to Easton's and Smith's Bible Dictionaries. Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests he is the same man as Shema, a son of Elpaal mentioned a few verses earlier in the same chapter. Because several men in this genealogy bear similar names, his exact place in the family line is uncertain. Nothing else is recorded about him.

Shimon was a man named in the genealogy of the tribe of Judah in 1 Chronicles, where his four sons are listed as Amnon, Rinnah, Ben-hanan and Tilon (1 Chr 4:20). Nothing else is recorded about him, and the passage does not say how he connects to the surrounding family lines. Smith's Bible Dictionary calls this an obscure genealogy of Judah. STEPBible's proper-name index (Tyndale House) places him among the descendants of Judah through Caleb. Smith's gives the name's meaning as "desert," while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "providing well" or "fatness." He should not be confused with Simeon, the son of Jacob, whose name is similar.

Shimrath was a man of the tribe of Benjamin, named only in the genealogy of Benjamin's descendants in 1 Chr 8:21. He was a son of Shimhi, also spelled Shimei, and the last of nine sons listed. His brothers were Jakim, Zichri, Zabdi, Elienai, Zilthai, Eliel, Adaiah and Beraiah. The STEPBible Proper Names index connects his father with Shimei, son of Elpaal. Nothing else is recorded about his life. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "guard", while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "hearing" or "obedient".

Shimri was a man of the tribe of Simeon, the son of Shemaiah and the father of Jedaiah. He appears only once, in the genealogy of Ziza in 1 Chr 4:37. That list traces Ziza back through Shiphi, Allon and Jedaiah to Shimri and Shemaiah. The surrounding passage presents Ziza as one of the Simeonite clan leaders who, in the days of King Hezekiah, moved into the region of Gedor in search of pasture. Shimri would therefore have lived several generations before Hezekiah's reign. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both identify him as a Simeonite. Nothing else is recorded about him. Several other people in the Bible share the name Shimri, so he should not be confused with them.

Shimri was the father of Jediael and Joha, two men named among the mighty warriors of King David's army in 1 Chr 11:45. The verse adds the description "the Tizite," which may apply to Joha alone or to the whole family. If it applies to the family, it probably points to a home town or clan called Tiz or Tizi, though no such place is otherwise known. Nothing more is recorded about Shimri himself. His sons' service under David places him, by inference, in or just before the time of David's reign. Several other people in the Bible share the name Shimri, and this one should not be confused with them. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "vigilant," while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "thorn" or "dregs."

Shimri was a Levite of the family of Elizaphan who took part in cleansing the temple during the reign of King Hezekiah. He is named with Jeiel as the representatives of the sons of Elizaphan among the Levites who prepared themselves and purified the house of the Lord (2 Chr 29:13). Elizaphan was a leader of the Kohathite clan (Num 3:30), so Smith's Bible Dictionary describes Shimri as a Kohathite Levite. Nothing more is recorded about him. Several other men in the Bible share the name Shimri, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia counts four in all. This entry concerns only the Levite of Hezekiah's time. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "vigilant."

Shinab was the king of Admah, one of the five cities of the plain, in the time of Abraham. Genesis 14:2 names him among the five kings, along with Bera of Sodom, Birsha of Gomorrah, Shemeber of Zeboiim and the king of Bela (Zoar), who were attacked by Chedorlaomer king of Elam and his allies. The surrounding passage explains that these kings had served Chedorlaomer for twelve years and then rebelled, and that they fought and lost in the valley of Siddim (Gen 14:4, 8–10). Shinab is not mentioned again. Later passages such as Deut 29:23 recall Admah as destroyed along with Sodom and Gomorrah. The meaning of his name is uncertain: Easton's Bible Dictionary gives "cooling," Smith's Bible Dictionary "splendor of the father," and Hitchcock's Bible Names "father of changing."

Shiphi was a man of the tribe of Simeon, named only in the genealogy at 1 Chr 4:37. He was the son of Allon and the father of Ziza, and his line is traced back through Jedaiah, Shimri and Shemaiah. The surrounding passage lists Ziza among the Simeonite clan leaders whose families grew numerous. By inference from 1 Chr 4:41, these leaders moved to seize pasture land in the days of King Hezekiah of Judah. Smith's Bible Dictionary calls Ziza a prince of the tribe in that period, which would place Shiphi a generation or so earlier, in the late eighth century BC. Nothing else is recorded about Shiphi himself. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "abundant," and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "multitude."

Shiphrah was one of two midwives, with Puah, whom the king of Egypt addressed during the oppression of the Israelites in Egypt (Exod 1:15). The following verses (Exod 1:16–21) say the king ordered them to kill Hebrew baby boys at birth. Because they feared God, they let the boys live and told Pharaoh that Hebrew women gave birth before a midwife arrived. God treated the midwives well and gave them families of their own. The text calls them the "Hebrew midwives." Most references take this to mean they were Hebrews, though Easton's Bible Dictionary describes them as Egyptian midwives serving the Hebrews. This entry follows the reading that they were Hebrew. Her name is usually understood to mean "beauty" or "fairness" (International Standard Bible Encyclopedia). The Septuagint renders it Sepphora, the same form it uses for Zipporah, Moses' wife.

Shiphtan was an Ephraimite, known only as the father of Kemuel. Kemuel was the prince, or leader, of the tribe of Ephraim chosen to help divide the land of Canaan among the tribes of Israel (Num 34:24). That verse belongs to the list of tribal leaders who were to work with Eleazar the priest and Joshua in giving out the inheritance. Nothing else is recorded about Shiphtan himself. Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary give the meaning of his name as "judicial." Easton's describes him as the Ephraimite prince, though the verse gives that title to his son Kemuel. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that Greek manuscripts spell the name in forms such as Sabatha and Saphatan.

Shitrai was a man from Sharon who served King David as the official in charge of the royal herds that grazed in the plain of Sharon, the fertile coastal plain along the Mediterranean (1 Chr 27:29). He is called "the Sharonite," which probably marks him as a native of that region. He appears in a list of stewards who managed David's property, alongside Shaphat son of Adlai, who oversaw the herds in the valleys. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia describes him as David's chief shepherd. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of his name as "gatherer of money." Nothing else is recorded about him.

Shiza was a man of the tribe of Reuben, known only as the father of Adina. His son Adina appears in the list of David's mighty warriors in 1 Chr 11:42, where he is described as a captain of the Reubenites with thirty men under him. Nothing else is recorded about Shiza himself. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia reads the verse as making Shiza one of David's leading warriors, while Smith's Bible Dictionary and the Tyndale House proper-names index treat the warrior as his son Adina, which matches the plain wording of the verse. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "splendor," and Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "this gift."

Shobab was a son of Caleb son of Hezron, of the tribe of Judah, named in the genealogy at 1 Chr 2:18 together with his brothers Jesher and Ardon. The verse says Caleb had children by Azubah his wife and by Jerioth, then lists "her sons" without making clear which woman is meant. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the Tyndale House proper-names list take Azubah to be Shobab's mother. The other half-brothers counted with him in this entry, such as Hur and Mesha, appear elsewhere in the same chapter as sons of Caleb by other wives. Nothing else is recorded about him. He should not be confused with Shobab the son of David, a different man who shares the name. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "returned" or "turned back," and Smith's gives "rebellious."

Shobek was one of the men who set their seal to the covenant made in Nehemiah's day, when the community that had returned from the Babylonian exile formally pledged to keep God's law. He is known only from a single name in the list of signers (Neh 10:24), where he appears between Hallohesh and Pileha. Smith's Bible Dictionary counts him among the heads of the people, which matches his place in the part of the list introduced as 'the chief of the people' (Neh 10:14). STEPBible's proper-names index describes him as a Levite. This entry follows the 'heads of the people' reading. Smith's dates the covenant to about 446 BC, an estimate inferred from context. Nothing else is recorded about him. Smith's gives the meaning of his name as 'free', while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives 'made void; forsaken'.

Shobi was an Ammonite, the son of Nahash of Rabbah, the Ammonite capital. When David fled from his son Absalom and reached Mahanaim, east of the Jordan, Shobi met him along with Machir son of Ammiel of Lodebar and Barzillai the Gileadite of Rogelim. The following verses (2 Sam 17:28–29) say these men brought bedding, bowls and food such as wheat, barley, beans, honey and cheese for David and his people. His father is probably the Ammonite king Nahash whose kindness David remembered (2 Sam 10:2). If so, Shobi was the brother of King Hanun, whose city of Rabbah David later captured, and he may have governed there under David, though the text does not say so. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "captor", while Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "glorious".

Shoham was a Levite of the clan of Merari, named once in the Bible as a son of Jaaziah, alongside his brothers Beno, Zaccur and Ibri (1 Chr 24:27). He appears in the lists of Levitical families that 1 Chronicles places in David's time, when the Levites were organized for service at the sanctuary. Beyond his place in this genealogy, nothing more is recorded of him. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia give the meaning of his name as "onyx," while Hitchcock's Bible Names renders it "keeping back." Smith's Bible Dictionary dates him to about 1043 BC, an estimate inferred from the context of David's reign.

Shua was a woman of the tribe of Asher, the daughter of Heber. She appears only once, in the Asherite genealogy of 1 Chr 7:32, which names her as the sister of Japhlet, Shomer (also spelled Shamer) and Hotham. The verses just before it (1 Chr 7:30–31) make Heber a son of Beriah and a grandson of Asher, which places Shua in the fourth generation from Asher. Women are seldom named in these lists, but the text gives no further details about her. She should not be confused with others in the Bible who bear similar names, such as the Canaanite Shua whose daughter married Judah. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "crying" or "saving."

Shuah was a man of the tribe of Judah, named only once, in the genealogy of 1 Chr 4:11. There he appears as the brother of Chelub, who became the father of Mehir and the grandfather of Eshton. Nothing else is recorded about him. This entry gives his father as Rechah, probably by inference from the next verse, 1 Chr 4:12, which ends the short family list with "These are the men of Rechah." Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that the Hebrew form of his name is properly Shuchah, and the STEPBible name index spells it Shuhah. This sets him apart from other men called Shuah, such as the son of Abraham and Keturah. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meanings "ditch," "swimming" or "humiliation," while Smith's gives "wealth."

Shuppim was a Levite gatekeeper at the sanctuary, named with Hosah in the list of gatekeeping divisions drawn up in the time of King David. When duties were assigned by lot, Shuppim and Hosah received the west side, including the gate called Shallecheth by the ascending causeway, with guard posts set opposite one another (1 Chr 26:16). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia lists him as one of the temple porters. Nothing more is recorded about him. Because the previous verse ends with the Hebrew word for storehouses (asuppim), which looks very similar, some interpreters think the name may have come from a copying repetition. This entry treats Shuppim as a person, as the text reads. The name is shared by others in the Bible, including a Benjamite in the genealogies of 1 Chr 7, who should not be confused with this gatekeeper.

Shuthelah was a man of the tribe of Ephraim, one of the two tribes descended from Joseph, and the son of Zabad. He is named once, in the genealogy of Ephraim's descendants in 1 Chr 7:21. The verse goes on to mention Ezer and Elead, who were killed by the men of Gath when they went down to take the Gathites' cattle. It is not clear whether Shuthelah himself was involved in that raid. The name also belongs to an earlier Shuthelah, a son of Ephraim, who appears in the verse just before (1 Chr 7:20). The repetition suggests the family reused the name, but the two are treated as separate people here. The STEPBible Proper Names index identifies this Shuthelah as Zabad's son. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "plant" or "verdure."

Simeon is an ancestor of Jesus named only in Luke's genealogy, which traces Jesus' line back through Joseph, his legal father (Luke 3:30). He is listed as the son of Juda and the father of Levi. Since Luke's list runs from Jesus back through David's son Nathan, Simeon belongs to a generation after David and before the Babylonian exile, and so to the tribe of Judah. Nothing else is recorded about him. He is one of several men in the Bible named Simeon and is distinct from Jacob's son Simeon, who appears further back in the same genealogy. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the Revised Version spells his name "Symeon." Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "that hears or obeys."

Simeon, also called Niger, was one of the prophets and teachers in the church at Antioch, named alongside Barnabas, Lucius of Cyrene, Manaen and Saul (Acts 13:1). Easton's Bible Dictionary explains Niger as meaning "black," perhaps describing his complexion. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests Simeon was his Hebrew name and Niger a Latin name he also used. The verses that follow describe this group fasting, praying and setting Barnabas and Saul apart for the work they had been called to. Simeon was therefore probably among those who sent them out on the first missionary journey, about AD 45 by inference from context. Easton's notes a suggestion that he was the Simon of Cyrene who carried Jesus' cross. This entry treats him simply as the Antioch teacher. Nothing more is recorded of him. The name Simeon is shared by several other people in the Bible.

Simri was a Levite of the family of Merari and a son of Hosah, named in the lists of temple gatekeepers organized in David's reign. Although he was not the firstborn, his father made him chief among his sons (1 Chr 26:10). His brothers were Hilkiah, Tebaliah and Zechariah. Hosah's family is listed among the gatekeeper divisions, so Simri probably served as a gatekeeper too, which is how STEPBible's proper-name index describes him. Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that the name is properly Shimri and gives its meaning as "vigilant," while Easton's Bible Dictionary renders it "watchman." He is mentioned only in this one verse.

Sisamai was a man of the tribe of Judah, named only in the genealogy of 1 Chr 2:40, where he is the son of Eleasah and the father of Shallum. The surrounding list traces the family line of Jerahmeel through Sheshan, whose daughter married his Egyptian servant Jarha. Smith's Bible Dictionary accordingly describes Sisamai as a descendant of Sheshan in the line of Jerahmeel. Nothing else is recorded about his life. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia lists him under the alternative spelling Sismai. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "house" or "blindness."

So was a king of Egypt, named only in 2 Kgs 17:4. Hoshea, the last king of Israel, sent messengers to him and stopped paying the yearly tribute to the king of Assyria. The verse calls this a conspiracy, and probably means Hoshea was seeking Egyptian help against Assyria. When the Assyrian king discovered it, he imprisoned Hoshea. The text does not say whether So answered. His identity is uncertain. Easton's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia identify him with Shabaka (Sabako), the Ethiopian, or Nubian, ruler who founded Egypt's twenty-fifth dynasty. Smith's Bible Dictionary notes that writers have linked him with either the first or the second king of that dynasty. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests he may have been regent before taking the throne, and that he was defeated by the Assyrian king Sargon at Raphia about 720 BC.

Sodi was a man of the tribe of Zebulun and the father of Gaddiel, mentioned only once in the Bible. Gaddiel was the man chosen from Zebulun as one of the twelve leaders Moses sent to explore the land of Canaan (Num 13:10). Sodi himself is named only to identify his son, and nothing else is recorded about him. By inference from the setting, he belonged to the generation that came out of Egypt, during the wilderness period. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "intimate", while Hitchcock's Bible Names renders it "my secret".

The son of Abinadab was one of the twelve officers King Solomon appointed over districts of Israel, each responsible for supplying the royal household with provisions for one month of the year, as the surrounding passage explains. His own name is not given; the Hebrew calls him Ben-abinadab, "son of Abinadab." He governed all the region of Dor, the coastal area around the town of Dor south of Mount Carmel, and he was married to Taphath, a daughter of Solomon (1 Kgs 4:11). This made him the king's son-in-law. Which Abinadab was his father is not stated. Some interpreters suggest he was Abinadab the brother of David, which would make him Solomon's cousin, but the text does not confirm this.

The son of Dekar was one of the twelve district officers King Solomon appointed over Israel. According to 1 Kgs 4:7, each of these officers supplied food for the king and his household for one month of the year. His own name is not given; he is known only as Dekar's son, and some modern translations render the phrase as a name, "Ben-Deker." His district included Makaz, Shaalbim, Beth-shemesh and Elon-beth-hanan. Judging by the known towns of Shaalbim and Beth-shemesh, this was probably the lowland country west of Jerusalem, in the area once allotted to the tribe of Dan. Nothing else is recorded about him or his father.

Son of Geber (in Hebrew, Ben-geber) was one of the twelve officers King Solomon appointed over Israel. According to 1 Kgs 4:7, each officer supplied food for the king and his household for one month of the year. His personal name is not given. He was based at Ramoth-gilead, east of the Jordan. His district took in the towns of Jair son of Manasseh in Gilead and the region of Argob in Bashan, which is described as sixty large cities with walls and bronze bars. A Geber son of Uri appears a few verses later (1 Kgs 4:19) as the officer over Gilead. Whether he was this man's father, or the two simply share a name, is not stated.

Son of Hesed was one of the twelve district officers King Solomon appointed over Israel. Each officer supplied food for the king and his household for one month of the year, as the surrounding passage explains. His personal name is not given; he is identified only as the son of a man named Hesed. He was based in Aruboth, and his district included Sochoh and all the land of Hepher (1 Kgs 4:10). The exact location of Aruboth is uncertain. By inference from the places named with it, the district probably lay in the central hill country or the Sharon plain west of Manasseh. Hepher was an old Canaanite town whose king Joshua defeated, and Sochoh here is probably a town in that same area, not the better-known Sochoh in Judah. Nothing else is recorded about him.

Son of Hur is the name given to the first of King Solomon's twelve district officers listed in 1 Kgs 4:8. These officers each supplied food for the king and his household for one month of the year. His own personal name is not given. The text identifies him only by his father, Hur, and his district was the hill country of Ephraim, the central highlands of Israel. Many translations render the title as Ben-Hur, since "ben" is the Hebrew word for "son". Nothing else is recorded about him. It is uncertain whether his father Hur is connected with any other Hur mentioned in the Bible.

The son of Joiada is an unnamed priest of the tribe of Levi. He was a grandson of Eliashib the high priest, and Johanan was his brother. According to Neh 13:28 he married a daughter of Sanballat the Horonite, one of Nehemiah's leading opponents. Because of this marriage Nehemiah drove him away from his presence. In the surrounding passage this is one of several steps Nehemiah took against marriages with foreigners and the defiling of the priesthood. The text does not give his name. The Jewish historian Josephus tells a similar story about a priest named Manasseh who married Sanballat's daughter and was expelled from Jerusalem, but Josephus places those events later, so whether the two accounts describe the same man is uncertain.

Stachys was a Christian living in Rome whom Paul greets near the end of his letter to the Romans, calling him "my beloved" (Rom 16:9). He is named alongside Urbane, whom Paul describes as a helper in Christ. Nothing else is recorded about him, and the letter gives no details of his work or background. His name is Greek and means "ear of grain" (Hitchcock's Bible Names; Easton's Bible Dictionary). The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that the name is uncommon and has been found in inscriptions connected with the Roman imperial household. Paul's affectionate description suggests he knew Stachys personally, though how they met is not stated. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates the letter to about AD 56.

Suah was a man of the tribe of Asher, the first named of the sons of Zophah in the Asherite genealogy of 1 Chr 7:36. His brothers listed there and in the following verse include Harnepher, Beri, Imrah, Bezer, Hod, Shamma, Shilshah, Ithran or Jether, and Beera, with Ulla also counted among Zophah's sons in this entry. Nothing else is recorded about him beyond his place in this family list. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "sweeping" and dates him to about 1020 BC, an estimate drawn from the genealogy rather than stated in the text. Hitchcock's Bible Names offers "speaking" or "entreating" as possible meanings.

Susanna was one of the women who traveled with Jesus and his twelve disciples in Galilee and supported them from their own resources. She is named only once, in Luke 8:3, alongside Mary Magdalene (named in the preceding verse) and Joanna, the wife of Chuza, Herod's steward, among "many others" who provided for Jesus. By inference from the surrounding passage, these women had been healed of evil spirits and illnesses. This entry places the mention during Jesus' second tour of Galilee, about AD 28, an estimate inferred from context. Nothing else is recorded about her family or later life. Her name is usually understood to mean "lily," as both Easton's Bible Dictionary and Smith's Bible Dictionary give it.

Susi was a man of the tribe of Manasseh, named only as the father of Gaddi. Gaddi was the man chosen to represent Manasseh, counted as part of the tribe of Joseph, among the twelve sent by Moses to scout the land of Canaan (Num 13:11). Nothing else is recorded about Susi himself. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of his name as "horse," "swallow" or "moth."

Syntyche was a Christian woman in the church at Philippi whom Paul names in his letter to that church. He urges her and another woman, Euodias (Euodia in many modern translations), to "be of the same mind in the Lord" (Phil 4:2), which suggests some disagreement between them. In the next verse, Phil 4:3, Paul asks an unnamed "true yokefellow" to help these women, saying they had labored with him in the gospel, so she was evidently one of his co-workers. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia infers that she and Euodia were among the early converts from Paul's first visit to Philippi, described in Acts 16. Her name is Greek and is usually taken to mean "fortunate" or "affable" (Easton's Bible Dictionary). Nothing else is recorded about her.

Tabeal was the father of a man whom the kings of Syria and Israel planned to set on the throne of Judah, according to Isa 7:6. The surrounding passage identifies these kings as Rezin of Syria and Pekah son of Remaliah, who marched against Jerusalem in the reign of Ahaz. Their plan was to break into Judah and install "the son of Tabeal" as king in place of Ahaz. The name is usually explained as meaning "God is good" (Easton's Bible Dictionary; Smith's Bible Dictionary). Neither Tabeal nor his son is mentioned anywhere else, so who they were is uncertain. Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests the son was either an Ephraimite serving with Pekah or a Syrian serving with Rezin, and notes that the Aramaic form of the name points to a Syrian. Some references, such as the Tyndale House proper-names list, use the name Tabeal for the intended king himself.

Tabeel was one of the officials who, together with Bishlam, Mithredath and their companions, wrote a letter to Artaxerxes king of Persia. The letter was written in the Syrian (Aramaic) tongue (Ezra 4:7). The surrounding chapter makes clear that it opposed the Jews who had returned from exile and were rebuilding Jerusalem. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes him as a Persian governor of Samaria. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia calls him a Persian official in Samaria and says his name means "good is God." Nothing more is known of him. The name is not unique: a different man, spelled Tabeal in the King James Version, appears in Isa 7:6 as the father of a man Israel and Syria planned to set up as king in Judah.

Tabrimon was the son of Hezion and the father of Ben-hadad, the king of Syria who ruled from Damascus. He is named only once, in a genealogy identifying the Ben-hadad to whom King Asa of Judah sent silver and gold from the temple and palace treasuries (1 Kgs 15:18). The following verse and the parallel in 2 Chronicles 16 show that Asa was asking Ben-hadad to break his treaty with Baasha of Israel. The verse does not say whether Tabrimon himself was king, though his place in this line suggests he belonged to the ruling family of Damascus. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the name's meaning as "Good is Rimmon." Smith's Bible Dictionary spells it Tabrimmon, explains Rimmon as a Syrian god, and places Tabrimon before 928 BC. This dating is an estimate inferred from Asa's reign.

Tahan was a son of Ephraim, Joseph's son, and the ancestor of the Tahanites, one of the Ephraimite clans counted in the census Moses took on the plains of Moab (Num 26:35). In that list he appears with Shuthelah and Becher as heads of Ephraim's families. His other brothers, Elead, Ezer and Beriah, come from the genealogy in 1 Chr 7:20–23, which says Elead and Ezer were killed by men of Gath and that Beriah was born afterward. The same name appears again in 1 Chr 7:25 for a later descendant of Ephraim, so the name belongs to more than one person. The Tahan of 1 Chr 7:25 is probably a separate man, though he may carry the name of his clan's founder. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as “beseeching” or “merciful.”

Tahan was a descendant of Ephraim, son of Joseph, named in the genealogy of Ephraim's line in 1 Chr 7:25. He was the son of Telah, and the following verse continues the line with his son Laadan, which leads in turn to Elishama and eventually to Joshua, son of Nun (1 Chr 7:26–27). This places Tahan among Joshua's ancestors. He is known only from this list, and nothing more is recorded about him. Another Tahan, a son of Ephraim who founded the Tahanite clan, appears in Num 26:35. That is a different person, though the name probably reflects a family tradition within the tribe. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "beseeching" or "merciful."

Tahath was a descendant of Ephraim, son of Joseph, named in the Ephraimite genealogy of 1 Chr 7:20. He was the son of Bered and the father of Eladah. The verse lists the names in a chain joined by "his son," which suggests a single line of descent from Ephraim through Shuthelah and Bered, making Tahath probably Ephraim's great-grandson. The same verse names a second Tahath, a son of Eladah and so probably this Tahath's grandson, likely named after him. Nothing else is recorded about him. The name is also borne by other people in the Bible, so the verse should be read carefully to tell them apart. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "fear" or "going down."

Tahath was a descendant of Ephraim, son of Joseph, named in the Ephraimite genealogy of 1 Chr 7:20. He was the son of Eladah and the father of Zabad, and so belonged to the tribe of Joseph through its Ephraim branch. The same verse names an earlier Tahath, son of Bered, as Eladah's father. This Tahath therefore probably shared his name with his grandfather, a common practice in Israelite families. The list continues in the next verse with Zabad and further descendants. Nothing else is recorded about his life. The name is also borne by other people in the Bible, including a Levite of the family of Kohath, and it is the name of a camping place of Israel in the wilderness. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives its meaning as "fear" or "going down."

Tamar was the only daughter of Absalom, the son of King David, and is described as a woman of beautiful appearance (2 Sam 14:27). She had three brothers. Her name means "palm tree," and the STEPBible Proper Names index notes that she shared it with Absalom's sister Tamar, whose story is told in 2 Sam 13. She was probably born in Jerusalem, where her father lived. This entry identifies her as the wife of Uriel of Gibeah and the mother of Maachah. That link is inferred from connected passages. 2 Chr 13:2 calls Maachah (there spelled Michaiah), the mother of King Abijah, a daughter of Uriel of Gibeah, while 1 Kgs 15:2 and 2 Chr 11:20 call her a daughter of Absalom. These accounts are reconciled if Maachah was Absalom's granddaughter through Tamar. The name Tamar belongs to several women in the Bible.

Taphath was a daughter of King Solomon. Her only mention is in the list of the twelve officers who supplied food for Solomon's household. There she is named as the wife of the son of Abinadab, usually called Ben-abinadab, who governed the region of Dor on the Mediterranean coast (1 Kgs 4:11). Marrying the king's daughter to a district governor probably tied that official closely to the royal house. Her sister Basmath was likewise married to another of these officers, Ahimaaz (1 Kgs 4:15), and Rehoboam, who succeeded Solomon as king, was her brother. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates her to about 1000 BC, an estimate drawn from Solomon's reign. The meaning of her name is explained differently: Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "ornament," while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "distillation" or "drop."

Tappuah was a man of the tribe of Judah, named in the genealogy of Caleb's descendants as one of the sons of Hebron, along with his brothers Korah, Rekem and Shema (1 Chr 2:43). Nothing else is recorded about him. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "apple" or "swelling." Tappuah is also the name of towns in Judah and on the border of Ephraim (for example Josh 15:34). Several names in this part of the Chronicles genealogy match places in Judah, and Hebron itself is a well-known city. For that reason, the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia puts "son" in quotation marks, which suggests the list may partly describe clans or settlements rather than individual people. This entry treats Tappuah as a person, as the verse presents him.

Tarshish (Prince of Persia) was one of the seven princes of Persia and Media at the court of King Ahasuerus. Esth 1:14 lists him fourth among these men, who "saw the king's face" and "sat the first in the kingdom." In other words, they had direct access to the king and held the highest rank in his government. Judging from the surrounding passage, he was one of the advisers the king consulted, along with the other princes, about Queen Vashti's refusal to appear at his feast. Memucan spoke for the group on that occasion. Nothing else is recorded about Tarshish, and he should not be confused with the place or the other people of the same name in the Bible. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "contemplation" or "examination."

Tebah was a son of Nahor, Abraham's brother, by Nahor's concubine Reumah. He is named first among her four children, listed with Gaham, Thahash and a daughter, Maachah, in Gen 22:24. Smith's Bible Dictionary calls him the eldest of Reumah's sons, probably because his name comes first in the list. Through his father he was a half-brother of the eight sons Nahor had by his wife Milcah, among them Huz, Buz, Kemuel and Bethuel, the father of Rebekah. The list appears in a report brought to Abraham after the episode on Mount Moriah. Nothing else is recorded about Tebah's life. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of the name as "slaughter," and Hitchcock's Bible Names offers related senses such as "butchery" or "a cook."

Tebaliah was a Levite, the third son of Hosah, named in the list of temple gatekeepers in 1 Chr 26:11. His brothers Hilkiah and Zechariah appear beside him in that verse. Simri, another brother, appears in the surrounding passage, which says Hosah had thirteen sons and brothers in all. Hosah belonged to the clan of Merari, so Tebaliah was a Merarite, and he served among the gatekeepers organized in the time of David. Smith's Bible Dictionary dates this to about 1014 BC, an estimate drawn from context. The name is usually taken to mean "the Lord has dipped" or "purified." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests the original form may have been Tobiah, meaning "the Lord is good." Nothing else is recorded about him.

Tehinnah was a son of Eshton, named in the genealogy of Judah in 1 Chr 4:12 alongside his brothers Beth-rapha and Paseah. He is called "the father of Irnahash," which may mean the founder or chief settler of a town called Ir-nahash ("city of Nahash") rather than the parent of a person. Smith's Bible Dictionary reads it this way. The family group is described as "the men of Rechah," a place or clan that is otherwise unknown. The STEPBible names index places him among the descendants of Chelub in the tribe of Judah, following the surrounding verses of the genealogy. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia suggests the verse may refer to a settlement after the exile, though it calls the passage very obscure. His name means "supplication" or "entreaty." Nothing else is recorded about him.

Telah was a descendant of Ephraim, son of Joseph, named once in the genealogy of Ephraim's line in 1 Chr 7:25. He was the son of Resheph and the father of Tahan. The list continues for several more generations and ends with Joshua the son of Nun (1 Chr 7:27), so Telah appears among Joshua's ancestors, as Smith's Bible Dictionary notes. Because the verse's wording is compressed, it is not entirely clear how each name links to the next. This entry follows the usual reading, which makes Telah Resheph's son. Nothing else is recorded about him. Smith's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning of his name as "vigor", while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "moistening" or "greenness."

Telem was a gatekeeper (a "porter" in the King James Version) at the temple in Jerusalem in the time of Ezra. He is named with Shallum and Uri among the gatekeepers in the list of men who had married foreign wives (Ezra 10:24). From the surrounding chapter, these men agreed to send their wives away as part of Ezra's reforms after the return from exile. Smith's Bible Dictionary and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia both suggest he may be the same person as Talmon, a gatekeeper named in Nehemiah, though this is uncertain. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia also notes that the parallel list in 1 Esdras gives his name as Tolbanes. Telem is a different man from the southern town of Telem in Judah. Hitchcock's Bible Names gives the meaning of the name as "their dew" or "their shadow."

Temeni was a man of the tribe of Judah, named only in the genealogy of 1 Chr 4:6 as one of the four sons Naarah bore to Ashur. His full brothers were Ahuzam, Hepher and Haahashtari. The preceding verse (1 Chr 4:5) calls Ashur "the father of Tekoa" and says he had two wives, Helah and Naarah. The following verse (1 Chr 4:7) names Helah's sons, Zereth, Jezoar and Ethnan, who were Temeni's half-brothers. Coz, listed in 1 Chr 4:8, is also counted here as a half-brother. Nothing else is recorded about him. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia explains the name as meaning "a southerner," that is, someone from southern Judah. Smith's Bible Dictionary places him at about 1450 BC, an estimate drawn from the genealogy.

Tertius was the scribe who wrote down Paul's letter to the Romans, presumably at Paul's dictation. In the middle of the closing greetings he added one of his own, "I Tertius, who wrote this epistle, salute you in the Lord" (Rom 16:22), which is the only mention of him in the Bible. His name is Latin for "third." Smith's Bible Dictionary suggests he was probably a Roman. Others have thought he was a Roman Christian living in Corinth, where the letter is generally thought to have been written. Some have identified him with Silas, because the Hebrew word shalish also means "third." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes that Paul seems to have regularly dictated his letters and added only the closing lines in his own hand (2 Thess 3:17; Col 4:18; 1 Cor 16:21). Nothing more is known about Tertius.

Thahash was a son of Nahor, the brother of Abraham, and Nahor's concubine Reumah. He appears once, in Gen 22:24, among the four children Reumah bore: Tebah, Gaham, Thahash and Maachah. Through his father he was a half-brother of Nahor's eight sons by Milcah, including Huz, Buz, Kemuel and Bethuel, the father of Rebekah. Nothing further is recorded about his life. The name is also spelled Tahash in some modern translations and reference works. Easton's Bible Dictionary gives its meaning as "badger," while Hitchcock's Bible Names offers "that makes haste" or "that keeps silence." Like several of Nahor's sons, his name may also have been carried by a later tribe or clan descended from him, but the text itself does not say so.

Tharshish was a member of the tribe of Benjamin, named in a genealogy as one of the seven sons of Bilhan, who was the son of Jediael (1 Chr 7:10). His brothers were Jeush, Benjamin, Ehud, Chenaanah, Zethan and Ahishahar. The brother called Benjamin shares his name with the tribe's ancestor but is a different person. The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia treats Tharshish as the ancestor who gave his name to a Benjamite family. The surrounding passage lists these descendants of Jediael as heads of their fathers' houses and warriors. Nothing else is recorded about him. The same name, usually spelled Tarshish in English, belongs elsewhere in the Bible to other people and to a distant seaport, but those are unrelated to this man.

Theudas was a man who led a short-lived uprising, mentioned only in the speech of the Pharisee Gamaliel to the Jewish council during the trial of the apostles. Gamaliel recalls that some time earlier Theudas claimed to be someone important and gathered about four hundred followers. He was killed, and his followers were scattered and came to nothing (Acts 5:36). Gamaliel used his case, along with that of Judas of Galilee in the next verse, to argue that a movement of merely human origin would fail by itself. Easton's Bible Dictionary describes him as leading an insurrection against Roman authority. The historian Josephus tells of a Theudas who led a similar movement under the emperor Claudius, about AD 44. Smith's Bible Dictionary treats Luke's Theudas as a different and earlier man, probably one of the rebel leaders active near the end of Herod the Great's reign. Beyond this nothing is known of him.

Tiberius was the Roman emperor whose reign Luke uses to date the start of John the Baptist's preaching: "the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar" (Luke 3:1). Luke 3:1 is the only place he is named in the Bible. In the same verse Luke lists the local rulers of the time, including Pontius Pilate as governor of Judea and Herod as tetrarch of Galilee. Smith's Bible Dictionary and Easton's Bible Dictionary identify him as Tiberius Claudius Nero, the stepson and successor of Augustus, who reigned from AD 14 until his death in AD 37. On that basis Jesus' ministry and crucifixion took place under him. Easton's notes that the "Caesar" mentioned in the Gospel debates about paying tribute, and in Pilate's trial of Jesus (as in John 19:12), would by inference be Tiberius.

Tikvah was the father of Jahaziah, a man named in Ezra 10:15 during the crisis over Israelite men who had married foreign wives after the return from exile. His son Jahaziah and Jonathan son of Asahel are singled out in that verse. The King James Version says they were "employed about this matter," but many modern translations read the Hebrew as saying they opposed the plan. STEPBible's proper-names index follows the opposing reading. Nothing else is recorded about Tikvah himself. His name means "hope" (Smith's Bible Dictionary). The same name belongs to another man in the Bible, the father-in-law of the prophetess Huldah in the time of King Josiah, who is a different person from this Tikvah.

Tilon was a son of Shimon and one of four brothers, with Amnon, Rinnah and Ben-hanan, named in the genealogies of the tribe of Judah (1 Chr 4:20). Nothing more is recorded about him, and Shimon himself is not otherwise identified or linked to the families around him in the list. Ancient manuscripts and translations spell the name differently, and the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia notes Greek forms such as Thilan and Tholeim. The meaning of the name is uncertain: Smith's Bible Dictionary gives "gift," while Hitchcock's Bible Names gives "murmuring."

Timaeus was the father of Bartimaeus, the blind beggar who sat by the roadside as Jesus left Jericho with his disciples and a large crowd (Mark 10:46). He is named only in this verse, and nothing else is recorded about him. His name appears in Greek form, and the name Bartimaeus is itself a combination of the Aramaic word bar, meaning "son," with his father's name, so it simply means "son of Timaeus." The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia takes the Greek name Timaeus to mean "honorable," while Easton's Bible Dictionary gives the meaning "defiled."
